title: Syllabus
text:
The course has 11 modules and 149 lessons. Module 0 covers the prerequisites. Modules 1 and 2 match the certificate’s two required courses, and Modules 3–10 match its eight electives. The order is chosen so each module only uses ideas from earlier ones.
Lessons are numbered module.lesson, so 2.5 is the fifth lesson of Module 2.
Module 0 · Foundations
Course: prerequisite material
Length: 14 lessons and a project
Study plan: weeks 1–15
Before this: nothing, start here
Everything the certificate assumes you already know: R programming from the first line of code, describing data, probability, statistical inference, and the matrix algebra that regression is built on.
What it covers: Stands in for the prerequisite every course lists: one semester of applied statistics. It adds an introduction to R programming and the linear algebra used from Module 2 onward.


0.1 Welcome to R
the console, R as a calculator, objects and assignment, functions and arguments, getting help, reading error messages
0.2 Vectors and data types
creating vectors, sequences, vectorized arithmetic, numeric, character and logical types, comparisons, indexing, missing values, factors
0.3 Data frames
observations and variables, built-in datasets, inspecting data, selecting rows and columns, summaries by group, reading CSV files
0.4 Programming basics
if and else, for and while loops, writing your own functions, the apply family, debugging
0.5 Visualizing data with ggplot2
the grammar of graphics, histograms, boxplots, scatterplots, bar charts, facets, habits of good charts
0.6 Transforming data with dplyr
filter, select, mutate, arrange, summarise, group_by, the pipe
0.7 Describing data
center (mean, median), spread (variance, standard deviation, IQR), shape, outliers, z-scores, correlation
0.8 Probability
sample spaces and events, probability rules, conditional probability, independence, Bayes’ theorem, simulation
0.9 Discrete random variables
probability mass functions, expected value and variance, Bernoulli, binomial and Poisson distributions, R’s d/p/q/r functions
0.10 Continuous distributions
densities and integrals, cumulative distribution functions, uniform, exponential and normal distributions, standardizing, Q-Q plots
0.11 Sampling distributions and the CLT
sampling variability, the law of large numbers, the central limit theorem, standard errors
0.12 Confidence intervals
estimators, the t distribution, intervals for means and proportions, what 95% confidence means, sample size
0.13 Hypothesis testing
null and alternative hypotheses, p-values, Type I and II errors, power, one- and two-sample t-tests, paired tests, chi-square tests
0.14 Matrices for statistics
vectors and matrices in R, matrix multiplication, transpose, inverse, solving linear systems, determinants, a first look at eigenvalues


Project: Exploratory data analysis report. Pick a dataset, ask three questions about it, and answer them with graphs, summaries, a confidence interval and a hypothesis test, written up as a Quarto report in RStudio.
Open the Module 0 page


Module 1 · Statistical Data Management
Course: STAT 580
Length: 14 lessons and a project
Study plan: weeks 16–30
Before this: Module 0
How data is organized, stored, cleaned, combined and moved between software, and how to analyze data with missing values.
What it covers: Data organization and structures, designing statistical databases, analysis with statistical software, importing and exporting data between software, and missing data analysis.


1.1 Reproducible data workflows
RStudio projects, folder structure, file paths, naming conventions, Quarto reports, version control with Git
1.2 Data structures in R
vectors, lists, matrices, arrays, data frames and tibbles, attributes, choosing the right structure
1.3 Tidy data and reshaping
tidy data principles, pivot_longer and pivot_wider, separating and uniting columns, wide and long formats
1.4 Advanced data transformation
across(), case_when(), window functions, ranks, cumulative and lagged values, grouped operations
1.5 Combining datasets
keys, inner, left and full joins, semi and anti joins, binding rows and columns, join pitfalls
1.6 Designing statistical databases
the relational model, entity-relationship diagrams, primary and foreign keys, normalization, data dictionaries
1.7 SQL fundamentals
databases from R with DBI and SQLite, SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, aggregate functions
1.8 SQL beyond the basics
joins in SQL, subqueries, common table expressions, window functions, creating tables and indexes, dbplyr
1.9 Importing and exporting data
CSV, Excel, JSON and fixed-width files, SAS, SPSS and Stata files with haven, labelled data, encodings, Parquet
1.10 Text, dates and categories
strings and regular expressions with stringr, dates and times with lubridate, factors with forcats
1.11 Data quality and validation
finding errors and duplicates, validation rules, outlier checks, documenting cleaning decisions
1.12 Missing data I: patterns and mechanisms
MCAR, MAR and MNAR, visualizing missingness, what deleting incomplete cases does, single imputation and its problems
1.13 Missing data II: multiple imputation
multiple imputation with mice, Rubin’s rules, imputation diagnostics, sensitivity analysis
1.14 Working across statistical software
reading SAS, SPSS and Stata code, R equivalents of common procedures, moving data and results between tools


Project: Build an analysis-ready database. Take messy data spread over several files and formats, design a database for it, clean and validate it, handle the missing values, load it into SQLite and document it in a codebook.
Open the Module 1 page


Module 2 · Regression and ANOVA
Course: STAT 665 / STAT 562
Length: 15 lessons and a project
Study plan: weeks 31–46
Before this: Modules 0 and 1
Modeling how a response depends on predictors: simple and multiple regression, checking and repairing models, ANOVA for designed experiments, and logistic regression for yes/no outcomes.
What it covers: Correlation; simple and multiple linear regression with least squares and matrix notation; model building and checking; estimation and hypothesis tests; outliers, influence, multicollinearity and transformations; categorical regressors; logistic regression; and (from STAT 562) multifactor analysis of variance.


2.1 Correlation
scatterplots, Pearson and Spearman correlation, inference for a correlation, correlation and causation, regression to the mean
2.2 Simple linear regression
the linear model, least squares derived with calculus, interpreting slope and intercept, residuals, R-squared
2.3 Inference in simple regression
sampling distributions of the estimates, t-tests and confidence intervals, the ANOVA F-test, confidence and prediction intervals
2.4 Regression in matrix notation
the design matrix, normal equations, the least squares solution in matrix form, the hat matrix, variance of the estimates
2.5 Multiple linear regression
partial effects, interpreting coefficients, adjusted R-squared, added-variable plots, confounding
2.6 Hypothesis tests in multiple regression
overall and partial F-tests, nested models, general linear hypotheses, sequential and partial sums of squares
2.7 Categorical regressors and interactions
dummy variables, contrasts, interactions, centering
2.8 Checking model assumptions
residual plots, checking linearity, constant variance, normality and independence, formal tests
2.9 Transformations
log and power transformations, Box-Cox, polynomial terms, weighted least squares
2.10 Outliers and influence
leverage, studentized residuals, Cook’s distance, DFFITS and DFBETAS, what to do about unusual points
2.11 Multicollinearity
correlated predictors, variance inflation factors, condition numbers, remedies
2.12 Model building and selection
modeling strategies, AIC, BIC and Mallows’ Cp, stepwise and best-subset selection, cross-validation, overfitting
2.13 One-way ANOVA
ANOVA as regression, the F-test, multiple comparisons with Tukey and Bonferroni, contrasts, assumptions
2.14 Multifactor ANOVA
two-way factorial designs, interaction plots, blocking, unbalanced designs, ANCOVA
2.15 Logistic regression
odds and log-odds, maximum likelihood, odds ratios, deviance tests, predicted probabilities and classification


Project: A complete regression analysis. Build, check and interpret a regression model that answers a real question, then write it up as a report someone else could act on.
Open the Module 2 page


Module 3 · Multivariate Statistical Methods
Course: STAT 668
Length: 13 lessons and a project
Study plan: weeks 47–60
Before this: Modules 0 and 2
Analyzing several response variables at once: statistical distance, the multivariate normal distribution, Hotelling’s T², MANOVA, repeated-measures and nested designs, canonical correlation and discriminant analysis.
What it covers: Distance concepts; Hotelling’s T²; multivariate ANOVA; multivariate regression and correlation; linear contrasts; factorial, nested and repeated-measures designs; Bonferroni and chi-square tests; linear discriminant analysis; canonical correlation; applications.


3.1 Multivariate data and matrix algebra
data matrices, mean vectors, covariance and correlation matrices, linear combinations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors
3.2 Statistical distance
Euclidean and Mahalanobis distance, standardization, ellipses of constant distance
3.3 The multivariate normal distribution
the density and its properties, marginal and conditional distributions, checking multivariate normality
3.4 Inference for a mean vector
Hotelling’s T², confidence regions, simultaneous intervals, Bonferroni intervals, large-sample chi-square tests
3.5 Comparing two mean vectors
paired comparisons, the two-sample T² test, unequal covariance matrices, profile plots
3.6 One-way MANOVA
Wilks’ lambda, Pillai’s trace and related statistics, assumptions, Box’s M test
3.7 Linear contrasts and simultaneous inference
contrast matrices, simultaneous confidence intervals, follow-up comparisons after MANOVA
3.8 Factorial MANOVA
two-way multivariate designs, interaction effects, univariate follow-up tests
3.9 Repeated-measures designs
profile analysis, repeated-measures ANOVA and the multivariate approach, sphericity
3.10 Nested designs
nested factors, hierarchical data, nested MANOVA, a first look at mixed models
3.11 Multivariate regression and correlation
multivariate multiple regression, partial and multiple correlation, inference
3.12 Canonical correlation analysis
canonical variates, significance tests, interpretation
3.13 Linear discriminant analysis
Fisher’s discriminant function, classification rules, error rates, quadratic discriminant analysis


Project: A multivariate study. Analyze a dataset with several outcomes: test group differences with MANOVA, follow up with contrasts, and build a discriminant rule that classifies new cases.
Open the Module 3 page


Module 4 · Advanced Statistical Computing
Course: STAT 583
Length: 14 lessons and a project
Study plan: weeks 61–75
Before this: Modules 0, 1 and 2
The algorithms behind modern statistics: random number generation, simulation, resampling, numerical optimization, the EM algorithm, MCMC, smoothing, and clustering and classification.
What it covers: Data management, random number generation, resampling methods, numerical optimization, Markov chain Monte Carlo, smoothing methods, and data mining with clustering and classification.


4.1 Efficient and reliable R
vectorization, profiling and benchmarking, memory, functional programming, managing large data
4.2 Numbers inside the computer
floating-point arithmetic, rounding error, numerically stable algorithms
4.3 Random number generation
pseudo-random generators, seeds, testing randomness, the inverse-transform method
4.4 Simulating from distributions
rejection sampling, transformation methods, mixtures, designing simulation studies
4.5 Monte Carlo integration
Monte Carlo estimates and their error, importance sampling, antithetic and control variates
4.6 The bootstrap
nonparametric and parametric bootstrap, bootstrap confidence intervals, bootstrapping regression
4.7 Permutation tests, the jackknife and cross-validation
permutation tests, jackknife estimates of bias and variance, cross-validation
4.8 Root finding and one-dimensional optimization
bisection, Newton-Raphson, golden-section search, convergence
4.9 Multivariate optimization and maximum likelihood
gradient descent, Newton’s method, quasi-Newton methods, Nelder-Mead, optim(), Fisher scoring
4.10 The EM algorithm
missing data and latent variables, mixture models, convergence
4.11 Markov chain Monte Carlo
Markov chains, the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, tuning, convergence diagnostics
4.12 Gibbs sampling
full conditional distributions, data augmentation, blocking
4.13 Smoothing methods
kernel density estimation, kernel regression, loess, smoothing splines, choosing the bandwidth
4.14 Data mining: clustering and classification
k-means, hierarchical clustering, k-nearest neighbors, classification trees, judging the results


Project: A simulation study. Design and run a simulation study that compares statistical methods, implementing at least one of them (the bootstrap, EM or MCMC) from scratch.
Open the Module 4 page


Module 5 · Bayesian Statistics
Course: STAT 576
Length: 13 lessons and a project
Study plan: weeks 76–89
Before this: Modules 0, 2 and 4
Treating unknown quantities as probability distributions: priors and posteriors, conjugate models, sampling methods, MCMC, hierarchical models and Bayesian model checking.
What it covers: Basic concepts of Bayesian theory, sampling methods, Markov chain Monte Carlo and hierarchical modeling, applied to problems in the natural and physical sciences and engineering.


5.1 Bayesian thinking
probability as uncertainty, prior, likelihood and posterior, grid approximation
5.2 The beta-binomial model
conjugate priors, the posterior as a compromise, credible intervals
5.3 Choosing priors
informative, weakly informative and noninformative priors, Jeffreys priors, prior predictive checks, sensitivity analysis
5.4 More conjugate models
gamma-Poisson and normal-normal models, the posterior predictive distribution
5.5 Posterior inference
point estimates, credible and HPD intervals, Bayesian hypothesis tests, Bayes factors
5.6 Multiparameter models
the normal model with unknown mean and variance, marginal posteriors, Monte Carlo summaries
5.7 Sampling from posteriors
direct simulation, rejection sampling, importance sampling
5.8 MCMC in practice
Metropolis and Gibbs revisited, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, trace plots, R-hat and effective sample size
5.9 Probabilistic programming with Stan
writing models in Stan, fitting them from R with brms, reading the output
5.10 Bayesian linear regression
priors on coefficients, posterior predictive checks, comparison with least squares
5.11 Hierarchical models I
partial pooling, exchangeability, the eight-schools model
5.12 Hierarchical models II
hierarchical regression, varying intercepts and slopes, hierarchical logistic and Poisson models
5.13 Model checking and comparison
posterior predictive checks, WAIC and leave-one-out cross-validation, the Bayesian workflow, scientific applications


Project: A Bayesian hierarchical analysis. Fit, check and compare hierarchical models for grouped data from science or engineering, and explain what partial pooling changed.
Open the Module 5 page


Module 6 · Time Series Analysis
Course: STAT 577
Length: 13 lessons and a project
Study plan: weeks 90–103
Before this: Modules 0 and 2
Data collected over time: stationarity, ARIMA and seasonal models, forecasting, regression with autocorrelated errors, multivariate series, cointegration, volatility and long memory.
What it covers: Stationarity; ARIMA modeling with seasonality; parameter estimation, diagnostics and forecasting; regression with autocorrelated errors; cointegration and multivariate ARMA models; heteroscedasticity and long-memory models.


6.1 Time series data
time series objects, time plots, seasonal and lag plots, trend, seasonality and cycles
6.2 Decomposition and smoothing
moving averages, classical and STL decomposition, exponential smoothing
6.3 Stationarity and autocorrelation
white noise, random walks, the ACF and PACF, differencing, unit-root tests
6.4 Autoregressive models
AR(p) processes, stationarity conditions, Yule-Walker estimation
6.5 Moving-average and ARMA models
MA(q) processes, invertibility, ARMA(p, q), identifying models from the ACF and PACF
6.6 ARIMA modeling
the Box-Jenkins approach, maximum likelihood estimation, choosing models with AIC
6.7 Model diagnostics
residual analysis, the Ljung-Box test, overfitting checks
6.8 Forecasting
point forecasts and prediction intervals, accuracy measures, time-series cross-validation, benchmark methods
6.9 Seasonal ARIMA
seasonal differencing, SARIMA models, identification and fitting
6.10 Regression with autocorrelated errors
dynamic regression, ARIMA errors, generalized least squares, spurious regression
6.11 Multivariate time series
vector autoregression, Granger causality, impulse responses, VARMA models
6.12 Cointegration
common stochastic trends, the Engle-Granger and Johansen methods, error-correction models
6.13 Volatility and long memory
ARCH and GARCH models, long-memory processes, ARFIMA


Project: A forecasting study. Model and forecast a realistic seasonal series, compare several methods with time-series cross-validation, and report forecasts with honest uncertainty.
Open the Module 6 page


Module 7 · Introduction to Machine Learning
Course: STAT 584
Length: 14 lessons and a project
Study plan: weeks 104–118
Before this: Modules 0, 2 and 3
Statistical learning for prediction and pattern-finding: resampling, classification, regularization, nonlinear models, support vector machines, neural networks, principal components and clustering.
What it covers: Methods of statistical learning, including generalized (multinomial) logistic regression, ridge regression, neural networks, support vector machines, principal components analysis, and k-means and hierarchical clustering.


7.1 What is statistical learning?
prediction and inference, supervised and unsupervised learning, the bias-variance trade-off
7.2 Resampling and model assessment
training and test sets, k-fold cross-validation, the bootstrap, data leakage
7.3 k-nearest neighbors
kNN for regression and classification, choosing k, the curse of dimensionality
7.4 Logistic and multinomial regression
multiple logistic regression, multinomial (generalized) logistic regression, decision boundaries
7.5 Discriminant analysis and naive Bayes
LDA, QDA and naive Bayes as generative classifiers, when each works best
7.6 Evaluating classifiers
confusion matrices, sensitivity and specificity, ROC curves and AUC, precision and recall, class imbalance
7.7 Ridge regression
shrinkage, the bias-variance trade-off, choosing lambda by cross-validation, standardizing predictors
7.8 Lasso and elastic net
sparsity and variable selection, glmnet, regularized logistic regression
7.9 Beyond linearity
polynomial regression, step functions, splines, generalized additive models
7.10 Support vector machines
maximal-margin classifiers, soft margins, kernels, multiclass SVMs
7.11 Neural networks
perceptrons, multilayer networks, backpropagation, gradient descent, regularization
7.12 Principal components analysis
directions of maximum variance, scree plots, biplots, principal components regression
7.13 Clustering
k-means, hierarchical clustering and linkage, choosing the number of clusters
7.14 The machine-learning workflow
tidymodels recipes and workflows, hyperparameter tuning, final models, interpretability and fairness


Project: A prediction challenge. Build, tune and compare several models on a realistic prediction problem, and explain which one you would deploy and why.
Open the Module 7 page


Module 8 · Applied Analytics: Decision Trees
Course: STAT 585
Length: 13 lessons and a project
Study plan: weeks 119–132
Before this: Modules 0, 2 and 7
Predictive modeling for business problems with CHAID, CART, logistic regression and neural networks, plus the tree ensembles that grew out of them.
What it covers: Selected topics in predictive modeling using CHAID, classification and regression trees (CART), logistic regression and neural networks.


8.1 Predictive modeling in practice
the analytics workflow, business objectives, target variables, training, validation and test partitions
8.2 How decision trees work
recursive partitioning, impurity measures (Gini and entropy), stopping rules, reading a tree
8.3 CART classification trees
growing trees with rpart, class probabilities, priors and misclassification costs
8.4 CART regression trees
variance-reduction splits, piecewise-constant predictions, comparison with linear regression
8.5 Pruning and tree size
cost-complexity pruning, cross-validation, the one-standard-error rule
8.6 CHAID
chi-square splitting, merging categories, Bonferroni adjustments, multiway splits
8.7 Conditional inference trees and C5.0
unbiased variable selection, ctree, C5.0, comparing tree algorithms
8.8 Missing values and categorical inputs
surrogate splits, high-cardinality categories, preparing data for trees
8.9 Logistic regression for prediction
selecting and transforming inputs, scoring new data, comparison with trees
8.10 Neural networks for prediction
multilayer perceptrons, training and early stopping, interpretation
8.11 Assessing and comparing models
lift and gains charts, ROC curves, profit and cost matrices, choosing a cutoff
8.12 Bagging and random forests
bootstrap aggregation, random forests, out-of-bag error, variable importance
8.13 Boosting
gradient boosting, XGBoost, tuning, partial dependence and SHAP explanations


Project: A business analytics case study. Predict customer churn or credit risk with CHAID, CART, logistic regression, a neural network and an ensemble, then recommend one using profit-based assessment.
Open the Module 8 page


Module 9 · Spatial-temporal Statistics
Course: STAT 586
Length: 13 lessons and a project
Study plan: weeks 133–146
Before this: Modules 0, 2 and 6
Data tied to places and times: geostatistics and kriging, models for areal data, point patterns, and models for large spatio-temporal datasets.
What it covers: Basic concepts of geostatistics, point patterns and areal units; spatio-temporal modeling of high-dimensional data; applications in the natural and physical sciences and engineering.


9.1 Spatial data and maps
geostatistical, areal and point-pattern data, coordinate reference systems, sf objects, making maps
9.2 Spatial dependence
spatial autocorrelation, Moran’s I and Geary’s C, local indicators of spatial association
9.3 Variograms
stationarity and isotropy, empirical variograms, spherical, exponential and Matérn models
9.4 Kriging
simple and ordinary kriging, kriging variance, cross-validation with gstat
9.5 Beyond ordinary kriging
universal and regression kriging, anisotropy, the Gaussian-process view
9.6 Areal data and spatial weights
neighborhoods, spatial weight matrices, choropleth maps, testing for autocorrelation
9.7 Models for areal data
SAR and CAR models, spatial regression, disease mapping
9.8 Point patterns I
intensity, complete spatial randomness, quadrat tests, kernel estimates of intensity
9.9 Point patterns II
Ripley’s K and L functions, clustering and inhibition, Poisson and Cox process models
9.10 Spatio-temporal data
data structures, Hovmöller plots and animations, exploratory analysis
9.11 Spatio-temporal covariance and kriging
separable and non-separable covariances, spatio-temporal variograms, prediction
9.12 High-dimensional spatio-temporal data
empirical orthogonal functions, basis functions, dimension reduction
9.13 Dynamic spatio-temporal models
hierarchical and state-space models, environmental applications


Project: An environmental spatio-temporal analysis. Map, model and predict an environmental variable such as air pollution or temperature across space and time, including maps of the uncertainty.
Open the Module 9 page


Module 10 · Introduction to Bioinformatics
Course: CPSC 545
Length: 13 lessons and a project
Study plan: weeks 147–160
Before this: Modules 0, 1 and 4
Statistics and algorithms for biological data: molecular genetics, biological databases, sequence alignment and database search, phylogenetic trees, structure prediction and microarray analysis.
What it covers: Concepts of molecular genetics, biological databases, database searching, sequence alignment, phylogenetic trees, structure prediction and microarray data analysis.


10.1 Molecular genetics for data scientists
DNA, RNA and proteins, genes and the genetic code, mutation, the central dogma
10.2 Biological databases and file formats
GenBank, UniProt, PDB and Ensembl, FASTA, FASTQ and GenBank files, Bioconductor
10.3 Working with sequences in R
Biostrings, reverse complements, translation, GC content, motifs and k-mers
10.4 Pairwise alignment I: global alignment
dot plots, dynamic programming, the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm
10.5 Pairwise alignment II: local alignment and scoring
Smith-Waterman, gap penalties, PAM and BLOSUM matrices, statistical significance of scores
10.6 Database searching
BLAST and FASTA heuristics, E-values, interpreting search results
10.7 Multiple sequence alignment
progressive alignment, profiles, conserved regions
10.8 Phylogenetic trees I
tree terminology, distance methods, UPGMA and neighbor joining
10.9 Phylogenetic trees II
parsimony, maximum likelihood, bootstrap support
10.10 Hidden Markov models for sequences
CpG islands and gene finding, the Viterbi and forward algorithms
10.11 Protein structure prediction
levels of protein structure, secondary-structure prediction, homology modeling, AlphaFold
10.12 Microarray data analysis I
how microarrays work, preprocessing, normalization, quality control
10.13 Microarray data analysis II
differential expression with limma, multiple testing and false discovery rates, clustering and heatmaps


Project: From sequences to expression. Identify ten new bacterial isolates with a 16S tree and its bootstrap support, check whether their ketoreductase genes are intact, and find the genes that respond to high substrate load in a microarray experiment, then recommend a production strain.
Open the Module 10 page

title: Module 10 project: from sequences to expression
text:
The ketoreductase step works: PL-7’s KRED reduces the plant’s ketone to the alcohol the customer wants, with the right handedness. Now Amaya wants to scale it up, and before her group spends six months on fermentation trials, she wants to know whether a better strain is sitting in the plant’s own wastewater basin. They’ve isolated ten bacteria from it, sequenced their 16S rRNA genes and their kred-like genes, and run a microarray experiment on PL-7 at high and low substrate load.
That’s a typical bioinformatics question: from sequences to identities, from genes to function, and from expression to biology, with a decision at the end.

title: Module 10 project: from sequences to expression
text:
What you’ll make
One report, written in Quarto in your plant-study RStudio project, that Amaya could take to her group meeting. It should contain:

A summary for Amaya, at the top, in plain words: what the isolates are, which carry an intact kred gene, which strain(s) you recommend for the trials, and what high substrate load does to PL-7.
The data and its problems: what you found, and what you did about each.
The isolates: a 16S tree with the reference strains and bootstrap support, and what it does and doesn’t tell you.
The kred genes: for each isolate, whether the gene is intact, with the evidence (the catalytic residues, the motif, the reading frame).
The expression experiment: the quality checks, the model, and the genes that respond to high load, with the false discovery rate.
Limitations, and a recommendation.

Nobody grades it, but write it as if Amaya’s group will check every claim at the bench. In real life, they would.

title: Module 10 project: from sequences to expression
text:
The handover
Download these files into a new folder in your project, data-raw/strain/, and don’t edit them:

README.txt: Amaya’s note, with the three questions and notes from the lab. Read it first.
isolates_16s.fasta: the 16S rRNA sequences of the ten isolates and six reference strains.
isolates_kred.fasta: each isolate’s kred-like gene, as sequenced.
process_array.csv, process_samples.csv and process_probes.csv: the microarray intensities, the design and the genes’ functions.
pl7_fragment.gb: PL-7’s GenBank record from Lesson 2, with the KRED protein sequence.

Then download the project template, save it in the top folder of your project as strain-choice.qmd, and click Render. It reads the data and summarizes it, with headings and code skeletons for every step. Fill it in one section at a time, and render often. It uses Biostrings, pwalign, ape and limma (install the Bioconductor ones with BiocManager::install()).

title: Module 10 project: from sequences to expression
text:
The brief, step by step

Explore (Lessons 2 and 3). How long is each sequence? Do any contain Ns? Is every kred gene a whole number of codons? How many probes, genes and arrays are there, and how was the experiment designed?
The isolates (Lessons 4, 5, 8 and 9). Check each 16S read’s orientation against the PL-7 reference. Put the reads on a common coordinate system, compute distances, and build a neighbour-joining tree rooted on the most distant reference. Bootstrap it. Which isolates are close relatives of PL-7, and which are other genera?
The kred genes (Lessons 1, 3 and 4). Translate each gene on the right strand, align the protein with PL-7’s KRED, and check the catalytic serine, tyrosine and lysine and the TGxxxGxG motif. For any gene that doesn’t translate cleanly, find out what’s wrong.
The expression experiment (Lessons 12 and 13). Background-correct, log-transform and normalize. Average the genes with two probes. Check the arrays: do they all look like the other arrays of their group? Look at the scan days: is the design balanced? Fit a limma model, and report the genes that respond to high load at an FDR of 5%, with their fold changes and functions.
Write it up. Summary first. Then the data, the cleaning, the isolates, the kred genes, the expression experiment, the limitations and a recommendation, and the cleaning log at the end.

Stretch goal. Build the 16S tree by maximum likelihood instead, with your loglik() function from Lesson 9 or, in RStudio, with phangorn’s pml() and optim.pml(). Does it agree with neighbour joining on the clades that matter for the recommendation? Then compare the KRED proteins of the intact isolates in a tree of their own: does the protein tree agree with the 16S tree?

title: Module 10 project: from sequences to expression
text:
Check your own work
When you’ve finished, assess your project against this rubric. Aim for the right-hand column.










Needs work

Excellent




The data

title: Module 10 project: from sequences to expression
text:
Tips

Orientation. Score each read and its reverse complement against REF_Rhodococcus_PL7 with pairwiseAlignment(..., type = "global-local", scoreOnly = TRUE) (Lesson 5). The backwards one scores far higher reversed.
No multiple aligner? You don’t need one here. The 16S reads differ from each other only by substitutions and by where they were trimmed, so aligning each read with the PL-7 reference and taking aligned() puts them all on the reference’s coordinates. dist.dna(..., pairwise.deletion = TRUE) leaves out the gaps and the Ns pair by pair.
Bootstrap support (Lesson 9). boot.phylo() needs a function that rebuilds the whole tree, distances and rooting included, from a resampled alignment. Report how often each clade appears; within a genus, low support is expected for so few differences.
Frames and stops. A gene that translates without internal stops on the minus strand is just backwards. A gene that has internal stops on both strands, and whose length isn’t a multiple of three, has lost or gained a base: align its DNA with PL-7’s kred DNA (complement 1101..1859 in the GenBank record) and look for the gap.
Catalytic residues. Use aligned() on the protein alignment to read each isolate’s residue at PL-7’s positions 141, 154 and 158. A substitution elsewhere may not matter; one there almost certainly does.
Swapped labels. If an array correlates best with the other group’s arrays, and another array does the same the other way round, the labels were probably swapped. Look at both the load and the scan day of each suspect: do the data match the label? Fix the sample sheet, not the data, and log it. Without the fix, almost nothing is significant.
Unbalanced batches. With three high-load arrays and one low-load array on day 1, the scan day and the load are partly confounded (Lesson 12). Put the scan day in the design; then limma estimates the load effect within days.
Don’t over-claim. A 16S tree identifies a genus, not a strain’s performance; a kred gene that’s intact may still be poorly expressed; an array experiment on PL-7 says nothing about the isolates. Say what the trials need to test.


When it’s done, you’ll have carried out a complete bioinformatics analysis, from raw sequences to a tree, a gene check, an expression experiment and a recommendation. And that’s the course: eleven modules, 160 weeks, from your first data frame to the trees of life. Congratulations!

title: Microarray data analysis II
text:
Module 10 · Lesson 13 of 13 Week 159 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Last lesson turned the raw intensities into normalized log₂ expression values, and found two problems: a scratch on array C3 and a day effect. Now the question Amaya’s group asked: which of PL-7’s 4,000 genes change when toluene is added?
For one gene, that’s a two-sample comparison you’ve done since Module 1. The difficulty is doing it 4,000 times with only 12 arrays: each gene’s variance is estimated from a handful of values, and 4,000 tests at the 5% level give about 200 false positives even if nothing changes. limma (“linear models for microarray data”, Gordon Smyth, 2004) answers both problems, and it’s among the most-used statistical packages in biology.
In this lesson you’ll:
The setup code preprocesses the arrays as in the last lesson (normexp background correction, log₂, quantile normalization, the scratched spots on C3 set to missing) into N, with genes as row names. Because the data are simulated, we also know the truth: solvent_array_truth.csv has each gene’s true log₂ fold change, and truly_de marks the 160 genes that really respond.

title: Microarray data analysis II
section: A linear model for every gene
text:
A linear model for every gene
limma fits the same linear model (Module 2) to every gene separately: here, each gene’s log₂ expression on array j is
y_j = \beta_0 + \beta_{\text{day2}}\,[\text{day 2}] + \beta_{\text{day3}}\,[\text{day 3}] + \beta_{\text{tol}}\,[\text{toluene}] + \varepsilon_j,
where the brackets are 0/1 indicators. \beta_{\text{tol}} is the gene’s log₂ fold change for toluene, adjusted for the day. The model is written once, as a design matrix with one row per array.
Your turn. Build the design matrix with the day and the condition.









Add condition.


design <- model.matrix(~ day + condition, data = samples)
print(cbind(samples[, c("array", "condition", "day")], design))
colnames(design)
Four columns: the intercept (a control array on day 1), the shifts for days 2 and 3, and the toluene effect. Each row is one array: B2, for example, is (1, 1, 0, 1), a toluene array on day 2. Because every day has two arrays of each condition, the day and toluene effects can be estimated separately.




Your turn. Fit the model to all genes with lmFit(), apply empirical Bayes moderation with eBayes(), and list the top five genes with topTable().









eBayes(fit).


design <- model.matrix(~ day + condition, data = samples)
fit <- lmFit(N, design)
fit <- eBayes(fit)
top <- topTable(fit, coef = "conditiontoluene", number = 5)
cbind(round(top[, c("logFC", "AveExpr", "t", "adj.P.Val")], 3), product = probes$product[match(rownames(top), probes$gene)])
The top five: the chaperone HtpG, two unannotated genes, the chaperone DnaJ and efflux pump subunit H, all up by about 2.5 on the log₂ scale (2^{2.5} \approx 5.7 times), with moderated t statistics of 25 to 30. Their adjusted p-values round to 0. topTable() sorts by p-value by default; AveExpr is the gene’s mean log₂ expression over all arrays.

title: Microarray data analysis II
text:
The moderated t statistic
With 12 arrays and 4 coefficients, each gene’s residual variance s_g^2 rests on just 8 degrees of freedom. Some genes get a tiny s_g^2 by luck, and a tiny variance makes a huge t statistic out of a small difference. limma’s empirical Bayes step (Module 5’s idea of a prior estimated from the data) assumes the genes’ true variances come from a common distribution, estimates it from all 4,000 genes, and shrinks each gene’s variance toward it:
\tilde s_g^2 = \frac{d_0 s_0^2 + d\, s_g^2}{d_0 + d}.
Here s_0^2 is the typical variance, d_0 how much information the prior carries (in degrees of freedom) and d the gene’s own degrees of freedom. The moderated t uses \tilde s_g and has d_0 + d degrees of freedom.
Your turn. Look at the prior, and at the gene with the smallest residual standard deviation: its ordinary and moderated t statistics.









The residual standard deviations are fit$sigma.


fit <- eBayes(lmFit(N, model.matrix(~ day + condition, data = samples)))
g <- which.min(fit$sigma)
ordinary_t <- fit$coefficients[g, 4] / (fit$stdev.unscaled[g, 4] * fit$sigma[g])
c(s0_squared = fit$s2.prior, d0 = fit$df.prior, d = fit$df.residual[g],
  gene_sd = fit$sigma[g], moderated_sd = sqrt(fit$s2.post[g]),
  ordinary_t = ordinary_t, moderated_t = fit$t[g, 4], truly_de = truly_de[g])
The prior: s_0^2 = 0.049 (a typical SD of 0.22) worth d_0 = 4.1 degrees of freedom, against each gene’s own 8. Gene PL7_03635 has the smallest residual SD, 0.050, which by itself would give an ordinary t of −3.72, ranked 189th of 4,000. Moderation pulls its SD up to 0.136 and its t down to −1.36. It doesn’t really respond to toluene: its tiny variance was luck, and its ordinary t a false lead.




Your turn. Moderation matters most when arrays are few. Use only the four day-1 arrays (2 controls, 2 with toluene), rank the genes by ordinary and by moderated t, and count the genes in each top 50 that don’t really respond.









The top 50.


d1 <- samples$day == "day1"
fit4 <- lmFit(N[, d1], model.matrix(~ condition, data = samples[d1, ]))
ordinary_t <- fit4$coefficients[, 2] / (fit4$stdev.unscaled[, 2] * fit4$sigma)
moderated_t <- suppressWarnings(eBayes(fit4))$t[, 2]   # a few genes have zero variance
c(false_in_top50_ordinary = sum(!truly_de[order(-abs(ordinary_t))[1:50]]),
  false_in_top50_moderated = sum(!truly_de[order(-abs(moderated_t))[1:50]]))
With two arrays per group, the ordinary t’s top 50 holds 19 genes that don’t really respond; the moderated t’s holds 2. With 2 residual degrees of freedom, a gene’s variance is almost pure noise: some genes even have a variance of exactly zero, and an infinite ordinary t. Borrowing strength across genes is what makes small experiments usable, and small experiments are the norm in biology.

title: Microarray data analysis II
text:
Thousands of tests
With 4,000 tests, the usual 5% level isn’t the right protection. The family-wise error rate (Bonferroni: test each gene at 0.05/4000) protects against even one false positive, and loses many real ones. The false discovery rate (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995) controls something more useful for a screen: the expected share of false positives among the genes called significant. The BH procedure sorts the m p-values, finds the largest k with p_{(k)} \le 0.05\,k/m, and calls the k smallest significant. Its adjusted p-values (adj.P.Val) are compared directly with 0.05.
Your turn. Count the genes significant by raw p < 0.05, by BH and by Bonferroni.









"BH".


fit <- eBayes(lmFit(N, model.matrix(~ day + condition, data = samples)))
p <- fit$p.value[, "conditiontoluene"]
c(raw = sum(p < 0.05), BH = sum(p.adjust(p, "BH") < 0.05), Bonferroni = sum(p.adjust(p, "bonferroni") < 0.05),
  expected_false_by_raw = 0.05 * (nrow(N) - 160))
Raw p < 0.05 calls 423 genes, but about 192 false positives are expected among the 3,840 that don’t change, nearly half the list. BH calls 161, Bonferroni 129: Bonferroni’s guarantee against even one false positive costs 32 genes.













The p-value histogram above is the first plot to look at after any screen. Genes that don’t change have uniformly distributed p-values, the flat floor; genes that do change pile up near zero. A floor that slopes, or a bump in the middle, means the model is wrong for these data. Here the floor is nearly flat, with a small excess just above zero: partly responding genes with weak signals, partly the unchanged genes’ p-values being slightly too small (the next exercise shows it).
Your turn. The data are simulated, so check the FDR: of the BH-significant genes, how many really respond?









truly_de.


fit <- eBayes(lmFit(N, model.matrix(~ day + condition, data = samples)))
tt <- topTable(fit, coef = "conditiontoluene", number = Inf, sort.by = "none")
sig <- tt$adj.P.Val < 0.05
c(significant = sum(sig), truly_respond = sum(sig & truly_de), false = sum(sig & !truly_de),
  false_share = mean(!truly_de[sig]), missed = sum(!sig & truly_de))
161 genes called, 150 of which really respond: 11 false, a false share of 6.8%, close to the 5% promised. (The FDR is an average over repeated experiments, so one experiment can land a little above or below. Here the unchanged genes’ p-values are also slightly too small, 6.9% of them below 0.05 instead of 5%: the model’s assumptions hold only approximately.) And 10 of the 160 responding genes are missed.

title: Microarray data analysis II
text:
The batch effect
Your turn. What did including the day buy? Fit the model without it, and count the genes with a significant day effect (an F test of the two day coefficients).









Only condition.


fit <- eBayes(lmFit(N, model.matrix(~ day + condition, data = samples)))
fit_noday <- eBayes(lmFit(N, model.matrix(~ condition, data = samples)))
c(residual_sd_with_day = median(fit$sigma, na.rm = TRUE), residual_sd_without_day = median(fit_noday$sigma, na.rm = TRUE),
  t_of_true_genes_with_day = median(abs(fit$t[truly_de, 4])), t_of_true_genes_without_day = median(abs(fit_noday$t[truly_de, 2])),
  found_with_day = sum(p.adjust(fit$p.value[, 4], "BH") < 0.05 & truly_de),
  found_without_day = sum(p.adjust(fit_noday$p.value[, 2], "BH") < 0.05 & truly_de),
  genes_with_day_effect = sum(topTable(fit, coef = 2:3, number = Inf)$adj.P.Val < 0.05))
The day matters: 1,204 genes have a significant day effect. Including it in the model lowers the median residual SD from 0.31 to 0.22, and raises the median |t| of the truly responding genes from 8.5 to 11.1. Here, though, the toluene effects are so large (all at least a doubling) that both models find 150 of them; with subtler effects, that extra precision is what separates a gene from the noise. And because every day has both conditions, leaving the day out doesn’t bias the fold changes. When conditions and batches are unbalanced, it does (the project has an example).

title: Microarray data analysis II
text:
Big enough to matter
Statistical significance isn’t biological importance: with enough precision, a 5% change can be significant. Biologists often also require a minimum fold change, such as a doubling (|\log_2 \text{FC}| > 1). Filtering the significant genes by fold change afterwards is common but muddles the error rate; limma’s treat() tests the right hypothesis directly, H_0: |\beta| \le 1 against |\beta| > 1.
Your turn. Compare filtering by fold change with treat() at a log₂ threshold of 1.









lfc = 1.


design <- model.matrix(~ day + condition, data = samples)
fit <- eBayes(lmFit(N, design))
tt <- topTable(fit, coef = "conditiontoluene", number = Inf, sort.by = "none")
filt <- tt$adj.P.Val < 0.05 & abs(tt$logFC) > 1
tr <- topTreat(treat(lmFit(N, design), lfc = 1), coef = "conditiontoluene", number = Inf, sort.by = "none")
c(filtered = sum(filt), filtered_true = sum(filt & truly_de),
  treat = sum(tr$adj.P.Val < 0.05), treat_true = sum(tr$adj.P.Val < 0.05 & truly_de))
Filtering the significant genes by fold change leaves 140, all real here; treat() calls 77, also all real. treat() is stricter because it needs evidence that the change exceeds a doubling, not just an estimate above it, so genes whose true change is only just over a doubling aren’t called. The filter’s error rate isn’t controlled: a gene with an estimate of 1.05 and a wide interval passes. Use treat() when the threshold matters scientifically.

title: Microarray data analysis II
text:
How PL-7 copes
Your turn. The annotation names 12 efflux pump subunits (pumps that push solvent back out of the cell) and 8 chaperones (proteins that refold damaged proteins). How many are significant, and which one is missed?









Search the product names for "efflux".


fit <- eBayes(lmFit(N, model.matrix(~ day + condition, data = samples)))
tt <- topTable(fit, coef = "conditiontoluene", number = Inf, sort.by = "none")
pump <- grepl("efflux", probes$product)
chap <- probes$product %in% c("GroEL", "GroES", "DnaK", "DnaJ", "GrpE", "ClpB", "IbpA", "HtpG")
miss <- which(chap & tt$adj.P.Val >= 0.05)
list(pumps_significant = sum(pump & tt$adj.P.Val < 0.05), chaperones_significant = sum(chap & tt$adj.P.Val < 0.05),
     missed = probes$product[miss], missed_logFC = tt$logFC[miss], missed_true_logFC = truth$true_log2fc[miss],
     missed_AveExpr = tt$AveExpr[miss], median_AveExpr = median(tt$AveExpr))
All 12 efflux pump subunits are significant, and 7 of the 8 chaperones. The one missed is IbpA: its true log₂ fold change is 1.81, but its estimate only 0.69. It’s weakly expressed (average log₂ expression 5.66, against a median of 7.91), near the background, where the background correction compresses fold changes and adds noise. The low-intensity end is microarrays’ weak point, and one of the reasons RNA sequencing replaced them.




Your turn. Do the top genes separate the arrays by condition? Remove the day effect with removeBatchEffect() (for display only: the model already handles it), cluster the arrays on the 50 top genes (Module 7), and cut the tree into two groups.









The batch is samples$day.


fit <- eBayes(lmFit(N, model.matrix(~ day + condition, data = samples)))
top50 <- order(fit$p.value[, "conditiontoluene"])[1:50]
Nc <- removeBatchEffect(N, batch = samples$day, design = model.matrix(~ condition, data = samples))
hc <- hclust(dist(t(Nc[top50, ])), method = "average")
table(cluster = cutree(hc, 2), condition = samples$condition)
A perfect split: six controls in one cluster, six toluene arrays in the other. That’s expected, since these genes were chosen for differing between the conditions; clustering on the genes you selected can’t confirm the selection. The heatmap below shows the pattern.



















NoteGo deeper: from microarrays to RNA-seq





RNA sequencing counts reads per gene instead of measuring fluorescence, so the data are counts, with a variance that grows with the mean. Three approaches dominate, all descended from the ideas in this lesson. limma-voom (Law and others, 2014) log-transforms the counts and estimates each observation’s precision from the mean-variance trend, then runs the usual limma pipeline with weights. edgeR (Robinson and others, 2010) and DESeq2 (Love and others, 2014) model the counts with a negative binomial distribution (Module 3’s overdispersed Poisson) and shrink each gene’s dispersion toward a trend, the counterpart of the moderated variance. All three use generalized linear models with design matrices, so batch effects, paired designs and interactions work exactly as here, and all report BH-adjusted p-values. Gordon Smyth, “Linear models and empirical Bayes methods for assessing differential expression in microarray experiments”, Statistical Applications in Genetics and Molecular Biology 3, 2004, article 3; Yoav Benjamini and Yosef Hochberg, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 57, 1995, pages 289 to 300.

title: Microarray data analysis II
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Gene set testing. Instead of single genes, ask whether a whole functional category shifts up. geneSetTest() compares the moderated t statistics of a category’s genes with all the others (a rank test). Test each category in probes$func.









alternative = "up".


fit <- eBayes(lmFit(N, model.matrix(~ day + condition, data = samples)))
t_tol <- fit$t[, "conditiontoluene"]
p_up <- sapply(split(seq_along(t_tol), probes$func), function(idx) geneSetTest(idx, t_tol, alternative = "up"))
round(sort(p_up), 3)
Only transport shifts up, and barely (p = 0.043). Stress response, with 13 significant genes all going up, gets p = 0.32: its other 169 genes don’t change, and dilute the signal. Gene set tests answer “does the category as a whole move?”, which isn’t the same as “does it contain responding genes?”. Curated sets (the efflux pumps alone, or a pathway) give sharper answers than broad categories.




Challenge 2 · RNA-seq. In RStudio, install edgeR and work through the first case study in the edgeR User’s Guide. Then run the same counts through voom() and limma. Do the two methods agree on the top 100 genes?

title: Microarray data analysis II
text:
Quick quiz

1. limma fits, for each gene:

The same linear model, from one design matrix
A different model chosen for that gene
One model for all genes together


The empirical Bayes step then links the genes through their variances.



2. The moderated t statistic differs from the ordinary one because:

It uses a larger fold change
Each gene’s variance is shrunk toward a value estimated from all genes
It ignores the variance


That stops genes with a tiny variance by chance from topping the list.



3. Testing 4,000 genes at p < 0.05 when none change gives about:

0 false positives
5 false positives
200 false positives


5% of 4,000.



4. Controlling the false discovery rate at 5% means:

At most 5% of all genes are false positives
On average, at most 5% of the genes called significant are false positives
The probability of any false positive is 5%


The last is the family-wise error rate (Bonferroni).



5. Including the day in the design:

Takes the day-to-day variation out of the residual variance, making the tests more precise
Is never needed when every day has both conditions
Removes the toluene effect


With balanced days, leaving it out doesn’t bias the fold changes, but the residual SD here rose from 0.22 to 0.31. With unbalanced days, leaving it out would also bias them.



6. IbpA was missed although it truly responds, because:

It doesn’t respond to toluene
It’s weakly expressed, near background, where fold changes are compressed and noisy
It’s on the scratch


Low-intensity spots are microarrays’ weak point.

title: Microarray data analysis II
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve run a complete expression analysis, from raw intensities to biology. Here’s what you’ve learned:

limma fits one linear model per gene from a design matrix, here with the day as a batch effect; 1,204 genes have a significant day effect.
The moderated t shrinks each gene’s variance toward the common value; with only four arrays it cut the false genes in the top 50 from 19 to 2.
Multiple testing: raw p < 0.05 called 423 genes; BH called 161, of which 150 really respond, close to the promised 5% false share.
Fold-change thresholds belong in the hypothesis (treat()), and volcano plots and heatmaps show the results.
PL-7 under toluene switches on all 12 efflux pump subunits and 7 of 8 chaperones: it pumps the solvent out and repairs its proteins.

That’s the end of the course’s last lesson. The project puts Module 10 together: Amaya’s group needs a production strain.






TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download the four solvent_array files (samples, probes, truth) into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install limma and pheatmap.

Array weights. Refit the model with weights = arrayWeights(N, design) instead of setting C3’s scratch to missing. How many genes are significant, and how many really respond?
The mean-variance trend. Run plotSA(fit). Does the variance depend on expression? Refit with eBayes(fit, trend = TRUE) and compare.
Precision and recall. Plot the share of truly responding genes against the number called, for the moderated and ordinary t. Where do they differ most?
Down-regulated genes. The analysis found more genes going up than down. What functions are the down-regulated genes in?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Design matrix

The matrix of predictors (one row per sample) that specifies the linear model.

Differential expression

A change in a gene’s expression between conditions.

Empirical Bayes

Estimating a prior distribution from the data, here for the genes’ variances.

Moderated t statistic

A t statistic using a variance shrunk toward a common value, with extra degrees of freedom.

False discovery rate (FDR)

The expected share of false positives among the results called significant.

Benjamini-Hochberg procedure

The step-up procedure that controls the FDR; it gives adjusted p-values.

Family-wise error rate

The probability of at least one false positive, controlled by Bonferroni’s correction.

Volcano plot

Fold change against significance for every gene.

Gene set test

A test of whether a group of genes, such as a functional category, shifts as a whole.











NoteWant to read more?






Gordon Smyth and others, the limma User’s Guide, chapters 8 and 9, on linear models and many worked case studies.
Susan Holmes and Wolfgang Huber, Modern Statistics for Modern Biology (free online), chapter 6 on testing, including the false discovery rate.
Bradley Efron, Large-Scale Inference (Cambridge, 2010; free on the author’s website), on empirical Bayes and FDR for thousands of tests.

title: Protein structure prediction
text:
Module 10 · Lesson 11 of 13 Week 157 of 160 About 5–7 hours
A protein folds into a specific 3D shape, and the shape does the work: the KRED enzyme holds its NADPH cofactor and the ketone substrate in a pocket where the catalytic serine, tyrosine and lysine (Lesson 7) meet. Amaya’s group wants to engineer the enzyme to accept a bulkier ketone, which means knowing which residues line the pocket, which means knowing the structure.
Structure is described at four levels: the primary structure is the sequence; the secondary structure, local regular shapes stabilized by hydrogen bonds between the backbone’s atoms, mainly α-helices (H) and β-strands (E, which pair into sheets), with coils or loops (C) in between; the tertiary structure, the 3D fold of the whole chain; and the quaternary structure, how several chains assemble (SDRs are usually tetramers).
kred_structure.csv lists PL7_KRED’s 252 residues with the secondary structure assigned from its (fictional) crystal structure, and the confidence of an AlphaFold-style prediction for each residue. The fold is the SDR family’s Rossmann fold: a sheet of parallel strands sandwiched between helices.
In this lesson you’ll:
The setup code reads the three files: the structure, the Chou-Fasman propensities with the Kyte-Doolittle hydropathy scale, and 120 homology models with their templates’ sequence identity and their errors.
Your turn. What share of the enzyme is helix, strand and coil, and how many helices and strands are there?

title: Protein structure prediction
text:
Hydropathy
Hydrophobic residues (I, V, L, F) avoid water and pack into a protein’s core; charged and polar ones (R, K, D, E) sit on the surface. The Kyte-Doolittle scale scores each amino acid’s hydropathy, from +4.5 (isoleucine) to −4.5 (arginine). Averaged in a sliding window, it gives a hydropathy profile; a window of 19 residues averaging above about 1.6 suggests a helix that crosses a membrane, the first clue that a protein is a membrane protein.
Your turn. Compute the profile with a window of 19, and find its maximum and the number of windows above 1.6.









The membrane threshold is 1.6.


h <- cf$hydropathy[match(st$aa, cf$aa)]
prof <- stats::filter(h, rep(1 / 19, 19), sides = 2)
c(max = max(prof, na.rm = TRUE), at = which.max(prof), membrane_windows = sum(prof > 1.6, na.rm = TRUE))
The most hydrophobic 19-residue window, centred on residue 214, averages 1.09, and no window exceeds 1.6: KRED has no membrane-spanning helix, as expected for a soluble enzyme in the cytoplasm. Its hydrophobic stretches are the buried strands and the faces of helices that pack against them.

title: Protein structure prediction
text:
Chou-Fasman: propensities
Peter Chou and Gerald Fasman (1974) counted how often each amino acid appeared in helices, strands and turns of the few structures then known, relative to its overall frequency. A propensity above 1 means “found in this structure more often than average”: alanine, glutamate and leucine for helices; valine, isoleucine and tyrosine for strands; glycine, proline and asparagine for turns, which is why proline breaks helices.
Your turn. Check the propensities against PL7_KRED’s own structure: the mean helix and sheet propensity of the residues in each kind of structure.









Group by st$ss.


ph <- cf$helix[match(st$aa, cf$aa)]; pe <- cf$sheet[match(st$aa, cf$aa)]
round(rbind(helix_propensity = tapply(ph, st$ss, mean), sheet_propensity = tapply(pe, st$ss, mean)), 3)
Residues in helices have a mean helix propensity of 1.106, against 0.98 to 0.99 for the others; residues in strands a mean sheet propensity of 1.174, against 0.97 to 1.02. The differences are real but small: a residue’s own propensity says a little about its structure, not a lot.




Your turn. Turn propensities into a prediction: average them over a window of 7 residues, and predict helix where the helix average is above 1.03 and above the sheet average, strand where the sheet average is above 1.05 and above the helix average, and coil otherwise. Measure the Q3 accuracy, the share of residues predicted correctly.









The strand threshold is 1.05.


ph <- cf$helix[match(st$aa, cf$aa)]; pe <- cf$sheet[match(st$aa, cf$aa)]
wh <- stats::filter(ph, rep(1 / 7, 7), sides = 2); we <- stats::filter(pe, rep(1 / 7, 7), sides = 2)
pred <- ifelse(!is.na(wh) & wh > 1.03 & wh > we, "H", ifelse(!is.na(we) & we > 1.05 & we > wh, "E", "C"))
c(Q3 = mean(pred == st$ss), all_coil_baseline = mean(st$ss == "C"))
A Q3 of 54.4%, against 36.5% for predicting coil everywhere. That’s roughly what Chou-Fasman achieved on real proteins (50 to 60%): better than nothing, far from useful for engineering.




Your turn. Where does it go wrong? Tabulate the predictions against the truth, and compute the accuracy for each true class.









Divide by the row totals of tab.


ph <- cf$helix[match(st$aa, cf$aa)]; pe <- cf$sheet[match(st$aa, cf$aa)]
wh <- stats::filter(ph, rep(1 / 7, 7), sides = 2); we <- stats::filter(pe, rep(1 / 7, 7), sides = 2)
pred <- ifelse(!is.na(wh) & wh > 1.03 & wh > we, "H", ifelse(!is.na(we) & we > 1.05 & we > wh, "E", "C"))
tab <- table(truth = st$ss, predicted = pred)
print(tab)
round(diag(tab) / rowSums(tab), 3)
Strands are found best (68.2% of strand residues predicted as strands), helices next (59.5%), coil worst (41.3%): many coil residues are predicted as strand or helix, and 26 helix residues as strands. Local propensities can’t see what decides structure: contacts with residues far away in the sequence.

title: Protein structure prediction
text:
AlphaFold and its confidence
Propensities look at one residue and its neighbours, but structure is decided by contacts between residues far apart in the sequence. In 2020, DeepMind’s AlphaFold 2 predicted structures with close to experimental accuracy for most proteins, by learning from the PDB and from coevolution in multiple alignments (Lesson 7): residues in contact tend to change together. Its prediction comes with a per-residue confidence, the pLDDT (predicted local distance difference test, 0 to 100): above 90 is very high confidence, 70 to 90 confident, 50 to 70 low, below 50 very low (often disordered regions).
Your turn. Summarize the predicted structure’s pLDDT, and find the low-confidence stretches.









Low confidence is below 70.


low <- st$plddt < 70
r <- rle(low); ends <- cumsum(r$lengths); starts <- ends - r$lengths + 1
long_low <- r$values & r$lengths >= 5
list(summary = c(median = median(st$plddt), very_high = mean(st$plddt > 90), low = mean(low)),
     low_stretches = paste(starts[long_low], ends[long_low], sep = "-"))
A median pLDDT of 90.1; 51.6% of residues have very high confidence (above 90) and 11.9% low confidence (below 70), in three stretches: residues 140 to 144, just before the catalytic serine; 186 to 194, a loop that in real SDRs often covers the substrate pocket; and 241 to 252, the C-terminal tail. For the engineers, that’s the important news: two of the low-confidence loops are near the active site, so those are the parts of the model to treat with caution, or to check experimentally.













Your turn. Compare the mean pLDDT of helices, strands and coils.









Group by st$ss.


round(tapply(st$plddt, st$ss, mean), 1)
Helices 91.9 and strands 92.1, coils 76.8: the regular, buried elements are predicted with confidence, and the loops, which are more flexible in reality too, less. A low pLDDT often reflects real flexibility, not just a failure of prediction.

title: Protein structure prediction
text:
Homology modelling
Before AlphaFold, and still for many applications, the most reliable prediction was a homology model: align the protein with a relative of known structure (a template, found by a database search like Lesson 6’s against the PDB), copy the template’s backbone, and rebuild the side chains and loops. Its accuracy depends on how similar the sequences are. Cyrus Chothia and Arthur Lesk (1986) found that the error, measured as the root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of the core’s atoms from the true structure, grows roughly exponentially as sequence identity falls.
homology_models.csv has 120 models with their template’s identity and their RMSD (in ångströms, Å; a C–C bond is 1.5 Å).
Your turn. Fit \log(\text{RMSD}) = a + b\,(1 - \text{identity}), and predict the RMSD of models from templates with 30% and 50% identity.









50% identity is 0.5.


fit <- lm(log(rmsd) ~ I(1 - identity), data = hm)
print(coef(fit))
exp(predict(fit, data.frame(identity = c(0.3, 0.5))))
\log(\text{RMSD}) = -0.96 + 2.00\,(1 - \text{identity}): the error roughly doubles for every 35 points of identity lost. Models from 50%-identical templates are expected to be within about 1.0 Å of the truth over their core, and from 30% templates about 1.5 Å. The relation is for the conserved core; loops and side chains are worse.













Your turn. Compare the models from templates in the twilight zone (identity below 25%) with those from close templates (above 50%): their median RMSD and their median coverage (the share of the protein the template covers).









The coverage column is coverage.


zone <- cut(hm$identity, c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 1), labels = c("below 25%", "25-50%", "above 50%"))
rbind(n = table(zone), median_rmsd = tapply(hm$rmsd, zone, median), median_coverage = tapply(hm$coverage, zone, median))
Below 25% identity, the 27 models have a median RMSD of 1.93 Å and their templates cover a median of 66% of the protein; from 25 to 50%, 1.25 Å and 95%; above 50%, 0.64 Å and 96%. In the twilight zone, the models aren’t just less accurate: a third of the protein, often including loops near the active site, has no template at all.










NoteGo deeper: from Anfinsen to AlphaFold





Christian Anfinsen showed in the 1960s that a protein’s sequence alone determines its fold (denatured ribonuclease refolds by itself), which made prediction a well-posed problem; Cyrus Levinthal pointed out that a protein can’t find its fold by random search, since there are astronomically many conformations. The CASP competition, every two years since 1994, tested predictions blind against structures about to be published. Secondary-structure prediction improved from Chou-Fasman’s Q3 of about 60% to about 80% with neural networks on multiple-alignment profiles (PSIPRED, 1999). For tertiary structure, coevolution-based contact prediction (2011 onward) and then deep learning culminated in AlphaFold 2 at CASP14 (2020), with a median error near 1 Å for most targets; its database now covers over 200 million proteins, and its successors model complexes with ligands. John Jumper and others, “Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold”, Nature 596, 2021, pages 583 to 589.

title: Protein structure prediction
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Good enough for engineering? Protein engineers want a model accurate to about 2 Å in the active site. Using the fitted Chothia-Lesk relation, find the lowest template identity whose predicted RMSD is below 2 Å.









The target RMSD is 2 Å.


fit <- lm(log(rmsd) ~ I(1 - identity), data = hm)
a <- coef(fit)[1]; b <- coef(fit)[2]
identity_needed <- 1 - (log(2) - a) / b               # solve a + b (1 - id) = log(2)
unname(identity_needed)
About 17% identity, by the fitted curve. But that’s the average core error, for models whose alignment was correct; at 17% identity, the alignment itself is often wrong, and the coverage is poor (previous exercise). In practice, engineers want templates of 40% identity or more for active-site work, or an AlphaFold model with high pLDDT there.




Challenge 2 · A real structure. In RStudio, install bio3d, download the structure of a real SDR with read.pdb("1ZEM") (a xylitol dehydrogenase), and find the residues within 8 Å of its bound NAD cofactor with binding.site(). Then find the same structure in the AlphaFold database, and compare.

title: Protein structure prediction
text:
Quick quiz

1. An α-helix and a β-strand are examples of:

Primary structure
Secondary structure
Quaternary structure


Local regular shapes held by backbone hydrogen bonds.



2. A window of 19 residues with a Kyte-Doolittle average above 1.6 suggests:

A membrane-spanning helix
A β-strand
A disordered region


19 residues span a membrane’s hydrophobic core as a helix.



3. A Chou-Fasman propensity of 1.5 for helices means:

The residue is 50% likely to be in a helix
The residue is found in helices 1.5 times as often as its overall frequency would predict
The residue breaks helices


Proline, with 0.57, is the classic helix breaker.



4. Why is Q3 alone a misleading measure?

It’s always 100%
Predicting “coil” everywhere already gets a fair share right, so accuracy must be compared with that baseline
It ignores helices


As with unbalanced classes in Module 7.



5. A pLDDT of 45 for a stretch of residues suggests:

A well-predicted helix
Very low confidence, often a flexible or disordered region
A membrane segment


Below 50 is “very low”.



6. Homology models from templates below about 25% identity:

Are as accurate as experimental structures
Have large errors and often cover only part of the protein
Can’t be built


The twilight zone again, now in 3D.

title: Protein structure prediction
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve gone from sequence to structure. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Four levels of structure: sequence, secondary (helix, strand, coil), tertiary fold and quaternary assembly; KRED has the SDR family’s Rossmann fold, 46% helix and 18% strand.
Hydropathy profiles find hydrophobic stretches; KRED has no membrane-spanning helix.
Chou-Fasman propensities predict secondary structure with a Q3 of 54%, against 37% for predicting coil everywhere.
AlphaFold’s pLDDT is high in the enzyme’s core and low in two loops and the C-terminal tail.
Homology models are only as good as their templates: by Chothia-Lesk, about 1.5 Å of error at 30% identity, and a template of at least 17% identity for a 2 Å model.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download kred_structure.csv, chou_fasman.csv and homology_models.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Tune the predictor. Try windows of 5 to 15 and thresholds from 0.95 to 1.15. How much can Q3 improve, and is that improvement real or over-fitting to one protein?
A logistic predictor. Fit a multinomial logistic regression (Module 7) of the structure on the propensities of the residues in a window. Compare its Q3, by cross-validation over residues, with the rule.
Helical wheels. For the helix at residues 150 to 170, plot each residue’s hydropathy around a helical wheel (100° per residue). Is one face more hydrophobic? (Amphipathic helices pack one face against the protein’s core.)
AlphaFold database. Search the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database for a real Rhodococcus short-chain dehydrogenase, and look at its pLDDT colouring. Where is it low?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure

The sequence, local regular shapes, the chain’s 3D fold, and the assembly of several chains.

α-helix, β-strand, coil

The main secondary-structure elements, and the irregular regions between them.

Rossmann fold

A fold of parallel β-strands alternating with α-helices, typical of NAD(P)-binding enzymes.

Hydropathy profile

A sliding-window average of a hydrophobicity scale along a sequence.

Propensity

How often an amino acid occurs in a structure relative to its overall frequency.

Q3 accuracy

The share of residues whose three-state secondary structure is predicted correctly.

Homology modelling

Building a structure from an aligned relative of known structure.

RMSD

Root-mean-square deviation between two structures’ atoms, in ångströms.

pLDDT

AlphaFold’s per-residue confidence score, from 0 to 100.











NoteWant to read more?






Carl Branden and John Tooze, Introduction to Protein Structure (2nd edition, Garland, 1999), chapters 1 to 4, the classic, beautifully illustrated introduction.
Cyrus Chothia and Arthur Lesk, “The relation between the divergence of sequence and structure in proteins”, EMBO Journal 5, 1986, pages 823 to 826.
John Jumper and others, “Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold”, Nature 596, 2021, pages 583 to 589, and the AlphaFold database’s guide to pLDDT.

title: Phylogenetic trees II
text:
Module 10 · Lesson 9 of 13 Week 155 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Distance methods squeeze each pair of sequences into one number. Character-based methods use the alignment itself, site by site: a tree is good if it explains the observed bases well. Maximum parsimony prefers the tree that needs the fewest changes; maximum likelihood prefers the tree under which the data are most probable, given a model of evolution. And whatever the method, the bootstrap asks how much each branch would survive if the data had been a little different.
The usual R package for both, phangorn, doesn’t run in the browser version of R, so this lesson writes the two classic algorithms by hand, which is the best way to understand them anyway, and uses ape for the bootstrap.
In this lesson you’ll:
The setup code reads the alignment as a character matrix, and defines two functions you’ll use: fitch() and loglik(). Both work on all 1,200 sites at once.

title: Phylogenetic trees II
text:
Parsimony
Fitch’s algorithm (1971) counts the minimum number of changes a tree needs at one site. Working from the tips toward the root, give each node a set of bases: if its two children’s sets overlap, take the intersection; if not, take the union and count one change. The total over all sites is the tree’s parsimony score; the most parsimonious tree has the smallest.
Your turn. Do one site by hand. Four taxa on the tree ((A,B),(C,D)) have bases a, a, g and a at some site. Run Fitch’s rule: the (A,B) node, the (C,D) node, then the root.









At the root, intersect the two children’s sets: ab and cd.


ab <- intersect("a", "a")                                   # A and B agree
cd <- if (length(intersect("g", "a")) > 0) intersect("g", "a") else union("g", "a")
root <- if (length(intersect(ab, cd)) > 0) intersect(ab, cd) else union(ab, cd)
changes <- (length(intersect("g", "a")) == 0) + (length(intersect(ab, cd)) == 0)
list(ab = ab, cd = cd, root = root, changes = changes)
The (A,B) node gets {a}; the (C,D) node gets {g, a} (no overlap: one change); the root gets {a} (overlap: no change). One change in all: an A→G on the branch to C. The fitch() function in the setup does exactly this for every site at once, with bases coded as bits so that intersection and union are bitwAnd() and bitwOr().




Your turn. Compute the parsimony score of the neighbour-joining tree from Lesson 8.









The alignment as characters is X.


nj_tree <- nj(dist.dna(s16, model = "JC69"))
fitch(nj_tree, X)
1,385 changes, over 1,200 sites. On its own, the number means little; it’s for comparing trees on the same data.




Your turn. Compare the parsimony scores of the true tree, the neighbour-joining tree and the UPGMA tree.









The UPGMA tree is up_tree.


truth <- read.tree("data/bioreactor_true_tree.nwk")
nj_tree <- nj(dist.dna(s16, model = "JC69"))
up_tree <- as.phylo(hclust(dist.dna(s16, model = "K80"), "average"))
sapply(list(truth = truth, nj = nj_tree, upgma = up_tree), function(tr) fitch(tr, X))
The true tree and the neighbour-joining tree both need 1,385 changes (they have the same topology; parsimony ignores branch lengths), and the UPGMA tree 1,416: 31 more, the price of tearing the Accumulibacter pair apart. Parsimony agrees with Lesson 8’s verdict.




Your turn. Not every site helps choose between trees. A site is parsimony-informative if at least two bases each occur in at least two sequences; a constant site, or one with a single odd base out, costs the same on every tree. Count them.









Bases occurring at least twice: >= 2.


informative <- apply(X, 2, function(col) sum(table(col) >= 2) >= 2)
constant <- apply(X, 2, function(col) length(unique(col)) == 1)
c(sites = ncol(X), constant = sum(constant), informative = sum(informative))
Of the 1,200 sites, 594 are constant and 432 are parsimony-informative; the other 174 vary, but with only one sequence different, which costs one change on any tree. Only the informative sites decide between trees. Constant sites still matter for likelihood, because they tell the model how slowly the gene evolves.

title: Phylogenetic trees II
text:
Maximum likelihood
Parsimony ignores branch lengths and multiple changes, and it can be inconsistent: with long branches, it can prefer a wrong tree more and more strongly as data accumulate (Felsenstein, 1978). Maximum likelihood uses a model instead. Under the Jukes-Cantor model, the probability that a base stays the same along a branch of length t (substitutions per site) is

P_{ii}(t) = \tfrac14 + \tfrac34 e^{-4t/3}, \qquad P_{ij}(t) = \tfrac14 - \tfrac14 e^{-4t/3}\ (i \ne j).

Your turn. Compute the 4 \times 4 probability matrix for t = 0.1 and for a very long branch, and check that its rows sum to 1.









A very long branch: try 10.


P1 <- jc_P(0.1); P10 <- jc_P(10)
c(same_0.1 = P1[1, 1], change_0.1 = P1[1, 2], row_sum = sum(P1[1, ]), same_long = P10[1, 1])
For a branch of 0.1 substitutions per site, a base stays the same with probability 0.906 and changes to each particular other base with 0.031 (the three add up to 0.094; rows sum to 1). After a very long branch, every base has probability 0.25: the sequence has forgotten where it started, which is why the Jukes-Cantor distance goes to infinity at 75% difference.




The likelihood of a tree sums over every possible base at every ancestor: 4^{12} combinations per site for 14 taxa. Felsenstein’s pruning algorithm (1981) does it in one pass from the tips to the root: each node’s partial likelihood for each base is the product, over its children, of \sum_y P_{xy}(t)\,L_{\text{child}}(y), a matrix product. The setup’s loglik() is that algorithm, for all sites at once.
Your turn. Compute the log-likelihoods of the true, neighbour-joining and UPGMA trees, each with its own branch lengths.









Apply loglik.


truth <- read.tree("data/bioreactor_true_tree.nwk")
nj_tree <- nj(dist.dna(s16, model = "JC69"))
up_tree <- as.phylo(hclust(dist.dna(s16, model = "JC69"), "average"))
sapply(list(truth = truth, nj = nj_tree, upgma = up_tree), function(tr) loglik(tr, X))
-8{,}507 for the neighbour-joining tree, -8{,}522 for the true tree, and -8{,}606 for UPGMA. The NJ tree beats even the true tree, because the two have the same topology but NJ’s branch lengths were estimated from these data, while the true tree carries the simulation’s lengths, and the Jukes-Cantor model ignores the simulation’s rate variation. UPGMA’s tree is 99 log-likelihood units worse: an enormous difference.




Maximum likelihood also fits the branch lengths, which is where the work is. For four taxa there are only three unrooted trees, so we can fit each and compare.
Your turn. For PL-7, Gordonia, Mycobacterium and Nitrosomonas_A, fit the five branch lengths of each of the three possible trees by maximizing the likelihood with optim(), and compare.









optim() returns the minimum it found as value.


four <- c("Rhodococcus_PL7", "Gordonia", "Mycobacterium", "Nitrosomonas_A")
X4 <- X[four, ]
topologies <- c(PL7_Gordonia = "((Rhodococcus_PL7,Gordonia),Mycobacterium,Nitrosomonas_A);",
                PL7_Myco = "((Rhodococcus_PL7,Mycobacterium),Gordonia,Nitrosomonas_A);",
                PL7_Nitro = "((Rhodococcus_PL7,Nitrosomonas_A),Gordonia,Mycobacterium);")
fit_one <- function(newick) {
  tr <- read.tree(text = newick)
  negll <- function(logt) { tr$edge.length <- exp(logt); -loglik(tr, X4) }
  opt <- optim(rep(log(0.05), nrow(tr$edge)), negll, method = "BFGS")
  -opt$value
}
sapply(topologies, fit_one)
-3{,}294 for PL-7 with Gordonia, against -3{,}326 and -3{,}326 for the other two: a difference of 31 log-likelihood units, so the data are about e^{31} \approx 10^{13} times more probable under the first tree. With 14 taxa there would be (2 \times 14 - 5)!! \approx 3 \times 10^{11} trees, too many to fit one by one, which is why ML programs search.

title: Phylogenetic trees II
text:
The bootstrap
How sure are we of each branch? Felsenstein’s bootstrap (1985) resamples the alignment’s columns with replacement (Module 4’s bootstrap, applied to sites), builds a tree from each resample, and reports for each branch of the original tree the percentage of bootstrap trees that contain it. Values above about 70% are usually taken as good support; low values flag branches the data can’t settle.
Your turn. Bootstrap the neighbour-joining tree with 100 resamples using boot.phylo().









100 resamples.


build <- function(x) root(nj(dist.dna(x, model = "JC69")), outgroup = outgroup, resolve.root = TRUE)
tr <- build(s16)
set.seed(10091)
support <- boot.phylo(tr, s16, build, B = 100, quiet = TRUE)
c(nodes = length(support), min = min(support, na.rm = TRUE), at_least_70 = sum(support >= 70, na.rm = TRUE))
13 internal nodes (the first, the root, gets no value); 12 have at least 70% support, and the weakest has 59%.













Your turn. Find the weakest branch: the clade with the lowest support, and its members.









Node number Ntip(tr) + k.


build <- function(x) root(nj(dist.dna(x, model = "JC69")), outgroup = outgroup, resolve.root = TRUE)
tr <- build(s16)
set.seed(10091)
