support <- boot.phylo(tr, s16, build, B = 100, quiet = TRUE)
k <- which.min(support)                                     # support[k] belongs to node Ntip + k
weak <- extract.clade(tr, Ntip(tr) + k)
list(support = support[k], members = sort(weak$tip.label))
59% for the clade grouping the two Accumulibacter with Zoogloea and Thauera: the short internal branch that the Kimura NJ tree got wrong in Lesson 8. The data favour this grouping, but not decisively; a careful report would say so, or show the branch as unresolved.










NoteGo deeper: tree search, model choice and what bootstrap values mean





With more than a handful of taxa, the likelihood can’t be computed for every tree; programs search: start from a good tree (often neighbour joining), then try rearrangements (nearest-neighbour interchanges, subtree pruning and regrafting) and keep the improvements, fitting branch lengths for each. RAxML and IQ-TREE do this for thousands of taxa, under models chosen by AIC or BIC (Module 2) from a menu like JC, K80, HKY and GTR, each with or without gamma-distributed rates (+G) and invariant sites (+I). A Bayesian analysis (MrBayes, BEAST; Module 5’s MCMC) samples trees from their posterior instead, and reports posterior probabilities for clades. Bootstrap values are not probabilities that a clade is true: they measure how consistently the data support it, and they’re conservative for well-supported clades and sometimes misleading under a wrong model. Joseph Felsenstein’s Inferring Phylogenies (Sinauer, 2004), chapters 7, 16 and 20.

title: Phylogenetic trees II
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · UPGMA’s confidence. Bootstrap the UPGMA tree the same way (100 resamples, Kimura distances), and look at the support of the clade it wrongly built. Does the bootstrap warn you?









100 resamples again.


build_up <- function(x) as.phylo(hclust(dist.dna(x, model = "K80"), "average"))
up <- build_up(s16)
set.seed(10092)
support <- boot.phylo(up, s16, build_up, B = 100, quiet = TRUE)
c(min = min(support, na.rm = TRUE), median = median(support, na.rm = TRUE))
Most of UPGMA’s branches have 100% support (the median), and the weakest 23%. The bootstrap measures how consistently the method gives the same answer from resampled data, not whether the answer is right: UPGMA’s misplacement of the fast lineage is a bias, not noise, and resampling the same sites reproduces the same bias. A method that’s wrong can be confidently wrong.




Challenge 2 · Search for the ML tree. In RStudio, install phangorn (it works there) and run optim.pml(pml(nj_tree, phyDat(s16)), optNni = TRUE, model = "K80", optGamma = TRUE). Does the maximum likelihood tree match the true tree? Is the estimated gamma shape close to the simulation’s 0.5?

title: Phylogenetic trees II
text:
Quick quiz

1. Fitch’s algorithm counts a change at a node when:

The two children have the same base
The two children’s sets of bases don’t overlap
The node is the root


Then the node takes the union, at the cost of one change.



2. A parsimony-informative site needs:

Any variation
At least two bases each present in at least two sequences
No gaps


Other sites cost the same on every tree.



3. Under Jukes-Cantor, after a very long branch, the probability that a base is unchanged tends to:

0
1/4
1


The base becomes random.



4. Felsenstein’s pruning algorithm avoids:

Summing over all 4^{n-2} combinations of ancestral bases explicitly
Computing branch lengths
Using a model


Partial likelihoods are combined node by node.



5. A bootstrap support of 45% for a clade means:

The clade is 45% likely to be true
The clade appeared in 45% of trees built from resampled alignments; the data don’t settle it
The clade is wrong


Bootstrap values measure consistency, not probability.



6. Why can parsimony go wrong with long branches?

It counts too many changes
It ignores multiple changes on long branches, and can group them together (long-branch attraction)
It needs a molecular clock


Likelihood with a suitable model accounts for multiple hits.

title: Phylogenetic trees II
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve judged trees by their characters. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Parsimony: Fitch’s algorithm counts the minimum changes; the neighbour-joining and true trees need 1,385 changes, UPGMA’s more; 432 of the 1,200 sites are informative.
Likelihood: Jukes-Cantor transition probabilities and Felsenstein’s pruning give a tree’s likelihood; for four taxa, maximum likelihood picks PL-7 with Gordonia.
The bootstrap: resampling sites gives support for each branch; most of the NJ tree’s branches have strong support, and the weakest is the one Lesson 8 found uncertain.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download bioreactor_16s.fasta and bioreactor_true_tree.nwk into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install ape and phangorn.

Check your functions. Compare fitch() with phangorn::parsimony() and loglik() with phangorn::pml(tree, phyDat(s16))$logLik for the NJ tree. They should agree.
Parsimony search. optim.parsimony(nj_tree, phyDat(s16)) searches for the most parsimonious tree. Is it the true tree?
Long-branch attraction. Simulate four taxa with two long branches on opposite sides of the tree (phangorn’s simSeq()), and compare parsimony and maximum likelihood as the number of sites grows from 100 to 10,000.
Model choice. phangorn::modelTest(phyDat(s16), tree = nj_tree) compares substitution models by AIC and BIC. Which model wins? (The data were simulated under K80 with gamma rates.)










NoteKey words from this lesson






Maximum parsimony

Choosing the tree that requires the fewest character changes.

Fitch’s algorithm

Computing the minimum number of changes for a site on a tree, with sets of states at the nodes.

Parsimony-informative site

A site with at least two states, each in at least two sequences.

Maximum likelihood

Choosing the tree and parameters under which the data are most probable.

Felsenstein’s pruning algorithm

Computing a tree’s likelihood by combining partial likelihoods from the tips to the root.

Bootstrap support

The percentage of trees from column-resampled alignments that contain a given clade.

Long-branch attraction

The tendency of some methods to group long branches together, wrongly.

Consistency

A method’s property of converging to the true answer as the data grow.











NoteWant to read more?






Joseph Felsenstein, Inferring Phylogenies (Sinauer, 2004), chapters 2, 16 and 20, on parsimony, likelihood and the bootstrap, by the inventor of the last two.
Joseph Felsenstein, “Evolutionary trees from DNA sequences: a maximum likelihood approach”, Journal of Molecular Evolution 17, 1981, pages 368 to 376, where the pruning algorithm appeared.
Klaus Schliep, “phangorn: phylogenetic analysis in R”, Bioinformatics 27, 2011, pages 592 to 593, and the package’s vignettes, for doing all of this in RStudio.

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
Module 10 · Lesson 7 of 13 Week 153 of 160 About 5–7 hours
A pairwise alignment compares two sequences. A multiple sequence alignment (MSA) puts a whole family in one table, one row per sequence, so that each column holds residues that descend from the same position in the family’s ancestor. It’s the starting point for almost everything else: finding the residues that matter (they’re the ones that never change), building profiles for more sensitive searches, and inferring the family tree (Lessons 8 and 9).
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
How multiple alignments are made
Aligning N sequences optimally by dynamic programming would need an N-dimensional table: for 25 sequences of 250 residues, 250^{25} cells. So practical aligners use heuristics, most often progressive alignment (Feng and Doolittle, 1987; Clustal, 1988):

Align every pair, and compute their distances.
Build a guide tree from the distances (by UPGMA or neighbour joining, Lesson 8).
Following the tree from the leaves, align the closest pair, then align the next sequence (or group) to that pair’s profile, and so on until all are in.

“Once a gap, always a gap”: a gap placed early is never removed, so early mistakes propagate. Modern aligners refine the result iteratively (MUSCLE, MAFFT) or add consistency information from all the pairwise alignments (T-Coffee). None of them runs in the browser version of R, so this lesson uses the family’s alignment as delivered (made from the simulation that created the family, so it’s the true alignment that aligners aim for); the practice section shows how to make your own in RStudio.
The setup code reads the alignment as a character matrix: 25 rows, one column per alignment position, with - for gaps.












Your turn. How many columns does the alignment have, what share of its cells are gaps, and how long is each sequence without its gaps?









Count the cells that aren’t "-".


ungapped <- rowSums(al != "-")
c(columns = ncol(al), gap_share = mean(al == "-"), shortest = min(ungapped), longest = max(ungapped))
276 columns, of which 8.6% of the cells are gaps; without their gaps, the sequences are 250 to 259 residues long. Every column is a hypothesis: that its residues all descend from one residue of the ancestral enzyme.




Your turn. Residue numbers refer to one sequence; columns to the alignment. Map PL7_KRED’s residues 12 (the start of the TGxxxGxG motif), 141, 154 and 158 (the catalytic serine, tyrosine and lysine) to their columns.









The catalytic lysine is residue 158.


col_of <- which(al["PL7_KRED", ] != "-")          # col_of[k] is the column of residue k
cols <- col_of[c(12, 141, 154, 158)]
rbind(column = cols, residue = al["PL7_KRED", cols])
Residue 12 (T) is in column 12, but the catalytic S, Y and K are in columns 164, 177 and 181: 23 columns later than their residue numbers, because other family members have insertions before them. Biologists refer to positions by residue number in a reference sequence; the alignment translates between sequences.

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
Identities and the guide tree
Your turn. Compute the percentage identity of every pair of sequences, counting only columns where both have a residue, and find the closest and the most distant pairs.









Compare row i with row j.


n <- nrow(al)
id <- matrix(1, n, n, dimnames = list(rownames(al), rownames(al)))
for (i in 1:(n - 1)) for (j in (i + 1):n) {
  both <- al[i, ] != "-" & al[j, ] != "-"
  id[i, j] <- id[j, i] <- mean(al[i, both] == al[j, both])
}
off <- id; diag(off) <- NA
c(closest = max(off, na.rm = TRUE), most_distant = min(off, na.rm = TRUE), pl7_mean = mean(off["PL7_KRED", ], na.rm = TRUE))
The closest pair is 90.4% identical and the most distant 22.9%: the family spans near-twins to the twilight zone. PL7_KRED is, on average, 51% identical to the others. Identities computed from a multiple alignment differ a little from pairwise ones, because the multiple alignment places some gaps differently.




Your turn. Build a guide tree by average-linkage clustering (UPGMA) of the distances 1 - \text{identity}, and find which pair a progressive aligner would align first.









Average linkage is UPGMA: "average".


n <- nrow(al)
id <- matrix(1, n, n, dimnames = list(rownames(al), rownames(al)))
for (i in 1:(n - 1)) for (j in (i + 1):n) {
  both <- al[i, ] != "-" & al[j, ] != "-"
  id[i, j] <- id[j, i] <- mean(al[i, both] == al[j, both])
}
guide <- hclust(as.dist(1 - id), method = "average")
first <- guide$merge[1, ]                                   # negative numbers are single sequences
c(first_pair = paste(rownames(al)[-first], collapse = " + "), height = guide$height[1])
SDR_10 and SDR_16, at a distance of 0.096 (90.4% identity), the closest pair, would be aligned first. hclust()’s merge matrix lists the merges in order; negative entries are single sequences, positive ones clusters formed earlier.

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
Consensus and conservation
Your turn. Compute the consensus sequence: the most common residue in each column (ignoring gaps), and its share. Then compare PL7_KRED with the consensus.









Use the same positions on both sides: where PL7_KRED isn’t a gap.


top_res <- apply(al, 2, function(col) { col <- col[col != "-"]; names(which.max(table(col))) })
top_share <- apply(al, 2, function(col) { col <- col[col != "-"]; max(table(col)) / length(col) })
pl7 <- al["PL7_KRED", ]
c(consensus_start = paste(top_res[1:20], collapse = ""), pl7_start = paste(pl7[1:20], collapse = ""),
  pl7_matches = mean(pl7[pl7 != "-"] == top_res[pl7 != "-"]))
The consensus starts VCEKHTMKESEGGAASGIGL and PL7_KRED starts MCRKHPMKESGTGAASGIGL: both have the motif region GAASGIG, and overall PL7_KRED carries the consensus residue at 67.9% of its positions. A consensus is a summary, not a real protein: no family member needs to match it everywhere.




Your turn. How conserved are the motif and the catalytic residues? Compute the share of sequences carrying PL7_KRED’s residue in each of their columns.









The column of residue k.


col_of <- which(al["PL7_KRED", ] != "-")
sites <- c(T12 = 12, G13 = 13, G17 = 17, G19 = 19, S141 = 141, Y154 = 154, K158 = 158)
sapply(sites, function(k) { col <- al[, col_of[k]]; mean(col == al["PL7_KRED", col_of[k]]) })
The glycines G17 and G19 and the catalytic lysine K158 are in every sequence; the serine S141 in 96%, the tyrosine Y154 in 92%, G13 in 84%. The motif’s first position, T12, is shared by only 36%. The glycines let the NADPH cofactor sit close to the protein’s backbone, and the serine, tyrosine and lysine do the chemistry, so the family can’t afford to change them; the occasional exception is either a very old divergence or an enzyme that has lost its activity (the project has one).




Your turn. A column’s Shannon entropy, H = -\sum_a p_a \log_2 p_a over the residues present, is 0 for a column of one residue and up to \log_2 20 = 4.3 bits for a column with all 20 equally. Compute it for every column, count the invariant columns, and compare the motif region with the rest.









\log_2 p: log2(p).


H <- apply(al, 2, function(col) { col <- col[col != "-"]; p <- table(col) / length(col); -sum(p * log2(p)) })
c(invariant = sum(H == 0), median = median(H), motif_mean = mean(H[12:19]), others_mean = mean(H[-(12:19)]))
38 of the 276 columns are invariant, the median entropy is 1.61 bits, and the motif region (columns 12 to 19) averages 0.56 bits against 1.45 elsewhere. The plot below shows where the conserved positions lie.













Your turn. Columns that are mostly gaps (an insertion in one or two sequences) carry little information and are often removed before building trees. Count the columns with more than half gaps, and the width after removing them.









More than half: 0.5.


gap_share <- colMeans(al == "-")
gappy <- gap_share > 0.5
c(gappy_columns = sum(gappy), width_after = sum(!gappy), any_gaps = sum(gap_share > 0))
25 columns are more than half gaps: insertions in a few sequences. Removing them leaves 251 columns. 34 columns have at least one gap.

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
Profiles
A profile, or position-specific scoring matrix (PSSM), turns an alignment into scores: for each column k and residue a, s_k(a) = \log_2(f_k(a) / p_a), where f_k(a) is the residue’s frequency in the column and p_a its background frequency. A conserved glycine column gives G a high score and everything else a very low one; a variable column scores everything near 0. Pseudocounts (adding a little of the background to each column) keep unseen residues from scoring -\infty.
Your turn. Build a PSSM for the alignment’s first 60 columns, with pseudocounts, and score PL7_KRED’s own first 60 columns.









Divide by the background, bg.


bg <- c(7.8, 5.1, 4.5, 5.4, 1.9, 4.3, 6.3, 7.4, 2.6, 6.8, 9.9, 5.8, 2.5, 4.7, 3.9, 5.7, 5.1, 1.3, 3.2, 6.6)
bg <- setNames(bg / sum(bg), aa)
cols <- 1:60
pssm <- sapply(cols, function(k) {
  col <- al[, k]; col <- col[col %in% aa]
  f <- (table(factor(col, levels = aa)) + 20 * bg) / (length(col) + 20)     # 20 pseudocounts, spread like the background
  log2(f / bg)
})
pl7 <- al["PL7_KRED", cols]; ok <- pl7 %in% aa                       # skip PL7_KRED's gaps
c(score_pl7 = sum(pssm[cbind(match(pl7[ok], aa), seq_along(cols)[ok])]), best_possible = sum(apply(pssm, 2, max)), G17 = pssm["G", 17], A17 = pssm["A", 17])
PL7_KRED’s first 60 residues score 125.9 bits against the profile, out of a best possible 150.7 (if every column had its best residue). In column 17, the motif’s first G, a G scores +3.0 bits and an A -1.2: the profile rewards the residues the family keeps and penalizes the others, column by column.










NoteGo deeper: from profiles to profile HMMs





A PSSM has no gaps: it scores a fixed-width window. A profile hidden Markov model (Krogh and others, 1994; Lesson 10’s machinery) adds, for each column, an insert state (extra residues between columns) and a delete state (skipping the column), with position-specific transition probabilities, so that a family’s indel patterns are modelled too. HMMER (Sean Eddy) searches databases with profile HMMs, and the Pfam database holds profile HMMs for about 20,000 protein families; the SDR family is Pfam’s PF00106, “adh_short”. Profile searches are much more sensitive than pairwise ones, because a profile knows which positions matter. Richard Durbin and others, Biological Sequence Analysis, chapters 5 and 6, explains profile HMMs and their training from alignments.

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · A profile search. Score every protein in the database with the PSSM: slide the 60-column profile along each sequence (ignoring gaps, so using a window of 60 residues) and keep the best window. Compare the family members’ best scores with the unrelated proteins’.









The unrelated proteins: other.


bg <- c(7.8, 5.1, 4.5, 5.4, 1.9, 4.3, 6.3, 7.4, 2.6, 6.8, 9.9, 5.8, 2.5, 4.7, 3.9, 5.7, 5.1, 1.3, 3.2, 6.6)
bg <- setNames(bg / sum(bg), aa)
pssm <- sapply(1:60, function(k) { col <- al[, k]; col <- col[col %in% aa]
  log2(((table(factor(col, levels = aa)) + 20 * bg) / (length(col) + 20)) / bg) })
db <- readAAStringSet("data/protein_db.fasta")
best_window <- function(s) {
  s <- match(strsplit(as.character(s), "")[[1]], aa); L <- ncol(pssm)
  max(sapply(1:(length(s) - L + 1), function(st) sum(pssm[cbind(s[st:(st + L - 1)], 1:L)])))
}
best <- sapply(db, best_window)
sdr <- grepl("^(PL7|SDR)", names(db)); other <- !grepl("^(PL7|SDR|RMT)", names(db))
c(sdr_min = min(best[sdr]), other_max = max(best[other]), sdr_above_other_max = sum(best[sdr] > max(best[other])))
The SDR members’ best windows score from 5.3 upward, and the best unrelated protein 7.1: 24 of the 25 SDR members score above every unrelated protein. The one that doesn’t has diverged in its first 60 residues. A 60-column ungapped profile is a short ruler; full-length profiles with gaps (the profile HMMs of the box above) do better.




Challenge 2 · Align it yourself. In RStudio, install msa from Bioconductor (BiocManager::install("msa")), remove the gaps from kred_family_aligned.fasta (AAStringSet(gsub("-", "", ...))), and realign with msa(..., method = "ClustalOmega") and "Muscle". In what share of columns does each aligner agree with the true alignment? (Compare which residues share a column, not the column numbers.)

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why don’t multiple aligners use exact dynamic programming?

It gives worse alignments
The table grows exponentially with the number of sequences
Gaps can’t be handled


L^N cells for N sequences of length L.



2. In progressive alignment, the guide tree decides:

The final phylogeny
The order in which sequences and groups are aligned
The gap penalties


Closest pairs first; it’s a heuristic, not the inferred tree.



3. “Once a gap, always a gap” refers to:

Progressive alignment never revisiting gaps placed in early steps
Gaps being penalized twice
Gappy columns being removed


Iterative refinement (MUSCLE, MAFFT) addresses it.



4. A column’s entropy of 0 means:

Every residue is different
Every sequence has the same residue there
The column is all gaps


Invariant columns are often functionally essential.



5. Why add pseudocounts to a profile?

To make the scores positive
So residues not seen in a column, with only 25 sequences, don’t score minus infinity
To remove gaps


Unseen doesn’t mean impossible.



6. Why can a profile search be more sensitive than a pairwise one?

It uses more memory
It knows which positions are conserved and weights them accordingly
It ignores the background frequencies


A pairwise search treats every position of the query equally.

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve worked with a family alignment. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Progressive alignment builds an MSA from a guide tree; “once a gap, always a gap” is its weakness.
The family’s alignment: 25 sequences in 276 columns; the catalytic S, Y and K of PL7_KRED sit in columns 164, 177 and 181.
Identities and a guide tree from the alignment; a consensus that PL7_KRED matches at 68% of its residues.
Conservation: 38 invariant columns; the motif’s glycines and the catalytic lysine are (almost) invariant.
Profiles: a PSSM scores sequences position by position, and separates the SDR family from unrelated proteins in a database search.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download kred_family_aligned.fasta and protein_db.fasta into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

A sequence logo. Install ggseqlogo and draw a logo of the motif region (columns 5 to 30). Which positions stand out?
Sum-of-pairs score. Compute the alignment’s sum-of-pairs score with BLOSUM62 and a gap penalty of -4 per gap position. Then shift one sequence’s residues one column to the right in a region, and recompute. How much does the score drop?
Weighting. Close relatives are over-represented in most families. Compute Henikoff position-based sequence weights, rebuild the PSSM with them, and see whether the profile search improves.
Pfam. Look up Pfam family PF00106 on the InterPro website and look at its HMM logo. Do you recognize the TGxxxGxG motif?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Multiple sequence alignment (MSA)

An alignment of three or more sequences, one per row, with homologous residues in the same column.

Progressive alignment

Building an MSA by aligning sequences and groups in the order of a guide tree.

Guide tree

A quick clustering of the sequences that fixes the order of progressive alignment.

Consensus sequence

The most common residue in each column.

Conservation, Shannon entropy

How little a column varies; entropy measures its diversity, 0 for an invariant column.

Position-specific scoring matrix (PSSM), profile

Log-odds scores for each residue at each alignment position.

Pseudocounts

Small counts added to observed frequencies so that unseen residues get a finite score.

Profile HMM

A hidden Markov model of a family alignment with match, insert and delete states.











NoteWant to read more?






Richard Durbin and others, Biological Sequence Analysis (Cambridge, 1998), chapters 5 and 6, on profiles, profile HMMs and multiple alignment.
Kazutaka Katoh and Daron Standley, “MAFFT multiple sequence alignment software version 7”, Molecular Biology and Evolution 30, 2013, pages 772 to 780, on one of today’s standard aligners.
Ulrich Bodenhofer and others, “msa: an R package for multiple sequence alignment”, Bioinformatics 31, 2015, pages 3997 to 3999, the Bioconductor package for RStudio.

title: Pairwise alignment II: local alignment and scoring
text:
Module 10 · Lesson 5 of 13 Week 151 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Global alignment assumes two sequences correspond from end to end. Often they don’t: two proteins may share one domain and nothing else, or a gene may be compared with a whole genome. Local alignment finds the best-matching parts. And it raises a question that global alignment hides: every pair of sequences has a best local alignment, even two random ones. When is a score high enough to mean the proteins are related?
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Pairwise alignment II: local alignment and scoring
text:
Smith-Waterman
Temple Smith and Michael Waterman (1981) changed one thing in Needleman-Wunsch: a cell can’t go below zero,

F(i, j) = \max\{0,\ F(i-1, j-1) + s(x_i, y_j),\ F(i-1, j) + g,\ F(i, j-1) + g\},

so a bad region “resets” the alignment instead of dragging it down. The first row and column are all zeros, the best score is the largest cell anywhere in the matrix, and the traceback starts there and stops at the first zero. For this to find local regions, the expected score of aligning two random letters must be negative; otherwise long random alignments would always win.
The setup code reads the family and pwalign’s BLOSUM matrices.












Your turn. Compute the Smith-Waterman matrix for the classic textbook pair HEAGAWGHEE and PAWHEAE (Durbin and others, 1998), with BLOSUM50 and a gap score of -8, and find the best local score.









The floor is 0.


x <- strsplit("HEAGAWGHEE", "")[[1]]; y <- strsplit("PAWHEAE", "")[[1]]
g <- -8
F <- matrix(0, length(x) + 1, length(y) + 1)              # zeros in the first row and column
for (i in 2:(length(x) + 1)) for (j in 2:(length(y) + 1))
  F[i, j] <- max(0, F[i - 1, j - 1] + BLOSUM50[x[i - 1], y[j - 1]], F[i - 1, j] + g, F[i, j - 1] + g)
c(best = max(F), row = which(F == max(F), arr.ind = TRUE)[1, 1] - 1, col = which(F == max(F), arr.ind = TRUE)[1, 2] - 1)
A best score of 28, ending at the 9th letter of HEAGAWGHEE (the second-to-last E) and the 5th of PAWHEAE (its E): the local alignment AWGHE over AW-HE. The rest of each sequence is simply left out.




Your turn. Check it with pairwiseAlignment(type = "local"), with a linear gap penalty of 8.









type = "local".


al <- pairwiseAlignment(AAString("HEAGAWGHEE"), AAString("PAWHEAE"), type = "local",
                        substitutionMatrix = BLOSUM50, gapOpening = 0, gapExtension = 8)
c(score = score(al), pattern = as.character(alignedPattern(al)), subject = as.character(alignedSubject(al)))
Score 28, AWGHE over AW-HE, as by hand.




Your turn. A domain hidden in an unrelated protein: take residues 60 to 160 of SDR_05, embed them in 300 random residues, and align PL7_KRED with the result, globally and locally.









The local alignment: "local".


set.seed(10051)
aa <- c("A", "R", "N", "D", "C", "Q", "E", "G", "H", "I", "L", "K", "M", "F", "P", "S", "T", "W", "Y", "V")
junk <- function(n) paste(sample(aa, n, TRUE), collapse = "")
chimera <- AAString(paste0(junk(150), as.character(subseq(fam[[6]], 60, 160)), junk(150)))
loc <- pairwiseAlignment(fam[[1]], chimera, type = "local", substitutionMatrix = "BLOSUM62", gapOpening = 10, gapExtension = 1)
glo <- pairwiseAlignment(fam[[1]], chimera, type = "global", substitutionMatrix = "BLOSUM62", gapOpening = 10, gapExtension = 1)
c(local = score(loc), global = score(glo), subject_start = start(subject(loc)), subject_end = end(subject(loc)))
Locally, a score of 139, aligning PL7_KRED with residues 152 to 251 of the chimera: exactly where the 101-residue domain was put (positions 151 to 251). Globally, -27: the 300 random residues drown the signal in gap and mismatch penalties.

title: Pairwise alignment II: local alignment and scoring
text:
Where the scores come from
A substitution score is a log-odds ratio:

s(a, b) = \frac{1}{\lambda}\log\frac{q_{ab}}{p_a\,p_b},

where q_{ab} is the frequency with which a and b are aligned in true alignments of related proteins, and p_a p_b the frequency expected by chance. Positive scores mean “aligned more often than chance”. BLOSUM62 (Henikoff and Henikoff, 1992) estimated q_{ab} from conserved blocks of proteins clustered at 62% identity, and reports scores in half-bits (\lambda = \ln 2 / 2), rounded to integers. PAM matrices (Dayhoff, 1978) were built instead from close alignments and extrapolated to more distant ones by matrix powers: PAM250 for distant proteins, PAM30 for close ones. With BLOSUM, a higher number is for closer proteins.
Your turn. Look up a few BLOSUM62 scores, and compute the expected score of two random residues, \sum_a\sum_b p_a p_b\, s(a, b), with typical amino-acid frequencies.









Weight the scores, S.


p <- c(A = 7.8, R = 5.1, N = 4.5, D = 5.4, C = 1.9, Q = 4.3, E = 6.3, G = 7.4, H = 2.6, I = 6.8,
       L = 9.9, K = 5.8, M = 2.5, F = 4.7, P = 3.9, S = 5.7, T = 5.1, W = 1.3, Y = 3.2, V = 6.6)
p <- p / sum(p)
S <- BLOSUM62[names(p), names(p)]
c(LL = S["L", "L"], LI = S["L", "I"], LD = S["L", "D"], WW = S["W", "W"], expected = sum(outer(p, p) * S))
L with L scores 4, L with I 2 (similar residues, often swapped), L with D -4 (rarely swapped), and W with W 11 (tryptophan is rare, so a shared W is strong evidence). The expected score of two random residues is -0.98: negative, as local alignment requires.




Your turn. Estimate log-odds scores yourself from the aligned KRED family: count how often each pair of residues occurs in the same column (over all pairs of sequences), compare with chance, and convert to half-bits. Compare a few with BLOSUM62.









Round to 2 decimals.


al <- as.matrix(readAAStringSet("data/kred_family_aligned.fasta"))   # 25 x columns
aa <- c("A", "R", "N", "D", "C", "Q", "E", "G", "H", "I", "L", "K", "M", "F", "P", "S", "T", "W", "Y", "V")
Q <- matrix(0, 20, 20, dimnames = list(aa, aa))
for (k in seq_len(ncol(al))) {
  col <- al[, k]; col <- col[col %in% aa]
  tab <- table(factor(col, levels = aa)); Q <- Q + outer(tab, tab) - diag(as.numeric(tab))   # pairs in this column
}
q <- Q / sum(Q); pa <- rowSums(q)
s_est <- 2 * log2(q / outer(pa, pa))                                  # half-bits
round(c(LL = s_est["L", "L"], LI = s_est["L", "I"], LD = s_est["L", "D"], cor_with_blosum = cor(as.vector(s_est[is.finite(s_est)]), as.vector(BLOSUM62[aa, aa][is.finite(s_est)]))), 2)
From the family’s own alignment: L with L 5.2, L with I 0.1, L with D -3.1, and overall the estimated scores correlate 0.75 with BLOSUM62. They’re noisier (some pairs are rare in 25 sequences), and they’re specific to this family’s degree of divergence. That’s what BLOSUM did on a large scale, from thousands of conserved blocks.

title: Pairwise alignment II: local alignment and scoring
text:
Is the score significant?
The most distant family member, SDR_24, aligns locally with PL7_KRED with some score. Is that more than two unrelated proteins of the same lengths and compositions would get? The simplest answer is a permutation test: shuffle one sequence many times (keeping its composition, destroying its order), align each shuffle, and see where the real score falls.
Your turn. Align PL7_KRED with SDR_24, then with 200 shuffles of SDR_24.









200 shuffles.


target <- fam[[25]]
sw <- function(s) score(pairwiseAlignment(fam[[1]], s, type = "local", substitutionMatrix = "BLOSUM62", gapOpening = 10, gapExtension = 1))
observed <- sw(target)
set.seed(10052)
shuffled <- replicate(200, sw(AAString(paste(sample(strsplit(as.character(target), "")[[1]]), collapse = ""))))
c(observed = observed, max_shuffled = max(shuffled), mean = mean(shuffled), sd = sd(shuffled),
  p_empirical = (sum(shuffled >= observed) + 1) / (200 + 1))
The real score is 344; the 200 shuffles score at most 51, with a mean of 32 and an SD of 5.2. None comes close: the empirical p-value is 1/201 = 0.005, the smallest that 200 shuffles can give. SDR_24 shares only about 35% of its residues with PL7_KRED, but that’s far beyond chance.




A permutation p-value can’t go below 1/(n+1), so to say how significant a score of several hundred is, we need the distribution’s shape. The best local alignment score is a maximum over many possible alignments, and maxima don’t follow the normal distribution: they follow an extreme-value distribution. For local alignment scores, Karlin and Altschul (1990) proved it’s the Gumbel distribution:

P(S \ge x) \approx 1 - \exp\left(-e^{-\lambda(x - \mu)}\right),

with a long right tail. Its mean is \mu + 0.5772/\lambda and its standard deviation \pi/(\lambda\sqrt6), so the parameters can be estimated from a sample’s mean and standard deviation (the method of moments).
Your turn. Fit the Gumbel distribution to the shuffled scores, and compute the p-value of the observed score.









The standard deviation is \pi/(\lambda\sqrt 6).


target <- fam[[25]]
sw <- function(s) score(pairwiseAlignment(fam[[1]], s, type = "local", substitutionMatrix = "BLOSUM62", gapOpening = 10, gapExtension = 1))
observed <- sw(target)
set.seed(10052)
shuffled <- replicate(200, sw(AAString(paste(sample(strsplit(as.character(target), "")[[1]]), collapse = ""))))
lambda <- pi / (sd(shuffled) * sqrt(6))
mu <- mean(shuffled) - 0.5772 / lambda
p_gumbel <- function(x) 1 - exp(-exp(-lambda * (x - mu)))
c(lambda = lambda, mu = mu, p_at_60 = p_gumbel(60), log10_p_observed = -lambda * (observed - mu) / log(10))   # the tail, on the log scale
\lambda = 0.248 and \mu = 29.9. A score of 60 already has a p-value of 0.0006, and the observed 344 has \log_{10} p = -34. For large scores, P \approx e^{-\lambda(x - \mu)}, which the code computes on the log scale, because the exact formula rounds to 0 in floating point. The histogram below shows the fit.

title: Pairwise alignment II: local alignment and scoring
text:
E-values and bit scores
In a database search, a query is compared with many sequences, and some random hit will score well. The E-value is the expected number of hits with a score at least S by chance, in a search of this size. Karlin and Altschul’s formula for a query of length m against a database of total length n is

E = K\,m\,n\,e^{-\lambda S},

with constants \lambda and K that depend on the scoring system. For one comparison, E \approx P when both are small; for a database of N comparable sequences, E \approx N \times P. An E-value below about 0.001 is strong evidence of homology; near 1, a hit is what chance alone would give. The bit score S' = (\lambda S - \ln K)/\ln 2 normalizes a raw score so that E = m\,n\,2^{-S'}, comparable between scoring systems.
Your turn. Using the Gumbel fit, find the score that would have an E-value of 0.001 in a search of 600 sequences like these, and of 250 million (the size of UniProt).









Divide by lambda.


target <- fam[[25]]
sw <- function(s) score(pairwiseAlignment(fam[[1]], s, type = "local", substitutionMatrix = "BLOSUM62", gapOpening = 10, gapExtension = 1))
set.seed(10052)
shuffled <- replicate(200, sw(AAString(paste(sample(strsplit(as.character(target), "")[[1]]), collapse = ""))))
lambda <- pi / (sd(shuffled) * sqrt(6)); mu <- mean(shuffled) - 0.5772 / lambda
score_for_E <- function(E, N) mu - log(-log(1 - E / N)) / lambda         # solve N * P(S >= x) = E for x
c(db600 = score_for_E(0.001, 600), uniprot = score_for_E(0.001, 2.5e8))
For an E-value of 0.001, a score of 84 is needed among 600 sequences, and 136 among UniProt’s 250 million. The bigger the database, the higher the bar: the same alignment can be convincing in a small search and borderline in a large one.




Your turn. Estimate K from the fit (\mu = \ln(Kmn)/\lambda, with m and n the two sequences’ lengths), and compute the observed alignment’s bit score.









Bits: divide by \ln 2.


target <- fam[[25]]
sw <- function(s) score(pairwiseAlignment(fam[[1]], s, type = "local", substitutionMatrix = "BLOSUM62", gapOpening = 10, gapExtension = 1))
observed <- sw(target)
set.seed(10052)
shuffled <- replicate(200, sw(AAString(paste(sample(strsplit(as.character(target), "")[[1]]), collapse = ""))))
lambda <- pi / (sd(shuffled) * sqrt(6)); mu <- mean(shuffled) - 0.5772 / lambda
m <- length(fam[[1]]); n <- length(target)
K <- exp(lambda * mu) / (m * n)
c(K = K, bits = (lambda * observed - log(K)) / log(2))
K = 0.026 and a bit score of 128. With bits, E = mn\,2^{-S'}: here about 252 \times 250 \times 2^{-128}, around 10^{-34}, the same conclusion in the currency BLAST reports.










NoteGo deeper: why the Gumbel, and why it’s only approximate with gaps





For ungapped local alignments, Karlin and Altschul (1990) proved that the maximal segment score has, asymptotically, a Gumbel distribution, with \lambda the unique positive solution of \sum_{a,b} p_a p_b e^{\lambda s(a,b)} = 1 (which exists exactly when the expected score is negative and some score is positive), and K given by a more complicated formula. The intuition: an alignment’s running score is a random walk with negative drift; a high-scoring segment is a rare excursion upward, and the maximum of many nearly independent excursions, each with an exponential tail, is Gumbel. With gaps there’s no proof, but simulations show the Gumbel form still holds, and BLAST uses \lambda and K estimated by simulation for each scoring system. Also, \lambda connects to the matrix: for BLOSUM62 in half-bits, the ungapped \lambda is close to \ln 2/2 = 0.347. Samuel Karlin and Stephen Altschul, “Methods for assessing the statistical significance of molecular sequence features by using general scoring schemes”, PNAS 87, 1990, pages 2264 to 2268.

title: Pairwise alignment II: local alignment and scoring
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Which matrix? Align PL7_KRED with a close relative (SDR_01) and with the most distant one (SDR_24) using BLOSUM45, BLOSUM62 and BLOSUM80, and compare the scores, each relative to its best.









The third is "BLOSUM80".


mats <- c("BLOSUM45", "BLOSUM62", "BLOSUM80")
sc <- sapply(mats, function(mx) sapply(c(close = 2, far = 25), function(i)
  score(pairwiseAlignment(fam[[1]], fam[[i]], type = "local", substitutionMatrix = mx, gapOpening = 10, gapExtension = 1))))
sc
Raw scores aren’t comparable between matrices (they’re on different scales), so compare the ratio of far to close in each column: 0.49 with BLOSUM45, 0.45 with BLOSUM62 and 0.40 with BLOSUM80. Relative to the close relative, the distant one holds up best under BLOSUM45, which was built from more divergent blocks. Search programs default to BLOSUM62 as a compromise.




Challenge 2 · λ from the matrix. In RStudio, solve \sum_{a,b} p_a p_b\, e^{\lambda s(a,b)} = 1 for \lambda > 0 with uniroot(), for BLOSUM62 with the frequencies of the exercise above. Compare it with \ln 2 / 2 and with your Gumbel fit’s \lambda (which includes gaps).

title: Pairwise alignment II: local alignment and scoring
text:
Quick quiz

1. What makes Smith-Waterman local?

It uses a different substitution matrix
Cells can’t go below zero, and the best cell anywhere is the end of the alignment
It ignores gaps


A bad region resets the score instead of penalizing the whole alignment.



2. A positive BLOSUM62 score for a pair of amino acids means:

They’re aligned in related proteins more often than chance would predict
They’re chemically identical
They never replace each other


It’s a log-odds ratio of observed to expected frequency.



3. Why must the expected score of two random residues be negative for local alignment?

To make the scores integers
Otherwise random alignments would grow with length and always cover everything
Because of the gap penalty


With negative drift, only real similarity produces high-scoring segments.



4. Local alignment scores of unrelated sequences follow:

A normal distribution
An extreme-value (Gumbel) distribution
A uniform distribution


The score is a maximum over many possible alignments.



5. An E-value of 0.5 means:

The hit is 50% likely to be a true homolog
Half a hit this good is expected by chance in a search of this size
The score is half the maximum


E-values depend on the database size.



6. For aligning two distant proteins, which matrix is usually better?

BLOSUM45
BLOSUM80
It doesn’t matter


Lower BLOSUM numbers come from more divergent blocks.

title: Pairwise alignment II: local alignment and scoring
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve found local similarities and judged them. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Smith-Waterman adds a zero floor to the recurrence; the textbook pair scores 28 (AWGHE over AW-HE), and a hidden domain is found where global alignment fails.
Substitution scores are log-odds ratios in half-bits; the family’s own estimates correlate 0.75 with BLOSUM62; the expected random score is negative.
Significance: shuffling gives a null distribution, which is Gumbel; PL7_KRED against its most distant relative is far beyond any shuffle.
E-values (E = Kmn\,e^{-\lambda S}) and bit scores put scores on a common, database-aware scale.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download kred_family.fasta and kred_family_aligned.fasta into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

More shuffles. Repeat the shuffle test with 2,000 shuffles, and fit the Gumbel by maximum likelihood (optim() on the log-likelihood). How much do \lambda and \mu change from the moment estimates?
Length dependence. Generate random protein pairs of lengths 100, 200, 400 and 800, and plot the mean best local score against \log(mn). Karlin-Altschul theory says the relation is a straight line with slope 1/\lambda.
Smith-Waterman traceback. Add a traceback to your Smith-Waterman code, starting from the largest cell and stopping at a zero.
PAM by matrix powers. Build a substitution probability matrix P from the family’s pair counts, and compute P^{250} with repeated multiplication. What share of residues are unchanged after “250 PAMs”?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Local alignment

An alignment of the best-matching parts of two sequences.

Smith-Waterman algorithm

Dynamic programming for optimal local alignment, with a floor of zero.

Log-odds score

The logarithm of the ratio of the observed pairing frequency to the frequency expected by chance.

BLOSUM and PAM matrices

Families of amino-acid substitution matrices for different evolutionary distances.

Permutation (shuffle) test

Comparing a score with scores of shuffled sequences that keep the composition but destroy the order.

Gumbel (extreme-value) distribution

The distribution of maxima, which local alignment scores of random sequences follow.

E-value

The expected number of chance hits with at least a given score in a search.

Bit score

A normalized score, independent of the scoring system’s scale.











NoteWant to read more?






Richard Durbin and others, Biological Sequence Analysis (Cambridge, 1998), chapter 2, sections 2.3 to 2.7, on local alignment, scoring matrices and significance.
Steven Henikoff and Jorja Henikoff, “Amino acid substitution matrices from protein blocks”, PNAS 89, 1992, pages 10915 to 10919, where BLOSUM was introduced.
Warren Ewens and Gregory Grant, Statistical Methods in Bioinformatics (2nd edition, Springer, 2005), chapters 6 and 9, on extreme-value theory and BLAST statistics.

title: Working with sequences in R
text:
Module 10 · Lesson 3 of 13 Week 149 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 1 did everything with strsplit() and loops, which is fine for 3,000 bases and hopeless for a genome of 6 million (PL-7’s size) or 3 billion (a human’s). Biostrings stores sequences compactly and does the common operations in compiled code. This lesson is a tour of what it does, on PL-7’s fragment and reads.
In this lesson you’ll:
The setup code reads the fragment as a DNAString, and the reads.

title: Working with sequences in R
text:
The basics, fast
Your turn. Extract the kred gene with subseq(), reverse-complement it, and translate it.









The gene ends at 1,859.


gene <- reverseComplement(subseq(frag, start = 1101, end = 1859))
prot <- translate(gene)
c(gene = length(gene), protein = length(prot), last = as.character(subseq(prot, length(prot), length(prot))))
759 bases, 253 characters of protein ending in *: the same as Lesson 1’s hand-made translation, in three function calls. translate() uses the standard genetic code by default (getGeneticCode() gives others, such as the mitochondrial ones), and warns if the length isn’t a multiple of 3.




Your turn. Compute the GC content in sliding windows of 200 bases with letterFrequencyInSlidingView(), and compare the windows inside the kred gene with the rest.









Windows of 200 bases.


gc <- letterFrequencyInSlidingView(frag, view.width = 200, letters = "GC", as.prob = TRUE)[, 1]
centre <- seq_along(gc) + 99                              # each window's middle position
in_gene <- centre >= 1101 & centre <= 1859
c(min = min(gc), max = max(gc), gene = mean(gc[in_gene]), outside = mean(gc[!in_gene]))
The windows range from 0.50 to 0.74 GC. Inside the kred gene the average is 0.58, lower than the 0.65 outside it. A gene’s GC content is held back by its protein: its first and second codon positions (47% and 43% GC in Lesson 1) are set by the amino acids, and only the third (83%) follows the genome’s preference. Windows like these are how genomic islands (stretches acquired from other organisms, with a different composition) are spotted.

title: Working with sequences in R
text:
Words in the sequence
Counting short words, k-mers, is one of the most useful things to do with a sequence: their frequencies are a signature of the organism, they power database search (Lesson 6) and genome assembly, and some carry biology, like the dinucleotide CG.
Your turn. Count dinucleotides with dinucleotideFrequency(), and compute the CpG observed-to-expected ratio, f(\text{CG}) / (f(\text{C})\,f(\text{G})), which is about 1 if CG occurs as often as its bases’ frequencies predict.









The expected frequency of CG is f(C) \times f(G).


di <- dinucleotideFrequency(frag, as.prob = TRUE)
mono <- letterFrequency(frag, c("A", "C", "G", "T"), as.prob = TRUE)
c(CG = di[["CG"]], GC = di[["GC"]], cpg_ratio = di[["CG"]] / (mono[["C"]] * mono[["G"]]))
CG makes up 10.5% of the dinucleotides, and the observed-to-expected ratio is 1.05: in this bacterium, CG occurs as often as chance predicts. In vertebrate genomes, it’s about 0.2, because methylated cytosines in CG mutate easily to T, and CG survives mainly in CpG islands, which Lesson 10 hunts for with a hidden Markov model.




Your turn. Count all 64 trinucleotides on the forward strand with oligonucleotideFrequency(), and list the most and least common.









Trinucleotides have width 3.


tri <- oligonucleotideFrequency(frag, width = 3)
c(head(sort(tri, decreasing = TRUE), 3), head(sort(tri), 3))
The most common trinucleotides are GCG (99), CCG and CGC (97 each); the rarest AAT (10), TAT and TTA (14 each). In a GC-rich genome, AT-rich words are rare, and that includes the stop codons TAA and TAG, which is why long open reading frames are commoner by chance in GC-rich DNA (see the ORF search below).

title: Working with sequences in R
text:
Searching for motifs
matchPattern() finds every occurrence of a pattern. Restriction enzymes, the scissors of molecular cloning, cut DNA at specific short sites: EcoRI at GAATTC, BamHI at GGATCC, NotI at GCGGCCGC. These sites are palindromes (each is its own reverse complement), so searching one strand finds them on both.
Your turn. Count the sites of the three enzymes in the fragment.









Search the fragment, frag.


sites <- c(EcoRI = "GAATTC", BamHI = "GGATCC", NotI = "GCGGCCGC")
sapply(sites, function(s) countPattern(s, frag))
No EcoRI sites, two BamHI sites, no NotI sites. EcoRI’s site is AT-rich, so it’s rare in a GC-rich genome; NotI’s 8-base site would occur by chance only once every 4^8 = 65{,}536 bases in a random sequence with equal bases. That’s why rare-cutters like NotI are used to cut whole genomes into a few large pieces.




Your turn. Biological motifs are rarely exact. The bacterial ribosome-binding site (Shine-Dalgarno) is about AGGAGG, 5 to 10 bases upstream of the start codon. Search the kred gene’s strand, from 30 bases before its start, allowing one mismatch.









Allow one mismatch.


upstream <- reverseComplement(subseq(frag, 1860, 1889))      # the 30 bases before the start codon, gene strand
m <- matchPattern("AGGAGG", upstream, max.mismatch = 1)
c(upstream = as.character(upstream), found_at = paste(start(m), collapse = ","), match = paste(as.character(m), collapse = ","))
AGGAGG, exactly, at position 20 of the 30 upstream bases: it ends 5 bases before the start codon, the classic spacing. A one-mismatch search would also have found AGGAGA or GGGAGG, which real ribosome-binding sites often are.




Your turn. Count the codons of the kred gene with trinucleotideFrequency(..., step = 3), and find the most-used codon for leucine (CTN and TTA/TTG) and for alanine (GCN).









Step through the gene one codon at a time: step = 3.


gene <- reverseComplement(subseq(frag, 1101, 1859))
cu <- trinucleotideFrequency(gene, step = 3)
leu <- cu[c("CTT", "CTC", "CTA", "CTG", "TTA", "TTG")]
ala <- cu[c("GCT", "GCC", "GCA", "GCG")]
list(leucine = leu, alanine = ala)
For leucine, TTG (6), CTC and CTG (4 each), then CTA and TTA (1 each) and CTT (0); for alanine, GCC (10), GCG (6), GCT (3) and GCA (0). The codons ending in G or C dominate, as the GC-rich genome predicts. Codon usage differs between organisms, which matters when a gene is moved into a production host: a gene full of codons the host rarely uses can be translated slowly, and biotech companies routinely “codon-optimize” genes before expressing them.

title: Working with sequences in R
text:
Finding genes: open reading frames
Your turn. Translate all six reading frames of the fragment, and find every ORF of at least 80 codons (a methionine followed by at least 79 non-stop residues and a stop).









Keep the frames whose list of ORFs isn’t empty: Filter(length, orfs).


frames <- c(lapply(0:2, function(o) subseq(frag, 1 + o, 1 + o + 3 * floor((3000 - o) / 3) - 1)),
            lapply(0:2, function(o) subseq(reverseComplement(frag), 1 + o, 1 + o + 3 * floor((3000 - o) / 3) - 1)))
names(frames) <- c("+1", "+2", "+3", "-1", "-2", "-3")
orfs <- lapply(frames, function(f) {
  p <- as.character(translate(f))
  m <- gregexpr("M[^*]{79,}\\*", p)[[1]]
  if (m[1] < 0) integer(0) else attr(m, "match.length") / 1          # residues incl. the stop
})
lengths <- unlist(orfs)
c(n_orfs = length(lengths), longest = max(lengths), frames_with_orfs = paste(names(Filter(length, orfs)), collapse = " "))
Three ORFs of at least 80 codons. In frame +1, the hypothetical protein’s 100 codons (with its stop). In frame -2, the kred gene, but 263 codons long, not 253: the search starts at the first ATG after the previous stop, and there’s an in-frame ATG 10 codons upstream of the real start. An ORF search can’t tell which start is real; the ribosome-binding site, 5 bases before the true ATG, can, and so can comparison with related genes (Lesson 6). And in frame +2, a 110-codon ORF that’s no gene at all: it lies on the opposite strand inside the kred gene, a “shadow” ORF of the kind that GC-rich DNA, poor in the AT-rich stop codons, produces by chance. Gene finders score ORFs by their codon usage to reject these.

title: Working with sequences in R
text:
Mapping reads
A read comes from one strand or the other of some place in the genome. Mapping finds where. Real mappers (BWA, Bowtie 2) index the genome and allow mismatches and gaps; for a 3,000-base fragment, a direct search will do.
Your turn. Find where the first read’s first 30 bases occur, on either strand, allowing up to 2 mismatches (sequencing errors).









On the other strand, search for the seed’s reverse complement.


seed <- subseq(reads[[1]], 1, 30)
fwd <- matchPattern(seed, frag, max.mismatch = 2)
rev <- matchPattern(reverseComplement(seed), frag, max.mismatch = 2)
c(forward_hits = length(fwd), reverse_hits = length(rev), position = c(start(fwd), start(rev))[1])
One hit, on the reverse strand, at position 2,111: the read was sequenced from the reverse strand, and its first 30 bases match positions 2,111 to 2,140 of the forward sequence, reverse-complemented, with at most 2 mismatches.










NoteGo deeper: how real mappers and assemblers use k-mers





A genome of billions of bases can’t be searched read by read. Mappers build an index of the genome first: a suffix array or its compressed cousin, the Burrows-Wheeler transform with an FM-index, which finds every occurrence of a short string in time proportional to its length, regardless of the genome’s size. They then extend exact seed matches into full alignments with mismatches and gaps (seed-and-extend, as BLAST does in Lesson 6). Genome assembly works without a reference: it breaks the reads into k-mers and builds a de Bruijn graph, whose nodes are (k-1)-mers and whose edges are k-mers, then walks it to reconstruct the genome. Ben Langmead and others, “Ultrafast and memory-efficient alignment of short DNA sequences to the human genome”, Genome Biology 10, 2009 (Bowtie), and Phillip Compeau, Pavel Pevzner and Glenn Tesler, “How to apply de Bruijn graphs to genome assembly”, Nature Biotechnology 29, 2011, are readable introductions.

title: Working with sequences in R
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Map them all. Map every read’s first 30 bases (up to 2 mismatches, either strand), and count the reads that map exactly once.









The same 2 mismatches on both strands.


hits <- sapply(seq_along(reads), function(i) {
  seed <- subseq(reads[[i]], 1, 30)
  length(matchPattern(seed, frag, max.mismatch = 2)) + length(matchPattern(reverseComplement(seed), frag, max.mismatch = 2))
})
table(hits)
399 of the 400 reads map exactly once; one doesn’t map at all (one of the poor reads, with more than 2 errors in its first 30 bases). In a real genome, some reads map to several places (repeats, or genes in more than one copy), and mappers report a mapping quality for how sure they are of the place.




Challenge 2 · Coverage. In RStudio, record each mapped read’s start, strand and length, and compute the coverage: how many reads cover each base of the fragment. With 400 reads of 150 bases on 3,000 bases, the average should be 20. Plot it. Is it even, and what does Lander-Waterman theory (coverage is Poisson) predict for the share of bases with no read at all?

title: Working with sequences in R
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why use Biostrings instead of character strings?

It gives different answers
It stores long sequences compactly and does common operations in fast compiled code
Base R can’t read FASTA


Lesson 1’s methods work, but don’t scale to genomes.



2. A CpG observed-to-expected ratio well below 1 means:

The sequence is GC-poor
The dinucleotide CG is rarer than the frequencies of C and G predict
CG is overrepresented


In vertebrates, methylated CpGs mutate to TpG, depleting CG except in CpG islands (Lesson 10).



3. Why does one search find a palindromic restriction site on both strands?

Restriction enzymes only cut one strand
The site is its own reverse complement
Biostrings searches both strands automatically


GAATTC reverse-complemented is GAATTC.



4. In a six-frame translation, how many frames are on the reverse strand?

One
Three
Six


Three offsets on each strand.



5. Why allow mismatches when mapping reads?

Reads have sequencing errors, and the genome may differ slightly from the reference
To find more genes
To make the search faster


Exact matching would lose reads with even one error.



6. A k-mer is:

A protein of length k
A substring of length k
A gene with k exons


k-mer counting is a workhorse of genome analysis.

title: Working with sequences in R
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve used Bioconductor’s sequence toolkit. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Biostrings basics: subseq(), reverseComplement(), translate() on DNAString objects reproduce Lesson 1 in three calls.
Composition: GC in sliding windows, dinucleotide and k-mer frequencies, and the CpG observed-to-expected ratio (1.05 here).
Searching: matchPattern() and countPattern() for exact sites and approximate motifs.
Gene finding: a six-frame search for long ORFs finds the two annotated genes (one with a start 10 codons too early) and a chance ORF hidden inside one of them.
Mapping: reads map back to one place on one strand, allowing a few mismatches.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download pl7_fragment.fasta and pl7_reads.fastq into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

A real genome. Install BSgenome.Ecoli.NCBI.20080805 from Bioconductor and repeat this lesson’s composition statistics on a whole E. coli genome. How long do they take?
k-mer spectra. Count the 6-mers in the fragment and in a random sequence with the same base composition (sample()). Compare the two distributions of counts. Which 6-mers are over- or under-represented, and by how much compared with random variation?
Codon adaptation. Compare the codon usage of kred with that of the hypothetical protein gene. Highly expressed genes in bacteria tend to use a narrower set of codons. Which looks more “highly expressed”?
A de Bruijn graph. Break the fragment into 20-mers, build the de Bruijn graph of 19-mers with igraph, and check that it’s a single path.










NoteKey words from this lesson






DNAString, DNAStringSet

Biostrings’ classes for one DNA sequence and for many.

Sliding window

A fixed-width window moved along a sequence one position at a time.

k-mer

A substring of length k.

CpG observed-to-expected ratio

f(\text{CG})/(f(\text{C})f(\text{G})), the CG dinucleotide’s frequency relative to chance.

Restriction site

A short DNA sequence, often a palindrome, cut by a restriction enzyme.

Palindrome (in DNA)

A sequence equal to its own reverse complement.

Six-frame translation

Translating a DNA sequence in all three offsets on both strands.

Read mapping

Finding where in a reference genome each sequencing read comes from.

Coverage

The number of reads covering each base.











NoteWant to read more?






Hervé Pagès and others, the Biostrings vignettes on bioconductor.org, especially “A short presentation of the basic classes” and “Pairwise Sequence Alignments”.
Susan Holmes and Wolfgang Huber, Modern Statistics for Modern Biology (free online), chapter 2, section 2.9, on Markov chain models of DNA, k-mers and CpG islands.
Phillip Compeau and Pavel Pevzner, Bioinformatics Algorithms: An Active Learning Approach (3rd edition, Active Learning Publishers, 2018), chapters 1 to 3, on k-mers, motifs and assembly.

title: Molecular genetics for data scientists
text:
Module 10 · Lesson 1 of 13 Week 147 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The last module of the course follows CPSC 545, bioinformatics: statistics and algorithms for biological sequences and measurements. It might seem far from a chemical plant, but it isn’t. The plant’s parent company has a biocatalysis group that uses enzymes instead of metal catalysts for some of its fine-chemical steps, because enzymes work in water, at room temperature, and make one mirror-image form of a molecule instead of both. One of their best enzymes came from a bacterium that lives in the plant’s own wastewater treatment basin: Rhodococcus sp. PL-7. (The organism, its genome and every sequence in this module are fictional, simulated for the course.)
Dr. Amaya Rossi, who leads the group, has the bacterium’s genome sequenced and wants to know everything about its ketoreductase (KRED), the enzyme that reduces a ketone to an alcohol in their process. This module follows that enzyme from its gene to its family, its evolution, its structure, and the bacterium’s response to the solvents it has to work in.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Molecular genetics for data scientists
text:
DNA as data
DNA is a chain of four kinds of nucleotides, named by their bases: A (adenine), C (cytosine), G (guanine) and T (thymine). Two chains wind together into the double helix, with A always paired to T and C to G, so each strand determines the other. The two strands run in opposite directions, conventionally labelled 5′ to 3′; sequences are written 5′ to 3′.
A gene is a stretch of DNA that’s copied (transcribed) into RNA; for most genes, the RNA is then translated into a protein, three bases (a codon) per amino acid. That’s the central dogma: DNA → RNA → protein. RNA uses U (uracil) instead of T.
The setup code reads a 3,000-base fragment of the PL-7 genome from a FASTA file (a text format: a header line starting with >, then the sequence) using nothing but base R, and builds the genetic code: a named vector from the 64 codons to the 20 amino acids (one-letter codes) and * for the three stop codons.












Your turn. How long is the fragment, and how many of each base does it have?









Tabulate bases.


bases <- strsplit(fragment, "")[[1]]              # one letter per element
c(length = length(bases), table(bases))
3,000 bases: 543 A, 934 C, 964 G and 559 T. The counts of A and T are close, and so are those of C and G. Within a single strand they don’t have to be (only the two strands together are exactly balanced), but in long sequences they usually are, a regularity known as Chargaff’s second rule.




Your turn. The GC content, the share of G and C, varies a lot between organisms (from about 25% to 75% in bacteria) and between regions of one genome. Compute it.









G or C.


bases <- strsplit(fragment, "")[[1]]
mean(bases %in% c("G", "C"))
63.3%: PL-7’s genome is GC-rich, like other Rhodococcus species. A G-C pair is held by three hydrogen bonds and an A-T pair by two, so GC-rich DNA is more stable, and the GC content shapes which codons an organism uses, as you’ll see below.

title: Molecular genetics for data scientists
text:
The other strand
The sequence in the file is one strand. The other strand is its reverse complement: swap A↔︎T and C↔︎G (the complement), then reverse the order (because the strands run in opposite directions, and we always write 5′ to 3′). Genes can lie on either strand.
Your turn. Write a function for the reverse complement with chartr() (character translation) and rev(), and apply it to the first 12 bases.









A becomes T, C becomes G, G becomes C, T becomes A: "TGCA".


revcomp <- function(s) paste(rev(strsplit(chartr("ACGT", "TGCA", s), "")[[1]]), collapse = "")
c(forward = substr(fragment, 1, 12), reverse_complement = revcomp(substr(fragment, 1, 12)))
GCTGTGGGCCAA becomes TTGGCCCACAGC: read backwards, with every base swapped. Applying revcomp() twice gives the original back, a quick check worth making whenever you write sequence code.

title: Molecular genetics for data scientists
text:
From gene to protein
The genome annotation says the kred gene is at complement(1101..1859): positions 1,101 to 1,859, on the reverse strand. To read it, take those bases and reverse-complement them. The result is the gene’s coding strand, which has the same sequence as its messenger RNA, with T for U.
Your turn. Extract the gene, and check how it starts and ends.









The gene ends at 1,859.


revcomp <- function(s) paste(rev(strsplit(chartr("ACGT", "TGCA", s), "")[[1]]), collapse = "")
kred <- revcomp(substr(fragment, 1101, 1859))
mrna <- chartr("T", "U", kred)                      # transcription: T becomes U
c(length = nchar(kred), first = substr(mrna, 1, 15), last = substr(mrna, nchar(mrna) - 2, nchar(mrna)))
759 bases, starting with AUG and ending with UGA. 759 is a multiple of 3: 253 codons.




Your turn. Split the gene into codons with substring(), and count them.









A codon is 3 bases.


revcomp <- function(s) paste(rev(strsplit(chartr("ACGT", "TGCA", s), "")[[1]]), collapse = "")
kred <- revcomp(substr(fragment, 1101, 1859))
starts <- seq(1, nchar(kred), by = 3)
cod <- substring(kred, starts, starts + 2)
c(n_codons = length(cod), first = cod[1], last = cod[length(cod)], n_stops = sum(genetic_code[cod] == "*"))
253 codons: ATG, the start codon (which also codes for methionine), then 251 more, and TGA, a stop codon, at the end, and no other stop in between. A stretch from a start codon to the next stop in the same frame, with no stop in between, is an open reading frame (ORF); long ORFs are how gene-finding programs spot genes in bacterial genomes.




Your turn. Translate the gene with the genetic code, and look at the protein.









Look up each codon: genetic_code[cod].


revcomp <- function(s) paste(rev(strsplit(chartr("ACGT", "TGCA", s), "")[[1]]), collapse = "")
kred <- revcomp(substr(fragment, 1101, 1859))
cod <- substring(kred, seq(1, nchar(kred), 3), seq(3, nchar(kred), 3))
protein <- paste(genetic_code[cod], collapse = "")
c(length = nchar(protein), start = substr(protein, 1, 25), motif_at = regexpr("TG...G.G", protein))
253 characters: 252 amino acids, then * for the stop. The protein starts MCRKHPMKESG, and the regular expression TG...G.G (a dot matches any amino acid) finds the cofactor-binding motif TGAASGIG at position 12. That’s the signature of the short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) family, where the enzyme binds its NADPH cofactor; Lesson 7 shows that it’s conserved in every member of the family.

title: Molecular genetics for data scientists
text:
Codon usage
The genetic code is degenerate: 61 codons for 20 amino acids, so most amino acids have two to six codons, usually differing at the third position. Organisms don’t use synonymous codons equally, and a GC-rich genome like PL-7’s favours G and C at the third position, where the choice doesn’t change the protein.
Your turn. Compute the GC content at each of the three codon positions.









Group by pos.


revcomp <- function(s) paste(rev(strsplit(chartr("ACGT", "TGCA", s), "")[[1]]), collapse = "")
kred <- revcomp(substr(fragment, 1101, 1859))
x <- strsplit(kred, "")[[1]]
pos <- rep(1:3, length.out = length(x))
round(tapply(x %in% c("G", "C"), pos, mean), 3)
47.4% at the first position, 42.7% at the second and 82.6% at the third. The first two positions mostly decide the amino acid, so their composition follows the protein; the third is mostly free, and there the genome’s GC preference shows almost unchecked.

title: Molecular genetics for data scientists
text:
Mutations
A point mutation changes one base. If the new codon codes for the same amino acid, the mutation is synonymous (silent); if not, it’s non-synonymous (missense), or nonsense if it creates a stop codon. The share of possible changes that are synonymous matters for measuring selection: a gene under strong selection to keep its protein accumulates synonymous changes faster than non-synonymous ones.
Your turn. For every codon of the gene (without the stop), try all 9 possible single-base changes, and classify them.









Compare with the original codon, cd.


revcomp <- function(s) paste(rev(strsplit(chartr("ACGT", "TGCA", s), "")[[1]]), collapse = "")
kred <- revcomp(substr(fragment, 1101, 1859))
cod <- substring(kred, seq(1, 756, 3), seq(3, 756, 3))                 # 252 codons, no stop
kind <- unlist(lapply(cod, function(cd) {
  unlist(lapply(1:3, function(p) sapply(setdiff(c("A", "C", "G", "T"), substr(cd, p, p)), function(nb) {
    new <- cd; substr(new, p, p) <- nb
    if (genetic_code[new] == "*") "nonsense" else if (genetic_code[new] == genetic_code[cd]) "synonymous" else "missense"
  })))
}))
round(prop.table(table(kind)), 3)
21.6% synonymous, 74.3% missense and 4.1% nonsense, and almost all the synonymous changes are at third positions. When genes are compared between species, the ratio of non-synonymous to synonymous differences, each per possible site (called dN/dS, or ω), is the classic measure of selection: well below 1 for a gene whose protein is under constraint.




Your turn. A frameshift, an insertion or deletion of a number of bases that isn’t a multiple of 3, shifts every codon after it. Delete the 301st base of the gene, translate, and find the first stop codon.









Continue from base 302.


revcomp <- function(s) paste(rev(strsplit(chartr("ACGT", "TGCA", s), "")[[1]]), collapse = "")
kred <- revcomp(substr(fragment, 1101, 1859))
mut <- paste0(substr(kred, 1, 300), substr(kred, 302, nchar(kred)))   # skip base 301
cod <- substring(mut, seq(1, nchar(mut) - 2, 3), seq(3, nchar(mut), 3))
p <- genetic_code[cod]
c(first_stop = which(p == "*")[1], same_until = which(p != genetic_code[substring(kred, seq(1, 756, 3), seq(3, 756, 3))][seq_along(p)])[1])
The protein is unchanged up to codon 100; every amino acid from codon 101 on is different, and a stop codon appears at codon 159. The result is a truncated protein of 158 residues, the last 58 of them scrambled, almost certainly inactive. That’s why a frameshift in an enzyme gene is a red flag (the project has one).










NoteGo deeper: what the central dogma leaves out





Real genes are messier. In bacteria, genes are mostly continuous ORFs, often grouped in operons transcribed together; in eukaryotes, genes are split into exons separated by introns, which are spliced out of the RNA, and one gene can be spliced several ways into different proteins. Many genes make RNA that’s never translated (ribosomal RNA, which Lessons 8 and 9 use for phylogenetics, transfer RNA, and many regulatory RNAs). Translation starts at a start codon downstream of a ribosome-binding site (in bacteria, the Shine-Dalgarno sequence, AGGAGG, about 8 bases before the start). Some organisms use slightly different genetic codes (mitochondria, for instance). And proteins are modified after translation. Bruce Alberts and others’ Molecular Biology of the Cell (7th edition, Norton, 2022), chapters 4 to 7, is the standard account.

title: Molecular genetics for data scientists
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Six reading frames. A DNA sequence can be read in three frames on each strand. Count the stop codons in each of the six frames of the gene region (positions 1,101 to 1,859).









The reverse frames read revcomp(region).


revcomp <- function(s) paste(rev(strsplit(chartr("ACGT", "TGCA", s), "")[[1]]), collapse = "")
region <- substr(fragment, 1101, 1859)
stops_in <- function(s, offset) {
  st <- seq(1 + offset, nchar(s) - 2, by = 3)
  sum(genetic_code[substring(s, st, st + 2)] == "*")
}
c(forward = sapply(0:2, function(o) stops_in(region, o)),
  reverse = sapply(0:2, function(o) stops_in(revcomp(region), o)))
The gene’s own frame (reverse strand, first frame) has a single stop, at the very end; the other five frames have 4 to 12 stops each in the same 759 bases. In random sequence, a stop appears on average every 21 codons (3 of the 64), a little less often in GC-rich DNA, where the AT-rich stop codons are rarer. So an open frame of 252 codons is very unlikely by chance, and that’s the statistical basis of bacterial gene finding.




Challenge 2 · The ribosome-binding site. In RStudio, look at the 15 bases just upstream of the gene’s start codon, on the gene’s strand (that’s revcomp(substr(fragment, 1860, 1874))). Can you find the Shine-Dalgarno sequence, AGGAGG or something close to it?

title: Molecular genetics for data scientists
text:
Quick quiz

1. The complement of the DNA sequence 5′-ATGC-3′, written 5′ to 3′, is:

TACG
GCAT
CGTA


Complement (TACG), then reverse, because the strands run in opposite directions.



2. A codon is:

One base
Three bases that code for one amino acid or a stop
A whole gene


64 codons, 20 amino acids and stop.



3. The gene is at complement(1101..1859). To read it 5′ to 3′:

Take positions 1,101 to 1,859 as they are
Take them and reverse-complement them
Translate the forward strand


“complement” means the gene is on the other strand.



4. Why is the GC content highest at the third codon position in PL-7’s genes?

Third positions are always G or C
Changes there are often synonymous, so the GC-rich genome’s bias shows most freely there
The ribosome reads third positions twice


The degeneracy of the code is mostly at the third position.



5. A mutation that changes a codon into a stop codon is:

Synonymous
Missense
Nonsense


It truncates the protein.



6. Deleting one base inside a gene:

Changes one amino acid
Shifts the reading frame, changing every codon after it, usually until a premature stop
Has no effect


A frameshift; deleting three bases would remove one amino acid instead.

title: Molecular genetics for data scientists
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve turned a genome fragment into a protein. Here’s what you’ve learned:

DNA as a string: 3,000 bases of A, C, G and T, with 63% GC; the other strand is the reverse complement.
From gene to protein: the kred gene, on the reverse strand at 1,101 to 1,859, is 759 bases: 252 codons from ATG plus a stop, translated through the genetic code into a 252-residue protein with the cofactor motif TGxxxGxG at position 12.
Codon usage: GC-rich genomes favour G and C at the third codon position.
Mutations: about 22% of possible point changes are synonymous; a frameshift scrambles everything after it.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download pl7_fragment.fasta into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Find all ORFs. Write a function that finds every ORF of at least 100 codons in all six frames of the fragment. How many are there, and where?
A GC skew plot. Compute the GC content in sliding windows of 200 bases, and the GC skew (G - C)/(G + C). Plot both along the fragment.
Codon usage table. Count every codon in the kred gene and compute the relative synonymous codon usage (each codon’s count divided by the average for its amino acid).
Rosalind. Solve the first ten problems of the Rosalind “Bioinformatics Stronghold” in R. Several are this lesson’s exercises.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Nucleotide, base

A unit of DNA or RNA; the bases are A, C, G, T (U in RNA).

Strand, reverse complement

DNA is double-stranded; the other strand, read 5′ to 3′, is the reverse complement.

Gene

A stretch of DNA transcribed into RNA, most often coding for a protein.

Central dogma

DNA is transcribed into RNA, which is translated into protein.

Codon, genetic code

Three bases specifying one amino acid or a stop; the code maps the 64 codons to amino acids.

Open reading frame (ORF)

A run of codons from a start codon to the next in-frame stop codon.

GC content

The share of G and C bases in a sequence.

Synonymous, missense, nonsense mutation

A base change that keeps the amino acid, changes it, or creates a stop codon.

Frameshift

An insertion or deletion that shifts the reading frame.











NoteWant to read more?






Susan Holmes and Wolfgang Huber, Modern Statistics for Modern Biology (Cambridge, 2019, free online), chapter 2, “Statistical Modeling”, with sequence data from the start. This module’s main reading.
Bruce Alberts and others, Molecular Biology of the Cell (7th edition, Norton, 2022), chapters 4 to 7, on DNA, genes and the central dogma.
Rosalind, a collection of bioinformatics problems to solve by programming, from counting bases to assembling genomes.

title: High-dimensional spatio-temporal data
text:
Module 9 · Lesson 12 of 13 Week 144 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The plant draws its cooling water from the reservoir to its north-west, and returns it about 8 °C warmer through an outfall on the south shore. Its environmental permit limits how much the lake may warm. The regulator’s satellite team sends Hana a thermal image of the lake’s surface every week that the sky is clear: 258 pixels of 250 × 250 m, for 2023 to 2025.
That’s 32,000 numbers, and a model for each pixel would miss the point: the pixels move together. This lesson finds the few patterns that carry most of the variation. It’s Module 7’s principal components analysis, applied to a space-time matrix, which climate scientists call empirical orthogonal functions (EOFs).
In this lesson you’ll:

title: High-dimensional spatio-temporal data
text:
The space-time matrix
lake_temperature.csv has one row per pixel per cloud-free week: cell, x, y (UTM metres), week, temp_c. plant_weekly.csv has, for every week, the plant’s load (as a fraction of full load) and the east-west wind (m/s, positive from the west).
The setup code reads both.












Your turn. Make the matrix of weeks × pixels, and count the cloudy weeks (weeks with no image).









Columns by cell.


Z <- tapply(lake$temp_c, list(lake$week, lake$cell), mean)
c(weeks = nrow(Z), pixels = ncol(Z), missing_values = sum(is.na(Z)), cloudy_weeks = nrow(plant) - nrow(Z))
124 clear weeks × 258 pixels, with no missing values inside the matrix: a cloudy week has no image at all, so 32 of the 156 weeks are simply absent. This lesson uses the 124 complete weeks; Lesson 13 fills in the cloudy ones.




Your turn. The seasonal cycle dwarfs everything else. Compute the lake’s mean temperature each week, its range, and how much of the variation around each pixel’s own mean is left after removing it.









Centre the columns of A.


Z <- tapply(lake$temp_c, list(lake$week, lake$cell), mean)
lake_mean <- rowMeans(Z)                                    # one value per week
A <- sweep(Z, 1, lake_mean)                                 # remove each week's lake mean
A <- sweep(A, 2, colMeans(A))                               # and each pixel's average anomaly
c(range(lake_mean), share_left = sum(A^2) / sum(sweep(Z, 2, colMeans(Z))^2))
The lake’s weekly mean runs from 4.3 °C in winter to 22.7 °C in summer, and removing it leaves only 0.34% of the variation: almost everything is the whole lake warming and cooling together. That 0.34% is where the plant, the wind and the lake’s shape show up. Without removing the common signal first, the first EOF would just be “the season”, and the interesting patterns would be squeezed into the rest.

title: High-dimensional spatio-temporal data
text:
Empirical orthogonal functions
The singular value decomposition writes any matrix as A = U D V^\top: V’s columns are orthonormal patterns over the pixels, the EOFs; U D’s columns are their amplitudes over time, the principal component (PC) time series; and the squared singular values d_k^2, divided by their sum, are the shares of the variance each pattern carries. It’s PCA (Module 7) with the weeks as observations and the pixels as variables:

a_{t,s} = \sum_k d_k \, u_{t,k} \, v_{s,k},

each week’s anomaly map is a weighted sum of the same few maps v_{\cdot,k}, with weights d_k u_{t,k} that change from week to week.
Your turn. Compute the SVD of the anomaly matrix, and the share of variance of the first six EOFs.









The variance is the singular value squared: ^2.


Z <- tapply(lake$temp_c, list(lake$week, lake$cell), mean)
A <- sweep(Z, 1, rowMeans(Z)); A <- sweep(A, 2, colMeans(A))
sv <- svd(A)
share <- sv$d^2 / sum(sv$d^2)
round(share[1:6], 3)
23.4%, 17.5% and 6.8% for the first three EOFs, then 4.2%, 2.9%, 2.7% and a long, slowly falling tail. Three patterns stand out; the rest look like noise: small-scale, short-lived variations that no single pattern describes.




Your turn. How many EOFs are needed for half the variance? And how much do the first three carry together?









Half: 0.5.


Z <- tapply(lake$temp_c, list(lake$week, lake$cell), mean)
A <- sweep(Z, 1, rowMeans(Z)); A <- sweep(A, 2, colMeans(A))
sv <- svd(A)
cum <- cumsum(sv$d^2) / sum(sv$d^2)
c(first_three = cum[3], needed_for_half = which(cum >= 0.5)[1])
The first three carry 47.6%, and 4 EOFs are needed for half. Unlike Module 7’s sensors, where three components carried 87%, a field like this has a lot of small-scale noise, spread over many dimensions. The usual ways to decide how many EOFs to keep are the same as for PCA: the scree plot’s elbow (here after 3), or North’s rule of thumb, which flags EOFs whose sampling errors overlap their neighbours’ and so can’t be interpreted separately.

title: High-dimensional spatio-temporal data
text:
What the patterns mean
An EOF is a statistical pattern, not a physical one, and its sign is arbitrary (the SVD can flip u_k and v_k together). Interpreting it means comparing its map with what we know about the lake, and its time series with what we know about the forcing.
