Your turn. EOF 2 looks like a patch on the south shore. Correlate its pattern with a plume-shaped function of the distance from the outfall, and find its strongest pixel.









EOF 2 is column 2 of sv$v.


Z <- tapply(lake$temp_c, list(lake$week, lake$cell), mean)
A <- sweep(Z, 1, rowMeans(Z)); A <- sweep(A, 2, colMeans(A))
sv <- svd(A)
cc <- cells[match(colnames(Z), cells$cell), ]
outfall <- c(mean(range(cc$x)), mean(range(cc$y)) - 1500)     # middle of the south shore
plume_shape <- exp(-sqrt((cc$x - outfall[1])^2 + (cc$y - outfall[2])^2) / 1200)
c(correlation = cor(sv$v[, 2], plume_shape), strongest_x = cc$x[which.max(abs(sv$v[, 2]))],
  strongest_y = cc$y[which.max(abs(sv$v[, 2]))])
A correlation of -0.94 (the sign is arbitrary: this EOF came out negative at the outfall), and the strongest pixel is at (477125, 5707125), on the south shore next to the outfall. EOF 2 is the cooling-water plume: warm water spreading from the outfall over about a kilometre and a half.




Your turn. If EOF 2 is the plume, its time series should follow the plant’s load. Correlate them.









Match on the week column.


Z <- tapply(lake$temp_c, list(lake$week, lake$cell), mean)
A <- sweep(Z, 1, rowMeans(Z)); A <- sweep(A, 2, colMeans(A))
sv <- svd(A)
pc <- sv$u %*% diag(sv$d)                                     # PC time series
p <- plant[match(rownames(Z), plant$week), ]                 # the same weeks
c(cor_load = cor(pc[, 2], p$load), r_squared = summary(lm(pc[, 2] ~ p$load))$r.squared)
r = -0.80: the load explains 65% of the plume’s week-to-week variation (the negative sign matches the negative pattern; together, more load means a warmer plume). In April 2024, during the plant’s four-week turnaround, the plume disappears from the images. The rest of PC 2’s variation reflects the plume’s one-week memory: the water warmed last week is still there.













Your turn. EOF 1 looked like a west-east gradient. Correlate its pattern with the pixels’ x coordinate, and its time series with the east-west wind.









The wind is wind_ew_ms.


Z <- tapply(lake$temp_c, list(lake$week, lake$cell), mean)
A <- sweep(Z, 1, rowMeans(Z)); A <- sweep(A, 2, colMeans(A))
sv <- svd(A)
cc <- cells[match(colnames(Z), cells$cell), ]
p <- plant[match(rownames(Z), plant$week), ]
c(pattern_vs_x = cor(sv$v[, 1], cc$x), series_vs_wind = cor(sv$u[, 1], p$wind_ew_ms))
The pattern correlates -0.94 with the x coordinate, and its time series +0.74 with the east-west wind: when the wind blows from the west, it pushes warm surface water to the east end and cold water wells up at the west end, tilting the lake’s temperature. (Its time series also correlates -0.49 with the season, because in this period the west wind happened to be stronger in winter; EOFs can mix things that happen at the same time.) EOF 3, a patch on the north shore that’s strong in summer, is a shallow bay that warms faster than the deep lake.

title: High-dimensional spatio-temporal data
text:
Dimension reduction
Your turn. Reconstruct the anomalies from the first k EOFs, for k = 1, 2, 3, 5 and 10, and compute the root mean squared reconstruction error.









Rebuild from k EOFs.


Z <- tapply(lake$temp_c, list(lake$week, lake$cell), mean)
A <- sweep(Z, 1, rowMeans(Z)); A <- sweep(A, 2, colMeans(A))
sv <- svd(A)
rebuild <- function(k) sv$u[, 1:k, drop = FALSE] %*% diag(sv$d[1:k], k) %*% t(sv$v[, 1:k, drop = FALSE])
c(none = sqrt(mean(A^2)), sapply(c(k1 = 1, k2 = 2, k3 = 3, k5 = 5, k10 = 10), function(k) sqrt(mean((A - rebuild(k))^2))))
The anomalies have an RMS of 0.37 °C. Three EOFs bring the error down to 0.27 °C, ten to 0.22. So 124 \times 258 = 32{,}000 numbers are summarized, to within about 0.27 °C, by 3 maps and 3 time series: 3 \times 258 + 3 \times 124 = 1{,}146 numbers. That’s the point of dimension reduction for spatio-temporal data: models (Lesson 13) can work on 3 time series instead of 258.




EOFs are learned from the data. The other way to reduce dimension is to fix the patterns in advance: basis functions, such as Gaussian bumps \phi_j(s) = \exp(-\lVert s - c_j\rVert^2 / 2\sigma^2) centred on a grid of points c_j. A field is then approximated by \sum_j \alpha_j \phi_j(s), a regression on the bumps. Basis functions work for any location (not just the pixels), handle irregular data, and are how large-data spatial models (fixed rank kriging, the FRK package) stay fast.
Your turn. Represent one image, 15 July 2024, with grids of 8, 18, 32 and 72 Gaussian bumps, and compare their leave-one-out errors (for a linear regression, \text{residual}_i / (1 - h_{ii}) gives the leave-one-out residuals without refitting).









The leverages of fit.


Z <- tapply(lake$temp_c, list(lake$week, lake$cell), mean)
cc <- cells[match(colnames(Z), cells$cell), ]
z <- Z["2024-07-15", ]
loo_rmse <- function(n) {
  ctr <- expand.grid(cx = seq(min(cc$x), max(cc$x), length.out = n),
                     cy = seq(min(cc$y), max(cc$y), length.out = max(2, round(n / 2))))
  s <- 1.5 * (max(cc$x) - min(cc$x)) / n                      # bump width
  B <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(ctr)), function(j) exp(-((cc$x - ctr$cx[j])^2 + (cc$y - ctr$cy[j])^2) / (2 * s^2)))
  fit <- lm(z ~ B)
  sqrt(mean((residuals(fit) / (1 - hatvalues(fit)))^2))
}
sapply(c(b8 = 4, b18 = 6, b32 = 8, b72 = 12), loo_rmse)
Leave-one-out errors of 0.31 °C with 8 bumps, 0.25 with 18, 0.23 with 32, and back up to 0.28 with 72, which start to fit the noise. 32 bumps represent the 258 pixels well (the image’s SD is 0.78 °C): the usual bias-variance trade-off, with the number of basis functions as the complexity knob. Unlike EOFs, these bumps know nothing about lakes; they just impose smoothness.










NoteGo deeper: EOFs, Karhunen-Loève, and their limits





EOFs are the empirical version of the Karhunen-Loève expansion: any random field with a finite variance can be written as \sum_k \sqrt{\lambda_k}\,\xi_k(t)\,\phi_k(s), with uncorrelated coefficients \xi_k and orthonormal eigenfunctions \phi_k of the covariance, ordered by eigenvalue \lambda_k; it’s the most efficient expansion, in the sense of mean squared error, for any number of terms. Their limits: they need complete data (or an EM-style iteration to fill the gaps); they’re orthogonal by construction, so physical modes that aren’t orthogonal get mixed (EOF 1’s touch of season); and their sign and, when eigenvalues are close, their order are arbitrary. Rotated EOFs (varimax, as in factor analysis) and extended EOFs (patterns in space and time lag) address some of this. Hannachi, Jolliffe and Stephenson, “Empirical Orthogonal Functions and Related Techniques in Atmospheric Science: A Review”, International Journal of Climatology 27, 2007, is a thorough guide.

title: High-dimensional spatio-temporal data
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The same with prcomp(). Run prcomp() on the anomaly matrix (no centring, since it’s already centred) and compare its variance shares with the SVD’s.









center = FALSE.


Z <- tapply(lake$temp_c, list(lake$week, lake$cell), mean)
A <- sweep(Z, 1, rowMeans(Z)); A <- sweep(A, 2, colMeans(A))
pr <- prcomp(A, center = FALSE)
round(summary(pr)$importance[2, 1:4], 3)
The same 0.234, 0.175, 0.068 and 0.042. prcomp() is an SVD: pr$rotation holds the EOFs (V) and pr$x the PC time series (UD), possibly with flipped signs. Climate scientists say EOF, statisticians PCA, engineers proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), signal processors the Karhunen-Loève transform; it’s the same computation.




Challenge 2 · Without removing the season. In RStudio, compute the SVD of the matrix with only each pixel’s mean removed (not the lake’s weekly mean). What does EOF 1 look like, how much variance does it carry, and where do the plume and the tilt end up?

title: High-dimensional spatio-temporal data
text:
Quick quiz

1. In the SVD A = UDV^\top of a weeks × pixels matrix, the EOFs are:

The columns of U
The columns of V: patterns over the pixels
The singular values


UD gives their amplitudes over time.



2. Why remove each week’s lake mean before computing EOFs?

To make the matrix square
The common seasonal signal would dominate EOF 1 and hide the spatial patterns
To remove the clouds


It was 99.7% of the variation.



3. An EOF’s sign is:

Always positive at the largest value
Arbitrary: the SVD can flip a pattern and its time series together
Positive for warm patterns


Interpretation looks at the product of the two.



4. Which evidence identified EOF 2 as the cooling-water plume?

Its variance share
Its map peaks at the outfall, and its time series follows the plant’s load
It’s the second largest


Both the spatial pattern and the temporal behaviour must make physical sense.



5. Three EOFs reconstruct the anomalies to 0.27 °C. What’s gained?

Better accuracy than the data
32,000 numbers summarized by about 1,100, with the noise left out
The missing weeks are filled in


Dimension reduction; Lesson 13 models the three time series.



6. How do basis functions differ from EOFs?

They’re fixed in advance (such as Gaussian bumps), rather than learned from the data
They’re always more accurate
They can’t be used for prediction


Basis functions work anywhere and with irregular data; EOFs adapt to the field.

title: High-dimensional spatio-temporal data
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve reduced a big spatio-temporal dataset to a few patterns. Here’s what you’ve learned:

The space-time matrix: 124 clear weeks × 258 pixels; the lake-wide seasonal cycle is 99.7% of the variation, and is removed first.
EOFs by SVD: 23.4%, 17.5% and 6.8% for the first three; their maps are V, their time series UD.
Interpretation: EOF 1 is the wind’s tilt (time series r = 0.74 with the east-west wind), EOF 2 the cooling-water plume (r = -0.80 with the load, map peaked at the outfall), EOF 3 the shallow north bay.
Dimension reduction: three EOFs reconstruct the anomalies to 0.27 °C (from 0.37), with 1,146 numbers instead of 32,000.
Basis functions: 32 Gaussian bumps represent one image best, by leave-one-out cross-validation.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download lake_temperature.csv and plant_weekly.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Map the EOFs. Map the first four EOFs with geom_raster() and a diverging scale. Does EOF 4 look like anything physical?
Rotated EOFs. Apply varimax() to the first three EOFs (varimax(sv$v[, 1:3] %*% diag(sv$d[1:3]))). Does rotation separate the wind and the season more cleanly?
The permit. The permit says the plume may not warm more than 1 km² of the lake by more than 3 °C above the lake’s mean. Using the anomalies, count the weeks in which more than 16 pixels (1 km²) were 3 °C above that week’s mean.
Fixed rank kriging. Install FRK and fit FRK(temp_c ~ 1, data = list(one_week_sf)) to one image, with its automatic basis functions. Compare its predictions with your 32-bump regression.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Space-time data matrix

A matrix with one row per time and one column per location.

Empirical orthogonal functions (EOFs)

The principal component patterns of a space-time matrix: orthonormal maps ordered by the variance they carry.

Principal component time series

The amplitude of each EOF over time.

Singular value decomposition (SVD)

A = UDV^\top, with orthonormal U and V and non-negative singular values in D.

Dimension reduction

Representing many variables (pixels) by a few derived ones (EOF amplitudes or basis coefficients).

Basis functions

Fixed functions (such as Gaussian bumps on a grid) whose weighted sum represents a field.

Karhunen-Loève expansion

The theoretical, optimal orthogonal expansion of a random field, of which EOFs are the empirical version.











NoteWant to read more?






Christopher Wikle, Andrew Zammit-Mangion and Noel Cressie, Spatio-Temporal Statistics with R (CRC Press, 2019, free online), chapter 2.4 on EOFs and chapter 4 on basis functions.
Ian Jolliffe, Principal Component Analysis (2nd edition, Springer, 2002), chapter 12, on PCA for time series and spatial data, and on rotation.
Hans von Storch and Francis Zwiers, Statistical Analysis in Climate Research (Cambridge, 1999), chapter 13, on EOFs, their sampling errors and North’s rule.

title: Spatio-temporal data
text:
Module 9 · Lesson 10 of 13 Week 142 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lessons 1 to 9 froze time: the soil survey, the districts’ five-year totals and the leak survey were each a single snapshot. Most environmental data aren’t like that. Air quality, river temperatures, groundwater levels and weather are measured at fixed places, again and again, and they change in both space and time, together.
The county runs 24 monitoring stations for nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), a gas from combustion: traffic above all, but also the plant’s boilers and furnaces. The air-quality officer, Tomás, has sent Hana the 2025 daily means. The EU limit for the annual mean is 40 µg/m³; the World Health Organization’s 2021 guideline is 10.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Spatio-temporal data
text:
Long and wide
Three files: air_stations.csv (station, type, x, y in UTM metres), air_no2_daily.csv (station, date, no2, one row per station and day: the long form) and weather_daily.csv (date, wind direction, wind speed, temperature). The station types are urban background, roadside (along the motorway), industrial (around the plant) and rural background.
For many analyses, the wide form is more convenient: a matrix with one row per day and one column per station, the space-time data matrix. Lessons 12 and 13 do linear algebra on it.
The setup code reads the three files.












Your turn. How many rows are there, and how many (and what share of) daily values are missing?









The values are in no2.


c(rows = nrow(air), stations = length(unique(air$station)), days = length(unique(air$date)),
  missing = sum(is.na(air$no2)), share_missing = mean(is.na(air$no2)))
8,760 rows: 24 stations × 365 days. 181 daily values (2.1%) are missing, scattered over the year, plus a block of three weeks in June at A09, whose analyzer was sent for repair. A complete grid of stations and times, with some missing values, is the commonest kind of spatio-temporal data (a spatio-temporal full grid, in the spacetime package’s terms).




Your turn. Make the wide matrix with tapply(), and find the three stations with the highest annual mean.









Columns by station.


M <- tapply(air$no2, list(air$date, air$station), mean)   # 365 days x 24 stations
print(dim(M))
round(sort(colMeans(M, na.rm = TRUE), decreasing = TRUE)[1:3], 1)
A01 (urban, the town centre) has the highest annual mean, 31.5 µg/m³, then A09 (roadside) at 28.9 and A12 (industrial, 3.6 km north-east of the plant) at 27.9. No station exceeds the EU limit of 40; all but one exceed the WHO guideline of 10. (colMeans(..., na.rm = TRUE) skips the missing days; for A09, with its June gap, that slightly overweights the rest of the year.)

title: Spatio-temporal data
section: Summaries in space and in time
text:
Summaries in space and in time
Your turn. Average the stations’ annual means by station type.









Match on the station column.


M <- tapply(air$no2, list(air$date, air$station), mean)
annual <- colMeans(M, na.rm = TRUE)
type <- stations$type[match(names(annual), stations$station)]
round(tapply(annual, type, mean), 1)
Urban stations average 23.4 µg/m³, roadside 23.1, industrial 19.2, rural 10.3. Traffic dominates NO₂ almost everywhere; the industrial stations’ average hides large differences between those downwind of the plant and those upwind, as you’ll see.




Your turn. Now in time: compute the network’s daily mean (over stations), and average it by month.









The month as a number: "%m".


M <- tapply(air$no2, list(air$date, air$station), mean)
network <- rowMeans(M, na.rm = TRUE)
round(tapply(network, format(as.Date(names(network)), "%m"), mean), 1)
From 23.9 µg/m³ in December and 21.0 in January to 14.6 in June and 14.3 in July. NO₂ peaks in winter: more heating, and a lower boundary layer that traps pollution near the ground. Module 6’s tools (decomposition, seasonal models) apply to each station’s series, but here every station shares the same seasonal cycle, and that’s part of the space-time structure.




Your turn. Average the network mean by day of the week, and compute the ratio of Sunday to Thursday.









Thursday is day 4.


M <- tapply(air$no2, list(air$date, air$station), mean)
network <- rowMeans(M, na.rm = TRUE)
wd <- tapply(network, format(as.Date(names(network)), "%u"), mean)   # 1 = Monday ... 7 = Sunday
c(round(wd, 1), sunday_over_thursday = wd[["7"]] / wd[["4"]])
18.4 to 19.8 µg/m³ on weekdays, 16.1 on Saturday and 13.9 on Sunday: 30% lower on Sunday than on Thursday. A weekly cycle is the fingerprint of human activity, traffic and work; natural sources don’t know what day it is.

title: Spatio-temporal data
text:
Place, day, and what’s left
A simple model for the log values, \log y_{st} = \mu + a_s + b_t + r_{st}, splits each value into a station effect a_s (place: traffic, the town), a day effect b_t (time: season, weekday, weather, shared by all stations), and a residual r_{st}, the space-time interaction: what’s specific to that station on that day. It’s two-way ANOVA (Module 2) on the space-time matrix.
Your turn. Remove the station means and then the day means from the log matrix, and find how much of the variance each part accounts for.









Subtract the day effects, b, from each row.


M <- tapply(air$no2, list(air$date, air$station), mean)
L <- log(M)
mu <- mean(L, na.rm = TRUE)
a <- colMeans(L, na.rm = TRUE) - mu                         # station effects
b <- rowMeans(sweep(L, 2, a + mu), na.rm = TRUE)           # day effects
R <- sweep(sweep(L, 2, a + mu), 1, b)                      # residuals
ok <- !is.na(L)
total <- sum((L[ok] - mu)^2)
c(station = sum(matrix(a, nrow(L), ncol(L), byrow = TRUE)[ok]^2) / total,
  day = sum(matrix(b, nrow(L), ncol(L))[ok]^2) / total,
  interaction = sum(R[ok]^2) / total)
53% of the variation in log NO₂ is between stations, 34% between days, and 13% is the interaction. (With missing values, the three parts add up to almost exactly 100%.) The interaction is small, but it’s where the interesting space-time structure lives: weather that’s local, a traffic jam, the plant’s plume. The next two exercises look inside it.




A Hovmöller plot (after the meteorologist Ernest Hovmöller, 1949) shows one spatial coordinate against time, coloured by the value. Below, the stations are sorted from west to east, and the colour is the interaction r_{st}:









Reading it: vertical stripes would be days when every station is unusual (there are none: the day effect removed them); horizontal stripes would be stations that are always high (removed by the station effect). What’s left is speckle: short streaks of a few days, some shared by neighbouring stations. The eye can’t find much structure in it; the next exercises measure it, and the last section finds a pattern at the industrial stations that the plot hides.
Your turn. Is the interaction correlated between stations? Correlate every pair of stations’ residual series, and compare pairs less than 5 km apart with pairs more than 15 km apart.









More than 15 km apart.


M <- tapply(air$no2, list(air$date, air$station), mean)
L <- log(M)
R <- sweep(L, 2, colMeans(L, na.rm = TRUE))
R <- sweep(R, 1, rowMeans(R, na.rm = TRUE))                     # the interaction
cors <- cor(R, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
xy <- stations[match(colnames(R), stations$station), c("x", "y")]
D <- as.matrix(dist(xy)) / 1000                                # km
pair <- lower.tri(D)
c(near = mean(cors[pair][D[pair] < 5]), far = mean(cors[pair][D[pair] > 15]))
0.27 for the 71 pairs within 5 km, and -0.015 for pairs more than 15 km apart. The interaction is spatially correlated over a few kilometres: on a given day, two nearby stations tend to be unusual in the same direction. (This is with the network-wide day effect removed; with it, every pair is strongly correlated, because they share the season and the weather.)




Your turn. And in time? Compute each station’s lag-1 autocorrelation of the interaction, and average them.









Pair each day with the previous one: drop the last value, z[-length(z)].


M <- tapply(air$no2, list(air$date, air$station), mean)
L <- log(M)
R <- sweep(L, 2, colMeans(L, na.rm = TRUE))
R <- sweep(R, 1, rowMeans(R, na.rm = TRUE))
lag1 <- apply(R, 2, function(z) cor(z[-1], z[-length(z)], use = "complete.obs"))
mean(lag1)
0.38: an unusual day at a station tends to be followed by another unusual day there. So the interaction is correlated in space (a few km) and in time (a few days). Lesson 11 models both at once with a spatio-temporal covariance, and uses it to predict where and when there are no measurements.

title: Spatio-temporal data
text:
The plant’s plume
The plant’s emissions should show up at the industrial stations, but only when the wind carries them there. On days when it blows from the south-west (from 200° to 250°, 38% of the year’s days), the plant’s emissions are carried toward the north-east.
Your turn. Compare station A11’s NO₂ (1.8 km north-east of the plant) on south-westerly days and other days, and estimate the ratio from its interaction values.









South-westerly: up to 250°.


M <- tapply(air$no2, list(air$date, air$station), mean)
L <- log(M)
R <- sweep(L, 2, colMeans(L, na.rm = TRUE)); R <- sweep(R, 1, rowMeans(R, na.rm = TRUE))
sw <- weather$wind_dir_deg >= 200 & weather$wind_dir_deg <= 250
fit <- lm(R[, "A11"] ~ sw)
c(share_sw_days = mean(sw), mean_sw = mean(M[sw, "A11"], na.rm = TRUE), mean_other = mean(M[!sw, "A11"], na.rm = TRUE),
  ratio = exp(coef(fit)[["swTRUE"]]))
On south-westerly days, A11 averages 28.2 µg/m³, against 19.0 on other days; after removing the network’s day effect, the plume raises A11’s NO₂ by a factor of 1.40. The weather table and the air table share their dates (both are sorted by date, with all 365 days), which is why sw lines up with the rows of R. Joining by date with match() is the safer habit.










NoteGo deeper: storing and drawing spatio-temporal data





R has several classes for spatio-temporal data. The spacetime package (Pebesma, 2012) defines STFDF (a full grid of locations × times, like this network), STSDF (sparse: only some combinations observed) and STIDF (irregular: every observation has its own place and time, like a moving sensor), on which gstat’s spatio-temporal functions work (Lesson 11). The newer stars package stores data cubes (x, y, time, variable) for gridded data such as satellite images and model output, and works with sf. Animations (one map per day, with gganimate) are the most intuitive display, but hard to read quantitatively; Hovmöller plots and small multiples are better for analysis. Wikle, Zammit-Mangion and Cressie’s Spatio-Temporal Statistics with R (2019, free online), chapter 2, covers data structures and exploratory plots.

title: Spatio-temporal data
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Upwind and downwind. Estimate the south-westerly effect on the interaction for each industrial station (A11 to A16), and for rural A20. Where are the stations relative to the plant, and does the pattern make sense?









na.rm = TRUE.


M <- tapply(air$no2, list(air$date, air$station), mean)
L <- log(M)
R <- sweep(L, 2, colMeans(L, na.rm = TRUE)); R <- sweep(R, 1, rowMeans(R, na.rm = TRUE))
sw <- weather$wind_dir_deg >= 200 & weather$wind_dir_deg <= 250
effect <- sapply(c("A11", "A12", "A13", "A14", "A15", "A16", "A20"),
                 function(s) mean(R[sw, s], na.rm = TRUE) - mean(R[!sw, s], na.rm = TRUE))
round(effect, 3)
On the log scale: A11 +0.34 (1.8 km north-east of the plant), A12 +0.19 (3.6 km north-east), A13 +0.08 (5.7 km north-east): a plume that fades with distance along the wind. A14 and A15, south and west of the plant, are lower on south-westerly days (-0.24 and -0.23): they’re upwind, getting clean air from the countryside, and the network’s day effect, raised by the plume, makes them look lower still. A16, north of the plant, is slightly raised (+0.07), and rural A20, far to the south-east, slightly lowered. A wind-dependent footprint like this is a space-time interaction with a physical cause, and the strongest evidence that the plant contributes to NO₂ at A11 and A12.




Challenge 2 · The weather. In RStudio, regress the log of the network’s daily mean on the wind speed and the temperature. Each m/s of wind lowers NO₂ by about 8%, and each °C by about 2.5%. Why would wind speed and temperature matter? (Think of dilution and of the boundary layer.) Then add the weekday and the month: how much of the day effect does the weather explain?

title: Spatio-temporal data
text:
Quick quiz

1. The “wide” form of spatio-temporal data is:

One row per measurement
A matrix with one row per time and one column per location
A map for each day


The space-time data matrix, used in Lessons 12 and 13.



2. A weekly cycle in NO₂ points to:

Weather
Human activity, mainly traffic
The season


Natural processes don’t follow the calendar week.



3. In \log y_{st} = \mu + a_s + b_t + r_{st}, the term r_{st} is:

The station effect
The day effect
The space-time interaction: what’s specific to that station on that day


13% of the variation here.



4. A Hovmöller plot shows:

Two spatial coordinates
One spatial coordinate against time
A variogram


Here, stations sorted west to east against the days of the year.



5. The interaction’s correlation was 0.27 for stations within 5 km and about 0 beyond 15 km, and its lag-1 autocorrelation 0.38. So it’s:

Independent
Correlated over a few kilometres and a few days
Correlated only in time


That’s what a spatio-temporal covariance model describes.



6. Stations upwind of the plant were lower on south-westerly days. Why?

Measurement error
They get clean country air then, and the network’s day effect is raised by the plume
The wind direction was recorded wrongly


A wind-dependent footprint is a space-time interaction with a physical cause.

title: Spatio-temporal data
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve looked at a year of data from 24 places. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Long and wide forms: 8,760 rows, or a 365 × 24 space-time matrix with 2.1% missing.
Space: A01 in the town centre has the highest mean (31.5 µg/m³); urban and roadside about 23, rural 10.3; all under the EU limit, nearly all above the WHO guideline.
Time: a winter peak (23.9 in December, 14.3 to 14.6 in summer) and a weekly cycle (Sunday 30% below Thursday).
Decomposition: 53% station, 34% day, 13% interaction; the interaction is correlated over a few km and a few days.
The plume: downwind of the plant, NO₂ is 40% higher on south-westerly days at 1.8 km, fading with distance, while upwind stations are lower.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download air_stations.csv, air_no2_daily.csv and weather_daily.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Small multiples. Plot every station’s daily series with facet_wrap(~ station). Which look alike?
An animation. Install gganimate and animate a map of the stations, coloured by NO₂, day by day, with transition_time(date).
A spacetime object. Install spacetime and build an STFDF from the stations (as SpatialPoints), the dates, and the values in the order station-fastest-within-day. stplot() draws it.
Wind roses. For A11, bin the days by wind direction (30° sectors) and plot the mean NO₂ in each sector as a polar bar chart (coord_polar()). Which sector points to the plant?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Spatio-temporal data

Measurements indexed by both location and time.

Long and wide forms

One row per location and time, or a time × location matrix (the space-time data matrix).

Spatio-temporal full grid

Data observed at every combination of a fixed set of locations and times (possibly with missing values).

Space-time interaction

Variation that isn’t explained by a location effect plus a time effect.

Hovmöller plot

A plot of one spatial coordinate against time, coloured by the value.

Separable structure (preview)

Dependence that factors into a purely spatial and a purely temporal part.











NoteWant to read more?






Christopher Wikle, Andrew Zammit-Mangion and Noel Cressie, Spatio-Temporal Statistics with R (CRC Press, 2019, free online), chapter 2, “Exploring Spatio-Temporal Data”. This module’s main reading for Lessons 10 to 13.
Edzer Pebesma, “spacetime: Spatio-Temporal Data in R”, Journal of Statistical Software 51(7), 2012, on the data classes.
The World Health Organization’s Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021), chapter 3, for the evidence behind the 10 µg/m³ guideline for NO₂.

title: Point patterns I
text:
Module 9 · Lesson 8 of 13 Week 140 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Every year, the plant’s leak detection and repair (LDAR) team walks the site with a gas detector and checks thousands of flanges, valves, pump seals and connectors. In 2025 they found 205 leaks. The maintenance manager wants to know whether leaks happen everywhere alike (in which case the inspection plan should cover the site evenly) or concentrate somewhere (in which case it shouldn’t).
This is the third kind of spatial data from Lesson 1: a point pattern. The locations themselves are the data. Nobody chose where to measure; the question is how the points are arranged.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Point patterns I
section: A point pattern and its window
text:
A point pattern and its window
A point pattern has two parts: the points, and the window in which they could have occurred. The window matters as much as the points: “205 leaks” means nothing without “in 0.9 km²”, and an empty corner of the window is information too. The leak survey covered the whole fenced site, whose corners are in site_boundary.csv, in site coordinates (metres from the south-west corner of the fence).
The intensity \lambda(u) is the expected number of points per unit area at location u. The simplest model, complete spatial randomness (CSR), is the homogeneous Poisson process: the intensity is the same everywhere, and the points are independent of each other. CSR is the null hypothesis of point-pattern analysis, like independence in Lesson 2.
The setup code reads the leaks and the fence, and loads spatstat.












Your turn. Make the window from the fence with owin(poly = ...), the pattern with ppp(), and compute the average intensity per hectare.









The window is W.


W <- owin(poly = list(x = fence$x, y = fence$y))
X <- ppp(leaks$x, leaks$y, window = W)
print(X)
c(area_ha = area(W) / 1e4, leaks_per_ha = npoints(X) / area(W) * 1e4)
205 points in a window of 89.6 ha, an average intensity of 2.29 leaks per hectare. spatstat checks that every point lies inside the window; points outside are dropped with a warning (a useful check on coordinates). The polygon’s vertices must go anticlockwise; clockwise means a hole.

title: Point patterns I
text:
Quadrat counts
The oldest test of CSR divides the window into quadrats, counts the points in each, and compares the counts with what CSR predicts (expected counts proportional to the quadrats’ areas) with a chi-squared test.
Your turn. Count the leaks in a 4 × 3 grid of quadrats, and run the test.









Three rows: ny = 3.


W <- owin(poly = list(x = fence$x, y = fence$y))
X <- ppp(leaks$x, leaks$y, window = W)
print(quadratcount(X, nx = 4, ny = 3))
qt <- quadrat.test(X, nx = 4, ny = 3)
c(statistic = unname(qt$statistic), df = unname(qt$parameter), p = qt$p.value)
The counts range from 38 and 37 in the second column (around x = 300 to 575 m) to 0 in the south-east corner, the tank farm. X^2 = 99.2 on 11 degrees of freedom, p = 5 \times 10^{-16}: the leaks are not spread uniformly. (The quadrats on the north-east edge are cut by the fence, which quadrat.test() allows for by using each tile’s actual area.)




Your turn. What does the test give for a pattern that really is CSR? Simulate 205 uniform points in the same window with runifpoint() and test them.









As many points as leaks: 205.


W <- owin(poly = list(x = fence$x, y = fence$y))
set.seed(9081)
U <- runifpoint(205, win = W)
quadrat.test(U, nx = 4, ny = 3)$p.value
p = 0.60, as expected for CSR. Quadrat tests are simple, but their answer depends on the quadrat size: too large and they average away local structure, too small and the expected counts are too low for the chi-squared approximation. They also only say whether the pattern departs from CSR, not how.

title: Point patterns I
text:
Kernel estimates of the intensity
A smoother picture comes from a kernel estimate: put a little bump (a Gaussian, with standard deviation \sigma, the bandwidth) on every point, and add them up,

\hat\lambda(u) = \frac{1}{e(u)} \sum_i k_\sigma(u - x_i),

where e(u) is an edge correction: the share of the kernel around u that lies inside the window. As with Module 4’s density estimates, the bandwidth decides everything: small \sigma gives a spiky map, large \sigma a blur.
Your turn. Compare two automatic bandwidths: Diggle’s (by mean squared error) and the likelihood cross-validation choice (bw.ppl()).









bw.ppl.


W <- owin(poly = list(x = fence$x, y = fence$y))
X <- ppp(leaks$x, leaks$y, window = W)
c(diggle = unname(bw.diggle(X)), ppl = unname(bw.ppl(X)))
51 m by Diggle’s method, 143 m by likelihood cross-validation. Diggle’s choice is known to undersmooth patterns with large-scale trends (it reacts to the local clumping that every inhomogeneous pattern has), and likelihood cross-validation is usually better for a smooth map of intensity. The lesson uses \sigma = 100 m, between the two; try both in RStudio.




Your turn. Estimate the intensity with \sigma = 100 m, and compare it at the oldest units, (300, 560), and in the tank farm, (1000, 150), in leaks per hectare.









sigma = 100.


W <- owin(poly = list(x = fence$x, y = fence$y))
X <- ppp(leaks$x, leaks$y, window = W)
D <- density(X, sigma = 100)                       # leaks per m2
c(old_units = D[ppp(300, 560, window = W)], tank_farm = D[ppp(1000, 150, window = W)]) * 1e4
4.6 leaks per hectare at the oldest units, 0.065 in the tank farm: a ratio of 70. The map below shows the whole surface; its peak, 5.3 per hectare, is at about (430, 670), in the oldest part of the plant. density() returns an image (class im), and D[points] reads its value at those points.













Your turn. Why correct for edges? Near the fence, part of each kernel falls outside the window, where there can’t be leaks, so an uncorrected estimate is biased down there. Compare the corrected and uncorrected estimates near the west fence, at (20, 400), and the two surfaces’ totals over the window.









edge = FALSE.


W <- owin(poly = list(x = fence$x, y = fence$y))
X <- ppp(leaks$x, leaks$y, window = W)
D1 <- density(X, sigma = 100, edge = TRUE)
D0 <- density(X, sigma = 100, edge = FALSE)
c(corrected = D1[ppp(20, 400, window = W)] * 1e4, uncorrected = D0[ppp(20, 400, window = W)] * 1e4,
  total_corrected = integral(D1), total_uncorrected = integral(D0))
At the fence, 1.78 leaks per hectare with the correction against 1.05 without: the uncorrected estimate is 41% too low there, because almost half of each kernel near the fence lies outside the site. Over the whole window, the uncorrected surface adds up to only 180 leaks instead of 205; the corrected one to 208. Edges are a recurring problem in point-pattern analysis; every statistic in Lesson 9 needs a correction too.

title: Point patterns I
text:
Intensity and a covariate
The 1960s units around (300, 560) have the oldest flanges and gaskets. Does the intensity follow the distance from them?
Your turn. Compare the share of leaks within 300 m of the old units with the share of the site’s area within 300 m. as.im() turns a function into a fine image of the window, whose pixels give the area.









Within 300 m.


W <- owin(poly = list(x = fence$x, y = fence$y))
d_leak <- sqrt((leaks$x - 300)^2 + (leaks$y - 560)^2)
Z <- as.im(function(x, y) sqrt((x - 300)^2 + (y - 560)^2), W = W, dimyx = 256)
c(share_of_leaks = mean(d_leak < 300), share_of_area = mean(Z$v[!is.na(Z$v)] < 300))
56% of the leaks are within 300 m of the old units, which cover only 29% of the site. The pixels outside the window are NA in the image, which is why they’re removed before taking the mean.




Your turn. Go further: compute the intensity (leaks per hectare) in distance bands from the old units: 0 to 200 m, 200 to 400, 400 to 600, 600 to 800, and beyond.









A pixel’s area is Z$xstep * Z$ystep.


W <- owin(poly = list(x = fence$x, y = fence$y))
d_leak <- sqrt((leaks$x - 300)^2 + (leaks$y - 560)^2)
Z <- as.im(function(x, y) sqrt((x - 300)^2 + (y - 560)^2), W = W, dimyx = 256)
bands <- c(0, 200, 400, 600, 800, 1200)
n_leaks <- table(cut(d_leak, bands))
area_m2 <- table(cut(Z$v[!is.na(Z$v)], bands)) * Z$xstep * Z$ystep
round(n_leaks / area_m2 * 1e4, 2)
4.70 leaks per hectare within 200 m, then 3.32, 1.86, 0.57, and 0.14 beyond 800 m: the intensity falls steadily, by a factor of about 34 across the site, roughly halving every 150 to 200 m. That’s a covariate effect on the intensity, an inhomogeneous Poisson process, and Lesson 9 fits it as a model. For the maintenance manager, it’s a clear answer: inspect the old units more often. (rhohat() estimates the same relation nonparametrically, as a smooth curve.)

title: Point patterns I
text:
Nearest-neighbour distances
Another classical idea compares the distances from each point to its nearest neighbour with what CSR predicts: for a Poisson process of intensity \lambda, the mean nearest-neighbour distance is 1/(2\sqrt\lambda). The Clark-Evans ratio R is the observed mean divided by that: R < 1 suggests clustering, R > 1 regularity.
Your turn. Compute R by hand and with clarkevans(), and its test.









The expected distance uses the intensity, lambda.


W <- owin(poly = list(x = fence$x, y = fence$y))
X <- ppp(leaks$x, leaks$y, window = W)
lambda <- npoints(X) / area(W)
R_hand <- mean(nndist(X)) / (0.5 / sqrt(lambda))
c(R_hand = R_hand, clarkevans(X), p = clarkevans.test(X, correction = "cdf")$p.value)
R = 0.98 (0.95 with an edge correction), p = 0.15: no evidence against CSR! The test compares nearest-neighbour distances, which only see a few metres around each point, with a global average intensity. Locally, the leaks are spread like a Poisson process (each leak is independent of the others); the departure from CSR is in the large-scale intensity, which this test doesn’t look at. Different tests see different scales, and a pattern can be inhomogeneous without being clustered, which is exactly the distinction Lesson 9 makes.

title: Point patterns I
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Marks. Each leak has a mark, its component type. Make a marked pattern and compute the intensity of each type per hectare.









The marks are the component column.


W <- owin(poly = list(x = fence$x, y = fence$y))
Xm <- ppp(leaks$x, leaks$y, window = W, marks = factor(leaks$component))
round(intensity(Xm) * 1e4, 3)
Flanges 0.95 per hectare, valves 0.77, connectors 0.32 and pump seals 0.25. A marked point pattern can be split by type (split(Xm)) and each part analyzed separately, or the types compared: do pump seals follow the same intensity surface as flanges? relrisk(Xm) estimates the probability of each type at every location.




Challenge 2 · A smooth relation. In RStudio, plot rhohat(X, Z), with Z the distance image from the exercises. It estimates the intensity as a smooth function of the distance, with a confidence band. Does it look like an exponential decay? Plot it on a log scale.

title: Point patterns I
text:
Quick quiz

1. What is the intensity of a point pattern?

The number of points
The expected number of points per unit area, possibly varying with location
The mean nearest-neighbour distance


An average intensity is the count divided by the window’s area.



2. Complete spatial randomness means:

Points are evenly spaced
A constant intensity, and points independent of each other
Points cluster at random places


It’s the homogeneous Poisson process.



3. Why does a kernel estimate need an edge correction?

Because points near the edge are less reliable
Near the edge, part of each kernel falls outside the window, biasing the estimate down
Because the bandwidth is too large


Without correction, the leaks’ surface lost 25 of its 205 leaks at the edges.



4. A larger kernel bandwidth gives:

A spikier map
A smoother map
More points


Bandwidth is the usual bias-variance trade-off.



5. The intensity fell from 4.7 to 0.14 leaks per hectare with distance from the old units. That’s:

An inhomogeneous intensity, driven by a covariate
Clustering of leaks around each other
An edge effect


Lesson 9 separates inhomogeneity from clustering.



6. The Clark-Evans test found no departure from CSR. Why?

The leaks are random
It only looks at nearest-neighbour distances, and the departure is in the large-scale intensity
The edge correction was wrong


Different statistics are sensitive at different scales.

title: Point patterns I
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve analyzed your first point pattern. Here’s what you’ve learned:

A point pattern is points plus a window; the average intensity of leaks is 2.29 per hectare.
Quadrat counts reject complete spatial randomness (X^2 = 99.2, p = 5 \times 10^{-16}); a simulated random pattern doesn’t (p = 0.60).
Kernel estimates of intensity depend on the bandwidth (51 m by Diggle’s method, 143 m by likelihood cross-validation) and need edge correction (41% too low at the fence without it).
A covariate: the intensity falls from 4.7 leaks per hectare within 200 m of the oldest units to 0.14 beyond 800 m.
Nearest-neighbour tests look at small scales and can miss large-scale inhomogeneity (Clark-Evans R = 0.98).







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download site_leaks.csv and site_boundary.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install spatstat.

Plot it. plot(density(X, sigma = 100)); plot(X, add = TRUE) draws the intensity map with the leaks. Try sigma = 50 and 200.
Quadrat size. Repeat the quadrat test with 2 × 2, 4 × 3, 8 × 6 and 16 × 12 quadrats. How do the statistic and the p-value change?
A Monte Carlo test. quadrat.test(X, 4, 3, method = "MonteCarlo", nsim = 999) avoids the chi-squared approximation. Does the conclusion change?
Relative risk. With the marked pattern, plot(relrisk(Xm)) maps the probability of each component type. Are pump seals concentrated anywhere?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Point pattern

The locations of events in a window, where the locations themselves are the data.

Window

The region in which points could have been observed.

Intensity

The expected number of points per unit area; constant for a homogeneous pattern, varying for an inhomogeneous one.

Complete spatial randomness (CSR)

The homogeneous Poisson process: constant intensity and independent points.

Quadrat test

A chi-squared test of CSR from counts in subregions.

Kernel intensity estimate

A smooth estimate of the intensity from a sum of kernels on the points, with a bandwidth \sigma.

Edge correction

An adjustment for the parts of a kernel or a neighbourhood that fall outside the window.

Clark-Evans ratio

The mean nearest-neighbour distance divided by its expected value under CSR.

Marked point pattern

A point pattern with a value (a mark) attached to each point.











NoteWant to read more?






Adrian Baddeley, Ege Rubak and Rolf Turner, Spatial Point Patterns: Methodology and Applications with R (CRC Press, 2015), chapters 3, 6 and 8, by spatstat’s authors: the standard reference.
Edzer Pebesma and Roger Bivand, Spatial Data Science with Applications in R (free online), chapter 11, “Point Pattern Analysis”, a short introduction.
Peter Diggle, Statistical Analysis of Spatial and Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns (3rd edition, CRC Press, 2013), chapters 2 to 5, on exploratory methods and tests of CSR.

title: Areal data and spatial weights
text:
Module 9 · Lesson 6 of 13 Week 138 of 160 About 5–7 hours
In March, the local newspaper printed a map of respiratory hospital admissions by district, from public health data. The darkest districts were around the plant, and the headline asked whether the plant was making people ill. Hana has been asked to look at the numbers properly, with the county’s public health officer. This lesson and the next are that analysis.
The data are areal: one number per district, for a partition of the county into 60 districts. There’s nothing to interpolate between districts; the questions are whether the pattern is real, and what explains it.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Areal data and spatial weights
text:
Standardized ratios
district_health.csv has, for each district, its population, the share aged 65 or more, a deprivation index (0 is the national average, in standard deviations), the density of main roads, the distance from the plant, and the number of respiratory hospital admissions over five years, 2021 to 2025. Raw counts mostly measure population, and older people are admitted more often, so the public health office has also computed the number expected if the district had the national admission rates for each age group. The standardized admission ratio (SAR; for deaths, the standardized mortality ratio, SMR) is

\text{SMR}_i = \frac{O_i}{E_i} \quad \text{(observed over expected)}.

1 means “as expected for its age structure”, 1.5 means 50% more admissions than expected.
The setup code reads the districts, transforms them to UTM, attaches the health data, and loads spdep.













Your turn. Compute each district’s ratio, the county’s overall ratio (\sum O / \sum E), and list the five highest.









Divide by expected.


dis$smr <- dis$admissions / dis$expected
print(sum(dis$admissions) / sum(dis$expected))
st_drop_geometry(dis[order(-dis$smr), c("name", "expected", "admissions", "smr", "dist_plant_km")])[1:5, ]
The county as a whole has 5,023 admissions against 4,892 expected, a ratio of 1.03, about the national average. The districts range from 0.55 to 1.80. The highest, Ashby (1.80) and North Park (1.76), are 8.4 and 5.6 km from the plant, with only 44.5 and 40.9 admissions expected: small districts, whose ratios are noisy. Riverside, St Anne’s and Market Hill, in the town, follow.

title: Areal data and spatial weights
text:
Neighbours by contiguity
For areas, the natural neighbours are those that share a border: contiguity. Two versions, named after chess pieces: queen contiguity counts any shared boundary point, even a single corner; rook contiguity needs a shared edge of positive length. spdep::poly2nb() finds them from the polygons.
Your turn. Find the queen neighbours, and summarize how many each district has.









queen = TRUE (the default).


nb <- poly2nb(dis, queen = TRUE)
print(nb)
c(links = sum(card(nb)), mean = mean(card(nb)), min = min(card(nb)), max = max(card(nb)))
310 links: on average, a district has 5.2 neighbours, from 2 (three districts on the county’s edge) to 10 (Canal Side, the plant’s own district, a large district that touches many town districts). Contiguity neighbours are symmetric by construction: if i borders j, j borders i.




Your turn. Now rook contiguity. How many links differ?









Rook is queen = FALSE.


nb_q <- poly2nb(dis, queen = TRUE)
nb_r <- poly2nb(dis, queen = FALSE)
c(queen = sum(card(nb_q)), rook = sum(card(nb_r)))
None: 310 both ways. These districts are irregular polygons (they were drawn as Voronoi cells), and in such a tiling, borders meet three at a time, so two districts never touch at a corner only. On a regular grid of squares, like a raster, every cell has 4 rook neighbours and 8 queen neighbours, and the choice matters a lot. Real administrative boundaries are in between.

title: Areal data and spatial weights
text:
Spatial weights and Moran’s I
Your turn. Build row-standardized weights, compute the spatial lag of the ratios (the average of each district’s neighbours), and correlate it with the ratios.









The lag of smr.


dis$smr <- dis$admissions / dis$expected
lw <- nb2listw(poly2nb(dis), style = "W")
lag <- lag.listw(lw, dis$smr)
cor(dis$smr, lag)
0.73: districts with high ratios tend to have neighbours with high ratios. Something that varies smoothly across the county is raising or lowering admissions.




Your turn. Compute Moran’s I with row-standardized ("W") and binary ("B", every link weighs 1) weights.









Binary weights are style "B".


dis$smr <- dis$admissions / dis$expected
nb <- poly2nb(dis)
c(W = unname(moran.test(dis$smr, nb2listw(nb, style = "W"))$estimate[1]),
  B = unname(moran.test(dis$smr, nb2listw(nb, style = "B"))$estimate[1]))
0.51 with row-standardized weights and 0.49 with binary ones; both far above the expected -1/59 = -0.017 (the row-standardized test’s standard deviate is 6.6). Row standardization gives each district’s neighbours a total weight of 1, so a district with 10 neighbours counts each one less; binary weights let districts with many neighbours (Canal Side, the town) weigh more in the total. The choice is a modelling decision, and it should be reported.




Your turn. With only 60 districts, the normal approximation is shaky. Run a permutation test with 999 shuffles.









The function is moran.mc.


dis$smr <- dis$admissions / dis$expected
lw <- nb2listw(poly2nb(dis), style = "W")
set.seed(9061)
mc <- moran.mc(dis$smr, lw, nsim = 999)
c(I = unname(mc$statistic), p = mc$p.value)
p = 0.001: none of the 999 random rearrangements of the 60 ratios over the map gave an I as large as the real one. The clustering is real. What causes it is another question (Lesson 7).

title: Areal data and spatial weights
text:
The small-numbers problem
A ratio from a district expecting 30 admissions is much noisier than one from a district expecting 300. If admissions are Poisson, \text{SD}(O_i/E_i) \approx \sqrt{\text{RR}_i / E_i}: with no real differences at all, a district expecting 25 would have ratios scattered with an SD of 0.2, one expecting 250 with 0.06. So the extremes of a map of ratios are dominated by the smallest districts, which is why Ashby and North Park topped the list.
Your turn. Compare the spread of the ratios in districts expecting fewer than 40 admissions with those expecting 100 or more.









100 or more.


dis$smr <- dis$admissions / dis$expected
small <- dis$expected < 40
big <- dis$expected >= 100
c(n_small = sum(small), sd_small = sd(dis$smr[small]), n_big = sum(big), sd_big = sd(dis$smr[big]))
The 19 small districts’ ratios have an SD of 0.31, the 16 large ones’ 0.17: nearly twice the spread, for the same kind of places. Part of every small district’s ratio is Poisson noise, and a map can’t show the difference.




Empirical Bayes smoothing shrinks each district’s ratio toward the county’s mean, more for small districts. Suppose the true relative risks \theta_i vary around a mean b with variance a, and O_i \mid \theta_i \sim \text{Poisson}(E_i\theta_i). The best estimate of \theta_i is then a weighted average,

\hat\theta_i = w_i \, \frac{O_i}{E_i} + (1 - w_i)\, b, \qquad w_i = \frac{a}{a + b/E_i},

with a and b estimated from all the districts by the method of moments (Marshall, 1991). It’s Module 5’s partial pooling, done quickly.
Your turn. Smooth the ratios with EBest(), and compare the ranges before and after.









The counts and the expected counts: dis$expected.


dis$smr <- dis$admissions / dis$expected
eb <- EBest(dis$admissions, dis$expected)
print(attr(eb, "parameters"))
dis$eb <- eb$estmm
c(range(dis$smr), range(dis$eb))
The estimated mean is b = 1.03 and the variance of the true risks a = 0.058 (an SD of 0.24: the districts really do differ). The range shrinks from 0.55–1.80 to 0.63–1.58. Ashby, expecting 44.5, keeps a weight of 0.058/(0.058 + 1.03/44.5) = 0.72 on its own ratio, and moves from 1.80 to 1.58; a district expecting 300 would keep 94%. The ranking changes too: the smoothed map’s highest districts are those with high ratios and enough data to believe them.




Your turn. Is the clustering only noise? Assunção and Reis’s empirical Bayes Moran’s I standardizes each ratio by its own Poisson uncertainty before computing I. Run it.









999 permutations.


lw <- nb2listw(poly2nb(dis), style = "W")
set.seed(9062)
ebm <- EBImoran.mc(dis$admissions, dis$expected, lw, nsim = 999)
c(I = unname(ebm$statistic), p = ebm$p.value)
0.51, p = 0.001: the same answer. With these district sizes, the clustering isn’t an artefact of unequal noise. The pattern on the newspaper’s map is real; the next question is what explains it.

title: Areal data and spatial weights
section: Choropleth maps and their class breaks
text:
Choropleth maps and their class breaks









A choropleth map colours each area by its value in classes. The classes’ breaks decide what the eye sees. Quantile breaks put the same number of areas in each class (every class appears, whatever the values); equal-interval breaks split the range evenly (honest about the values, but one outlier can push everything else into a couple of classes). The classInt package computes both, and several others.
Your turn. Compute five quantile classes and five equal-interval classes of the raw ratios, and count the districts in each equal-interval class.









Equal intervals are style "equal".


dis$smr <- dis$admissions / dis$expected
q <- classIntervals(dis$smr, n = 5, style = "quantile")
e <- classIntervals(dis$smr, n = 5, style = "equal")
print(round(q$brks, 2)); print(round(e$brks, 2))
table(cut(dis$smr, e$brks, include.lowest = TRUE))
The quantile breaks are 0.55, 0.83, 0.96, 1.14, 1.37 and 1.80: the darkest class starts at 1.37, so 12 districts look alarming. With equal intervals (0.55, 0.80, 1.05, 1.30, 1.55, 1.80), only 6 districts are in the darkest class, and 21 are in the second-lightest. Same data, two different stories. A careful map states its breaks, uses ones with a meaning when it can (1 = as expected, 1.25, 1.5), and maps the smoothed estimates, or the probability that the risk exceeds 1, rather than raw ratios.










NoteGo deeper: the modifiable areal unit problem





Areal data come from aggregating individuals into areas whose boundaries someone chose. Draw the boundaries differently, at the same scale (the zoning effect) or at a different scale (the scale effect), and correlations, regression slopes and Moran’s I can all change, sometimes even sign. This is the modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP), named by Stan Openshaw in 1984. A related trap is the ecological fallacy: a correlation between district averages (deprivation and admissions) doesn’t say that the deprived individuals are the ones admitted. Neither problem has a general solution; the defences are to analyze at the finest scale available, to check whether conclusions survive a change of units, and to phrase conclusions about areas as conclusions about areas. Openshaw’s short book The Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (Geo Books, 1984) is still worth reading.

title: Areal data and spatial weights
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Before blaming the plant. Correlate the ratios with the distance from the plant, the ratios with deprivation, and deprivation with the distance from the plant.









The distance column is dist_plant_km.


dis$smr <- dis$admissions / dis$expected
c(smr_distance = cor(dis$smr, dis$dist_plant_km),
  smr_deprivation = cor(dis$smr, dis$deprivation),
  deprivation_distance = cor(dis$deprivation, dis$dist_plant_km))
-0.62: the ratios fall with the distance from the plant, as the newspaper said. But they rise with deprivation even more strongly (+0.73), and deprivation itself falls with the distance from the plant (-0.68): the old industrial housing around the plant and in the town is the most deprived. The distance could be standing in for deprivation, or the other way round. Correlations can’t separate them; a regression with both can, and since the residuals will be spatially correlated, it has to be a spatial regression. That’s Lesson 7. (And the plant’s own district, Canal Side? A ratio of 0.95.)




Challenge 2 · Distance-based neighbours. In RStudio, define neighbours as each district’s 4 nearest centroids (knn2nb(knearneigh(st_coordinates(st_centroid(dis)), k = 4))) and recompute Moran’s I. It’s 0.54, close to the contiguity version’s 0.51. When would the two definitions disagree badly? (Think of a county with one huge rural district and many small town districts.)

title: Areal data and spatial weights
text:
Quick quiz

1. A standardized ratio of 1.3 means:

1.3 admissions per 1,000 people
30% more admissions than expected from the district’s age structure
30% of the county’s admissions


Observed over expected, where expected uses national age-specific rates.



2. Queen contiguity differs from rook contiguity in:

Counting areas that touch only at a corner
Using distances
Giving more weight to larger areas


Here it made no difference, because the districts never meet only at a corner.



3. Why did the two highest ratios belong to small districts?

Small districts are unhealthier
Ratios from small expected counts are noisier, so they dominate the extremes
The expected counts were wrong


The small-numbers problem: \text{SD} \approx \sqrt{\text{RR}/E}.



4. Empirical Bayes smoothing:

Averages each district with its neighbours
Shrinks each ratio toward the overall mean, more when its expected count is small
Removes the spatial pattern


It’s partial pooling; spatial smoothing (Lesson 7’s CAR model) also borrows from neighbours.



5. With quantile classes, the darkest class always contains:

About a fifth of the areas (with five classes), whatever their values
Only the areas significantly above 1
The areas above the mean


That’s why quantile maps can make small differences look alarming.



6. The ratios fall with the distance from the plant (r = -0.62). What does that show?

The plant raises admissions
Nothing yet: deprivation is correlated with both
The data are wrong


A confounder; Lesson 7 separates the two.

title: Areal data and spatial weights
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve checked the newspaper’s map. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Standardized ratios (observed over expected) compare districts with different age structures; the county overall is at 1.03, the districts between 0.55 and 1.80.
Contiguity neighbours (queen or rook) and row-standardized or binary weights; here, 310 links and 5.2 neighbours per district.
The clustering is real: Moran’s I 0.51 (p = 0.001 by permutation, and the same with the empirical Bayes version for rates).
The small-numbers problem: small districts’ ratios are twice as variable. Empirical Bayes shrinks them (Ashby from 1.80 to 1.58).
Class breaks change a map’s message: 12 alarming districts with quantiles, 6 with equal intervals.
Before blaming the plant: distance and deprivation are entangled (r = -0.68).







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download districts.geojson and district_health.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install spdep and classInt.

Draw the neighbours. plot(st_geometry(dis)); plot(nb, st_coordinates(st_centroid(dis)), add = TRUE, col = "red") draws the neighbour graph.
Local smoothing. EBlocal() shrinks each ratio toward its neighbours’ mean instead of the county’s. Map both smoothings side by side.
A probability map. Using the empirical Bayes prior (a gamma distribution with mean b and variance a), compute each district’s posterior probability that its relative risk exceeds 1.2, and map it.
Jenks breaks. Try classIntervals(..., style = "jenks"), which minimizes the variance within classes. How does it compare?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Standardized ratio (SMR, SAR)

Observed over expected cases, where the expected count uses reference rates for each age group.

Contiguity (queen, rook)

Neighbours defined by a shared boundary: any shared point (queen) or a shared edge (rook).

Row-standardized and binary weights

Each area’s neighbour weights sum to 1, or every link has weight 1.

Small-numbers problem

The extra variability of rates from small populations, which dominates the extremes of a map.

Empirical Bayes smoothing

Shrinking each area’s rate toward an overall (or local) mean, by an amount that depends on its expected count.

Choropleth map

A map with areas coloured by classes of a value.

Modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP)

The dependence of results for areal data on how the areas were drawn.

Ecological fallacy

Concluding about individuals from relationships between area averages.











NoteWant to read more?






Edzer Pebesma and Roger Bivand, Spatial Data Science with Applications in R (free online), chapters 14 and 15, on contiguity, weights and Moran’s I for areal data.
Lance Waller and Carol Gotway, Applied Spatial Statistics for Public Health Data (Wiley, 2004), chapters 4 and 7, on standardized ratios, smoothing and tests for clustering of disease.
Renato Assunção and Edna Reis, “A New Proposal to Adjust Moran’s I for Population Density”, Statistics in Medicine 18, 1999, pages 2147 to 2162, the empirical Bayes Moran’s I.

title: Kriging
text:
Module 9 · Lesson 4 of 13 Week 136 of 160 About 5–7 hours
A family on the north-eastern edge of the plant wants to know whether their vegetable garden is safe. Nobody took a sample in it: the nearest one is 97 m away. Hana has to give them a number, and an honest idea of how sure that number is. That’s the problem kriging solves: the best linear prediction of the value at an unsampled place, with its prediction variance, using the variogram to decide how much each sample should count.
The method is named after Danie Krige, a South African mining engineer who in the 1950s estimated gold grades in new blocks of ore from nearby boreholes; Georges Matheron, in Fontainebleau, turned his practice into theory in the 1960s.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Kriging
text:
The variogram, once more
Kriging uses the variogram at the distances between the target and its nearby samples, mostly a few hundred metres. So we fit it up to 1 km, where the trend matters less, and to log mercury itself (Lesson 5 brings the trend back in).
The setup code reads the data and fits that model. Its coordinates for the garden, and a 50 m prediction grid over the survey square, come with it.













Your turn. Print the fitted model, and evaluate it at 100, 500 and 1,000 m with variogramLine().









Add 1000.


print(m)
variogramLine(m, dist_vector = c(100, 500, 1000))
A tiny nugget (0.006), and an exponential with a partial sill of 4.6 and a range parameter of 3,887 m, far beyond the survey: over the first kilometre, this model is almost a straight line, \gamma(100) = 0.12, \gamma(500) = 0.57, \gamma(1000) = 1.06. That’s the trend’s doing (the variogram doesn’t level off, Lesson 3), and the fitted sill means nothing on its own. It doesn’t matter much here: ordinary kriging only uses the variogram’s shape over the distances to the neighbours, and that’s well estimated.

title: Kriging
text:
A baseline: inverse distance weighting
The simplest spatial predictor is a weighted average of the nearby samples, with weights proportional to 1/d^p: inverse distance weighting (IDW), usually with p = 2. It’s intuitive and quick, but its weights ignore the variogram, ignore how the samples cluster, and give no measure of uncertainty.
Your turn. Predict log mercury in the garden by IDW from its 10 nearest samples, and back-transform to mg/kg.









The usual power is 2.


d <- sqrt((soil$x - garden$x)^2 + (soil$y - garden$y)^2)
nn <- order(d)[1:10]                                          # the 10 nearest samples
w <- 1 / d[nn]^2
w <- w / sum(w)
c(nearest_m = d[nn[1]], prediction = sum(w * soil$z[nn]), mg_kg = exp(sum(w * soil$z[nn])))
The nearest sample is 97 m away. IDW predicts a log value of 0.048, about 1.05 mg/kg: right at the 1 mg/kg screening value. The 10 neighbours range from 0.39 to 2.16 mg/kg, so the answer depends a lot on how they’re weighted.

title: Kriging
text:
Ordinary kriging by hand
Kriging also predicts with a weighted sum, \hat Z(s_0) = \sum_i \lambda_i Z(s_i), but chooses the weights to minimize the expected squared error, subject to \sum_i \lambda_i = 1 (so the prediction is unbiased whatever the mean, which is what makes it ordinary kriging; simple kriging assumes the mean is known). With a variogram, the minimization gives a linear system: for n neighbours, with \Gamma_{ij} = \gamma(s_i - s_j), \gamma_{0i} = \gamma(s_0 - s_i) and a Lagrange multiplier \mu for the constraint,

\begin{pmatrix} \Gamma & \mathbf 1 \\ \mathbf 1^\top & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol\lambda \\ \mu \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol\gamma_0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\sigma^2_{\text{OK}} = \boldsymbol\lambda^\top \boldsymbol\gamma_0 + \mu .

\sigma^2_{\text{OK}} is the kriging variance, the expected squared prediction error. It depends on where the samples are and on the variogram, but not on the values measured.
Your turn. Build the system for the garden’s 10 nearest samples, solve it, and predict.









The last equation says the weights sum to 1.


d <- sqrt((soil$x - garden$x)^2 + (soil$y - garden$y)^2)
nn <- order(d)[1:10]
gam <- function(h) variogramLine(m, dist_vector = h)$gamma
Gamma <- matrix(gam(as.vector(as.matrix(dist(soil[nn, c("x", "y")])))), 10)
A <- rbind(cbind(Gamma, 1), c(rep(1, 10), 0))                 # the 11 x 11 system
b <- c(gam(d[nn]), 1)
sol <- solve(A, b)
lambda <- sol[1:10]
c(sum_weights = sum(lambda), prediction = sum(lambda * soil$z[nn]))
A prediction of 0.0135 on the log scale, 1.01 mg/kg. Look at the weights (round(lambda, 3)): 0.50 for the nearest sample, 0.40 for the second, and only 0.06 or less for the other eight, some of them slightly negative. Kriging notices that the farther samples are screened by the two near ones: once you know the values 97 and 123 m away, a sample 400 m away in the same direction adds little. IDW can’t do that: it gave the eight farther samples 32% of the weight between them, kriging only 10%.




Your turn. Compute the kriging variance, \boldsymbol\lambda^\top\boldsymbol\gamma_0 + \mu, and the standard error.









Add the Lagrange multiplier, mu.


d <- sqrt((soil$x - garden$x)^2 + (soil$y - garden$y)^2)
nn <- order(d)[1:10]
gam <- function(h) variogramLine(m, dist_vector = h)$gamma
Gamma <- matrix(gam(as.vector(as.matrix(dist(soil[nn, c("x", "y")])))), 10)
A <- rbind(cbind(Gamma, 1), c(rep(1, 10), 0))
b <- c(gam(d[nn]), 1)
sol <- solve(A, b)
lambda <- sol[1:10]; mu <- sol[11]
ok_var <- sum(lambda * gam(d[nn])) + mu
c(variance = ok_var, se = sqrt(ok_var))
A variance of 0.136, a standard error of 0.37 on the log scale. A 95% prediction interval for log mercury is 0.014 \pm 1.96 \times 0.37, which back-transforms to 0.49 to 2.1 mg/kg. So the honest answer for the family is: “probably about 1 mg/kg, possibly as low as 0.5 or as high as 2; we should sample the garden.” That’s what the kriging variance is for.

title: Kriging
text:
Kriging with gstat
Your turn. krige() does all of this. Krige the garden from its 10 nearest samples (nmax = 10), and compare.









nmax = 10.


k <- krige(z ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = soil, newdata = garden, model = m, nmax = 10)
k
The same 0.01354 and 0.1356. z ~ 1 asks for ordinary kriging (a constant but unknown mean); nmax limits it to the nearest samples, a local neighbourhood, which is faster and lets the mean drift slowly across the map. Without nmax, gstat uses all 200 samples.




Your turn. Krige the whole 60 × 60 grid from all the samples, and find the area (each cell is 0.0025 km²) where the predicted log value is above 0, that is, where the predicted median is above 1 mg/kg.









Predict at the grid.


kg <- krige(z ~ 1, ~x + y, soil, newdata = grid, model = m, debug.level = 0)
print(summary(kg$var1.pred))
sum(kg$var1.pred > 0) * 0.0025                                 # km2
The predictions run from -3.7 (0.025 mg/kg) to 1.29 (3.6 mg/kg), and 1.21 km² of the 9 km² square has a predicted median above 1 mg/kg. Kriging is an exact interpolator with no nugget: at a sampled location, the prediction equals the measurement. With this tiny nugget, it nearly does.













Your turn. The standard-error map (right, above) looks like a map of the samples. Correlate each cell’s kriging standard error with its distance to the nearest sample.









The kriging variance is kg$var1.var.


kg <- krige(z ~ 1, ~x + y, soil, newdata = grid, model = m, debug.level = 0)
nearest <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) min(sqrt((soil$x - grid$x[i])^2 + (soil$y - grid$y[i])^2)))
c(max_se = max(sqrt(kg$var1.var)), correlation = cor(sqrt(kg$var1.var), nearest))
A correlation of 0.90 with the distance to the nearest sample; the largest standard error, 0.69, is in a corner of the square, where there are samples on one side only. The kriging variance depends on the geometry of the samples and on the variogram, not on the data values, so it can be computed before sampling. That’s how sampling campaigns are designed: put the next samples where the kriging variance is largest, or where it matters most.

title: Kriging
text:
Cross-validation
Did kriging get it right? Leave-one-out cross-validation removes each sample in turn, predicts it from the other 199, and compares. Three numbers matter: the mean error (bias, should be near 0), the root mean squared error (accuracy), and the mean squared z-score, the squared error divided by the kriging variance (calibration: near 1 if the kriging variances are honest).
Your turn. Run krige.cv(), and compute the three.









The z-scores are in cv$zscore.


cv <- krige.cv(z ~ 1, ~x + y, soil, model = m, debug.level = 0)
c(mean_error = mean(cv$residual), rmse = sqrt(mean(cv$residual^2)),
  mean_sq_z = mean(cv$zscore^2))
A mean error of -0.0002, an RMSE of 0.443 on the log scale (predictions typically within a factor of e^{0.44} = 1.6), and a mean squared z-score of 1.03: the kriging variances are almost exactly as large as the real errors, and 5.5% of the z-scores fall outside \pm 1.96, close to the 5% they should. The model’s uncertainty is honest.




Your turn. Cross-validate IDW too (krige.cv() without a model does IDW; set = list(idp = 2) sets the power), and compare with predicting every sample by the mean of the others.









idp = 2.


cvi <- krige.cv(z ~ 1, ~x + y, soil, debug.level = 0, set = list(idp = 2))
loo_mean <- (sum(soil$z) - soil$z) / (nrow(soil) - 1)
c(idw = sqrt(mean(cvi$residual^2)), mean_only = sqrt(mean((soil$z - loo_mean)^2)))
IDW (from all the samples) has an RMSE of 0.630, and the mean alone 1.161, against kriging’s 0.443. Kriging’s errors are 30% smaller than IDW’s. IDW is a reasonable quick look; for decisions, krige.

title: Kriging
text:
From predictions to decisions
On the log scale, the kriging prediction and its standard error describe an approximately normal distribution for the true value in each cell. So the probability that a cell exceeds 1 mg/kg (\log 1 = 0) is

P(Z(s_0) > \log 1) = 1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{\log 1 - \hat Z(s_0)}{\sigma_{\text{OK}}(s_0)}\right).

A map of that probability is what a regulator can act on: clean up where it’s high, sample more where it’s in between.
Your turn. Compute the exceedance probability for every cell, and the area where it’s above 0.9, 0.5 and 0.1.









The third threshold is 0.1.


kg <- krige(z ~ 1, ~x + y, soil, newdata = grid, model = m, debug.level = 0)
p1 <- 1 - pnorm((log(1) - kg$var1.pred) / sqrt(kg$var1.var))
sapply(c(p90 = 0.9, p50 = 0.5, p10 = 0.1), function(p) sum(p1 > p) * 0.0025)
0.49 km² is almost certainly above 1 mg/kg (probability over 90%), 1.21 km² probably (over 50%, the same as the predicted-median area), and 2.53 km² possibly (over 10%). In the residential area north-east of the plant, 0.24 km² has a probability above 10%: that’s where Hana would recommend garden sampling. The gap between the 90% and 10% areas is the price of having only 200 samples; more samples would shrink it.










NoteGo deeper: simple kriging, and why kriging is “BLUP”





If the mean m is known, simple kriging predicts \hat Z(s_0) = m + \mathbf c_0^\top C^{-1}(\mathbf z - m\mathbf 1), with covariances C(h) = C(0) - \gamma(h) instead of the variogram, and no constraint on the weights; its variance C(0) - \mathbf c_0^\top C^{-1}\mathbf c_0 is smaller than ordinary kriging’s, because it doesn’t have to estimate the mean. (With gstat, give the mean as beta in krige().) That formula is exactly the conditional mean of a multivariate normal distribution (Module 3), which is the Gaussian-process view of Lesson 5. Ordinary kriging is the best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP) when the mean is unknown, the same BLUP that appears in mixed models (Module 3, Lesson 11), where the “random effects” are predicted by the same algebra. Cressie’s Statistics for Spatial Data, chapter 3, derives all of them.

title: Kriging
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The garden, in mg/kg. The kriging prediction on the log scale back-transforms to the median, e^{\hat Z}. If the log value is normal, the mean is e^{\hat Z + \sigma^2/2}. For the garden, compute both, and the probability of exceeding 1 mg/kg.









The mean adds half the variance: divide by 2.


k <- krige(z ~ 1, ~x + y, soil, newdata = garden, model = m, nmax = 10, debug.level = 0)
pr <- k$var1.pred; s2 <- k$var1.var
c(median = exp(pr), mean = exp(pr + s2 / 2), p_above_1 = 1 - pnorm((0 - pr) / sqrt(s2)))
A median of 1.01 mg/kg, a mean of 1.08, and a probability of 51% of exceeding 1 mg/kg: a coin toss. For a health question, the mean matters (exposure adds up over the garden), and so does the probability. Both say the same thing: take a sample. Back-transforming a kriged log value with e^{\hat Z} alone underestimates the mean everywhere, more where the uncertainty is larger.




Challenge 2 · Where to sample next. In RStudio, add a hypothetical sample at the cell with the largest kriging standard error inside the residential area (any value will do: the variance doesn’t depend on it), re-krige, and see how much the standard errors around it shrink. Then try the cell with the exceedance probability closest to 0.5 instead. Which is the better place to sample, and for whom?

title: Kriging
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why do ordinary kriging’s weights sum to 1?

To make the prediction positive
To make the prediction unbiased when the mean is unknown
To make the variance smallest


With weights summing to 1, the unknown constant mean cancels out of the error.



2. The kriging variance depends on:

The measured values
The sample locations and the variogram, not the measured values
Only the number of samples


That’s why it can be used to design sampling before any value is known.



3. Some kriging weights were slightly negative. Why?

Rounding errors
Screening: far samples behind near ones add little, and the weights adjust for redundancy
The nugget was negative


Kriging accounts for the samples’ correlation with each other, not just with the target.



4. Cross-validation gave a mean squared z-score of 1.03. That means:

The predictions are biased
The kriging variances match the real errors
The RMSE is 1.03


Near 1 is well calibrated; much above 1 means the model is overconfident.



5. Which method had the smallest cross-validated RMSE?

Ordinary kriging (0.443)
Inverse distance weighting (0.630)
The overall mean (1.16)


Kriging uses the variogram and accounts for clustering.



6. e^{\hat Z} of a kriged log value estimates:

The mean concentration
The median concentration
The 95th percentile


The mean is e^{\hat Z + \sigma^2/2}, larger.

title: Kriging
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve predicted where nobody measured, and said how sure you are. Here’s what you’ve learned:

IDW is a quick weighted average; ordinary kriging chooses the weights from the variogram to minimize the error, with weights summing to 1, and gives a kriging variance.
By hand and with gstat: the garden’s prediction is 1.01 mg/kg (log 0.014, standard error 0.37), with half the weight on the nearest sample and screening of the far ones.
The standard-error map follows the sampling gaps (correlation 0.90 with the distance to the nearest sample).
Cross-validation: RMSE 0.443 for kriging against 0.630 for IDW, with honest variances (mean squared z-score 1.03).
Decisions: 0.49 km² is almost certainly above 1 mg/kg, 2.53 km² possibly, and the garden is a coin toss: sample it.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download soil_mercury.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Neighbourhood size. Cross-validate ordinary kriging with nmax = 5, 10, 20, 50 and all samples. Which is best, and why might a local neighbourhood help here?
The model’s influence. Cross-validate with the spherical and Gaussian models fitted in Lesson 3 (to the residuals’ variogram). How much does the model matter?
A probability map. Map p1 with geom_raster() and a diverging color scale centred on 0.5, and overlay the samples.
Block kriging. Remediation is decided for 50 × 50 m blocks, not points. Add block = c(50, 50) to krige(). How do the predictions and the variances change?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Inverse distance weighting (IDW)

Prediction by a weighted average with weights proportional to 1/d^p.

Ordinary kriging

The best linear unbiased prediction with an unknown constant mean, from a variogram; its weights sum to 1.

Simple kriging

Kriging with a known mean, using covariances.

Kriging variance

The expected squared prediction error of kriging; it depends on the sampling geometry and the variogram, not on the values.

Screening

The reduction of a sample’s kriging weight when nearer samples lie between it and the target.

Local neighbourhood

Kriging from only the nearest samples (nmax).

Leave-one-out cross-validation

Predicting each sample from all the others, to measure bias, accuracy and calibration.

Exceedance probability

The probability that the true value at a location exceeds a threshold, from the prediction and its standard error.











NoteWant to read more?






Edzer Pebesma and Roger Bivand, Spatial Data Science with Applications in R (free online), chapter 12, on kriging with gstat, cross-validation and block kriging.
Edward Isaaks and R. Mohan Srivastava, An Introduction to Applied Geostatistics (Oxford, 1989), chapters 12 to 13, the most readable account of ordinary kriging and its weights, from mining practice.
Peter Diggle and Paulo Ribeiro, Model-based Geostatistics (Springer, 2007), chapter 6, on prediction and on exceedance probabilities.

title: Spatial dependence
text:
Module 9 · Lesson 2 of 13 Week 134 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Waldo Tobler’s “first law of geography” says that everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things. For the soil survey, it means a sample tells you something about the soil 100 m away, less about the soil 1 km away, and nothing about the soil 3 km away. This lesson measures that resemblance, the spatial autocorrelation, the same way Module 6 measured how much today resembles yesterday.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Spatial dependence
text:
Neighbours and weights
Every measure of spatial dependence compares each observation with its neighbours, so the first step is to decide who they are. For points, the usual choices are the k nearest points, or all points within a distance d. The neighbours are then turned into a spatial weights matrix W, with w_{ij} > 0 if j is a neighbour of i and 0 otherwise.
