Most often the rows are standardized to sum to 1 (style "W" in spdep), so that \sum_j w_{ij} z_j is the average of i’s neighbours.
The setup code reads the soil data, takes the logarithm of mercury (it’s skewed, and the log is what the module works with from here on), and loads spdep.












Your turn. Find each sample’s 6 nearest neighbours with knearneigh(), convert them to a neighbour list with knn2nb(), and count the links. Is the relation symmetric (is every sample a neighbour of its neighbours)?









Six neighbours: k = 6.


nb <- knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 6))
c(links = sum(card(nb)), symmetric = is.symmetric.nb(nb))
1,200 links, six for each of the 200 samples, and the relation isn’t symmetric: a sample on the edge of the survey has neighbours that are closer to other samples than to it. That’s fine for Moran’s I; card(nb) counts each sample’s neighbours.




Your turn. Make row-standardized weights with nb2listw(), compute the spatial lag (each sample’s neighbour average) with lag.listw(), and correlate it with the samples’ own values.









Row-standardized is style "W".


nb <- knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 6))
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W")
lag <- lag.listw(lw, z)
cor(z, lag)
0.915: a sample’s log mercury is very close to its neighbours’ average. That’s the spatial version of the lag-1 autocorrelation of Module 6. Plotted against each other (lag against value), the samples form the Moran scatterplot, whose slope is Moran’s I.

title: Spatial dependence
text:
Moran’s I
Moran’s I is the most used measure of spatial autocorrelation. With z_i centred on their mean,

I = \frac{n}{S_0} \, \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij} z_i z_j}{\sum_i z_i^2}, \qquad S_0 = \sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}.

It’s a correlation-like number: near 0 when neighbours are unrelated (its expected value under no autocorrelation is -1/(n-1), slightly negative), positive when neighbours are alike, negative when they differ (a checkerboard). With row-standardized weights, S_0 = n and I is the slope of the Moran scatterplot.
Your turn. Compute Moran’s I by hand, with the weights as a matrix from listw2mat().









W z, with the centred values: W %*% zc.


lw <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 6)), style = "W")
W <- listw2mat(lw)                          # 200 x 200, rows sum to 1
zc <- z - mean(z)
(length(z) / sum(W)) * sum(zc * (W %*% zc)) / sum(zc^2)
I = 0.822, very strong positive autocorrelation. It’s close to, but not the same as, the correlation of 0.915 with the lag: Moran’s I is a regression slope rather than a correlation, and it uses the overall mean for both the values and their lags.




Your turn. moran.test() computes the same I, and its variance under the hypothesis of no autocorrelation, for a z-test. Run it.









Give it the values and the weights, lw.


lw <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 6)), style = "W")
mt <- moran.test(z, lw)
print(mt)
mt$statistic
I = 0.822 against an expected -0.005, with a standard deviate of 21.7: overwhelming evidence that nearby samples are alike, which nobody doubted. The test’s real use is on residuals, where the answer matters: if a regression’s residuals are autocorrelated, its standard errors are wrong (Lesson 7).




The z-test relies on approximations. A permutation test needs none: shuffle the values among the locations many times, recompute I each time, and see where the real I falls among the shuffled ones. A shuffle destroys any spatial pattern while keeping the values, so the shuffled I’s show what I looks like by chance.
Your turn. Run moran.mc() with 999 permutations, and find the largest of the 999 permuted values.









nsim = 999.


lw <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 6)), style = "W")
set.seed(9021)
mc <- moran.mc(z, lw, nsim = 999)
c(I = unname(mc$statistic), p = mc$p.value, max_permuted = max(mc$res[1:999]))
None of the 999 shuffles came anywhere near: the largest permuted I was 0.160, against the real 0.822. The p-value, (0 + 1)/(999 + 1) = 0.001, is the smallest 999 permutations can give. (mc$res holds the permuted values, plus the observed one at the end.)




Geary’s C looks at squared differences between neighbours instead of products:

C = \frac{(n-1)}{2 S_0} \, \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij} (z_i - z_j)^2}{\sum_i (z_i - \bar z)^2}.

It’s 1 with no autocorrelation, below 1 when neighbours are alike, and above 1 when they differ. It’s more sensitive to local differences, Moran’s I to the global pattern.
Your turn. Run geary.test().









The function is geary.test.


lw <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 6)), style = "W")
geary.test(z, lw)$estimate
C = 0.19, far below its expected value of 1: neighbours differ much less than random pairs. Moran’s I and Geary’s C almost always agree on the direction; they differ in what they weigh most.

title: Spatial dependence
text:
Trend or dependence?
Some of that resemblance is easy to explain: samples near the cell room are high, and their neighbours are near the cell room too. That’s a trend, a large-scale change in the mean. What’s left after the trend is removed is the small-scale dependence, and the two need different treatment (Lessons 3 to 5).
Your turn. Fit a straight-line trend of log mercury on the distance to the cell room, and compute Moran’s I of the residuals with lm.morantest(), which accounts for the fitted coefficients.









Regress on d_cell.


lw <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 6)), style = "W")
fit <- lm(z ~ d_cell)
print(coef(fit))
lm.morantest(fit, lw)$estimate[1]
Log mercury falls by about 0.0017 per metre (a factor of 5.2 per kilometre), and the residuals’ Moran’s I is 0.620: lower than 0.822, but still very strong. The distance trend explains part of the resemblance, and the rest is genuine small-scale dependence, from the patchy way mercury settled and the soil holds it. That’s what kriging will use.




Your turn. A correlogram shows how the autocorrelation fades with distance: Moran’s I computed with neighbours in distance bands, 0 to 250 m, 250 to 500 m, and so on. Compute it for the trend’s residuals.









Name each value by its band’s upper limit: bands[-1].


r <- residuals(lm(z ~ d_cell))
bands <- seq(0, 2000, by = 250)
I_band <- sapply(1:8, function(i) {
  nb_i <- dnearneigh(xy, bands[i], bands[i + 1])             # neighbours in this band
  moran.test(r, nb2listw(nb_i, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE), zero.policy = TRUE)$estimate[1]
})
round(setNames(I_band, bands[-1]), 3)
0.666 for pairs up to 250 m apart, 0.437 for 250 to 500 m, 0.209 at 500 to 750 m, then about 0 beyond 1 km (slightly negative at the largest distances, as residuals that average to zero must be). The dependence reaches about a kilometre. The variogram, next lesson, says the same thing in a form that’s easier to model. (zero.policy = TRUE allows samples with no neighbours in a band, which happens at the short distances near the edges.)













Without the trend, Moran’s I of log mercury itself turns strongly negative at large distances: samples 1.5 km apart are typically one near the cell room and one far away, so they differ. That’s what a trend does to a correlogram, and why you look at the residuals.

title: Spatial dependence
text:
Local clusters: LISA
Moran’s I is one number for the whole survey. Its local version (Anselin’s LISA, local indicators of spatial association) gives one number per sample, I_i = z_i \sum_j w_{ij} z_j / m_2 (with m_2 = \sum z_i^2 / n), whose average is the global I. A large positive I_i with a high value is a high-high cluster, a hot spot surrounded by hot neighbours; low-low is a cold spot; negative I_i marks an outlier unlike its neighbours.
Your turn. Compute the local Moran’s I with localmoran(), and count the samples that are significant high-high clusters at the 5% level.









Significant at 5%: p < 0.05.


lw <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 6)), style = "W")
loc <- localmoran(z, lw)
p <- loc[, 5]                                            # the p-values
lag <- lag.listw(lw, z)
high_high <- z > mean(z) & lag > mean(z) & p < 0.05
c(high_high = sum(high_high), median_distance = median(d_cell[high_high]))
51 high-high samples, with a median distance of 368 m from the cell room and none farther than 840 m: 46 on the plant site, 3 on farmland and 2 in residential areas. There are also 34 low-low samples, far out. The average of the 200 local I’s is exactly the global I, 0.822.










NoteGo deeper: why local p-values need care





Each local test uses a sample and its neighbours, so neighbouring tests share data and aren’t independent, and there are 200 of them. At the 5% level, about 10 would be “significant” by chance even with no pattern at all. The local p-values are also computed under randomization assumptions that the strong global autocorrelation violates. Anselin (1995) recommended treating them as exploratory, and a correction for multiple testing (Bonferroni, which is very strict here, or a false discovery rate) as the minimum. Even then, a LISA map is a map of where to look, not a set of findings. Luc Anselin, “Local Indicators of Spatial Association: LISA”, Geographical Analysis 27(2), 1995, introduced them.

title: Spatial dependence
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Fewer false alarms. Adjust the local p-values for multiple testing with the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (p.adjust(..., method = "BH")), and count the high-high samples that survive.









method = "BH".


lw <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 6)), style = "W")
p_adj <- p.adjust(localmoran(z, lw)[, 5], method = "BH")
lag <- lag.listw(lw, z)
sum(z > mean(z) & lag > mean(z) & p_adj < 0.05)
30 of the 51 survive: the core of the hot spot, around the cell room. The others are on its fringes, where the evidence is weaker. A false discovery rate of 5% means that, of the samples flagged, about 5% are expected to be false alarms, which is a sensible standard for a map of where to look next.




Challenge 2 · Raw or log? In RStudio, compute Moran’s I for the raw mercury values (not the log) with the same weights. It’s 0.79, slightly lower than the log’s 0.82. Which would you report, and why? (Think about what a few very high values do to a statistic built from products.)

title: Spatial dependence
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does a row-standardized weights matrix do to the spatial lag?

It sums the neighbours’ values
It averages the neighbours’ values
It removes the trend


Rows that sum to 1 turn \sum_j w_{ij} z_j into an average.



2. Moran’s I is near -1/(n-1) when:

Neighbours are alike
There’s no spatial autocorrelation
Neighbours differ systematically


That’s its expected value under independence; it’s slightly negative because the values are centred.



3. Geary’s C below 1 means:

Positive autocorrelation: neighbours are alike
Negative autocorrelation
No autocorrelation


Geary’s C measures squared differences, so it’s small when neighbours are alike.



4. Why does a permutation test shuffle the values among the locations?

To increase the sample size
To see what the statistic looks like when there’s no spatial pattern
To remove the trend


Each shuffle keeps the values but destroys their arrangement.



5. Moran’s I fell from 0.82 to 0.62 after removing the distance trend. What does that show?

The trend was wrong
Part of the resemblance was the trend; the rest is small-scale dependence
Moran’s I can’t be used on residuals


Trend and small-scale dependence both make neighbours alike; models treat them differently.



6. Why are LISA p-values treated as exploratory?

They’re computed with the wrong formula
There are many correlated tests, so some “clusters” appear by chance
They can only be negative


200 tests at 5% give about 10 false alarms even with no pattern.

title: Spatial dependence
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve measured the resemblance between neighbours. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Neighbours and weights: six nearest neighbours, row-standardized, so the spatial lag is the neighbours’ average (correlation 0.915 with the values).
Moran’s I is 0.822 for log mercury (standard deviate 21.7; no permutation out of 999 came close), and Geary’s C is 0.19.
Trend versus dependence: after a distance trend, the residuals’ I is 0.62, and the correlogram shows the dependence fading over about a kilometre.
LISA finds 51 high-high samples around the cell room (30 after a false-discovery-rate adjustment): a map of where to look.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download soil_mercury.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install spdep.

Other neighbours. Repeat Moran’s I with k = 3, 6, 12 and 24 nearest neighbours, and with distance bands dnearneigh(xy, 0, 300). How does I change, and why?
The Moran scatterplot. Draw it with moran.plot(z, lw). Which samples does it flag as influential?
A LISA map. Classify every sample as high-high, low-low, high-low, low-high or not significant, and map the classes with ggplot2.
Getis-Ord. Compute localG(z, lw), another hot-spot statistic, and compare its map with LISA’s.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Spatial autocorrelation

The resemblance between observations at nearby locations.

Neighbour list

For each observation, the observations counted as its neighbours (k nearest, within a distance, or sharing a border).

Spatial weights matrix

The matrix W of weights w_{ij} given to neighbour j of observation i, often row-standardized.

Spatial lag

The weighted average of an observation’s neighbours, \sum_j w_{ij} z_j.

Moran’s I

A global measure of spatial autocorrelation built from products of centred neighbouring values.

Geary’s C

A global measure built from squared differences between neighbours; below 1 for positive autocorrelation.

Correlogram

Moran’s I (or another autocorrelation) as a function of the distance between pairs.

LISA

Local indicators of spatial association: a local Moran’s I for each observation, to find clusters and outliers.











NoteWant to read more?






Edzer Pebesma and Roger Bivand, Spatial Data Science with Applications in R (free online), chapters 14 and 15, on neighbours, weights and measures of autocorrelation, by spdep’s author.
Luc Anselin, “Local Indicators of Spatial Association: LISA”, Geographical Analysis 27(2), 1995, pages 93 to 115.
Waldo Tobler, “A Computer Movie Simulating Urban Growth in the Detroit Region”, Economic Geography 46, 1970, pages 234 to 240, where the “first law of geography” appears, almost in passing.

title: Module 8 project: a business analytics case study
text:
The plant’s parent company also runs a distribution business, which sells chemicals in smaller quantities to about 3,000 business customers, on credit: they pay their invoices 30 to 90 days after delivery. Most pay. About one in six, each year, ends up 90 or more days overdue, and most of that money is never fully recovered.
Pieter, in credit control, wants a scorecard: a model and a rule that say which customers get credit and which pay cash in advance. Management likes decision trees, because they can read them, but will accept whatever works best, if it can be explained. That’s a business analytics case study: several models, compared by what they would earn, with a recommendation that management can act on.

title: Module 8 project: a business analytics case study
text:
What you’ll make
One report, written in Quarto in your plant-study RStudio project, that Pieter could take to the finance director. It should contain:

A summary for Pieter, at the top, in plain words: the rule you recommend, what it would have earned on the 600 new applications compared with granting credit to everyone, which factors matter most, and a one-page tree that management can read, with what it gives up compared with the best model.
The data and its problems: what you found, and what you did about each.
The model comparison: at least CHAID (by hand, as in Lesson 6, or with the CHAID package in RStudio), a pruned CART tree, a logistic regression, a neural network and an ensemble (a random forest or boosting), compared on a validation set by AUC, gains and profit.
The chosen rule, with its cut-off derived from the profit matrix, and its test on the new applications.
An explanation, and a list of limitations.

Nobody grades it, but write it as if the finance director will check your numbers. In real life, they would.

title: Module 8 project: a business analytics case study
text:
The handover
Download the four files into a new folder in your project, data-raw/credit/, and don’t edit them:

README.txt: Pieter’s note, with the economics, the questions, the columns and a known issue. Read it first.
credit_accounts.csv: the accounts at the start of last year, with what happened during the year.
new_applications.csv: 600 applications from this year.
new_application_outcomes.csv: what happened to those 600 (they were all given credit, as a trial). Don’t open it until you’ve chosen your model and your rule.

Then download the project template, save it in the top folder of your project as credit-scorecard.qmd, and click Render. It reads the data and summarizes it, with headings and code skeletons for every step. Fill it in one section at a time, and render often. It uses the tidyverse, rpart, rpart.plot, partykit, nnet, randomForest and gbm.

title: Module 8 project: a business analytics case study
text:
The brief, step by step

Explore (Lessons 1 and 2). The bad rate, overall and by company type, industry and credit score band. Which columns would be known when the credit decision is made, and which wouldn’t?
Clean (Lesson 8, and Module 1). Look for duplicated accounts, and for inputs recorded after the outcome. Small private companies often don’t file accounts: is the missingness of the financial ratios informative? Code it so that every model can use it. Look at the rare levels of the categorical inputs.
Partition (Lesson 1). Split the cleaned accounts into training (60%) and validation (40%) sets, stratified by the outcome. The 600 new applications are your test set.
Build the models (Lessons 2 to 13). CHAID; CART, grown with cp = 0 and pruned (Lesson 5); a conditional inference tree if you like (Lesson 7); a logistic regression, with inputs suggested by the trees (Lesson 9); a neural network with weight decay (Lesson 10); and a random forest or a boosted model (Lessons 12 and 13).
Compare (Lesson 11). Validation AUC, a gains chart, and the profit of each model at its profit-maximizing cut-off.
Choose the rule (Lessons 3 and 11). From the profit matrix in the README, derive the break-even probability of default. Check the chosen model’s calibration before relying on it.
Test once (Lesson 11). Score the 600 new applications, then open the outcomes, and report the AUC, the number refused, the bad debts avoided and the profit, against granting credit to everyone.
Explain (Lessons 3, 9, 12 and 13). Which factors drive the risk, in words a credit controller can use: importance, partial dependence, and the one-page tree’s rules.
Write it up. Summary first. Then the data, the cleaning, the comparison, the rule and its test, the explanation, the limitations, and the cleaning log at the end.

Stretch goal. Credit isn’t all or nothing: Pieter could also grant a reduced limit, half the usual one, which halves both the margin and the loss on a bad account. Work out the expected profit of the three options (full credit, half credit, cash in advance) as a function of the probability of default, and turn your model into a three-band rule. How much more would it earn?

title: Module 8 project: a business analytics case study
text:
Check your own work
When you’ve finished, assess your project against this rubric. Aim for the right-hand column.










Needs work
Good
Excellent

Used as received

The models
One or two

CHAID, pruned CART, an engineered logistic regression, a regularized network and an ensemble, each tuned on the training data or by the validation set, not the test set

Accuracy

A cut-off of 0.5
A cut-off from the costs

title: Module 8 project: a business analytics case study
text:
Tips

Ask “when is this known?” of every column. A column about what happened during the year can’t be used to decide at the start of it. Its AUC alone will tell you something’s wrong.
Missing ratios are information. Compare the bad rates of accounts with and without filed accounts. For trees, a missingness indicator plus a code value outside the real range works well; for logistic regression and networks, an indicator plus a typical value.
The break-even probability. Granting credit to a customer with default probability p earns 6{,}000(1 - p) - 25{,}000\,p on average. Refuse when that’s negative.
Profit at each model’s best cut-off. Compare models at their own best cut-offs on the validation set, then use the break-even cut-off for the final rule, as in Lesson 11.
A tree for management. Prune a CART or CHAID tree to 6 to 10 leaves, draw it with rpart.plot, and write its rules. State how much profit it gives up against your best model: that’s the price of readability, and it’s management’s decision whether to pay it.
Don’t tune on the test set. Choose everything (model, inputs, cut-off) on the training and validation data, then score the 600 applications once.


When it’s done, you’ll have run a complete business analytics study, from a messy credit file to a rule with a euro value. Congratulations on finishing Module 8! Module 9 changes scale: statistics for data that live in space and time, from contaminated soil to air quality maps.

title: Boosting
text:
Module 8 · Lesson 13 of 13 Week 131 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Random forests average many deep, independent trees to cut variance. Boosting does the opposite: it grows many small trees in sequence, each one fitted to what the trees before it got wrong, and adds them up. Each small tree is a weak, biased model; the sum is strong. Boosted trees are, by most accounts, the most accurate off-the-shelf method for tables of data, and they win most prediction competitions on business data. Lesson 7’s boosted C5.0 was a first taste. This lesson builds gradient boosting from scratch, then uses the gbm package.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Boosting
text:
Boosting by hand
For squared-error regression, gradient boosting is beautifully simple:

Start with a constant prediction, \hat f_0 = \bar y.
For m = 1, \ldots, M: compute the residuals r_i = y_i - \hat f_{m-1}(x_i), fit a small tree h_m to them, and update \hat f_m = \hat f_{m-1} + \nu\, h_m.

The learning rate (or shrinkage) \nu, typically 0.01 to 0.1, makes each tree’s contribution small, so that no single tree’s mistakes matter much. For other losses (like the churn model’s log loss), the residuals are replaced by the loss’s negative gradient, which is where “gradient” boosting gets its name.
The setup code reads Lesson 4’s catalyst-life charges (400 for training, 200 for testing), and the churn accounts prepared for gbm: the sales reps dropped, and the target as a 0/1 column churn (gbm handles the missing satisfaction scores itself).












Your turn. Boost depth-2 regression trees for catalyst life, 100 rounds with a learning rate of 0.1, and find the test RMSE.









The test predictions get the same learning rate, 0.1.


f_train <- rep(mean(ctrain$life_days), nrow(ctrain))
f_test <- rep(mean(ctrain$life_days), nrow(ctest))
for (m in 1:100) {
  d <- ctrain
  d$life_days <- ctrain$life_days - f_train
  h <- rpart(life_days ~ ., data = d, control = small)
  f_train <- f_train + 0.1 * predict(h, ctrain)
  f_test <- f_test + 0.1 * predict(h, ctest)
}
c(train_rmse = sqrt(mean((ctrain$life_days - f_train)^2)), test_rmse = sqrt(mean((ctest$life_days - f_test)^2)))
A training RMSE of 43 days and a test RMSE of 66: better than Lesson 4’s single tree (85) and Lesson 12’s random forest (69 to 74), from a hundred trees with only four leaves each. No single tree here is any good; each one nudges the prediction a tenth of the way toward fixing the current errors. Together they build the hinge in temperature and the H₂S step out of many small steps.




Your turn. Record the test RMSE after each round, for 300 rounds, and look at it after 1, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200 and 300.









The last round is 300.


f_train <- rep(mean(ctrain$life_days), nrow(ctrain))
f_test <- rep(mean(ctrain$life_days), nrow(ctest))
test_rmse <- numeric(300)
for (m in 1:300) {
  d <- ctrain; d$life_days <- ctrain$life_days - f_train
  h <- rpart(life_days ~ ., data = d, control = small)
  f_train <- f_train + 0.1 * predict(h, ctrain)
  f_test <- f_test + 0.1 * predict(h, ctest)
  test_rmse[m] <- sqrt(mean((ctest$life_days - f_test)^2))
}
round(test_rmse[c(1, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 300)], 1)
155.4 days after one round, 109.9 after 10, 83.3 after 25, 70.1 after 50, 66.2 after 100 and 200, and 66.8 after 300. The error falls fast, levels off, then starts, slowly, to rise. Unlike a random forest, boosting can overfit with too many trees: each new tree fits the residuals harder, and eventually it fits noise. The number of trees is boosting’s main tuning parameter.

title: Boosting
text:
gbm
The gbm package does gradient boosting properly, for many losses (distribution = "bernoulli" for a 0/1 target), with a few refinements: each tree is fitted to a random half of the data (stochastic gradient boosting, bag.fraction = 0.5), and trees are grown to a fixed number of splits (interaction.depth). The model stores every tree, so its prediction after any number of trees is available with predict(..., n.trees = k).
Your turn. Boost 1,500 trees of depth 3 for churn, with a learning rate of 0.02, and find the validation AUC after 10, 50, 100, 200, 400, 600, 1,000 and 1,500 trees.









A 0/1 target is distribution = "bernoulli".


set.seed(8132)
gb <- gbm(churn ~ ., data = train, distribution = "bernoulli", n.trees = 1500, interaction.depth = 3, shrinkage = 0.02)
k <- c(10, 50, 100, 200, 400, 600, 1000, 1500)
round(setNames(sapply(k, function(n) auc(predict(gb, valid, n.trees = n, type = "response"), valid$churn)), k), 4)
0.780 after 10 trees, 0.831 after 100, 0.843 after 400, then a slow decline, to 0.837 after 1,500. Scanning every 25 trees, the best validation AUC is 0.844 at 550 trees: better than the random forest (0.832), and close to the engineered logistic regression (0.853), with no feature engineering at all. In practice, gbm’s cv.folds option can choose the number of trees by cross-validation instead (gbm.perf(gb, method = "cv")); here, the validation set does it.




Your turn. The learning rate and the number of trees trade off. Boost with learning rates of 0.1, 0.02 and 0.005 (3,000 trees each), and find each one’s best number of trees and validation AUC, scanning every 25 trees.









Use the function’s argument: shrinkage = nu.


t(sapply(c(0.1, 0.02, 0.005), function(nu) {
  set.seed(8133)
  g <- gbm(churn ~ ., data = train, distribution = "bernoulli", n.trees = 3000, interaction.depth = 3, shrinkage = nu)
  k <- seq(25, 3000, by = 25)
  a <- sapply(k, function(n) auc(predict(g, valid, n.trees = n, type = "response"), valid$churn))
  c(shrinkage = nu, best_trees = k[which.max(a)], best_auc = max(a))
}))
With a learning rate of 0.1, the best is 75 trees (AUC 0.841); with 0.02, 500 trees (0.844); with 0.005, 1,975 trees (0.844). A smaller learning rate needs proportionally more trees and does a little better, up to a point: slow learning averages more trees and is less sensitive to exactly when you stop. The usual advice: pick the smallest learning rate you can afford the computing time for, then tune the number of trees.




Your turn. The tree depth sets how many inputs can interact within one tree. Compare interaction.depth of 1, 2, 3 and 5.









Use interaction.depth = dp.


k <- c(10, 50, 100, 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000, 1500)
t(sapply(c(1, 2, 3, 5), function(dp) {
  set.seed(8134)
  g <- gbm(churn ~ ., data = train, distribution = "bernoulli", n.trees = 1500, interaction.depth = dp, shrinkage = 0.02)
  a <- sapply(k, function(n) auc(predict(g, valid, n.trees = n, type = "response"), valid$churn))
  c(depth = dp, best_trees = k[which.max(a)], best_auc = max(a))
}))
Depth 1 (stumps, each splitting on a single input) reaches 0.832; depths 2, 3 and 5 reach 0.844, 0.846 and 0.843. A sum of stumps is an additive model, with no interactions, and the churn data have a real one (price by service contract). Depth 2 or 3 is enough to capture it; deeper trees need fewer rounds (200 at depth 5) but don’t do better. Depths of 2 to 8 are typical in practice.

title: Boosting
text:
Explaining a boosted model
A boosted model is hundreds of trees: no one can read it. Three tools explain it:

Relative influence: each input’s share of the total improvement from all the splits on it, the boosting version of Gini importance;
Partial dependence: the average prediction as one input (or two) is set to each value for every account (Lesson 10);
Shapley values: for one prediction, each input’s fair share of the difference between that prediction and the average.

Your turn. Find the relative influence of each input in the 550-tree model.









Use the best number of trees, 550.


set.seed(8132)
gb <- gbm(churn ~ ., data = train, distribution = "bernoulli", n.trees = 1500, interaction.depth = 3, shrinkage = 0.02)
ri <- summary(gb, n.trees = 550, plotit = FALSE)
head(ri, 8)
The late deliveries (24.3%), the price (15.8%), the volume change (14.7%), the account’s age (10.3%) and the segment (9.2%) lead, followed by the satisfaction score, the service contract and the complaints. The same story as every model in this module. Relative influence is computed from the training splits, like the Gini importance, so it shares the bias toward inputs with many split points; a permutation importance on the validation set is the safer check.




Your turn. Compute the boosted model’s partial dependence on the late deliveries, from 0 to 6.









Set the column to v.


set.seed(8132)
gb <- gbm(churn ~ ., data = train, distribution = "bernoulli", n.trees = 1500, interaction.depth = 3, shrinkage = 0.02)
pd <- sapply(0:6, function(v) {
  d <- valid
  d$late_deliveries <- v
  mean(predict(gb, d, n.trees = 550, type = "response"))
})
round(setNames(pd, 0:6), 3)
13.0% with no late deliveries, 13.8% with one, 14.7% with two, then a jump to 46.8% with three, and 51.8% from four on. A clean step at three, exactly as in the data: where Lesson 10’s network drew a smooth S-curve, the boosted trees, built from splits, find the threshold naturally. It’s the strength of tree ensembles on business data, where thresholds (“three strikes”) are common.




Your turn. A two-way partial dependence varies two inputs together. Compute it for the price index (0.95 to 1.08) and the service contract.









Use the training data’s levels: levels(train$tech_service).


set.seed(8132)
gb <- gbm(churn ~ ., data = train, distribution = "bernoulli", n.trees = 1500, interaction.depth = 3, shrinkage = 0.02)
grid <- expand.grid(price_index = c(0.95, 1.00, 1.03, 1.05, 1.08), tech_service = c("no", "yes"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
grid$pd <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) {
  d <- valid
  d$price_index <- grid$price_index[i]
  d$tech_service <- factor(grid$tech_service[i], levels = levels(train$tech_service))
  mean(predict(gb, d, n.trees = 550, type = "response"))
})
xtabs(round(pd, 3) ~ price_index + tech_service, data = grid)
Below a price index of 1.03, the churn probability is about 15% without a service contract and 12% to 15% with one. At 1.05, it jumps to 45% without a contract, but only to 25% with one. The boosted model has found the price-by-service interaction on its own, threshold and all, which Lesson 9 had to build by hand from ctree’s hint. A one-way partial dependence on the price would average the two curves and hide this.





gp <- expand.grid(price_index = seq(0.92, 1.12, by = 0.005), tech_service = c("no", "yes"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
gp$pd <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(gp)), function(i) { d <- valid; d$price_index <- gp$price_index[i]
  d$tech_service <- factor(gp$tech_service[i], levels = levels(train$tech_service)); mean(predict(gb, d, n.trees = 550, type = "response")) })
ggplot(gp, aes(price_index, pd, color = tech_service)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(no = "#C2416C", yes = "#2a78d6"), name = "Service contract") +
  labs(x = "Price index (our price / market price)", y = "Churn probability (partial dependence)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "top")














NoteGo deeper: Shapley values





For a prediction f(x) with inputs 1, \ldots, p, let v(S) be the expected prediction when the inputs in the set S are fixed at x’s values and the others vary as in the data. Lloyd Shapley’s 1953 solution to sharing a payoff fairly among players gives input j the value

\phi_j = \sum_{S \subseteq \{1..p\} \setminus \{j\}} \frac{|S|!\,(p - |S| - 1)!}{p!} \big(v(S \cup \{j\}) - v(S)\big),

its marginal contribution averaged over every order in which inputs could be added. The \phi_j add up exactly to f(x) - E f(X). The sum has 2^{p-1} terms per input, so exact Shapley values are only feasible for a few inputs; the SHAP methods (Lundberg and Lee, 2017) approximate them quickly, and exactly for trees (TreeSHAP). The challenge below computes them exactly for four inputs, on the log-odds scale, with the other inputs held at the account’s values. Molnar’s Interpretable Machine Learning has a clear chapter on them.

title: Boosting
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Why this account? The validation account with the highest predicted churn risk (0.986) is a one-year-old Adhesives account with one late delivery, a 36% volume drop, a price 7.7% above the market, no service contract and a satisfaction score of 4. Compute exact Shapley values, on the log-odds scale, for four of its inputs (late deliveries, volume change, price and service contract), using 200 random validation accounts as the background.









Each term is the contribution of adding j to the set S: v(c(S, j)) - v(S).


set.seed(8132)
gb <- gbm(churn ~ ., data = train, distribution = "bernoulli", n.trees = 1500, interaction.depth = 3, shrinkage = 0.02)
x <- valid[which.max(predict(gb, valid, n.trees = 550, type = "response")), ]
feats <- c("late_deliveries", "volume_change_pct", "price_index", "tech_service")
set.seed(8135)
bg <- valid[sample(nrow(valid), 200), ]
v <- function(S) {
  d <- bg; for (f in S) d[[f]] <- x[[f]]
  mean(predict(gb, d, n.trees = 550))
}
p <- length(feats)
shap <- sapply(feats, function(j) {
  others <- setdiff(feats, j); total <- 0
  for (k in 0:length(others)) {
    subsets <- if (k == 0) list(character(0)) else combn(others, k, simplify = FALSE)
    for (S in subsets) total <- total + factorial(length(S)) * factorial(p - length(S) - 1) / factorial(p) * (v(c(S, j)) - v(S))
  }
  total
})
round(c(shap, sum = sum(shap), check = v(feats) - v(character(0))), 3)
On the log-odds scale, the volume drop contributes +1.87, the high price +1.72 and the missing service contract +0.37, and the single late delivery -0.12 (it’s slightly below the average account’s 1.1). Together, +3.85: exactly the difference between these four inputs fixed at the account’s values and the background average, as Shapley values guarantee. For the engineer visiting this account, that’s a to-do list: the price and the falling volume are the problems, not the deliveries. Shapley values turn a black-box prediction into a reason that can be acted on.




Challenge 2 · The final table. Compare the module’s three strongest models on the test set: the boosted model (550 trees), a random forest (300 trees, Lesson 12’s settings) and Lesson 9’s engineered logistic regression.









Compare with the test target, test$churn.


set.seed(8132)
gb <- gbm(churn ~ ., data = train, distribution = "bernoulli", n.trees = 1500, interaction.depth = 3, shrinkage = 0.02)
fill <- function(d) {
  d$sat_missing <- as.integer(is.na(d$satisfaction)); d$satisfaction[is.na(d$satisfaction)] <- 7
  d$churned <- factor(ifelse(d$churn == 1, "yes", "no"), levels = c("no", "yes")); d$churn <- NULL; d
}
set.seed(8123)
rf <- randomForest(churned ~ ., data = fill(train), ntree = 300)
eng <- function(d) {
  d <- fill(d)
  d$late_grp <- cut(d$late_deliveries, c(-1, 0, 2, Inf), labels = c("0", "1-2", "3+"))
  d$vol_drop <- as.integer(d$volume_change_pct < -15); d$high_price <- as.integer(d$price_index > 1.04)
  d$new_account <- as.integer(d$account_years <= 2); d
}
logit <- glm(churned ~ late_grp + vol_drop + high_price * tech_service + new_account + segment +
               complaints + satisfaction + sat_missing + visits, family = binomial, data = eng(train))
round(c(boosting = auc(predict(gb, test, n.trees = 550, type = "response"), test$churn),
        random_forest = auc(predict(rf, fill(test), type = "prob")[, "yes"], test$churn),
        engineered_logistic = auc(predict(logit, eng(test), type = "response"), test$churn)), 3)
0.850 for boosting, 0.840 for the random forest and 0.865 for the engineered logistic regression. The ensembles are excellent with no feature engineering at all, and they would be the default choice on a new problem. But the logistic regression, with four inputs suggested by the trees, wins here, and it’s the model a sales team can read. The module’s lesson in one line: use trees to find the structure, and choose the final model by what it earns and who has to trust it.

title: Boosting
text:
Quick quiz

1. How does boosting differ from a random forest?

Boosting uses deeper trees
Boosting grows small trees in sequence, each fitted to the current errors, and adds them up; a forest averages independent deep trees
They’re the same


Forests reduce variance; boosting reduces bias, step by step.



2. What does each tree fit in gradient boosting with squared error?

The original target
The residuals of the current model
A bootstrap sample of the target


For other losses, the negative gradient of the loss.



3. Can boosting overfit by adding more trees?

Yes, so the number of trees must be tuned
No, like random forests
Only with a large learning rate


The catalyst model’s test error started rising after about 200 rounds.



4. What happens when you lower the learning rate?

Fewer trees are needed
More trees are needed, and performance is usually a little better
The model can’t learn interactions


0.005 needed about 2,000 trees to 0.1’s 75.



5. What does interaction.depth = 1 give?

The most flexible model
An additive model of stumps, with no interactions
A single tree


It was the weakest depth for churn, which has a real interaction.



6. What do one account’s Shapley values add up to?

1
The difference between its prediction and the average prediction
The model’s AUC


That’s what makes them a fair split of one prediction among the inputs.

title: Boosting
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve finished the module with its most powerful method. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Gradient boosting adds small trees fitted to the residuals, each scaled by a learning rate. By hand, 100 depth-2 trees cut the catalyst test RMSE from 155 to 66 days.
The number of trees must be tuned: the churn model’s validation AUC peaked at 0.844 around 550 trees, then declined.
A smaller learning rate needs more trees and does a little better; depth sets the order of interactions, and depth 1 was the weakest.
Relative influence, partial dependence and Shapley values explain the model: the boosted trees found the step at three late deliveries and the price-by-service interaction, without being told.
The final comparison on the test set: boosting and the random forest close behind the engineered logistic regression, which won because the trees had shown it where to look.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download customer_churn.csv and catalyst_life.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install gbm (and, if you like, xgboost).

Cross-validate the number of trees. Refit the churn model with cv.folds = 5, and use gbm.perf(gb, method = "cv"). Does it agree with the validation set’s choice?
gbm’s partial dependence. plot(gb, i.var = "late_deliveries", n.trees = 550) and plot(gb, i.var = c("price_index", "tech_service"), n.trees = 550) draw what you computed by hand.
XGBoost. Fit the churn model with xgboost::xgboost() on a numeric matrix (use model.matrix()), with eta = 0.02, max_depth = 3 and early stopping on the validation set. Compare its AUC and speed.
SHAP for every account. Install fastshap or treeshap, compute SHAP values for the validation accounts, and plot them for the late deliveries against its value. Where’s the step?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Boosting

Building a strong model as a sum of weak models fitted in sequence, each to the current model’s errors.

Gradient boosting

Boosting in which each new model is fitted to the negative gradient of the loss: the residuals, for squared error.

Learning rate (shrinkage)

The factor \nu by which each new tree is scaled before it’s added.

Stochastic gradient boosting

Fitting each tree to a random subsample of the data (bag.fraction in gbm).

Interaction depth

The number of splits in each tree, which limits the order of interactions the model can represent.

Relative influence

Each input’s share of the total improvement from the splits on it, across all the trees.

Shapley values

Each input’s average marginal contribution to one prediction, over all orders of adding the inputs.











NoteWant to read more?






James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition), section 8.2.3, “Boosting”.
Boehmke and Greenwell, Hands-On Machine Learning with R, chapter 12, “Gradient Boosting”, and chapter 16, “Interpretable Machine Learning”.
Jerome Friedman, “Greedy function approximation: A gradient boosting machine”, Annals of Statistics 29(5), 2001, doi:10.1214/aos/1013203451. The paper that defined gradient boosting.
Scott Lundberg and Su-In Lee, “A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions”, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30, 2017, arXiv:1705.07874. SHAP.

title: Assessing and comparing models
text:
Module 8 · Lesson 11 of 13 Week 129 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Ten lessons have produced a dozen churn models. The AUC has been the yardstick so far, and it’s a good one for comparing rankings. But Lena doesn’t care about the AUC. She cares about what happens when her engineers visit the accounts at the top of the list: how many leavers they reach, and what it’s worth. This lesson measures the models in her terms, with the tools STAT 585 uses: gains and lift charts, and a profit matrix.
The three contenders are the module’s best of each kind: Lesson 9’s engineered logistic regression, Lesson 5’s pruned CART tree (20 leaves), and Lesson 7’s conditional inference tree.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Assessing and comparing models
section: Three models on the validation set
text:
Three models on the validation set
The setup code refits the three models on the training accounts, and puts their validation churn probabilities in the data frame scores, with a column per model. y is TRUE for the validation accounts that churned.












Your turn. Find each model’s validation AUC.









Pass the target, y.


round(sapply(scores, auc, y = y), 3)
0.853 for the engineered logistic regression, 0.767 for the pruned CART tree and 0.792 for ctree, as in earlier lessons. The AUC averages the ranking over the whole list, including its bottom, where nobody will be visited. The next charts look at the part of the list that matters.

title: Assessing and comparing models
text:
Gains and lift
Sort the accounts from the highest score to the lowest. The cumulative gains at depth d is the share of all the leavers found in the top d of the list. The lift of a decile is its churn rate divided by the base rate.
Your turn. Find each model’s cumulative gains at depths of 10%, 20%, 30% and 50%.









Divide by the total number of leavers, sum(y).


gains <- function(p, y, depths = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5)) {
  o <- order(p, decreasing = TRUE)
  found <- cumsum(y[o]) / sum(y)
  setNames(sapply(depths, function(d) found[ceiling(d * length(y))]), paste0(depths * 100, "%"))
}
round(sapply(scores, gains, y = y), 3)
In the top 10% of the list, the logistic regression finds 35.7% of the leavers, CART 28.1% and ctree 29.4%; in the top 20%, 59.7%, 51.1% and 52.0%. Visiting a fifth of the accounts by the logistic regression’s list reaches six leavers in ten; by CART’s, five in ten. A model with no skill would find 10% in the top 10%, 20% in the top 20%, and so on: the diagonal of the gains chart below.





gcurve <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(scores), function(m) { o <- order(scores[[m]], decreasing = TRUE)
  data.frame(depth = seq_along(o) / length(o), found = cumsum(y[o]) / sum(y), model = m) }))
ggplot(gcurve, aes(depth, found, color = model)) + geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(logistic = "#C2416C", cart = "#1baf7a", ctree = "#2a78d6"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Share of accounts visited (highest scores first)", y = "Share of leavers found") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "top")








Your turn. Find the lift in each decile for each model.









Divide by the base rate, mean(y).


lift <- function(p, y) {
  o <- order(p, decreasing = TRUE)
  decile <- ceiling(seq_along(o) / length(o) * 10)
  tapply(y[o], decile, mean) / mean(y)
}
round(sapply(scores, lift, y = y), 2)
The logistic regression’s top decile has a lift of 3.57: its accounts are 3.6 times as likely to leave as average. Its lift then falls steadily, to 0.09 in the bottom decile, the shape of a good ranking. The trees’ lifts are lower at the top (2.81 and 2.94) and bumpy lower down: CART’s bottom decile has a lift of 0.86, because a tree gives whole leaves the same score, and ties at the bottom are broken arbitrarily.

title: Assessing and comparing models
text:
Comparing in euros
Finance has estimated the economics of a visit. A visit costs about €500 of an engineer’s time. A customer who would have left and is kept is worth €15,000 a year in margin. And a visit to an account that was going to leave keeps it about 40% of the time. That’s a profit matrix:




the account would leave
the account would stay




visit
0.4 \times 15{,}000 - 500 = 5{,}500
-500


don’t visit
0
0



(The “don’t visit” row is 0 because profits are measured against doing nothing.) Lena has 15 engineers who can each make 10 visits before the renewal round: 150 visits for the validation set’s 1,030 accounts.
Your turn. For each model, find the profit of visiting the 150 accounts it ranks highest.









Each of the n_visits visits costs 500.


value <- function(p, y, n_visits) {
  top <- order(p, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(n_visits)]
  sum(y[top]) * (0.4 * 15000) - 500 * n_visits
}
sapply(scores, value, y = y, n_visits = 150)
€543,000 with the logistic regression’s list, €441,000 with CART’s and €459,000 with ctree’s. The difference between the best model and the best tree is €84,000 on 1,030 accounts, in one renewal round, from a better ranking of the same accounts. That’s a number Lena can weigh against the extra effort of maintaining a regression with engineered inputs, which an AUC difference of 0.06 isn’t.

title: Assessing and comparing models
text:
How many visits?
Without the capacity limit, the question becomes: which accounts are worth a visit at all? The expected value of visiting an account with churn probability p is

p \times 5{,}500 + (1 - p) \times (-500) = 6{,}000\,p - 500,

which is positive when p > 500/6{,}000 = 0.083.
Your turn. Compute the break-even probability, and the expected value of a visit at churn probabilities of 0.05, 0.2 and 0.5.









If the account would stay, the visit loses loss_stay.


gain_leave <- 0.4 * 15000 - 500
loss_stay <- -500
ev <- function(p) p * gain_leave + (1 - p) * loss_stay
c(break_even = -loss_stay / (gain_leave - loss_stay), ev_0.05 = ev(0.05), ev_0.2 = ev(0.2), ev_0.5 = ev(0.5))
A break-even of 0.083: an account with a 1-in-12 chance of leaving is worth a visit. At 5%, a visit loses €200 on average; at 20%, it earns €700; at 50%, €2,500. Because a kept customer is worth so much more than a visit costs, the break-even is low, and many accounts qualify. The calculation is only as good as the probabilities, which is why Lesson 9 checked the model’s calibration.




Your turn. For each model, compute the profit of visiting the top n accounts, for n from 0 to 1,030 in steps of 10, and find the best n and its profit.









Use the inner function’s argument: n.


value <- function(p, y, n_visits) {
  top <- order(p, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(n_visits)]
  sum(y[top]) * 6000 - 500 * n_visits
}
ns <- seq(0, 1030, by = 10)
prof <- sapply(scores, function(p) sapply(ns, function(n) value(p, y, n)))
rbind(best_n = ns[apply(prof, 2, which.max)], best_profit = apply(prof, 2, max), visit_all = prof[nrow(prof), ])
The logistic regression’s best is to visit 680 accounts, for €926,000; ctree’s, 650 accounts for €857,000. CART’s profit keeps rising to the end: its best is to visit everyone, for €811,000, because its bottom leaves still hold leavers. With this generous profit matrix, even a mediocre model says “visit most accounts”, and the good model’s advantage is that it knows which third to skip: €115,000 more than visiting everyone.





ns <- seq(0, 1030, by = 10)
pc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(scores), function(m) { o <- order(scores[[m]], decreasing = TRUE)
  data.frame(n = ns, profit = sapply(ns, function(k) sum(y[o[seq_len(k)]]) * 6000 - 500 * k), model = m) }))
ggplot(pc, aes(n, profit / 1000, color = model)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 150, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(logistic = "#C2416C", cart = "#1baf7a", ctree = "#2a78d6"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Accounts visited (highest scores first)", y = "Profit (thousand €)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "top")








Your turn. In practice, the rule is a cut-off on the probability rather than a number of visits. Find the cut-off from 0.02 to 0.60 that maximizes the logistic regression’s validation profit, and compare it with the theoretical break-even, 0.083.









The theoretical cut-off is 500 / 6000.


profit_at <- function(p, y, t) { visit <- p >= t; sum(y[visit]) * 6000 - 500 * sum(visit) }
ts <- seq(0.02, 0.60, by = 0.01)
pr <- sapply(ts, function(t) profit_at(scores$logistic, y, t))
c(best_cutoff = ts[which.max(pr)], best_profit = max(pr),
  theory_profit = profit_at(scores$logistic, y, 500 / 6000), theory_visits = sum(scores$logistic >= 500 / 6000))
The best validation cut-off is 0.06, for €922,500; the theoretical 0.083 gives €913,500, with 501 visits. Within 1%. The empirical optimum is a little lower than theory because the model’s probabilities are a little low on this validation set (Lesson 9). Use the theoretical cut-off, which depends only on the costs, unless the model’s calibration is known to be off; the empirical one is tuned to one set of accounts’ luck.

title: Assessing and comparing models
text:
The test set, once
The model (the engineered logistic regression) and the rule (visit when \hat p \ge 0.083) are chosen. Now, and only now, the test set gives the honest estimate.
Your turn. Score the 1,008 test accounts, and find the test AUC, the number of visits, the leavers reached, and the profit, against visiting everyone.









Visiting everyone costs 500 for each of the length(y_test) accounts.


p_test <- predict(logit, prep(raw_test), type = "response")
y_test <- raw_test$churned == "yes"
visit <- p_test >= 500 / 6000
c(test_auc = auc(p_test, y_test), visits = sum(visit), leavers_reached = sum(y_test[visit]), leavers = sum(y_test),
  profit = sum(y_test[visit]) * 6000 - 500 * sum(visit), visit_everyone = sum(y_test) * 6000 - 500 * length(y_test))
A test AUC of 0.865, a little above the validation estimate (0.853): the model generalizes. The rule visits 482 of 1,008 accounts, reaches 185 of the 204 leavers, and earns €869,000, against €720,000 for visiting everyone and nothing for visiting no one. That’s the number for Lena’s report: about €149,000 per 1,000 accounts better than the blanket policy, and almost €870,000 better than doing nothing, per renewal round.










NoteGo deeper: what a profit matrix assumes





The calculation assumes that a visit’s effect is the same for every leaver (a 40% save rate), that visits don’t change the behavior of customers who would have stayed, and that the model’s probabilities are calibrated. The first two are strong: a visit may save a customer annoyed by late deliveries far more easily than one leaving because of a competitor’s price. Estimating who responds to a visit, rather than who will leave, is uplift modeling, and it needs data from a randomized trial: visited and unvisited accounts with similar scores. Without it, a churn model can send engineers to customers who will leave whatever anyone does. Gutierrez and Gérardy’s “Causal Inference and Uplift Modeling: A Review of the Literature” (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 67, 2017) is an accessible start.

title: Assessing and comparing models
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · A lower save rate. Suppose a visit saves only 20% of the leavers. Find the new break-even probability, and the logistic regression’s validation profit and number of visits at it.









Break even when p \times 3{,}000 = 500: divide by gain.


gain <- 0.2 * 15000
t20 <- 500 / gain
visit <- scores$logistic >= t20
c(cutoff = t20, visits = sum(visit), profit = sum(y[visit]) * gain - 500 * sum(visit))
The break-even doubles, to 1/6 = 0.167, the rule visits 358 accounts instead of 501, and the validation profit falls to €331,000, about a third of the 40% case. When visits work less well, fewer accounts are worth one, and the model’s ranking matters more, because the margin for error at the top of the list is smaller. The save rate is the most uncertain number in the profit matrix, so a report should show how the decision changes with it.




Challenge 2 · Did the ranking hold? Find the test AUCs of the pruned CART tree and ctree too. (Strictly, this is a second look at the test set; it’s fine after the choice is made, as a report, not as a reason to change the choice.)









Compare with y_test.


set.seed(8072)
ct2 <- ctree(churned ~ ., data = raw_train)
p_ct_test <- predict(ct2, raw_test, type = "prob")[, "yes"]
y_test <- raw_test$churned == "yes"
round(c(logistic = auc(predict(logit, prep(raw_test), type = "response"), y_test),
        cart = auc(predict(cart, raw_test)[, "yes"], y_test), ctree = auc(p_ct_test, y_test)), 3)
0.865 for the logistic regression, 0.783 for CART and 0.794 for ctree: the same order as on the validation set, and the same gaps. The choice holds up. If the order had changed, the right response would be to report it, and to wonder whether the validation comparison was luck, not to switch models on the strength of the test set.

title: Assessing and comparing models
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does the cumulative gains at 20% measure?

The churn rate of the top 20%
The share of all the leavers found in the top 20% of the list
The model’s accuracy


The logistic regression found 60% of the leavers in its top 20%.



2. A decile’s lift is 3.6. What does that mean?

Its accounts churn at 3.6 times the overall rate
It contains 3.6% of the leavers
The model is 3.6 times more accurate


Lift is a rate relative to the base rate.



3. A visit costs €500 and saves 40% of leavers worth €15,000. Above what churn probability is a visit worth it?

0.5
About 0.083
0.033


6{,}000p - 500 > 0 when p > 1/12.



4. Why compare models at a fixed number of visits (150)?

It’s required by the AUC
It’s the business’s real constraint, and it turns ranking quality into euros
It removes the need for a test set


The best model earned €84,000 more than the best tree at 150 visits.



5. Why use the theoretical cut-off rather than the one that maximized validation profit?

The theoretical one is always higher
It depends only on the costs; the empirical one is partly tuned to one set of accounts’ luck
The empirical one can’t be computed


Here they were within 1% of each other.



6. When should the test set be used?

To choose between the models
To tune the cut-off
Once, after the model and the rule are chosen, for an honest estimate


Changing the choice after looking makes the test set part of the tuning.

title: Assessing and comparing models
text:
Wrap-up
You can now compare models the way a business decides. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Gains and lift show the top of the list: the logistic regression found 60% of the leavers in its top 20%, with a top-decile lift of 3.57; the trees found about 51%.
Under a capacity limit of 150 visits, the logistic regression’s list was worth €543,000, against €441,000 and €459,000 for the trees.
A profit matrix gives the value of a visit, 6{,}000p - 500, and a break-even probability of 0.083.
The profit curve peaked at 680 visits (€926,000); the profit-maximizing cut-off (0.06) and the theoretical one (0.083) were within 1%.
On the test set, once: AUC 0.865, 482 visits reaching 185 of 204 leavers, and €869,000, against €720,000 for visiting everyone.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download customer_churn.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

ROC curves. Install pROC and draw the three models’ validation ROC curves on one plot. Test whether the logistic regression’s AUC is significantly better than ctree’s with pROC::roc.test().
A bootstrap interval for the profit. Resample the test accounts 1,000 times and recompute the profit of the chosen rule. What’s a 95% interval for the €869,000?
Sensitivity analysis. Recompute the best number of visits for save rates from 10% to 60% and margins from €5,000 to €25,000. When does the model stop being worth using?
Add the boosted C5.0 model from Lesson 7 to the gains chart and the 150-visit comparison.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Cumulative gains

The share of all positive cases found in the top d of a list sorted by score.

Lift

The positive rate in a part of the list divided by the overall rate.

Gains chart

Cumulative gains plotted against the depth of the list, with the diagonal for random selection.

Profit matrix

The profit or cost of each combination of decision and outcome.

Break-even probability

The predicted probability above which an action has a positive expected profit.

Profit curve

The total profit of acting on the top n cases, plotted against n.

Uplift modeling

Predicting the effect of an action on each case, rather than the outcome itself.











NoteWant to read more?






Provost and Fawcett, Data Science for Business (O’Reilly, 2013), chapters 7 and 8, “Decision Analytic Thinking” and “Visualizing Model Performance”, on expected value, profit curves and lift.
Linoff and Berry, Data Mining Techniques (3rd edition, Wiley, 2011), chapter 5, on lift and gains charts and choosing a cut-off, from STAT 585’s tradition.
Boehmke and Greenwell, Hands-On Machine Learning with R, section 2.6, “Model evaluation”.

title: Logistic regression for prediction
text:
Module 8 · Lesson 9 of 13 Week 127 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Trees are easy to read, but a single tree is a coarse predictor: Lesson 7’s best, the conditional inference tree, reached a validation AUC of 0.792. Logistic regression is the other workhorse of business analytics, especially in credit scoring and marketing, where regulators and managers want a model whose every coefficient can be explained. Its weakness is the opposite of a tree’s: it assumes each input has a straight-line effect on the log-odds, with no thresholds and no interactions unless you add them.
So the two work well together. The trees of Lessons 2 to 7 found the structure in the churn data: three or more late deliveries, a volume drop past 15%, accounts under three years old, and a price above the market that matters mainly without a service contract. This lesson builds those findings into a logistic regression, and shows what they’re worth.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Logistic regression for prediction
text:
A first model
Logistic regression can’t handle missing values, so the setup code’s prep() function fills the missing satisfaction scores with 7 and adds an indicator sat_missing (1 when the score was missing), following Lesson 8. It also drops the sales reps. It makes Lesson 1’s partition, prepares the training and validation sets, and defines auc() and a shortcut, vauc(), for a model’s validation AUC.












Your turn. Fit a logistic regression with every input, and find its number of coefficients and its training and validation AUCs.









Logistic regression is family = binomial.


m0 <- glm(churned ~ ., family = binomial, data = train)
c(n_coef = length(coef(m0)), train = auc(fitted(m0), train$churned), valid = vauc(m0))
23 coefficients, a training AUC of 0.807 and a validation AUC of 0.787. Already about as good as the best single tree (0.792), with every effect a straight line on the log-odds scale. glm models the probability of the second level of the response, “yes”, which is what we want here.

title: Logistic regression for prediction
text:
Selecting inputs
Business models are often trimmed to the inputs that earn their place. Stepwise selection by AIC (Module 2) drops inputs one at a time while the AIC improves.
Your turn. Run backward stepwise selection from the full model, and list the inputs it keeps and the validation AUC.









trace = 0 keeps step() quiet.


m0 <- glm(churned ~ ., family = binomial, data = train)
ms <- step(m0, trace = 0)
print(attr(terms(ms), "term.labels"))
vauc(ms)
It keeps 10 of the 13 inputs, dropping the region, the volume and the payment terms, which the trees never used either, and the validation AUC stays at 0.787. Stepwise selection here simplifies without losing anything. It can’t add what isn’t in the candidate list, though: no thresholds and no interactions. That’s the next step’s job.

title: Logistic regression for prediction
text:
Inputs the trees suggested
Each tree in this module split the late deliveries at three, and CHAID grouped them into 0, 1 to 2, and 3 or more. Every tree also split the volume change near -15\%. Binning an input at a threshold, or adding a flag for it, lets the logistic regression model a step where a straight line can’t.
Your turn. Replace the late deliveries by CHAID’s three groups, and add a flag for a volume drop of more than 15%. Fit the model with these and the inputs stepwise selection kept, and find its validation AUC.









The last group is open-ended: Inf.


add_bins <- function(d) {
  d$late_grp <- cut(d$late_deliveries, breaks = c(-1, 0, 2, Inf), labels = c("0", "1-2", "3+"))
  d$vol_drop <- as.integer(d$volume_change_pct < -15)
  d
}
tr <- add_bins(train); vl <- add_bins(valid)
m1 <- glm(churned ~ late_grp + vol_drop + price_index + tech_service + account_years + segment +
            complaints + satisfaction + sat_missing + visits, family = binomial, data = tr)
vauc(m1, vl)
0.816, up from 0.787, from two transformations. A straight line in the number of late deliveries says each one adds the same risk; the data say that the first two hardly matter and the third is a tipping point. The groups capture that. cut(..., breaks = c(-1, 0, 2, Inf)) makes the intervals (-1, 0], (0, 2] and (2, \infty).




Your turn. ctree found that a price above about 1.04 times the market matters mainly for accounts without a technical service contract. Add a high-price flag and its interaction with the service contract.









a * b fits both main effects and their interaction.


add_more <- function(d) {
  d$late_grp <- cut(d$late_deliveries, breaks = c(-1, 0, 2, Inf), labels = c("0", "1-2", "3+"))
  d$vol_drop <- as.integer(d$volume_change_pct < -15)
  d$high_price <- as.integer(d$price_index > 1.04)
  d
}
tr <- add_more(train); vl <- add_more(valid)
m2 <- glm(churned ~ late_grp + vol_drop + high_price * tech_service + account_years + segment +
            complaints + satisfaction + sat_missing + visits, family = binomial, data = tr)
print(round(coef(m2)[c("high_price", "tech_serviceyes", "high_price:tech_serviceyes")], 3))
vauc(m2, vl)
The validation AUC jumps to 0.843. A high price raises the log-odds by 2.27 for an account without a service contract (odds times 9.7), but only by 2.27 - 1.49 = 0.78 for one with a contract (odds times 2.2). For Lena, that’s a pricing insight: price increases above the market are dangerous mainly where there’s no technical relationship to hold the customer. The tree found it; the regression measures it.




Your turn. Every tree split the account’s age near 2.5 years. Replace account_years with a flag for accounts of two years or less, and find the validation and training AUCs.









Two years or less: <= 2.


engineer <- function(d) {
  d$late_grp <- cut(d$late_deliveries, breaks = c(-1, 0, 2, Inf), labels = c("0", "1-2", "3+"))
  d$vol_drop <- as.integer(d$volume_change_pct < -15)
  d$high_price <- as.integer(d$price_index > 1.04)
  d$new_account <- as.integer(d$account_years <= 2)
  d
}
tr <- engineer(train); vl <- engineer(valid)
m3 <- glm(churned ~ late_grp + vol_drop + high_price * tech_service + new_account + segment +
            complaints + satisfaction + sat_missing + visits, family = binomial, data = tr)
c(train = auc(fitted(m3), tr$churned), valid = vauc(m3, vl))
A validation AUC of 0.853, with a training AUC of 0.879: the gap is small, so the engineered model isn’t overfitting. From 0.787 to 0.853 with four engineered inputs, and well past every tree. On these data, the structure is a few thresholds and one interaction, which is exactly what a logistic regression with the right inputs can represent, and a tree only approximates with its coarse leaves.

title: Logistic regression for prediction
text:
Scoring and scorecards
Scoring means applying the fitted model to new accounts: the same preparation, the same engineered inputs, then predict().
Your turn. Score an account in Coatings with three or more late deliveries, a volume drop of more than 15%, a price above 1.04, no service contract, three years as a customer, one complaint, a satisfaction score of 6 and four visits.









type = "response" gives the probability.


engineer <- function(d) {
  d$late_grp <- cut(d$late_deliveries, breaks = c(-1, 0, 2, Inf), labels = c("0", "1-2", "3+"))
  d$vol_drop <- as.integer(d$volume_change_pct < -15)
  d$high_price <- as.integer(d$price_index > 1.04)
  d$new_account <- as.integer(d$account_years <= 2)
  d
}
m3 <- glm(churned ~ late_grp + vol_drop + high_price * tech_service + new_account + segment +
            complaints + satisfaction + sat_missing + visits, family = binomial, data = engineer(train))
new <- data.frame(late_deliveries = 3, volume_change_pct = -20, price_index = 1.06,
                  tech_service = factor("no", levels = c("no", "yes")), account_years = 3,
                  segment = factor("Coatings", levels = levels(train$segment)), complaints = 1,
                  satisfaction = 6, sat_missing = 0, visits = 4)
predict(m3, engineer(new), type = "response")
A churn probability of 0.985: three warning signs at once (late deliveries, falling volume, a high price without a service contract), each multiplying the odds. A deployed model is exactly this: a preparation function and a fitted model, applied every month to every account. The factor levels of new data must match the training data’s, which is why segment is built with levels = levels(train$segment).




In credit scoring, logistic regressions are traditionally deployed as scorecards: each input value earns a number of points, and the points add up to a score. The usual scaling makes every 20 points double the odds (“points to double the odds”, PDO = 20), so each coefficient \beta becomes \beta \times 20/\ln 2 points.
Your turn. Convert the engineered model’s coefficients to scorecard points.









Doubling the odds: log(2).


m3 <- glm(churned ~ late_grp + vol_drop + high_price * tech_service + new_account + segment +
            complaints + satisfaction + sat_missing + visits, family = binomial,
          data = within(train, {
            late_grp <- cut(late_deliveries, c(-1, 0, 2, Inf), labels = c("0", "1-2", "3+"))
            vol_drop <- as.integer(volume_change_pct < -15)
            high_price <- as.integer(price_index > 1.04)
            new_account <- as.integer(account_years <= 2)
          }))
points <- round(coef(m3) * 20 / log(2), 1)
points[c("late_grp3+", "vol_drop", "high_price", "high_price:tech_serviceyes", "new_account", "segmentPharma")]
Three or more late deliveries: 76.8 points; a volume drop: 61.7; a high price: 70.0, minus 48.9 if there’s a service contract; a new account: 45.6; being in Pharma: minus 29.8. A sales manager can compute a score with a pencil, and see that fixing deliveries removes almost 77 points. Scorecards are logistic regressions in a form that people trust and can audit, which is why they still dominate credit decisions. (Credit scorecards usually count points against risk, so the signs are flipped there.)




Your turn. Check the engineered model’s calibration: split the validation accounts into five groups by predicted probability, and compare each group’s average prediction with its churn rate.









The observed rate is the share with churned == "yes".


engineer <- function(d) {
  d$late_grp <- cut(d$late_deliveries, breaks = c(-1, 0, 2, Inf), labels = c("0", "1-2", "3+"))
  d$vol_drop <- as.integer(d$volume_change_pct < -15)
  d$high_price <- as.integer(d$price_index > 1.04)
  d$new_account <- as.integer(d$account_years <= 2)
  d
}
m3 <- glm(churned ~ late_grp + vol_drop + high_price * tech_service + new_account + segment +
            complaints + satisfaction + sat_missing + visits, family = binomial, data = engineer(train))
p <- predict(m3, engineer(valid), type = "response")
g <- cut(p, breaks = quantile(p, probs = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2)), include.lowest = TRUE)
round(cbind(predicted = tapply(p, g, mean), observed = tapply(valid$churned == "yes", g, mean)), 3)
From 1.5% predicted and 2.9% observed in the lowest fifth, to 59.4% predicted and 64.1% observed in the highest. The model is a little low in every group, by about 2 to 5 points, because the validation set happens to have more churners (21.5%) than the training set (19.8%). The ranking is excellent and the probabilities are close: good enough for Lesson 11’s profit calculations, and a reminder to recheck calibration when the model runs on a new year’s data.










NoteGo deeper: weight of evidence and information value





Credit scoring has its own tradition for binning inputs. Each bin of an input gets its weight of evidence, \text{WoE} = \ln\big(\%\text{goods in the bin} / \%\text{bads in the bin}\big), which is the bin’s log-odds relative to the whole population, and the input’s information value, \sum (\%\text{goods} - \%\text{bads}) \times \text{WoE}, ranks inputs by predictive power (below 0.02 useless, above 0.3 strong, by the usual rules of thumb). Replacing each input by its WoE makes every input’s effect monotone and linear on the log-odds scale, which is exactly what logistic regression wants. It’s a cousin of Lesson 8’s target encoding, on the log-odds scale, and it carries the same leakage risk if computed on the data used to fit. Naeem Siddiqi’s Intelligent Credit Scoring (2nd edition, Wiley, 2017) is the practitioner’s guide. The R package scorecard implements it.

title: Logistic regression for prediction
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Against the trees. Compare the engineered logistic regression’s validation AUC with Lesson 5’s pruned CART tree (20 leaves) and Lesson 7’s conditional inference tree.









The engineered model needs the engineered validation data, vl.


raw_train <- churn[part == "train", ]; raw_valid <- churn[part == "valid", ]
set.seed(8051)
big <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = raw_train, method = "class", cp = 0)
pruned <- prune(big, cp = big$cptable[which.min(big$cptable[, "xerror"]), "CP"])
set.seed(8072)
ct <- ctree(churned ~ ., data = raw_train)
p_ct <- predict(ct, raw_valid, type = "prob")[, "yes"]
tr <- within(train, { late_grp <- cut(late_deliveries, c(-1, 0, 2, Inf), labels = c("0", "1-2", "3+"));
  vol_drop <- as.integer(volume_change_pct < -15); high_price <- as.integer(price_index > 1.04); new_account <- as.integer(account_years <= 2) })
vl <- within(valid, { late_grp <- cut(late_deliveries, c(-1, 0, 2, Inf), labels = c("0", "1-2", "3+"));
  vol_drop <- as.integer(volume_change_pct < -15); high_price <- as.integer(price_index > 1.04); new_account <- as.integer(account_years <= 2) })
m3 <- glm(churned ~ late_grp + vol_drop + high_price * tech_service + new_account + segment +
            complaints + satisfaction + sat_missing + visits, family = binomial, data = tr)
round(c(pruned_cart = auc(predict(pruned, raw_valid)[, "yes"], raw_valid$churned),
        ctree = auc(p_ct, raw_valid$churned), engineered_logistic = vauc(m3, vl)), 3)
0.767 for the pruned tree, 0.792 for ctree and 0.853 for the engineered logistic regression. The regression wins by six points, but it’s standing on the trees’ shoulders: every engineered input came from a tree’s split. A good workflow uses both: trees to explore, a well-specified regression (or an ensemble, Lessons 12 and 13) to predict.




Challenge 2 · Interactions by brute force. Instead of choosing interactions from the trees, add every pairwise interaction among nine numeric and binary inputs. Count the coefficients, and compare the training and validation AUCs.









(a + b + ...)^2 gives every main effect and every pairwise interaction.


m4 <- glm(churned ~ (late_deliveries + volume_change_pct + price_index + tech_service + account_years +
                       complaints + satisfaction + visits + volume_t)^2, family = binomial, data = train)
c(n_coef = length(coef(m4)), train = auc(fitted(m4), train$churned), valid = vauc(m4))
46 coefficients, a training AUC of 0.827 and a validation AUC of 0.785, no better than the main-effects model (0.787), and far below the engineered one (0.853). The 36 interactions include the one that matters, but they’re all straight lines in the raw inputs, so none of them is a threshold, and most are noise. Knowing which structure to add is worth more than adding everything.

title: Logistic regression for prediction
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does a logistic regression assume about each numeric input, unless you transform it?

Nothing
A straight-line effect on the log-odds
A threshold


Bins, flags and splines let it model other shapes.



2. What did grouping the late deliveries into 0, 1 to 2, and 3 or more do?

Nothing
Let the model capture the tipping point at three, raising the validation AUC
Removed an input


From 0.787 to 0.816, with the volume-drop flag.



3. A high price raised the log-odds by 2.27 without a service contract and by 0.78 with one. What’s that?

Two main effects
An interaction between price and the service contract
Multicollinearity


The interaction coefficient was -1.49.



4. In a scorecard with 20 points to double the odds, how many points is a coefficient of 0.693?

0.693
13.9
20


0.693 \times 20/\ln 2 = 20: a coefficient of \ln 2 doubles the odds.



5. Why build new data’s factors with the training data’s levels?

So the model’s coding of the categories matches, and predict() works
To make them alphabetical
It isn’t necessary


A new data frame with only one level would otherwise code it differently.



6. Adding every pairwise interaction gave a validation AUC no better than main effects. Why?

Interactions never help
They were straight-line interactions of raw inputs, mostly noise, and none modeled a threshold
There were too few accounts for logistic regression


The one useful interaction, built from tree thresholds, was worth six points of AUC.

title: Logistic regression for prediction
text:
Wrap-up
You can now build a logistic regression that predicts as well as anything. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Main effects with every input: a validation AUC of 0.787, already level with the best single tree. Stepwise AIC kept 10 inputs at the same AUC.
Engineering from the trees: grouped late deliveries and a volume-drop flag (0.816), a high-price-by-service interaction (0.843), and a new-account flag (0.853).
Interpretation: a high price multiplies the odds by 9.7 without a service contract, by 2.2 with one.
Scoring applies the same preparation to new accounts; a scorecard turns coefficients into points (76.8 for three or more late deliveries).
Calibration was close, a few points low throughout, because the validation year had more churn.
Trees to explore, regression to predict: the engineered model beat the best tree by six points, and brute-force interactions didn’t help.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download customer_churn.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Splines instead of bins. Replace the bins and flags with natural splines (splines::ns(late_deliveries, 3) and so on, Module 7). Does the AUC match the engineered model? Which is easier to explain?
A lasso version. Fit the engineered model with glmnet and cv.glmnet(..., family = "binomial", type.measure = "auc"). Which terms does the lasso drop?
Write the scorecard. Make a one-page table of points for every input value, and a few example accounts with their total scores.
Weight of evidence. Install the scorecard package, and use woebin() to bin the inputs. Compare its bins with the trees’ thresholds.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Binning

Replacing a numeric input by groups of its values, so that the model can fit a step-shaped effect.

Indicator (flag)

A 0/1 input marking whether a condition holds, such as a volume drop of more than 15%.

Feature engineering

Building new inputs from the raw ones to capture structure the model can’t find on its own.

Stepwise selection

Adding or removing inputs one at a time to improve a criterion such as AIC.

Scoring

Applying a fitted model to new cases to get their predictions.

Scorecard

A logistic regression written as points for each input value, which add up to a score.

Points to double the odds (PDO)

The scorecard scaling: the number of points that corresponds to doubling the odds.











NoteWant to read more?






Boehmke and Greenwell, Hands-On Machine Learning with R, chapter 5, “Logistic Regression”.
Frank Harrell, Regression Modeling Strategies (2nd edition, Springer, 2015), chapters 2 and 4, on choosing and transforming predictors, and on the dangers of stepwise selection.
Naeem Siddiqi, Intelligent Credit Scoring: Building and Implementing Better Credit Risk Scorecards (2nd edition, Wiley, 2017). The practitioner’s book on scorecards, binning and weight of evidence, useful for this module’s project.

title: Conditional inference trees and C5.0
text:
Module 8 · Lesson 7 of 13 Week 125 of 160 About 5–7 hours
CART and CHAID aren’t the only tree algorithms. This lesson covers the two others you’re most likely to meet: conditional inference trees (ctree), from statistics, which fix a bias in CART, and C5.0, from machine learning, the last of a line of algorithms (ID3, C4.5, C5.0) by the computer scientist Ross Quinlan.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Conditional inference trees and C5.0
text:
CART’s selection bias
