CART tries every split of every input and picks the best. An input with many ways to split has many chances to look good by luck. A numeric input with 300 distinct values has 299 candidate thresholds; a 20-level factor has 2^{19} - 1 = 524{,}287 possible groupings.
The setup code makes Lesson 1’s partition, and defines auc().











Your turn. Simulate 200 datasets in which the target is pure noise and there are three inputs, all noise too: a numeric one, a binary one and a 20-level factor. Grow a one-split CART tree on each, and count how often each input is chosen.









One split: maxdepth = 1.


set.seed(8071)
pick <- replicate(200, {
  d <- data.frame(y = factor(sample(c("a", "b"), 300, replace = TRUE)),
                  x_num = rnorm(300),
                  x_bin = factor(sample(c("u", "v"), 300, replace = TRUE)),
                  x_cat = factor(sample(LETTERS[1:20], 300, replace = TRUE)))
  fit <- rpart(y ~ ., data = d, control = rpart.control(cp = 0, maxdepth = 1, minbucket = 5))
  if (nrow(fit$frame) > 1) as.character(fit$frame$var[1]) else "none"
})
table(pick)
The 20-level factor is chosen 191 times out of 200, the numeric input 5 times, and the binary input never (4 trees didn’t split at all). All three are equally useless; a fair method would pick each about a third of the time. In real data, that means a high-cardinality input, like a customer’s postcode or the sales rep, gets into the tree, and high up, whether it matters or not. That’s variable selection bias.




Your turn. Count the candidate binary splits of each input in one such dataset.









A factor with k levels has 2^{k-1} - 1 binary splits.


set.seed(8071)
x_num <- rnorm(300)
c(numeric = length(unique(x_num)) - 1, binary = 2^(2 - 1) - 1, factor_20 = 2^(20 - 1) - 1)
299, 1 and 524,287. (CART’s ordering trick checks only 19 of the factor’s splits, but they’re the 19 best of all 524,287, so the factor gets the benefit of the whole search.) The binary input has one chance; the factor, half a million. The impurity decrease of the best split grows with the number of chances, so the comparison between inputs isn’t fair.




Your turn. Grow a default CART tree on the churn data with the 60 sales reps, and look at its variable importance and validation AUC.









Compare with the validation target, valid$churned.


cart_rep <- rpart(churned ~ ., data = train, method = "class")
print(round(cart_rep$variable.importance, 1))
auc(predict(cart_rep, valid)[, "yes"], valid$churned)
The sales rep is now the second most important input (64.6), ahead of the volume change and the price, and the validation AUC is 0.743. Three of the 60 reps really do lose customers, so there’s some signal, but CART’s importance is wildly inflated by the search: a grouping of 60 reps into “good” and “bad” can always be found that fits the training data well, and most of it is noise. Lesson 8 shows a better way to use an input like this.

title: Conditional inference trees and C5.0
text:
Conditional inference trees
Torsten Hothorn, Kurt Hornik and Achim Zeileis’s conditional inference trees (2006) separate the two questions CART answers at once:

Which input? At each node, test the association between each input and the target with a permutation test, which gives a p-value that’s comparable across inputs of every type and number of levels. Adjust the p-values for the number of inputs (Bonferroni, by default). Pick the input with the smallest adjusted p-value.
Where to split it? Only then, for the chosen input, find the best binary split.

If no input’s adjusted p-value is below the threshold (by default, $1 - $ mincriterion = 0.05), the node isn’t split. Like CHAID, it stops by significance and doesn’t prune. On the same 200 noise datasets, a ctree forced to split at the root picks the numeric input 71 times, the binary one 69 times and the 20-level factor 60 times: about equally often, as a fair method should. With its default threshold, it splits only 8 of the 200 datasets at all (4%, close to the 5% a 0.05 test should give), which is the right answer for noise.
Your turn. Grow a conditional inference tree on the churn data, with all the inputs, sales reps included. Count its leaves, and find its validation AUC.









The churn probability is the "yes" column.


set.seed(8072)
ct <- ctree(churned ~ ., data = train)
print(ct)
c(leaves = length(nodeids(ct, terminal = TRUE)),
  auc = auc(predict(ct, valid, type = "prob")[, "yes"], valid$churned))
14 leaves, a validation AUC of 0.792, the best single tree so far, and no sales reps anywhere in it. The tree also found something CART missed: under the late-delivery split, it splits on the price index, then, for accounts priced above the market, on the technical service contract, which is the interaction built into the data. It uses the satisfaction score several times, and it splits once on the payment terms, deep in the tree, which is probably noise: a significance test at 5% will pass a useless split now and then. The set.seed() matters here for two reasons. For some inputs, ctree computes its p-values with a randomized algorithm; and by default ctree has no surrogate splits, so an account whose satisfaction score is missing is sent down a random branch when it’s predicted. (ctree_control(maxsurrogate = 3) turns surrogates on, but ctree can’t search surrogate splits on a factor with 31 or more levels, like the sales reps.) That’s why the exercises predict right after fitting, with nothing random in between.




Your turn. Look at the permutation tests at the root: each input’s test statistic and p-value.









The test results are in the node’s criterion element.


set.seed(8072)
ct <- ctree(churned ~ ., data = train)
crit <- info_node(node_party(ct))$criterion
signif(sort(crit["p.value", ]), 3)
The late deliveries are by far the most significant (p = 8 \times 10^{-43}), then the satisfaction, the complaints, the price index and the volume change. The sales rep’s p-value is 1: tested fairly, as one input with 59 degrees of freedom, its association with churn is no stronger than chance would give. (These p-values are already Bonferroni-adjusted for the 13 inputs.) The real effect of three bad reps is too diluted among 60 to show; that’s the other side of a fair test.




Your turn. ctree’s mincriterion is 1 - \alpha. Grow the tree with mincriterion = 0.99 and 0.90, and compare their leaves and validation AUCs.









Use the function’s argument: mincriterion = m.


sapply(c(0.99, 0.95, 0.90), function(m) {
  set.seed(8072)
  fit <- ctree(churned ~ ., data = train, control = ctree_control(mincriterion = m))
  c(mincriterion = m, leaves = length(nodeids(fit, terminal = TRUE)),
    auc = auc(predict(fit, valid, type = "prob")[, "yes"], valid$churned))
})
11, 14 and 15 leaves, with validation AUCs of 0.783, 0.792 and 0.797. The threshold acts like CART’s complexity parameter, but in units anyone can understand: “split only when the evidence is significant at 1%”. The top of the tree is the same at every threshold, because the strong effects pass any of them; the threshold only decides how many weak splits are added at the bottom.

title: Conditional inference trees and C5.0
text:
C5.0
Quinlan’s C5.0 grows trees by information gain ratio, an entropy-based criterion divided by the split’s own entropy, which penalizes splits into many small groups. It splits categorical inputs into one branch per level (or groups of levels), prunes by an error-based estimate rather than cross-validation, and has two extras: it can convert its tree into a compact rule set, and it has boosting built in.
The entropy of a node, in bits, is H = -\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k, where p_k is the share of class k: 0 for a pure node, 1 for a 50/50 node. A split’s information gain is the parent’s entropy minus the children’s average entropy, weighted by their sizes. Its split information is the entropy of the split itself, -\sum_j w_j \log_2 w_j, where w_j is the share of accounts sent to branch j: it grows with the number of branches. The gain ratio is the gain divided by the split information.
Your turn. Compute the gain, the split information and the gain ratio of three splits of the training accounts: late deliveries (3 or more against fewer), the segment (8 branches) and the sales rep (60 branches).









The split information is the entropy of the split itself: of x, not of y.


H <- function(y) {                                         # entropy, in bits
  p <- prop.table(table(y)); p <- p[p > 0]
  -sum(p * log2(p))
}
gain_ratio <- function(x, y) {
  w <- prop.table(table(x))                                # the branch shares
  gain <- H(y) - sum(w * tapply(y, x, H))
  split_info <- H(x)
  c(gain = gain, split_info = split_info, ratio = gain / split_info)
}
round(rbind(late_3plus = gain_ratio(train$late_deliveries >= 3, train$churned),
            segment = gain_ratio(train$segment, train$churned),
            sales_rep = gain_ratio(train$sales_rep, train$churned)), 4)
The late-delivery split gains 0.083 bits, with a split information of 0.56, so a gain ratio of 0.150: far ahead of the others. Look at the other two. On gain alone, the 60 sales reps (0.0223) look three times as good as the 8 segments (0.0074), because 60 small groups are purer by chance: the same bias as CART’s. Their split information is 5.9 bits against 2.9, and dividing by it shrinks the reps’ advantage to 0.0038 against 0.0025. The gain ratio reduces the bias, but doesn’t remove it; ctree’s tests are the cleaner fix.










ImportantC5.0 runs in RStudio, not in the browser



The C50 package’s C code crashes in the browser version of R that these pages use, so the C5.0 code below isn’t an exercise: it was run, and its output recorded, when this page was built. Run it in RStudio (install C50 first) to try it yourself.


A C5.0 tree, grown without the sales reps, with its size and validation AUC:

c5 <- C5.0(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train)
c(size = c5$size, auc = auc(predict(c5, valid, type = "prob")[, "yes"], valid$churned))
#>    size     auc 
#> 6.00000 0.68811

A tree with 6 leaves, and a validation AUC of 0.688, much like CART’s default tree (0.690). C5.0’s pruning is aggressive on these data; summary(c5) prints the tree, and C5.0Control(CF = 0.5) prunes less.
With rules = TRUE, C5.0 turns its tree into a rule set. Here are the rules from its summary:

c5r <- C5.0(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, rules = TRUE)
summary(c5r)


#> Rule 1: (974/53, lift 1.2)
#>  account_years > 2
#>  price_index <= 1.048
#>  late_deliveries <= 2
#>  ->  class no  [0.945]
#> 
#> Rule 2: (1480/152, lift 1.1)
#>  late_deliveries <= 2
#>  volume_change_pct > -15
#>  ->  class no  [0.897]
#> 
#> Rule 3: (433/55, lift 1.1)
#>  segment in {Food, Pharma}
#>  ->  class no  [0.871]
#> 
#> Rule 4: (48/12, lift 3.7)
#>  price_index > 1.048
#>  volume_change_pct <= -15
#>  ->  class yes  [0.740]
#> 
#> Rule 5: (80/26, lift 3.4)
#>  account_years <= 2
#>  volume_change_pct <= -15
#>  ->  class yes  [0.671]
#> 
#> Rule 6: (255/105, lift 3.0)
#>  late_deliveries > 2
#>  ->  class yes  [0.588]

Six rules. Each shows how many training accounts it covers and how many it gets wrong (48/12: 48 covered, 12 wrong), its lift (how many times the overall churn rate its accounts have), and its confidence in brackets. The strongest “yes” rule, Rule 4: a price more than 1.048 times the market and a volume drop of 15% or more. Unlike a tree’s leaves, rules can overlap; an account can match several, and they vote. Rule sets are often shorter and easier to act on than the tree they came from: these six could go on one slide for the sales meeting.
Your turn. Check Rule 4 on the training accounts: how many it covers, what share of them churned, and its lift, that share divided by the overall churn rate.









A volume change of -15 or less.


covered <- train$price_index > 1.048 & train$volume_change_pct <= -15
rate <- mean(train$churned[covered] == "yes")
c(covered = sum(covered), churn_rate = rate, lift = rate / mean(train$churned == "yes"))
48 accounts, of which 36 churned (75%), against 19.8% overall: a lift of 3.79. C5.0 reports 3.7 and a confidence of 0.740 because it uses a cautious estimate of the rate, (36 + 1) / (48 + 2) = 0.74 (the Laplace correction), which pulls small rules toward 50%. A rule is just a filter on the data, so anyone with a spreadsheet can check it, which is part of its appeal.




C5.0’s trials argument grows a sequence of trees, each focusing on the accounts the previous ones got wrong, and lets them vote. That’s boosting, the subject of Lesson 13. Here it is with 10 trials:

c5b <- C5.0(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, trials = 10)
c(trials_used = c5b$trials[["Actual"]], auc = auc(predict(c5b, valid, type = "prob")[, "yes"], valid$churned))
#> trials_used         auc 
#>   7.0000000   0.8185515

A validation AUC of 0.819, far above any single tree. C5.0 stopped after 7 of the 10 trials, because the later trees were no longer improving the training fit. A committee of small trees ranks accounts much more finely than one tree can, which is the idea behind every ensemble in Lessons 12 and 13. The price: no single tree or rule set to read any more.






NoteGo deeper: how ctree’s tests work





For an input X and target Y, ctree computes a linear statistic T = \sum_i g(X_i) h(Y_i)^\top, where g and h code the variables (indicator columns for factors, the values themselves for numbers). Under the null hypothesis that X and Y are independent, every permutation of Y against X is equally likely, and Strasser and Weber (1999) gave the exact mean and covariance of T over all permutations. A standardized quadratic form of T is then approximately chi-squared, with degrees of freedom equal to the dimension of T: 1 for a numeric input with a binary target, 59 for the sales reps. Because every input’s p-value refers to its own degrees of freedom, a 60-level factor gets no free advantage. The framework covers numeric, categorical, censored and multivariate targets with the same machinery. Hothorn, Hornik and Zeileis, “Unbiased Recursive Partitioning: A Conditional Inference Framework”, Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics 15(3), 2006, is the reference.

title: Conditional inference trees and C5.0
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Every tree so far. Put the validation AUCs of the trees you can grow here side by side: CART’s default tree (without the reps), CART with the reps, and ctree.









churned ~ . uses every input, the reps included.


set.seed(8072)
ct <- ctree(churned ~ ., data = train)
p_ctree <- predict(ct, valid, type = "prob")[, "yes"]        # predict right after fitting
p <- list(
  cart = predict(rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class"), valid)[, "yes"],
  cart_with_reps = predict(rpart(churned ~ ., data = train, method = "class"), valid)[, "yes"],
  ctree = p_ctree)
round(sapply(p, auc, y = valid$churned), 3)
0.690 for CART, 0.743 for CART with the reps and 0.792 for ctree; add C5.0’s 0.688 and boosted C5.0’s 0.819 from above (Lesson 5’s pruned CART tree had 0.767). Among single trees, ctree wins here, with an honest test for every split; among everything, the ensemble wins. Single trees are all within a few points of each other once they’re the right size, and which wins depends on the data. The real jump comes from combining trees.

title: Conditional inference trees and C5.0
text:
Quick quiz

1. On pure noise, why does CART prefer a 20-level factor?

Factors are more informative
It has far more possible splits, so its best split looks good by chance more often
rpart handles factors first


That’s variable selection bias.



2. How does ctree choose the input to split on?

By the largest impurity decrease
By the smallest adjusted p-value of a permutation test of independence
At random


It chooses the split point afterwards, only for that input.



3. When does ctree stop splitting a node?

When the node is pure
When no input’s adjusted p-value is below 1 - mincriterion
After cross-validation


Like CHAID, it stops by significance and doesn’t prune.



4. The sales rep’s ctree p-value was 1, though three reps really lose customers. Why?

ctree ignores factors
The effect is concentrated in 3 of 60 levels, so a test over all 59 degrees of freedom can’t detect it
The test is wrong


A fair test can also be a weak one for sparse effects.



5. What can C5.0 produce besides a tree?

A regression line
A rule set, and a boosted ensemble of trees
A neural network


rules = TRUE and trials = ....



6. Which gave the highest validation AUC?

CART with the sales reps
ctree
Boosted C5.0


0.819: ensembles of trees beat single trees.

title: Conditional inference trees and C5.0
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve met the other two families of trees. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Selection bias: on noise, CART picked a 20-level factor 191 times out of 200; on churn, it promoted the 60 sales reps to the second most important input.
Conditional inference trees choose inputs by permutation tests with adjusted p-values, then choose the split, and stop when nothing is significant. On churn: 14 leaves, no sales reps, the price-by-service interaction found, and a validation AUC of 0.792.
mincriterion sets the significance threshold: 11 to 15 leaves between 0.99 and 0.90.
C5.0 grows trees by gain ratio, which penalizes many-branch splits (but doesn’t remove their advantage), writes rule sets (6 rules here) that anyone can check, and boosts: 0.688 as a single tree, 0.819 boosted. It runs in RStudio, not in the browser.
The lesson: right-sized single trees are all similar; combining trees is what makes the big difference.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download customer_churn.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install partykit and C50.

Plot the ctree. plot(ct) draws the tree with a bar chart of the churn rate in every leaf, and each inner node’s p-value. Try plot(ct, type = "simple").
The noise simulation with ctree. Repeat the 200 noise datasets with ctree(..., control = ctree_control(mincriterion = 0)) and record which input it picks at the root. Then with the default mincriterion: how often does it split at all?
C5.0 with the sales reps. Grow C5.0 with the reps included. Does it use them? Compare with CART and ctree.
Winnowing. C5.0Control(winnow = TRUE) lets C5.0 drop inputs it thinks are useless before growing the tree. Which does it drop?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Variable selection bias

A tree’s tendency to choose inputs with many possible splits, whether or not they matter.

Conditional inference tree (ctree)

A tree that chooses inputs by permutation tests of independence, then chooses the split, and stops when nothing is significant.

Permutation test

A test that compares a statistic with its distribution over all permutations of the data under the null hypothesis.

mincriterion

In ctree, one minus the significance threshold for splitting.

C5.0

Quinlan’s tree algorithm, using the information gain ratio, with rule sets and boosting.

Information gain ratio

The decrease in entropy from a split, divided by the entropy of the split itself.

Rule set

A list of if-then rules, possibly overlapping, extracted from a tree.











NoteWant to read more?






Torsten Hothorn, Kurt Hornik and Achim Zeileis, “Unbiased Recursive Partitioning: A Conditional Inference Framework”, Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics 15(3), 2006, doi:10.1198/106186006X133933.
Torsten Hothorn and Achim Zeileis, “partykit: A Toolkit for Recursive Partytioning”, the package’s vignette, and its “ctree” vignette.
Max Kuhn and Kjell Johnson, Applied Predictive Modeling (Springer, 2013), sections 14.2 to 14.6, on CART, C4.5, C5.0 and their rules, with a careful comparison.

title: Pruning and tree size
text:
Module 8 · Lesson 5 of 13 Week 123 of 160 About 5–7 hours
How big should a tree be? Lesson 2’s stopping rules (a minimum leaf size, a maximum depth, a minimum improvement) all decide while the tree grows, and they have a known flaw: a split that looks useless can make a very useful split possible further down. The interaction between price and the technical service contract is like that: price alone splits the churn data weakly, but under it, the service contract splits strongly.
CART’s answer, from Breiman and colleagues’ 1984 book, is to grow the tree too big, then prune it back. Pruning removes the branches that add the least, one at a time, which gives a nested sequence of smaller and smaller subtrees. Cross-validation, or a validation set, then picks the best one.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Pruning and tree size
text:
A tree grown too far
With cp = 0, rpart keeps splitting as long as a split improves the fit at all, until the leaves get too small (by default, a node needs 20 cases to be split, and a leaf needs 7).
The setup code makes Lesson 1’s partition, and defines auc() and a helper, err(), which gives a tree’s misclassification rate on some data.











Your turn. Grow the tree with cp = 0, and compare its training and validation error rates.









No complexity penalty: cp = 0.


set.seed(8051)
big <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class", cp = 0)
c(leaves = sum(big$frame$var == "<leaf>"), train_error = err(big, train), valid_error = err(big, valid))
36 leaves, a training error of 11.2% and a validation error of 20.2%. The tree misclassifies almost twice as often on accounts it hasn’t seen, and on the validation set it’s barely better than predicting “no” for everyone (21.5%). The set.seed() is there because rpart cross-validates every tree it grows, with random folds, and the next step uses the results.

title: Pruning and tree size
text:
Cost-complexity pruning
Write R(T) for a tree’s misclassification rate on the training data and |T| for its number of leaves. Cost-complexity pruning finds, for each penalty \alpha \ge 0, the subtree that minimizes

R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha |T| .

At \alpha = 0, that’s the full tree. As \alpha grows, extra leaves cost more, and the best subtree shrinks, down to the root alone. Breiman and colleagues showed that the best subtrees for all values of \alpha form a nested sequence, and that it can be found by repeatedly cutting the “weakest link”, the branch with the smallest improvement per leaf removed.
rpart reports the sequence in its complexity table, cptable. Each row is a subtree, with:

CP: the penalty at which it becomes optimal, scaled by the root’s error (rpart’s \alpha divided by R(\text{root}));
nsplit: its number of splits (leaves minus one);
rel error: its training error, relative to the root’s;
xerror and xstd: its 10-fold cross-validated error, relative to the root’s, and that estimate’s standard error.

Your turn. Print the big tree’s complexity table, and find the row with the smallest cross-validated error.









The cross-validated error is the "xerror" column.


set.seed(8051)
big <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class", cp = 0)
ct <- big$cptable
print(round(ct, 4))
ct[which.min(ct[, "xerror"]), ]
The smallest cross-validated error, 0.802, is at 19 splits (20 leaves), with CP 0.0064. Look at the whole column, though: the training error (rel error) falls steadily from 1 to 0.567, but the cross-validated error falls to about 0.80 by 5 splits, then wanders between 0.80 and 0.82 up to 24 splits, and rises to 0.91 at 35. Every size between 5 and 24 splits is, within its standard error (about 0.042), as good as any other. That’s typical, and it’s what the one-standard-error rule is for.




Here’s the same table as a picture, made with plotcp()’s logic: the cross-validated error against the tree size, with one-standard-error bars, and a dashed line one standard error above the minimum.

ct <- big$cptable
d <- data.frame(leaves = ct[, "nsplit"] + 1, xerror = ct[, "xerror"], xstd = ct[, "xstd"], rel = ct[, "rel error"])
lim <- min(d$xerror) + d$xstd[which.min(d$xerror)]
ggplot(d, aes(leaves)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = lim, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(aes(y = rel), color = "grey60") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = xerror - xstd, ymax = xerror + xstd), width = 0.6, color = "#C2416C") +
  geom_line(aes(y = xerror), color = "#C2416C") + geom_point(aes(y = xerror), color = "#C2416C", size = 1.8) +
  labs(x = "Number of leaves", y = "Error relative to the root") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: Pruning and tree size
text:
Two ways to choose
Your turn. Prune the big tree at the CP with the smallest cross-validated error, and find its leaves, validation error and validation AUC.









Prune at best_cp.


set.seed(8051)
big <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class", cp = 0)
ct <- big$cptable
best_cp <- ct[which.min(ct[, "xerror"]), "CP"]
t_min <- prune(big, cp = best_cp)
c(leaves = sum(t_min$frame$var == "<leaf>"), valid_error = err(t_min, valid),
  valid_auc = auc(predict(t_min, valid)[, "yes"], valid$churned))
20 leaves, a validation error of 19.6% and a validation AUC of 0.767, the best AUC of any churn tree so far, as good as Lesson 1’s logistic regression. Pruning took away 16 leaves and lost nothing on new accounts.




The one-standard-error rule (Breiman and colleagues’ own recommendation) chooses the smallest tree whose cross-validated error is within one standard error of the minimum: given that the estimates are noisy, prefer the simplest tree that’s statistically as good.
Your turn. Apply the one-standard-error rule, and find the tree’s leaves, validation error and validation AUC.









Add the minimum’s standard error, the "xstd" column.


set.seed(8051)
big <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class", cp = 0)
ct <- big$cptable
i <- which.min(ct[, "xerror"])
limit <- ct[i, "xerror"] + ct[i, "xstd"]
j <- which(ct[, "xerror"] <= limit)[1]
t_1se <- prune(big, cp = ct[j, "CP"])
c(leaves = sum(t_1se$frame$var == "<leaf>"), valid_error = err(t_1se, valid),
  valid_auc = auc(predict(t_1se, valid)[, "yes"], valid$churned))
Just 3 leaves (late deliveries, then a volume drop), a validation error of 19.5%, slightly lower than the 20-leaf tree’s, and a validation AUC of only 0.628. Both rules did their job: they chose by misclassification error, which is what xerror measures, and on that measure the two trees are equal. But a 3-leaf tree ranks accounts into only three groups, and Lena needs a ranking. Pruning should be judged by the measure the business will use.

title: Pruning and tree size
text:
Pruning with the validation set
The complexity table gives every subtree in the sequence, so the validation set can pick one directly, by whatever measure matters.
Your turn. For every CP in the table, prune the big tree and find the subtree’s leaves, validation error and validation AUC.









Prune at the function’s argument, cp.


set.seed(8051)
big <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class", cp = 0)
path <- t(sapply(big$cptable[, "CP"], function(cp) {
  sub <- prune(big, cp = cp)
  c(leaves = sum(sub$frame$var == "<leaf>"), valid_error = err(sub, valid),
    valid_auc = auc(predict(sub, valid)[, "yes"], valid$churned))
}))
round(path, 4)
By validation error, the best subtrees have 7 or 12 leaves (18.6%), and everything from 6 to 23 leaves is within a point of them. By AUC, there’s a jump: subtrees with 6 to 14 leaves have about 0.69, and from 20 leaves on about 0.76 to 0.77, with the best at 22 leaves (0.768). The splits between 14 and 20 leaves are small ones, which hardly change any account’s predicted class, but they break up big leaves and so improve the ranking. For a visit list, a tree of about 20 leaves is the right choice.




Your turn. The cost-complexity criterion trades errors against leaves. With R(T) = relative training error × the root’s error rate (388/1,962), compare R_\alpha(T) for the 20-leaf and the 3-leaf subtrees at \alpha = 0.002 and \alpha = 0.005.









The 3-leaf tree pays for 3 leaves.


set.seed(8051)
big <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class", cp = 0)
ct <- big$cptable
R <- ct[, "rel error"] * 388 / 1962
leaves <- ct[, "nsplit"] + 1
r20 <- which(leaves == 20); r3 <- which(leaves == 3)
sapply(c(0.002, 0.005), function(a) c(leaves20 = R[r20] + a * 20, leaves3 = R[r3] + a * 3))
At \alpha = 0.002, the 20-leaf tree wins (0.162 against 0.170): its training error of 12.2% is worth its extra 17 leaves. At \alpha = 0.005, the 3-leaf tree wins (0.179 against 0.222). Somewhere between, the preferred subtree switches, and as \alpha rises through the CP values in the table (times 388/1,962), each subtree in turn becomes the best. Cross-validation’s job is to choose \alpha; the training error alone would always choose \alpha = 0 and the biggest tree.




Your turn. The pruned trees are nested: each is the big tree with some branches removed. Check that the 3-leaf tree’s splits are the same as the first splits of the 20-leaf tree, by comparing the variables of the nodes that both trees have.









Look up the same node numbers in the 20-leaf tree: t20$frame[nodes3, "var"].


set.seed(8051)
big <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class", cp = 0)
ct <- big$cptable
t20 <- prune(big, cp = ct[ct[, "nsplit"] == 19, "CP"])
t3 <- prune(big, cp = ct[ct[, "nsplit"] == 2, "CP"])
nodes3 <- rownames(t3$frame)
identical(as.character(t3$frame[nodes3, "var"])[t3$frame$var != "<leaf>"],
          as.character(t20$frame[nodes3, "var"])[t3$frame$var != "<leaf>"])
TRUE: the 3-leaf tree’s two splits (late deliveries, then the volume change) are exactly the top of the 20-leaf tree. rpart numbers its nodes so that node k’s children are 2k and 2k + 1, which makes the comparison easy. Because the subtrees are nested, choosing a size never means choosing different splits, only how far down to keep them.










NoteGo deeper: the weakest link





For an internal node t with branch T_t below it, collapsing the branch into a leaf changes R_\alpha by R(t) - R(T_t) - \alpha(|T_t| - 1). The branch is worth keeping while \alpha < g(t) = \frac{R(t) - R(T_t)}{|T_t| - 1}: the improvement it buys per extra leaf. Weakest-link pruning repeatedly collapses the node with the smallest g(t); the successive values of g are the CP values in rpart’s table (divided by R(\text{root})), and each collapse gives the next subtree in the sequence. Breiman and colleagues proved that this sequence contains the optimal subtree for every \alpha. Cross-validation then works on \alpha rather than on trees: rpart grows a tree on each fold’s training part, prunes it at each CP, and measures the held-out error. ISLR’s Algorithm 8.1 summarizes it.

title: Pruning and tree size
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The folds matter. rpart’s cross-validation uses random folds. Grow the big tree with seeds 1 to 5, and for each, find the number of splits chosen by the minimum rule and by the one-standard-error rule.









Use the function’s argument: set.seed(s).


t(sapply(1:5, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  b <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class", cp = 0)
  ct <- b$cptable
  i <- which.min(ct[, "xerror"])
  j <- which(ct[, "xerror"] <= ct[i, "xerror"] + ct[i, "xstd"])[1]
  c(seed = s, min_rule = ct[i, "nsplit"], one_se = ct[j, "nsplit"])
}))
The minimum rule picks 6 splits for four of the seeds and 9 for the fifth, and the one-standard-error rule picks 2 to 6. With seed 8051, they had picked 19 and 2. When the cross-validated error curve is this flat, which size wins is close to a coin toss, which is another reason to look at the whole path, and at the measure you care about, before trusting one number.




Challenge 2 · Pruning the catalyst tree. Grow the catalyst-life regression tree with cp = 0 (after set.seed(8052)), prune it by the minimum rule and by the one-standard-error rule, and compare the test RMSEs of the three trees.









The one-standard-error tree is row j.


cat_life <- read.csv("data/catalyst_life.csv", stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
cat_life$charge <- NULL
set.seed(8022); tr <- sample(600, 400)
ctrain <- cat_life[tr, ]; ctest <- cat_life[-tr, ]
set.seed(8052)
big_c <- rpart(life_days ~ ., data = ctrain, method = "anova", cp = 0)
ct <- big_c$cptable
i <- which.min(ct[, "xerror"])
j <- which(ct[, "xerror"] <= ct[i, "xerror"] + ct[i, "xstd"])[1]
rmse <- function(tree) sqrt(mean((ctest$life_days - predict(tree, ctest))^2))
c(full = rmse(big_c), min_rule = rmse(prune(big_c, cp = ct[i, "CP"])), one_se = rmse(prune(big_c, cp = ct[j, "CP"])),
  leaves_min = ct[i, "nsplit"] + 1, leaves_1se = ct[j, "nsplit"] + 1)
The full tree (32 leaves) has a test RMSE of 79.7 days, the minimum-rule tree (29 leaves) 78.5, and the one-standard-error tree (18 leaves) 82.2. All three beat Lesson 4’s default tree (12 leaves, 85.4): with a strong, structured signal and 400 charges, bigger trees keep finding real detail, and pruning removes little. The one-standard-error tree gives up 4 days of RMSE for a tree about half the size, a trade worth making if the planners want to read it.

title: Pruning and tree size
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why grow a big tree and prune it, rather than stop early?

It’s faster
A weak split can enable strong splits below it, which early stopping would never see
Pruned trees are always smaller


Pruning judges whole branches, not single splits.



2. What does xerror in rpart’s complexity table measure?

The training error
The 10-fold cross-validated misclassification error, relative to the root’s
The validation AUC


For regression trees, it’s the cross-validated sum of squares, relative to the root’s.



3. What does the one-standard-error rule choose?

The tree with the smallest cross-validated error
The smallest tree whose cross-validated error is within one standard error of the minimum
A tree one level smaller than the minimum


It prefers simplicity when the estimates can’t tell trees apart.



4. The 3-leaf tree had the same validation error as the 20-leaf tree, but a much lower AUC. Why?

The AUC was miscalculated
Error counts only class labels; with 3 leaves, the tree can rank accounts into only 3 groups
The 3-leaf tree overfits


Prune by the measure the decision depends on.



5. In R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha|T|, what happens as \alpha grows?

The best tree gets bigger
The best tree gets smaller, down to the root alone
Nothing


Each leaf costs \alpha.



6. Running rpart with different seeds chose different tree sizes. Why?

rpart is buggy
Its cross-validation uses random folds, and the error curve is flat, so small changes move the minimum
The data changed


With a flat curve, many sizes are equally good.

title: Pruning and tree size
text:
Wrap-up
You can now size a tree properly. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Grow, then prune: with cp = 0, the churn tree grew 36 leaves and overfitted (11.2% training error, 20.2% validation).
Cost-complexity pruning gives a nested sequence of subtrees, one for each range of \alpha; rpart’s complexity table lists them with their cross-validated errors.
The minimum rule chose 20 leaves (validation AUC 0.767); the one-standard-error rule chose 3 (equally accurate, but an AUC of 0.628).
The validation path showed why: error and ranking disagree. For a visit list, about 20 leaves.
The choice is noisy: different folds chose 2 to 19 splits, because the error curve is flat.
The catalyst tree kept improving with size: 29 leaves gave a test RMSE of 78.5 days.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download customer_churn.csv and catalyst_life.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

plotcp. Run plotcp(big) and printcp(big) for both big trees, and find the minimum and one-standard-error trees on the plot.
Repeated cross-validation. rpart’s xval argument sets the folds. Average xerror over 20 different seeds, and choose the size from the averaged curve. Is it more stable?
Prune for AUC. Write your own 10-fold cross-validation that prunes each fold’s tree at every CP and computes the held-out AUC. Which size does it choose?
Draw them. Plot the 3-leaf and 20-leaf trees with rpart.plot, and write each as rules. Which would you give Lena?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Pruning

Removing branches from a fully grown tree to reduce overfitting.

Cost-complexity criterion

R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha|T|: the training error plus a penalty per leaf.

Complexity parameter (CP)

rpart’s scaled version of \alpha; a split must improve the fit by at least CP (relative to the root) to be kept.

Weakest-link pruning

Repeatedly collapsing the branch with the smallest improvement per leaf, which gives the nested sequence of optimal subtrees.

Cross-validated error (xerror)

The error of each subtree size, estimated by cross-validation, relative to the root’s.

One-standard-error rule

Choosing the smallest tree whose cross-validated error is within one standard error of the minimum.











NoteWant to read more?






James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition), section 8.1.1, “Tree Pruning”, and Algorithm 8.1.
Therneau and Atkinson, “An Introduction to Recursive Partitioning Using the RPART Routines”, sections 4.2 and 6, on the complexity parameter and cross-validation.
Boehmke and Greenwell, Hands-On Machine Learning with R, section 9.4, “How deep?”.

title: CART classification trees
text:
Module 8 · Lesson 3 of 13 Week 121 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 2 grew a tree two levels deep, by hand and with rpart(). This lesson lets rpart grow a full tree with its default settings, and looks at it the way a business analyst would: as a set of rules, as a source of probabilities, and as a classifier that can be told what its mistakes cost.
That last part matters for Lena’s problem. A visit to an account that wasn’t going to leave wastes an engineer’s day: call it a cost of 1. Missing an account that leaves loses a customer, and the margin with it: much more, say 4. A tree grown to minimize the plain error rate treats both mistakes alike. CART has two ways to make it care: prior probabilities and a loss matrix.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: CART classification trees
text:
A full tree
The setup code makes Lesson 1’s partition, and defines the auc() function from Lesson 1. The trees in this lesson leave out the 60 sales reps (Lesson 8 deals with them), but include the satisfaction score, with its missing values: rpart handles them with surrogate splits, also in Lesson 8.











Your turn. Grow a tree with rpart’s defaults, and count its leaves.









A classification tree is method = "class". (rpart would guess it from the factor response, but it’s good practice to say so.)


tree <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class")
print(tree)
sum(tree$frame$var == "<leaf>")
10 leaves. Below the first split (late deliveries), the low-risk branch splits on a volume drop of 14.5%, then on the account’s age and the price index; the high-risk branch splits on the segment, then on age and complaints. These are the effects built into the data, found in the order of their strength, and the interactions too: the price index matters only for established accounts whose volume is falling. The satisfaction score doesn’t appear: its information is mostly carried by the complaints and late deliveries, which cause it.





tree <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class")
rpart.plot(tree, type = 4, extra = 106, box.palette = list("#F4C0D1", "#C2416C"), branch.lty = 1, roundint = FALSE, digits = 3, tweak = 1.05)

title: CART classification trees
text:
Classes and probabilities
predict(tree, newdata, type = "class") gives each account’s predicted class, the majority class of its leaf; type = "prob" gives the leaf’s class proportions.
Your turn. Predict the classes of the validation accounts, and make the confusion matrix and the accuracy.









type = "class".


tree <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class")
cl <- predict(tree, valid, type = "class")
print(table(predicted = cl, actual = valid$churned))
mean(cl == valid$churned)
81.2% accurate, against 78.5% for predicting that nobody leaves. But of the 221 validation leavers, the tree flags only 79, and misses 142. The majority-class rule predicts “yes” only in leaves where more than half the accounts churned, and most leavers are in leaves where they’re a minority.




Your turn. Find the validation AUC of the tree’s probabilities, and how many different probabilities it gives.









The churn probability is the "yes" column.


tree <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class")
p <- predict(tree, valid, type = "prob")[, "yes"]
c(auc = auc(p, valid$churned), distinct = length(unique(p)))
An AUC of 0.690, with only 10 distinct probabilities, one per leaf. Lesson 1’s five-input logistic regression had 0.766. The tree’s ranking is coarse: 1,480 training accounts share the lowest leaf, so the tree can’t rank them against each other at all. That’s the price of a tree’s readability. Pruning (Lesson 5) finds the right size, and Lessons 12 and 13 average hundreds of trees to get a fine ranking back.

title: CART classification trees
section: What the tree thinks is important
text:
What the tree thinks is important
rpart’s variable importance adds up, for each input, the impurity decreases of the splits it made, plus a share of those it would have made as a surrogate. It’s a quick summary of what the tree relies on.
Your turn. Look at the tree’s variable importance.









It’s stored in tree$variable.importance.


tree <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class")
round(tree$variable.importance, 1)
The late deliveries (89.4) far ahead, then the volume change (30.0), the account’s age (22.2), the price index (15.5) and the segment (11.6). For Lena, that’s a priority list for the operations side as much as for sales: fixing deliveries would do more for retention than any visit. The technical service contract, which matters a lot in the data (it changes the effect of price), doesn’t appear at all, because the tree splits on price only once, in a small branch, and has no room left to split on service under it. Importance only describes what this tree used.

title: CART classification trees
text:
Moving the cut-off
The simplest way to catch more leavers is to classify with a lower cut-off on the probability, as in Module 7. If missing a leaver costs 4 and a wasted visit 1, the break-even probability is 1/(1 + 4) = 0.2: visit an account when its churn probability is above 0.2.
Your turn. Classify the validation accounts as leavers when the tree’s probability is at least 0.2, and make the confusion matrix.









Use 0.2.


tree <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class")
p <- predict(tree, valid, type = "prob")[, "yes"]
cl <- ifelse(p >= 0.2, "yes", "no")
table(predicted = cl, actual = valid$churned)
83 leavers caught instead of 79, and 55 wasted visits instead of 52: hardly any change. With only 10 leaf probabilities, moving the cut-off from 0.5 to 0.2 only re-labels the leaves whose churn rate lies in between, and only one does: a small leaf with a rate of 0.22 and 9 training accounts. Moving the cut-off can only use the ranking the tree already has. Priors and losses change the tree itself.

title: CART classification trees
text:
Prior probabilities
By default, rpart takes the class proportions in the training data as the prior probabilities: 80% stayers, 20% leavers. Setting the priors to 50/50 makes the tree behave as if leavers were as common as stayers. Every leaver then counts four times as much in the impurity calculations, so the tree looks harder for splits that isolate them, and calls a leaf “yes” much more easily.
Your turn. Grow the tree with equal priors, and make its validation confusion matrix. Also find its leaves and its AUC.









The priors are for the classes in level order, “no” then “yes”: c(0.5, 0.5).


tree_p <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class", parms = list(prior = c(0.5, 0.5)))
print(table(predicted = predict(tree_p, valid, type = "class"), actual = valid$churned))
c(leaves = sum(tree_p$frame$var == "<leaf>"), auc = auc(predict(tree_p, valid)[, "yes"], valid$churned))
Now 158 leavers caught (63 missed), at the cost of 186 wasted visits. The tree is different: 5 leaves instead of 10, a simpler tree aimed at separating leavers, with a validation AUC of 0.759, better than the default tree’s 0.690. Its “probabilities” are now adjusted to the 50/50 priors, so they’re no longer the real churn rates: a leaf with 30% leavers shows up as about 63%. Use them to rank, not as probabilities.

title: CART classification trees
text:
A loss matrix
The more direct way is to tell rpart what each mistake costs. The loss matrix has the true classes in its rows and the predicted classes in its columns, with zeros on the diagonal:




predicted no
predicted yes




actually no
0
1 (a wasted visit)


actually yes
4 (a lost customer)
0



rpart then labels each leaf with the class that has the lower expected loss, and takes the losses into account when it chooses splits (by altering the priors, as the Go deeper box explains).
Your turn. Grow the tree with this loss matrix, and make its validation confusion matrix.









Pass the matrix: loss = L. Check that L[2, 1], true “yes” predicted “no”, is 4.


L <- matrix(c(0, 4,
              1, 0), nrow = 2)
L
tree_l <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class", parms = list(loss = L))
print(table(predicted = predict(tree_l, valid, type = "class"), actual = valid$churned))
sum(tree_l$frame$var == "<leaf>")
The same 5-leaf tree as with equal priors, and the same confusion matrix: 158 leavers caught, 186 wasted visits. That’s no coincidence: with two classes, a loss of 4 for missing a leaver is equivalent to raising the leavers’ prior from 0.2 to exactly 0.5 (the Go deeper box below shows why). The difference is in what you write down: the loss matrix says what the business believes, in its own units, so it’s the clearer way to set up the problem.










NoteGo deeper: priors and losses are two views of one thing





For two classes, a loss matrix with costs L_{12} (true class 1 predicted as 2) and L_{21} is equivalent, for labeling the leaves, to altered priors

\tilde\pi_j = \frac{\pi_j L_{j\cdot}}{\sum_k \pi_k L_{k\cdot}},

where L_{j\cdot} is the cost of misclassifying class j. rpart grows the tree with these altered priors, so a loss of 4 for missing a leaver acts like raising the leavers’ prior from 0.20 to 0.2 \times 4/(0.8 \times 1 + 0.2 \times 4) = 0.5: exactly the equal priors of the previous step. That’s why the two trees here are similar. With more than two classes, a loss matrix can’t always be expressed as priors, and rpart’s “generalized Gini” handles it. Therneau and Atkinson’s rpart vignette, section 4, gives the details.

title: CART classification trees
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Which policy costs least? With a wasted visit costing 1 and a lost customer 4, find the total validation cost of four policies: the default tree’s classes, the default tree with a cut-off of 0.2, the equal-priors tree, and the loss-matrix tree.









A missed leaver costs 4.


cost <- function(cl) sum(cl == "yes" & valid$churned == "no") * 1 + sum(cl == "no" & valid$churned == "yes") * 4
tree <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class")
tree_p <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class", parms = list(prior = c(0.5, 0.5)))
tree_l <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class", parms = list(loss = matrix(c(0, 4, 1, 0), 2)))
c(default = cost(predict(tree, valid, type = "class")),
  cutoff_0.2 = cost(ifelse(predict(tree, valid)[, "yes"] >= 0.2, "yes", "no")),
  priors = cost(predict(tree_p, valid, type = "class")),
  loss = cost(predict(tree_l, valid, type = "class")))
620 for the default tree, 607 with the 0.2 cut-off, and 438 for both the equal-priors and the loss-matrix trees. Building the costs into the tree saved 29% against the default; moving the cut-off saved 2%, because a cut-off can only re-label the leaves of a tree that was grown for a different goal. When the costs of mistakes are unequal, tell the tree while it grows. Lesson 11 does the same with euros instead of a 1-to-4 ratio.




Challenge 2 · Rules for the sales team. rpart.plot::rpart.rules() writes each leaf of a tree as an if-then rule. Print the rules of the default tree, and find the rule with the highest churn rate.









Count the rules: nrow(rules).


tree <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train, method = "class")
rules <- rpart.rules(tree, roundint = FALSE)
print(rules)
nrow(rules)
Ten rules, one per leaf, sorted by churn rate. The riskiest, at 75%: three or more late deliveries, not in Food or Pharma, and at least one complaint. The next, at 73%: three or more late deliveries in Food or Pharma, but a new account. Rules like these go straight into a sales playbook, which is why trees are so popular in business, whatever their AUC.

title: CART classification trees
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does predict(tree, type = "class") return for an account?

The class with the highest predicted probability across all leaves
The majority class of the leaf the account falls into (or the lower-loss class, with a loss matrix)
A random class


With default priors and losses, that’s the class with more than half of the leaf’s training cases.



2. Why did the default tree have a lower AUC than the logistic regression?

Trees can’t do classification
It gives only 10 distinct probabilities, so it can’t rank accounts within a leaf
It used fewer inputs


A coarse ranking loses AUC. Ensembles of trees fix that.



3. What does setting equal priors do?

Makes the tree’s probabilities more accurate
Makes the tree treat the classes as equally common, so it works harder to isolate the rare one
Removes the rare class


The resulting probabilities are adjusted to the priors, so they’re for ranking.



4. In rpart’s loss matrix, what is L[2, 1]?

The cost of a case of class 2 (here “yes”) predicted as class 1 (“no”)
The cost of a case of class 1 predicted as class 2
Always 1


Rows are the true classes, columns the predicted ones.



5. Why did moving the cut-off from 0.5 to 0.2 change so little?

The cut-off doesn’t matter for trees
With only 10 leaf probabilities, few leaves lie between 0.2 and 0.5
The cut-off should be 0.8


A cut-off can only re-label whole leaves.



6. What does rpart’s variable importance measure?

The coefficient of each input
The total impurity decrease from each input’s splits, including surrogate splits
The correlation of each input with the target


It describes what this particular tree relied on.

title: CART classification trees
text:
Wrap-up
You can now grow a classification tree, read it, and make it care about costs. Here’s what you’ve learned:

A default tree for churn had 10 leaves, and found the planted thresholds and interactions in order of strength.
Its predictions are leaf proportions: a validation AUC of 0.690 from only 10 distinct values, and 81.2% accuracy that missed 142 of 221 leavers.
Variable importance put the late deliveries far ahead of the volume change, the account’s age and the price.
Moving the cut-off re-labels whole leaves, so it changed little here.
Priors and a loss matrix change the tree itself: equal priors gave a 5-leaf tree that caught 158 leavers, with an AUC of 0.759.
Costs compare the policies directly: building the 4-to-1 cost into the tree cost far less than the default tree’s 620.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download customer_churn.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install rpart.plot.

Draw the three trees (default, equal priors, loss matrix) side by side with rpart.plot(). How do their shapes differ?
Other costs. Repeat the loss-matrix tree for costs of 2, 3, 6 and 10 for a missed leaver. Plot the number of leavers caught and the number of wasted visits against the cost.
The summary. summary(tree) prints every node with its primary and surrogate splits. Find a node where the satisfaction score appears as a surrogate.
Real probabilities from the priors tree. The equal-priors tree’s probabilities are adjusted. Convert them back to the true scale with Bayes’ theorem, using the real priors 0.8 and 0.2.










NoteKey words from this lesson






CART

Classification and regression trees: binary recursive partitioning with impurity-based splits and cost-complexity pruning.

Class probability (tree)

The share of each class among the training cases in a leaf.

Prior probabilities

The class probabilities a tree assumes; by default, the training proportions.

Loss matrix

A matrix of misclassification costs, with true classes in the rows and predicted classes in the columns.

Variable importance (rpart)

The sum of the impurity decreases from an input’s primary and surrogate splits.

Decision rule

A leaf written as the conditions on its path from the root: “if … and … then …”.











NoteWant to read more?






Therneau and Atkinson, “An Introduction to Recursive Partitioning Using the RPART Routines”, sections 3 and 4, on priors, losses and variable importance.
Stephen Milborrow, “Plotting rpart trees with the rpart.plot package”, the package’s vignette, with every type and extra option.
Boehmke and Greenwell, Hands-On Machine Learning with R, chapter 9, “Decision Trees”.

title: Predictive modeling in practice
text:
Module 8 · Lesson 1 of 13 Week 119 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Module 7 was about methods. Module 8 follows STAT 585, a course in applied analytics: using those methods, and a few new ones, to answer business questions, with decision trees at the center. Trees are the workhorse of business analytics because a manager can read one, and because, combined into forests and boosted ensembles, they’re among the most accurate models there are for tables of data.
The plant’s parent company sells specialty chemicals (coatings resins, plastic additives, adhesives, process chemicals) to about 4,000 industrial customers on annual supply contracts. Each year, about one customer in five doesn’t renew. Lena, the commercial director, has a team of technical sales engineers who can visit an account before its renewal, sort out its problems, and often keep it. But there are 4,000 accounts and 15 engineers. Which accounts should they visit?
customer_churn.csv has last year’s 4,000 accounts, with what was known about each one three months before its renewal date, and whether it renewed:
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Predictive modeling in practice
text:
The question and the target
A predictive model needs three things from the business before any data is touched:

The decision it supports. Here: which accounts get a visit before renewal.
The target: what exactly is being predicted, and when. Here: churned, “didn’t renew”, predicted three months before the renewal date, when there’s still time to visit.
The unit: one row per account per renewal.

The setup code reads the data (as factors, which tree functions like), and drops the account numbers, which identify the rows but carry no information.












Your turn. Find the share of accounts that churned.









A churned account has churned == "yes".


mean(churn$churned == "yes")
20.3%: 813 of the 4,000 accounts didn’t renew. That’s the base rate, and every model will be compared with it. A list of accounts chosen at random would contain 20.3% leavers; a good model should do much better at the top of its list.




Your turn. Find the churn rate in each segment, sorted from lowest to highest.









Group by churn$segment.


round(sort(tapply(churn$churned == "yes", churn$segment, mean)), 3)
From 12.8% in Pharma and 15.0% in Food to 26.3% in Mining. Pharmaceutical customers rarely switch suppliers, because every change of raw material means requalifying the product with the regulators; mining customers buy flotation chemicals on price. A segment’s rate is a useful first fact, but within each segment there are accounts at very different risk, and that’s what the model has to find.

title: Predictive modeling in practice
text:
Inputs that exist in time
A model can only use what’s known when it’s used. Every input here was taken from the records three months before each renewal. That’s the most important check in predictive modeling, and the easiest to get wrong: a column like “number of retention calls made” or “final invoice value” would make a model look brilliant, and it couldn’t be used, because it’s recorded after the fact. Module 7’s project had one such column; this module’s project has one too.
Some inputs are known but awkward. satisfaction is missing for 31% of accounts, because those customers didn’t answer the survey, and Lesson 8 shows that the missingness itself is informative. sales_rep has 60 levels, and Lesson 8 shows what that does to trees. For now, the first models leave both out.

title: Predictive modeling in practice
text:
Training, validation and test
STAT 585’s way of working, which comes from SAS Enterprise Miner and is standard in business analytics, splits the data three ways:

a training set (here 50%), to fit the models;
a validation set (25%), to compare the models, choose their settings and pick a cut-off;
a test set (25%), set aside and used once, at the very end, for an honest estimate of the chosen model’s performance.

With thousands of rows, a fixed validation set is simpler than cross-validation, and with business data it has another advantage: everyone can see exactly which accounts each model was judged on.
Your turn. Assign each account at random to training (50%), validation (25%) or test (25%), and find the size and the churn rate of each part.









The test set gets the last 25%: 0.25.


set.seed(8012)
part <- sample(c("train", "valid", "test"), nrow(churn), replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.5, 0.25, 0.25))
rbind(n = table(part), churn_rate = round(tapply(churn$churned == "yes", part, mean), 4))
1,962 accounts for training, 1,030 for validation and 1,008 for testing, with churn rates of 19.8%, 21.5% and 20.2%. Assigning each account independently gives sizes and rates that wander a little around the targets. This module’s lessons all use this split, so their results can be compared.




Your turn. A stratified split assigns the leavers and the stayers separately, so that every part gets the same churn rate. Do it, by giving each class’s accounts a shuffled sequence of “train”, “train”, “valid”, “test”.









Make as many labels as there are accounts in the class: length(i).


set.seed(8012)
strat <- character(nrow(churn))
for (cl in c("no", "yes")) {
  i <- which(churn$churned == cl)
  strat[i] <- sample(rep_len(c("train", "train", "valid", "test"), length(i)))
}
rbind(n = table(strat), churn_rate = round(tapply(churn$churned == "yes", strat, mean), 4))
2,001, 1,000 and 999 accounts, each with a churn rate of 20.3%. Stratifying matters most when the target is rare (a 1% fraud rate can leave a small validation set with almost no frauds). At 20% and 4,000 rows, the simple split is fine, and the lessons keep it.

title: Predictive modeling in practice
section: A baseline and a first model
text:
A baseline and a first model
The rest of the lesson works with the random split: train and valid come from part exactly as in your exercise.
Your turn. What’s the validation accuracy of the “model” that predicts that nobody churns?









“Nobody churns” is right for every account with churned == "no".


set.seed(8012)
part <- sample(c("train", "valid", "test"), nrow(churn), replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.5, 0.25, 0.25))
valid <- churn[part == "valid", ]
mean(valid$churned == "no")
78.5% accurate, and useless: it never finds a leaver. As in Module 7, accuracy is the wrong yardstick here. What Lena needs is a ranking of the accounts, so that the engineers’ visits go where they matter most.




Your turn. Fit a logistic regression with five inputs on the training set, and find its AUC on the training and the validation sets.









Fit on the training set, train.


set.seed(8012)
part <- sample(c("train", "valid", "test"), nrow(churn), replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.5, 0.25, 0.25))
train <- churn[part == "train", ]; valid <- churn[part == "valid", ]
m1 <- glm(churned ~ late_deliveries + volume_change_pct + price_index + tech_service + account_years,
          family = binomial, data = train)
c(train = auc(fitted(m1), train$churned), valid = auc(predict(m1, valid, type = "response"), valid$churned))
0.787 on the training set and 0.766 on validation. The validation AUC is the honest one: the model has never seen those accounts. Every input pulls in the expected direction: more late deliveries, a falling volume, a higher price and a shorter relationship raise the risk, and a technical service contract lowers it.




Your turn. Now throw everything in: all 13 inputs, with the missing satisfaction scores filled in with 7, a typical score. Compare the training and validation AUCs.









Predict the validation set, valid.


set.seed(8012)
part <- sample(c("train", "valid", "test"), nrow(churn), replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.5, 0.25, 0.25))
filled <- churn
filled$satisfaction[is.na(filled$satisfaction)] <- 7
train <- filled[part == "train", ]; valid <- filled[part == "valid", ]
m_all <- glm(churned ~ ., family = binomial, data = train)
c(n_coef = length(coef(m_all)), train = auc(fitted(m_all), train$churned),
  valid = auc(predict(m_all, valid, type = "response"), valid$churned))
81 coefficients, 59 of them for the sales reps. The training AUC rises to 0.829, and the validation AUC falls, to 0.758, below the five-input model’s 0.766. Without the sales reps, the same model gets 0.807 and 0.783: the other inputs help, and the 59 rep coefficients mostly fit noise. The gap between training and validation is how overfitting shows up in practice, and it’s why the validation set, not the training set, chooses the model.

title: Predictive modeling in practice
text:
What the business sees: lift
The engineers can visit perhaps 10% of the accounts before each renewal round. So the question isn’t “how good is the AUC?” but “if we visit the 10% of accounts with the highest scores, how many of them are real risks?” The lift of the top decile is its churn rate divided by the base rate: how many times better than picking at random.
Your turn. Score the validation accounts with the five-input model, and find the churn rate and the lift in the top 10%.









The top 10% are the scores at or above the 90th percentile: quantile(score, 0.9).


set.seed(8012)
part <- sample(c("train", "valid", "test"), nrow(churn), replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.5, 0.25, 0.25))
train <- churn[part == "train", ]; valid <- churn[part == "valid", ]
m1 <- glm(churned ~ late_deliveries + volume_change_pct + price_index + tech_service + account_years,
          family = binomial, data = train)
score <- predict(m1, valid, type = "response")
top <- score >= quantile(score, 0.9)
rate_top <- mean(valid$churned[top] == "yes")
c(n_top = sum(top), churn_rate_top = rate_top, lift = rate_top / mean(valid$churned == "yes"))
Of the 103 highest-scored validation accounts, 66% churned: a lift of 3.1. Two of every three visits would go to an account that’s about to leave, against one in five at random. That’s a sentence Lena can take to the sales meeting. Lesson 11 turns lift into gains charts and profit.

title: Predictive modeling in practice
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Capture. If the engineers could visit the top 20% of the list, what share of all the validation leavers would they reach?









Divide by all the validation leavers: valid$churned == "yes".


set.seed(8012)
part <- sample(c("train", "valid", "test"), nrow(churn), replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.5, 0.25, 0.25))
train <- churn[part == "train", ]; valid <- churn[part == "valid", ]
m1 <- glm(churned ~ late_deliveries + volume_change_pct + price_index + tech_service + account_years,
          family = binomial, data = train)
score <- predict(m1, valid, type = "response")
top20 <- score >= quantile(score, 0.8)
sum(valid$churned[top20] == "yes") / sum(valid$churned == "yes")
50%: visiting a fifth of the accounts reaches half of the leavers. That’s called the capture rate (or the gain) at 20%. The other half are spread thinly over the remaining 80% of the list, where visits would mostly be wasted. Lesson 11’s gains chart draws this for every depth of the list.




Challenge 2 · The one look at the test set. Suppose the five-input model is the final choice. Report its AUC on the test set.









The test set is part == "test".


set.seed(8012)
part <- sample(c("train", "valid", "test"), nrow(churn), replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.5, 0.25, 0.25))
train <- churn[part == "train", ]; test <- churn[part == "test", ]
m1 <- glm(churned ~ late_deliveries + volume_change_pct + price_index + tech_service + account_years,
          family = binomial, data = train)
auc(predict(m1, test, type = "response"), test$churned)
0.771, close to the validation estimate of 0.766. The validation AUC was used to choose the model, which makes it slightly optimistic in general (the winner of a comparison tends to have been a little lucky); the test AUC wasn’t used for anything, so it’s the one to report. In this module, the test set comes out only in Lessons 11 and 13, for the final comparison.

title: Predictive modeling in practice
text:
Quick quiz

1. Which comes first in a predictive modeling project?

Choosing the algorithm
Defining the decision the model supports, and the target
Tuning the model


The decision defines the target, the timing, and how the model will be judged.



2. A column records “retention discount offered”. Can a churn model three months before renewal use it?

Yes, it’s in the data
Not if the discount is offered after the prediction would be made
Only in the test set


Inputs must be known at the time the model is used. Otherwise it’s leakage.



3. What’s the validation set for?

Fitting the models
Comparing models and choosing their settings
The final, honest estimate


The test set gives the final estimate, once.



4. Adding inputs raised the training AUC and lowered the validation AUC. What happened?

The validation set is too small
The model overfitted the training data
The new inputs are leaks


59 sales-rep coefficients mostly fitted noise.



5. The top decile’s churn rate is 66% and the base rate is 21.5%. What’s the lift?

0.33
44.5
About 3.1


0.66 / 0.215 = 3.1: three times better than picking at random.



6. When does stratifying the split matter most?

When the data are large
When the target is rare, so a random split could leave a part with very few positives
Never


At a 20% rate and 4,000 rows, a simple random split is fine.

title: Predictive modeling in practice
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve set up a predictive modeling project the way it’s done in business analytics. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Start from the decision: which accounts to visit, three months before renewal. That fixes the target and the timing.
Check the inputs’ timing: only what’s known when the model is used.
Split three ways: training to fit, validation to compare and choose, test to report once. The lessons use a 50/25/25 random split: 1,962, 1,030 and 1,008 accounts.
Judge on validation: a five-input logistic regression had a validation AUC of 0.766; throwing in every input raised the training AUC and lowered the validation AUC.
Speak the business’s language: the top 10% of the list had a lift of 3.1, and the top 20% held half the leavers.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download customer_churn.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Explore. Plot the churn rate against each numeric input, in bins. Which look like thresholds rather than smooth trends? (Trees, next lesson, love thresholds.)
Another split. Repeat the five-input model with seeds 1 to 20 for the partition, and look at the spread of the validation AUCs. How much does a single validation set’s estimate vary?
Lift for each segment. Does the model work as well in Pharma as in Mining? Compare the AUC by segment on the validation set.
Write the brief. In five sentences, describe the decision, the target, the inputs, the partition and the success measure, as you would for Lena.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Predictive modeling

Building a model to predict an outcome for new cases, judged by how well it predicts rather than by what its parameters mean.

Target variable

The outcome the model predicts, defined precisely, including when it’s predicted.

Base rate

The share of cases with the outcome, without any model.

Training, validation and test sets

The three parts of the data: to fit models, to compare and tune them, and to estimate the final model’s performance once.

Stratified sampling

Sampling within each class separately, so that each part has the same class proportions.

Lift

The outcome rate among the top-scored cases divided by the base rate.

Capture rate (gain)

The share of all positive cases found in the top-scored part of the list.











NoteWant to read more?






Bradley Boehmke and Brandon Greenwell, Hands-On Machine Learning with R (free online), chapter 2, “Modeling Process”. This module’s main reading.
Foster Provost and Tom Fawcett, Data Science for Business (O’Reilly, 2013), chapters 2 and 7, on framing business problems and on expected-value thinking. The best book on the business side of predictive modeling.
Gordon Linoff and Michael Berry, Data Mining Techniques (3rd edition, Wiley, 2011), chapter 5, on lift, gains and the three-way partition, from practitioners.

title: Clustering
text:
Module 7 · Lesson 13 of 14 Week 116 of 160 About 5–7 hours
A refinery buys crude oil from many sources, and each one behaves differently in the units: light crudes give more gasoline and less residue, sour crudes need more desulfurization, acidic ones corrode, waxy ones gel in tanks in winter. The refinery’s assay library has 48 crudes, each with eight measured properties:
The planners want to know which crudes are alike, so that a crude that’s hard to get can be replaced with a similar one, and so that blends can be planned by type. There’s no response here and no labels: just 48 points in eight dimensions, and the question of whether they fall into groups. That’s clustering.
(This dataset has a secret. The assay lab does know what type each crude is, and that’s in a separate file, which this lesson opens only at the end, to check whether clustering found the truth.)
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Clustering
text:
Preparing the data
Clustering works with distances, so everything from Lesson 3 applies: the properties need comparable scales. Viscosity runs from 1.7 to 372 cSt and the metals from 3 to 414 ppm; both are strongly skewed, and on their raw scales a few heavy crudes would dominate every distance. The setup code takes their logs, standardizes all eight properties into the matrix Z, and labels its rows with the crudes’ names.

title: Clustering
text:
k-means by hand
k-means clustering splits the data into k clusters so that the total within-cluster sum of squares (WSS), the squared distances from each point to its cluster’s center, is as small as possible. Checking every possible split is hopeless (there are about 10^{27} ways to split 48 crudes into 4 groups), so it uses a simple iteration, Lloyd’s algorithm:

Choose k starting centers.
Assign each point to its nearest center.
Update each center to the mean of its points.
Repeat steps 2 and 3 until nothing changes.

Each step can only lower the WSS, so it always converges, but only to a local minimum, which depends on the start.
Your turn. Use the first four crudes as starting centers. Do one assignment step and one update step, and find the cluster sizes and the WSS.









Each cluster’s points are compared with that cluster’s own new center: centers[k, ].


centers <- Z[1:4, ]
d2 <- sapply(1:4, function(k) colSums((t(Z) - centers[k, ])^2))
cl <- max.col(-d2)
centers <- t(sapply(1:4, function(k) colMeans(Z[cl == k, , drop = FALSE])))
wss <- sum(sapply(1:4, function(k) sum((t(Z[cl == k, , drop = FALSE]) - centers[k, ])^2)))
c(table(cl), wss = wss)
Clusters of 12, 11, 14 and 11 crudes, with a WSS of 30.1. max.col(-d2) finds the column with the smallest distance in each row. The first four crudes were a poor start: two of them (Kestrel Blend and Alder Crude) turn out to be the same kind, so two centers began in one group. More iterations would move them apart, and the next exercise lets kmeans() do that.

title: Clustering
text:
kmeans()
Your turn. Run kmeans() with 4 clusters and 25 random starts. Find the cluster sizes, the total WSS, and the share of the total sum of squares that lies between the clusters.









25 random starts: nstart = 25.


set.seed(7131)
km <- kmeans(Z, centers = 4, nstart = 25)
c(km$size, wss = km$tot.withinss, between_share = km$betweenss / km$totss)
Clusters of 14, 11, 10 and 13 crudes, with a WSS of 15.5, half of what one hand step reached. 95.9% of the total variation is between the clusters: the crudes are very close to their cluster’s center and far from the others. That’s an unusually clean clustering, and the next steps check whether 4 is the right number.

title: Clustering
text:
How many clusters?
With no labels, there’s no test error to minimize, and the WSS always falls as k grows (with k = 48, it’s 0). Two common aids:

The elbow plot: plot the WSS against k and look for the point where adding clusters stops helping much.
The silhouette: for each point, compare a, its average distance to the other points in its own cluster, with b, its average distance to the points of the nearest other cluster: s = (b - a)/\max(a, b). It’s near 1 if the point sits snugly in its cluster, near 0 if it’s on a border, and negative if it’s probably in the wrong one. The best k maximizes the average silhouette.

Your turn. Find the WSS for k = 1 to 8.









Use the function’s argument: centers = k.


wss <- sapply(1:8, function(k) {
  set.seed(7131)
  kmeans(Z, centers = k, nstart = 25)$tot.withinss
})
round(wss, 1)
376, 136, 72, 15.5, 14.0, 12.6, 11.3 and 10.6. The WSS falls steeply up to k = 4 and then hardly at all: a sharp elbow at 4. Real data rarely give such a clear elbow, which is why the silhouette helps.





wss <- sapply(1:8, function(k) { set.seed(7131); kmeans(Z, k, nstart = 25)$tot.withinss })
ggplot(data.frame(k = 1:8, wss), aes(k, wss)) + geom_line(color = "#C2416C") + geom_point(color = "#C2416C", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) + labs(x = "Number of clusters, k", y = "Within-cluster sum of squares") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Your turn. Compute the average silhouette width for k = 2 to 7 with cluster::silhouette().









silhouette() needs the clusters and the distances, d.


d <- dist(Z)
sil <- sapply(2:7, function(k) {
  set.seed(7131)
  cl <- kmeans(Z, centers = k, nstart = 25)$cluster
  mean(cluster::silhouette(cl, d)[, "sil_width"])
})
round(sil, 3)
(2:7)[which.max(sil)]
k = 4, with an average silhouette of 0.755; next best is k = 2 (0.607) and k = 5 (0.623). Silhouettes above 0.7 are usually read as strong structure. Two clusters score well too, because the heavy crudes are very different from all the rest: there’s a hierarchy of structure, which the dendrogram below shows directly.

title: Clustering
text:
Why many starts?
Your turn. Run kmeans() with 4 clusters and a single random start, for seeds 1 to 10, and compare the WSS of each.









A single start: nstart = 1.


sapply(1:10, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  round(kmeans(Z, centers = 4, nstart = 1)$tot.withinss, 1)
})
Five of the ten starts find the best solution (15.5), four get stuck at about 70, and one at 110. A WSS of 70 means two true groups merged and another split in two: a completely different answer from a single unlucky start. nstart = 25 runs 25 starts and keeps the best, which makes such failures very unlikely. Always use many starts.

title: Clustering
text:
Hierarchical clustering
k-means needs k in advance. Hierarchical clustering builds the whole hierarchy instead: start with every crude as its own cluster, and repeatedly merge the two closest clusters until only one is left. The result is a dendrogram, a tree whose merge heights are the distances at which clusters joined. Cutting it at any height gives a clustering.
“The distance between two clusters” needs a definition, the linkage:

complete: the largest distance between a point in one and a point in the other (compact clusters);
single: the smallest such distance (which can “chain” a string of points into one long cluster);
average: the average over all pairs;
Ward’s: the increase in WSS from merging (the hierarchical cousin of k-means).


hc <- hclust(dist(Z), method = "complete")
par(mar = c(7, 4, 1, 1), cex = 0.6)
plot(hc, hang = -1, main = "", xlab = "", sub = "", ylab = "Merge height (distance)")
rect.hclust(hc, k = 4, border = c("#C2416C", "#2a78d6", "#1baf7a", "#8a5a00"))








Your turn. Cut the complete-linkage dendrogram into 4 clusters, and cross-tabulate them with the k-means clusters.









Cut into 4 clusters: k = 4.


set.seed(7131)
km <- kmeans(Z, centers = 4, nstart = 25)
hc <- hclust(dist(Z), method = "complete")
table(hierarchical = cutree(hc, k = 4), kmeans = km$cluster)
A perfect match: each hierarchical cluster is exactly one k-means cluster, with different numbers (cluster numbers are arbitrary labels). Single and average linkage find the same four groups too. Different methods agreeing is good evidence that the groups are real. With less separated data they often disagree, and single linkage in particular tends to chain clusters together.

title: Clustering
text:
Naming the clusters
A cluster is useful only once someone can say what it is. Its profile, the average of each property on the original scale, usually tells.
Your turn. Find each k-means cluster’s average properties.









Group by km$cluster.


set.seed(7131)
km <- kmeans(Z, centers = 4, nstart = 25)
prof <- aggregate(crude[, -1], by = list(cluster = km$cluster), FUN = mean)
round(prof, 2)

Cluster 3 is the interesting one: light and sweet by its gravity and sulfur, but with a pour point of 30 °C, it’s solid at room temperature. It would be lumped with cluster 1 by anyone looking at gravity and sulfur alone, the two numbers on every crude’s price sheet, and it needs heated tanks.




Your turn. What if the properties hadn’t been logged and standardized? Run kmeans() with 4 clusters on the raw assays, and look at the cluster sizes.









Drop the name column: crude[, -1].


set.seed(7131)
km_raw <- kmeans(as.matrix(crude[, -1]), centers = 4, nstart = 25)
km_raw$size
Clusters of 37, 6, 4 and 1. In raw units, the viscosity (SD 107 cSt) and the metals (SD 114 ppm) dwarf every other property (the sulfur’s SD is 1.4%), so the distances measure almost nothing else. k-means spends three of its four clusters splitting the 11 heavy crudes by viscosity and metals, and lumps the light sweet, medium sour and waxy crudes together in one cluster of 37. Nothing in the output warns you: it’s a perfectly good minimum of the wrong problem.










NoteGo deeper: what k-means assumes





k-means minimizes squared Euclidean distances to the cluster means, so it works best for clusters that are roughly spherical (after scaling), of similar size and spread, and well separated. It struggles with elongated or curved clusters, and with clusters of very different sizes or densities. Every point is forced into a cluster, outliers included.
