Alternatives drop some of those assumptions: model-based clustering fits a mixture of multivariate normal distributions, each with its own covariance, by the EM algorithm of Module 4 (the mclust package; the number of clusters can then be chosen by BIC), and DBSCAN finds clusters as dense regions of any shape and leaves sparse points unclustered (the dbscan package). ISLR’s section 12.4.3 discusses the practical issues: scaling, the choice of dissimilarity, and checking that clusters aren’t just noise.

title: Clustering
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The answer key. The assay lab’s classification of each crude is in crude_kinds.csv. Read it, and cross-tabulate it with the k-means clusters.









The column is kind.


kinds <- read_csv("data/crude_kinds.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(identical(kinds$crude, crude$crude))
set.seed(7131)
km <- kmeans(Z, centers = 4, nstart = 25)
table(cluster = km$cluster, kind = kinds$kind)
Every crude is in the right group: cluster 1 is the 14 light sweet crudes, 2 the 11 heavy sour, 3 the 10 waxy and 4 the 13 medium sour, exactly as the profiles suggested. Real clustering rarely comes with an answer key, which is why the profiles, the agreement between methods and the silhouette matter: they’re how you build confidence without one. And the raw-units clustering of the last exercise, run on the same data, would have been just as confident and badly wrong.




Challenge 2 · A new crude. A trader offers a crude with an API gravity of 33, 0.3% sulfur, a TAN of 0.06, a viscosity of 8 cSt, a pour point of 18 °C, 6 ppm of metals, 20% naphtha and 27% residue. Standardize it with the library’s means and SDs, and find its squared distance to each cluster center.









scale() stores the means in "scaled:center" and the SDs in "scaled:scale".


set.seed(7131)
km <- kmeans(Z, centers = 4, nstart = 25)
new <- c(api = 33, sulfur = 0.3, tan = 0.06, log_visc = log(8), pour = 18, log_metals = log(6), naphtha = 20, resid = 27)
z_new <- (new - attr(Z, "scaled:center")) / attr(Z, "scaled:scale")
round(colSums((t(km$centers) - z_new)^2), 2)
0.80 to the waxy cluster’s center, against 6.1 to the medium sour, 7.8 to the light sweet and 29 to the heavy sour: it’s a waxy crude, and the planners should budget for heated storage. Its pour point of 18 °C, lower than the waxy cluster’s average, doesn’t change the verdict, because its other properties match too. Assigning new points to the nearest center turns a clustering into a simple classifier, as long as the new point really resembles one of the groups.

title: Clustering
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does k-means minimize?

The number of clusters
The total within-cluster sum of squared distances to the cluster means
The distance between cluster centers


Lloyd’s algorithm alternates assigning points and updating means, lowering it at every step.



2. Why use nstart = 25?

To get 25 clusters
Lloyd’s algorithm finds a local minimum that depends on the start; many starts make a poor one unlikely
To make the clusters equal in size


Half of the single starts on the crudes got stuck at a WSS of 70 or more.



3. A point has a silhouette near 0. What does that mean?

It’s an outlier
It lies between two clusters, about as close to the neighboring cluster as to its own
It’s at its cluster’s center


Near 1 means snugly in its cluster; negative means probably in the wrong one.



4. What does a dendrogram’s merge height show?

The number of points in a cluster
The distance (by the chosen linkage) at which two clusters were joined
The order of the data


Cutting the tree at a height gives a clustering.



5. Which linkage tends to chain points into long, straggly clusters?

Complete
Single
Ward’s


Single linkage merges on the closest pair, so a string of close points joins up.



6. Clustering the raw assays put 37 crudes in one cluster. Why?

There are only two kinds of crude
Viscosity and metals have the largest numbers, so the distances mostly measured them
k-means can’t handle 8 variables


Logs and standardizing gave every property a fair say.

title: Clustering
text:
Wrap-up
You can now find groups in unlabeled data, and check whether they’re real. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Prepare first: logs for skewed properties, then standardize, because clustering is about distances.
k-means alternates assigning points to the nearest center and moving the centers to the means. It finds local minima, so use many starts: single starts got stuck at a WSS of 70 or 110, against 15.5.
Choosing k: a sharp elbow at 4, and the best average silhouette, 0.755.
Hierarchical clustering builds a dendrogram; the linkage defines the distance between clusters. Complete, single and average linkage all found the same four groups as k-means.
Profiles name the clusters: light sweet, heavy sour, waxy and medium sour, with the waxy crudes invisible on gravity and sulfur alone.
Unscaled data gave a confident and wrong answer. The answer key confirmed the scaled clustering perfectly.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download crude_assays.csv and crude_kinds.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Plot the silhouettes. plot(cluster::silhouette(km$cluster, dist(Z))). Which crudes have the lowest silhouettes, and why?
Clusters on principal components. Plot the crudes’ first two principal component scores, colored by cluster. How much of the separation do two components show?
Ward’s method. Cluster with hclust(dist(Z), method = "ward.D2"), and compare its dendrogram with complete linkage’s.
Robustness. Drop one property at a time, recluster, and compare with the original clusters using table(). Which property, if dropped, loses the waxy cluster?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Clustering

Dividing observations into groups so that observations in the same group are similar, with no labels to learn from.

k-means

A clustering method that minimizes the total within-cluster sum of squared distances to the cluster means.

Lloyd’s algorithm

The iteration behind k-means: assign each point to the nearest center, move each center to its points’ mean, repeat.

Within-cluster sum of squares (WSS)

The sum, over all points, of the squared distance to their cluster’s center.

Elbow plot

The WSS against k, used to choose the number of clusters.

Silhouette

For each point, (b - a)/\max(a, b), comparing its distance to its own cluster with its distance to the nearest other cluster.

Hierarchical clustering

Building a tree of nested clusters by repeatedly merging the closest pair.

Dendrogram

The tree that hierarchical clustering produces, with merge heights as distances.

Linkage

The rule for the distance between two clusters: complete, single, average or Ward’s.











NoteWant to read more?






James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition), section 12.4, “Clustering Methods”, with its lab in section 12.5.3.
Leonard Kaufman and Peter Rousseeuw, Finding Groups in Data: An Introduction to Cluster Analysis (Wiley, 1990, reissued 2005). The book behind the cluster package, including the silhouette.
Peter Rousseeuw, “Silhouettes: a graphical aid to the interpretation and validation of cluster analysis”, Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics 20, 1987, doi:10.1016/0377-0427(87)90125-7.

title: Neural networks
text:
Module 7 · Lesson 11 of 14 Week 114 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Neural networks are behind almost every headline about artificial intelligence: image recognition, translation, chatbots. Those networks have billions of parameters and need specialized hardware. But the idea underneath is old and small, and you already know its building block. This lesson builds a neural network from that block, trains one by hand, and then uses R’s nnet package for the kind of small networks that suit plant data: a few inputs, a few hundred or thousand samples, and one hidden layer.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Neural networks
text:
One neuron
A neuron (or unit) takes inputs x_1, \ldots, x_p, forms a weighted sum plus a bias, and passes it through an activation function g:

a = g\big(b + w_1 x_1 + \cdots + w_p x_p\big) .

With the sigmoid activation g(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z}), the output is between 0 and 1, and the neuron is exactly a logistic regression: the weights are its coefficients, the bias its intercept. Other common activations are \tanh(z), which is a sigmoid stretched to run from -1 to 1, and the ReLU, \max(0, z), the default in deep learning:

z <- seq(-4, 4, by = 0.05)
act <- rbind(data.frame(z, g = 1 / (1 + exp(-z)), f = "sigmoid"), data.frame(z, g = tanh(z), f = "tanh"),
             data.frame(z, g = pmax(0, z), f = "ReLU"))
act$f <- factor(act$f, c("sigmoid", "tanh", "ReLU"))
ggplot(act, aes(z, g)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey80") + geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~f) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-1.1, 2)) + labs(x = "z", y = "g(z)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The setup code loads the boiler data (scaled, in B), the reactor alarms (standardized, in Fz), and the soft sensor’s four chemistry tags (standardized, in S), with the folds from earlier lessons. Scaling the inputs matters for networks, as it does for kNN and SVMs, for a reason explained below.












Your turn. Lesson 4’s logistic regression of fault on the temperature deviation and the valve’s SD had coefficients -2.989, 1.419 and 1.594. Treat it as a neuron: compute its output for alarm A001 by hand.









The sigmoid of the weighted sum: exp(-z).


w <- coef(glm(fault ~ temp_dev_C + valve_sd_pct, family = binomial, data = faults))
x <- c(1, faults$temp_dev_C[1], faults$valve_sd_pct[1])
z <- sum(w * x)
1 / (1 + exp(-z))
0.781, exactly Lesson 4’s predicted probability for A001. The neuron’s weighted sum is the log-odds, and its sigmoid turns it into a probability. Every unit in a network does this, with its own weights.

title: Neural networks
text:
Training by gradient descent
glm() fits a logistic regression with Newton’s method (iteratively reweighted least squares). Neural networks are trained with something simpler: gradient descent. Start with some weights, compute the gradient of the loss (here, the average log loss) with respect to every weight, and take a small step downhill:

w \leftarrow w - \eta \, \nabla L(w) .

\eta is the learning rate. For a single sigmoid neuron with the log loss, the gradient has a famously simple form: \nabla L = \frac{1}{n} X^\top(\hat p - y), the inputs weighted by the errors.
Your turn. Starting from zero weights, run 2,000 steps of gradient descent with \eta = 0.5 on the standardized inputs, and compare the weights with glm()’s coefficients on the same inputs.









The gradient uses the errors, p - y.


Z <- cbind(1, scale(faults$temp_dev_C), scale(faults$valve_sd_pct))
y <- faults$fault
w <- c(0, 0, 0)
for (step in 1:2000) {
  p <- 1 / (1 + exp(-Z %*% w))
  w <- w - 0.5 * t(Z) %*% (p - y) / nrow(Z)
}
rbind(gradient_descent = as.numeric(w), glm = coef(glm(y ~ Z[, 2] + Z[, 3], family = binomial)))
The same to four decimals: 0.1875, 1.6673 and 1.4117. After only 100 steps, they’d be 0.16, 1.61 and 1.32: close, but not there. Gradient descent is slower than Newton’s method, but each step is cheap, and it works for any differentiable model, however many layers it has. With inputs on very different scales, it crawls, because one learning rate has to suit every weight; that’s one reason networks need scaled inputs.

title: Neural networks
section: A network with a hidden layer
text:
A network with a hidden layer
A single neuron draws a straight boundary. Put several neurons side by side in a hidden layer, each looking at the inputs with its own weights, and feed their outputs to an output unit:

h_k = g\big(b_k + w_k^\top x\big), \quad k = 1, \ldots, H, \qquad \hat y = c_0 + \sum_{k=1}^H c_k h_k .

The hidden units create new features, each a smooth step in some direction of the input space, and the output combines them. With enough hidden units, this can approximate any continuous function: that’s the universal approximation theorem. For regression, the output is linear; for classification, it goes through a sigmoid (two classes) or a softmax (several), as in Lesson 4.
Your turn. Compute the output of a network with 2 inputs, 2 tanh hidden units and a linear output, for the input x = (1, 2). The hidden weights are the rows of W1, the hidden biases b1, the output weights W2 and the output bias b2.









Each hidden unit adds its bias, b1.


W1 <- matrix(c(0.5, -1,
               2, 0.3), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
b1 <- c(0.1, -0.2)
W2 <- c(1.5, -0.8)
b2 <- 0.4
x <- c(1, 2)
h <- tanh(W1 %*% x + b1)
b2 + sum(W2 * h)
-1.715. The hidden units’ weighted sums are -1.4 and 2.4, their tanh outputs -0.885 and 0.984, and the output is 0.4 + 1.5 \times (-0.885) - 0.8 \times 0.984. With many inputs, many hidden units and many samples, this is two matrix products and an elementwise function, which is why networks run so fast on hardware built for matrix arithmetic.

title: Neural networks
text:
Backpropagation
Training a network means gradient descent on all its weights at once. The gradient with respect to the output weights is easy: it’s like a linear regression’s. For the hidden weights, the chain rule carries the error backwards through the network: each hidden unit’s share of the error is the output error times its output weight times the slope of its activation (1 - h^2 for tanh). That’s backpropagation: one forward pass to compute the predictions, one backward pass to compute every gradient.
Your turn. Fit a network with 3 tanh hidden units to the boiler’s efficiency against load (both scaled), with 3,000 steps of gradient descent at \eta = 0.1. Complete the backward pass, and find the RMSE in efficiency points.









The derivative of \tanh(z) is 1 - \tanh(z)^2: (1 - hid^2).


x <- B$load
y <- (B$eff - 84) / 2
set.seed(7111)
H <- 3
W1 <- rnorm(H); b1 <- rnorm(H); W2 <- rnorm(H); b2 <- 0
for (step in 1:3000) {
  hid <- tanh(outer(x, W1) + matrix(b1, length(x), H, byrow = TRUE))
  e <- as.numeric(hid %*% W2 + b2 - y)
  gW2 <- colMeans(hid * e); gb2 <- mean(e)
  d_hid <- outer(e, W2) * (1 - hid^2)
  gW1 <- colMeans(d_hid * x); gb1 <- colMeans(d_hid)
  W2 <- W2 - 0.1 * gW2; b2 <- b2 - 0.1 * gb2; W1 <- W1 - 0.1 * gW1; b1 <- b1 - 0.1 * gb1
}
2 * sqrt(mean(e^2))
An RMSE of 0.80 points with load alone, against 1.74 for a straight line in load, and 0.76 for Lesson 9’s natural spline. Ten parameters and 3,000 small steps have bent three tanh curves into the boiler’s efficiency curve. Every deep-learning library does exactly this, with automatic differentiation instead of hand-written gradients, and with smarter step rules than a fixed \eta.





x <- (boiler$load_pct - 65) / 20; y <- (boiler$efficiency_pct - 84) / 2
set.seed(7111); H <- 3; W1 <- rnorm(H); b1 <- rnorm(H); W2 <- rnorm(H); b2 <- 0
for (step in 1:3000) {
  hid <- tanh(outer(x, W1) + matrix(b1, length(x), H, byrow = TRUE)); e <- as.numeric(hid %*% W2 + b2 - y)
  gW2 <- colMeans(hid * e); gb2 <- mean(e); d_hid <- outer(e, W2) * (1 - hid^2)
  gW1 <- colMeans(d_hid * x); gb1 <- colMeans(d_hid)
  W2 <- W2 - 0.1 * gW2; b2 <- b2 - 0.1 * gb2; W1 <- W1 - 0.1 * gW1; b1 <- b1 - 0.1 * gb1
}
gx <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = 200)
gh <- tanh(outer(gx, W1) + matrix(b1, 200, H, byrow = TRUE))
fitdf <- data.frame(load = 65 + 20 * gx, eff = 84 + 2 * (gh %*% W2 + b2))
units <- data.frame(load = rep(65 + 20 * gx, H), eff = 78 + as.vector(sweep(gh, 2, W2, "*")), unit = rep(1:H, each = 200))
ggplot(boiler, aes(load_pct, efficiency_pct)) + geom_point(color = "grey70", size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = units, aes(load, eff, group = unit), linetype = "dashed", color = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = fitdf, aes(load, eff), color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Load (%)", y = "Efficiency (%)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12)














NoteGo deeper: the chain rule, written out





Take one sample, with squared-error loss L = \tfrac12 e^2, e = \hat y - y, \hat y = b_2 + \sum_k c_k h_k and h_k = \tanh(a_k), a_k = b_{1k} + w_k x. Then

\frac{\partial L}{\partial c_k} = e\,h_k, \qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_k} = \underbrace{e \, c_k}_{\partial L/\partial h_k} \cdot \underbrace{(1 - h_k^2)}_{\partial h_k/\partial a_k} \cdot \underbrace{x}_{\partial a_k/\partial w_k} .

The code averages these over the samples. The middle factor is why activations matter: a sigmoid’s slope is at most 1/4, and in a deep network the product of many such factors shrinks toward zero (the vanishing gradient problem). ReLU’s slope is 1 wherever it’s active, which is one reason deep learning switched to it. The Elements of Statistical Learning, section 11.4, derives backpropagation for a general single-hidden-layer network.

title: Neural networks
text:
Networks with nnet
nnet::nnet() fits networks with one hidden layer, using a quasi-Newton optimizer (BFGS) instead of plain gradient descent. Its main arguments:

size: the number of hidden units;
decay: weight decay, a ridge penalty \lambda\sum w^2 on all the weights, which keeps the network smooth;
linout = TRUE for a linear output (regression); the default is a sigmoid output (classification);
maxit: the maximum number of iterations.

Weight decay penalizes all weights alike, so the inputs should be on similar scales. That’s the other reason for scaling.
Your turn. Fit a network with 5 hidden units and a decay of 0.01 to the boiler’s efficiency, using all three scaled inputs. Find the training RMSE and the number of weights.









For regression, the output is linear: linout = TRUE.


set.seed(7112)
net <- nnet::nnet(eff ~ load + o2 + air, data = B, size = 5, decay = 0.01, linout = TRUE, maxit = 1000, trace = FALSE)
c(train_rmse = sqrt(mean((B$eff - predict(net))^2)), n_weights = length(net$wts))
A training RMSE of 0.44 points, with 26 weights: (3 + 1) \times 5 into the hidden layer, and (5 + 1) into the output. That’s close to the noise level of 0.45. Without linout = TRUE, the output would pass through a sigmoid and could never exceed 1, so every prediction of an efficiency of 85% would fail silently: a classic nnet mistake.




Your turn. A network’s loss surface has many local minima, and nnet() starts from random weights. Fit the same network without weight decay from 5 different random starts (seeds 1 to 5), and compare the training RMSEs.









Each start uses its own seed, s.


sapply(1:5, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  net <- nnet::nnet(eff ~ load + o2 + air, data = B, size = 5, decay = 0, linout = TRUE, maxit = 1000, trace = FALSE)
  sqrt(mean((B$eff - predict(net))^2))
})
About 2.47, 0.45, 0.73, 0.44 and 0.48: the same network, five answers. The first start got stuck in a poor local minimum, with an error worse than a straight line’s, and the third is mediocre. Weight decay helps (it smooths the loss surface), and in practice, you fit several starts and keep the best, or average their predictions. The exact numbers can differ slightly between computers, because the optimizer’s path is sensitive to tiny rounding differences.

title: Neural networks
text:
Tuning a network
The size and the decay are tuning parameters, and cross-validation chooses them, as always. On these data, sizes of 2, 5 and 10 and decays of 0.001, 0.01 and 0.1 give CV RMSEs from 0.47 (size 5, decay 0.01) to 0.71 (size 2): two hidden units are too few for the curves, and ten overfit unless the decay restrains them.
Your turn. Cross-validate the network with 5 hidden units and a decay of 0.01, on Lesson 9’s folds.









Predict the held-out fold, B[fold == j, ].


err <- numeric(400)
for (j in 1:10) {
  set.seed(7113)
  net <- nnet::nnet(eff ~ load + o2 + air, data = B[fold != j, ], size = 5, decay = 0.01,
                    linout = TRUE, maxit = 1000, trace = FALSE)
  err[fold == j] <- B$eff[fold == j] - predict(net, B[fold == j, ])
}
sqrt(mean(err^2))
About 0.47, essentially tied with Lesson 9’s GAM (0.462) on the same folds, and four times better than the linear model (1.70). The network found the load curve, the oxygen sweet spot and the air temperature’s effect without being told any of their shapes. But the GAM got there with a model you can plot term by term and test, and the network is a set of 26 weights that mean nothing on their own. When the two tie, the interpretable one usually wins.




Your turn. Classify the reactor alarms with a network: 3 hidden units, a decay of 0.1, and a softmax output (nnet() uses one automatically when the response is a factor with more than two levels). Cross-validate it on Lessons 4 and 5’s folds.









type = "class" returns the predicted classes.


pred <- factor(rep(NA, 800), levels = levels(Fz$cause))
for (j in 1:10) {
  set.seed(7114)
  net <- nnet::nnet(cause ~ ., data = Fz[ffold != j, ], size = 3, decay = 0.1, maxit = 1000, trace = FALSE)
  pred[ffold == j] <- predict(net, Fz[ffold == j, ], type = "class")
}
mean(pred != Fz$cause)
18.25% wrong: better than multinomial regression (20.1%), about the same as LDA, and not as good as QDA (15.6%). Over sizes of 3 to 10 and decays of 0.01 to 1, the best is 18.1%. The network can, in principle, learn QDA’s curved boundaries, but with 800 alarms and a hundred-odd weights, it can’t find them as reliably as a model that assumes the right shape. Flexible models need data in proportion to their flexibility.

title: Neural networks
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The soft sensor. Cross-validate a network with 2 hidden units and a decay of 0.01 on the soft sensor’s four chemistry tags, with Lesson 2’s time blocks as folds, and compare it with a linear model on the same blocks.









Predict the held-out block, S[block == j, ].


e_net <- numeric(500); e_lin <- numeric(500)
for (j in 1:10) {
  set.seed(7115)
  net <- nnet::nnet(y ~ ., data = S[block != j, ], size = 2, decay = 0.01, linout = TRUE, maxit = 1000, trace = FALSE)
  e_net[block == j] <- S$y[block == j] - predict(net, S[block == j, ])
  e_lin[block == j] <- S$y[block == j] - predict(lm(y ~ ., data = S[block != j, ]), S[block == j, ])
}
c(network = sqrt(mean(e_net^2)), linear = sqrt(mean(e_lin^2)))
About 0.205 for the network and 0.194 for the linear model: the network is worse. The chemistry makes \log(\text{MI}) nearly linear in these tags, so the network’s flexibility only adds variance, and the blocked folds, which ask it to predict weeks it hasn’t seen, punish that. Larger networks did no better (0.21). A neural network is a tool for unknown, strongly nonlinear relationships with plenty of data, not a universal upgrade.




Challenge 2 · Counting weights. How many weights does a network with p inputs, one hidden layer of H units and K outputs have, counting the biases? Write a function, and use it for the alarm network with 10 hidden units (p = 6, K = 4) and for a network with 100 inputs (a spectrum), 20 hidden units and one output.









Each output unit has a weight from each hidden unit, plus a bias: H + 1.


n_weights <- function(p, H, K) (p + 1) * H + (H + 1) * K
c(alarms = n_weights(6, 10, 4), spectra = n_weights(100, 20, 1))
114 for the alarm network and 2,041 for the spectrum network, which would be trained on 80 calibration samples. Without a strong decay penalty, that network would interpolate the calibration data perfectly and predict nothing. nnet() refuses networks with more than 1,000 weights unless you raise MaxNWts, a hint that small networks are what it’s for.

title: Neural networks
text:
Quick quiz

1. A single neuron with a sigmoid activation is equivalent to what?

A decision tree
Logistic regression
kNN


Its weighted sum is the log-odds, and the sigmoid turns it into a probability.



2. What does backpropagation compute?

The predictions
The gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, by the chain rule
The best number of hidden units


A forward pass gives the predictions; the backward pass gives the gradients.



3. What is weight decay?

Shrinking the learning rate over time
A ridge penalty on the network’s weights
Removing hidden units


It keeps the network smooth, and it’s tuned by cross-validation like ridge’s \lambda.



4. Why did five fits of the same network give different errors?

The data changed
Training starts from random weights, and the loss surface has many local minima
nnet() has a bug


Fit several starts and keep the best, or average them.



5. What happens if you forget linout = TRUE for a regression?

The output goes through a sigmoid, so it can’t predict values above 1
Nothing
The network becomes linear


For an efficiency near 85, every prediction would be wrong.



6. On the soft sensor, the linear model beat the network. Why?

Networks can’t do regression
The relationship is nearly linear, so the network’s flexibility only added variance
The network had too few inputs


Flexibility pays only when there’s nonlinearity to find, and enough data to find it.

title: Neural networks
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve built a neural network from its parts, and learned when to use one. Here’s what you’ve learned:

A neuron is a weighted sum and an activation. With a sigmoid, it’s a logistic regression.
Gradient descent steps downhill on the loss. For the neuron, 2,000 steps reproduced glm()’s coefficients.
A hidden layer builds new features from the inputs, and backpropagation gets every gradient with the chain rule. Your hand-written network fitted the efficiency curve with an RMSE of 0.80.
nnet fits one-hidden-layer networks. Scale the inputs, use linout = TRUE for regression, use weight decay, and try several random starts.
Tuned by CV, the network tied the boiler GAM (about 0.47 against 0.462), was beaten by QDA on the alarms (18% against 15.6%), and lost to a linear model on the soft sensor.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download the three data files into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Plot the network. Install NeuralNetTools and run plotnet(net) on the boiler network. Then garson(net) and olden(net) give two measures of each input’s importance. Do they agree with the GAM?
Average several starts. Fit the boiler network from 10 random starts, average their predictions, and cross-validate the average. Is it better than one network?
A ReLU network. Change your backpropagation code to use ReLU, \max(0, z), whose derivative is 1 for positive z and 0 otherwise. How many hidden units does it need to match the tanh network?
Learning rate. Rerun your backpropagation with \eta = 0.01, 0.1 and 1, and plot the RMSE against the step number for each.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Neuron (unit)

A function that forms a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, and applies an activation function.

Activation function

The nonlinear function in a neuron: sigmoid, tanh or ReLU, for example.

Hidden layer

A layer of neurons between the inputs and the output.

Gradient descent

Minimizing a function by repeatedly stepping against its gradient.

Learning rate

The size of each gradient descent step, \eta.

Backpropagation

Computing the gradient of a network’s loss with respect to all its weights, with the chain rule, from the output back to the inputs.

Weight decay

A ridge penalty on a network’s weights.

Universal approximation theorem

The result that a network with one hidden layer and enough units can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region.

Local minimum

A point where the loss is lower than all nearby points, but not the lowest overall.











NoteWant to read more?






James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition), chapter 10, “Deep Learning”, sections 10.1, 10.2 and 10.7 (fitting a network).
Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, chapter 11, “Neural Networks”, including the issues in training them (section 11.5).
Michael Nielsen, Neural Networks and Deep Learning (free online book), chapter 2, “How the backpropagation algorithm works”.
William Venables and Brian Ripley, Modern Applied Statistics with S (4th edition, Springer, 2002), section 8.10, on nnet(), by its authors.

title: Beyond linearity
text:
Module 7 · Lesson 9 of 14 Week 112 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The plant’s main boiler burns natural gas to raise steam, and every percentage point of efficiency is worth about €150,000 a year in gas. The utilities engineer logged 400 hours of operation: the load (steam output as a percentage of the boiler’s rating), the excess oxygen in the flue gas, the air temperature at the burner inlet, and the efficiency computed from the gas and steam flows.
Boiler engineers know the shapes to expect. Efficiency peaks somewhere around three-quarters load and falls off steeply at low load, where the fixed heat losses become a bigger share. Excess oxygen has a sweet spot: too much means heating air that does nothing but carry heat up the stack, and too little means incomplete combustion. Neither is a straight line:
long <- rbind(data.frame(x = boiler$load_pct, eff = boiler$efficiency_pct, v = "Load (%)"),
              data.frame(x = boiler$excess_o2_pct, eff = boiler$efficiency_pct, v = "Excess oxygen (%)"))
ggplot(long, aes(x, eff)) + geom_point(color = "#C2416C", size = 0.9, alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~v, scales = "free_x") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Efficiency (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
Machine learning has very flexible methods for curves like these, coming in Lessons 10 and 11. This lesson stays closer to home: it extends the linear model, so that each predictor can have a curved effect, while the model stays easy to fit, to interpret and to test. These methods are workhorses of applied statistics, and in engineering they’re often all you need.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Beyond linearity
section: The linear model, and what it misses
text:
The linear model, and what it misses
The setup code reads the 400 hours and makes 10 random folds. It also defines cv_rmse(), which returns the 10-fold CV RMSE of any lm() formula. (These are hourly averages from a steady boiler, so their errors are close to independent, and random folds are fine here.)












Your turn. Fit a linear model of efficiency on all three predictors, and find its R^2 and its 10-fold CV RMSE.









Cross-validate the same formula, f_lin.


f_lin <- efficiency_pct ~ load_pct + excess_o2_pct + air_temp_C
c(r_squared = summary(lm(f_lin, data = boiler))$r.squared, cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_lin))
An R^2 of 0.53 and a CV RMSE of 1.70 points. A straight line through a curve with a peak in the middle captures only the overall rise, and the residuals carry the rest of the shape. The rest of this lesson brings the CV RMSE down to 0.46.

title: Beyond linearity
text:
Polynomials and step functions
The first two ways to bend a line, using load alone for now:

Polynomial regression adds x^2, x^3, \ldots, x^d as predictors. It’s still a linear model, linear in the coefficients, so lm() fits it. Its weakness is that it’s global: every coefficient affects the curve everywhere, and high-degree polynomials swing wildly at the ends of the data.
Step functions cut x into bins and fit a constant in each: cut(x, breaks) makes a factor. They’re local, but blocky, and the bins’ edges are arbitrary.

Your turn. Find the CV RMSE of polynomials in load of degree 1 to 8.









The degree is the function’s argument, d.


cv_poly <- sapply(1:8, function(d) cv_rmse(efficiency_pct ~ poly(load_pct, d)))
round(cv_poly, 3)
which.min(cv_poly)
Degree 4 is best, at 0.767, and degrees 3 to 8 are all within 0.01 of it. With load alone, about 0.77 is as low as any curve gets: the rest of the variation comes from the oxygen and the air temperature.




Your turn. Cut the load into 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 equal-width bins, and find each step function’s CV RMSE.









k bins need k + 1 break points: length.out = k + 1.


sapply(c(2, 4, 8, 16, 32), function(k) {
  breaks <- seq(29, 101, length.out = k + 1)
  cv_rmse(efficiency_pct ~ cut(load_pct, breaks))
})
2.05 with 2 bins, 1.24 with 4, 0.97 with 8, 0.84 with 16 and 0.85 with 32. More bins follow the curve better, until each bin holds too few hours to estimate its level well. Even the best step function is worse than the degree-4 polynomial (0.767), because inside each bin it ignores the slope, and on a curve as steep as this one at low load, that costs a lot. Step functions are most useful when the effect really does jump, at a regulation threshold or a change of equipment.

title: Beyond linearity
text:
Regression splines
A spline combines the best of both: it’s a polynomial within each region, like a step function with sloping, curving pieces, and the pieces join smoothly at the boundaries, called knots. A cubic spline uses cubic pieces that join with matching values, slopes and curvatures, so the joins are invisible. It’s fitted by least squares on a set of basis functions, so lm() fits it too:

bs(x, df) makes a cubic spline basis with df - 3 interior knots, placed at quantiles of x;
ns(x, df) makes a natural spline: a cubic spline that’s forced to be linear beyond the outermost knots. That tames the wild ends that plague polynomials, and costs fewer degrees of freedom.

Your turn. Find the CV RMSE of natural splines in load with 2 to 10 degrees of freedom.









Use df = d.


cv_ns <- sapply(2:10, function(d) cv_rmse(efficiency_pct ~ ns(load_pct, df = d)))
round(cv_ns, 4)
(2:10)[which.min(cv_ns)]
7 degrees of freedom is best, at 0.771, very close to the best polynomial (0.767). On a smooth curve over a well-covered range, splines and polynomials do about equally well. The difference shows in extrapolation, below: a natural spline continues as a straight line, and a polynomial goes wherever its highest power takes it. Here the gap is modest, a few points just outside the data, but it grows quickly with the distance, and with higher degrees.





grid <- data.frame(load_pct = seq(20, 110, by = 0.5))
fits <- rbind(
  data.frame(grid, eff = predict(lm(efficiency_pct ~ cut(load_pct, seq(29, 101, length.out = 9)), boiler),
                                 data.frame(load_pct = pmin(pmax(grid$load_pct, 29.5), 100.5))), m = "step, 8 bins"),
  data.frame(grid, eff = predict(lm(efficiency_pct ~ poly(load_pct, 4), boiler), grid), m = "polynomial, degree 4"),
  data.frame(grid, eff = predict(lm(efficiency_pct ~ ns(load_pct, df = 7), boiler), grid), m = "natural spline, df 7"))
ggplot(boiler, aes(load_pct, efficiency_pct)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 20, xmax = 30, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey92") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 100, xmax = 110, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey92") +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = fits, aes(y = eff, color = m), linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`step, 8 bins` = "#1baf7a", `polynomial, degree 4` = "#2a78d6", `natural spline, df 7` = "#C2416C"), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(65, 90)) +
  labs(x = "Load (%), gray: outside the data", y = "Efficiency (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Beyond linearity
text:
Smoothing splines
Regression splines need you to choose the knots, or at least how many. A smoothing spline sidesteps that: it puts a knot at every distinct x, and controls the wiggliness with a penalty instead, minimizing

\sum_i \big(y_i - g(x_i)\big)^2 + \lambda \int g''(t)^2 \, dt .

The integral of the squared second derivative measures roughness. With \lambda = 0, g interpolates the data; as \lambda \to \infty, it becomes a straight line. It’s the same idea as ridge regression, in Lesson 7: a penalty on complexity, with \lambda as the dial. smooth.spline() chooses \lambda automatically by generalized cross-validation (GCV), a fast approximation to leave-one-out CV, and reports the result as effective degrees of freedom.
Your turn. Fit a smoothing spline of efficiency on load, and find the effective degrees of freedom that GCV chose.









The response is efficiency_pct.


ss <- smooth.spline(boiler$load_pct, boiler$efficiency_pct)
ss$df
10.2 effective degrees of freedom, a little more flexible than the best natural spline (7). That’s common: GCV tends to choose slightly wigglier fits than k-fold CV, and with a smooth true curve, the differences in prediction are tiny. smooth.spline(..., df = 7) would fix the flexibility instead of choosing it.

title: Beyond linearity
text:
Generalized additive models
So far, one predictor at a time. A generalized additive model (GAM) gives each predictor its own smooth function, and adds them up:

y_i = \beta_0 + f_1(x_{i1}) + f_2(x_{i2}) + \cdots + f_p(x_{ip}) + \varepsilon_i .

Each f_j can be a spline, or linear, or a factor. The model keeps the most useful property of the linear model, additivity: each predictor’s effect can be plotted and understood on its own, holding the others fixed. “Generalized” means it extends to other response types, like logistic regression, through family =.
The mgcv package fits GAMs with penalized regression splines, s(x), and chooses each one’s smoothness automatically, much as smooth.spline() does.
Your turn. Fit a GAM with smooth functions of load and excess oxygen, and a linear term in the air temperature. Look at the smooth terms’ table and the R^2.









The second smooth is of excess_o2_pct.


g <- mgcv::gam(efficiency_pct ~ s(load_pct) + s(excess_o2_pct) + air_temp_C, data = boiler)
print(summary(g)$s.table)
summary(g)$r.sq
An R^2 of 0.967, against the linear model’s 0.53. The load’s smooth has 8.3 effective degrees of freedom (edf), and the oxygen’s 7.4: both are strongly curved. An edf near 1 would mean the term is close to a straight line. The air temperature’s linear coefficient, from coef(g), is 0.029: each extra degree of air temperature is worth 0.03 points of efficiency (warmer air needs less heating). The residual SD, 0.45, is the measurement noise: the GAM has captured essentially all the structure.




Each smooth term is a partial effect: the change in efficiency as that predictor varies, with the others held fixed. Here are both, with their 95% confidence bands:

g <- gam(efficiency_pct ~ s(load_pct) + s(excess_o2_pct) + air_temp_C, data = boiler)
mk <- function(v, lab) {
  nd <- data.frame(load_pct = 70, excess_o2_pct = 3, air_temp_C = 12)[rep(1, 200), ]
  nd[[v]] <- seq(min(boiler[[v]]), max(boiler[[v]]), length.out = 200)
  pr <- predict(g, nd, type = "terms", se.fit = TRUE)
  k <- paste0("s(", v, ")")
  data.frame(x = nd[[v]], fit = pr$fit[, k], lo = pr$fit[, k] - 2 * pr$se.fit[, k], hi = pr$fit[, k] + 2 * pr$se.fit[, k], v = lab)
}
pe <- rbind(mk("load_pct", "Load (%)"), mk("excess_o2_pct", "Excess oxygen (%)"))
ggplot(pe, aes(x, fit)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#F4C0D1") +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.9) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  facet_wrap(~v, scales = "free_x") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Partial effect on efficiency (points)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Your turn. Predict the efficiency at 75% load and an air temperature of 12 °C, for excess oxygen of 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4 and 5%.









The air temperature is 12 °C.


g <- mgcv::gam(efficiency_pct ~ s(load_pct) + s(excess_o2_pct) + air_temp_C, data = boiler)
nd <- data.frame(load_pct = 75, excess_o2_pct = c(1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5), air_temp_C = 12)
round(predict(g, nd), 2)
85.0% at 1.5% oxygen, 86.3 at 2%, 86.4 at 2.5%, 86.1 at 3%, 85.6 at 4% and 85.0 at 5%. The sweet spot is between 2 and 2.5%, the curve is steep on the low side (incomplete combustion) and gentle on the high side (heating extra air). The boiler’s operators typically run at 3.4% (the median), which is safe but costs about 0.5 points: roughly €75,000 a year, by the engineer’s rule of thumb. A good reason to tune the oxygen trim controller, carefully, given the cliff below 2%.




Your turn. Compare the 10-fold CV RMSE of the linear model and the GAM, on the same folds.









Predict the held-out fold, boiler[fold == j, ].


err <- numeric(400)
for (j in 1:10) {
  fit <- mgcv::gam(efficiency_pct ~ s(load_pct) + s(excess_o2_pct) + air_temp_C, data = boiler[fold != j, ])
  err[fold == j] <- boiler$efficiency_pct[fold == j] - predict(fit, boiler[fold == j, ])
}
c(linear = cv_rmse(efficiency_pct ~ load_pct + excess_o2_pct + air_temp_C), gam = sqrt(mean(err^2)))
1.70 for the linear model, 0.46 for the GAM: almost four times smaller, and at the noise level. An additive model with natural splines (ns(load_pct, 5) + ns(excess_o2_pct, 5) + air_temp_C, fitted by lm()) gets 0.48, nearly as good: the automatic smoothness selection gains a little, and saves choosing the knots.










NoteGo deeper: how mgcv chooses the smoothness





s(x) builds a thin-plate regression spline: a basis of (by default) 10 functions, with a penalty \lambda_j \beta_j^\top S_j \beta_j on each term’s wiggliness, like a smoothing spline’s \int g''^2. The GAM is then a penalized least-squares (or penalized likelihood) problem, and the \lambda_j are chosen by GCV (the default for gam()) or by REML, which treats the penalized coefficients as random effects, as in Module 3’s mixed models. Simon Wood, mgcv’s author, recommends method = "REML": it’s less prone to undersmoothing. The edf of each term is the trace of its part of the “hat” matrix, the same effective degrees of freedom as in ridge regression. If an edf is close to the basis size minus one (9, by default), the basis may be too small: gam.check() tests that, and s(x, k = 20) enlarges it.

title: Beyond linearity
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Is there an interaction? Additivity assumes that the oxygen’s effect is the same at every load. Add a tensor-product interaction, ti(load_pct, excess_o2_pct), and test it against the additive model with anova(..., test = "F"). Fit both with method = "REML".









The interaction term is ti(load_pct, excess_o2_pct).


g_add <- mgcv::gam(efficiency_pct ~ s(load_pct) + s(excess_o2_pct) + air_temp_C, data = boiler, method = "REML")
g_int <- mgcv::gam(efficiency_pct ~ s(load_pct) + s(excess_o2_pct) + ti(load_pct, excess_o2_pct) + air_temp_C,
                   data = boiler, method = "REML")
a <- anova(g_add, g_int, test = "F")
a$`Pr(>F)`[2]
p = 0.39: no evidence of an interaction. The interaction term’s edf is 1.0, the smallest it can be, so REML has shrunk it to almost nothing. The additive model is enough: the best oxygen level is the same at every load. ti() adds only the interaction, on top of the main effects; te() would fit the whole two-dimensional surface in one term.




Challenge 2 · The best load. The plant can share steam demand between two boilers, so it can choose each one’s load. Use optimize() on the GAM’s prediction to find the load with the highest efficiency, at 2.5% oxygen and 12 °C air.









optimize() minimizes unless maximum = TRUE.


g <- mgcv::gam(efficiency_pct ~ s(load_pct) + s(excess_o2_pct) + air_temp_C, data = boiler)
best <- optimize(function(l) predict(g, data.frame(load_pct = l, excess_o2_pct = 2.5, air_temp_C = 12)),
                 interval = c(30, 100), maximum = TRUE)
c(load = best$maximum, efficiency = unname(best$objective))
74% load, for an efficiency of 86.4%. The peak is broad: from the partial effect, anywhere between about 65% and 85% load is within a few tenths of a point of it. For two identical boilers sharing a total demand of 150%, running both at 75% (86.4% each) beats running one at 100% (85.2%) and the other at 50% (84.4%). That’s the kind of decision a smooth, interpretable model supports and a black box makes harder. Because the model is additive, the best load doesn’t depend on the oxygen level or the air temperature.

title: Beyond linearity
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why can lm() fit a degree-4 polynomial?

It can’t; you need nls()
The model is still linear in its coefficients; the powers of x are just new predictors
lm() approximates it


Splines work the same way: lm() on a set of basis functions.



2. What’s the main weakness of a high-degree polynomial?

It can’t fit curves
It’s global, and it swings wildly near and beyond the ends of the data
It needs too many knots


Splines are local, and natural splines are linear beyond the outer knots.



3. What is a knot?

A point where the spline is discontinuous
A point where two polynomial pieces join
An outlier


In a cubic spline, the pieces join with matching values, slopes and curvatures.



4. What controls a smoothing spline’s flexibility?

The number of knots
A penalty \lambda on its roughness, \int g''^2
The polynomial degree


It has a knot at every data point; the penalty does the smoothing, chosen by GCV.



5. What does “additive” mean in a GAM?

It adds more data
The predictors’ effects add up, so each can be plotted with the others held fixed
It adds an interaction for every pair of predictors


Interactions can be added explicitly, with ti() or te().



6. A smooth term in a GAM has an edf of 1.0. What does that mean?

It’s a constant
It’s effectively a straight line
It’s very wiggly


Larger edf means more curvature.

title: Beyond linearity
text:
Wrap-up
You can now fit curved relationships while keeping a model you can read. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Polynomials are linear models in powers of x: degree 4 in load gave a CV RMSE of 0.767. They’re global, and wild at the edges.
Step functions cut x into bins: local but blocky.
Regression splines join polynomial pieces smoothly at knots. Natural splines are linear beyond the outer knots: 7 df was best, at 0.771.
Smoothing splines penalize roughness, and GCV chose 10 df.
GAMs add a smooth function of each predictor: the boiler GAM’s CV RMSE was 0.46, against 1.70 for the linear model, with R^2 = 0.967.
Partial effects showed an efficiency peak near 74% load and an oxygen sweet spot between 2 and 2.5%, and a test found no interaction.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download boiler_efficiency.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and use mgcv (it comes with R).

Plot the GAM. plot(g, pages = 1, residuals = TRUE) draws the partial effects with partial residuals. Do the residuals show any pattern the smooth missed?
Check the basis. Run gam.check(g). Is the default basis size big enough for load?
Local regression. Fit loess(efficiency_pct ~ load_pct, span = s) for spans of 0.2, 0.4 and 0.75, and compare their fits with the natural spline.
A logistic GAM. Define a “poor hour” as efficiency below 84%, and fit gam(poor ~ s(load_pct) + s(excess_o2_pct), family = binomial). Plot the partial effects on the log-odds scale.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Polynomial regression

A linear model with powers of a predictor, x, x^2, \ldots, x^d, as terms.

Step function

A piecewise-constant fit, made by cutting a predictor into bins.

Knot

A point where the pieces of a spline join.

Cubic spline

A piecewise cubic polynomial whose pieces join with continuous first and second derivatives.

Natural spline

A cubic spline constrained to be linear beyond its boundary knots.

Smoothing spline

A function that minimizes the residual sum of squares plus a penalty on its roughness, \lambda\int g''(t)^2dt.

Generalized additive model (GAM)

A model in which the response (or its link) is a sum of smooth functions of the predictors.

Partial effect

The change in the response as one predictor varies with the others held fixed.

Generalized cross-validation (GCV)

A fast approximation to leave-one-out CV for linear smoothers.











NoteWant to read more?






James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition), chapter 7, “Moving Beyond Linearity”, which covers every method in this lesson.
Simon Wood, Generalized Additive Models: An Introduction with R (2nd edition, CRC Press, 2017). The book by mgcv’s author.
Noam Ross, GAMs in R, a free, interactive online course on mgcv.

title: Ridge regression
text:
Module 7 · Lesson 7 of 14 Week 110 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The solvent plant blends ethanol, water and glycerol, and the blend’s ethanol content has to be right. The lab’s gas chromatograph takes 40 minutes per sample. A near-infrared (NIR) analyzer on the line takes a spectrum every few seconds: the light absorbed at each of 100 wavelengths from 1,100 to 2,486 nm. Ethanol absorbs at some wavelengths, water and glycerol at others, and their bands overlap. The analyzer needs a calibration: a model that turns 100 absorbances into an ethanol percentage.
nir_spectra.csv has 120 calibration samples, each with its spectrum and its ethanol content from the GC. Here are 20 of them:
sp <- data.frame(wl = rep(wl, each = 20), A = as.vector(X[1:20, ]), ethanol = rep(y[1:20], 100), id = rep(1:20, 100))
ggplot(sp, aes(wl, A, group = id, color = ethanol)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_color_gradient(low = "#F4C0D1", high = "#3A1F35", name = "Ethanol (%)") +
  labs(x = "Wavelength (nm)", y = "Absorbance") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
The differences that carry the ethanol information are small, they’re spread across many wavelengths, and they’re mixed with the other components’ bands and a random offset for each sample. This is the classic setting for regularization: many correlated predictors, few samples. Chemometricians have calibrated spectrometers this way for decades, and this lesson and the next two use their problem.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Ridge regression
text:
Least squares with 100 predictors
The setup code reads the spectra into a 120 \times 100 matrix X, with the ethanol in y, and picks 80 samples at random for calibration (train); the other 40 are for testing. It also defines a grid of \lambda values, lam, which you’ll need later.













Your turn. Find the correlations between neighboring wavelengths: wavelength 1 with 2, 2 with 3, and so on.









The neighbor of wavelength i is wavelength i + 1: 2:100.


r <- cor(X)
range(r[cbind(1:99, 2:100)])
From 0.90 to 0.9987. Neighboring wavelengths carry almost the same information, and so, to a lesser degree, do wavelengths far apart, since all of them move with the sample’s offset. r[cbind(i, j)] picks the elements (i_1, j_1), (i_2, j_2), \ldots of a matrix, here the entries just above the diagonal.




With 80 calibration samples and 101 coefficients (an intercept and 100 slopes), least squares has more unknowns than equations. There are infinitely many coefficient vectors that fit the 80 samples exactly.
Your turn. Fit least squares to the 80 calibration samples. Find the fit’s rank, the number of coefficients lm() sets to NA, the training RMSE and the test RMSE (with the NA coefficients set to 0).









The test samples are y[-train].


ols <- lm(y[train] ~ X[train, ])
b <- coef(ols)
b[is.na(b)] <- 0
pred <- cbind(1, X[-train, ]) %*% b
c(rank = ols$rank, n_na = sum(is.na(coef(ols))),
  train_rmse = sqrt(mean(resid(ols)^2)), test_rmse = sqrt(mean((y[-train] - pred)^2)))
A rank of 80, so 21 coefficients are NA. The training RMSE is 0, a perfect fit, and the test RMSE is 9.9 percentage points, when the ethanol content itself only ranges from 5% to 30% (its SD is about 7). This is Lesson 1’s overfitting at its most extreme: with as many parameters as samples, the model can fit anything, noise included. Even with only every fifth wavelength (20 predictors), the test RMSE is 1.13, and the coefficients reach \pm 85, enormous positive and negative weights on neighboring wavelengths that nearly cancel.

title: Ridge regression
text:
Ridge regression
Ridge regression keeps all the predictors but stops the coefficients from growing large. It minimizes the residual sum of squares plus a penalty on the size of the coefficients:

\hat\beta^{\text{ridge}} = \arg\min_\beta \; \sum_{i=1}^n \Big(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^p x_{ij}\beta_j\Big)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j^2 .

The tuning parameter \lambda \ge 0 sets the trade-off. At \lambda = 0, it’s least squares. As \lambda grows, the coefficients shrink toward zero, and at \lambda = \infty, they’re all zero and the model predicts the mean. The intercept isn’t penalized.
The penalty treats every \beta_j alike, so the predictors should be on comparable scales: the usual practice is to standardize them first. With standardized predictors Z and a centered response, ridge has a closed-form solution, just like least squares:

\hat\beta^{\text{ridge}} = (Z^\top Z + \lambda I)^{-1} Z^\top y .

Adding \lambda to the diagonal makes the matrix invertible however many predictors there are. That’s where the name comes from: a “ridge” added along the diagonal.
Your turn. Standardize the calibration spectra, compute the ridge coefficients for \lambda = 1 by hand, and find the test RMSE. Standardize the test spectra with the calibration means and SDs.









The identity matrix is 100 \times 100: diag(100).


mu <- colMeans(X[train, ])
s <- apply(X[train, ], 2, sd)
Z <- scale(X[train, ], center = mu, scale = s)
yc <- y[train] - mean(y[train])
beta <- solve(crossprod(Z) + 1 * diag(100), crossprod(Z, yc))
pred <- mean(y[train]) + scale(X[-train, ], center = mu, scale = s) %*% beta
sqrt(mean((y[-train] - pred)^2))
A test RMSE of 0.41 percentage points: 24 times better than least squares, from one extra term. crossprod(Z) is Z^\top Z, and crossprod(Z, yc) is Z^\top y. The intercept is the mean of the calibration y, because the predictors are centered.

title: Ridge regression
text:
The penalty’s dial
Your turn. Repeat the calculation for \lambda = 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10 and 100, and find the test RMSE for each.









The penalty is the function’s argument, l.


mu <- colMeans(X[train, ])
s <- apply(X[train, ], 2, sd)
Z <- scale(X[train, ], center = mu, scale = s)
yc <- y[train] - mean(y[train])
Ztest <- scale(X[-train, ], center = mu, scale = s)
sapply(c(0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100), function(l) {
  beta <- solve(crossprod(Z) + l * diag(100), crossprod(Z, yc))
  sqrt(mean((y[-train] - mean(y[train]) - Ztest %*% beta)^2))
})
0.68, 0.51, 0.41, 0.72 and 2.34. Lesson 1’s U-shape again, with \lambda as the dial: too little penalty lets the coefficients chase the noise (high variance), too much shrinks away the real signal (high bias). \lambda = 1 is the best of these five. But choosing \lambda by the test set uses up the test set, so in practice it’s chosen by cross-validation, below.




How flexible is a ridge fit? Least squares with p predictors uses p degrees of freedom. Ridge uses fewer, because the penalty restrains them. Its effective degrees of freedom come from the singular values d_j of Z:

\text{df}(\lambda) = \sum_j \frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2 + \lambda} .

Each direction in the data counts as one degree of freedom if its d_j^2 is much larger than \lambda, and as almost nothing if it’s much smaller.
Your turn. Compute the effective degrees of freedom at \lambda = 1.









Use \lambda = 1.


mu <- colMeans(X[train, ])
s <- apply(X[train, ], 2, sd)
Z <- scale(X[train, ], center = mu, scale = s)
d <- svd(Z)$d
sum(d^2 / (d^2 + 1))
34 effective degrees of freedom, from 100 predictors. At \lambda = 0.01, 10 and 100, it’s 75, 11 and 4. The first three squared singular values are 5,328, 2,016 and 389, and they fall below 1 after a few dozen: most of the 100 directions carry almost no variation, and ridge spends almost nothing on them. Lesson 12 looks at these directions directly: they’re the principal components.










NoteGo deeper: ridge as shrinkage along principal directions





Write the singular value decomposition Z = UDV^\top. Least squares’ fitted values are U U^\top y = \sum_j u_j (u_j^\top y). Ridge’s are

Z\hat\beta^{\text{ridge}} = \sum_j u_j \, \frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2 + \lambda} \, (u_j^\top y) .

So ridge takes least squares’ fit along each principal direction u_j and shrinks it by the factor d_j^2/(d_j^2 + \lambda). Directions with large d_j (lots of spread in the predictors) are barely shrunk; directions with small d_j, where the data give little information and the coefficients are the most variable, are shrunk hard. Challenge 2 computes these factors. There’s also a Bayesian view, from Module 5: ridge’s \hat\beta is the posterior mode (and mean) when each \beta_j has a N(0, \sigma^2/\lambda) prior. A bigger \lambda is a tighter prior around zero. The Elements of Statistical Learning, section 3.4.1, has both derivations.

title: Ridge regression
text:
Ridge with glmnet
The glmnet package fits ridge (and the lasso, next lesson) efficiently for a whole sequence of \lambda values at once, and cross-validates them. glmnet(x, y, alpha = 0) is ridge. It standardizes the predictors internally and reports the coefficients on the original scale. Its \lambda is scaled differently from the formula above (it divides the sum of squares by 2n), so don’t compare its \lambda values with yours.
cv.glmnet() runs k-fold CV (10 folds by default) over the \lambda sequence, and reports two choices: lambda.min, with the smallest CV error, and lambda.1se, the largest \lambda whose CV error is within one standard error of the minimum.
Your turn. Run cv.glmnet() for ridge on the calibration samples, with glmnet’s default \lambda sequence. Compare lambda.min with the smallest \lambda in the sequence, and find the test RMSE.









Ridge is alpha = 0.


set.seed(7053)
cv0 <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = 0)
c(lambda_min = cv0$lambda.min, smallest_in_grid = min(cv0$lambda),
  test_rmse = sqrt(mean((y[-train] - predict(cv0, X[-train, ], s = "lambda.min"))^2)))
The best \lambda is 62.1, which is the smallest value in the grid, and the test RMSE is 3.45, eight times worse than your hand-made ridge. When the best value of a tuning parameter is at the edge of the range searched, the search was too narrow: the true optimum is somewhere beyond it. glmnet’s default sequence stops at 1% of its largest \lambda when there are more predictors than samples, which leaves far too much shrinkage for spectra. Always check.




Your turn. Cross-validate again with the longer grid lam, from 100 down to 10^{-6}, and find lambda.min and its test RMSE.









Pass the grid: lambda = lam.


set.seed(7053)
cv <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = 0, lambda = lam)
c(lambda_min = cv$lambda.min,
  test_rmse = sqrt(mean((y[-train] - predict(cv, X[-train, ], s = "lambda.min"))^2)))
lambda.min is 0.059, well inside the grid, and the test RMSE is 0.416, essentially the same as the best hand-made ridge (0.41). CV found it without touching the test set. plot(cv) draws the CV error against \log\lambda, with error bars: a U-shape with its bottom near \log\lambda = -3.




As \lambda falls, the coefficients grow from zero, each along its own path:

fit <- glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = 0, lambda = lam)
B <- as.matrix(fit$beta)
paths <- data.frame(loglam = rep(log(fit$lambda), each = 100), beta = as.vector(B), wl = rep(1:100, length(fit$lambda)))
set.seed(7053); cvf <- cv.glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = 0, lambda = lam)
ggplot(paths, aes(loglam, beta, group = wl)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey55", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log(cvf$lambda.min), linetype = "dashed", color = "#C2416C") +
  labs(x = "log(λ)", y = "Coefficient") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: Ridge regression
text:
The one-standard-error rule
The CV error curve is itself an estimate, with noise. Often many values of \lambda are statistically indistinguishable. The one-standard-error rule picks the simplest model (here, the most shrunk) whose CV error is within one standard error of the minimum: it gives up a little estimated accuracy for a model that’s less likely to have been chosen by luck.
Your turn. Find lambda.1se, and its test RMSE.









Ask for s = "lambda.1se".


set.seed(7053)
cv <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = 0, lambda = lam)
c(lambda_1se = cv$lambda.1se,
  test_rmse = sqrt(mean((y[-train] - predict(cv, X[-train, ], s = "lambda.1se"))^2)))
\lambda = 0.148, two and a half times more shrinkage, and a test RMSE of 0.417, no worse than lambda.min’s 0.416. Here the two rules agree on the test set; in general, lambda.1se gives a slightly simpler, more conservative model. Which to use is a judgment call, and many practitioners default to lambda.1se.




Your turn. Compare the range of the ridge coefficients at lambda.min with the range of least squares’ coefficients.









Least squares has NA coefficients: na.rm = TRUE.


set.seed(7053)
cv <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = 0, lambda = lam)
b_ridge <- as.numeric(coef(cv, s = "lambda.min"))[-1]
b_ols <- coef(lm(y[train] ~ X[train, ]))[-1]
rbind(ridge = range(b_ridge), ols = range(b_ols, na.rm = TRUE))
Ridge’s coefficients run from -18 to 23; least squares’ from -546 to 495. Those huge least-squares coefficients are positive and negative weights on neighboring wavelengths, nearly cancelling, and they amplify the noise in each new spectrum. The penalty forbids such delicate balancing acts.

title: Ridge regression
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · To standardize or not? glmnet standardizes by default. Spectra are all absorbances, in the same units, and chemometricians often don’t standardize them. Cross-validate ridge with standardize = FALSE, and compare the test RMSE.









standardize = FALSE.


set.seed(7053)
cv_raw <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = 0, lambda = lam, standardize = FALSE)
c(lambda_min = cv_raw$lambda.min,
  test_rmse = sqrt(mean((y[-train] - predict(cv_raw, X[-train, ], s = "lambda.min"))^2)))
A test RMSE of 0.400, slightly better than 0.416, with a much smaller \lambda (0.00018), because unstandardized absorbances have small SDs (0.04 to 0.14). Standardizing gives every wavelength an equal say, including the ones that barely vary and carry mostly noise. Without it, the strongly varying wavelengths, which carry the chemistry, dominate. Like kNN’s distances in Lesson 3, the penalty depends on the scales, and standardizing is a choice to make, not a ritual. When predictors are in different units (temperatures and pressures), standardize; when they’re in the same units and their spread means something, think twice.




Challenge 2 · Shrinkage factors. Compute ridge’s shrinkage factor d_j^2/(d_j^2 + \lambda) along the first 8 principal directions of the standardized calibration spectra, for \lambda = 1.









\lambda = 1.


mu <- colMeans(X[train, ])
s <- apply(X[train, ], 2, sd)
d <- svd(scale(X[train, ], center = mu, scale = s))$d
round(d[1:8]^2 / (d[1:8]^2 + 1), 4)
0.9998, 0.9995, 0.9974, 0.98, 0.98, then 0.80, 0.78 and 0.77. The first five directions are kept almost intact, and from the sixth on, everything is shrunk by about 20% or more. The data have five strong directions: the three components (ethanol, water and glycerol), the offset and the slope of each sample’s baseline. Everything beyond is mostly noise. That’s the structure Lesson 12’s principal components regression uses directly.

title: Ridge regression
text:
Quick quiz

1. What happens to least squares with more predictors than samples?

It can’t be computed at all
It fits the training data exactly and predicts new data badly
It sets the extra coefficients to zero and works fine


Infinitely many coefficient vectors fit exactly. lm() picks one by setting some to NA.



2. What does ridge regression add to least squares?

A penalty on the number of nonzero coefficients
A penalty \lambda \sum \beta_j^2 on the squared size of the coefficients
A penalty on the residuals’ size


The lasso, next lesson, penalizes \sum |\beta_j| instead.



3. What happens as \lambda grows?

The coefficients grow
The coefficients shrink toward zero: lower variance, higher bias
Predictors are dropped one by one


Ridge shrinks all the coefficients, but none becomes exactly zero.



4. lambda.min equals the smallest value in the \lambda grid. What should you do?

Use it: it’s the best
Extend the grid to smaller values: the best \lambda is probably beyond it
Use lambda.1se instead


glmnet’s default grid stopped too early for the spectra, and the test error was 8 times too high.



5. What does the one-standard-error rule choose?

The \lambda with the smallest CV error
The largest \lambda whose CV error is within one standard error of the smallest
The \lambda one standard error below the minimum


It prefers a simpler (more shrunk) model that’s statistically as good.



6. Ridge with \lambda = 1 had 34 effective degrees of freedom from 100 predictors. What does that mean?

It used 34 of the 100 wavelengths
Its flexibility is like that of a least-squares fit with 34 predictors
66 coefficients are zero


All 100 coefficients are nonzero, but the penalty restrains them.

title: Ridge regression
text:
Wrap-up
You can now fit a model with more predictors than samples. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Least squares fails with p \ge n: 80 samples and 100 wavelengths gave a perfect fit and a test RMSE of 9.9.
Ridge regression adds \lambda\sum\beta_j^2, with the closed form (Z^\top Z + \lambda I)^{-1}Z^\top y. At \lambda = 1, by hand, the test RMSE was 0.41.
\lambda is the dial: too small overfits, too large underfits. The effective degrees of freedom, 34 at \lambda = 1, measure the flexibility.
glmnet (alpha = 0) fits the whole path and cross-validates it. Its default grid stopped too early here, at a test RMSE of 3.45; a longer grid gave 0.416.
The one-standard-error rule picks a more shrunk model that’s statistically as good.
Standardizing is a choice: for spectra in one unit, not standardizing did slightly better.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download nir_spectra.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install glmnet.

The CV curve. plot(cv) for the ridge fit with the long grid. Where are lambda.min and lambda.1se?
The coefficient spectrum. Plot the ridge coefficients against the wavelength. Do the large ones line up with ethanol’s absorption bands (near 1,700 and 2,270 nm)?
Preprocessing. Spectroscopists remove baseline offsets by taking the first derivative of each spectrum: t(apply(X, 1, diff)). Fit ridge to the derivative spectra. Does the test RMSE improve?
Learning curve. Fit ridge with 20, 40, 60 and 80 calibration samples, and plot the test RMSE against the number of samples. How many samples does the calibration really need?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Regularization

Adding a penalty to a model’s fitting criterion to restrain its flexibility.

Ridge regression

Least squares with a penalty \lambda\sum_j\beta_j^2, which shrinks all the coefficients toward zero.

Shrinkage

Pulling estimates toward zero (or another value), trading a little bias for less variance.

Tuning parameter

A setting that controls a method’s flexibility and isn’t estimated by the fit itself, like \lambda or k.

Effective degrees of freedom

A measure of a regularized fit’s flexibility, \sum_j d_j^2/(d_j^2 + \lambda) for ridge.

One-standard-error rule

Choosing the simplest model whose CV error is within one standard error of the best.

Calibration (chemometrics)

A model that converts an instrument’s signal, such as a spectrum, into a concentration.











NoteWant to read more?






James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition), section 6.2.1, “Ridge Regression”, and the lab in section 6.5.2.
Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, section 3.4.1, with the SVD view of ridge.
Trevor Hastie, Junyang Qian and Kenneth Tay, “An Introduction to glmnet”, the package’s vignette.
Arthur Hoerl and Robert Kennard, “Ridge Regression: Biased Estimation for Nonorthogonal Problems”, Technometrics 12(1), 1970, doi:10.1080/00401706.1970.10488634. The original paper, written by two statisticians at a chemical company (DuPont).

title: Discriminant analysis and naive Bayes
text:
Module 7 · Lesson 5 of 14 Week 108 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Logistic regression models P(Y = k \mid x) directly: given the measurements, how likely is each cause? That’s a discriminative model. There’s another way round. Model what the measurements look like for each cause, f_k(x), which is often natural for an engineer (“a sticking valve makes the valve hunt, so its SD is high”), and how common each cause is, \pi_k. Then Bayes’ theorem turns them into the probabilities you want:
P(Y = k \mid X = x) = \frac{\pi_k f_k(x)}{\sum_{l=1}^K \pi_l f_l(x)} .
That’s a generative model: it describes how the data for each class are generated. This lesson covers the three classic generative classifiers. They differ only in what they assume about f_k: linear discriminant analysis (LDA), which you met in Module 3, quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA), and naive Bayes.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Discriminant analysis and naive Bayes
text:
One measurement, by hand
LDA assumes that, within each class, X is normal, with a mean \mu_k of its own and a variance \sigma^2 shared by every class. The setup code reads the alarms and makes the same 10 folds as Lesson 4.












Your turn. Using the valve’s SD alone, estimate each cause’s prior probability (its share of the alarms), its mean, and the pooled within-class variance. Then use Bayes’ theorem to find the probability of each cause for an alarm with a valve SD of 2.5%.









The normal density’s SD is the square root of the pooled variance, s2.


x <- faults$valve_sd_pct
prior <- prop.table(table(faults$cause))
mu <- tapply(x, faults$cause, mean)
s2 <- sum(tapply(x, faults$cause, function(v) sum((v - mean(v))^2))) / (800 - 4)
num <- prior * dnorm(2.5, mean = mu, sd = sqrt(s2))
num / sum(num)
35% sticking valve, 28% normal, 20% feed upset and 17% cooling loss. A valve SD of 2.5% is far above the normal mean (1.18%) and below the sticking valve’s (2.91%). The sticking valve wins, but only narrowly, for two reasons: it’s the rarest cause (a prior of 1/8), and the pooled SD, 0.70, is wide enough to make 2.5% plausible for every class. The pooled variance divides by n - K, just as a one-way ANOVA’s error mean square does.




Here’s the picture: each cause’s normal curve, scaled by its prior. Where a curve is on top, that cause is the most probable.

x <- faults$valve_sd_pct
prior <- prop.table(table(faults$cause)); mu <- tapply(x, faults$cause, mean)
s <- sqrt(sum(tapply(x, faults$cause, function(v) sum((v - mean(v))^2))) / 796)
g <- expand.grid(x = seq(-1, 6, by = 0.02), cause = levels(faults$cause))
g$y <- prior[g$cause] * dnorm(g$x, mu[g$cause], s)
ggplot(g, aes(x, y, color = cause)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cols, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Valve position SD (%)", y = "prior × density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "top")
#> Don't know how to automatically pick scale for object of type <table>.
#> Defaulting to continuous.








Your turn. Check your answer with MASS::lda().









Predict at a valve SD of 2.5.


fit <- MASS::lda(cause ~ valve_sd_pct, data = faults)
predict(fit, data.frame(valve_sd_pct = 2.5))$posterior
The same four probabilities, to every digit. lda() estimates the priors, the means and the pooled variance exactly as you did. With one predictor and a shared variance, the log of \pi_k f_k(x) is linear in x (the x^2 terms are the same for every class and cancel), which is where the “linear” in LDA comes from.

title: Discriminant analysis and naive Bayes
text:
LDA with all six measurements
With p predictors, LDA assumes each class is multivariate normal, N(\mu_k, \Sigma), with its own mean vector and a covariance matrix \Sigma shared by all the classes. The boundaries between classes are still straight: lines, planes or hyperplanes. It’s the same LDA as Module 3’s, used here as a classifier.
Your turn. Cross-validate LDA on all six measurements.









predict() on an LDA fit returns a list; the predicted classes are in $class.


f6 <- reformulate(vars, response = "cause")
pred <- factor(rep(NA, 800), levels = levels(faults$cause))
for (j in 1:10) {
  fit <- MASS::lda(f6, data = faults[fold != j, ])
  pred[fold == j] <- predict(fit, faults[fold == j, ])$class
}
print(table(predicted = pred, actual = faults$cause))
mean(pred != faults$cause)
18.25% wrong, better than multinomial logistic regression (20.1%) on the same folds. Both have linear boundaries, so why the difference? When the classes really are close to normal, LDA uses that knowledge, and its estimates are more efficient. Logistic regression assumes less, and when the normality assumption is badly wrong, it’s the safer choice. But the sticking valve is still a problem: only 54 of 100 are recognized.

title: Discriminant analysis and naive Bayes
text:
Unequal spreads: QDA
LDA’s shared covariance matrix is a strong assumption. Is it true here?
Your turn. Find the SD of each measurement within each cause.









Apply sd to each column.


sds <- sapply(split(faults[vars], faults$cause), function(d) apply(d, 2, sd))
round(sds, 2)
For the first three causes, the SDs are similar. For the sticking valve, every measurement is about twice as spread out: the valve’s SD has an SD of 1.55, against 0.42 to 0.51 for the others, and its position 16.8 against 7 to 9. A sticking valve doesn’t just shift the measurements; it makes them erratic. A shared covariance matrix can’t describe that.




QDA gives each class its own covariance matrix, N(\mu_k, \Sigma_k). Then the x^\top \Sigma_k^{-1} x terms no longer cancel, and the boundaries become quadratic curves.
Your turn. Cross-validate QDA.









The function is MASS::qda().


f6 <- reformulate(vars, response = "cause")
pred <- factor(rep(NA, 800), levels = levels(faults$cause))
for (j in 1:10) {
  fit <- MASS::qda(f6, data = faults[fold != j, ])
  pred[fold == j] <- predict(fit, faults[fold == j, ])$class
}
print(table(predicted = pred, actual = faults$cause))
mean(pred != faults$cause)
15.6% wrong: the best so far. The gain is almost all in the sticking valve: 78 of 100 recognized, against LDA’s 54. QDA wraps a wide boundary around the sticking valve’s wide cloud, and narrow ones around the others.




The boundaries, in two of the six dimensions:

grid2 <- expand.grid(temp_dev_C = seq(-3, 5, length.out = 160), valve_sd_pct = seq(0, 8, length.out = 160))
f2 <- cause ~ temp_dev_C + valve_sd_pct
reg <- rbind(cbind(grid2, cause = predict(lda(f2, faults), grid2)$class, method = "LDA: straight boundaries"),
             cbind(grid2, cause = predict(qda(f2, faults), grid2)$class, method = "QDA: curved boundaries"))
ggplot(reg, aes(temp_dev_C, valve_sd_pct)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = cause), alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_point(data = faults, aes(color = cause), size = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols, name = "Cause") + scale_color_manual(values = cols, guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~method) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-3, 5), ylim = c(0, 8), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Temperature deviation (°C)", y = "Valve position SD (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "top")








QDA’s flexibility has a price: a covariance matrix for every class. The challenge round counts the parameters. With few data per class and many predictors, QDA’s extra variance can cost more than its lower bias gains, the same trade-off as in Lesson 1.

title: Discriminant analysis and naive Bayes
text:
Naive Bayes
Estimating a full covariance matrix for each class takes a lot of data. Naive Bayes makes the opposite simplification: within each class, the predictors are independent. Then each class’s density is a product of one-dimensional densities,

f_k(x) = f_{k1}(x_1) \times f_{k2}(x_2) \times \cdots \times f_{kp}(x_p),

and each f_{kj} is easy to estimate, from a normal distribution, a histogram or a kernel density, or a table of frequencies for a categorical predictor. That makes naive Bayes cheap, stable with many predictors, and happy with mixed types. The independence is almost never true, which is why it’s “naive”, but naive Bayes often classifies well anyway.
Your turn. Cross-validate e1071::naiveBayes(), which uses a normal density for each numeric predictor.









Predict the held-out fold, faults[fold == j, ]. For naive Bayes, predict() returns the classes directly.


f6 <- reformulate(vars, response = "cause")
pred <- factor(rep(NA, 800), levels = levels(faults$cause))
for (j in 1:10) {
  fit <- e1071::naiveBayes(f6, data = faults[fold != j, ])
  pred[fold == j] <- predict(fit, faults[fold == j, ])
}
mean(pred != faults$cause)
17.9% wrong: better than LDA (18.25%), though not as good as QDA (15.6%). Naive Bayes gets each class’s own spread for each measurement, which is what helped QDA, but it ignores every correlation. Here that trade comes out in between.




The temperature and pressure deviations are correlated at 0.87 within every class: they carry nearly the same information. Naive Bayes multiplies their densities as if they were independent, so it counts that information twice.
Your turn. Cross-validate naive Bayes again without the pressure deviation.









Drop "pressure_dev_bar".


f5 <- reformulate(setdiff(vars, "pressure_dev_bar"), response = "cause")
pred <- factor(rep(NA, 800), levels = levels(faults$cause))
for (j in 1:10) {
  fit <- e1071::naiveBayes(f5, data = faults[fold != j, ])
  pred[fold == j] <- predict(fit, faults[fold == j, ])
}
mean(pred != faults$cause)
17.25%: removing a measurement made naive Bayes better. With both, the temperature evidence was counted twice, which made the model overconfident about anything that runs hot. LDA and QDA estimate the correlation and aren’t fooled: dropping pressure changes their errors by less than 1 point. For naive Bayes, it pays to leave out near-duplicate predictors, or to combine them first.




Here’s the scoreboard so far, all on the same 10 folds:



Method
CV error
Sticking valves recognized




kNN, k = 9 (Lesson 3, other folds)
20.1%



Multinomial logistic regression
20.1%
52 of 100


Multinomial, with squared terms
16.9%



LDA
18.25%
54 of 100


Naive Bayes
17.9%



QDA
15.6%
78 of 100









NoteGo deeper: when does each method win?





All three generative methods compute \log \pi_k f_k(x) and pick the largest. With normal f_k:

LDA: \delta_k(x) = x^\top \Sigma^{-1}\mu_k - \tfrac12 \mu_k^\top \Sigma^{-1} \mu_k + \log \pi_k, linear in x.
QDA: \delta_k(x) = -\tfrac12 \log|\Sigma_k| - \tfrac12 (x - \mu_k)^\top \Sigma_k^{-1}(x - \mu_k) + \log \pi_k, quadratic in x.
Naive Bayes: QDA with every \Sigma_k forced to be diagonal.

So naive Bayes and LDA are both special cases of QDA, simplified in different directions. LDA keeps the correlations but forces equal spreads; naive Bayes allows unequal spreads but drops the correlations. Which simplification costs less depends on the data. With p large and n small, both beat QDA, because QDA’s Kp(p+1)/2 covariance parameters are estimated badly. ISLR’s section 4.5 compares all of these, and logistic regression and kNN, in six simulated scenarios. A further fact: LDA’s log-odds between two classes are linear in x, exactly the form of logistic regression. The two differ only in how the coefficients are estimated.

title: Discriminant analysis and naive Bayes
section: Priors and the cost of mistakes
text:
Priors and the cost of mistakes
The priors \pi_k come from the training data unless you say otherwise: half the alarms are false, so “normal” starts with a big advantage. But the costs of mistakes aren’t equal. Calling a real fault “normal” means nobody acts on it; calling a false alarm a fault means an operator checks something that was fine.
Your turn. Cross-validate LDA with equal priors for the four causes, and count the real faults that are called “normal”, compared with the default priors.









Equal priors for four classes: rep(0.25, 4).


f6 <- reformulate(vars, response = "cause")
missed <- function(prior) {
