  pred <- factor(rep(NA, 800), levels = levels(faults$cause))
  for (j in 1:10) {
    fit <- if (is.null(prior)) MASS::lda(f6, data = faults[fold != j, ]) else MASS::lda(f6, data = faults[fold != j, ], prior = prior)
    pred[fold == j] <- predict(fit, faults[fold == j, ])$class
  }
  c(error = mean(pred != faults$cause), faults_called_normal = sum(pred == "normal" & faults$cause != "normal"))
}
rbind(default = missed(NULL), equal = missed(rep(0.25, 4)))
With the default priors, 85 real faults are called “normal” and the error rate is 18.25%. With equal priors, only 47 are missed, but the error rate rises to 21%, because 71 false alarms are now diagnosed as faults, against 28 before. The overall error rate treats every mistake as equally bad, and it’s often the wrong measure. Lesson 6 makes this precise, with costs and thresholds.

title: Discriminant analysis and naive Bayes
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Counting parameters. How many parameters do LDA and QDA estimate for these data, with K = 4 classes and p = 6 predictors? Count the means and the covariance entries (a p \times p covariance matrix has p(p+1)/2 distinct entries), and leave out the priors.









QDA has a covariance matrix for each of the K classes.


K <- 4
p <- 6
c(LDA = K * p + p * (p + 1) / 2,
  QDA = K * p + K * p * (p + 1) / 2)
45 for LDA and 108 for QDA. With 100 sticking-valve alarms, estimating that class’s 21 covariance entries is fine. With 50 predictors, QDA would need 4 \times 1{,}275 = 5{,}100 covariance entries, and each class’s matrix would need more observations than predictors just to be invertible. Naive Bayes needs only 2Kp = 48 here (a mean and an SD per class and predictor), and 400 with 50 predictors.




Challenge 2 · LDA as a map. With K classes, LDA’s information lies in at most K - 1 directions, the linear discriminants, which Module 3 used to plot the classes. Find how much of the between-class separation each of the three discriminants carries.









The proportions are the squared singular values over their sum: fit$svd^2.


fit <- MASS::lda(reformulate(vars, "cause"), data = faults)
fit$svd^2 / sum(fit$svd^2)
46%, 31% and 23%. All three directions matter: the four causes differ from each other in three different ways, so no single direction, and no two-dimensional plot, separates them all. fit$scaling holds each direction’s coefficients (multiply them by each measurement’s within-class SD to compare their weights), and plot(fit) draws the alarms on the first two.

title: Discriminant analysis and naive Bayes
text:
Quick quiz

1. What makes a classifier “generative”?

It generates new training data
It models the distribution of X within each class, and uses Bayes’ theorem to get P(Y \mid X)
It uses a neural network


Logistic regression, which models P(Y \mid X) directly, is discriminative.



2. What does LDA assume that QDA doesn’t?

Normal distributions within each class
The same covariance matrix for every class
Independent predictors


Both assume normality. QDA gives each class its own covariance matrix.



3. Why did QDA beat LDA on the alarms?

It used more predictors
The sticking valve’s measurements are much more spread out than the other causes’, which a shared covariance can’t describe
QDA always beats LDA


With few data per class or many predictors, QDA’s extra parameters can make it worse.



4. What does naive Bayes assume?

The classes are equally likely
The predictors are independent within each class
The predictors are normal and share a covariance matrix


Its density for each class is a product of one-dimensional densities.



5. Dropping the pressure deviation made naive Bayes better. Why?

Pressure is irrelevant
Pressure duplicates the temperature’s information, and naive Bayes counted it twice
There were too many parameters


LDA and QDA estimate the correlation, so they weren’t affected.



6. Making the priors equal raised the error rate. Was it a mistake?

Yes, a lower error rate is always better
Not necessarily: it missed far fewer real faults, which may matter more than extra false alarms
Yes, priors must match the training data


The error rate treats every mistake as equally costly. Lesson 6 deals with unequal costs.

title: Discriminant analysis and naive Bayes
text:
Wrap-up
You can now classify by modeling each class. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Generative classifiers model \pi_k and f_k(x), then apply Bayes’ theorem. With one measurement, LDA by hand matched lda() exactly.
LDA assumes normal classes with a shared covariance: linear boundaries, 18.25% wrong on the alarms.
QDA gives each class its own covariance: quadratic boundaries, and 15.6% wrong, because the sticking valve’s measurements are about twice as spread out. It estimates 108 parameters to LDA’s 45.
Naive Bayes assumes independent predictors within each class: cheap and robust, 17.9% wrong, but it double-counts correlated predictors. Dropping pressure improved it.
Priors shift the balance between kinds of mistakes: equal priors missed 47 faults instead of 85, with more false alarms.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download process_faults.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Check normality. Make Q-Q plots of each measurement within each cause. Which are clearly not normal? (The valve’s SD can’t be negative.) Try LDA and QDA on log(valve_sd_pct).
Kernel naive Bayes. The naivebayes package’s naive_bayes(..., usekernel = TRUE) estimates each f_{kj} with a kernel density. Does it beat the normal version?
Regularized discriminant analysis. klaR::rda() blends LDA and QDA, with a tuning parameter \lambda between them. Find the best \lambda by cross-validation.
Plot LD1 against LD2, colored by cause. Which causes overlap?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Generative classifier

A classifier that models the distribution of the predictors within each class, and the classes’ prior probabilities, and combines them with Bayes’ theorem.

Discriminative classifier

A classifier that models P(Y \mid X) directly, like logistic regression.

Prior probability

\pi_k, the probability of class k before seeing the predictors.

Posterior probability

P(Y = k \mid X = x), the probability of class k given the predictors.

Linear discriminant analysis (LDA)

A generative classifier that assumes multivariate normal classes with a shared covariance matrix, giving linear boundaries.

Quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA)

Like LDA, but with a separate covariance matrix for each class, giving quadratic boundaries.

Naive Bayes

A generative classifier that assumes the predictors are independent within each class.

Linear discriminants

The at most K - 1 directions in which LDA separates the classes.











NoteWant to read more?






James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition), sections 4.4 and 4.5, “Generative Models for Classification” and the comparison of classification methods.
Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, section 4.3, including regularized discriminant analysis.
David Hand and Keming Yu, “Idiot’s Bayes: Not So Stupid After All?”, International Statistical Review 69(3), 2001, doi:10.1111/j.1751-5823.2001.tb00465.x. Why naive Bayes works better than its assumptions deserve.

title: k-nearest neighbors
text:
Module 7 · Lesson 3 of 14 Week 106 of 160 About 5–7 hours
An experienced operator, asked what the melt index is doing right now, might say: “The last time we ran at this hydrogen ratio, it was about 0.9.” That’s a prediction method, and a good one. It assumes nothing about the shape of f. It just finds the most similar past cases and reports what happened then.
k-nearest neighbors (kNN) is that method, made precise. To predict at a new input x_0, find the k training points closest to x_0, the set \mathcal{N}_0, and average their responses:
\hat f(x_0) = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}_0} y_i .
For classification, take a vote instead: predict the most common class among the k neighbors. kNN is the purest non-parametric method, and it’s a useful yardstick: if a fancy model can’t beat kNN, something is wrong with it. It also shows, very clearly, a problem that every flexible method has to face.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: k-nearest neighbors
text:
Neighbors by hand
The setup code reads the soft-sensor data from Lesson 2, with the logs, and lists the four chemistry tags in chem and all 20 tags in tags. It makes the same 10 folds as Lesson 2, so that the CV errors here can be compared with that lesson’s. It also reads the alarm data, for the end of the lesson.












Your turn. The operators are about to run at a hydrogen ratio of 0.25. Find the 5 past samples whose \log(\text{H}_2) is closest to \log(0.25), and predict the MI as the geometric mean of their MIs (the mean on the log scale, transformed back).









order(dist0) lists the samples from nearest to farthest. Take the first 5.


dist0 <- abs(mi$log_h2 - log(0.25))
nearest <- order(dist0)[1:5]
mi[nearest, c("sample", "h2_ratio", "melt_index")]
exp(mean(mi$log_mi[nearest]))
The five neighbors ran at hydrogen ratios of 0.228 to 0.239, all a little below 0.25, and their MIs range from 0.68 to 1.16. The prediction is 0.88. Notice that there’s no sample above 0.25 among them: the nearest neighbors can all lie on one side of x_0, which biases the prediction toward their side. Here, that probably makes 0.88 a little low.




FNN::knn.reg(train, test, y, k) does the same, for many test points at once. Its first two arguments are matrices of predictors.
Your turn. Write a function that computes the 10-fold CV RMSE of kNN regression on log(MI), for a given set of predictor columns and a given k. Use it with log_h2 alone and k = 5.









Pass the function’s argument: k = k.


cv_knn <- function(cols, k) {
  X <- as.matrix(mi[cols])
  err <- numeric(nrow(mi))
  for (j in 1:10) {
    tr <- fold != j
    pred <- FNN::knn.reg(X[tr, , drop = FALSE], X[!tr, , drop = FALSE], mi$log_mi[tr], k = k)$pred
    err[!tr] <- mi$log_mi[!tr] - pred
  }
  sqrt(mean(err^2))
}
cv_knn("log_h2", 5)
0.230. Lesson 2’s straight line in log_h2 had a CV RMSE of 0.217 on the same folds, so kNN with k = 5 is a little worse. drop = FALSE keeps a one-column matrix a matrix, instead of letting R turn it into a vector.

title: k-nearest neighbors
text:
Choosing k
k is kNN’s flexibility dial, turned the opposite way from a polynomial’s degree. With k = 1, each prediction copies a single past sample, noise and all: low bias, high variance. With large k, each prediction averages many samples, some of them far from x_0: low variance, but biased, because far-away samples have a different f. At the extreme, k = n predicts the overall mean everywhere.

g <- seq(min(mi$log_h2), max(mi$log_h2), length.out = 400)
fits <- rbind(data.frame(x = g, y = FNN::knn.reg(as.matrix(mi$log_h2), as.matrix(g), mi$log_mi, k = 1)$pred, k = "k = 1"),
              data.frame(x = g, y = FNN::knn.reg(as.matrix(mi$log_h2), as.matrix(g), mi$log_mi, k = 30)$pred, k = "k = 30"))
ggplot(mi, aes(log_h2, log_mi)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey70", size = 1) +
  geom_line(data = fits, aes(x, y), color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~k) +
  labs(x = "log(hydrogen/ethylene ratio)", y = "log(melt index)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Your turn. Find the CV RMSE with log_h2 alone for k = 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 10, 15, 20, 30 and 50, and the best k.









Each call uses that iteration’s k.


cv_knn <- function(cols, k) {
  X <- as.matrix(mi[cols])
  err <- numeric(nrow(mi))
  for (j in 1:10) {
    tr <- fold != j
    pred <- FNN::knn.reg(X[tr, , drop = FALSE], X[!tr, , drop = FALSE], mi$log_mi[tr], k = k)$pred
    err[!tr] <- mi$log_mi[!tr] - pred
  }
  sqrt(mean(err^2))
}
ks <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50)
cv <- sapply(ks, function(k) cv_knn("log_h2", k))
round(cv, 4)
ks[which.min(cv)]
The CV RMSE falls from 0.297 at k = 1 to 0.2145 at k = 30, and rises again to 0.217 at k = 50. With one predictor and 450 training samples, k can be large, because 30 neighbors still lie close together. The best kNN is now slightly better than the straight line (0.217), which tells you the relationship is very nearly a straight line: kNN has to work hard to match a model that assumed the right shape.

title: k-nearest neighbors
text:
Units matter
With more than one predictor, “nearest” means smallest Euclidean distance, \sqrt{\sum_j (x_{0j} - x_{ij})^2}, and that adds up differences in whatever units the predictors happen to be in. A difference of 1 °C counts the same as a difference of 1 in the comonomer ratio, which is 25 times the ratio’s whole range.
Your turn. Cross-validate kNN with k = 8 on the four chemistry tags, as they are. Then express the comonomer ratio in mol% (multiply by 100), and do it again.









A ratio of 0.05 is 5 mol%: multiply by 100.


cv_knn_data <- function(data, cols, k) {
  X <- as.matrix(data[cols])
  err <- numeric(nrow(data))
  for (j in 1:10) {
    tr <- fold != j
    pred <- FNN::knn.reg(X[tr, , drop = FALSE], X[!tr, , drop = FALSE], data$log_mi[tr], k = k)$pred
    err[!tr] <- data$log_mi[!tr] - pred
  }
  sqrt(mean(err^2))
}
mi_pct <- mi
mi_pct$comonomer_ratio <- mi$comonomer_ratio * 100
c(ratio = cv_knn_data(mi, chem, 8), mol_pct = cv_knn_data(mi_pct, chem, 8))
0.192 with the ratio, and 0.211 with mol%: the same data and the same method give a different model, only because of the units. With the ratio, whose SD is 0.009, differences in comonomer are tiny next to differences in temperature (SD 1.1 °C), so kNN effectively ignores the comonomer. In mol%, its SD is 0.9, and it counts as much as temperature. Ignoring it happens to work better here, but by luck, not by design.




The usual fix is to standardize every predictor: subtract its mean and divide by its SD, so that each one is measured in SDs. Then the units no longer matter. But it’s a choice too: it makes every predictor equally important in the distance. To avoid the leakage of Lesson 2, the means and SDs should come from each fold’s training rows only.
Your turn. Add standardization to the CV function, using the training rows’ means and SDs, and cross-validate the four chemistry tags with k = 8, in both units.









Scale the test rows with the training rows’ SDs, s.


cv_knn_std <- function(data, cols, k) {
  X <- as.matrix(data[cols])
  err <- numeric(nrow(data))
  for (j in 1:10) {
    tr <- fold != j
    mu <- colMeans(X[tr, , drop = FALSE])
    s <- apply(X[tr, , drop = FALSE], 2, sd)
    Xtr <- scale(X[tr, , drop = FALSE], center = mu, scale = s)
    Xte <- scale(X[!tr, , drop = FALSE], center = mu, scale = s)
    err[!tr] <- data$log_mi[!tr] - FNN::knn.reg(Xtr, Xte, data$log_mi[tr], k = k)$pred
  }
  sqrt(mean(err^2))
}
mi_pct <- mi
mi_pct$comonomer_ratio <- mi$comonomer_ratio * 100
c(ratio = cv_knn_std(mi, chem, 8), mol_pct = cv_knn_std(mi_pct, chem, 8))
0.227 both ways: once each predictor is measured in its own SDs, the units no longer matter. But it’s worse than either unscaled version, because standardizing gives the comonomer ratio a full say, and the comonomer matters much less than hydrogen. kNN has no way to learn that some predictors matter more than others. Every predictor you give it counts fully, so choosing the predictors is up to you.

title: k-nearest neighbors
text:
The curse of dimensionality
Standardizing gave the comonomer ratio an equal say, and it hurt, because the comonomer matters much less than hydrogen. Now imagine giving an equal say to 16 tags that don’t matter at all.
Your turn. Compare standardized kNN with k = 10 on the four chemistry tags and on all 20 tags.









All 20 tags are in tags.


cv_knn_std <- function(data, cols, k) {
  X <- as.matrix(data[cols])
  err <- numeric(nrow(data))
  for (j in 1:10) {
    tr <- fold != j
    mu <- colMeans(X[tr, , drop = FALSE])
    s <- apply(X[tr, , drop = FALSE], 2, sd)
    Xtr <- scale(X[tr, , drop = FALSE], center = mu, scale = s)
    Xte <- scale(X[!tr, , drop = FALSE], center = mu, scale = s)
    err[!tr] <- data$log_mi[!tr] - FNN::knn.reg(Xtr, Xte, data$log_mi[tr], k = k)$pred
  }
  sqrt(mean(err^2))
}
c(chemistry = cv_knn_std(mi, chem, 10), all_tags = cv_knn_std(mi, tags, 10))
0.229 with the four chemistry tags, and 0.509 with all 20: more than twice the error, and much worse than hydrogen alone (0.2145). The best k with 20 tags, 5 to 10, doesn’t help: it’s still above 0.5. Compare Lesson 2, where adding the same 16 tags to a linear model cost almost nothing (0.170 to 0.174): least squares can give an irrelevant tag a coefficient near zero, but kNN can’t ignore anything. Every tag counts fully in every distance, so with 20 tags, the “nearest” samples are mostly the ones that happen to match on 16 irrelevant numbers.




There’s a deeper problem, even when every predictor matters. In many dimensions, everything is far from everything. To capture 10% of uniformly spread data in a neighborhood, you need 10% of the range of one predictor, but 0.1^{1/10} = 79\% of the range of each of ten predictors. “Local” stops being local. This is the curse of dimensionality, and it hits every method that relies on nearness.
Your turn. Simulate 500 points spread uniformly in p dimensions, and find the ratio of the nearest to the farthest distance from the first point to the others, for p = 2 and p = 100.









Divide the nearest distance by the farthest: max(d).


set.seed(7033)
ratio <- sapply(c(2, 100), function(p) {
  X <- matrix(runif(500 * p), nrow = 500)
  d <- sqrt(colSums((t(X[-1, ]) - X[1, ])^2))
  min(d) / max(d)
})
ratio
0.012 in 2 dimensions: the nearest point is 90 times closer than the farthest. In 100 dimensions, 0.70: the nearest of 499 random points is 70% as far away as the farthest. When all the distances are about the same, “nearest” means very little.










NoteGo deeper: why distances concentrate





For two independent points uniform on [0, 1]^p, the squared distance is a sum of p independent terms (u_j - v_j)^2, each with mean 1/6 and variance 7/180. So E\|u - v\|^2 = p/6, and its standard deviation is \sqrt{7p/180}. The relative spread of the squared distance, \sqrt{7p/180}\,/\,(p/6) \approx 1.18/\sqrt{p}, shrinks like 1/\sqrt p: with p = 100, almost every squared distance is within about 12% of p/6. Beyer and colleagues (“When Is ‘Nearest Neighbor’ Meaningful?”, 1999) showed that this happens for a broad class of distributions, not only uniform ones. Real data escape the worst of it when their predictors are correlated, so that the data live near a low-dimensional surface. That’s what Lesson 12’s principal components exploit.

title: k-nearest neighbors
text:
kNN for classification
For a categorical response, kNN takes a vote among the k neighbors, and the share of the votes for each class is an estimate of P(Y = \text{class} \mid x_0). class::knn(train, test, cl, k) returns the winning class for each test row.
The alarm data hold 800 high-temperature alarms on a reactor, each summarized by six measurements over the following 10 minutes, and labeled with the cause the engineers found afterwards: normal (a false alarm from a load change), loss of cooling, a feed upset, or a sticking control valve. Lessons 4 and 5 model them properly. Here, they test kNN.
Your turn. Cross-validate kNN with k = 9 on the six standardized measurements, and find the error rate.









Use 9 neighbors. The second set.seed() is there because knn() breaks ties at random.


vars <- c("temp_dev_C", "pressure_dev_bar", "coolant_dt_C", "feed_dev_pct", "valve_pos_pct", "valve_sd_pct")
X <- as.matrix(faults[vars])
set.seed(7034)
ffold <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(faults)))
pred <- factor(rep(NA, nrow(faults)), levels = levels(faults$cause))
set.seed(7035)
for (j in 1:10) {
  tr <- ffold != j
  mu <- colMeans(X[tr, ])
  s <- apply(X[tr, ], 2, sd)
  pred[!tr] <- class::knn(scale(X[tr, ], mu, s), scale(X[!tr, ], mu, s), faults$cause[tr], k = 9)
}
mean(pred != faults$cause)
20.1% of the alarms are misdiagnosed. The CV error is between 19% and 21% for any k from 5 to 15, and it rises on both sides: 26% at k = 1, and 24% at k = 60. Half the alarms are normal, so always guessing “normal” would be wrong 50% of the time: kNN has learned a lot. Lessons 4 and 5 will beat it, with models that use the shape of each class.




Here’s what kNN’s decision regions look like, with just two of the measurements, the temperature deviation and the valve’s variability:

z <- scale(faults[c("temp_dev_C", "valve_sd_pct")])
grid2 <- expand.grid(temp_dev_C = seq(-2.5, 4.5, length.out = 150), valve_sd_pct = seq(0, 8, length.out = 150))
zg <- scale(grid2, attr(z, "scaled:center"), attr(z, "scaled:scale"))
regions <- rbind(cbind(grid2, cause = class::knn(z, zg, faults$cause, k = 1), k = "k = 1"),
                 cbind(grid2, cause = class::knn(z, zg, faults$cause, k = 25), k = "k = 25"))
cols <- c(normal = "grey55", cooling_loss = "#2a78d6", feed_upset = "#1baf7a", sticking_valve = "#C2416C")
ggplot(regions, aes(temp_dev_C, valve_sd_pct)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = cause), alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_point(data = faults, aes(color = cause), size = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols, name = "Cause") + scale_color_manual(values = cols, guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~k) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-2.5, 4.5), ylim = c(0, 8), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Temperature deviation (°C)", y = "Valve position SD (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "top")








With k = 1, every alarm gets its own little island: the boundary is overfitted to the training data. With k = 25, the regions are smooth and sensible. With only these two measurements, the CV error is much higher, about 33% at its best (k = 25): loss of cooling and feed upsets overlap on these two axes, and only the other measurements tell them apart.

title: k-nearest neighbors
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · No extrapolation. The highest hydrogen ratio in the data is 2.89. Predict log(MI) at a ratio of 4 with kNN (k = 30, on log_h2 alone) and with the straight line lm(log_mi ~ log_h2), both fitted to all the data. Transform both back to the MI scale.









Predict the line at x_new.


x_new <- log(4)
knn_pred <- FNN::knn.reg(as.matrix(mi$log_h2), as.matrix(x_new), mi$log_mi, k = 30)$pred
lm_pred <- predict(lm(log_mi ~ log_h2, data = mi), data.frame(log_h2 = x_new))
exp(c(knn = knn_pred, line = unname(lm_pred)))
kNN predicts an MI of 11.8, and the line 17.3. The 30 nearest neighbors of a ratio of 4 are the 30 samples with the highest ratios, all below 2.9, so kNN predicts about what they had. The line carries the trend on. If the chemistry holds, the line is right and kNN is badly low; if something new happens at a ratio of 4, neither knows. kNN’s predictions are always averages of responses it has seen, so they can never leave the range of the data. That’s a safety feature and a limitation: a soft sensor built on kNN can’t warn you about a grade you’ve never made.




Challenge 2 · The votes. With prob = TRUE, class::knn() also returns the share of votes for the winning class. Fit kNN with k = 9 to all the alarms but the first, on the six standardized measurements, and classify the first. What’s its predicted cause, and what share of the 9 neighbors voted for it?









Ask for the vote shares with prob = TRUE.


vars <- c("temp_dev_C", "pressure_dev_bar", "coolant_dt_C", "feed_dev_pct", "valve_pos_pct", "valve_sd_pct")
Z <- scale(as.matrix(faults[vars]))
set.seed(7036)
p1 <- class::knn(Z[-1, ], Z[1, , drop = FALSE], faults$cause[-1], k = 9, prob = TRUE)
c(as.character(p1), round(attr(p1, "prob"), 3), as.character(faults$cause[1]))
kNN says “normal”, with 6 of the 9 votes (0.667), but the engineers found that alarm A001 was a loss of cooling. Its measurements are borderline: a temperature 1.2 °C high, a coolant temperature rise of 7.5 °C (normal runs about 8, and a cooling loss about 6) and the valve 63% open. The vote share is a rough probability: 0.667 says that this diagnosis is far from sure, and an alarm like this one deserves a second look. Lessons 4 to 6 build classifiers whose probabilities are better calibrated.

title: k-nearest neighbors
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does kNN regression predict at a new point?

The value of a fitted line there
The average response of the k nearest training points
The response of the single nearest point, always


With k = 1, it’s the nearest point’s response. With larger k, an average.



2. How does increasing k change the bias and variance?

Both increase
Variance falls and bias rises
Bias falls and variance rises


Larger k averages more points, some farther away. k = 1 is the most flexible.



3. Why standardize the predictors before kNN?

It makes the model linear
Otherwise the distances depend on the arbitrary units of the predictors
kNN can’t handle negative numbers


Standardizing makes each predictor count equally, which is itself a choice.



4. Adding 16 irrelevant tags hardly hurt the linear model but doubled kNN’s error. Why?

Least squares can give an irrelevant tag a coefficient near zero, but kNN weights every tag fully in every distance
kNN can’t use more than 4 predictors
The linear model was overfitting


That’s one face of the curse of dimensionality.



5. What happens to distances between random points as the number of dimensions grows?

They become more varied
They become nearly equal, so the nearest point is almost as far as the farthest
They shrink to zero


In 100 dimensions, the ratio of nearest to farthest distance was about 0.7.



6. What does kNN predict far outside the range of the training data?

An extrapolation of the trend
The average of the training points nearest the edge
An error


Its predictions are always averages of observed responses, so it can’t go beyond them.

title: k-nearest neighbors
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve met the simplest flexible method, and the problem that haunts all of them. Here’s what you’ve learned:

kNN predicts the average of the k nearest training responses, or their majority class.
k is the flexibility dial: small k overfits, large k oversmooths. Cross-validation chose k = 30 for the melt index on hydrogen alone, with a CV RMSE of 0.2145.
Units matter: distances add up the predictors’ units. Standardizing (inside each fold) removes that, but it gives every predictor an equal say.
The curse of dimensionality: 16 irrelevant tags doubled kNN’s error, to 0.509, and in 100 dimensions, the nearest point is almost as far as the farthest.
kNN classification misdiagnosed 20.1% of the reactor alarms, with k = 9. Its vote shares estimate the class probabilities.
kNN can’t extrapolate. Its predictions are always averages of observed values.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download soft_sensor.csv and process_faults.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install FNN.

Weighting by importance. Standardize the four chemistry tags, then multiply each one by the size of its effect in Lesson 2’s chemistry model (its coefficient times its SD). Does kNN do better with these weighted distances?
Adding noise tags one at a time. Add the 16 irrelevant tags to the chemistry tags one by one, and plot kNN’s CV RMSE against the number of tags.
Plot the curse. Repeat the distance simulation for p = 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100 and 500, and plot the nearest-to-farthest ratio against p.
The confusion matrix. Make table(pred, faults$cause) for the cross-validated kNN predictions. Which causes does kNN confuse most?










NoteKey words from this lesson






k-nearest neighbors (kNN)

A method that predicts from the k training points closest to the new point: their average response, or their majority class.

Euclidean distance

The straight-line distance between two points, \sqrt{\sum_j (x_j - z_j)^2}.

Standardizing

Subtracting a variable’s mean and dividing by its standard deviation, so that it’s measured in standard deviations.

Curse of dimensionality

The ways that data become sparse, and distances less informative, as the number of dimensions grows.

Decision boundary

The boundary between the regions of input space that a classifier assigns to different classes.

Extrapolation

Predicting outside the range of the training data.











NoteWant to read more?






James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition), section 2.2.3 (kNN classification) and section 3.5 (kNN regression against linear regression, with the curse of dimensionality).
Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, sections 2.3 and 2.5, “Local Methods in High Dimensions”.
Kevin Beyer, Jonathan Goldstein, Raghu Ramakrishnan and Uri Shaft, “When Is ‘Nearest Neighbor’ Meaningful?”, International Conference on Database Theory, 1999, doi:10.1007/3-540-49257-7_15.

title: What is statistical learning?
text:
Module 7 · Lesson 1 of 14 Week 104 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Machine learning sounds like something new, but most of it is statistics you’ve already met, with a change of emphasis. In regression, you fitted a model and asked what its coefficients mean. In machine learning, the main question is usually different: how well will this model predict data it has never seen? That one question changes how you choose models, how you judge them, and how flexible you let them be.
This module follows the course STAT 584 and its textbook, An Introduction to Statistical Learning. It’s about statistical learning: methods that learn, from data, the relationship between some inputs and an output. The first lesson sets up the ideas that every later lesson uses, on the simplest possible example: one input, one output, 40 runs.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: What is statistical learning?
text:
The function behind the data
The pilot plant ran a new catalyst at 40 temperatures between 150 and 225 °C and measured the yield of each run:

grid <- data.frame(temp_C = seq(150, 225, by = 0.5))
ggplot(runs, aes(temp_C, yield_pct)) +
  geom_line(data = transform(grid, yield_pct = f_true(temp_C)), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_point(color = "#C2416C", size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Yield (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Statistical learning assumes that the output Y (yield) depends on the input X (temperature) through some fixed but unknown function f, plus random error:

Y = f(X) + \varepsilon .

f is the systematic part: the yield you’d get, on average, at each temperature. \varepsilon is everything else: measurement error, small differences in the feed, things nobody recorded. It has mean zero, and it’s independent of X. Statistical learning is a set of ways to estimate f from data, written \hat f.
There are two reasons to want \hat f:

Prediction. You want good values of \hat Y = \hat f(X) for new inputs, and you don’t much care what \hat f looks like inside. A soft sensor that predicts a lab result from process tags is a prediction problem.
Inference. You want to understand f: which inputs matter, in which direction, by how much. “How much does yield fall for each degree above the optimum?” is an inference question.

Modules 2 and 3 were mostly about inference. This module is mostly about prediction, which frees you to use models whose insides are hard to read, as long as they predict well.
One unusual thing about these runs: they’re simulated, so the true f is known. It’s the dashed curve, with its optimum at 190 °C, and the error has a standard deviation of 3 points. In real life, you never know f. Here, knowing it lets you measure things that are normally invisible. The setup code below defines it as f_true(), and it also makes 2,000 new runs from the same process: data that no model gets to see while it’s being fitted.












Your turn. Fit a straight line and a quadratic to the 40 runs, and compare their training mean squared error, the average squared residual.









A quadratic is a polynomial of degree 2.


line <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C, data = runs)
quad <- lm(yield_pct ~ poly(temp_C, 2), data = runs)
c(line = mean(resid(line)^2), quadratic = mean(resid(quad)^2))
60.6 for the line, 13.7 for the quadratic. The line can’t bend, so it misses the peak entirely: its slope, 0.06 points per °C, says that temperature hardly matters, which is badly wrong. The quadratic bends once, and it does much better. poly(temp_C, 2) uses orthogonal polynomials, which give the same fit as temp_C + I(temp_C^2) but are numerically safer at high degrees.

title: What is statistical learning?
text:
Supervised and unsupervised learning
In the pilot runs, every input comes with its output: each temperature has a measured yield. A method can learn f by comparing its predictions with the right answers. That’s supervised learning, and it covers regression (a numeric output, like yield) and classification (a categorical output, like the cause of an alarm).
Sometimes there’s no output at all: just inputs, and a question about their structure. Do these 48 crude oils fall into natural groups? Does the plant run in a few distinct modes? That’s unsupervised learning: there’s no right answer to learn from, so there’s no simple error rate to judge it by. Lessons 12 and 13 cover it.
Your turn. Label each of the four tasks below “supervised” or “unsupervised”.









Ask: is there a known right answer for each past example, to learn from?


c(
  predict_melt_index = "supervised",
  group_crude_oils = "unsupervised",
  diagnose_alarm = "supervised",
  find_operating_modes = "unsupervised"
)
The melt index and the alarm causes have known answers in the past data: supervised (regression and classification). The crude oils and the operating modes don’t: unsupervised. There’s also a middle ground, semi-supervised learning, where only some examples have answers, as when the lab tests only one batch in ten.

title: What is statistical learning?
text:
Flexibility and the training error
The line and the quadratic are two points on a scale of flexibility. A polynomial of degree d has d + 1 coefficients, and the higher d is, the more shapes it can take. Flexible models can follow f more closely. They can also follow the noise.
Your turn. Compute the training MSE for polynomials of degree 1 to 12.









The degree is the function’s argument, d.


train_mse <- sapply(1:12, function(d) {
  fit <- lm(yield_pct ~ poly(temp_C, d), data = runs)
  mean(resid(fit)^2)
})
round(train_mse, 2)
60.58, 13.67, 9.63, 7.91, 7.86, … down to 5.39 at degree 12. It never goes up: a degree-12 polynomial contains every lower-degree polynomial as a special case, so least squares can always fit the training data at least as well. If the training error were the measure, the most flexible model would always win. But the error variance is 9 (an SD of 3), so a training MSE of 5.39 is better than the truth: the model has started fitting the noise.

title: What is statistical learning?
text:
The test error
What matters for prediction is the error on new data: the test MSE, \text{Ave}\big(y_0 - \hat f(x_0)\big)^2 over runs (x_0, y_0) that weren’t used to fit \hat f. Here, the 2,000 new runs play that part.
Your turn. Compute the test MSE for each degree, and find the degree with the smallest.









Predict for the new runs: predict(fit, new_runs).


test_mse <- sapply(1:12, function(d) {
  fit <- lm(yield_pct ~ poly(temp_C, d), data = runs)
  mean((new_runs$yield_pct - predict(fit, new_runs))^2)
})
round(test_mse, 2)
which.min(test_mse)
Degree 5 wins, with a test MSE of 11.50. The line’s test MSE is 93.2, the quadratic’s 18.2, and past degree 5 the test error creeps up again, to 13.56 at degree 12, while the training error keeps falling. That U-shape is the most important picture in machine learning.




Here are both curves together:

mse <- t(sapply(1:12, function(d) {
  fit <- lm(yield_pct ~ poly(temp_C, d), data = runs)
  c(training = mean(resid(fit)^2), test = mean((new_runs$yield_pct - predict(fit, new_runs))^2))
}))
df <- data.frame(degree = rep(1:12, 2), mse = c(mse), set = rep(c("training", "test"), each = 12))
ggplot(df, aes(degree, mse, color = set)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 9, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_log10() + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(training = "grey45", test = "#C2416C"), name = NULL) +
  annotate("text", x = 11.5, y = 8.3, label = "irreducible error", size = 3.5, color = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Polynomial degree (flexibility)", y = "Mean squared error (log scale)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "top")








A model whose training error is much lower than its test error is overfitting: it has learned patterns in the training data, the noise, that won’t come back. A model that’s too rigid, like the line, is underfitting: both errors are high. The art is to find the flexibility in between, and the next lesson shows how to do it without a convenient set of 2,000 extra runs.

title: What is statistical learning?
text:
The irreducible error
Even a perfect estimate, \hat f = f, wouldn’t predict perfectly, because each new run has its own \varepsilon. For any \hat f, the expected test error at an input x_0 splits into two parts:

E\big(Y - \hat f(x_0)\big)^2 = \underbrace{\big(f(x_0) - \hat f(x_0)\big)^2}_{\text{reducible}} + \underbrace{\text{Var}(\varepsilon)}_{\text{irreducible}} .

Better models shrink the first part. Nothing shrinks the second: it’s the noise floor. The only way below it is to measure more inputs, which might explain some of what is now noise.
Your turn. Find the test MSE of the true function itself, on the new runs.









The true function is f_true().


mean((new_runs$yield_pct - f_true(new_runs$temp_C))^2)
9.47, close to the true error variance, 3^2 = 9 (2,000 runs are a sample too). The best model’s test MSE, 11.50, is only about 2 above this floor: most of its error is noise that no model could remove. In real problems, you don’t know the floor, but replicate measurements can estimate it: the lab’s repeatability is a floor for any soft sensor.

title: What is statistical learning?
text:
Bias and variance
Why does the test error go down and then up? Imagine running the 40-run study again and again, each time with new runs, and fitting the same kind of model each time. At a given temperature, \hat f(x_0) would come out different every time. Its expected squared error splits into three parts:

E\big(Y_0 - \hat f(x_0)\big)^2 = \underbrace{\big(E\hat f(x_0) - f(x_0)\big)^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\text{Var}\big(\hat f(x_0)\big)}_{\text{variance}} + \text{Var}(\varepsilon).


Bias is how far the model’s average fit is from the truth. A straight line through a curved f is biased however many runs you collect.
Variance is how much the fit changes from one dataset to the next. A degree-12 polynomial chases each dataset’s noise, so it changes a lot.

More flexibility lowers the bias and raises the variance. The test error is their sum plus the noise, so it’s lowest where the trade-off balances. That’s the bias-variance trade-off.
Your turn. Simulate 300 new 40-run studies, fit a polynomial of degree d to each, and predict the yield at 205 °C. Estimate the squared bias and the variance for degree 1, then change it to 5 and 10.









Start with d <- 1. The check wants degree 10’s answer.


d <- 10
set.seed(7013)
pred <- replicate(300, {
  t <- runif(40, 150, 225)
  y <- f_true(t) + rnorm(40, 0, 3)
  predict(lm(y ~ poly(t, d)), data.frame(t = 205))
})
c(bias2 = (mean(pred) - f_true(205))^2, variance = var(pred))
At 205 °C:



Degree
Bias²
Variance




1
3.78
4.24


5
0.28
1.15


10
0.00
2.76



The line is biased: on average it predicts 1.9 points too low at 205 °C. Degree 10 is unbiased, but its predictions scatter more than degree 5’s. Degree 5 has the smallest sum. The line’s variance is surprisingly high too: a rigid model that’s wrong swings around, because where it misses depends on where each study’s runs happened to fall.




Averaged over the whole temperature range, the same simulation draws the classic picture:

bv_all <- function(d, n = 40, reps = 200) {
  set.seed(7014)
  g <- seq(152, 223, length.out = 50)
  P <- replicate(reps, { t <- runif(n, 150, 225); y <- f_true(t) + rnorm(n, 0, 3); predict(lm(y ~ poly(t, d)), data.frame(t = g)) })
  c(bias2 = mean((rowMeans(P) - f_true(g))^2), variance = mean(apply(P, 1, var)))
}
tab <- t(sapply(1:10, bv_all))
df <- data.frame(degree = rep(1:10, 3), value = c(tab[, 1], tab[, 2], tab[, 1] + tab[, 2] + 9),
                 part = rep(c("bias²", "variance", "test MSE"), each = 10))
ggplot(df, aes(degree, value, color = part)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_log10() + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`bias²` = "#2a78d6", variance = "#1baf7a", `test MSE` = "#C2416C"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Polynomial degree", y = "Average over 152–223 °C (log scale)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "top")








The variance explodes at high degrees because high-degree polynomials go wild near the ends of the data, where there are few runs to hold them down. Over the whole range, degree 4 balances best, with an expected test MSE of about 10.6.






NoteGo deeper: deriving the decomposition





Write \hat f = \hat f(x_0), f = f(x_0), and Y_0 = f + \varepsilon, with \varepsilon independent of the training data (and so of \hat f). Then

E(Y_0 - \hat f)^2 = E(f - \hat f)^2 + 2E\big[\varepsilon (f - \hat f)\big] + E\varepsilon^2 = E(f - \hat f)^2 + \sigma^2,

because the middle term is 2E[\varepsilon]\,E[f - \hat f] = 0. Now add and subtract E\hat f:

E(f - \hat f)^2 = (f - E\hat f)^2 + E(\hat f - E\hat f)^2 + 2(f - E\hat f)\,E(E\hat f - \hat f) = \text{bias}^2 + \text{Var}(\hat f),

since E(E\hat f - \hat f) = 0. The expectations are over training sets: the “imagine running the study again” in the text. The Elements of Statistical Learning, section 7.3, works it out for linear models and for k-nearest neighbors.

title: What is statistical learning?
text:
Parametric and non-parametric methods
A polynomial is a parametric method: you choose a form for f with a fixed number of parameters, then estimate them. If the form is wrong, as a line is here, no amount of data fixes it. Non-parametric methods don’t assume a form. They let the data shape \hat f, with a tuning setting that controls how smooth it is. They need more data, but they can follow any reasonable f.
A smoothing spline is one. Its tuning setting is the effective degrees of freedom, df: about 2 is nearly a straight line, and 40 would pass through every run.
Your turn. Fit smoothing splines with 4, 8 and 20 degrees of freedom, and compare their test MSEs.









The degrees of freedom are the function’s argument, k.


sapply(c(4, 8, 20), function(k) {
  fit <- smooth.spline(runs$temp_C, runs$yield_pct, df = k)
  mean((new_runs$yield_pct - predict(fit, new_runs$temp_C)$y)^2)
})
14.3 with 4 degrees of freedom, 11.7 with 8, and 14.1 with 20: the same U-shape as the polynomials, with a different dial. The best spline is about as good as the best polynomial (11.5), without having had to guess the form of f. Lesson 9 covers splines properly, and every flexible method in this module has a dial like df that has to be set from the data.

title: What is statistical learning?
text:
Classification and the Bayes classifier
When the output is a category, the error is the error rate: the share of cases put in the wrong class. Suppose the plant only cares whether a run is a high-yield run, above 75%. A classifier takes a temperature and answers “high” or “not high”.
The best possible classifier assigns each input to its most probable class. It’s called the Bayes classifier, and its error rate, the Bayes error rate, is the classification version of the irreducible error: no classifier can do better on average. Here, since Y = f(X) + \varepsilon with \varepsilon \sim N(0, 3^2),

P(\text{high} \mid X = x) = P\big(f(x) + \varepsilon > 75\big) = 1 - \Phi\left(\frac{75 - f(x)}{3}\right),

which is above 0.5 exactly when f(x) > 75, that is, between 172.2 and 207.5 °C.
Your turn. Compute the Bayes classifier’s error rate on the new runs.









The Bayes classifier picks the more probable class: “high” when its probability is over 0.5.


high <- new_runs$yield_pct > 75
p_high <- 1 - pnorm(75, mean = f_true(new_runs$temp_C), sd = 3)
mean((p_high > 0.5) != high)
7.75%. Even knowing f exactly, about 1 run in 13 lands on the wrong side of 75%, because the noise pushes runs near the boundary across it. A classifier built from the degree-5 polynomial (high when \hat f(x) > 75) gets 8.1% wrong, close to the floor. Real classifiers never know P(Y \mid X), so most of this module is about estimating it: logistic regression, discriminant analysis, nearest neighbors and more.

title: What is statistical learning?
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Fewer runs. Suppose only 15 of the 40 runs had been done. Pick them with set.seed(7015); small <- runs[sample(40, 15), ], and find the test MSE of polynomials of degree 1 to 6 fitted to them. Which degree is best now?









Fit to small.


set.seed(7015)
small <- runs[sample(40, 15), ]
test_small <- sapply(1:6, function(d) {
  fit <- lm(yield_pct ~ poly(temp_C, d), data = small)
  mean((new_runs$yield_pct - predict(fit, new_runs))^2)
})
which.min(test_small)
Degree 3, with a test MSE of 19.4, and degrees 5 and 6 are disastrous (500 and 716). With less data, every model’s variance is higher, so the best balance moves toward simpler models. The right flexibility isn’t a property of the problem alone: it depends on how much data you have.




Challenge 2 · More runs. Now simulate 400 runs from the same process, and repeat the comparison for degrees 1 to 12.









The error’s standard deviation is 3.


set.seed(7016)
big <- data.frame(temp_C = runif(400, 150, 225))
big$yield_pct <- f_true(big$temp_C) + rnorm(400, 0, 3)
test_big <- sapply(1:12, function(d) {
  fit <- lm(yield_pct ~ poly(temp_C, d), data = big)
  mean((new_runs$yield_pct - predict(fit, new_runs))^2)
})
round(test_big, 2)
The minimum is now at degree 6 (9.68), and everything from degree 4 to 12 is within 0.25 of it, just above the floor of 9.47. With ten times the data, the variance of flexible models falls so much that overfitting hardly costs anything. That’s why big datasets let machine learning use very flexible models, and why small plant datasets usually reward simple ones.

title: What is statistical learning?
text:
Quick quiz

1. A soft sensor estimates a lab result from process tags every minute. Is that mainly prediction or inference?

Prediction
Inference
Neither


What matters is the accuracy of each estimate, not what the model’s insides say.



2. As a model gets more flexible, what happens to its training error?

It never goes up
It falls, then rises
It rises


The test error is the one that falls, then rises.



3. A model’s training MSE is 2 and its test MSE is 15. What’s happening?

Underfitting
Overfitting
It’s the irreducible error


It has learned patterns in the training data that don’t carry over to new data.



4. What does more flexibility usually do?

Raises the bias and lowers the variance
Lowers the bias and raises the variance
Lowers both


That’s the bias-variance trade-off. The best test error balances the two.



5. What can reduce the irreducible error?

A more flexible model
More training data
Measuring new inputs that explain part of the noise


The irreducible error is irreducible for the inputs you have. New inputs can explain part of what was noise.



6. What is the Bayes error rate?

The error rate of naive Bayes
The lowest error rate any classifier could achieve
The error rate of a Bayesian model


It’s the error of the classifier that knows the true class probabilities.

title: What is statistical learning?
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve met the ideas that the rest of this module builds on. Here’s what you’ve learned:

The setup: Y = f(X) + \varepsilon. Statistical learning estimates f, for prediction or for inference.
Supervised learning has an output to learn from (regression and classification), and unsupervised learning doesn’t.
Training error always falls with flexibility. Test error falls, then rises: for the 40 pilot runs, a degree-5 polynomial was best, at 11.50, and the line was worst, at 93.2.
The irreducible error, here about 9, is a floor that no model can get under.
Bias and variance: rigid models are biased, flexible models are variable, and the test error is their sum plus the noise. Less data favors simpler models, and more data allows flexible ones.
The Bayes classifier knows the true class probabilities. Its error rate, 7.75% here, is the floor for classification.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download pilot_runs.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and copy f_true() from this lesson.

Watch the overfit. Plot the 40 runs with the fitted curves of degree 1, 5 and 12 over them. Where does the degree-12 curve go wrong? Add xlim(140, 235) to see what happens just outside the data.
Bias and variance by temperature. Repeat the bias-variance simulation at 155, 170, 190, 205 and 220 °C, for degrees 3 and 10. Where is the variance highest, and why?
The noise level. Simulate studies with a noise SD of 1 and of 6, and redo the test-error curve for each. How does the best degree change?
Classification. Fit a logistic regression of high on poly(temp_C, 2) to the 40 runs, and find its error rate on the new runs. How close does it get to the Bayes error rate?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Statistical learning

A set of methods for estimating, from data, the function that links inputs to an output.

Supervised learning

Learning from examples whose outputs are known: regression for a numeric output, classification for a category.

Unsupervised learning

Finding structure in inputs with no output to learn from, such as groups or main directions of variation.

Training error

The average loss on the data the model was fitted to.

Test error

The average loss on new data that wasn’t used to fit the model.

Overfitting

Fitting the noise in the training data, so that the test error is much larger than the training error.

Irreducible error

The variance of \varepsilon: the part of the test error that no model of the same inputs can remove.

Bias-variance trade-off

Flexible models have low bias and high variance, rigid models the reverse. The test error is lowest where they balance.

Parametric method

A method that assumes a form for f with a fixed number of parameters.

Bayes classifier

The classifier that assigns each input to its most probable class. Its error rate is the lowest possible.











NoteWant to read more?






Gareth James, Daniela Witten, Trevor Hastie and Robert Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition, free PDF), chapter 2, “Statistical Learning”. This module’s textbook: chapter 2 covers everything in this lesson.
Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani and Jerome Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning (2nd edition, free PDF), sections 2.9 and 7.3, on model complexity and the bias-variance decomposition.
Leo Breiman, “Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures”, Statistical Science 16(3), 2001, doi:10.1214/ss/1009213726. A famous essay on prediction and inference, with replies from statisticians who disagreed.
