title: Cointegration
text:
Module 6 · Lesson 12 of 13 Week 101 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 10 ended with a warning: regressing one wandering series on another gives “significant” results that mean nothing. But some wandering series really are tied together. The plant’s boilers burn natural gas, so its steam cost follows the gas price. Gas prices wander like a random walk: there’s no level they return to. The steam cost wanders too. But the two can’t drift apart for long, because if the steam cost ran far ahead of the gas price, the next contract renegotiation would bring it back.
Two non-stationary series that share a common stochastic trend, so that some combination of them is stationary, are cointegrated. Clive Granger and Robert Engle shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in economics partly for this idea. The data are 1,000 trading days of the gas price (€/MWh) and the plant’s daily steam cost (€ per tonne), from January 2022 to October 2025.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Cointegration
text:
Two wandering series













long <- rbind(data.frame(date = as.Date(gp$date), value = gp$gas_eur_mwh, series = "natural gas (€/MWh)"),
              data.frame(date = as.Date(gp$date), value = gp$steam_cost_eur_t, series = "steam cost (€/t)"))
ggplot(long, aes(x = date, y = value)) +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ series, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Your turn. Check that each series has a unit root, and that its daily changes don’t, with the ADF test.









Test the steam cost’s changes too: diff(steam).


c(gas = tseries::adf.test(gas)$p.value, steam = tseries::adf.test(steam)$p.value,
  gas_changes = tseries::adf.test(diff(gas))$p.value, steam_changes = tseries::adf.test(diff(steam))$p.value)
p = 0.73 for the gas price and 0.65 for the steam cost: no evidence against a unit root in either. Their daily changes: p = 0.01 (or less) for both. So both are I(1). Cointegration only makes sense for series like these: two stationary series need no leash, and two series with different orders of integration can’t share one.

title: Cointegration
text:
The Engle-Granger method
If the two series are cointegrated, there’s a combination \text{steam}_t - \beta_0 - \beta_1\,\text{gas}_t that’s stationary. The Engle-Granger method estimates it in two steps:

Regress one series on the other by least squares: the cointegrating regression. Unlike Lesson 10’s spurious regression, this one is meaningful if the series are cointegrated, and its estimates are even unusually precise (“superconsistent”).
Test the residuals for a unit root. If they’re stationary, the series are cointegrated.

Your turn. Step 1: regress the steam cost on the gas price.









Regress on the gas price, gas.


long_run <- lm(steam ~ gas)
c(coef(long_run), r2 = summary(long_run)$r.squared)
In the long run, steam costs €8.13 per tonne plus €0.618 for every €/MWh of gas: about 0.62 MWh of gas per tonne of steam, priced in, which is a plausible boiler efficiency. R² = 0.97. That R² alone proves nothing, as Lesson 10’s spurious pair showed with 0.62. The test is whether the residuals, the steam cost’s deviation from its long-run relationship, are stationary.




Step 2 has a catch. The residuals come from a regression that chose \beta to make them as small as possible, so they look more stationary than they are, and the ordinary ADF critical values are too lenient. The Phillips-Ouliaris test, tseries::po.test(), uses the right critical values for residuals of a cointegrating regression. Its null hypothesis is no cointegration.
Your turn. Run it on the two series.









The second column is the gas price. The first column is the one regressed on the others.


tseries::po.test(cbind(steam, gas))$p.value
p = 0.01 (the smallest the test reports): strong evidence against “no cointegration”. The deviations from the long-run relationship are stationary: the steam cost wanders with the gas price, but always comes back to its line.




Your turn. For contrast, run the same test on two independent random walks.









Both walks have 1,000 steps.


set.seed(6121)
a <- cumsum(rnorm(1000))
b <- cumsum(rnorm(1000))
tseries::po.test(cbind(b, a))$p.value
p = 0.15 (the largest it reports): no evidence of cointegration. A regression of b on a would still give a large R² and a tiny p-value, but its residuals wander, and the cointegration test sees through it. That’s the practical rule: before trusting a regression between two I(1) series, test for cointegration. If they’re cointegrated, the levels regression is meaningful. If not, use their differences.

title: Cointegration
text:
Johansen’s test
The Engle-Granger method has two weaknesses: the result can depend on which series you put on the left, and with more than two series, there can be more than one cointegrating relationship. Johansen’s method works within a VAR (Lesson 11) and tests the cointegrating rank r, the number of independent stationary combinations, one value at a time: is r = 0? If not, is r \leq 1? And so on. The urca package’s ca.jo() does it.
Your turn. Run the Johansen trace test, with 2 lags in the VAR and a constant in the cointegrating relationship, and compare the test statistics with the 5% critical values.









A constant in the cointegrating relationship: ecdet = "const".


jo <- urca::ca.jo(data.frame(steam = steam, gas = gas), type = "trace", K = 2, ecdet = "const")
cbind(statistic = jo@teststat, critical_5pct = jo@cval[, "5pct"])
Read from the bottom up. r = 0: a statistic of 92.5, far above its 5% critical value of 20.0, so reject “no cointegration”. r \leq 1: 1.2, far below 9.2, so don’t reject. The rank is 1: one cointegrating relationship, one common stochastic trend, as expected for two series tied by one physical process.




Your turn. The cointegrating vector is the first column of jo@V. Normalize it so that the steam cost’s coefficient is 1, and compare it with the Engle-Granger estimates.









Divide by the steam cost’s entry, the first.


jo <- urca::ca.jo(data.frame(steam = steam, gas = gas), type = "trace", K = 2, ecdet = "const")
jo@V[, 1] / jo@V[1, 1]
(1, -0.617, -8.19): the stationary combination is \text{steam}_t - 0.617\,\text{gas}_t - 8.19. Engle-Granger’s least squares said 0.618 and 8.13. Two different methods, the same long-run relationship.

title: Cointegration
text:
The error-correction model
Cointegration says the deviations are stationary. The error-correction model (ECM) says how they get corrected. It models the steam cost’s daily change with two terms: how far it was from its long-run relationship yesterday, and today’s change in the gas price:

\Delta\text{steam}_t = \alpha + \gamma\, e_{t-1} + \delta\,\Delta\text{gas}_t + \varepsilon_t,

where e_{t-1} is yesterday’s Engle-Granger residual. If the series are cointegrated, \gamma is negative: a positive deviation, steam too expensive for the gas price, is followed by a fall. Granger’s representation theorem says that cointegration and error correction are two sides of the same coin.
Your turn. Fit the ECM by least squares.









Drop the last residual: e[-length(e)], or e[-1000].


e <- resid(lm(steam ~ gas))
d_steam <- diff(steam)
d_gas <- diff(gas)
e_lag <- e[-1000]                   # yesterday's deviation: drop the last one
ecm <- lm(d_steam ~ e_lag + d_gas)
rbind(estimate = coef(ecm), se = summary(ecm)$coefficients[, "Std. Error"])
\hat\gamma = -0.179 (SE 0.018): each day, 18% of any deviation from the long-run relationship is corrected. And \hat\delta = 0.633 (SE 0.021): a €1/MWh rise in the gas price raises the steam cost by €0.63 the same day. Unlike Lesson 10’s regressions, every term here is stationary, so the ordinary standard errors are valid.




Your turn. How long does it take for half of a deviation to disappear? With a correction of \gamma per day, the deviation shrinks by (1 + \gamma) a day, so its half-life is \log(0.5)/\log(1 + \gamma) days.









Use the correction coefficient, gamma.


gamma <- -0.179452014
log(0.5) / log(1 + gamma)
3.5 trading days. A deviation, for example from a shift in the plant’s steam demand that briefly moves its cost, halves in three and a half days, and is mostly gone within two weeks. The cost accountants can treat the long-run relationship as the “fair” steam cost, and expect the actual cost to return to it quickly.

title: Cointegration
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Short run and long run. Compare the ECM’s short-run effect of the gas price, \hat\delta, with the long-run one from the cointegrating regression. Are gas price changes passed through to the steam cost fully, and at once?









The short-run effect is the coefficient on the gas price’s changes, diff(gas).


long_run <- coef(lm(steam ~ gas))[["gas"]]
e <- resid(lm(steam ~ gas))
short_run <- coef(lm(diff(steam) ~ e[-1000] + diff(gas)))[[3]]
c(long_run = long_run, short_run = short_run, ratio = short_run / long_run)
0.618 in the long run and 0.633 the same day: the ratio is 1.02, so price changes pass through fully and at once, with a little overshoot that the error correction then removes. In many markets, the short-run pass-through is much smaller than the long-run one, and the ECM shows how the gap closes over time.




Challenge 2 · Where’s the deviation going? On the last day, the steam cost was above its long-run relationship. Find the deviation, and its expected size ten trading days later, if the gas price doesn’t change.









Ten days: raise (1 + \gamma) to the power 10.


e <- resid(lm(steam ~ gas))
gamma <- coef(lm(diff(steam) ~ e[-1000] + diff(gas)))[[2]]
c(today = e[[1000]], in_10_days = e[[1000]] * (1 + gamma)^10)
€0.29 per tonne above the long-run relationship today, and an expected €0.04 in ten trading days. This is the forecast a cointegrated system makes that a VAR in differences can’t: it knows the levels are tied, so it predicts the gap closing. For long-horizon forecasts of cointegrated series, that matters a lot.

title: Cointegration
text:
Quick quiz

1. When are two series cointegrated?

When they’re highly correlated
When both are I(1), but some linear combination of them is stationary
When both are stationary


They share a common stochastic trend, so they can’t drift apart.



2. Why can’t you use the ordinary ADF critical values on the residuals of a cointegrating regression?

Because the residuals are always stationary
Because least squares chose the coefficients to make the residuals small, so they look more stationary than they are
Because the residuals have a trend


Engle-Granger and Phillips-Ouliaris tests use adjusted critical values.



3. A Johansen trace test rejects r = 0 but not r \leq 1. What’s the cointegrating rank?

0
1
2


Test from r = 0 upward, and stop at the first hypothesis you can’t reject.



4. In an error-correction model, the coefficient on the lagged deviation is −0.18. What does that mean?

The series diverge by 18% a day
18% of any deviation from the long-run relationship is corrected each period
The short-run effect is −0.18


A negative coefficient pulls the series back toward equilibrium. Its half-life here is 3.5 days.



5. Two I(1) series are not cointegrated. How should you model their relationship?

Regress one on the other in levels
Work with their differences, for example a VAR in differences
Use an error-correction model


Without cointegration, a levels regression is spurious, and there’s no error to correct.



6. What can an error-correction model forecast that a VAR in differences can’t?

Short-run changes
That a gap between the two series’ levels will close
Seasonality


A VAR in differences forgets the levels, and with them the long-run relationship.

title: Cointegration
text:
Wrap-up
You can now find and use long-run relationships between wandering series. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Both series are I(1): ADF p = 0.73 for the gas price and 0.65 for the steam cost, and their changes are stationary.
Engle-Granger: in the long run, steam costs €8.13 per tonne plus €0.618 per €/MWh of gas, and the Phillips-Ouliaris test confirms cointegration (p = 0.01), while two independent random walks fail it (p = 0.15).
Johansen: the cointegrating rank is 1 (trace statistics 92.5 and 1.2), and the cointegrating vector, (1, -0.617, -8.19), matches Engle-Granger.
Error correction: 18% of a deviation is corrected each day, a half-life of 3.5 trading days, and gas price changes pass through fully and at once (0.63 against 0.62).







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download gas_prices.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install urca: install.packages("urca").

Plot the deviation. Plot the Engle-Granger residuals over time, with a horizontal line at 0. Do they look stationary? Compare with the residuals of a regression of b on a for two independent random walks.
The other direction. Regress the gas price on the steam cost instead. Is the implied long-run slope 1/0.618? Why not exactly? (Hint: least squares isn’t symmetric.)
A vector error-correction model. Run summary(urca::cajorls(jo, r = 1)). It fits the ECM for both series. Which one does the correcting: does the gas price respond to deviations, or only the steam cost?
The Engle-Granger critical values. Use urca::ur.df(e, type = "none", lags = 1) on the residuals, and compare its test statistic with the Engle-Granger 5% critical value for two series, about −3.37.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Cointegration

Two or more I(1) series with a linear combination that’s stationary.

Common stochastic trend

The shared random-walk component that cointegrated series follow.

Cointegrating regression

A levels regression between cointegrated series, which estimates their long-run relationship.

Engle-Granger method

Estimating the cointegrating regression by least squares, then testing its residuals for a unit root.

Phillips-Ouliaris test

A test of the null hypothesis of no cointegration, with critical values for regression residuals.

Johansen’s method

A VAR-based test of the cointegrating rank, and an estimate of the cointegrating vectors.

Error-correction model

A model for the changes of cointegrated series, including the previous deviation from their long-run relationship.

Half-life

The time it takes for half of a deviation to be corrected.











NoteWant to read more?






Robert Engle and Clive Granger, “Co-integration and error correction: representation, estimation, and testing”, Econometrica (1987). The paper that introduced the idea, and the representation theorem.
Bernhard Pfaff, Analysis of Integrated and Cointegrated Time Series with R (2nd edition, Springer, 2008). By the author of the urca and vars packages.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, “Time-series econometrics: cointegration and autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity” (2003). The scientific background to Engle and Granger’s Nobel Prize, which also covers Lesson 13’s ARCH models.

title: Regression with autocorrelated errors
text:
Module 6 · Lesson 10 of 13 Week 99 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 9’s seasonal models forecast the steam demand from the calendar alone, and left behind structure only the weather could explain. The natural fix is a regression: steam demand depends on the heating degree days, and on the plant’s slow growth,
y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{HDD}_t + \beta_2\, t + \eta_t .
Module 2 would fit that by least squares, and trust its standard errors. But here the error term \eta_t is a time series itself: a cold spell, a slow month of production or a long shutdown affects several months in a row. Ordinary least squares assumes the errors are independent. When they aren’t, its estimates are still unbiased, but its standard errors are wrong, usually too small, and every test and interval built on them is overconfident.
The fix is to model the errors too: regression with ARIMA errors, where \eta_t follows an ARMA model, and its white-noise part, \varepsilon_t, is what’s left.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Regression with autocorrelated errors
text:
Least squares, and its residuals












Your turn. Fit the regression by least squares, and look at the coefficients, their standard errors, and the residuals’ lag-1 autocorrelation.









Lag 1 is the second element of the ACF.


ols <- lm(steam_kt ~ hdd + t, data = steam)
c(coef(ols), se = summary(ols)$coefficients[, "Std. Error"], lag1 = acf(resid(ols), plot = FALSE)$acf[2])
Each extra heating degree day adds 0.0229 kt of steam (SE 0.0005), and demand grows by 0.051 kt a month (SE 0.0022), on top of the weather. But the residuals have a lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.57: a month with more steam than the weather explains is usually followed by another. So these standard errors can’t be trusted.




The classical check for this is the Durbin-Watson statistic,

DW = \frac{\sum_{t=2}^n (e_t - e_{t-1})^2}{\sum_{t=1}^n e_t^2} \approx 2(1 - r_1),

which is near 2 for independent residuals, and near 0 for strongly positively autocorrelated ones.
Your turn. Compute it.









The numerator adds up the squared changes, diff(e)^2.


e <- resid(lm(steam_kt ~ hdd + t, data = steam))
sum(diff(e)^2) / sum(e^2)
0.84, far below 2, and close to 2(1 - 0.57) = 0.86. lmtest::dwtest() turns it into a formal test, but with a value this low, there’s no doubt. Module 2 met the Durbin-Watson test as a regression diagnostic. For time series data, it should be the first thing you check.

title: Regression with autocorrelated errors
text:
Regression with AR(1) errors
Arima() fits the regression and the error model together, by maximum likelihood, when you give it the predictors as xreg. With order = c(1, 0, 0), the errors are AR(1): \eta_t = \phi\,\eta_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t.
Your turn. Fit it, and compare the coefficients and standard errors with least squares.









The predictors are in the setup code’s matrix X.


fit <- Arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = X)
rbind(estimate = coef(fit), se = sqrt(diag(vcov(fit))))
The error AR coefficient is 0.58. The coefficients barely move, 0.0226 kt per degree day and 0.051 kt a month of growth, but their standard errors grow: from 0.0005 to 0.0007 for the heating degree days, and from 0.0022 to 0.0041 for the trend, almost twice as large. Least squares claimed the growth rate was known twice as precisely as it is. With the honest standard error, the 95% interval for the yearly growth is 12 \times (0.051 \pm 1.96 \times 0.0041), from 0.52 to 0.71 kt a year.




Your turn. Now the decisive check. Lesson 9’s seasonal model left residual autocorrelation at lags 5, 9 and 18. Test this model’s residuals over 24 lags, and count how many autocorrelations are outside \pm 1.96/\sqrt{144}.









One ARMA coefficient in the errors: fitdf = 1.


fit <- Arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = X)
r <- acf(residuals(fit), lag.max = 24, plot = FALSE)$acf[-1]
c(ljung_box_p = Box.test(residuals(fit), lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 1)$p.value,
  outside = sum(abs(r) > 1.96 / sqrt(144)), lag5 = r[5], lag9 = r[9], lag18 = r[18])
The residuals pass easily, p = 0.62, and none of the 24 autocorrelations is outside the bounds. Lags 5, 9 and 18 are now −0.06, 0.00 and 0.12. The weather was the missing piece. A model built on the cause of the seasonality, rather than its calendar, explained it better, with fewer parameters, and with no seasonal differencing at all.

title: Regression with autocorrelated errors
text:
Generalized least squares
Another route to the same model is generalized least squares (GLS), from Module 2, with a correlation structure for the errors. The nlme package’s gls() fits a regression with AR(1) errors, correlation = corAR1(), using the formula interface.
Your turn. Fit the model with gls(), and find the coefficients, the estimated AR coefficient \phi and the standard errors.









The AR(1) correlation structure is corAR1().


g <- nlme::gls(steam_kt ~ hdd + t, data = steam, correlation = nlme::corAR1())
c(coef(g), phi = coef(g$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE), se = sqrt(diag(vcov(g))))
Nearly the same as Arima(): 0.0226 per degree day and 0.051 a month, with standard errors 0.0007 and 0.0044, and \hat\phi = 0.60. (gls() maximizes the restricted likelihood, REML, so its numbers differ slightly.) gls() fits into the usual regression workflow, with summary(), anova() and predict(), and handles irregularly spaced data with corCAR1(). Arima() is the better tool for forecasting, and for more complex error models.

title: Regression with autocorrelated errors
text:
Forecasting with a predictor
There’s a catch to forecasting with a regression: you need the predictors’ future values. The trend is easy. Next year’s heating degree days aren’t known, so the forecast has to assume something. A common choice is the climatology: each month’s average over past years.
Your turn. Forecast 2026 with the average heating degree days for each calendar month, and find January’s forecast, its 95% interval, and July’s.









2026 is months 145 to 156.


fit <- Arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = X)
normal_hdd <- tapply(steam$hdd, as.integer(substr(steam$month, 6, 7)), mean)     # the average for each month
future_X <- cbind(hdd = as.numeric(normal_hdd), t = 145:156)
fc <- forecast(fit, xreg = future_X)
c(normal_jan_hdd = normal_hdd[[1]], january = fc$mean[1], lo95 = fc$lower[1, 2], hi95 = fc$upper[1, 2], july = fc$mean[7])
With a normal January, 515 degree days, the forecast is 50.0 kt, with a 95% interval from 48.2 to 51.8, and July 38.5. That interval is narrower than Lesson 9’s, 47.6 to 52.9, but it’s not a fair comparison: it’s conditional on January’s weather being exactly normal. It leaves out the weather’s own uncertainty, which is the biggest uncertainty of all. Forecasts with predictors are best presented as scenarios.




Your turn. The weather service forecasts a cold January, 600 degree days. How much does that change January’s steam forecast?









January’s degree days are 600.


fit <- Arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = X)
normal_hdd <- tapply(steam$hdd, as.integer(substr(steam$month, 6, 7)), mean)
normal <- forecast(fit, xreg = cbind(hdd = as.numeric(normal_hdd), t = 145:156))
cold <- forecast(fit, xreg = cbind(hdd = c(600, normal_hdd[2:12]), t = 145:156))
c(normal = normal$mean[1], cold = cold$mean[1], difference = cold$mean[1] - normal$mean[1])
51.9 kt instead of 50.0: 85 extra degree days, times 0.0226 kt each, is 1.9 kt more steam. That’s what the boiler house can plan for: “if January is as cold as forecast, we’ll need about 2 kt more steam than usual.” A calendar model like Lesson 9’s can’t answer that question at all.

title: Regression with autocorrelated errors
text:
Spurious regression
The opposite danger: two series that seem related, but aren’t. Any two series that both trend, or both wander, will be correlated over a stretch of time, and a regression of one on the other will look highly significant. Granger and Newbold called it spurious regression in 1974.
Your turn. Simulate two independent random walks of 200 steps, regress one on the other, and look at the R² and the slope’s p-value. Then do the same with their differences.









Regress the changes on the changes: diff(a).


set.seed(6101)
a <- cumsum(rnorm(200))
b <- cumsum(rnorm(200))
levels <- summary(lm(b ~ a))
changes <- summary(lm(diff(b) ~ diff(a)))
c(r2_levels = levels$r.squared, p_levels = levels$coefficients[2, 4], r2_changes = changes$r.squared, p_changes = changes$coefficients[2, 4])
In levels: R² = 0.62, and a p-value of 10^{-43}, for two series that have nothing to do with each other. In differences: R² = 0.004, p = 0.38, the truth. Each random walk wanders, and over 200 steps, their wanderings happen to line up. The regression’s residuals are a random walk too, so the independence assumption fails completely. The rule: never regress one non-stationary series on another without checking the residuals, or differencing. Lesson 12 covers the one exception, cointegration.

title: Regression with autocorrelated errors
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · How often? One spurious regression could be bad luck. Repeat the simulation 1,000 times, and find how often the slope is “significant” at the 5% level.









The 5% level is 0.05.


set.seed(6102)
p_values <- replicate(1000, {
  a <- cumsum(rnorm(200))
  b <- cumsum(rnorm(200))
  summary(lm(b ~ a))$coefficients[2, 4]
})
mean(p_values < 0.05)
83% of the regressions find a “significant” relationship, where a valid test would find one 5% of the time. And the rate gets worse with longer series, not better. Plant data are full of slowly drifting series, such as fouling, catalyst age, ambient temperature and inventories. Regressing one on another is a reliable way to discover relationships that aren’t there.




Challenge 2 · How much did the weather explain? Compare the shock variance of the regression with AR(1) errors with that of Lesson 9’s best seasonal model, ARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)_{12}.









Lesson 9’s model has a seasonal MA(1): seasonal = c(0, 1, 1).


with_weather <- Arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = X)
calendar_only <- Arima(y, order = c(1, 1, 1), seasonal = c(0, 1, 1))
c(with_weather = with_weather$sigma2, calendar_only = calendar_only$sigma2, ratio = with_weather$sigma2 / calendar_only$sigma2)
0.82 against 1.80: knowing the month’s weather removes more than half of the one-step-ahead forecast variance. Most of what the calendar model calls “noise” is weather. That’s the general lesson of this module’s first half: a good predictor beats a clever model of the series’ own past.

title: Regression with autocorrelated errors
text:
Quick quiz

1. What goes wrong with ordinary least squares when the errors are positively autocorrelated?

The coefficients are biased
The standard errors are too small, so tests and intervals are overconfident
The R² is always 0


The estimates are still unbiased. It’s their claimed precision that’s wrong.



2. A regression has a Durbin-Watson statistic of 0.8. What does that suggest?

No autocorrelation
Strong positive autocorrelation in the residuals, about r_1 = 0.6
Negative autocorrelation


DW \approx 2(1 - r_1). Values near 2 are fine.



3. What does Arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = X) fit?

An AR(1) model for y, ignoring X
A regression of y on X, with AR(1) errors
A regression of X on y


The ARIMA order describes the errors, not y itself.



4. Why is the regression’s forecast interval for January narrower than the seasonal ARIMA’s?

Because the regression is always better
Because it assumes January’s weather is known, so it leaves out the weather’s uncertainty
Because it has fewer parameters


Forecasts with predictors are conditional on the predictors’ future values.



5. Two independent random walks are regressed on each other. What usually happens?

The slope is near 0 and insignificant
A “significant” slope and a large R², with random-walk residuals
The regression fails to run


That’s spurious regression. Regress the differences instead, or test for cointegration.



6. What’s the advantage of gls() over Arima() for a regression with AR(1) errors?

It’s more accurate
It fits into the usual regression workflow, and handles irregularly spaced data
It doesn’t need the errors to be stationary


Arima() is the better tool for forecasting.

title: Regression with autocorrelated errors
text:
Wrap-up
You can now regress one series on another without fooling yourself. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Least squares found 0.0229 kt of steam per degree day and 0.051 kt a month of growth, but its residuals had a lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.57 and a Durbin-Watson statistic of 0.84.
Regression with AR(1) errors (\hat\phi = 0.58) kept the coefficients, and nearly doubled the trend’s standard error, to 0.0041. gls() with corAR1() agrees.
The weather explained the leftovers: the residuals pass the Ljung-Box test (p = 0.62), and the shock variance is less than half the seasonal ARIMA’s (0.82 against 1.80).
Forecasts are conditional on the predictors: 50.0 kt for a normal January, and 1.9 kt more if it’s as cold as 600 degree days.
Spurious regression: two unrelated random walks gave R² = 0.62, and 83% of such pairs look “significant”.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download steam_demand.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

auto.arima() with predictors. Run auto.arima(y, xreg = X). Which error model does it choose? Is the difference from AR(1) errors worth it?
A weather scenario fan. Draw 1,000 Januaries’ degree days from the past twelve (with sample()), forecast with each, and plot the distribution of January’s steam forecasts. How much wider is it than the conditional interval?
Lagged weather. Does last month’s weather matter, for example through cold buildings? Add lag_hdd = c(NA, hdd[-144]) as a predictor, and check its coefficient.
Durbin-Watson, formally. Run lmtest::dwtest(lm(steam_kt ~ hdd + t, data = steam)). Then compare summary(ols) with lmtest::coeftest(ols, vcov = sandwich::NeweyWest(ols)), which corrects the standard errors for autocorrelation without modeling it.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Regression with ARIMA errors

A regression whose error term follows an ARIMA model, fitted with the regression by maximum likelihood.

Durbin-Watson statistic

\sum(e_t - e_{t-1})^2/\sum e_t^2, about 2(1 - r_1): a check for autocorrelated regression residuals.

Generalized least squares (GLS)

Least squares that allows for correlated or unequal-variance errors, such as gls() with corAR1().

Conditional forecast

A forecast that assumes given future values of the predictors.

Climatology

The average weather for each time of year, used as a “normal” scenario.

Spurious regression

An apparently significant relationship between unrelated non-stationary series.











NoteWant to read more?






Rob Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd edition), chapter 10, “Dynamic regression models”, including forecasting with predictors and scenarios.
Penn State’s STAT 510, lesson 8, “Regression with ARIMA errors, cross correlation functions, and relationships between two time series”.
Clive Granger and Paul Newbold, “Spurious regressions in econometrics”, Journal of Econometrics (1974). A short paper that changed how time series regressions are done.

title: Forecasting
text:
Module 6 · Lesson 8 of 13 Week 97 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Every model in this module can produce a forecast. The question this lesson asks is the one a plant manager should always ask back: how accurate is it likely to be? A model’s fit to the data it was estimated on is no answer. With enough parameters, any model fits the past well, and that tells you nothing about the future.
The honest test is to forecast data the model hasn’t seen. Split the series into a training set, to fit the models, and a test set, to judge them. Here, the steam demand from 2014 to 2023 is the training set, and the 24 months of 2024 and 2025 are the test set, as if it were January 2024 and you had to plan the boilers for two years.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Forecasting
text:
Training and test sets












Your turn. Split the series with window(): training to December 2023, testing from January 2024. Check the lengths.









The test set starts in January 2024.


train <- window(y, end = c(2023, 12))
test <- window(y, start = c(2024, 1))
c(train = length(train), test = length(test))
120 months to train on and 24 to test. The test set should be at least as long as the horizon you care about, here two years. Never tune a model by looking at the test set: once you’ve used it to choose, it’s no longer a fair test.

title: Forecasting
text:
Benchmarks
Before building anything clever, try the four simple methods that every forecast should beat:

Mean: the average of all the training data, meanf().
Naive: the last observation, naive(). The random walk’s forecast.
Seasonal naive: the value from the same month a year earlier, snaive().
Drift: the last observation, plus the average change per period, rwf(drift = TRUE).

Accuracy is measured from the test-set errors, e = y - \hat y. The root mean squared error (RMSE), \sqrt{\text{mean}(e^2)}, punishes big errors most. The mean absolute error (MAE), \text{mean}(|e|), is easier to explain: the typical error. accuracy(forecast, test) computes them, and more.
Your turn. Forecast the test period with all four, and compare their test-set RMSE.









The drift method is rwf() with drift = TRUE.


fcs <- list(mean = meanf(train, h = 24), naive = naive(train, h = 24),
            snaive = snaive(train, h = 24), drift = rwf(train, drift = TRUE, h = 24))
sapply(fcs, function(f) accuracy(f, test)["Test set", "RMSE"])
The seasonal naive method wins by far: an RMSE of 1.70 kt, against 6.0 to 7.0 for the other three, which ignore the season. “This month will be like the same month last year” is a strong benchmark for any seasonal series. A model that can’t beat it isn’t worth its complexity.




Your turn. Check what the seasonal naive method does: compare its forecast for January 2024 with the training data’s January 2023.









January is period 1.


fc <- snaive(train, h = 24)
c(forecast_jan_2024 = fc$mean[1], actual_jan_2023 = window(train, start = c(2023, 1), end = c(2023, 1)))
Both are 47.5 kt: the forecast simply copies last January. For 2025, the seasonal naive method copies 2023 again, since it can’t see 2024. It ignores the trend, which is why a model with a trend should beat it at longer horizons.

title: Forecasting
text:
ETS against ARIMA
Your turn. Fit ets() to the training data, forecast the test period, and find the test-set RMSE, MAPE (mean absolute percentage error) and MASE (explained below).









Compare the forecast with test.


fit <- ets(train)
fc <- forecast(fit, h = 24)
c(fit$method, round(accuracy(fc, test)["Test set", c("RMSE", "MAPE", "MASE")], 3))
ets() chose ETS(M,A,A) on the training data: multiplicative errors, with an additive trend and season. Its test-set RMSE is 1.64 kt, a little better than the seasonal naive’s 1.70, and its MAPE says it’s off by 2.8% in a typical month. That’s a smaller margin than you might expect from a model with a trend. The weather in 2024 and 2025 is what no model of steam alone can foresee.




On the training data, auto.arima() chooses ARIMA(1,0,0)(1,1,1)[12] with drift, a seasonal model (Lesson 9 explains the notation). The search takes a while in the browser, so here’s the model, specified directly.
Your turn. Fit it, forecast the test period, and compare its RMSE and MASE with ETS’s.









The third measure is "MASE".


fit <- Arima(train, order = c(1, 0, 0), seasonal = c(1, 1, 1), include.drift = TRUE)
fc <- forecast(fit, h = 24)
accuracy(fc, test)["Test set", c("RMSE", "MAE", "MASE")]
An RMSE of 1.59, slightly better than ETS’s 1.64, but a MASE of 0.83, worse than ETS’s 0.69. The two measures disagree because ARIMA made fewer large errors but more middling ones. With 24 test months, neither difference means much: that’s the limitation of a single test set, which the cross-validation below addresses.




Here are both forecasts, against what happened:

fe <- forecast(ets(train), h = 24)
fa <- forecast(Arima(train, order = c(1, 0, 0), seasonal = c(1, 1, 1), include.drift = TRUE), h = 24)
df <- rbind(data.frame(t = as.numeric(time(window(y, start = 2020))), v = as.numeric(window(y, start = 2020)), what = "actual"),
            data.frame(t = as.numeric(time(fe$mean)), v = as.numeric(fe$mean), what = "ETS forecast"),
            data.frame(t = as.numeric(time(fa$mean)), v = as.numeric(fa$mean), what = "ARIMA forecast"))
ggplot(df, aes(x = t, y = v, color = what)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2024, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(actual = "#3A1F35", `ETS forecast` = "#C2416C", `ARIMA forecast` = "#2a78d6"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Steam demand (kt per month)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Forecasting
section: Do the intervals keep their promise?
text:
Do the intervals keep their promise?
A forecast’s prediction intervals are part of the forecast. An 80% interval should contain the actual value about 80% of the time. That’s called coverage.
Your turn. Find the share of the 24 test months that fell inside ETS’s 80% and 95% intervals.









The 95% interval is the second column.


fc <- forecast(ets(train), h = 24)
c(inside_80 = mean(test >= fc$lower[, 1] & test <= fc$upper[, 1]),
  inside_95 = mean(test >= fc$lower[, 2] & test <= fc$upper[, 2]))
20 of 24 months inside the 80% intervals (83%), and 21 inside the 95% intervals (88%). The 80% intervals did well. The 95% intervals missed three months, about twice as many as they should, but with 24 months, that could easily be chance. Model-based intervals tend to be a bit too narrow in practice, because they ignore the uncertainty about the model itself. Keep track of coverage over time: it’s the honest test of whether a forecaster’s uncertainty can be trusted.

title: Forecasting
text:
Scale-free accuracy: MASE
RMSE and MAE are in the series’ units, so you can’t compare them across series. MAPE is unit-free, but it explodes near 0, and it treats over- and under-forecasts unequally. The mean absolute scaled error (MASE), from Hyndman and Koehler, divides the MAE by the in-sample MAE of the seasonal naive method on the training data:

\text{MASE} = \frac{\text{MAE of the forecast}}{\text{mean}\big(|y_t - y_{t-m}|\big)\text{ over the training data}}.

Below 1, the forecast beats a typical seasonal naive one-step forecast.
Your turn. Compute ETS’s MASE by hand.









The seasonal naive differences are 12 months apart.


fc <- forecast(ets(train), h = 24)
scale <- mean(abs(diff(train, lag = 12)))          # the seasonal naive's in-sample MAE
mae <- mean(abs(test - fc$mean))
c(scale = scale, mae = mae, mase = mae / scale)
The seasonal naive method’s typical in-sample error is 1.69 kt, and ETS’s test MAE is 1.17, so its MASE is 0.69, matching accuracy(). ETS’s errors, up to two years ahead, were about 30% smaller than the seasonal naive’s one-year-ahead errors on the past data.

title: Forecasting
text:
Time-series cross-validation
A single test set gives a single, noisy answer. Time-series cross-validation uses many: for each origin t, fit the model to the data up to t, forecast t + h, and record the error. The training set grows as the origin moves forward, and the model never sees the future. (Ordinary cross-validation, which leaves out random observations, would let the model peek at the future.)
tsCV(y, method, h) does it, and returns the errors.
Your turn. Compare the one-step-ahead cross-validated RMSE of the seasonal naive, naive and drift methods, using the whole series.









One step ahead: h = 1.


e_snaive <- tsCV(y, snaive, h = 1)
e_naive <- tsCV(y, naive, h = 1)
e_drift <- tsCV(y, rwf, drift = TRUE, h = 1)
c(snaive = sqrt(mean(e_snaive^2, na.rm = TRUE)), naive = sqrt(mean(e_naive^2, na.rm = TRUE)),
  drift = sqrt(mean(e_drift^2, na.rm = TRUE)), forecasts = sum(!is.na(e_snaive)))
The seasonal naive method’s cross-validated RMSE is 1.99 kt, over 131 forecasts, against 2.59 for naive and 2.63 for drift. One step ahead, last month is a better guide than it was two years ahead, but still worse than last year’s same month. Run on ETS(A,A,A), refitted at every origin from 60 months on, cross-validation gives a one-step RMSE of 1.50: a clear improvement, measured over 84 forecasts, not 24. (That takes 84 model fits, which is why it isn’t a browser exercise.)

title: Forecasting
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Combine the forecasts. One of the most robust findings in forecasting is that the average of several reasonable forecasts often beats each of them. Average the ETS and seasonal ARIMA forecasts, and find the test-set RMSE.









Average the two point forecasts, fe$mean and fa$mean.


fe <- forecast(ets(train), h = 24)
fa <- forecast(Arima(train, order = c(1, 0, 0), seasonal = c(1, 1, 1), include.drift = TRUE), h = 24)
combo <- (fe$mean + fa$mean) / 2
sqrt(mean((test - combo)^2))
1.22 kt, better than either alone (1.64 and 1.59). Their errors weren’t perfectly correlated, so averaging canceled some of them out. Forecast competitions, from Makridakis’s M competitions onward, have found this again and again. When in doubt, combine.




Challenge 2 · Accuracy by horizon. tsCV() with h = 6 returns a matrix with a column for each horizon. Find the seasonal naive method’s cross-validated RMSE at horizons 1 to 6.









Six horizons: h = 6.


e <- tsCV(y, snaive, h = 6)
round(sqrt(colMeans(e^2, na.rm = TRUE)), 4)
About 1.99 kt at every horizon from 1 to 6. That’s special to the seasonal naive method: every forecast up to 12 months ahead uses data from a year earlier, so they’re all equally old. For models like ETS and ARIMA, the error grows with the horizon, and comparing methods at the horizon you actually need is essential.

title: Forecasting
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why judge a forecasting model on a test set rather than on its fit to the training data?

Because the test set is larger
Because a model can fit the past well and still forecast badly, and only new data reveal that
Because the residuals are always zero on the training set


In-sample fit rewards complexity. Out-of-sample accuracy is what matters.



2. For a monthly seasonal series, which benchmark is usually hardest to beat?

The mean
Naive
Seasonal naive


Last year’s same month already captures the seasonal pattern.



3. What does a MASE of 0.7 mean?

The forecast is 70% accurate
The forecast’s MAE is 70% of the seasonal naive method’s in-sample MAE
70% of the forecasts were inside their intervals


Below 1 means better than a typical seasonal naive forecast.



4. In time-series cross-validation, why must the training set only contain data before each forecast origin?

To save computing time
Because using later data would let the model see the future, making its accuracy look too good
Because ARIMA can’t handle gaps


Ordinary cross-validation leaves out random points, which breaks the time order.



5. Of 24 test months, 21 fell inside the 95% prediction intervals. What should you conclude?

The intervals are much too narrow
Slightly fewer than expected, but with 24 months, that’s within chance; keep tracking coverage
The model is wrong


You’d expect about 23. Three misses instead of one can easily happen.



6. Why do combined forecasts often beat their components?

Because they use more data
Because the components’ errors are imperfectly correlated, so averaging cancels some of them
Because the average is always closer to the truth than any single forecast


Not always closer, but more robust on average.

title: Forecasting
text:
Wrap-up
You can now judge forecasts fairly. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Training and test sets: fit on 2014 to 2023, judge on 2024 and 2025.
Benchmarks: seasonal naive is the one to beat, with a test RMSE of 1.70 kt, against 6.0 to 7.0 for the mean, naive and drift methods.
ETS(M,A,A) and seasonal ARIMA beat it modestly: RMSE 1.64 and 1.59, MASE 0.69 and 0.83. The measures can disagree, and 24 months can’t settle it.
Coverage: 83% of test months inside ETS’s 80% intervals, and 88% inside its 95% intervals.
Time-series cross-validation compares methods over many origins: seasonal naive’s one-step RMSE is 1.99 kt over 131 forecasts, and ETS’s 1.50.
Combining the ETS and ARIMA forecasts gave the best test RMSE, 1.22 kt.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download steam_demand.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

All the measures. Run accuracy(fc, test) for the ETS forecast, and read every column: ME, RMSE, MAE, MPE, MAPE, MASE and ACF1. What does ME say about bias?
Cross-validate ETS and ARIMA. Write a function fets <- function(x, h) forecast(ets(x), h = h), and run tsCV(y, fets, h = 12, initial = 60). Do the same for auto.arima(). (It takes a few minutes.) Plot the RMSE against the horizon for both, with the seasonal naive’s.
A different test period. Repeat the test-set comparison with 2022 to 2023 as the test set. Does the ranking of ETS and ARIMA change?
Bootstrap intervals. Compare forecast(ets(train), h = 24) with forecast(ets(train), h = 24, bootstrap = TRUE). Are the intervals much different? What does that suggest about the residuals’ distribution?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Training set and test set

The data used to fit a model, and the later data used to judge its forecasts.

Benchmark methods

Simple forecasts that every model must beat: mean, naive, seasonal naive and drift.

RMSE and MAE

The root mean squared error and the mean absolute error of the forecasts, in the series’ units.

MAPE

The mean absolute percentage error. Unit-free, but unstable near 0.

MASE

The mean absolute scaled error: the MAE divided by the seasonal naive method’s in-sample MAE.

Coverage

The share of actual values that fall inside the prediction intervals.

Time-series cross-validation

Repeated forecasting from many origins, each using only the data before it.

Forecast combination

Averaging the forecasts of several methods.











NoteWant to read more?






Rob Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd edition), chapter 5, “The forecaster’s toolbox”: the benchmark methods, the accuracy measures and time-series cross-validation, and section 13.4, “Forecast combinations”.
Rob Hyndman and Anne Koehler, “Another look at measures of forecast accuracy”, International Journal of Forecasting (2006). Where MASE comes from, and what’s wrong with the alternatives.
Spyros Makridakis, Evangelos Spiliotis and Vassilios Assimakopoulos, “The M4 Competition: 100,000 time series and 61 forecasting methods”, International Journal of Forecasting (2020). What the largest forecasting competition learned, including about combinations.

title: ARIMA modeling
text:
Module 6 · Lesson 6 of 13 Week 95 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The plant’s crude unit processes a blend of crudes that changes as cargoes arrive, so the sulfur content of the feed drifts from week to week. Sulfur matters: it poisons catalysts downstream and decides how hard the hydrotreaters have to work. The lab has measured it weekly since January 2019, 364 weeks in all, and the planners want a forecast for the next quarter.
The series wanders, from a high of 1.9 wt% in 2019 to lows near 0.4 in 2022 and 2025, so it isn’t stationary. An ARIMA(p, d, q) model handles that: difference the series d times, then fit an ARMA(p, q) to the result. The “I” stands for integrated: the model for the original series is the ARMA model, summed up d times. George Box and Gwilym Jenkins turned that into a method in 1970, and it’s still the standard approach:
In this lesson you’ll:

title: ARIMA modeling
text:
Step 1: identification













ggplot(feed, aes(x = as.Date(week), y = sulfur_wt_pct)) +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Sulfur in the feed (wt%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Your turn. How many differences does the series need? Ask ndiffs(), and run the ADF test on the series and on its differences.









Test the differences, diff(x).


c(ndiffs = forecast::ndiffs(x),
  adf_level = tseries::adf.test(x)$p.value,
  adf_changes = tseries::adf.test(diff(x))$p.value)
One difference: the ADF test can’t reject a unit root for the level (p = 0.31), and rejects it for the weekly changes (p = 0.01). So d = 1. Physically, that makes sense: the crude slate drifts with the market and the cargoes, with nothing pulling it back to a fixed sulfur level.




Your turn. Now look at the differenced series’ ACF and PACF at lags 1 to 3.









Lags 1 to 3 of the PACF are elements 1 to 3.


dx <- diff(x)
rbind(acf = acf(dx, lag.max = 3, plot = FALSE)$acf[2:4],
      pacf = pacf(dx, lag.max = 3, plot = FALSE)$acf[1:3])
The ACF decays geometrically, 0.57, 0.29, 0.15, roughly halving each lag, and the PACF has one spike, 0.57, then nothing (−0.05 and 0.00). That’s the AR(1) pattern from Lesson 5’s table, so the candidate is ARIMA(1,1,0): the weekly changes follow an AR(1). A change in the crude slate tends to continue for a few weeks, as a supply shift works its way through the tanks.

title: ARIMA modeling
text:
Step 2: estimation
The forecast package’s Arima() is a front end to R’s arima() with a few conveniences, such as a drift term and forecasting from the fit.
Your turn. Fit ARIMA(1,1,0), and look at the AR coefficient, its standard error, the shock variance and the log-likelihood.









One difference: d = 1.


fit <- forecast::Arima(x, order = c(1, 1, 0))
c(coef(fit), se = sqrt(vcov(fit)[1, 1]), sigma2 = fit$sigma2, loglik = fit$loglik)
\hat\phi = 0.575 (SE 0.043), close to the 0.6 the series was simulated with, and a shock variance of 0.00069, an SD of 0.026 wt% a week. The model is \Delta y_t = 0.575\,\Delta y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t. With d = 1, there’s no mean or constant, because a constant in the differences would mean a steady drift. That’s a separate choice, tested below.




Your turn. Models are compared by an information criterion, which rewards fit and penalizes parameters. AIC is -2\log L + 2k, where k counts the estimated parameters, including the shock variance. Compute it by hand, and compare it with fit$aic.









The penalty is 2k.


fit <- forecast::Arima(x, order = c(1, 1, 0))
k <- 2                               # phi and sigma^2
c(by_hand = -2 * fit$loglik + 2 * k, reported = fit$aic)
−1607.4 both ways. Only differences in AIC between models matter. Lower is better, and a difference of 2 or more is worth noticing. AICc corrects AIC for small samples, and auto.arima() uses it. But AIC values can only be compared between models with the same d: differencing changes the data the likelihood is computed on.




Your turn. Fit every ARIMA(p, 1, q) with p and q from 0 to 2, and rank them by AICc.









The second argument comes from the grid’s q column.


grid <- expand.grid(p = 0:2, q = 0:2)
grid$aicc <- mapply(function(p, q) forecast::Arima(x, order = c(p, 1, q))$aicc, grid$p, grid$q)
head(grid[order(grid$aicc), ], 4)
ARIMA(1,1,0) comes first, at −1607.4. Next are ARIMA(1,1,1) and ARIMA(2,1,0), about 1.2 worse: each adds a parameter for almost no gain in fit. The identification and the information criterion agree, which is the reassuring case. When they don’t, prefer the simpler model, and let the diagnostics of Lesson 7 decide.

title: ARIMA modeling
text:
Letting auto.arima() choose
auto.arima() automates the same steps: it chooses d with repeated KPSS tests, then searches over p and q by AICc. By default, the search is stepwise: it starts from a few simple models and moves to neighbors while AICc improves. That’s fast, but it can miss the best model. stepwise = FALSE searches all models up to a maximum order.
Your turn. Run both searches.









The full search has stepwise = FALSE.


stepwise <- forecast::auto.arima(x)
full <- forecast::auto.arima(x, stepwise = FALSE, approximation = FALSE)
rbind(stepwise = forecast::arimaorder(stepwise), full = forecast::arimaorder(full))
Both choose (1, 1, 0). That’s three methods agreeing: the ACF and PACF, the hand-made grid and the automatic search. (approximation = FALSE makes it compute exact likelihoods, slower for long series. Rob Hyndman, who wrote the package, recommends checking an automatic choice by hand, as you just did.)




Your turn. Is there a steady drift, an average change per week? Fit the model with include.drift = TRUE, and look at the drift’s estimate and standard error.









Set include.drift = TRUE.


fit <- forecast::Arima(x, order = c(1, 1, 0), include.drift = TRUE)
rbind(estimate = coef(fit), se = sqrt(diag(vcov(fit))))
A drift of −0.002 wt% a week, with a standard error of 0.003: indistinguishable from 0. Over seven years, the series fell from 1.62 to 0.77, which looks like a downward trend, but a random walk wanders that far easily. Keep the model without drift. A drift term in a model with d = 1 means a straight-line trend in the forecasts, and assuming one without evidence would make long-range forecasts confidently wrong.

title: ARIMA modeling
text:
Forecasting
An ARIMA(1,1,0) forecast continues the latest change for a while, decaying by \phi each week, and then stays flat. Its prediction intervals keep widening, because the model has a unit root: the series could drift anywhere, given time.
Your turn. Forecast the next 12 weeks, and find the forecasts and 95% intervals one and twelve weeks ahead.









Week 12’s upper limit is in row 12.


fit <- forecast::Arima(x, order = c(1, 1, 0))
fc <- forecast::forecast(fit, h = 12)
rbind(week_1 = c(fc$mean[1], fc$lower[1, 2], fc$upper[1, 2]),
      week_12 = c(fc$mean[12], fc$lower[12, 2], fc$upper[12, 2]))
Next week: 0.775 wt% (95% interval 0.72 to 0.83). Twelve weeks out: 0.784, with an interval from 0.40 to 1.16. The last change was up, +0.012 wt%, so the forecast continues upward a little and then levels off. The interval at twelve weeks is seven times as wide as at one week. For planning the hydrotreaters, that’s the honest message: next week is predictable, next quarter much less so.





fit <- Arima(feed$sulfur_wt_pct, order = c(1, 1, 0))
fc <- forecast(fit, h = 12)
hist_df <- data.frame(week = 261:364, y = feed$sulfur_wt_pct[261:364])
fc_df <- data.frame(week = 365:376, m = as.numeric(fc$mean), lo80 = fc$lower[, 1], hi80 = fc$upper[, 1], lo95 = fc$lower[, 2], hi95 = fc$upper[, 2])
ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = fc_df, aes(x = week, ymin = lo95, ymax = hi95), fill = "#F4C0D1", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_ribbon(data = fc_df, aes(x = week, ymin = lo80, ymax = hi80), fill = "#F4C0D1") +
  geom_line(data = hist_df, aes(x = week, y = y), color = "#C2416C") +
  geom_line(data = fc_df, aes(x = week, y = m), color = "#3A1F35", linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "Week (since January 2019)", y = "Sulfur (wt%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
#> Don't know how to automatically pick scale for object of type <ts>. Defaulting
#> to continuous.
#> Don't know how to automatically pick scale for object of type <ts>. Defaulting
#> to continuous.
#> Don't know how to automatically pick scale for object of type <ts>. Defaulting
#> to continuous.

#> to continuous.

title: ARIMA modeling
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · ARIMA and exponential smoothing. Lesson 2’s simple exponential smoothing is exactly the forecast of an ARIMA(0,1,1) model, with \alpha = 1 + \theta. Fit ARIMA(0,1,1) to the pressure drop from Lesson 2, and compare 1 + \hat\theta with the \alpha that ses() chose, 0.349.









One MA term: q = 1.


dp <- read_csv("data/pressure_drop.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)$dp_bar
fit <- forecast::Arima(dp, order = c(0, 1, 1))
c(theta = coef(fit)[[1]], one_plus_theta = 1 + coef(fit)[[1]])
\hat\theta = -0.648, so 1 + \hat\theta = 0.352, close to ses()’s 0.349 (the two estimate the starting values differently). The two families overlap: every linear exponential smoothing model is an ARIMA model, and ARIMA(0,1,1) is SES. Holt’s linear method is ARIMA(0,2,2). Many seasonal ARIMA models and ETS models have no equivalent in the other family, though, which is why Lesson 8 compares them on the data.




Challenge 2 · A sweet-crude quarter? The refinery earns a premium in any quarter when the feed’s sulfur is below 0.5 wt%. Using the forecast distribution twelve weeks ahead, which is normal with the forecast as its mean, find the probability that the sulfur is below 0.5. The 95% interval’s half-width is 1.96 standard errors.









The 95% interval’s half-width is qnorm(0.975) standard errors.


fit <- forecast::Arima(x, order = c(1, 1, 0))
fc <- forecast::forecast(fit, h = 12)
se12 <- (fc$upper[12, 2] - fc$mean[12]) / qnorm(0.975)
c(se = se12, p_below_0.5 = pnorm(0.5, fc$mean[12], se12))
A forecast standard error of 0.19 wt% at twelve weeks, and a 7% probability that the sulfur is below 0.5 by then. Unlikely, but not negligible: the series was below 0.5 for weeks at a time in 2022 and 2025. Probabilities like this, from the full forecast distribution, are usually more useful to planners than a single number.

title: ARIMA modeling
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does ARIMA(1,1,0) mean?

An AR(1) and an MA(1), with no differencing
One difference, then an AR(1) model for the differences
An AR(1) with a trend


The middle number, d, is the number of differences.



2. What are the four steps of the Box-Jenkins approach?

Identify, estimate, check, forecast
Difference, smooth, decompose, forecast
Plot, test, fit, publish


And if the check fails, back to identification.



3. Can you compare the AIC of an ARIMA(1,1,0) with that of an ARIMA(1,0,0)?

Yes, always
No: the differencing changes the data the likelihood is computed on
Only if both have drift


Choose d first, by unit-root tests, then compare models with the same d.



4. What does a drift term do in a model with one difference?

It makes the series stationary
It adds a constant average change per period, so the forecasts follow a straight-line trend
It removes the seasonality


Include it only if the data support a steady trend.



5. Why do an ARIMA(1,1,0)’s prediction intervals keep widening with the horizon?

Because the AR coefficient is positive
Because the model has a unit root, so the series’ level can drift without limit
Because the shocks get larger


A stationary model’s intervals would level off at a fixed width.



6. Which ARIMA model gives the same forecasts as simple exponential smoothing?

ARIMA(1,0,0)
ARIMA(0,1,0)
ARIMA(0,1,1)


With \alpha = 1 + \theta. ARIMA(0,1,0) is the random walk, whose forecast is the last value.

title: ARIMA modeling
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve built an ARIMA model the Box-Jenkins way. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Differencing: the feed’s sulfur needs one difference (d = 1): ADF p = 0.31 for the level, 0.01 for the changes.
Identification: the changes’ ACF decays and their PACF cuts off after lag 1, pointing to ARIMA(1,1,0).
Estimation: \hat\phi = 0.575 (SE 0.043). AIC is -2\log L + 2k, −1607.4 here, and it’s the lowest AICc in a grid of nine models.
auto.arima() agrees, stepwise and with a full search. A drift term isn’t needed (−0.002, SE 0.003).
Forecasts: 0.775 wt% next week (0.72 to 0.83), and 0.784 in twelve weeks (0.40 to 1.16), with a 7% chance of being below 0.5.
ARIMA(0,1,1) is simple exponential smoothing, with \alpha = 1 + \theta.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download feed_impurity.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

The full display. Run ggtsdisplay(diff(x)), which shows a series with its ACF and PACF. Then autoplot(forecast(fit, h = 26)) for a half-year forecast.
auto.arima()’s search. Run auto.arima(x, trace = TRUE) to see every model it tries. How many does the stepwise search fit? And stepwise = FALSE?
A held-out test. Fit ARIMA(1,1,0) to the first 312 weeks only, forecast the last 52, and compare the forecasts with what happened. How many of the 52 weeks fell outside the 95% intervals?
The constant. Fit Arima(x, order = c(1, 0, 0)), an AR(1) without differencing. What does it estimate for \phi? Why is it so close to 1? Compare its 52-week forecast with ARIMA(1,1,0)’s.










NoteKey words from this lesson






ARIMA(p, d, q) model

An ARMA(p, q) model for the series differenced d times.

Integrated

A series that needs differencing to become stationary. The I in ARIMA.

Box-Jenkins approach

Identify, estimate, check, forecast, and repeat until the check passes.

Akaike information criterion (AIC)

-2\log L + 2k: a measure of fit penalized for the number of parameters. Lower is better.

AICc

AIC with a small-sample correction, used by auto.arima().

Drift

A constant in a differenced model, which gives the forecasts a straight-line trend.

Stepwise search

A model search that moves from model to neighboring model while the criterion improves.











NoteWant to read more?






Rob Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd edition), sections 9.7, “ARIMA modelling in fable” and 9.8, “Forecasting”, with the automatic algorithm explained. The 2nd edition covers the same with auto.arima().
Penn State’s STAT 510, lesson 3, “Identifying and estimating ARIMA models”, and lesson 4, on seasonal models.
Rob Hyndman and Yeasmin Khandakar, “Automatic time series forecasting: the forecast package for R”, Journal of Statistical Software (2008). How auto.arima() and ets() work.

title: Autoregressive models
text:
Module 6 · Lesson 4 of 13 Week 93 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 3 found that the reactor temperature’s partial autocorrelations cut off after lag 2: each minute depends directly on the previous two, and on nothing earlier. That’s the defining property of an autoregressive model, the most natural model for a process with memory. An AR(p) model regresses the series on its own past:
y_t = c + \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \phi_2 y_{t-2} + \cdots + \phi_p y_{t-p} + \varepsilon_t,
where \varepsilon_t is white noise. It’s a multiple regression whose predictors are the series itself, lagged. This lesson builds the simplest case by hand, then fits an AR(2) to the reactor temperature and reads it like a control engineer.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Autoregressive models
text:
AR(1)
The AR(1) model, y_t = \phi y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, is the discrete-time version of a first-order lag: each step keeps a fraction \phi of the last value and adds a new shock. If |\phi| < 1, shocks die away geometrically, and the process is stationary, with

\text{Var}(y_t) = \frac{\sigma^2}{1 - \phi^2}, \qquad \rho_k = \phi^k.

With \phi = 1, shocks never die away: that’s Lesson 3’s random walk.












Your turn. Simulate 5,000 steps of an AR(1) with \phi = 0.8 and \sigma = 1, and compare its variance with 1/(1 - 0.8^2), and its lag-1 autocorrelation with 0.8.









Each value depends on the previous one, y[t - 1].


set.seed(6041)
n <- 5000
y <- numeric(n)
e <- rnorm(n)
for (t in 2:n) y[t] <- 0.8 * y[t - 1] + e[t]
c(variance = var(y), theory = 1 / (1 - 0.8^2), lag1 = acf(y, plot = FALSE)$acf[2])
A variance of 2.82, against the theoretical 2.78, and a lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.80. The process’s variance is almost three times the shocks’ variance, because each shock lingers: with \phi = 0.8, it takes about 10 steps to fall to a tenth of its size. R’s arima.sim() simulates any ARMA model, but writing the loop once shows what the model is.




Your turn. ARMAacf() gives the theoretical ACF of any ARMA model. Find it for the AR(1) with \phi = 0.8, up to lag 5.









The AR coefficient is 0.8.


ARMAacf(ar = 0.8, lag.max = 5)
1, 0.8, 0.64, 0.512, 0.410, 0.328: exactly 0.8^k, a geometric decay. An AR(1)’s ACF decays smoothly, and its PACF has a single spike at lag 1. If \phi were negative, the ACF would alternate in sign.

title: Autoregressive models
section: When is an AR model stationary?
text:
When is an AR model stationary?
For AR(1), the condition is |\phi| < 1. For AR(p), it’s a condition on the characteristic polynomial, 1 - \phi_1 z - \phi_2 z^2 - \cdots - \phi_p z^p: the model is stationary if every root of it lies outside the unit circle, |z| > 1. (For AR(1), the root is z = 1/\phi, so that’s |\phi| < 1 again.) polyroot() finds the roots, coefficients first, starting with the constant term.
Your turn. Check two AR(2) models: \phi = (1.3, -0.6), close to the reactor temperature, and \phi = (0.5, 0.6).









The polynomial is 1 - \phi_1 z - \phi_2 z^2, so for \phi_2 = 0.6, the last coefficient is −0.6.


c(model_a = Mod(polyroot(c(1, -1.3, 0.6))), model_b = Mod(polyroot(c(1, -0.5, -0.6))))
Model A’s two roots both have modulus 1.29, outside the unit circle: stationary. They’re complex, a conjugate pair, which means the process oscillates. Model B has a root of modulus 0.94, inside the unit circle: not stationary, and a simulation of it would explode. Its coefficients add up to more than 1, which is always a sign of trouble for an AR(2).

title: Autoregressive models
text:
Yule-Walker estimation
How do you estimate the \phis? Multiply the AR(p) equation by y_{t-k} and take expectations, and you get the Yule-Walker equations, which link the coefficients to the autocorrelations. For AR(2):

\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \rho_1 \\ \rho_1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 \\ \phi_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \rho_1 \\ \rho_2 \end{pmatrix}.

Put the sample autocorrelations in, and solve.
Your turn. Estimate the reactor temperature’s AR(2) coefficients by Yule-Walker, by hand.









solve(R, r) solves the linear system.


r <- acf(temp, lag.max = 2, plot = FALSE)$acf[2:3]          # r1 and r2
R <- matrix(c(1, r[1], r[1], 1), 2)
solve(R, r)                                                  # solve R phi = r
\hat\phi_1 = 1.296 and \hat\phi_2 = -0.593, close to the values the temperature was simulated with, 1.3 and −0.6. A neat fact: \hat\phi_2 is exactly the lag-2 partial autocorrelation from Lesson 3, −0.593. For any AR(p) fitted by Yule-Walker, the last coefficient is the partial autocorrelation at lag p. That’s where the PACF comes from.




Your turn. R’s ar() fits AR models by Yule-Walker, and chooses the order p by AIC. Let it choose for the temperature.









The method is "yule-walker".


fit <- ar(temp, method = "yule-walker")
c(order = fit$order, fit$ar, shock_variance = fit$var.pred)
It chose order 2, with the same coefficients as by hand, and a shock variance of 0.0137, an SD of 0.12 °C. The minute-to-minute disturbances are small. The process’s own dynamics, the controller fighting each disturbance and overshooting, turn them into the larger swings you saw in Lesson 3’s plot.

title: Autoregressive models
text:
Maximum likelihood
Yule-Walker is fast but not the most efficient estimator. arima() fits by maximum likelihood, assuming normal shocks, and gives standard errors. The model is specified by its order (p, d, q): here, (2, 0, 0), an AR(2) with no differencing and no moving-average terms. The ARIMA lessons explain d and q.
Your turn. Fit the AR(2) by maximum likelihood, and look at the coefficients and their standard errors.









An AR(2) has p = 2.


fit <- arima(temp, order = c(2, 0, 0))
rbind(estimate = coef(fit), se = sqrt(diag(vcov(fit))))
\hat\phi_1 = 1.298 (SE 0.033), \hat\phi_2 = -0.596 (SE 0.033), almost the same as Yule-Walker’s, as they should be with 600 observations. Careful with the name of the last term: arima() calls it “intercept”, but it’s the mean of the series, −0.023 °C (SE 0.016), not the constant c in the equation. The two are related by c = \mu(1 - \phi_1 - \phi_2). The mean isn’t significantly different from 0: the controller holds the set point, on average.

title: Autoregressive models
text:
Reading the oscillation
The complex roots of an AR(2) say how it oscillates. If the root is z = |z|e^{i\theta}, the oscillation’s period is 2\pi/\theta time steps, and its damping, how fast it dies out, is set by |z|: each period, the swing shrinks by a factor of |z|^{-2\pi/\theta}.
Your turn. Find the period of the fitted model’s oscillation, in minutes, and the roots’ modulus.









The angle of a complex number is Arg().


fit <- arima(temp, order = c(2, 0, 0))
z <- polyroot(c(1, -coef(fit)[1:2]))[1]
c(period_minutes = 2 * pi / abs(Arg(z)), modulus = Mod(z))
A period of 11.0 minutes, and a modulus of 1.30. Each disturbance sets off an oscillation that repeats every 11 minutes and shrinks by a factor of 1.30^{-11} \approx 0.06 per cycle: about one overshoot, then it’s gone. That’s a fairly well-tuned loop. A control engineer would read the same numbers off a step response. Here, they came from 600 minutes of routine operating data, without disturbing the process.

title: Autoregressive models
text:
Forecasting with an AR model
An AR model forecasts by running its equation forward, with future shocks set to their mean, 0. The forecasts start from the last observations and return to the series’ mean, along the model’s own dynamics, and their standard errors grow to the series’ SD.
Your turn. Forecast the next 10 minutes with predict().









Ten minutes ahead: n.ahead = 10.


fit <- arima(temp, order = c(2, 0, 0))
fc <- predict(fit, n.ahead = 10)
round(rbind(forecast = fc$pred, se = fc$se), 4)
The last two minutes were −0.13 and −0.00 °C, recovering upward. The forecast continues the swing, overshooting to +0.08 two minutes ahead, then dipping to −0.05 at minute 607, and settling toward the mean of −0.02. Its standard error grows from 0.12 to 0.25, the SD of the process itself. Beyond about ten minutes, this model can’t say more than “around the set point, give or take 0.5 °C”.





fit <- arima(temp, order = c(2, 0, 0))
fc <- predict(fit, n.ahead = 10)
hist_df <- data.frame(minute = 541:600, value = temp[541:600])
fc_df <- data.frame(minute = 601:610, value = as.numeric(fc$pred), lo = as.numeric(fc$pred - 1.96 * fc$se), hi = as.numeric(fc$pred + 1.96 * fc$se))
ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = fc_df, aes(x = minute, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "grey85") +
  geom_line(data = hist_df, aes(x = minute, y = value), color = "#C2416C") +
  geom_line(data = fc_df, aes(x = minute, y = value), color = "#3A1F35", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Minute", y = "Temperature deviation (°C)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: Autoregressive models
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · AR by least squares. An AR model is a regression on lagged values, so ordinary least squares estimates it too. Regress each minute’s temperature on the previous two.









Two minutes earlier than temp[3:600] is temp[1:598].


y <- temp[3:600]
lag1 <- temp[2:599]
lag2 <- temp[1:598]
coef(lm(y ~ lag1 + lag2))
1.299 and −0.596, essentially the maximum likelihood estimates. With a long series, all three estimators agree. They differ for short series, or near the stationarity boundary, where Yule-Walker is biased toward 0 and least squares can give a non-stationary model.




Challenge 2 · Does the model reproduce the ACF? Compare the sample ACF of the temperature at lags 1 to 6 with the theoretical ACF of the fitted AR(2).









The AR coefficients are the first two: coef(fit)[1:2].


fit <- arima(temp, order = c(2, 0, 0))
rbind(sample = acf(temp, lag.max = 6, plot = FALSE)$acf[2:7],
      model = ARMAacf(ar = coef(fit)[1:2], lag.max = 6)[2:7])
They agree well: 0.81 and 0.81 at lag 1, 0.46 and 0.46 at lag 2, and a damped oscillation in both, going negative from lag 4. The fit is a little more negative at lags 5 and 6, −0.23 against the sample’s −0.21 and −0.17, which is within the sampling error of autocorrelations from 600 points (about ±0.08). A model that reproduces the data’s correlation structure has captured its dynamics. Lesson 7 makes that check formal.

title: Autoregressive models
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does an AR(p) model regress the series on?

Time
Its own previous p values
Its previous p forecast errors


Regressing on previous errors is the moving-average model, in Lesson 5.



2. An AR(1) has \phi = 0.9 and shock variance 1. What is its variance?

0.9
1
About 5.3


1/(1 - 0.81) = 5.26. Persistent shocks pile up.



3. When is an AR(p) model stationary?

When all its coefficients are positive
When all the roots of its characteristic polynomial lie outside the unit circle
When its coefficients sum to 1


For AR(1), that’s |\phi| < 1.



4. What do complex roots of an AR(2) mean?

The model is non-stationary
The process oscillates, with a period of 2\pi/\theta steps
The estimation failed


The reactor temperature’s controller makes it oscillate with an 11-minute period.



5. In arima()’s output for an AR model, what is “intercept”?

The constant c in the AR equation
The mean of the series
The first observation


c = \mu(1 - \phi_1 - \cdots - \phi_p). It’s a common source of confusion.



6. What happens to an AR model’s forecasts far into the future?

They grow without limit
They return to the series’ mean, with standard errors approaching the series’ SD
They repeat the last value


A stationary model’s long-run forecast is its mean. A random walk’s would be its last value.

title: Autoregressive models
text:
Wrap-up
You can now fit and interpret autoregressive models. Here’s what you’ve learned:

AR(1): y_t = \phi y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t has variance \sigma^2/(1 - \phi^2) and ACF \phi^k, checked by simulation.
Stationarity: every root of the characteristic polynomial must lie outside the unit circle. \phi = (1.3, -0.6) passes, with complex roots of modulus 1.29, and (0.5, 0.6) fails.
Estimation: Yule-Walker, maximum likelihood and least squares all give about \hat\phi = (1.30, -0.60) for the reactor temperature, and ar() chooses order 2 by AIC.
Interpretation: the complex roots mean an oscillation with an 11-minute period, damped to 6% per cycle: the controller’s tuning, read from routine data.
Forecasts run the model forward: an overshoot, then a return to the mean, with intervals widening to the process’s own SD.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download process_signals.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Simulate AR(2) models. Use arima.sim(list(ar = c(phi1, phi2)), n = 300) for \phi = (0.5, 0.3), (1.3, -0.6), (0.2, -0.8) and (-0.5, -0.3). Plot each, with its ACF and PACF. Which oscillate? Check with polyroot().
The stationarity triangle. An AR(2) is stationary when \phi_1 + \phi_2 < 1, \phi_2 - \phi_1 < 1 and |\phi_2| < 1. Plot that triangle in the (\phi_1, \phi_2) plane, and shade the region with complex roots, \phi_1^2 + 4\phi_2 < 0. Where is the reactor’s model?
The impulse response. ARMAtoMA(ar = c(1.3, -0.6), lag.max = 20) gives the effect of one shock on the following minutes. Plot it. It’s the discrete-time impulse response of the closed loop.
Order selection. Fit AR models of orders 1 to 6 with arima(), and compare their AIC values. Does AIC agree with the PACF?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Autoregressive model, AR(p)

A model in which each value is a linear combination of the previous p values plus white noise.

Characteristic polynomial

1 - \phi_1 z - \cdots - \phi_p z^p. Its roots decide whether an AR model is stationary, and how it behaves.

Unit circle

The complex numbers with modulus 1. An AR model is stationary if all its roots lie outside it.

Yule-Walker equations

Equations linking an AR model’s coefficients to its autocorrelations, used to estimate them.

Maximum likelihood estimation

Choosing the parameters that make the observed series most probable, as arima() does.

Period of oscillation

For complex roots |z|e^{\pm i\theta}, the number of time steps per cycle, 2\pi/\theta.

Impulse response

The effect of a single shock on the series’ future values.











NoteWant to read more?






Rob Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd edition), section 9.3, “Autoregressive models”.
Penn State’s STAT 510, lesson 1, section 1.2, on the AR(1) model, and lesson 2, on AR(p) and the PACF.
George Box, Gwilym Jenkins, Gregory Reinsel and Greta Ljung, Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control (5th edition, Wiley, 2015). The classic, written by statisticians who worked with chemical plants: its examples include chemical process concentrations and temperatures, and a gas furnace.

title: Decomposition and smoothing
text:
Module 6 · Lesson 2 of 13 Week 91 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 1 saw three things at once in the steam demand: a rising trend, a winter-summer season, and month-to-month noise. To understand a series, and to forecast it, it helps to pull those apart. A decomposition writes the series as
y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t,
a trend-cycle T_t, a seasonal component S_t and a remainder R_t. (When the seasonal swings grow with the level, a multiplicative version, y_t = T_t \times S_t \times R_t, fits better.) The second half of this lesson turns to the simplest forecasting methods that work in practice, exponential smoothing, which weight recent observations more than old ones.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Decomposition and smoothing
text:
Moving averages
A moving average smooths out short-term noise by averaging each observation with its neighbors. To remove a monthly seasonal pattern completely, average over exactly a year. Twelve is even, so a centered version averages 13 months, giving the two end months half weight: the 2×12 moving average,

\hat T_t = \tfrac{1}{12}\left(\tfrac12 y_{t-6} + y_{t-5} + \cdots + y_{t+5} + \tfrac12 y_{t+6}\right).

Every month of the year gets the same total weight, so the seasonal pattern averages out, and what’s left is the trend-cycle.












Your turn. Compute the 2×12 moving average of the steam demand with stats::filter(), which multiplies each window by a vector of weights. Find the first month it’s defined for, its value there, and its value for December 2019, month 72.









The last of the 13 weights is a half, like the first.


weights <- c(0.5, rep(1, 11), 0.5) / 12
trend <- stats::filter(y, weights, sides = 2)      # sides = 2: centered on each month
c(first_month = which(!is.na(trend))[1], first_value = trend[7], december_2019 = trend[72])
The first defined value is for month 7, July 2014, at 37.2 kt: it needs six months on each side. The last is for month 138, June 2025. So the trend is missing at both ends, which is exactly where you’d want it most. In December 2019, it’s 38.4. (Write stats::filter() in full: dplyr also has a filter(), which does something else.)

title: Decomposition and smoothing
text:
Classical decomposition
Classical decomposition goes one step further. It estimates the trend with the 2×12 moving average, subtracts it, and averages what’s left for each calendar month, to get the seasonal component. Those twelve seasonal indices are adjusted to sum to 0. The remainder is whatever is left over. decompose() does all of it.
Your turn. Decompose the steam demand, and look at the seasonal indices for January and August, in $figure.









August is month 8.


d <- decompose(y)
c(january = d$figure[1], august = d$figure[8], total = sum(d$figure))
January is 6.0 kt above the trend, and August 5.2 below, and the twelve indices sum to 0 (to within rounding error, 10^{-15}). Classical decomposition assumes that the seasonal pattern is the same every year, which can’t be quite true: Lesson 1 found the peak in December some years and February in others.




Removing the seasonal component gives the seasonally adjusted series, the trend plus the remainder. It’s what official statistics usually report, so that a month can be compared with the month before it.
Your turn. Compute the seasonally adjusted series, and compare December 2025, the last month, with its raw value.









Subtract the seasonal component, d$seasonal, which repeats the twelve indices over every year.


d <- decompose(y)
adjusted <- y - d$seasonal
c(raw = y[144], adjusted = adjusted[144])
December 2025 used 49.5 kt, the most of any month in the twelve years. But December is always high: seasonally adjusted, it’s 44.9. Comparing adjusted values tells you whether demand is really rising, rather than just being winter.

title: Decomposition and smoothing
text:
STL decomposition
STL (Seasonal and Trend decomposition using Loess) is the modern replacement. It estimates the trend and the seasonal component with local regression (Module 4’s smoothing), so the trend is defined right to the ends, and the seasonal pattern can change slowly over the years.
