Its main setting, s.window, is how many years the seasonal pattern is smoothed over: "periodic" forces it to be the same every year, and a number such as 13 lets it evolve.

st <- stl(y, s.window = 13)
autoplot(st) +
  labs(x = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








How strong are the trend and the seasonality? Compare the remainder’s variance with the variance of each component plus the remainder. The strength of seasonality and the strength of trend (Hyndman and Athanasopoulos’s definitions) are

F_S = \max\left(0,\ 1 - \frac{\text{Var}(R_t)}{\text{Var}(S_t + R_t)}\right), \qquad F_T = \max\left(0,\ 1 - \frac{\text{Var}(R_t)}{\text{Var}(T_t + R_t)}\right),

each between 0 (none) and 1 (all of the variation, apart from the remainder).
Your turn. Compute both from the STL decomposition.









The trend column is "trend".


st <- stl(y, s.window = 13)
R <- st$time.series[, "remainder"]
S <- st$time.series[, "seasonal"]
Tr <- st$time.series[, "trend"]
c(seasonal_strength = max(0, 1 - var(R) / var(S + R)), trend_strength = max(0, 1 - var(R) / var(Tr + R)))
A seasonal strength of 0.94 and a trend strength of 0.82. Both are strong, the seasonality especially. The remainder’s SD, 1.05 kt, is the month-to-month variation that neither the trend nor the season explains. A forecast can’t do much better than that, unless it brings in more information, like next month’s weather forecast.

title: Decomposition and smoothing
text:
Simple exponential smoothing
The plant’s hydrotreater has a catalyst bed whose pressure drop creeps up as it fouls and settles, and the operators read it every day. The readings are noisy, and the level they’re measuring drifts. What’s the best estimate of today’s level, and of tomorrow’s reading?
Taking the last reading trusts the noise. Taking the average of all 200 days ignores the drift. Simple exponential smoothing (SES) is in between: each new estimate of the level is a weighted average of the newest reading and the previous estimate,

\ell_t = \alpha\, y_t + (1 - \alpha)\,\ell_{t-1}, \qquad \hat y_{t+1} = \ell_t,

with a smoothing parameter \alpha between 0 and 1. Unrolled, \ell_t is a weighted average of all past readings, with weights \alpha(1-\alpha)^k that fall off exponentially with age k. With \alpha near 1, it’s the last reading, and near 0, an average over a long memory.

sm <- ses(dp, alpha = 0.35)
ggplot(data.frame(day = 1:200, dp = dp, level = as.numeric(fitted(sm))), aes(x = day)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = dp), color = "grey60", size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = level), color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "Day", y = "Pressure drop (bar)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Your turn. Run SES by hand, with \alpha = 0.3, starting the level at the first reading. At each step, record the one-step-ahead forecast error, y_t - \ell_{t-1}. Report the sum of squared errors and the final level.









The new level combines the new reading with the previous level.


ses_by_hand <- function(alpha) {
  level <- dp[1]
  err <- numeric(length(dp) - 1)
  for (t in 2:length(dp)) {
    err[t - 1] <- dp[t] - level                         # the forecast error
    level <- alpha * dp[t] + (1 - alpha) * level         # the new level
  }
  c(sse = sum(err^2), level = level)
}
ses_by_hand(0.3)
A sum of squared errors of 0.357, and a final level of 1.301 bar: the forecast for day 201. With \alpha = 1, the naive “last reading” forecast, the SSE is 0.492, and with \alpha = 0.05, 0.945. Neither extreme is as good as smoothing.




Your turn. Which \alpha is best? Minimize the sum of squared one-step errors with optimize().









Minimize the "sse" element.


ses_by_hand <- function(alpha) {
  level <- dp[1]; err <- numeric(length(dp) - 1)
  for (t in 2:length(dp)) { err[t - 1] <- dp[t] - level; level <- alpha * dp[t] + (1 - alpha) * level }
  c(sse = sum(err^2), level = level)
}
best <- optimize(function(a) ses_by_hand(a)[["sse"]], interval = c(0.01, 1))
c(alpha = best$minimum, sse = best$objective)
\alpha = 0.35, with an SSE of 0.355. About a third of each new reading goes into the level, so the forecast “remembers” roughly the last week of readings. The best \alpha depends on how much the level really drifts compared with the noise: more drift, larger \alpha.

title: Decomposition and smoothing
section: Exponential smoothing with the forecast package
text:
Exponential smoothing with the forecast package
The forecast package’s ses() does the same, estimating \alpha and the starting level by maximum likelihood, and adds prediction intervals. Its relatives add a trend, holt(), and seasonality, hw(). And ets() chooses among the whole family of ETS models (Error, Trend, Seasonal), each component additive, multiplicative or absent, by AICc.
Your turn. Forecast the pressure drop 7 days ahead with ses(), and find \alpha, the forecast for day 201, its 80% interval, and the 95% interval for day 207.









Seven days ahead: h = 7.


fc <- forecast::ses(dp, h = 7)
c(alpha = fc$model$par[["alpha"]], day_201 = fc$mean[1], lo80 = fc$lower[1, 1], hi80 = fc$upper[1, 1],
  lo95_day207 = fc$lower[7, 2], hi95_day207 = fc$upper[7, 2])
\alpha = 0.349, as by hand. Tomorrow’s reading: 1.300 bar, with an 80% interval from 1.246 to 1.354. SES forecasts are flat, the same for every future day, but their intervals widen: a week out, the 95% interval runs from 1.19 to 1.41. The level could have drifted by then, and SES knows it.




Your turn. For the steam demand, let ets() choose the model, and forecast January 2026 with its 95% interval.









Forecast a year ahead, h = 12. (Any h of 1 or more gives the same January forecast.)


fit <- forecast::ets(y)
fit$method
fc <- forecast::forecast(fit, h = 12)
c(january_2026 = fc$mean[1], lo95 = fc$lower[1, 2], hi95 = fc$upper[1, 2])
ets() chose ETS(A,A,A): additive errors, an additive trend and an additive seasonal pattern, Holt-Winters’ additive method in statistical form. It forecasts 50.0 kt for January 2026, with a 95% prediction interval from 47.4 to 52.6. Its smoothing parameters for the trend and the season are tiny, 0.0001: the data say both are nearly constant, so the model barely updates them.

title: Decomposition and smoothing
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Is there a trend? The pressure drop is creeping up. Holt’s method adds a trend term to SES. Compare the two methods’ forecasts 30 days ahead.









Holt’s method is forecast::holt().


ses_fc <- forecast::ses(dp, h = 30)
holt_fc <- forecast::holt(dp, h = 30)
c(ses_day_230 = ses_fc$mean[30], holt_day_230 = holt_fc$mean[30], holt_beta = holt_fc$model$par[["beta"]])
SES says 1.30 bar on day 230, and Holt 1.38. Holt estimates a steady rise of about 0.0025 bar a day, with a trend smoothing parameter near 0, so the trend is treated as fixed. If the bed’s design limit were 1.4 bar, that difference would decide when to plan a catalyst change. Which forecast is better? Lesson 8 answers that with time-series cross-validation, not by eye.




Challenge 2 · Multiplicative seasonality. R’s built-in AirPassengers, monthly airline passengers from 1949 to 1960, is the classic multiplicative series: its seasonal swings grow with its level. Decompose it multiplicatively, and find the seasonal indices for July and November.









The type is "multiplicative".


d <- decompose(AirPassengers, type = "multiplicative")
c(july = d$figure[7], november = d$figure[11])
July is 23% above the trend and November 20% below. Multiplicative seasonal indices are ratios that average 1, so the swing in passengers grows as the airline grows. Taking logs turns a multiplicative series into an additive one, \log y_t = \log T_t + \log S_t + \log R_t, which is often the simplest way to handle it.

title: Decomposition and smoothing
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why does a 2×12 moving average remove a monthly seasonal pattern?

Because it’s centered
Because every calendar month gets the same total weight in each average
Because it has 13 terms


The seasonal ups and downs cancel over a full year.



2. What does a seasonally adjusted series show?

Only the trend
The trend and the remainder, without the seasonal component
Only the seasonal pattern


It lets you compare consecutive months without the season getting in the way.



3. Name two advantages of STL over classical decomposition.

It needs no data and no settings
The trend is estimated up to the ends of the series, and the seasonal pattern can change over time
It always gives a multiplicative decomposition


Classical decomposition loses six months at each end and forces the same seasonal pattern every year.



4. In simple exponential smoothing, what happens as \alpha approaches 1?

The forecast becomes the average of all the data
The forecast becomes the last observation
The forecast becomes 0


All the weight goes to the newest observation: the naive forecast.



5. Why do SES prediction intervals widen with the forecast horizon, even though the point forecast is flat?

Because of rounding
Because the level may keep drifting, so the further ahead, the more it can have moved
Because the smoothing parameter changes


The model treats the level as wandering, so its uncertainty grows with time.



6. What does ETS(A,A,A) mean?

Three additive seasonal patterns
Additive errors, an additive trend and additive seasonality
An ARIMA model with three terms


ETS names its Error, Trend and Seasonal components, each N (none), A (additive) or M (multiplicative).

title: Decomposition and smoothing
text:
Wrap-up
You can now take a series apart, and forecast it with smoothing. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Moving averages: a 2×12 moving average estimates the trend of monthly data, but loses six months at each end.
Classical decomposition: January’s steam demand is 6.0 kt above the trend and August’s 5.2 below. December 2025’s record 49.5 kt is 44.9 seasonally adjusted.
STL handles the ends and an evolving season. The steam demand has a seasonal strength of 0.94 and a trend strength of 0.82.
Simple exponential smoothing weights recent readings exponentially more. For the pressure drop, the best \alpha is 0.35, and tomorrow’s forecast is 1.30 bar (80% interval 1.25 to 1.35).
The ETS family adds trends and seasons, and ets() chooses among them: ETS(A,A,A) for the steam demand, forecasting 50.0 kt for January 2026.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download steam_demand.csv and pressure_drop.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

The STL window. Decompose the steam demand with s.window = "periodic", 7 and 25, and plot each with autoplot(). How does the seasonal component change? Which would you choose, and why?
Exponential weights. For \alpha = 0.35, plot the weight SES gives to the readings from 0 to 20 days ago, \alpha(1-\alpha)^k. After how many days have the weights added up to 90%?
Holt-Winters. Fit hw(y, seasonal = "additive") and hw(y, seasonal = "multiplicative") to the steam demand, and compare their forecasts for 2026 with autoplot(). Does it matter which one you use for this series?
The SES-ARIMA link. Fit Arima(dp, order = c(0, 1, 1)). Its MA coefficient, \theta, should be close to \alpha - 1. Is it? (Lesson 6 explains why.)










NoteKey words from this lesson






Decomposition

Writing a series as a trend-cycle, a seasonal component and a remainder, added or multiplied.

Moving average

An average of each observation with its neighbors. A 2×12 moving average estimates the trend of monthly data.

Seasonally adjusted series

The series with its seasonal component removed.

STL

Seasonal and Trend decomposition using Loess, which allows a changing seasonal pattern and estimates the trend to the ends.

Strength of seasonality, strength of trend

How much of the variation, apart from the remainder, each component explains, on a scale from 0 to 1.

Simple exponential smoothing

Forecasting with a level that’s a weighted average of past observations, with weights falling off exponentially with age.

Smoothing parameter

The weight \alpha that SES gives to each new observation.

ETS model

A model of the exponential smoothing family, named by its Error, Trend and Seasonal components.











NoteWant to read more?






Rob Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd edition), chapters 3, “Time series decomposition” and 8, “Exponential smoothing”, including the strength measures in section 4.3.
Robert Cleveland, William Cleveland, Jean McRae and Irma Terpenning, “STL: A seasonal-trend decomposition procedure based on loess”, Journal of Official Statistics (1990). The original STL paper, from a statistics office.
Penn State’s STAT 510, lesson 5, on decomposition and smoothing.

title: Module 5 project: a Bayesian hierarchical analysis
text:
The plant’s cooling water runs through 16 heat exchangers, coolers and headers, and all of them are carbon steel. To watch for corrosion, water treatment hangs small steel coupons at each location, about 90 days at a time, and the lab weighs them before and after. The weight lost, over the coupon’s area and the exposure time, gives a corrosion rate in mm per year. The treatment program’s target is 0.125 mm/yr at every location.
Ines, the water treatment engineer, has budget to act at three locations this year: change the inhibitor dosing, or the metallurgy. But some locations have had eight coupons over two years, and some only one or two. Ranking them by their raw average rates would put the locations with the fewest coupons at the top and the bottom, by chance. That’s a job for a hierarchical model.

title: Module 5 project: a Bayesian hierarchical analysis
text:
What you’ll make
One report, written in Quarto in your plant-study RStudio project, that Ines could take to the plant’s maintenance planning meeting. It should contain:

A summary for Ines, at the top, in plain words: which locations are probably above the target, which three to act at and why, how the water temperature matters, and what to expect at the new chiller, E-401.
The data and its cleaning: the corrosion rates, how you computed them, and every problem you found.
The models: complete pooling, no pooling, partial pooling, and partial pooling with the water temperature, with their priors and prior predictive checks.
The checks and the comparison: convergence diagnostics, posterior predictive checks, and LOO.
The answers: each location’s typical corrosion rate with a credible interval, the probability that it’s above 0.125 mm/yr, and a prediction for E-401.
What partial pooling changed, a cleaning log, and the limitations.

Nobody grades it, but write it as if the plant’s corrosion specialist will read it. In real life, one would.

title: Module 5 project: a Bayesian hierarchical analysis
text:
The handover
Download the three files into a new folder in your project, data-raw/corrosion/, and don’t edit them:

README.txt: Ines’s note, with the corrosion-rate formula, the target, the questions, the columns and a known issue. Read it first.
coupons_2026.csv: every coupon since October 2024, 98 of them.
locations.csv: the 16 locations, with their typical water temperatures.

Then download the project template, save it in the top folder of your project as corrosion-study.qmd, and click Render. It reads the data, computes the rates, and plots them by location, with headings and code skeletons for every step. Fill it in one section at a time, and render often.
The models need brms with Stan, so follow the installation steps in Lesson 9’s practice section first. If you can’t install Stan, there’s a route without it: see the tips.

title: Module 5 project: a Bayesian hierarchical analysis
text:
The brief, step by step

Explore and clean (Module 1, Lesson 13 of this module). Compute each coupon’s exposure time from its dates, and compare it with the exposure_days column. Then compute each coupon’s corrosion rate with Ines’s formula. Plot the rates by location, on a log scale, with the target. Is any coupon’s rate impossible, or nearly so? Fix what you can justify, and log every decision.
Choose the scale and the priors (Lessons 3 and 10). Corrosion rates are positive and skewed, so model the log rate. Write down weakly informative priors: a typical carbon-steel coupon in treated cooling water corrodes at roughly 0.02 to 0.2 mm/yr, and locations differ by perhaps a factor of 2. Check them with a prior predictive simulation: do they predict plausible rates?
Fit four models (Lessons 9, 11 and 12):

complete pooling, log_rate ~ 1
no pooling, log_rate ~ 0 + loc_id
partial pooling, log_rate ~ 1 + (1 | loc_id)
partial pooling with the water temperature, centered at 37 °C, log_rate ~ temp_c + (1 | loc_id)

Check them (Lessons 8, 10 and 13). Every R-hat below 1.01, enough ESS, no divergences (raise adapt_delta if you see any). Then posterior predictive checks with pp_check(), including one aimed at the differences between locations.
Compare them (Lesson 13). Use loo() and loo_compare(). Then think about what each comparison predicts: leaving out one coupon isn’t the same as leaving out a whole location. Which matters for E-401?
Answer Ines (Lessons 5, 11 and 12). With the model your checks and comparison support, report each location’s typical corrosion rate (the posterior median of its exponentiated mean log rate) with a 90% credible interval, and the probability that it’s above 0.125 mm/yr. Which three locations would you act at, and on what criterion? What does the temperature model predict for E-401’s next coupon?
Show what partial pooling changed. A table or plot of the no-pooling and partial-pooling estimates side by side. Which locations moved most, and why? Did the ranking change?
Write it up. Summary first, then the data, the models, the checks and comparison, the answers, and the limitations, with the cleaning log at the end.

Stretch goal. Ines’s question is really about future coupons. Fit the model with a location-level predictor that’s leave-one-location-out cross-validated: kfold(fit, group = "loc_id") in brms. Does the temperature model win now? Or take it further: corrosion rates often fall during a coupon’s exposure as a protective film forms, so add the exposure days as a coupon-level predictor, and see whether the data support it.

title: Module 5 project: a Bayesian hierarchical analysis
text:
Check your own work
When you’ve finished, assess your project against this rubric. Aim for the right-hand column.










Needs work
Good
Excellent




The data
Used as received
Rates computed from the dates, and the lost coupons handled
The inconsistent exposure time is found, fixed with a justification, and its effect on the results shown; everything is in the cleaning log


The priors
Defaults, unexamined
Weakly informative priors on the log scale
Priors justified from engineering knowledge, checked with a prior predictive simulation, and a sensitivity analysis for the between-location SD


The models
One model
The four models
The four models, all converged, with the diagnostics reported and any divergences dealt with


The checks
None
pp_check() plots
Posterior predictive checks aimed at the models’ assumptions, and a LOO comparison read with its standard errors and Pareto k values


The answers
Point estimates only
Rates with credible intervals and probabilities of exceeding the target
A clear recommendation of three locations with the criterion stated, a predictive interval for E-401, and what partial pooling changed


Communication
Code output with little text
A report that explains its steps
A report Ines could take to the planning meeting: a plain summary, honest uncertainty, and stated limitations

title: Module 5 project: a Bayesian hierarchical analysis
text:
Tips

Trust the dates, not the log. The exposure time is the difference between removed and installed. If a typed column disagrees with the dates, and the dates agree with the 90-day routine, the typed column is wrong.
Work on the log scale, report on the rate scale. A location’s typical rate is e^{\mu_j}, the median of its coupons’ rates, and its credible interval comes from exponentiating the draws of \mu_j. Transform the draws, not the summaries.
Center the temperature. With temp_c = temperature minus 37 °C, the intercept is the log rate at a typical location, which is easy to put a prior on, and the sampler is happier.
Divergences in hierarchical models usually mean the funnel (Lesson 11). brms is already non-centered, so raise adapt_delta to 0.95 or 0.99.
“Probably above the target” needs a threshold you state: a posterior probability above 50%? Above 10%? With Ines’s budget of three, ranking by the probability, or by the posterior median, are both defensible. Say which, and whether the top three differ.
E-401 has one coupon. Predict its next coupon with posterior_predict(), which includes the coupon-to-coupon scatter. A credible interval for its typical rate is a different, narrower thing. Ines asked for a prediction.
Without Stan, write a Gibbs sampler for the varying-intercepts model (Module 4, Lesson 12): the conditional posteriors of the location means, the overall mean, and the two variances are all normal or scaled inverse chi-squared. Check it against lme4::lmer(log_rate ~ 1 + (1 | loc_id)), which gives similar point estimates.
Say what partial pooling did, and why. “The model is more conservative” isn’t enough. Name the locations that moved, and connect it to how many coupons they had.


When it’s done, you’ll have built the kind of model that real reliability and process-monitoring teams use, and checked it like a statistician. Congratulations on finishing Module 5! Module 6 adds the one thing all of this module’s data had but never used: time order. Next stop, time series.

title: Model checking and comparison
text:
Module 5 · Lesson 13 of 13 Week 88 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 12 fitted three models to the eight reactors’ catalyst activity:
All three converged, and all three give a posterior. That’s not the same as being right. This lesson asks two questions every analysis should end with. Does each model reproduce the important features of the data? That’s model checking, with Lesson 10’s posterior predictive checks. And which model would predict new data best? That’s model comparison, with cross-validation. Then it puts everything in this module together, as the Bayesian workflow.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Model checking and comparison
text:
Posterior predictive checks











The pooled model assumes that every reactor is the same. A test statistic that targets that assumption is the spread of the reactor means: the SD of the eight reactors’ average activities. The setup code has 1,000 posterior draws of each model, in pooled, intercepts and slopes.
Your turn. For each draw of the pooled model, simulate a replicated dataset at the same reactors and days, compute the SD of its reactor means, and find the posterior predictive p-value.









Compare with the observed activities, deact$activity_pct.


spread <- function(y) sd(tapply(y, deact$reactor, mean))       # the SD of the 8 reactor means
set.seed(5131)
T_rep <- sapply(1:nrow(pooled), function(s) spread(pooled$a[s] + pooled$b[s] * deact$day100 + rnorm(nrow(deact), 0, pooled$sigma[s])))
c(T_observed = spread(deact$activity_pct), p_value = mean(T_rep >= spread(deact$activity_pct)))
The real reactor means have an SD of 3.3 points, and only 1.5% of the pooled model’s replicated datasets spread that much. The pooled model can’t reproduce the differences between reactors. (Some of the spread in the real means comes from R8, whose three measurements are all early, when activity is high. The replicated datasets have the same design, so the check allows for that.)




Here’s the same check for all three models: the histograms are the replicated datasets’ spreads, and the line is the real data’s:

intercepts <- read_csv("data/brms_deact_intercepts_draws.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
spread <- function(y) sd(tapply(y, deact$reactor, mean))
rep_varying <- function(draws, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  A <- as.matrix(draws[, paste0("a_", deact$reactor)]); B <- as.matrix(draws[, paste0("b_", deact$reactor)])
  sapply(1:nrow(draws), function(s) spread(A[s, ] + B[s, ] * deact$day100 + rnorm(nrow(deact), 0, draws$sigma[s])))
}
set.seed(5131)
rp <- sapply(1:nrow(pooled), function(s) spread(pooled$a[s] + pooled$b[s] * deact$day100 + rnorm(nrow(deact), 0, pooled$sigma[s])))
reps <- rbind(data.frame(T = rp, model = "pooled"),
              data.frame(T = rep_varying(intercepts, 5135), model = "varying intercepts"),
              data.frame(T = rep_varying(slopes, 5136), model = "varying slopes"))
ggplot(reps, aes(x = T)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#F4C0D1", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = spread(deact$activity_pct), color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "SD of the 8 reactor means, in replicated data", y = "Replicated datasets") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The varying-intercepts model passes this check, because it lets each reactor have its own level. But it assumes that every reactor declines at the same rate, and a check of that assumption is the challenge at the end of the lesson. Each check tests one aspect of a model. A model that passes many well-chosen checks earns some trust. None can prove it right.

title: Model checking and comparison
text:
Predicting new data
Checks say whether a model is good enough. To choose between models that pass, the natural question is which one would predict new data best. The best measure of a prediction is the probability it gave to what actually happened. For a Bayesian model, that’s the posterior predictive density of a new observation, p(\tilde y \mid y) = \int p(\tilde y \mid \theta)\, p(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta, averaged over the posterior, and on the log scale.
We don’t have new data, but each observation can stand in for one. The first step is the log pointwise predictive density (lppd): for each observation, average its likelihood over the posterior draws, take the log, and add them up:

\text{lppd} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log\left(\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S} p(y_i \mid \theta^{(s)})\right).

The setup code’s log_lik_matrix() computes \log p(y_i \mid \theta^{(s)}) for every draw s and every observation i: a matrix with 1,000 rows and 114 columns.
Your turn. Compute the log-likelihood matrix for the varying-slopes model, and its lppd.









Average the likelihood, exp(ll), down each column, then take logs and sum.


ll <- log_lik_matrix(slopes)
dim(ll)
sum(log(colMeans(exp(ll))))
An lppd of −176.5, from 1,000 draws of 114 observations. But it’s too optimistic: each observation was used to fit the model it’s now predicting, so it’s a little easier to predict than a genuinely new one would be. That optimism grows with the model’s flexibility, and the varying-slopes model is the most flexible of the three. A fair comparison has to correct for it.

title: Model checking and comparison
text:
WAIC
The widely applicable information criterion (WAIC) corrects the lppd by subtracting an estimate of the effective number of parameters, p_{\text{WAIC}}: the sum, over observations, of the posterior variance of the log-likelihood. An observation whose log-likelihood changes a lot from draw to draw is one the model bends to fit.

\widehat{\text{elpd}}_{\text{WAIC}} = \text{lppd} - p_{\text{WAIC}}, \qquad p_{\text{WAIC}} = \sum_{i=1}^n \text{Var}_s\big(\log p(y_i \mid \theta^{(s)})\big).

“elpd” is the expected log predictive density for new data, the quantity we want. Higher is better. (WAIC itself is -2 times this, on the “deviance” scale, where lower is better. Modern practice reports the elpd.)
Your turn. Compute p_{\text{WAIC}} and the elpd by hand, and compare them with loo::waic().









p_{\text{WAIC}} adds up the variance of each column: var.


ll <- log_lik_matrix(slopes)
lppd <- sum(log(colMeans(exp(ll))))
p_waic <- sum(apply(ll, 2, var))
c(p_waic = p_waic, elpd_waic = lppd - p_waic, loo_package = loo::waic(ll)$estimates["elpd_waic", "Estimate"])
p_{\text{WAIC}} = 14.7 and elpd = −191.2, as the loo package says. The model has 2 × 8 reactor coefficients, plus the hyperparameters and \sigma, more than 20 in all, but they’re shrunk toward each other, so they behave like about 15 free parameters. The loo package also warned that some observations’ variances are large, and recommended leave-one-out cross-validation instead. Take its advice.

title: Model checking and comparison
text:
Leave-one-out cross-validation
The most direct estimate of out-of-sample prediction is leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO, Module 4, Lesson 7): fit the model without observation i, predict y_i, and repeat for every i. Refitting 114 times would be slow. Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS-LOO) avoids it: it reweights the existing draws, by importance sampling (Lesson 7), to approximate the posterior without each observation. The weights are 1/p(y_i \mid \theta^{(s)}), and their tail is stabilized by fitting a Pareto distribution to the largest ones.
Your turn. Compute PSIS-LOO for the varying-slopes model with loo::loo().









The table of estimates is fit_loo$estimates.


ll <- log_lik_matrix(slopes)
fit_loo <- loo::loo(ll)
fit_loo$estimates
An elpd of −191.6, with a standard error of 7.5, and an effective number of parameters, p_{\text{loo}}, of 15.1: very close to WAIC. The standard error comes from the 114 pointwise values, and it matters when comparing models. (The loo package also warns that the “relative effective sample sizes” weren’t given. With brms, loo(fit) supplies them automatically. They only refine the Monte Carlo error of the estimate.)

title: Model checking and comparison
text:
Comparing the three models
loo::loo_compare() lines up several models’ LOO results, best first, with each one’s elpd difference from the best, and the standard error of that difference. A difference of several standard errors is a clear preference.
Your turn. Compute LOO for all three models, and compare them.









The third model’s draws are in pooled.


loo_slopes <- loo::loo(log_lik_matrix(slopes))
loo_intercepts <- loo::loo(log_lik_matrix(intercepts))
loo_pooled <- loo::loo(log_lik_matrix(pooled))
comparison <- loo::loo_compare(list(slopes = loo_slopes, intercepts = loo_intercepts, pooled = loo_pooled))
comparison[, c("elpd_diff", "se_diff")]



Model
elpd difference
SE




Varying slopes
0



Varying intercepts
−24.6
6.6


Pooled
−48.2
7.6



The varying-slopes model predicts best, by 24.6 points of elpd over varying intercepts, almost four standard errors: a clear win, even after paying for its extra flexibility. A rough rule: differences under 4 are small whatever their SE, and beyond that, compare them with their SE.

title: Model checking and comparison
text:
Pareto k diagnostics
PSIS-LOO comes with its own warning light. For each observation, the fitted Pareto distribution’s shape, k, says how reliable the importance sampling was. Below 0.7, the estimate is fine. Above it, the observation is so influential that removing it changes the posterior too much for reweighting to work, and that observation’s LOO estimate can’t be trusted. Then refit the model without it (loo(fit, reloo = TRUE) in brms), or use a more robust model.
Your turn. Find the varying-slopes model’s largest Pareto k, and which observation it belongs to.









Find the largest value of k.


fit_loo <- loo::loo(log_lik_matrix(slopes))
k <- loo::pareto_k_values(fit_loo)
i <- which.max(k)
c(max_k = k[i], n_over_0.7 = sum(k > 0.7))
deact[i, ]
One observation has k = 0.77: R2’s measurement at day 282, 88.0%, which sits well above R2’s line (look back at Lesson 12’s plot), near the end of its series, where it pulls on R2’s slope. One mildly high k out of 114 doesn’t change the conclusion, since the models differ by 24.6, but it’s worth a sentence in a report. It’s also worth a look in the lab’s records: was something different that day?




Your turn. Which reactors’ observations favor the varying-slopes model most? The pointwise element of a LOO result has each observation’s elpd. Sum the differences between the two varying models by reactor.









Use the same column for both: "elpd_loo".


loo_slopes <- loo::loo(log_lik_matrix(slopes))
loo_intercepts <- loo::loo(log_lik_matrix(intercepts))
diff <- loo_slopes$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"] - loo_intercepts$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"]
round(tapply(diff, deact$reactor, sum), 2)
Most of the advantage comes from R6, with 13.8 points, and R7, with 6.2: the reactors whose decline rates are furthest from the average, 3.6 and 6.8 points per 100 days. R8, the reason Lesson 12 was interested in varying slopes, contributes only 0.6: three early measurements can’t tell the two models apart. Pointwise comparisons show why one model wins, which is often more useful than the total.

title: Model checking and comparison
text:
The Bayesian workflow
This module has used every step of what Gelman and colleagues call the Bayesian workflow. It isn’t a recipe, but it’s a good checklist:

Start from the question, and the data that answer it: what will the plant do with the answer? (Lesson 5’s decision.)
Build a model of how the data arose, starting simple: the pooled model first, then the extensions.
Choose priors, and check them with prior predictive simulations (Lesson 3).
Fit the model, and check the computation: R-hat, ESS, divergences, and agreement with another method when you can (Lessons 8 and 9).
Check the model against the data with posterior predictive checks aimed at its assumptions (Lessons 10 and 13).
Improve and compare models, with LOO, and understand why one predicts better (this lesson).
Use the posterior for what the question needs: probabilities, predictions and decisions (Lessons 5, 11 and 12).
Report the model, the priors and their sensitivity, the checks, and the uncertainty, in words a decision-maker can use.

And Bayesian methods are everywhere in science and engineering: calibrating instruments and combining interlaboratory studies (Lesson 11), reliability and maintenance planning (Lessons 9 and 12), pharmacokinetics and dose-finding, process safety (Lesson 7), the search for lost ships and planes, climate and astrophysical models, and fitting computer simulations to measurements. They’re most valuable where data are scarce and expensive, prior knowledge is real, and decisions depend on the full uncertainty. Chemical engineering has all three.

title: Model checking and comparison
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Do the reactors decline at the same rate? The varying-intercepts model assumes they do. A test statistic that targets that assumption is the SD of the decline rates of R1 to R7, each fitted by its own least-squares line (R8, with three points, would only add noise). Compute its posterior predictive p-value for both varying models.









The second model’s draws are in slopes.


old <- deact$reactor != "R8"
slope_sd <- function(y) {                  # the SD of R1 to R7's least-squares slopes
  b <- sapply(split(which(old), deact$reactor[old]), function(i) cov(deact$day100[i], y[i]) / var(deact$day100[i]))
  sd(b)
}
ppp <- function(draws, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  A <- as.matrix(draws[, paste0("a_", deact$reactor)]); B <- as.matrix(draws[, paste0("b_", deact$reactor)])
  T_rep <- sapply(1:nrow(draws), function(s) slope_sd(A[s, ] + B[s, ] * deact$day100 + rnorm(nrow(deact), 0, draws$sigma[s])))
  mean(T_rep >= slope_sd(deact$activity_pct))
}
c(T_observed = slope_sd(deact$activity_pct), intercepts = ppp(intercepts, 5133), slopes = ppp(slopes, 5134))
The real slopes have an SD of 1.08 points per 100 days. Not one of the varying-intercepts model’s 1,000 replicated datasets came close: their largest was 0.96. Its p-value is 0, and the varying-slopes model’s is 0.45. The check and the LOO comparison agree, which is reassuring. They don’t always: a check asks whether a model is wrong in some respect, LOO asks which model predicts best, and a model can be wrong in a way that hardly matters for prediction.




Challenge 2 · Model weights. Instead of choosing one model, you can combine their predictions. Stacking finds the weights that make the combined predictive distribution best under LOO. Compute them with loo::loo_model_weights().









The function is loo::loo_model_weights().


loos <- list(slopes = loo::loo(log_lik_matrix(slopes)), intercepts = loo::loo(log_lik_matrix(intercepts)), pooled = loo::loo(log_lik_matrix(pooled)))
loo::loo_model_weights(loos)
All the weight goes to the varying-slopes model: the others add nothing to its predictions. When models are closer, stacking often spreads the weight, and the combined predictions beat any single model. It’s a good default when no model is clearly right, which in science is most of the time.

title: Model checking and comparison
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does a posterior predictive check test?

Whether the sampler has converged
Whether data simulated from the fitted model reproduce a chosen feature of the real data
Which model has the highest likelihood


It’s aimed at one aspect of the model, through the test statistic.



2. Why is the lppd too optimistic as an estimate of predictive accuracy?

Because it uses too few draws
Because each observation helped fit the model that’s predicting it
Because it ignores the prior


WAIC and LOO correct for that, by estimating the effective number of parameters, or by leaving each observation out.



3. In a LOO comparison, model A’s elpd is 3 higher than model B’s, with a standard error of 4. What should you conclude?

Model A is clearly better
The models predict about equally well
Model B is better


A difference smaller than about 4, or than a couple of its standard errors, isn’t a clear preference.



4. An observation has a Pareto k of 1.2. What does that mean?

The observation is an error
Its PSIS-LOO estimate is unreliable, because leaving it out changes the posterior too much: refit without it, or rethink the model
The model fits it perfectly


Values below 0.7 are fine. High values flag very influential observations.



5. What is p_{\text{loo}}?

The number of parameters in the model
The effective number of parameters, which is smaller than the actual count when hierarchical models shrink parameters toward each other
A p-value


The varying-slopes model has more than 20 parameters, and a p_{\text{loo}} of 15.



6. Which step comes first in the Bayesian workflow?

Fitting the most complex model
Understanding the question, and the data that answer it
Computing LOO


Every later choice, from the model to the report, depends on what the answer is for.

title: Model checking and comparison
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve finished Module 5. Here’s what you’ve learned in this lesson:

Posterior predictive checks aimed at a model’s assumptions found that the pooled model can’t reproduce the differences between reactors (p = 0.015), and the varying-intercepts model can’t reproduce the differences in their decline rates (p = 0).
The lppd measures how well a model predicts its own data, too optimistically. WAIC and PSIS-LOO correct for that, with about 15 effective parameters for the varying-slopes model.
LOO comparison ranks varying slopes first, by 24.6 points of elpd (SE 6.6) over varying intercepts, and 48.2 over the pooled model.
Pareto k flagged one influential observation, R2 at day 282, which doesn’t change the conclusion.
Pointwise differences show that R6 and R7, whose decline rates are furthest from the average, drive the comparison.
The Bayesian workflow ties it all together: question, model, priors, computation, checks, comparison, use, and report.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download deactivation.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder. These steps need brms (Lesson 9).

Fit the three models with brms, with Lesson 12’s priors, and run loo(fit) for each and loo_compare(). Do you get the same ranking? (Your draws will differ from the lesson’s, so the numbers will too, a little.)
brms’s checks. Try pp_check(fit, type = "stat_grouped", stat = "mean", group = "reactor") and pp_check(fit, type = "intervals_grouped", group = "reactor") for the pooled and the varying-slopes models. What does each show?
Refit for the high k. Run loo(fit_slopes, reloo = TRUE), which refits the model without each observation that has k > 0.7. Does the elpd change?
K-fold cross-validation. Leave out a whole reactor at a time with kfold(fit, group = "reactor"). That asks a different question: how well does each model predict a new reactor? Which model wins now?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Model checking

Asking whether a model reproduces the important features of the data, for example with posterior predictive checks.

Model comparison

Asking which of several models would predict new data best.

Log pointwise predictive density (lppd)

The sum over observations of the log of each one’s likelihood, averaged over the posterior draws.

Expected log predictive density (elpd)

The expected value of the lppd for new data, which WAIC and LOO estimate. Higher is better.

WAIC

The widely applicable information criterion: the lppd minus the effective number of parameters, estimated from the variance of the log-likelihood.

PSIS-LOO

Leave-one-out cross-validation approximated by Pareto-smoothed importance sampling of the posterior draws, without refitting.

Pareto k

The diagnostic of PSIS-LOO for each observation. Values above 0.7 mean that observation’s estimate is unreliable.

Effective number of parameters

How many free parameters a model behaves as if it had. Hierarchical shrinkage makes it smaller than the actual count.

Stacking

Choosing weights for several models’ predictions to make their combination predict best under cross-validation.

Bayesian workflow

The iterative process of building, fitting, checking, comparing and using Bayesian models.











NoteWant to read more?






Aki Vehtari, Andrew Gelman and Jonah Gabry, “Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC”, Statistics and Computing (2017). The paper behind the loo package, PSIS-LOO and the Pareto k diagnostic.
Aki Vehtari, “Cross-validation FAQ”. Short, practical answers to the questions everyone has about LOO, including how to read differences and their standard errors.
Andrew Gelman, Aki Vehtari, Daniel Simpson and others, “Bayesian workflow” (2020). The long paper that describes this lesson’s checklist, with many examples.
Alicia Johnson, Miles Ott and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, chapter 10, “Evaluating regression models”, and chapter 11, “Extending the normal regression model”, for model comparison in practice.

title: Hierarchical models I
text:
Module 5 · Lesson 11 of 13 Week 86 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The plant’s fuel oil is sold on its sulfur content, so the lab’s sulfur results have to be right. Every year, the lab joins an interlaboratory study: a reference fuel goes to ten labs, each analyzes it several times, and each reports its mean and standard error. The results disagree by more than their standard errors allow. Each lab has a small bias of its own. The question is: what is each lab’s true mean, which labs are biased, and how far apart would a new lab’s results be?
Labs E and J ran only two replicates each, and they have the two lowest means. Is that a real bias, or just noise? There are two extreme answers. Complete pooling says all ten labs measure the same thing, so combine everything into one number. No pooling says each lab is its own world, so take each mean at face value. A hierarchical model says the truth is in between, and lets the data decide where.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Hierarchical models I
text:
Complete pooling and no pooling











Complete pooling estimates the common mean by weighting each lab by its precision, 1/\text{se}_j^2: Lesson 4’s precision-weighted average.
Your turn. Compute it, and its standard error.









Divide by the sum of the weights, w.


w <- 1 / se^2
c(pooled = sum(w * y) / sum(w), se = sqrt(1 / sum(w)))
48.61 mg/kg, with a standard error of 0.16. That’s suspiciously precise. It assumes that every lab measures exactly the same thing, so the only differences are each lab’s random error. But lab A, with a standard error of 0.38, is 3.7 standard errors below it, and lab H, 1.9 above. The labs disagree more than their own errors can explain, so complete pooling is wrong, and its standard error is too small.




No pooling is the other extreme: each lab’s true mean is estimated by its own mean. That’s fine for lab F, with 12 replicates, but for E and J, with 2 each, it takes the noise at face value. And it can’t say anything about a lab that wasn’t in the study.

title: Hierarchical models I
text:
The hierarchical model
The hierarchical model treats the labs’ true means \theta_j as draws from a common distribution, whose mean \mu is the consensus value, and whose SD \tau is the between-lab SD:

y_j \sim N(\theta_j, \text{se}_j^2), \qquad \theta_j \sim N(\mu, \tau^2), \qquad \tau \sim \text{half-normal}(0, 2), \qquad p(\mu) \propto 1.

The second line is what makes it hierarchical: the labs’ parameters have a distribution, and its parameters, \mu and \tau, are estimated from the data too. They’re called hyperparameters, and their priors hyperpriors. Two limits explain the model. If \tau = 0, every lab has the same true mean: complete pooling. If \tau = \infty, the labs are unrelated: no pooling. The data choose \tau, and with it, how much pooling there is.
The assumption behind it is exchangeability: before seeing the results, we had no reason to expect any particular lab to be higher or lower than another, so their \theta_j are like draws from one distribution. If we did know something, for example that some labs use a different method, the model should include it, as a predictor (Lesson 12).
Given \mu and \tau, each lab’s posterior mean is a precision-weighted compromise between its own mean and \mu, Lesson 4’s normal-normal model again. The weight on \mu is the shrinkage factor

B_j = \frac{\text{se}_j^2}{\text{se}_j^2 + \tau^2}, \qquad E(\theta_j \mid \mu, \tau, y) = B_j\,\mu + (1 - B_j)\, y_j .

Noisy labs, with a large \text{se}_j, are shrunk a lot. Precise ones keep their own mean.
Your turn. With \tau = 1 and \mu at the pooled 48.61, compute every lab’s shrinkage factor and its shrunken estimate. Return them for lab E, the fifth.









The denominator adds the between-lab variance, tau^2.


tau <- 1
mu <- 48.61273
B <- se^2 / (se^2 + tau^2)
theta <- B * mu + (1 - B) * y
c(B_E = B[5], theta_E = theta[5], B_F = B[6], theta_F = theta[6])
Lab E’s mean, 46.89, is shrunk 77% of the way to the consensus, to 48.22: with two replicates and a standard error of 1.84, its low result is mostly noise. Lab F’s, 48.95, is shrunk only 6%, to 48.93: its 12 replicates are trusted. Shrinkage isn’t a penalty for being different. It’s a penalty for being imprecise.

title: Hierarchical models I
text:
The posterior, exactly
For this model, the posterior can be computed without MCMC, in three steps (Gelman and others’ Bayesian Data Analysis, section 5.4):

The between-lab SD, \tau. Integrating out \mu and the \theta_j leaves its marginal posterior as a formula, p(\tau \mid y) \propto p(\tau)\, V_\mu^{1/2} \prod_j N(y_j \mid \hat\mu_\tau, \text{se}_j^2 + \tau^2), which can go on a grid. The setup code’s log_p_tau() computes its logarithm.
The consensus, \mu, given \tau: normal, centered at the precision-weighted mean \hat\mu_\tau with weights 1/(\text{se}_j^2 + \tau^2).
Each lab, \theta_j, given \mu and \tau: the normal-normal shrinkage above.

Your turn. Put the posterior of \tau on the setup code’s grid, taus, and find its median and 95% credible interval.









Normalize the posterior by its own sum.


lp <- sapply(taus, log_p_tau)
post <- exp(lp - max(lp))
post <- post / sum(post)
cdf <- cumsum(post)
c(median = taus[min(which(cdf >= 0.5))], lower = taus[min(which(cdf >= 0.025))], upper = taus[min(which(cdf >= 0.975))])
A posterior median between-lab SD of 1.03 mg/kg, with a 95% credible interval from 0.51 to 2.06. The interval excludes 0, so complete pooling is ruled out: the labs really do differ. But \tau is uncertain, as between-group SDs usually are with only ten groups. A full analysis averages over that uncertainty, instead of plugging in one value.




Your turn. Now all three steps: draw 4,000 values of \tau from the grid, then \mu given each \tau, then each lab’s \theta_j given both, and report the posterior means of the labs’ true means.









The conditional mean is the precision-weighted sum divided by the total precision, prec.


lp <- sapply(taus, log_p_tau)
post <- exp(lp - max(lp)) / sum(exp(lp - max(lp)))
set.seed(5111)
S <- 4000
tau <- sample(taus, S, replace = TRUE, prob = post)                       # step 1
v <- outer(tau^2, se^2, "+")                                              # se_j^2 + tau^2, one row per draw
mu <- rnorm(S, rowSums(sweep(1 / v, 2, y, "*")) / rowSums(1 / v), sqrt(1 / rowSums(1 / v)))     # step 2
prec <- outer(1 / tau^2, 1 / se^2, "+")                                   # step 3: precisions add
theta_mean <- sweep(matrix(mu / tau^2, S, 10), 2, y / se^2, "+") / prec
theta <- matrix(rnorm(S * 10, theta_mean, sqrt(1 / prec)), S, 10)
setNames(round(colMeans(theta), 3), labs$lab)
Labs E and J, whose means were 46.9 and 47.1, have posterior means of 48.25 and 48.26: pulled most of the way to the consensus. Lab A, at 47.18 with 10 replicates, stays low, at 47.40. The posterior mean of \mu is 48.72. The ranking changed, too: without pooling, E and J were the two lowest labs, and now A and D are.




Here’s the shrinkage, lab by lab:

ord <- order(labs$n)
sh <- data.frame(lab = factor(labs$lab, levels = labs$lab[ord]), n = labs$n, own = y, partial = colMeans(th))
ggplot(sh, aes(y = lab)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(md), linetype = "dashed", color = "#3A1F35") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = own, xend = partial, yend = lab), arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm")), color = "#C2416C") +
  geom_point(aes(x = own), color = "#2a78d6", size = 2.4) +
  geom_point(aes(x = partial), color = "#C2416C", size = 2.4) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 50.9, label = paste0(n, " reps")), size = 3.2, color = "grey40", hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 46.75, y = 10.45, label = "own mean", color = "#2a78d6", hjust = 0, size = 3.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 47.75, y = 10.45, label = "partial pooling", color = "#C2416C", hjust = 0, size = 3.4) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(46.7, 51.4), clip = "off") +
  labs(x = "Sulfur (mg/kg)", y = "Lab, by number of replicates") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: Hierarchical models I
section: The same model in Stan, and the funnel

title: Hierarchical models I
text:
Which labs are biased?
Each lab’s bias is \theta_j - \mu, its true mean’s distance from the consensus. The reference fuel’s specification allows a lab to be 1 mg/kg off.
Your turn. Using the exact draws, find each lab’s posterior probability of a bias of more than 1 mg/kg in either direction.









Subtract the consensus draws, mu. R recycles the vector down each column.


lp <- sapply(taus, log_p_tau)
post <- exp(lp - max(lp)) / sum(exp(lp - max(lp)))
set.seed(5111)
S <- 4000
tau <- sample(taus, S, replace = TRUE, prob = post)
v <- outer(tau^2, se^2, "+")
mu <- rnorm(S, rowSums(sweep(1 / v, 2, y, "*")) / rowSums(1 / v), sqrt(1 / rowSums(1 / v)))
prec <- outer(1 / tau^2, 1 / se^2, "+")
theta <- matrix(rnorm(S * 10, sweep(matrix(mu / tau^2, S, 10), 2, y / se^2, "+") / prec, sqrt(1 / prec)), S, 10)
bias <- theta - mu                              # subtract each draw's consensus from every lab
setNames(round(colMeans(abs(bias) > 1), 3), labs$lab)
Lab A has a 72% probability of being more than 1 mg/kg off, the only lab where it’s more likely than not. B (43%) and H (42%) come next. Labs E and J, with the most extreme raw means, are at 33%: their results were too noisy to convict them. A no-pooling analysis would have flagged E and J first. The hierarchical model flags A, which has 10 replicates and a consistent low result. That’s the lab to visit.




Your turn. A new lab joins next year’s study. Where will its true mean be? For each draw, a new lab’s \theta is a draw from N(\mu, \tau^2). Find the 95% predictive interval.









The new lab’s SD around the consensus is the between-lab SD, tau.


lp <- sapply(taus, log_p_tau)
post <- exp(lp - max(lp)) / sum(exp(lp - max(lp)))
set.seed(5111)
S <- 4000
tau <- sample(taus, S, replace = TRUE, prob = post)
v <- outer(tau^2, se^2, "+")
mu <- rnorm(S, rowSums(sweep(1 / v, 2, y, "*")) / rowSums(1 / v), sqrt(1 / rowSums(1 / v)))
set.seed(5112)
theta_new <- rnorm(S, mu, tau)
quantile(theta_new, c(0.025, 0.975))
From 46.2 to 51.3 mg/kg. That’s the range a buyer’s lab could get for the same fuel, even with perfect repeatability, and it’s why fuel contracts specify a reproducibility limit. Neither extreme model can answer this: complete pooling says every lab gets 48.6, and no pooling knows nothing about labs it hasn’t seen. Predicting new groups is one of the hierarchical model’s main uses.

title: Hierarchical models I
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The eight schools. The most famous hierarchical example is from education: coaching programs for a test in eight schools, with estimated effects y = 28, 8, −3, 7, −1, 1, 18, 12 points and standard errors 15, 10, 16, 11, 9, 11, 10, 18 (Rubin, 1981). Repeat the exact analysis with a flat prior for \tau (the setup code’s log_p_tau() works for the labs only, so it’s written out here), and find school A’s posterior mean effect. Its own estimate was 28.









School A is the first column.


y8 <- c(28, 8, -3, 7, -1, 1, 18, 12)
s8 <- c(15, 10, 16, 11, 9, 11, 10, 18)
log_p_tau8 <- function(tau) {
  v <- s8^2 + tau^2
  mu_hat <- sum(y8 / v) / sum(1 / v)
  0.5 * log(1 / sum(1 / v)) + sum(dnorm(y8, mu_hat, sqrt(v), log = TRUE))     # flat prior on tau
}
t8 <- seq(0.01, 40, length.out = 4000)
lp <- sapply(t8, log_p_tau8)
set.seed(5113)
tau <- sample(t8, 4000, replace = TRUE, prob = exp(lp - max(lp)))
v <- outer(tau^2, s8^2, "+")
mu <- rnorm(4000, rowSums(sweep(1 / v, 2, y8, "*")) / rowSums(1 / v), sqrt(1 / rowSums(1 / v)))
prec <- outer(1 / tau^2, 1 / s8^2, "+")
theta <- matrix(rnorm(4000 * 8, sweep(matrix(mu / tau^2, 4000, 8), 2, y8 / s8^2, "+") / prec, sqrt(1 / prec)), 4000, 8)
c(school_A = mean(theta[, 1]), quantile(theta[, 1], c(0.025, 0.975)), median_tau = median(tau))
School A’s effect shrinks from 28 to a posterior mean of 11, with a 95% interval from −2 to 32. Here, the standard errors are large compared with the spread of the estimates, so the data can’t rule out \tau = 0, and every school is pulled strongly toward the overall 8 points. These eight numbers appear in almost every Bayesian textbook since Gelman and others’ Bayesian Data Analysis (section 5.5), and in Stan’s own documentation of the funnel.




Challenge 2 · How much does the hyperprior matter? With only ten labs, the prior on \tau deserves a sensitivity analysis (Lesson 3). Find the posterior median of \tau with three hyperpriors: half-normal(0, 2), flat, and a tighter half-normal(0, 0.5), which says that labs rarely differ by more than 1 mg/kg. The setup code’s log_p_tau() takes a log_prior function.









The tight hyperprior has an SD of 0.5.


median_tau <- function(log_prior) {
  lp <- sapply(taus, log_p_tau, log_prior = log_prior)
  post <- exp(lp - max(lp)) / sum(exp(lp - max(lp)))
  taus[min(which(cumsum(post) >= 0.5))]
}
c(half_normal_2 = median_tau(function(t) dnorm(t, 0, 2, log = TRUE)),
  flat = median_tau(function(t) 0),
  half_normal_0.5 = median_tau(function(t) dnorm(t, 0, 0.5, log = TRUE)))
1.03, 1.08 and 0.76. The two weak hyperpriors agree, so the data are doing the work. The tight one pulls \tau down by a quarter, and with it, the labs closer together. A hyperprior that strong would have to come from earlier interlaboratory studies, and should be reported as such.

title: Hierarchical models I
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does a hierarchical model assume about the groups’ parameters?

That they’re all equal
That they’re unrelated
That they come from a common distribution, whose parameters are estimated too


That’s between the two extremes: complete pooling (\tau = 0) and no pooling (\tau = \infty).



2. Which lab’s estimate is shrunk most toward the consensus?

The one furthest from the consensus
The one with the largest standard error
The one with the most replicates


The shrinkage factor \text{se}_j^2/(\text{se}_j^2 + \tau^2) depends on the lab’s precision, not on how far off it is.



3. What does exchangeability mean?

The groups have identical data
Before seeing the data, nothing distinguishes the groups, so their parameters can be treated as draws from one distribution
The groups can be analyzed in any order


If something does distinguish them, such as the method a lab uses, add it to the model as a predictor.



4. Why does the centered parameterization of a hierarchical model cause divergent transitions?

Because its priors are improper
Because its posterior is funnel-shaped: very narrow at small \tau and wide at large \tau, so no single step size fits
Because it has too many parameters


The non-centered version, \theta_j = \mu + \tau z_j, removes the funnel.



5. Lab E’s raw mean is the lowest, but its probability of a bias over 1 mg/kg is only 33%. Why?

Because its mean is close to the consensus
Because with two replicates, its low result is too uncertain to be strong evidence of a bias
Because the hyperprior protects it


Partial pooling protects against over-reacting to noisy groups.



6. Which question can only the hierarchical model answer?

What is lab F’s mean?
Where will a new lab’s true mean be?
What is the average of the ten means?


The distribution of the \theta_j, with \mu and \tau, describes the population of labs, including ones not yet seen.

title: Hierarchical models I
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve fitted your first hierarchical model. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Complete pooling (48.61 ± 0.16) ignores real differences between groups, and no pooling over-trusts noisy ones.
Partial pooling shrinks each group toward the consensus by its shrinkage factor, \text{se}_j^2/(\text{se}_j^2 + \tau^2): labs E and J moved from about 47 to 48.25, and precise lab F hardly moved.
The between-lab SD is estimated from the data: 1.03 mg/kg (0.51 to 2.06).
The exact posterior agrees with Stan. The non-centered parameterization removed the centered version’s divergences, which sat in the funnel’s neck.
Lab A is the one most probably biased (72%), not the labs with the most extreme raw means, and a new lab’s true mean could be anywhere from 46.2 to 51.3 mg/kg.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download interlab_sulfur.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder. Step 3 needs brms (Lesson 9).

Plot the posterior of \tau, from the grid, and add vertical lines at its median and 95% interval. Then plot each lab’s posterior mean against \tau, for \tau from 0 to 4 (the shrinkage formula with \mu at its conditional mean). Where do the lines meet, and where do they end?
The classical version. The metafor package fits the same model by restricted maximum likelihood: metafor::rma(yi = mean_mgkg, sei = se_mgkg, data = labs). Compare its estimate of \tau (it reports \tau^2) with the posterior.
brms. Fit brm(mean_mgkg | se(se_mgkg) ~ 1 + (1 | lab), data = labs, prior = prior(normal(0, 2), class = sd)). The se() term tells brms that the standard errors are known. Compare its estimates with this lesson’s.
Leave one lab out. Drop lab A, refit, and predict lab A’s mean from the other nine. Is lab A’s result surprising for a new lab?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Complete pooling

Treating all groups as one, with a single shared parameter.

No pooling

Estimating each group separately, ignoring the others.

Partial pooling

Estimating each group with information borrowed from the others, through a common distribution: what hierarchical models do.

Hierarchical (multilevel) model

A model whose group-level parameters have a distribution, with its own parameters (hyperparameters) estimated from the data.

Hyperparameter

A parameter of the distribution of group-level parameters, such as \mu and \tau here. Its prior is a hyperprior.

Shrinkage factor

The weight a group’s estimate puts on the overall mean, \text{se}_j^2/(\text{se}_j^2 + \tau^2).

Exchangeability

The assumption that, before seeing the data, nothing distinguishes the groups.

Non-centered parameterization

Writing \theta_j = \mu + \tau z_j with standard normal z_j, which removes the funnel and helps HMC sample hierarchical models.











NoteWant to read more?






Andrew Gelman and others, Bayesian Data Analysis (3rd edition), chapter 5, “Hierarchical models”: the exact computation of section 5.4, and the eight schools in section 5.5.
Alicia Johnson, Miles Ott and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, chapters 15, “Hierarchical models are exciting” and 16, “(Normal) hierarchical models without predictors”, on complete, no and partial pooling.
Michael Betancourt and Mark Girolami, “Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for hierarchical models” (2013). Why the funnel defeats samplers, and how non-centering helps.
Bradley Efron and Carl Morris, “Stein’s paradox in statistics”, Scientific American (1977). The classic popular account of why shrinkage beats separate estimates, with baseball batting averages.

title: Probabilistic programming with Stan
text:
Module 5 · Lesson 9 of 13 Week 84 of 160 About 5–7 hours
In Module 4, sampling the pumps’ posterior took a page of R: the log-likelihood with its censoring, the log-prior, a Metropolis sampler, its tuning, and the convergence checks. And every new model would need all of that again, by hand.
Stan turns that around. You write down the model, the data, the parameters, the priors and the likelihood, in a short program, and Stan does the rest: it computes the gradient by automatic differentiation, runs Lesson 8’s Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with an adaptive trajectory length (the No-U-Turn Sampler, NUTS), tunes the step size and the mass matrix during warmup, and reports the diagnostics. It’s what most Bayesian analyses in science and engineering use today. And brms goes one step further: it writes the Stan program for you, from an R formula like the ones you used with lm() and glm() in Module 2.
Stan compiles each model to C++, so it can’t run in your browser. This lesson shows the Stan programs and their output, fitted on a computer, and the live exercises work with the saved posterior draws. The practice section at the end says how to install Stan, so you can fit the models yourself in RStudio.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Probabilistic programming with Stan
Probabilistic programming with Stan
text:
Fitting it from R
The cmdstanr package compiles the program and runs the sampler. This code ran on a computer with Stan installed:
library(cmdstanr)
pumps <- read.csv("data-raw/pump_field.csv")
model <- cmdstan_model("pumps.stan")                      # compile to C++ (takes a minute, once)
fit <- model$sample(
  data = list(N = nrow(pumps), days = pumps$days, failed = pumps$failed),
  seed = 5091, chains = 4, parallel_chains = 4
)
fit$summary(c("shape", "scale", "b10"))
fit$diagnostic_summary()
By default, it ran 4 chains, each with 1,000 warmup iterations (discarded, used to tune the sampler) and 1,000 kept draws: 4,000 posterior draws in all. Here is the summary:

#>  variable     mean  median       sd      mad       q5      q95  rhat ess_bulk
#>     shape    1.863    1.85   0.2941   0.2857    1.402    2.365 1.001     2399
#>     scale 1784.437 1773.68 191.4859 181.6137 1498.260 2113.433 1.003     2563
#>       b10  526.815  522.68 113.0345 113.8632  341.497  710.727 1.000     2442
#>  ess_tail
#>      2567
#>      2116
#>      2463

And the sampler’s diagnostics: no divergent transitions in any chain, no chain that hit the maximum tree depth (the cap on a trajectory’s length), and an energy diagnostic (E-BFMI) well above its warning level of 0.3:

#> $num_divergent
#> [1] 0 0 0 0
#> 
#> $num_max_treedepth
#> [1] 0 0 0 0
#> 
#> $ebfmi
#> [1] 1.0633188 1.1567346 1.0953391 0.9861281












Your turn. The setup code has Stan’s 4,000 draws in pumps_draws, with columns chain, iteration, shape, scale and b10. Find the posterior mean and 95% credible interval of the shape. Module 4’s hand-written Metropolis sampler gave 1.86 (1.26 to 2.48).









The column is shape.


c(mean = mean(pumps_draws$shape), quantile(pumps_draws$shape, c(0.025, 0.975)))
A posterior mean of 1.863, with a 95% credible interval from 1.32 to 2.49: the same posterior as Module 4’s, within Monte Carlo error. Two samplers, one posterior. That’s the most reassuring check there is, and it’s worth doing whenever you write your first Stan version of a model you’ve fitted another way.




Your turn. The Stan program computed the B10 life for every draw, in its generated quantities block. What’s the posterior probability that it’s longer than a year?









A year is 365 days.


c(mean = mean(pumps_draws$b10), p_over_a_year = mean(pumps_draws$b10 > 365))
A posterior mean of 527 days, and a 93% probability that it’s more than a year. Module 4 got 91% from its 9,000 Metropolis draws, which were worth only about 700 independent ones; Stan’s 4,000 are worth about 2,400. The difference is within Monte Carlo error.

title: Probabilistic programming with Stan
text:
Checking the draws yourself
The posterior package, from Lesson 8, reads draws in a standard format. as_draws_df() wants the chain and iteration in columns named .chain and .iteration, and then summarise_draws() gives the same summary as Stan, with any statistics you ask for.
Your turn. Convert the pumps draws, and summarize the shape and scale with their mean, SD, R-hat, and bulk and tail ESS.









The iteration number is in pumps_draws$iteration.


draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(data.frame(shape = pumps_draws$shape, scale = pumps_draws$scale,
                                           .chain = pumps_draws$chain, .iteration = pumps_draws$iteration))
posterior::summarise_draws(draws, "mean", "sd", "rhat", "ess_bulk", "ess_tail")
R-hat is 1.001 for the shape and 1.003 for the scale, and every ESS is above 2,000: these draws pass every check from Lesson 8. Because R-hat compares the chains, it needs to know which draw came from which chain. That’s why the .chain column matters.




Your turn. How precisely do 4,000 draws pin down the posterior mean of the shape? Compute its Monte Carlo standard error.









Lesson 8’s function for the MCSE of a mean is posterior::mcse_mean().


posterior::mcse_mean(pumps_draws$shape)
0.006, so the posterior mean is 1.863 ± 0.006, and “1.86” is the right way to report it. The posterior SD is 0.29, about 50 times larger: nearly all the uncertainty is about the pumps, not about the simulation.

title: Probabilistic programming with Stan
text:
brms: models from formulas
Writing Stan programs is the most flexible way to work, but for the common models, brms (Bayesian regression models using Stan) is faster. You write an R formula, choose a family and priors, and brms writes the Stan program, compiles it and samples. Here’s Lesson 7’s flammability model, with the same priors:
library(brms)
flam <- read.csv("data-raw/flammability.csv")
flam$x <- flam$conc_pct - 1.4
fit <- brm(
  ignitions | trials(tests) ~ x, family = binomial(), data = flam,
  prior = c(prior(normal(0, 2.5), class = Intercept),
            prior(normal(0, 25), class = b)),
  seed = 5092
)
summary(fit)
The formula reads “ignitions out of tests trials, depending on x”. The left-hand side’s | trials(tests) is brms’s way of giving the binomial its number of trials, like cbind(ignitions, tests - ignitions) in glm(). Here’s the summary:

#>  Family: binomial 
#>   Links: mu = logit 
#> Formula: ignitions | trials(tests) ~ x 
#>    Data: flam (Number of observations: 5) 
#>   Draws: 4 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1;
#>          total post-warmup draws = 4000
#> 
#> Regression Coefficients:
#>           Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> Intercept    -0.38      0.61    -1.62     0.78 1.00     2223     1812
#> x            11.55      3.82     5.21    20.47 1.00     2525     1634
#> 
#> Draws were sampled using sample(hmc). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
#> and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
#> scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).

Read it like a glm() summary, with Bayesian columns: Estimate is the posterior mean, Est.Error the posterior SD, and l-95% CI and u-95% CI the 95% credible interval. Then come the convergence diagnostics, R-hat and the two ESS. The slope, 11.55, and its interval from 5.2 to 20.5 match Lesson 7’s grid. stancode(fit) shows the Stan program brms wrote, about 40 lines. Its main difference from a hand-written one is that it centers the predictors, which helps the sampler.
Your turn. The setup code has brms’s draws in flam_draws, with columns alpha (the intercept) and beta (the slope). Compute the posterior of the LFL50, 1.4 - \alpha/\beta, and compare it with Lesson 7’s 1.43% (1.32% to 1.54%).









Divide by the slope, flam_draws$beta.


lfl50 <- 1.4 - flam_draws$alpha / flam_draws$beta
c(mean = mean(lfl50), quantile(lfl50, c(0.025, 0.975)))
1.434% (1.325% to 1.546%). Lesson 7’s grid, rejection and importance samplers, Lesson 8’s HMC, and now brms: five methods, one posterior.




Your turn. And the safety question: the posterior mean ignition probability at 1.1%, its 95% interval, and the probability that it’s above 5%.









5% is 0.05.


p_low <- plogis(flam_draws$alpha + flam_draws$beta * (1.1 - 1.4))
c(mean = mean(p_low), quantile(p_low, c(0.025, 0.975)), p_over_5pct = mean(p_low > 0.05))
A mean of 4.0% and an interval up to 16.6%, as in Lesson 7, and a 27% probability that the ignition probability at 1.1% is above 5%. That’s a number the process safety team can act on: more than a one-in-four chance that the safe-sounding limit isn’t safe enough.

title: Probabilistic programming with Stan
text:
brms formulas
brms formulas extend R’s usual ones. A few that you’ll meet in the next lessons:







Formula
Model




y ~ x
linear regression (with family = gaussian(), the default)


y | trials(n) ~ x
binomial: y successes out of n


y ~ x + (1 | group)
a separate intercept for each group, drawn from a common distribution (Lesson 11)


y ~ x + (x | group)
a separate intercept and slope for each group (Lesson 12)


days | cens(censored) ~ 1
censored data, with a variable that’s "right" for censored and "none" otherwise



The terms in parentheses, (1 | group), are the same as in lme4’s lmer() in Module 3.
Your turn. Write the brms formula for Lesson 12’s leak survey: leaks found out of components inspected in each unit, with a separate intercept for each unit and no predictors. Return the formula itself.









The number of trials is the number of components inspected.


leaks | trials(components) ~ 1 + (1 | unit)
A binomial model with one intercept for the whole plant, plus a deviation for each unit. Typing a formula at the console just returns it, without evaluating anything, so you can build formulas without data. With brms installed, brm(that formula, family = binomial(), data = ldar) would fit it.

title: Probabilistic programming with Stan
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · A pump in its first year. A new pump has just been installed. What’s the posterior predictive probability that its seal fails within a year? For each draw of the shape and scale, the probability is the Weibull CDF at 365 days, pweibull(365, shape, scale). Average it over the draws.









Use the scale draws, pumps_draws$scale.


mean(pweibull(365, shape = pumps_draws$shape, scale = pumps_draws$scale))
5.7%. Averaging the probability over the posterior gives the posterior predictive probability directly, with no need to simulate lifetimes. (Simulating one lifetime per draw with rweibull() and counting the ones below 365 would estimate the same number, with more noise.)




Challenge 2 · Stan against Metropolis. Rerun Module 4’s Metropolis sampler for the pumps, and compare the 5%, 50% and 95% quantiles of its shape draws with Stan’s.









The log shape is the first column of the draws.


pumps <- read_csv("data/pump_field.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
nll <- function(theta) {
  k <- exp(theta[1]); lambda <- exp(theta[2])
  -(sum(pumps$failed * (log(k) - log(lambda) + (k - 1) * log(pumps$days / lambda))) - sum((pumps$days / lambda)^k))
}
log_post <- function(theta) -nll(theta) + dnorm(theta[1], 0, 1, log = TRUE) + dnorm(theta[2], 7.5, 1, log = TRUE)
set.seed(4113)
draws <- matrix(NA, 10000, 2); current <- c(0, 7); lp <- log_post(current)
for (i in 1:10000) {
  proposal <- current + rnorm(2, 0, 0.15); lp_prop <- log_post(proposal)
  if (log(runif(1)) < lp_prop - lp) { current <- proposal; lp <- lp_prop }
  draws[i, ] <- current
}
rbind(stan = quantile(pumps_draws$shape, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)),
      metropolis = quantile(exp(draws[-(1:1000), 1]), c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)))
Stan: 1.40, 1.85 and 2.36. Metropolis: 1.36, 1.86 and 2.39. They agree to within the Metropolis chain’s Monte Carlo error, which is several times larger than Stan’s: its 9,000 draws are worth about 730 independent ones, and Stan’s 4,000 about 2,400. Stan did it with no tuning, and in a fraction of the time.

title: Probabilistic programming with Stan
text:
Quick quiz

1. In a Stan program, where do the priors and the likelihood go?

In the data block
In the generated quantities block
In the model block


The model block builds the log-posterior, with ~ statements and target +=.



2. What does target += weibull_lccdf(days[i] | shape, scale) add for a pump that’s still running?

The log-density of failing at days[i]
The log of the probability of surviving at least days[i] days
Nothing, censored pumps are dropped


That’s the censored likelihood: all we know is that the pump lasted at least that long.



3. What does Stan do during warmup?

It produces the draws you use
It tunes the step size and the mass matrix, and those draws are discarded
It compiles the model


Compilation happens once, before sampling. Warmup adapts the sampler to the posterior.



4. In a brms summary, what is “Est.Error”?

The Monte Carlo standard error
The posterior standard deviation
The residual standard error


It’s the Bayesian counterpart of a standard error. The Monte Carlo error is much smaller, and depends on the ESS.



5. What does y | trials(n) ~ x mean in brms?

y is predicted by n and x
y successes out of n trials, with a success probability depending on x
A model run n times


With family = binomial(), it’s logistic regression for counts out of a known total.



6. Why should you compare a new Stan model with an earlier fit of the same model, when you have one?

Stan needs it to converge
Agreement between two independent methods is strong evidence that both are right
Because Stan’s results are always different


Bugs in a model’s code are common. Two methods with the same bug are rare.

title: Probabilistic programming with Stan
text:
Wrap-up
You can now read and write Stan programs, and fit models with brms. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Stan separates the model from the sampler. A program’s blocks declare the data, the parameters and their transformations, the log-posterior, and quantities to compute from each draw.
Censoring takes one line: weibull_lccdf() for the pumps still running. Stan’s posterior for the shape, 1.86 (1.32 to 2.49), matches Module 4’s.
cmdstanr compiles and samples from R, with 4 chains of 1,000 warmup and 1,000 kept draws by default, and reports R-hat, the bulk and tail ESS, and the sampler’s diagnostics.
brms writes the Stan program from an R formula. The flammability model took one call, and gave the same LFL50, 1.43%, as every method before it.
Posterior draws answer the questions: a 93% probability that the pumps’ B10 life is over a year, a 5.7% chance that a new pump fails in its first year, and a 27% chance that 1.1% vapor isn’t safe enough.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about two hours, the first time)





Install Stan. This takes about 30 minutes and 2 GB of disk space, once.

On Windows, install Rtools for your version of R, from CRAN’s Rtools page. (On a Mac, install the Xcode command line tools by running xcode-select --install in the Terminal.)
In R, install cmdstanr and brms:
install.packages("cmdstanr", repos = c("https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev", getOption("repos")))
install.packages("brms")
Install CmdStan itself, Stan’s command-line program, and check it:
cmdstanr::check_cmdstan_toolchain(fix = TRUE)
cmdstanr::install_cmdstan(cores = 4)
Tell brms to use it: options(brms.backend = "cmdstanr"), in your .Rprofile or at the top of each script.

Then download pump_field.csv, flammability.csv and pumps.stan, and:

Fit the pumps model with the cmdstanr code above. Check that your summary matches this lesson’s. (With the same seed on a different computer, the draws may differ slightly, but the summary should agree within Monte Carlo error.)
Fit the flammability model with brms, and try plot(fit) (trace and density plots), pp_check(fit) and conditional_effects(fit).
Change the prior. Refit the flammability model with prior(normal(0, 5), class = b), a much narrower prior for the slope. How much does the LFL50 change? And the ignition probability at 1.1%?
Read brms’s Stan code with stancode(fit). Find the likelihood, the priors and the centering of the predictor.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Probabilistic programming language

A language for writing statistical models, whose software then does the inference. Stan is the most widely used.

Stan blocks

The sections of a Stan program: data, transformed data, parameters, transformed parameters, model and generated quantities.

No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS)

Stan’s version of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, which chooses each trajectory’s length automatically, stopping when it starts to turn back.

Warmup

The first part of each chain, used to tune the step size and the mass matrix, and then discarded.

Automatic differentiation

Computing exact gradients of a program’s output with respect to its inputs, automatically. Stan uses it to get the gradients HMC needs.

cmdstanr

The R interface to CmdStan, Stan’s command-line program.

brms

An R package that fits Bayesian regression models in Stan from R formulas.

Generated quantities

Values computed from each posterior draw after sampling, such as predictions or derived quantities.











NoteWant to read more?






Stan Development Team, Stan User’s Guide. Examples of every common model, written in Stan, including censored data in the chapter on truncated or censored data.
Paul-Christian Bürkner, “brms: An R package for Bayesian multilevel models using Stan”, Journal of Statistical Software (2017). The paper that introduced brms, with many examples of its formulas.
cmdstanr’s getting started guide, the vignette that walks through installation, fitting and the output, step by step.
Alicia Johnson, Miles Ott and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, chapter 6, “Approximating the posterior”, whose second half introduces rstan, another R interface to Stan.

title: Sampling from posteriors
text:
Module 5 · Lesson 7 of 13 Week 82 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The plant is introducing a new cleaning solvent, and the process safety team needs to know at what concentration its vapor becomes flammable in air.
