The safety lab ran the standard test: a spark in a vessel of vapor and air, at five concentrations, six times each, recording whether the mixture ignited.
A logistic model describes it: the probability of ignition at concentration c is
P(\text{ignition}) = \text{logit}^{-1}\big(\alpha + \beta\,(c - 1.4)\big),
centered at 1.4% so that \alpha is the log-odds at 1.4%. The safety question is about the concentration where ignition becomes likely, and especially about how sure we are that low concentrations are safe.
There’s no conjugate prior for logistic regression, so the posterior has no formula. Module 4 sampled such posteriors with MCMC. This lesson covers the simpler methods that came first, which still matter: they’re exact, they’re easy to check, and for one or two parameters, they’re often all you need.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Sampling from posteriors
text:
The log-posterior
The prior is weakly informative: a normal distribution with mean 0 and SD 2.5 for \alpha, which allows ignition probabilities at 1.4% from about 1% to 99%, and a normal with mean 0 and SD 25 for \beta, which allows the probability to go from near 0 to near 1 within a fraction of a percent of concentration, or hardly change at all. The setup code has the data, x (the concentration minus 1.4), y (ignitions) and m (tests), and a function log_lik(a, b) that computes the log-likelihood for vectors of \alpha and \beta values at once.










Your turn. Write the log-posterior, up to its constant, and evaluate it at \alpha = 0, \beta = 10.









Add the log-prior, log_prior(a, b).


log_post <- function(a, b) log_lik(a, b) + log_prior(a, b)
log_post(0, 10)
−10.54. As in Module 4, the value itself doesn’t mean anything, but differences between values do. Because log_lik() works on vectors, so does log_post(): you can evaluate it at 40,000 points in one call.

title: Sampling from posteriors
text:
Direct sampling from a grid
With two parameters, a grid still works. Evaluate the posterior on a 200 × 200 grid, sample grid points in proportion to it, and add a little uniform jitter within each cell so the draws aren’t stuck on grid lines. The draws are exact, apart from the grid’s resolution.
The quantity the safety team wants is the LFL50, the concentration with a 50% chance of ignition. At that concentration, \alpha + \beta(c - 1.4) = 0, so it’s 1.4 - \alpha/\beta: a function of both parameters, whose posterior comes straight from the draws.
Your turn. Make the grid, sample 10,000 draws, and summarize the LFL50.









Sample the grid points with their posterior probabilities, post.


log_post <- function(a, b) log_lik(a, b) + log_prior(a, b)
g <- expand.grid(a = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 200), b = seq(0, 60, length.out = 200))
lp <- log_post(g$a, g$b)
post <- exp(lp - max(lp))
post <- post / sum(post)
set.seed(5071)
i <- sample(nrow(g), 10000, replace = TRUE, prob = post)
a <- g$a[i] + runif(10000, -0.02, 0.02)               # jitter within each grid cell
b <- g$b[i] + runif(10000, -0.15, 0.15)
lfl50 <- 1.4 - a / b
c(mean = mean(lfl50), quantile(lfl50, c(0.025, 0.975)))
A posterior mean LFL50 of 1.43%, with a 95% credible interval from 1.32% to 1.54%. Two practical checks matter with grids. Subtracting max(lp) before exp() avoids underflow (Module 4, Lesson 2). And the grid must cover the posterior: here, only about two parts in a million of the posterior lie near its edges.




Here are 100 of the posterior’s ignition curves, with the observed proportions:

cc <- seq(0.9, 1.9, by = 0.01)
curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:100, function(k) data.frame(id = k, conc = cc, p = plogis(a_draws[k] + b_draws[k] * (cc - 1.4)))))
ggplot(curves, aes(x = conc, y = p, group = id)) +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_point(data = flam, aes(x = conc_pct, y = ignitions / tests), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3, color = "#3A1F35") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Vapor in air (% by volume)", y = "Probability of ignition") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Your turn. The safety case for the solvent store assumes that vapor never exceeds 1.1%. What’s the posterior of the ignition probability at 1.1%? Use the grid draws, a and b.









The concentration is 1.1%.


log_post <- function(a, b) log_lik(a, b) + log_prior(a, b)
g <- expand.grid(a = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 200), b = seq(0, 60, length.out = 200))
lp <- log_post(g$a, g$b)
post <- exp(lp - max(lp)) / sum(exp(lp - max(lp)))
set.seed(5071)
i <- sample(nrow(g), 10000, replace = TRUE, prob = post)
a <- g$a[i] + runif(10000, -0.02, 0.02)
b <- g$b[i] + runif(10000, -0.15, 0.15)
p_low <- plogis(a + b * (1.1 - 1.4))
c(mean = mean(p_low), quantile(p_low, c(0.025, 0.975)))
A posterior mean of 4.2%, but a 95% credible interval from 0.1% to 17%. Nothing ignited at 1.0% or 1.2%, yet 30 tests can’t rule out a substantial ignition probability at 1.1%, because the curve’s steepness is so uncertain. For a safety case, that upper end is what matters. The honest conclusion is that 1.1% isn’t demonstrably safe, and the lab should run more tests between 1.0% and 1.3%, where the uncertainty is.

title: Sampling from posteriors
text:
Rejection sampling
A grid in 5 dimensions would need 200^5 points, so we need methods that don’t. Rejection sampling (Module 4, Lesson 4) draws from a proposal and accepts each draw with a probability that corrects for the difference from the target. With the prior as the proposal there’s a neat version: accept a prior draw with probability L(\theta)/L_{\max}, its likelihood divided by the largest possible likelihood. Prior times likelihood is proportional to the posterior, so the accepted draws are exact posterior draws.
Your turn. Draw 100,000 values from the prior, accept them with probability L(\theta)/L_{\max} (on the log scale), and report the acceptance rate and the posterior mean LFL50. The maximum log-likelihood is −4.3146.









Subtract the maximum log-likelihood, max_ll.


set.seed(5072)
a0 <- rnorm(100000, 0, 2.5)                  # draws from the prior
b0 <- rnorm(100000, 0, 25)
max_ll <- -4.314570629                       # the maximum of the log-likelihood
keep <- log(runif(100000)) < log_lik(a0, b0) - max_ll
c(acceptance = mean(keep), lfl50 = mean(1.4 - a0[keep] / b0[keep]))
Only 3.0% of the prior draws survived, about 3,000 out of 100,000, but they’re exact posterior draws, and their mean LFL50, 1.432%, agrees with the grid’s 1.431%. The acceptance rate is the problem: the more the data say, the narrower the posterior is compared with the prior, and the more draws are wasted. With a few more parameters, or a little more data, it drops to one in a million.

title: Sampling from posteriors
text:
The normal approximation
A much better proposal starts from the posterior’s mode, found by optimization, as in Module 4, Lesson 9. Near its mode, a posterior is often roughly normal, with a covariance matrix equal to the inverse of the Hessian of the negative log-posterior there. That’s the Laplace approximation, or normal approximation. With lots of data it’s very accurate on its own, and even when it isn’t, it makes an excellent proposal.
Your turn. Find the mode with optim(), and the approximate posterior SDs from the Hessian.









Invert the Hessian, fit$hessian.


log_post <- function(a, b) log_lik(a, b) + log_prior(a, b)
fit <- optim(c(0, 10), function(t) -log_post(t[1], t[2]), hessian = TRUE)
V <- solve(fit$hessian)                       # the approximate posterior covariance
c(mode = fit$par, sd = sqrt(diag(V)))
The mode is at \alpha = -0.31, \beta = 9.67, with approximate SDs of 0.56 and 3.28. But the grid’s posterior mean of \beta was 11.5, well above the mode: the posterior of \beta is skewed, with a long right tail toward very steep curves. A normal approximation can’t capture that. It’s a good proposal, though, especially if you fatten its tails.

title: Sampling from posteriors
text:
Importance sampling
Importance sampling (Module 4, Lesson 5) keeps every draw from a proposal q, and weights it by w = p(\theta \mid y)/q(\theta), which only needs the posterior up to its constant if the weights are normalized to sum to 1. A posterior expectation is then the weighted average. As a proposal, use a t distribution with 4 degrees of freedom, centered at the mode with the Laplace covariance: like the normal approximation, but with heavier tails, so it covers the posterior’s skew.
The effective sample size of the weights, 1/\sum w_i^2, says how many equally weighted draws they’re worth. If a few draws have nearly all the weight, it’s tiny, and the estimate can’t be trusted.
Your turn. Draw 10,000 values from the t proposal, compute the normalized weights, and find the weighted mean LFL50 and the effective sample size.









The effective sample size uses the normalized weights, w.


log_post <- function(a, b) log_lik(a, b) + log_prior(a, b)
fit <- optim(c(0, 10), function(t) -log_post(t[1], t[2]), hessian = TRUE)
V <- solve(fit$hessian)
set.seed(5073)
th <- mvtnorm::rmvt(10000, sigma = V, df = 4, delta = fit$par)
log_w <- log_post(th[, 1], th[, 2]) - mvtnorm::dmvt(th, delta = fit$par, sigma = V, df = 4, log = TRUE)
w <- exp(log_w - max(log_w))
w <- w / sum(w)
lfl50 <- 1.4 - th[, 1] / th[, 2]
c(lfl50 = sum(w * lfl50), ess = 1 / sum(w^2))
An LFL50 of 1.430%, matching the other two methods, and the 10,000 weighted draws are worth 7,844 independent ones: a 78% efficiency, against rejection sampling’s 3%. A good proposal makes all the difference. (mvtnorm::dmvt() returns the log-density with log = TRUE, but note that its default is log = TRUE anyway, an unusual choice.)

title: Sampling from posteriors
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · From weights to draws. Many tools want plain, unweighted draws. Sampling importance resampling (SIR) gets them: resample the proposal draws with their weights as probabilities. Draw 4,000, and compare the LFL50’s 2.5%, 50% and 97.5% quantiles with the grid’s: 1.320%, 1.432% and 1.542%.









Resample with the importance weights, w.


log_post <- function(a, b) log_lik(a, b) + log_prior(a, b)
fit <- optim(c(0, 10), function(t) -log_post(t[1], t[2]), hessian = TRUE)
V <- solve(fit$hessian)
set.seed(5073)
th <- mvtnorm::rmvt(10000, sigma = V, df = 4, delta = fit$par)
log_w <- log_post(th[, 1], th[, 2]) - mvtnorm::dmvt(th, delta = fit$par, sigma = V, df = 4, log = TRUE)
w <- exp(log_w - max(log_w)) / sum(exp(log_w - max(log_w)))
lfl50 <- 1.4 - th[, 1] / th[, 2]
set.seed(5074)
r <- sample(10000, 4000, replace = TRUE, prob = w)
quantile(lfl50[r], c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
1.323%, 1.429% and 1.540%: three methods, one posterior. Resampling with replacement repeats the heavily weighted draws, so the 4,000 aren’t all distinct, but they’re draws from (approximately) the posterior. The same idea, run as a sequence, is behind particle filters, which track the state of a process in real time.




Challenge 2 · A proposal that’s too narrow. Importance sampling fails quietly when the proposal is narrower than the posterior: the tails are rarely sampled, and the few draws that land there get enormous weights. Repeat it with a normal proposal with a quarter of the Laplace SDs (V / 16), and look at the effective sample size and the largest weight.









The proposal density must be the one you drew from: V / 16.


log_post <- function(a, b) log_lik(a, b) + log_prior(a, b)
fit <- optim(c(0, 10), function(t) -log_post(t[1], t[2]), hessian = TRUE)
V <- solve(fit$hessian)
set.seed(5075)
th <- mvtnorm::rmvnorm(10000, fit$par, V / 16)
log_w <- log_post(th[, 1], th[, 2]) - mvtnorm::dmvnorm(th, fit$par, V / 16, log = TRUE)
w <- exp(log_w - max(log_w))
w <- w / sum(w)
c(ess = 1 / sum(w^2), largest_weight = max(w))
10,000 draws worth 10, and a single draw carrying 31% of the total weight. Estimates from these weights would be dominated by a handful of draws, and they’d change completely with another seed. Always check the effective sample size. Better still, choose a proposal with heavier tails than the posterior, like the t, so that the weights stay bounded. This weakness is why MCMC, the next lesson’s subject, took over for anything beyond a few parameters.

title: Sampling from posteriors
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why subtract the maximum log-posterior before exponentiating on a grid?

It changes the posterior’s shape
It keeps the numbers in a range the computer can represent, without changing the normalized posterior
It removes the prior


Log-posteriors like −1,000 would underflow to 0. The constant cancels when you normalize.



2. With the prior as the proposal, what is the acceptance probability in rejection sampling?

The prior density
The likelihood divided by its maximum
Always 50%


Prior × L/L_{\max} is proportional to the posterior, so the accepted draws come from the posterior.



3. Why does rejection sampling from the prior get worse with more data?

Because the prior changes
Because the posterior gets narrower than the prior, so a smaller share of prior draws is accepted
Because the likelihood gets flatter


Here, 3% were accepted. With ten times the data, it would be far fewer.



4. What is the Laplace approximation?

A normal distribution at the posterior mode, with covariance equal to the inverse Hessian of the negative log-posterior
A uniform distribution over the grid
The prior with its mean moved to the data


It’s accurate when the posterior is close to normal, and a good proposal when it isn’t quite.



5. 10,000 importance draws have an effective sample size of 12. What does that tell you?

The estimate is very precise
A few draws carry nearly all the weight, so the estimate is unreliable: the proposal is too narrow or in the wrong place
You need to normalize the weights


Use a proposal with heavier tails, centered on the posterior mode.



6. Why use a t proposal rather than a normal one for importance sampling?

Because t draws are faster
Its heavier tails cover the posterior’s tails, so no draw gets an enormous weight
Because the posterior is always a t distribution


A proposal should be wider than the target in every direction.

title: Sampling from posteriors
text:
Wrap-up
You can now sample a posterior that has no formula, three ways. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Grid sampling is exact up to the grid’s resolution, and it works for one or two parameters: the solvent’s LFL50 is 1.43% (95% credible interval 1.32% to 1.54%).
The posterior of any function of the parameters comes from the draws: the ignition probability at 1.1% could be as high as 17%, so more tests are needed at low concentrations.
Rejection sampling with the prior as the proposal is exact but wasteful: 3% acceptance here.
The Laplace approximation puts a normal distribution at the mode. Here it missed the skew in \beta, whose posterior mean is 11.5 against a mode of 9.7.
Importance sampling with a t proposal at the mode was 78% efficient. Always check the effective sample size: a too-narrow proposal gave 10 from 10,000.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download flammability.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Compare with glm(). Fit glm(cbind(ignitions, tests - ignitions) ~ I(conc_pct - 1.4), family = binomial, data = flam). How do its estimates compare with the posterior mode? Why are they close but not equal?
Contour plot. Plot the grid posterior of (\alpha, \beta) with geom_contour(), and overlay the Laplace approximation’s 95% ellipse (the ellipse package, or by hand with chol(V)). Where does the approximation fail?
Design the next tests. Suppose the lab can run 12 more tests. Simulate the posterior’s 95% upper bound for the ignition probability at 1.1% after running them all at 1.1%, or all at 1.3%, or six at each. Which design teaches the most about the safety question?
The safe concentration. Find the posterior distribution of the concentration with a 1% ignition probability, 1.4 + (\text{logit}(0.01) - \alpha)/\beta, and its 5th percentile. Would you write that number into a safety case?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Grid sampling

Drawing grid points in proportion to the posterior, with jitter within each cell. Exact up to the resolution, practical in one or two dimensions.

Rejection sampling

Drawing from a proposal and accepting each draw with a probability that corrects for the difference from the target.

Mode

The parameter value with the highest posterior density, found by optimization.

Laplace (normal) approximation

A normal distribution centered at the posterior mode, with covariance equal to the inverse Hessian of the negative log-posterior.

Importance sampling

Weighting draws from a proposal by the ratio of the target to the proposal density.

Effective sample size of importance weights

1/\sum w_i^2 for normalized weights: how many equally weighted draws the weighted draws are worth.

Sampling importance resampling (SIR)

Resampling importance draws with their weights as probabilities, to get unweighted draws.











NoteWant to read more?






Andrew Gelman and others, Bayesian Data Analysis (3rd edition), section 3.7, the bioassay experiment, which is this lesson’s analysis with rats instead of sparks, and chapter 10, “Introduction to Bayesian computation”, on rejection and importance sampling.
Alicia Johnson, Miles Ott and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, chapter 6, “Approximating the posterior”, on grid approximation and its limits.
Roger Peng, Advanced Statistical Computing, the sections on rejection sampling and importance sampling, the reading for Module 4’s lessons on them.

title: Posterior inference
text:
Module 5 · Lesson 5 of 13 Week 80 of 160 About 5–7 hours
A posterior distribution is the complete answer to a Bayesian analysis. But a plant manager doesn’t want a distribution: she wants a number, a range, a yes or a no. This lesson is about getting those from a posterior, and about doing it in a way that matches the question.
We’ll stay with the new recipe. With the team’s prior, its off-spec rate has the posterior Beta(3, 47), and the old recipe’s rate is 38/480 = 7.9%. That posterior is skewed, with a long right tail, which is exactly when the different summaries disagree.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Posterior inference
text:
Point estimates
If you must report one number, which? Each common choice is the best answer to a different question, and the question is described by a loss function: how bad it is to report \hat\theta when the truth is \theta.








Estimate
Minimizes the expected
Loss




Posterior mean
squared error
(\hat\theta - \theta)^2


Posterior median
absolute error
\lvert\hat\theta - \theta\rvert


Posterior mode (MAP)
“all or nothing” loss
0 if exactly right, 1 otherwise



The mode is also called the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate. For a symmetric posterior, all three agree. For a skewed one, they don’t.











Your turn. Compute the three point estimates for Beta(3, 47).









The median is the 50th percentile.


c(mean = a / (a + b), median = qbeta(0.5, a, b), mode = (a - 1) / (a + b - 2))
A mean of 6.0%, a median of 5.4% and a mode of 4.2%. The right tail pulls the mean up. For reporting an off-spec rate, where an error in either direction costs about the same, the median or the mean is a better choice than the mode, which sits at the low end of the plausible range.




Your turn. Check the table with posterior draws. For each candidate estimate from 0 to 0.2, compute the average squared error and the average absolute error over 20,000 draws, and find the candidates that minimize them.









The absolute error is abs(draws - e).


set.seed(5051)
draws <- rbeta(20000, a, b)
candidates <- seq(0, 0.2, by = 0.0005)
squared <- sapply(candidates, function(e) mean((draws - e)^2))
absolute <- sapply(candidates, function(e) mean(abs(draws - e)))
c(best_squared = candidates[which.min(squared)], best_absolute = candidates[which.min(absolute)])
5.95% and 5.35%: the draws’ mean and median, 5.97% and 5.37%, to the nearest step of the candidate grid. A loss function turns “what’s the best estimate?” into a question with an answer. And if the costs aren’t symmetric, for example if underestimating the off-spec rate is three times as bad as overestimating it, the best estimate is a different quantile of the posterior.

title: Posterior inference
text:
Highest posterior density intervals
A 95% credible interval is any interval with 95% posterior probability, and there are infinitely many. The equal-tailed interval cuts 2.5% off each end. The highest posterior density (HPD) interval is the shortest one: every value inside it has a higher posterior density than every value outside. For a skewed posterior, it shifts toward the peak.
To find it for a beta posterior, slide a window of 95% probability along the distribution, starting at lower-tail probability p and ending at p + 0.95, and find the p that makes it narrowest.
Your turn. Use optimize() to find the HPD interval of Beta(3, 47), and compare its width with the equal-tailed interval’s.









The window ends at best$minimum + 0.95.


width <- function(p) qbeta(p + 0.95, a, b) - qbeta(p, a, b)
best <- optimize(width, interval = c(0, 0.05))
c(hpd = qbeta(c(best$minimum, best$minimum + 0.95), a, b), hpd_width = best$objective, equal_tailed_width = width(0.025))
The HPD interval runs from 0.7% to 12.5%, 11.9 points wide, against the equal-tailed 1.3% to 14.0%, 12.7 points wide. It’s shifted toward the low rates, where the posterior is densest. At its two ends, the posterior density is the same, 1.84: that’s the property that defines it.





th <- seq(0, 0.25, by = 0.0005)
ggplot(data.frame(theta = th, density = dbeta(th, 3, 47)), aes(x = theta, y = density)) +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0.00674, xend = 0.1253, y = 1.84, yend = 1.84, linetype = "dashed", color = "#3A1F35") +
  annotate("segment", x = 0.00674, xend = 0.1253, y = -1.3, yend = -1.3, linewidth = 3, color = "#C2416C") +
  annotate("segment", x = 0.0128, xend = 0.1398, y = -2.8, yend = -2.8, linewidth = 3, color = "#2a78d6") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.1300, y = -1.3, label = "highest density, 0.7% to 12.5%", hjust = 0, size = 3.5, color = "#3A1F35") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.1445, y = -2.8, label = "equal-tailed, 1.3% to 14.0%", hjust = 0, size = 3.5, color = "#3A1F35") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.25)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 12, by = 4)) +
  labs(x = "Off-spec rate", y = "Posterior density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








With posterior draws instead of a formula, the HPD interval is the shortest stretch of the sorted draws that contains 95% of them.
Your turn. Find it from the 20,000 draws.









You want the narrowest window: which.min(widths).


set.seed(5051)
s <- sort(rbeta(20000, a, b))
k <- floor(0.95 * length(s))                              # each window holds k + 1 draws
widths <- s[(k + 1):length(s)] - s[1:(length(s) - k)]     # the width of every window
i <- which.min(widths)
c(s[i], s[i + k])
From 0.6% to 12.4%, close to the exact 0.7% to 12.5%. coda::HPDinterval() does the same calculation. HPD intervals have one drawback: unlike equal-tailed ones, they change if you transform the parameter. The HPD interval for the log of the rate isn’t the log of this one.

title: Posterior inference
text:
Testing hypotheses
A Bayesian test of a hypothesis is direct: compute its posterior probability. “The new recipe is better” is H_1: \theta < 0.079, and its posterior probability is pbeta(old_rate, 3, 47), 76%. Its alternative, H_0: \theta \geq 0.079, has 24%.
But how much of that 76% came from the data, and how much from the team’s optimistic prior? The Bayes factor separates the two. It’s the factor by which the data multiplied the odds:

\underbrace{\frac{P(H_1 \mid y)}{P(H_0 \mid y)}}_{\text{posterior odds}} = \underbrace{\frac{p(y \mid H_1)}{p(y \mid H_0)}}_{\text{Bayes factor } BF_{10}} \times \underbrace{\frac{P(H_1)}{P(H_0)}}_{\text{prior odds}}.

A Bayes factor above 1 means that the data favor H_1, and below 1, that they favor H_0. A common rough scale, from Kass and Raftery (1995), calls 1 to 3 “not worth more than a bare mention”, 3 to 20 “positive”, 20 to 150 “strong” and over 150 “very strong” evidence.
Your turn. Compute the prior odds that the recipe is better, under the Beta(1, 19) prior, the posterior odds under Beta(3, 47), and the Bayes factor.









The Bayes factor is the posterior odds divided by the prior odds.


prior_odds <- pbeta(old_rate, 1, 19) / pbeta(old_rate, 1, 19, lower.tail = FALSE)
post_odds <- pbeta(old_rate, 3, 47) / pbeta(old_rate, 3, 47, lower.tail = FALSE)
c(prior_odds = prior_odds, post_odds = post_odds, bayes_factor = post_odds / prior_odds)
A surprise. The prior odds were 3.8 to 1 in favor of “better”, a prior probability of 79%, and the posterior odds are 3.1 to 1. The Bayes factor is 0.82: the trial slightly favored “not better”. All of the 76% came from the prior. The trial’s 6.7% was a bit worse than the team expected, so it moved them back a little. Posterior probabilities answer “what should I believe now?”, and Bayes factors answer “what did these data say?”. Report both when the prior is doing a lot of work.

title: Posterior inference
text:
Bayes factors for point hypotheses
A different kind of question: “Is the new recipe’s rate the same as the old one’s?” That’s a point hypothesis, H_0: \theta = 0.079 exactly, against H_1: \theta \sim \text{Beta}(1, 19). A continuous posterior gives a single point zero probability, so here the Bayes factor is computed from the marginal likelihood of each hypothesis: the probability of the data averaged over its prior.

Under H_0, it’s just the binomial probability, dbinom(2, 30, old_rate).
Under H_1, it’s the beta-binomial probability from Lesson 2: \binom{30}{2} B(2 + a, 28 + b)/B(a, b).

Your turn. Compute both, and the Bayes factor BF_{01} in favor of “the same”.









BF_{01} puts H_0’s marginal likelihood on top: p_y_h0 / p_y_h1.


p_y_h0 <- dbinom(2, 30, old_rate)
p_y_h1 <- choose(30, 2) * beta(2 + 1, 28 + 19) / beta(1, 19)
c(p_y_h0 = p_y_h0, p_y_h1 = p_y_h1, bf01 = p_y_h0 / p_y_h1)
The data are 1.8 times as probable if the rate is exactly the old one’s. That’s evidence “not worth more than a bare mention” for “no change”: 30 batches can’t distinguish a rate of 7.9% from the nearby rates H_1 allows.




Bayes factors for point hypotheses have a notorious property: they depend heavily on the prior under H_1, even when the posterior under H_1 hardly does.
Your turn. Recompute BF_{01} with four priors for H_1: flat Beta(1, 1), the team’s Beta(1, 19), Beta(0.5, 9.5) and Beta(0.1, 1.9). The last three all have a mean of 5%, worth 20, 10 and 2 batches.









The prior’s beta function is beta(a1, b1).


bf01 <- function(a1, b1) dbinom(2, 30, old_rate) / (choose(30, 2) * beta(2 + a1, 28 + b1) / beta(a1, b1))
c(flat = bf01(1, 1), team = bf01(1, 19), weaker = bf01(0.5, 9.5), vague = bf01(0.1, 1.9))
From 1.8 to 8.4. The vaguer H_1’s prior, the more the Bayes factor favors H_0, because a vague H_1 spreads its predictions over rates the data rule out, and so predicts the actual data poorly. Make the prior vague enough, and any data at all will favor the point hypothesis. That’s Lindley’s paradox. The lesson: never use a “noninformative” prior when computing a Bayes factor, and for estimating a rate, a posterior interval is usually more informative than a test of a point hypothesis that nobody believed anyway.

title: Posterior inference
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Should the plant switch? “Is the new recipe better?” is the wrong question. The plant manager’s real question is whether to switch, and that depends on money. The new recipe saves €1,500 of steam per batch, and every off-spec batch costs €12,000 to rework. Over the next 100 batches, switching gains 100 \times (1500 - 12000\,(\theta - 0.079)) euros. Find its posterior expected value and the probability that switching pays.









The extra off-spec cost compares \theta with the old rate, old_rate.


set.seed(5052)
theta <- rbeta(100000, a, b)
gain <- 100 * (1500 - 12000 * (theta - old_rate))
c(expected_gain = mean(gain), p_pays = mean(gain > 0))
An expected gain of €173,000 over 100 batches, and a 99.9% probability that switching pays. The steam savings are so large that the new recipe would have to run off spec 12.5 points more often than the old one to lose money, and the posterior says that’s almost impossible. The probability that it’s better is only 76%, but the decision is easy. Bayesian decision theory chooses the action with the highest expected value under the posterior. It’s the right tool whenever a test result has to turn into an action.




Challenge 2 · The Savage-Dickey shortcut. When H_0 is a point inside H_1’s prior, the Bayes factor has a shortcut: BF_{01} is the posterior density at the point divided by the prior density there, both under H_1. Check that it gives the 1.81 you found with the team’s prior.









Divide by the prior density, Beta(1, 19).


dbeta(old_rate, 3, 47) / dbeta(old_rate, 1, 19)
1.81, exactly. The data raised the density at 7.9% by a factor of 1.81, from the prior to the posterior. This Savage-Dickey density ratio makes Bayes factors for point hypotheses easy to get from MCMC draws: estimate the two densities at the point, with a kernel density estimate (Module 4) if there’s no formula.

title: Posterior inference
text:
Quick quiz

1. Which point estimate minimizes the expected absolute error?

The posterior mean
The posterior median
The posterior mode


The mean minimizes squared error, the median absolute error, and the mode the “all or nothing” loss.



2. What defines the highest posterior density interval?

It cuts equal probability off each tail
It’s the shortest interval with the stated probability: every point inside has a higher density than every point outside
It’s centered on the posterior mean


For a symmetric posterior it’s the same as the equal-tailed interval. For a skewed one, it shifts toward the peak.



3. The posterior probability of H_1 is 76%, but the Bayes factor is 0.82. What does that mean?

There’s an error in one of them
The prior already favored H_1, and the data slightly lowered its probability
The data strongly support H_1


The Bayes factor measures what the data did to the odds, separately from where the odds started.



4. What is the marginal likelihood of a hypothesis?

The probability of the data, averaged over the hypothesis’s prior
The maximum of the likelihood
The posterior probability of the hypothesis


A Bayes factor is the ratio of two marginal likelihoods. That’s why it depends on the priors.



5. Testing a point hypothesis, you make the prior under H_1 vaguer and vaguer. What happens to BF_{01}?

It approaches 1
It grows without limit, favoring the point hypothesis whatever the data
It stays the same


That’s Lindley’s paradox. Bayes factors need real, informative priors under each hypothesis.



6. The new recipe has only a 76% probability of being better, yet switching to it has a 99.9% probability of paying off. How?

The two numbers contradict each other
The steam savings outweigh any plausible increase in off-spec costs, so the decision doesn’t depend on whether it’s better
The decision used a different prior


Decisions depend on costs and benefits, not just on probabilities.

title: Posterior inference
text:
Wrap-up
You can now turn any posterior into the answer a question needs. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Point estimates answer different questions: for Beta(3, 47), the mean 6.0% minimizes squared error, the median 5.4% absolute error, and the mode 4.2% the all-or-nothing loss.
HPD intervals are the shortest credible intervals: 0.7% to 12.5%, against the equal-tailed 1.3% to 14.0%.
Posterior probabilities test hypotheses directly, and Bayes factors say what the data contributed: 0.82, so the 76% for “better” came from the prior.
Point hypotheses need marginal likelihoods, and their Bayes factors depend strongly on the prior under the alternative: from 1.8 to 8.4 here.
Decisions maximize posterior expected value: switching gains an expected €173,000 per 100 batches.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)






Asymmetric loss. Suppose underestimating the off-spec rate costs three times as much as overestimating it. Show with draws that the best estimate is the posterior’s 75th percentile. (Hint: the loss is 3(\theta - \hat\theta) if \hat\theta < \theta, and \hat\theta - \theta otherwise.)
HPD for a bimodal posterior. Mix two normal distributions, 60% N(0, 1) and 40% N(5, 1), draw 100,000 values, and plot them. Compute an equal-tailed 80% interval and an 80% highest-density region (it may come in two pieces). Which describes the distribution better?
The break-even. In the switching decision, how much would rework have to cost per batch before the probability that switching pays fell below 90%?
coda. Compare your HPD intervals with coda::HPDinterval(coda::mcmc(draws)).










NoteKey words from this lesson






Loss function

How bad it is to report an estimate when the truth is something else. Each common point estimate minimizes the expected value of one loss.

Maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate

The posterior mode, the single most probable value.

Highest posterior density (HPD) interval

The shortest interval with a stated posterior probability.

Bayes factor

The ratio of the marginal likelihoods of two hypotheses: how much the data change the odds between them.

Marginal likelihood

The probability of the data under a hypothesis, averaged over that hypothesis’s prior.

Lindley’s paradox

With a vague enough prior under the alternative, a Bayes factor favors a point hypothesis whatever the data say.

Savage-Dickey density ratio

For a point hypothesis nested in the alternative, the Bayes factor is the posterior density at the point divided by the prior density there.

Bayesian decision theory

Choosing the action with the best expected outcome, averaged over the posterior.











NoteWant to read more?






Alicia Johnson, Miles Ott and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, chapter 8, “Posterior inference & prediction”, on credible intervals, hypothesis tests and Bayes factors.
Robert Kass and Adrian Raftery, “Bayes factors”, Journal of the American Statistical Association (1995). The classic review, with the evidence scale used in this lesson.
Andrew Gelman and others, Bayesian Data Analysis (3rd edition), chapter 9, “Decision analysis”, with worked examples of choosing actions by expected value.

title: Choosing priors
text:
Module 5 · Lesson 3 of 13 Week 78 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The high-pressure steam line is getting a new kind of gasket. Before it goes into service, the maintenance team pressure-tested 25 of them on the test rig at 1.5 times the design pressure, and none leaked. The plant’s rule is that a new gasket needs a leak probability below 5% under test conditions. Does this one qualify?
Zero events is where the prior matters most. The data say the leak probability is “small”, but not how small, and different reasonable priors give different answers. So how do you choose? This lesson is about the main kinds of prior, and about two tools that keep you honest: prior predictive checks, which ask whether a prior makes sense before you see the data, and sensitivity analysis, which asks how much the conclusions depend on it.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Choosing priors
text:
Noninformative priors
The natural first idea is a prior that says nothing: the flat Beta(1, 1). With 0 leaks in 25 tests, the posterior is Beta(1, 26).











Your turn. Find the flat-prior posterior mean, and the 95% upper credible bound: the value the leak probability is below with 95% probability.









The upper bound is the 95th percentile, 0.95.


a <- 1 + y
b <- 1 + n - y
c(mean = a / (a + b), upper_95 = qbeta(0.95, a, b))
A posterior mean of 3.7%, and a 95% upper bound of 10.9%. So with a flat prior, the gasket doesn’t demonstrably meet the 5% rule: leak probabilities up to 11% are still plausible after 25 clean tests. Classical statistics has a famous shortcut for zero events, the rule of three: the 95% upper confidence bound is about 3/n, here 12%. Challenge 2 compares the two.




But is “flat” really “uninformative”? Flat on the leak probability \theta says that a probability between 0% and 1% is as likely as one between 50% and 51%. On the log-odds scale, \log(\theta/(1-\theta)), which logistic regression uses, the same prior isn’t flat at all: it piles up near 0. Every prior is flat on some scale and informative on others, so “flat” isn’t a property of your knowledge, it’s a property of your parameterization.
The Jeffreys prior is a way around that. It’s built from the Fisher information (Module 4’s curvature of the log-likelihood), and it gives the same answers whichever way you parameterize the model. For a binomial probability, it’s Beta(½, ½), which puts a little more weight near 0 and 1 than the flat prior does.
Your turn. Repeat the analysis with the Jeffreys prior.









The Jeffreys prior is Beta(0.5, 0.5).


a <- 0.5 + y
b <- 0.5 + n - y
c(mean = a / (a + b), upper_95 = qbeta(0.95, a, b))
A mean of 1.9% and an upper bound of 7.3%. Two “noninformative” priors, and the posterior means differ by a factor of two. With 25 tests and no leaks, the data are too thin for the choice not to matter. (Don’t try Beta(0, 0), the Haldane prior, here. It isn’t a proper distribution, and with zero events its posterior, Beta(0, 25), isn’t either. An improper prior is sometimes fine, but you must always check that the posterior is proper.)




Your turn. The opposite trap: a “vague” prior on the log-odds scale. A normal prior with mean 0 and SD 10 looks harmless there. Draw 100,000 values from it, turn them into probabilities with plogis(), and see what it says about \theta.









The SD is 10.


set.seed(5031)
theta <- plogis(rnorm(100000, mean = 0, sd = 10))
c(below_1pct = mean(theta < 0.01), above_99pct = mean(theta > 0.99))
65% of the prior is below 1% or above 99%: 32% for “almost never leaks” and 32% for “almost always leaks”. That’s a strong, strange belief, not a vague one. With an SD of 1.5 on the log-odds scale, only 0.2% of the prior is that extreme. Lesson 10 uses priors like that for regression coefficients.

title: Choosing priors
section: Informative priors, and prior predictive checks
text:
Informative priors, and prior predictive checks
The gasket’s vendor has its own test data: 2 leaks in 200 gaskets, at the same test pressure. If the plant’s conditions match the vendor’s, that’s real information, and an informative prior uses it: roughly Beta(2, 198), with a mean of 1%, worth 200 tests.
How do you check a prior? You can’t compare it with the data you’re about to analyze, but you can ask what data it predicts. That’s a prior predictive check: simulate data from the prior, before looking at yours, and see whether they’re plausible. For the gasket, the prior predictive probability of 0 leaks in 25 is the beta-binomial probability from Lesson 2, B(a, b + 25)/B(a, b).
Your turn. Compute it for the flat prior and for the vendor’s prior.









The denominator is the beta function of the vendor’s prior, beta(2, 198).


c(flat = beta(1, 1 + 25) / beta(1, 1), vendor = beta(2, 198 + 25) / beta(2, 198))
The flat prior predicted 0 leaks in 25 with probability 3.8%. It thought a clean test run was unusual, because it gave as much weight to a 60% leak rate as to a 1% one. Nobody at the plant thought that. The vendor’s prior gave it 79%: the result it expected. Neither number proves that a prior is right, but a prior that’s surprised by the data everyone expected deserves a second look.




Prior predictive checks matter even more for models with several parameters, where nobody can picture the joint prior. Take Module 2’s yield model, \text{yield} = \alpha + \beta\,(T - 180), for reactor temperatures T from 160 to 200 °C. “Vague” priors such as normal distributions with mean 0 and SD 100 for both \alpha and \beta look safe.
Your turn. Simulate 10,000 pairs (\alpha, \beta) from those priors, compute the yields they imply at the five temperatures in the setup code’s temps, and find the share of predicted yields that are impossible, below 0% or above 100%.









The model uses T - 180.


set.seed(5032)
alpha <- rnorm(10000, 0, 100)
beta <- rnorm(10000, 0, 100)
yields <- outer(alpha, rep(1, 5)) + outer(beta, temps - 180)    # a row of 5 yields for each pair
mean(yields < 0 | yields > 100)
91% of the predicted yields are impossible. The “vague” priors say the yield is most likely thousands of percent, or negative. With 40 batches of data, the likelihood will overwhelm them, so the posterior will be fine. But in bigger models with less data, priors like these can cause real trouble, and they always make the sampler’s job harder.

title: Choosing priors
text:
Weakly informative priors
Between “nothing” and “the vendor’s data” is the most useful kind of prior in practice: a weakly informative one. It rules out the absurd without pretending to know the answer. For the yield model: the yield at 180 °C is probably 60% to 100% (a normal prior for \alpha with mean 80 and SD 8), and a 1 °C change in temperature probably changes it by less than 1 percentage point (a normal prior for \beta with mean 0 and SD 0.5).
Your turn. Repeat the prior predictive check with these priors.









The SD for \beta is 0.5.


set.seed(5032)
alpha <- rnorm(10000, 80, 8)
beta <- rnorm(10000, 0, 0.5)
yields <- outer(alpha, rep(1, 5)) + outer(beta, temps - 180)
mean(yields < 0 | yields > 100)
3%. The weakly informative priors still allow a wide range, yields from about 55% to 105% at 200 °C, and only a few impossible ones. They weren’t made up from the data; they come from knowing what a yield is and roughly how chemistry responds to temperature. That’s the kind of knowledge priors are for.




Here are 40 lines from each prior, the yield against temperature that each (\alpha, \beta) pair implies:

set.seed(5033)
draw_lines <- function(a, b, label) {
  data.frame(id = rep(1:40, each = 2), temp = rep(c(160, 200), 40),
             yield = rep(a, each = 2) + rep(b, each = 2) * (rep(c(160, 200), 40) - 180), prior = label)
}
lines <- rbind(draw_lines(rnorm(40, 0, 100), rnorm(40, 0, 100), "vague: SD 100 for both"),
               draw_lines(rnorm(40, 80, 8), rnorm(40, 0, 0.5), "weakly informative"))
lines$prior <- factor(lines$prior, levels = c("vague: SD 100 for both", "weakly informative"))
ggplot(lines, aes(x = temp, y = yield, group = id)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 160, xmax = 200, ymin = 0, ymax = 100, fill = "#F4C0D1", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ prior, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Predicted yield (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The shaded band is the possible range. Note the y-axes: the vague priors’ lines run off into thousands of percent.

title: Choosing priors
text:
Sensitivity analysis
When different reasonable priors could be argued for, analyze the data with several, and report how much the conclusions move. If they hardly move, the data have spoken. If they move a lot, that’s an important finding too: it says the data alone can’t settle the question.
Your turn. For the gasket, compute the posterior mean and the 95% upper bound with four priors: flat, Jeffreys, a weakly informative Beta(1, 9) (a leak rate of about 10% or less, worth 10 tests) and the vendor’s Beta(2, 198).









The number of tests without a leak, n - y, goes to the second parameter.


priors <- list(flat = c(1, 1), jeffreys = c(0.5, 0.5), weak = c(1, 9), vendor = c(2, 198))
t(sapply(priors, function(ab) {
  a <- ab[1] + y
  b <- ab[2] + n - y
  c(mean = a / (a + b), upper_95 = qbeta(0.95, a, b))
}))



Prior
Posterior mean
95% upper bound




Flat
3.7%
10.9%


Jeffreys
1.9%
7.3%


Weakly informative
2.9%
8.4%


Vendor’s data
0.9%
2.1%



Only the vendor’s prior says the gasket meets the 5% rule. So the honest report is: “On our own 25 tests, the gasket hasn’t yet shown that its leak probability is below 5%; it will if the vendor’s tests apply to our conditions.” That puts the real question, whether the vendor’s test rig is like the plant’s, in front of the people who can answer it. About 50 tests without a leak would settle it with the weakly informative prior alone.

title: Choosing priors
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · A prior that knows when to back off. The risk with the vendor’s prior is that the vendor’s conditions might not match the plant’s. A mixture prior hedges: 70% weight on the vendor’s Beta(2, 198), and 30% on a flat Beta(1, 1), in case the vendor’s data don’t apply. Compute the posterior on a fine grid, and the posterior weight of the vendor’s part. Then imagine the 25 tests had found 3 leaks instead, and do it again.









The denominator adds both parts of the prior: vendor_part + flat_part.


grid <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.0001)
vendor_part <- 0.7 * dbeta(grid, 2, 198)
flat_part <- 0.3 * dbeta(grid, 1, 1)
weight_vendor <- function(leaks) {
  lik <- dbinom(leaks, 25, grid)
  sum(vendor_part * lik) / sum((vendor_part + flat_part) * lik)
}
c(no_leaks = weight_vendor(0), three_leaks = weight_vendor(3))
With no leaks, the vendor’s part gains weight, from 70% to 98%: the plant’s data agree with the vendor’s, so the posterior trusts them more, with a mean of 0.95%. With 3 leaks, its weight falls to 20%, and the posterior mean is 12%. The vendor’s prior on its own would have said 2.2%, explaining the leaks away. The mixture prior lets the data decide whether the prior applies. That’s often the right compromise when prior information comes from somewhere else.




Challenge 2 · The rule of three. Compare the classical rule of three, 3/n, with the flat-prior Bayesian 95% upper bound, qbeta(0.95, 1, n + 1), for 0 events in n = 10, 25, 100 and 1,000 tests.









With 0 events, the flat-prior posterior is Beta(1, n + 1): n_tests + 1.


n_tests <- c(10, 25, 100, 1000)
rbind(rule_of_three = 3 / n_tests, bayes_flat = qbeta(0.95, 1, n_tests + 1))
With 10 tests, 30% against 24%. With 1,000, 0.30% against 0.30%. The two agree more and more closely as n grows, and with so many tests, the prior hardly matters. The rule comes from (1 - \theta)^n = 0.05, so \theta = 1 - 0.05^{1/n} \approx -\log(0.05)/n \approx 3/n, and the flat-prior bound is 1 - 0.05^{1/(n + 1)}, almost the same formula.

title: Choosing priors
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why isn’t a flat prior on a probability “uninformative” in an absolute sense?

Because it’s improper
Because it isn’t flat on other scales, such as the log-odds, so it still says something
Because it favors 0.5


Flatness depends on the parameterization. The Jeffreys prior is one way to get answers that don’t.



2. What is a prior predictive check?

Comparing the posterior with the data
Simulating data from the prior, before seeing your own, to check that the prior predicts plausible data
Testing whether the prior is normal


If a prior predicts yields of 3,000%, it doesn’t express what you know.



3. What does a weakly informative prior do?

It expresses a precise belief from earlier data
It rules out implausible values without claiming to know the answer
It’s always flat


For example, a normal prior with mean 80% and SD 8% for a yield: wide, but no impossible values to speak of.



4. Four reasonable priors give posterior 95% upper bounds from 2% to 11%. What should you report?

The one closest to the answer you wanted
The average of the four
That the conclusion depends on the prior, what each prior assumes, and what data would settle it


That’s the point of a sensitivity analysis: it shows how much the data alone can tell you.



5. You use an improper prior, such as Beta(0, 0). What must you check?

That the prior integrates to 1
That the posterior is proper, integrating to a finite value
Nothing, improper priors are always fine


With zero events, the Beta(0, 0) prior gives a Beta(0, n) posterior, which isn’t a proper distribution.



6. What’s the advantage of a mixture prior, such as 70% vendor data and 30% flat?

It always gives narrower intervals
If the data conflict with the vendor’s information, the posterior shifts weight away from it
It removes the need for a likelihood


A robust prior lets the data decide whether outside information applies.

title: Choosing priors
text:
Wrap-up
You can now choose priors with your eyes open. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Noninformative priors aren’t unique: with 0 leaks in 25 tests, the flat prior gives a mean of 3.7% and the Jeffreys prior 1.9%.
Flat depends on the scale: a normal prior with SD 10 on the log-odds puts 65% of its weight below 1% or above 99%.
Prior predictive checks: the “vague” yield priors predicted 91% impossible yields, the weakly informative ones 3%.
Informative priors carry real knowledge, such as the vendor’s tests, but only if it applies.
Sensitivity analysis: the gasket meets the 5% rule only with the vendor’s prior. That’s the finding to report.
Robust mixture priors trust outside information when the data agree with it, and drop it when they don’t.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)






Plot the four priors and their posteriors. For the gasket’s four priors, plot each prior and its posterior side by side with facet_wrap(). Which posteriors look almost alike, and which stand out?
How many tests? For each of the four priors, find the smallest number of tests without a leak that puts the 95% upper bound below 5%.
A prior predictive check you can see. For the yield model’s weakly informative priors, simulate 20 datasets of 40 batches each (yields with a residual SD of 3), and plot each with geom_point() in small multiples. Do they look like real plant data?
Reparameterize. Draw 100,000 values from the flat Beta(1, 1), convert them to log-odds with qlogis(), and plot their histogram. Then do the same for Beta(0.5, 0.5). What does each “noninformative” prior say about the log-odds?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Noninformative prior

A prior meant to add as little information as possible, such as a flat or Jeffreys prior. No prior is noninformative on every scale.

Jeffreys prior

A prior proportional to the square root of the Fisher information. It gives the same answers however the model is parameterized. For a binomial probability, it’s Beta(½, ½).

Improper prior

A “prior” that doesn’t integrate to a finite value, such as a flat prior on the whole real line. It’s acceptable only if the posterior is proper.

Informative prior

A prior that carries real knowledge, for example from earlier studies.

Weakly informative prior

A prior that rules out implausible values without claiming to know the answer.

Prior predictive check

Simulating data from the prior to see whether it predicts plausible data.

Sensitivity analysis

Repeating the analysis with different reasonable priors, and reporting how much the conclusions change.

Mixture prior

A weighted combination of priors, such as outside information and a vague prior. The posterior shifts its weight toward the part that agrees with the data.











NoteWant to read more?






Alicia Johnson, Miles Ott and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, chapter 4, “Balance and sequentiality in Bayesian analyses”, on how different priors meet the same data.
The Stan Development Team, “Prior choice recommendations”, a living page of practical advice on weakly informative priors, from the people who use them most.
Jonah Gabry, Daniel Simpson, Aki Vehtari, Michael Betancourt and Andrew Gelman, “Visualization in Bayesian workflow”, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society A (2019). The paper that made prior predictive checks routine, with a vivid example of a vague prior predicting absurd data.
Andrew Gelman and others, Bayesian Data Analysis (3rd edition), section 2.8, “Noninformative prior distributions”, and section 2.9, “Weakly informative prior distributions”.

title: Bayesian thinking
text:
Module 5 · Lesson 1 of 13 Week 76 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The plant has a new recipe. It runs the reaction 15 °C cooler, which saves steam, and the development team thinks it also makes fewer off-spec batches. The old recipe ran off spec in 38 of its last 480 batches, 7.9%. The new one has now been trialled on 30 batches, and 2 were off spec, 6.7%.
So is the new recipe better? A classical test says: with only 30 batches, you can’t tell. Its 95% confidence interval for the off-spec rate runs from 0.8% to 22%, and the plant manager can’t do much with that. What she’d like is an answer to the question she actually has: how probable is it that the new recipe is better?
That’s a question about the probability of a parameter, and classical statistics doesn’t allow it: the rate is a fixed number, not a random one. Bayesian statistics does. It uses probability for anything you’re uncertain about, including parameters. You saw the machinery in Module 4: the posterior distribution, sampled by MCMC. This module is about the ideas behind it, and how to use them well.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Bayesian thinking
text:
Probability as uncertainty
There are two ways to read “the probability is 30%”. The frequentist reading is about repetition: in a long run of identical trials, 30% would turn out that way. The Bayesian reading is about knowledge: given what you know, you’d bet on it at odds of 30 to 70. The second reading works even for one-off things, like “the new recipe’s off-spec rate is below 7.9%”, which isn’t a repeatable trial at all.
The rule for updating knowledge is Bayes’ theorem. For a hypothesis H and evidence E,

P(H \mid E) = \frac{P(E \mid H)\, P(H)}{P(E)}, \qquad P(E) = P(E \mid H)\,P(H) + P(E \mid \text{not } H)\,P(\text{not } H).

Here’s a classic case. An online analyzer watches the product for a contaminant. About 2% of batches are contaminated. The analyzer catches 95% of them (its sensitivity), and it raises a false alarm on 5% of clean batches.












Your turn. The alarm goes off. What’s the probability that the batch is really contaminated?









The second part of the denominator is P(\text{alarm} \mid \text{clean})\,P(\text{clean}), so it uses false_alarm.


prior <- 0.02                   # P(contaminated)
sens <- 0.95                    # P(alarm | contaminated)
false_alarm <- 0.05             # P(alarm | clean)
prior * sens / (prior * sens + (1 - prior) * false_alarm)
Only 28%. Most alarms are false, because clean batches are so much more common: out of 1,000 batches, 19 are contaminated and caught, but 49 clean ones also raise the alarm. The 2% you knew before the alarm, the prior probability, matters as much as the analyzer’s accuracy. People who ignore it make the base-rate fallacy, and it’s one of the most common mistakes in reasoning about evidence.




Your turn. The plant adds a second, independent analyzer with the same accuracy. Both alarm. Now what’s the probability? (With independent analyzers, the chance of two alarms is the product of the chances.)









Two false alarms happen with probability false_alarm^2.


prior <- 0.02
sens <- 0.95
false_alarm <- 0.05
prior * sens^2 / (prior * sens^2 + (1 - prior) * false_alarm^2)
88%. You’d get the same answer by updating twice: the 28% after the first alarm becomes the prior for the second. Yesterday’s posterior is today’s prior. That’s how Bayesian learning works, and you’ll see it again with the recipe.

title: Bayesian thinking
text:
Prior, likelihood and posterior
Now the recipe. The unknown is \theta, the new recipe’s off-spec rate. Every Bayesian analysis has three parts:

The prior p(\theta): what you believed about \theta before the trial.
The likelihood p(\text{data} \mid \theta): how probable the data are for each value of \theta. For 2 off-spec batches out of 30, it’s the binomial probability, dbinom(2, 30, theta).
The posterior p(\theta \mid \text{data}): what you believe afterwards. By Bayes’ theorem, it’s proportional to the prior times the likelihood.


p(\theta \mid \text{data}) \;\propto\; p(\text{data} \mid \theta)\; p(\theta)

To start simply, suppose the development team had narrowed it to three possibilities: the new recipe’s rate is 3% (much better), 8% (the same as the old one) or 15% (worse), and they thought each equally likely.
Your turn. Find the posterior probability of each.









Divide by the sum of prior * lik, so that the posterior probabilities add up to 1.


theta <- c(0.03, 0.08, 0.15)
prior <- c(1, 1, 1) / 3
lik <- dbinom(2, 30, theta)                      # P(2 off spec out of 30 | theta)
prior * lik / sum(prior * lik)
31% for “much better”, 50% for “the same” and 19% for “worse”. The trial moved the team’s beliefs, but not far: 30 batches is a small trial. The sum in the denominator is P(\text{data}), the same for all three hypotheses. Its only job is to make the posterior add up to 1.

title: Bayesian thinking
text:
Grid approximation
Of course, the rate isn’t limited to three values. It could be anything from 0 to 1. The simplest way to handle that is a grid: try 1,001 values, \theta = 0, 0.001, 0.002, \ldots, 1, and do exactly what you did for three. With a flat prior, every rate equally plausible, the posterior is the likelihood, scaled to sum to 1.
Your turn. The setup code has the grid. Compute the posterior on it, then its mean and its mode, the most probable value.









Same as before: divide by sum(prior * lik).


prior <- rep(1, length(grid))                                   # flat
lik <- dbinom(sum(trial$off_spec), nrow(trial), grid)
post <- prior * lik / sum(prior * lik)
c(mean = sum(grid * post), mode = grid[which.max(post)])
The most probable rate is 6.7%, the trial’s own rate, 2 out of 30. The posterior mean is higher, 9.4%, because the posterior has a long right tail: rates of 15% or 20% are still possible after only 30 batches, but rates below 0 aren’t. With a flat prior, the mode is always the maximum likelihood estimate.




Here’s the posterior. With a flat prior, it has the same shape as the likelihood:

ggplot(data.frame(theta = grid, post = post)[grid <= 0.3, ], aes(x = theta, y = post)) +
  geom_area(data = function(d) d[d$theta < 38 / 480, ], fill = "#F4C0D1") +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 38 / 480, linetype = "dashed", color = "#3A1F35") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.083, y = max(post) * 1.02, label = "old recipe, 7.9%", hjust = 0, size = 3.6, color = "#3A1F35") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "New recipe's off-spec rate", y = "Posterior probability") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The shaded area is the probability that the new recipe is better than the old one.
Your turn. Compute it: add up the posterior probabilities of all the rates below the old recipe’s, 38/480.









The old recipe’s rate is 38 / 480.


lik <- dbinom(sum(trial$off_spec), nrow(trial), grid)
post <- lik / sum(lik)                                          # the flat-prior posterior
sum(post[grid < 38 / 480])
45%. That’s the direct answer to the plant manager’s question: given this trial and a flat prior, there’s a 45% probability that the new recipe makes fewer off-spec batches than the old one. It’s a coin toss. A good outcome from 30 batches, but not yet evidence of an improvement. (For now, we treat the old rate as known exactly. Challenge 2 drops that.)

title: Bayesian thinking
text:
The prior matters
A flat prior says that an off-spec rate of 90% was as plausible as 5% before the trial. Nobody at the plant believed that. The development team’s lab work suggested the new recipe would run off spec about 5% of the time, perhaps less, rarely more than 15%. One way to write that down is an exponential prior with mean 5%: highest at 0, and falling away smoothly.
Your turn. Use the prior dexp(grid, rate = 20) (an exponential with mean 1/20 = 5%), and recompute the posterior mean and the probability of an improvement.









The posterior is proportional to prior * lik.


prior <- dexp(grid, rate = 20)
lik <- dbinom(sum(trial$off_spec), nrow(trial), grid)
post <- prior * lik / sum(prior * lik)
c(mean = sum(grid * post), p_better = sum(post[grid < 38 / 480]))
With the team’s prior, the posterior mean is 5.9%, and the probability of an improvement is 76%. The same 30 batches, a different conclusion, because the team brought in what it knew from the lab. Is that cheating? Not if the prior is stated openly, was set before the data came in, and is backed by real knowledge. But a skeptical plant manager could reasonably say the lab results were optimistic. Lesson 3 is about choosing priors, and about checking how much the conclusions depend on them.

title: Bayesian thinking
text:
Updating as the data arrive
The trial didn’t happen all at once. The first 15 batches ran in March, with 1 off spec, and the second 15 in April, with another 1. Suppose the team had computed the posterior after March. In April, that posterior is the prior.
Your turn. Update the flat prior with the first 15 batches, then update that posterior with the second 15. Compare the result with the posterior from all 30 at once.









April’s prior is post_march.


march <- trial$off_spec[1:15]
april <- trial$off_spec[16:30]
post_march <- dbinom(sum(march), 15, grid)                           # flat prior times the likelihood
post_march <- post_march / sum(post_march)
post_april <- post_march * dbinom(sum(april), 15, grid)              # March's posterior is April's prior
post_april <- post_april / sum(post_april)
post_all <- dbinom(2, 30, grid) / sum(dbinom(2, 30, grid))
c(mean_after_march = sum(grid * post_march), biggest_difference = max(abs(post_april - post_all)))
After March, the posterior mean was 11.8%. After April, the posterior is the same as the one from all 30 batches at once, to 17 decimal places. It makes no difference whether you learn in one step or in two, or batch by batch. That’s a property classical tests don’t have: a Bayesian analysis can be updated whenever new data arrive, without any penalty for “peeking”.

title: Bayesian thinking
text:
Predicting the next batches
The posterior also predicts. The probability that the next batch is off spec is the off-spec rate averaged over the posterior, \sum_\theta \theta\, p(\theta \mid \text{data}): the posterior mean. The probability that the next 10 batches are all on spec averages (1 - \theta)^{10} in the same way. This is the posterior predictive distribution, and it carries all the uncertainty about \theta into the prediction.
Your turn. With the flat-prior posterior, find both probabilities.









Ten batches in a row on spec: (1 - grid)^10.


post <- dbinom(2, 30, grid) / sum(dbinom(2, 30, grid))
c(next_off_spec = sum(grid * post), next_10_on_spec = sum(post * (1 - grid)^10))
A 9.4% chance that the next batch is off spec, and a 42% chance that the next 10 are all fine. If you’d plugged in the single best estimate, 6.7%, you’d have said (1 - 0.067)^{10} = 50\%: too confident, because it ignores the chance that the true rate is higher. Prediction intervals in Module 2 allowed for the same thing.

title: Bayesian thinking
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Draws from a grid. Most of this module works with posterior draws, as Module 4 did. You can get them from a grid too: sample grid values with the posterior probabilities as weights. Draw 10,000, and use them for the posterior mean and a 95% credible interval, the middle 95% of the draws.









The weights are the posterior probabilities, post.


post <- dbinom(2, 30, grid) / sum(dbinom(2, 30, grid))
set.seed(5011)
draws <- sample(grid, 10000, replace = TRUE, prob = post)
c(mean = mean(draws), quantile(draws, c(0.025, 0.975)))
A mean of 9.4%, as before, and a 95% credible interval from 2.1% to 21.6%: given the trial and a flat prior, there’s a 95% probability that the new recipe’s off-spec rate is in that range. From draws, any summary is one line of R.




Challenge 2 · The old recipe was uncertain too. The old recipe’s 7.9% came from 480 batches, so it isn’t known exactly either. Give it its own flat-prior posterior on the grid, draw 10,000 values from each posterior, and find the probability that the new rate is below the old one.









The old recipe’s draws come from post_old.


post_new <- dbinom(2, 30, grid) / sum(dbinom(2, 30, grid))
post_old <- dbinom(38, 480, grid) / sum(dbinom(38, 480, grid))
set.seed(5012)
new <- sample(grid, 10000, replace = TRUE, prob = post_new)
old <- sample(grid, 10000, replace = TRUE, prob = post_old)
c(p_new_better = mean(new < old), quantile(old, c(0.025, 0.975)))
46%, almost the same as the 45% before. The old rate’s 95% credible interval is narrow, 5.9% to 10.7%, so its uncertainty hardly matters next to the new recipe’s. That’s the usual pattern: the smaller study dominates the uncertainty in a comparison. To learn more, the plant needs more batches of the new recipe.

title: Bayesian thinking
text:
Quick quiz

1. In the Bayesian view, what does “a 76% probability that the new recipe is better” describe?

How often the new recipe would be better in repeated trials
How strongly the evidence and the prior support the claim, as a degree of belief
The p-value of a test


Bayesian probability describes uncertainty about anything, including one-off claims about parameters.



2. A test for a rare condition (1 in 1,000) is 99% accurate both ways. Someone tests positive. What’s the probability that they have the condition?

99%
About 50%
About 9%


Out of 100,000 people, 99 of the 100 with the condition test positive, but so do 999 of the 99,900 without it. So 99/(99 + 999) = 9\%. That’s the base-rate fallacy again.



3. What is the posterior proportional to?

The prior plus the likelihood
The prior times the likelihood
The likelihood divided by the prior


p(\theta \mid \text{data}) \propto p(\text{data} \mid \theta)\, p(\theta). The constant of proportionality, 1/p(\text{data}), just makes it sum to 1.



4. With a flat prior, what is the mode of the posterior?

The maximum likelihood estimate
The posterior mean
Always 0.5


A flat prior makes the posterior proportional to the likelihood, so they peak at the same place.



5. You analyze March’s data, then use the posterior as the prior for April’s. How does the result compare with analyzing March and April together?

It’s less accurate, because of the extra step
It’s identical
It depends on which month had more data


Multiplying by March’s likelihood and then by April’s is the same as multiplying by both at once.



6. Why is the posterior predictive probability that the next 10 batches are on spec (42%) lower than (1 - 0.067)^{10} = 50\%?

Because of rounding
Because it averages over the uncertainty in the rate, including the chance that the rate is higher
Because the prior was flat


Plugging in a single estimate ignores the uncertainty in it, and predictions made that way are too confident.

title: Bayesian thinking
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve done your first Bayesian analyses. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Probability as uncertainty: Bayesian probability measures what you know, so it can describe parameters and one-off claims.
Bayes’ theorem: a 95%-sensitive analyzer’s alarm means only a 28% chance of contamination when the base rate is 2%. Two alarms make it 88%.
Prior × likelihood ∝ posterior: the posterior is the prior, reweighted by how well each value of the parameter explains the data.
Grid approximation: with a flat prior, the new recipe’s off-spec rate has a posterior mean of 9.4% and a 45% probability of being below the old recipe’s 7.9%. With the team’s prior, it’s 76%.
Updating: analyzing the data in two steps gives exactly the same posterior as one.
Prediction: the posterior predictive probability that the next 10 batches are all on spec is 42%, not the 50% a plug-in estimate gives.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download recipe_trial.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Watch the posterior learn. Compute the flat-prior posterior after 5, 10, 15, …, 30 batches, and plot them all on one chart, with a color for each. How does the posterior change shape as the data come in?
A coarser grid. Repeat the grid analysis with steps of 0.05 instead of 0.001. How much do the posterior mean and the probability of an improvement change? How coarse can the grid be before the answers are wrong in the second digit?
Two parameters on a grid. Suppose 40 temperature readings are normal with an unknown mean and SD. Make a grid of 200 means by 200 SDs with expand.grid(), compute the log-likelihood at each point, and plot the posterior with geom_raster(). A grid with k points per parameter has k^d points in d dimensions. How many would a model with 10 parameters need?
Your own base-rate problem. Find a real case at work, or in the news, where a test or an alarm has a low base rate. What’s the probability that a positive result is real?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Bayesian probability

Probability as a degree of belief, given what you know. It can describe parameters and one-off events.

Bayes’ theorem

P(H \mid E) = P(E \mid H)\,P(H)/P(E): how to update the probability of a hypothesis with evidence.

Base-rate fallacy

Ignoring the prior probability when interpreting evidence, for example taking an alarm from an accurate analyzer at face value when the condition is rare.

Prior distribution

What you believe about a parameter before seeing the data.

Likelihood

The probability of the observed data for each value of the parameter.

Posterior distribution

What you believe about the parameter after seeing the data, proportional to the prior times the likelihood.

Grid approximation

Computing the posterior at a grid of parameter values, and normalizing it to sum to 1.

Posterior predictive distribution

The distribution of future data, averaged over the posterior uncertainty in the parameters.











NoteWant to read more?






Alicia Johnson, Miles Ott and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, chapters 1, “The big (Bayesian) picture” and 2, “Bayes’ rule”. The friendliest introduction there is, with R. Free online.
Richard McElreath, Statistical Rethinking lectures. Lecture 2, “The Garden of Forking Data”, builds grid approximation from counting, with globe tossing instead of batches.
Andrew Gelman and others, Bayesian Data Analysis (3rd edition), chapter 1. The graduate reference for this module, free as a PDF on the book’s site. Section 1.5 is about the meaning of probability.

title: Smoothing methods
text:
Module 4 · Lesson 13 of 14 Week 73 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Most of this course’s models have a shape decided in advance: a straight line, a normal distribution, a mixture of two normals. Smoothing lets the data decide the shape. You give up a formula, and in exchange you see the data’s real structure: two humps where a normal distribution would show one, or a peak where a polynomial would put a wiggle.
This lesson has two problems. The first is Lesson 10’s crystal sizes, without assuming that they’re a mixture of normals. The second is new. The safety lab heated a sample of the reaction mixture in a differential scanning calorimeter (DSC), which measures the heat the sample releases as its temperature rises at a steady rate. The scan shows an exotherm, a peak of released heat, and its temperature matters for safety: it says where a runaway could start. But the scan is noisy:
ggplot(dsc, aes(x = temp_C, y = heat_flow_Wg)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, color = "#C2416C", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Heat flow (W/g)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
The highest single reading is at 213.0 °C, but with noise this big, the highest point says little about where the true peak is. A smooth curve through the points says much more.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Smoothing methods
text:
Kernel density estimation
A histogram depends on where its bins start and how wide they are. A kernel density estimate (KDE) avoids the bins: it places a small bump, the kernel, on every data point, and adds them up. With a normal kernel of standard deviation h, the bandwidth,

\hat{f}(x) = \frac{1}{n h} \sum_{i=1}^n \phi\!\left(\frac{x - x_i}{h}\right),

where \phi is the standard normal density. Each bump has area 1/n, so the total area is 1. The bandwidth decides everything: a small h gives a spiky estimate that follows every quirk of the sample, and a large h blurs real features away.










Your turn. Write the kernel density estimate as a function, and evaluate it at 85, 150 and 215 µm with a bandwidth of 15 µm.









The formula divides by nh. mean() already divides by n, so divide by h.


kde <- function(x0, h) mean(dnorm((x0 - x) / h)) / h
c(at_85 = kde(85, 15), at_150 = kde(150, 15), at_215 = kde(215, 15))
0.0065 at both 85 and 215 µm, the two humps, and 0.0019 at 150 µm, in the valley between them. R’s density(x, bw = 15) gives the same values to four digits (it uses a fast approximation on a grid). With 250 crystals, the estimate at 150 µm says that about 0.19% of crystals per micrometer are near 150 µm.

title: Smoothing methods
text:
Choosing the bandwidth
density() chooses a bandwidth automatically, with Silverman’s rule of thumb, bw.nrd0(), which would be the best choice if the data were normal. For data with two humps, it oversmooths. The Sheather-Jones method, bw.SJ(), estimates the curvature of the density from the data instead, and usually does better.
Your turn. Compare the two bandwidths, and count the peaks of each density estimate. The setup code has n_modes(h), which counts the peaks for a bandwidth h.









The Sheather-Jones bandwidth is bw.SJ(x).


bws <- c(silverman = bw.nrd0(x), sheather_jones = bw.SJ(x))
rbind(bandwidth = bws, peaks = sapply(bws, n_modes))
Silverman’s rule picks 21.3 µm, and Sheather-Jones 10.7 µm, half as wide. Both find the two populations, but Silverman’s estimate flattens the fines’ peak and fills in the valley. Sheather-Jones finds a third, tiny peak at 316 µm: the two largest crystals, far out in the tail. Is that a real third population, or noise? Two crystals can’t tell you. The number of peaks depends on the bandwidth, so be careful about reading too much into small ones.





dens <- do.call(rbind, lapply(list(c("h = 4 (too small)", 4), c("Sheather-Jones, h = 10.7", bw.SJ(x)), c("Silverman, h = 21.3", bw.nrd0(x))), function(b) {
  d <- density(x, bw = as.numeric(b[2]), n = 1024, from = 0, to = 380)
  data.frame(size = d$x, density = d$y, rule = b[1])
}))
dens$rule <- factor(dens$rule, levels = c("h = 4 (too small)", "Sheather-Jones, h = 10.7", "Silverman, h = 21.3"))
ggplot(dens, aes(x = size, y = density, color = rule)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_rug(data = crystals, aes(x = size_um), inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.4, color = "#3A1F35") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("grey60", "#C2416C", "#2a78d6"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Crystal size (µm)", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Smoothing methods
text:
Kernel regression
The same idea smooths a curve through points. To estimate the heat flow at a temperature x_0, average the readings near x_0, giving more weight to the closer ones. With normal kernel weights w_i = \phi\big((x_0 - x_i)/h\big), that’s the Nadaraya-Watson estimator:

\hat{m}(x_0) = \frac{\sum_i w_i\, y_i}{\sum_i w_i}.

It’s a weighted mean that slides along the temperature axis. The bandwidth h is now in °C, and says how far from x_0 the readings still count.
Your turn. Write the estimator, compute the smooth curve on the setup code’s fine grid of temperatures with h = 2 °C, and find the peak.









Weight the heat-flow readings, heat.


nw <- function(x0, h) {
  w <- dnorm((x0 - temp) / h)
  sum(w * heat) / sum(w)
}
smooth <- sapply(grid, nw, h = 2)
c(peak_temp = grid[which.max(smooth)], peak_height = max(smooth))
The smoothed peak is at 214.2 °C, with a height of 0.929 W/g. The noisy maximum was at 213.0 °C. (The scan was simulated with its true peak at 214.0 °C, so the smoother got within 0.2 degrees.) Try h = 5: the peak stays near 214 °C, but its height drops to 0.81, because a wide kernel averages the peak with its lower shoulders. Oversmoothing flattens peaks.

title: Smoothing methods
text:
Loess
Kernel regression fits a weighted constant near each point. Loess (local regression) fits a weighted line or quadratic instead, which follows slopes and peaks better, especially near the ends of the data. Its bandwidth is the span: the fraction of the data used for each local fit. It’s what geom_smooth() draws by default for fewer than 1,000 points.
Your turn. Fit a loess curve with a span of 0.1 (each local fit uses the nearest 10% of the readings), and find the peak.









span = 0.1.


fit <- loess(heat_flow_Wg ~ temp_C, data = dsc, span = 0.1)
curve <- predict(fit, data.frame(temp_C = grid))
c(peak_temp = grid[which.max(curve)], peak_height = max(curve))
A peak at 214.4 °C, 0.954 W/g high: higher than the kernel regression’s, because the local quadratics follow the peak’s curvature instead of averaging across it. The default span, 0.75, would be a disaster here: each local fit would use three quarters of the scan, and the peak would flatten to 0.49 W/g, at 218 °C.

title: Smoothing methods
text:
Smoothing splines
A smoothing spline takes a different route. It looks for the function f that balances fitting the data against being smooth:

\sum_i \big(y_i - f(x_i)\big)^2 + \lambda \int f''(x)^2\, dx,

where f'' is the second derivative, which measures wiggliness. With \lambda = 0, the curve passes through every point. With \lambda \to \infty, it becomes a straight line. The answer is always a cubic spline (cubic polynomials joined smoothly at the data points), and smooth.spline() chooses \lambda by generalized cross-validation (GCV), a fast approximation to leave-one-out cross-validation. Its smoothness is reported as the equivalent degrees of freedom: 2 for a straight line, more for wigglier curves.
Your turn. Fit a smoothing spline with the GCV choice, and find its degrees of freedom and its peak.









The responses are the heat-flow readings, heat.


fit <- smooth.spline(temp, heat)
curve <- predict(fit, grid)$y
c(df = fit$df, peak_temp = grid[which.max(curve)], peak_height = max(curve))
GCV chose 27.4 equivalent degrees of freedom, and the peak is at 214.1 °C, 0.939 W/g high. Three different smoothers, three peak temperatures between 214.1 and 214.4 °C: the data say “about 214 °C” clearly, whatever the method. The raw maximum, 213.0 °C, was a degree off.

title: Smoothing methods
text:
Choosing the bandwidth by cross-validation
The bandwidth trades bias against variance. A wide kernel averages many readings, so the curve has little noise (low variance), but it flattens real features (high bias). A narrow kernel follows the features, but also the noise. Lesson 7’s cross-validation finds the balance: predict each reading from all the others, and choose the bandwidth that predicts best.
For kernel regression, leave-one-out is quick. Put all the kernel weights in a matrix K, with K_{ij} = \phi\big((x_i - x_j)/h\big). Setting its diagonal to 0 removes each reading from its own prediction, and then the leave-one-out predictions are the row-weighted averages, all at once.
Your turn. Compute the leave-one-out error for bandwidths from 0.5 to 10 °C.









Set the diagonal to 0.


cv_error <- function(h) {
  K <- dnorm(outer(temp, temp, "-") / h)     # all the kernel weights
  diag(K) <- 0                                 # leave each reading out of its own prediction
  pred <- drop(K %*% heat) / rowSums(K)
  mean((heat - pred)^2)
}
