hs <- c(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10)
round(sapply(hs, cv_error), 5)
The error is smallest at h = 2 °C (0.00294), rises slowly for smaller bandwidths, where the noise gets through, and quickly for larger ones, where the peak gets flattened. optimize(cv_error, c(0.5, 10)) puts the best bandwidth at 1.9 °C. The minimum error, 0.0029, is a typical prediction error of \sqrt{0.0029} = 0.054 W/g, about the size of the instrument’s noise.




Here’s the scan with the cross-validated kernel regression, and an oversmoothed loess for contrast:

smooth2 <- sapply(grid, nw, h = 2)
lo4 <- predict(loess(heat_flow_Wg ~ temp_C, data = dsc, span = 0.4), data.frame(temp_C = grid))
curves <- rbind(data.frame(temp = grid, heat = smooth2, method = "kernel regression, h = 2 °C"),
                data.frame(temp = grid, heat = lo4, method = "loess, span 0.4 (too smooth)"))
ggplot(dsc, aes(x = temp_C, y = heat_flow_Wg)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.7, color = "grey70") +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(x = temp, y = heat, color = method), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#C2416C", "#2a78d6"), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(150, 280)) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Heat flow (W/g)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")














NoteGo deeper: the curse of dimensionality





Smoothing works beautifully in one dimension, and reasonably in two or three. In ten, it fails. To keep a “neighborhood” containing 10% of uniformly spread data in d dimensions, its side must cover a fraction 0.1^{1/d} of each variable’s range: 10% in one dimension, 32% in two, and 79% in ten. The neighborhoods stop being local, and the estimates stop being smooth versions of the data. That’s the curse of dimensionality, and it’s why many-variable problems need models with structure, such as additive models, which smooth one variable at a time, or the trees and other methods of Modules 7 and 8.

title: Smoothing methods
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · How precise is the peak temperature? Bootstrap it, with Lesson 6’s residual resampling: compute the smooth curve at the readings’ temperatures, add resampled residuals to make 1,000 new scans, smooth each one, and find its peak. To make it fast, the code computes the kernel weights for every grid point once, as a matrix W with rows that sum to 1, so that smoothing a scan is a single matrix product.









Resample the residuals, res.


h <- 2
W <- dnorm(outer(grid, temp, "-") / h); W <- W / rowSums(W)          # smoothing weights on the grid
K <- dnorm(outer(temp, temp, "-") / h); K <- K / rowSums(K)          # and at the readings
fitted_heat <- drop(K %*% heat)
res <- heat - fitted_heat
set.seed(4131)
peaks <- replicate(1000, {
  new_scan <- fitted_heat + sample(res, replace = TRUE)
  grid[which.max(W %*% new_scan)]
})
c(peak = grid[which.max(W %*% heat)], se = sd(peaks), quantile(peaks, c(0.025, 0.975)))
The peak is at 214.2 °C, with a bootstrap standard error of 0.33 °C and a 95% interval from 213.4 to 214.7 °C. For the safety report: the exotherm peaks at 214.2 \pm 0.7 °C. (This interval ignores the smoother’s bias, which is small here because the bandwidth is narrow compared with the peak’s width.)




Challenge 2 · How smooth is too smooth? The height of the peak matters too: it’s related to how violently the reaction releases heat. Fit smoothing splines with 8, 15, 27.4 (GCV’s choice) and 80 degrees of freedom, and compare their peak heights. The true peak height of this simulated scan is 0.956 W/g.









Inside the function, the degrees of freedom are d.


sapply(c(8, 15, 27.4, 80), function(d) {
  fit <- smooth.spline(temp, heat, df = d)
  max(predict(fit, grid)$y)
})
0.65, 0.86, 0.94 and 0.97 W/g. With 8 degrees of freedom, the spline is too stiff to bend sharply, and it shaves a third off the peak. GCV’s 27.4 gets within 2% of the true 0.956. With 80, the curve is noisy, and its maximum is pushed up by the noise, a little above the truth. Oversmoothing biases peaks down, and undersmoothing makes them noisy and, if anything, too high.

title: Smoothing methods
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does a kernel density estimate put on each data point?

A bar of a histogram
A small bump, the kernel, of area 1/n
A normal distribution fitted to all the data


The estimate is the sum of all the bumps.



2. What happens with a very small bandwidth?

The estimate becomes a straight line
The estimate becomes spiky, following the noise of the sample
The estimate becomes normal


Small bandwidths mean low bias and high variance. Large ones, the reverse.



3. Why does Silverman’s rule oversmooth the crystal sizes?

Because it ignores the sample size
Because it’s the best bandwidth for normal data, and these data have two humps
Because it uses the wrong kernel


Sheather-Jones adapts to the data’s curvature and picks a narrower bandwidth here.



4. What’s the difference between kernel regression and loess?

Loess uses no weights
Kernel regression fits a weighted constant near each point, and loess fits a weighted line or quadratic
Kernel regression only works for densities


Local lines or quadratics follow slopes and peaks better.



5. In a smoothing spline, what does a larger \lambda do?

It makes the curve wigglier
It penalizes curvature more, making the curve smoother, down to a straight line
It removes outliers


\lambda trades the fit to the data against the curve’s roughness.



6. How does leave-one-out cross-validation choose a bandwidth?

By choosing the bandwidth with the smallest residuals
By predicting each point from all the others, and choosing the bandwidth that predicts best
By choosing the middle of the range


The smallest residuals always come from the smallest bandwidth, which just follows the noise.

title: Smoothing methods
text:
Wrap-up
You can now let the data choose the shape of a curve. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Kernel density estimates add a bump for every data point. The bandwidth decides what you see: Silverman’s 21.3 µm flattens the crystals’ fines, and Sheather-Jones’s 10.7 µm shows both populations clearly.
Kernel regression is a sliding weighted mean. Loess fits local lines or quadratics, and smoothing splines balance the fit against the curvature.
The DSC exotherm peaks at about 214 °C by every method (214.1 to 214.4), where the noisiest point said 213.0.
The bias-variance trade-off: too wide and peaks flatten (a spline with 8 degrees of freedom lost a third of the peak), too narrow and the noise gets through.
Cross-validation chose a bandwidth of about 2 °C, and the bootstrap gave the peak temperature as 214.2 \pm 0.7 °C.
Smoothing struggles in many dimensions, where neighborhoods stop being local.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download crystal_sizes.csv and dsc_scan.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Other kernels. density() has a kernel argument: try "epanechnikov", "rectangular" and "triangular" with the Sheather-Jones bandwidth. Does the kernel’s shape matter as much as its width?
Onset temperature. Safety reports often use the exotherm’s onset: the temperature where the heat flow first rises clearly above the baseline. Fit a straight line to the baseline between 120 and 170 °C, and find where the smoothed curve first exceeds it by 0.05 W/g. How sensitive is the onset to the bandwidth?
The derivative. The steepest rise of the exotherm is where the derivative of the smooth curve is largest. predict(fit, grid, deriv = 1) gives the derivative of a smoothing spline. Find the temperature of the steepest rise.
geom_smooth. Plot the scan with geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.1) and with the default span. Then try geom_smooth(method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x, k = 40)), which uses a penalized spline from the mgcv package (it comes with R). Which one would you show in a safety report?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Smoothing

Estimating a curve or a density from data without assuming a fixed functional form.

Kernel density estimate

A density estimate made by placing a kernel (a small bump) on every data point and adding them up.

Bandwidth

The width of the kernel, which controls how smooth the estimate is.

Kernel regression

A smooth curve made of weighted local averages: the Nadaraya-Watson estimator.

Loess

Local regression: a smooth curve made of weighted local lines or quadratics, with a span that controls its smoothness.

Smoothing spline

The curve that minimizes the residual sum of squares plus a penalty \lambda on its curvature.

Bias-variance trade-off

Smoother estimates have less noise but more distortion of real features, and rougher ones the reverse.

Curse of dimensionality

The difficulty of smoothing in many dimensions, where any neighborhood holding enough data is no longer local.











NoteWant to read more?






Gareth James and others, An Introduction to Statistical Learning, chapter 7, “Moving beyond linearity”. Smoothing splines, local regression and generalized additive models, with R labs.
Larry Wasserman, All of Nonparametric Statistics (Springer, 2006), chapters 5 and 6. Kernel regression, density estimation, bandwidth choice and the bias-variance trade-off, concisely. Not free.
R’s help pages for density(), bw.SJ(), loess() and smooth.spline(). Their arguments and the methods behind them.

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
text:
Module 4 · Lesson 11 of 14 Week 71 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 9 estimated the Weibull shape and scale of the plant’s pumps by maximum likelihood: the single best pair of values, with a standard error from the curvature. Bayesian statistics, the subject of Module 5, asks a different question: given the data, how probable is each value of the parameters? The answer is the posterior distribution, and by Bayes’ theorem it’s
p(\theta \mid \text{data}) = \frac{p(\text{data} \mid \theta)\; p(\theta)}{p(\text{data})} \;\propto\; \text{likelihood} \times \text{prior}.
The likelihood and the prior are easy to compute. The denominator is an integral over every possible \theta, and for most models nobody can compute it. So the posterior is known only up to a constant. Lesson 4’s rejection sampling could work with that in one or two dimensions, but it gets hopeless as the dimension grows. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) doesn’t. It builds a random walk that wanders through the parameter space, spending time in each region in proportion to its posterior probability. Run it long enough, and its path is a sample from the posterior.
It’s one of the most important algorithms of the 20th century. It was invented by physicists in 1953 to simulate molecules (by Metropolis, the Rosenbluths and the Tellers, on one of the first computers), and it transformed statistics in the 1990s.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
text:
Markov chains
A Markov chain is a sequence of random states where the next state depends only on the current one, not on the history. Reactor R3’s state each morning is one of three: running, fouled (running, but its heat-transfer surfaces are fouling and it needs cleaning soon), or cleaning. From the maintenance logs, the chances of tomorrow’s state given today’s are the transition matrix P:



Today \ Tomorrow
running
fouled
cleaning




running
0.90
0.08
0.02


fouled
0
0.70
0.30


cleaning
0.80
0
0.20



Each row sums to 1. Whatever state it starts in, a chain like this settles into a long-run pattern: the share of days spent in each state converges to the stationary distribution \boldsymbol\pi, which satisfies \boldsymbol\pi P = \boldsymbol\pi. Once the chain’s distribution is \boldsymbol\pi, one more step leaves it unchanged.











Your turn. Simulate 10,000 days of the reactor, starting from running. Each day’s state is drawn with the probabilities in the row of yesterday’s state.









The probabilities are the row of yesterday’s state: P[state[t - 1], ].


set.seed(4111)
state <- integer(10000)
state[1] <- 1                                       # 1 = running, 2 = fouled, 3 = cleaning
for (t in 2:10000) state[t] <- sample(1:3, 1, prob = P[state[t - 1], ])
round(table(factor(state, 1:3, rownames(P))) / 10000, 4)
Over 10,000 days, the reactor was running 70.8% of the time, fouled 20.1%, and being cleaned 9.1%. A typical running spell lasted about 10 days. The days are far from independent: a running day is usually followed by another, and the chain moves through the states in long stretches. But in the long run, the shares settle down.




Your turn. Find the stationary distribution exactly. The rows of P^n (the matrix multiplied by itself n times) give the chances of each state n days later, so as n grows, every row converges to \boldsymbol\pi. Compute P^{100}.









Multiply by P each time.


Pn <- diag(3)                          # the identity matrix: P to the power 0
for (i in 1:100) Pn <- Pn %*% P
round(Pn, 4)
Every row is the same, \boldsymbol\pi = (0.7186, 0.1916, 0.0898): after 100 days, the starting state is forgotten. The simulation’s shares, 0.708, 0.201 and 0.091, were close. (You could also solve \boldsymbol\pi P = \boldsymbol\pi directly: \boldsymbol\pi is the eigenvector of P^\top with eigenvalue 1, scaled to sum to 1.) So the reactor can produce on about 91% of days, running or fouled.

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
text:
The Metropolis algorithm
MCMC runs this idea backwards. Instead of finding the stationary distribution of a given chain, it builds a chain whose stationary distribution is the one you want. The random-walk Metropolis algorithm, for a target density \pi(\theta) known up to a constant:

From the current value \theta, propose a nearby value \theta^* = \theta + \varepsilon, with \varepsilon a normal step with mean 0.
Accept it with probability \min\left(1, \pi(\theta^*)/\pi(\theta)\right). Otherwise, stay at \theta (and count \theta again).
Repeat.

Uphill moves are always accepted, and downhill moves only sometimes, so the chain spends more time where \pi is high. The unknown constant cancels in the ratio, which is the whole trick. On the log scale, the acceptance test is \log u < \log\pi(\theta^*) - \log\pi(\theta) for a uniform u, which avoids underflow (Lesson 2).






NoteGo deeper: why the chain’s stationary distribution is \pi





A chain with transition probabilities q(\theta \to \theta') has stationary distribution \pi if it satisfies detailed balance: \pi(\theta)\, q(\theta \to \theta') = \pi(\theta')\, q(\theta' \to \theta) for every pair. In words, in the long run, there’s as much flow from \theta to \theta' as back. For Metropolis, the proposal is symmetric, and the move from \theta to \theta' happens with probability proportional to \min(1, \pi(\theta')/\pi(\theta)). If \pi(\theta') < \pi(\theta), then \pi(\theta) \cdot \frac{\pi(\theta')}{\pi(\theta)} = \pi(\theta'), and \pi(\theta') \cdot 1 = \pi(\theta'): the two sides balance. The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm extends this to asymmetric proposals, by multiplying the acceptance ratio by q(\theta^* \to \theta)/q(\theta \to \theta^*).



Your turn. Try it on a target where you know the answer: the density \pi(x) \propto x^2 e^{-x} for x > 0, a gamma distribution with shape 3, whose mean is 3 and variance 3. Complete the acceptance test.









Compare the proposal with the current value.


log_target <- function(x) if (x <= 0) -Inf else 2 * log(x) - x     # log of x^2 exp(-x)
set.seed(4112)
draws <- numeric(10000)
current <- 1
accepted <- 0
for (i in 1:10000) {
  proposal <- current + rnorm(1, 0, 2)
  if (log(runif(1)) < log_target(proposal) - log_target(current)) {
    current <- proposal
    accepted <- accepted + 1
  }
  draws[i] <- current
}
c(mean = mean(draws), var = var(draws), acceptance = accepted / 10000)
A mean of 2.98 and a variance of 2.81, against the true 3 and 3, with 63% of the proposals accepted. The algorithm never used the gamma function, the normalizing constant of this density. Proposals below 0 have a log-density of -\infty, so they’re always rejected. The draws are correlated, so 10,000 of them are worth fewer independent draws, which is why the variance is a little off. You’ll measure that shortly.

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
text:
The pumps’ posterior
Now the real thing: the posterior distribution of the pumps’ shape and scale. We’ll keep Lesson 9’s log scale, \theta = (\log k, \log\lambda), and the likelihood, nll(). The prior says what the engineers believed before seeing these data: not much. The shape is probably within a factor of seven of 1 (a normal prior for \log k with mean 0 and SD 1), and the scale somewhere between eight months and 37 years (a normal prior for \log\lambda with mean 7.5, which is 1,800 days, and SD 1).
Your turn. The setup code has nll() and the prior, log_prior(). Write the log-posterior, up to its constant, and evaluate it at \theta = (0.5, 7.5).









Add the log-prior, log_prior(theta).


log_post <- function(theta) -nll(theta) + log_prior(theta)      # log-likelihood + log-prior
log_post(c(0.5, 7.5))
−226.0. The number itself means nothing, because the constant is missing. Only differences between log-posterior values matter, which is exactly what the Metropolis algorithm uses.




Your turn. Run the Metropolis algorithm in two dimensions for 10,000 steps, from \theta = (0, 7), with normal steps of SD 0.15 in each direction. The setup code’s log_post_pumps() is the log-posterior. Discard the first 1,000 draws as burn-in, the stretch where the chain is still finding its way from the starting point.









The step SD is 0.15.


set.seed(4113)
draws <- matrix(NA, 10000, 2)
current <- c(0, 7)
lp <- log_post_pumps(current)
accepted <- 0
for (i in 1:10000) {
  proposal <- current + rnorm(2, 0, 0.15)
  lp_prop <- log_post_pumps(proposal)
  if (log(runif(1)) < lp_prop - lp) { current <- proposal; lp <- lp_prop; accepted <- accepted + 1 }
  draws[i, ] <- current
}
keep <- draws[-(1:1000), ]
c(acceptance = accepted / 10000, shape = mean(exp(keep[, 1])), scale = mean(exp(keep[, 2])))
48% of the proposals were accepted. The posterior mean shape is 1.86, and the scale 1,788 days. A 95% credible interval, the middle 95% of the draws, runs from 1.26 to 2.48 for the shape. Unlike a confidence interval, it has the direct meaning people often want: given the data and the prior, there’s a 95% probability that the shape is in it. The shape is a little below the maximum likelihood estimate, 1.94, because the posterior averages over all the plausible scales, while maximum likelihood picks the single best pair. Challenge 2 shows that the prior is only a small part of the difference.




Here are the 9,000 kept draws, with Lesson 9’s maximum likelihood estimate:

set.seed(4113)
run <- metropolis(log_post, 10000, c(0, 7), 0.15)
keep <- run$draws[-(1:1000), ]
ggplot(data.frame(shape = exp(keep[, 1]), scale = exp(keep[, 2])), aes(x = shape, y = scale)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.25, color = "#C2416C") +
  annotate("point", x = 1.941, y = 1758, color = "#3A1F35", size = 3.2, shape = 4, stroke = 1.6) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.0, y = 1700, label = "maximum likelihood", hjust = 0, size = 3.6, color = "#3A1F35") +
  labs(x = "Weibull shape", y = "Weibull scale (days)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
text:
Tuning the step size
The step size matters a lot. With tiny steps, nearly every proposal is accepted, but the chain creeps along and takes forever to explore. With huge steps, almost every proposal lands in an improbable region and is rejected, so the chain sits still for long stretches. Both make the draws highly correlated, so 10,000 draws carry much less information than 10,000 independent ones.
The effective sample size (ESS) measures that: the number of independent draws that would give the same precision. The coda package computes it from the chain’s autocorrelation. For random-walk Metropolis, the best acceptance rate is around 44% in one dimension and 23% in many dimensions, with somewhere between 20% and 50% as a reasonable target.
Your turn. Run 5,000 steps with step SDs of 0.01, 0.15 and 2, starting at the posterior’s center, and compare the acceptance rates and the ESS for \log k. The setup code has a metropolis() function that takes the log-posterior, the number of steps, the start and the step SD.









Inside the function, the step SD is s.


t(sapply(c(0.01, 0.15, 2), function(s) {
  set.seed(4114)
  run <- metropolis(log_post_pumps, 5000, c(0.66, 7.47), step = s)
  c(step = s, acceptance = run$acceptance, ess = coda::effectiveSize(run$draws[, 1]))
}))
With steps of 0.01, 96% are accepted, but the 5,000 draws are worth only 9 independent ones. With 2, only 0.6% are accepted, worth 43. With 0.15, 48% are accepted, and they’re worth 377: 40 times better than the timid chain, from the same work.




The trace plots, each draw against its step number, show the three behaviors at a glance:

traces <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.01, 0.15, 2), function(s) {
  set.seed(4114)
  run <- metropolis(log_post, 5000, c(0.66, 7.47), s)
  data.frame(step = 1:5000, logk = run$draws[, 1],
             size = factor(paste("step SD", s), levels = paste("step SD", c(0.01, 0.15, 2))))
}))
ggplot(traces, aes(x = step, y = logk)) +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ size, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Step", y = "log shape") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The middle one is what a healthy chain looks like: a “fuzzy caterpillar” that crosses its whole range again and again.

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
text:
Has it converged?
You can never be sure that a chain has explored the whole posterior, but you can look for evidence that it hasn’t. The most useful check runs several chains from very different starting points. If they’ve all converged, they should look alike. The Gelman-Rubin statistic \hat R (R-hat, the “potential scale reduction factor”) compares the variation between the chains with the variation within them. It’s close to 1 when they agree, and values above about 1.01 to 1.05 are a warning sign that the chains haven’t mixed yet.
Your turn. Run three chains of 6,000 steps from widely spread starting points, drop 1,000 draws of burn-in from each, and compute \hat R.









Combine the chains with coda::mcmc.list().


set.seed(4115)
starts <- list(c(-1, 6), c(0.66, 7.47), c(2, 9))     # shapes 0.37, 1.9 and 7.4; scales 400 to 8,100 days
chains <- lapply(starts, function(s) coda::mcmc(metropolis(log_post_pumps, 6000, s, 0.15)$draws[-(1:1000), ]))
coda::gelman.diag(coda::mcmc.list(chains))
\hat R is 1.01 for \log k and 1.00 for \log\lambda: the three chains, started far apart, agree. The “upper C.I.” column is an upper bound on \hat R that allows for the chains’ finite length. If you want it closer to 1 too, run the chains longer. Starting from a shape of 7.4, the third chain needed only about 50 steps to reach the posterior, so 1,000 steps of burn-in was plenty.

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The B10 life, the Bayesian way. With posterior draws, the posterior of any function of the parameters is just that function applied to each draw. Lesson 9 needed a normal approximation for the B10 life. Here, compute it for every draw. What’s the posterior probability that the B10 life is more than a year?









A year is 365 days.


set.seed(4113)
keep <- metropolis(log_post_pumps, 10000, c(0, 7), 0.15)$draws[-(1:1000), ]
b10_draws <- apply(keep, 1, b10)                 # the setup code has b10() from Lesson 9
c(mean = mean(b10_draws), quantile(b10_draws, c(0.025, 0.975)), p_over_a_year = mean(b10_draws > 365))
A posterior mean B10 life of 528 days, with a 95% credible interval from 284 to 762 days, and a 91% probability that it’s longer than a year. That last number is exactly what a maintenance planner wants to know, and the Bayesian answer gives it directly. A yearly seal inspection catches the first 10% of failures with 91% probability.




Challenge 2 · Did the prior matter? Run the same chain with a flat prior, which adds nothing to the log-likelihood, so the posterior is proportional to the likelihood alone. Compare the posterior mean shape with the 1.86 above.









The log-likelihood is minus the negative log-likelihood: -nll(theta).


log_post_flat <- function(theta) -nll(theta)       # the log-likelihood alone
set.seed(4113)
keep_flat <- metropolis(log_post_flat, 10000, c(0, 7), 0.15)$draws[-(1:1000), ]
c(shape = mean(exp(keep_flat[, 1])), scale = mean(exp(keep_flat[, 2])))
A posterior mean shape of 1.90, a little above the 1.86 with the weak prior, which pulled the shape slightly toward 1. (With 9,000 correlated draws, each of these estimates has a Monte Carlo error of 0.01 to 0.02; much longer chains give 1.88 and 1.85.) Either way, the prior moved the shape by less than 2%, because 36 pumps overwhelm such a weak prior. Most of the gap to the maximum likelihood estimate, 1.94, comes from the method: averaging over the posterior is not the same as maximizing. With 27 failures, the two differ a little. With 2,700, they’d agree. Module 5 is all about priors, and when they matter.

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
text:
Quick quiz

1. What makes a sequence of random states a Markov chain?

The states are independent
The next state depends only on the current state, not on earlier ones
The states are normally distributed


That’s the Markov property. MCMC draws are dependent, but only through the current state.



2. Why can the Metropolis algorithm sample a posterior known only up to a constant?

It estimates the constant first
It only uses the ratio \pi(\theta^*)/\pi(\theta), in which the constant cancels
Posteriors don’t have constants


That’s what makes MCMC work for almost any Bayesian model.



3. A random-walk Metropolis chain accepts 98% of its proposals. What should you do?

Nothing, a high acceptance rate is ideal
Increase the step size: the chain is taking tiny steps and exploring slowly
Decrease the step size


Aim for roughly 20% to 50%. A very high rate usually means very small, nearly useless steps.



4. A chain of 10,000 draws has an effective sample size of 400. What does that mean?

9,600 draws were rejected
Because the draws are correlated, they’re worth about 400 independent draws
Only the last 400 draws can be used


The Monte Carlo standard error of a posterior mean uses the ESS, not the number of draws.



5. What does a Gelman-Rubin \hat R of 1.4 tell you?

The posterior has a large variance
The chains disagree, so they haven’t converged: run them longer, or improve the sampler
The chains have converged


Values close to 1, below about 1.01 to 1.05, are what you want.



6. What is burn-in?

The first draws, discarded because the chain was still moving from its starting point toward the posterior
The time it takes to compile the code
The last draws, discarded to save memory


A chain that starts in an improbable place needs some steps to get to where the posterior is.

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
text:
Wrap-up
You can now sample from distributions that have no formula. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Markov chains settle into a stationary distribution: reactor R3 runs 72% of days, is fouled 19% and is cleaned 9%.
The Metropolis algorithm proposes a random step and accepts it with probability \min(1, \pi(\theta^*)/\pi(\theta)). The unknown constant cancels, so it works for any posterior.
The pumps’ posterior: a shape of 1.86 (95% credible interval 1.26 to 2.48) and a scale of 1,788 days, and a 91% probability that the B10 life exceeds a year.
Tuning: a step SD of 0.15 accepted 48% and gave 40 times the effective sample size of a step of 0.01.
Diagnostics: trace plots should look like fuzzy caterpillars, the effective sample size says what the draws are worth, and \hat R near 1 says that chains from different starts agree.
Bayes in one line: any quantity of interest gets its posterior by applying it to each draw.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download pump_field.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

The coda toolkit. Make chain <- coda::mcmc(keep) with colnames(keep) <- c("log_shape", "log_scale"), and try plot(chain) (trace and density plots), summary(chain) (with Monte Carlo standard errors), coda::autocorr.plot(chain) and coda::HPDinterval(chain).
A different prior. Suppose the seal manufacturer’s data say the shape is about 3, give or take 0.5. Use a normal prior for \log k with mean \log 3 and SD 0.17. How much does the posterior change? Plot the two posteriors of the shape together.
Thinning. Keep only every 10th draw of a long chain. Does it improve the ESS per draw kept? Does it improve the ESS overall? (Thinning saves memory, but it throws information away.)
A smarter proposal. The pumps’ posterior is roughly normal with the covariance V from Lesson 9’s Hessian. Propose steps from N(0, 2.4^2 V/2), using chol(V), instead of independent steps. Compare the acceptance rate and the ESS with the step SD of 0.15.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Markov chain

A sequence of random states in which the next state depends only on the current one.

Stationary distribution

The distribution a Markov chain settles into, which one more step leaves unchanged: \boldsymbol\pi P = \boldsymbol\pi.

Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)

Simulating a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the target, and using its states as (dependent) draws from it.

Metropolis algorithm

An MCMC method that proposes a random step and accepts it with probability \min(1, \pi(\theta^*)/\pi(\theta)).

Posterior distribution

The distribution of the parameters given the data, proportional to the likelihood times the prior.

Credible interval

An interval that contains the parameter with a stated posterior probability, such as the middle 95% of the posterior draws.

Burn-in

The early draws of a chain, discarded because the chain hadn’t yet reached the target distribution.

Effective sample size

The number of independent draws that would carry the same information as a chain’s correlated draws.

Gelman-Rubin statistic (\hat R)

A comparison of the variation between several chains with the variation within them. Values near 1 suggest convergence.











NoteWant to read more?






Roger Peng, Advanced Statistical Computing, chapter 7, “Markov chain Monte Carlo”, with sections on the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm and on monitoring convergence.
Andrew Gelman and others, Bayesian Data Analysis (3rd edition), free PDF on the book’s site. Chapter 11 covers Metropolis and the convergence checks of this lesson, by the inventor of \hat R. A preview of Module 5.
Nicholas Metropolis, Arianna and Marshall Rosenbluth, and Augusta and Edward Teller, “Equation of state calculations by fast computing machines”, Journal of Chemical Physics (1953). The original paper, about simulating molecules in a box: chemistry gave statistics its most important algorithm.

title: Multivariate optimization and maximum likelihood
text:
Module 4 · Lesson 9 of 14 Week 69 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 8’s seals were run to failure on a test rig. The plant’s own pumps tell a messier story. The maintenance team followed the 36 pumps installed between 2019 and 2022 until 31 October 2026, and recorded the days from installation to each pump’s first seal failure:
head(pumps)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   pump_id installed   days failed
#>   <chr>   <date>     <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 P-101   2019-01-01  2860      0
#> 2 P-102   2019-01-10  1685      1
#> 3 P-103   2019-01-16  2397      1
#> 4 P-104   2019-03-01  1185      1
#> 5 P-105   2019-03-25   566      1
#> 6 P-106   2019-04-10  2457      1
table(failed = pumps$failed)
#> failed
#>  0  1 
#>  9 27
27 pumps had a seal failure. The other 9 are still running: for them, days is how long they’ve lasted so far. Their true lifetimes are longer, but we don’t know by how much. Such observations are right-censored. They can’t be thrown away, because they’re the toughest pumps, and dropping them would make the seals look worse than they are. And they can’t be treated as failures either.
Maximum likelihood handles censoring naturally, but it leaves you with two parameters to estimate at once, and no score equation to solve by hand. This lesson is about optimization in several dimensions: the algorithms inside R’s optim(), and inside glm().
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Multivariate optimization and maximum likelihood
text:
A likelihood for censored data
A pump that failed at x_i days contributes the probability density of failing then, f(x_i), as in Lesson 8. A pump still running at x_i days contributes the probability of lasting at least that long, the survival function S(x_i) = P(T > x_i). For the Weibull distribution, S(x) = \exp[-(x/\lambda)^k]. With \delta_i = 1 for a failure and 0 for a censored pump, the log-likelihood is

\ell(k, \lambda) = \sum_i \delta_i \left[\log k - \log\lambda + (k - 1)\log\frac{x_i}{\lambda}\right] - \sum_i \left(\frac{x_i}{\lambda}\right)^k ,

because \log f = \log k - \log\lambda + (k-1)\log(x/\lambda) - (x/\lambda)^k and \log S = -(x/\lambda)^k: every pump contributes the last term, and only the failures contribute the first.
Optimizers conventionally minimize, so we’ll work with the negative log-likelihood. And we’ll give the optimizer \theta = (\log k, \log\lambda) instead of (k, \lambda). Then any value it tries corresponds to a positive shape and scale, and the two parameters are on similar scales (about 0.7 and 7.5, instead of 2 and 1,800).









Your turn. Complete the negative log-likelihood, and minimize it with optim(), starting from \theta = (0, 7): a shape of 1 and a scale of e^7 \approx 1100 days. Without a method, optim() uses Nelder-Mead.









The last term is \sum (x_i/\lambda)^k: the exponent is k.


nll <- function(theta) {
  k <- exp(theta[1]); lambda <- exp(theta[2])
  -(sum(failed * (log(k) - log(lambda) + (k - 1) * log(days / lambda))) - sum((days / lambda)^k))
}
fit_nm <- optim(c(0, 7), nll)
c(shape = exp(fit_nm$par[1]), scale = exp(fit_nm$par[2]), evaluations = fit_nm$counts[["function"]])
A shape of 1.94 and a scale of 1,758 days, after 101 evaluations of the likelihood. The shape is above 1, so the seals wear out, as on the test rig. The scale is the age by which 63% of seals have failed, about 4.8 years. Always check fit_nm$convergence too: 0 means optim() thinks it converged.

title: Multivariate optimization and maximum likelihood
text:
Inside optim(): Nelder-Mead and BFGS
Nelder-Mead uses function values only. In two dimensions, it keeps a triangle of three points, called a simplex. At each step, it replaces the worst point by reflecting it through the other two, stretching the triangle when that goes well, and shrinking it when it doesn’t. The triangle tumbles downhill and contracts around the minimum. It’s robust and needs no derivatives, but it’s slow, and in many dimensions it can stall. Here are the points it tried, on the contours of the negative log-likelihood:

tried <- matrix(numeric(0), ncol = 2)
nll_logged <- function(theta) { tried <<- rbind(tried, theta); nll(theta) }
invisible(optim(c(0, 7), nll_logged))
grid <- expand.grid(logk = seq(-0.2, 1.2, length.out = 120), loglam = seq(6.8, 8.0, length.out = 120))
grid$nll <- apply(grid, 1, function(th) nll(th))
path <- data.frame(logk = tried[, 1], loglam = tried[, 2], step = seq_len(nrow(tried)))
ggplot(grid, aes(x = logk, y = loglam)) +
  geom_contour(aes(z = nll), breaks = 223.53 + c(0.5, 2, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80), color = "grey70") +
  geom_path(data = path, color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(data = path, color = "#C2416C", size = 1.3) +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = 7, color = "#3A1F35", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.03, y = 6.93, label = "start", hjust = 0, size = 3.6, color = "#3A1F35") +
  labs(x = "log shape", y = "log scale (log days)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








BFGS (Broyden, Fletcher, Goldfarb and Shanno, who found it independently in 1970) is a quasi-Newton method. It uses the gradient, the vector of partial derivatives, which optim() approximates by finite differences unless you supply it. And it builds up an estimate of the curvature as it goes, which lets it take Newton-like steps without ever computing second derivatives. With hessian = TRUE, optim() also returns the matrix of second derivatives at the answer, which you’ll need for standard errors.
Your turn. Fit the model with BFGS, and compare its answer and its work with Nelder-Mead’s.









method = "BFGS".


fit_nm <- optim(c(0, 7), nll)
fit_bfgs <- optim(c(0, 7), nll, method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE)
rbind(nelder_mead = c(exp(fit_nm$par), fit_nm$counts),
      bfgs = c(exp(fit_bfgs$par), fit_bfgs$counts))
The same answer, a shape of 1.94 and a scale of 1,758 days, from 35 function and 9 gradient evaluations, against Nelder-Mead’s 101 (it uses no gradients, so that column is NA). Each finite-difference gradient costs a few function evaluations, but BFGS still needs far fewer steps. With more parameters, the gap grows. survival::survreg(), the standard function for censored lifetimes, gives the same estimates.




The log scale isn’t just tidy. Here’s BFGS on the original scale, starting from a shape of 1 and a scale of 1,000 days:

nll_raw <- function(th) {
  k <- th[1]; lambda <- th[2]
  if (k <= 0 || lambda <= 0) return(Inf)
  -(sum(failed * (log(k) - log(lambda) + (k - 1) * log(days / lambda))) - sum((days / lambda)^k))
}
raw <- optim(c(1, 1000), nll_raw, method = "BFGS")
c(raw$par, value = raw$value, convergence = raw$convergence)
#>                               value convergence 
#>    1.214661 1052.372917  234.141146    1.000000

It stopped at a shape of 1.21 and a scale of 1,052, far from the answer, with a worse negative log-likelihood (234.1 against 223.5). Its convergence code, 1, says it ran out of iterations. A change of 1 in the scale barely moves the likelihood, while a change of 1 in the shape is enormous, so the gradient points almost entirely along the shape, and progress along the scale is painfully slow. On the log scale, both parameters move the likelihood about equally. Rescale and transform your parameters, and always check convergence.

title: Multivariate optimization and maximum likelihood
text:
Standard errors from the Hessian
Near its maximum, a log-likelihood is shaped like an upside-down bowl. A sharply curved bowl pins the estimate down, and a flat one doesn’t. The curvature is measured by the Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives of the negative log-likelihood. At the maximum, it’s called the observed information, and its inverse estimates the covariance matrix of the estimates:

\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\theta) \approx H^{-1}.

The square roots of its diagonal are the standard errors. They’re for \log k and \log\lambda, so build the 95% intervals on the log scale and take the exponential of the ends.
Your turn. The setup code has fitted fit_bfgs with hessian = TRUE. Compute 95% confidence intervals for the shape and the scale.









Invert the Hessian: fit_bfgs$hessian.


V <- solve(fit_bfgs$hessian)         # the estimated covariance matrix of the log parameters
se <- sqrt(diag(V))
est <- fit_bfgs$par
rbind(estimate = exp(est), lower = exp(est - 1.96 * se), upper = exp(est + 1.96 * se))
The shape is between 1.42 and 2.65, and the scale between 1,447 and 2,135 days. The shape’s interval is entirely above 1, so the wear-out is clear even with 36 pumps. The intervals are asymmetric on the original scale, which is right for positive quantities. And on the log scale, the two estimates are almost uncorrelated (a correlation of 0.02), another sign that it’s a good parameterization.

title: Multivariate optimization and maximum likelihood
text:
Gradient descent
The simplest optimizer of all steps downhill: compute the gradient \nabla f(\theta), and move a little way against it,

\theta \leftarrow \theta - \alpha\, \nabla f(\theta),

with a step size (or learning rate) \alpha. It’s how most neural networks are trained (Module 7). It needs no second derivatives, but it’s slow when the bowl is long and narrow, and the step size needs tuning: too small and it crawls, too large and it overshoots and diverges.
Try it on a logistic regression (Lesson 2.15). The plant pressure-tested 80 gaskets at different pressures and temperatures, and 23 of them leaked. The model is \operatorname{logit} P(\text{leak}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{pressure} + \beta_2 \cdot \text{temperature}, and its negative log-likelihood has the gradient

\nabla = -X^\top(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{p}),

where X is the model matrix and \mathbf{p} the fitted leak probabilities. The setup code has standardized both predictors (mean 0, SD 1), which makes the bowl rounder and gradient descent much happier.
Your turn. Run 500 steps of gradient descent with a step size of 0.01.









The step size is 0.01.


beta <- c(0, 0, 0)
for (i in 1:500) {
  p <- plogis(X %*% beta)                      # fitted probabilities
  gradient <- -t(X) %*% (y - p)                # gradient of the negative log-likelihood
  beta <- beta - 0.01 * gradient               # a small step downhill
}
drop(beta)
After 500 steps, \boldsymbol\beta = (-2.0065, 2.6016, 0.6204), correct to about 3 digits: glm() gives (-2.0068, 2.6019, 0.6205). It took 2,000 steps to match all the printed digits. Pressure matters most: one SD more pressure (8.8 bar) multiplies the odds of a leak by e^{2.6} \approx 13.

title: Multivariate optimization and maximum likelihood
text:
Newton’s method and Fisher scoring
Newton’s method in several dimensions uses the curvature as well as the slope. It replaces the function by the quadratic bowl that matches its gradient and Hessian, and jumps straight to that bowl’s bottom:

\theta \leftarrow \theta - H^{-1} \nabla f(\theta).

For logistic regression, the Hessian is X^\top W X, with W the diagonal matrix of p_i(1 - p_i). So the Newton step solves

(X^\top W X)\, \Delta = X^\top(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{p}).

Fisher scoring uses the expected information instead of the observed Hessian. For logistic regression the two are the same, and so is a third name for the algorithm, iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS), because each step is a weighted least squares fit. It’s exactly what glm() does, and it’s what the “Number of Fisher Scoring iterations” in summary() of a glm() counts.
Your turn. Run Newton’s method from \boldsymbol\beta = \mathbf{0} for 8 steps, and watch the digits settle.









The right-hand side is X^\top(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{p}).


beta <- c(0, 0, 0)
for (i in 1:8) {
  p <- drop(plogis(X %*% beta))
  W <- p * (1 - p)                                          # the weights
  beta <- beta + solve(t(X) %*% (W * X), t(X) %*% (y - p))
  cat(i, format(drop(beta), digits = 10), "\n")
}
drop(beta)
Six steps reach 8 digits, and the seventh changes nothing that a double can show: quadratic convergence again. Gradient descent needed 2,000 steps for the same answer. glm(leak ~ scale(pressure_bar) + scale(temp_C), family = binomial, data = leaks) reports “Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 6”. (W * X multiplies each row of X by its weight, which is WX without building the diagonal matrix.)










NoteGo deeper: which optimizer when?






Newton’s method is the fastest near the answer, but it needs second derivatives, and each step solves a linear system with one row per parameter, which is expensive for thousands of parameters. Far from the answer, it can jump the wrong way, as in Lesson 8, so good implementations add a line search that shortens a step that doesn’t improve the function.
Quasi-Newton methods (BFGS, and L-BFGS-B with bounds on the parameters) are the general-purpose default: fast, and they need only gradients.
Nelder-Mead is for small problems where the function isn’t smooth, or the gradient is unreliable.
Gradient descent, and its random-subsample version, stochastic gradient descent, wins for huge problems such as neural networks, where even storing a Hessian is impossible.

All of them find a local minimum. If a likelihood has several, try several starting points.

title: Multivariate optimization and maximum likelihood
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Throwing away the survivors. What if the analyst had simply dropped the 9 pumps that are still running, and fitted a Weibull distribution to the 27 failures alone?









Keep the pumps that failed: failed == 1.


fail_days <- days[failed == 1]
nll_fail <- function(theta) -sum(dweibull(fail_days, exp(theta[1]), exp(theta[2]), log = TRUE))
fit_fail <- optim(c(0, 7), nll_fail, method = "BFGS")
c(shape = exp(fit_fail$par[1]), scale = exp(fit_fail$par[2]))
A scale of 1,429 days instead of 1,758: the seals look 19% shorter-lived than they are, because the 9 longest-lived pumps were thrown out. The shape barely changes (2.03 against 1.94). Censored observations carry real information: “this pump lasted at least 2,860 days” is a lot of evidence for long lives.




Challenge 2 · The B10 life. Maintenance planners use the B10 life: the age by which 10% of seals have failed, t_{10} = \lambda\,(-\log 0.9)^{1/k}. To get a confidence interval, simulate 5,000 parameter vectors from the estimates’ approximate normal distribution, N(\hat\theta, V), and compute the B10 life for each. (Multiplying independent normals by chol(V) gives them the covariance V.)









Apply the function b10 to each row.


V <- solve(fit_bfgs$hessian)
est <- fit_bfgs$par
b10 <- function(theta) exp(theta[2]) * (-log(0.9))^(1 / exp(theta[1]))
set.seed(4091)
draws <- sweep(matrix(rnorm(10000), ncol = 2) %*% chol(V), 2, est, "+")   # 5,000 rows of (log k, log lambda)
b10_draws <- apply(draws, 1, b10)
c(b10 = b10(est), quantile(b10_draws, c(0.025, 0.975)))
A B10 life of 551 days, with a 95% interval from 344 to 804 days. So inspecting the seals at about a year (365 days) would be a cautious plan. The model that dropped the survivors would have said 471 days. Simulating from the estimates’ distribution like this is a quick alternative to the delta method, and to the bootstrap of Lesson 6 (which would refit the model for every resample).

title: Multivariate optimization and maximum likelihood
text:
Quick quiz

1. How does a right-censored observation enter the likelihood?

It’s left out
As a failure at the censoring time
Through the survival function S(x) = P(T > x), the probability of lasting at least that long


It’s evidence that the lifetime is longer than x, and that’s exactly what S(x) measures.



2. Why optimize over \log k and \log\lambda instead of k and \lambda?

It changes the maximum likelihood estimates
Every value the optimizer tries is valid, and the two parameters are on similar scales
optim() can’t handle positive numbers


On the original scale, BFGS ran out of iterations far from the answer.



3. What does Nelder-Mead use to find a minimum?

The gradient and the Hessian
Function values only, at the corners of a moving simplex
Random guesses


That makes it robust, but slow.



4. What does the inverse of the Hessian of the negative log-likelihood at its minimum estimate?

The maximum likelihood estimates
The covariance matrix of the estimates
The gradient


Sharp curvature means a well-determined estimate and a small standard error.



5. What does glm() use to fit a logistic regression?

Gradient descent
Nelder-Mead
Fisher scoring, which for logistic regression is Newton’s method, also called IRLS


That’s why it reports the number of Fisher scoring iterations.



6. Gradient descent needed 2,000 steps and Newton’s method 6. Why use gradient descent at all?

It’s more accurate
Each step is much cheaper: it needs no Hessian, which matters with thousands or millions of parameters
It always finds the global minimum


For three parameters, Newton wins easily. For a neural network, a Hessian wouldn’t even fit in memory.

title: Multivariate optimization and maximum likelihood
text:
Wrap-up
You can now maximize likelihoods with many parameters, and get their uncertainty too. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Censored data: failures contribute the density, and survivors the survival function. The pumps’ seals have a Weibull shape of 1.94 and a scale of 1,758 days.
optim(): Nelder-Mead uses function values only (101 evaluations here), and BFGS uses gradients and a built-up curvature (35).
Transform the parameters: on the log scale they stay positive and comparable. On the original scale, BFGS stalled far from the answer, and said so with convergence = 1.
Standard errors come from the inverse Hessian: a shape between 1.42 and 2.65, clear wear-out.
Gradient descent vs Newton: 2,000 cheap steps against 6 expensive ones for the gasket logistic regression. Newton’s method for logistic regression is Fisher scoring, the IRLS inside glm().
Don’t drop the survivors: without the censored pumps, the scale falls by 19%, and the B10 life from 551 to 471 days.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download pump_field.csv and leak_tests.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

The standard tool. Install nothing: survival comes with R. Fit survival::survreg(survival::Surv(days, failed) ~ 1, data = pumps, dist = "weibull"). Its scale is 1/k, and its intercept is \log\lambda. Check that they match your optim() fit. Then draw the Kaplan-Meier curve, plot(survival::survfit(survival::Surv(days, failed) ~ 1, data = pumps)), and add the Weibull survival curve with curve(exp(-(x / 1758)^1.94), add = TRUE).
An analytic gradient. Write the gradient of nll() with respect to (\log k, \log\lambda) by hand (use the chain rule), check it against a finite difference, and pass it to optim(..., gr = ...). How many evaluations does BFGS need now?
Unscaled predictors. Run gradient descent on the gasket data with the original pressure and temperature (and a column of ones). Find a step size that doesn’t diverge, and count the steps needed. Why is it so much worse?
A profile interval. For a fixed shape k, the best scale is \hat\lambda(k) (as in Lesson 8, but with censoring, \hat\lambda(k)^k = \sum x_i^k / \sum \delta_i). Plot the profile log-likelihood of k, and find the shapes where it’s 1.92 below its maximum. That’s a likelihood-based 95% interval. Compare it with the Hessian interval, 1.42 to 2.65.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Right-censored observation

An observation known only to be larger than a recorded value, such as a pump that hasn’t failed yet.

Survival function

S(x) = P(T > x), the probability of lasting longer than x.

Nelder-Mead

A derivative-free optimizer that moves and reshapes a simplex of points.

Quasi-Newton method

An optimizer, such as BFGS, that uses gradients and builds up an approximation to the curvature.

Hessian

The matrix of second derivatives. For a negative log-likelihood at its minimum, it’s the observed information, and its inverse estimates the covariance matrix of the estimates.

Gradient descent

An optimizer that repeatedly steps against the gradient, with a chosen step size.

Fisher scoring

Newton’s method with the expected information in place of the Hessian. For logistic regression, it’s the same as iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS).

B10 life

The age by which 10% of items have failed.











NoteWant to read more?






Roger Peng, Advanced Statistical Computing, chapter 3, “General optimization”, especially sections 3.2, “The Newton direction” (with generalized linear models), and 3.3, “Quasi-Newton”.
R’s help page for optim(). Its methods, their options, and what each convergence code means.
William Meeker, Luis Escobar and Francis Pascual, Statistical Methods for Reliability Data (Wiley, 2nd edition, 2021). Censored data, Weibull analysis and B10 lives, for engineers. Not free.

title: Permutation tests, the jackknife and cross-validation
text:
Module 4 · Lesson 7 of 14 Week 67 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The bootstrap resamples the data to ask “how uncertain is my estimate?”. This lesson’s three methods also reuse the data, each in its own way, for three other jobs:
All three are older than the bootstrap, and you can write each of them in a few lines of R.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Permutation tests, the jackknife and cross-validation
text:
Permutation tests
Dana ran a trial of a new catalyst, B, against the current one, A: 16 runs, 8 with each catalyst, in random order.

ggplot(trial, aes(x = yield_pct, y = catalyst, color = catalyst)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(A = "#2a78d6", B = "#C2416C"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Yield (%)", y = "Catalyst") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Catalyst B’s mean yield is 2.66 points higher. Is that the catalyst, or the luck of which runs got which catalyst?
The permutation test answers by taking the null hypothesis literally. If the catalyst makes no difference, each run’s yield would have been the same whichever catalyst it got, and the labels “A” and “B” are just the random assignment. So shuffle the labels: every shuffle is a result that the null hypothesis says was just as likely. Do it thousands of times, and see how often a shuffle gives a difference as big as the one observed. That share is the p-value.
The test makes no assumption of normality. It relies on one thing: that the runs were randomly assigned to the catalysts (or, for observational data, that the observations are exchangeable under the null hypothesis).









Your turn. The setup code has a function diff_means(y, g), which returns B’s mean minus A’s, and the observed difference, obs. Shuffle the labels 10,000 times with sample(), and compute the two-sided p-value.









Shuffle the catalyst labels: sample(trial$catalyst).


set.seed(4071)
perm <- replicate(10000, diff_means(trial$yield_pct, sample(trial$catalyst)))
c(observed = obs, p_value = mean(abs(perm) >= abs(obs)))
A p-value of 0.042: only 4.2% of the shuffles gave a difference of 2.66 points or more, in either direction. The two-sample t-test gives 0.043, almost the same, because these data are close to normal. The permutation test got there without assuming it. sample(x) without other arguments returns x in a random order, so each shuffle keeps eight A’s and eight B’s.




Here are the 10,000 shuffled differences. The p-value is the share beyond the dashed lines, at ±2.66:

set.seed(4071)
perm <- replicate(10000, diff_means(trial$yield_pct, sample(trial$catalyst)))
ggplot(data.frame(d = perm), aes(x = d, fill = abs(d) >= abs(obs))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-obs, obs), linetype = "dashed", color = "#3A1F35") +
  annotate("text", x = obs + 0.15, y = 600, label = "observed, 2.66", hjust = 0, size = 3.6, color = "#3A1F35") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#F4C0D1", `TRUE` = "#C2416C"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Difference in mean yield, B minus A, after shuffling (points)", y = "Number of shuffles") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








A permutation test can use any statistic you like. The difference in medians, for example, is less sensitive to an outlying run.
Your turn. Repeat the test with the difference in medians.









Compare with the observed difference in medians, obs_med.


diff_medians <- function(y, g) median(y[g == "B"]) - median(y[g == "A"])
obs_med <- diff_medians(trial$yield_pct, trial$catalyst)
set.seed(4073)
perm_med <- replicate(10000, diff_medians(trial$yield_pct, sample(trial$catalyst)))
c(observed = obs_med, p_value = mean(abs(perm_med) >= abs(obs_med)))
The medians differ by 1.8 points, and the p-value is 0.14. With normal-looking data like these, the median throws away information, so its test has less power. The choice of statistic is part of the test, and it should be made before looking at the results. Trying several statistics and reporting the smallest p-value is cheating, even by accident.

title: Permutation tests, the jackknife and cross-validation
text:
The jackknife
The lab’s precision is reported as a coefficient of variation, the SD as a percentage of the mean. Over 15 analyses of the certified reference material, it’s 2.29%. A customer’s audit asks: how precisely do you know that?
The jackknife, from the 1950s, answers by leaving out one observation at a time. With \hat\theta_{(i)} the statistic computed without observation i, and \bar\theta_{(\cdot)} the average of the n of them, the jackknife estimates the standard error and the bias as

\text{SE}_{\text{jack}} = \sqrt{\frac{n-1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\hat\theta_{(i)} - \bar\theta_{(\cdot)}\right)^2}, \qquad
\text{bias}_{\text{jack}} = (n - 1)\left(\bar\theta_{(\cdot)} - \hat\theta\right).

The leave-one-out values hardly vary, because each one shares n - 2 observations with any other, so the factor n - 1 scales them up to the size of a real sample-to-sample variation.
Your turn. The setup code has a function cv_pct(). Compute the 15 leave-one-out values, and the jackknife standard error and bias.









x[-i] is x without its ith element.


x <- qc$iron_mgkg
n <- length(x)
theta_i <- sapply(1:n, function(i) cv_pct(x[-i]))
c(cv = cv_pct(x),
  jack_se = sqrt((n - 1) / n * sum((theta_i - mean(theta_i))^2)),
  jack_bias = (n - 1) * (mean(theta_i) - cv_pct(x)))
A CV of 2.29%, with a jackknife standard error of 0.36 percentage points: from 15 analyses, the lab’s precision is somewhere between about 1.6% and 3.0%. The estimated bias is small, −0.03. A bootstrap of the same statistic gives a standard error of 0.33, close to the jackknife’s. The jackknife values also show which analysis matters most: leaving out run 4, the highest result (53.27 mg/kg), drops the CV to 2.05%.




The jackknife needs only n recomputations, where the bootstrap needs thousands, and it gives the same answer every time. Its limitation: it works for smooth statistics such as means, SDs and correlations, but not for the median or other quantiles, which jump in steps when one observation is removed. For those, use the bootstrap.

title: Permutation tests, the jackknife and cross-validation
text:
Cross-validation
The lab measured a resin’s viscosity at 40 temperatures between 20 and 80 °C, and wants a curve to look up the viscosity at any temperature. A polynomial in temperature seems sensible. But what degree? Every extra term makes the curve fit the 40 points better: the training error, the mean squared residual, can only go down. A curve that follows the noise, though, will predict new measurements worse.
Cross-validation estimates the error on new data with the data you have. In k-fold cross-validation, you divide the data at random into k groups, called folds. Each fold takes a turn as the test set: fit the model to the other k - 1 folds, and measure its squared prediction error on the fold that was left out. The average over all folds is the cross-validated error. Lesson 2.12 used it to compare regression models. Now you’ll write it yourself.
Your turn. Complete the function that computes the 5-fold cross-validated error of a polynomial of a given degree, and compute it for degrees 1 to 6.









The test set is fold k.


set.seed(4072)
folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(visc)))      # a random fold for each measurement
cv_mse <- function(degree) {
  errors <- sapply(1:5, function(k) {
    train <- visc[folds != k, ]
    test <- visc[folds == k, ]
    fit <- lm(viscosity_mPas ~ poly(temp_C, degree), data = train)
    mean((test$viscosity_mPas - predict(fit, test))^2)
  })
  mean(errors)
}
round(sapply(1:6, cv_mse), 4)
A straight line is poor (0.206), degree 2 is far better (0.0234), and degree 3 is best (0.0224). Beyond that, the error rises again: 0.0229, 0.0246, 0.0254. Choose the cubic. Its cross-validated error, 0.0224, corresponds to a typical prediction error of \sqrt{0.0224} = 0.15 mPa·s, which is about the measurement noise.




Here’s the training error against the cross-validated error, for degrees 2 to 6 (the straight line’s errors, near 0.2, would be far off the top):

set.seed(4072)
folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(visc)))
cv_mse <- function(degree) mean(sapply(1:5, function(k) {
  fit <- lm(viscosity_mPas ~ poly(temp_C, degree), data = visc[folds != k, ])
  mean((visc$viscosity_mPas[folds == k] - predict(fit, visc[folds == k, ]))^2)
}))
train_mse <- function(degree) mean(resid(lm(viscosity_mPas ~ poly(temp_C, degree), data = visc))^2)
errs <- rbind(data.frame(degree = 2:6, error = sapply(2:6, train_mse), kind = "training"),
              data.frame(degree = 2:6, error = sapply(2:6, cv_mse), kind = "cross-validated"))
ggplot(errs, aes(x = degree, y = error, color = kind)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 5.5, y = 0.0261, label = "cross-validated", color = "#C2416C", size = 3.6) +
  annotate("text", x = 5.5, y = 0.0187, label = "training", color = "#2a78d6", size = 3.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(training = "#2a78d6", `cross-validated` = "#C2416C"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:6) +
  labs(x = "Degree of the polynomial", y = "Mean squared error") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The training error says “more is always better”. The cross-validated error says “stop at 3”.

title: Permutation tests, the jackknife and cross-validation
text:
The leave-one-out shortcut
With k = n, every fold holds one observation, and cross-validation becomes leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV). It needs n fits in general. For linear models fitted by least squares, though, there’s a shortcut: the prediction error for observation i, from a fit without it, is

y_i - \hat{y}_{(i)} = \frac{e_i}{1 - h_{ii}},

where e_i is the ordinary residual and h_{ii} the leverage from Lesson 2.10. So LOOCV needs just one fit. The sum of the squared leave-one-out errors is called PRESS, the prediction error sum of squares.
Your turn. Compute the LOOCV error with the shortcut, for degrees 1 to 6.









The leverages come from the fitted model: hatvalues(fit).


loocv <- function(degree) {
  fit <- lm(viscosity_mPas ~ poly(temp_C, degree), data = visc)
  mean((resid(fit) / (1 - hatvalues(fit)))^2)
}
round(sapply(1:6, loocv), 4)
0.221, 0.0236, 0.0231, 0.0242, 0.0253 and 0.0263: degree 3 again. These are exactly the numbers you’d get by refitting 40 times, at a fortieth of the cost. LOOCV has no random folds, so it gives the same answer every time.










NoteGo deeper: which k?





Small k (such as 5) trains each model on less data, so it slightly overestimates the error of a model fitted to all the data: a small bias. LOOCV trains on almost all the data, so its bias is tiny, but its n fitted models are nearly identical, so their errors are highly correlated, and the average can be quite variable. Five or 10 folds are the usual compromise. The randomness of the folds adds variation too, which Challenge 2 measures. For choosing between models, the differences in cross-validated error matter, and a common rule is to pick the simplest model whose error is within one standard error of the best (the “one-standard-error rule”).

title: Permutation tests, the jackknife and cross-validation
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · An exact p-value. With 16 runs, there are only \binom{16}{8} = 12{,}870 ways to choose which 8 got catalyst B. combn(16, 8) lists them all, one per column. Compute the difference in means for every one of them, and the exact two-sided p-value.









The other 8 runs are y[-b].


y <- trial$yield_pct
groups <- combn(16, 8)                       # each column: the 8 runs labeled B
d <- apply(groups, 2, function(b) mean(y[b]) - mean(y[-b]))
c(shuffles = ncol(groups), exact_p = mean(abs(d) >= abs(obs) - 1e-9))
The exact p-value is 0.0429: 552 of the 12,870 assignments give a difference of 2.66 or more. The 10,000 random shuffles estimated 0.042, within their Monte Carlo error. (The - 1e-9 is Lesson 2’s tolerance: the observed assignment itself must count, even if its difference is computed with a different rounding error.) With 30 runs, there would be 155 million assignments, and random shuffles would be the only practical way.




Challenge 2 · Does the choice depend on the folds? Repeat the 5-fold cross-validation with 20 different random fold assignments (seeds 1 to 20), and count how often each degree wins.









which.min(cv) gives the position of the smallest error, which is the degree.


best <- sapply(1:20, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = 40))
  cv <- sapply(1:6, function(degree) mean(sapply(1:5, function(k) {
    fit <- lm(viscosity_mPas ~ poly(temp_C, degree), data = visc[folds != k, ])
    mean((visc$viscosity_mPas[folds == k] - predict(fit, visc[folds == k, ]))^2)
  })))
  which.min(cv)              # the degree with the smallest error
})
table(best)
Degree 3 wins 14 times and degree 2 wins 6 times. Degree 1 and degrees 4 to 6 never win. So cross-validation is sure about “2 or 3, not more”, and not sure between those two. That’s honest: the curve’s true shape (Andrade’s equation, \ln \mu = A + B/T) isn’t a polynomial at all, and degrees 2 and 3 approximate it about equally well. Averaging the errors over several fold assignments, called repeated cross-validation, makes the choice more stable.

title: Permutation tests, the jackknife and cross-validation
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does a permutation test shuffle?

The measurements within each group
The group labels, which under the null hypothesis are just a random assignment
The order of the runs


If the catalyst makes no difference, every assignment of labels to yields was equally likely.



2. What does a permutation test assume?

That the data are normal
That the groups were randomly assigned, or that the observations are exchangeable under the null hypothesis
That the groups have equal sizes


It needs no distributional assumption, which is why it’s called distribution-free.



3. How many recomputations does the jackknife need for a sample of 15?

2,000
15
2^{15}


One for each observation left out.



4. For which statistic is the jackknife a bad choice?

The mean
The coefficient of variation
The median


The median jumps in steps when one observation is removed, so the jackknife’s standard error is unreliable. Use the bootstrap.



5. Why can’t you choose a polynomial’s degree by its training error?

Because it’s hard to compute
Because the training error can only go down as terms are added, even when the extra terms are fitting noise
Because it ignores the intercept


Cross-validation measures the error on data that the model didn’t see.



6. What’s the leave-one-out prediction error of observation i for a linear model?

e_i
e_i/(1 - h_{ii})
e_i \times h_{ii}


High-leverage points pull the fit toward themselves, so their residuals understate their prediction errors the most.

title: Permutation tests, the jackknife and cross-validation
text:
Wrap-up
You now have three more resampling tools, each for its own job. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Permutation tests shuffle the labels to see what the null hypothesis would produce. Catalyst B’s 2.66-point advantage has a p-value of 0.042 from 10,000 shuffles, and 0.0429 exactly, from all 12,870.
Any statistic can be tested, but choose it before you look: the difference in medians gives p = 0.14.
The jackknife leaves out one observation at a time. The lab’s CV of 2.29% has a standard error of 0.36 percentage points and a negligible bias. It’s quick and exact, but only for smooth statistics.
k-fold cross-validation estimates prediction error on new data. It chose a cubic for the viscosity curve, while the training error kept falling.
LOOCV for linear models needs one fit: the leave-one-out errors are e_i/(1 - h_{ii}).
Cross-validation has its own randomness: across 20 fold assignments, degree 3 won 14 times and degree 2 won 6.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download catalyst_trial.csv, qc_repeats.csv and viscosity.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

A permutation test for correlation. Is the iron result correlated with the run number (a drift in the method)? Compute cor(qc$run, qc$iron_mgkg), then shuffle iron_mgkg 10,000 times and compute the share of shuffled correlations at least as big in absolute value. Compare with cor.test().
The power of a permutation test. Simulate 500 trials of 8 against 8 runs with a true difference of 2.5 points and an SD of 2.2. For each, run a permutation test with 1,000 shuffles. What share of trials gives p < 0.05? Compare it with power.t.test(n = 8, delta = 2.5, sd = 2.2).
The jackknife and the median. Compute the jackknife standard error of the median of the 15 iron results, and compare it with a bootstrap standard error. Why do they differ?
Andrade’s equation. Fit lm(log(viscosity_mPas) ~ I(1 / (temp_C + 273.15)), data = visc) and compute its LOOCV error on the viscosity scale (back-transform its leave-one-out predictions with exp(); you’ll need to refit 40 times, because the shortcut works on the log scale). Is the physical model better than the cubic?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Permutation test

A test that compares the observed statistic with its values over random (or all) reassignments of the group labels.

Exact test

A permutation test that enumerates every possible reassignment, instead of sampling them.

Jackknife

A resampling method that recomputes a statistic with each observation left out, to estimate its bias and standard error.

Coefficient of variation

The standard deviation as a percentage of the mean, a common measure of a method’s precision.

Cross-validation

Estimating a model’s prediction error on new data by fitting it to part of the data and testing it on the rest.

Fold

One of the k groups that k-fold cross-validation divides the data into.

Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV)

Cross-validation with one observation per fold. For linear models, its errors are e_i/(1 - h_{ii}).

PRESS

The prediction error sum of squares: the sum of the squared leave-one-out errors.











NoteWant to read more?






Gareth James and others, An Introduction to Statistical Learning, section 5.1, “Cross-validation”, and the R lab in section 5.3. LOOCV, k-fold cross-validation and the bias-variance trade-off, with pictures.
Tim Hesterberg, “What teachers should know about the bootstrap”, section 3 on permutation tests. Why they’re often the best way to teach and to do hypothesis tests.
Bradley Efron and Robert Tibshirani, An Introduction to the Bootstrap (Chapman & Hall, 1993), chapters 11 (the jackknife), 15 (permutation tests) and 17 (cross-validation). Not free.

title: Monte Carlo integration
text:
Module 4 · Lesson 5 of 14 Week 65 of 160 About 5–7 hours
A batch reactor runs a first-order reaction for 30 minutes, so its conversion is
X = 1 - e^{-kt}, \qquad t = 30 \text{ min}.
If every batch had the same rate constant, k = 0.05 per minute, every batch would reach X = 0.777. But the catalyst’s activity varies from batch to batch, and so does k: from the plant’s records, it’s lognormal, with a median of 0.05 per minute and a sdlog of 0.3. Dana wants to know the average conversion, to plan the downstream separation. That’s an expected value, which is an integral:
E[X] = \int_0^\infty \left(1 - e^{-30k}\right) f(k)\, dk,
with f the lognormal density. There’s no formula for it. You could use numerical integration, but there’s a simpler and more general way: simulate many batches, and average their conversions. That’s Monte Carlo integration, named after the casino, and it’s the workhorse of modern statistical computing.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Monte Carlo integration
text:
Integrals as averages
The idea fits in one line. If X_1, \dots, X_n are independent draws from the density f, the law of large numbers says that

\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n h(X_i) \;\longrightarrow\; E[h(X)] = \int h(x)\, f(x)\, dx .

So any integral that you can write as an expectation, you can estimate by an average. Even an ordinary integral over (0, 1) is one: \int_0^1 h(x)\,dx = E[h(U)] with U uniform, because the uniform density is 1 on (0, 1).
Your turn. The integral \int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx has no formula (it’s related to the normal CDF). Estimate it from 10,000 uniform draws, and compare with R’s numerical integration, integrate().









The integrand is e^{-x^2}: exp(-u^2).


integrate(function(x) exp(-x^2), 0, 1)$value       # numerical integration, to compare
set.seed(4051)
u <- runif(10000)
mean(exp(-u^2))
0.7458, against the true value 0.7468. Close, but only to about two and a half digits. For a one-dimensional integral like this, integrate() is far more accurate. Monte Carlo wins in many dimensions, where grids of points become impossibly large, and for expectations over complicated random processes, where there’s nothing to integrate on a grid.

title: Monte Carlo integration
text:
The average conversion
Now Dana’s question. Simulate the rate constants of many batches, compute each batch’s conversion, and average.
Your turn. Estimate the expected conversion after 30 minutes from 10,000 simulated batches, and compare it with the conversion of a batch that has the average rate constant.









The reaction time is 30 minutes.


set.seed(4052)
k <- rlnorm(10000, log(0.05), 0.3)      # rate constants of 10,000 batches, per minute
X <- 1 - exp(-k * 30)                    # each batch's conversion after 30 minutes
c(mean_conversion = mean(X), at_mean_k = 1 - exp(-mean(k) * 30))
The average batch converts 77.0%. But a batch with the average rate constant would convert 79.2%: plugging the average input into the formula overestimates the average output by over 2 percentage points. The reason is that the conversion is a concave function of k: it flattens out as k grows. A fast batch gains less than a slow batch loses, so the variation in k costs conversion on average. That’s Jensen’s inequality, and it’s why engineers simulate their uncertainty instead of plugging in averages.

title: Monte Carlo integration
text:
How precise is it?
A Monte Carlo estimate is a sample mean, so it has a standard error like any other: the Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE),

\text{MCSE} = \frac{s_h}{\sqrt{n}},

where s_h is the standard deviation of the h(X_i), here the conversions. By the central limit theorem, the estimate \pm\, 1.96 \times \text{MCSE} is a 95% confidence interval for the true integral. The \sqrt{n} is the catch: to get one more decimal digit, 10 times more precision, you need 100 times more draws. Here’s the estimate of the average conversion as the simulation runs, with its 95% band:

set.seed(4052)
k <- rlnorm(10000, log(0.05), 0.3)
X <- 1 - exp(-k * 30)
n <- seq_along(X)
running <- data.frame(n = n, estimate = cumsum(X) / n, se = sd(X) / sqrt(n))[n >= 10, ]
ggplot(running, aes(x = n, y = estimate)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = estimate - 1.96 * se, ymax = estimate + 1.96 * se), fill = "#F4C0D1", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.76957339, color = "#3A1F35", linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 2500, y = 0.7615, label = "true value, 0.7696", hjust = 0.5, size = 3.6, color = "#3A1F35") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10, 100, 1000, 10000), labels = c("10", "100", "1,000", "10,000")) +
  labs(x = "Number of simulated batches", y = "Estimated average conversion") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Your turn. Compute the MCSE of the average conversion, and a 95% interval for it.









Divide by the square root of the number of draws, length(X).


set.seed(4052)
k <- rlnorm(10000, log(0.05), 0.3)
X <- 1 - exp(-k * 30)
mcse <- sd(X) / sqrt(length(X))
c(estimate = mean(X), mcse = mcse, lower = mean(X) - 1.96 * mcse, upper = mean(X) + 1.96 * mcse)
An MCSE of 0.001, so the average conversion is between 76.8% and 77.2%. The true value, 76.96% (from careful numerical integration), is inside. For a precision of ±0.05 percentage points, you’d need about 140,000 batches. That’s still quick, but later in this lesson you’ll get there with far fewer.

title: Monte Carlo integration
text:
Rare events: importance sampling
The reactor’s peak pressure during a batch is normal, with a mean of 8.0 bar and an SD of 0.4 bar. Its relief valve opens at 9.8 bar, 4.5 standard deviations above the mean. The safety review needs the probability that a batch lifts the valve:

P(Z > 4.5) = \int_{4.5}^{\infty} \phi(z)\, dz = E\big[\mathbf{1}(Z > 4.5)\big],

where \phi is the standard normal density and \mathbf{1}(\cdot) is 1 when the condition holds and 0 otherwise. Here, pnorm() knows the answer, 3.4 \times 10^{-6}, so we can check our methods. In a real safety study, the peak pressure would come from a simulation of the whole reactor, and there would be no formula.
Plain Monte Carlo is hopeless for rare events. With 100,000 simulated batches, you’d expect a third of one to exceed 4.5. Almost all your draws land where nothing happens.
Importance sampling draws from a different density g that puts more draws where it matters, and corrects with weights:

E_f[h(X)] = \int h(x)\, \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\, g(x)\, dx = E_g\!\left[h(X)\, w(X)\right], \qquad w(x) = \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}.

So draw from g, and average h(x)\,w(x). Here, a good g is a normal centered at the threshold, N(4.5, 1): half its draws exceed 4.5, and each one is weighted down by \phi(x)/\phi(x - 4.5), the ratio of the two densities.
Your turn. Compare plain Monte Carlo with importance sampling, 100,000 draws each.









Center the proposals at the threshold: mean = 4.5.


pnorm(4.5, lower.tail = FALSE)                  # the true value, to compare
set.seed(4053)
z <- rnorm(1e5)
mean(z > 4.5)                                   # plain Monte Carlo
y <- rnorm(1e5, mean = 4.5)                     # draws centered on the rare event
w <- dnorm(y) / dnorm(y, mean = 4.5)            # importance weights f / g
mean((y > 4.5) * w)                             # importance sampling
Plain Monte Carlo found exactly one batch above 4.5, so it estimates 10^{-5}: three times too high, and with another seed it would just as likely say 0. Importance sampling gives 3.3995 \times 10^{-6}, within 0.05% of the truth, from the same number of draws. Its MCSE is 0.7% of the estimate. For the safety review: with 2,000 batches a year, the valve should lift about once every 150 years.










NoteGo deeper: choosing g





The variance of the importance sampling estimate is small when h(x)\,f(x)/g(x) is nearly constant wherever g puts its draws. The ideal g is proportional to |h(x)|\,f(x), but you’d need the answer to normalize it. Good proposals imitate it: here, the normal density beyond 4.5, which an exponential tail starting at 4.5 copies closely (Challenge 2). Two rules of thumb: g must never be zero where h f isn’t, and g’s tails should be at least as heavy as f’s. If g has lighter tails, a rare draw far out gets a huge weight, and the estimate’s variance can be infinite.

title: Monte Carlo integration
text:
Antithetic variates
Monte Carlo estimates get more precise with more draws. They also get more precise with better draws. The rate constant came from a uniform number, through the lognormal quantile function: k = F^{-1}(U). A small U gives a slow batch, and a large U a fast one. Antithetic variates pair each U with its mirror image 1 - U: each pair contains one slow and one fast batch, so their average conversion is close to the overall average. The pairs’ errors partly cancel.
Your turn. Make 5,000 antithetic pairs, and compare the variance of their estimate with the variance of plain Monte Carlo with the same number of conversions, 10,000.









The antithetic partner of u is 1 - u.


set.seed(4054)
u <- runif(5000)
X1 <- 1 - exp(-30 * qlnorm(u, log(0.05), 0.3))
X2 <- 1 - exp(-30 * qlnorm(1 - u, log(0.05), 0.3))     # the mirror-image batches
