pairs <- (X1 + X2) / 2
c(estimate = mean(pairs), var_plain = var(X1) / 10000, var_antithetic = var(pairs) / 5000)
The estimate is 0.7696, almost exactly the true 0.76957, and its variance is 47 times smaller than plain Monte Carlo’s with the same 10,000 conversions. To match it, plain Monte Carlo would need 470,000 draws. The two halves of each pair have a correlation of −0.98. Antithetic variates help whenever the result rises or falls steadily with the uniform number, as it does here.

title: Monte Carlo integration
text:
Control variates
Another trick uses something you already know. The conversion X is strongly correlated with k, and the mean of k is known exactly: for a lognormal, E[k] = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2} = 0.0523. If a simulation’s \bar{k} comes out above 0.0523, its batches were faster than average, so its \bar{X} is probably too high too. The control variate estimate corrects for that:

\hat\theta_{\text{cv}} = \bar{X} - b\,\big(\bar{k} - E[k]\big),

with b the slope of X on k, b = \operatorname{cov}(X, k)/\operatorname{var}(k). Its variance is smaller by a factor of 1/(1 - \rho^2), where \rho is the correlation between X and k.
Your turn. Compute the control variate estimate.









Subtract the known mean, Ek.


set.seed(4055)
k <- rlnorm(10000, log(0.05), 0.3)
X <- 1 - exp(-30 * k)
Ek <- exp(log(0.05) + 0.3^2 / 2)                  # the known mean of k
b <- cov(X, k) / var(k)
X_cv <- X - b * (k - Ek)
c(plain = mean(X), control = mean(X_cv), var_ratio = var(X) / var(X_cv))
The plain estimate is 0.7701, and the control variate estimate 0.7695, closer to the truth, with a variance 10 times smaller. The correlation between X and k is 0.95, and 1/(1 - 0.95^2) = 10.3. Here, the antithetic pairs did even better, but control variates work in situations where antithetic pairs can’t, as long as you know the exact mean of something correlated with the result.

title: Monte Carlo integration
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · In specification on both counts. A batch’s purity is normal with mean 99.1% and SD 0.3%, and its water is normal with mean 150 ppm and SD 25 ppm, with a correlation of −0.6 (wet batches are less pure). A batch is in specification if its purity is at least 98.6% and its water is at most 200 ppm. That’s a two-dimensional integral. Estimate it by simulation, building the correlated pair from two independent normals as in Lesson 4, and compare with mvtnorm::pmvnorm(), which computes such probabilities numerically.









The water limit is 200 ppm.


set.seed(4056)
z1 <- rnorm(20000)
z2 <- rnorm(20000)
purity <- 99.1 + 0.3 * z1
water <- 150 + 25 * (-0.6 * z1 + sqrt(1 - 0.6^2) * z2)    # correlation -0.6 with purity
S <- matrix(c(0.3^2, -0.6 * 0.3 * 25, -0.6 * 0.3 * 25, 25^2), 2)
as.numeric(mvtnorm::pmvnorm(lower = c(98.6, -Inf), upper = c(Inf, 200), mean = c(99.1, 150), sigma = S))
mean(purity >= 98.6 & water <= 200)
93.7% by simulation, and 93.8% numerically. If purity and water were independent, the answer would be 0.952 \times 0.977 = 93.1\%. The negative correlation helps a little: the batches that fail on water tend to be the ones that fail on purity too, so the failures overlap. In ten dimensions, numerical integration struggles, and simulation works just as well as here.




Challenge 2 · A better proposal. The Go deeper box says that the best proposal imitates the target beyond 4.5. The normal tail beyond 4.5 looks very much like an exponential distribution starting at 4.5, with rate 4.5. Use it as the proposal, and compare the relative MCSE (the MCSE divided by the estimate) with the 0.7% of the shifted normal.









The proposal’s rate is 4.5.


set.seed(4057)
y <- 4.5 + rexp(1e5, rate = 4.5)              # every draw is beyond 4.5
w <- dnorm(y) / dexp(y - 4.5, rate = 4.5)
c(estimate = mean(w), relative_mcse = sd(w) / sqrt(1e5) / mean(w))
3.3967 \times 10^{-6}, with a relative MCSE of 0.027%, which is 26 times smaller than the shifted normal’s, so it’s worth about 700 times as many draws. Every draw lands in the region that matters, and the weights hardly vary, because the proposal is shaped almost exactly like the target. (There’s no need for (y > 4.5) here: it’s always true.)

title: Monte Carlo integration
text:
Quick quiz

1. How does Monte Carlo estimate \int h(x) f(x)\,dx, where f is a density?

By evaluating h on a fine grid
By averaging h(X_i) over many random draws X_i from f
By drawing from h


The law of large numbers makes the average converge to the expectation.



2. A Monte Carlo estimate has an MCSE of 0.004 with 10,000 draws. How many draws would give an MCSE of 0.001?

40,000
160,000
1,000,000


The MCSE shrinks like 1/\sqrt{n}: four times smaller needs 16 times the draws.



3. The conversion of the batch with the average rate constant is 79.2%, but the average conversion is 77.0%. Why?

Simulation error
The conversion is a concave function of k, so the variation in k lowers the average conversion
The rate constants aren’t normal


Jensen’s inequality: for a concave function, the average of the outputs is below the output at the average.



4. Why does plain Monte Carlo struggle with a probability of 10^{-6}?

Because the random numbers aren’t random enough
Because almost no draws land in the rare region, so the estimate is usually 0 or wildly off
Because the MCSE formula doesn’t apply


Its relative error is about 1/\sqrt{np}, which needs n in the hundreds of millions for p = 10^{-6}.



5. In importance sampling with proposal density g, what weight does each draw get?

g(x)/f(x)
f(x)/g(x)
1


Draws where g is generous compared with f are weighted down.



6. When do antithetic variates help most?

When the result doesn’t depend on the random numbers
When the result rises or falls steadily with the underlying uniform number, so that U and 1 - U give negatively correlated results
When the sample size is small


Here, the two halves of each pair had a correlation of −0.98, and the variance dropped 47-fold.

title: Monte Carlo integration
text:
Wrap-up
You can now compute integrals with dice, and know how far to trust them. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Monte Carlo integration: an integral written as an expectation, E[h(X)], is estimated by the average of h(X_i) over random draws.
The Monte Carlo standard error, s_h/\sqrt{n}, measures the precision. Each extra digit costs 100 times more draws.
Jensen’s inequality: the average batch converts 77.0%, not the 79.2% of a batch with the average rate constant. Simulate the uncertainty; don’t plug in averages.
Importance sampling draws from a proposal g and weights by f/g. It turned a hopeless one-in-a-million estimate into one with a 0.7% error, and 0.03% with a proposal shaped like the target.
Antithetic variates pair U with 1 - U, and cut the variance 47-fold here.
Control variates correct with a correlated quantity whose mean is known, and cut it 10-fold.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)






Longer reactions. Repeat the average-conversion simulation for reaction times of 10, 30, 60 and 120 minutes. Does the gap between the average conversion and the conversion at the average k grow or shrink? Why? (Hint: think about the curvature of 1 - e^{-kt} at each time.)
Both tricks at once. Combine antithetic pairs with the control variate k. Is the variance smaller than with either trick alone?
A bad proposal. Redo the relief-valve estimate with the proposal N(6, 0.5), centered too far out and too narrow. Look at the largest weights with sort(w, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5], and at the estimate. What goes wrong?
π by darts. Estimate \pi as four times the share of uniform points in the unit square that land inside the quarter circle x^2 + y^2 \le 1. How many points do you need for 3 correct decimals? Check your answer against the MCSE formula.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Monte Carlo integration

Estimating an integral or expected value by averaging a function over random draws.

Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE)

The standard error of a Monte Carlo estimate, s_h/\sqrt{n} for an average of n independent draws.

Jensen’s inequality

For a concave function h, E[h(X)] \le h(E[X]), and the reverse for a convex one.

Importance sampling

Estimating an expectation under f from draws from another density g, weighting each draw by f/g.

Variance reduction

Methods that make a Monte Carlo estimate more precise without more draws.

Antithetic variates

Pairing each random draw with a negatively correlated partner, such as U with 1 - U.

Control variate

A quantity with a known mean, correlated with the result, used to correct the estimate.











NoteWant to read more?






Roger Peng, Advanced Statistical Computing, section 6.4, “Importance sampling”. The method, its properties, and an example from Bayesian statistics.
Art Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, free online. Chapters 2 (simple Monte Carlo), 8 (variance reduction) and 9 (importance sampling) go much deeper, with many examples.
Christian Robert and George Casella, Introducing Monte Carlo Methods with R (Springer, 2010). Chapters 3 and 4 cover Monte Carlo integration and its precision, with R code. Not free.

title: Random number generation
text:
Module 4 · Lesson 3 of 14 Week 63 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The plant has 36 pumps, and their mechanical seals fail at unpredictable times. The maintenance team wants to know how many spare seals to keep in stock: too few, and a pump waits days for a part; too many, and money sits on a shelf. The usual way to answer questions like that is simulation: imagine thousands of years of seal failures, and count how often the stock runs out.
Every simulation starts from random numbers. But a computer follows its instructions exactly, and does the same thing every time. So where do its random numbers come from? This lesson opens up the generator, and then shows how to turn its numbers into the random failure times and demands that a simulation needs.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Random number generation
text:
Pseudo-random numbers
Computers make pseudo-random numbers: numbers that come from a fixed formula, but look random. The oldest widely used formula is the linear congruential generator (LCG). Start from a whole number x_0, the seed, and repeat

x_{n+1} = (a\,x_n + c) \bmod m,

where “mod m” means the remainder after dividing by m (R’s %%). Every x_n is a whole number from 0 to m - 1, and u_n = x_n/m is a number between 0 and 1. With well-chosen constants, the u_n look like independent draws from the uniform distribution.
There are only m possible values, so the sequence must eventually repeat, and from then on it repeats forever. The length of the cycle is the generator’s period.










Your turn. Write a tiny LCG with a = 5, c = 3 and m = 16, and generate 20 numbers from the seed 1.









Take the remainder after dividing by m.


lcg <- function(n, seed, a = 5, c = 3, m = 16) {
  x <- numeric(n)
  for (i in 1:n) {
    seed <- (a * seed + c) %% m
    x[i] <- seed
  }
  x
}
lcg(20, seed = 1)
8, 11, 10, 5, 12, … : it looks patternless, and it visits every number from 0 to 15 once. Then, at the 17th number, it starts again: 8, 11, 10, 5. The period is 16, the longest possible with m = 16. Real LCGs use m = 2^{31} or more, so their period is billions of numbers long, but they still repeat in the end.

title: Random number generation
text:
A famous bad generator
In the 1960s, IBM’s computers shipped with an LCG called RANDU: a = 65539, c = 0 and m = 2^{31}. It was fast, and its numbers passed the usual tests. It was used for years, in thousands of scientific studies. Then people noticed that it has a fatal flaw. Because 65539 = 2^{16} + 3, every three consecutive numbers satisfy

9\,u_n - 6\,u_{n+1} + u_{n+2} = \text{a whole number}.

So if you plot the triples (u_n, u_{n+1}, u_{n+2}) as points in a cube, they don’t fill it: they all lie on just 15 parallel planes, with nothing in between. Any simulation in three or more dimensions, such as a particle moving in space, was quietly wrong.
Your turn. The setup code has a randu() function. Generate 3,002 numbers and compute the combination for 3,000 triples. How many different values does it take?









The combination is 9u_n - 6u_{n+1} + u_{n+2}.


u <- randu(3002)
k <- 9 * u[1:3000] - 6 * u[2:3001] + u[3:3002]
table(round(k, 6))
Only 15 values, the whole numbers from −5 to 9: one for each plane. A good generator would give 3,000 different values, spread over the range from −6 to 10.




Here’s the same combination for RANDU and for R’s own generator, plotted against u_n:

u <- randu(3002)
set.seed(4032)
v <- runif(3002)
triples <- rbind(
  data.frame(generator = "RANDU", u1 = u[1:3000], k = 9 * u[1:3000] - 6 * u[2:3001] + u[3:3002]),
  data.frame(generator = "R's Mersenne Twister", u1 = v[1:3000], k = 9 * v[1:3000] - 6 * v[2:3001] + v[3:3002])
)
triples$generator <- factor(triples$generator, levels = c("RANDU", "R's Mersenne Twister"))
ggplot(triples, aes(x = u1, y = k)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.35, alpha = 0.6, color = "#3A1F35") +
  facet_wrap(~ generator) +
  labs(x = expression(u[n]), y = expression(9*u[n] - 6*u[n+1] + u[n+2])) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The lesson: a generator can look fine in one dimension and be badly wrong in three. All LCGs have some such structure, which is why modern software uses better generators.

title: Random number generation
text:
Seeds and R’s generator
R’s default generator is the Mersenne Twister, from 1998. It’s still deterministic, but its period is 2^{19937} - 1, a number with 6,002 digits, and its output passes almost every test of randomness that’s been invented. You can see what R is using:

RNGkind()
#> [1] "Mersenne-Twister" "Inversion"        "Rejection"

The three parts are the uniform generator, the method for normal numbers (Lesson 4.4 has more about that), and the method sample() uses.
Because the generator is deterministic, the same seed always gives the same numbers. set.seed() sets it. That’s what makes a simulation reproducible: anyone who runs your code with your seed gets exactly your results. Set the seed once, at the start, and then let the generator run.
The classic seed bug is to set it in the wrong place. Here’s a function that simulates the mean of 10 measurements, with the seed set inside it:

one_batch <- function() {
  set.seed(1)
  mean(rnorm(10))
}
replicate(5, one_batch())
#> [1] 0.1322028 0.1322028 0.1322028 0.1322028 0.1322028

Five “random” means, all identical: each call restarts the generator from the same place. A simulation study written this way would report a standard error of zero.
Your turn. Fix it: take set.seed() out of the function, and set the seed once, to 2026, before the simulation.









set.seed(2026).


one_batch <- function() mean(rnorm(10))
set.seed(2026)
replicate(5, one_batch())
Five different means, and run it again and you get the same five: reproducible and random. The simulation continues the generator’s stream from one call to the next, as it should.

title: Random number generation
text:
Testing randomness
How do you know a generator’s numbers look random? You test them, as you’d test any hypothesis. If the numbers are uniform, then about a tenth of them should fall between 0 and 0.1, a tenth between 0.1 and 0.2, and so on. The chi-square goodness-of-fit test compares the counts in each bin with the expected counts, here 100 per bin for 1,000 numbers:

\chi^2 = \sum_{\text{bins}} \frac{(\text{observed} - \text{expected})^2}{\text{expected}},

with 9 degrees of freedom for 10 bins. A tiny p-value says the numbers don’t look uniform.
Your turn. Test 1,000 numbers from R’s generator, with 10 equal bins.









Ten equal bins between 0 and 1 are 0.1 wide.


set.seed(4031)
u <- runif(1000)
counts <- table(cut(u, breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.1)))
counts
chisq.test(counts)$p.value
The counts run from 84 to 115, and the p-value is 0.35: no evidence against uniformity. But RANDU passes this test too (with 10,000 numbers, its p-value is 0.45), because its flaw is in the triples, not in the single numbers. So generators are checked with batteries of hundreds of tests, looking at pairs, triples, gaps, runs and more. The Mersenne Twister passes nearly all of them, and RANDU fails many.

title: Random number generation
text:
The inverse-transform method
Generators make uniform numbers between 0 and 1. A simulation needs other distributions: seal lifetimes, demands, measurement errors. The simplest way to convert is the inverse-transform method: if U is uniform on (0, 1) and F is a continuous cumulative distribution function (CDF), then

X = F^{-1}(U)

has the CDF F. In words: pick a random height on the CDF’s vertical axis, and read off the value on the horizontal axis where the CDF reaches that height. Values where the CDF rises steeply, where the density is high, catch the most heights.






NoteGo deeper: why it works





F is increasing, so F^{-1}(U) \le x exactly when U \le F(x). Therefore

P(X \le x) = P\big(F^{-1}(U) \le x\big) = P\big(U \le F(x)\big) = F(x),

because P(U \le t) = t for a uniform U. So X has the CDF F. The reverse is true as well: if X has a continuous CDF F, then F(X) is uniform. That’s the probability integral transform, and it’s behind Q-Q plots and many goodness-of-fit tests.



Seal lifetimes are often described by the Weibull distribution, whose CDF is

F(x) = 1 - \exp\!\left[-\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^{k}\right], \qquad x > 0,

with a scale \lambda and a shape k. A shape above 1 means that seals wear out: the older a seal, the more likely it is to fail soon. Solving u = F(x) for x gives x = \lambda\,[-\log(1 - u)]^{1/k}. And since 1 - U is uniform whenever U is, \lambda\,[-\log U]^{1/k} works just as well.
Your turn. On the test rig, seal lifetimes follow a Weibull distribution with shape 2.3 and scale 480 hours. Generate five lifetimes by the inverse-transform method, and compare them with R’s rweibull() from the same seed.









The exponent is one over the shape: 1 / shape.


shape <- 2.3
scale <- 480      # hours
set.seed(42)
mine <- scale * (-log(runif(5)))^(1 / shape)
set.seed(42)
theirs <- rweibull(5, shape, scale)
rbind(mine, theirs)
Identical, to the last digit: 168, 146, 529, 231 and 337 hours. That’s because R’s rweibull() is the inverse-transform method, with exactly this formula. Many of R’s random number functions are just a uniform generator plus a clever transformation.




Here are 10,000 lifetimes made the same way, with the Weibull density on top:

set.seed(42)
lifetimes <- data.frame(hours = 480 * (-log(runif(10000)))^(1 / 2.3))
ggplot(lifetimes, aes(x = hours)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 40, boundary = 0, fill = "#F4C0D1", color = "white") +
  stat_function(fun = dweibull, args = list(shape = 2.3, scale = 480), color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Seal lifetime (hours)", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: Random number generation
text:
Discrete distributions
The inverse-transform method works for discrete distributions too. From the plant’s maintenance records, the number of seals needed in a month has this distribution:



Seals needed
0
1
2
3
4




Probability
0.30
0.36
0.22
0.09
0.03


Cumulative
0.30
0.66
0.88
0.97
1.00



Divide the interval from 0 to 1 into pieces with these lengths. A uniform number u below 0.30 means 0 seals, between 0.30 and 0.66 means 1 seal, and so on. In other words, the number of seals is how many cumulative probabilities are at or below u. R’s findInterval(u, breaks) counts exactly that, for a whole vector of u at once.
Your turn. Simulate 10,000 months of seal demand, and compare the proportions with the probabilities.









The breaks are the cumulative probabilities, cumsum(p).


p <- c(0.30, 0.36, 0.22, 0.09, 0.03)     # P(0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 seals)
set.seed(7)
u <- runif(10000)
seals <- findInterval(u, cumsum(p))
round(table(seals) / 10000, 3)
0.301, 0.358, 0.220, 0.088 and 0.033: all within a percentage point of the probabilities, as they should be with 10,000 months. sample(0:4, 10000, replace = TRUE, prob = p) does the same job.

title: Random number generation
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · How many spare seals? The spare seals are ordered once a year. Simulate 10,000 years, each of 12 months, and estimate the chance that a stock of 20 seals isn’t enough.









Each simulated year has 12 months, so it needs runif(12).


p <- c(0.30, 0.36, 0.22, 0.09, 0.03)
set.seed(12)
yearly <- replicate(10000, sum(findInterval(runif(12), cumsum(p))))
mean(yearly)              # the average number of seals needed in a year
mean(yearly > 20)         # the chance that 20 seals aren't enough
A year needs 14.3 seals on average (the exact mean is 12 \times 1.19 = 14.28). But a stock of 14 would run out almost half the time. With 20 seals, the chance of running out is 5.0%, and with 22, it’s 1.5%. The team can now choose its risk. How precise is that 5.0%? Lesson 5 shows how to put an error bar on a simulation result.




Challenge 2 · A triangular distribution. Engineers often describe an uncertain quantity with three numbers: the lowest, the most likely and the highest value. The next plant turnaround will take between 10 and 18 days, most likely 12. That’s a triangular distribution, whose density rises in a straight line from 10 to 12, and falls in a straight line to 18. Its CDF reaches F_m = (12 - 10)/(18 - 10) = 0.25 at the mode, and inverting it gives

x = \begin{cases} \text{lo} + \sqrt{u\,(\text{hi} - \text{lo})(\text{mode} - \text{lo})} & \text{if } u < F_m, \\ \text{hi} - \sqrt{(1 - u)(\text{hi} - \text{lo})(\text{hi} - \text{mode})} & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}

Complete the generator, and estimate the mean duration and the chance that the turnaround takes more than 15 days.









The last factor is hi - mode.


lo <- 10; mode <- 12; hi <- 18
r_triangle <- function(n) {
  u <- runif(n)
  Fm <- (mode - lo) / (hi - lo)
  ifelse(u < Fm,
         lo + sqrt(u * (hi - lo) * (mode - lo)),
         hi - sqrt((1 - u) * (hi - lo) * (hi - mode)))
}
set.seed(11)
x <- r_triangle(10000)
c(mean = mean(x), more_than_15 = mean(x > 15))
A mean of 13.36 days (the exact mean is (10 + 12 + 18)/3 = 13.33), and an 18.5% chance of more than 15 days (exactly 3^2/(8 \times 6) = 0.1875). The mean is well above the most likely value, 12 days, because the long tail toward 18 pulls it up. Plans built on the “most likely” duration run late more often than not.

title: Random number generation
text:
Quick quiz

1. What’s a pseudo-random number generator?

A device that measures physical noise
A deterministic formula whose output looks random, and which repeats exactly from the same seed
A list of random numbers stored in R


Deterministic is the point: it’s what makes simulations reproducible.



2. A function sets set.seed(1) and then simulates. What happens when you call it 1,000 times in a simulation?

You get 1,000 different results
You get the same result 1,000 times
R gives an error


Each call restarts the generator from the same seed. Set the seed once, outside.



3. What was wrong with RANDU?

Its numbers weren’t uniform
Its period was only 16
Consecutive triples of its numbers lie on just 15 planes


It passed one-dimensional tests. Its flaw only shows up when you look at several numbers together.



4. 1,000 numbers pass a chi-square test of uniformity, with a p-value of 0.35. What can you conclude?

The generator is good
These numbers show no evidence of non-uniformity, which says nothing about other kinds of patterns
The generator is bad


That’s why generators are tested with batteries of many different tests.



5. If U is uniform on (0, 1), what is the distribution of F^{-1}(U)?

Uniform
The distribution whose CDF is F
Normal


That’s the inverse-transform method: P(F^{-1}(U) \le x) = P(U \le F(x)) = F(x).



6. The exponential distribution has CDF F(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}. Which formula generates it from a uniform U?

e^{-\lambda U}
-\log(1 - U)/\lambda
\lambda U


Solve u = 1 - e^{-\lambda x} for x. Since 1 - U is uniform too, -\log(U)/\lambda works as well. It’s a Weibull with shape 1.

title: Random number generation
text:
Wrap-up
You can now make the random numbers a simulation needs. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Pseudo-random numbers come from deterministic formulas, such as the linear congruential generator x_{n+1} = (a x_n + c) \bmod m. They repeat after their period.
RANDU shows that a generator can look random one number at a time and still be badly patterned: its triples fall on 15 planes. R’s default, the Mersenne Twister, has a period of 2^{19937} - 1 and passes nearly every test.
Seeds make simulations reproducible. Set the seed once, at the start, never inside a function that’s called repeatedly.
Testing randomness is hypothesis testing: a chi-square test checks uniformity, but no single test can prove a generator good.
The inverse-transform method, X = F^{-1}(U), turns uniform numbers into any distribution whose CDF you can invert. R’s rweibull() is exactly this.
Discrete distributions by inversion: findInterval(u, cumsum(p)). A stock of 20 seals runs out in about 5% of years.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)






See RANDU’s planes in 3D. Install plotly, make 10,000 RANDU triples, and plot them with plotly::plot_ly(x = u1, y = u2, z = u3, type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers", marker = list(size = 1)). Rotate the cube with the mouse until the 15 planes appear. Do the same with runif().
Other generators. Run RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG"), then set.seed(1); runif(3). Compare with the default generator’s set.seed(1); runif(3). Switch back with RNGkind("default"). (L’Ecuyer’s generator is the one used for parallel simulations, because it can split into many independent streams.)
Exponential failures. Generate 10,000 exponential lifetimes with rate 0.002 per hour by inversion, and compare them with rexp(10000, 0.002) in a Q-Q plot (qqplot()). Are the numbers identical, as with rweibull()? (R’s rexp() uses a different algorithm.)
An older plant. At an older plant, the monthly demand is 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 seals with probabilities 0.20, 0.30, 0.30, 0.15 and 0.05. How many seals should it stock to keep the chance of running out below 5%?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Pseudo-random numbers

Numbers produced by a deterministic formula that look like independent random draws.

Seed

The starting value of a pseudo-random number generator. The same seed gives the same sequence.

Linear congruential generator

A generator of the form x_{n+1} = (a x_n + c) \bmod m.

Period

The length of a generator’s cycle, after which its sequence repeats.

Mersenne Twister

R’s default generator, with a period of 2^{19937} - 1.

Inverse-transform method

Generating a random variable as F^{-1}(U), where U is uniform and F is the target CDF.

Weibull distribution

A distribution for lifetimes, with a scale and a shape. A shape above 1 means wear-out failures.











NoteWant to read more?






Roger Peng, Advanced Statistical Computing, sections 6.1, “Random number generation” and 6.2, “Non-uniform random numbers”. Linear congruential generators and the inverse-transform method, briefly and clearly.
R’s help page for random number generation, ?Random. The generators R offers, and how set.seed() works.
Luc Devroye, Non-Uniform Random Variate Generation (1986), free online. The encyclopedia of methods for turning uniform numbers into everything else.

title: Efficient and reliable R
text:
Module 4 · Lesson 1 of 14 Week 61 of 160 About 5–7 hours
So far in this course, you’ve mostly called functions that other people wrote: lm(), t.test(), manova(). This module opens them up. You’ll generate random numbers, simulate, resample, optimize, and draw samples from distributions that have no formula, and you’ll write the algorithms yourself. Statisticians call this statistical computing, and it’s what you reach for when the formulas run out.
Writing your own algorithms means writing code that runs fast enough, and that gives answers you can trust. This lesson is about both. The data come from reactor R3’s historian, the plant’s database of sensor readings, which logs the reactor temperature once a minute. All of 2026 is 525,600 readings:
length(temp_C)
#> [1] 525600
round(temp_C[1:8], 2)
#> [1] 183.65 183.75 183.90 183.78 183.84 183.80 183.81 183.68
Dana, the process engineer, wants three things from them: the reaction’s rate constant at every minute, a smoothed temperature for the control chart, and a summary for each month.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Efficient and reliable R
text:
Loops and vectors
The rate constant follows the Arrhenius equation from Lesson 2.9:

k = A \exp\!\left(-\frac{E_a}{RT}\right),

with the temperature T in kelvin. For this reaction, A = 1.1 \times 10^8 per minute and E_a = 82{,}000 J/mol, so at 185 °C, k is about 0.049 per minute.
You could compute k with a loop, one reading at a time. In most languages, that’s the natural way. In R, it’s slow, because R is an interpreted language: for every pass through the loop, R reads the code again, looks up every name, checks every type, and calls exp() for a single number. Do that 525,600 times and it adds up.
The alternative is vectorized code: write the formula once for the whole vector, temp_C + 273.15, and R hands all 525,600 numbers to its compiled C code in one call. Arithmetic, exp(), log(), comparisons and most of R’s math functions work this way.











Your turn. The setup code has loaded the year’s readings as temp_C, with n = 525,600. The code below computes k with a loop, and times it with system.time(). Fill in the vectorized version, and compare the times.









Use the whole vector, temp_C, where the loop used one element, temp_C[i].


A <- 1.1e8       # pre-exponential factor, per minute
Ea <- 82000      # activation energy, J/mol
R <- 8.314       # gas constant, J/(mol K)
loop_time <- system.time({
  k_loop <- numeric(n)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) k_loop[i] <- A * exp(-Ea / (R * (temp_C[i] + 273.15)))
})
vector_time <- system.time({
  k <- A * exp(-Ea / (R * (temp_C + 273.15)))
})
summary(k)
c(loop = loop_time[["elapsed"]], vector = vector_time[["elapsed"]])
The elapsed time is the wall-clock time in seconds. In the browser, the loop takes most of a second and the vector a few thousandths: a hundred times faster or more. (Your computer’s R runs loops faster than the browser’s does, but the vector still wins easily.)
Now look at the summary. The median, 0.049 per minute, is what you’d expect at 185 °C. But the maximum is about 300 million, and it has dragged the mean up to over a thousand. Something in the data is badly wrong. Hold that thought: you’ll find it later in this lesson.

title: Efficient and reliable R
section: When a loop is the only way
text:
When a loop is the only way
Some calculations can’t be written as one formula for the whole vector, because each step needs the result of the step before. The smoothed temperature for Dana’s control chart is one of them. It’s an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA): each smoothed value is a weighted average of the new reading and the previous smoothed value,

z_t = \lambda x_t + (1 - \lambda) z_{t-1},

with a small weight such as \lambda = 0.05. So z_t remembers the recent past, and the minute-to-minute noise averages out.
A loop is fine here, as long as you avoid one trap: growing a vector. Code like z <- c(z, new_value) makes R allocate a new, longer vector and copy everything into it, every single time. With 20,000 values, on a typical computer:

system.time({ z <- c(); for (i in 1:20000) z <- c(z, temp_C[i]) })[["elapsed"]]
#> [1] 0.41
system.time({ z <- numeric(20000); for (i in 1:20000) z[i] <- temp_C[i] })[["elapsed"]]
#> [1] 0

The second loop preallocates: it creates the full-length vector first with numeric(), and then fills it in place. It’s so fast that system.time() can hardly measure it, and the gap grows with the length, because the copying in the first loop grows like the square of the length. For a whole year of readings, growing the vector would take minutes instead of a fraction of a second.






NoteGo deeper: why growing a vector is so slow





To add value number i, c(z, new_value) copies the i - 1 values already in z. Over n values, that’s

0 + 1 + 2 + \cdots + (n - 1) = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}

copies: about 200 million for n = 20{,}000, and 138 billion for a year of readings. The preallocated loop copies nothing. The total work of the first grows like n^2, and of the second like n: computer scientists write these as O(n^2) and O(n). Doubling n doubles the time of an O(n) algorithm, and quadruples the time of an O(n^2) one.



Your turn. Compute the EWMA of the whole year with a loop. Preallocate the vector ewma with the right length.









The vector needs one value for every reading: numeric(n).


lambda <- 0.05
ewma <- numeric(n)
ewma[1] <- temp_C[1]
for (i in 2:n) ewma[i] <- lambda * temp_C[i] + (1 - lambda) * ewma[i - 1]
round(tail(ewma), 2)
The year ends with a smoothed temperature of about 184.4 °C. The loop runs 525,600 times, but each pass only does a little arithmetic and writes one number into a vector that already exists, so it finishes in about a second, even in the browser.




Better still: someone may already have written your loop in C. The EWMA is a recursive filter, and base R’s stats::filter() runs recursive filters in compiled code. With method = "recursive", it computes y_t = x_t + f\,y_{t-1}, which is the EWMA when x_t is \lambda times the reading and f = 1 - \lambda.
Your turn. Compute the same EWMA with stats::filter(). The init argument sets the value before the first reading, so that the first smoothed value is the first reading.









The method is "recursive".


lambda <- 0.05
ewma2 <- stats::filter(lambda * temp_C, 1 - lambda, method = "recursive", init = temp_C[1])
ewma2 <- as.numeric(ewma2)
round(tail(ewma2), 2)
The same numbers as your loop, in a few thousandths of a second. Before writing a loop, it’s worth a quick search for a function that already does it: cumsum(), cumprod(), diff(), stats::filter() and rle() are all loops written in C.




Here’s one day of readings, January 2nd, with the EWMA:

ewma_static <- as.numeric(stats::filter(0.05 * temp_C, 0.95, method = "recursive", init = temp_C[1]))
one_day <- data.frame(hour = (0:1439) / 60, reading = temp_C[1441:2880], smoothed = ewma_static[1441:2880])
ggplot(one_day, aes(x = hour)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = reading), color = "grey65", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = smoothed), color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.3, y = max(one_day$reading) + 0.25, label = "readings", hjust = 0, color = "grey40", size = 3.6) +
  annotate("text", x = 18.5, y = one_day$smoothed[18.5 * 60] + 0.7, label = "EWMA", hjust = 0, color = "#C2416C", size = 3.6, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 6)) +
  labs(x = "Hour of January 2nd", y = "Temperature (°C)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The temperature drifts by several degrees over the day, as the cooling water warms and cools and the controller doesn’t quite keep up. The EWMA follows the drift without the noise, a few minutes behind.

title: Efficient and reliable R
text:
Timing code: benchmarks
system.time() times one run, and a single run is noisy: your computer is doing other things, too. Benchmarking runs code many times and summarizes the times. The bench package’s bench::mark() does that, and two more useful things: it checks that every version gives the same answer, and it reports how much memory each one allocated.
Dana wants the mean temperature of each day. tapply(temp_C, day, mean) does it, by splitting the vector into 365 groups. But this data has a special structure: every day has exactly 1,440 readings. So matrix(temp_C, nrow = 1440) puts each day in its own column, without copying anything into groups, and colMeans() averages the columns in compiled code.
Your turn. Benchmark the two ways. as.numeric() drops the names that tapply() adds, so that bench::mark() can compare the answers.









Each column holds one day: nrow = 1440.


bench::mark(
  tapply = as.numeric(tapply(temp_C, day, mean)),
  matrix = colMeans(matrix(temp_C, nrow = 1440)),
  min_iterations = 5
)
The median column is the typical time. The matrix version is about 8 times faster in the browser, and more than 10 times faster in RStudio, because tapply() copies every reading into its group. In RStudio, the mem_alloc column shows the memory each version allocated: about 22 MB against 4 MB. (The browser’s R can’t measure memory, so there it shows NA.) If you put nrow = 60 instead, bench::mark() stops with an error: the answers wouldn’t match, which is exactly the check you want before trusting a faster version.

title: Efficient and reliable R
text:
Finding the slow part: profiling
In a long analysis, you rarely know which part is slow, and guesses are often wrong. A profiler finds out. While your code runs, R’s profiler, Rprof(), stops it every few milliseconds and writes down which functions are running. Afterwards, summaryRprof() adds up where the time went.
Here’s a function that computes Dana’s daily report, with three steps: the rate constants (with a loop), the daily means of k (with tapply()), and the EWMA (with stats::filter()). The profiler shows what share of the time each step takes:

rate_loop <- function(temp_C) {
  k <- numeric(length(temp_C))
  for (i in seq_along(temp_C)) k[i] <- 1.1e8 * exp(-82000 / (8.314 * (temp_C[i] + 273.15)))
  k
}
daily_means <- function(x) tapply(x, day, mean)
smooth_temp <- function(x) stats::filter(0.05 * x, 0.95, method = "recursive", init = x[1])
daily_report <- function(temp_C) {
  k <- rate_loop(temp_C)
  list(daily_k = daily_means(k), smooth = smooth_temp(temp_C))
}

prof_file <- tempfile()
Rprof(prof_file, interval = 0.005)
for (run in 1:20) report <- daily_report(temp_C)
Rprof(NULL)
prof <- summaryRprof(prof_file)$by.total
rownames(prof) <- gsub('"', "", rownames(prof))     # the names come with quotes around them
prof[c("rate_loop", "daily_means", "smooth_temp"), c("total.time", "total.pct")]
#>             total.time total.pct
#> rate_loop        0.305     53.04
#> daily_means      0.155     26.96
#> smooth_temp      0.115     20.00

The loop takes the biggest share, about half the time, so that’s the step to fix first: it’s the one-line change you made in the first exercise. That’s the profiler’s lesson in general: measure first, then speed up the part that matters.
The browser’s R can’t run Rprof(), so the profiler is for RStudio. There, the profvis package draws the profile as an interactive chart, line by line: you’ll try it in the practice section.

title: Efficient and reliable R
text:
How much memory?
R keeps all your data in memory. A number stored as a double (R’s usual numeric type) takes 8 bytes, so a year of readings from one sensor takes about 4 megabytes:

format(object.size(temp_C), units = "MB")
#> [1] "4 Mb"

The type matters. An integer takes 4 bytes, half as much. Text takes much more. Here’s one month of timestamps, stored as date-times and as text:

stamps <- as.POSIXct("2026-01-01", tz = "UTC") + 60 * (0:44639)
format(object.size(stamps), units = "MB")
#> [1] "0.3 Mb"
format(object.size(format(stamps, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")), units = "MB")
#> [1] "3.7 Mb"

The text takes about ten times more memory on a typical (64-bit) computer, because R stores each distinct string separately, with some overhead. Store dates as dates and categories as factors, not as text.
Your turn. The plant’s historian records 2,000 sensors, or “tags”: temperatures, pressures, flows and levels. How many gigabytes would a year of all of them take, as doubles?









Multiply by the number of tags, 2000.


bytes <- as.numeric(object.size(temp_C))
bytes / 1e6                  # megabytes for one tag, for one year
bytes * 2000 / 1e9           # gigabytes for all the tags
About 8.4 GB. A typical laptop has 8 to 16 GB of memory, which R shares with everything else. And many calculations make temporary copies, so in practice R needs two or three times the size of the data. A year of the whole historian won’t fit.




When the data don’t fit, don’t load them all. The usual strategies:

Load only what you need. readr::read_csv(..., col_select = ...) reads just some columns. A database query (Lessons 1.7 and 1.8) or a Parquet file (Lesson 1.9) can hand you just the rows and columns you ask for.
Summarize early. Hourly means of 2,000 tags for a year are 17.5 million numbers instead of a billion. Many questions only need the summary.
Work in pieces. Process one month, or one tag, at a time, and keep only the results.
Use tools built for it. The arrow and duckdb packages query files much bigger than memory, with dplyr code that you already know.

title: Efficient and reliable R
section: Applying a function to every piece
text:
Applying a function to every piece
A common pattern is split, apply, combine: split the data into pieces, apply a function to each piece, and combine the results. You’ve done it with group_by() and summarize(). Base R does it with split(), which makes a list with one element per group, and the apply family of functions, which run a function on every element of a list. It’s an example of functional programming: passing a function, such as max, as an argument to another function.
vapply() is the safest member of the family: you tell it what each result should look like, such as numeric(1) (one number), and it stops with an error if one of them doesn’t. sapply() guesses instead, and sometimes guesses wrong.
Your turn. Find the lowest temperature of each month.









Pass the function min, without parentheses.


monthly_min <- vapply(split(temp_C, month), min, numeric(1))
round(monthly_min, 1)
Found it! Ten months bottom out around 180 °C, but March and July have a reading of −9999 °C, colder than absolute zero. That’s the historian’s code for a sensor fault: a minute when it had no valid reading. Two fake readings out of 525,600 were enough to wreck the mean rate constant in the first exercise, because k at −9999 °C is about 300 million.

title: Efficient and reliable R
text:
Functions you can trust
The rate-constant formula didn’t complain about −9999 °C. It just returned a number, and the number was nonsense. Reliable code fails loudly instead: a function should check that its inputs make sense, and stop with a clear message if they don’t. stopifnot() is the quickest way. It stops unless every condition you give it is TRUE.
Should the function stop for a missing value, NA? Here, no. A missing reading should give a missing rate constant, not stop a whole year’s calculation. That’s what na.rm = TRUE inside all() allows.
Your turn. Make rate_constant() refuse temperatures at or below absolute zero, −273.15 °C.









Every temperature must be above -273.15.


rate_constant <- function(temp_C, A = 1.1e8, Ea = 82000) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(temp_C), all(temp_C > -273.15, na.rm = TRUE))
  A * exp(-Ea / (8.314 * (temp_C + 273.15)))
}
rate_constant(185)
0.0492 per minute at 185 °C. Now try rate_constant(temp_C): it stops with “all(temp_C > -273.15, na.rm = TRUE) is not TRUE”. The real fix is in the data. Mark the faults as missing with temp_C[temp_C == -9999] <- NA, and then rate_constant(temp_C) works, with NA for the two faulty minutes, and mean(k, na.rm = TRUE) is 0.0494 per minute.




Input checks are one habit of reliable code. Three more:

Test your functions on cases where you know the answer. Here, k at 185 °C should be 0.049. In RStudio, the testthat package turns such checks into tests that run with one click.
Set the seed whenever your code uses random numbers (Lesson 3), so that the results can be reproduced.
Keep the raw data raw. Fix problems in code, such as the line that turns −9999 into NA, so that every change is written down.

title: Efficient and reliable R
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · A grid of rate constants. The activation energy isn’t known exactly: it might be anywhere from 78 to 86 kJ/mol. outer(x, y, f) applies a vectorized function f to every combination of the values in x and y, and returns a matrix. Compute k for every combination of seven temperatures and three activation energies.









Inside the function, the temperature is called T.


temps <- seq(170, 200, by = 5)
Eas <- c(78000, 82000, 86000)
grid <- outer(temps, Eas, function(T, E) 1.1e8 * exp(-E / (8.314 * (T + 273.15))))
dimnames(grid) <- list(temp_C = temps, Ea = Eas)
signif(grid, 3)
At 185 °C, k is 0.141 per minute if E_a is 78 kJ/mol, and 0.0172 if it’s 86 kJ/mol: an 8-fold range from an uncertainty of 5% either way in E_a. outer() passed it all 21 combinations at once, as two vectors, so the function ran just once.




Challenge 2 · The longest excursion. The alarm sounds when the temperature goes above 188 °C. What’s the longest stretch of consecutive minutes above it? It looks like a job for a loop, but rle() (run-length encoding) does it in C: it turns a vector into runs of identical values, with each run’s lengths and values.









Keep only the runs whose value is TRUE: runs$lengths[runs$values].


runs <- rle(temp_C > 188)
sum(runs$values)                         # how many excursions above 188 °C
max(runs$lengths[runs$values])           # the longest one, in minutes
726 excursions in the year, and the longest lasted 204 minutes, nearly three and a half hours, in March. Each run’s values is TRUE (above 188 °C) or FALSE, and runs$lengths[runs$values] keeps the lengths of the TRUE runs.

title: Efficient and reliable R
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why is exp(x) on a whole vector so much faster than a loop over its elements?

It uses a different formula
It makes one call to compiled code, instead of interpreting the loop’s code once per element
It skips some of the elements


The work per number is the same. The loop’s overhead is R reading and checking the code 525,600 times.



2. Why is z <- c(z, x[i]) inside a loop slow?

Because c() is a slow function
Because R copies the whole vector every time it grows, so the total work grows like the square of the length
Because the result isn’t numeric


Preallocate with numeric(n) and fill in place, and the work grows only like the length.



3. What does bench::mark() do that one system.time() doesn’t?

It makes the code faster
It runs each version many times, checks that they give the same answer, and reports memory too
It works only for loops


One timing is noisy. Many timings, summarized by the median, are reliable.



4. Your analysis takes ten minutes. What should you do first?

Rewrite the part you think is slow
Profile it, to find where the time actually goes
Buy a faster computer


Speeding up a step that takes 5% of the time can save at most 5%. The profiler tells you which step matters.



5. About how much memory does a vector of one million doubles take?

1 MB
8 MB
64 MB


Each double takes 8 bytes.



6. A function returns nonsense for an impossible input. What’s the better design?

Return 0 for impossible inputs
Check the inputs and stop with a clear error message
Leave it to the user to notice


A loud error is found at once. A quiet wrong number can spoil a whole analysis, as two −9999 readings spoiled the mean rate constant.

title: Efficient and reliable R
text:
Wrap-up
Your code is faster now, and harder to fool. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Vectorize: write the formula for the whole vector, and let R’s compiled code do the loop. Here, it was a hundred times faster or more.
Preallocate when a loop is unavoidable, and never grow a vector inside a loop. Better still, look for a function that runs the loop in C, such as stats::filter() or rle().
Measure: system.time() for one run, bench::mark() for a fair comparison that checks the answers, and a profiler to find the slow part before you fix anything.
Memory: a double takes 8 bytes. A year of the whole historian wouldn’t fit, so load only what you need, summarize early, and work in pieces.
Split, apply, combine with split() and vapply(), which checks the type of every result.
Fail loudly: check inputs with stopifnot(), test functions on known answers, set seeds, and fix data in code. Two sensor faults coded as −9999 would otherwise have spoiled the mean rate constant.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Copy the setup code at the top of this lesson’s exercises into a script in your project, to recreate the year of readings.

Profile it. Install the profiler with install.packages("profvis"). Run profvis::profvis(daily_report(temp_C)) with this lesson’s daily_report() function. Which line takes the most time? Replace the loop with vectorized code, profile again, and see what’s slowest now.
Test it. Install testthat, and write tests for rate_constant(): testthat::expect_equal(rate_constant(185), 0.0492, tolerance = 1e-3) and testthat::expect_error(rate_constant(-9999)). What other cases deserve a test?
Files on disk. Save the year as a CSV file with readr::write_csv() and as a Parquet file with nanoparquet::write_parquet() (Lesson 1.9). Compare the file sizes, and the time each takes to read back in.
Your computer against the browser. Rerun the loop-against-vector benchmark in RStudio. How much faster are loops there? Is the vector still faster?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Vectorized code

Code that applies an operation to a whole vector at once, so that the work is done in compiled code.

Preallocation

Creating an object at its final size before a loop fills it, instead of growing it.

Benchmark

A careful timing that runs code many times, often comparing several versions.

Profiler

A tool that records where a program spends its time, such as Rprof() or profvis.

Split, apply, combine

Splitting data into groups, applying a function to each group, and combining the results.

Functional programming

A style of programming that passes functions as arguments to other functions, as in vapply(x, max, numeric(1)).

Defensive programming

Writing code that checks its inputs and assumptions, and fails with a clear message when they’re wrong.











NoteWant to read more?






Hadley Wickham, Advanced R, chapters 23, “Measuring performance” and 24, “Improving performance”. Profiling with profvis, benchmarking with bench, and the main ways to speed code up.
Colin Gillespie and Robin Lovelace, Efficient R Programming, chapter 3, “Efficient programming”. Vectorization, preallocation and the apply family, with benchmarks.
Patrick Burns, The R Inferno, circles 2 and 3, “Growing objects” and “Failing to vectorize”. A short, funny tour of R’s traps.

title: Module 3 · Multivariate Statistical Methods
text:
Analyzing several response variables at once: statistical distance, the multivariate normal distribution, Hotelling’s T², MANOVA, repeated-measures and nested designs, canonical correlation and discriminant analysis. Real studies measure many things on each subject. Analyzing them together answers questions that one-at-a-time tests get wrong.
0 of 13 lessons complete




3.1 Multivariate data and matrix algebra
data matrices, mean vectors, covariance and correlation matrices, linear combinations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors

title: Canonical correlation analysis
text:
Module 3 · Lesson 12 of 13 Week 58 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 11 related the quality properties to the process conditions one property at a time. Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) asks a symmetric question about the two sets as wholes. Which combination of the process conditions is most strongly correlated with which combination of the quality properties? And how many separate links between the two sets are there?
With four variables in each set, there are 16 correlations between the sets: too many to take in at once. CCA boils them down to a few pairs of combinations, ordered from the strongest link to the weakest.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Canonical correlation analysis
text:
Two sets of variables
The first set is the process conditions, with the catalyst coded as a 0/1 column. The second is the quality properties, with the color on the log scale as in Lesson 11. FS73 is left out again.

bq <- read_csv("data/batch_quality.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(batch_id != "FS73") |>
  mutate(log_color = log(color_apha), catalyst_B = as.numeric(catalyst == "B"))
X <- as.matrix(bq[, c("temp_C", "residence_min", "feed_water_ppm", "catalyst_B")])
Y <- as.matrix(bq[, c("purity_pct", "water_ppm", "log_color", "acid_mgKOH")])











Your turn. The setup code has stored the process conditions as the matrix X and the quality properties as Y. Compute the 16 correlations between the two sets.









cor(X, Y) correlates every column of X with every column of Y.


round(cor(X, Y), 2)
The strongest links are the temperature’s with the purity (−0.87) and the log color (+0.87), and the feed water’s with the product’s water (+0.81). The acid is linked to both the temperature (+0.55) and the feed water (+0.52). The residence time and the catalyst have only weak correlations with anything.

title: Canonical correlation analysis
text:
Canonical variates
CCA looks for a combination of the process conditions, U_1 = \mathbf{a}_1^\top\mathbf{x}, and a combination of the quality properties, V_1 = \mathbf{b}_1^\top\mathbf{y}, whose correlation is as large as possible. That largest correlation is the first canonical correlation, r_1, and U_1 and V_1 are the first pair of canonical variates.
Then it looks for a second pair, U_2 and V_2, with the largest correlation among the combinations that are uncorrelated with the first pair, and so on. With p variables in one set and q in the other, there are \min(p, q) pairs, here 4.
The squared canonical correlations are the eigenvalues of a product of correlation matrices. Split the correlation matrix of all eight variables into blocks: R_{11} for the process conditions, R_{22} for the quality properties, and R_{12} for the correlations between them. Then r_1^2, r_2^2, \ldots are the eigenvalues of

R_{11}^{-1} R_{12} R_{22}^{-1} R_{21} ,

with R_{21} = R_{12}^\top, and the eigenvectors give the coefficients \mathbf{a}_i of the standardized variables. If that looks familiar, it should: one-way MANOVA’s statistics came from the eigenvalues of E^{-1}H in Lesson 6. Both look for the directions where one matrix is largest relative to another.
Your turn. Compute the four canonical correlations as the square roots of the eigenvalues.









R_{21} is the transpose of R_{12}: t(R12).


R11 <- cor(X)
R22 <- cor(Y)
R12 <- cor(X, Y)
M <- solve(R11) %*% R12 %*% solve(R22) %*% t(R12)
sqrt(Re(eigen(M)$values))
0.97, 0.87, 0.36 and 0.30. Two very strong links, and two weak ones. (Re() drops the zero imaginary parts that eigen() can return for a matrix like M, which isn’t symmetric.)

title: Canonical correlation analysis
text:
CCA in R
Base R has cancor(), but the candisc package adds the tests and the interpretation tools. candisc::cancor(X, Y) prints the canonical correlations, their squares, and a test for each.
Your turn. Run the canonical correlation analysis.









The two sets are X and Y.


cc <- candisc::cancor(X, Y)
cc
The same four canonical correlations. The first pair’s squared correlation is 0.94, so U_1 and V_1 share 94% of their variance. The Eigen column holds r^2/(1 - r^2), the eigenvalues in the MANOVA form, and the first pair accounts for 81% of their total.

title: Canonical correlation analysis
text:
How many pairs matter?
The tests in the printout are sequential. Row k tests the hypothesis that the k-th canonical correlation and all the ones after it are zero. The test statistic is a Wilks’ lambda built from the squared canonical correlations, \Lambda_k = \prod_{i \ge k} (1 - r_i^2), and Bartlett’s chi-square approximation turns it into a p-value:

\chi^2 = -\left(n - 1 - \frac{p + q + 1}{2}\right)\ln \Lambda_k
\quad \text{on } (p - k + 1)(q - k + 1) \text{ degrees of freedom.}

(candisc reports an F approximation instead, which gives nearly the same p-values.) You keep the pairs up to the last significant row. Here, every row is significant, even the fourth (p = 0.008): with 79 batches, even a correlation of 0.30 is detectable.
But statistical significance isn’t the same as importance. The third and fourth pairs have squared correlations of 0.13 and 0.09, and they’re hard to interpret: they mix the catalyst with the residence time, and pick up small effects like catalyst B’s on the purity. Most analysts would report the first two pairs and mention the other two.
Your turn. Compute Bartlett’s test for k = 3: are the third and fourth canonical correlations both zero?









Wilks’ lambda uses the squared canonical correlations: r[k:4]^2.


r <- cc$cancor
n <- 79; p <- 4; q <- 4; k <- 3
Lambda <- prod(1 - r[k:4]^2)
chi2 <- -(n - 1 - (p + q + 1) / 2) * log(Lambda)
c(chi2 = chi2, p = pchisq(chi2, (p - k + 1) * (q - k + 1), lower.tail = FALSE))
\chi^2 = 17.3 on 4 degrees of freedom, p = 0.002, the same p-value as candisc’s F approximation gives. The last two pairs aren’t both zero, but together they’re a small part of the story.

title: Canonical correlation analysis
text:
What the variates mean
To interpret a canonical variate, look at its structure correlations: the correlations between the variate and each of the original variables in its set. The raw coefficients \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{b} depend on the units, and when the variables in a set are correlated with each other they can be unstable, with misleading signs. The structure correlations show what each variate is.
The setup code has stored the result as cc. Its scores component holds the canonical variates, one column per pair, scaled to variance 1: cc$scores$X for the process variates U, and cc$scores$Y for the quality variates V. Here are the first two pairs:

cc <- candisc::cancor(X, Y)
scores <- bind_rows(
  tibble(pair = "First pair, r = 0.97", U = cc$scores$X[, 1], V = cc$scores$Y[, 1]),
  tibble(pair = "Second pair, r = 0.87", U = cc$scores$X[, 2], V = cc$scores$Y[, 2])
)
ggplot(scores, aes(x = U, y = V)) +
  geom_point(color = "#3A1F35", alpha = 0.7, size = 1.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ pair) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Process variate, U", y = "Quality variate, V") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Your turn. What is the first quality variate? Compute the correlations between the quality properties and V_1.









The first variate is the first column: cc$scores$Y[, 1].


round(cor(Y, cc$scores$Y[, 1]), 2)
Purity +0.97, water −0.05, log color −0.89, acid −0.71. V_1 is a quality score: high when the product is pure, pale and low in acid. The water plays no part.




Your turn. And the first process variate? Compute the correlations between the process conditions and U_1.









Correlate the process conditions, X, with the first process variate.


round(cor(X, cc$scores$X[, 1]), 2)
Temperature −0.96, and the other three conditions near zero. U_1 is essentially minus the temperature. So the first, and strongest, link between the sets says: cool batches are good batches. The heat degrades the product, which loses purity and gains color and acid. (The signs of a canonical pair are arbitrary: flipping both U_1 and V_1 leaves their correlation unchanged.)
The second pair tells the wetness story. U_2 correlates +0.92 with the feed water and −0.27 with the residence time, and V_2 correlates +0.99 with the product’s water and +0.60 with the acid. Wet feed and a short residence time make a wet, acidic product.

title: Canonical correlation analysis
text:
Canonical correlation and regression
When one of the sets has a single variable, there’s only one canonical pair, and its correlation is that variable’s multiple correlation with the other set (Lesson 11). So canonical correlation extends multiple correlation from one response to several. It also explains why r_1 = 0.97 is larger than any single property’s multiple correlation, the largest of which was the purity’s 0.95: V_1 can combine the properties.
A related summary is the redundancy index: the average squared correlation between the quality properties and a process variate, which says how much of the properties’ variance that variate explains. For U_1, it’s 52%. Added over all four process variates, it’s 80%, which is the average R^2 of Lesson 11’s four regressions.

title: Canonical correlation analysis
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · One response. Base R’s stats::cancor() gives the canonical correlations, without the tests, and handles a single response, which candisc’s version doesn’t. (Write stats:: in front: the live boxes load candisc, whose cancor() would be used otherwise.) Use it to compute the canonical correlation between the process conditions and the purity alone, and compare it with the purity’s multiple correlation from Lesson 11, R = \sqrt{0.893}.









The purity’s column is purity_pct. drop = FALSE keeps it a one-column matrix.


stats::cancor(X, Y[, "purity_pct", drop = FALSE])$cor
0.945, exactly the multiple correlation \sqrt{0.893}. With one response, CCA is multiple regression.




Challenge 2 · Units don’t matter. Convert the temperature to degrees Fahrenheit and the product’s water to percent, then recompute the canonical correlations.









1% is 10,000 ppm, so divide by 1e4.


X_new <- X
X_new[, "temp_C"] <- X[, "temp_C"] * 9 / 5 + 32
Y_new <- Y
Y_new[, "water_ppm"] <- Y[, "water_ppm"] / 1e4
stats::cancor(X_new, Y_new)$cor
The same four numbers. Rescaling or shifting a variable rescales its coefficient, and leaves every correlation unchanged, like T^2 in Lesson 4. Unlike principal components (Lesson 1’s eigenvectors), CCA doesn’t care about units.

title: Canonical correlation analysis
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does the first canonical correlation measure?

The average correlation between the two sets
The largest correlation between any linear combination of one set and any linear combination of the other
The correlation between the first variable of each set


The first pair of canonical variates achieves it.



2. With 4 process conditions and 4 quality properties, how many pairs of canonical variates are there?

16
8
4


There are \min(p, q) = 4 pairs.



3. Row 3 of the sequential tests has p = 0.002. What does it test?

That the third canonical correlation alone is zero
That the third and all later canonical correlations are zero
That the first three canonical correlations are equal


Each row tests its own correlation and all the smaller ones after it.



4. Why interpret canonical variates with structure correlations rather than raw coefficients?

Because the raw coefficients are always zero
Because raw coefficients depend on the units and can be unstable when the variables in a set are correlated
Because structure correlations are always larger


Structure correlations show how each variate relates to each original variable.



5. The first pair has U_1 correlated −0.96 with the temperature, and V_1 correlated +0.97 with the purity and −0.89 with the log color. What’s the story?

Hot batches are purer
Cool batches are purer and paler: the heat degrades the product
The temperature doesn’t matter


U_1 is high for cool batches, and V_1 is high for pure, pale product. Their correlation is 0.97.



6. With a single response, what does the canonical correlation equal?

Zero
The correlation between the response and the first predictor
The response’s multiple correlation R with the predictors


CCA extends multiple correlation to several responses.

title: Canonical correlation analysis
text:
Wrap-up
You can now summarize the links between two sets of variables! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Canonical variates are pairs of linear combinations, one from each set, with the largest possible correlation, each pair uncorrelated with the earlier ones.
Canonical correlations are the square roots of the eigenvalues of R_{11}^{-1}R_{12}R_{22}^{-1}R_{21}, and they don’t depend on the units.
candisc::cancor() gives the canonical correlations, the variates and the tests.
Bartlett’s sequential tests decide how many pairs differ from zero, but report the pairs that matter in practice.
Structure correlations interpret the variates. Here, pair 1 is the heat story (cool batches are good batches), and pair 2 is the wetness story.
With one response, the canonical correlation is the multiple correlation.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download batch_quality.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Redundancy. Compute the redundancy index of the quality properties for each process variate, the average of the squared correlations between the properties and U_i. Check that they add up to the average R^2 of Lesson 11’s four regressions.
A plot of the first pair. plot(cc) draws the first pair’s canonical scores, with a data ellipse and a regression line. Try plot(cc, which = 2) for the second pair too. How do the plots show the strength of each link?
With FS73. Repeat the analysis with FS73 included. Does one unusual batch change the canonical correlations? Which pair moves the most?
Raw against standardized coefficients. Compare the raw coefficients in cc$coef$X with the coefficients for standardized variables, the raw ones multiplied by each variable’s standard deviation. Which is easier to compare across variables?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Canonical correlation analysis

A method that finds the linear combinations of two sets of variables with the largest correlations.

Canonical variates

The pairs of linear combinations, U_i = \mathbf{a}_i^\top\mathbf{x} and V_i = \mathbf{b}_i^\top\mathbf{y}, found by CCA.

Canonical correlation

The correlation between a pair of canonical variates.

Bartlett’s sequential test

A chi-square test that the k-th and all later canonical correlations are zero.

Structure correlations

The correlations between a canonical variate and the original variables, used to interpret it.

Redundancy index

The proportion of one set’s variance explained by a canonical variate of the other set.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 505, Lesson 13: Canonical Correlation Analysis. The method, its tests, and how to interpret the variates, with a worked example.
Johnson and Wichern, Applied Multivariate Statistical Analysis, chapter 10, “Canonical correlation analysis”. The theory, sample variates, and large-sample tests.
Michael Friendly and John Fox, candisc: visualizing generalized canonical discriminant and canonical correlation analysis, the package’s CRAN page, with its vignettes.

title: Nested designs
text:
Module 3 · Lesson 10 of 13 Week 56 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The plant and its biggest customer keep disagreeing about the product’s water content: the customer’s lab finds more water than the plant’s lab does. Is the product changing in transit, or are the labs measuring differently? To find out, the quality department organized an interlaboratory study. One well-mixed reference sample went to four labs: the plant’s, the customer’s, and two contract labs. In each lab, three analysts each measured it three times, for purity and water.
It’s the same sample everywhere, so every difference in the 36 results is a measurement difference. The questions: do the labs disagree? Do the analysts within a lab? And how much of the variation comes from each source?
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Nested designs
text:
The interlaboratory study
Here are the 36 results, one panel per lab, with each analyst’s mean as a bar:

interlab |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(purity_pct, water_ppm), names_to = "property", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(property = factor(property, labels = c("Purity (%)", "Water (ppm)"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = analyst, y = value)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.6, color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(color = "#3A1F35", size = 1.6, alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_grid(property ~ lab, scales = "free", switch = "y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(strip.placement = "outside", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))








Two things stand out. The customer lab’s purity results are higher than everyone else’s, and contract lab 2’s water results are well above everyone else’s. Within each lab, the analysts’ means also differ, though by less.










Your turn. The setup code has loaded the 36 results as interlab. Compute each lab’s mean purity and mean water content.









Group by lab.


interlab |>
  group_by(lab) |>
  summarise(purity = mean(purity_pct), water = mean(water_ppm))
The plant lab finds 137.7 ppm of water and the customer lab 149.5 ppm, so the complaint is real. Contract lab 2 finds even more, 162.3 ppm. For purity, the customer lab is the odd one out, at 99.25% against 99.00% to 99.07% elsewhere.

title: Nested designs
text:
Nested, not crossed
In Lesson 8, the factors were crossed: every catalyst was run at every temperature. Here, the analysts are nested in the labs: each analyst works in only one lab, so “analyst 1” at the plant lab has nothing to do with “analyst 1” at the customer lab. There’s no lab × analyst interaction to estimate, since no analyst appears in two labs. (That’s why the data give the analysts lab-specific codes, PL-A1 and so on.)
The model for repeat k by analyst j in lab i is

y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_{j(i)} + e_{ijk},

where \beta_{j(i)} is the effect of analyst j within lab i. In R, lab / analyst means “lab, and analyst within lab”, and expands to lab + lab:analyst. The degrees of freedom are 3 for the labs, 4 \times (3 - 1) = 8 for the analysts within the labs, and 12 \times (3 - 1) = 24 for the repeats.
Your turn. Fit the nested ANOVA of the purity.









The nesting operator is /.


summary(aov(purity_pct ~ lab / analyst, data = interlab))
Three rows: the labs (3 degrees of freedom), the analysts within the labs (8) and the residuals, the repeats (24). The analysts’ F-test is right: F = 4.69, p = 0.0015, so the analysts within a lab do differ. But the labs’ F-test, F = 89.4, is wrong, as the next section explains.

title: Nested designs
text:
The right error term
By default, aov() tests every term against the residuals, the variation between repeats by the same analyst. For the analysts, that’s the right comparison. For the labs, it isn’t.
A lab’s mean is the average of its three analysts’ results, so it carries those analysts’ quirks along with the lab’s own bias. Even if the four labs were identical, their means would differ because their analysts differ. So the labs must be compared with the variation between analysts within the labs:

F = \frac{\text{MS}_{\text{lab}}}{\text{MS}_{\text{analyst(lab)}}} \quad \text{on 3 and 8 degrees of freedom.}

The rule: test a factor against the mean square of the random factor nested directly below it. The analysts are random here: they stand for all the analysts who might ever run the test, not just these twelve.
Your turn. The setup code has stored the nested ANOVA table as tab. Compute the right F-test for the labs.









The analysts’ mean square is in the second row of the table.


F_lab <- tab[["Mean Sq"]][1] / tab[["Mean Sq"]][2]
c(F = F_lab, p = pf(F_lab, 3, 8, lower.tail = FALSE))
F = 19.1 on 3 and 8 degrees of freedom, p = 0.0005. The labs really do disagree, but the evidence is much weaker than the wrong test’s F = 89.4 on 3 and 24 suggested. With only 3 analysts per lab, there are only 8 degrees of freedom for the error.
aov() can do this itself, if you tell it the error structure: aov(purity_pct ~ lab + Error(analyst), data = interlab) tests the labs in the analyst stratum. Try it!

title: Nested designs
text:
Variance components
The labs disagree. But the more useful question for a measurement method is: how much variation does each source add? Treat the labs as random too, a sample of all the labs that might measure the product. Then the model has three variance components: \sigma^2_L between labs, \sigma^2_A between analysts within a lab, and \sigma^2_e between repeats. A single result from a random lab and analyst has variance \sigma^2_L + \sigma^2_A + \sigma^2_e.
Each mean square estimates a combination of the components. With 3 analysts per lab and 3 repeats per analyst,

E(\text{MS}_e) = \sigma^2_e, \qquad
E(\text{MS}_{A(L)}) = \sigma^2_e + 3\sigma^2_A, \qquad
E(\text{MS}_L) = \sigma^2_e + 3\sigma^2_A + 9\sigma^2_L .

Solving gives the estimates: \hat\sigma^2_e = \text{MS}_e, \hat\sigma^2_A = (\text{MS}_{A(L)} - \text{MS}_e)/3 and \hat\sigma^2_L = (\text{MS}_L - \text{MS}_{A(L)})/9.
Your turn. Estimate the three variance components of the purity.









Each analyst made 3 repeats, so divide by 3.


ms <- tab[["Mean Sq"]]
c(lab = (ms[1] - ms[2]) / 9,
  analyst = (ms[2] - ms[3]) / 3,
  repeat_ = ms[3])
In standard deviations: 0.103 percentage points between labs, 0.037 between analysts, and 0.034 between repeats. The labs contribute 81% of the total variance: the analysts are fine, and the labs are the problem.




Measurement scientists summarize such a study with two standard deviations:

The repeatability standard deviation, s_r = \hat\sigma_e = 0.034: how much repeats by the same analyst, in the same lab, scatter.
The reproducibility standard deviation, s_R = \sqrt{\hat\sigma^2_L + \hat\sigma^2_A + \hat\sigma^2_e} = 0.115: how much results from different labs scatter.

Here, s_R is more than three times s_r. A purity result is very repeatable within a lab, but results from two labs can easily differ by 0.2 or 0.3 percentage points.

title: Nested designs
section: A first look at mixed models
text:
A first look at mixed models
The ANOVA formulas need a balanced design, and they can even give negative variance estimates when a mean square comes out smaller than the one below it. A mixed model estimates the variance components directly, by REML (restricted maximum likelihood), and copes with unbalanced data. The lme4 package fits them. In its formula, (1 | lab/analyst) means a random effect for each lab and for each analyst within a lab:

m_purity <- lme4::lmer(purity_pct ~ 1 + (1 | lab / analyst), data = interlab)
lme4::VarCorr(m_purity)
#>  Groups      Name        Std.Dev.
#>  analyst:lab (Intercept) 0.037382
#>  lab         (Intercept) 0.103457
#>  Residual                0.033718

The standard deviations are the same as the ANOVA estimates: for balanced data with positive estimates, the two methods agree. Module 5 comes back to models like this one as Bayesian hierarchical models.
Your turn. Fit the same mixed model for the water content, and look at its variance components.









The water’s column is water_ppm.


m_water <- lme4::lmer(water_ppm ~ 1 + (1 | lab / analyst), data = interlab)
lme4::VarCorr(m_water)
Standard deviations of 10.5 ppm between labs, 3.4 ppm between analysts, and 4.5 ppm between repeats. So s_r = 4.5 ppm and s_R = 11.9 ppm. Again, the labs dominate.

title: Nested designs
text:
Nested MANOVA
To test the labs and the analysts on both properties at once, fit a nested MANOVA. The same rule about error terms holds, with SSCP matrices in place of mean squares. manova() tests the analysts within the labs against the repeats, which is right. Its test of the labs uses the same error, which is wrong again: the labs must be tested against the analysts’ SSCP matrix, H_{A(L)}.
With a balanced design, there’s an easy way to get that test. Average each analyst’s three repeats, and run a one-way MANOVA of the 12 analyst means on the labs. The variation of the analyst means within a lab is exactly the analyst-level variation, so the test has the right error, with 8 degrees of freedom.
Your turn. Fit the nested MANOVA of purity and water.









Nest the analysts in the labs: lab / analyst.


fit <- manova(cbind(purity_pct, water_ppm) ~ lab / analyst, data = interlab)
summary(fit)
The analysts within the labs differ: Pillai’s trace 1.11, F = 3.74 on 16 and 48 degrees of freedom, p = 0.0002. Ignore the lab line, which uses the wrong error.

title: Nested designs
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The labs, tested right. The setup code has stored the 12 analysts’ means as analyst_means, with columns lab, analyst, purity and water. Test the labs on both properties with a one-way MANOVA of the analyst means.









Use analyst_means, not interlab.


summary(manova(cbind(purity, water) ~ lab, data = analyst_means))
Pillai’s trace 1.74, F = 17.7 on 6 and 16 degrees of freedom, p = 3 \times 10^{-6}. The labs disagree, on the pair of properties, even when tested against the analyst-to-analyst variation. You’d get the same Wilks’ lambda, 0.016, from \det(H_{A(L)})/\det(H_{A(L)} + H_L) with the SSCP matrices of the nested MANOVA.




Challenge 2 · Settling the dispute. Does the customer’s lab find more water than the plant’s lab, by more than the analysts’ variation explains? Fit the water of the analyst means on the lab. The plant lab is the first level, so each coefficient compares a lab with the plant lab.









The analyst means’ water column is water.


water_fit <- lm(water ~ lab, data = analyst_means)
summary(water_fit)$coefficients
The customer lab reads 11.8 ppm more water than the plant lab (standard error 3.5, p = 0.01), and contract lab 2 reads 24.6 ppm more (p = 0.0001). So the dispute is about measurement, not the product. Every lab measured the same sample.
The study can’t say which lab is right, though. For that, the labs would measure a certified reference material whose water content is known. Then each lab’s bias could be estimated, and corrected.

title: Nested designs
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why are the analysts nested in the labs, and not crossed with them?

Because there are more analysts than labs
Because each analyst works in only one lab
Because the analysts are random


Crossed factors appear in every combination. Here, “analyst 1” means a different person in each lab.



2. What should the labs’ F-test use as its denominator?

The residual mean square, the repeats
The mean square of the analysts within the labs
The total mean square


A lab’s mean carries its analysts’ differences, so the labs are compared with the analyst-to-analyst variation.



3. With 3 analysts per lab and 3 repeats per analyst, what does \text{MS}_{A(L)} estimate?

\sigma^2_A
\sigma^2_e + 3\sigma^2_A
\sigma^2_e + 3\sigma^2_A + 9\sigma^2_L


Each analyst’s mean averages 3 repeats, so it varies by \sigma^2_A + \sigma^2_e/3, and the mean square multiplies that by 3.



4. The repeatability standard deviation is 4.5 ppm and the reproducibility standard deviation 11.9 ppm. What does that tell you?

The analysts are careless
Results from different labs scatter much more than repeats within a lab
The sample wasn’t well mixed


Most of the reproducibility variance comes from the labs. (A badly mixed sample would show up as large repeat-to-repeat scatter.)



5. What does (1 | lab / analyst) mean in an lme4 formula?

Labs divided by analysts
A random effect for each lab, and one for each analyst within a lab
A fixed effect for each lab


It expands to (1 | lab) + (1 | lab:analyst).



6. Why does a one-way MANOVA of the 12 analyst means test the labs correctly?

Because means are always normally distributed
Because the variation of the analyst means within a lab is the analyst-level variation, the right error for the labs
Because it has more degrees of freedom


With a balanced design, it gives exactly the test of H_L against H_{A(L)}, with 8 error degrees of freedom.

title: Nested designs
text:
Wrap-up
You can now analyze nested designs! Here’s what you’ve learned:
