Nested factors appear within only one level of another factor, like analysts within labs. In R, lab / analyst expands to lab + lab:analyst, with no interaction.
The right error term: test a factor against the mean square of the random factor nested directly below it. Error() terms in aov() do that automatically.
Variance components come from the expected mean squares, or directly from a mixed model, lme4::lmer() with (1 | lab / analyst).
Repeatability and reproducibility summarize a measurement method: here, the labs contribute most of the variance in both properties.
Nested MANOVA uses the same rules with SSCP matrices. With a balanced design, a MANOVA of the analyst means tests the labs correctly.
The dispute: the customer’s lab reads 11.8 ppm more water than the plant’s lab. The labs measure differently, and a certified reference material would show which one is right.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download interlab.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Fixed labs, random analysts. If you care about these four labs in particular, the labs are fixed and the analysts random. Fit nlme::lme(purity_pct ~ lab, random = ~ 1 | analyst, data = interlab) and look at anova() of it. Is the labs’ F-test the one you computed by hand?
Repeatability and reproducibility limits. The ISO 5725 standard defines the repeatability limit r = 2.8\,s_r and the reproducibility limit R = 2.8\,s_R: about 95% of the differences between two results (by one analyst, or from two labs) fall within them. Compute both for the water. Is the customer’s complaint, a difference of about 12 ppm between two labs, surprising?
An unbalanced study. Delete a few rows at random, and compare the ANOVA formulas’ variance components with lme4::lmer()’s. When do they disagree?
A negative estimate. What does the ANOVA formula give for \hat\sigma^2_A if \text{MS}_{A(L)} < \text{MS}_e? What does lmer() report in that case?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Nested factor

A factor whose levels appear within only one level of another factor, such as analysts within labs.

Crossed factors

Factors whose levels appear in every combination, such as catalysts and temperatures.

Random factor

A factor whose levels are a sample from a larger population of levels, such as analysts. Its effects are described by a variance.

Variance components

The variances contributed by each random factor and by the residual error.

Repeatability and reproducibility

The scatter of repeated results within one lab (s_r), and of results from different labs (s_R).

Mixed model

A model with both fixed and random effects, fitted by REML in lme4::lmer() or nlme::lme().











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 502, Lesson 6: Random Effects and Introduction to Mixed Models, especially section 6.4, “Fully Nested Random Effects Model: Quality Control Example”. Expected mean squares and variance components, worked through.
NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 2.4.4 Analysis of variability, with its pages on repeatability and reproducibility. How measurement scientists analyze nested studies of a measurement process.
Paul Roback and Julie Legler, Beyond Multiple Linear Regression, chapter 8, “Introduction to Multilevel Models”. A friendly introduction to mixed models for nested data, in R.
Douglas Bates and others, “Fitting linear mixed-effects models using lme4”, Journal of Statistical Software (2015). The lme4 package’s own guide, for when you want the details.

title: Factorial MANOVA
text:
Module 3 · Lesson 8 of 13 Week 54 of 160 About 5–7 hours
In Lesson 2.14, a follow-up experiment tested the new catalyst F2 against the standard one at three temperatures, and found that F2’s yield advantage grows with the heat. Before switching catalysts, the plant repeated the experiment at the pilot plant, this time measuring three responses on every run. The yield is why F2 was bought. The purity and the color are what the customers pay for.
Two factors and three responses make a factorial MANOVA. The questions are the ones of Lesson 2.14, asked of all three responses at once. Does the catalyst change the product? Does the temperature? And does the catalyst’s effect depend on the temperature?
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Factorial MANOVA
text:
The pilot-plant experiment
Each of the 2 × 3 combinations of catalyst and temperature was run 6 times, 36 runs in all, in random order. Here’s each response against the temperature, with the cell means joined up, one line per catalyst:

long <- fq |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(yield_pct, purity_pct, color_apha), names_to = "response", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(response = factor(response, levels = c("yield_pct", "purity_pct", "color_apha"),
                           labels = c("Yield (%)", "Purity (%)", "Color (APHA)")))
cell_means <- long |> group_by(response, catalyst, temp_C) |> summarise(value = mean(value), .groups = "drop")
ggplot(long, aes(x = temp_C, y = value, color = catalyst)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.8, height = 0, seed = 1), alpha = 0.35, size = 1.2) +
  geom_line(data = cell_means, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = cell_means, size = 2.4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(standard = "#2a78d6", F2 = "#C2416C"), name = "Catalyst") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(175, 185, 195)) +
  facet_wrap(~ response, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Each response tells its own story:

Yield: both catalysts gain from the heat, and F2 gains more. Its advantage is 1.6 points at 175 °C, 4.2 at 185 °C and 7.4 at 195 °C. The lines spread apart: an interaction, as in Lesson 2.14.
Purity falls with the heat, by about 0.3 percentage points per 10 °C, the same with both catalysts.
Color rises with the heat, and F2’s product is a little darker, by 1 to 2 APHA units at each temperature. The lines are close to parallel.











Your turn. The setup code has loaded the 36 runs as fq, with the catalyst and the temperature as factors (catalyst and temp) and the temperature as a number (temp_C). Compute the cell mean vectors: the mean of each response for every combination of catalyst and temperature.









Group by both factors: the catalyst and the temperature, temp_C.


fq |>
  group_by(catalyst, temp_C) |>
  summarise(across(c(yield_pct, purity_pct, color_apha), mean), .groups = "drop")
Six rows, one mean vector per cell. The yield climbs from 57.8% to 64.7% with the standard catalyst, and from 59.4% to 72.2% with F2.

title: Factorial MANOVA
text:
The two-way MANOVA model
With a levels of factor A (the catalyst), b levels of factor B (the temperature) and n runs per cell, the model for run k in cell (i, j) is the two-way ANOVA model of Lesson 2.14 with vectors in place of numbers:

\mathbf{x}_{ijk} = \boldsymbol\mu + \boldsymbol\alpha_i + \boldsymbol\beta_j + \boldsymbol\gamma_{ij} + \mathbf{e}_{ijk},
\qquad \mathbf{e}_{ijk} \sim N_p(\mathbf{0}, \Sigma) ,

where \boldsymbol\alpha_i and \boldsymbol\beta_j are the main effects and \boldsymbol\gamma_{ij} is the interaction. The total SSCP matrix splits into four parts, and so do its degrees of freedom:

T = H_A + H_B + H_{AB} + E, \qquad
abn - 1 = (a-1) + (b-1) + (a-1)(b-1) + ab(n-1) .

Here, that’s 35 = 1 + 2 + 2 + 30. Each H matrix is tested against E exactly as in one-way MANOVA (Lesson 6): Wilks’ lambda for the interaction is \det(E)/\det(E + H_{AB}), and all four statistics come from the eigenvalues of E^{-1}H_{AB}. A term with h degrees of freedom has at most \min(p, h) non-zero eigenvalues.
In a balanced design like this one, with the same number of runs in every cell, the split is unique, and the order of the terms in the model doesn’t matter. (The end of the lesson shows what happens when a run is lost.)
Your turn. Fit the two-way MANOVA with both main effects and the interaction.









catalyst * temp is shorthand for catalyst + temp + catalyst:temp.


fit <- manova(cbind(yield_pct, purity_pct, color_apha) ~ catalyst * temp, data = fq)
summary(fit)
All three terms are significant. The interaction has Pillai’s trace 0.58, F = 3.97 on 6 and 58 degrees of freedom, p = 0.002. The catalyst’s main effect has p = 2 \times 10^{-10}, and the temperature’s p = 10^{-6}.




The SS part of summary(fit) holds the four SSCP matrices. E/30 is the pooled covariance matrix within the cells, and its correlations show why a joint analysis pays. Within a cell, the runs with a higher yield had a lower purity: the correlation is −0.50. A MANOVA uses that correlation, and three separate ANOVAs ignore it.
Your turn. Compute Wilks’ lambda for the interaction from the SSCP matrices.









names(ss) shows the names of the four matrices. The interaction’s is "catalyst:temp".


ss <- summary(fit)$SS
names(ss)
E <- ss[["Residuals"]]
H_AB <- ss[["catalyst:temp"]]
det(E) / det(E + H_AB)
\Lambda = 0.43, the same as summary(fit, test = "Wilks") gives. The eigenvalues of E^{-1}H_{AB} are 1.26 and 0.025 (the third is zero, since the interaction has 2 degrees of freedom). So nearly all of the interaction lies in a single direction.

title: Factorial MANOVA
text:
Interaction first, then follow-ups
As in Lesson 2.14, look at the interaction before the main effects. Here, it’s real: the catalyst’s effect on the product depends on the temperature. So “F2 adds 4.4 points of yield” is an average over three different advantages, and the catalyst’s main effect, significant as it is, doesn’t tell the whole story.
Which responses carry the effects? Univariate ANOVAs of each response answer that, as in Lesson 6, and summary.aov(fit) runs all three at once. For the yield, the interaction is strong (F = 13.1, p = 0.00008). For the purity, only the temperature matters: the catalyst has no detectable effect (p = 0.71), and neither does the interaction (p = 0.81). With three responses, a cautious analyst compares each p-value with 0.05/3 = 0.017, and these conclusions survive that.
The assumptions are those of Lesson 6, cell by cell. With only six runs per cell, the cells’ standard deviations bounce around a lot by chance (from 0.55 to 1.65 for the yield), and Box’s M test across the six cells gives p = 0.07: no clear evidence that the covariance matrices differ.
Your turn. Run the univariate ANOVA for the color.









The color’s column is color_apha.


anova(lm(color_apha ~ catalyst * temp, data = fq))
No interaction for the color (p = 0.38), but both main effects (p = 0.001 for the catalyst). The temperature darkens the product, and F2 darkens it by 1.4 APHA units more, on average. F2’s extra color ranges from 1.0 to 2.2 units across the three temperatures, but that’s no more variation than chance explains: that’s what p = 0.38 says. Without an interaction, the main effect is a fair summary.

title: Factorial MANOVA
text:
Simple effects
When the interaction is real, report simple effects: the catalyst’s effect at each temperature. For one response, a simple effect is the difference of two cell means. Each cell mean averages 6 runs, so its standard error is \sqrt{\text{MSE}\,(1/6 + 1/6)}, which for the yield is 0.81 points.
For all three responses at once, a simple effect is a contrast of two cell mean vectors, tested with T^2 as in Lesson 7. The easiest way is the cell-means model of Lesson 7, with one mean vector per cell, ~ 0 + cell. The setup code has made the factor cell, whose six levels are standard_175, F2_175, standard_185, F2_185, standard_195 and F2_195, in that order.
Your turn. The setup code has stored the cell means as cm. Compute F2’s yield advantage at each temperature.









Subtract the standard catalyst’s mean: catalyst == "standard".


cm |>
  group_by(temp_C) |>
  summarise(advantage = yield_pct[catalyst == "F2"] - yield_pct[catalyst == "standard"])
1.6, 4.2 and 7.4 points. With a standard error of 0.81, the advantage at 175 °C is only 2 standard errors from zero (p = 0.06), and the other two are far from it.




Your turn. Test the catalyst’s simple effect at 195 °C on all three responses: F2 at 195 °C against the standard catalyst at 195 °C.









F2_195 is the sixth cell, so it gets the weight +1.


cells <- lm(cbind(yield_pct, purity_pct, color_apha) ~ 0 + cell, data = fq)
car::linearHypothesis(cells, hypothesis.matrix = rbind(c(0, 0, 0, 0, -1, 1)))
F = 40.2 on 3 and 28 degrees of freedom, p = 3 \times 10^{-10}. The same test at 185 °C gives p = 0.00006, and at 175 °C p = 0.07. So the plant’s recommendation writes itself. At 195 °C, F2 gives 7.4 points more yield, the same purity, and 2.2 APHA units more color: worth it, if the customers’ color limit has room. At 175 °C, F2 barely makes a difference.

title: Factorial MANOVA
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Temperature is a number. The model spends 2 degrees of freedom on the temperature’s main effect and 2 more on the interaction, because it treats the three temperatures as categories. But temperature is a number, and the lines in the figure look nearly straight. Fit the model with temp_C, the temperature as a number, and compare it with the categorical model. If the straight lines fit as well, the p-value will be large.









Use temp_C, the numeric column, in the second model.


full <- lm(cbind(yield_pct, purity_pct, color_apha) ~ catalyst * temp, data = fq)
straight <- lm(cbind(yield_pct, purity_pct, color_apha) ~ catalyst * temp_C, data = fq)
anova(full, straight)
p = 0.76: no evidence of curvature, so straight lines are enough. That’s a lack-of-fit test, and it pays off. In the straight-line model, the interaction has 1 degree of freedom instead of 2, and its test is much sharper (F = 11.8 on 3 and 30, p = 0.00003, against 0.002). The slopes also make a tidy report: the standard catalyst gains 3.5 points of yield per 10 °C, and F2 gains 6.4.




Challenge 2 · A lost run. Suppose run 1, a standard run at 185 °C, had been lost. With 5 runs in one cell and 6 in the others, the design is unbalanced, the SSCP matrices no longer split T uniquely, and the sequential tests of manova() depend on the order of the terms, as in Lesson 2.14:

lost <- filter(fq, run != 1)
rbind(
  catalyst_first = summary(manova(cbind(yield_pct, purity_pct, color_apha) ~ catalyst * temp, data = lost))$stats["catalyst", ],
  catalyst_second = summary(manova(cbind(yield_pct, purity_pct, color_apha) ~ temp * catalyst, data = lost))$stats["catalyst", ]
)
#>                 Df    Pillai approx F num Df den Df       Pr(>F)
#> catalyst_first   1 0.8194824 40.85664      3     27 3.568150e-10
#> catalyst_second  1 0.8180007 40.45075      3     27 3.981148e-10

With one run missing, the difference is small, but with messier data it can be large. Run the Type II tests with car::Anova(), which test each main effect after the other.









Fit the model to lost, the 35 remaining runs.


lost <- filter(fq, run != 1)
car::Anova(lm(cbind(yield_pct, purity_pct, color_apha) ~ catalyst * temp, data = lost))
The catalyst’s Type II test has Pillai’s trace 0.818, the same as the sequential test with the catalyst second: it’s tested after the temperature. The interaction’s test, 0.601, is the same in every version, because it’s always tested after both main effects. The conclusions don’t change.

title: Factorial MANOVA
text:
Quick quiz

1. With 2 catalysts and 3 temperatures, how many degrees of freedom does the interaction have?

1
2
6


(a - 1)(b - 1) = 1 \times 2 = 2.



2. Why test the interaction before the main effects?

Because R prints it last
Because if it’s real, a main effect averages over effects that differ, and the simple effects are what to report
Because the main effects can’t be tested when there’s an interaction


The main effects can be tested, but with a real interaction, they summarize the factor’s effect poorly.



3. The MANOVA’s interaction is significant. How do you find out which responses carry it?

From the size of Pillai’s trace
With univariate ANOVAs of each response, such as summary.aov(fit)
By fitting the MANOVA again without the interaction


Here, the yield carries it, and the purity and the color don’t.



4. Within the cells, the yield and the purity are correlated (−0.50). What does the MANOVA do with that correlation?

It ignores it, like separate ANOVAs
It uses it, through the within-cell SSCP matrix E
It removes the purity from the analysis


E holds the cross-products as well as the sums of squares, so the tests account for the correlations between the responses.



5. Why treat the temperature as a number instead of a factor?

It’s always more accurate
If its effect is linear, the model uses fewer degrees of freedom and the tests are sharper
Factors can’t have more than two levels


Check the straight lines with a lack-of-fit test first, as in the challenge. Here, p = 0.76.



6. One run is lost, so the design is unbalanced. What changes?

The interaction’s test now depends on the order of the terms
The sequential tests of the main effects now depend on the order of the terms
MANOVA can no longer be used


The interaction is tested last in every order. For the main effects, use Type II tests, car::Anova().

title: Factorial MANOVA
text:
Wrap-up
You can now analyze a factorial experiment with several responses! Here’s what you’ve learned:

The two-way MANOVA model splits the total SSCP matrix into H_A, H_B, H_{AB} and E, and tests each H against E with the usual four statistics.
Interaction first: if it’s real, report simple effects instead of main effects. A multivariate simple effect is a contrast of cell mean vectors, tested as in Lesson 7.
Univariate follow-ups show which responses carry each effect. Here, the yield carries the interaction, the purity only depends on the temperature, and the color has two additive main effects.
A quantitative factor can be treated as a number. A lack-of-fit test checks the straight lines, and fewer degrees of freedom make sharper tests.
Unbalanced data make sequential tests depend on the order of the terms. Type II tests, car::Anova(), don’t.
The pilot plant’s answer: at 195 °C, F2 gives 7.4 points more yield with the same purity and slightly more color. At 175 °C, it barely helps.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download factorial_quality.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

HE plots. The heplots package draws a picture of a MANOVA: an ellipse for each term’s H matrix and one for E. Make temp a factor as in this lesson, then try heplots::heplot(lm(cbind(yield_pct, color_apha) ~ catalyst * temp, data = fq)). With the default scaling, a term is significant by Roy’s test exactly when its ellipse sticks out of the error ellipse somewhere. Which directions do the three terms point in?
Effect sizes. heplots::etasq(fit) gives a multivariate effect size for each term, Pillai’s trace divided by the number of eigenvalues it can have. Which term has the largest effect?
All simple effects at once. Write a three-row hypothesis matrix that tests the catalyst at all three temperatures jointly in car::linearHypothesis(). What does it test, in terms of the model’s main effects and interaction?
Compare with Lesson 2.14. Lesson 2.14’s lab experiment found F2 advantages of 2.7, 4.5 and 7.9 points at the three temperatures. Are the pilot plant’s advantages (1.6, 4.2 and 7.4) consistent with them, given their standard errors?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Factorial MANOVA

A MANOVA with two or more crossed factors, which tests their main effects and interactions on several responses at once.

Interaction (multivariate)

An effect of one factor on the mean vector that depends on the level of another factor.

Simple effect

The effect of one factor at a single level of another factor, reported when the interaction is real.

Univariate follow-up

An ANOVA of a single response after a significant MANOVA, to see which responses carry an effect.

Lack-of-fit test

A test of whether a simpler model, such as straight lines in a quantitative factor, fits as well as the full categorical model.

Type II tests

Tests of each term after all the other terms that don’t contain it, which don’t depend on the order of the terms in unbalanced designs.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 505, Lesson 8: Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA), sections 8.9 to 8.11. A two-way MANOVA for a randomized block design, and how to form the MANOVA table.
Johnson and Wichern, Applied Multivariate Statistical Analysis, chapter 6, section 6.7, “Two-way multivariate analysis of variance”. The model, the SSCP split and the tests, with a worked example.
Penn State STAT 502, Lesson 5: Multi-Factor ANOVA. The univariate background: interactions, interaction plots and simple effects.

title: One-way MANOVA
text:
Module 3 · Lesson 6 of 13 Week 52 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Last lesson compared two suppliers. The plant has four, and the purchasing department wants the full picture: do the four suppliers’ feed lots differ, taking all four inspection results into account? With one response, that would be a one-way ANOVA (Lesson 2.13). With several, it’s a multivariate analysis of variance, or MANOVA. The ideas are the same, with one twist: sums of squares become matrices, and a test now has to summarize a whole matrix in one number. There are four popular ways to do that, and this lesson explains all of them.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: One-way MANOVA
text:
Four suppliers, four properties
Here are the 58 lots, one panel per property:

feed |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(all_of(vars), names_to = "property", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(property = factor(property, levels = vars, labels = c("Water (ppm)", "Aldehyde (ppm)", "Acid (mg KOH/g)", "Iron (ppb)"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = supplier, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#F4C0D1", color = "#C2416C", outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.6) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, size = 1.3, color = "#3A1F35", alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ property, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)








The fingerprints are clear: Kestrel is wet and acidic, Rosewater carries aldehyde, Plum Valley a little iron. You could run four one-way ANOVAs, one per property. But that has the problems you’ve seen before: four tests inflate the chance of a false alarm, and they ignore the correlations, so they can miss differences in combinations of properties, as the NIR analyzer showed in Lesson 5. MANOVA asks one question:

H_0: \boldsymbol\mu_1 = \boldsymbol\mu_2 = \boldsymbol\mu_3 = \boldsymbol\mu_4 ,

where each \boldsymbol\mu_i is a supplier’s mean vector of all four properties.

title: One-way MANOVA
text:
Sums of squares become matrices
One-way ANOVA splits the total sum of squares into a between-group and a within-group part: \text{SST} = \text{SSB} + \text{SSW}. MANOVA does the same with matrices of sums of squares and cross-products (SSCP matrices). With k groups, group mean vectors \bar{\mathbf{x}}_i and grand mean vector \bar{\mathbf{x}}:

\underbrace{\sum_{i}\sum_{j} (\mathbf{x}_{ij} - \bar{\mathbf{x}})(\mathbf{x}_{ij} - \bar{\mathbf{x}})^\top}_{T,\ \text{total}}
= \underbrace{\sum_{i} n_i (\bar{\mathbf{x}}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}})(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}})^\top}_{H,\ \text{between (hypothesis)}}
+ \underbrace{\sum_{i}\sum_{j} (\mathbf{x}_{ij} - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_i)(\mathbf{x}_{ij} - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_i)^\top}_{E,\ \text{within (error)}} .

Each matrix is p \times p. Its diagonal holds the ordinary ANOVA sums of squares, one per variable, and its off-diagonal entries are the matching sums of cross-products, which carry the correlations. H measures how far apart the group means are, and E how much the lots vary within each supplier. (Dividing E by N - k gives the pooled covariance matrix S_p from Lesson 5.)










Your turn. The setup code has built E and H for you. Compute the total matrix T directly from the data, and check that H + E = T.









The total matrix is centered at the grand mean vector, grand.


T_total <- crossprod(sweep(X, 2, grand))
max(abs(H + E - T_total))
About 10^{-11}: zero, up to rounding. And diag(H) holds the four ANOVA “between” sums of squares: 113,070 for the water, 4,954 for the aldehyde, 0.021 for the acid and 1,283 for the iron.

title: One-way MANOVA
text:
Wilks’ lambda and its friends
In ANOVA, the F statistic compares SSB with SSW. Here, you need to compare the matrix H with the matrix E. The natural comparison is E^{-1}H, the matrix version of the ratio SSB/SSW, and its eigenvalues, \lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots, sum it up. Each eigenvalue measures how far apart the groups are along one direction, compared with the within-group spread in that direction. There are s = \min(p, k - 1) non-zero eigenvalues: here \min(4, 3) = 3, because four group means always lie in a three-dimensional space.
Four test statistics combine the eigenvalues in different ways:








Statistic
Formula
Large values mean




Wilks’ lambda
\Lambda = \dfrac{|E|}{|H + E|} = \prod_i \dfrac{1}{1 + \lambda_i}
small \Lambda is evidence of a difference


Pillai’s trace
V = \sum_i \dfrac{\lambda_i}{1 + \lambda_i}
a difference


Hotelling-Lawley trace
U = \sum_i \lambda_i
a difference


Roy’s largest root
\theta = \lambda_1
a difference



Wilks’ lambda has the most intuitive form: the generalized variance within the groups, divided by the generalized variance overall (Lesson 1). If the groups are all the same, the two are about equal and \Lambda is close to 1. If the groups differ a lot, most of the variation is between groups, and \Lambda is close to 0. It’s the likelihood-ratio test for MANOVA. Each statistic has an approximate F distribution, which is how R computes the p-values.
With one variable, all four reduce to the ordinary ANOVA F-test. With two groups, they all reduce to the two-sample T^2.
Your turn. Compute Wilks’ lambda from the determinants.









The denominator is the determinant of the total matrix, H + E.


det(E) / det(H + E)
\Lambda = 0.034: within-supplier variation is only about 3% of the total generalized variance. The suppliers’ lots differ enormously.




Your turn. Compute the eigenvalues of E^{-1}H.









The matrix is E^{-1}H: solve(E) %*% H. (Re() drops the zero imaginary parts that eigen() can return for a non-symmetric matrix.)


lambda <- Re(eigen(solve(E) %*% H)$values)
round(lambda, 3)
5.499, 2.141, 0.460 and 0. Three non-zero eigenvalues, as promised, and the first two carry 94% of their total: the four suppliers are spread out in mainly two directions. (The directions themselves, the eigenvectors, are the linear discriminants of Lesson 13.) Check that prod(1 / (1 + lambda)) gives Wilks’ lambda.

title: One-way MANOVA
text:
MANOVA in R
manova() fits the model, with the responses bound into a matrix on the left of the formula, and summary() runs the test. Pillai’s trace is R’s default:

fit <- manova(cbind(water_ppm, aldehyde_ppm, acid_mgKOH, iron_ppb) ~ supplier, data = feed)
summary(fit)
#>           Df Pillai approx F num Df den Df    Pr(>F)    
#> supplier   3 1.8428   21.101     12    159 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> Residuals 54                                            
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
summary(fit, test = "Wilks")
#>           Df    Wilks approx F num Df den Df    Pr(>F)    
#> supplier   3 0.033553   29.385     12 135.22 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> Residuals 54                                              
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Pillai’s trace is 1.84, with F = 21.1 on 12 and 159 degrees of freedom: p = 4 \times 10^{-27}. Wilks, Hotelling-Lawley and Roy all agree, with even smaller p-values. No surprise there: the boxplots showed differences you could see from across the room. The real work starts after the test: which suppliers differ, and on what? That’s the next lesson.
Your turn. Run the MANOVA and pull out the p-value for Wilks’ lambda.









The test’s name is "Wilks".


fit <- manova(cbind(water_ppm, aldehyde_ppm, acid_mgKOH, iron_ppb) ~ supplier, data = feed)
summary(fit, test = "Wilks")$stats[1, "Pr(>F)"]
6 \times 10^{-32}. Wilks’ \Lambda = 0.034 converts to F = 29.4 on 12 and 135.2 degrees of freedom (Rao’s approximation, which is why the degrees of freedom aren’t whole numbers).

title: One-way MANOVA
text:
Which statistic should you report?
They usually agree, as they do here. When they don’t, it’s because they weigh the eigenvalues differently:

Roy’s largest root looks only at \lambda_1, so it’s the most powerful when the groups differ along a single direction, and the least when they differ along several. Its F approximation is an upper bound, so its p-values are too small: treat it with care.
Wilks’ lambda and Hotelling-Lawley sit in the middle. Wilks is the traditional choice and the likelihood-ratio test.
Pillai’s trace is the most robust when the assumptions are shaky, especially unequal covariance matrices, as long as the groups are of similar sizes. That’s why R uses it by default, and it’s a safe choice to report.

Whichever you choose, choose it before you look at the results, and report it with its F, degrees of freedom and p-value.

title: One-way MANOVA
text:
Checking the assumptions
MANOVA assumes the same things as a two-sample T^2, for every group:

Independent observations. Each lot is its own delivery, so that’s reasonable.
Multivariate normality within each group. Check the residuals, each observation minus its group’s mean vector: one-variable Q-Q plots and Shapiro-Wilk tests, and a chi-square Q-Q plot of their Mahalanobis distances (Lesson 3). Here, all four residuals pass Shapiro-Wilk comfortably (every p-value is above 0.5). MANOVA, like ANOVA, is fairly robust to moderate non-normality.
Equal covariance matrices. That’s the multivariate version of ANOVA’s equal variances, and it’s checked with Box’s M test: H_0: \Sigma_1 = \Sigma_2 = \dots = \Sigma_k.

Box’s M has two well-known faults: it’s very sensitive to non-normality (it can reject because of heavy tails, not because of the covariances), and with big samples it flags differences too small to matter. So the usual advice is to take it seriously only at small significance levels, like 0.001. If it does reject, prefer Pillai’s trace, and look at the group standard deviations and correlations to see what differs.
Your turn. Run Box’s M test for the four suppliers.









The grouping variable is supplier.


bm <- heplots::boxM(X, supplier)
bm$p.value
p = 0.0008: the covariance matrices differ, even by Box’s strict standard. sapply(levels(supplier), function(s) apply(X[supplier == s, ], 2, sd)) shows the culprit: Kestrel’s water has a standard deviation of 29 ppm, against 11 to 20 for the others. Since the groups are of similar sizes (13 to 16 lots) and the differences between suppliers are huge, Pillai’s trace is still trustworthy here.

title: One-way MANOVA
text:
Following up with ANOVAs
A significant MANOVA says that the mean vectors differ somewhere. The simplest follow-up is an ordinary ANOVA for each response, which summary.aov() runs straight from the MANOVA fit:

summary.aov(fit)
#>  Response water_ppm :
#>             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
#> supplier     3 113070   37690  94.813 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> Residuals   54  21466     398                      
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#>  Response aldehyde_ppm :
#>             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
#> supplier     3 4953.8 1651.26  38.408 1.997e-13 ***
#> Residuals   54 2321.6   42.99                      
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#>  Response acid_mgKOH :
#>             Df   Sum Sq   Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
#> supplier     3 0.020871 0.0069570  19.551 1.04e-08 ***
#> Residuals   54 0.019215 0.0003558                     
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#>  Response iron_ppb :
#>             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
#> supplier     3 1283.4  427.80  7.6749 0.0002316 ***
#> Residuals   54 3009.9   55.74                      
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

All four properties differ between suppliers: water with F = 94.8, aldehyde 38.4, acid 19.6, and iron 7.7 (p = 0.0002). Running ANOVAs only after a significant MANOVA is called a protected approach: the MANOVA guards against the false alarms of fishing through many responses, at least partly. It still doesn’t say which suppliers differ on what, or account for the correlations between the responses. For that, the next lesson builds contrasts and simultaneous intervals.
Your turn. Find the p-value of the iron’s ANOVA.









The p-value column is called "Pr(>F)".


fit <- manova(cbind(water_ppm, aldehyde_ppm, acid_mgKOH, iron_ppb) ~ supplier, data = feed)
anovas <- summary.aov(fit)
anovas[[4]][1, "Pr(>F)"]
p = 0.00023. The iron, the property that told Fizzwell and Plum Valley apart, is the weakest of the four overall: its differences are modest, and mostly involve Plum Valley, while the water and the aldehyde each set one supplier far apart from the rest.

title: One-way MANOVA
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Pillai’s trace by hand. Compute Pillai’s trace from the eigenvalues of E^{-1}H, and compare it with summary(fit).









Pillai’s trace is \sum \lambda_i/(1 + \lambda_i).


lambda <- Re(eigen(solve(E) %*% H)$values)
sum(lambda / (1 + lambda))
1.843, as summary(fit) reports. Pillai’s trace can’t exceed s = 3, one for each non-zero eigenvalue, and each term is a squared canonical correlation between the properties and the supplier, an idea you’ll meet in Lesson 12.




Challenge 2 · Without Kestrel. Leave Kestrel out, and redo Box’s M test and the MANOVA for the other three suppliers.









Leave out "Kestrel".


three <- filter(feed, supplier != "Kestrel")
fit3 <- manova(cbind(water_ppm, aldehyde_ppm, acid_mgKOH, iron_ppb) ~ supplier, data = three)
c(box_m = heplots::boxM(as.matrix(three[, vars]), three$supplier)$p.value,
  pillai = summary(fit3)$stats[1, "Pr(>F)"])
Box’s M now gives p = 0.23: the other three suppliers share a covariance matrix, so Kestrel was the odd one out. And the three still differ clearly (p = 10^{-10}), mostly through Rosewater’s aldehyde and Plum Valley’s iron.

title: One-way MANOVA
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does MANOVA’s null hypothesis say?

Each property has the same mean in every group, tested one property at a time
All the groups have the same mean vector
All the groups have the same covariance matrix


H_0: \boldsymbol\mu_1 = \dots = \boldsymbol\mu_k, one hypothesis about all the properties together. Equal covariance matrices are an assumption, checked with Box’s M.



2. What’s on the diagonal of the between-group SSCP matrix H?

The ordinary between-group sums of squares, one for each variable
The group means
The correlations between the variables


The diagonals of H and E are the ANOVA sums of squares. The off-diagonal cross-products carry the correlations.



3. Wilks’ lambda is 0.034. What does it mean?

The groups barely differ
The within-group generalized variance is only 3.4% of the total, so the groups differ a lot
3.4% of the lots are misclassified


\Lambda = |E|/|H + E|. Values near 1 mean no difference, and values near 0 a big one.



4. With 4 groups and 4 variables, how many non-zero eigenvalues does E^{-1}H have?

4
3
1


s = \min(p, k - 1) = \min(4, 3) = 3: four group means span at most a three-dimensional space.



5. Box’s M test rejects equal covariance matrices. What’s a sensible reaction?

Abandon the MANOVA
Report Pillai’s trace, which is the most robust, and look at which group’s spread differs
Switch to Roy’s largest root


Box’s M is oversensitive, and Pillai’s trace holds up well when the groups are of similar sizes. Here, the culprit was Kestrel’s variable water content.



6. Why run the univariate ANOVAs only after a significant MANOVA?

Because ANOVA can’t be run without MANOVA
The MANOVA protects, at least partly, against false alarms from testing many responses separately
Because they give the same p-values


That’s the “protected” approach. Contrasts and simultaneous intervals, in the next lesson, give fuller protection.

title: One-way MANOVA
text:
Wrap-up
You can now compare several groups on several variables at once! Here’s what you’ve learned:

MANOVA tests H_0: \boldsymbol\mu_1 = \dots = \boldsymbol\mu_k in one go, without the multiple testing of separate ANOVAs, and with the correlations taken into account.
SSCP matrices: T = H + E, between and within groups. Their diagonals are the ANOVA sums of squares.
The test statistics all come from the eigenvalues of E^{-1}H: Wilks’ \Lambda = |E|/|H + E|, Pillai’s \sum\lambda_i/(1 + \lambda_i), Hotelling-Lawley’s \sum\lambda_i and Roy’s \lambda_1. There are \min(p, k - 1) non-zero eigenvalues.
In R: manova(cbind(y1, y2, ...) ~ group) and summary(fit, test = "Pillai"). Pillai is the robust default, and Roy is liberal.
Assumptions: independence, multivariate normal residuals, and equal covariance matrices (Box’s M, heplots::boxM(), at a strict level). Kestrel’s covariance matrix differs, the other three suppliers’ don’t.
Follow-ups: summary.aov(fit) runs one ANOVA per response. All four properties differ between the suppliers.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download feed_lots.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install the heplots and car packages.

HE plots. Fit mlm <- lm(cbind(water_ppm, aldehyde_ppm, acid_mgKOH, iron_ppb) ~ supplier, data = feed) and run heplots::heplot(mlm). It draws the H and E matrices as ellipses: if the H ellipse pokes outside the E ellipse, the effect is significant. Try heplots::pairs(mlm) for every pair of properties.
car’s Manova. Run car::Manova(mlm) and summary(car::Manova(mlm)). It prints all four statistics, and the H and E matrices.
A smaller difference. Run the MANOVA for Fizzwell and Plum Valley only, and compare it with your two-sample T^2 from Lesson 5. All four statistics should give the same F.
Residual checks. Compute the residuals, resid(mlm), and draw a chi-square Q-Q plot of their squared Mahalanobis distances (use the pooled covariance, crossprod(resid(mlm)) / (58 - 4)). Are any lots unusual?










NoteKey words from this lesson






MANOVA (multivariate analysis of variance)

A test of whether several groups have the same mean vector on several response variables.

SSCP matrix

A matrix of sums of squares and cross-products. In MANOVA, the total matrix T splits into a between-groups matrix H and a within-groups matrix E.

Wilks’ lambda

|E|/|H + E|, the ratio of the within-group to the total generalized variance. It’s the likelihood-ratio statistic for MANOVA.

Pillai’s trace

\sum \lambda_i/(1 + \lambda_i), the most robust of the four MANOVA statistics.

Hotelling-Lawley trace

\sum \lambda_i, the sum of the eigenvalues of E^{-1}H.

Roy’s largest root

\lambda_1, the largest eigenvalue of E^{-1}H, most powerful when the groups differ in a single direction.

Box’s M test

A test that several groups share the same covariance matrix. It’s sensitive to non-normality, so it’s usually read at a strict level.

Protected univariate tests

Ordinary ANOVAs for each response, run only after a significant MANOVA.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 505, Lesson 8: Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA), sections 8.1 to 8.5. The SSCP matrices, the four test statistics, and a complete worked example with checks.
John Fox, Michael Friendly and Georges Monette, “Visualizing hypothesis tests in multivariate linear models: the heplots package for R”, Computational Statistics (2009). Where HE plots come from, and how to read them.
Johnson and Wichern, Applied Multivariate Statistical Analysis, chapter 6, sections 6.4 to 6.6. One-way MANOVA, its test statistics and its assumptions.

title: Inference for a mean vector
text:
Module 3 · Lesson 4 of 13 Week 50 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Our product’s data sheet, the document that customers design their processes around, lists typical values for the four properties: 99.2% purity, 135 ppm of water, a color of 15 APHA, and an acid value of 0.205 mg KOH/g. Is the plant still making the product the data sheet describes? That’s a question about four means at once. You could run four t-tests, but this lesson shows two problems with that: it asks four questions instead of one, and, more surprisingly, it can miss a difference that’s really there. The fix is a test named after Harold Hotelling, who introduced it in 1931.
In this lesson you’ll:
FS73, the batch with the acid-wash residue (Lessons 2 and 3), is left out from here on: it isn’t an example of normal production.

title: Inference for a mean vector
text:
One question instead of four
The question is a single null hypothesis about the whole mean vector:

H_0: \boldsymbol\mu = \boldsymbol\mu_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 99.2 \\ 135 \\ 15 \\ 0.205 \end{pmatrix}.

In one dimension, the t statistic is t = (\bar{x} - \mu_0)/(s/\sqrt{n}), and its square is t^2 = n(\bar{x} - \mu_0)(s^2)^{-1}(\bar{x} - \mu_0). Replace each piece by its matrix version, and you get Hotelling’s T^2:

T^2 = n\,(\bar{\mathbf{x}} - \boldsymbol\mu_0)^\top S^{-1} (\bar{\mathbf{x}} - \boldsymbol\mu_0) .

It’s n times the squared Mahalanobis distance of the sample mean from the target. If H_0 is true and the data are multivariate normal, a rescaled T^2 follows an F distribution:

\frac{n - p}{p\,(n - 1)}\, T^2 \sim F_{p,\ n - p} .

With 79 batches and 4 properties, that’s an F distribution with 4 and 75 degrees of freedom.










Your turn. Compute T^2, the F statistic and the p-value.









The denominator degrees of freedom are n - p.


d <- colMeans(Y) - target
T2 <- n * t(d) %*% solve(cov(Y)) %*% d
F_stat <- (n - p) / (p * (n - 1)) * T2
c(T2 = T2, F = F_stat, p = pf(F_stat, p, n - p, lower.tail = FALSE))
T^2 = 11.1, F = 2.67 on 4 and 75 degrees of freedom, p = 0.039. At the 5% level, the product isn’t what the data sheet describes.

title: Inference for a mean vector
section: One at a time says no, together says yes
text:
One at a time says no, together says yes
Now the separate t-tests. Here are the means, the targets and the four p-values:

tibble(property = colnames(Y), mean = colMeans(Y), target = target,
       p_value = sapply(1:4, function(j) t.test(Y[, j], mu = target[j])$p.value))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   property      mean  target p_value
#>   <chr>        <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 purity_pct  99.2    99.2     0.404
#> 2 water_ppm  132.    135       0.282
#> 3 color_apha  15.4    15       0.373
#> 4 acid_mgKOH   0.209   0.205   0.231

None of the four comes anywhere near significance: the p-values run from 0.23 to 0.40. Each mean, on its own, is consistent with its typical value. Yet the joint test rejects. How?
Look at water and acid together. The product has 3.4 ppm less water than the data sheet says, and 0.004 mg KOH/g more acid. Each difference alone is small. But water and acid are positively correlated (water makes acid), so in this process they tend to move up or down together. A product that’s drier yet more acidic is moving against the grain, in a direction where the sample mean is precise. Here’s the picture: the ellipse is the 95% confidence region for the two means, and the dashed rectangle is made of the two ordinary 95% confidence intervals:

W <- Y[, c("water_ppm", "acid_mgKOH")]
n <- nrow(W)
c2 <- 2 * (n - 1) / (n - 2) * qf(0.95, 2, n - 2)
theta <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200)
region <- t(colMeans(W) + sqrt(c2 / n) * t(chol(cov(W))) %*% rbind(cos(theta), sin(theta)))
ci <- sapply(1:2, function(j) t.test(W[, j])$conf.int)
ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = ci[1, 1], xmax = ci[2, 1], ymin = ci[1, 2], ymax = ci[2, 2],
           fill = NA, color = "grey55", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_path(aes(x = region[, 1], y = region[, 2]), color = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(x = mean(W[, 1]), y = mean(W[, 2])), color = "#2a78d6", size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = 135, y = 0.205), color = "#C2416C", size = 3, shape = 17) +
  annotate("text", x = 135, y = 0.205, label = "data sheet", vjust = 2, size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(W[, 1]), y = mean(W[, 2]), label = "sample mean", vjust = -1.2, size = 3.5) +
  labs(x = "Mean water (ppm)", y = "Mean acid (mg KOH/g)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The data sheet’s values (the triangle) are inside the rectangle, so each t-test lets them through. But they’re outside the tilted ellipse, which follows the correlation between the two means. The rectangle’s corners are full of combinations that the data actually rule out, like “drier and more acidic”, and that’s exactly where the data sheet’s values sit. For these two properties alone, T^2 = 7.3, p = 0.032.
That’s the second reason to test jointly. The first was multiple testing (Lesson 2.6): four tests at 5% each have a much bigger chance of a false alarm than 5%. The joint test fixes that, and it uses the correlations, which can make it more powerful than any of the separate tests.
Your turn. Run the four separate t-tests against the data sheet’s values, and collect their p-values.









Each test uses its own target: target[j].


sapply(1:4, function(j) t.test(Y[, j], mu = target[j])$p.value)
0.40, 0.28, 0.37 and 0.23. Four “no difference” verdicts, and one joint “yes, there’s a difference”.










NoteGo deeper: T² is the worst-case t-test





Take any linear combination of the properties, \mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x}, and test whether its mean equals \mathbf{a}^\top\boldsymbol\mu_0. Its squared t statistic is

t^2(\mathbf{a}) = \frac{n\,[\mathbf{a}^\top(\bar{\mathbf{x}} - \boldsymbol\mu_0)]^2}{\mathbf{a}^\top S\,\mathbf{a}} .

Hotelling’s T^2 is the largest value that t^2(\mathbf{a}) can take, over every possible \mathbf{a}. (That’s the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, and the maximum is reached at \mathbf{a} \propto S^{-1}(\bar{\mathbf{x}} - \boldsymbol\mu_0).) So T^2 searches every combination of the properties for the one that differs most from its target, and it reports how big that difference is.
That’s why T^2 can’t follow a t distribution: it’s the maximum of infinitely many correlated t^2s, so it’s naturally larger, and its F distribution allows for the search. And it’s why the confidence region gives simultaneous intervals, in the next section: they’re all consistent with one another, because they all come from the same ellipse.

title: Inference for a mean vector
text:
Confidence regions
The 95% confidence region for \boldsymbol\mu is the set of all mean vectors that the T^2 test wouldn’t reject:

\left\{ \boldsymbol\mu : n(\bar{\mathbf{x}} - \boldsymbol\mu)^\top S^{-1}(\bar{\mathbf{x}} - \boldsymbol\mu) \le c^2 \right\}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{p(n - 1)}{n - p}\,F_{p,\,n-p}(0.95) .

It’s an ellipsoid centered at \bar{\mathbf{x}}, with axes along the eigenvectors of S, and half-lengths \sqrt{\lambda_j}\,c/\sqrt{n}. With two variables, you can draw it, as above. With four, you can’t, but you can still check whether a given vector is inside it: compute its T^2, and compare it with c^2.
Your turn. For water and acid alone, is the data sheet’s pair of values inside the 95% confidence region? Compute its T^2 and the critical value c^2, with p = 2.









With p = 2, the denominator degrees of freedom are n - 2.


W <- Y[, c("water_ppm", "acid_mgKOH")]
d <- colMeans(W) - c(135, 0.205)
T2 <- n * t(d) %*% solve(cov(W)) %*% d
c2 <- 2 * (n - 1) / (n - 2) * qf(0.95, 2, n - 2)
c(T2 = T2, critical = c2)
T^2 = 7.31, above the critical value of 6.31: the data sheet’s water and acid lie outside the confidence ellipse, as the plot showed.

title: Inference for a mean vector
text:
Simultaneous intervals
The joint test says something differs. To report what, you want an interval for each mean, but four ordinary 95% intervals don’t have a 95% chance of being right together. Two ways to fix that:

Simultaneous T^2 intervals: \bar{x}_j \pm c\, s_j/\sqrt{n}, with c the square root of the critical value above. These are the shadows of the confidence ellipsoid on each axis. Their great strength is that the same c works for every linear combination you might look at, \mathbf{a}^\top\bar{\mathbf{x}} \pm c\sqrt{\mathbf{a}^\top S\mathbf{a}/n}, even ones you think of after seeing the data, and all of them are right together 95% of the time.
Bonferroni intervals: \bar{x}_j \pm t_{n-1}\!\left(\tfrac{\alpha}{2p}\right) s_j/\sqrt{n}. Each interval gets an error rate of \alpha/p, so together they’re wrong at most \alpha of the time (Lesson 2.13). For a few planned intervals, they’re narrower than the T^2 ones.

They differ only in the multiplier. For p = 4 and n = 79:



Intervals
Multiplier
Covers all four together




ordinary t, one at a time
1.99
no


Bonferroni
2.56
yes, at least 95%


simultaneous T^2
3.22
yes, 95%, and any other combination too



Here, every interval contains its typical value, even the narrowest. That isn’t a contradiction of the joint test. The difference the test found isn’t in any single property: it’s in a combination, acid relative to water, and only an interval for that combination would show it. The first challenge finds it.
Your turn. Compute the three multipliers.









The F quantile has p and n - p degrees of freedom.


c(t = qt(0.975, n - 1),
  bonferroni = qt(1 - 0.05 / (2 * p), n - 1),
  T2 = sqrt(p * (n - 1) / (n - p) * qf(0.95, p, n - p)))
1.99, 2.56 and 3.22. The price of covering every possible combination is a wider interval for each one.




Your turn. Compute the simultaneous T^2 interval for the mean acid value.









The standard error of a mean is s/\sqrt{n}.


c_mult <- sqrt(p * (n - 1) / (n - p) * qf(0.95, p, n - p))
acid <- Y[, "acid_mgKOH"]
mean(acid) + c(-1, 1) * c_mult * sd(acid) / sqrt(n)
From 0.198 to 0.220 mg KOH/g: it contains the data sheet’s 0.205, comfortably.

title: Inference for a mean vector
text:
Large samples: the chi-square version
When n is large, S is a very good estimate of \Sigma, and T^2 behaves like the squared Mahalanobis distance with a known covariance matrix. By last lesson’s property 4, that’s chi-square:

T^2 \approx \chi^2_p \quad \text{for large } n - p .

That has two advantages. It doesn’t need multivariate normality, only the central limit theorem, so it works for skewed data when n is large. And chi-square quantiles are easy to remember: the 95% point for p = 4 is 9.49, against 10.37 for the exact T^2 critical value here. With n = 79, the two still differ noticeably. The chi-square version is a little too liberal, and the F version is the one to report.
Your turn. Compute the large-sample chi-square p-value for T^2 = 11.11.









The degrees of freedom are the number of variables, p.


d <- colMeans(Y) - target
T2 <- n * t(d) %*% solve(cov(Y)) %*% d
pchisq(T2, df = p, lower.tail = FALSE)
p = 0.025, against 0.039 from the F distribution. The approximation ignores the uncertainty in S, so it’s a little too confident.

title: Inference for a mean vector
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The combination that differs. The Go deeper box says that T^2 is the squared t statistic of the best combination, \mathbf{a} = S^{-1}(\bar{\mathbf{x}} - \boldsymbol\mu_0). Compute that combination for every batch, test its mean against \mathbf{a}^\top\boldsymbol\mu_0 with a t-test, and square the t statistic.









The combination’s target is \mathbf{a}^\top\boldsymbol\mu_0: sum(a * target).


a <- solve(cov(Y)) %*% (colMeans(Y) - target)
z <- Y %*% a
t_best <- t.test(z, mu = sum(a * target))$statistic
unname(t_best^2)
11.11, exactly T^2. Scale each weight by its variable’s standard deviation, a * sqrt(diag(cov(Y))), to compare them: the biggest are +1.0 for the acid and -0.8 for the water, with smaller weights for the purity (+0.3) and the color (-0.2). The difference is “acid relative to water”: for its water content, our product is more acidic than the data sheet suggests. Not by much, but consistently.




Challenge 2 · Units don’t matter. Express the water in percent instead of ppm, and the acid in mg KOH per kg instead of per g, convert the targets the same way, and recompute T^2.









The acid was multiplied by 1000, so its target is too.


Y2 <- Y
Y2[, "water_ppm"] <- Y2[, "water_ppm"] / 10000
Y2[, "acid_mgKOH"] <- Y2[, "acid_mgKOH"] * 1000
target2 <- target * c(1, 1 / 10000, 1, 1000)
d2 <- colMeans(Y2) - target2
n * t(d2) %*% solve(cov(Y2)) %*% d2
11.11 again. T^2 doesn’t care about units, because S^{-1} undoes any rescaling. A test based on plain Euclidean distances would give a different answer in every set of units, which is no way to make a decision.

title: Inference for a mean vector
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does Hotelling’s T^2 test?

Whether each mean equals its target, one at a time
Whether the whole mean vector equals a target vector, in one test
Whether the variables are correlated


H_0: \boldsymbol\mu = \boldsymbol\mu_0, a single hypothesis about all the means together.



2. Four t-tests are all non-significant, but T^2 rejects. How can that be?

It can’t: one of the calculations is wrong
The difference lies in a combination of the variables that goes against their correlation
T^2 always rejects more often


T^2 is the largest t^2 over all combinations. Here, the product is drier yet more acidic, a direction in which the mean is estimated precisely.



3. What’s the distribution of \frac{n-p}{p(n-1)}T^2 under H_0, for multivariate normal data?

t_{n-1}
F_{p,\,n-p}
\chi^2_{n}


And for large n, T^2 itself is approximately \chi^2_p.



4. What shape is a confidence region for a mean vector of two variables?

A rectangle made of two confidence intervals
An ellipse, tilted by the correlation between the two means
A circle


It’s the set of mean vectors with T^2 below the critical value. The rectangle includes combinations that the ellipse rules out.



5. Why are simultaneous T^2 intervals wider than Bonferroni intervals for the four means?

They use a different estimate of the variance
They cover every possible linear combination of the means, not just the four you planned
Bonferroni intervals aren’t valid


For a few planned intervals, Bonferroni is narrower. For exploring combinations after seeing the data, the T^2 intervals keep their promise.



6. You change the water’s units from ppm to percent. What happens to T^2?

It shrinks by a factor of 10,000
Nothing: it’s the same in any units
It becomes invalid


S^{-1} undoes any rescaling of the variables, so T^2 (like the Mahalanobis distance) is unit-free.

title: Inference for a mean vector
text:
Wrap-up
You can now test several means at once, and say where they differ! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Hotelling’s T^2 = n(\bar{\mathbf{x}} - \boldsymbol\mu_0)^\top S^{-1}(\bar{\mathbf{x}} - \boldsymbol\mu_0) tests a whole mean vector at once, with \frac{n-p}{p(n-1)}T^2 \sim F_{p,\,n-p}.
Joint beats separate: one test instead of four, and it uses the correlations. The product matched every typical value on its own, yet jointly it didn’t (p = 0.039): it’s more acidic for its water content than the data sheet suggests.
Confidence regions are ellipsoids. Check whether a vector is inside by comparing its T^2 with c^2 = \frac{p(n-1)}{n-p}F_{p,\,n-p}(0.95).
Simultaneous intervals: T^2 intervals (multiplier c) cover every combination together, and Bonferroni intervals (t_{n-1}(\alpha/2p)) are narrower for a few planned ones.
T^2 is the worst-case t^2, reached at \mathbf{a} \propto S^{-1}(\bar{\mathbf{x}} - \boldsymbol\mu_0), and it doesn’t depend on the units.
Large samples: T^2 \approx \chi^2_p, without needing normality, but the F version is more accurate for moderate n.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download batch_quality.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Packages that do it for you. Install the DescTools package and run DescTools::HotellingsT2Test(Y, mu = target). Check that it matches your T^2 test.
With and without FS73. Rerun the test with FS73 included. How much does one batch change the result, and in which direction? Why?
Coverage by simulation. Simulate 2,000 samples of 79 batches from a multivariate normal with mean target and covariance cov(Y), and count how often the T^2 test rejects at 5%. Then count how often at least one of the four t-tests rejects. Which one keeps its promise of 5%?
An ellipse for purity and color. Draw the 95% confidence region for the mean purity and color, which are strongly negatively correlated, and add the data sheet’s values. Which way does the ellipse tilt?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Hotelling’s T^2

The multivariate version of the squared t statistic, n(\bar{\mathbf{x}} - \boldsymbol\mu_0)^\top S^{-1}(\bar{\mathbf{x}} - \boldsymbol\mu_0), used to test a mean vector.

Confidence region

The set of all mean vectors that a test wouldn’t reject: an ellipsoid for T^2.

Simultaneous confidence intervals

A set of intervals that are all correct together with a stated probability, such as 95%.

T^2 intervals

Simultaneous intervals with the multiplier c = \sqrt{\frac{p(n-1)}{n-p}F_{p,\,n-p}(0.95)}, valid for every linear combination of the means.

Bonferroni intervals

Simultaneous intervals for a planned set of m combinations, each built at the level 1 - \alpha/m.

Affine invariance

A statistic’s property of not changing when the variables are rescaled or recombined linearly, as T^2 doesn’t.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 505, Lesson 7: Inferences Regarding Multivariate Population Mean, sections 7.1.1 to 7.1.5 and 7.2.4. Hotelling’s T^2, confidence ellipses, and simultaneous and Bonferroni intervals, with worked examples.
Johnson and Wichern, Applied Multivariate Statistical Analysis, chapter 5. The full treatment, including the proofs and the large-sample results.
Harold Hotelling, “The generalization of Student’s ratio”, Annals of Mathematical Statistics 2 (1931). The paper where it all started.

title: Statistical distance
text:
Module 3 · Lesson 2 of 13 Week 48 of 160 About 5–7 hours
With one variable, “unusual” is easy: a z-score of 3 is unusual. With four, it’s harder than it looks. A batch can be perfectly ordinary on every property separately and still be very strange as a whole, because the combination doesn’t fit the way the properties usually go together. This lesson builds the right ruler for multivariate data, the Mahalanobis distance, and uses it to catch a batch that every one-at-a-time check would let through.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Statistical distance
text:
Euclidean distance
The obvious way to measure how far a batch is from the average batch is the straight-line, Euclidean distance between their observation vectors:

d(\mathbf{x}, \bar{\mathbf{x}}) = \sqrt{(x_1 - \bar{x}_1)^2 + \dots + (x_p - \bar{x}_p)^2} = \sqrt{(\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}})^\top(\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}})} .

It treats every direction as equally important, and that’s the problem. A difference of 10 ppm of water counts as much as a difference of 10 percentage points of purity, which would be a catastrophe. In practice, the Euclidean distance between batches is just the difference in water content, because water is measured in big numbers.










Your turn. Compute every batch’s Euclidean distance from the mean vector, and find the most distant batch.









sweep(Y, 2, xbar) subtracts the mean vector from every row. Find the batch with the largest d.


d <- sqrt(rowSums(sweep(Y, 2, xbar)^2))
names(which.max(d))
FS51, at a distance of 87. It’s the wettest batch, with 218 ppm of water. That might be genuinely unusual, but this ruler couldn’t tell us anything else: the purity, color and acid barely contribute.

title: Statistical distance
section: Standardizing is better, but not enough
text:
Standardizing is better, but not enough
The units problem has an easy fix: convert every variable to z-scores first, so that each one counts in standard deviations. The standardized distance is

d_z = \sqrt{z_1^2 + \dots + z_p^2}, \qquad z_j = \frac{x_j - \bar{x}_j}{s_j} .

Now every property gets a fair say. But one problem remains. Look at water against acid, in standard units, with two batches picked out:

Z <- scale(Y)
r <- cor(Y)[2, 4]
theta <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200)
e2 <- eigen(matrix(c(1, r, r, 1), 2))
ellipse <- function(c2) {
  pts <- t(e2$vectors %*% diag(sqrt(c2 * e2$values)) %*% rbind(cos(theta), sin(theta)))
  tibble(x = pts[, 1], y = pts[, 2])
}
circle <- tibble(x = sqrt(qchisq(0.99, 2)) * cos(theta), y = sqrt(qchisq(0.99, 2)) * sin(theta))
pts <- tibble(batch = rownames(Z), x = Z[, "water_ppm"], y = Z[, "acid_mgKOH"]) |>
  mutate(type = case_when(batch == "FS73" ~ "FS73", batch == "FS51" ~ "FS51", TRUE ~ "other"))
ggplot(pts, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_path(data = circle, color = "grey65", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_path(data = ellipse(qchisq(0.99, 2)), color = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_path(data = ellipse(qchisq(0.5, 2)), color = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_path(data = ellipse(13.3), color = "#C2416C", linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(color = type, size = type)) +
  geom_text(data = filter(pts, type != "other"), aes(label = batch), nudge_x = 0.45, size = 3.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(FS73 = "#C2416C", FS51 = "#1baf7a", other = "grey55")) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(FS73 = 3, FS51 = 3, other = 1.6)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Water (z-score)", y = "Acid (z-score)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "none")








The dashed circle is a set of points at the same standardized distance from the center. But the data don’t fill a circle. Water and acid are correlated (r = 0.58), so the cloud is stretched along the diagonal, an ellipse, not a circle. FS51 (green) sits at the far end of the cloud: extreme, but in a direction the data often go. FS73 (rose) is closer to the center by standardized distance, but it sits in a direction where the data almost never go: low water with high acid. Water makes acid, so that combination needs explaining.
Your turn. Compute FS73’s standardized distance from the center, using all four properties.









Square the z-scores and add them up across each row: rowSums(Z^2).


Z <- scale(Y)
dz <- sqrt(rowSums(Z^2))
dz["FS73"]
2.62. That’s only the 16th largest of the 80 batches: by this ruler, FS73 is unremarkable. Its z-scores are 1.1 for purity, −1.6 for water, −0.3 for color and 1.7 for acid. None of them would raise an eyebrow on its own.

title: Statistical distance
text:
The Mahalanobis distance
The right ruler accounts for the correlations as well as the spreads. It’s the Mahalanobis distance, introduced by the Indian statistician P. C. Mahalanobis in 1936:

D^2(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}})^\top S^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}}) .

It’s the squared Euclidean distance with S^{-1} in the middle, and the inverse covariance matrix is what does the work. Remember the end of last lesson: S^{-1} magnifies the directions in which the data hardly vary. So a step in a direction the data often take counts for little, and the same step in a direction the data rarely take counts for a lot. With uncorrelated variables, D^2 is exactly the sum of the squared z-scores, and with one variable it’s just z^2.
R’s mahalanobis(x, center, cov) returns D^2, already squared, for every row:

d2 <- mahalanobis(Y, colMeans(Y), cov(Y))
head(sort(d2, decreasing = TRUE), 4)
#>      FS73      FS51      FS08      FS24 
#> 34.616060 12.354437  9.574946  9.462807

FS73’s squared distance is 34.6. The next most unusual batch is at 12.4. FS73 is by far the strangest batch of the quarter, and no single property says so.






NoteGo deeper: Mahalanobis distance is Euclidean distance after “whitening”





Use the spectral decomposition, S = P\Lambda P^\top, so that S^{-1} = P\Lambda^{-1}P^\top. Then

D^2 = (\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}})^\top P \Lambda^{-1} P^\top (\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}}) = \sum_{j=1}^{p} \frac{y_j^2}{\lambda_j}, \qquad \mathbf{y} = P^\top(\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}}) .

In words: rotate the data onto the principal axes (the eigenvectors), divide each coordinate by its standard deviation along that axis, \sqrt{\lambda_j}, and measure ordinary distance. That turns the elliptical cloud into a round one, with every direction equally variable and no correlations left. It’s called whitening, and the matrix that does it is S^{-1/2} = P\Lambda^{-1/2}P^\top. The second challenge has you check it.
A small eigenvalue \lambda_j is a direction where the data barely spread, so dividing by it makes even a modest step there count a lot. FS73 stepped out in one of those directions.



Your turn. Find the batch with the largest Mahalanobis distance.









The covariance matrix is S.


d2 <- mahalanobis(Y, center = xbar, cov = S)
sort(d2, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
FS73 with 34.6, then FS51 with 12.4 and FS08 with 9.6. FS51, the “most distant” batch by the Euclidean ruler, is second here: it’s extreme, but in a typical direction.




Your turn. Compute FS73’s squared distance by hand, from the formula.









solve(S) is the inverse of the covariance matrix.


dev <- Y["FS73", ] - xbar
t(dev) %*% solve(S) %*% dev
34.6, the same as mahalanobis(). FS73’s deviations from the mean are +0.41 points of purity, −47 ppm of water, −1.2 APHA and +0.051 mg KOH/g of acid. Purer than average but more acidic, and drier but more acidic: both clash with how the properties usually move together.

title: Statistical distance
text:
Ellipses of constant distance
All the points at the same Mahalanobis distance from the center form an ellipse (in more dimensions, an ellipsoid). In the plot above, the blue curves are two such ellipses, for water and acid: the inner one at the distance that half the batches fall within, the outer one at the 99% mark. Their shape comes straight from the eigen-decomposition:

the axes point along the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix;
the half-length of each axis is \sqrt{c\,\lambda_j}, for an ellipse at squared distance c.

So the ellipse is long in the direction of the biggest eigenvalue, where the data spread most, and short where they spread least. In standard units, the two eigenvalues of a 2 \times 2 correlation matrix are 1 + r and 1 - r (Lesson 0.14), so the stronger the correlation, the longer and thinner the ellipse. FS51 and FS73 both lie outside the 99% ellipse. But FS51 is far out along the ellipse’s long axis, 4.1 standard units from the center, while FS73 is only 2.4 standard units out, across the short axis. Measured with the ellipse, FS73 is the more unusual of the two: the dotted rose ellipse passes through FS73, at a squared distance of 13.3 for this pair, and FS51, at 10.6, lies inside it.

title: Statistical distance
text:
How far is far?
If the data come from a multivariate normal distribution (next lesson), the squared Mahalanobis distances of the observations follow, approximately, a chi-square distribution with p degrees of freedom: one for each variable. That’s the multivariate version of “a squared z-score is chi-square with one degree of freedom”. It gives a yardstick:

qchisq(c(0.95, 0.99, 0.999), df = 4)
#> [1]  9.487729 13.276704 18.466827

About 1 batch in 100 should have D^2 above 13.3. Among the 80 batches, three are above the 95% mark, about the four you’d expect by chance, and only FS73 is above the 99% mark. Plotting every batch’s D^2 in production order gives a multivariate control chart, also called a Hotelling T^2 chart, which many chemical plants run alongside their single-variable charts precisely to catch batches like FS73:

tibble(order = seq_along(d2), d2 = d2, batch = names(d2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = order, y = d2)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = qchisq(0.99, 4), color = "#C2416C", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(color = "grey75") +
  geom_point(color = "#2a78d6", size = 1.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 73, y = 34.6, label = "FS73", hjust = 1.3, size = 3.5) +
  labs(x = "Batch, in production order", y = "Squared Mahalanobis distance") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Two cautions. First, the chi-square yardstick is only approximate: the mean and covariance are estimated from the same data, and the outlier itself inflates S, which makes it look a little less extreme than it is. With 80 batches and 4 variables, the approximation is reasonable. Second, with 80 batches checked, the most extreme one is always somewhat large, so judge the largest distance with a Bonferroni-style correction, as in Lesson 2.10.
So what happened to FS73? The production records show that its reactor had been cleaned with a dilute acid wash just before the batch, and it seems not all of the wash was rinsed out. No single test flagged the batch, and it passed its specification. The customer, whose process is sensitive to acid, noticed.
Your turn. Compute the chi-square p-value for FS73’s squared distance, and its Bonferroni-adjusted value for having checked 80 batches.









The degrees of freedom are the number of variables, p = 4.


d2 <- mahalanobis(Y, xbar, S)
p <- pchisq(d2["FS73"], df = 4, lower.tail = FALSE)
c(p = unname(p), bonferroni = min(1, 80 * unname(p)))
p = 5.6 \times 10^{-7}, and 4.5 \times 10^{-5} even after the correction. FS73 doesn’t belong with the others.




Your turn. Which pair of properties makes FS73 unusual? Compute its squared Mahalanobis distance using water and acid only.









The second column is "acid_mgKOH".


W <- Y[, c("water_ppm", "acid_mgKOH")]
mahalanobis(W, colMeans(W), cov(W))["FS73"]
13.3, the largest of all 80 batches for this pair, and beyond the 99.8% point of a chi-square with 2 degrees of freedom. Purity with acid gives 11.5. Every other pair gives about 4 or less. FS73 is unusual because its acid doesn’t match its water, or its purity.

title: Statistical distance
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Whitening. Build S^{-1/2} = P\Lambda^{-1/2}P^\top from the eigen-decomposition of S, transform the centered data with it, and compute FS73’s squared Euclidean distance in the transformed (“whitened”) space.









Take the square roots of the eigenvalues, e$values.


e <- eigen(S)
S_inv_half <- e$vectors %*% diag(1 / sqrt(e$values)) %*% t(e$vectors)
white <- sweep(Y, 2, xbar) %*% S_inv_half
sum(white[which(rownames(Y) == "FS73"), ]^2)
34.6 again. In the whitened space, ordinary Euclidean distance is the Mahalanobis distance. Check round(cov(white), 10): it’s the identity matrix, so the whitened variables are uncorrelated, with variance 1.




Challenge 2 · The ellipse’s axes. For water and acid in standard units, the correlation matrix has eigenvalues 1 + r and 1 - r. Compute the half-lengths of the axes of the 95% ellipse, \sqrt{c\,\lambda_j} with c the 95% point of the chi-square distribution with 2 degrees of freedom.









The second eigenvalue is 1 - r.


r <- cor(Y[, "water_ppm"], Y[, "acid_mgKOH"])
c95 <- qchisq(0.95, df = 2)
sqrt(c95 * c(1 + r, 1 - r))
3.08 along the diagonal “wetter and more acid” direction, and 1.58 across it. The ellipse is twice as long as it is wide. With r = 0.9, it would be more than four times as long: \sqrt{1.9/0.1} = 4.4.

title: Statistical distance
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why is the Euclidean distance a poor measure of how unusual a batch is?

It’s hard to compute
It depends on the units, and it ignores the correlations between the variables
It’s always too small


In ppm, water dominates it. Standardizing fixes the units, but not the correlations.



2. Two variables are strongly positively correlated. Which of these points is more unusual, at the same standardized distance from the center?

A point that’s high on both
A point that’s high on one and low on the other
They’re equally unusual


High-high is a direction the data often take. High-low goes against the correlation, so its Mahalanobis distance is larger.



3. What does the inverse covariance matrix do in D^2 = (\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}})^\top S^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}})?

It turns the distance into a probability
It shrinks steps in directions where the data vary a lot, and magnifies steps in directions where they vary little
It removes the mean


S^{-1} divides by the variance along each principal axis, so rare directions count more.



4. With uncorrelated variables, the squared Mahalanobis distance equals…

the sum of the squared z-scores
the squared Euclidean distance in the original units
the number of variables


With a diagonal S, S^{-1} just divides each squared deviation by its variance.



5. What shape is a set of points at the same Mahalanobis distance from the center of two correlated variables?

A circle
A square
An ellipse, with its axes along the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix


The half-length of each axis is \sqrt{c\lambda_j}, so the ellipse is longest in the direction of greatest spread.



6. For multivariate normal data with p = 4 variables, what distribution do the squared Mahalanobis distances approximately follow?

A normal distribution
A chi-square distribution with 4 degrees of freedom
A t distribution with 4 degrees of freedom


One degree of freedom per variable. The 99% point, 13.3, makes a convenient flag for unusual observations.

title: Statistical distance
text:
Wrap-up
You now have the right ruler for multivariate data! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Euclidean distance treats every direction alike. With mixed units, the variable with the biggest numbers dominates it.
Standardized distance fixes the units, but still ignores the correlations, so it misses unusual combinations.
The Mahalanobis distance, D^2 = (\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}})^\top S^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}}), accounts for both. mahalanobis() computes it. It’s Euclidean distance after whitening the data with S^{-1/2}.
Ellipses of constant distance have axes along the eigenvectors, with half-lengths \sqrt{c\lambda_j}.
How far is far: for multivariate normal data, D^2 is approximately chi-square with p degrees of freedom. Plotted over time, it’s a multivariate control chart.
FS73 was ordinary on every property, but its acid didn’t fit its water or its purity: D^2 = 34.6, with a Bonferroni-adjusted p = 4.5 \times 10^{-5}. An acid wash residue was the culprit.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download batch_quality.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

A robust center. FS73 itself inflates the covariance matrix it’s judged against. Recompute every batch’s distance using the mean and covariance of the other 79 batches (leave one out). How much bigger does FS73’s distance get?
Robust covariance. The MASS package’s cov.rob() estimates a mean and covariance that ignore the most unusual points. Compare mahalanobis(Y, cov.rob(Y)$center, cov.rob(Y)$cov) with the ordinary distances.
A control chart for new batches. Use the first 60 batches to estimate the mean and covariance, then compute the distances of batches 61 to 80 from them. For new batches, the exact limit is based on an F distribution, \frac{p(n+1)(n-1)}{n(n-p)}F_{p,\,n-p}. Compare it with the chi-square limit.
Your own example. Think of two measurements in your own experience that usually move together. What would an unusual combination look like, and what might cause it?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Euclidean distance

The straight-line distance between two vectors, \sqrt{(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y})^\top(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y})}.

Standardized distance

The Euclidean distance between the z-scores.

Mahalanobis distance

A distance that accounts for the variances and correlations of the variables: D^2 = (\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}})^\top S^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}}).

Whitening

Transforming data with S^{-1/2} so that the variables become uncorrelated with variance 1. Euclidean distance after whitening is the Mahalanobis distance.

Ellipse (ellipsoid) of constant distance

The set of points at a given Mahalanobis distance from the center, with axes along the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix.

Multivariate control chart

A plot of each observation’s squared Mahalanobis distance in time order, with a control limit, used to monitor several variables at once. Also called a Hotelling T^2 chart.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 505, Lesson 4: Multivariate Normal Distribution, sections 4.3 to 4.6. The Mahalanobis distance, its chi-square distribution, outliers and the geometry of the ellipses.
NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, “What are multivariate control charts?”. How plants monitor several variables at once with Hotelling’s T^2.
Johnson and Wichern, Applied Multivariate Statistical Analysis, chapter 1, section 1.5, “Distance”. The textbook’s careful development of statistical distance.

title: Module 2 project: a complete regression analysis
text:
The plant has built a new reactor, R3: 2,000 liters, ten times the size of the pilot reactors. Between September and mid-October, the process engineers ran it 64 times to commission it, varying the temperature, the residence time and the agitator speed, and trying both catalysts. Production on R3 starts in November, and Dana, the process engineer in charge, has a question for you: how should we run it?
That’s the whole of Module 2 in one project: exploring relationships, building a multiple regression with curves and categories, checking it, finding the runs that don’t belong, choosing between models, and turning the result into a decision with honest uncertainty.

title: Module 2 project: a complete regression analysis
text:
What you’ll make
One report, written in Quarto in your plant-study RStudio project, that Dana could act on tomorrow. It should contain:

A summary for Dana, at the top, in plain words: the settings you recommend, the yield she can expect, whether catalyst B is worth its price, and the main caveats.
The evidence: what you found in the data, the models you built for the yield and the purity, how you checked them, and what you changed because of the checks.
The uncertainty: confidence intervals for what’s known, and prediction intervals for what a single batch might do.
A cleaning log and a list of limitations: every decision about the data, and everything that these 64 runs can’t tell you.

Nobody grades it, but write it as if Dana will base November’s production plan on it. Because in real work, she would.

title: Module 2 project: a complete regression analysis
text:
The handover
Download both files into a new folder in your project, data-raw/r3/, and don’t edit them:

README.txt: Dana’s note, with the question, the columns and the known issues. Read it first.
r3_runs.csv: the 64 commissioning runs.

Then download the project template, save it in the top folder of your project as r3-analysis.qmd, and click Render. It reads the data, prints a first look at it and draws some scatterplots, with headings for every step. Fill it in one section at a time, and render often.

title: Module 2 project: a complete regression analysis
text:
The brief, step by step

Explore (Lessons 1, 5). Plot the yield and the purity against every predictor. Look at the ranges, the notes and anything odd. What relationships do you expect from the pilot plant, and which ones look different at this scale?
Check the records (Lessons 8, 10). The run sheets were typed in by hand. Fit a first, simple model and look for runs that don’t fit, with studentized residuals, leverage and Cook’s distance. For each suspect, look for an explanation in the notes and the other columns. Correct what you can confirm, exclude only with a reason, and write every decision in the cleaning log.
