Build a model for the yield (Lessons 5, 7, 9). Start from what you learned on the pilot reactors: which terms should be in the model, and in what form? Does the yield curve with temperature? Dana’s note asks you to check the agitator speed again, so look at it carefully: does it matter, and does it matter everywhere in its range? Center the temperature.
Check the model (Lessons 8, 10, 11). Residuals against the fitted values, against every predictor and in run order, a Q-Q plot, the influence measures, and the VIFs. If a residual plot shows a pattern, change the model and look again.
Compare candidate models (Lessons 6, 12). Use partial F-tests for nested models, and AIC, BIC or cross-validation to choose between a few serious candidates. Prefer the simplest model that the diagnostics are happy with.
Model the purity (Lessons 5, 9). It’s the constraint: the customer’s limit is 98.5%. Which conditions lower it? Two purity results are missing: note why, and check that leaving them out is reasonable (Module 1, Lesson 12).
Choose the operating conditions (Lessons 3, 9). Search a grid of settings inside the range of the data, keep only those where the purity is safely above 98.5%, and find the highest predicted yield. “Safely” is your call: the template suggests using the lower end of the purity’s 95% prediction interval, so that a single batch would rarely fall below the limit. Say what you chose, and why.
Say how sure you are (Lessons 3, 6). At your recommended settings, give a confidence interval for the average batch’s yield and a prediction interval for a single batch, and explain the difference in words Dana would use. For catalyst B, the question is whether it adds at least 2 points: give its interval, and test it against 2 (an offset() from Lesson 6 does it).
Write it up. Summary first, then the details. Plots that make each point, tables that are easy to read, and the limitations at the end.

Stretch goal. Kestrel’s feed lots run at 260 ppm of water or more. How should the operating conditions change for a wet lot, and what yield should Dana expect then? And here’s a different angle on the purity constraint: turn the purity into a yes-or-no outcome, “at least 98.5%”, and fit a logistic regression for it (Lesson 15). With only about 60 runs, how does that compare with modeling the purity itself? (It throws away information, which is a lesson in itself.)

title: Module 2 project: a complete regression analysis
text:
Check your own work
When you’ve finished, assess your project against this rubric. Aim for the right-hand column.










Needs work
Good
Excellent




The records
The data are used as received
The obvious problems are found and fixed
Every suspect run is investigated with diagnostics and the notes, each decision is justified, and the cleaning log is complete


Model building
A single model with every predictor as a straight line
A sensible model with the right terms
A model built from subject knowledge, checked against alternatives with tests and criteria, with each term’s form justified


Diagnostics
No checks
Residual plots are shown
Every assumption is checked, the plots are interpreted, and the model is changed where they demanded it


Uncertainty
Point estimates only
Confidence intervals for the coefficients
Confidence and prediction intervals at the recommended settings, correctly explained, and catalyst B tested against the 2-point bar


Recommendation
Settings that maximize yield alone
Settings that respect the purity limit
Settings that respect the purity limit with a stated safety margin, stay inside the data, and come with a wet-feed caveat


Communication
Code output with little text
A report that explains its steps
A report Dana could act on: a clear summary, plots that make each point, honest limitations

title: Module 2 project: a complete regression analysis
text:
Tips

Look before you model. Many of this project’s surprises are visible in a scatterplot. One run’s yield is more than eight points above any other run’s. Is that believable?
Use the notes, and be fair about them. A note can explain an outlier, but not every note means a run is bad.
Don’t trust the pilot plant blindly. R3 is ten times bigger. Things that didn’t matter in 200 liters, like mixing, can matter in 2,000.
A curve in the residuals is a clue about the physics. If yield stops improving above some agitator speed, that’s a statement about mixing, and it suggests a simple model term. Try a few forms and compare them.
Stay inside the data. The best settings often sit at the edge of what was tried. Say so, and suggest runs that would confirm them.
Two kinds of “how sure”. Dana’s planners care about the average batch (a confidence interval). The customer cares about their batch (a prediction interval).
Write for the reader. Dana knows the chemistry better than you do. She doesn’t need the formula for Cook’s distance. She needs to know which runs you set aside, and why.


When it’s done, you’ll have taken a real question from data to decision: cleaning, modeling, checking, choosing and communicating. That’s what applied statisticians do all day. Congratulations on finishing Module 2! Module 3 looks at several responses at once, with multivariate methods.

title: Logistic regression
text:
Module 2 · Lesson 15 of 15 Week 45 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Every response so far has been a number: a yield, an absorbance, a rate constant. But many of the plant’s most important outcomes are yes or no. Did the batch pass the customer’s specification? Did the filter clog? Did the reactor trip? A batch is on spec or it isn’t, and what you want to know is the probability, and how the process conditions change it. That’s the job of logistic regression, the last tool of this module, and the first of a whole family of models you’ll meet again in Modules 5 and 7.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Logistic regression
text:
Yes-or-no outcomes
The full-scale plant’s quality records for last year cover 400 batches. For each one, they give the feed supplier and its water content, the reactor temperature, the catalyst, and whether the batch passed the customer’s specification:

production <- read_csv("data/production.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(production)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   batch_id month supplier  feed_water_ppm temp_C catalyst on_spec
#>   <chr>    <chr> <chr>              <dbl>  <dbl> <chr>    <lgl>  
#> 1 Q0001    Jan   Rosewater            208   188. B        TRUE   
#> 2 Q0002    Jan   Kestrel              328   179. B        TRUE   
#> 3 Q0003    Jan   Fizzwell             220   193. A        FALSE  
#> 4 Q0004    Jan   Rosewater            197   188. B        FALSE  
#> 5 Q0005    Jan   Rosewater            203   184  A        TRUE   
#> 6 Q0006    Jan   Kestrel              291   190. A        FALSE
production |>
  group_by(supplier) |>
  summarise(batches = n(), on_spec_rate = mean(on_spec), water_ppm = mean(feed_water_ppm))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   supplier    batches on_spec_rate water_ppm
#>   <chr>         <int>        <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 Fizzwell        134        0.806      196.
#> 2 Kestrel          71        0.634      292.
#> 3 Plum Valley      97        0.804      194.
#> 4 Rosewater        98        0.857      195.

Overall, 78.8% of the batches were on spec, but only 63% of the batches made with Kestrel’s wet feed. The response, on_spec, is TRUE or FALSE, which R treats as 1 or 0.
Why not use ordinary regression, with 1 for on spec and 0 for not? Its fitted values would estimate the probability of being on spec, which sounds fine. But a straight line goes on forever, and probabilities stop at 0 and 1. The linear probability model below predicts a 134% chance of being on spec at 160 °C. And a yes-or-no response can’t have normal errors or a constant variance: its variance, p(1 - p), is biggest at p = 0.5 and shrinks to nothing near 0 and 1. The model needs an S-shaped curve that bends to stay between 0 and 1:

fit_lpm <- lm(as.numeric(on_spec) ~ temp_C, data = production)
fit_1 <- glm(on_spec ~ temp_C, family = binomial, data = production)
curves <- tibble(temp_C = seq(160, 212, by = 0.5)) |>
  mutate(`straight line` = predict(fit_lpm, pick(temp_C)),
         `logistic curve` = predict(fit_1, pick(temp_C), type = "response")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-temp_C, names_to = "model", values_to = "p")
ggplot(production, aes(x = temp_C, y = as.numeric(on_spec))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 1), color = "grey75") +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.03, seed = 1), alpha = 0.3, size = 1.2, color = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(y = p, color = model), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("straight line" = "#2a78d6", "logistic curve" = "#C2416C")) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "On spec (1) or not (0)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Each grey point is a batch, at 1 if it was on spec and 0 if not (jittered a little so they don’t sit on top of one another). Hotter batches fail more often, and the rose curve follows that, staying inside the 0-to-1 range at every temperature.

title: Logistic regression
text:
Probabilities, odds and log-odds
Logistic regression works on the scale of odds. If the probability of being on spec is p, the odds are

\text{odds} = \frac{p}{1 - p} .

A probability of 0.8 is odds of 4 (four on spec for every one off). Probability 0.5 is odds of 1, “evens”. Odds run from 0 to infinity. Take their logarithm, and you get the log-odds, or logit, which runs over the whole number line, from minus to plus infinity:

\text{logit}(p) = \ln\frac{p}{1 - p} .

That’s what makes it the natural scale for a linear model: a line in x can go anywhere, and so can the logit. Logistic regression says that the log-odds are linear in the predictors:

\ln\frac{p}{1 - p} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_k x_k
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_k x_k)}} .

The second form, the logistic function (plogis() in R), is the S-curve. Its inverse, qlogis(), turns a probability into log-odds.
To compare two groups, use the odds ratio: the odds in one group divided by the odds in the other. An odds ratio of 1 means no difference, and below 1 means lower odds.











Your turn. Compute the odds of being on spec for Kestrel’s batches and for everyone else’s, and their odds ratio.









Divide by the other suppliers’ odds: odds(p_others).


p_kestrel <- mean(production$on_spec[production$supplier == "Kestrel"])
p_others <- mean(production$on_spec[production$supplier != "Kestrel"])
odds <- function(p) p / (1 - p)
odds(p_kestrel) / odds(p_others)
0.38. Kestrel’s batches had odds of 1.7 (63% on spec), against 4.6 for the others (82%), so their odds of passing were only 38% as high.

title: Logistic regression
text:
The logistic regression model
glm() fits generalized linear models, which include logistic regression. family = binomial says the response is yes or no, and the logit is its default link:

fit_1 <- glm(on_spec ~ temp_C, family = binomial, data = production)
summary(fit_1)$coefficients
#>               Estimate Std. Error   z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept) 27.4148071 4.59829903  5.961945 2.492527e-09
#> temp_C      -0.1399452 0.02451027 -5.709653 1.132066e-08

The slope is −0.140 per °C, on the log-odds scale: each extra degree lowers the log-odds of being on spec by 0.140. Log-odds are hard to feel, so exponentiate: e^{-0.140} = 0.87, an odds ratio of 0.87 per degree. Each degree multiplies the odds of passing by 0.87, a 13% drop. Over 10 degrees, the odds ratio is e^{-1.40} = 0.25: a batch at 195 °C has a quarter of the odds of passing that a batch at 185 °C has.
On the probability scale, the effect isn’t constant, because the curve is S-shaped. The fitted probability of passing is 95% at 175 °C, 82% at 185 °C, and only 53% at 195 °C. The same 10 degrees cost 13 points of probability in the first step and 29 in the second. That’s why logistic coefficients are reported as odds ratios, which are constant.
The z value column tests each coefficient with a Wald test: the estimate divided by its standard error, compared with a normal distribution. It’s the logistic counterpart of the t-test.
Your turn. Compute the odds ratio for 10 degrees from fit_1.









For a 10-degree change, multiply the slope by 10 before exponentiating.


fit_1 <- glm(on_spec ~ temp_C, family = binomial, data = production)
b <- coef(fit_1)["temp_C"]
unname(exp(10 * b))
0.25: ten degrees hotter cuts the odds of passing to a quarter. (Note that it’s e^{10b}, not 10 \times e^{b}: odds ratios multiply.)

title: Logistic regression
text:
Several predictors and odds ratios
Add the water content and the catalyst, exactly as in lm():

fit <- glm(on_spec ~ temp_C + feed_water_ppm + catalyst, family = binomial, data = production)
summary(fit)$coefficients
#>                   Estimate  Std. Error   z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept)    31.88574980 4.977259687  6.406286 1.491070e-10
#> temp_C         -0.15110092 0.025845675 -5.846275 5.027034e-09
#> feed_water_ppm -0.01264207 0.002895932 -4.365456 1.268577e-05
#> catalystB       0.79097973 0.272872986  2.898710 3.747009e-03
exp(cbind(odds_ratio = coef(fit), confint(fit)))
#> Waiting for profiling to be done...
#>                  odds_ratio        2.5 %       97.5 %
#> (Intercept)    7.043770e+13 5.731334e+09 1.801854e+18
#> temp_C         8.597609e-01 8.157588e-01 9.030065e-01
#> feed_water_ppm 9.874375e-01 9.817647e-01 9.930117e-01
#> catalystB      2.205556e+00 1.299947e+00 3.800169e+00

Each coefficient is now a partial effect on the log-odds, with the other predictors held fixed, just as in Lesson 5. In odds ratios, with 95% confidence intervals:



Change
Odds ratio
95% interval




10 °C hotter
0.22
0.13 to 0.36


100 ppm more water
0.28
0.16 to 0.50


catalyst B instead of A
2.21
1.30 to 3.80



So catalyst B more than doubles the odds of passing, at the same temperature and water content, and 100 ppm of extra water cuts them to about a quarter. confint() on a glm computes profile-likelihood intervals, which are more accurate than “estimate ± 2 SE” for logistic models. Exponentiate both ends to get the interval for the odds ratio. (The intercept’s “odds ratio” is the odds at 0 °C and 0 ppm, a meaningless extrapolation, so ignore it.)
Your turn. What’s the odds ratio for 100 ppm more water, in the full model?









For 100 ppm, exponentiate 100 * b_water.


b_water <- coef(fit)["feed_water_ppm"]
unname(exp(100 * b_water))
0.28: at the same temperature and with the same catalyst, a feed with 100 ppm more water has about 28% of the odds of producing an on-spec batch. Kestrel’s lots average about 95 ppm more water than the others’, which explains their poor record.

title: Logistic regression
section: How the model is fitted: maximum likelihood
text:
How the model is fitted: maximum likelihood
Least squares makes no sense for 0s and 1s, so logistic regression uses maximum likelihood: choose the coefficients that make the observed outcomes as probable as possible. For a set of coefficients, each batch gets a predicted probability \hat{p}_i. If the batch was on spec, the model gave that outcome probability \hat{p}_i; if it wasn’t, 1 - \hat{p}_i. Since the batches are independent, the probability of the whole dataset is the product, and its logarithm is the log-likelihood:

\ell = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Big[ y_i \ln \hat{p}_i + (1 - y_i) \ln(1 - \hat{p}_i) \Big] .

Maximum likelihood finds the coefficients with the largest \ell. There’s no formula like the normal equations, so glm() climbs to the top iteratively: the “Number of Fisher Scoring iterations” in its summary says how many steps it took (5 here).






NoteGo deeper: Newton’s method in disguise





Fisher scoring is Newton’s method for finding where the gradient of \ell is zero. For logistic regression, the gradient is X^\top(\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{p}}) and the matrix of second derivatives is -X^\top W X, with W diagonal with entries \hat{p}_i(1 - \hat{p}_i). So each step is

\mathbf{b}_{\text{new}} = \mathbf{b} + (X^\top W X)^{-1} X^\top (\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{p}}),

which turns out to be a weighted least squares fit (Lesson 9) to a “working response”. That’s why it’s also called iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS). At the maximum, X^\top(\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{p}}) = \mathbf{0}: the logistic version of Lesson 4’s X^\top\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}, and it means that the fitted probabilities add up to the number of on-spec batches.
The standard errors come from the curvature at the top, (X^\top W X)^{-1}: a sharply peaked likelihood means precise estimates. Maximum likelihood is the workhorse of modern statistics, and Module 5 shows how Bayesian methods build on the same likelihood.



Your turn. Compute the log-likelihood of fit by hand from its fitted probabilities, and compare it with logLik(fit).









An off-spec batch contributes the log of its probability of being off spec, 1 - p_hat.


p_hat <- fitted(fit)
y <- as.numeric(production$on_spec)
sum(y * log(p_hat) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p_hat))
−174.1, the same as logLik(fit). Any other set of coefficients would give a lower (more negative) number.

title: Logistic regression
text:
Testing with deviance
In linear regression, tests compare sums of squares. In logistic regression, they compare deviances. For yes-or-no data, a model’s deviance is simply -2\ell, minus twice its log-likelihood: the smaller it is, the better the model fits. summary() reports two:

the null deviance, 413.8, for a model with only an intercept (the same probability for every batch);
the residual deviance, 348.2, for the fitted model.

To compare nested models, use the likelihood-ratio test: the drop in deviance between them. If the extra coefficients are really zero, the drop follows a chi-square distribution, with degrees of freedom equal to the number of extra coefficients. Here, the three predictors together cut the deviance by 65.6 on 3 degrees of freedom, p = 4 \times 10^{-14}.
anova(reduced, full, test = "Chisq") runs the test, and drop1(fit, test = "LRT") tests each term in turn, like the partial F-tests of Lesson 6. The likelihood-ratio test and the Wald z-test usually agree, but when they don’t, trust the likelihood-ratio test: it’s more reliable in small samples and for large effects.
Your turn. Does the catalyst matter, once temperature and water are accounted for? Run the likelihood-ratio test.









The likelihood-ratio test is test = "Chisq".


without <- glm(on_spec ~ temp_C + feed_water_ppm, family = binomial, data = production)
anova(without, fit, test = "Chisq")
The catalyst cuts the deviance by 8.7 on 1 degree of freedom, p = 0.003. The Wald test in summary() gave p = 0.004: close, as they usually are.

title: Logistic regression
text:
Predicted probabilities
predict() on a glm works on the log-odds scale by default. Add type = "response" to get probabilities:

new <- tibble(temp_C = c(180, 190), feed_water_ppm = c(200, 300), catalyst = c("B", "A"))
predict(fit, newdata = new, type = "response")
#>         1         2 
#> 0.9502706 0.3506816

A catalyst B batch at 180 °C with dry feed has a 95% chance of passing. A catalyst A batch at 190 °C with Kestrel-wet feed has 35%.
For a confidence interval around a predicted probability, build it on the log-odds scale, where the estimate is roughly normal, then transform both ends with plogis(). That keeps the interval inside 0 to 1:

lp <- predict(fit, newdata = tibble(temp_C = 190, feed_water_ppm = 300, catalyst = "B"), se.fit = TRUE)
plogis(lp$fit + c(-1.96, 1.96) * lp$se.fit)
#> [1] 0.3947763 0.6850654

Your turn. A wet lot (300 ppm) is going to be run at 190 °C. How much does switching from catalyst A to B raise its chance of passing?









For probabilities, use type = "response".


runs <- tibble(temp_C = 190, feed_water_ppm = 300, catalyst = c("A", "B"))
predict(fit, newdata = runs, type = "response")
From 35% to 54%. Better, but still close to a coin toss: for a lot this wet, running cooler would help more, as the challenge will show.

title: Logistic regression
text:
From probabilities to decisions
Suppose the plant wants to flag batches that are likely to fail, so that it can test them more carefully, or adjust them before they’re finished. A simple rule: flag a batch if its predicted probability of passing is below some threshold. Comparing the flags with what really happened gives a confusion matrix. With a threshold of 0.5:

flagged <- fitted(fit) < 0.5
table(flagged, off_spec = !production$on_spec)
#>        off_spec
#> flagged FALSE TRUE
#>   FALSE   302   67
#>   TRUE     13   18

The rule is right about 80% of the batches. That sounds good, until you notice that “never flag anything” is right about 78.8% of them, because most batches pass anyway. Accuracy is a poor guide when one outcome is rare. What matters is the two kinds of error:

Missed failures: of the 85 batches that really failed, the rule flagged only 18. Its sensitivity, the fraction of failures caught, is 21%.
False alarms: it flagged 13 batches that passed. Its specificity, the fraction of passing batches left alone, is 96%.

Moving the threshold trades one error for the other. Flag every batch below 0.7, and it catches 48 of the 85 failures, at the price of 46 false alarms. Flag below 0.8, and it catches 59, with 104 false alarms. The right threshold depends on the costs: if a failed batch that reaches the customer costs much more than an extra lab test, flag generously. Plotting the sensitivity against the false-alarm rate for every threshold gives the ROC curve, and the area under it (0.77 here) measures how well the model separates the passes from the failures, whatever the threshold. You’ll use these tools a lot in Module 7.
Your turn. With a threshold of 0.7, how many of the failed batches are caught?









The new threshold is 0.7.


flagged <- fitted(fit) < 0.7
off_spec <- !production$on_spec
sum(flagged & off_spec)
48 of the 85 failures (56%), with sum(flagged & !off_spec) = 46 false alarms. Whether that’s a good trade is a question for the plant’s accountants as much as its statisticians.

title: Logistic regression
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · A safe operating temperature. The customer wants at least a 90% chance that each batch passes. With catalyst B and normal feed (200 ppm of water), what’s the highest temperature that still gives 90%? Solve the model’s equation for the temperature: set the log-odds equal to qlogis(0.9).









Catalyst B adds its coefficient, "catalystB", to the log-odds.


b <- coef(fit)
target <- qlogis(0.9)
unname((target - b["(Intercept)"] - b["feed_water_ppm"] * 200 - b["catalystB"]) / b["temp_C"])
185.0 °C. With Kestrel-wet feed at 300 ppm, the same calculation gives 176.6 °C: the wet lots need to run about 8 degrees cooler for the same chance of passing. Of course, cooler runs make less yield (Lesson 9), so the plant faces a trade-off that combines both models.




Challenge 2 · Is it the supplier or the water? Kestrel’s batches fail more because their feed is wetter. Or is there something else wrong with Kestrel’s feed? Add the supplier to the model, which already has the water, and test it with a likelihood-ratio test.









Add supplier.


with_supplier <- glm(on_spec ~ temp_C + feed_water_ppm + catalyst + supplier, family = binomial, data = production)
anova(fit, with_supplier, test = "Chisq")
A drop in deviance of only 2.4 on 3 degrees of freedom, p = 0.50. Once the water content is known, the supplier tells you nothing more. That’s good news for purchasing: the problem is the water, which can be specified in a contract, measured on delivery, or dried out, rather than something mysterious about Kestrel.

title: Logistic regression
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why is ordinary linear regression a poor choice for a yes-or-no response?

It can’t handle more than one predictor
Its predictions can fall below 0 or above 1, and a 0/1 response can’t have a constant variance
It’s too slow


A straight line ignores the limits of a probability, and the variance p(1 - p) changes with p.



2. A batch has a 0.75 probability of passing. What are its odds?

0.75
3
1.33


0.75/0.25 = 3: three passes for every failure.



3. A logistic coefficient for temperature is −0.15 per °C. What does e^{-0.15} = 0.86 mean?

Each degree lowers the probability of passing by 0.86
Each degree multiplies the odds of passing by 0.86
86% of the batches pass


Exponentiated logistic coefficients are odds ratios. The change in probability depends on where you are on the S-curve.



4. How are the coefficients of a logistic regression estimated?

By least squares
By maximum likelihood: the coefficients that make the observed outcomes most probable
By averaging the 0s and 1s


There’s no formula, so glm() maximizes the log-likelihood iteratively (Fisher scoring, or IRLS).



5. How do you test whether a predictor matters in a logistic regression?

With an F-test of sums of squares
With a likelihood-ratio test: the drop in deviance, compared with a chi-square distribution (or the Wald z-test)
By checking whether R^2 goes up


Deviance plays the role of the residual sum of squares. anova(reduced, full, test = "Chisq") and drop1(fit, test = "LRT") do the tests.



6. A model flags batches likely to fail, with 80% accuracy, but 79% of batches pass anyway. What should you look at?

Nothing: 80% is good
How many failures it catches (sensitivity) and how many false alarms it raises, at a threshold chosen from the costs
Only the p-values


When one outcome is common, accuracy hides the errors that matter. A rule that never flags anything would be 79% accurate.

title: Logistic regression
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve modeled your first yes-or-no outcome, and finished Module 2! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Yes-or-no responses need a model that keeps probabilities between 0 and 1. Linear regression doesn’t.
Odds are p/(1 - p), and log-odds (the logit) run over the whole number line. Logistic regression makes the log-odds linear in the predictors: \text{logit}(p) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots
glm(y ~ ..., family = binomial) fits it. Exponentiated coefficients are odds ratios: 10 °C hotter cut the odds of passing to 0.22, 100 ppm more water to 0.28, and catalyst B multiplied them by 2.2.
Maximum likelihood fits the model, iteratively. The deviance, -2\ell, measures lack of fit, and likelihood-ratio tests compare nested models with chi-square tests.
Predicted probabilities come from predict(..., type = "response"). Build their confidence intervals on the log-odds scale.
Decisions: a threshold turns probabilities into flags. Judge it by its sensitivity and false alarms, not by its accuracy, and choose it from the costs.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download production.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

The S-curves. Plot the fitted probability of passing against the temperature, with one curve for each catalyst, at 200 ppm of water. Then add curves for 300 ppm. Where do the curves for catalyst B at 300 ppm and catalyst A at 200 ppm cross?
An interaction. Does the catalyst’s effect depend on the water? Add feed_water_ppm:catalyst to the model and test it with a likelihood-ratio test.
The ROC curve. Install the pROC package, and run plot(pROC::roc(production$on_spec, fitted(fit))) and pROC::auc(...). Then do it without the package: for thresholds from 0 to 1, compute the sensitivity and the false-alarm rate, and plot one against the other.
Checking the calibration. Group the batches into ten groups by their fitted probability (dplyr::ntile(fitted(fit), 10)), and compare each group’s average fitted probability with its actual on-spec rate. Do the model’s probabilities mean what they say? (This is the idea behind the Hosmer-Lemeshow test.)










NoteKey words from this lesson






Odds

p/(1 - p), the probability of an event divided by the probability that it doesn’t happen.

Log-odds (logit)

\ln\left(p/(1 - p)\right), which runs from minus to plus infinity.

Logistic regression

A model in which the log-odds of a yes-or-no outcome are a linear function of the predictors.

Odds ratio

The odds in one situation divided by the odds in another. In logistic regression, e^{b} is the odds ratio for a one-unit increase in the predictor.

Maximum likelihood

Estimating coefficients by choosing the values that make the observed data most probable.

Deviance

For a yes-or-no response, -2 times the log-likelihood. Smaller means a better fit.

Likelihood-ratio test

A test of nested models that compares their deviances with a chi-square distribution.

Confusion matrix

A table of predicted against actual outcomes, used to count correct decisions and the two kinds of error.

Sensitivity and specificity

The fraction of real events that a rule detects, and the fraction of non-events that it correctly leaves alone.











NoteWant to read more?






Paul Roback and Julie Legler, Beyond Multiple Linear Regression, chapters 2, 5 and 6. Likelihoods, generalized linear models and logistic regression, with clear case studies.
Penn State STAT 501, Lesson 13: Weighted Least Squares & Logistic Regressions, section 13.2. Logistic regression, odds ratios and deviance tests.
Introduction to Modern Statistics, “Logistic regression”. A gentle introduction with many pictures.

title: One-way ANOVA
text:
Module 2 · Lesson 13 of 15 Week 43 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lessons 5 to 12 squeezed answers out of an observational study, where the plant ran as it ran and the analysis had to untangle confounding, collinearity and unlucky runs. This lesson and the next are about the other way to learn: an experiment, where you decide the conditions yourself. A catalyst supplier sent four new formulations, and the process-development team tested them against the standard catalyst. The question sounds simple: are any of them better? Answering it properly takes one of statistics’ best-known tools, the analysis of variance, and a little care about asking many questions at once.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: One-way ANOVA
text:
The screening experiment
The design was simple and careful. Each of the five formulations, the standard catalyst and the new F1 to F4, was tested in 6 runs, all at the standard conditions of 185 °C and 45 minutes, with feed from the same well-mixed lot. The 30 runs were done in a random order:

screening <- read_csv("data/catalyst_screening.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(formulation = factor(formulation, levels = c("standard", "F1", "F2", "F3", "F4")))
head(screening, 8)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>     run formulation yield_pct
#>   <dbl> <fct>           <dbl>
#> 1     1 F1               60.2
#> 2     2 F3               59.2
#> 3     3 F3               61.9
#> 4     4 F4               63.1
#> 5     5 F2               71  
#> 6     6 F4               67.2
#> 7     7 F1               64.7
#> 8     8 F3               62.3

Two features make it a good experiment:

Replication. Six runs per formulation show how much the yield varies when nothing changes. Without that, you couldn’t tell a real difference from run-to-run noise.
Randomization. If all the standard runs had been done first and all the F4 runs last, any drift during the experiment (a catalyst bed ageing, a sensor drifting, the weather changing) would have looked like a difference between formulations. Remember the sawtooth in Lesson 8? A random order spreads any drift evenly over the groups, so it can’t masquerade as an effect.

The factor(..., levels = ...) line puts the standard catalyst first, so that it’ll be the baseline. Here are the results:

ggplot(screening, aes(x = formulation, y = yield_pct)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.5, color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, size = 2.2, color = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(x = "Formulation", y = "Yield (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The bars mark each group’s mean. F2 looks best, and F4 second, with the standard, F1 and F3 grouped together lower down. But with six noisy runs per group, which of those differences are real?

title: One-way ANOVA
text:
Between and within
The analysis of variance compares two ways in which the yields vary:

Between groups: how far each formulation’s mean is from the grand mean of all 30 runs.
Within groups: how far each run is from its own formulation’s mean. That’s pure run-to-run noise, since the runs within a group had identical conditions.

If the formulations are all the same, the group means should differ only by about as much as the noise allows. The sums of squares make this precise. With k groups of n_i runs, group means \bar{y}_i and grand mean \bar{y}:

\underbrace{\sum_{i}\sum_{j} (y_{ij} - \bar{y})^2}_{\text{SST}}
= \underbrace{\sum_{i} n_i (\bar{y}_i - \bar{y})^2}_{\text{SSB, between}}
+ \underbrace{\sum_{i}\sum_{j} (y_{ij} - \bar{y}_i)^2}_{\text{SSW, within}} .

Each sum of squares gets its degrees of freedom: k - 1 = 4 between, and N - k = 25 within, for N = 30 runs. The mean squares compare them:

F = \frac{\text{MSB}}{\text{MSW}} = \frac{\text{SSB}/(k - 1)}{\text{SSW}/(N - k)} .

MSW estimates the noise variance \sigma^2, whatever the group means are. MSB estimates \sigma^2 too, if the groups are all equal, but it’s inflated if they differ. So an F near 1 is what equal groups look like, and a big F is evidence that they differ. Under the null hypothesis that all the true means are equal, F follows an F distribution with 4 and 25 degrees of freedom.










Your turn. Compute SSB, SSW and the F statistic by hand.









The within-group degrees of freedom are N - k = 30 - 5 = 25.


grand <- mean(screening$yield_pct)
groups <- screening |>
  group_by(formulation) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(yield_pct), ss_within = sum((yield_pct - mean(yield_pct))^2))
ssb <- sum(groups$n * (groups$mean - grand)^2)
ssw <- sum(groups$ss_within)
(ssb / 4) / (ssw / 25)
\text{SSB} = 188.9 and \text{SSW} = 127.4, so F = (188.9/4)/(127.4/25) = 47.2/5.09 = 9.27. The group means are spread out about nine times more than the noise alone would spread them.




aov() does it all in one go, and summary() prints the ANOVA table:

fit_aov <- aov(yield_pct ~ formulation, data = screening)
summary(fit_aov)
#>             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
#> formulation  4  188.9   47.23    9.27 9.78e-05 ***
#> Residuals   25  127.4    5.09                     
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

p = 0.0001: strong evidence that the formulations don’t all give the same yield. That’s all the F-test says. It doesn’t say which formulations differ, or by how much. That’s the next two steps’ job.

title: One-way ANOVA
text:
ANOVA is regression
There’s nothing new under the hood. A one-way ANOVA is exactly a linear regression on the formulation’s dummy variables (Lesson 7), and aov() is just lm() with ANOVA-style printing:

fit_lm <- lm(yield_pct ~ formulation, data = screening)
anova(fit_lm)
#> Analysis of Variance Table
#> 
#> Response: yield_pct
#>             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
#> formulation  4 188.91  47.229  9.2697 9.775e-05 ***
#> Residuals   25 127.37   5.095                      
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The same table, and the same F-test: it’s the partial F-test of all four dummies together (Lesson 6). The regression’s coefficients add something useful, because each one is a formulation’s difference from the baseline, the standard catalyst:

summary(fit_lm)$coefficients
#>                  Estimate Std. Error     t value     Pr(>|t|)
#> (Intercept)   61.53333333  0.9214964 66.77544860 1.067161e-29
#> formulationF1 -0.03333333  1.3031927 -0.02557821 9.797968e-01
#> formulationF2  5.70000000  1.3031927  4.37387362 1.888209e-04
#> formulationF3 -1.06666667  1.3031927 -0.81850267 4.208040e-01
#> formulationF4  3.13333333  1.3031927  2.40435158 2.393523e-02

Your turn. How much more yield did F2 give than the standard catalyst? Find it among the regression coefficients.









The dummy for F2 is called "formulationF2".


fit_lm <- lm(yield_pct ~ formulation, data = screening)
coef(fit_lm)["formulationF2"]
5.70 points: F2’s mean, 67.23%, minus the standard’s, 61.53%. Its t-test, p = 0.0002, compares just those two groups. But you’re about to see why one t-test among many needs care.

title: One-way ANOVA
text:
Which ones differ?
With five groups, there are 10 pairs to compare. Here’s the trouble: if you test each pair at the 5% level, each test has a 5% chance of a false alarm, and over 10 tests the chance of at least one false alarm grows to about 1 - 0.95^{10} = 40\%, even if nothing differs at all. That’s the fishing problem from Lesson 6 again. The probability of at least one false alarm in a family of tests is called the family-wise error rate, and multiple comparison methods keep it at 5%.
Bonferroni’s method is the simplest: multiply each p-value by the number of comparisons (here, 10), or equivalently test each one at the 0.5% level. It works for any set of tests, but it’s conservative: when there are many comparisons, it misses real differences.
Tukey’s honestly significant difference (HSD) is designed for exactly this job, all the pairwise comparisons of group means, and it’s less conservative than Bonferroni for it. It gives adjusted p-values and simultaneous confidence intervals: intervals that, all together, cover the true differences 95% of the time.

TukeyHSD(fit_aov)
#>   Tukey multiple comparisons of means
#>     95% family-wise confidence level
#> 
#> Fit: aov(formula = yield_pct ~ formulation, data = screening)
#> 
#> $formulation
#>                    diff         lwr       upr     p adj
#> F1-standard -0.03333333  -3.8606423  3.793976 0.9999999
#> F2-standard  5.70000000   1.8726910  9.527309 0.0016215
#> F3-standard -1.06666667  -4.8939757  2.760642 0.9224295
#> F4-standard  3.13333333  -0.6939757  6.960642 0.1471647
#> F2-F1        5.73333333   1.9060243  9.560642 0.0015204
#> F3-F1       -1.03333333  -4.8606423  2.793976 0.9302619
#> F4-F1        3.16666667  -0.6606423  6.993976 0.1402664
#> F3-F2       -6.76666667 -10.5939757 -2.939358 0.0002036
#> F4-F2       -2.56666667  -6.3939757  1.260642 0.3092134
#> F4-F3        4.20000000   0.3726910  8.027309 0.0264499


TukeyHSD(fit_aov)$formulation |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("pair") |>
  mutate(pair = factor(pair, levels = rev(pair))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = diff, y = pair)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey60") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lwr, xmax = upr), width = 0.25, orientation = "y", color = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, color = "#C2416C") +
  labs(x = "Difference in mean yield (points), with 95% simultaneous intervals", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Intervals that miss zero mark differences you can trust. F2 beats the standard (by 5.7 points, somewhere from 1.9 to 9.5), F1 and F3. F4 beats F3. Everything else is uncertain: F4 might be better than the standard (by up to 7 points), or slightly worse.
Your turn. Without any adjustment, does F4 look better than the standard? Use pairwise.t.test(), which does all the pairwise t-tests with the pooled standard deviation.









No adjustment is p.adjust.method = "none".


unadjusted <- pairwise.t.test(screening$yield_pct, screening$formulation, p.adjust.method = "none")
unadjusted$p.value["F4", "standard"]
p = 0.024: “significant” on its own. With the Bonferroni adjustment (p.adjust.method = "bonferroni") it becomes 0.24, and Tukey’s method gives 0.15. Which is right? It depends on the question you set out to ask. If “is F4 better than the standard?” was the only question, planned in advance, the unadjusted test is fine. If it’s one of ten comparisons you scanned for the most exciting one, it isn’t.




Your turn. Find Tukey’s adjusted p-value for F4 against the standard.









The rows are named like "F4-standard".


tk <- TukeyHSD(fit_aov)$formulation
tk["F4-standard", "p adj"]
0.15. Allowing for all ten comparisons, the evidence that F4 beats the standard isn’t convincing. F4 deserves a second look, perhaps a follow-up experiment, but not a purchase order.




When every new formulation is compared only with a control, as here, Dunnett’s method is the specialist: it adjusts for just the four comparisons with the standard, and it’s a little more powerful than Tukey’s for that job. The emmeans and multcomp packages provide it (see the practice exercises).

title: One-way ANOVA
text:
Contrasts: asking a planned question
Sometimes the question isn’t about one pair. The supplier’s sales pitch was “our new formulations are better than your standard catalyst”. On average? That’s a contrast: a weighted combination of the group means whose weights add up to zero,

L = \sum_i c_i \bar{y}_i, \qquad \sum_i c_i = 0 .

“The average of the new formulations minus the standard” has weights -1 for the standard and \tfrac14 for each of F1 to F4. A contrast’s standard error comes from the pooled noise variance, MSW:

\text{SE}(L) = \sqrt{\text{MSW} \sum_i \frac{c_i^2}{n_i}}, \qquad t = \frac{L}{\text{SE}(L)} \text{ with } N - k \text{ degrees of freedom.}

Contrasts are the most efficient way to ask a specific question, and if you choose them before seeing the data, a few of them need no multiple-comparison adjustment.
Your turn. Test the supplier’s claim with that contrast.









Each group has n_i = 6 runs.


means <- tapply(screening$yield_pct, screening$formulation, mean)
weights <- c(-1, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4)
msw <- sum(resid(fit_aov)^2) / 25
L <- sum(weights * means)
se <- sqrt(msw * sum(weights^2 / 6))
t <- L / se
c(L = L, t = t, p = 2 * pt(-abs(t), df = 25))
On average, the new formulations beat the standard by 1.9 points, but p = 0.072. Not convincing, because the average mixes one clear winner (F2) with two that are no better (F1, F3). The right claim isn’t “the new formulations are better”, it’s “F2 is better”. That’s why the question matters as much as the analysis.

title: One-way ANOVA
text:
Checking the assumptions
One-way ANOVA is a linear model, so it makes Lesson 8’s assumptions: independent runs (the randomization helps), normal errors, and the same variance in every group. The last one matters most when the groups have different sizes. With equal groups, as here, ANOVA is fairly robust to moderate differences in spread.
The group standard deviations run from 1.8 to 3.2 points: F2 is the most variable. Is that more than chance? Two tests check:

Bartlett’s test (Lesson 8), bartlett.test(), is powerful but very sensitive to non-normality.
Levene’s test is more robust. It’s simply an ANOVA of each run’s absolute distance from its group’s median: if one group is more spread out, its distances are bigger. car::leveneTest() does it, or you can do it by hand.

For the shape, a Q-Q plot of the residuals, and shapiro.test(resid(fit_aov)) gives p = 0.75: nothing to worry about.
If the assumptions failed badly, the Kruskal-Wallis test is the rank-based alternative: it replaces the yields by their ranks and asks whether the groups’ ranks differ, much as Spearman’s correlation did in Lesson 1. It assumes much less, but it says less too: it tests whether some group tends to give higher values, not anything about the size of the differences in means.
Your turn. Run Levene’s test by hand: compute each run’s absolute deviation from its group’s median, and run a one-way ANOVA on those.









The deviation from the group’s median: median(yield_pct) inside the grouped mutate().


spread <- screening |>
  group_by(formulation) |>
  mutate(abs_dev = abs(yield_pct - median(yield_pct))) |>
  ungroup()
summary(aov(abs_dev ~ formulation, data = spread))
F = 0.56, p = 0.70: no evidence that the spreads differ. F2’s larger standard deviation is within what chance produces with six runs per group. (Bartlett’s test agrees: p = 0.66.)

title: One-way ANOVA
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · How many runs were needed? Before an experiment, you can work out how many runs per group you’d need to detect differences of a given size. power.anova.test() does it for a one-way design, from the variance of the true group means (between.var) and the noise variance (within.var). Suppose the true means were spread like the observed ones (variance 7.87) and the noise variance was 5.09. How many runs per formulation would give 90% power?









90% power is power = 0.9.


pw <- power.anova.test(groups = 5, between.var = 7.87, within.var = 5.09, power = 0.9)
pw$n
3.6, so 4 runs per formulation would have been enough to detect differences like these, and 6 gave a power of over 99%. But “differences like these” is doing a lot of work: to detect F4’s 3-point advantage over the standard on its own, with Tukey’s adjustment, you’d need many more runs. Base the calculation on the smallest difference that would matter to the plant.




Challenge 2 · The rank-based test. Run the Kruskal-Wallis test on the screening data. Does it agree with the ANOVA?









The function is kruskal.test().


kruskal.test(yield_pct ~ formulation, data = screening)
\chi^2 = 17.2 on 4 degrees of freedom, p = 0.0018. It agrees that the formulations differ, though with a larger p-value than the ANOVA’s 0.0001: ranks throw away some information, so when the ANOVA’s assumptions hold, ANOVA is more powerful.

title: One-way ANOVA
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why were the 30 runs done in a random order?

To make the analysis easier
So that any drift during the experiment can’t line up with the formulations and look like an effect
Because ANOVA requires unequal group sizes


Randomization protects against confounders you didn’t think of, by making them unrelated to the treatments.



2. The ANOVA gives F = 9.27 with p = 0.0001. What can you conclude?

Every formulation differs from every other
At least one formulation’s mean yield differs from the others
F2 is the best formulation


The F-test only says the means aren’t all equal. Multiple comparisons say which ones differ.



3. How is a one-way ANOVA related to regression?

They’re unrelated methods
It’s a regression on the group’s dummy variables, and its F-test is the partial F-test of all the dummies
ANOVA is only for numerical predictors


aov() and lm() fit the same model. The coefficients are differences from the baseline group.



4. You compare all 10 pairs of five groups, each at the 5% level, and none of the groups really differ. What’s the chance of at least one “significant” result?

5%
About 40%
50%


1 - 0.95^{10} = 0.40 (for independent tests, which is roughly right). That’s the family-wise error rate, which Tukey’s and Bonferroni’s methods keep at 5%.



5. What’s the difference between Tukey’s and Bonferroni’s methods?

Bonferroni’s is only for two groups
Tukey’s is designed for all pairwise comparisons and is less conservative there. Bonferroni’s works for any set of tests but is more conservative
Tukey’s doesn’t control the family-wise error rate


Both keep the chance of any false alarm at 5%. Tukey’s uses the exact distribution of the largest pairwise difference, so it gives narrower intervals for that particular job.



6. What is a contrast?

Any difference between two observations
A test that the variances are equal
A weighted combination of group means, with weights that add up to zero, chosen to answer a specific question


For example, -1 for the standard and \tfrac14 for each new formulation compares the average of the new ones with the standard.

title: One-way ANOVA
text:
Wrap-up
You can now analyze a comparative experiment from start to finish! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Good experiments replicate (to measure the noise) and randomize (to protect against drifts and hidden confounders).
ANOVA splits the total variation into between-group and within-group parts: F = \text{MSB}/\text{MSW}, with k - 1 and N - k degrees of freedom. aov() and summary() print the table.
ANOVA is regression on dummy variables. Put the control group first with factor(..., levels = ), and the coefficients compare each group with it.
Multiple comparisons: many tests inflate the family-wise error rate. Tukey’s HSD (TukeyHSD()) handles all pairs, Bonferroni (pairwise.t.test(..., p.adjust.method = "bonferroni")) handles anything, and Dunnett’s handles comparisons with a control.
Contrasts answer planned questions efficiently: L = \sum c_i\bar{y}_i, with \text{SE} = \sqrt{\text{MSW}\sum c_i^2/n_i}.
Assumptions: check equal spreads with Levene’s or Bartlett’s test and the residuals’ shape with a Q-Q plot. The Kruskal-Wallis test is the rank-based alternative.
The verdict: F2 is better than the standard by about 6 points (Tukey interval 1.9 to 9.5). F4 might be, and the others aren’t.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download catalyst_screening.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install the emmeans package.

emmeans. Run emm <- emmeans::emmeans(fit_aov, ~ formulation), then pairs(emm) (Tukey-adjusted pairs), emmeans::contrast(emm, "trt.vs.ctrl") (Dunnett’s comparisons with the standard), and plot(emm, comparisons = TRUE).
A custom contrast. With emmeans, test the contrast “F2 and F4 together against the standard”: emmeans::contrast(emm, list(best_vs_std = c(-1, 0, 0.5, 0, 0.5))).
Randomize your own experiment. Write the R code that would have produced a random run order for 6 runs of each of 5 formulations, using sample(). Then think about a constraint: if only 10 runs can be done per day, how would you make sure every day gets a fair mix? (That’s the idea behind blocking, in the next lesson.)
The residuals. Plot the residuals of fit_aov against the run order. Is there any sign of a drift during the experiment?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Analysis of variance (ANOVA)

A method that splits the variation in a response into parts due to different sources, and tests them with F statistics.

Replication and randomization

Repeating each treatment to measure the noise, and assigning the run order by chance to protect against drift and hidden confounders.

Between- and within-group sums of squares

The variation of the group means around the grand mean (SSB), and of the observations around their own group means (SSW).

Family-wise error rate

The probability of at least one false alarm in a set of tests.

Tukey’s honestly significant difference (HSD)

A method for all pairwise comparisons of group means that controls the family-wise error rate, with simultaneous confidence intervals.

Bonferroni correction

Multiplying each p-value by the number of tests, which controls the family-wise error rate for any set of tests.

Contrast

A weighted combination of group means, with weights that sum to zero, used to test a specific comparison.

Kruskal-Wallis test

A rank-based test of whether several groups differ, the nonparametric counterpart of one-way ANOVA.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 502, Lesson 2: ANOVA Foundations and Lesson 3: ANOVA Models Part I. The ANOVA table, Tukey’s test and contrasts, then the model, its assumptions and power.
NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, “Are the means equal?”. The handbook’s one-way ANOVA section: an engineering-flavored walk through the calculations, with multiple comparisons.
Douglas Montgomery, Design and Analysis of Experiments (Wiley), chapter 3. The standard engineering textbook on experiments, and a great companion for this lesson and the next.

title: Multicollinearity
text:
Module 2 · Lesson 11 of 15 Week 41 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The process study records the reactor temperature. It also records the temperature of the heating jacket around the reactor, and the reactor pressure, which rises with temperature. Three measurements of nearly the same thing. If more information is always better, why not put them all in the model? This lesson shows what happens when you do: the coefficients go haywire, the standard errors explode, and yet the predictions are fine. That’s multicollinearity, and knowing when it matters, and when it doesn’t, will save you a lot of confusion.
From this lesson on, we use the cleaned study from Lesson 10: P066’s temperature corrected to 185.1 °C, and P047, with its failed stirrer, left out.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Multicollinearity
text:
Predictors that move together
Here are the correlations between six of the process study’s predictors:

study <- read_csv("data/process_study.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(temp_C = if_else(run_id == "P066", 185.1, temp_C)) |>
  filter(run_id != "P047")
round(cor(select(study, temp_C, jacket_C, pressure_bar, residence_min, feed_rate_Lmin, feed_water_ppm)), 2)
#>                temp_C jacket_C pressure_bar residence_min feed_rate_Lmin
#> temp_C           1.00     0.99         0.96         -0.07           0.10
#> jacket_C         0.99     1.00         0.95         -0.08           0.10
#> pressure_bar     0.96     0.95         1.00         -0.05           0.08
#> residence_min   -0.07    -0.08        -0.05          1.00          -0.95
#> feed_rate_Lmin   0.10     0.10         0.08         -0.95           1.00
#> feed_water_ppm   0.05     0.05         0.05          0.40          -0.38
#>                feed_water_ppm
#> temp_C                   0.05
#> jacket_C                 0.05
#> pressure_bar             0.05
#> residence_min            0.40
#> feed_rate_Lmin          -0.38
#> feed_water_ppm           1.00

Three tight clusters, each with a physical reason:

Temperature, jacket and pressure (correlations 0.95 to 0.99). The jacket heats the reactor, so it runs about 11 °C hotter; and in a closed reactor, the vapor pressure rises with the temperature.
Residence time and feed rate (−0.95). The residence time is the reactor volume divided by the flow rate: a slower feed means a longer stay.
Residence time and feed water (0.40), from the operators’ habit you met in Lesson 5.

This is completely normal for process data. Many variables are measured because they’re easy to measure, not because they’re independent.

title: Multicollinearity
text:
What collinearity does
Start with Lesson 5’s three-predictor model, and then add the jacket temperature:

fit1 <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm, data = study)
fit2 <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + jacket_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm, data = study)
summary(fit1)$coefficients
#>                   Estimate  Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
#> (Intercept)    -56.1138294 6.123064512 -9.164337 2.295926e-15
#> temp_C           0.5984626 0.031165642 19.202641 1.130589e-37
#> residence_min    0.3303743 0.029331362 11.263517 2.766609e-20
#> feed_water_ppm  -0.0554867 0.008431755 -6.580682 1.451738e-09
summary(fit2)$coefficients
#>                    Estimate  Std. Error    t value     Pr(>|t|)
#> (Intercept)    -53.66436728 7.088488352 -7.5706363 1.048213e-11
#> temp_C           0.79860302 0.291521480  2.7394312 7.144914e-03
#> jacket_C        -0.20123827 0.291433073 -0.6905128 4.912753e-01
#> residence_min    0.32941521 0.029431104 11.1927575 4.527337e-20
#> feed_water_ppm  -0.05539789 0.008451979 -6.5544279 1.690387e-09

Look at what happened:

The temperature’s standard error jumped from 0.031 to 0.29, almost ten times bigger. Its confidence interval now runs from about 0.2 to 1.4 points per degree.
The jacket has a negative coefficient, −0.20 per degree. Taken literally, a hotter jacket lowers the yield, which makes no physical sense.
Neither temperature looks very important on its own, yet together they’re clearly essential, and on its own, the jacket temperature works just as well as the reactor’s (0.59 per degree, t = 18).
The fit hasn’t changed: R^2 is 0.799 in one model and 0.800 in the other, and the partial F-test for the jacket says p = 0.49.

Why? Each coefficient is a partial effect: the change in yield when one temperature rises and the other stays fixed. But in this study, the two temperatures never move apart: the jacket is always 8 to 14 °C hotter. The data contain almost no information about what happens when one changes without the other, so the model can’t split the credit between them. It knows that their combined effect is about 0.6 points per degree, and almost nothing about how to share it out. That’s why the individual coefficients are so uncertain, and so sensitive: drop or add a few runs, and the split can swing wildly.
Predictions are a different matter. As long as you predict for conditions like the data, where the jacket runs about 11 °C above the reactor, both models agree. Multicollinearity is a problem for interpreting coefficients, not for prediction within the pattern of the data.










Your turn. By what factor did adding the jacket inflate the temperature’s standard error?









The model with the jacket is fit2.


se1 <- summary(fit1)$coefficients["temp_C", "Std. Error"]
se2 <- summary(fit2)$coefficients["temp_C", "Std. Error"]
se2 / se1
9.4 times bigger. To get the temperature’s coefficient back to its old precision while keeping the jacket in the model, you’d need about 9.4^2 = 88 times as many runs.

title: Multicollinearity
text:
Perfect collinearity
At the extreme, one predictor is an exact linear combination of others. Then the model can’t be fitted at all, because X^\top X has no inverse (Lesson 4). It happens more often than you’d think: the same temperature in °C and °F, a total and all of its parts, or a dummy for every category of a factor. R doesn’t stop with an error. It quietly drops a column and reports NA for its coefficient, so watch out for NAs in a coefficient table.
Your turn. Add the temperature in Fahrenheit to a model that already has it in Celsius. Which coefficient comes out as NA?









is.na(b) is TRUE for the missing coefficient.


study_f <- mutate(study, temp_F = 1.8 * temp_C + 32)
fit_f <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + temp_F + residence_min, data = study_f)
b <- coef(fit_f)
names(b)[is.na(b)]
temp_F. R noticed that it’s exactly 1.8 \times temp_C + 32, a combination of the temperature and the intercept, and dropped it. alias(fit_f) shows the exact relationship it found.

title: Multicollinearity
text:
Variance inflation factors
How do you measure multicollinearity? Ask how well each predictor can be predicted from the others. Regress predictor j on all the other predictors, and call that regression’s R^2 R_j^2. Then the variance inflation factor is

\text{VIF}_j = \frac{1}{1 - R_j^2} .

It’s exactly the factor by which predictor j’s variance is inflated, compared with a world where it was uncorrelated with the others. So its standard error is inflated by \sqrt{\text{VIF}_j}. A VIF of 1 means no collinearity at all. Common rules of thumb call a VIF above 5, or above 10, a problem: that’s R_j^2 above 0.8 or 0.9, and a standard error more than about twice or three times as big as it could be.
The car package’s vif() computes them for every predictor:

car::vif(fit1)
#>         temp_C  residence_min feed_water_ppm 
#>       1.013209       1.202594       1.200013
car::vif(fit2)
#>         temp_C       jacket_C  residence_min feed_water_ppm 
#>      88.248540      88.322925       1.205278       1.200291

Without the jacket, every VIF is below 1.3. With it, both temperatures have VIFs of 88. Put all six correlated predictors in, and the VIFs reach 104 for the temperature, 89 for the jacket, 13 for the pressure, and about 11 for the residence time and the feed rate.
For a categorical predictor, or a predictor with interactions or polynomial terms, a single VIF per coefficient can mislead. car::vif() then reports a generalized VIF (GVIF) for each term, and its GVIF^(1/(2*Df)) column is comparable to \sqrt{\text{VIF}}.
Your turn. Compute the temperature’s VIF in fit2 by hand: regress the temperature on the model’s other predictors, and use that regression’s R^2.









The other predictors in fit2 are jacket_C, residence_min and feed_water_ppm.


r2_temp <- summary(lm(temp_C ~ jacket_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm, data = study))$r.squared
1 / (1 - r2_temp)
88.2: the other predictors explain 98.9% of the temperature’s variation. And \sqrt{88.2} = 9.4, just the inflation you found in the standard error.

title: Multicollinearity
text:
Condition numbers
VIFs look at one predictor at a time. The condition number looks at all of them together. Standardize the predictors, and compute the eigenvalues of their correlation matrix (Lesson 0.14). Each eigenvalue measures how much the data spread out in one direction of the predictor space. A tiny eigenvalue means a direction in which the data hardly vary at all: a combination of predictors that’s almost constant, like “jacket minus temperature”. The condition number compares the biggest spread with the smallest:

\kappa = \sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}}} .

A common rule of thumb says that values above about 30 mean serious trouble, and above 10 to 15 deserve a look. (R’s kappa() computes a condition number for any matrix. Use kappa(scale(X), exact = TRUE) for the standardized version.) The eigenvectors that go with the small eigenvalues even tell you which predictors are tangled together.
Your turn. Compute the condition number of all six predictors from the eigenvalues of their correlation matrix.









Divide by the smallest eigenvalue, min(ev).


X <- select(study, temp_C, jacket_C, pressure_bar, residence_min, feed_rate_Lmin, feed_water_ppm)
ev <- eigen(cor(X))$values
round(ev, 4)
sqrt(max(ev) / min(ev))
23.6. The smallest eigenvalue, 0.005, belongs to the jacket-minus-temperature direction, and the next two to the residence-feed-rate pair (0.047) and the pressure (0.056). With only the temperature, residence time and water, the condition number is 1.6.

title: Multicollinearity
section: Collinearity you make yourself: polynomials and interactions
text:
Collinearity you make yourself: polynomials and interactions
Some collinearity comes from the model, not the data. Over the study’s range, from 167 to 206 °C, the temperature and its square are almost perfectly correlated: both just get bigger together. Fit a quadratic without centering, and the VIFs are over 1,300:

fit_raw <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + I(temp_C^2) + residence_min + feed_water_ppm, data = study)
fit_cen <- lm(yield_pct ~ I(temp_C - 185) + I((temp_C - 185)^2) + residence_min + feed_water_ppm, data = study)
car::vif(fit_raw)
#>         temp_C    I(temp_C^2)  residence_min feed_water_ppm 
#>    1349.858814    1351.459696       1.242972       1.218138
car::vif(fit_cen)
#>     I(temp_C - 185) I((temp_C - 185)^2)       residence_min      feed_water_ppm 
#>            1.241224            1.285389            1.242972            1.218138

Centered at 185 °C, they drop to about 1.3. The two models fit identically: same fitted values, same residuals, same squared-term coefficient. What changes is the linear term. Uncentered, it’s the slope at 0 °C, 6.8 ± 1.0 points per degree, a useless extrapolation. Centered, it’s the slope at 185 °C, 0.68 ± 0.03. That’s the collinearity Lesson 7 removed by centering the interaction, too. This kind is harmless once you know about it, because centering removes it completely, but it’s a common reason for alarming VIFs in perfectly good models.
Your turn. Compare the correlation between the temperature and its square, uncentered and centered at 185 °C.









Center at 185 °C.


t <- study$temp_C
tc <- t - 185
c(uncentered = cor(t, t^2), centered = cor(tc, tc^2))
0.9996 uncentered, 0.44 centered. (It isn’t zero, because the temperatures aren’t perfectly symmetric around 185 °C. Centering at the mean would get it closer still.)

title: Multicollinearity
text:
Remedies
What should you do about multicollinearity? It depends on what you want the model for.

Nothing, if you only need predictions for conditions like the data. The combined effect is well estimated, and so are the predictions.
Drop redundant predictors. The jacket temperature adds nothing that the reactor temperature doesn’t already say, and the reactor temperature is the one that drives the chemistry. Keep the variable with the clearest physical meaning.
Combine them. If several sensors measure the same thing, like three thermocouples in a reactor, average them into one better measurement.
Center polynomial and interaction terms.
Collect data that break the pattern. The only way to learn the separate effects of two variables is to see them move apart. In a designed experiment, you set the factors independently, so there’s no collinearity at all. That’s the deep reason the next three lessons are about experiments.
Use methods built for it. Ridge regression and the lasso (Module 7) trade a little bias for much smaller variance, and principal components (Module 3) replace correlated predictors with uncorrelated combinations.

One trap to avoid: never interpret the sign of a coefficient with a big VIF. The jacket’s “negative effect” is noise, not chemistry.
Your turn. Predictions are fine within the pattern of the data. What about outside it? Use fit2 to predict the yield at 190 °C, 50 minutes and 200 ppm, with a jacket at 201 °C (normal, 11 degrees hotter) and at 215 °C (25 degrees hotter, never seen in the study). Compare the widths of their 95% confidence intervals.









The second jacket temperature is 215.


new <- tibble(temp_C = 190, jacket_C = c(201, 215), residence_min = 50, feed_water_ppm = 200)
p <- predict(fit2, newdata = new, interval = "confidence")
p[, "upr"] - p[, "lwr"]
1.8 points wide for the normal jacket, and 16.3 for the unusual one. Each value, 190 °C and 215 °C, is within the range of its own variable, but the combination is far outside the data: an extrapolation in a direction the data never explored. With correlated predictors, “inside the range of each variable” isn’t the same as “inside the data”.

title: Multicollinearity
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Residence time or feed rate? The residence time and the feed rate are two views of the same thing. Put both in a model with the temperature and the water, and look at their VIFs. Then compare the R^2 of the model with the residence time alone and the model with the feed rate alone. Which would you keep?









The second model uses feed_rate_Lmin instead of residence_min.


r2_res <- summary(lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm, data = study))$r.squared
r2_feed <- summary(lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + feed_rate_Lmin + feed_water_ppm, data = study))$r.squared
c(residence = r2_res, feed_rate = r2_feed)
0.799 with the residence time, 0.784 with the feed rate. In a model with both, their VIFs are about 10.6, and the feed rate isn’t significant (p = 0.42). Keep the residence time: it fits better, because the yield depends on how long the reactants spend together, which is proportional to the residence time and only inversely related to the feed rate. The chemistry and the data agree.




Challenge 2 · The two-predictor formula. With only two predictors, R_j^2 is simply their squared correlation, so \text{VIF} = 1/(1 - r^2). Compute it from the correlation between the reactor and jacket temperatures. Why is it a little smaller than fit2’s VIF of 88.2?









1 / (1 - r^2).


r <- cor(study$temp_C, study$jacket_C)
1 / (1 - r^2)
About 84. In fit2, the temperature is predicted from the jacket and the residence time and water, which explain a sliver more of it, so its R_j^2 is a little higher and its VIF a little bigger. The formula also shows how fast things get worse: a correlation of 0.9 gives a VIF of 5.3, 0.99 gives 50, and 0.999 gives 500.

title: Multicollinearity
text:
Quick quiz

1. Two predictors have a correlation of 0.99. What happens when both are in the model?

The model can’t be fitted
Their coefficients get large standard errors and can have odd signs, while the overall fit is fine
R^2 drops sharply


The data can’t separate their effects, so the split between them is very uncertain. Their combined effect, and the fit, are well determined.



2. A predictor has a VIF of 25. What does that mean?

It explains 25% of the response
Its coefficient’s variance is 25 times what it would be if it were uncorrelated with the other predictors, so its standard error is 5 times bigger
It should be multiplied by 25


\text{VIF} = 1/(1 - R_j^2) inflates the variance, and its square root inflates the standard error. Here R_j^2 = 0.96.



3. The coefficient table shows NA for one predictor. What’s the likeliest reason?

The predictor has missing values
The predictor is an exact linear combination of others, so R dropped it
Its effect is exactly zero


That’s perfect collinearity: the same quantity in two units, a total and all its parts, or one dummy too many.



4. A quadratic model in temperature has VIFs over 1,000. What’s the simplest fix?

Center the temperature before squaring it
Drop the squared term
Collect more data


Uncentered x and x^2 are almost perfectly correlated over a range far from zero. Centering removes that without changing the fit.



5. Your model has severe multicollinearity, but you only need it to predict yields for conditions like the ones in the data. What should you do?

Drop predictors until every VIF is below 5
Not much: predictions within the pattern of the data are fine
Never use the model


Multicollinearity hurts the interpretation of individual coefficients. Predictions within the data’s pattern are well estimated. Beware of combinations outside it, though.



6. What’s the only way to learn the separate effects of two variables that always move together in your plant?

Use a bigger computer
Standardize both variables
Collect data in which they move independently, for example with a designed experiment


No analysis can extract information that isn’t in the data. An experiment that sets them independently puts it there.

title: Multicollinearity
text:
Wrap-up
You can now spot predictors that are stepping on each other’s toes! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Multicollinearity means correlated predictors. It’s normal in process data: sensors that track each other, quantities defined from each other, and operators’ habits.
Its effects: large standard errors, unstable and sometimes nonsensical coefficients, but a good overall fit and good predictions within the data’s pattern.
Perfect collinearity makes a coefficient NA: R drops a column that’s an exact combination of others.
VIFs, 1/(1 - R_j^2) from car::vif(), say how much each predictor’s variance is inflated. Above 5 or 10 is worth a look.
Condition numbers, \sqrt{\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}} from the standardized predictors, measure the collinearity of the whole set. Above 30 is serious.
Model-made collinearity from polynomials and interactions disappears with centering.
Remedies: do nothing (for prediction), drop or combine redundant predictors, center, collect data that break the pattern, or use ridge regression or principal components.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download process_study.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and apply Lesson 10’s cleaning (P066’s temperature to 185.1, and P047 out).

Unstable coefficients. Fit fit2 to 200 bootstrap resamples of the runs (slice_sample(study, prop = 1, replace = TRUE)), and plot the temperature coefficient against the jacket coefficient. What shape do you see, and what does it say about the two estimates?
Eigenvectors. Look at eigen(cor(X))$vectors[, 6], the eigenvector of the smallest eigenvalue. Which predictors carry the biggest weights, and with which signs? That’s the near-constant combination.
The GVIF. Run car::vif() on the full cleaned model from Lesson 10, yield_pct ~ temp_C * catalyst + I((temp_C - 185)^2) + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst_age, with and without centering the temperature. Compare the GVIF^(1/(2*Df)) columns.
Ridge regression, a preview. Install the glmnet package and fit glmnet::glmnet(as.matrix(X), study$yield_pct, alpha = 0) with all six predictors. Plot the coefficient paths with plot(). Module 7 explains what you’re seeing.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Multicollinearity

Strong correlation among predictors, which makes their separate effects hard to estimate.

Perfect collinearity

An exact linear relationship among predictors, which makes X^\top X singular and some coefficients impossible to estimate.

Variance inflation factor (VIF)

1/(1 - R_j^2), the factor by which a coefficient’s variance is inflated by its predictor’s correlation with the others.

Generalized VIF (GVIF)

A version of the VIF for terms with several coefficients, like factors, polynomials and interactions.

Condition number

\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}} for the eigenvalues of the standardized predictors’ correlation matrix, a measure of the collinearity of the whole set.

Extrapolation in the predictor space

Predicting for a combination of predictor values unlike any in the data, even if each value is within its own range.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 501, Lesson 12: Multicollinearity & Other Regression Pitfalls. The effects, the VIF, and remedies, with worked examples.
John Fox, Applied Regression Analysis and Generalized Linear Models (Sage), the chapter “Collinearity and its purported remedies”. A clear, skeptical look at what the usual fixes can and can’t do.
David Belsley, Edwin Kuh and Roy Welsch, Regression Diagnostics: Identifying Influential Data and Sources of Collinearity (Wiley, 1980). The classic that introduced condition-number diagnostics, along with much of Lesson 10.

title: Transformations
text:
Module 2 · Lesson 9 of 15 Week 39 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Last lesson’s residuals found curves and funnels. “Linear regression” sounds as if it can only fit straight lines with equal scatter, but it’s more flexible than that. Linear means linear in the coefficients: you can transform the response, transform the predictors, and add squared terms, and it’s still least squares with a design matrix. This lesson shows you the four standard tools, starting with one every chemical engineer already uses.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Transformations
text:
Arrhenius: logs make it straight
The kinetics lab measured the reaction’s rate constant, k, twice at each of eight temperatures from 140 to 210 °C:

kinetics <- read_csv("data/kinetics.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ggplot(kinetics, aes(x = temp_C, y = k_per_min)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, color = "#C2416C") +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Rate constant k (1/min)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The rate climbs faster and faster: a straight line fits it badly (R^2 = 0.85). But you know the law it should follow, the Arrhenius equation:

k = A\, e^{-E_a/(RT)} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \ln k = \ln A - \frac{E_a}{R} \cdot \frac{1}{T},

with T in kelvin and R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). Take logs, and \ln k is a straight line in 1/T, with slope -E_a/R. That’s a simple regression, with a transformed response and a transformed predictor:

kinetics <- mutate(kinetics, inv_T = 1 / (temp_C + 273.15))
fit_arr <- lm(log(k_per_min) ~ inv_T, data = kinetics)
coef(fit_arr)
#> (Intercept)       inv_T 
#>    18.76305 -9899.49717
ggplot(kinetics, aes(x = 1000 * inv_T, y = log(k_per_min))) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, color = "#C2416C") +
  labs(x = "1000 / T (1/K)", y = "ln k") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The points fall on the line (R^2 = 0.998). The slope is −9,899 K, so E_a = 9899 \times 8.314 = 82{,}300 J/mol, about 82 kJ/mol.
The log helped twice. It straightened the curve, and it evened out the scatter. Rate constants have multiplicative errors: each measurement is off by a few percent, so the absolute errors are tiny at 140 °C and big at 210 °C, a funnel. On the log scale, a 6% error is the same size everywhere. Whenever a variable’s errors scale with its size, a log is the natural first try. (In R, log() is the natural log, ln. Use log10() for base 10.)










Your turn. Compute the activation energy, in kJ/mol, from the slope of fit_arr, and its 95% confidence interval from confint().









Divide by 1000 to turn J/mol into kJ/mol, the same as for the estimate. (The interval’s ends swap places because of the minus sign.)


R <- 8.314
slope <- coef(fit_arr)["inv_T"]
slope_ci <- confint(fit_arr)["inv_T", ]
c(Ea = unname(-slope * R / 1000), lower = unname(-slope_ci[2] * R / 1000), upper = unname(-slope_ci[1] * R / 1000))
E_a = 82.3 kJ/mol, with a 95% interval from 80.4 to 84.2 kJ/mol. A transformation plus a confidence interval gives you a physical constant with honest error bars.

title: Transformations
section: Reading a model on the log scale
text:
Reading a model on the log scale
When the response is logged, the coefficients describe ratios, not differences. If \ln y = b_0 + b_1 x, then raising x by one unit multiplies y by e^{b_1}. For small b_1, that’s roughly a 100 \times b_1 percent change. For example, a fit of \ln k against the temperature in °C, over this range, has a slope of 0.0495 per degree: each degree speeds the reaction up by about e^{0.0495} - 1 = 5.1\%.







Model
Meaning of the slope b_1




y = b_0 + b_1 x
one more unit of x adds b_1 to y


\ln y = b_0 + b_1 x
one more unit of x multiplies y by e^{b_1} (about 100 b_1 percent)


y = b_0 + b_1 \ln x
multiplying x by e adds b_1 to y. Doubling x adds 0.69\,b_1


\ln y = b_0 + b_1 \ln x
a 1% increase in x goes with about a b_1% increase in y (an elasticity, or a power law y = a x^{b_1})



To predict, work on the log scale, then transform back with exp(). Back-transformed prediction intervals stay valid: if \ln k is inside its interval 95% of the time, so is k. But they’re no longer symmetric, because the log scale stretches small values and squashes big ones.






NoteGo deeper: the back-transformed mean is a median





If \ln Y is normal with mean \mu and standard deviation \sigma, then e^{\mu} is the median of Y, not its mean. The mean of a lognormal variable is e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}, a little higher, because the exponential stretches the upper tail.
So exp(predict(fit)) estimates the median rate constant at a temperature. For the Arrhenius fit, \sigma = 0.048, and the correction factor e^{\sigma^2/2} is 1.001: a tenth of a percent, which doesn’t matter. With noisier data, say \sigma = 0.5, it would be 13%, and it would matter whenever you need averages, like total production over a year. Then use the correction, or Duan’s “smearing” estimate, which multiplies by the average of the exponentiated residuals instead of assuming normality.



Your turn. How many times faster is the reaction at 200 °C than at 180 °C? Predict \ln k at both temperatures, and take the exponential of the difference.









The difference of two logs is the log of their ratio: log_k[2] - log_k[1].


temps <- tibble(inv_T = 1 / (c(180, 200) + 273.15))
log_k <- predict(fit_arr, newdata = temps)
exp(log_k[2] - log_k[1])
2.5 times faster: the old rule of thumb that “reaction rates double for every 10 degrees” is roughly right here, since 1.6 \times 1.6 = 2.5 for the two 10-degree steps. It’s not a law, though: it depends on the activation energy and the temperature.

title: Transformations
text:
Box-Cox: let the data choose
Without a physical law to guide you, how do you choose a transformation? The Box-Cox family is a ladder of powers for the response:

y^{(\lambda)} = \begin{cases} \dfrac{y^\lambda - 1}{\lambda} & \lambda \ne 0 \\[2mm] \ln y & \lambda = 0 \end{cases}

\lambda = 1 leaves y alone, \lambda = 0.5 is a square root, \lambda = 0 is the log, and \lambda = -1 is a reciprocal.
