(The odd-looking form makes the family change smoothly with \lambda, with the log as the limit at 0.) For each \lambda, the Box-Cox method fits the model to the transformed response and computes how likely the data are. MASS::boxcox() computes that profile, and you can draw it with a 95% confidence interval for \lambda. (Fit the model with y = TRUE, which keeps a copy of the response inside it for boxcox() to use.)

bc <- MASS::boxcox(lm(k_per_min ~ inv_T, data = kinetics, y = TRUE), plotit = FALSE, lambda = seq(-1, 1, by = 0.01))
ci <- range(bc$x[bc$y > max(bc$y) - qchisq(0.95, 1) / 2])
ggplot(tibble(lambda = bc$x, loglik = bc$y), aes(x = lambda, y = loglik)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = ci[1], xmax = ci[2], ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "#F4C0D1", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "λ", y = "Profile log-likelihood") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The peak is at \lambda = 0.02, and the interval runs from −0.02 to 0.05: the data ask for a log, just as Arrhenius said. In practice, choose a simple value inside the interval (1, 0.5, 0 or −1) that makes sense to explain, rather than 0.02 exactly.
Three things to know about Box-Cox. It transforms the response only (the kinetics model already used 1/T as the predictor). The response must be positive. And it chooses the power that makes the residuals most normal-looking and the variance most even for that model, so a different set of predictors can ask for a different \lambda.
Your turn. Find the \lambda with the highest profile log-likelihood.









bc$y holds the log-likelihood for each \lambda in bc$x.


bc <- MASS::boxcox(lm(k_per_min ~ inv_T, data = kinetics, y = TRUE), plotit = FALSE,
                   lambda = seq(-1, 1, by = 0.01))
bc$x[which.max(bc$y)]
\lambda = 0.02, practically 0: take logs.

title: Transformations
text:
Polynomial terms
Sometimes no transformation is natural, and you just need the line to bend. Add a squared term: y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \varepsilon. It’s still a linear model, because it’s linear in the \betas: x^2 is simply another column of X. In R, write it as I(x^2), because inside a formula ^ has a different meaning. The I() says “compute this as arithmetic”.
The calibration curve. Lesson 8 found that the absorbance bends down at high concentrations. A quadratic term lets it:

calibration <- read_csv("data/calibration.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fit_q <- lm(absorbance ~ conc_mgL + I(conc_mgL^2), data = calibration)
summary(fit_q)$coefficients
#>                    Estimate   Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
#> (Intercept)    4.345280e-03 2.810847e-03  1.545897 1.370673e-01
#> conc_mgL       2.109992e-02 2.871805e-04 73.472692 8.191895e-27
#> I(conc_mgL^2) -3.825203e-05 5.557115e-06 -6.883434 8.389428e-07
anova(fit_q, lm(absorbance ~ factor(conc_mgL), data = calibration))
#> Analysis of Variance Table
#> 
#> Model 1: absorbance ~ conc_mgL + I(conc_mgL^2)
#> Model 2: absorbance ~ factor(conc_mgL)
#>   Res.Df        RSS Df  Sum of Sq      F Pr(>F)
#> 1     21 0.00081866                            
#> 2     16 0.00071282  5 0.00010584 0.4751 0.7895

The squared term is small but clearly real (t = -6.9), and the lack-of-fit test is now happy (p = 0.79). The intercept, 0.0043, finally agrees with the blanks (0.0052 on average). That was the clue from Lesson 2: the straight line’s intercept, 0.0173, was a symptom of the curve.
The process study. Lesson 8 found an arch in the residuals against temperature, too, along with one run, P066, whose temperature looks wrong. Until Lesson 10 settles P066’s case, let’s set it aside and add a squared temperature term, centered at 185 °C as in Lesson 7:

study <- read_csv("data/process_study.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
no66 <- filter(study, run_id != "P066")
fit_lin <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C * catalyst + residence_min + feed_water_ppm, data = no66)
fit_quad <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C * catalyst + I((temp_C - 185)^2) + residence_min + feed_water_ppm, data = no66)
summary(fit_quad)$coefficients["I((temp_C - 185)^2)", ]
#>      Estimate    Std. Error       t value      Pr(>|t|) 
#> -1.275272e-02  2.189003e-03 -5.825811e+00  5.738707e-08

The yield’s rise does flatten at high temperatures. With the curve in the model, the arch in the residuals disappears: the mean residual is within half a point of zero in every temperature band. (And notice that catalyst B’s slope now matches A’s almost exactly, p = 0.92 for the difference. Lesson 10 will explain.)
Where’s the peak? For catalyst A, the fitted curve tops out at about 206 °C, right at the edge of the study, and for C it would be beyond the data. Polynomials are dangerous outside the range of the data: a parabola must come back down eventually, whether the chemistry does or not. Use them to describe a curve where you have data, not to predict where you don’t.
Three rules for polynomial terms:

Keep the lower terms. A model with x^2 should have x too, or its shape depends on where zero is.
Center first (or use poly()): x and x^2 are almost perfectly correlated when x is far from zero, which inflates the standard errors. Lesson 11 shows this.
Rarely go beyond a cubic. High-degree polynomials wiggle wildly between and beyond the data. Lesson 12 shows how they overfit.

Your turn. A sample’s absorbance was 0.462. In Lesson 2, the straight line said 23.2 mg/L. What does the quadratic calibration say? Solve b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 x^2 = 0.462 for x with uniroot(), which finds where a function crosses zero.









The function should be zero where the curve’s prediction equals the measured absorbance, 0.462.


fit_q <- lm(absorbance ~ conc_mgL + I(conc_mgL^2), data = calibration)
gap <- function(x) predict(fit_q, newdata = tibble(conc_mgL = x)) - 0.462
uniroot(gap, interval = c(0, 50))$root
22.6 mg/L, against 23.2 from the straight line. That’s a 2.4% difference, which is bigger than the 0.35 mg/L standard error Lesson 3 put on the straight-line result. The line wasn’t just slightly imprecise; it was biased, and its error bars didn’t know it. A high R^2 hid a real error, and the residual plot found it.




Your turn. Test the squared temperature term in the process model with a partial F-test (P066 is set aside, as above).









The linear model is nested in the quadratic one: anova(fit_lin, fit_quad).


no66 <- filter(study, run_id != "P066")
fit_lin <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C * catalyst + residence_min + feed_water_ppm, data = no66)
fit_quad <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C * catalyst + I((temp_C - 185)^2) + residence_min + feed_water_ppm, data = no66)
anova(fit_lin, fit_quad)
F = 33.9, p = 6 \times 10^{-8}: the curve clearly belongs. In practice, it matters most at the top of the range. For catalyst A, the straight line promised 4.9 points from raising the temperature from 195 to 205 °C. The curve says only 1.7.

title: Transformations
text:
Weighted least squares
The calibration’s funnel is still there: the quadratic fixed the shape, not the scatter. When you know (or can estimate) how the variance changes, weighted least squares (WLS) uses it. It minimizes

\sum w_i\, (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2, \qquad w_i = \frac{1}{\sigma_i^2},

so precise observations, with small \sigma_i, get big weights, and noisy ones get small weights. That’s exactly what an analyst would do by instinct: trust the precise standards more. By the Gauss-Markov reasoning from Lesson 4, the right weights give the most precise estimates.
Where do the \sigma_i come from? With replicates, from the data. The triplicates’ standard deviations are rough (three readings each), so it’s better to smooth them: fit a line to the SD against concentration, and use that line’s predictions:

sds <- calibration |> group_by(conc_mgL) |> summarise(sd = sd(absorbance))
sd_fit <- lm(sd ~ conc_mgL, data = sds)
coef(sd_fit)
#>  (Intercept)     conc_mgL 
#> 0.0008564546 0.0002073208
calibration <- mutate(calibration, w = 1 / predict(sd_fit, newdata = calibration)^2)
fit_w <- lm(absorbance ~ conc_mgL + I(conc_mgL^2), data = calibration, weights = w)
summary(fit_w)$coefficients
#>                    Estimate   Std. Error    t value     Pr(>|t|)
#> (Intercept)    0.0049421653 5.482200e-04   9.014931 1.152928e-08
#> conc_mgL       0.0209602226 1.532365e-04 136.783507 1.808687e-32
#> I(conc_mgL^2) -0.0000349522 4.519530e-06  -7.733593 1.411239e-07

The SD grows from about 0.0009 for a blank to 0.011 at 50 mg/L, so the blanks get about 170 times the weight of the top standards. The coefficients barely move. Least squares was unbiased all along. The gain is in the uncertainty: the intercept’s standard error drops from 0.0028 to 0.0005, because the precise low standards now pin it down. And prediction intervals finally get the right shape: to predict, tell predict() the weight of the new observation as well.
Your turn. Compute the WLS model’s 95% prediction interval for a new reading of a 5 mg/L standard, and its width. The OLS quadratic’s interval at 5 mg/L is 0.027 wide.









The new reading’s weight is w_new.


sds <- calibration |> group_by(conc_mgL) |> summarise(sd = sd(absorbance))
sd_fit <- lm(sd ~ conc_mgL, data = sds)
calibration <- mutate(calibration, w = 1 / predict(sd_fit, newdata = calibration)^2)
fit_w <- lm(absorbance ~ conc_mgL + I(conc_mgL^2), data = calibration, weights = w)
new <- tibble(conc_mgL = 5)
w_new <- 1 / predict(sd_fit, newdata = new)^2
p <- predict(fit_w, newdata = new, interval = "prediction", weights = w_new)
p[, "upr"] - p[, "lwr"]
0.0094, about a third of the OLS interval’s 0.027. At 45 mg/L, it goes the other way: the WLS interval is 0.052 wide, against OLS’s 0.028. OLS gave every concentration the same, average-sized interval: too wide at the bottom and too narrow at the top. WLS gets both ends right.

title: Transformations
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · A half-life from Arrhenius. For a first-order reaction, the half-life is t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / k. Use the Arrhenius fit to predict k at 160 °C, and compute the half-life in minutes.









The model predicts \ln k, so transform back with exp(log_k).


log_k <- predict(fit_arr, newdata = tibble(inv_T = 1 / (160 + 273.15)))
k_160 <- exp(log_k)
log(2) / k_160
k = 0.0167 per minute, so the half-life is 41.5 minutes. At 180 °C, it would be about 15 minutes. (Strictly, e^{\widehat{\ln k}} estimates the median k, but with \sigma = 0.048, that makes no practical difference.)




Challenge 2 · Transforming the response to a rate law. For the first-order batch reaction from Lesson 1, X = 1 - e^{-kt}, so -\ln(1 - X) = kt: a straight line through the origin. Fit it to the conversion data, with no intercept, to estimate k. Use only the samples after time 0 with a conversion below 90%: near full conversion, 1 - X is tiny, and the log blows up its measurement noise.









0 + removes the intercept, as in Lesson 2’s line through the origin.


early <- filter(conversion, time_min > 0, conversion_pct < 90)
fit_k <- lm(-log(1 - conversion_pct / 100) ~ 0 + time_min, data = early)
coef(fit_k)
k = 0.0452 per minute, from the 9 early samples. With all the samples, you’d get 0.0499: the near-complete conversions at the end, magnified by the log, pull it up. A transformation changes the error structure too, so check where it makes the noise explode. This run was at 180 °C, and the Arrhenius fit predicts 0.0458 there, so two completely separate experiments agree to within about 1%.

title: Transformations
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why does \ln k against 1/T give a straight line for rate constants?

Because logs make every relationship straight
Because the Arrhenius equation is linear in 1/T after taking logs
Because rate constants are normally distributed


\ln k = \ln A - (E_a/R)(1/T). Theory chose the transformation, and the slope estimates -E_a/R.



2. In a model for \ln y, a coefficient is 0.05. What does a one-unit increase in that predictor do?

Adds 0.05 to y
Multiplies y by e^{0.05}, about a 5% increase
Adds 5 to y


On the log scale, adding b means multiplying by e^b on the original scale.



3. The Box-Cox interval for \lambda runs from 0.3 to 0.7. Which transformation would you use?

The log
The square root
None


Pick a simple value inside the interval: 0.5, the square root. 0 (log) and 1 (none) are both outside it.



4. Why write I(x^2) in a formula instead of x^2?

It’s faster
Inside a formula, ^ means something else, and I() makes R compute the arithmetic
x^2 would center the variable


In formulas, ^ builds interactions: (a + b)^2 means a + b + a:b. I() protects arithmetic from that.



5. A quadratic fits a yield curve well between 170 and 205 °C, and peaks at 206 °C. What should you be careful about?

Nothing: the peak is where the yield is highest
Using the curve near or beyond the edge of the data, where a parabola’s shape is an assumption, not evidence
The squared term must be removed


The data say the curve flattens. They say little about what happens beyond 206 °C. More runs up there would settle it.



6. What does weighted least squares do with the noisiest observations?

Removes them
Gives them less weight, in proportion to 1/\sigma_i^2
Gives them more weight, because they carry more information


Precise observations get more say. The estimates stay unbiased, and their standard errors and prediction intervals become right for each observation.

title: Transformations
text:
Wrap-up
Your models can now bend and weigh! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Linear means linear in the coefficients. Transformations and polynomial terms are just new columns of X.
Logs straighten multiplicative relationships and even out multiplicative errors. Arrhenius: \ln k = \ln A - (E_a/R)(1/T) gave E_a = 82.3 \pm 1.9 kJ/mol.
Interpreting logs: a coefficient in a log-y model is a multiplicative effect, e^{b}. Back-transform predictions with exp(). They estimate the median.
Box-Cox (MASS::boxcox()) chooses a power of the response. Pick a simple value in its interval.
Polynomials: I(x^2) bends a line. It fixed the calibration’s lack of fit (the unknown is 22.6 mg/L, not 23.2) and the process study’s arch. Keep the lower terms, center, and don’t extrapolate.
Weighted least squares (lm(..., weights = )) handles known non-constant variance, with w_i = 1/\sigma_i^2. Smooth the variances first, and give predict() the new weights.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download kinetics.csv, calibration.csv and conversion.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Nonlinear least squares. Fit the Arrhenius equation directly, without logs: nls(k_per_min ~ A * exp(-Ea / (8.314 * (temp_C + 273.15))), data = kinetics, start = list(A = 1e8, Ea = 80000)). Compare E_a with the log-scale fit. Why are they slightly different? (Think about which errors each one minimizes.)
First-order kinetics, nonlinearly. Fit nls(conversion_pct ~ 100 * (1 - exp(-k * time_min)), data = conversion, start = list(k = 0.05)) to all the samples. Does it need you to drop the late ones?
poly(). Fit the calibration with poly(conc_mgL, 2) instead of conc_mgL + I(conc_mgL^2). The coefficients differ, but the fitted values are the same. Why? Look up “orthogonal polynomials”.
Your own Box-Cox. Fit the yield of the March batches (batches.csv) against residence time, and run MASS::boxcox() on it. Does it ask for a transformation?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Transformation

Replacing a variable by a function of it, like \ln y or 1/x, to straighten a relationship or even out the variance.

Multiplicative error

An error proportional to the size of the measurement, like “±6%”. Logs turn it into an additive, constant-size error.

Elasticity

In a log-log model, the percentage change in y for a 1% change in x.

Box-Cox transformation

The family of power transformations (y^\lambda - 1)/\lambda, with the log at \lambda = 0, and a likelihood method for choosing \lambda.

Polynomial regression

A linear model with powers of a predictor, like x and x^2, as columns.

Weighted least squares

Least squares in which each squared residual is multiplied by a weight, usually 1/\sigma_i^2, so that precise observations count more.

Activation energy

In the Arrhenius equation, the energy barrier E_a that sets how strongly a reaction rate depends on temperature.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 501, Lesson 9: Data Transformations and Lesson 13: Weighted Least Squares & Logistic Regressions. Transformations, polynomial terms and weighting, with examples.
NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, “Weighted least squares regression”. When and how to weight, from an engineering point of view.
H. Scott Fogler, Elements of Chemical Reaction Engineering, chapter 7, “Collection and analysis of rate data”. The integral and differential methods for finding rate laws, which use exactly these transformations.

title: Categorical regressors and interactions
text:
Module 2 · Lesson 7 of 15 Week 37 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Regression was born for numbers, but half the interesting questions in a plant are about categories: this catalyst or that one, this supplier, this reactor, this shift. You’ve already seen R slip categories into a model as dummy columns. This lesson explains exactly what those columns do, and how to choose them. Then it tackles a bigger idea: what if a predictor’s effect depends on another predictor? What if one catalyst likes heat more than the others?
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Categorical regressors and interactions
text:
Dummy variables
The catalyst has three values, A, B and C. To use it in a regression, R makes dummy variables (also called indicator variables): columns of 0s and 1s that say which catalyst each run used.

head(cbind(catalyst = study$catalyst, model.matrix(~ catalyst, data = study)), 4)
#>   catalyst (Intercept) catalystB catalystC
#> 1 "A"      "1"         "0"       "0"      
#> 2 "B"      "1"         "1"       "0"      
#> 3 "A"      "1"         "0"       "0"      
#> 4 "B"      "1"         "1"       "0"

There’s a column for B and a column for C, but none for A. A run with catalyst A has zeros in both, so A is the baseline (or reference) category, and the others are measured against it. Why not a column for A as well? Because then the three dummy columns would always add up to 1, exactly the intercept’s column, and X^\top X would have no inverse (Lesson 4): the model couldn’t tell the intercept from the catalysts. With k categories, you always get k - 1 dummies.
In a model without interactions, each dummy coefficient shifts the whole fitted surface up or down:

fit_add <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst, data = study)
coef(fit_add)
#>    (Intercept)         temp_C  residence_min feed_water_ppm      catalystB 
#>   -45.42220294     0.53924571     0.35844052    -0.06217914     3.60735634 
#>      catalystC 
#>    -1.94985024

For runs with the same temperature, residence time and water, catalyst B makes 3.6 points more than A, and C makes 1.9 points less. Here are the three catalysts’ fitted lines against temperature, at 50 minutes and 200 ppm of water. Each point is a run, with its yield adjusted to those same conditions using the model’s coefficients, so that only the temperature and the catalyst differ:

b <- coef(fit_add)
study |>
  mutate(adjusted = yield_pct - b["residence_min"] * (residence_min - 50) - b["feed_water_ppm"] * (feed_water_ppm - 200)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = temp_C, y = adjusted, color = catalyst)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(data = expand.grid(temp_C = c(168, 207), catalyst = c("A", "B", "C"), residence_min = 50, feed_water_ppm = 200) |>
              mutate(adjusted = predict(fit_add, pick(everything()))), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cat_colors) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Yield at 50 min and 200 ppm (%)", color = "Catalyst") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Three parallel lines: the model says each catalyst responds to temperature in exactly the same way, and only their heights differ. Keep an eye on the green points at the high-temperature end, though.









Your turn. Predict the yield of a catalyst B run and a catalyst C run, both at 190 °C, 50 minutes and 200 ppm, with fit_add. How far apart are they?









The C run is the second row, so p[2] - p[1] is C minus B.


runs <- tibble(temp_C = 190, residence_min = 50, feed_water_ppm = 200, catalyst = c("B", "C"))
p <- predict(fit_add, newdata = runs)
p[2] - p[1]
C makes 5.56 points less than B: -1.95 - 3.61, the difference of their two dummy coefficients. In this model, that’s true at every temperature, residence time and water content, because the lines are parallel.

title: Categorical regressors and interactions
text:
Choosing the baseline
R picks the baseline alphabetically, which is rarely the most useful choice. If B is the plant’s standard catalyst, you’d want every other catalyst compared with B. relevel() sets the reference level of a factor:

study_b <- mutate(study, catalyst = relevel(factor(catalyst), ref = "B"))
coef(lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst, data = study_b))
#>    (Intercept)         temp_C  residence_min feed_water_ppm      catalystA 
#>   -41.81484661     0.53924571     0.35844052    -0.06217914    -3.60735634 
#>      catalystC 
#>    -5.55720658

Now the dummies are for A and C, and each coefficient is a difference from B. Notice what didn’t change: the other coefficients, the fitted values, the residuals, R^2. Changing the baseline only changes which comparisons the coefficients report. It’s the same model, described from a different starting point.
Your turn. With B as the baseline, how does catalyst C compare?









The new reference level is "B".


study_b <- mutate(study, catalyst = relevel(factor(catalyst), ref = "B"))
fit_b <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst, data = study_b)
coef(fit_b)["catalystC"]
−5.56, the same B-against-C difference you predicted, now read straight off the coefficient table, with its own standard error and t-test.

title: Categorical regressors and interactions
text:
Sum-to-zero contrasts
Dummy coding, which R calls treatment contrasts, is one way of turning a category into columns. Another popular one is sum-to-zero contrasts (or effect coding). With them, each coefficient is a category’s difference from the average of all the categories, rather than from a baseline, and the deviations add up to zero:

fit_sum <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst, data = study,
              contrasts = list(catalyst = "contr.sum"))
coef(fit_sum)
#>    (Intercept)         temp_C  residence_min feed_water_ppm      catalyst1 
#>   -44.86970091     0.53924571     0.35844052    -0.06217914    -0.55250203 
#>      catalyst2 
#>     3.05485431

catalyst1 is A’s deviation from the average catalyst, −0.55, and catalyst2 is B’s, +3.05. There’s no coefficient for C, because its deviation is whatever makes the three add up to zero. Again, the fit itself is identical. Sum-to-zero contrasts are handy when no category is a natural baseline, and in designed experiments, where they make the main effects easier to interpret (Lesson 14).
Your turn. Work out catalyst C’s deviation from the average catalyst.









The three deviations add up to zero, so C’s is minus the sum of the other two: -(b["catalyst1"] + b["catalyst2"]).


fit_sum <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst, data = study,
              contrasts = list(catalyst = "contr.sum"))
b <- coef(fit_sum)
-(b["catalyst1"] + b["catalyst2"])
−2.50. So B is 3.05 above the average catalyst, A is 0.55 below it, and C 2.50 below. The differences between catalysts are the same as with dummy coding: B − C = 3.05 - (-2.50) = 5.56.

title: Categorical regressors and interactions
text:
Interactions
Back to those green points: catalyst C’s runs seem to rise more steeply with temperature than the others. An additive model can’t capture that, because its lines are parallel by construction. An interaction lets them differ. In R’s formula language, temp_C * catalyst means “temperature, catalyst, and their interaction”, temp_C:catalyst:

fit_int <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C * catalyst + residence_min + feed_water_ppm, data = study)
summary(fit_int)$coefficients
#>                      Estimate   Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
#> (Intercept)      -36.62072717  8.972596445 -4.081397 8.421438e-05
#> temp_C             0.49475944  0.046949673 10.538081 1.860372e-18
#> catalystB         29.01782771 12.460312910  2.328820 2.166255e-02
#> catalystC        -53.69976607 12.508506320 -4.293060 3.763438e-05
#> residence_min      0.35726401  0.026643451 13.409074 4.901465e-25
#> feed_water_ppm    -0.06402694  0.007557655 -8.471799 1.075018e-13
#> temp_C:catalystB  -0.13368561  0.066153522 -2.020839 4.568189e-02
#> temp_C:catalystC   0.27846031  0.067034269  4.153999 6.407346e-05

The interaction terms are new columns of the design matrix: the temperature multiplied by each dummy. For a catalyst A run, both are zero. For a C run, temp_C:catalystC equals its temperature. So the model is really three lines with their own slopes:

\begin{aligned}
\text{A:}\quad & \text{slope} = b_{\text{temp}} = 0.495 \\
\text{B:}\quad & \text{slope} = b_{\text{temp}} + b_{\text{temp:B}} = 0.495 - 0.134 = 0.361 \\
\text{C:}\quad & \text{slope} = b_{\text{temp}} + b_{\text{temp:C}} = 0.495 + 0.278 = 0.773
\end{aligned}

Each interaction coefficient is a difference in slopes: catalyst C gains 0.28 points per degree more than A does. Here are the three lines:

b <- coef(fit_int)
study |>
  mutate(adjusted = yield_pct - b["residence_min"] * (residence_min - 50) - b["feed_water_ppm"] * (feed_water_ppm - 200)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = temp_C, y = adjusted, color = catalyst)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(data = expand.grid(temp_C = c(168, 207), catalyst = c("A", "B", "C"), residence_min = 50, feed_water_ppm = 200) |>
              mutate(adjusted = predict(fit_int, pick(everything()))), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cat_colors) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Yield at 50 min and 200 ppm (%)", color = "Catalyst") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Is the interaction real? It’s two coefficients, so test them together, with a partial F-test of the additive model against the interaction model:

anova(fit_add, fit_int)
#> Analysis of Variance Table
#> 
#> Model 1: yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst
#> Model 2: yield_pct ~ temp_C * catalyst + residence_min + feed_water_ppm
#>   Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
#> 1    114 1895.3                                  
#> 2    112 1398.6  2    496.73 19.889 4.059e-08 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

F = 19.9 on 2 and 112 degrees of freedom: very clear evidence that the catalysts respond differently to temperature. C is the most temperature-sensitive, which a chemist might explain by a higher activation energy.
And B’s slope, 0.36, flatter than A’s with p = 0.046? That’s borderline, and it’s worth a little suspicion. Can you spot the lonely blue point, far to the left of all the others? Lesson 10 will show you that this single run is behind it.
Two rules for interactions:

Keep the main effects. If a model has temp_C:catalyst, it should also have temp_C and catalyst on their own. The * shorthand does this for you. An interaction without its main effects forces strange constraints on the lines, like making them all cross at 0 °C.
Don’t interpret a main effect alone. In this model, “the effect of temperature” isn’t one number any more: it depends on the catalyst. And the catalystC coefficient, −53.7, isn’t “C against A”: it’s C against A at 0 °C, where the C line would be if you extended it that far. Nobody runs this reactor at 0 °C. The next section fixes that.

Your turn. Compute catalyst C’s temperature slope from the interaction model’s coefficients.









Add C’s interaction coefficient, named "temp_C:catalystC", to the baseline slope.


b <- coef(fit_int)
unname(b["temp_C"] + b["temp_C:catalystC"])
0.77 points per degree for catalyst C, against 0.49 for A. Over the study’s 35-degree range, that’s a difference of almost 10 points.

title: Categorical regressors and interactions
text:
Centering
The fix for meaningless main effects is to center the numerical predictor: subtract a sensible reference value, so that “0” means something. The temperature set points ran from 170 to 205 °C, and 185 °C is the plant’s usual setting, so subtract 185:

study_c <- mutate(study, temp_c = temp_C - 185)
fit_c <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_c * catalyst + residence_min + feed_water_ppm, data = study_c)
summary(fit_c)$coefficients
#>                     Estimate  Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
#> (Intercept)      54.90976995 1.857455738 29.561819 1.008326e-54
#> temp_c            0.49475944 0.046949673 10.538081 1.860372e-18
#> catalystB         4.28598922 0.833072640  5.144797 1.151554e-06
#> catalystC        -2.18460788 0.806964011 -2.707194 7.848912e-03
#> residence_min     0.35726401 0.026643451 13.409074 4.901465e-25
#> feed_water_ppm   -0.06402694 0.007557655 -8.471799 1.075018e-13
#> temp_c:catalystB -0.13368561 0.066153522 -2.020839 4.568189e-02
#> temp_c:catalystC  0.27846031 0.067034269  4.153999 6.407346e-05

Look at what changed, and what didn’t:

The catalyst coefficients now compare the catalysts at 185 °C: B makes 4.3 points more than A there, and C 2.2 points less. Those are numbers you can use.
The interaction coefficients, the residence and water coefficients, the residuals and the fit are all exactly the same. Centering is just a change of reference point.
The standard errors of the catalyst coefficients shrank from about 12.5 to 0.8! An estimate at 0 °C, far outside the data, was hopelessly uncertain. An estimate at 185 °C, in the middle of the data, isn’t. Centering also removes most of the correlation between a dummy and its interaction column, from 0.997 to 0.04: that’s the multicollinearity you’ll meet properly in Lesson 11.

Center at a value that means something to the reader: the usual set point, the mean, or a round number in the middle of the data.
Your turn. Fit the centered interaction model, and report catalyst B’s advantage over A at 185 °C.









Center at the usual set point: temp_C - 185.


study_c <- mutate(study, temp_c = temp_C - 185)
fit_c <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_c * catalyst + residence_min + feed_water_ppm, data = study_c)
coef(fit_c)["catalystB"]
4.29 points at 185 °C, with a standard error of only 0.83. Before centering, the same coefficient was 29.0 ± 12.5: B’s advantage at 0 °C.

title: Categorical regressors and interactions
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The best catalyst depends on the temperature. Use the interaction model to predict the yield of each catalyst at 175 °C and at 205 °C, with 50 minutes of residence and 200 ppm of water. Which catalyst would you choose at each temperature?









predict(fit_int, newdata = grid) gives one prediction per row of the grid.


grid <- expand.grid(temp_C = c(175, 205), catalyst = c("A", "B", "C"),
                    residence_min = 50, feed_water_ppm = 200)
grid$predicted <- predict(fit_int, newdata = grid)
grid
At 175 °C, B is the clear winner: 60.6% against 55.0% for A and 50.1% for C. At 205 °C, the order flips: C makes 73.2%, B 71.5% and A 69.9%. When lines cross like this, there’s no single “best catalyst”, and an additive model would have hidden that. (205 °C is right at the top edge of the study, though. Before switching the plant to C at 205 °C, you’d want more runs up there, and a look at the purity, which falls with temperature.)




Challenge 2 · Two numbers interacting. Interactions between two numerical predictors work the same way: residence_min * feed_water_ppm adds their product as a column, and its coefficient says how much the residence slope changes per ppm of water. Maybe wet feed makes extra residence time more valuable? Add that interaction to fit_int and test it.









The other half of the interaction is feed_water_ppm.


fit_rw <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C * catalyst + residence_min * feed_water_ppm, data = study)
anova(fit_int, fit_rw)
F = 0.17, p = 0.68. No evidence that the residence-time effect depends on the water content: an extra minute seems to be worth the same whatever the feed. Not every interaction you can imagine is there, and testing them all is fishing (Lesson 6). Test the ones that the chemistry suggests.

title: Categorical regressors and interactions
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why does a category with three values get only two dummy columns?

To save memory
Because three dummies would always add up to the intercept’s column of 1s, so the model couldn’t be fitted
Because R ignores the least common category


With the intercept and k dummies, X^\top X has no inverse. Dropping one category, the baseline, fixes it.



2. You change the baseline catalyst from A to B. What changes?

The fitted values and R^2
Only which comparisons the catalyst coefficients report
The coefficients of temperature and residence time


It’s the same model with a different starting point: the fit, residuals and other coefficients are unchanged.



3. In a model with temperature and catalyst but no interaction, the fitted lines of yield against temperature for the three catalysts are…

parallel
all through the origin
free to have any slopes


Without an interaction, the catalyst only shifts the line up or down, so all three share the temperature slope.



4. The coefficient of temp_C:catalystC is 0.28. What does it mean?

Catalyst C makes 0.28 points more yield than A
Catalyst C’s yield rises 0.28 points per degree faster than catalyst A’s
Temperature explains 28% of catalyst C’s yield


An interaction coefficient between a numerical predictor and a dummy is a difference in slopes.



5. In the uncentered interaction model, the catalystC coefficient is −53.7. Why so extreme?

Catalyst C ruins the reaction
It’s the difference between C and A at 0 °C, far outside the data
It’s a rounding error


With an interaction, a main effect is the effect where the other predictor is zero. Centering the temperature at 185 °C turns it into a useful comparison.



6. What does centering the temperature change in the interaction model?

The fitted values and residuals
The interaction coefficients
The meaning (and standard errors) of the catalyst coefficients and the intercept


Centering moves the reference point. The fit and the interaction coefficients stay the same, while the main effects become comparisons at the new reference point.

title: Categorical regressors and interactions
text:
Wrap-up
Your models can now handle categories and nuance! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Dummy variables: a category with k values becomes k - 1 columns of 0s and 1s. Each coefficient compares a category with the baseline.
The baseline is the first level alphabetically, unless you relevel(). Changing it changes the comparisons, not the model.
Sum-to-zero contrasts (contr.sum) compare each category with the average category instead.
Interactions: x * group gives each group its own slope. Each interaction coefficient is a difference in slopes. Test interactions as a group, with a partial F-test.
Rules: keep the main effects with their interaction, and don’t interpret a main effect on its own when there’s an interaction.
Centering a numerical predictor makes the main effects comparisons at a sensible value, and shrinks their standard errors, without changing the fit.
Numerical interactions (x1 * x2) let one slope change steadily with another predictor.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download process_study.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Separate fits. Fit yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm separately for each catalyst (try dplyr::group_by() with group_modify(), or a loop). Compare the three temperature slopes with the interaction model’s. Why are they a little different? (Hint: the separate fits also give each catalyst its own residence and water slopes.)
The emmeans package. Install it and run emmeans::emtrends(fit_int, ~ catalyst, var = "temp_C"). It reports each catalyst’s temperature slope with a confidence interval. Then try emmeans::emmeans(fit_int, pairwise ~ catalyst, at = list(temp_C = 185)) for the catalyst comparisons at 185 °C.
Reactor and supplier. Add reactor to the model. Does the reactor matter? Then try the supplier instead of the feed water. Why shouldn’t you put both the supplier and the water in, and interpret both?
Interaction plots for data. Draw the raw yields against temperature with geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) for each catalyst. How does it compare with this lesson’s adjusted plot, and why?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Dummy (indicator) variable

A column of 0s and 1s that marks which observations belong to one category.

Baseline (reference) category

The category without a dummy column. The other categories’ coefficients are differences from it.

Treatment contrasts

R’s default coding of a category: dummy variables compared with a baseline.

Sum-to-zero contrasts

A coding in which each coefficient is a category’s difference from the average of all the categories.

Interaction

A term that lets one predictor’s effect depend on the value of another, built from the product of their columns.

Main effect

A predictor’s own term in a model. With an interaction present, it’s the predictor’s effect where the other predictor equals zero.

Hierarchy (marginality) principle

Keep a predictor’s main effect in the model whenever one of its interactions is in it.

Centering

Subtracting a reference value from a numerical predictor, so that zero means something and the main effects become comparisons at that value.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 501, Lesson 8: Categorical Predictors. Dummy variables and interactions, with many worked examples.
Andrew Gelman, Jennifer Hill and Aki Vehtari, Regression and Other Stories, sections 10.3 and 12.2. Interactions, and why centering makes them easier to read.
UCLA’s statistical consulting group, “R library contrast coding systems for categorical variables”. A tour of the many ways to code a category, with R code for each.

title: Multiple linear regression
text:
Module 2 · Lesson 5 of 15 Week 35 of 160 About 5–7 hours
A yield doesn’t depend on one thing. Temperature, residence time, the feed, the catalyst and a dozen other things all push it around at once. Simple regression looks at one of them and lumps the rest into the error. Multiple regression looks at several together, and that changes what you can learn, sometimes completely. In this lesson, a relationship that’s invisible in a scatterplot turns out to cost the plant six points of yield.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Multiple linear regression
text:
The process study
In April and May, the process-development team ran 120 batches on the two pilot reactors, to learn how the process responds. They varied the temperature and residence time on purpose, rotated three catalysts, and recorded much more than in March:

study <- read_csv("data/process_study.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(study)
#> Rows: 120
#> Columns: 19

#> $ purity_pct     <dbl> 98.69, 98.46, 99.44, 98.73, 99.25, 99.32, 99.58, 98.55,…
#> $ notes          <chr> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, "Sample tak…

Each row is a run. Most columns explain themselves, and a few are new:







Column
What it is




catalyst, catalyst_age
the catalyst charge in the reactor (A, B or C), and how many runs that charge has done, from 1 to 10


lot_id, supplier
the feed lot, and who supplied it. Kestrel is the supplier whose lots were wet in Module 1

the water content of the feed, measured by the lab for every run
