  largest_imputed = max(unlist(imp$imp$analyzer_gL)))
Both are 50.9 g/L. No imputed value can ever exceed the largest observed one, because PMM only borrows observed values.




Your turn. Impute with method = "norm" instead, and pool the mean again.









The method’s name goes in quotes: method = "norm".


imp <- mice(d, m = 5, method = "norm", seed = 2026, printFlag = FALSE)
summary(pool(with(imp, lm(analyzer_gL ~ 1))))
About 39.6 g/L, right on the lab’s true mean. PMM is an excellent default, because it keeps imputations realistic. But when the missing values lie beyond the observed ones, as they do here, a model-based method like norm is the better choice.




Your turn. Pool the regression on temperature and flow again, this time with norm imputations. Has the temperature slope recovered?









Inside with(), write the analysis as you would on a complete dataset: lm(analyzer_gL ~ temp_C + flow_Lmin).


imp <- mice(d, m = 5, method = "norm", seed = 2026, printFlag = FALSE)
fit <- with(imp, lm(analyzer_gL ~ temp_C + flow_Lmin))
summary(pool(fit))
About 0.64 g/L per °C, up from PMM’s 0.57, and in line with the complete-case regression from the last lesson. Remember that the complete cases were already fine for this slope, because the missingness depends on the temperature, which is in the model. The real gain from imputation here is the overall mean.

title: Missing data II: multiple imputation
text:
How many imputations?
The classic advice was that 5 imputations are enough, and for the estimates themselves they often are. But standard errors and p-values need more to be stable from one run to the next. A common modern rule of thumb is to use at least as many imputations as the percentage of incomplete cases. Here, 26% of the samples are incomplete, so about 25 imputations would be a good choice. With modern computers, that’s rarely a problem: 20 imputations of this dataset take only moments.
A few more choices matter more than the number of imputations:

Include every variable in your analysis in the imputation model, the outcome too. Leaving one out tells mice that it’s unrelated to the missing values, and that weakens its relationships in the completed data.
Add auxiliary variables: variables that aren’t in your analysis but that predict the missing values, or predict which values are missing. They make the imputations both more accurate and less uncertain. You’ll try one in the challenge round.
Leave out ID columns and anything else that’s meaningless as a predictor, like sample_id.

title: Missing data II: multiple imputation
section: What if the data are MNAR?
text:
What if the data are MNAR?
Everything so far assumed that the readings are missing at random, given the temperature and the flow. What if they aren’t? Suppose that the analyzer also tends to fail at high concentrations, regardless of the temperature. Then the missing readings would be even higher than MAR predicts, and no amount of data could reveal it.
You can’t test that assumption, but you can test how much it matters. That’s a sensitivity analysis. The simplest kind is a delta adjustment: shift every imputed value by some amount \delta, and see how the conclusions change. mice’s post argument runs a line of code after each imputation step, so it can add \delta:

post <- make.post(d)
post["analyzer_gL"] <- "imp[[j]][, i] <- imp[[j]][, i] + 4"    # add 4 g/L to each imputed reading
imp_mnar <- mice(d, m = 5, method = "norm", seed = 2026, printFlag = FALSE, post = post)
summary(pool(with(imp_mnar, lm(analyzer_gL ~ 1))))
#>          term estimate std.error statistic       df      p.value
#> 1 (Intercept) 40.55281 0.7091857  57.18221 114.7593 3.521603e-86

If the missing readings were 4 g/L higher than MAR predicts, the mean would be about 40.6 g/L instead of 39.6. Is a shift of 4 g/L plausible? That’s a question for the analyzer’s engineers, not for the data. A good report shows the results for a range of \delta values, and lets the reader see where the conclusions would change.

title: Missing data II: multiple imputation
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · An auxiliary variable. Suppose that the lab’s results were available for this study. They aren’t part of the analysis, but they predict the analyzer readings extremely well. Include lab_gL in the imputation, with norm, and pool the mean of the analyzer readings. Compare the fraction of missing information, fmi, with the version without it.









Add the lab’s column, lab_gL, to the selection.


d_aux <- select(analyzer, temp_C, flow_Lmin, analyzer_gL, lab_gL)
imp <- mice(d_aux, m = 5, method = "norm", seed = 2026, printFlag = FALSE)
pool(with(imp, lm(analyzer_gL ~ 1)))$pooled[, c("estimate", "fmi")]
The pooled mean is about 39.6 g/L, and the fraction of missing information drops to around 0.02, from about 0.12 without the lab’s results. With a variable that predicts the missing readings so well, the imputations hardly need to guess. In real studies, auxiliary variables are rarely this good, but even modest ones help.




Challenge 2 · A sensitivity table. Compute the pooled mean concentration for \delta = 0, 2 and 4 g/L, with norm imputations. Complete the function, and sapply() does the rest.









Pass the post object that the function just built: post = post.


pooled_mean <- function(delta) {
  post <- make.post(d)
  post["analyzer_gL"] <- paste("imp[[j]][, i] <- imp[[j]][, i] +", delta)
  imp <- mice(d, m = 5, method = "norm", seed = 2026, printFlag = FALSE, post = post)
  summary(pool(with(imp, lm(analyzer_gL ~ 1))))$estimate
}
sapply(c(0, 2, 4), pooled_mean)
About 39.6, 40.1 and 40.6 g/L. Each extra 2 g/L of \delta raises the mean by about 0.45 g/L, because 22.5% of the readings are imputed (0.225 × 2 = 0.45). That’s a simple, honest way to report what the MAR assumption is worth.

title: Missing data II: multiple imputation
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why does multiple imputation create several completed datasets, instead of one?

So that the disagreement between them can measure the uncertainty caused by the missing values
Because one dataset would be too small
To make the analysis run faster


A single imputation hides the uncertainty. The spread between several imputations shows it, and Rubin’s rules add it to the standard error.



2. In Rubin’s rules, what does the between-imputation variance B measure?

The sampling uncertainty you’d have without any missing data
How much the estimates from the different imputations disagree
The number of missing values


W is the ordinary sampling uncertainty, and B is the extra uncertainty from the missing data. The total is T = W + (1 + 1/m)B.



3. What’s the order of the three steps in a mice analysis?

mice() to impute, with() to analyze, pool() to combine
pool(), then mice(), then with()
with(), then pool(), then mice()


Impute, analyze, pool, in that order.



4. Why did predictive mean matching underestimate the mean concentration in the analyzer study?

Because it ignores the temperature
Because it only borrows observed values, and the missing readings were higher than any observed one
Because 5 imputations are too few


PMM can’t impute beyond the observed range. When the missing values lie beyond it, a method that extrapolates, like norm, is better.



5. Which of these improves an imputation model?

Leaving out the analysis’s outcome variable
Including the sample ID as a predictor
Adding auxiliary variables that predict the missing values


Include the analysis variables, outcome and all, plus any good auxiliary variables. Leave out IDs.



6. What does a delta-adjustment sensitivity analysis show?

Whether the data are MAR
How much the results would change if the missing values differed from the MAR predictions by \delta
The best value of \delta for the analysis


The MAR assumption can’t be tested from the data, but a sensitivity analysis shows how much the conclusions depend on it.

title: Missing data II: multiple imputation
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve learned the most powerful general tool for missing data! Here’s the summary:

The idea: impute several times, analyze each completed dataset, and pool, so that the uncertainty from the missing values is kept, not hidden.
mice: mice(data, m, method, seed), then with(imp, analysis), then summary(pool(fit)). complete() gives the completed datasets.
Rubin’s rules: average the estimates, and add the within-imputation variance W to the between-imputation variance B: T = W + (1 + 1/m)B. The fraction of missing information shows how much the gaps matter.
Diagnostics: plot(imp) for convergence, and plots of imputed against observed values. PMM is realistic but can’t extrapolate. norm can.
Choices: use more imputations than the percentage of incomplete cases, include all the analysis variables plus auxiliary ones, and leave out IDs.
Sensitivity: shift the imputations by \delta with post, and report how the conclusions change.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Install mice with install.packages("mice"), and download analyzer_study.csv.

mice’s own plots. Try densityplot(imp) and stripplot(imp) on PMM and norm imputations. Can you see PMM’s ceiling?
The rule of thumb. Pool the mean with m = 5, m = 25 and m = 100, each with several different seeds. How much do the estimate and its standard error move between seeds, for each m?
Imputation versus truth. For the 36 missing readings, compare the mean of the imputed values (from complete(imp, "long")) with the lab’s values for the same samples. How close are PMM and norm?
A full sensitivity analysis. Extend Challenge 2 to \delta from −4 to 8 g/L, and plot the pooled mean against \delta, with error bars of ±1.96 standard errors.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Multiple imputation

Filling in each missing value several times, analyzing every completed dataset, and pooling the results.

Chained equations (mice)

Imputing one variable at a time, each from all the others, and cycling round until the imputations settle.

Predictive mean matching (PMM)

Imputing a value by borrowing the observed value of a case with a similar prediction.

Rubin’s rules

The formulas that pool estimates and their variances across imputations: T = W + (1 + 1/m)B.

Fraction of missing information (fmi)

The share of an estimate’s uncertainty that’s caused by the missing data.

Auxiliary variable

A variable that’s not in the analysis, but that helps to predict the missing values.

Sensitivity analysis

Checking how much the conclusions change under different assumptions, for example a delta adjustment for MNAR data.











NoteWant to read more?






Stef van Buuren, Flexible Imputation of Missing Data, chapters 2 to 6. The author of mice explains multiple imputation, Rubin’s rules, the imputation methods and diagnostics.
Ian White, Patrick Royston and Angela Wood, “Multiple imputation using chained equations: Issues and guidance for practice”, Statistics in Medicine (2011). A very practical guide, and the source of the rule of thumb for m.

title: Data quality and validation
text:
Module 1 · Lesson 11 of 14 Week 26 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Last lesson, you fixed how things were written: batch codes, test names and times. This lesson asks a harder question: is the data right? Are there results typed in twice? Values that can’t be true? Numbers hiding inside text? By the end, you’ll have turned the lab’s messy spreadsheet into a table that you can trust, and you’ll be able to say exactly what you changed, and why.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Data quality and validation
text:
Clean names
Lesson 1 promised a function that tidies messy column names. It’s clean_names(), from the janitor package. It makes every name lower case, replaces spaces and symbols with underscores, and spells out % and #:

library(janitor)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'janitor'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     chisq.test, fisher.test
messy <- tibble(`Batch ID` = 1, `Temp (°C)` = 2, `Yield %` = 3, pressureBar = 4, `Batch ID ` = 5)
names(clean_names(messy))
#> [1] "batch_id"      "temp_c"        "yield_percent" "pressure_bar" 
#> [5] "batch_id_2"

Notice that pressureBar became pressure_bar, and the second Batch ID became batch_id_2, so that the names stay unique. Automatic cleaning is a great start, but always look at the result. Here are the cooling-water names from Lesson 9:

cw <- read_csv2("data/cooling_water_eu.csv", locale = locale(encoding = "latin1"), show_col_types = FALSE)
names(clean_names(cw))
#> [1] "sample"              "date"                "temperature_c"      
#> [4] "conductivity_m_s_cm" "p_h"

The µ became an m (so microsiemens now look like millisiemens, a thousand times bigger!), and pH was split into p_h. janitor even warns you about the µ. A quick rename() fixes both.









Your turn. Clean the cooling-water names, then rename the two that went wrong: call them conductivity_uS_cm and ph.









rename() takes new_name = old_name. The old names are the ones clean_names() produced: conductivity_m_s_cm and p_h.


read_csv2("data/cooling_water_eu.csv", locale = locale(encoding = "latin1"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  clean_names() |>
  rename(conductivity_uS_cm = conductivity_m_s_cm, ph = p_h) |>
  names()

title: Data quality and validation
text:
Numbers hiding in text
Here’s last lesson’s work on the raw lab file, in one step: clean batch codes, analytes and times. The value column is still text, though, because not every value is a number:

raw <- read_csv("data/lab_results_raw.csv", col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))
lab_raw <- raw |>
  mutate(batch_id = str_c("B", str_pad(str_extract(batch, "\\d+"), 2, pad = "0")),
         analyte = case_when(str_detect(test, regex("pur", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "purity",
                             str_detect(test, regex("water|h2o", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "water",
                             str_detect(test, regex("colou?r|apha", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "color"),
         measured_at = parse_date_time(measured, orders = c("Ymd HM", "dmY HM", "bdY IMp"), tz = "UTC")) |>
  select(batch_id, analyte, measured_at, value, instrument, analyst)

lab_raw |>
  filter(is.na(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(value)))) |>
  count(value, sort = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 23 × 2
#>    value       n
#>    <chr>   <int>
#>  1 154 ppm     3
#>  2 99,9        2
#>  3 <20         2
#>  4 n/a         2
#>  5 -           1
#>  6 174 ppm     1
#>  7 201 ppm     1
#>  8 202 ppm     1
#>  9 217 ppm     1
#> 10 221 ppm     1
#> # ℹ 13 more rows

as.numeric() turns anything that isn’t a plain number into NA, so this lists every troublemaker: units typed into the cell (154 ppm), decimal commas (99,9), values below the detection limit (<20), and three different ways of saying “missing” (n/a, - and a blank cell, which readr has already made NA).
readr’s parse_number() looks like the perfect tool, because it ignores any text around a number. But watch what it does with the tricky ones:

parse_number(c("154 ppm", "98,83", "<20", "n/a"))
#> Warning: 1 parsing failure.
#> row col expected actual
#>   4  -- a number    n/a
#> [1]  154 9883   20   NA
#> attr(,"problems")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>     row   col expected actual
#>   <int> <int> <chr>    <chr> 
#> 1     4    NA a number n/a

154 ppm is fine. But 98,83 became 9,883, because the comma was taken for a thousands separator, just like the pH of 782 in Lesson 9. <20 became 20, which is wrong: it means less than 20. And n/a gave a parsing failure. Each one needs handling on purpose: replace the commas first, tell parse_number() which strings mean missing, and keep a note of the values that were below the detection limit.
Values below the detection limit. The lab’s water titrator can’t measure below 20 ppm, so it reports <20. The true value is somewhere between 0 and 20. That’s a censored value: you know a range, not a number. Turning it into NA throws away real information (we know the water was low), and using 20 overstates it. A common convention, and the one the plant’s database uses, is half the limit: 10 ppm. Whichever you choose, keep a below_lod column, so that the choice can be revisited, and say what you did in your report.
Your turn. Parse the values. Replace each decimal comma with a point first, then count the missing values, and find the highest purity.









Replace a comma with a point: str_replace(value, ",", ".").


lab_raw |>
  mutate(value = parse_number(str_replace(value, ",", "."), na = c("", "NA", "n/a", "-"))) |>
  summarise(missing = sum(is.na(value)),
            max_purity = max(value[analyte == "purity"], na.rm = TRUE))
Four missing values, and a highest purity of 101.2%. A purity above 100% is impossible, so that’s a problem for the next steps.

title: Data quality and validation
text:
Duplicates and repeats
A duplicate is the same observation recorded twice, usually by accident. janitor’s get_dupes() shows the rows that share the same values in the columns you name:

get_dupes(lab_raw, batch_id, analyte, measured_at)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   batch_id analyte measured_at         dupe_count value instrument analyst
#>   <chr>    <chr>   <dttm>                   <int> <chr> <chr>      <chr>  
#> 1 B02      color   2026-03-02 15:20:00          2 13    COL-1      A1     
#> 2 B02      color   2026-03-02 15:20:00          2 13    COL-1      A1     
#> 3 B30      purity  2026-03-17 04:22:00          2 101.2 GC-1       A2     
#> 4 B30      purity  2026-03-17 04:22:00          2 101.2 GC-1       A2     
#> 5 B32      water   2026-03-18 03:25:00          2 330   KF-1       A3     
#> 6 B32      water   2026-03-18 03:25:00          2 330   KF-1       A3

Three results were typed in twice. But be careful: not every repeated batch and analyte is a mistake. Six batches had their purity re-tested, and those are genuine, separate measurements, taken at different times:

lab_raw |>
  distinct(batch_id, analyte, measured_at) |>
  count(batch_id, analyte) |>
  filter(n > 1)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   batch_id analyte     n
#>   <chr>    <chr>   <int>
#> 1 B19      purity      2
#> 2 B21      purity      2
#> 3 B25      purity      2
#> 4 B34      purity      2
#> 5 B35      purity      2
#> 6 B39      purity      2

That’s why the key matters. A result is identified by its batch, its analyte and its time, as you saw in Lesson 6. Two rows that agree on all three are duplicates. Two rows that differ only in time are a re-test, and both belong in the data.
One more trap: duplicates can hide behind messy spellings. B2 and B02 aren’t duplicates as text, but they’re the same batch. Always look for duplicates after standardizing the keys, as you just did.
Your turn. Remove the duplicates, keeping one row for each batch, analyte and time. How many rows are left?









List the three key columns: batch_id, analyte, measured_at. .keep_all = TRUE keeps the other columns too.


lab_raw |>
  distinct(batch_id, analyte, measured_at, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  nrow()
124 rows, exactly as many as the lab’s database holds.

title: Data quality and validation
text:
Validation rules
You can write down what “correct” means as a list of validation rules, and then check the data against all of them at once. That’s what the validate package is for. First, here’s the parsed, de-duplicated table:

lab <- lab_raw |>
  mutate(below_lod = str_detect(value, "^<") %in% TRUE,
         value = parse_number(str_replace(value, ",", "."), na = c("", "NA", "n/a", "-"))) |>
  distinct(batch_id, analyte, measured_at, .keep_all = TRUE)

validator() holds the rules, each one a condition that should be true for every row, and confront() checks the data against them:

library(validate)
rules <- validator(
  code_ok = grepl("^B[0-9]{2}$", batch_id),
  not_missing = !is.na(value),
  purity_max = if (analyte == "purity") value <= 100
)
out <- confront(lab, rules)
summary(out)[, 1:5]
#>          name items passes fails nNA
#> 1     code_ok   124    124     0   0
#> 2 not_missing   124    120     4   0
#> 3  purity_max   124    121     1   2

Every batch code is fine, four values are missing, and one purity is above 100%. (nNA counts the rows that couldn’t be checked: the two missing purities.) violating() pulls out the rows that broke a rule:

violating(lab, out["purity_max"])
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   batch_id analyte measured_at         value instrument analyst below_lod
#>   <chr>    <chr>   <dttm>              <dbl> <chr>      <chr>   <lgl>    
#> 1 B30      purity  2026-03-17 04:22:00  101. GC-1       A2      FALSE

Some rules span two tables. Every lab result must belong to a real batch, so this should return nothing:

batches <- read_csv("data/batches.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
anti_join(lab, batches, by = "batch_id")
#> # A tibble: 0 × 7
#> # ℹ 7 variables: batch_id <chr>, analyte <chr>, measured_at <dttm>,
#> #   value <dbl>, instrument <chr>, analyst <chr>, below_lod <lgl>

It doesn’t, which means that the batch codes were cleaned well. Remember B5 and B41, the orphans from Lesson 5? This is the check that catches them, before they’re loaded. A quick cross-table, with janitor’s tabyl(), checks something else that should hold: each analyte comes from the right instruments.

tabyl(lab, analyte, instrument)
#>  analyte COL-1 GC-1 GC-2 KF-1
#>    color    40    0    0    0
#>   purity     0   26   20    0
#>    water     0    0    0   38

Your turn. Add a rule that water contents can’t be negative, and find the row that breaks it.









Follow the pattern of the purity rule: if (analyte == "water") value >= 0.


rules <- validator(
  purity_max = if (analyte == "purity") value <= 100,
  water_min = if (analyte == "water") value >= 0
)
out <- confront(lab, rules)
violating(lab, out["water_min"])
B25’s water content is −15 ppm. Most likely, someone typed a minus sign by mistake.

title: Data quality and validation
text:
Outliers: errors or discoveries?
An outlier is a value far from the rest. It might be an error, or it might be the most interesting thing in your data! There are three common ways to flag them:

Range checks use what’s physically possible. The reactors can’t reach 999.9 °C, so the sensor log’s reading from Lesson 3 is a glitch:


sensor <- read_csv("data/sensor_log.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
sensor$R1_temp_C[sensor$R1_temp_C > 300]
#> [1] 999.9


The IQR rule flags values more than 1.5 interquartile ranges below the first quartile, or above the third. It’s the rule that a boxplot uses to draw its separate points, and boxplot.stats(x)$out lists them.
Z-scores, the distance from the mean in standard deviations, flag values beyond 3 or so. But a big outlier inflates the standard deviation itself, so it can hide behind its own z-score. The IQR rule is more robust.

A flag is a question, not a verdict. Before you change or delete anything, look at the context.
Your turn. Flag the water results outside the IQR fences.









The upper fence is the third quartile plus the fence: q[2] + fence.


water <- lab |> filter(analyte == "water", !is.na(value))
q <- quantile(water$value, c(0.25, 0.75))
fence <- 1.5 * (q[2] - q[1])
water |>
  filter(value < q[1] - fence | value > q[2] + fence) |>
  select(batch_id, value, below_lod)
Six flags, but look closer. B18, B19 and B32 used Kestrel’s wet lots (Lesson 5), so their high water is real, and it’s the most important finding in the whole dataset! B16 and B28 are the two results below the detection limit: real, just low. Only B25’s −15 ppm is an error. Deleting all six “outliers” would have thrown away the discovery.

title: Data quality and validation
text:
Writing it all down
Every cleaning step is a decision, and decisions should be written down. Three habits make cleaning trustworthy:

Never edit the raw data. It stays in data-raw/, exactly as you received it. Every change happens in a script, so it can be re-run, and checked, by anyone.
Keep a cleaning log. List each decision, the reason for it, and how many rows it touched. It’s a small table, and it answers the questions that every reviewer asks.
End with assertions. An assertion is a check that stops the script, loudly, if the data breaks a rule. stopifnot() takes conditions, each with a message:


cleaning_log <- tribble(
  ~decision,                                     ~reason,                          ~rows,
  "Standardized the batch codes to B01-B40",     "82 spellings of 40 codes",       127,
  "Read decimal commas as decimal points",       "European number format",          10,
  "Removed units typed into the cells",          "values must be numbers",          12,
  "Recoded n/a, - and blanks as missing",        "three ways of saying missing",     4,
  "Set <20 ppm to 10 ppm, flagged in below_lod", "half the detection limit",         2,
  "Removed rows that were typed in twice",       "exact duplicates",                 3,
  "Set purity 101.2% and water -15 ppm to NA",   "physically impossible",            2
)
cleaning_log
#> # A tibble: 7 × 3
#>   decision                                    reason                        rows
#>   <chr>                                       <chr>                        <dbl>
#> 1 Standardized the batch codes to B01-B40     82 spellings of 40 codes       127
#> 2 Read decimal commas as decimal points       European number format          10
#> 3 Removed units typed into the cells          values must be numbers          12
#> 4 Recoded n/a, - and blanks as missing        three ways of saying missing     4
#> 5 Set <20 ppm to 10 ppm, flagged in below_lod half the detection limit         2
#> 6 Removed rows that were typed in twice       exact duplicates                 3
#> 7 Set purity 101.2% and water -15 ppm to NA   physically impossible            2


stopifnot(
  "one row per result" = !anyDuplicated(lab[c("batch_id", "analyte", "measured_at")]),
  "purity can't exceed 100%" = all(lab$value[lab$analyte == "purity"] <= 100, na.rm = TRUE)
)
#> Error:
#> ! purity can't exceed 100%

The first condition holds, but the second doesn’t, so the script stops right there, before the impossible purity can sneak into an analysis. Once the impossible values are dealt with, the same lines pass in silence.
One last trap, for when you compare your cleaned values with another source. Decimal numbers are stored in binary, so two ways of computing “the same” number can differ in the 15th decimal place. For example, parse_number() and as.numeric() don’t always agree exactly. So never compare decimals with ==. Use dplyr’s near() instead, which allows for a tiny tolerance:

0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3
#> [1] FALSE
near(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)
#> [1] TRUE

title: Data quality and validation
Data quality and validation
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does clean_names() turn the column name Yield % into?

yield_percent
Yield_%
yield


It makes names lower case, joins words with underscores, and spells out % as “percent”.



2. What does parse_number("98,83") return?

98.83
9883
NA


With the default locale, the comma is a thousands separator, so it’s dropped. Replace decimal commas with points first, or set the locale’s decimal_mark.



3. A water result is recorded as <20. What do you know about the true value?

It’s exactly 20
It’s somewhere between 0 and 20, below what the instrument can measure
Nothing: it’s a typing error


It’s a censored value. Keep a flag for it, and document how you handled it, for example by using half the detection limit.



4. Batch B19 has two purity results, measured at different times. What are they?

Duplicates, so delete one
A first test and a re-test: two genuine measurements
An error in the batch code


Duplicates agree on the whole key, including the time. Results at different times are separate measurements.



5. The IQR rule flags B18’s water content of 410 ppm. What should you do?

Delete it, because it’s an outlier
Replace it with the median
Look at its context first: B18 used a wet lot, so the value is real


A flag is a question, not a verdict. Here, the “outlier” is the most important finding in the data.



6. Why end a cleaning script with stopifnot() assertions?

So that the script stops loudly if the cleaned data ever breaks a rule
To make the script run faster
To delete the rows that break the rules


Assertions turn silent problems into loud ones, every time the script runs, even when new data arrives.

title: Data quality and validation
text:
Wrap-up
You can turn a messy spreadsheet into data you trust! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Names: clean_names() from janitor, followed by a careful look and a rename() where needed.
Values: find the non-numbers with as.numeric(), and parse them with care: decimal commas first, missing codes in na, and censored values flagged.
Detection limits: a value like <20 is censored. Keep a flag, choose a convention such as half the limit, and document it.
Duplicates: get_dupes() and distinct() on the full key, after standardizing it. Re-tests aren’t duplicates.
Rules: validator(), confront(), summary() and violating(), plus anti_join() checks across tables.
Outliers: range checks, the IQR rule and z-scores flag values. Context decides whether they’re errors.
Documentation: raw data stays read-only, a cleaning log records each decision, and stopifnot() assertions guard the result. Compare decimals with near(), not ==.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)






Finish the cleaning script. Complete R/02-clean-lab.R from the last lesson. Add every step from this lesson, end it with your assertions, and save the result as data/lab_results_clean.csv, with your cleaning log next to it as data/cleaning_log.csv. Then delete both files, re-run the script, and check that you get them back.
Plot the rules. plot(out) draws a bar for each validation rule, showing its passes, fails and missing values. Add rules for the color results (between 0 and 500 on the APHA scale) and for the measurement times (every test after its batch ended).
See the discovery. Join the cleaned water results to the batches, lots and suppliers, and draw a boxplot of water content by supplier. Kestrel Industrial’s lots should stand out.
Try the other conventions. Set the <20 values to 0, then to 20, and recompute the mean water content of the campaign. How much does the choice matter here?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Validation rule

A condition that every row of correct data should meet, like “purity is at most 100%”.

Duplicate

The same observation recorded more than once, usually by accident.

Re-test

A genuine second measurement of the same thing, at a different time. Not a duplicate.

Detection limit and censored value

The smallest amount an instrument can measure, and a value known only to lie beyond such a limit, like <20.

Outlier

A value far from the rest of the data. It may be an error, or a real and important result.

IQR rule

Flags values more than 1.5 interquartile ranges beyond the quartiles, as a boxplot does.

Referential integrity

Every foreign key value has a matching row in the table it points to.

Cleaning log

A record of each cleaning decision, its reason, and the number of rows it touched.

Assertion

A check that stops a script with an error if the data breaks a rule.











NoteWant to read more?






Mark van der Loo, The Data Validation Cookbook. A friendly, practical guide to the validate package.
The janitor documentation. clean_names(), get_dupes(), tabyl() and other small tools that make cleaning faster.
Mark van der Loo and Edwin de Jonge, Statistical Data Cleaning with Applications in R (Wiley, 2018). The textbook on the subject, if you want to go deeper.

title: Importing and exporting data
text:
Module 1 · Lesson 9 of 14 Week 24 of 160 About 5–7 hours
So far, your data has mostly arrived as tidy CSV files. Real data is rarely that polite. In the plant alone, the cooling-water contractor’s lab in Europe sends CSV files with commas for decimal points, the batch system exports Excel workbooks with a title on top, the online analyzer speaks JSON, the old chromatograph writes a fixed-width log, and the operator survey comes from SPSS. This lesson is a tour of the readers, and writers, for all of them.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Importing and exporting data
text:
Delimited files and locales
A delimited file is plain text, with one row per line and a special character between the values. CSV stands for comma-separated values, but in much of Europe the comma is the decimal mark, so files there put semicolons between the values instead. Here are the first lines of the cooling-water file:

readLines("data/cooling_water_eu.csv", n = 3, encoding = "latin1")
#> [1] "sample;date;temperature (°C);conductivity (µS/cm);pH"
#> [2] "CW-01;02.03.2026;21,7;805;7,82"                      
#> [3] "CW-02;03.03.2026;24,2;803;7,82"

Semicolons between the values, commas inside the numbers, and dates written day first. Read it with the wrong settings, and R does exactly what you asked, and the result is nonsense:

library(readr)
wrong <- read_delim("data/cooling_water_eu.csv", delim = ";",
                    locale = locale(encoding = "latin1"))
head(wrong, 3)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   sample date       `temperature (°C)` `conductivity (µS/cm)`    pH
#>   <chr>  <chr>                   <dbl>                  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 CW-01  02.03.2026                217                    805   782
#> 2 CW-02  03.03.2026                242                    803   782
#> 3 CW-03  04.03.2026                232                    828   761

A pH of 782! readr took each comma for a thousands separator, as in 1,000, and quietly dropped it. No error and no warning, just wrong numbers. That’s why you should always look at your data, and check that the values are plausible, right after importing it.
The fix is a locale, readr’s name for a file’s local conventions. read_csv2() is the shortcut for semicolons with decimal commas, and locale() sets the rest:

cw <- read_csv2("data/cooling_water_eu.csv",
                locale = locale(encoding = "latin1", date_format = "%d.%m.%Y"))
cw
#> # A tibble: 20 × 5
#>    sample date       `temperature (°C)` `conductivity (µS/cm)`    pH
#>    <chr>  <date>                  <dbl>                  <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1 CW-01  2026-03-02               21.7                    805  7.82
#>  2 CW-02  2026-03-03               24.2                    803  7.82
#>  3 CW-03  2026-03-04               23.2                    828  7.61
#>  4 CW-04  2026-03-05               24.7                    837  7.66
#>  5 CW-05  2026-03-06               22.8                    908  7.65
#>  6 CW-06  2026-03-07               24                      839  7.82
#>  7 CW-07  2026-03-08               26.2                    868  7.88
#>  8 CW-08  2026-03-09               22                      907  7.81
#>  9 CW-09  2026-03-10               24.8                    757  7.84
#> 10 CW-10  2026-03-11               24.9                    935  7.82
#> 11 CW-11  2026-03-12               23.6                    900  7.64
#> 12 CW-12  2026-03-13               25.7                    881  7.67
#> 13 CW-13  2026-03-14               21.3                    925  7.84
#> 14 CW-14  2026-03-15               23.5                    901  7.61
#> 15 CW-15  2026-03-16               27.5                    918  7.77
#> 16 CW-16  2026-03-17               26.8                    818  8.13
#> 17 CW-17  2026-03-18               22.5                    938  7.78
#> 18 CW-18  2026-03-19               25.8                    855  7.64
#> 19 CW-19  2026-03-20               24.7                    867  7.71
#> 20 CW-20  2026-03-21               27.6                    888  8.16

date_format = "%d.%m.%Y" describes the dates: day, dot, month, dot, four-digit year. (Next lesson is all about dates.) A few other arguments are worth knowing:

col_types tells readr each column’s type, when you know better than its guess, for example col_types = cols(sample = col_character(), .default = col_double()).
na lists the strings that mean “missing”, for example na = c("", "NA", "n/a", "-").
spec(cw) shows the types that readr guessed, and problems(cw) lists any values that didn’t fit.












Your turn. Read the cooling-water file with read_delim(), and tell readr that the decimal mark is a comma. Then compute the mean pH.









The decimal mark is a comma, written as text: decimal_mark = ",".


cw <- read_delim("data/cooling_water_eu.csv", delim = ";",
                 locale = locale(encoding = "latin1", decimal_mark = ","))
mean(cw$pH)
A mean pH of 7.78, slightly alkaline, which is normal for cooling water.

title: Importing and exporting data
text:
Text encodings
Computers store text as numbers. An encoding is the table that says which number stands for which character. For plain English letters, nearly all encodings agree. The trouble starts with everything else: é, ü, °, µ, and every non-Latin alphabet.
Today almost everything uses UTF-8, which can store every character of every language. But older software, especially on European Windows computers, often writes Latin-1 (also called ISO-8859-1). In Latin-1, ° is the single byte B0. In UTF-8 it’s two bytes, C2 B0. So if you read a Latin-1 file as if it were UTF-8, the lone B0 makes no sense:

names(read_csv2("data/cooling_water_eu.csv", show_col_types = FALSE))
#> [1] "sample"                  "date"                   
#> [3] "temperature (\xb0C)"     "conductivity (\xb5S/cm)"
#> [5] "pH"

R shows the bytes it couldn’t decode, \xb0 and \xb5. (Without show_col_types = FALSE, readr would even stop with an “invalid multibyte string” error, because it can’t print the broken names in its summary of the columns.) The opposite mistake, reading UTF-8 as Latin-1, gives the famous mojibake: °C turns into Â°C. If you’ve ever seen that on a website, now you know why!
guess_encoding() makes an educated guess from the bytes, and then locale(encoding = ...) tells readr what to expect:

guess_encoding("data/cooling_water_eu.csv")
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   encoding   confidence
#>   <chr>           <dbl>
#> 1 ISO-8859-1       0.22
#> 2 ISO-8859-2       0.22

With only two special characters to go on, it’s a weak guess, but a good one. The golden rule of encodings: whatever comes in, write UTF-8 out. readr’s write_csv() always does.
Your turn. Read the file with the right encoding, and give the two awkward columns simple names, temp_C and cond_uS_cm. Column names with spaces and symbols need backticks.









The file is Latin-1: encoding = "latin1". With the wrong encoding, readr stops with an “invalid multibyte string” error, or rename() can’t find the columns, because their names don’t contain a real °.


read_csv2("data/cooling_water_eu.csv", locale = locale(encoding = "latin1")) |>
  rename(temp_C = `temperature (°C)`, cond_uS_cm = `conductivity (µS/cm)`) |>
  names()

title: Importing and exporting data
text:
Excel workbooks
An Excel file holds several sheets, and people decorate them with titles, notes and blank rows. The readxl package reads them, with no need for Excel itself:

library(readxl)
excel_sheets("data/batch_records.xlsx")
#> [1] "Batches" "Lots"    "Notes"
read_excel("data/batch_records.xlsx", sheet = "Batches", range = "A1:B5", col_names = FALSE)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>   ...1                                                         ...2   
#>   <chr>                                                        <chr>  
#> 1 Pilot plant batch records, March 2026                        <NA>   
#> 2 Exported from the batch system on 2026-04-01. Times are UTC. <NA>   
#> 3 <NA>                                                         <NA>   
#> 4 batch_id                                                     reactor
#> 5 B01                                                          R1

The title is in cell A1, a note in A2, and the real header on row 4. skip = 3 jumps over the first three rows:

batches <- read_excel("data/batch_records.xlsx", sheet = "Batches", skip = 3)
batches
#> # A tibble: 40 × 12
#>    batch_id reactor start_time          end_time            operator_id lot_id 
#>    <chr>    <chr>   <dttm>              <dttm>              <chr>       <chr>  
#>  1 B01      R1      2026-03-02 14:59:00 2026-03-02 16:30:00 OP3         L26-001
#>  2 B02      R2      2026-03-02 09:00:00 2026-03-02 10:22:00 OP1         L26-001
#>  3 B03      R1      2026-03-03 11:46:00 2026-03-03 13:03:00 OP2         L26-001
#>  4 B04      R2      2026-03-04 03:27:00 2026-03-04 05:12:00 OP4         L26-001
#>  5 B05      R1      2026-03-04 13:10:00 2026-03-04 14:21:00 OP1         L26-002
#>  6 B06      R2      2026-03-04 10:10:00 2026-03-04 11:30:00 OP3         L26-002
#>  7 B07      R1      2026-03-05 21:50:00 2026-03-05 23:34:00 OP6         L26-002
#>  8 B08      R2      2026-03-05 13:50:00 2026-03-05 14:57:00 OP2         L26-003
#>  9 B09      R1      2026-03-06 19:55:00 2026-03-06 21:15:00 OP5         L26-003
#> 10 B10      R2      2026-03-07 00:28:00 2026-03-07 01:29:00 OP5         L26-003
#> # ℹ 30 more rows
#> # ℹ 6 more variables: catalyst <chr>, temp_C <dbl>, pressure_bar <dbl>,
#> #   residence_min <dbl>, alarms <dbl>, yield_pct <dbl>

The start and end times arrive as proper date-times. Excel stores a date as a number of days since the end of 1899, and readxl converts it for you. Other useful arguments are range (like range = "A4:L44") to read just a block of cells, col_types to set the types, and na for the strings that mean “missing”.
Your turn. The workbook’s Notes sheet holds the operators’ comments on a few batches. Read both sheets, join them, and find the mean yield of the batches that have a note.









Skip the 3 rows above the header, and name the sheet in quotes: sheet = "Notes".


batches <- read_excel("data/batch_records.xlsx", sheet = "Batches", skip = 3)
notes <- read_excel("data/batch_records.xlsx", sheet = "Notes")
batches |>
  inner_join(notes, by = "batch_id") |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_yield = mean(yield_pct))
The five batches with a note averaged 44.6%, against 59.5% for the rest. Look at the notes to see why: tripped pumps, a sticking valve, short runs.

title: Importing and exporting data
text:
JSON
Web services and instrument software often speak JSON (JavaScript Object Notation). Like CSV it’s plain text, but unlike a table it can nest: an object can hold lists, which can hold more objects. Here’s the start of the online analyzer’s export:

cat(readLines("data/analyzer_export.json", n = 16), sep = "\n")
#> {
#>   "instrument": {
#>     "id": "GC-ONLINE-2",
#>     "location": "Reactor R2 outlet",
#>     "software": "ChromaLog 3.1"
#>   },
#>   "runs": [
#>     {
#>       "run_id": 101,
#>       "time": "2026-03-10T07:30:00Z",
#>       "batch": "B18",
#>       "peaks": [
#>         {
#>           "compound": "solvent",
#>           "rt_min": 1.06,
#>           "area_pct": 2.54

Curly brackets { } hold named fields, and square brackets [ ] hold a list. The export describes the instrument, and then lists its runs. Each run has an ID, a time, a batch, and a list of peaks, one for each compound the chromatograph found. jsonlite’s fromJSON() turns it all into R lists and data frames:

library(jsonlite)
analyzer <- fromJSON("data/analyzer_export.json")
analyzer$instrument
#> $id
#> [1] "GC-ONLINE-2"
#> 
#> $location
#> [1] "Reactor R2 outlet"
#> 
#> $software
#> [1] "ChromaLog 3.1"
runs <- as_tibble(analyzer$runs)
runs
#> # A tibble: 9 × 4
#>   run_id time                 batch peaks       
#>    <int> <chr>                <chr> <list>      
#> 1    101 2026-03-10T07:30:00Z B18   <df [3 × 3]>
#> 2    102 2026-03-10T07:35:00Z B18   <df [3 × 3]>
#> 3    103 2026-03-10T07:40:00Z B18   <df [3 × 3]>
#> 4    104 2026-03-10T07:45:00Z B18   <df [3 × 3]>
#> 5    105 2026-03-10T07:50:00Z B18   <df [3 × 3]>
#> 6    106 2026-03-10T07:55:00Z B18   <df [3 × 3]>
#> 7    107 2026-03-10T08:00:00Z B18   <df [3 × 3]>
#> 8    108 2026-03-10T08:05:00Z B18   <df [3 × 3]>
#> 9    109 2026-03-10T08:10:00Z B18   <df [3 × 3]>

The peaks column is a list-column: each of its cells holds a whole little data frame. unnest() from tidyr spreads them out, with one row per peak:

library(tidyr)
unnest(runs, peaks)
#> # A tibble: 27 × 6
#>    run_id time                 batch compound  rt_min area_pct
#>     <int> <chr>                <chr> <chr>      <dbl>    <dbl>
#>  1    101 2026-03-10T07:30:00Z B18   solvent     1.06     2.54
#>  2    101 2026-03-10T07:30:00Z B18   product     4.11    95.8 
#>  3    101 2026-03-10T07:30:00Z B18   byproduct   5.3      1.61
#>  4    102 2026-03-10T07:35:00Z B18   solvent     1.03     2.03
#>  5    102 2026-03-10T07:35:00Z B18   product     4.12    96.2 
#>  6    102 2026-03-10T07:35:00Z B18   byproduct   5.29     1.72
#>  7    103 2026-03-10T07:40:00Z B18   solvent     1.06     2.46
#>  8    103 2026-03-10T07:40:00Z B18   product     4.11    96.1 
#>  9    103 2026-03-10T07:40:00Z B18   byproduct   5.28     1.41
#> 10    104 2026-03-10T07:45:00Z B18   solvent     1.05     2.23
#> # ℹ 17 more rows

Nine runs with three peaks each make 27 rows, in tidy form. Writing JSON is just as easy: write_json(df, "file.json") saves a data frame, and toJSON(df, pretty = TRUE) shows you what it would look like.
Your turn. The analyzer watched batch B18 as it ran. Unnest the peaks, keep the "product" peak of each run, and see how its area changed.









Unnest the list-column peaks, then keep compound == "product".


fromJSON("data/analyzer_export.json")$runs |>
  unnest(peaks) |>
  filter(compound == "product") |>
  select(run_id, time, area_pct)
The product peak climbed from 95.9% to 98.8% over 40 minutes, as the reaction ran towards completion.

title: Importing and exporting data
text:
Fixed-width files
Some older instruments and mainframe systems write fixed-width files. They have no delimiters at all: each column simply starts at the same position on every line. Here’s the start of the GC-1 chromatograph’s log:

cat(readLines("data/gc1_log.txt", n = 5), sep = "\n")
#> GC-1 RUN LOG  exported 2026-04-01
#> RUN  DATE    TIMESAMPLE  AREA%  RT
#> 00101202603021455B02-1     98.70  4.12
#> 00102202603022147B01-1     98.90  4.13
#> 00103202603031426B03-1     99.60  4.11

Without a description, that’s gibberish. The lab’s manual says that each line holds the run number (5 characters), the date (8), the time (4), the sample (8), the peak area in % (7) and the retention time in minutes (6). read_fwf() cuts each line at those widths, and skip = 2 skips the two header lines:

gc1 <- read_fwf("data/gc1_log.txt",
                col_positions = fwf_widths(c(5, 8, 4, 8, 7, 6),
                                           c("run", "date", "time", "sample", "area_pct", "rt")),
                col_types = cols(date = col_date("%Y%m%d"), time = col_character()),
                skip = 2)
gc1
#> # A tibble: 26 × 6
#>    run   date       time  sample area_pct    rt
#>    <chr> <date>     <chr> <chr>     <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1 00101 2026-03-02 1455  B02-1      98.7  4.12
#>  2 00102 2026-03-02 2147  B01-1      98.9  4.13
#>  3 00103 2026-03-03 1426  B03-1      99.6  4.11
#>  4 00104 2026-03-04 1813  B05-1      99.2  4.13
#>  5 00105 2026-03-06 0513  B07-1      99.2  4.13
#>  6 00106 2026-03-07 1607  B12-1      99.9  4.12
#>  7 00107 2026-03-08 0618  B11-1      99.1  4.12
#>  8 00108 2026-03-08 1257  B13-1      98.0  4.12
#>  9 00109 2026-03-09 0937  B14-1      99    4.13
#> 10 00110 2026-03-09 1803  B15-1      99.7  4.12
#> # ℹ 16 more rows

col_types reads the date as a real date, and keeps the time as text, so that 0513 doesn’t become the number 513. You can also give the columns as fwf_cols(run = 5, date = 8, ...), or by their start and end positions with fwf_positions().
Your turn. Some batches were tested twice on GC-1. Read the log, count the runs for each sample, and keep the samples with more than one run.









The widths are 5, 8, 4, 8, 7 and 6: c(5, 8, 4, 8, 7, 6).


read_fwf("data/gc1_log.txt",
         col_positions = fwf_widths(c(5, 8, 4, 8, 7, 6), c("run", "date", "time", "sample", "area_pct", "rt")),
         skip = 2, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  count(sample) |>
  filter(n > 1)
B21, B25, B35 and B39 were re-tested on GC-1. The other two re-tested batches, B19 and B34, were tested on GC-2.

title: Importing and exporting data
text:
SAS, SPSS and Stata files
Statistics has three classic commercial packages, each with its own file format, and the haven package reads and writes them all:



Software
File
Read with
Write with




SAS
.sas7bdat
read_sas()
use .xpt instead


SAS transport
.xpt
read_xpt()
write_xpt()


SPSS
.sav
read_sav()
write_sav()


Stata
.dta
read_dta()
write_dta()



Here’s the batch table as a Stata file, and as a SAS transport file. The US Food and Drug Administration requires transport files for clinical trial data, so they’re everywhere in the pharmaceutical industry.

library(haven)
read_dta("data/batches.dta") |> head(3)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 12
#>   batch_id reactor start_time          end_time            operator_id lot_id 
#>   <chr>    <chr>   <dttm>              <dttm>              <chr>       <chr>  
#> 1 B01      R1      2026-03-02 14:59:00 2026-03-02 16:30:00 OP3         L26-001
#> 2 B02      R2      2026-03-02 09:00:00 2026-03-02 10:22:00 OP1         L26-001
#> 3 B03      R1      2026-03-03 11:46:00 2026-03-03 13:03:00 OP2         L26-001
#> # ℹ 6 more variables: catalyst <chr>, temp_C <dbl>, pressure_bar <dbl>,
#> #   residence_min <dbl>, alarms <dbl>, yield_pct <dbl>
names(read_xpt("data/batches.xpt"))
#>  [1] "batch_id"      "reactor"       "start_time"    "end_time"     
#>  [5] "operator_id"   "lot_id"        "catalyst"      "temp_C"       
#>  [9] "pressure_bar"  "residence_min" "alarms"        "yield_pct"

Unlike CSV, these formats store each column’s type, so the date-times survive the trip.
SPSS and Stata files also carry information that ordinary R data frames don’t: value labels, which give names to codes (1 = “operator”), and variable labels, which describe a column in words. haven keeps both. Here’s the operator survey:

survey <- read_sav("data/operator_survey.sav")
survey
#> # A tibble: 48 × 5
#>       id role           shift     workload        overtime_h
#>    <dbl> <dbl+lbl>      <dbl+lbl> <dbl+lbl>            <dbl>
#>  1     1 3 [engineer]   2 [night] 2 [low]                  2
#>  2     2 1 [operator]   1 [day]   3 [about right]         12
#>  3     3 2 [technician] 1 [day]   1 [very low]             9
#>  4     4 2 [technician] 1 [day]   4 [high]                 4
#>  5     5 1 [operator]   2 [night] 3 [about right]          7
#>  6     6 1 [operator]   2 [night] 4 [high]                 9
#>  7     7 2 [technician] 1 [day]   1 [very low]            13
#>  8     8 1 [operator]   2 [night] 5 [very high]            7
#>  9     9 1 [operator]   2 [night] 3 [about right]         11
#> 10    10 1 [operator]   1 [day]   2 [low]                 10
#> # ℹ 38 more rows
attr(survey$workload, "label")
#> [1] "How would you rate your workload?"

<dbl+lbl> marks a labelled column: numbers, with names attached. Before analyzing, you usually want a factor instead, and as_factor() makes one from the labels:

count(survey, role = as_factor(role))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   role           n
#>   <fct>      <int>
#> 1 operator      24
#> 2 technician    15
#> 3 engineer       9

zap_labels() does the opposite: it drops the labels and keeps the bare numbers.
SPSS also lets you declare certain codes to be missing, like 9 = “no answer”. By default, read_sav() turns those user-defined missing values into NA, which is safe. But if you keep them with user_na = TRUE, and then convert carelessly, the 9s sneak into your numbers:

survey_9 <- read_sav("data/operator_survey.sav", user_na = TRUE)
mean(survey$workload, na.rm = TRUE)    # "no answer" is NA: correct
#> [1] 2.977778
mean(as.numeric(survey_9$workload))    # "no answer" counts as a 9: wrong!
#> [1] 3.354167

Three “no answer”s, counted as scores of 9, push the mean workload from 2.98 to 3.35. Always look at a variable’s labels before you compute with it!
Your turn. Compute the mean overtime for each role, with the roles’ names rather than their codes.









as_factor(role) turns the codes 1, 2 and 3 into the labels operator, technician and engineer.


read_sav("data/operator_survey.sav") |>
  mutate(role = as_factor(role)) |>
  group_by(role) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_overtime = mean(overtime_h))
The technicians worked the most overtime: almost 9 hours last month, on average.

title: Importing and exporting data
text:
Exporting, and Parquet
Every reader has a writer: write_csv(), write_xlsx() from writexl, write_json(), and haven’s write_sav(), write_dta() and write_xpt(). So which format should you choose? That depends on who, or what, is going to read the file.
CSV can be read by everything, and will be forever, but it only stores text. Every column’s type has to be guessed again when the file is read back, and some types can’t be recovered at all:

test <- tibble(
  id = 1:3,
  grade = factor(c("low", "high", "low"), levels = c("low", "high")),
  time = as.POSIXct("2026-03-02 06:00", tz = "UTC") + 3600 * 0:2
)
write_csv(test, "test.csv")
read_csv("test.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>      id grade time               
#>   <dbl> <chr> <dttm>             
#> 1     1 low   2026-03-02 06:00:00
#> 2     2 high  2026-03-02 07:00:00
#> 3     3 low   2026-03-02 08:00:00

The whole numbers came back as decimals (dbl instead of int), and the factor came back as plain text, with its level order lost.
Parquet is a modern file format, designed for data analysis. It stores each column’s type, it’s compressed, and it’s fast to read. Python, R, Spark, DuckDB and Arrow all understand it. The small nanoparquet package reads and writes it:

library(nanoparquet)
write_parquet(test, "test.parquet")
read_parquet("test.parquet")
#> # A data frame: 3 × 3
#>      id grade time               
#>   <int> <fct> <dttm>             
#> 1     1 low   2026-03-02 06:00:00
#> 2     2 high  2026-03-02 07:00:00
#> 3     3 low   2026-03-02 08:00:00
file.size(c("data/sensor_log.csv", "data/sensor_log.parquet"))
#> [1] 12142  4627

Every type survived. And as Parquet, the sensor log takes up less than half the space it does as CSV. For files that only R will ever read, saveRDS() and readRDS() store any R object exactly, but no other software can open them.








Format
Good for
Keeps the types?




CSV
sharing with anyone, forever
no


Excel (.xlsx)
people who’ll open it in Excel
partly


JSON
web services, and nested data
partly


Parquet
large data, and other data tools
yes


.sav, .dta, .xpt
colleagues who use SPSS, Stata or SAS
yes, with labels


.rds
R, and only R
everything



Your turn. A colleague wants the batches and the notes in one Excel file, with a sheet for each. write_xlsx() makes one sheet for each data frame in a named list.









The names in the list become the sheet names: list(batches = batches, notes = notes).


batches <- read_excel("data/batch_records.xlsx", sheet = "Batches", skip = 3)
notes <- read_excel("data/batch_records.xlsx", sheet = "Notes")
writexl::write_xlsx(list(batches = batches, notes = notes), "plant_export.xlsx")
excel_sheets("plant_export.xlsx")
Reading your own export back is a good habit: it proves that the file really contains what you think it does.

title: Importing and exporting data
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The hottest day. Read the cooling-water file properly, with real numbers and real dates, and find the date of the highest water temperature.









You need three settings: semicolons with decimal commas (read_csv2()), the encoding, and the date format.


read_csv2("data/cooling_water_eu.csv", locale = locale(encoding = "latin1", date_format = "%d.%m.%Y"))


cw <- read_csv2("data/cooling_water_eu.csv",
                locale = locale(encoding = "latin1", date_format = "%d.%m.%Y"))
cw$date[which.max(cw$`temperature (°C)`)]
21 March 2026, the last day of the campaign, at 27.6 °C.




Challenge 2 · Workload by shift. Compute the mean workload score on each shift, with the shifts’ names. Make sure that “no answer” doesn’t count as a score! Also count how many people on each shift actually answered.









With the default settings, “no answer” is already NA. Turn shift into a factor, group by it, and use na.rm = TRUE. sum(!is.na(workload)) counts the answers.


mutate(shift = as_factor(shift)) |>
  group_by(shift) |>
  summarise(answered = sum(!is.na(workload)), mean_workload = mean(workload, na.rm = TRUE))


read_sav("data/operator_survey.sav") |>
  mutate(shift = as_factor(shift)) |>
  group_by(shift) |>
  summarise(answered = sum(!is.na(workload)), mean_workload = mean(workload, na.rm = TRUE))
All three “no answer”s came from the day shift, where 23 of 26 people answered. The two shifts rate their workload about the same, just below 3, “about right”.

title: Importing and exporting data
text:
Quick quiz

1. A European CSV file shows 7,82 in its pH column. What does read_csv2() assume?

Semicolons between the values, and commas as decimal marks
Commas between the values, and dots as decimal marks
Tabs between the values


That’s the usual convention wherever the comma is the decimal mark. For anything else, use read_delim() with a locale().



2. A web page shows Â°C where it should say °C. What went wrong?

Text written in UTF-8 was read as Latin-1
The file was damaged
Latin-1 can’t store the ° sign


In UTF-8, ° is the two bytes C2 B0. Read as Latin-1, each byte becomes its own character: C2 is Â, and B0 is °.



3. An Excel sheet has a title in row 1, a note in row 2, an empty row 3, and the column names in row 4. How do you read it?

read_excel(path, skip = 4)
read_excel(path, skip = 3)
read_excel(path, col_names = FALSE)


skip = 3 skips the first three rows, so that row 4 is read as the header.



4. After fromJSON(), a column holds a small data frame in every cell. What does unnest() do with it?

It spreads each cell’s rows out into rows of the main table
It deletes the column
It converts the column to text


Nine runs, each with three peaks, become 27 rows, one for each peak.



5. An SPSS column has the codes 1, 2 and 3, labelled operator, technician and engineer. What does as_factor() give you?

A factor with the levels operator, technician and engineer
The numbers 1, 2 and 3, without labels
An error, because the column is numeric


as_factor() uses the value labels. zap_labels() would give you the bare numbers instead.



6. You’re sharing a large dataset with a colleague who works in Python. Why might you choose Parquet over CSV?

Parquet files can be opened in Notepad
Parquet keeps every column’s type, and its files are smaller and faster to read
Python can’t read CSV files


Both formats work in Python. But Parquet saves your colleague from guessing the types, and it’s much faster for big files.

title: Importing and exporting data
text:
Wrap-up
Data can arrive in any shape now, and you’ll get it in! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Delimited files: read_csv(), read_csv2() and read_delim(), with a locale() for the decimal mark, encoding and date format. Always check that the values are plausible after importing.
Encodings: UTF-8 can store everything, while older files are often Latin-1. Mismatches show up as \xb0 or as mojibake like Â°C. Write UTF-8 out.
Excel: excel_sheets(), then read_excel() with sheet, skip and range. write_xlsx() writes one sheet for each data frame in a named list.
JSON: fromJSON() makes lists and data frames, and unnest() flattens list-columns.
Fixed-width: read_fwf() with fwf_widths(), plus a description of the columns.
SAS, SPSS and Stata: haven’s read_sas(), read_xpt(), read_sav() and read_dta(). Use as_factor() for value labels, and watch out for user-defined missing codes.
Choosing a format: CSV for anyone, Parquet for types and speed, .rds for R alone.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download the files into your project’s data-raw/ folder: cooling_water_eu.csv, batch_records.xlsx, analyzer_export.json, gc1_log.txt, operator_survey.sav and sensor_log.parquet. Install the packages with install.packages(c("readxl", "writexl", "haven", "jsonlite", "nanoparquet")).

One script to import them all. Write R/01-import.R, which reads every file, cleans the column names, and saves each table to data/ as Parquet. Then restart R and check that your script rebuilds data/ from scratch.
A format bake-off. Save the batch table as CSV, Excel, Parquet, .rds and .dta. Compare the file sizes, then read each one back and compare the column classes with sapply(df, class). Which formats kept the date-times?
Look inside the workbook. If you have Excel or LibreOffice, open batch_records.xlsx, and change a start time cell’s format to “Number”. The date-time becomes a day count, with the time of day as a fraction.
Labels of your own. Create a labelled column with labelled(c(1, 2, 1), c(day = 1, night = 2), label = "Usual shift"), put it in a data frame, and save that with write_sav(). If you can, open the file in SPSS, or in its free alternative PSPP, and look for your labels.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Delimiter

The character that separates the values in a text file, like a comma, semicolon or tab.

Locale

A file’s local conventions: its decimal mark, grouping mark, encoding and date format.

Encoding

The table that maps bytes to characters. UTF-8 is the modern standard, and Latin-1 is a common older one.

Mojibake

Garbled text, like Â°C, caused by reading text with the wrong encoding.

List-column

A data frame column whose cells hold whole lists or data frames, often the result of reading JSON.

Fixed-width file

A text file in which every column starts at the same position on every line.

Value label and variable label

In SPSS and Stata, a name for a code (1 = “operator”), and a description of a whole column.

User-defined missing value

A code, like 9 = “no answer”, that SPSS treats as missing.

Parquet

A compressed, column-based file format that stores each column’s type.











NoteWant to read more?






R for Data Science (2e): “Data import”, “Spreadsheets” and “Hierarchical data”, for CSV, Excel and JSON.
haven’s article on conversion semantics. How labels and missing values from SAS, SPSS and Stata are carried into R.
Joel Spolsky, “The Absolute Minimum Every Software Developer Absolutely, Positively Must Know About Unicode and Character Sets”. A classic, friendly explanation of encodings.

title: SQL fundamentals
text:
Module 1 · Lesson 7 of 14 Week 22 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Most of the world’s data lives in databases: the plant’s laboratory system, a hospital’s patient records, every online shop’s orders. And the language almost every database speaks is SQL (Structured Query Language, often pronounced “sequel”). It’s over fifty years old, it’s on every data job description, and the good news is that you already know its ideas, because dplyr was designed after it. In this lesson you’ll query the plant’s database directly, in SQL, from R.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: SQL fundamentals
text:
Databases and SQL
A database management system (DBMS) stores tables and answers questions about them. Big organizations use servers like PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server or Oracle. SQLite is different: the whole database is a single file, with no server needed. It’s the most widely used database in the world (every smartphone has dozens of SQLite files on it), and it’s perfect for learning and for small projects.
The plant’s data is in plant.sqlite, with the same six tables as Lessons 5 and 6. In R, the DBI package talks to databases, and RSQLite is its driver for SQLite:

library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "data/plant.sqlite")
dbListTables(con)
#> [1] "batches"     "instruments" "lab_results" "lots"        "operators"  
#> [6] "suppliers"
dbListFields(con, "batches")
#>  [1] "batch_id"      "reactor"       "start_time"    "end_time"     
#>  [5] "operator_id"   "lot_id"        "catalyst"      "temp_C"       
#>  [9] "pressure_bar"  "residence_min" "alarms"        "yield_pct"

con is a connection: think of it as a phone line to the database. dbGetQuery() sends a query down the line and brings the answer back as a data frame:

dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT batch_id, reactor, yield_pct FROM batches LIMIT 5")
#>   batch_id reactor yield_pct
#> 1      B01      R1      70.2
#> 2      B02      R2      53.7
#> 3      B03      R1      49.2
#> 4      B04      R2      65.3
#> 5      B05      R1      53.4

The query is just a piece of text. By convention, SQL keywords are written in capitals, but SQL doesn’t actually care. When you’re finished, hang up with dbDisconnect(con).








SELECT * means “every column”. It’s handy for a quick look, but in real queries it’s better to name the columns you need.

title: SQL fundamentals
text:
SELECT: choosing columns
SELECT lists the columns you want, separated by commas, and FROM names the table. You can also compute new columns, and name them with AS:

dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT batch_id, yield_pct / 100 AS yield_fraction FROM batches LIMIT 3")
#>   batch_id yield_fraction
#> 1      B01          0.702
#> 2      B02          0.537
#> 3      B03          0.492

That’s select() and mutate() from dplyr, rolled into one.










Your turn. Get the batch_id, catalyst and yield_pct of every batch. (con is ready in every exercise.)









List the three columns after SELECT, separated by commas: batch_id, catalyst, yield_pct.


dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT batch_id, catalyst, yield_pct FROM batches")

title: SQL fundamentals
text:
WHERE: filtering rows
WHERE keeps the rows where a condition is true, just like filter(). A few things look a little different from R:








In SQL
In R
Meaning




=
==
equals


<> or !=
!=
doesn’t equal


AND, OR, NOT
&, |, !
combine conditions


'R1'
"R1"
text, in single quotes


IN ('A', 'D')
%in% c("A", "D")
is one of


BETWEEN 170 AND 180
>= 170 & <= 180
in a range, ends included


LIKE 'B1%'
startsWith(x, "B1")
matches a pattern: % means “anything”


IS NULL
is.na()
missing (SQL calls it NULL)




dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT batch_id, residence_min, yield_pct FROM batches WHERE residence_min > 60")
#>   batch_id residence_min yield_pct
#> 1      B04          60.7      65.3
#> 2      B07          64.0      74.1
#> 3      B29          71.7      74.0
#> 4      B33          65.4      69.5
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT batch_id, temp_C FROM batches WHERE temp_C IS NULL")
#>   batch_id temp_C
#> 1      B07     NA
#> 2      B23     NA







Warning= NULL never matches



In SQL, a comparison with a missing value is never true, so WHERE temp_C = NULL returns nothing at all, just like x == NA in R. Always write IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.


Because the whole query is inside R’s double quotes, text values in SQL use single quotes. That’s a happy accident: the two kinds of quotes don’t clash.
Your turn. Find the batches that ran on reactor 'R2' and had a yield above 60%.









Two conditions joined with AND: reactor = 'R2' AND yield_pct > 60. Note the single quotes around R2.


dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT batch_id, yield_pct FROM batches WHERE reactor = 'R2' AND yield_pct > 60")
Only five of R2’s 20 batches beat 60%.




Your turn. Which batch has a missing alarm count?









Missing values in SQL are NULL, and you test for them with IS NULL.


dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT batch_id, alarms FROM batches WHERE alarms IS NULL")

title: SQL fundamentals
text:
ORDER BY and LIMIT
ORDER BY sorts the result, smallest first; add DESC for largest first. LIMIT keeps only the first few rows. Together they find the top or bottom of anything:

dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT batch_id, yield_pct FROM batches ORDER BY yield_pct DESC LIMIT 3")
#>   batch_id yield_pct
#> 1      B11      74.8
#> 2      B07      74.1
#> 3      B29      74.0

Your turn. From lab_results, find the three lowest purity results, with their batch_id and value.









Sort by value, smallest first (the default), and keep three rows: ORDER BY value LIMIT 3.


dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT batch_id, value FROM lab_results WHERE analyte = 'purity' ORDER BY value LIMIT 3")
B10, B08 and B13, three batches that all ran hotter than 185 °C.

title: SQL fundamentals
text:
Aggregate functions
SQL’s aggregate functions summarize many rows into one, like summarise():



Function
Gives




COUNT(*)
the number of rows


COUNT(column)
the number of non-missing values in a column


SUM(), AVG()
the total and the mean


MIN(), MAX()
the smallest and largest




dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, MIN(yield_pct) AS worst, MAX(yield_pct) AS best FROM batches")
#>    n worst best
#> 1 40  31.1 74.8

Unlike R’s mean(), SQL’s aggregates quietly skip missing values, with no na.rm needed. That’s convenient, but it’s also why you should know how many values were missing.
Your turn. In one query, count all the batches (n), count the batches that have a temperature (n_temp), and compute the mean yield (mean_yield).









COUNT(temp_C) counts only the non-missing temperatures, and AVG(yield_pct) is the mean yield.


dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, COUNT(temp_C) AS n_temp, AVG(yield_pct) AS mean_yield FROM batches")
40 batches, 38 of them with a temperature, and a mean yield of 57.6%.

title: SQL fundamentals
text:
GROUP BY and HAVING
GROUP BY splits the rows into groups, so the aggregates are computed once per group. It’s group_by() plus summarise():

dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT catalyst, COUNT(*) AS n, ROUND(AVG(yield_pct), 1) AS mean_yield
  FROM batches
  GROUP BY catalyst
")
#>   catalyst  n mean_yield
#> 1        A 10       60.0
#> 2        B 12       55.7
#> 3        C  9       54.8
#> 4        D  9       60.5

A query can span several lines, which makes longer ones much easier to read.
To filter groups by their summaries, use HAVING. WHERE filters rows before they’re grouped, and HAVING filters groups after:

dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT catalyst, COUNT(*) AS n, ROUND(AVG(yield_pct), 1) AS mean_yield
  FROM batches
  GROUP BY catalyst
  HAVING AVG(yield_pct) > 57
")
#>   catalyst  n mean_yield
#> 1        A 10       60.0
#> 2        D  9       60.5

Your turn. For each reactor, count the batches (n) and compute their mean yield (mean_yield).









Add GROUP BY reactor at the end.


dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT reactor, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(yield_pct) AS mean_yield
  FROM batches
  GROUP BY reactor
")
R1 averages about 61% and R2 about 54%, the same gap you found with dplyr in Lesson 4.

title: SQL fundamentals
section: SQL and dplyr side by side
text:
SQL and dplyr side by side
You’ve now met the core of SQL, and every piece has a dplyr twin:



SQL
dplyr




SELECT a, b
select(a, b)


SELECT a / 100 AS c
mutate(c = a / 100)


FROM table
the data you pipe in


WHERE condition
filter(condition)


GROUP BY g
group_by(g)


COUNT(*), AVG(x)
n(), mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)


HAVING condition
filter() after summarise()


ORDER BY x DESC
arrange(desc(x))


LIMIT 5
head(5) or slice_head(n = 5)



One difference catches everyone out. You write the clauses in the order SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, but the database runs them in this order:

FROM: find the table.
WHERE: filter the rows.
GROUP BY: form the groups.
HAVING: filter the groups.
SELECT: compute the output columns.
ORDER BY, then LIMIT.

That explains a classic puzzle: you can’t use a name from SELECT ... AS inside WHERE, because WHERE runs before the name exists. (SQLite is lenient here, but most databases aren’t.)

title: SQL fundamentals
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Busy operators. Which operators ran more than 8 batches? Return their operator_id and the number of batches, n.









Group by operator first, then filter the groups by their count.


GROUP BY operator_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 8


dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT operator_id, COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM batches
  GROUP BY operator_id
  HAVING COUNT(*) > 8
")
OP1 (Maya, 11 batches) and OP5 (Lena, 9). Next lesson, you’ll join in their names with SQL.




Challenge 2 · A lab summary. For each analyte, count the results and compute their mean value, leaving out the re-tests, and sort by analyte. In the database, retest is stored as 0 for a first test and 1 for a re-test, because SQLite has no TRUE and FALSE.









Three clauses, in this order: WHERE to drop the re-tests, GROUP BY the analyte, ORDER BY the analyte.


WHERE retest = 0 GROUP BY analyte ORDER BY analyte


dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT analyte, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(value) AS mean_value
  FROM lab_results
  WHERE retest = 0
  GROUP BY analyte
  ORDER BY analyte
")
40 color results, 40 purity and 38 water. The water count is 38, not 40, because two tests were never run.

title: SQL fundamentals
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does SELECT * FROM lots return?

Every column and every row of the lots table
Only the first row
The number of lots


* means all the columns, and with no WHERE you get all the rows.



2. How do you write the text value R1 in a SQL condition?

'R1', in single quotes
R1, with no quotes
[R1]


Text values in SQL use single quotes, which conveniently don’t clash with the double quotes around the query in R.



3. WHERE temp_C = NULL returns no rows, even though two temperatures are missing. Why?

Comparisons with NULL are never true. You need IS NULL
SQLite can’t store missing values
The column name is wrong


Just like x == NA in R, comparing with an unknown gives an unknown. IS NULL asks the right question.



4. What’s the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(temp_C)?

COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(temp_C) counts only the non-missing temperatures
They’re the same
COUNT(temp_C) adds up the temperatures


40 rows, but only 38 temperatures.



5. What’s the difference between WHERE and HAVING?

WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after
They’re interchangeable
HAVING only works with ORDER BY


Use WHERE for conditions on single rows, and HAVING for conditions on group summaries, like COUNT(*) > 8.



6. Which dplyr verb matches SQL’s ORDER BY yield_pct DESC?

filter(yield_pct)
arrange(desc(yield_pct))
group_by(yield_pct)


ORDER BY sorts, like arrange(), and DESC is desc().

title: SQL fundamentals
text:
Wrap-up
You can talk to databases now! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Connect: dbConnect() opens a connection, dbGetQuery() sends SQL and returns a data frame, and dbDisconnect() closes it.
Choose and filter: SELECT picks and computes columns, FROM names the table, and WHERE filters rows, with IN, BETWEEN, LIKE and IS NULL.
Sort: ORDER BY ... DESC and LIMIT find the top and bottom of anything.
Summarize: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX skip missing values; GROUP BY makes one row per group; HAVING filters the groups.
Order of execution: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)






Install the drivers. Run install.packages(c("DBI", "RSQLite")), then download plant.sqlite into your project’s data-raw/ folder.
Look around. Connect with con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "data-raw/plant.sqlite"), then list the tables and their fields. dbReadTable(con, "operators") reads a whole table into a data frame, which is handy for small tables.
Write SQL chunks. In a Quarto document, you can write SQL directly in a chunk that starts with ```{sql, connection = con}, and the result appears as a table. Rewrite three of this lesson’s queries that way.
Answer with SQL. Using SQL only: Which catalyst has the lowest minimum yield? How many lab results did each analyst produce? What’s the average residence time of the batches with 2 or more alarms?
Try a GUI. The free DB Browser for SQLite opens plant.sqlite in a spreadsheet-like window, with a tab for running SQL. It’s a great way to explore a database you’ve been given.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Database management system (DBMS)

Software that stores tables and answers queries about them, like SQLite, PostgreSQL or SQL Server.

SQL

Structured Query Language, the standard language for asking databases questions.

Connection

An open link between R and a database, created with dbConnect().

Query

A request written in SQL, such as SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ....

NULL

SQL’s word for a missing value. Test for it with IS NULL.

Aggregate function

A function that summarizes many rows into one value: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX.

GROUP BY and HAVING

Make one summary row per group, and filter those groups by their summaries.











NoteWant to read more?






R for Data Science (2e), “Databases”. DBI, SQL basics and dbplyr, from the R side.
SQLBolt. Short interactive SQL lessons in the browser, perfect extra practice for this lesson and the next.

title: Combining datasets
text:
Module 1 · Lesson 5 of 14 Week 20 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Batch B18’s product had 410 ppm of water, twice the usual. Why? The answer isn’t in any single table. The lab results hold the water content, the batch records say which raw-material lot each batch used, the lots table says which supplier delivered each lot, and the suppliers table has their names. To connect them, you need joins. They’re among the most useful tools in all of data analysis, and by the end of this lesson you’ll have solved the mystery of B18.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Combining datasets
text:
Tables and their keys
Here’s how the plant’s tables fit together:









Table
One row per…
Key
Links to




suppliers
supplier
supplier_id



lots
delivered lot of raw material
lot_id
suppliers through supplier_id


operators
operator
operator_id



batches
batch
batch_id
lots through lot_id, operators through operator_id


lab_results
lab measurement
result_id
batches through batch_id



A primary key is a column (or set of columns) that identifies each row uniquely, like batch_id in batches. A foreign key is a column that points to another table’s primary key, like lot_id in batches, which points to a row of lots. Joins work by matching keys.
A primary key must be unique, so it’s worth checking:

batches <- read.csv("data/batches.csv")
lab <- read.csv("data/lab_results.csv")
lots <- read.csv("data/lots.csv")
suppliers <- read.csv("data/suppliers.csv")
operators <- read.csv("data/operators.csv")

batches |> count(batch_id) |> filter(n > 1)
#> [1] batch_id n       
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

No duplicates, so batch_id really is a key of batches. In lab_results, though, each batch appears several times, once for each measurement, so there batch_id is a foreign key, and the primary key is result_id.











Your turn. Most batches have three lab results: one each for purity, water and color. Which batches appear four times in lab? (All five tables are ready in every exercise.)









count() makes a column called n. Keep the rows where n == 4.


lab |>
  count(batch_id) |>
  filter(n == 4)
Six batches: their purity was tested twice, because the first result was close to the 98.5% spec.

title: Combining datasets
section: left_join(): add columns from another table

title: Combining datasets
Combining datasets
section: Inner, left, right and full joins
text:
Inner, left, right and full joins
Two batches, B12 and B33, have no water result. What happens to them depends on the kind of join:

water <- lab |> filter(analyte == "water") |> select(batch_id, water_ppm = value)
nrow(left_join(batches, water, by = "batch_id"))     # every batch; NA water for B12 and B33
#> [1] 40
nrow(inner_join(batches, water, by = "batch_id"))    # only batches with a match in both
#> [1] 38
nrow(full_join(batches, water, by = "batch_id"))     # everything from both tables
#> [1] 40




Join
Keeps




left_join(x, y)
every row of x


right_join(x, y)
every row of y


inner_join(x, y)
only the rows with a match in both


full_join(x, y)
every row of both, matched where possible
