left_join() is the one you’ll use most, because it never loses rows from your main table. An inner_join() silently drops anything without a match, which is easy to miss.
Your turn. How many rows does an inner join of the batches with the color results give?









The function is inner_join.


color <- lab |> filter(analyte == "color") |> select(batch_id, color_apha = value)
nrow(inner_join(batches, color, by = "batch_id"))
40: every batch had its color measured, so nothing is dropped.

title: Combining datasets
section: Filtering joins: who has a match?
text:
Filtering joins: who has a match?
Sometimes you don’t want columns from the other table, just to know whether a match exists. Filtering joins keep or drop rows of x without adding anything:

semi_join(x, y) keeps the rows of x that have a match in y.
anti_join(x, y) keeps the rows of x that don’t.

anti_join() is a data detective’s best friend. It finds the batches missing a test, lab results for batches that don’t exist, and lots that were never used:

semi_join(batches, water, by = "batch_id") |> nrow()
#> [1] 38

Your turn. Which batches have no water result?









You want the batches without a match: anti_join.


water <- lab |> filter(analyte == "water")
batches |>
  anti_join(water, by = "batch_id") |>
  select(batch_id)
B12 and B33. Someone should ask the lab what happened to those samples.

title: Combining datasets
text:
Join pitfalls
Joins are powerful, and they go wrong in a few classic ways.
Duplicate keys multiply rows. Join the purity results to the batches, and you get 46 rows, not 40, because the six re-tested batches match two purity results each:

purity <- lab |> filter(analyte == "purity") |> select(batch_id, purity = value, retest)
nrow(left_join(batches, purity, by = "batch_id"))
#> [1] 46

If you expect one match per row, say so with relationship = "one-to-one", and dplyr stops with an error when it isn’t true, instead of quietly adding rows:

left_join(batches, purity, by = "batch_id", relationship = "one-to-one")
#> Error in `left_join()`:
#> ! Each row in `x` must match at most 1 row in `y`.
#> ℹ Row 19 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.

Keys with different names. When the key columns are named differently, use join_by(), which reads like a sentence: “match batch in the first table with batch_id in the second”.

notes <- data.frame(batch = c("B07", "B18"), note = c("re-sampled", "high water"))
notes |> left_join(batches, by = join_by(batch == batch_id)) |> select(batch, note, reactor)
#>   batch       note reactor
#> 1   B07 re-sampled      R1
#> 2   B18 high water      R2

Keys that look the same but aren’t. "B07" and "b07" don’t match, and nor do "B07" and "B07 " with a trailing space, or the number 7 and the text "7". A mismatched key doesn’t cause an error. It just quietly gives NAs. Lesson 10 shows how to clean keys like these, and an anti_join() is the quickest way to check for them.
Your turn. Join the purity results to the batches without duplicating any batch: keep only the first tests, and add relationship = "one-to-one" to prove it.









The re-tests have retest equal to TRUE, so keep the rows where it isn’t: !retest.


purity <- lab |> filter(analyte == "purity", !retest) |> select(batch_id, purity = value)
batches |>
  left_join(purity, by = "batch_id", relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  nrow()




Your turn. The shift notes below use the column name batch instead of batch_id. Join them to the batches with join_by(), keeping the note, the reactor and the yield.









Inside join_by(), put the first table’s column on the left: batch == batch_id.


notes <- data.frame(batch = c("B07", "B18", "B33"), note = c("re-sampled", "high water", "no water test"))
notes |>
  left_join(batches, by = join_by(batch == batch_id)) |>
  select(batch, note, reactor, yield_pct)

title: Combining datasets
text:
Stacking tables: bind_rows()
Joins combine tables side by side, by key. Sometimes you just want to stack tables with the same columns on top of each other, like two shifts’ logs or two months of results. That’s bind_rows(), from Lesson 2:

day_log <- data.frame(batch_id = c("B01", "B02"), shift = "day")
night_log <- data.frame(batch_id = c("B04", "B07"), shift = "night")
bind_rows(day_log, night_log)
#>   batch_id shift
#> 1      B01   day
#> 2      B02   day
#> 3      B04 night
#> 4      B07 night

There’s also bind_cols(), which glues tables side by side by row position. Avoid it unless you’re certain the rows line up. One unnoticed sort, and every row is matched with the wrong partner. A join by key is always safer.

title: Combining datasets
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Does experience matter? Do operators with more years of experience get better yields? Join the operators to the batches, and compute the correlation between years_experience and yield_pct.









left_join(operators, by = "operator_id") brings each batch’s operator’s experience along.


joined <- batches |> left_join(operators, by = "operator_id")
cor(joined$years_experience, joined$yield_pct)
About 0.08: practically no relationship. The plant’s yields depend on residence time and alarms (Module 0), not on who’s running the batch. That’s good news for the newer operators!




Challenge 2 · Find the orphans. Some late color results arrived, keyed by a column called batch. Which of them belong to a batch that doesn’t exist in batches?









You want the rows of late without a match in batches, matching batch with batch_id.


anti_join(batches, by = join_by(batch == batch_id))


late <- data.frame(batch = c("B05", "B5", "B41", "B22"), analyte = "color", value = c(14, 15, 22, 18))
late |>
  anti_join(batches, by = join_by(batch == batch_id))
B5 is probably B05 typed without its zero, and B41 belongs to April’s campaign, which isn’t in this table. Both need checking before they’re loaded, which is exactly what Lesson 11 is about.

title: Combining datasets
text:
Quick quiz

1. What makes a column a primary key?

Its values identify each row uniquely
It’s the first column in the table
It’s numeric


A primary key has one distinct value per row. Check with count(table, key) |> filter(n > 1).



2. batches has 40 rows, and every batch has one lot. What does left_join(batches, lots, by = "lot_id") return?

40 rows, each with its lot’s columns added
12 rows, one per lot
52 rows


A left join keeps every row of the first table and adds columns from the second.



3. Which join keeps only the rows with a match in both tables?

left_join()
inner_join()
full_join()


An inner join silently drops rows without a match, so check row counts before and after.



4. You want the batches that have no lab result at all. Which function finds them?

semi_join(batches, lab)
anti_join(batches, lab)
inner_join(batches, lab)


anti_join() keeps the rows of the first table that have no match in the second.



5. After a left join, your table has more rows than before. What’s the most likely reason?

Some keys appear more than once in the second table
The join dropped some rows
The key columns have different names


Each duplicate match adds a row. Use relationship = "one-to-one" when you expect exactly one match.



6. A join gives NAs where you expected matches. Which is a likely cause?

The keys differ slightly, like "B07" and "b07"
The tables are too big
You used left_join() instead of bind_rows()


Keys must match exactly. Case, spaces and types all matter. An anti_join() shows which ones failed.

title: Combining datasets
text:
Wrap-up
You can now connect any tables you’re given. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Keys: a primary key identifies each row of a table; a foreign key points to another table’s primary key.
Mutating joins add columns: left_join() keeps every row of the first table, inner_join() only the matches, full_join() everything.
Filtering joins keep or drop rows: semi_join() keeps those with a match, anti_join() those without.
Pitfalls: duplicate keys multiply rows (use relationship), differently named keys need join_by(), and nearly identical keys don’t match at all.
Stacking: bind_rows() stacks tables with the same columns. Prefer joins to bind_cols().







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download all five tables used in this lesson into your project’s data-raw/ folder: batches.csv, lab_results.csv, lots.csv, suppliers.csv and operators.csv.

One big analysis table. Build a single table with one row per batch: its batch record, its lot and supplier, its operator, and its first-test purity, water and color as three columns. (You’ll need Lesson 3’s pivot_wider().) Check that it has exactly 40 rows.
Purity by supplier. Using your table, compare the mean purity and the on-spec rate (98.5% or more) across suppliers. Does the wet raw material from Kestrel Industrial also hurt purity?
Check every key. Use anti_join() to check that every lot_id in batches exists in lots, every supplier_id in lots exists in suppliers, and every operator_id in batches exists in operators.
A plot. Draw boxplots of water content by supplier name, with the points jittered on top. Give it a title that states the finding.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Primary key

A column, or set of columns, whose values identify each row of a table uniquely.

Foreign key

A column whose values point to the primary key of another table.

Mutating join

A join that adds columns from one table to another: left_join(), inner_join(), right_join(), full_join().

Filtering join

A join that keeps or drops rows without adding columns: semi_join() and anti_join().

join_by()

Describes how the keys match, including keys with different names, like join_by(batch == batch_id).

Relationship

How many rows of each table can match: one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many.

Orphan

A row whose foreign key matches nothing in the table it should point to.











NoteWant to read more?






R for Data Science (2e), “Joins”. Keys, every kind of join, and how joins go wrong, with excellent diagrams.

title: Tidy data and reshaping
text:
Module 1 · Lesson 3 of 14 Week 18 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The plant’s historian, the system that records every sensor, exports its data like a spreadsheet: one row per time stamp, one column per sensor. That’s easy to read by eye, but awkward to plot or summarize. The lab’s system does the opposite: one long column of results, with another column saying what each result is. The same information can be laid out in many ways, and this lesson is about the layout that makes analysis easy, called tidy data, and the tools that reshape data into it.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Tidy data and reshaping
text:
What is tidy data?
Tidy data follows three simple rules:

Each variable is a column.
Each observation is a row.
Each value is a cell.

Here’s the same information, from two reactors at two times, in three layouts:

WideLongTidy





timestamp
R1_temp_C
R1_press_bar
R2_temp_C
R2_press_bar

4.72

29.3

…

R1

R1

The wide layout hides a variable, the reactor, inside the column names. The tidy one has a column for each real variable: the time, the reactor, the temperature and the pressure. Each row is one observation: one reactor at one moment. With data like that, every dplyr verb and every ggplot works directly.
What counts as “a variable” depends on your question, and that’s fine. The long layout is often the most useful working form, because it’s easy to filter, group and plot.

title: Tidy data and reshaping
text:
Meet the sensor log
Here’s the historian’s export for 10 March 2026: a reading every 5 minutes from both reactors.

sensor <- read.csv("data/sensor_log.csv")
dim(sensor)
#> [1] 288   5
head(sensor, 3)
#>             timestamp R1_temp_C R1_press_bar R2_temp_C R2_press_bar
#> 1 2026-03-10 00:00:00      29.6         1.06      27.1         1.01
#> 2 2026-03-10 00:05:00      28.3         1.02      27.4         1.02
#> 3 2026-03-10 00:10:00      26.9         1.00      28.8         1.00

Each column name packs three pieces of information: the reactor, the variable and the unit. R2_temp_C means “reactor R2, temperature, in °C”. That’s very common in instrument data, and very untidy. Let’s fix it.

title: Tidy data and reshaping
text:
pivot_longer(): wide to long
pivot_longer() takes a set of columns and stacks them into two: one column for the old column names, and one for the values:

long <- sensor |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -timestamp, names_to = "tag", values_to = "value")
long
#> # A tibble: 1,152 × 3
#>    timestamp           tag          value
#>    <chr>               <chr>        <dbl>
#>  1 2026-03-10 00:00:00 R1_temp_C    29.6 
#>  2 2026-03-10 00:00:00 R1_press_bar  1.06
#>  3 2026-03-10 00:00:00 R2_temp_C    27.1 
#>  4 2026-03-10 00:00:00 R2_press_bar  1.01
#>  5 2026-03-10 00:05:00 R1_temp_C    28.3 
#>  6 2026-03-10 00:05:00 R1_press_bar  1.02
#>  7 2026-03-10 00:05:00 R2_temp_C    27.4 
#>  8 2026-03-10 00:05:00 R2_press_bar  1.02
#>  9 2026-03-10 00:10:00 R1_temp_C    26.9 
#> 10 2026-03-10 00:10:00 R1_press_bar  1   
#> # ℹ 1,142 more rows

cols = -timestamp means “every column except the time stamp”. The result has 4 rows for every original row: 288 × 4 = 1,152.
The tag column still packs three things together. pivot_longer() can split the names as it goes. Give names_to one name per piece, and say what separates them with names_sep:

long <- sensor |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -timestamp, names_to = c("reactor", "variable", "unit"),
               names_sep = "_", values_to = "value")
head(long, 4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>   timestamp           reactor variable unit  value
#>   <chr>               <chr>   <chr>    <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 2026-03-10 00:00:00 R1      temp     C     29.6 
#> 2 2026-03-10 00:00:00 R1      press    bar    1.06
#> 3 2026-03-10 00:00:00 R2      temp     C     27.1 
#> 4 2026-03-10 00:00:00 R2      press    bar    1.01

Now every piece of information has its own column, and you can plot the whole day in one go:

long |>
  filter(value < 500) |>                 # drop one sensor glitch (Lesson 11)
  mutate(timestamp = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = timestamp, y = value, color = reactor)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(R1 = "#C2416C", R2 = "#2a78d6")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, color = "Reactor") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








You can see both batches of the day: B18 on reactor R2 in the morning, and B17 on R1 in the afternoon. Temperature and pressure rise together, hold, then fall.
Your turn. Pivot the sensor log longer, splitting the names into reactor, variable and unit, and count how many rows you get for each reactor.









names_to needs one new column name for each piece of the old names: c("reactor", "variable", "unit").


library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
sensor <- read.csv("data/sensor_log.csv")
sensor |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -timestamp, names_to = c("reactor", "variable", "unit"),
               names_sep = "_", values_to = "value") |>
  count(reactor)
576 rows per reactor: 288 time stamps, two variables each.

title: Tidy data and reshaping
text:
pivot_wider(): long to wide
pivot_wider() does the opposite: it spreads one column of values out across several new columns, named after another column. The lab results are long, with one row per measurement:

lab <- read.csv("data/lab_results.csv")
head(lab[, c("batch_id", "analyte", "value", "retest")], 4)
#>   batch_id analyte value retest
#> 1      B02  purity  98.7  FALSE
#> 2      B02   water 154.0  FALSE
#> 3      B02   color  13.0  FALSE
#> 4      B01  purity  98.9  FALSE

To compare analytes batch by batch, it helps to have one row per batch, with a column for each analyte:

lab_wide <- lab |>
  filter(!retest) |>
  select(batch_id, analyte, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = analyte, values_from = value)
lab_wide
#> # A tibble: 40 × 4
#>    batch_id purity water color
#>    <chr>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1 B02        98.7   154    13
#>  2 B01        98.9   184    21
#>  3 B03        99.6   221    15
#>  4 B04        98.8   219    21
#>  5 B06        98.9   174    14
#>  6 B05        99.2   221    11
#>  7 B08        97.7   195    32
#>  8 B07        99.2   217    17
#>  9 B09        98.6   154    21
#> 10 B10        97.6   238    22
#> # ℹ 30 more rows

names_from says which column supplies the new column names, and values_from which supplies the values. Look at batches B12 and B33: they get NA for water, because those two water tests were never run. pivot_wider() fills any missing combination with NA.






WarningDuplicates make lists



Why filter out the re-tests first? Without that, some batches have two purity results, so pivot_wider() doesn’t know which one to put in the cell. It warns you, and puts both into a list-column. Decide what you want first: the first test, the re-test, or their mean (values_fn = mean).


Your turn. Make a wide table of the re-tests only, with one row per batch and a column for each analyte.









The new column names come from analyte, and the values from value: names_from = analyte, values_from = value.


library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
lab <- read.csv("data/lab_results.csv")
lab |>
  filter(retest) |>
  select(batch_id, analyte, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = analyte, values_from = value)
Only purity was ever re-tested, so there’s just one analyte column.

title: Tidy data and reshaping
text:
Splitting and combining columns
Sometimes one column holds two variables. A time stamp holds a date and a time, and a sample code like B18-S2 holds a batch and a sample number. separate_wider_delim() splits a column at a delimiter:

samples <- data.frame(code = c("B18-S1", "B18-S2", "B07-S1"))
samples |>
  separate_wider_delim(code, delim = "-", names = c("batch_id", "sample"))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   batch_id sample
#>   <chr>    <chr> 
#> 1 B18      S1    
#> 2 B18      S2    
#> 3 B07      S1

unite() goes the other way, gluing columns together with a separator:

long |>
  unite("tag", reactor, variable, sep = "_") |>
  head(3)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   timestamp           tag      unit  value
#>   <chr>               <chr>    <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 2026-03-10 00:00:00 R1_temp  C     29.6 
#> 2 2026-03-10 00:00:00 R1_press bar    1.06
#> 3 2026-03-10 00:00:00 R2_temp  C     27.1

(Older code uses separate(), which still works. separate_wider_delim() is its newer, stricter replacement.)
Your turn. Split the sensor log’s timestamp into a date column and a time column. They’re separated by a space.









The delimiter is a single space: delim = " ".


library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
sensor <- read.csv("data/sensor_log.csv")
sensor |>
  separate_wider_delim(timestamp, delim = " ", names = c("date", "time"))
For real date and time work, Lesson 10’s lubridate package is better. But splitting is often all you need.

title: Tidy data and reshaping
section: Long data is easy to summarize
text:
Long data is easy to summarize
With data in long form, a summary for every reactor and variable is one pipeline:

long |>
  group_by(reactor, variable) |>
  summarise(max = max(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   reactor variable     max
#>   <chr>   <chr>      <dbl>
#> 1 R1      press       4.72
#> 2 R1      temp     1000.  
#> 3 R2      press       4.77
#> 4 R2      temp      167.

A maximum temperature of 999.9 °C on R1? That’s not a runaway reactor: it’s a sensor glitch, a single bogus reading. Real data is full of surprises like this, and Lesson 11 shows how to catch them systematically. For now, notice how quickly the long layout let you spot it.
Your turn. Find the highest real temperature on each reactor: pivot longer, keep only the temperatures below 500 °C, then summarize.









Add a second condition inside filter(): value < 500.


library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
sensor <- read.csv("data/sensor_log.csv")
sensor |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -timestamp, names_to = c("reactor", "variable", "unit"),
               names_sep = "_", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(variable == "temp", value < 500) |>
  group_by(reactor) |>
  summarise(max_temp = max(value, na.rm = TRUE))
About 175 °C on R1 (batch B17) and 167 °C on R2 (batch B18).

title: Tidy data and reshaping
text:
Which layout when?







Layout
Best for




Long (one row per measurement)
Plotting with ggplot2, summarizing by group, storing in a database


Tidy (one column per variable)
Most analysis: dplyr pipelines, models, correlations


Wide (one column per group or time)
Tables for people to read, matrices, some statistical methods



You’ll move between them constantly. That’s normal, and now it’s easy.

title: Tidy data and reshaping
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Straight to tidy. Turn the sensor log into the tidy layout in one step: columns timestamp, reactor, temp_C and press_bar, with one row per reactor per time stamp. pivot_longer() has a special name for this, ".value", which means “use this part of the old column name as a new column name”.









names_pattern is a regular expression with two groups in parentheses: one for the reactor, and one for the rest. "(R[12])_(.*)" captures R1 or R2, then everything after the first underscore.


library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
sensor <- read.csv("data/sensor_log.csv")
sensor |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -timestamp, names_to = c("reactor", ".value"),
               names_pattern = "(R[12])_(.*)")
Each old name like R2_temp_C is split into R2, which goes into the reactor column, and temp_C, which becomes a column name. 576 rows, one per reactor per time stamp.




Challenge 2 · A stability study. A lab tests how an impurity grows while three samples sit in storage. The results came as a wide table, with one column per week. Pivot it into long form with a numeric week column and an impurity_pct column.









names_prefix removes text from the start of every name: here "wk". Then names_transform = as.numeric turns what’s left, like "8", into a number.


library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
stability <- data.frame(sample = c("S1", "S2", "S3"),
                        wk0 = c(0.10, 0.12, 0.09), wk2 = c(0.14, 0.15, 0.13),
                        wk4 = c(0.19, 0.21, 0.17), wk8 = c(0.29, 0.30, 0.27))
stability |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -sample, names_to = "week", values_to = "impurity_pct",
               names_prefix = "wk", names_transform = as.numeric)
With a numeric week, you could now plot impurity against time, or fit a line to it (Module 2).

title: Tidy data and reshaping
text:
Quick quiz

1. Which of these is a rule of tidy data?

Each variable is a column
Each table has as few rows as possible
Every column is numeric


Tidy data has one column per variable, one row per observation and one value per cell.



2. A table has the columns batch_id, Jan, Feb and Mar, holding monthly yields. What’s untidy about it?

The month is a variable, but it’s hidden in the column names
It has too few columns
Nothing: it’s tidy


Pivoting longer would give the columns batch_id, month and yield.



3. Which function turns many columns into two: one of names, one of values?

pivot_longer()
pivot_wider()
unite()


pivot_longer() makes data longer. pivot_wider() spreads it out into more columns.



4. You run pivot_wider(), and it warns that values aren’t uniquely identified. What does that mean?

The data has missing values
Some combinations appear more than once, like a batch with two purity results
The column names are invalid


Decide how to handle the duplicates first: filter them, or summarize them with values_fn.



5. What does pivot_wider() put in a cell when that combination doesn’t exist in the long data?

NA
0
It drops the row


Missing combinations become NA, like the two water tests that were never run. You can choose a different filler with values_fill.



6. Which layout is usually easiest for plotting several groups with ggplot2?

Long, with a column saying which group each value belongs to
Wide, with one column per group
It makes no difference


In long data, the group is a variable you can map to color or facets.

title: Tidy data and reshaping
text:
Wrap-up
You can reshape anything now. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Tidy data: each variable a column, each observation a row, each value a cell.
Wide to long: pivot_longer(), with names_sep, names_pattern, names_prefix and names_transform to clean up the old names as you go.
Long to wide: pivot_wider(), with names_from and values_from. Duplicates make list-columns, and missing combinations make NAs.
Split and glue: separate_wider_delim() splits a column; unite() combines columns.
Choose the layout for the job: long for plotting and grouping, tidy for analysis, wide for people to read.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Work in your plant-study project. Download sensor_log.csv and lab_results.csv into data-raw/.

Tidy the historian. Write R/02_tidy_sensors.R, which reads the sensor log, makes it tidy with the .value trick, converts timestamp to a date-time with as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"), and writes data/sensors_tidy.csv.
Plot it. Recreate this lesson’s chart from your tidy file, and save it to output/.
A wide lab table. Make a table with one row per batch and columns for purity, water and color, using the mean of any re-tests (values_fn = mean). Save it as data/lab_wide.csv.
Round trip. Pivot your wide lab table back to long. Do you get the same number of rows you started with? Why not?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Tidy data

Data with one variable per column, one observation per row and one value per cell.

Wide format

A layout with one column per group or time point, such as one column per sensor.

Long format

A layout with one row per measurement, and columns saying what each value is.

pivot_longer()

Stacks many columns into a column of names and a column of values.

pivot_wider()

Spreads a column of values into many columns, named after another column.

.value

In pivot_longer(), the part of the old column names that should become new column names.

List-column

A column whose cells hold lists. pivot_wider() makes one when combinations aren’t unique.











NoteWant to read more?






R for Data Science (2e), “Data tidying”. Tidy data and pivoting, with many more examples.
Hadley Wickham, “Tidy Data”, Journal of Statistical Software (2014). The original paper: readable, and full of examples of untidy data in the wild.

title: Reproducible data workflows
text:
Module 1 · Lesson 1 of 14 Week 16 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Welcome to Module 1! In Module 0, every analysis was a single file. Real projects aren’t like that. A study of the pilot plant might involve the lab’s spreadsheets, the batch records, a sensor log, a cleaned dataset, a dozen scripts, twenty figures and a report. Six months later, your supervisor asks: “How exactly did you get that number?” This lesson is about the habits that let you answer in thirty seconds: projects, a sensible folder structure, good file names, reports that rebuild themselves, and version control.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Reproducible data workflows
text:
Why reproducibility matters
An analysis is reproducible when someone else (or you, later) can start from the raw data and get exactly the same results by rerunning your code. That sounds obvious, but it fails all the time. Somebody fixes a typo by hand in a spreadsheet, filters some rows with the mouse, copies a number into a report, and a week later nobody can say which version of the data the report came from.
The cure is a simple rule: every step from raw data to final result is done by code. Raw files are never edited. Cleaning, combining, analyzing and plotting all happen in scripts. If the lab sends a corrected file, you drop it in and rerun everything.
That’s how the rest of this module works too. You’ll meet the pilot plant’s whole data system: the batch records, the lab results, the raw-material lots and their suppliers, the operators, the instruments and a sensor log. All of it is for the same 40 batches you analyzed in Module 0.

title: Reproducible data workflows
text:
Projects and folders
An RStudio project is just a folder with a small .Rproj file in it. When you open the project, RStudio sets the working directory to that folder, so every file path can start from there. One project per analysis, always.
Inside it, a standard structure means you (and everyone you work with) always know where things are:
plant-study/
├── plant-study.Rproj
├── README.md      ← what this project is, and how to run it
├── data-raw/      ← files exactly as you received them. Never edit these!
├── data/          ← cleaned data, written by your scripts
├── R/             ← scripts and functions
├── output/        ← figures and tables, written by your scripts
└── reports/       ← Quarto reports
The split between data-raw/ and data/ is the important part. Raw data is read-only; anything in data/ can be deleted and rebuilt by rerunning the scripts.
The live boxes have a small file system of their own, so you can try this here. dir.create() makes a folder, and list.dirs() lists them:








The data folder already holds a few of the plant’s files, which this lesson uses.
Your turn. Create the folders data-raw, data, R and output with a loop.









Inside the loop, f holds one folder name at a time. Pass it to dir.create().


folders <- c("data-raw", "data", "R", "output")
for (f in folders) {
  dir.create(f, showWarnings = FALSE)
}
list.dirs(recursive = FALSE)
showWarnings = FALSE keeps dir.create() quiet when a folder already exists, like data here.

title: Reproducible data workflows
text:
File paths that work anywhere
A path tells R where a file is. An absolute path starts from the top of the computer, like C:/Users/maya/Desktop/plant-study/data-raw/lab.csv. It works on Maya’s laptop and nowhere else. A relative path starts from the working directory, like data-raw/lab.csv, and works for anyone who opens the project.
So two rules:

Use relative paths, from the project folder.
Never put setwd() in a script. If a script starts with setwd("C:/Users/maya/..."), it breaks on every other computer.

file.path() glues the pieces of a path together with /, which works on Windows, Mac and Linux alike:

file.path("data-raw", "lab", "results.csv")
#> [1] "data-raw/lab/results.csv"
basename("data-raw/lab/results.csv")    # just the file name
#> [1] "results.csv"
dirname("data-raw/lab/results.csv")     # just the folder
#> [1] "data-raw/lab"
tools::file_ext("data-raw/lab/results.csv")
#> [1] "csv"







WarningBackslashes are a trap



Windows shows paths with backslashes, like C:\new\test.csv, but in R a backslash starts a special character: "\n" is a new line and "\t" is a tab! Use forward slashes ("C:/new/test.csv"), which R understands on Windows too, or better, file.path().


list.files() lists the files in a folder, and its pattern argument picks out names matching a pattern. Here, names ending in .csv:








The pattern is a regular expression: \\. means a real dot, and $ means “at the end”. Lesson 10 covers these properly.
Your turn. Build the path data-raw/lab/results_2026-03.csv with file.path().









Give file.path() the three pieces as separate arguments: the two folders, then the file name.


file.path("data-raw", "lab", "results_2026-03.csv")

title: Reproducible data workflows
text:
Naming things
Good file names are a gift to your future self. They follow three principles:

Machine-readable. No spaces, no accents, no special characters. Use letters, numbers, - and _.
Human-readable. Say what’s in the file: lab_results_raw.csv, not data2_final_FINAL.csv.
Sorted sensibly. Put dates first in the form YYYY-MM-DD (the ISO 8601 standard), and pad numbers with zeros.

Watch what happens when numbers aren’t padded:

sort(c("batch_B1.csv", "batch_B2.csv", "batch_B10.csv"))
#> [1] "batch_B1.csv"  "batch_B10.csv" "batch_B2.csv"
sort(c("batch_B01.csv", "batch_B02.csv", "batch_B10.csv"))
#> [1] "batch_B01.csv" "batch_B02.csv" "batch_B10.csv"

Text sorts character by character, so B10 comes before B2. That’s why the plant numbers its batches B01 to B40. Dates have the same problem: 05-03-2026 and 03-05-2026 sort wrongly and mean different days in Europe and the US, while 2026-03-05 is unambiguous and sorts correctly.
sprintf() builds names like these. In its template, %02d means “a whole number, padded with zeros to 2 digits”, and %s means “a piece of text”:

sprintf("batch_B%02d_%s.csv", c(7, 18), "2026-03-10")
#> [1] "batch_B07_2026-03-10.csv" "batch_B18_2026-03-10.csv"

The same thinking applies to variable names: lower case, words joined by underscores, and units in the name, like temp_C and residence_min. Lesson 11 shows a function that cleans up messy names automatically.
Your turn. Create the file names sample_01.csv, sample_02.csv, … up to sample_12.csv, with sprintf().









The template is "sample_%02d.csv": %02d pads each number to two digits.


sprintf("sample_%02d.csv", 1:12)

title: Reproducible data workflows
section: Raw data in, clean data out
text:
Raw data in, clean data out
Here’s the whole idea in miniature. A script reads a raw file, does its work, and writes the result to a new file. It never overwrites the raw data:

lab <- read.csv("data/lab_results.csv")
purity <- lab[lab$analyte == "purity" & !lab$retest, ]
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
write.csv(purity, "output/purity_first_tests.csv", row.names = FALSE)
nrow(read.csv("output/purity_first_tests.csv"))
#> [1] 40

row.names = FALSE stops write.csv() adding a column of row numbers, which you almost never want. Because the output is made by code, it can always be deleted and rebuilt. That’s the whole point.

A handy habit: number your scripts in the order they run, like R/01_import.R, R/02_clean.R, R/03_analysis.R. Then anyone can rebuild your project by running them from top to bottom.

Your turn. Read data/lab_results.csv, keep only the water results, write them to output/water.csv (without row names), then read the new file back and return its number of rows.









The analyte is called "water", and the file to write is "output/water.csv".


dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
lab <- read.csv("data/lab_results.csv")
water <- lab[lab$analyte == "water", ]
write.csv(water, "output/water.csv", row.names = FALSE)
nrow(read.csv("output/water.csv"))
38 water results. Two batches were never tested for water, which Lesson 5 tracks down.

title: Reproducible data workflows
text:
Reports that rebuild themselves
You wrote a Quarto report in the Module 0 project. That’s the last piece of a reproducible workflow: the report contains the code, so every table, figure and number is recomputed whenever you render it. Quarto can even put a number from R right into a sentence: writing `r round(mean(yield), 1)` in your text prints the current mean yield there, and it updates whenever the data changes.
So never copy numbers from R into a report by hand. Copied numbers go stale, and stale numbers are how embarrassing mistakes end up in final reports.

title: Reproducible data workflows
text:
Version control with Git
Have you ever had files called report_v2.docx, report_v3_final.docx and report_v3_final_REALLY.docx? Version control solves that properly. Git, the most popular version-control system, keeps the complete history of a project folder:

A repository is a project folder whose history Git tracks.
A commit is a snapshot of the files at one moment, with a short message saying what changed, like “Remove duplicate lab results”.
The history is the list of commits. You can see exactly what changed between any two, and go back to any of them.
A remote, such as a repository on GitHub, is a copy on a server. You push your commits to it and pull other people’s.

RStudio has a Git pane built in, with buttons for committing, pushing and pulling, so you hardly ever need the command line. Commit whenever you finish a small piece of work, with a message that would make sense to a stranger.






ImportantSome things should never go into a repository



Passwords, API keys and confidential data don’t belong in Git, especially on a public site like GitHub: once pushed, they’re very hard to remove from the history. List files Git should ignore in a file called .gitignore. Very large data files are usually kept out too.

title: Reproducible data workflows
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Read a whole folder. Read every CSV file in the data folder, and return a named vector with the number of rows in each file.









lapply() applies a function to every element: here, read.csv to every file path. Then sapply(tables, nrow) counts the rows of each table.


files <- list.files("data", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
tables <- lapply(files, read.csv)
names(tables) <- basename(files)
sapply(tables, nrow)
full.names = TRUE keeps the folder in each path, so read.csv() can find the files.




Challenge 2 · Tidy up column names. A spreadsheet has the column names below. Turn them into clean variable names: lower case, % written as pct, and every run of other characters replaced by a single underscore, with no underscore at the start or end. You should get batch_id, temp_c, pressure_bar and yield_pct.









You want a pattern meaning “one or more characters that aren’t a lower-case letter or a digit”. In a regular expression, that’s "[^a-z0-9]+".


messy <- c("Batch ID", "Temp (C)", "Pressure (bar)", "Yield %")
x <- tolower(messy)
x <- gsub("%", "pct", x, fixed = TRUE)
x <- gsub("[^a-z0-9]+", "_", x)
x <- gsub("^_|_$", "", x)
x
The last line removes underscores at the start (^_) or end (_$), which is where (C) would otherwise leave one.

title: Reproducible data workflows
text:
Quick quiz

1. The lab sends you a spreadsheet with an obvious typo. What should you do?

Fix it in the spreadsheet and save it
Keep the raw file unchanged, and fix the typo with code, with a comment saying why
Delete the row with the typo


Raw data stays read-only. A fix in code is documented and repeatable, and it can be undone.



2. Which path will work when a colleague opens your project on their computer?

"data-raw/lab_results.csv"
"C:/Users/maya/Desktop/plant-study/data-raw/lab_results.csv"
Both


A relative path starts from the project folder, wherever that is. An absolute path only exists on one computer.



3. Which file name sorts correctly by date and means the same thing everywhere?

05-03-2026_lab.csv
2026-03-05_lab.csv
March 5 2026 lab.csv


ISO 8601 dates (year, month, day) sort correctly as text, and nobody mixes up the day and the month.



4. What does a Git commit record?

A snapshot of the project’s files, with a message describing the change
Only the files you deleted
A backup on GitHub


A commit is a saved snapshot in the project’s history. It only reaches GitHub when you push it.



5. What should never go into a public GitHub repository?

Your R scripts
A README file
Passwords and confidential data


Anything pushed to a public repository can be seen, and copied, by anyone. List sensitive files in .gitignore.



6. Why build reports with Quarto instead of pasting numbers into a word processor?

Quarto reports look nicer
Every number and figure is recomputed from the data whenever you render, so nothing goes stale
Word processors can’t show tables


Reports built by code stay in sync with the data. Pasted numbers quietly go out of date.

title: Reproducible data workflows
text:
Wrap-up
Your projects are about to get a lot tidier. Here’s what you can do now:

Work reproducibly: every step from raw data to result is done by code, and raw files are never edited.
Organize: one RStudio project per analysis, with folders like data-raw/, data/, R/ and output/.
Point to files well: relative paths, built with file.path(), and no setwd() in scripts.
Name things well: machine-readable, human-readable, ISO dates and zero-padded numbers.
Track your work: Git keeps a history of commits, and GitHub keeps a copy on a server. Secrets stay out.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)






Make the project. Create a new RStudio project called plant-study (File → New Project → New Directory). Add the folders data-raw, data, R, output and reports, and a README.md saying in two sentences what the project is for.
Get the data. Download batches.csv and lab_results.csv into data-raw/.
Write a pipeline. In R/01_clean.R, read both raw files, keep the first-test purity results, and write them to data/purity.csv. In R/02_summary.R, read data/purity.csv and save a histogram to output/purity_hist.png with ggsave().
Start version control. Install the usethis package and run usethis::use_git(). Restart RStudio when it asks, then open the Git pane, tick your files and make your first commit, with the message “Set up the plant study project”.
Prove it’s reproducible. Delete everything in data/ and output/, then run your scripts in order. Everything should come back, exactly the same.
Optional: GitHub. If you’d like an online copy, make a free GitHub account and follow Happy Git and GitHub for the useR (below) to connect it to RStudio.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Reproducible

An analysis that anyone can rerun from the raw data, with exactly the same results.

RStudio project

A folder with an .Rproj file. Opening it sets R’s working directory to that folder.

Relative path

A file path that starts from the working directory, such as data-raw/lab.csv.

Raw data

Data exactly as you received it. It’s kept read-only, and all changes are made by code.

ISO 8601

The international date format, YYYY-MM-DD, which sorts correctly and can’t be misread.

Version control

Keeping the full history of a project’s files, so you can see changes and go back to any version.

Git, repository and commit

Git is a version-control system. A repository is a folder it tracks, and a commit is one saved snapshot.

.gitignore

A file listing the files and folders Git should never track.











NoteWant to read more?






R for Data Science (2e), “Workflow: scripts and projects”. Projects, paths and the working directory.
Jenny Bryan, Happy Git and GitHub for the useR. The friendliest guide to installing Git and connecting RStudio to GitHub.
Crystal Lewis, Data Management in Large-Scale Education Research. Practical chapters on folder structures, file naming and documentation, useful far beyond education.

title: Hypothesis testing
text:
Module 0 · Lesson 13 of 14 Week 13 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Is the reactor really running below its 60% yield target? Does the night shift really get better results? Did cleaning the heat exchanger actually help? Data always contain some pattern, because random variation creates patterns all by itself. A hypothesis test asks whether the pattern you see is too strong to be explained by chance alone. This lesson covers the logic of testing, the tests you’ll use most often, and, just as important, the ways tests get misused.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Hypothesis testing
text:
The logic of a test
A hypothesis test works like a criminal trial. The defendant is presumed innocent, and the prosecution must present evidence strong enough to make innocence implausible. If it can’t, the verdict is “not guilty”, which isn’t the same as “innocent”.

State two hypotheses. The null hypothesis H_0 is the skeptical “nothing is going on” position: no difference, no effect, the supplier is telling the truth. The alternative hypothesis H_A is what you’re looking for evidence of.
Choose a test statistic: a number that measures how far the data are from what H_0 predicts.
Find its distribution if H_0 were true, called the null distribution, by theory or by simulation.
Compute the p-value: how likely a result at least as extreme as yours would be, if H_0 were true.
Conclude in context. A small p-value is evidence against H_0.

Here’s an example. A supplier promises that only 5% of their drums leak. You inspect 100 drums and find 11 leaky ones. Bad luck, or is the supplier’s claim wrong?

H_0: the leak rate is p = 0.05, as promised. H_A: it’s higher, p > 0.05.
The test statistic is the number of leaky drums, 11.
If H_0 is true, the count is binomial with n = 100 and p = 0.05, so we’d expect about 5.
You only care whether the rate is worse than promised, so “at least as extreme” means 11 or more.


1 - pbinom(10, size = 100, prob = 0.05)                          # P(X >= 11)
#> [1] 0.01147241
binom.test(11, 100, p = 0.05, alternative = "greater")$p.value  # the same, in one step
#> [1] 0.01147241

If the supplier were telling the truth, 11 or more leaky drums would turn up only about 1% of the time. That’s strong evidence that the true leak rate is higher than 5%. A simulation tells the same story:

set.seed(13)
null_counts <- rbinom(10000, size = 100, prob = 0.05)
mean(null_counts >= 11)
#> [1] 0.0124

Your turn. In a second shipment of 100 drums you find 8 leaky ones. Use binom.test() to get the one-sided p-value for the same hypotheses.









Change the 11 to 8: binom.test(8, 100, p = 0.05, alternative = "greater")$p.value.


binom.test(8, 100, p = 0.05, alternative = "greater")$p.value
About 0.13. Eight leaky drums can easily happen by chance when the true rate is 5%, so this shipment gives no real evidence against the supplier.

title: Hypothesis testing
text:
p-values
The p-value is the probability, computed assuming H_0 is true, of getting a result at least as extreme as the one you observed. A small p-value means the data would be surprising if H_0 were true.
Many fields compare the p-value with a significance level \alpha chosen in advance, usually 0.05. If p \le \alpha, you reject H_0 and call the result statistically significant. If p > \alpha, you fail to reject H_0. Not “accept”: absence of evidence isn’t evidence of absence.
The p-value is easy to misread. It is not:

the probability that H_0 is true;
the probability that the result is “due to chance”;
a measure of how big or important an effect is.

In 2016, the American Statistical Association issued a formal statement warning against exactly these misreadings, and against treating 0.05 as a magic line. Report the p-value itself, together with an estimate of the effect and its confidence interval.

title: Hypothesis testing
section: A test by simulation: the permutation test
text:
A test by simulation: the permutation test
Batches with 3 or more alarms seem to have much lower yields:

d <- batches[!is.na(batches$alarms), ]
many <- d$alarms >= 3
tapply(d$yield_pct, many, mean)
#>    FALSE     TRUE 
#> 59.21143 44.20000
observed <- mean(d$yield_pct[many]) - mean(d$yield_pct[!many])
observed
#> [1] -15.01143

A gap of 15 points! But only 4 batches had that many alarms. Could a gap like this arise by chance, with alarms having nothing to do with yield? If H_0 is true, the “many alarms” labels are just arbitrary tags, so shuffling them among the batches should produce gaps as big as ours fairly often. Shuffle 10,000 times and see:

set.seed(13)
null_diffs <- replicate(10000, {
  shuffled <- sample(many)        # the same labels, randomly reassigned
  mean(d$yield_pct[shuffled]) - mean(d$yield_pct[!shuffled])
})
mean(abs(null_diffs) >= abs(observed))   # two-sided p-value
#> [1] 0.0034



Show the code
ggplot(data.frame(diff = null_diffs), aes(x = diff)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#F4C0D1", color = NA) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(observed, -observed), color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Differences in mean yield after shuffling the alarm labels",
       subtitle = "Pink lines: the observed difference and its mirror image",
       x = "Difference in mean yield (3+ alarms minus fewer)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









This is a permutation test. It needs no formulas and no normality assumption, only the idea that under H_0 the labels don’t matter. That makes it perfect for small groups like these 4 batches, where a normality assumption would be impossible to check. Only about 3 shuffles in 1,000 give a gap as big as the real one, so that’s strong evidence that many-alarm batches really do yield less.
Even so, this is observational data, so it doesn’t prove that the alarms cause the low yields. A fouled heat exchanger or a bad lot of raw material could cause both. To show cause and effect, you’d need a designed experiment, which Module 2 covers.

title: Hypothesis testing
text:
t-tests
The t distribution from the last lesson gives formula-based tests for means.

One-sample t-test
The plant’s target yield is 60%, and our 40 batches average 57.6%. Is the process really below target? The test statistic counts how many standard errors \bar{x} is from the target value \mu_0:

t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}} ,

and under H_0 it follows a t distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom.

x <- batches$yield_pct
t_stat <- (mean(x) - 60) / (sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)))
t_stat
#> [1] -1.526084
2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), df = length(x) - 1)   # two-sided p-value
#> [1] 0.1350589
t.test(x, mu = 60)
#> 
#>  One Sample t-test
#> 
#> data:  x
#> t = -1.5261, df = 39, p-value = 0.1351
#> alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 60
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  54.52947 60.76553
#> sample estimates:
#> mean of x 
#>   57.6475

Now you can read the whole t.test() output: the t statistic, the degrees of freedom, the p-value, the alternative hypothesis, the confidence interval and the estimate. With p = 0.135, there isn’t convincing evidence that the process is off target: the shortfall could easily be batch-to-batch noise. Notice that the 95% interval, 54.5% to 60.8%, contains 60. Two-sided tests and confidence intervals always agree like this: the interval excludes \mu_0 exactly when p < 0.05.
If, before seeing the data, you only cared about one direction, you can use a one-sided test with alternative = "greater" or "less", as with the drums. Choosing the direction after looking at the data is cheating, because it halves the p-value.


Two-sample t-test
To compare the means of two independent groups, t.test() takes a formula, outcome ~ group. Do the day and night shifts get different yields?

t.test(yield_pct ~ shift, data = batches)
#> 
#>  Welch Two Sample t-test
#> 
#> data:  yield_pct by shift
#> t = -0.63222, df = 28.328, p-value = 0.5323
#> alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group day and group night is not equal to 0
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  -8.710029  4.599928
#> sample estimates:
#>   mean in group day mean in group night 
#>            56.72273            58.77778

The night shift averaged about 2 points more, but p = 0.53: a difference like that is very common by chance alone. There’s no evidence that the shifts differ. By default, R runs Welch’s t-test, which doesn’t assume the two groups have equal variances. That’s the safe choice.


Paired t-test
Sometimes the measurements come in pairs: the same heat exchanger before and after cleaning, or the same sample measured on two instruments. Then you analyze the differences within each pair. Here are some (made-up) heat-transfer coefficients, in W/(m²·K), for 8 exchangers before and after cleaning:

before <- c(410, 385, 450, 398, 420, 372, 440, 405)
after <- c(452, 401, 489, 431, 447, 398, 472, 438)
after - before
#> [1] 42 16 39 33 27 26 32 33
t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE)
#> 
#>  Paired t-test
#> 
#> data:  after and before
#> t = 10.816, df = 7, p-value = 1.273e-05
#> alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  24.22285 37.77715
#> sample estimates:
#> mean difference 
#>              31

Cleaning improved the coefficient by 31 W/(m²·K) on average, and the p-value is tiny. Now watch what happens if you wrongly treat the before and after measurements as two independent groups:

t.test(after, before)$p.value
#> [1] 0.05163782

The p-value is far larger, because the exchangers differ a lot from each other (from 372 to 450 before cleaning). Pairing removes those differences, leaving a much clearer view of the cleaning effect. Use a paired test whenever the design pairs the data.






Your turn. Is the mean purity of the batches different from 99%? Return the p-value of a one-sample t-test.









t.test(x, mu = 99)$p.value, with x the purity column.


t.test(batches$purity_pct, mu = 99)$p.value




Your turn. Compare the purity of the batches that ran hotter than 185 °C with the rest, using a Welch two-sample t-test. Return the p-value. (The two batches with no temperature are removed for you.)









t.test(purity_pct ~ hot, data = h)$p.value


h <- batches[!is.na(batches$temp_C), ]
h$hot <- h$temp_C > 185
t.test(purity_pct ~ hot, data = h)$p.value
About 0.00005. Hot batches average 98.3% purity against 99.1% for the rest, and that gap is far too big to be chance.




Your turn. Six samples were each measured on two instruments, an old one and a new one. Is there a systematic difference between them? Run a paired t-test and return the p-value.









Give t.test() both vectors and paired = TRUE, since each sample was measured twice.


old <- c(5.12, 4.87, 6.03, 5.55, 4.98, 5.71)
new <- c(5.20, 4.92, 6.14, 5.59, 5.07, 5.78)
t.test(new, old, paired = TRUE)$p.value
About 0.001: the new instrument reads about 0.07 units higher, consistently. An unpaired test would give p = 0.79 and miss this completely, because the samples differ from each other far more than the instruments do.

title: Hypothesis testing
text:
Errors and power
A test can go wrong in two ways:









H_0 is true
H_0 is false




Reject H_0
Type I error (false positive), probability \alpha
Correct: the test detected the effect


Don’t reject H_0
Correct
Type II error (false negative), probability \beta



The significance level \alpha is the Type I error rate you accept. The power of a test, 1 - \beta, is the probability of rejecting H_0 when it’s false: the chance of detecting a real effect. Power increases with:

a larger sample,
a larger true effect,
less variability in the data,
a larger \alpha, at the cost of more false positives.

power.t.test() computes the power of a two-sample t-test, or the sample size needed for a given power. Say a new catalyst really raises the yield by 5 points, and yields vary with an SD of 10. How many trial batches should you run with each catalyst?

power.t.test(n = 20, delta = 5, sd = 10)$power    # with 20 batches per catalyst
#> [1] 0.3377084
power.t.test(power = 0.80, delta = 5, sd = 10)$n  # batches per catalyst for 80% power
#> [1] 63.76576

With 20 batches each, the trial would miss a real 5-point improvement about two times in three! You’d need about 64 per catalyst for 80% power, the usual target. Underpowered studies are a real problem: they usually miss true effects, and when they do find one, its estimated size tends to be exaggerated.
Your turn. The same catalyst trial runs 30 batches with each catalyst. What’s its power?









power.t.test(n = ..., delta = ..., sd = ...)$power, where n is the size of each group.


power.t.test(n = 30, delta = 5, sd = 10)$power
About 48%: this trial would miss the real improvement about half the time.




Your turn: false positives. Simulate 2,000 two-sample t-tests where H_0 is true: both groups of 15 come from the same normal distribution. What proportion of the p-values are below 0.05?









The proportion of TRUEs in p_values < 0.05.


set.seed(11)
p_values <- replicate(2000, t.test(rnorm(15), rnorm(15))$p.value)
mean(p_values < 0.05)
About 5%: when H_0 is true, the test rejects it at the rate \alpha. Try hist(p_values). When H_0 is true, p-values are uniformly distributed!

title: Hypothesis testing
text:
Chi-square tests for counts

Goodness of fit
A plant has four identical pumps. Over a year, they fail 12, 7, 5 and 16 times. Are some pumps worse than others, or is this just chance?

fails <- c(12, 7, 5, 16)
expected <- rep(sum(fails) / 4, 4)
sum((fails - expected)^2 / expected)   # the chi-square statistic
#> [1] 7.4
chisq.test(fails)
#> 
#>  Chi-squared test for given probabilities
#> 
#> data:  fails
#> X-squared = 7.4, df = 3, p-value = 0.06018

The chi-square statistic, \chi^2 = \sum (O - E)^2 / E, adds up the squared gaps between the observed counts O and the counts expected under H_0, E. Under H_0, it follows a chi-square distribution with (number of categories − 1) degrees of freedom. Here p = 0.06: suggestive, but not quite significant at the 5% level. A sensible engineer would keep a close eye on pump 4, and collect another year of data.


Test of independence
Are two categorical variables related? Here’s on-spec against shift:

spec_shift <- table(batches$shift, batches$on_spec)
spec_shift
#>        
#>         FALSE TRUE
#>   day       6   16
#>   night     3   15
chisq.test(spec_shift)
#> Warning in chisq.test(spec_shift): Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect
#> 
#>  Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction
#> 
#> data:  spec_shift
#> X-squared = 0.17523, df = 1, p-value = 0.6755

p = 0.68, so there’s no evidence that the shifts differ in their on-spec rates. But notice the warning. The chi-square approximation needs every expected count to be at least about 5, and here two of them are only about 4 and 5, because there are so few off-spec batches. When counts are small, use Fisher’s exact test instead:

fisher.test(spec_shift)$p.value
#> [1] 0.4760915

Same conclusion: no evidence of a difference.


A significant test isn’t the end of the story
Here’s a (made-up) example that every engineer should see once. Two catalysts are tried on two grades of raw material:










High-grade feed
Low-grade feed
Overall




Catalyst X
81 of 87 on spec (93%)
192 of 263 on spec (73%)
273 of 350 (78%)


Catalyst Y
234 of 270 on spec (87%)
55 of 80 on spec (69%)
289 of 350 (83%)



Overall, Y looks better. But X is better on both feeds! X was mostly used on the difficult low-grade feed, and that dragged its overall rate down. A trend that reverses when you split the data into groups is called Simpson’s paradox, and the feed grade here is a confounder. A test on the overall table would correctly say “catalyst and on-spec are related”, but it can’t tell you why. Always think about what else differs between the groups.
Your turn. The plan was to use catalyst A in 40% of batches, and B, C and D in 20% each. The actual counts were 10, 12, 9 and 9. Did the plant stick to the plan? Return the p-value of the chi-square goodness-of-fit test.









chisq.test() takes the planned probabilities through its p argument: p = c(0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2).


counts <- c(10, 12, 9, 9)
chisq.test(counts, p = c(0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2))$p.value
About 0.21. Catalyst A was used less than planned, but not by more than chance could explain.




Your turn. Is being on spec related to running hot (above 185 °C)? The counts are small, so use Fisher’s exact test, and return its p-value.









fisher.test(tab)$p.value


tab <- table(hot = batches$temp_C > 185, on_spec = batches$on_spec)
tab
fisher.test(tab)$p.value
About 0.00008: very strong evidence that running hot and going off spec go together.

title: Hypothesis testing
text:
Significance is not importance

With huge samples, trivial differences become significant. A plant logging a million batches could find a 0.01-point difference in yield with a tiny p-value, and it would mean nothing in practice. Always report the size of the effect, with its confidence interval.
With small samples, important differences may not be significant. “Not significant” often just means “not enough data”.
Many tests, many false positives. Run 20 tests on pure noise at \alpha = 0.05, and you expect about one “significant” result. Testing lots of things and reporting only the significant ones (sometimes called p-hacking) fills the scientific literature with false findings. The simplest fix, the Bonferroni correction, tests each of m hypotheses at level \alpha/m. Module 10 covers better methods.

title: Hypothesis testing
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The multiple-testing trap. An analyst runs 20 t-tests on pure noise. What’s the chance that at least one of them comes out “significant”? Simulate it 300 times.









For one analyst, you want to know whether any of their 20 p-values is below 0.05.


any(p < 0.05)


set.seed(20)
any_false <- replicate(300, {
  p <- replicate(20, t.test(rnorm(10), rnorm(10))$p.value)
  any(p < 0.05)
})
mean(any_false)
About two-thirds! The exact answer is 1 - 0.95^{20} \approx 0.64. Run enough tests and “significant” results are almost guaranteed, even when nothing is going on.




Challenge 2 · Your own permutation test. Do batches with a residence time above 45 minutes have higher yields? Complete the permutation test of the difference in mean yields, and return the two-sided p-value.









Shuffle the labels with sample(long).


The p-value is the proportion of shuffled differences at least as far from zero as the observed one: mean(abs(null_diffs) >= abs(observed)).


long <- batches$residence_min > 45
observed <- mean(batches$yield_pct[long]) - mean(batches$yield_pct[!long])
set.seed(12)
null_diffs <- replicate(10000, {
  shuffled <- sample(long)
  mean(batches$yield_pct[shuffled]) - mean(batches$yield_pct[!shuffled])
})
mean(abs(null_diffs) >= abs(observed))
Only about 4 shuffles in 10,000 give a gap as big as the real 10 points, so the p-value is tiny: very strong evidence that longer residence times go with higher yields.

title: Hypothesis testing
text:
Quick quiz

1. What is a p-value?

The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The probability, if H_0 were true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed
The probability that the result is important


It’s computed assuming H_0, so it can’t be the probability that H_0 is true.



2. A test gives p = 0.40. Which statement is right?

H_0 is proven true
The data don’t give convincing evidence against H_0
There’s a 40% chance H_0 is true


Failing to reject isn’t the same as proving H_0. With more data, a real effect might become clear.



3. What is a Type I error?

Rejecting H_0 when it’s true: a false positive
Failing to reject H_0 when it’s false
Using the wrong test


Its probability is the significance level \alpha. Missing a real effect is a Type II error.



4. Which change increases the power of a test?

A larger sample
A smaller sample
More variable data


More data shrinks the standard error, which makes real effects easier to tell apart from noise.



5. Which design calls for a paired t-test?

The same 10 heat exchangers measured before and after cleaning
10 cleaned exchangers compared with 10 different uncleaned ones
Exchangers from two different plants


Before-and-after measurements on the same units come in pairs, so you analyze the within-unit differences.



6. A study of a million batches finds that a new stirrer raises the yield by 0.01 points, with p < 0.0001. What’s the best summary?

An important discovery
Statistically significant, but far too small to matter in practice
The test must be wrong


With huge samples, tiny effects become significant. Whether an effect matters is a question about its size, not its p-value.

title: Hypothesis testing
text:
Wrap-up
You can now tell real effects from noise. Here’s what you can do:

Set up a test: a null hypothesis H_0 (“nothing going on”) against an alternative H_A.
Read p-values: the probability, if H_0 were true, of a result at least as extreme as yours. Small is evidence against H_0; large doesn’t prove it.
Shuffle: permutation tests build the null distribution by shuffling labels, with no formulas needed.
Compare means: one-sample, two-sample (Welch, R’s default) and paired t-tests. Pair whenever the design pairs the data.
Compare counts: chi-square tests for goodness of fit and independence, or Fisher’s exact test when the counts are small.
Plan for power: larger samples, bigger effects and less noise all help you detect real effects.
Keep perspective: significance isn’t importance, many tests mean many false positives, and confounders can fool any test.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about 75 minutes)





Work in week13.R.

Three questions, three tests. Answer each with the right test, and write each conclusion in a full sentence with the estimate, a confidence interval and the p-value:

Is the mean residence time different from 45 minutes?
Do catalysts C and D differ in mean yield? (subset() the two catalysts first.)
Is the catalyst related to being on spec? (What does R’s warning mean, and what should you do about it?)

Power curves. Use power.t.test() to compute the power for group sizes from 5 to 100, with a difference of 5 and an SD of 10. Plot power against group size, and add a horizontal line at 0.8.
Bonferroni in action. Repeat Challenge 1, but count a result as significant only when p < 0.05/20. What fraction of analysts now find a false positive?
Simpson’s paradox. Rebuild the catalyst X and Y table in R as a three-way table with array(), compute the on-spec rates by feed grade, and plot them. Then explain the paradox in your own words, in a comment.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Null and alternative hypotheses

H_0 is the “no effect” claim being tested; H_A is the claim you’re looking for evidence of.

Test statistic

A number that measures how far the data are from what H_0 predicts.

Null distribution

The distribution of the test statistic if H_0 is true.

p-value

The probability, if H_0 were true, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.

Significance level

The threshold \alpha, chosen in advance, below which you reject H_0.

Permutation test

A test whose null distribution comes from repeatedly shuffling the group labels.

Type I and Type II errors

Rejecting a true H_0 (a false positive), and failing to reject a false H_0 (a false negative).

Power

The probability that a test rejects H_0 when a particular alternative is true.

Chi-square test

A test that compares observed counts with the counts expected under H_0.

Simpson’s paradox

A trend that appears in combined data but reverses within groups, because of a confounder.











NoteWant to read more?






Introduction to Modern Statistics, “Hypothesis testing with randomization”, “Decision errors”, “Inference for comparing paired means” and “Inference for two-way tables”.
Wasserstein and Lazar, “The ASA Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose”, The American Statistician (2016). Short, readable and influential: six principles for using p-values well.

title: Sampling distributions and the CLT
text:
Module 0 · Lesson 11 of 14 Week 11 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The lab analyzes 25 drums from a delivery of 100,000 and finds a mean impurity of 19 ppm. Would another 25 drums give 19 ppm too? Almost certainly not: maybe 24, maybe 31. Every statistic computed from a sample would come out differently with a different sample. This lesson studies that variability itself. It’s the most important idea in this module, because it’s what lets you say how far a sample result is likely to be from the truth. Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests, in the next two lessons, are built directly on it.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Sampling distributions and the CLT
text:
Populations, samples, parameters and statistics
The population is everything you want to learn about: all the drums in a delivery, every bag a filler will ever produce, all the batches a reactor could run. You usually can’t measure all of it, so you measure a sample. A number describing the population is a parameter, and the matching number computed from the sample is a statistic, which estimates it.




Population (parameter)
Sample (statistic)




Mean
\mu
\bar{x}


Standard deviation
\sigma
s


Proportion
p
\hat{p} (“p-hat”)



Parameters are fixed but unknown. Statistics are known, but they vary from sample to sample. For a statistic to tell you about the population, the sample must be random: every member of the population must have a known chance of being chosen, so that no part of it is systematically over- or under-represented.






WarningA huge sample doesn’t fix a biased one



If you take every sample from the top of a tank that hasn’t been mixed, a thousand samples will tell you very precisely about the top layer, and nothing at all about the bottom. Size can’t cure bias. The most famous example is the Literary Digest magazine, which polled about 2.4 million Americans in 1936 and predicted the wrong winner of the presidential election by a landslide, because its sample came mostly from wealthier households. A random sample of a few thousand would have done better.

title: Sampling distributions and the CLT
text:
A population you can see
To study sampling, it helps to have a population whose parameters you know. Here’s a made-up population: the impurity levels of 100,000 drums, in ppm. It’s right-skewed: most drums are fairly clean, and a few are quite contaminated.

set.seed(11)
population <- rgamma(100000, shape = 2, scale = 12.5)   # a skewed, positive distribution
mu <- mean(population)
sigma <- sd(population)
c(mu = mu, sigma = sigma)
#>       mu    sigma 
#> 24.97653 17.58144

rgamma() draws from the gamma distribution, a flexible family for positive, skewed quantities that you’ll meet in Module 5. Now take one random sample of 25 drums:

one_sample <- sample(population, 25)
mean(one_sample)
#> [1] 18.90201

The sample mean isn’t exactly \mu, and another sample would give yet another value.

title: Sampling distributions and the CLT
text:
The sampling distribution
Imagine taking every possible sample of 25 drums and computing \bar{x} for each one. The distribution of all those means is the sampling distribution of \bar{x}. You can’t take every sample, but you can take 10,000, which is close enough:

means_25 <- replicate(10000, mean(sample(population, 25)))
c(mean_of_means = mean(means_25), sd_of_means = sd(means_25))
#> mean_of_means   sd_of_means 
#>     25.007907      3.499725

Compare these with the population:

The means are centered on \mu: on average, \bar{x} hits the target. That makes \bar{x} an unbiased estimator of \mu.
They’re far less spread out than individual drums: their SD is about 3.5 ppm, against 17.6 for single drums. Averaging cancels out much of the drum-to-drum variation.
Their shape is close to normal, even though the population is strongly skewed.



Show the code
sims <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 5, 25, 100), function(n) {
  data.frame(n = paste("n =", n), xbar = replicate(10000, mean(sample(population, n))))
}))
sims$n <- factor(sims$n, levels = paste("n =", c(1, 5, 25, 100)))
ggplot(sims, aes(x = xbar)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#C2416C", color = NA) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu, color = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ n, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Sample means from a skewed population, for four sample sizes",
       subtitle = "The blue line is the population mean",
       x = "Mean impurity in the sample (ppm)", y = "Number of samples") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









With n = 1, the “sample mean” is just one drum, and its distribution has the population’s skewed shape. As n grows, the sampling distribution narrows around \mu and becomes more and more bell-shaped. Those two facts are the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem.

title: Sampling distributions and the CLT
text:
The standard error
The standard deviation of a sampling distribution is called the standard error (SE) of the statistic. For the sample mean,

\text{SE}(\bar{x}) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} .

Check it against the simulation:

sigma / sqrt(25)
#> [1] 3.516288
sd(means_25)
#> [1] 3.499725

In practice you don’t know \sigma, so you estimate the standard error with the sample standard deviation: \text{SE} \approx s / \sqrt{n}. For the mean yield of our 40 reactor batches:

batches <- read.csv("data/reactor_batches.csv")
sd(batches$yield_pct) / sqrt(nrow(batches))
#> [1] 1.541528

So the average yield of 57.6% is uncertain by about 1.5 percentage points.
Keep the two ideas apart. The standard deviation describes how much individual drums or batches vary. The standard error describes how much a statistic would vary from sample to sample: it measures the statistic’s precision.
Because of the square root, precision improves slowly. To halve the standard error, you need four times as many observations:










Sample size n
25
100
400
1,600




\text{SE} = \sigma / \sqrt{n} (with \sigma = 17.6)
3.52
1.76
0.88
0.44



That’s why labs often run measurements in replicate: four replicates halve the uncertainty of a single measurement.






NoteGo deeper: where σ/√n comes from





Let X_1, \dots, X_n be independent draws from a population with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2. Using the rules from Lesson 9,

E(\bar{X}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n E(X_i) = \frac{1}{n}\cdot n\mu = \mu ,
\qquad
\text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \text{Var}(X_i) = \frac{1}{n^2}\cdot n\sigma^2 = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} .

The second step needs independence, so that the variances add. Taking the square root gives \text{SE}(\bar{X}) = \sigma/\sqrt{n}. Strictly speaking, sampling without replacement from a finite population makes the draws slightly dependent, but the correction is negligible when the sample is a small fraction of the population.



Your turn. Bag weights have a standard deviation of \sigma = 0.3 kg. What’s the standard error of the mean weight of 9 bags?









\text{SE} = \sigma / \sqrt{n}.


0.3 / sqrt(9)




Your turn. How many bags do you need to weigh for the standard error to be 0.05 kg?









Solve 0.3/\sqrt{n} = 0.05 for n: \sqrt{n} = 0.3/0.05.


(0.3 / 0.05)^2




Your turn: simulate it. A concentration is measured with an SD of 4 mg/L around its true value of 100 mg/L, and the lab reports the mean of 4 replicates. Simulate 5,000 such reports, and return the standard deviation of the reported means. What does the formula predict?









Inside mean(), draw one set of replicates with rnorm(4, mean = 100, sd = 4).


set.seed(4)
means <- replicate(5000, mean(rnorm(4, mean = 100, sd = 4)))
sd(means)
The formula gives 4/\sqrt{4} = 2 mg/L.

title: Sampling distributions and the CLT
text:
The law of large numbers
As the sample size grows, the sample mean gets closer and closer to the population mean. That’s the law of large numbers, and the standard error says how fast: the typical error shrinks like 1/\sqrt{n}. It’s why the coin-flip proportion in Lesson 8 settled down, and why simulation works: more repetitions give more accurate estimates.
It does not say that chance “evens out” in the short run. After five heads in a row, the next flip is still 50:50. The law works by swamping early streaks with lots of later flips, not by correcting them. Believing otherwise is called the gambler’s fallacy.

A plant-floor version: if batches are truly independent, three off-spec batches in a row don’t make a good one “due”. But in a real plant, three bad batches in a row usually mean something has changed, so the independence assumption itself is the thing to question. Go and investigate!

title: Sampling distributions and the CLT
text:
The central limit theorem
The central limit theorem (CLT) is one of the most remarkable results in mathematics:

For a random sample of size n from any population with mean \mu and standard deviation \sigma, the sampling distribution of \bar{x} is approximately normal, N(\mu, \sigma/\sqrt{n}), when n is large.

The population can have any shape (skewed, lumpy, discrete), as long as \sigma is finite. That’s why normal distributions appear everywhere in statistics: most methods work with averages or sums, and those are approximately normal.
How large must n be? It depends on the population:

If the population is close to normal, the CLT works well even for small samples.
For moderate skew, n \ge 30 is a common rule of thumb.
For strong skew or extreme outliers, you may need many more. When in doubt, check by simulation.

The CLT lets you compute probabilities about a sample mean with pnorm(). What’s the chance that the mean impurity of 25 drums comes out above 30 ppm?

1 - pnorm(30, mean = mu, sd = sigma / sqrt(25))   # by the CLT
#> [1] 0.07655564
mean(means_25 > 30)                               # by simulation
#> [1] 0.0827

The two agree reasonably well. The small difference is because, with this skewed population and only n = 25, the sampling distribution is still slightly skewed itself.








Try n <- 1, n <- 30 and n <- 200. You can also swap in something lumpy, like c(rnorm(50000, 20, 3), rnorm(50000, 40, 3)).
Your turn. Bags have a mean weight of 25 kg and an SD of 0.3 kg. A pallet holds 40 bags. What’s the probability that the average bag on a pallet weighs less than 24.9 kg?









By the CLT, the average of 40 bags is approximately normal, with mean 25 and SD 0.3/\sqrt{40}.


pnorm(24.9, mean = 25, sd = 0.3 / sqrt(40))
About 0.018. A single bag below 24.9 kg is common, but a whole pallet averaging that low is rare.




Your turn: a skewed population. Pump lifetimes are exponential, with a mean of 2,000 hours (so the SD is also 2,000). For a fleet of 50 pumps, use the CLT to approximate the probability that their average lifetime is below 1,800 hours.









The standard error is 2000/\sqrt{50}. Then use pnorm() for the lower tail.


pnorm(1800, mean = 2000, sd = 2000 / sqrt(50))

title: Sampling distributions and the CLT
text:
Sample proportions
A proportion is a mean of 0s and 1s (Lesson 2), so everything above applies to it. If a fraction p of the population has some property, the sample proportion \hat{p} from a random sample of size n has

E(\hat{p}) = p, \qquad \text{SE}(\hat{p}) = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} ,

and it’s approximately normal when the sample contains enough of both outcomes. The usual check is the success–failure condition: np \ge 10 and n(1-p) \ge 10.
Say 4% of all drums leak, and QC inspects 500 of them:

p <- 0.04
n <- 500
se <- sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
se
#> [1] 0.008763561
set.seed(2)
p_hat <- rbinom(10000, size = n, prob = p) / n   # 10,000 simulated inspections
sd(p_hat)
#> [1] 0.008832803
mean(abs(p_hat - p) < 1.96 * se)
#> [1] 0.9472

The standard error is just under 0.9 percentage points, so about 95% of inspections land within about 1.7 points of the true leak rate. That’s also where the “margin of error of plus or minus 3 points” quoted with opinion polls of about 1,000 people comes from.
Your turn. The true leak rate is 4%. In an inspection of 500 drums, what’s the probability that the sample shows a leak rate above 6%?









\hat{p} is approximately normal with mean 0.04 and SD \sqrt{0.04 \times 0.96/500}.


1 - pnorm(0.06, mean = 0.04, sd = sqrt(0.04 * 0.96 / 500))
About 1.1%. So if an inspection does find more than 6% leaking, that’s a strong hint that the true rate has gone up.




Your turn. A rare defect affects 1% of products. For a sample of 300, check the success–failure condition. Return TRUE if it holds.









Both np \ge 10 and n(1-p) \ge 10 must hold. Combine them with &.


p <- 0.01
n <- 300
n * p >= 10 & n * (1 - p) >= 10
We’d expect only 3 defects, so the sampling distribution of \hat{p} is too skewed for a normal approximation. For rare events, use the binomial (or Poisson) directly.

title: Sampling distributions and the CLT
section: Other statistics have sampling distributions too
text:
Other statistics have sampling distributions too
Medians, standard deviations, correlations and regression slopes all vary from sample to sample, and each one has a sampling distribution and a standard error. For some there’s a formula. For all of them, simulation works: draw lots of samples, compute the statistic each time, and look at the spread.
