#>  Mean   :60.43   Mean   :21.1   Mean   :86.29   Mean   :17.52  
#>  3rd Qu.:62.00   3rd Qu.:24.0   3rd Qu.:89.00   3rd Qu.:19.00  
#>  Max.   :80.00   Max.   :27.0   Max.   :93.00   Max.   :42.00


In RStudio, View(stackloss) opens the data in a spreadsheet-style viewer, and ?stackloss explains every column. Other built-in datasets with a lab flavor: pressure (the vapor pressure of mercury), Puromycin (enzyme kinetics), BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) and airquality (air pollution in New York).

Your turn. Puromycin holds the results of an enzyme kinetics experiment. With one function call, find out how many rows and columns it has.









One function gives you both numbers at once, rows first.


dim(Puromycin)
23 measurements of 3 variables: the substrate concentration, the reaction rate, and whether the cells were treated.

title: Data frames
text:
Working with columns
The dollar sign pulls a single column out of a data frame, as a vector:

stackloss$stack.loss
#>  [1] 42 37 37 28 18 18 19 20 15 14 14 13 11 12  8  7  8  8  9 15 15
mean(stackloss$stack.loss)
#> [1] 17.52381

So on average, about 1.75% of the ammonia escaped (17.52 divided by 10).
Adding a column is just as easy: assign to a new name after the $. Let’s store the loss as a real percentage. We’ll work on a copy called plant, so the original stays untouched:

plant <- stackloss
plant$loss_pct <- plant$stack.loss / 10
head(plant, 3)
#>   Air.Flow Water.Temp Acid.Conc. stack.loss loss_pct
#> 1       80         27         89         42      4.2
#> 2       80         27         88         37      3.7
#> 3       75         25         90         37      3.7

Your turn. What was the average cooling-water temperature over the 21 days?









Pull out the column with stackloss$Water.Temp, then take its mean(). Capital letters matter!


mean(stackloss$Water.Temp)




Your turn. The built-in pressure data has the vapor pressure of mercury at temperatures from 0 to 360 °C. Add a column temp_K with the temperature in kelvin.









Take the temperature column of vp and add 273.15: vp$temperature + ....


vp <- pressure
vp$temp_K <- vp$temperature + 273.15
head(vp)

title: Data frames
text:
Picking rows and columns
A data frame has two dimensions, so square brackets take two positions, separated by a comma: [rows, columns]. Leave one empty to mean “all of them”:

runs[1, ]                            # row 1, every column
#>   run catalyst temp_C yield_pct
#> 1   1        A    160      52.1
runs[, "yield_pct"]                  # every row, one column
#> [1] 52.1 55.8 60.4 63.0
runs[2, "catalyst"]                  # row 2, the catalyst
#> [1] "B"
runs[, c("catalyst", "yield_pct")]   # two columns, by name
#>   catalyst yield_pct
#> 1        A      52.1
#> 2        B      55.8
#> 3        A      60.4
#> 4        B      63.0

The real power comes from conditions. Put a TRUE/FALSE question in the row position, and you keep the rows where the answer is TRUE:

runs[runs$temp_C == 180, ]
#>   run catalyst temp_C yield_pct
#> 3   3        A    180      60.4
#> 4   4        B    180      63.0

Read it as “runs, the rows where temp_C is 180, every column”. It’s the logical indexing from the last lesson, now picking whole rows.
To sort, order() gives the row positions in sorted order, and you use them as the row index:

runs[order(runs$yield_pct, decreasing = TRUE), ]
#>   run catalyst temp_C yield_pct
#> 4   4        B    180      63.0
#> 3   3        A    180      60.4
#> 2   2        B    160      55.8
#> 1   1        A    160      52.1

And subset() is a shortcut that lets you use the column names directly:

subset(runs, catalyst == "B", select = c(run, yield_pct))
#>   run yield_pct
#> 2   2      55.8
#> 4   4      63.0

In Lesson 6 you’ll meet dplyr, which makes all of this even easier to read. These base R tools are still worth knowing, because they work everywhere and you’ll see them in other people’s code.






WarningDon’t forget the comma



runs[runs$temp_C == 180], without the comma, gives an error (undefined columns selected), because a single index picks columns. To pick rows, write runs[runs$temp_C == 180, ].


Your turn. On which days did more than 2% of the ammonia escape? Careful with the units: stack.loss is 10 times the percentage. Return those rows, with every column.









2% is a stack.loss of 20. Put the condition in the row position and leave the column position empty: stackloss[ condition , ].


stackloss[stackloss$stack.loss > 20, ]
The first four days, when the plant was running hardest. subset(stackloss, stack.loss > 20) works too.

title: Data frames
text:
Reading a data file
Real data usually arrives as a file, and the most common format is CSV, for comma-separated values. It’s plain text: the first line has the column names, and every other line is one observation, with commas between the values. Here are the first lines of the file we’ll use from now on:

cat(readLines("data/reactor_batches.csv", n = 4), sep = "\n")
#> "batch_id","shift","catalyst","temp_C","pressure_bar","residence_min","alarms","yield_pct","purity_pct","on_spec"
#> "B01","day","B",185.3,3.72,47.2,1,70.2,98.9,TRUE
#> "B02","day","D",176,5.31,37.9,1,53.7,98.7,TRUE
#> "B03","day","C",177.9,5.12,32.5,1,49.2,99.6,TRUE

read.csv() reads it into a data frame:

batches <- read.csv("data/reactor_batches.csv")
str(batches)
#> 'data.frame':    40 obs. of  10 variables:
#>  $ batch_id     : chr  "B01" "B02" "B03" "B04" ...
#>  $ shift        : chr  "day" "day" "day" "night" ...
#>  $ catalyst     : chr  "B" "D" "C" "B" ...
#>  $ temp_C       : num  185 176 178 184 180 ...
#>  $ pressure_bar : num  3.72 5.31 5.12 4.93 5.22 5.36 4.53 6.02 4.49 5.81 ...
#>  $ residence_min: num  47.2 37.9 32.5 60.7 41.1 47.1 64 38.9 38.8 21 ...
#>  $ alarms       : int  1 1 1 1 1 0 1 1 1 3 ...
#>  $ yield_pct    : num  70.2 53.7 49.2 65.3 53.4 58.5 74.1 55.3 56.4 31.1 ...
#>  $ purity_pct   : num  98.9 98.7 99.6 98.8 99.2 ...
#>  $ on_spec      : logi  TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE ...

These are 40 batches from a pilot-plant reactor. The data is made up for this course, but it behaves like the real thing. Here’s what each column means:







Column
What it is




batch_id
the batch’s label, B01 to B40


shift
which shift ran it: day or night


catalyst
which of four catalysts was used: A, B, C or D


temp_C
the reactor temperature, in °C


pressure_bar
the reactor pressure, in bar


residence_min
the residence time: how long the mixture stays in the reactor, in minutes


alarms
how many process alarms went off during the batch


yield_pct
the yield: how much product you got, as a percentage of the theoretical maximum


purity_pct
the purity of the product, in %


on_spec
TRUE if the purity met the 98.5% spec



read.csv() guessed each column’s type from what’s in it: chr (text) for the shift, num for the temperature, int (whole numbers) for the alarms, and logi (TRUE/FALSE) for on_spec. Always check with str() after reading a file. A wrong type is often the first clue that something’s off in the data, like the “n/a” from the last lesson.
You can download reactor_batches.csv to use in RStudio. The path "data/reactor_batches.csv" is relative to R’s working directory, the folder where R looks for files. Lesson 1.1 shows how RStudio projects make that painless.
The data is ready in the live boxes too. Have a look around:















Your turn. Return the batch IDs of the three highest-yielding batches, best first. (batches is already loaded.)









Sort the rows by yield_pct from highest to lowest with order(..., decreasing = TRUE), pick the batch_id column, then keep the first three with [1:3].


batches[order(batches$yield_pct, decreasing = TRUE), "batch_id"][______]


batches[order(batches$yield_pct, decreasing = TRUE), "batch_id"][1:3]
head(batches[order(batches$yield_pct, decreasing = TRUE), ], 3) shows the whole rows instead.

title: Data frames
text:
Summaries by group
Now for the questions engineers actually ask. Which catalyst gives the best yield? Does the night shift run differently? table() counts each category, and with two variables it counts every combination:

table(batches$catalyst)
#> 
#>  A  B  C  D 
#> 10 12  9  9
table(batches$shift, batches$on_spec)
#>        
#>         FALSE TRUE
#>   day       6   16
#>   night     3   15

The second one is called a contingency table. Of the 22 day-shift batches, 6 were off spec (FALSE) and 16 were on spec.
To summarize a number separately for each group, use tapply() or aggregate():

tapply(batches$yield_pct, batches$catalyst, mean)
#>        A        B        C        D 
#> 59.98000 55.72500 54.80000 60.46667
aggregate(yield_pct ~ catalyst, data = batches, FUN = mean)
#>   catalyst yield_pct
#> 1        A  59.98000
#> 2        B  55.72500
#> 3        C  54.80000
#> 4        D  60.46667

Both give the mean yield for each catalyst. Catalysts A and D come out ahead at about 60%, with B and C closer to 55%. Whether those differences are real or just batch-to-batch noise is a question for Lesson 13!
aggregate() uses a formula, yield_pct ~ catalyst, which you read as “yield by catalyst”. You’ll see the tilde ~ all over R’s statistical functions: every regression model in Module 2 is written as a formula.
Your turn. Compute the on-spec rate, the proportion of batches on spec, for each catalyst.









Remember from the last lesson: the mean of TRUE/FALSE values is the proportion of TRUEs. So use tapply() with the on_spec column, grouped by catalyst, and mean.


tapply(batches$on_spec, batches$catalyst, mean)
aggregate(on_spec ~ catalyst, data = batches, FUN = mean) gives the same numbers as a data frame.

title: Data frames
section: Missing values in a data frame
text:
Missing values in a data frame
Real data has gaps, and this dataset is no exception. colSums(is.na(...)) counts the missing values in every column at once:

colSums(is.na(batches))
#>      batch_id         shift      catalyst        temp_C  pressure_bar 
#>             0             0             0             2             0 
#> residence_min        alarms     yield_pct    purity_pct       on_spec 
#>             0             1             0             0             0

The temperature sensor dropped out twice, and one batch’s alarm log was lost.
Missing values cause a sneaky problem when you pick rows with a condition. For a batch with no temperature, batches$temp_C > 185 is NA, and R hands you back a row full of NAs for it:

nrow(batches[batches$temp_C > 185, ])          # 14 rows, but 2 of them are all NA
#> [1] 14
nrow(subset(batches, temp_C > 185))            # only the 12 real matches
#> [1] 12
nrow(batches[which(batches$temp_C > 185), ])   # which() also skips the NAs
#> [1] 12

subset() and which() quietly drop the rows where the answer is unknown. na.omit() goes further, and drops every row with any missing value:

nrow(na.omit(batches))
#> [1] 37

That loses 3 of the 40 batches. Sometimes that’s fine. But if values are missing for a reason (say, the sensor fails only when the reactor runs hot), dropping them can bias your results. Module 1 has two whole lessons on this.
Your turn. Return the batches that ran hotter than 185 °C, with only their batch_id, temp_C and purity_pct. No NA rows allowed!









subset() takes the data, a condition, and select = c(...) for the columns. It drops the rows where the condition is NA for you.


subset(batches, temp_C > 185, select = c(batch_id, temp_C, purity_pct))
With square brackets: batches[which(batches$temp_C > 185), c("batch_id", "temp_C", "purity_pct")].

title: Data frames
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Does a longer stay pay off? The residence time is how long the mixture spends in the reactor. Compute the mean yield separately for batches with residence times of 45 minutes or less, and more than 45 minutes.









batches$residence_min > 45 splits the batches into two groups, FALSE and TRUE. You can use it as the groups in tapply().


tapply(batches$yield_pct, batches$residence_min > 45, ______)


tapply(batches$yield_pct, batches$residence_min > 45, mean)
With logical indexing instead:
c(mean(batches$yield_pct[batches$residence_min <= 45]),
  mean(batches$yield_pct[batches$residence_min > 45]))
About 53% for the short stays and 63% for the long ones. More time in the reactor means more of the reactants get converted.




Challenge 2 · The temperature trade-off. A hotter reactor runs faster, but it often makes more by-products, which lowers the purity. Compare the on-spec rate of the batches that ran hotter than 185 °C with the rest. Watch out: two batches have no temperature.









It’s the same idea as Challenge 1, with on_spec as the values and temp_C > 185 as the groups. The mean of on_spec is the on-spec rate.


tapply() simply leaves out the batches whose group is NA. If you use logical indexing instead, you’ll need na.rm = TRUE or which().


tapply(batches$on_spec, batches$temp_C > 185, mean)
About 96% of the cooler batches were on spec, but only a third of the hot ones. That’s a real trade-off engineers face: push the temperature for speed, and pay for it in purity.

title: Data frames
text:
Quick quiz

1. In the batches data, each row is…

one batch: an observation
one measurement type: a variable
one value


Rows are observations (the things you collected data on), and columns are variables (what you recorded about them).



2. Which of these variables is ordinal?

Catalyst type (A, B, C, D)
Batch ID
Agitator setting (low, medium, high)
Purity in %


The agitator settings are categories with a natural order. Catalyst type and batch ID are categories with no order, and purity is numerical.



3. What does batches[2, ] return?

The second row, with every column
The second column, with every row
The value in row 2, column 2


Inside [rows, columns], an empty column position means “all the columns”.



4. You run batches[batches$yield_pct > 70]. What happens?

An error, because without a comma R thinks you’re picking columns
You get the batches with yields above 70
You get the yields above 70


A single index picks columns. To pick rows, add the comma: batches[batches$yield_pct > 70, ].



5. What does aggregate(purity_pct ~ shift, data = batches, FUN = mean) compute?

The mean purity for each shift
The mean shift for each purity
The overall mean purity


Read the formula purity_pct ~ shift as “purity by shift”: the mean purity within each shift.



6. Only 12 batches ran above 185 °C, yet batches[batches$temp_C > 185, ] returns 14 rows. Why?

Two batches have missing temperatures, and they come back as rows of NA
Two batches are counted twice
read.csv() added two rows


For a missing temperature, the condition is NA, so R returns a row of NAs. subset() and which() avoid this.

title: Data frames
text:
Wrap-up
Great job: you can now work with real tables of data. Here’s what you can do:

Think in rows and columns: observations and variables, and the types of variables (continuous, discrete, nominal, ordinal).
Build and inspect data frames with data.frame(), str(), head(), summary() and dim().
Pick what you need: $ pulls out a column, and [rows, columns] picks by position, name or condition. Don’t forget the comma!
Summarize by group with table(), tapply() and aggregate().
Load data from a CSV file with read.csv(), then check it with str() and colSums(is.na()).







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





This week you’ll set up an RStudio project, which keeps all the files for a piece of work together and makes file paths simple.

Create a project. Choose File → New Project → Existing Directory and pick your stats-course folder. RStudio reopens inside the project, and the working directory is now that folder. Check with getwd().
Get the data. Download reactor_batches.csv and save it in a new folder called data inside your project.
Load and look. In a new script, week03.R, run batches <- read.csv("data/reactor_batches.csv"), then str(batches), summary(batches) and View(batches).
Answer questions with code.

Which catalyst has the highest average purity?
What’s the on-spec rate on each shift?
Do batches with 3 or more alarms have lower yields than the rest? (Watch out for the missing alarm count.)

Save a subset. Make a data frame of only the night-shift batches and save it with write.csv(night, "data/night_batches.csv", row.names = FALSE). Open the file in a spreadsheet program or a text editor to see what R wrote.
Try the import tool. In the Environment pane, choose Import Dataset → From Text (base), pick the CSV and look at the preview. RStudio writes the read.csv() code for you.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Observation

One row of a dataset: one thing data was collected on.

Variable

One column of a dataset: a characteristic that varies across observations.

Numerical variable

A measured quantity, either continuous (any value in a range) or discrete (a count).

Categorical variable

A variable that sorts observations into groups, either nominal (no order) or ordinal (ordered).

Data frame

R’s object for a table of data, made of equal-length column vectors.

CSV file

A plain-text table with commas between the values and the column names on the first line.

Working directory

The folder R looks in when you give it a relative file path.

Contingency table

A table that counts the observations in every combination of two categorical variables.

Formula

An expression with ~, like yield_pct ~ catalyst, describing how variables relate. Read the tilde as “by”.











NoteWant to read more?






Introduction to Modern Statistics, “Hello data”. Observations, variables and their types, with lots of examples.
R for Data Science (2e), “Data import”. Reading CSV files with readr, the tidyverse alternative to read.csv() that you’ll use from Module 1 on.

title: Welcome to R
text:
Module 0 · Lesson 1 of 14 Week 1 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Hi, and welcome! Chemists have the lab notebook, engineers have the spreadsheet, and statisticians have R: a free programming language built specifically for working with data. Today you’ll write your first lines of it. By the end of this lesson, R will be your calculator, your unit converter and your memory for numbers. It never makes an arithmetic slip, and it never forgets a value.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Welcome to R
text:
Your first line of R
Let’s start with the simplest possible conversation. Press Run Code in the box below. (The very first run on a page takes a few seconds while R loads. After that it’s instant.)








R read your line, worked it out, and answered [1] 2. The [1] just means “here’s the first value of the answer”. It’ll make more sense in the next lesson, so you can ignore it for now.
Now change the numbers and run it again. Try 40 + 2, or 273 * 2. This is how you’ll learn R: change something, run it, see what happens.
You’ll also see examples like this one, where I’ve already run the code for you. Lines starting with #> show what R printed:

10 - 3
#> [1] 7


Little tip: type the examples into a live box instead of copying them. Your fingers learn R faster than your eyes do. And guess the answer before you press Run!

title: Welcome to R
text:
R as a calculator
R knows all the usual arithmetic, plus a couple of extras:



You type
It means
Example
Answer




+ -
add, subtract
25 + 273.15
298.15


* /
multiply, divide
7 / 2
3.5


^
to the power of
2^10
1024


%%
remainder
17 %% 5
2



Here’s one you’ll use all the time in chemistry. To turn a temperature in °C into kelvin, you add 273.15:

25 + 273.15
#> [1] 298.15

So room temperature, 25 °C, is 298.15 K.
R follows the order of operations you know from school: powers first, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. Parentheses beat everything. Compare these:

2 + 3 * 4
#> [1] 14
(2 + 3) * 4
#> [1] 20

When in doubt, add parentheses. They’re free, and they make your intent obvious to anyone reading your code, including future you.

Really big and really tiny numbers
Science is full of numbers that are awkward to type. R uses scientific notation: 6.022e23 means 6.022 \times 10^{23} (Avogadro’s number), and 1.6e-19 means 1.6 \times 10^{-19} (the charge of an electron, in coulombs).

6.022e23 * 2      # molecules in two moles
#> [1] 1.2044e+24



Your first engineering calculation
Here’s the ideal gas law, PV = nRT, rearranged for the number of moles, n = \dfrac{PV}{RT}. Let’s find out how many moles of gas fill 0.0224 m³ at 1 atm (101,325 Pa) and 0 °C (273.15 K), with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K):

(101325 * 0.0224) / (8.314 * 273.15)
#> [1] 0.9994324

About one mole. That’s the famous “22.4 liters per mole” you may remember from chemistry class, and R just worked it out for you.
Your turn. A reactor runs at 350 °C. What’s that in kelvin?









Add 273.15 to the temperature in °C.


350 + 273.15




One more. A reactor heats up from 20 °C to 80 °C in 15 minutes. What’s the average heating rate, in °C per minute?









The rate is the temperature change divided by the time. Make sure R subtracts before it divides, so put the subtraction in parentheses.


(80 - 20) / 15
Without the parentheses, 80 - 20 / 15 would divide first and give about 78.7, which is nonsense as a heating rate.










NoteGo deeper: why 0.1 + 0.2 isn’t exactly 0.3





Computers store numbers in binary, and most decimal fractions, like 0.1, can’t be written exactly in binary, just as 1/3 can’t be written exactly in decimal. The errors are tiny, but they show up if you test whether two numbers are exactly equal (== asks “are these equal?”):

0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3
#> [1] FALSE
isTRUE(all.equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))
#> [1] TRUE

all.equal() allows for those tiny rounding differences, so use it to compare decimals. Module 4 explains how computers handle numbers.

title: Welcome to R
text:
Giving values names
Typing 273.15 or 8.314 again and again gets old fast. So let’s give values names. In R you store a value in an object with the arrow <-:

reactor_temp <- 350

Read it as “reactor_temp gets 350”. Nothing is printed, because you only stored the value. Type the name to see it, or use it in a calculation:

reactor_temp
#> [1] 350
reactor_temp + 273.15
#> [1] 623.15

Here’s the ideal gas law again, but now every quantity has a name. Notice how much easier it is to read:








Now change temp_K to 298.15 (room temperature) and run it again. One edit, and everything that depends on it updates. In a real analysis with hundreds of steps, this is a superpower: it makes your work reproducible, because anyone can rerun it and get exactly the same answer.

A few naming rules: names can use letters, numbers, _ and ., but must start with a letter. No spaces! Capitals matter, so Temp and temp are different objects. And avoid naming things T or F, because R uses those as shortcuts for TRUE and FALSE.

A good style is to join words with underscores and include units in the name, like flow_rate_Lmin or mass_kg. In RStudio, Alt + - types the arrow for you (Option + - on a Mac).
Your turn. A storage tank holds 2.5 m³ of water, and water’s density is 997 kg/m³. Compute the mass of the water (mass = density × volume).









Multiply the two objects: density_kgm3 * volume_m3.


density_kgm3 <- 997
volume_m3 <- 2.5
mass_kg <- density_kgm3 * volume_m3
mass_kg

title: Welcome to R
text:
Functions: R’s toolbox
R comes with thousands of built-in functions: little machines that take inputs and give back an answer. You call a function by writing its name followed by parentheses with the inputs, called arguments, inside:

sqrt(16)          # square root
#> [1] 4
abs(-3)           # absolute value
#> [1] 3
round(3.14159, digits = 2)
#> [1] 3.14

Look at round(): the first argument is the number, and digits says how many decimal places to keep. If you leave digits out, R uses its default, which is 0:

round(3.14159)
#> [1] 3


Logs, the chemist’s favorite
You’ll meet logarithms all the time: in pH, in reaction rates, in decibels. R has a few:

log10(1000)    # base 10: 10^3 = 1000
#> [1] 3
log(100)       # careful: plain log() is the natural log, base e
#> [1] 4.60517
exp(1)         # e itself
#> [1] 2.718282

So the pH of a solution, \text{pH} = -\log_{10}[\text{H}^+], is one line. Pure water has [\text{H}^+] = 10^{-7} mol/L:

-log10(1e-7)
#> [1] 7

pH 7, neutral, just as it should be.


Functions inside functions
You can put one function inside another, and R works from the inside out:

round(sqrt(2), digits = 3)
#> [1] 1.414

First sqrt(2) gives 1.41421…, then round() keeps three decimals.


Your first statistics
The function c() (for combine) bundles several values together. Say you ran the same titration five times and got these volumes, in mL:

titrations <- c(24.8, 25.1, 24.9, 25.3, 25.0)
mean(titrations)
#> [1] 25.02
median(titrations)
#> [1] 25

The mean is the average: add them all up and divide by how many there are. The median is the middle value once they’re sorted. You’ll use both constantly, and Lesson 7 is all about them.
Your turn. A solution has a hydrogen-ion concentration of 3.2 \times 10^{-4} mol/L. What’s its pH, rounded to two decimals?









Inside out: -log10(3.2e-4) gives the pH, then wrap it in round(..., digits = 2).


round(-log10(3.2e-4), digits = 2)
A pH of about 3.49: quite acidic, like orange juice.




And one with your own mean. Compute the mean of the titration volumes “by hand”, with sum() and length() instead of mean().









The mean is the total divided by the count: sum(titrations) divided by length(titrations).


titrations <- c(24.8, 25.1, 24.9, 25.3, 25.0)
sum(titrations) / length(titrations)

title: Welcome to R
text:
When R complains
Sooner or later, R will answer you with an error. That’s completely normal: experienced programmers see errors all day long. An error isn’t R saying “you’re bad at this”. It’s R saying “I didn’t understand, can you say that differently?” The message usually tells you exactly what went wrong.








You typed
R says
What it means




Reactor_temp
object 'Reactor_temp' not found
A typo or a capital letter, or you never created it


sqrt(16
unexpected end of input
A parenthesis or quote was never closed


flow rate <- 5
unexpected symbol
Something’s missing or extra. Here, the space in the name


sqrt("16")
non-numeric argument
Quotes make text, and you can’t take the square root of text



Try it: run this box and read the message. Then fix it.








Sometimes R gives you a warning instead. A warning means the code ran, but R suspects the answer isn’t what you wanted:

sqrt(-4)
#> Warning in sqrt(-4): NaNs produced
#> [1] NaN

The square root of a negative number isn’t a real number, so you get NaN (“not a number”) and a gentle warning. Never ignore a warning until you understand it.

Stuck on a function? In RStudio, type ?round (or any function name) to open its help page. The Examples at the bottom are often the most useful part. And anything after a # is a comment: R ignores it, so use comments to leave notes for yourself.

Your turn: fix the bug. This should work out the volume pumped in 8 minutes at 12.5 L/min, but it has one mistake.









Read the error. Which object can’t R find? Compare it with how that object was spelled when it was created.


flow_rate <- 12.5
time_min <- 8
volume_L <- flow_rate * time_min
volume_L
Flow_rate has a capital F, but the object is called flow_rate.

title: Welcome to R
text:
Challenge round
Feeling good? These two use everything from today. They’re harder, so take your time and use the hints.
Challenge 1 · Why water boils at 100 °C. The Antoine equation gives the vapor pressure of a liquid at temperature T (in °C): 
\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{C + T} ,
 with P in mmHg. For water, A = 8.07131, B = 1730.63 and C = 233.426. Compute water’s vapor pressure at 100 °C.









The equation gives \log_{10} P, so you need to undo the log: P = 10^{\,A - B/(C + T)}.


In R: 10^(A - B / (C + temp_C)). The parentheses around C + temp_C matter!


A <- 8.07131
B <- 1730.63
C <- 233.426
temp_C <- 100
10^(A - B / (C + temp_C))
About 760 mmHg, which is exactly 1 atmosphere. A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the pressure around it, so water boils at 100 °C at sea level.




Challenge 2 · The pH of a vinegar solution. Acetic acid, the acid in vinegar, only partly dissociates in water. For a 0.10 mol/L solution, the hydrogen-ion concentration x solves the quadratic equation 
x^2 + K_a x - K_a c = 0, \qquad K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5} .
 Use the quadratic formula, x = \dfrac{-K_a + \sqrt{K_a^2 + 4K_a c}}{2}, then find the pH.









Translate the formula piece by piece: (-Ka + sqrt(Ka^2 + 4 * Ka * conc)) / 2.


Ka <- 1.8e-5
conc <- 0.10
h_plus <- (-Ka + sqrt(Ka^2 + 4 * Ka * conc)) / 2
-log10(h_plus)
A pH of about 2.88. Household vinegar is about eight times more concentrated, and its pH is around 2.4.

title: Welcome to R
text:
Quick quiz
Six quick questions to check your understanding. Tap an answer to see if you’re right.

1. What does 2 + 3 * 2 give?

10
8
12


Multiplication goes first: 3 * 2 is 6, then 2 + 6 is 8. For 10 you’d need (2 + 3) * 2.



2. Which of these is a valid object name?

2nd_reading
flow rate
reactor_temp_2
inlet-pressure


Names must start with a letter and can’t contain spaces or hyphens. R would read inlet-pressure as “inlet minus pressure”.



3. You run Yield <- 85 and then yield + 5. What happens?

An error: object ‘yield’ not found
R prints 90
R prints 85


Capitals matter. Yield exists, but yield doesn’t.



4. What does round(2.567, digits = 1) give?

2.5
2.6
3


One decimal place, and 2.567 is closer to 2.6 than to 2.5.



5. What does log10(1000) give?

3
About 6.9
100


10^3 = 1000, so \log_{10}(1000) = 3. About 6.9 is the natural log, log(1000).



6. R prints an answer and a warning. What does that mean?

The code ran, but the answer might not be what you wanted
The code didn’t run at all
R needs restarting


Warnings don’t stop the code; errors do. A warning is R saying “this worked, but take another look”.

title: Welcome to R
text:
Wrap-up
That’s your first lesson done. Here’s what you can do now:

Calculate: R handles arithmetic, powers and scientific notation, with parentheses to control the order.
Name things: <- stores a value in an object, and capital letters matter.
Use functions: round(), sqrt(), log10(), mean() and many more, with arguments that can have defaults.
Stay calm with errors: the message usually says exactly what’s wrong, and a warning means “take another look”.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about 30 minutes)





The live boxes are perfect for learning, but real work happens in RStudio on your own computer.

Look around. Open RStudio. You’ll see the Console (where code runs), and once you open a script, the Source pane where you write it. Environment (top right) lists your objects.
Start clean every time. Go to Tools → Global Options → General, untick Restore .RData into workspace at startup, and set Save workspace to .RData on exit to Never.
Make a course folder, for example Documents/stats-course.
Write a script. Choose File → New File → R Script and save it as week01.R in that folder. Type the ideal gas example with named objects, then run each line with Ctrl + Enter (Cmd + Enter on a Mac). Watch the Environment pane fill up.
Read a help page. Run ?mean. What does its trim argument do? Try mean(c(1, 2, 3, 100), trim = 0.25). (You should get 2.5: trimming drops the extreme values 1 and 100.)










NoteKey words from this lesson






Console

Where R code runs and answers appear.

Script

A file of R code (ending in .R) that you can save and rerun.

Object

A named value stored in R, created with <-.

Function

A built-in tool such as sqrt() or mean() that takes arguments and returns an answer.

Argument and default

An input to a function, and the value it uses when you don’t give one.

Error and warning

An error stops your code. A warning lets it finish but flags something to check.











NoteWant to read more?






Hands-On Programming with R, “The Very Basics”. A friendly tour of the same ideas, built around a pair of dice.
R for Data Science (2e), “Workflow: basics”. Short and practical, with good advice on naming things.

title: How to use this course
text:
Lessons go one step at a time. Use Continue and Back at the bottom, or the Step 2 of 9 button at the top to jump to any step. If you’d rather scroll through everything, that menu also has Show the whole lesson on one page.
The Course button (top right) opens your current module: its lessons, your progress, the study plan and the full syllabus. Everything else stays out of the way until you need it.

title: How to use this course
text:
The big picture
The course has 11 modules. Module 0 builds the foundations: R programming, describing data, probability and statistical inference. Modules 1–10 each cover one graduate course. Study them in order, one lesson a week; the study plan turns that into dates. Each module page says which earlier modules it builds on.

title: How to use this course
text:
What’s in a lesson
Every lesson has the same parts, so you always know where you are.

What you’ll learn

The goals of the lesson. Come back to them at the end and check you can do each one.

Examples

Code with its result shown underneath. Lines starting with #> are what R printed.

Live R boxes

Code boxes with a Run Code button. They run real R in your browser. Change the code and run it again as often as you like. Start Over restores the original code.

Go deeper boxes

Collapsed boxes with the math behind an idea, such as a derivation or a proof. They’re optional the first time through, but worth coming back to.

Exercises

Live boxes that check your answer when you run them. Each has hints, revealed one at a time, and a full solution. Try for a few minutes before you open a hint, and don’t open the solution until you’ve either solved it or genuinely tried.

Quiz

Short multiple-choice questions. Click an answer to see whether it’s right and why.

Practice in RStudio

A small task in RStudio on your own computer, because that’s where real work happens. If you’re only using a phone or tablet, skip these and come back to them later.

Read more

Chapters from free textbooks that cover the same material in a different voice. Optional, but a second explanation often makes things click.


At the bottom of every lesson there’s a Mark lesson complete button. Completed lessons get a ✓ in the menu, and your progress shows on the home page and module pages.

title: How to use this course
text:
Live R boxes

The first time you press Run Code on a page, your browser downloads R. That takes a few seconds, sometimes longer on a slow connection; after that, code runs instantly.
Boxes on the same page share their objects, like one R session. If a box uses an object made earlier on the page, run the earlier box first.
Exercises run in their own space, so an exercise can’t break the rest of the page.
Your edits are saved in this browser, so you can close the page and come back. Start Over brings back the original code.
The boxes need an internet connection to load R. If a box doesn’t respond, reload the page.

title: How to use this course
text:
Studying on your phone
The course works on a phone like an app:

iPhone (Safari): tap the Share button, then Add to Home Screen.
Android (Chrome): tap the ⋮ menu, then Add to Home screen or Install app.

Reading, quizzes and small code changes work well on a phone. For exercises with a lot of typing, a laptop or tablet with a keyboard is much more comfortable.

title: How to use this course
text:
Your progress is private
Progress, quiz answers and your code edits are saved only in the browser you’re using. Nothing is sent anywhere, and nobody else can see it. That also means each device and browser keeps its own progress, and clearing your browser’s data for this site resets it.

title: How to use this course
section: R and RStudio on your own computer
text:
R and RStudio on your own computer
The live boxes are enough for the lessons, but projects and the Practice in RStudio tasks need R and RStudio installed. Both are free.

Install R from CRAN, the official R site. Pick your operating system and download the latest version.
Install RStudio Desktop from Posit. It’s the program you’ll write R in; it uses the R you installed in step 1.
Open RStudio, go to Tools → Global Options → General, untick Restore .RData into workspace at startup, and set Save workspace to .RData on exit to Never. That way every session starts clean, and your scripts are the record of your work.
Install the packages the course uses by running this in the RStudio console:

install.packages("tidyverse")
Later modules list any extra packages they need.

title: How to use this course
text:
Where the data come from
Almost all of the course’s datasets are simulated: written by a script to behave like real plant, lab or business data, with problems planted on purpose. The plant, its people and their numbers are made up. That’s what lets the lessons say what the right answer is, and let you check it against the truth.
A few are real measurements, such as R’s built-in stackloss (a nitric acid plant), Puromycin (enzyme kinetics), pressure (mercury vapor pressure) and AirPassengers, and the historical Nile minima in Module 6.
So treat the numbers as practice, never as facts about real chemicals, plants or suppliers. And expect real data to be harder: nobody plants its problems for you to find, nobody knows the true answer, and the question often isn’t clear until you’ve talked to the person asking. The best next step after any module is to try its methods on data of your own.

title: How to use this course
text:
Tips for learning statistics

Predict before you run. Guess what the code will print, then run it. Being wrong is how you learn.
Type, don’t copy. Your fingers learn the syntax faster than your eyes do.
Explain it out loud. If you can explain an idea to a friend in plain words, you understand it. If you can’t, reread that section.
Errors are normal. Read the message: it usually tells you what’s wrong. Lesson 0.1 shows you how.
Review a little, often. Ten minutes redoing old exercises each week beats a long cram before moving on.

text:
A self-study course in R

    From your very first line of R to graduate-level data science, with realistic chemical engineering examples, live code right on the page, and Fizz cheering you on.
    
      Start lesson 0.1 
      How it works
    
  
  



  You are here · Module 0
  Foundations
  R from zero, describing data, probability, inference and matrices.
  Open Module 0 



  The whole journey
  11 modules, one lesson a week
  Each circle is a module. At 5–7 hours a week the whole course takes about 160 weeks, and you only ever need to think about the next step.
  
  See every module and lesson · Plan your weeks
