title: Continuous distributions
text:
Module 0 · Lesson 10 of 14 Week 10 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Temperatures, pressures, fill weights and lifetimes can take any value in a range, not just whole numbers. These are continuous random variables, and they need a different kind of distribution. Instead of a probability for each value, there’s a curve, and probabilities are areas under it. This is where your calculus comes in, because areas under curves are integrals! This lesson introduces the three continuous distributions you’ll use most, above all the normal distribution, which much of statistics is built on.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Continuous distributions
text:
From histograms to density curves
For a continuous variable, the probability of any exact value is zero. The chance that a bag weighs exactly 25.000000… kg is nil. Only ranges, like “between 24.9 and 25.1 kg”, have a positive probability.
Draw a histogram on a density scale, where each bar’s area is the proportion of the data in its bin. As the data grows and the bins get narrower, the bars trace out a smooth curve:


Show the code
set.seed(10)
sim <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100000))
panels <- rbind(
  transform(sim[1:200, , drop = FALSE], panel = "200 values, wide bins"),
  transform(sim[1:5000, , drop = FALSE], panel = "5,000 values"),
  transform(sim, panel = "100,000 values, narrow bins")
)
panels$panel <- factor(panels$panel, levels = unique(panels$panel))
bw <- c("200 values, wide bins" = 0.5, "5,000 values" = 0.25, "100,000 values, narrow bins" = 0.05)
ggplot(panels, aes(x = x)) +
  lapply(names(bw), function(p) geom_histogram(data = panels[panels$panel == p, ], aes(y = after_stat(density)),
                                               binwidth = bw[[p]], fill = "#F4C0D1", color = NA)) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









That limiting curve is the variable’s probability density function (PDF), f(x).

title: Continuous distributions
text:
Densities, areas and integrals
A density function is never negative, and the total area under it is 1. Probabilities are areas:

P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx .

The cumulative distribution function (CDF) gives the area to the left of a point: F(x) = P(X \le x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(t)\,dt. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, the density is the derivative of the CDF, f(x) = F'(x). And because single points have zero probability, it makes no difference whether you write < or \le.
Here’s a simple example. A reaction’s conversion, the fraction of reactant that gets converted, always lies between 0 and 1. Say the conversion in a batch has the density f(x) = 2x on [0, 1], so high conversions are more likely than low ones. (It’s a triangle with base 1 and height 2, so its area is 1.) What’s the chance that a batch converts at most half its reactant? By hand,

P(X \le 0.5) = \int_0^{0.5} 2x\,dx = \Big[x^2\Big]_0^{0.5} = 0.25 .

R’s integrate() computes integrals numerically. Give it a function and the limits:

f <- function(x) 2 * x
integrate(f, lower = 0, upper = 0.5)
#> 0.25 with absolute error < 2.8e-15
integrate(f, lower = 0, upper = 1)   # the total area: 1
#> 1 with absolute error < 1.1e-14

The mean and variance work just like the discrete versions, with the sums replaced by integrals:

E(X) = \mu = \int x\,f(x)\,dx, \qquad \text{Var}(X) = \int (x - \mu)^2 f(x)\,dx = E(X^2) - \mu^2 .

For the conversion, E(X) = \int_0^1 2x^2\,dx = 2/3 and E(X^2) = \int_0^1 2x^3\,dx = 1/2, so \text{Var}(X) = 1/2 - 4/9 = 1/18:

mu <- integrate(function(x) x * f(x), 0, 1)$value
ex2 <- integrate(function(x) x^2 * f(x), 0, 1)$value
c(mean = mu, variance = ex2 - mu^2)
#>       mean   variance 
#> 0.66666667 0.05555556

$value pulls the number out of integrate()’s result. So the average conversion is 2/3, about 67%.
Your turn. With the same density, use integrate() to find the probability that the conversion is above 0.5.









integrate(f, lower, upper) returns an object. Add $value to get the number.


f <- function(x) 2 * x
integrate(f, lower = 0.5, upper = 1)$value
By hand: \big[x^2\big]_{0.5}^{1} = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75.

title: Continuous distributions
text:
The uniform distribution
The uniform distribution on [a, b] makes every value in the interval equally likely. Its density is flat, f(x) = 1/(b - a), so probabilities are just proportions of the interval’s length. Its mean is (a + b)/2 and its variance is (b - a)^2/12.
An autosampler draws a sample from the reactor every 20 minutes. If a disturbance starts at a random moment, the delay until the next sample can catch it is uniform on [0, 20] minutes:

punif(15, min = 0, max = 20)       # P(delay <= 15)
#> [1] 0.75
1 - punif(15, min = 0, max = 20)   # P(delay > 15)
#> [1] 0.25
qunif(0.5, min = 0, max = 20)      # the median delay
#> [1] 10

You’ve already used runif(), which draws uniform random numbers, in Lesson 8.






NoteGo deeper: the uniform’s variance





With f(x) = 1/(b-a) on [a, b],

E(X) = \int_a^b \frac{x}{b-a}\,dx = \frac{b^2 - a^2}{2(b-a)} = \frac{a+b}{2}, \qquad
E(X^2) = \int_a^b \frac{x^2}{b-a}\,dx = \frac{b^3 - a^3}{3(b-a)} = \frac{a^2 + ab + b^2}{3} .

So \text{Var}(X) = \frac{a^2 + ab + b^2}{3} - \frac{(a+b)^2}{4} = \frac{(b-a)^2}{12}. For the autosampler, the standard deviation of the delay is 20/\sqrt{12} \approx 5.8 minutes.



Your turn. What’s the probability that a disturbance is caught within 5 minutes?









The delay is uniform on [0, 20]. Use punif() with min and max.


punif(5, min = 0, max = 20)

title: Continuous distributions
text:
The exponential distribution: lifetimes
When events happen independently at a constant average rate \lambda, the Poisson distribution from the last lesson counts them. The waiting time until the next event follows the exponential distribution:

f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, \qquad F(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}, \qquad x \ge 0 .

Its mean and standard deviation are both 1/\lambda. Reliability engineers use it all the time for random failures. A pump with a mean time between failures (MTBF) of 2,000 hours fails at a rate of \lambda = 1/2000 per hour. What’s the chance that it survives a 1,000-hour production campaign?

1 - pexp(1000, rate = 1 / 2000)   # P(lifetime > 1000 hours) = e^(-0.5)
#> [1] 0.6065307
exp(-0.5)
#> [1] 0.6065307

About 61%. The exponential has an unusual property: it’s memoryless. If the pump has already run for 1,000 hours, the chance that it runs another 1,000 is exactly the same as for a brand-new pump:

P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = \frac{e^{-\lambda(s+t)}}{e^{-\lambda s}} = e^{-\lambda t} = P(X > t) .

That fits failures caused by random shocks, like a power surge or a stray piece of debris. It doesn’t fit things that wear out, like bearings, seals and catalysts, which get more likely to fail as they age. Reliability engineers use other distributions for those, such as the Weibull.
Your turn. A temperature sensor fails at random, with an MTBF of 5,000 hours. What’s the probability that it lasts more than a year (8,760 hours)?









The rate is 1 / 5000 per hour. pexp(8760, rate = 1 / 5000) is the chance it fails within a year.


1 - pexp(8760, rate = 1 / 5000)
About 0.17: most of these sensors won’t make it through a year, so plan for spares!




Your turn: check the memory. The same sensor has already run for 2,000 hours. What’s the probability that it runs at least 5,000 more? That’s P(X > 7000 \mid X > 2000).









P(X > 7000 \mid X > 2000) = P(X > 7000) / P(X > 2000), because lasting past 7,000 hours means it lasted past 2,000 too.


(1 - pexp(7000, rate = 1 / 5000)) / (1 - pexp(2000, rate = 1 / 5000))
About 0.368, exactly the same as P(X > 5000) for a brand-new sensor. The 2,000 hours it has already run make no difference.

title: Continuous distributions
text:
The normal distribution
The normal distribution is the famous bell curve. It has two parameters, its mean \mu and its standard deviation \sigma, and its density is

f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \, e^{-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}} .

It’s symmetric around \mu, and \sigma sets its width. We write X \sim N(\mu, \sigma). (Some books write the variance \sigma^2 as the second parameter instead, so always check.)
Why is it everywhere? Measurements affected by many small, independent influences, like fill weights or measurement errors, tend to be roughly normal. Even more important, averages of almost anything are approximately normal when the sample is large. That’s the central limit theorem, in the next lesson, and it’s why the normal distribution turns up in nearly every method you’ll learn.
A packing line fills bags of product labeled 25 kg. The filled weights are roughly normal, with mean 25 kg and standard deviation 0.3 kg:

pnorm(24.5, mean = 25, sd = 0.3)                    # P(lighter than 24.5 kg)
#> [1] 0.04779035
pnorm(25.3, 25, 0.3) - pnorm(24.7, 25, 0.3)         # P(between 24.7 and 25.3 kg)
#> [1] 0.6826895
qnorm(0.99, mean = 25, sd = 0.3)                    # the 99th percentile
#> [1] 25.6979



Show the code
curve_df <- data.frame(x = seq(23.8, 26.2, length.out = 400))
curve_df$density <- dnorm(curve_df$x, 25, 0.3)
ggplot(curve_df, aes(x = x, y = density)) +
  geom_area(data = subset(curve_df, x >= 24.7 & x <= 25.3), fill = "#F4C0D1") +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 25, y = 0.5, label = "about 68%", size = 4.5) +
  labs(title = "P(24.7 < weight < 25.3) is the shaded area",
       x = "Bag weight (kg)", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)










Standardizing: the standard normal
Every normal distribution is a stretched and shifted copy of the standard normal, Z \sim N(0, 1). Turning a value into a z-score, as in Lesson 7,

z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} ,

turns any normal probability into a standard normal one. A 24.5 kg bag is z = (24.5 - 25)/0.3 \approx -1.67 standard deviations below the mean, and

pnorm((24.5 - 25) / 0.3)
#> [1] 0.04779035

gives the same answer as before. Before computers, statistics students looked these numbers up in printed tables.
The 68–95–99.7 rule from Lesson 7 comes straight from the standard normal:

pnorm(1) - pnorm(-1)
#> [1] 0.6826895
pnorm(2) - pnorm(-2)
#> [1] 0.9544997
pnorm(3) - pnorm(-3)
#> [1] 0.9973002
qnorm(0.975)
#> [1] 1.959964

The last line is a number you’ll see again and again: 95% of a normal distribution lies within 1.96 standard deviations of its mean.








curve() is base R’s quick way to draw a function.
Your turn. What proportion of the bags weigh between 24.5 and 25.5 kg?









Subtract the area to the left of 24.5 from the area to the left of 25.5.


pnorm(25.5, 25, 0.3) - pnorm(24.5, 25, 0.3)




Your turn. Below what weight do the lightest 5% of bags fall?









The lightest 5% are below the 5th percentile. qnorm() turns a probability into a value.


qnorm(0.05, mean = 25, sd = 0.3)
About 24.51 kg.

title: Continuous distributions
text:
Checking normality: Q-Q plots
Many methods assume the data come from a normal distribution, so you need a way to check. A histogram is a start, but a normal quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plot is sharper. It plots the sorted data against the values you’d expect from a normal distribution of the same size. If the data are normal, the points fall close to a straight line.


Show the code
qq <- rbind(
  data.frame(dataset = "Speed of light (Michelson)", value = morley$Speed),
  data.frame(dataset = "Ozone in New York", value = airquality$Ozone)
)
ggplot(qq, aes(sample = value)) +
  geom_qq(color = "#C2416C", size = 1.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_qq_line(color = "#898781", na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ dataset, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Theoretical normal quantiles", y = "Data") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









Michelson’s measurements follow the line closely: they’re close to normal. The ozone points curve upward at the right, the signature of right skew: the largest values are much bigger than a normal distribution would produce. An S-shape means tails that are heavier or lighter than normal. In base R, qqnorm(x) followed by qqline(x) draws the same plot.
Real data are never exactly normal. What matters is whether they’re close enough for the method you’re using, which later modules discuss method by method.



Your turn. Draw a normal Q-Q plot of the batch yields, batches$yield_pct, with a reference line. Do they look normal?









In base R: qqnorm(batches$yield_pct), then qqline(batches$yield_pct) on the next line.


qqnorm(batches$yield_pct)
qqline(batches$yield_pct)
The middle of the data follows the line nicely, but the three poor batches fall well below it at the left end: a heavier lower tail than a normal distribution would have.

title: Continuous distributions
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · A mean by integration. Pump lifetimes, measured in thousands of hours, are exponential with rate 0.5. Use integrate() to compute the mean lifetime, E(X) = \int_0^\infty x\,\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\,dx, and check it against 1/\lambda.









Integrate function(x) x * dexp(x, rate = 0.5) from 0 to Inf. integrate() can handle infinite limits.


integrate(function(x) x * dexp(x, rate = 0.5), lower = 0, upper = Inf)$value
2, which is 1/\lambda: an MTBF of 2,000 hours. By hand, integration by parts gives \int_0^\infty x\lambda e^{-\lambda x}dx = \big[-xe^{-\lambda x}\big]_0^\infty + \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda x}dx = 1/\lambda.




Challenge 2 · Set the filling machine. Selling a bag that’s lighter than its 25 kg label is against the law, so the line is allowed to underfill at most 1% of the bags. The spread of the filler is fixed at \sigma = 0.3 kg, but you can choose its target mean \mu. What’s the smallest target that keeps underweight bags to 1%?









You need 25 kg to sit at the 1st percentile of the distribution. In z-scores, that’s $z = $ qnorm(0.01), which is negative.


25 = \mu + z\sigma with z = qnorm(0.01), so \mu = 25 - z\sigma. That’s the same as 25 + qnorm(0.99) * sigma.


sigma <- 0.3
25 + qnorm(0.99) * sigma
About 25.70 kg. Check it: pnorm(25, mean = 25.70, sd = 0.3) is about 0.01. Every bag gets about 0.7 kg of free product on average, which is why engineers work so hard to make fillers more precise: halve \sigma, and you halve the giveaway.

title: Continuous distributions
text:
Quick quiz

1. X is a continuous random variable. What is P(X = 3)?

0
f(3)
It depends on the distribution


A single point has no width, so the area above it is zero. Only intervals have positive probability.



2. What is the total area under any probability density function?

1
It depends on the mean
Infinity


The total probability of all values is 1, and probability is area.



3. What is pnorm(0)?

0.5
0
0.399


The standard normal is symmetric about 0, so half its area is to the left. (0.399 is dnorm(0), the height of the curve.)



4. What is qnorm(0.975), approximately?

0.83
1.96
2.58


97.5% of the standard normal lies below 1.96, so 95% lies between −1.96 and 1.96.



5. A pump’s lifetime is exponential, and it has already run 1,000 hours. What can you say about the next 1,000?

It’s now more likely to fail, because it’s getting old
Its chance of failing is the same as a brand-new pump’s
It’s now less likely to fail


The exponential is memoryless: the hours already run tell you nothing about the future. Real wear-out failures need other distributions.



6. In a normal Q-Q plot, the points curve upward, away from the line, at the right-hand end. What does that suggest?

The data are right-skewed
The data are exactly normal
The data have no outliers


The largest values are bigger than a normal distribution would produce: a long right tail.

title: Continuous distributions
text:
Wrap-up
Calculus and probability, together at last! Here’s what you can do now:

Think in areas: for continuous variables, probabilities are areas under the density, \int_a^b f(x)\,dx, and single values have probability zero.
Use the CDF: F(x) = P(X \le x) accumulates area, and its derivative is the density. integrate() computes areas numerically.
Pick the right model: the uniform is flat; the exponential models waiting times and random failures, with mean 1/\lambda, and it’s memoryless.
Use the normal: standardize with z = (x - \mu)/\sigma. About 68%, 95% and 99.7% of it lies within 1, 2 and 3 SDs, and 95% within 1.96.
Check normality with a Q-Q plot: points near a straight line suggest a normal distribution, and curves reveal skew or heavy tails.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Work in week10.R.

Draw the families. Plot normal densities with mean 0 and SDs 0.5, 1 and 2 on one chart, using stat_function() in ggplot2, or curve() with add = TRUE in base R. Do the same for exponential densities with rates 0.5, 1 and 2.
Simulation against theory. Draw 10,000 bag weights from N(25, 0.3). Plot a density-scale histogram (aes(y = after_stat(density))) and add the theoretical curve with stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 25, sd = 0.3)).
Is it normal? Make normal Q-Q plots of temp_C, residence_min and purity_pct from the batches. Which looks most normal? Back it up with histograms.
The cost of giveaway. For filler SDs from 0.1 to 0.5 kg, compute the target mean that keeps underweight bags to 1%, and plot the average giveaway (target minus 25 kg) against the SD. How much product does a more precise filler save on a million bags a year?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Continuous random variable

A random variable that can take any value in an interval.

Probability density function (PDF)

A curve whose area over an interval gives the probability of that interval.

Cumulative distribution function (CDF)

F(x) = P(X \le x), the area under the density to the left of x.

Uniform distribution

A distribution in which every value in an interval is equally likely.

Exponential distribution

The distribution of the waiting time until the next event in a process with a constant rate.

Memoryless property

The time already waited doesn’t change the distribution of the remaining waiting time.

Normal distribution

The symmetric, bell-shaped distribution N(\mu, \sigma).

Standard normal

The normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

Q-Q plot

A plot of sorted data against the quantiles of a theoretical distribution, used to check how well it fits.











NoteWant to read more?






Seeing Theory, “Probability Distributions”. Continuous distributions and their densities, interactively.
Introduction to Modern Statistics, “Inference with mathematical models”. The normal distribution as it’s used in statistics, with lots of worked examples.
Introduction to Probability by Blitzstein and Hwang, chapters 5–6, free PDF. Continuous random variables and the uniform, normal and exponential distributions, with full derivations.

title: Confidence intervals
text:
Module 0 · Lesson 12 of 14 Week 12 of 160 About 5–7 hours
“The reactor’s average yield is 57.6%” sounds precise. But that’s from just 40 batches, and the long-run average of the process could easily be a few points different. A confidence interval reports an estimate together with a range of plausible values for the true parameter, like “57.6%, give or take about 3 points”. It’s the most useful single tool in this module, and you’ll use it in every analysis you ever write up.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Confidence intervals
section: From a point estimate to an interval
text:
From a point estimate to an interval
A single value like \bar{x} is a point estimate. The last lesson showed that \bar{x} varies around \mu with standard error \sigma/\sqrt{n}, and that, by the central limit theorem, its sampling distribution is approximately normal. So in 95% of samples,

\bar{x} \text{ lies within } 1.96 \times \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \text{ of } \mu .

Turn that around: in 95% of samples, \mu lies within 1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt{n} of \bar{x}. That gives the 95% confidence interval

\bar{x} \pm 1.96\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} .

Every confidence interval in this course has the same form:

\text{estimate} \pm \underbrace{\text{critical value} \times \text{standard error}}_{\text{margin of error}} .

Here’s an example where \sigma is known. Years of records show that the bag filler’s weights vary with a standard deviation of 0.3 kg. A sample of 36 bags has a mean of 24.92 kg:

xbar <- 24.92
sigma <- 0.3
n <- 36
margin <- qnorm(0.975) * sigma / sqrt(n)
c(lower = xbar - margin, upper = xbar + margin)
#>  lower  upper 
#> 24.822 25.018

The filler’s true average is plausibly anywhere from about 24.82 to 25.02 kg. Since the label promises 25 kg, it’s worth checking the machine’s setting.

title: Confidence intervals
text:
What “95% confidence” means
This is the most misunderstood idea in introductory statistics, so it’s worth getting exactly right.
The 95% describes the method, not any single interval. If you took lots of random samples and built an interval from each one, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true \mu. Any particular interval either contains \mu or it doesn’t. You just don’t know which, and you’re “95% confident” in the sense that you used a method that works 95% of the time.
A simulation makes this concrete. Imagine 100 labs, each measuring a reference standard 25 times. The standard’s true concentration is 50 mg/L, and each lab builds a 95% interval from its own measurements:


Show the code
set.seed(12)
intervals <- t(replicate(100, {
  y <- rnorm(25, mean = 50, sd = 4)
  t.test(y)$conf.int
}))
ci <- data.frame(lab = 1:100, lower = intervals[, 1], upper = intervals[, 2])
ci$result <- ifelse(ci$lower <= 50 & ci$upper >= 50, "Contains 50", "Misses 50")
ggplot(ci, aes(y = lab, xmin = lower, xmax = upper, color = result)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 50, color = "#52514e") +
  geom_errorbar(orientation = "y", width = 0, linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Contains 50" = "#2a78d6", "Misses 50" = "#C2416C")) +
  labs(title = paste0("100 labs, 100 confidence intervals: ", sum(ci$result == "Misses 50"), " miss the truth"),
       x = "95% confidence interval (mg/L)", y = "Lab", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")









Each horizontal line is one lab’s interval. The intervals move around because the measurements do, and a few miss the vertical line at the true value. In the long run, 5% of them will.
Three things a 95% confidence interval does not mean:

It’s not the range containing 95% of the data. Individual values are much more spread out than the mean.
It’s not the range where 95% of future sample means will fall.
Strictly, it’s not “a 95% probability that \mu is in this interval”. \mu is a fixed number, so it’s either in or out. (Bayesian credible intervals, in Module 5, do mean that.)

A correct way to report it: “We are 95% confident that the filler’s mean weight is between 24.82 and 25.02 kg.”

Other confidence levels
A higher confidence level needs a larger critical value, so the interval gets wider. That’s the price of being more sure:

levels <- c(0.90, 0.95, 0.99)
data.frame(confidence = levels, critical_value = qnorm(1 - (1 - levels) / 2))
#>   confidence critical_value
#> 1       0.90       1.644854
#> 2       0.95       1.959964
#> 3       0.99       2.575829

The other way to get a narrower interval is a bigger sample. Because the standard error shrinks like 1/\sqrt{n}, four times the data halves the width.
Your turn. The filler’s SD is \sigma = 0.3 kg. After a repair, a sample of 36 bags has a mean of 25.05 kg. Compute the 95% confidence interval, returning the lower and upper limits.









The margin of error is qnorm(0.975) * sigma / sqrt(n).


xbar <- 25.05
sigma <- 0.3
n <- 36
margin <- qnorm(0.975) * sigma / sqrt(n)
c(xbar - margin, xbar + margin)
About 24.95 to 25.15 kg. The interval now includes 25 kg comfortably.

title: Confidence intervals
section: When σ is unknown: the t distribution
text:
When σ is unknown: the t distribution
In practice you almost never know \sigma, so you estimate it with s. That adds extra uncertainty, especially in small samples, and the normal critical value 1.96 becomes too small. The fix was found by William Sealy Gosset, a chemist at the Guinness brewery in Dublin, who had to judge the quality of barley and yeast from very small samples. He published it in 1908 under the pen name “Student”.
If the population is normal,

t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{s / \sqrt{n}}

follows a t distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom. It looks like the standard normal, but with heavier tails, and the fewer the degrees of freedom, the heavier the tails. With more data, it gets closer and closer to normal:

df <- c(2, 5, 10, 30, 100)
data.frame(df = df, t_critical = round(qt(0.975, df), 3), normal = round(qnorm(0.975), 3))
#>    df t_critical normal
#> 1   2      4.303   1.96
#> 2   5      2.571   1.96
#> 3  10      2.228   1.96
#> 4  30      2.042   1.96
#> 5 100      1.984   1.96

So the 95% interval for a mean, when \sigma is unknown, is

\bar{x} \pm t^*_{n-1} \, \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} ,

where t^*_{n-1} is qt(0.975, df = n - 1). Here it is for the mean yield of our batches, step by step:

x <- batches$yield_pct
n <- length(x)
se <- sd(x) / sqrt(n)
t_star <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1)
c(estimate = mean(x), lower = mean(x) - t_star * se, upper = mean(x) + t_star * se)
#> estimate    lower    upper 
#> 57.64750 54.52947 60.76553

t.test() does it all at once:

t.test(batches$yield_pct)
#> 
#>  One Sample t-test
#> 
#> data:  batches$yield_pct
#> t = 37.396, df = 39, p-value < 2.2e-16
#> alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 0
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  54.52947 60.76553
#> sample estimates:
#> mean of x 
#>   57.6475

For now, look at the last lines of the output: the 95% confidence interval and the sample mean. The rest is a hypothesis test, the topic of the next lesson. To pull out just the interval, use t.test(x)$conf.int. To change the level, use t.test(x, conf.level = 0.99).






ImportantWhen can you trust a t interval?




Independence. The data come from a random sample or a randomized experiment, and the observations don’t influence each other.
Normality, or a large enough sample. For small samples (n < 30), the population should be roughly normal, so check a histogram or Q-Q plot for strong skew and outliers. For larger samples the central limit theorem covers moderate skew, but extreme outliers still cause trouble.

A t interval from a biased sample is precisely wrong. No formula can fix how the data were collected.







Your turn. What’s the t critical value for a 95% interval from 8 replicate measurements?









qt(0.975, df = ...), with n - 1 degrees of freedom.


qt(0.975, df = 7)
About 2.365, noticeably larger than 1.96. Small samples pay a price for estimating \sigma.




Your turn. Here are those 8 replicate measurements of a standard solution, in mg/L. Compute the 95% confidence interval for its true concentration with the formula. Then compare it with t.test().









se <- sd(x) / sqrt(n) and t_star <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1).


x <- c(10.2, 10.5, 9.9, 10.1, 10.3, 10.4, 10.0, 10.2)
n <- length(x)
se <- sd(x) / sqrt(n)
t_star <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1)
c(mean(x) - t_star * se, mean(x) + t_star * se)




Your turn. Return the 95% confidence interval for the mean purity of the batches. (batches is ready.)









t.test(...)$conf.int pulls out the interval.


t.test(batches$purity_pct)$conf.int




Your turn. Return the 99% confidence interval for the mean yield. Is it wider or narrower than the 95% one (54.5% to 60.8%)?









t.test() has a conf.level argument.


t.test(batches$yield_pct, conf.level = 0.99)$conf.int

title: Confidence intervals
text:
An interval for a proportion
For a proportion, the estimate is \hat{p}, and its standard error is estimated by \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}, so

\hat{p} \pm z^* \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}} .

It’s reliable when the sample has at least 10 successes and 10 failures. An inspection of 400 drums finds 22 that leak:

p_hat <- 22 / 400
se <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / 400)
c(estimate = p_hat, lower = p_hat - 1.96 * se, upper = p_hat + 1.96 * se)
#>   estimate      lower      upper 
#> 0.05500000 0.03265793 0.07734207

The line’s true leak rate is plausibly between about 3.3% and 7.7%. R’s prop.test(22, 400) gives a slightly different interval, because it uses a more accurate method (the Wilson score interval, with a continuity correction). That matters most for small samples, and for proportions close to 0 or 1, like this one.
Your turn. A new purification step is tried on 80 batches, and 52 of them reach 99.5% purity. Compute the 95% confidence interval for the step’s success rate with the formula.









\text{SE} = \sqrt{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})/n}, with n = 80.


p_hat <- 52 / 80
se <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / 80)
c(p_hat - 1.96 * se, p_hat + 1.96 * se)

title: Confidence intervals
section: How many measurements do you need?
text:
How many measurements do you need?
Before you collect any data, you can choose n to get the margin of error E you want. For a mean, solve E = z^* \sigma/\sqrt{n}:

n = \left(\frac{z^*\,\sigma}{E}\right)^2 ,

using a guess for \sigma from earlier work or a small pilot study, and always rounding up. How many titrations do you need to pin a concentration down to within 0.05 mol/L, if single titrations vary with an SD of about 0.12 mol/L?

ceiling((qnorm(0.975) * 0.12 / 0.05)^2)
#> [1] 23

For a proportion, n = (z^*)^2\,p(1-p)/E^2. If you have no idea what p is, use p = 0.5, which gives the largest (safest) answer. An opinion poll with a margin of error of 3 percentage points needs

ceiling(qnorm(0.975)^2 * 0.5 * 0.5 / 0.03^2)
#> [1] 1068

about 1,000 people, whether the country has 5 million voters or 300 million. Precision depends on the size of the sample, not the size of the population.
Your turn. You want to estimate the reactor’s mean yield to within 2 percentage points, with 95% confidence. Batch yields vary with an SD of about 10 points. How many batches do you need?









n = (z^*\sigma/E)^2, rounded up with ceiling().


ceiling((qnorm(0.975) * 10 / 2)^2)
97 batches, more than twice our 40.




Your turn. A study will estimate a defect rate that’s probably around 4%, to within 1 percentage point (0.01), with 95% confidence. How many items must it inspect?









n = (z^*)^2\,p(1-p)/E^2 with p = 0.04 and E = 0.01, rounded up.


ceiling(qnorm(0.975)^2 * 0.04 * 0.96 / 0.01^2)
1,476 items. Using p = 0.5 instead would ask for 9,604, so a sensible guess for p saves a lot of work.

title: Confidence intervals
text:
The bootstrap: intervals without formulas
What if you want an interval for a median, which has no simple standard-error formula? The bootstrap offers a brilliant workaround. Your sample is your best picture of the population, so you resample from the sample itself, with replacement, and see how much the statistic varies:

Draw n values from your data, with replacement (some values appear twice, some not at all).
Compute the statistic for this “bootstrap sample”.
Repeat thousands of times.
The middle 95% of the bootstrap statistics is a 95% percentile bootstrap interval.


x <- batches$yield_pct
set.seed(12)
boot_medians <- replicate(10000, median(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))
quantile(boot_medians, c(0.025, 0.975))
#>  2.5% 97.5% 
#> 56.10 59.85

For the mean, the bootstrap gives almost the same answer as the t interval:

boot_means <- replicate(10000, mean(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))
quantile(boot_means, c(0.025, 0.975))
#>    2.5%   97.5% 
#> 54.5350 60.5775
t.test(x)$conf.int
#> [1] 54.52947 60.76553
#> attr(,"conf.level")
#> [1] 0.95

The bootstrap isn’t magic: it needs a reasonably large, representative sample, and it struggles with extreme statistics like the maximum. Module 4 covers when it works, and better versions of it.

title: Confidence intervals
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Check the coverage. Does a 95% t interval really capture the truth 95% of the time? Simulate 1,000 samples of size 10 from a standard normal distribution (true mean 0), and find the proportion of their 95% intervals that contain 0.









The interval contains 0 when its lower limit is below 0 and its upper limit is above 0: ci[1] < 0 & ci[2] > 0.


set.seed(10)
covers <- replicate(1000, {
  ci <- t.test(rnorm(10))$conf.int
  ci[1] < 0 & ci[2] > 0
})
mean(covers)




Challenge 2 · A bootstrap interval. Build a 95% percentile bootstrap interval for the median purity of the batches.









Each bootstrap median is median(sample(x, replace = TRUE)).


The interval is quantile(boot_medians, c(0.025, 0.975)).


x <- batches$purity_pct
set.seed(11)
boot_medians <- replicate(10000, median(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))
quantile(boot_medians, c(0.025, 0.975))

title: Confidence intervals
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does “95% confidence” mean?

The method produces intervals that contain the true parameter in 95% of samples
95% of the data lie inside the interval
There’s a 95% chance the sample mean is inside the interval


The confidence level describes how often the procedure works across repeated samples.



2. You switch from a 95% to a 99% confidence interval, with the same data. The interval…

gets wider
gets narrower
stays the same


To be more confident of catching the parameter, you need a wider net: 2.576 instead of 1.96.



3. You collect four times as much data. Roughly what happens to the width of the interval?

It’s divided by 4
It’s halved
It doesn’t change


The width is proportional to the standard error, s/\sqrt{n}, and \sqrt{4} = 2.



4. Why use the t distribution instead of the normal for an interval for a mean?

Because the data aren’t normal
Because \sigma is estimated by s, which adds uncertainty
Because the sample is large


Estimating \sigma adds variability, which the heavier-tailed t distribution accounts for. With large samples, the t and normal critical values are nearly the same.



5. A 95% confidence interval for the mean yield is 54.5% to 60.8%. Which statement is correct?

We’re 95% confident that the process’s true mean yield is between 54.5% and 60.8%
95% of batches have yields between 54.5% and 60.8%
95% of future samples will have a mean between 54.5% and 60.8%


The interval is about the process mean, not individual batches or future sample means. (Individual batches range from 31% to 75%!)



6. An engineer samples only the batches that “looked fine” on the control screen. Their 95% interval is very narrow. What’s the biggest concern?

The sample is too small
The sample isn’t random, so the interval may be precisely wrong
The confidence level is too high


Intervals measure sampling variability, not bias. A hand-picked sample can miss the truth by far more than any margin of error.

title: Confidence intervals
text:
Wrap-up
You can now put an honest error bar on any estimate. Here’s what you can do:

Build intervals: estimate ± critical value × standard error.
Interpret them right: “95% confidence” means the method catches the true parameter in 95% of samples. A single interval either contains it or doesn’t.
Trade off: higher confidence means wider intervals; larger samples mean narrower ones, at a rate of 1/\sqrt{n}.
Use t when σ is unknown: \bar{x} \pm t^* s/\sqrt{n}, or simply t.test(). It needs independence and, for small samples, a roughly normal population.
Handle proportions: \hat{p} \pm z^*\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}, with at least 10 successes and 10 failures.
Plan ahead: n = (z^*\sigma/E)^2 for a mean, or (z^*)^2 p(1-p)/E^2 for a proportion, always rounded up.
Bootstrap when there’s no formula, and remember: no interval can fix a biased sample.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Work in week12.R.

Intervals by group. For each catalyst, compute the mean yield and its 95% t interval. With dplyr: summarise(mean = mean(yield_pct), lower = t.test(yield_pct)$conf.int[1], upper = t.test(yield_pct)$conf.int[2]).
Plot them. Draw the intervals with geom_pointrange(aes(x = catalyst, y = mean, ymin = lower, ymax = upper)). Which catalysts’ intervals overlap? Why are some wider than others?
When the t interval struggles. Repeat Challenge 1 with samples of size 10 from a strongly skewed population, rexp(10), whose true mean is 1. What’s the coverage now? Try n = 30 and n = 100.
Compare methods for a proportion. For 22 leaky drums out of 400, compare the formula interval with prop.test(22, 400)$conf.int and binom.test(22, 400)$conf.int. Then try 2 out of 50. Which methods disagree most, and why?
Write it up. In two sentences, report the mean purity with its interval, as you would in a lab report, without using the word “probability”.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Point estimate

A single number used to estimate a parameter, such as \bar{x} for \mu.

Confidence interval

A range of plausible values for a parameter, from a method that captures the parameter a stated percentage of the time.

Confidence level

The long-run percentage of intervals that contain the true parameter, such as 95%.

Margin of error

The amount added to and subtracted from the estimate: a critical value times the standard error.

Critical value

The multiplier that sets the confidence level, such as 1.96 for 95% with a normal distribution.

t distribution

A bell-shaped distribution with heavier tails than the normal, used when \sigma is estimated from the data.

Degrees of freedom

The parameter of the t distribution. For a single mean, it’s n - 1.

Bootstrap

Resampling the observed data with replacement, to approximate a statistic’s sampling distribution.











NoteWant to read more?






Introduction to Modern Statistics, “Confidence intervals with bootstrapping” and “Inference for a single mean”. Intervals built both by resampling and with the t distribution.
Seeing Theory, “Frequentist Inference”. Watch confidence intervals succeed and fail as you draw samples.

title: Matrices for statistics
text:
Module 0 · Lesson 14 of 14 Week 14 of 160 About 5–7 hours
A dataset is a table of numbers, and the mathematics of tables of numbers is linear algebra. Chemical engineers use it constantly, often without calling it that: every material balance with several streams is a system of linear equations. Statisticians use it everywhere too. From Module 2 on, regression is written with matrices, and one compact formula gives the best-fitting coefficients for any number of predictors. Module 3 analyzes whole covariance matrices at once, and machine learning in Module 7 is linear algebra almost all the way down. This lesson teaches the matrix operations you’ll need, each with the intuition behind it, all in R.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Matrices for statistics
text:
Vectors and matrices
In linear algebra, a vector is an ordered list of numbers, usually written as a column. A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers with n rows and p columns, called an n \times p matrix. A dataset with n observations of p numerical variables is naturally an n \times p data matrix.
matrix() builds a matrix from a vector. It fills the matrix column by column, unless you say byrow = TRUE:

A <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)
A
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    3    5
#> [2,]    2    4    6
B <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
B
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    2    3
#> [2,]    4    5    6
dim(A)
#> [1] 2 3

You can also glue vectors together as columns with cbind(), or as rows with rbind(), and turn a numeric data frame into a matrix with as.matrix():

cbind(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(4, 5, 6))
#>      x y
#> [1,] 1 4
#> [2,] 2 5
#> [3,] 3 6
X <- as.matrix(stackloss[1:4, ])
X
#>   Air.Flow Water.Temp Acid.Conc. stack.loss
#> 1       80         27         89         42
#> 2       80         27         88         37
#> 3       75         25         90         37
#> 4       62         24         87         28

Indexing works just like for data frames: A[i, j] is the element in row i and column j, A[1, ] is the first row, and A[, 2] is the second column. A matrix holds a single type, usually numbers, which is what makes fast arithmetic on it possible.
Ordinary arithmetic operators work element by element, exactly as with vectors:

A + 10
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]   11   13   15
#> [2,]   12   14   16
A * A
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    9   25
#> [2,]    4   16   36

Your turn. Create the 3 \times 3 matrix with the numbers 1 to 9 filled in row by row, so the first row is 1, 2, 3.









matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ...), and tell it to fill by rows.


matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)

title: Matrices for statistics
text:
Matrix multiplication
The dot product of two vectors of the same length multiplies them element by element and adds up the results: x \cdot y = \sum_i x_i y_i. You’ve computed dot products already: the expected value \sum x\,p(x) in Lesson 9 is the dot product of the values and their probabilities.
The matrix product AB is built from dot products: the element in row i and column j of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. So the number of columns of A must equal the number of rows of B, and an n \times k matrix times a k \times p matrix gives an n \times p matrix. In R, matrix multiplication is %*%. A plain * is not matrix multiplication!

\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix} 1\cdot5 + 2\cdot7 & 1\cdot6 + 2\cdot8 \\ 3\cdot5 + 4\cdot7 & 3\cdot6 + 4\cdot8 \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix} 19 & 22 \\ 43 & 50 \end{pmatrix}


P <- matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
Q <- matrix(c(5, 6, 7, 8), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
P %*% Q
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]   19   22
#> [2,]   43   50
Q %*% P
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]   23   34
#> [2,]   31   46

Unlike ordinary multiplication, the order matters: PQ and QP are usually different.

Recipes and costs
A matrix times a vector is especially useful. A plant makes three products from three raw materials. The recipe matrix says how many kilograms of each raw material go into one tonne of each product, and the price vector gives each raw material’s price per kilogram. One multiplication gives the raw-material cost of every product:

recipe <- matrix(c(500, 300, 200,
                   200, 600, 200,
                   100, 100, 800), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
                 dimnames = list(c("P1", "P2", "P3"), c("M1", "M2", "M3")))
prices <- c(1.20, 0.80, 2.50)   # dollars per kg of M1, M2, M3
recipe %*% prices
#>    [,1]
#> P1 1340
#> P2 1220
#> P3 2200

Each cost is 500 \times 1.20 + 300 \times 0.80 + 200 \times 2.50, and so on: a linear combination of the prices. Regression predictions in Module 2 are computed in exactly the same way.
Your turn. Compute AB for these two matrices.









Matrix multiplication in R is %*%. A single * multiplies element by element.


A <- matrix(c(2, 0, 1, 3), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
B <- matrix(c(1, 4, 2, 5), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
A %*% B




Your turn. Raw-material prices change: M1 now costs 1.50 dollars per kg, M2 still 0.80 and M3 drops to 2.00. Compute the new cost of each product with one multiplication.









The prices are a vector in the same order as the columns: M1, M2, M3.


recipe <- matrix(c(500, 300, 200,
                   200, 600, 200,
                   100, 100, 800), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
prices <- c(1.50, 0.80, 2.00)
recipe %*% prices
P1 gets more expensive (1,390 dollars a tonne), while P2 and P3 get cheaper, especially P3, which uses lots of M3.

title: Matrices for statistics
text:
Transpose, identity and symmetric matrices
The transpose A^\top swaps rows and columns, so an n \times p matrix becomes p \times n. In R, it’s t():

t(A)
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    1    2
#> [2,]    3    4
#> [3,]    5    6

A useful rule: (AB)^\top = B^\top A^\top, with the order reversed.
A square matrix has as many rows as columns. The identity matrix I has 1s on its diagonal and 0s everywhere else, and it plays the role of the number 1: IA = AI = A. diag(n) creates an n \times n identity, and diag(c(...)) makes a matrix with the given numbers on its diagonal.

diag(3)
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    0    0
#> [2,]    0    1    0
#> [3,]    0    0    1

A matrix is symmetric if A^\top = A. Covariance and correlation matrices are symmetric, and so is X^\top X for any matrix X. That product appears so often in statistics that R has a shortcut for it: crossprod(X).

title: Matrices for statistics
text:
Inverses and determinants
The inverse of a square matrix A is the matrix A^{-1} with AA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = I, just like 1/a for a number. solve(A) computes it:

M <- matrix(c(4, 7, 2, 6), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
M_inv <- solve(M)
M_inv
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]  0.6 -0.7
#> [2,] -0.2  0.4
M %*% M_inv
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    1    0
#> [2,]    0    1

The product is the identity, up to tiny floating-point errors. To check a result like this, use all.equal(M %*% M_inv, diag(2)) rather than ==.
Not every square matrix has an inverse, just as 0 has no reciprocal. A matrix with no inverse is called singular, and the determinant tells you which matrices those are. For a 2 \times 2 matrix,

\det \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} = ad - bc ,

and in general det() computes it. A matrix is singular exactly when its determinant is 0, which happens when one column is a combination of the others:

det(M)
#> [1] 10
S <- matrix(c(1, 2, 2, 4), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)   # the second column is twice the first
det(S)
#> [1] 0

solve(S) would stop with an error saying the matrix is singular. In statistics, this happens when one predictor is an exact combination of others, like having the temperature in both °C and kelvin in the same model. Module 2’s lesson on multicollinearity deals with the trickier case, where predictors are nearly combinations of each other.
Your turn. Compute the inverse of M = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 7 \\ 2 & 6 \end{pmatrix}.









With a single argument, solve() returns the inverse.


M <- matrix(c(4, 7, 2, 6), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
solve(M)
For a 2 \times 2 matrix, the inverse is \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix}, here \frac{1}{10}\begin{pmatrix} 6 & -7 \\ -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}.




Your turn. The second column of S is three times the first. Return its determinant, and think about what that means for solve(S).









det(S)


S <- matrix(c(2, 6,
              1, 3), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
det(S)
The determinant is 0, so S is singular and has no inverse: solve(S) gives an error.

title: Matrices for statistics
text:
Solving mass balances
Here’s where linear algebra meets your engineering classes. Two streams are mixed: stream A is 10% ethanol, and stream B is 50% ethanol. You need 100 kg of a 20% ethanol mixture. How much of each stream should you use? Write a mass balance for the total and one for the ethanol:

\begin{aligned} a + b &= 100 \\ 0.10\,a + 0.50\,b &= 20 \end{aligned}
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0.10 & 0.50 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 100 \\ 20 \end{pmatrix} ,

that is, A\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{b}, with solution \mathbf{v} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}. Give solve() both A and \mathbf{b}:

A2 <- matrix(c(1, 1,
               0.10, 0.50), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
b <- c(100, 20)
solve(A2, b)
#> [1] 75 25

75 kg of stream A and 25 kg of stream B. solve(A, b) is faster and more accurate than computing the inverse first and then multiplying, solve(A) %*% b, so prefer it. And the same one line works for 3 streams, or 30.
Your turn: a three-stream blend. Three streams contain ethanol, water and methanol in these mass fractions:




Stream 1
Stream 2
Stream 3




Ethanol
0.6
0.2
0.0


Water
0.4
0.5
0.3


Methanol
0.0
0.3
0.7



You need a blend containing 30 kg of ethanol, 40 kg of water and 30 kg of methanol. How many kilograms of each stream should you use?









Each row of A is one component’s balance, so \mathbf{b} holds the kilograms of each component you need, in the same order: ethanol, water, methanol.


A <- matrix(c(0.6, 0.2, 0.0,
              0.4, 0.5, 0.3,
              0.0, 0.3, 0.7), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
b <- c(30, 40, 30)
solve(A, b)
40 kg of stream 1, and 30 kg each of streams 2 and 3. Check the ethanol: 0.6 \times 40 + 0.2 \times 30 = 30. ✓

title: Matrices for statistics
text:
Statistics with matrices
Let X be an n \times p data matrix. Its mean vector holds the mean of each column:

X <- as.matrix(stackloss)
colMeans(X)
#>   Air.Flow Water.Temp Acid.Conc. stack.loss 
#>   60.42857   21.09524   86.28571   17.52381

Centering subtracts each column’s mean from that column. The covariance matrix is then

S = \frac{1}{n-1}\, X_c^\top X_c ,

where X_c is the centered data. Its diagonal holds each variable’s variance, and the off-diagonal entries are the covariances between pairs of variables: positive when two variables tend to be above their means together, negative when one tends to be above while the other is below. Divide each covariance by the two standard deviations, and you get the correlations from Lesson 7.

Xc <- scale(X, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)   # subtract each column's mean
S <- crossprod(Xc) / (nrow(X) - 1)
round(S, 2)
#>            Air.Flow Water.Temp Acid.Conc. stack.loss
#> Air.Flow      84.06      22.66      24.57      85.76
#> Water.Temp    22.66       9.99       6.62      28.15
#> Acid.Conc.    24.57       6.62      28.71      21.79
#> stack.loss    85.76      28.15      21.79     103.46
all.equal(S, cov(X), check.attributes = FALSE)
#> [1] TRUE
round(cov2cor(S), 2)
#>            Air.Flow Water.Temp Acid.Conc. stack.loss
#> Air.Flow       1.00       0.78       0.50       0.92
#> Water.Temp     0.78       1.00       0.39       0.88
#> Acid.Conc.     0.50       0.39       1.00       0.40
#> stack.loss     0.92       0.88       0.40       1.00

The covariance matrix sums up how a whole set of variables varies and moves together. Here, the stack loss is strongly related to both the air flow (0.92) and the cooling-water temperature (0.88). Module 3 is largely about analyzing matrices like this one.
Your turn. Compute the covariance matrix of the batches’ temperature, residence time and yield from the formula X_c^\top X_c / (n - 1), without cov(). (The batches with a missing temperature are removed for you.)












t(Xc) %*% Xc (or crossprod(Xc)), divided by nrow(X) - 1.


X <- as.matrix(na.omit(batches[, c("temp_C", "residence_min", "yield_pct")]))
Xc <- scale(X, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
crossprod(Xc) / (nrow(X) - 1)

title: Matrices for statistics
text:
Regression in one formula
Here’s a preview of Module 2. To predict the stack loss from the air flow, regression finds the line \widehat{\text{loss}} = b_0 + b_1 \cdot \text{air flow} that minimizes the sum of squared prediction errors: the least-squares idea from Lesson 7. Put a column of 1s (for the intercept) next to the predictor to form the design matrix X, and the least-squares coefficients are

\mathbf{b} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y} .


y <- stackloss$stack.loss
X <- cbind(intercept = 1, air_flow = stackloss$Air.Flow)
solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, y))   # (X'X)^(-1) X'y, computed by solving
#>                 [,1]
#> intercept -44.132025
#> air_flow    1.020309
coef(lm(stack.loss ~ Air.Flow, data = stackloss))
#> (Intercept)    Air.Flow 
#>  -44.132025    1.020309

The two agree: each extra unit of air flow adds about 1 unit of stack loss. crossprod(X, y) computes X^\top y, and solving the system X^\top X\,\mathbf{b} = X^\top y avoids computing the inverse explicitly. The same formula handles any number of predictors: you just add columns to X.






NoteGo deeper: where the formula comes from





The sum of squared errors is f(\mathbf{b}) = (\mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{b})^\top(\mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{b}). Expanding it gives \mathbf{y}^\top\mathbf{y} - 2\mathbf{b}^\top X^\top\mathbf{y} + \mathbf{b}^\top X^\top X \mathbf{b}. Set its gradient (the vector of partial derivatives) to zero, just as you’d set a derivative to zero in one variable:

\nabla f(\mathbf{b}) = -2X^\top\mathbf{y} + 2X^\top X\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
X^\top X\,\mathbf{b} = X^\top\mathbf{y} .

These are the normal equations. When X^\top X is invertible, which needs no predictor to be an exact combination of the others, the unique solution is \mathbf{b} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\mathbf{y}. With a single predictor and an intercept, it reduces to formulas involving the means, standard deviations and correlation, as Lesson 2.2 shows.



Your turn. Compute the least-squares coefficients for predicting the stack loss from the cooling-water temperature, Water.Temp, with the normal equations.









solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, y)). (Or the long way: solve(t(X) %*% X) %*% t(X) %*% y.)


y <- stackloss$stack.loss
X <- cbind(1, stackloss$Water.Temp)
solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, y))
Compare with coef(lm(stack.loss ~ Water.Temp, data = stackloss)). Each degree warmer cooling water adds about 2.8 units of stack loss: warm water cools the absorption tower less well.

title: Matrices for statistics
text:
Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
Multiplying a vector by a square matrix usually changes its direction. But for special vectors, called eigenvectors, the matrix only stretches or shrinks them:

A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v} .

The stretch factor \lambda is the matching eigenvalue. eigen() finds both:

E <- eigen(M)
E$values
#> [1] 8.872983 1.127017
E$vectors
#>            [,1]       [,2]
#> [1,] -0.8207173 -0.9251135
#> [2,] -0.5713345  0.3796908
M %*% E$vectors[, 1]
#>           [,1]
#> [1,] -7.282211
#> [2,] -5.069442
E$values[1] * E$vectors[, 1]
#> [1] -7.282211 -5.069442

The last two lines are equal: multiplying the first eigenvector by M just scales it by the first eigenvalue.
For a covariance or correlation matrix, eigenvectors have a beautiful meaning: they point in the directions in which the data spread out most, and each eigenvalue is the variance of the data in its direction. Here’s the temperature–purity trade-off from our batches, with both variables standardized to z-scores:

tp <- na.omit(batches[, c("temp_C", "purity_pct")])
Z <- scale(tp)
R <- cor(tp)
R
#>                temp_C purity_pct
#> temp_C      1.0000000 -0.7217229
#> purity_pct -0.7217229  1.0000000
eig <- eigen(R)
eig$values
#> [1] 1.7217229 0.2782771
eig$vectors
#>            [,1]       [,2]
#> [1,] -0.7071068 -0.7071068
#> [2,]  0.7071068 -0.7071068



Show the code
arrows_df <- data.frame(xend = eig$vectors[1, ] * 2 * sqrt(eig$values),
                        yend = eig$vectors[2, ] * 2 * sqrt(eig$values),
                        which = c("First eigenvector", "Second eigenvector"))
ggplot(as.data.frame(Z), aes(x = temp_C, y = purity_pct)) +
  geom_point(color = "#C2416C", size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_segment(data = arrows_df, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = xend, yend = yend, linetype = which),
               arrow = arrow(length = grid::unit(0.15, "inches")), linewidth = 0.9, color = "#3A1F35") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Eigenvectors follow the data's spread",
       x = "Temperature (z-score)", y = "Purity (z-score)", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", plot.title.position = "plot")









The first eigenvector points along the long axis of the cloud of points: hotter and less pure, or cooler and purer. That’s the trade-off itself! Its eigenvalue, 1.72, says the data vary a lot in that direction. The second eigenvector points across the cloud, where there’s little variation (0.28). For a 2 \times 2 correlation matrix with correlation r, the eigenvalues are always 1 + |r| and 1 - |r|. Their sum, 2, equals the sum of the variances on the diagonal: the eigenvalues split the total variance among the directions. Turning many correlated variables into a few such directions is principal components analysis, in Module 7.








Your turn. Compute the eigenvalues of the correlation matrix of the air flow and the stack loss. Check that they add up to 2.









eigen(R)$values


R <- cor(stackloss[, c("Air.Flow", "stack.loss")])
eigen(R)$values
They’re 1 + r and 1 - r, with r \approx 0.92: almost all the variation lies along a single direction.

title: Matrices for statistics
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Two predictors. Predict the stack loss from both the air flow and the cooling-water temperature. Build the design matrix, and compute the coefficients with the normal equations.









The design matrix needs three columns: a column of 1s, then stackloss$Air.Flow, then stackloss$Water.Temp. Use cbind().


y <- stackloss$stack.loss
X <- cbind(1, stackloss$Air.Flow, stackloss$Water.Temp)
solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, y))
With both predictors in the model, the air-flow coefficient shrinks from 1.02 to about 0.67, and the water-temperature one from 2.82 to about 1.30. That’s because the two predictors are correlated: the plant tends to run harder on days with warmer cooling water, so each one was partly taking credit for the other. Lesson 2.5 explains this “holding the other variables fixed” interpretation.




Challenge 2 · The enthalpy of vaporization. In Lesson 5 you saw that \ln P against 1/T is a straight line for mercury, with slope -\Delta H_{\text{vap}}/R. Now fit that line with the normal equations, and turn the slope into \Delta H_{\text{vap}} in kJ/mol.









b is the solution of the normal equations, exactly as in Challenge 1: solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, y)).


y <- log(pressure$pressure)
X <- cbind(1, 1 / (pressure$temperature + 273.15))
b <- solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, y))
-b[2] * 8.314 / 1000
About 60.7 kJ/mol, close to the textbook 59 kJ/mol for mercury. You just measured a thermodynamic property with linear algebra!

title: Matrices for statistics
text:
Quick quiz

1. A is 2 \times 3 and B is 3 \times 4. What are the dimensions of AB?

2 \times 4
3 \times 3
AB isn’t defined


The inner dimensions (3 and 3) must match, and the result takes the outer ones: 2 rows and 4 columns.



2. What’s the difference between A * B and A %*% B in R?

* multiplies element by element; %*% is matrix multiplication
They’re the same
%*% multiplies element by element; * is matrix multiplication


* needs matrices of the same size and multiplies matching elements. %*% combines rows with columns.



3. Which matrix has no inverse?

A matrix with determinant 3
A matrix with determinant 0
The identity matrix


A determinant of 0 means the matrix is singular: some column is a combination of the others.



4. What does solve(A, b) compute?

The vector \mathbf{v} that solves A\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{b}
The product A\mathbf{b}
The inverse of \mathbf{b}


It solves the linear system, like a mass balance. That’s the same as A^{-1}\mathbf{b}, but faster and more accurate.



5. What’s on the diagonal of a covariance matrix?

The variance of each variable
Zeros
The correlations between pairs of variables


The covariance of a variable with itself is its variance. In a correlation matrix, the diagonal is all 1s.



6. What do the eigenvalues of a covariance matrix represent?

The variance of the data along each eigenvector’s direction
The means of the variables
The number of observations


Eigenvectors point along the directions of spread, and the eigenvalues measure the variance in each. Together they add up to the total variance.

title: Matrices for statistics
text:
Wrap-up
That’s Module 0 done. You’ve built the whole foundation! Here’s what you can do with matrices now:

Build and combine matrices with matrix(), cbind() and rbind(). +, -, * and / work element by element.
Multiply: %*% combines rows with columns, needs matching inner dimensions, and depends on the order. A matrix times a vector is a set of linear combinations, like recipe costs.
Transpose and invert: t() transposes, diag(n) is the identity, solve(A) inverts, and a determinant of 0 means there’s no inverse.
Solve systems: solve(A, b) solves A\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{b}, from a two-stream mix to any mass balance.
Summarize data: the covariance matrix is X_c^\top X_c/(n-1), with variances on the diagonal.
Fit regressions: least-squares coefficients solve the normal equations, \mathbf{b} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\mathbf{y}.
Find directions: eigenvectors of a covariance matrix point along the greatest spread, and eigenvalues are the variances in those directions.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Work in week14.R.

Check the rules. With two random 3 \times 3 matrices, matrix(rnorm(9), 3), verify with all.equal() that (AB)^\top = B^\top A^\top and (AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}, and that AB \ne BA.
Regression for the batches. Using the batches with complete data, build the design matrix for predicting yield_pct from temp_C, residence_min and alarms. Compute the coefficients with the normal equations, and compare them with lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + alarms, data = ...).
Covariance and correlation. Compute the covariance and correlation matrices of the batches’ numerical columns. Which pair has the strongest relationship? Why is the covariance matrix harder to read than the correlation matrix?
Eigen-decomposition. Compute the eigenvalues of the correlation matrix of stackloss. What fraction of the total (which is 4) does the largest eigenvalue capture? Look at its eigenvector: which variables does it weight most heavily?
Watch the intuition. Watch chapters 1–4 and 14 of 3Blue1Brown’s Essence of Linear Algebra (link below), about an hour in total. They show what matrix multiplication and eigenvectors look like geometrically.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Matrix

A rectangular array of numbers with a given number of rows and columns.

Matrix multiplication

The product AB, whose elements are dot products of the rows of A with the columns of B.

Transpose

The matrix A^\top you get by swapping rows and columns.

Identity matrix

A square matrix with 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere, written I.

Inverse

The matrix A^{-1} with AA^{-1} = I. Only nonsingular square matrices have one.

Determinant

A number computed from a square matrix, which is zero exactly when the matrix is singular.

Covariance matrix

A symmetric matrix of the variances and covariances of a set of variables.

Design matrix

In regression, the matrix whose columns are a column of 1s and the predictors.

Eigenvector and eigenvalue

A vector that a matrix only stretches, A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}, and its stretch factor \lambda.











NoteWant to read more?






3Blue1Brown, Essence of Linear Algebra. Short, beautifully animated videos that build geometric intuition for everything in this lesson.
Boyd and Vandenberghe, Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra (free PDF). Vectors, matrices and least squares, aimed at applications in data science.

title: Module 0 project: an exploratory data analysis
text: You’ve learned R, charts, data transformation, descriptive statistics, probability, confidence intervals and hypothesis tests. That’s a whole semester of foundations! This project puts it all together, the way a real analysis does. You’ll choose a dataset, ask three questions about it, answer them with charts, summaries and inference, and write it all up as a report that someone else could read.

title: Module 0 project: an exploratory data analysis
text:
What you’ll make
A Quarto report: one .qmd file that mixes your writing with your R code, rendered into a single web page with all the code, results and charts in it. It’s how professional data scientists share their analyses, and it makes your work reproducible: anyone with the file and the data can rerun it and get exactly the same results. Think of it as a lab report that writes its own tables and figures.
Nobody grades it, but write it as if someone will. Imagine your reader is a smart friend who knows no statistics.

title: Module 0 project: an exploratory data analysis
section: Getting started with Quarto in RStudio
text:
Getting started with Quarto in RStudio
RStudio comes with Quarto built in.

Download the report template and save it in your stats-course project, for example as project0.qmd. Make sure reactor_batches.csv is in your project’s data folder too (you saved it there in Lesson 3).
Open the template in RStudio and click Render (or press Ctrl + Shift + K). A finished mini-report about the reactor batches appears in the Viewer pane. Look at how the text, code and output fit together.
Replace the batches with your own dataset and questions, one section at a time. Render often, so that when something breaks, you know what you just changed.

A Quarto file has three kinds of content: the header between the --- lines (title, author, format), text written in Markdown (## Heading, **bold**, - lists), and code chunks that start with ```{r}. Quarto’s tutorial for RStudio and the Quarto chapter of R for Data Science explain more.

title: Module 0 project: an exploratory data analysis
text:
Choosing a dataset
Pick something you’re curious about, with at least one categorical and two numerical variables, and at least 30 observations. Some ideas:

From this course: reactor_batches.csv, the 40 pilot-plant batches. It’s the template’s example, so you’ll need your own questions, or choose another dataset for more of a challenge.
Built into R, with an engineering or science flavor:

CO2: carbon dioxide uptake by grass plants at different CO₂ concentrations and temperatures.
Theoph: how the drug theophylline is absorbed and eliminated by the body over time. A real-life kinetics problem!
warpbreaks: yarn breaks during weaving, for two wool types and three tensions. A classic quality-control dataset.
airquality: daily ozone, sunlight, wind and temperature in New York in 1973.
morley: Michelson’s 1879 speed-of-light measurements, from five experiments.

Your own data: results from one of your lab courses, or anything you track yourself, saved from a spreadsheet as a CSV file.
Public data: the NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods has many real engineering datasets, Our World in Data has data on energy, emissions, health and more, and TidyTuesday publishes a new, clean dataset every week.

title: Module 0 project: an exploratory data analysis
text:
What the report should include
Work through these sections, which the template already sets up for you:

Introduction. Where the data come from: who collected them, when and how.
The data. The number of observations, and each variable you use, with its meaning, units and type (numerical or categorical, and which kind).
Three questions. At least one should compare groups, and one should look at the relationship between two numerical variables.
Data preparation. How you loaded the data, checked it with str() or glimpse(), and handled missing values: how many there were, what you did about them, and why. Create any new variables with dplyr.
Exploration. For each question:

a summary table (center and spread by group, or proportions for categorical variables);
at least one well-designed chart, with a title, labeled axes and units;
one or two sentences saying what the table and chart show.

Inference.

one confidence interval, with a full-sentence interpretation in context;
one hypothesis test (a t-test, chi-square test or permutation test) with its hypotheses stated, its assumptions checked, the p-value, a conclusion in context, and the size of the effect.

Conclusions. A plain-language answer to each question.
Limitations. Was the sample random? Is this observational data, so that associations aren’t proof of causes? Could the missing values matter? What would you do next?

title: Module 0 project: an exploratory data analysis
text:
Check your own work
When you’ve finished, assess your report against this rubric. Aim for the right-hand column.










Needs work
Good
Excellent




Questions and data
Questions are vague; variables aren’t described
Clear questions; variables described
Interesting questions motivated by the data’s context; every variable’s type and units given


Data handling
Missing values ignored
Missing values counted and handled
Choices about missing values and new variables explained and justified


Charts
Default labels, or the wrong kind of chart
Right chart types, with titles and labels
Each chart answers a question, is easy to read, and is interpreted in the text


Inference
A test without hypotheses or interpretation
Correct interval and test, interpreted
Assumptions checked; effect size reported with its interval; significance kept separate from importance


Communication
Output without explanation
Clear explanations of each step
A reader who knows no statistics would understand the findings and their limits

title: Module 0 project: an exploratory data analysis
text:
Tips

Start with the charts. Look at your data from several angles before you compute anything.
Write the sentence, then the code. Decide what you want to show, then write the code that shows it.
Keep chunks small, one task each, and give each one a label.
Report numbers sensibly. “The mean yield was 57.6%” rather than “57.6475”.
Be honest about limitations. Saying what your analysis can’t show is a sign of good statistics, not of weakness.


When it’s done, give yourself a huge pat on the back: you now have the foundations of a full semester of applied statistics. Module 1 starts with how professionals organize data projects, which will make your next report even easier.

title: Data structures in R
text:
Module 1 · Lesson 2 of 14 Week 17 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Every piece of data in R lives in a container, and choosing the right one makes everything else easier. A set of temperature readings is a vector. A batch record, with its ID, its times, its readings and its lab results all bundled together, is a list. A grid of thermocouple readings is a matrix, readings by reactor, hour and day form an array, and a table of batches is a data frame. This lesson is a tour of all five, and how to move data between them.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Data structures in R
text:
Vectors and attributes
You know vectors from Module 0: an ordered set of values, all of the same type. typeof() tells you how R stores them:

typeof(c(178.2, 181.5))   # decimal numbers
#> [1] "double"
typeof(c(3L, 5L))         # whole numbers: the L makes an integer
#> [1] "integer"
typeof("B18")
#> [1] "character"
typeof(TRUE)
#> [1] "logical"

Vectors can carry attributes: extra information attached to them. The one you’ll use most is names:

setpoints <- c(R1 = 180, R2 = 175)
setpoints
#>  R1  R2 
#> 180 175
names(setpoints)
#> [1] "R1" "R2"
setpoints["R2"]
#>  R2 
#> 175

You can attach any attribute you like. Here’s a handy one for engineers, the units:

temps <- c(178.2, 181.5, 179.8)
attr(temps, "units") <- "°C"
attributes(temps)
#> $units
#> [1] "°C"
mean(temps)
#> [1] 179.8333

Attributes ride along with the data, but most functions ignore them: mean() doesn’t care about the units. Factors (Module 0, Lesson 2) are built the same way: integer codes, plus a levels attribute.
Your turn. Build a named vector pressure holding the pressures R1 = 5.1 and R2 = 4.7 bar, then pick out R2’s.









Write the names inside c(), like this: c(R1 = 5.1, ...).


pressure <- c(R1 = 5.1, R2 = 4.7)
pressure["R2"]

title: Data structures in R
text:
Lists: containers for anything
A vector holds one type. A list can hold anything: numbers, text, vectors of different lengths, data frames, even other lists. That makes it perfect for a record that bundles different kinds of information. Here’s batch B18, which ran on reactor R2 on the morning of 10 March:

b18 <- list(
  batch_id = "B18",
  reactor = "R2",
  operator = "Jonas",
  temps_C = c(28.5, 84.9, 139.3, 166.3, 166.8, 165.8),
  lab = list(purity_pct = 98.96, water_ppm = 410, color_apha = 5)
)
str(b18)
#> List of 5
#>  $ batch_id: chr "B18"
#>  $ reactor : chr "R2"
#>  $ operator: chr "Jonas"
#>  $ temps_C : num [1:6] 28.5 84.9 139.3 166.3 166.8 ...
#>  $ lab     :List of 3
#>   ..$ purity_pct: num 99
#>   ..$ water_ppm : num 410
#>   ..$ color_apha: num 5

str() shows the structure: five elements, the last one a list of its own. There are three ways to get things out, and the difference matters:

b18$operator          # $ by name: the element itself
#> [1] "Jonas"
b18[["temps_C"]]      # [[ ]]: also the element itself
#> [1]  28.5  84.9 139.3 166.3 166.8 165.8
b18["temps_C"]        # [ ]: a smaller LIST containing the element
#> $temps_C
#> [1]  28.5  84.9 139.3 166.3 166.8 165.8
b18$lab$water_ppm     # dig into a list inside a list
#> [1] 410

The rule: [[ ]] and $ take something out of the list; [ ] gives you back a list. If you think of a list as a box of labeled compartments, x["a"] hands you a smaller box holding compartment a, and x[["a"]] hands you what’s inside it.
You add or change elements just like with data frames:

b18$on_spec <- b18$lab$purity_pct >= 98.5
names(b18)
#> [1] "batch_id" "reactor"  "operator" "temps_C"  "lab"      "on_spec"


B18’s water content is 410 ppm, about twice the usual. Remember that number: you’ll find out why in Lesson 5, when you link the batches to their raw-material suppliers.

Your turn. Get B18’s color result, as a number, out of the nested lab list.









Chain two $s: first into lab, then to color_apha.


b18 <- list(
  batch_id = "B18",
  reactor = "R2",
  temps_C = c(28.5, 84.9, 139.3, 166.3, 166.8, 165.8),
  lab = list(purity_pct = 98.96, water_ppm = 410, color_apha = 5)
)
b18$lab$color_apha
b18[["lab"]][["color_apha"]] works too.

title: Data structures in R
text:
Matrices: grids of numbers
A matrix is a vector arranged in rows and columns, with one type throughout. Here are temperatures measured at four positions along a tubular reactor, in three runs:

profile <- matrix(c(150, 172, 181, 176,
                    148, 170, 183, 179,
                    152, 175, 184, 178), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
                  dimnames = list(c("run1", "run2", "run3"), c("z0.5m", "z1.0m", "z1.5m", "z2.0m")))
profile
#>      z0.5m z1.0m z1.5m z2.0m
#> run1   150   172   181   176
#> run2   148   170   183   179
#> run3   152   175   184   178
dim(profile)
#> [1] 3 4
profile["run2", "z1.5m"]
#> [1] 183

rowMeans() and colMeans() summarize each row or column. For any other function, apply() does the job: its second argument is the margin, 1 for rows and 2 for columns:

colMeans(profile)              # the average temperature at each position
#>    z0.5m    z1.0m    z1.5m    z2.0m 
#> 150.0000 172.3333 182.6667 177.6667
apply(profile, 1, max)         # the hottest reading in each run
#> run1 run2 run3 
#>  181  183  184

The column means show the classic hot spot of a tubular reactor: the temperature peaks about 1.5 m along the tube, where the reaction runs fastest, then falls as the reactants are used up.
Your turn. Use apply() and which.max() to find the position of the hottest reading in each run.









You want to apply which.max to each row, so the margin is 1.


profile <- matrix(c(150, 172, 181, 176,
                    148, 170, 183, 179,
                    152, 175, 184, 178), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
                  dimnames = list(c("run1", "run2", "run3"), c("z0.5m", "z1.0m", "z1.5m", "z2.0m")))
apply(profile, 1, which.max)
Position 3, the 1.5 m thermocouple, in every run.

title: Data structures in R
text:
Arrays: more than two dimensions
An array is a matrix with more dimensions. Here are average temperatures for two reactors, at four times of day, over three days: a 2 × 4 × 3 array.

temps <- array(
  c(175, 172, 177, 174, 179, 176, 176, 173,
    176, 173, 178, 175, 180, 177, 177, 174,
    174, 171, 176, 173, 178, 175, 175, 172),
  dim = c(2, 4, 3),
  dimnames = list(reactor = c("R1", "R2"), hour = c("06", "12", "18", "24"), day = c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed"))
)
temps[, , "Mon"]          # one day: a 2 x 4 matrix
#>        hour
#> reactor  06  12  18  24
#>      R1 175 177 179 176
#>      R2 172 174 176 173
temps["R1", "12", ]       # R1 at noon, every day
#> Mon Tue Wed 
#> 177 178 176

Indexing works just like a matrix, with one position per dimension, and a blank means “all”. apply() works too: a margin of c(1, 3) means “keep reactors and days, and summarize over hours”.
Your turn. Pull out reactor R2’s four readings on Tuesday.









Three positions: the reactor, then the hours (blank for all of them), then the day: temps["R2", , "Tue"].


temps <- array(
  c(175, 172, 177, 174, 179, 176, 176, 173,
    176, 173, 178, 175, 180, 177, 177, 174,
    174, 171, 176, 173, 178, 175, 175, 172),
  dim = c(2, 4, 3),
  dimnames = list(reactor = c("R1", "R2"), hour = c("06", "12", "18", "24"), day = c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed"))
)
temps["R2", , "Tue"]

title: Data structures in R
text:
Data frames and tibbles
A data frame is the structure you know best, and now you can see what it really is: a list of vectors of the same length, one per column, with a names attribute and a class attribute saying “treat me as a table”.

batches <- read.csv("data/batches.csv")
typeof(batches)
#> [1] "list"
class(batches)
#> [1] "data.frame"
length(batches)       # the number of columns, because it's a list of columns
#> [1] 12

A tibble is the tidyverse’s version. It’s still a data frame, so everything works the same, but it prints more helpfully and it’s a little stricter. One example: a data frame lets $ match part of a column name, which can quietly hand you the wrong column. A tibble refuses:

df <- data.frame(batch_id = c("B01", "B02"), yield_pct = c(70.2, 53.7))
df$yie                      # data frame: partial match, returns yield_pct!
#> [1] 70.2 53.7
tb <- dplyr::as_tibble(df)
tb$yie                      # tibble: NULL, with a warning
#> Warning: Unknown or uninitialised column: `yie`.
#> NULL

A tibble’s column can even hold a list, called a list-column, which is handy when each row has a small table of its own, like the chromatograph peaks in Lesson 9.
Your turn. Build a tibble with a column reactor holding "R1" and "R2", and a column setpoint_C holding 180 and 175.









tibble() works like data.frame(): name = values, separated by commas.


library(dplyr)
tibble(reactor = c("R1", "R2"), setpoint_C = c(180, 175))

title: Data structures in R
text:
Moving between structures
Real work keeps converting from one structure to another. The most useful conversions:








From
To
How




A list of vectors
One vector
unlist(x)


A matrix
A data frame
as.data.frame(m)


A data frame of numbers
A matrix
as.matrix(df)


A data frame
A list of data frames, one per group
split(df, df$group)


A list of data frames
One data frame
dplyr::bind_rows(x) or do.call(rbind, x)



split() is particularly useful: it breaks data into groups, so you can work on each group with lapply() or sapply(). Here are the lab results, split by analyte:

lab <- read.csv("data/lab_results.csv")
by_analyte <- split(lab$value, lab$analyte)
str(by_analyte)
#> List of 3
#>  $ color : num [1:40] 13 21 15 21 14 11 32 17 21 22 ...
#>  $ purity: num [1:46] 98.7 98.9 99.6 98.8 98.9 ...
#>  $ water : num [1:38] 154 184 221 219 174 221 195 217 154 238 ...
sapply(by_analyte, length)
#>  color purity  water 
#>     40     46     38

That’s exactly what tapply() did for you in Module 0, done in two steps you can see.
Your turn. Split the lab values by analyte, and compute the median of each group with sapply().









split(values, groups): the values are lab$value, and the groups are lab$analyte.


lab <- read.csv("data/lab_results.csv")
by_analyte <- split(lab$value, lab$analyte)
sapply(by_analyte, median)

title: Data structures in R
text:
Choosing the right structure







You have…
Use a…




Many values of one kind, like a column of readings
Vector


A record that mixes kinds of information
List
