A grid of numbers, like a temperature profile or a matrix for algebra
Matrix


Numbers organized by three or more factors
Array (or a long data frame, Lesson 3)


A table of observations and variables
Data frame or tibble


A table where each row has its own little table
Tibble with a list-column



Most of the time it’s a data frame. The others are the tools you reach for along the way.

title: Data structures in R
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Glue the runs together. Three runs were logged as separate data frames. Combine them into one data frame with 9 rows, and a column run saying which run each row came from.









bind_rows() takes the list, and its .id argument names a new column that records which list element each row came from: bind_rows(runs, .id = "run").


library(dplyr)
runs <- list(
  run1 = data.frame(position_m = c(0.5, 1.0, 1.5), temp_C = c(150, 172, 181)),
  run2 = data.frame(position_m = c(0.5, 1.0, 1.5), temp_C = c(148, 170, 183)),
  run3 = data.frame(position_m = c(0.5, 1.0, 1.5), temp_C = c(152, 175, 184))
)
bind_rows(runs, .id = "run")




Challenge 2 · Daily means from an array. Using the temps array, compute the mean temperature for each reactor on each day: a 2 × 3 table, with reactors in rows and days in columns.









The margin lists the dimensions you want to keep: reactors (dimension 1) and days (dimension 3). In R, that’s c(1, 3).


temps <- array(
  c(175, 172, 177, 174, 179, 176, 176, 173,
    176, 173, 178, 175, 180, 177, 177, 174,
    174, 171, 176, 173, 178, 175, 175, 172),
  dim = c(2, 4, 3),
  dimnames = list(reactor = c("R1", "R2"), hour = c("06", "12", "18", "24"), day = c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed"))
)
apply(temps, c(1, 3), mean)
R1 runs 3 °C hotter than R2 every day, and both were warmest on Tuesday.

title: Data structures in R
text:
Quick quiz

1. What’s the main difference between a vector and a list?

A vector holds one type of value; a list can hold anything, even other lists
A list is always longer
Only vectors can have names


Vectors are for many values of one kind. Lists are for records that mix different kinds of things.



2. x <- list(a = 1:3, b = "hi"). What does x["a"] return?

The vector 1 2 3
A list containing the vector 1 2 3
An error


Single brackets return a smaller list. To get the vector itself, use x[["a"]] or x$a.



3. What does apply(m, 2, mean) compute for a matrix m?

The mean of each row
The mean of each column
The mean of the whole matrix


The margin 1 means rows and 2 means columns, so this is the same as colMeans(m).



4. What is a data frame, underneath?

A list of equal-length vectors, one per column
A matrix
A text file


That’s why length() of a data frame counts its columns, and why columns can have different types.



5. df is a data frame with a column yield_pct. What does df$yie return?

The yield_pct column, because data frames allow partial matching
NULL
An error


Data frames quietly match partial names, which can return the wrong column. Tibbles refuse, which is safer.



6. You have a list of 20 data frames, one per batch, all with the same columns. How do you make one data frame?

unlist(x)
dplyr::bind_rows(x)
split(x)


bind_rows() stacks data frames on top of each other. split() goes the other way.

title: Data structures in R
text:
Wrap-up
You can now pick the right container for any data. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Vectors hold one type, and can carry attributes like names and units.
Lists hold anything. [[ ]] and $ take an element out; [ ] returns a smaller list.
Matrices and arrays are grids with two or more dimensions. Summarize them with rowMeans(), colMeans() and apply().
Data frames are lists of equal-length columns. Tibbles print better and are stricter.
Converting is everyday work: unlist(), as.data.frame(), as.matrix(), split() and bind_rows().







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about 45 minutes)





Work in your plant-study project from Lesson 1.

Explore a list. Read lab_results.csv, split it into a list of data frames with split(lab, lab$batch_id), and look at one element with str(). How many batches are there? Which one has the most results, and why?
Batch records. Write a function batch_record(id) that returns a list with the batch’s row from batches.csv and a named vector of its first-test lab results. Try it on B18 and B10.
Back to a table. Use lapply() to make a record for every batch, then turn the list back into one data frame with bind_rows(). Check that you get 40 rows.
Inspect structures. Run str(), class(), typeof() and attributes() on a factor, a matrix, a data frame and a tibble. Write down one thing that surprised you.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Attribute

Extra information attached to an object, such as names, dim, class or your own units.

List

A container that can hold objects of any type and length, including other lists.

[[ ]] and $

Extract a single element from a list. [ ] returns a smaller list instead.

Matrix

A two-dimensional grid of values of one type.

Array

A grid of values with any number of dimensions.

Margin

In apply(), the dimensions to keep: 1 for rows, 2 for columns, and so on.

Tibble

The tidyverse’s data frame: it prints compactly and never does partial matching.

List-column

A data frame column whose cells are lists, such as one small table per row.











NoteWant to read more?






Hands-On Programming with R, “R Objects”. Vectors, attributes, matrices, arrays, lists and data frames, built around a deck of cards.
Advanced R (2e), “Vectors”. The deep dive, when you want to know exactly how R stores things.

title: Advanced data transformation
text:
Module 1 · Lesson 4 of 14 Week 19 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Module 0 gave you dplyr’s five main verbs. Process data asks for more. You’ll want the same summary for twenty columns at once, the change from one sensor reading to the next, a running total of alarms over the campaign, or the best batch for each catalyst. This lesson adds those tools, and they all slot straight into the pipelines you already know.
In this lesson you’ll:
We’ll use the batch records and the tidy sensor log from Lesson 3:
batches <- read.csv("data/batches.csv")
sensor <- read.csv("data/sensor_log.csv") |>
  pivot_longer(-timestamp, names_to = c("reactor", ".value"), names_pattern = "(R[12])_(.*)")
head(sensor, 4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   timestamp           reactor temp_C press_bar
#>   <chr>               <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 2026-03-10 00:00:00 R1        29.6      1.06
#> 2 2026-03-10 00:00:00 R2        27.1      1.01
#> 3 2026-03-10 00:05:00 R1        28.3      1.02
#> 4 2026-03-10 00:05:00 R2        27.4      1.02

title: Advanced data transformation
Advanced data transformation
section: Neighbors in time: lag() and lead()
text:
Neighbors in time: lag() and lead()
lag(x) shifts a vector down by one position, so each row sees the previous value. lead(x) looks ahead to the next one. Together they let you compare each row with its neighbors:

x <- c(28, 56, 85, 110)
lag(x)
#> [1] NA 28 56 85
x - lag(x)
#> [1] NA 28 29 25
lead(x)
#> [1]  56  85 110  NA

The first value of lag(x) is NA, because nothing comes before it. In the sensor log, that’s exactly what you need for a heating rate: the change in temperature between readings, divided by the 5 minutes between them.
There’s a catch. The tidy sensor log alternates between the reactors, so a plain lag() would compare an R1 reading with an R2 one! Group by reactor first, and lag() works within each group:

sensor |>
  group_by(reactor) |>
  mutate(rate_C_per_min = (temp_C - lag(temp_C)) / 5) |>
  filter(timestamp >= "2026-03-10 07:10:00", timestamp <= "2026-03-10 07:35:00", reactor == "R2")
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#> # Groups:   reactor [1]
#>   timestamp           reactor temp_C press_bar rate_C_per_min
#>   <chr>               <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1 2026-03-10 07:10:00 R2        28.5      1             -0.3 
#> 2 2026-03-10 07:15:00 R2        55.9      1.78           5.48
#> 3 2026-03-10 07:20:00 R2        84.9      2.53           5.8 
#> 4 2026-03-10 07:25:00 R2       110.       3.25           5   
#> 5 2026-03-10 07:30:00 R2       139.       4.03           5.88
#> 6 2026-03-10 07:35:00 R2       166.       4.72           5.4

That’s batch B18 heating up on R2: about 5 to 6 °C per minute.

Always ask “neighbors within what?” before using lag(). The data must be sorted in the right order (use arrange() if you’re not sure) and grouped by whatever separates the series, like the reactor.

Your turn. Find the fastest heating rate on each reactor during the day. Drop the 999.9 °C glitch first, or it will win easily!









The previous reading is lag(temp_C).


sensor |>
  filter(temp_C < 500) |>
  group_by(reactor) |>
  mutate(rate = (temp_C - lag(temp_C)) / 5) |>
  summarise(max_rate = max(rate, na.rm = TRUE))
Both reactors heat at up to about 6 °C per minute.

title: Advanced data transformation
Advanced data transformation
section: Ranks and the top of each group
text:
Ranks and the top of each group
Ranking functions give each row its position in the order of a variable. They differ in how they handle ties:

y <- c(65.2, 74.8, 65.2, 58.1)
min_rank(desc(y))     # ties share the best rank, then a gap: 3 1 3 4
#> [1] 2 1 2 4
dense_rank(desc(y))   # ties share, with no gap: 2 1 2 3
#> [1] 2 1 2 3
row_number(desc(y))   # no ties at all: every row gets its own rank
#> [1] 2 1 3 4

desc() ranks from largest to smallest. To keep the top rows in each group, slice_max() is the quickest way. Here are the two best batches on each reactor:

batches |>
  slice_max(yield_pct, n = 2, by = reactor) |>
  select(batch_id, reactor, yield_pct)
#>   batch_id reactor yield_pct
#> 1      B11      R1      74.8
#> 2      B07      R1      74.1
#> 3      B16      R2      68.7
#> 4      B04      R2      65.3

by = reactor groups for just this one step, the same as group_by(reactor) before it.
Your turn. Find the highest-yielding batch for each catalyst with slice_max().









Order by yield_pct, within each catalyst.


batches |>
  slice_max(yield_pct, n = 1, by = catalyst) |>
  select(batch_id, catalyst, yield_pct)
Five rows for four catalysts? Catalyst C has a tie: B20 and B39 both reached 65.2%, and slice_max() keeps ties unless you add with_ties = FALSE.

title: Advanced data transformation
section: Grouped calculations that keep every row

title: Advanced data transformation
Advanced data transformation
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does summarise(across(c(a, b), mean)) compute?

The mean of column a and the mean of column b
The mean of a and b added together
The mean of each row


across() applies the function to each listed column separately.



2. What is lag(c(5, 8, 2))?

NA 5 8
8 2 NA
3 -6


Each element is replaced by the one before it. lead() would give 8 2 NA.



3. You compute temp - lag(temp) on sensor data from two reactors, stored in one long table. What else must you do?

Sort by time and group by reactor, so neighbors come from the same reactor
Nothing
Remove the NA values first


Without grouping, lag() would compare a reading from one reactor with a reading from the other.



4. What is cumsum(c(2, NA, 1))?

2 2 3
2 NA NA
An error


Once a running total meets a missing value, it stays missing. coalesce(x, 0) is one way around that, if 0 is a fair replacement.



5. Two batches tie for the highest yield in a group. What does slice_max(yield_pct, n = 1) return for that group?

Both batches
The first one only
Neither


slice_max() keeps ties by default. Add with_ties = FALSE to get exactly one row.



6. group_by(catalyst) |> mutate(m = mean(yield_pct)) gives…

One row per catalyst
Every batch, each with the mean yield of its own catalyst
The overall mean on every row


A grouped mutate() keeps every row and computes within groups. summarise() would collapse each group to one row.

title: Advanced data transformation
text:
Wrap-up
Your dplyr toolkit just got a lot bigger. Here’s what you can do now:

Work on many columns: across() applies one or more functions to a set of columns, inside summarise() or mutate().
Compare neighbors: lag() and lead() look back and ahead. Sort and group first!
Build up values: cumsum(), cummax() and friends give running totals and records. coalesce() fills NAs, when that’s justified.
Rank: min_rank(), dense_rank() and row_number() handle ties differently, and slice_max() keeps the top rows of each group.
Calculate within groups: a grouped mutate() or filter() compares each row with its own group, and .by groups for a single step.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Work in your plant-study project, with the tidy sensor file from Lesson 3.

A batch timeline. For each reactor, find when the temperature first rose above 150 °C and when it next fell below 150 °C. How long did each batch spend at temperature? Compare with residence_min in batches.csv for B17 and B18.
Smoothing. Compute a 3-point moving average of each reactor’s temperature, (temp_C + lag(temp_C) + lag(temp_C, 2)) / 3, and plot it on top of the raw readings. What does smoothing do at the start of a batch?
A campaign report. For each reactor, in time order, compute the running mean yield with cummean(). Plot both reactors’ running means against start_time. When did the gap between R1 and R2 open up?
Summaries for every column. Use across(where(is.numeric), list(mean = mean, sd = sd, min = min, max = max)) on the batches, by reactor, then pivot the result longer to make it readable. (Lesson 3 will help.)










NoteKey words from this lesson






across()

Applies one or more functions to a set of columns, inside summarise() or mutate().

Anonymous function

A function written where it’s used, like \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE).

lag() and lead()

Shift a vector so that each row sees the previous or the next value.

Window function

A function that returns one value per row, computed from the surrounding rows, like lag(), cumsum() or a rank.

Cumulative function

Builds up a value row by row: cumsum(), cummax(), cummin(), cummean().

Rank

A row’s position in the order of a variable. min_rank(), dense_rank() and row_number() treat ties differently.

coalesce()

Replaces missing values with a given value, or with the first non-missing value from other columns.











NoteWant to read more?






R for Data Science (2e), “Numbers”. Ranks, offsets like lag(), cumulative functions and more.
The dplyr documentation, “Column-wise operations” and “Window functions”. Short, clear guides with many examples.

title: Designing statistical databases
text:
Module 1 · Lesson 6 of 14 Week 21 of 160 About 5–7 hours
In the last lesson you joined five tables, and it worked smoothly. That’s not luck: somebody designed those tables. Each one is about one kind of thing, each has a key, and each fact is stored exactly once. Compare that with the classic lab spreadsheet: one giant sheet, the supplier’s name typed again on every row, three results crammed into one cell, and “n/a” meaning something different in every column. This lesson is about designing data so that mistakes are hard to make, and questions are easy to answer.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Designing statistical databases
text:
The relational model
Almost every database uses the relational model, invented by Edgar Codd at IBM in 1970. Its ideas are simple:

Data lives in tables, also called relations. Each table describes one kind of thing, an entity: a supplier, a lot, a batch, a lab result.
Each row is one instance of the entity, and each column is one of its attributes, like a lot’s delivery date.
Tables are connected by relationships, through keys: a batch uses a lot, a lot comes from a supplier.

The plant’s data is already designed this way. That’s why every table in Lesson 5 had a clear “one row per…”.

title: Designing statistical databases
text:
Entity-relationship diagrams
An entity-relationship diagram (ERD) is a picture of a database’s design: a box for each table, listing its columns, and lines for the relationships between them. Here’s the plant’s database:






erDiagram
  SUPPLIERS ||--o{ LOTS : delivers
  LOTS ||--o{ BATCHES : "is used in"
  OPERATORS ||--o{ BATCHES : runs
  BATCHES ||--o{ LAB_RESULTS : "is tested in"
  INSTRUMENTS ||--o{ LAB_RESULTS : measures
  SUPPLIERS {
    text supplier_id PK
    text name
    text country
  }
  LOTS {
    text lot_id PK
    text supplier_id FK
    date received
    real assay_pct
  }
  OPERATORS {
    text operator_id PK
    text name
    text shift
  }
  BATCHES {
    text batch_id PK
    text lot_id FK
    text operator_id FK
    text reactor
    real yield_pct
  }
  LAB_RESULTS {
    text result_id PK
    text batch_id FK
    text instrument_id FK
    text analyte
    real value
  }
  INSTRUMENTS {
    text instrument_id PK
    text type
    date last_calibrated
  }






PK marks a primary key and FK a foreign key. The ends of the lines are called crow’s feet, and they say how many rows can be on each side. || means “exactly one”, and o{ means “zero or more”. So reading the top line: each lot comes from exactly one supplier, and each supplier delivers zero or more lots. That’s a one-to-many relationship, the most common kind.






NoteGo deeper: many-to-many relationships





What if one batch could use several lots, and each lot could go into several batches? That’s many-to-many, and you can’t store it with a foreign key in either table. The standard fix is a third table, called a junction table, with one row per pair: batch_lots(batch_id, lot_id, kg_used). Each of its rows says “this batch used this much of this lot”. Both columns together form its primary key.

title: Designing statistical databases
text:
Choosing keys
A primary key must be unique and never missing. There are two kinds:

A natural key already means something, like a batch number B07 or a CAS number for a chemical.
A surrogate key is made up just to be an ID, like result_id (R0001, R0002, …). It never needs to change, even if everything else about the row does.

Sometimes no single column is unique, and the key is a composite key made of several columns together. In the lab results, is “batch plus analyte” enough to identify a result?

lab <- read.csv("data/lab_results.csv")
lab |> count(batch_id, analyte) |> filter(n > 1)
#>   batch_id analyte n
#> 1      B19  purity 2
#> 2      B21  purity 2
#> 3      B25  purity 2
#> 4      B34  purity 2
#> 5      B35  purity 2
#> 6      B39  purity 2

No: the six re-tested batches have two purity results each. Adding the measurement time makes it unique. That’s why the lab gave each result its own result_id: one simple column is much easier to work with than a key made of three.

Store IDs as text, even when they look like numbers. A lot number like 0042 stored as a number becomes 42, and suddenly it doesn’t match the label on the drum!








Your turn. Check that batch, analyte and measurement time together identify every lab result: count the combinations, and keep any that appear more than once. (The tables are ready in every exercise.)









Give count() all three columns: batch_id, analyte, measured_at.


lab |>
  count(batch_id, analyte, measured_at) |>
  filter(n > 1)
No rows, so the three columns together are a key.

title: Designing statistical databases
text:
Normalization: store each fact once
Here’s the “one big table” version of the plant’s data, made by joining the batches with their lots and suppliers:

batches <- read.csv("data/batches.csv")
lots <- read.csv("data/lots.csv")
suppliers <- read.csv("data/suppliers.csv")
flat <- batches |> left_join(lots, by = "lot_id") |> left_join(suppliers, by = "supplier_id")
flat |> select(batch_id, lot_id, supplier_id, name, country) |> head(5)
#>   batch_id  lot_id supplier_id               name country
#> 1      B01 L26-001          S1 Fizzwell Chemicals     USA
#> 2      B02 L26-001          S1 Fizzwell Chemicals     USA
#> 3      B03 L26-001          S1 Fizzwell Chemicals     USA
#> 4      B04 L26-001          S1 Fizzwell Chemicals     USA
#> 5      B05 L26-002          S2 Plum Valley Supply  Canada

It’s handy for analysis, but terrible for storing data. “Fizzwell Chemicals, USA” is repeated on 16 rows, and that causes three kinds of trouble, called anomalies:

Update anomaly. If a supplier changes its name, you must change it on every row, and if you miss one, the table contradicts itself.
Insertion anomaly. You can’t record a new supplier until it has delivered a lot that was used in a batch.
Deletion anomaly. Delete the only batch that used a lot, and you lose everything you knew about that lot.

Normalization fixes this by splitting the data into tables where each fact lives in exactly one place. Database theory defines a ladder of normal forms. The first three cover almost everything:








Normal form
Rule
Broken by…




First (1NF)
One value per cell, and no repeating groups of columns
"98.9; 410; 5" in a single cell, or columns result1, result2, result3


Second (2NF)
Every column depends on the whole key
In a table keyed by batch + analyte, a reactor column, which depends on the batch alone


Third (3NF)
Columns depend on the key, and on nothing else
A supplier’s country in the batches table: it depends on the supplier, not the batch



The practical version fits in one sentence: each fact goes in the table of the thing it describes. A supplier’s country belongs in suppliers, a lot’s delivery date in lots, and a batch’s yield in batches.
You can recover the normalized tables from the flat one with distinct(), which keeps each unique combination once:

flat |> distinct(supplier_id, name, country)
#>   supplier_id               name country
#> 1          S1 Fizzwell Chemicals     USA
#> 2          S2 Plum Valley Supply  Canada
#> 3          S3 Rosewater Reagents     USA
#> 4          S4 Kestrel Industrial Germany

Notice the connection with Lesson 3: tidy data is really normalization applied to a single table. In practice you store normalized tables, and join them into a flat table whenever an analysis needs one. The flat table is a result, never the source.
Your turn. Rebuild the lots table from flat: one row per lot, with lot_id, supplier_id, received and assay_pct.









distinct() takes the columns that describe a lot: lot_id, supplier_id, received, assay_pct.


flat |>
  distinct(lot_id, supplier_id, received, assay_pct)
12 rows, one per lot: exactly the original lots table.

title: Designing statistical databases
text:
Data dictionaries
A table is only useful if people know what its columns mean. A data dictionary (or codebook) documents every column: its name, type and units, its allowed values, how missing values are coded, and where it came from. Here’s the start of one for the batches table:









Column
Type
Units
Description




batch_id
text

Batch number, B01 to B40. Primary key.


reactor
text

R1 or R2


start_time
date-time
UTC
When the reactor was charged


lot_id
text

Raw-material lot used. Foreign key to lots.


temp_C
number
°C
Reactor temperature. NA when the sensor failed.


yield_pct
number
%
Product made, as a percentage of the theoretical maximum



Some of a dictionary, like the types and the counts of missing values, can be computed, so you only have to write the descriptions by hand:

data.frame(column = names(batches),
           type = sapply(batches, class),
           missing = colSums(is.na(batches)),
           row.names = NULL) |>
  head(4)
#>       column      type missing
#> 1   batch_id character       0
#> 2    reactor character       0
#> 3 start_time character       0
#> 4   end_time character       0

Your turn. Build that computed part of the dictionary for the whole batches table: one row per column, with its name, type and number of missing values.









sapply(batches, class) gives each column’s type, and colSums(is.na(batches)) counts its missing values.


data.frame(column = names(batches),
           type = sapply(batches, class),
           missing = colSums(is.na(batches)),
           row.names = NULL)
Two temperatures and one alarm count are missing, just as in Module 0.

title: Designing statistical databases
text:
Design rules for statistical data
A few habits make data far easier to analyze later:

Store raw measurements, not conclusions. Store the purity, and compute “on spec” from it. If the spec changes from 98.5% to 98.0%, you just rerun the code.
One value per cell, with units in the column name or the dictionary. 98.9 in a column called purity_pct, not "98.9 %".
One way to say “missing”. A real NA, not a mix of "n/a", -999 and blanks. (Lessons 11 and 12 show how much trouble the mix causes.)
Dates and times in ISO format, with the time zone stated. The plant stores everything in UTC, and Lesson 10 shows why.
IDs as text. Leading zeros matter, and nobody needs the average batch number.
Write the dictionary as you go. You’ll never remember later what flag2 meant.

title: Designing statistical databases
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · A key-checking function. Write is_key(df, cols), which returns TRUE if the columns cols together identify every row of df uniquely, and FALSE otherwise.









The columns are a key when the number of distinct combinations equals the number of rows. distinct(df, across(all_of(cols))) keeps one row per combination of the columns named in cols.


nrow(distinct(df, across(all_of(cols)))) == nrow(df)


is_key <- function(df, cols) {
  nrow(distinct(df, across(all_of(cols)))) == nrow(df)
}
c(is_key(lab, c("batch_id", "analyte")),
  is_key(lab, c("batch_id", "analyte", "measured_at")),
  is_key(batches, "lot_id"))
FALSE TRUE FALSE: batch + analyte isn’t a key (re-tests), adding the time makes one, and lot_id isn’t a key of batches, because each lot goes into several batches. all_of() lets you pass column names as text.




Challenge 2 · Spot an update anomaly. Someone edited a copy of the flat table by hand, and now one supplier appears under two different names. Find the supplier_id that has more than one name.









n_distinct(name) counts the different names within each supplier.


edited <- flat
edited$name[c(3, 25)] <- "Fizzwell Chemicals Inc."
edited |>
  group_by(supplier_id) |>
  summarise(n_names = n_distinct(name)) |>
  filter(n_names > 1)
Supplier S1 now has two names. In a normalized database, the name is stored once, in suppliers, so this can’t happen.

title: Designing statistical databases
text:
Quick quiz

1. In the relational model, what should each table describe?

One kind of thing, like batches or suppliers
Everything about one project
One week of data


Each table is one entity. Relationships between entities are stored as keys.



2. In an ERD, a line marked ||--o{ between SUPPLIERS and LOTS means…

Each lot has exactly one supplier, and each supplier has zero or more lots
Each supplier has exactly one lot
Suppliers and lots are unrelated


|| means “exactly one” and o{ means “zero or more”: a one-to-many relationship.



3. A supplier changes its name, and you have to edit 16 rows of a table. What problem is that?

An update anomaly, caused by storing the same fact many times
A deletion anomaly
A missing primary key


In a normalized design, the name lives in one row of suppliers, and changing it means changing one cell.



4. A cell contains "98.9; 410; 5" for purity, water and color. Which rule does that break?

First normal form: one value per cell
Third normal form
None: it saves space


Three values in one cell can’t be filtered, sorted or averaged without first splitting them apart.



5. Which of these should usually be computed rather than stored?

The measured purity
Whether the batch was on spec
The batch’s start time


“On spec” is a conclusion drawn from the purity. If the spec changes, you just recompute it.



6. Why store lot numbers like 0042 as text?

As numbers, the leading zeros disappear, so 0042 would no longer match the label
Text takes less space
Numbers can’t be used as keys


IDs are labels, not quantities. Nobody needs the mean lot number, but everyone needs it to match.

title: Designing statistical databases
text:
Wrap-up
You can now design data, not just analyze it. Here’s what you’ve learned:

The relational model: one table per entity, rows as instances, columns as attributes, and keys for relationships.
ERDs picture a database’s tables and relationships. Crow’s feet show one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many.
Keys: natural or surrogate, single or composite. Always check they’re unique.
Normalization: each fact in the table of the thing it describes, which avoids update, insertion and deletion anomalies. Store normalized, join for analysis.
Data dictionaries document every column. Compute what you can, and write the rest as you go.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)






Draw your own ERD. Pick something from your own life with at least three entities, like your coursework (courses, assignments, grades) or a hobby. Sketch its ERD on paper, with keys and crow’s feet.
Normalize a flat file. Using the plant data, build the flat table from this lesson, add the operators too, and save it as data/flat.csv. Then write a script that rebuilds suppliers, lots, operators and batches from the flat file alone, and checks each against the original with all.equal().
A real data dictionary. Write a full dictionary for lab_results.csv as a CSV file, with the columns column, type, units, allowed_values, missing_code and description. Save it in your project’s data/ folder, next to the data it describes.
Keys everywhere. Use your is_key() function to find the primary key of every table in the plant data.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Relational model

Organizing data as tables of rows and columns, connected through keys.

Entity and attribute

An entity is a kind of thing a table describes. An attribute is one of its properties, stored as a column.

Entity-relationship diagram (ERD)

A diagram of a database’s tables, their columns and the relationships between them.

Natural, surrogate and composite keys

A natural key already has a meaning, a surrogate key is an ID made up for the purpose, and a composite key combines several columns.

Normalization

Splitting data into tables so that each fact is stored exactly once.

Normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF)

Rules of increasing strictness: one value per cell, columns depending on the whole key, and on nothing but the key.

Anomaly

An inconsistency caused by storing a fact more than once: an update, insertion or deletion anomaly.

Data dictionary

A document describing every column of a dataset: its type, units, allowed values, missing codes and meaning.











NoteWant to read more?






Crystal Lewis, Data Management in Large-Scale Education Research. Its chapters on data structure and documentation cover data dictionaries in depth.
Karl Broman and Kara Woo, “Data Organization in Spreadsheets”, The American Statistician (2018). Twelve practical rules for spreadsheets that analysts will thank you for.

title: SQL beyond the basics
text:
Module 1 · Lesson 8 of 14 Week 23 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Last lesson, every query looked at a single table. But the interesting questions in the plant span several of them: which supplier’s lots make the wettest product? needs the lab results, the batches, the lots and the suppliers, all at once. In this lesson you’ll answer questions like that in SQL, build queries in readable steps, rank and accumulate with window functions, and create tables of your own. At the end, you’ll meet dbplyr, which writes the SQL for you.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: SQL beyond the basics
text:
Joins in SQL
A join in SQL names both tables, and says how their rows match with ON:

dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT b.batch_id, b.reactor, o.name, o.shift
  FROM batches AS b
  INNER JOIN operators AS o ON b.operator_id = o.operator_id
  LIMIT 4
")
#>   batch_id reactor  name shift
#> 1      B01      R1 Priya   day
#> 2      B02      R2  Maya   day
#> 3      B03      R1 Jonas   day
#> 4      B04      R2   Tom night

b and o are table aliases: short nicknames, given with AS. b.batch_id means “the batch_id column of b”. You need the prefix whenever both tables have a column with the same name, like operator_id, and it makes long queries easier to read anyway.
The SQL joins match the dplyr ones from Lesson 5:








SQL
dplyr
Keeps




INNER JOIN, or just JOIN
inner_join()
only the rows with a match in both tables


LEFT JOIN
left_join()
every row of the left table, matched or not


FULL JOIN
full_join()
every row of both tables



Once the tables are joined, everything from last lesson works on the combined rows. Here’s the mean yield on each shift:

dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT o.shift, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(b.yield_pct) AS mean_yield
  FROM batches AS b
  INNER JOIN operators AS o ON b.operator_id = o.operator_id
  GROUP BY o.shift
")
#>   shift  n mean_yield
#> 1   day 22   56.72273
#> 2 night 18   58.77778












Your turn. Last lesson you found that OP1 and OP5 ran more than 8 batches each. Now put names to them: join operators to batches, and count the batches for each operator’s name.









The two tables share the column operator_id. Match it with b.operator_id = o.operator_id.


dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT o.name, COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM batches AS b
  INNER JOIN operators AS o ON b.operator_id = o.operator_id
  GROUP BY o.name
  HAVING COUNT(*) > 8
")
Maya ran 11 batches and Lena ran 9.




A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table, and fills in NULL where there’s no match. That makes it the tool for finding what’s missing: join, then keep the rows where the right-hand side is NULL.
Your turn. Find the batches that have no water result.









A batch with no water result has nothing to match, so all of its l columns are NULL. Keep the rows where l.result_id IS NULL.


dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT b.batch_id
  FROM batches AS b
  LEFT JOIN lab_results AS l
    ON b.batch_id = l.batch_id AND l.analyte = 'water'
  WHERE l.result_id IS NULL
")
B12 and B33, the two batches whose water test was never run.




Notice that l.analyte = 'water' sits in the ON clause, as part of the matching rule. In WHERE, it would run after the join and throw away the unmatched rows, whose analyte is NULL. Those are exactly the rows you’re looking for, so you’d get nothing back!

title: SQL beyond the basics
text:
Subqueries
A subquery is a query inside another query, in brackets. The inner query runs first, and the outer one uses its answer. How many batches beat the average yield?

dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM batches
  WHERE yield_pct > (SELECT AVG(yield_pct) FROM batches)
")
#>    n
#> 1 19

You can’t write WHERE yield_pct > AVG(yield_pct), because WHERE looks at one row at a time, and an average needs all of them. The subquery works out the average first.
A subquery can also return a whole list of values, for use with IN. Which batches used one of Kestrel Industrial’s lots?

dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT batch_id, lot_id, yield_pct
  FROM batches
  WHERE lot_id IN (SELECT lot_id FROM lots WHERE supplier_id = 'S4')
")
#>   batch_id  lot_id yield_pct
#> 1      B18 L26-006      48.9
#> 2      B19 L26-006      58.4
#> 3      B20 L26-006      65.2
#> 4      B31 L26-010      56.7
#> 5      B32 L26-010      56.3
#> 6      B33 L26-010      69.5
#> 7      B34 L26-010      56.0

IN (subquery) is SQL’s semi join, and NOT IN (subquery) is its anti join. Be careful with NOT IN, though: if the subquery’s list contains a NULL, nothing matches at all. The LEFT JOIN with IS NULL from the last step is the safer anti join.
Your turn. Six batches had their purity re-tested. Use a subquery on lab_results to list them.









Inside the brackets, write a whole query that returns the batch_id of every re-test: SELECT batch_id FROM lab_results WHERE retest = 1.


dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT batch_id, catalyst, yield_pct
  FROM batches
  WHERE batch_id IN (SELECT batch_id FROM lab_results WHERE retest = 1)
")

title: SQL beyond the basics
text:
Common table expressions
Subqueries inside subqueries soon become hard to read. A common table expression (CTE) gives a query a name, with WITH, at the very top. After that, you can use it just like a table:

dbGetQuery(con, "
  WITH purity AS (
    SELECT batch_id, value AS purity
    FROM lab_results
    WHERE analyte = 'purity' AND retest = 0
  )
  SELECT b.catalyst, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(p.purity) AS mean_purity
  FROM batches AS b
  INNER JOIN purity AS p ON b.batch_id = p.batch_id
  GROUP BY b.catalyst
")
#>   catalyst  n mean_purity
#> 1        A 10    98.79400
#> 2        B 12    98.90917
#> 3        C  9    98.97000
#> 4        D  9    98.96667

Read it from top to bottom, like a pipe: first make purity, then join it to batches and summarize. CTEs are the closest thing SQL has to |>. You can define several, separated by commas, as in WITH a AS (...), b AS (...) SELECT ..., and each one can use the ones before it.
One more trick that you’ll often see inside CTEs: CASE WHEN ... THEN ... END is SQL’s case_when(). Combined with GROUP BY, it can even do the job of pivot_wider():

dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT batch_id,
    MAX(CASE WHEN analyte = 'purity' THEN value END) AS purity,
    MAX(CASE WHEN analyte = 'water' THEN value END) AS water,
    MAX(CASE WHEN analyte = 'color' THEN value END) AS color
  FROM lab_results
  WHERE retest = 0
  GROUP BY batch_id
  LIMIT 4
")
#>   batch_id purity water color
#> 1      B01  98.90   184    21
#> 2      B02  98.70   154    13
#> 3      B03  99.60   221    15
#> 4      B04  98.83   219    21

For each batch, the CASE picks out the value of one analyte, and MAX() collapses the group to that single value.
Your turn. Complete the CTE water, so that it holds the water results. The rest of the query then finds the mean water content for each catalyst.









Keep only the water results: analyte = 'water'.


dbGetQuery(con, "
  WITH water AS (
    SELECT batch_id, value AS water
    FROM lab_results
    WHERE analyte = 'water'
  )
  SELECT b.catalyst, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(w.water) AS mean_water
  FROM batches AS b
  INNER JOIN water AS w ON b.batch_id = w.batch_id
  GROUP BY b.catalyst
")
Catalyst D’s batches come out wettest, at about 242 ppm. But two of its eight water results come from Kestrel’s wet lots. So is it the catalyst, or the raw material? Untangling two causes like that is a job for regression, in Module 2.

title: SQL beyond the basics
text:
Window functions
In Lesson 4 you met window functions in dplyr: ranks, lag() and cumulative sums, which compute a value for every row by looking at its neighbors. SQL has them too, written with OVER:

dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT batch_id, reactor, yield_pct,
    RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY reactor ORDER BY yield_pct DESC) AS rank_in_reactor
  FROM batches
  ORDER BY reactor, rank_in_reactor
  LIMIT 5
")
#>   batch_id reactor yield_pct rank_in_reactor
#> 1      B11      R1      74.8               1
#> 2      B07      R1      74.1               2
#> 3      B29      R1      74.0               3
#> 4      B01      R1      70.2               4
#> 5      B33      R1      69.5               5

OVER (...) describes the window. PARTITION BY splits the rows into groups, like group_by(), and ORDER BY sets the order inside each group. Unlike GROUP BY, a window function keeps every row.








SQL
dplyr
Gives




ROW_NUMBER()
row_number()
1, 2, 3, … with no ties


RANK()
min_rank()
ranks, where ties share a rank, then a gap


DENSE_RANK()
dense_rank()
ranks, where ties share a rank, with no gap


LAG(x), LEAD(x)
lag(x), lead(x)
the previous or the next value


SUM(x) OVER (... ORDER BY ...)
cumsum(x)
a running total


AVG(x) OVER (PARTITION BY g)
mean(x) in a grouped mutate()
the group’s mean, on every row



Here’s a running total of the alarms on R1, around batch B31, whose alarm count is missing:

dbGetQuery(con, "
  WITH running AS (
    SELECT batch_id, reactor, alarms,
      SUM(alarms) OVER (PARTITION BY reactor ORDER BY start_time) AS running_alarms
    FROM batches
  )
  SELECT * FROM running
  WHERE reactor = 'R1' AND batch_id BETWEEN 'B27' AND 'B35'
")
#>   batch_id reactor alarms running_alarms
#> 1      B27      R1      3             19
#> 2      B29      R1      1             20
#> 3      B31      R1     NA             20
#> 4      B33      R1      1             21
#> 5      B35      R1      2             23

Two things to notice. First, at B31 the running total just carries on, because SQL’s SUM() skips the NULL. In Lesson 4, R’s cumsum() turned everything after B31 into NA. Second, the window is computed inside a CTE, and only filtered afterwards. Window functions run in the SELECT step, after WHERE, so filtering first would cut the windows short. For the same reason, you can’t use a window function inside WHERE at all.
Your turn. Find the best batch on each reactor. Number the batches within each reactor from the highest yield down, then keep number 1.









Partition by reactor, and order by yield_pct DESC, so that number 1 is the highest yield.


dbGetQuery(con, "
  WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT batch_id, reactor, yield_pct,
      ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY reactor ORDER BY yield_pct DESC) AS rn
    FROM batches
  )
  SELECT batch_id, reactor, yield_pct
  FROM ranked
  WHERE rn = 1
")
B11 on R1, at 74.8%, and B16 on R2, at 68.7%. That’s slice_max(yield_pct, n = 1) after group_by(reactor), in SQL.

title: SQL beyond the basics
text:
Creating tables and indexes
So far you’ve only read from the database, but SQL can also build one. To experiment safely, connect to ":memory:": a fresh, empty database that lives only in memory, and disappears when you disconnect.

mem <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
dbExecute(mem, "
  CREATE TABLE analysts (
    analyst_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    name       TEXT NOT NULL
  )
")
#> [1] 0
dbExecute(mem, "INSERT INTO analysts VALUES ('A1', 'Noor'), ('A2', 'Felix')")
#> [1] 2
dbGetQuery(mem, "SELECT * FROM analysts")
#>   analyst_id  name
#> 1         A1  Noor
#> 2         A2 Felix

dbExecute() is for SQL that changes something rather than asking a question, and it returns the number of rows it changed. CREATE TABLE lists each column with its type, plus constraints that the database enforces for you: PRIMARY KEY means that the values must be unique, and NOT NULL forbids missing values. Try breaking the rules:

dbExecute(mem, "INSERT INTO analysts VALUES ('A1', 'Someone else')")
#> Error:
#> ! UNIQUE constraint failed: analysts.analyst_id

That’s the primary key from Lesson 6, now guarded by the database itself. To copy a whole data frame into a database, use dbWriteTable():

dbWriteTable(mem, "lab_results", dbReadTable(con, "lab_results"))
dbListTables(mem)
#> [1] "analysts"    "lab_results"

dbAppendTable() adds rows to a table that already exists, and dbRemoveTable() deletes one. Be aware that dbWriteTable() doesn’t create any keys or constraints. For those, write the CREATE TABLE yourself first, and then append the data.
An index is like the index at the back of a book: a sorted list that lets the database jump straight to the rows it needs, instead of reading the whole table. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows how a query will run:

plan <- "EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM lab_results WHERE batch_id = 'B18'"
dbGetQuery(con, plan)$detail
#> [1] "SCAN lab_results"
dbExecute(con, "CREATE INDEX idx_lab_batch ON lab_results (batch_id)")
#> [1] 0
dbGetQuery(con, plan)$detail
#> [1] "SEARCH lab_results USING INDEX idx_lab_batch (batch_id=?)"

Before the index, SQLite has to SCAN all of lab_results. Afterwards, it can SEARCH the index. With 124 rows you’d never notice the difference, but with 124 million it’s the difference between milliseconds and minutes. Index the columns you join and filter on the most, usually the keys. The price is a little extra storage, and slightly slower inserts.
Your turn. The lab results mention three analysts, but in a fresh database the analysts table is empty. Fill it with all three: A1 is Noor, A2 is Felix and A3 is Ada.









Each row goes in brackets, with the text in single quotes, and the rows are separated by commas: ('A1', 'Noor'), ....


mem <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
dbExecute(mem, "CREATE TABLE analysts (analyst_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)")
dbExecute(mem, "INSERT INTO analysts VALUES ('A1', 'Noor'), ('A2', 'Felix'), ('A3', 'Ada')")
dbGetQuery(mem, "SELECT * FROM analysts")

title: SQL beyond the basics
text:
dbplyr: dplyr that writes SQL
Here’s the twist: you don’t always have to write SQL yourself. The dbplyr package lets you write ordinary dplyr code against a database table. tbl() points at a table without loading it into R:

library(dplyr)
batches_db <- tbl(con, "batches")
by_catalyst <- batches_db |>
  group_by(catalyst) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_yield = mean(yield_pct, na.rm = TRUE))
show_query(by_catalyst)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `catalyst`, COUNT(*) AS `n`, AVG(`yield_pct`) AS `mean_yield`
#> FROM `batches`
#> GROUP BY `catalyst`

show_query() reveals the SQL that dbplyr wrote for you. Nothing has actually run yet: by_catalyst is a lazy query, a recipe waiting to be cooked. collect() runs it in the database, and brings the result into R as a tibble:

collect(by_catalyst)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   catalyst     n mean_yield
#>   <chr>    <int>      <dbl>
#> 1 A           10       60.0
#> 2 B           12       55.7
#> 3 C            9       54.8
#> 4 D            9       60.5

Lazy queries are dbplyr’s superpower. The database does the heavy lifting, and only the small result travels to R, which matters when a table is too big for your computer’s memory. Writing na.rm = TRUE tells dbplyr that you know SQL always skips missing values. Leave it out, and dbplyr reminds you with a warning.
Not every R function has a SQL translation. dbplyr knows the common ones, like arithmetic, comparisons, mean(), n(), if_else() and case_when(). A function it doesn’t know is passed to the database as it is, and the database complains if it doesn’t know it either. When that happens, collect() first, and carry on in R.
Your turn. With dbplyr, compare the two gas chromatographs: count the first-test purity results from each instrument, and compute their mean. Then bring the answer into R.









Keep the purity first tests with filter(analyte == "purity", retest == 0). It’s ordinary dplyr!


The last step runs the query and brings the result into R: collect().


tbl(con, "lab_results") |>
  filter(analyte == "purity", retest == 0) |>
  group_by(instrument_id) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_purity = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  collect()
GC-1 ran 22 of the first tests and GC-2 ran 18, with means of 99.01% and 98.79%. Add show_query() in place of collect() to see the SQL.

title: SQL beyond the basics
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The wet supplier, in SQL. In Lesson 5, you traced batch B18’s wet product back to its supplier with a chain of dplyr joins. Do it again in SQL: find the mean water content for each supplier, from the wettest down.









Three joins, one after another: lab_results to batches by batch_id, batches to lots by lot_id, and lots to suppliers by supplier_id. The query already uses the aliases l and s.


INNER JOIN batches AS b ON l.batch_id = b.batch_id
INNER JOIN lots AS lo ON b.lot_id = lo.lot_id
INNER JOIN suppliers AS s ON lo.supplier_id = s.supplier_id


dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT s.name, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(l.value) AS mean_water
  FROM lab_results AS l
  INNER JOIN batches AS b ON l.batch_id = b.batch_id
  INNER JOIN lots AS lo ON b.lot_id = lo.lot_id
  INNER JOIN suppliers AS s ON lo.supplier_id = s.supplier_id
  WHERE l.analyte = 'water'
  GROUP BY s.name
  ORDER BY mean_water DESC
")
Kestrel Industrial comes out on top again, at about 319 ppm. Same answer, different language.




Challenge 2 · Ties at the top. Find the best batch for each catalyst. This time, use RANK() instead of ROW_NUMBER(), and keep every batch ranked 1. You’ll get one more row than you might expect. Why?









The same window as before, but partitioned by catalyst, and with RANK() in place of ROW_NUMBER().


RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY catalyst ORDER BY yield_pct DESC)


dbGetQuery(con, "
  WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT batch_id, catalyst, yield_pct,
      RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY catalyst ORDER BY yield_pct DESC) AS r
    FROM batches
  )
  SELECT batch_id, catalyst, yield_pct
  FROM ranked
  WHERE r = 1
")
Five rows for four catalysts: B20 and B39 tie at the top of catalyst C, both at 65.2%. RANK() gives both of them rank 1, while ROW_NUMBER() would keep just one of them, chosen arbitrarily. It’s the same tie that slice_max() kept in Lesson 4.

title: SQL beyond the basics
text:
Quick quiz

1. In FROM batches AS b, what is b?

A short nickname for the table, so you can write b.batch_id
A new table
The first column of batches


Table aliases keep queries short, and tell SQL which table a column comes from when two tables share a column name.



2. Which join keeps the batches that have no water result?

INNER JOIN
LEFT JOIN, with batches on the left
Neither: SQL always drops unmatched rows


A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table, filling in NULL where nothing matches. Adding WHERE l.result_id IS NULL then finds the missing tests.



3. Why can’t you write WHERE yield_pct > AVG(yield_pct)?

WHERE looks at one row at a time, so it can’t compute an average. A subquery can
AVG() doesn’t exist in SQLite
You have to use HAVING for every comparison


WHERE yield_pct > (SELECT AVG(yield_pct) FROM batches) computes the average in a subquery first.



4. What does a common table expression (WITH name AS (...)) do?

It names a query, so that the rest of the query can use it like a table
It permanently saves a new table in the database
It creates an index


A CTE only exists while its query runs. It’s a way of building a query in readable steps, much like a pipe.



5. Two batches tie for the highest yield in a group. What do RANK() and ROW_NUMBER() give them?

RANK() gives both of them 1, and ROW_NUMBER() gives them 1 and 2
Both give 1 and 2
Both give 1 and 1


RANK() shares ranks between ties, like dplyr’s min_rank(). ROW_NUMBER() always counts 1, 2, 3, … and breaks ties arbitrarily.



6. In dbplyr, what does collect() do?

It shows the SQL that dbplyr wrote
It runs the query in the database, and brings the result into R
It deletes the table from the database


Until you collect(), a dbplyr query is lazy: just a recipe. show_query() shows the recipe, and collect() cooks it.

title: SQL beyond the basics
text:
Wrap-up
That’s a seriously powerful toolkit! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Joins: INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN ... ON, with table aliases. A LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL finds what’s missing.
Subqueries: a query in brackets, giving a single value, or a list for IN.
CTEs: WITH name AS (...) builds a query in readable steps, like a pipe. CASE WHEN is SQL’s case_when().
Window functions: ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), LAG() and running sums, with OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...). They keep every row, and they run after WHERE.
Building: CREATE TABLE with PRIMARY KEY and NOT NULL constraints, INSERT INTO, dbWriteTable(), and CREATE INDEX for speed.
dbplyr: tbl(), the usual dplyr verbs, show_query() to see the SQL and collect() to run it.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





You’ll need plant.sqlite in your project’s data-raw/ folder, as in the last lesson.

Rebuild the database with keys. The tables in plant.sqlite were written with dbWriteTable(), so they have no keys at all. Create a new database, data/plant_keys.sqlite. Write a CREATE TABLE for each of the six tables, with the primary keys you chose in Lesson 6 and clauses like FOREIGN KEY (lot_id) REFERENCES lots (lot_id), then fill the tables with dbAppendTable(). SQLite only enforces foreign keys after you run dbExecute(con, "PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON"). Do that, then try inserting a batch with a lot that doesn’t exist.
Save a view. A view is a saved query that behaves like a table. Save this lesson’s CASE WHEN query (without the LIMIT) with CREATE VIEW lab_wide AS SELECT ..., and check that SELECT * FROM lab_wide works.
Time between batches. SQLite’s julianday() turns a timestamp into a number of days. With LAG(end_time), compute the gap in hours between each batch’s start and the previous batch’s end on the same reactor. Which reactor sat idle the longest?
Compare dbplyr’s SQL with yours. Write three of this lesson’s queries in dplyr, against tbl(). Use show_query(), and compare dbplyr’s SQL with your own. Which is easier to read?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Table alias

A short nickname for a table in a query, given with AS, as in FROM batches AS b.

INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN

Joins that keep only matched rows, or every row of the left table.

Subquery

A query inside another query, in brackets.

Common table expression (CTE)

A named query defined with WITH, which the rest of the query can use like a table.

Window function

A function that computes a value for every row from a window of related rows, like RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY ...).

Constraint

A rule that a database enforces, like PRIMARY KEY or NOT NULL.

Index

A sorted lookup structure that lets a database find rows without reading the whole table.

Lazy query

A dbplyr query that hasn’t run yet. collect() runs it.











NoteWant to read more?






R for Data Science (2e), “Databases”. Joins, dbplyr and SQL side by side.
The SQLite documentation on window functions. Every window function, with small examples.
“Introduction to dbplyr”. How to connect, which functions translate, and what lazy queries are.

title: Text, dates and categories
text:
Module 1 · Lesson 10 of 14 Week 25 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Meet the lab’s spreadsheet, as it looked before anybody cleaned it: lab_results_raw.csv. Different people typed it over three weeks, and it shows. Batch 1 appears as B01, B1 and " b01 ". Purity is called Purity, purity % and PURITY. And the times are written in three different styles. None of this is unusual: text typed by humans is always messy. This lesson gives you the three packages that tidy it up: stringr for text, lubridate for dates and times, and forcats for categories.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Text, dates and categories
text:
Strings: the basics
Here’s the raw file. Reading every column as text, with trim_ws = FALSE, shows exactly what was typed, stray spaces and all. (By default, readr trims spaces from the edges of each value. Base R’s read.csv() doesn’t.)

raw <- read_csv("data/lab_results_raw.csv",
                col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), trim_ws = FALSE)
n_distinct(raw$batch)
#> [1] 82
head(unique(raw$batch), 15)
#>  [1] "B02"   "B2"    " b01 " "B1"    "B01"   "B03"   "b03"   "B04"   "b06"  
#> [10] "B06"   "b05"   "B05"   "B-08"  " B08 " "B08"

There are 40 batches, spelled in 82 different ways! The stringr functions all start with str_, and they all take the text as their first argument, so they work nicely in pipes:

library(stringr)
x <- c(" b01 ", "B-07", "B 12", "B5", "b33")
str_trim(x)                   # remove spaces at the start and end
#> [1] "b01"  "B-07" "B 12" "B5"   "b33"
str_to_upper(x)               # also str_to_lower() and str_to_title()
#> [1] " B01 " "B-07"  "B 12"  "B5"    "B33"
str_length(x)                 # the number of characters
#> [1] 5 4 4 2 3
str_sub("L26-006", 1, 3)      # characters 1 to 3
#> [1] "L26"
str_pad("5", 2, pad = "0")    # pad to 2 characters, on the left
#> [1] "05"
str_c("B", "07")              # join strings together
#> [1] "B07"

A few more that you’ll use all the time: str_squish() removes spaces at the edges and squeezes repeated spaces inside, and str_glue() fills values into a template:

str_squish("  too   many    spaces  ")
#> [1] "too many spaces"
str_glue("Batch {c('B01', 'B02')} ran on reactor R{1:2}")
#> Batch B01 ran on reactor R1
#> Batch B02 ran on reactor R2












Your turn. Trim the spaces off the batch codes and make them all upper case. How many different spellings are left? (raw is ready in every exercise.)









str_trim() removes the spaces at the start and end of each value.


n_distinct(str_to_upper(str_trim(raw$batch)))
66, down from 82. That’s progress, but B-08, B 07 and B9 are still spelled their own way. You need a cleverer tool.

title: Text, dates and categories
text:
Regular expressions
A regular expression (regex for short) is a little language for describing patterns in text. Instead of saying “the text B07”, a regex can say “a B, then some digits”. Here are the pieces you’ll use most:







Regex
Matches




B, 07
those exact characters


.
any one character


\d
a digit, 0 to 9 (and \D is anything but a digit)


[A-Z], [a-z]
one character from a range


[- ]
one character from a set: here, a dash or a space


+, *, ?
the thing before it: one or more times, zero or more times, or optionally


{2}
the thing before it, exactly twice


^, $
the start and the end of the text


a|b
either a or b



In an R string, a backslash has to be written twice, so the regex \d is typed "\\d". (A real dot is "\\.", as in Lesson 1’s file names.) These stringr functions all take a pattern:

str_detect(x, "\\d")            # does it contain a digit?
#> [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE
str_extract(x, "\\d+")          # the first run of digits
#> [1] "01" "07" "12" "5"  "33"
str_remove_all(x, "[- ]")       # delete every dash and space
#> [1] "b01" "B07" "B12" "B5"  "b33"
str_replace(x, "^b", "B")       # replace a lower-case b at the start
#> [1] " b01 " "B-07"  "B 12"  "B5"    "B33"
str_detect(c("B07", "B7", "B-07"), "^B\\d{2}$")   # exactly B and two digits?
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE

The last line describes a clean batch code completely: ^ the start, B, \d{2} exactly two digits, $ the end. str_view() is great for testing a pattern, because it marks every match with <>:

str_view(c("Purity", "purity %", "PURITY"), regex("pur", ignore_case = TRUE))
#> [1] │ <Pur>ity
#> [2] │ <pur>ity %
#> [3] │ <PUR>ITY

regex(..., ignore_case = TRUE) makes the match ignore upper and lower case.
Your turn. Every spelling of a batch code contains the batch number. Extract the digits with a regex, pad them to two characters, and put a B in front. How many distinct batch codes do you get?









“One or more digits” is "\\d+".


raw |>
  mutate(batch_id = str_c("B", str_pad(str_extract(batch, "\\d+"), 2, pad = "0"))) |>
  count(batch_id)
Exactly 40 codes, from B01 to B40. Padding matters for sorting, too: as text, "B10" comes before "B9", but "B09" comes before "B10".

title: Text, dates and categories
text:
Matching text
The test names need the same treatment. They come in nine spellings for three analytes:

count(raw, test, sort = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 9 × 2
#>   test            n
#>   <chr>       <int>
#> 1 Purity         25
#> 2 APHA           16
#> 3 H2O ppm        15
#> 4 water          15
#> 5 color          13
#> 6 purity %       13
#> 7 Colour APHA    12
#> 8 PURITY          9
#> 9 Water (KF)      9

str_detect() inside case_when() sorts them out: each line tests for a pattern, and the first one that matches wins. In a regex, colou?r matches both the American “color” and the British “colour”, because u? means “an optional u”.
Your turn. Complete the patterns for water and color. The water tests are called “Water (KF)”, “water” and “H2O ppm”, and the color tests “Colour APHA”, “color” and “APHA”.









Use | for “or”: "water|h2o" matches either word.


For color: "colou?r|apha".


raw |>
  mutate(analyte = case_when(
    str_detect(test, regex("pur", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "purity",
    str_detect(test, regex("water|h2o", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "water",
    str_detect(test, regex("colou?r|apha", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "color"
  )) |>
  count(analyte)
No NA row, so every one of the 127 rows found its analyte. Always check for a leftover NA group after a case_when() like this one.

title: Text, dates and categories
text:
Dates and times
R has two main types for time. A Date is a day on the calendar, and a date-time (POSIXct) is an exact moment, down to the second. lubridate’s parsing functions are named after the order of the parts:

library(lubridate)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'lubridate'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     date, intersect, setdiff, union
ymd("2026-03-02")
#> [1] "2026-03-02"
dmy("02.03.2026")
#> [1] "2026-03-02"
mdy("March 2, 2026")
#> [1] "2026-03-02"
ymd_hms("2026-03-10T07:30:00Z")
#> [1] "2026-03-10 07:30:00 UTC"

All four understand many separators, so dmy() reads 02.03.2026, 02/03/2026 and 2 March 2026 alike. Once you have a date-time, you can take it apart:

t <- ymd_hms("2026-03-02 14:59:00")
year(t)
#> [1] 2026
month(t, label = TRUE)
#> [1] Mar
#> 12 Levels: Jan < Feb < Mar < Apr < May < Jun < Jul < Aug < Sep < ... < Dec
wday(t, label = TRUE)
#> [1] Mon
#> Levels: Sun < Mon < Tue < Wed < Thu < Fri < Sat
hour(t)
#> [1] 14
floor_date(t, "hour")
#> [1] "2026-03-02 14:00:00 UTC"

But what’s 02/03/2026? In Europe, it’s the 2nd of March. In the US, it’s February 3rd! A computer can’t know which, so you have to:

dmy("02/03/2026")
#> [1] "2026-03-02"
mdy("02/03/2026")
#> [1] "2026-02-03"

The lab’s campaign ran in March, so its dates are day first. The raw file mixes three styles: 2026-03-02 14:55, 02/03/2026 14:55 and Mar 03 2026 02:41 PM. parse_date_time() accepts a list of possible orders, and tries each one:

parse_date_time(c("2026-03-02 14:55", "02/03/2026 14:55", "Mar 03 2026 02:41 PM"),
                orders = c("Ymd HM", "dmY HM", "bdY IMp"), tz = "UTC")
#> [1] "2026-03-02 14:55:00 UTC" "2026-03-02 14:55:00 UTC"
#> [3] "2026-03-03 14:41:00 UTC"

In the orders, Y is a four-digit year, m a month number, b a month name, d a day, H an hour from 0 to 23, I an hour from 1 to 12, M the minutes and p AM or PM.
Your turn. Parse all of the measured times in the raw file, and find the first and last measurement.









The other two styles are day-month-year with a 24-hour time, and month name, day, year with a 12-hour time and AM or PM.


orders = c("Ymd HM", "dmY HM", "bdY IMp")


measured_at <- parse_date_time(raw$measured, orders = c("Ymd HM", "dmY HM", "bdY IMp"), tz = "UTC")
range(measured_at)
The first test was at 14:55 on 2 March, and the last at 11:48 on 22 March. If even one time had failed to parse, range() would have returned NA, and lubridate would have warned you.

title: Text, dates and categories
text:
Time spans and time zones
Subtracting two date-times gives a difftime, a time span with units. difftime() lets you choose the units, and as.numeric() turns the result into a plain number:

batches <- read_csv("data/batches.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
batches$end_time[1] - batches$start_time[1]
#> Time difference of 1.516667 hours
difftime(batches$end_time[1], batches$start_time[1], units = "mins")
#> Time difference of 91 mins

lubridate can also add time. It has two kinds of spans: a duration is an exact number of seconds (ddays(1) is always 86,400 seconds), while a period follows the calendar (days(1) means “the same time tomorrow”). Usually they agree. They disagree when the clocks change, and that’s where time zones come in.
Every date-time has a time zone. The plant’s batch system records UTC, Coordinated Universal Time, and with_tz() shows the same moment on another clock. Imagine that the plant is in Ohio, on US Eastern time. On the night of 8 March 2026, the clocks there jumped from 2:00 straight to 3:00, for daylight saving time. Here’s a batch that ran across that night:

start <- ymd_hm("2026-03-08 06:30", tz = "UTC")
end <- ymd_hm("2026-03-08 08:30", tz = "UTC")
end - start
#> Time difference of 2 hours
with_tz(c(start, end), "America/New_York")
#> [1] "2026-03-08 01:30:00 EST" "2026-03-08 04:30:00 EDT"

The batch ran for 2 hours, but a wall clock in Ohio went from 1:30 to 4:30, which looks like 3 hours. If the system had stored local times, as plain text without a time zone, every batch that crossed that night would seem an hour too long. In November, when the clocks fall back, durations would come out an hour too short, and some times would even happen twice. UTC never jumps. That’s why the plant, like almost every database, stores times in UTC and converts them to local time only for display, as Lesson 6 promised.
with_tz() changes the clock that a moment is shown on. force_tz() keeps the clock time and changes the zone, so it makes a different moment. Use it only to fix times that were recorded with the wrong zone.
Your turn. Compute each batch’s duration in minutes, and find the longest batch of the campaign.









The units for minutes are written "mins".


batches |>
  mutate(duration_min = as.numeric(difftime(end_time, start_time, units = "mins"))) |>
  slice_max(duration_min, n = 1) |>
  select(batch_id, start_time, end_time, duration_min)
B29 ran for 113 minutes. It also had the longest residence time of the campaign, 71.7 minutes.

title: Text, dates and categories
text:
Factors with forcats
A factor is R’s type for categorical data: a variable with a fixed set of possible values, called levels, in a chosen order. The levels exist even when no row uses them, which is just what you want in a table:

analyte <- factor(c("water", "purity", "water"), levels = c("purity", "water", "color"))
table(analyte)
#> analyte
#> purity  water  color 
#>      1      2      0

Unless you say otherwise, the levels are sorted alphabetically, and that order decides the order of tables, legends and the bars in a plot. The forcats functions (all starting with fct_) change the levels without touching the data:







Function
Does




fct_relevel(f, "C")
moves level C to the front


fct_infreq(f)
orders the levels from the most common to the least


fct_reorder(f, x)
orders the levels by the median of x in each group


fct_recode(f, new = "old")
renames levels


fct_collapse(f, AB = c("A", "B"))
merges levels into one


fct_lump_n(f, n)
keeps the n most common levels, and lumps the rest into “Other”




library(forcats)
table(fct_infreq(batches$catalyst))
#> 
#>  B  A  C  D 
#> 12 10  9  9
levels(fct_reorder(batches$catalyst, batches$yield_pct))
#> [1] "B" "A" "D" "C"

Ordering bars by their value, rather than alphabetically, makes plots far easier to read. That’s fct_reorder()’s favorite job.
Some categories have a natural order, like the workload scale in Lesson 9’s survey. An ordered factor knows that “low” comes before “high”, so comparisons work:

workload <- factor(c("low", "high", "about right"),
                   levels = c("very low", "low", "about right", "high", "very high"),
                   ordered = TRUE)
workload > "low"
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE

Your turn. Order the catalysts by their median yield, from lowest to highest.









Reorder by the yields: batches$yield_pct. fct_reorder() uses the median unless you choose another function.


levels(fct_reorder(batches$catalyst, batches$yield_pct))
B, A, D and then C. But try .fun = mean: then C comes first! Catalyst C has the highest median but the lowest mean, because a few very poor batches pull its mean down. Which summary you choose matters.




Your turn. Keep the three operators who ran the most batches, lump the rest into “Other”, and count.









n = 3 keeps the three most common levels.


table(fct_lump_n(batches$operator_id, n = 3))
OP1 (Maya), OP2 (Jonas) and OP5 (Lena) ran 27 batches between them, and the other three operators ran 13.

title: Text, dates and categories
Text, dates and categories
text:
Quick quiz

1. Which of these does the regex "^B\\d{2}$" match?

"B07"
"B7"
"B-07"


It needs a B at the start, then exactly two digits, and then the end of the text. "B7" has only one digit, and "B-07" has a dash.



2. Which function removes the spaces at the start and end of " B08 "?

str_pad()
str_trim()
str_to_upper()


str_trim() removes the spaces at the edges. str_squish() also squeezes repeated spaces in the middle.



3. A European lab writes 02/03/2026 for the 2nd of March. Which function reads it correctly?

dmy()
mdy()
ymd()


Day, month, year: dmy(). mdy() would read it as February 3rd.



4. Why does the plant’s database store times in UTC?

UTC never jumps for daylight saving time, so durations and the order of events always come out right
UTC takes less storage space
R can only read UTC times


Local clocks skip an hour in spring and repeat one in autumn. UTC does neither. Convert to local time only for display, with with_tz().



5. In what order are the levels of factor(c("low", "high", "medium"))?

low, high, medium, in the order they appear
high, low, medium, alphabetically
low, medium, high, in their natural order


Without levels = ..., R sorts the levels alphabetically. Give the levels yourself whenever the order matters.



6. What does fct_reorder(catalyst, yield_pct) do?

It orders the catalyst levels by the median yield of each catalyst
It sorts the rows of the data by yield
It renames the catalysts


Only the order of the levels changes, not the data. It’s perfect for ordering the bars of a plot.

title: Text, dates and categories
text:
Wrap-up
Messy text holds no fear for you now! Here’s what you’ve learned:

stringr basics: str_trim(), str_squish(), str_to_upper(), str_pad(), str_sub(), str_c() and str_glue().
Regular expressions: \d, [...], +, ?, {2}, ^, $ and |, typed with double backslashes in R, and used by str_detect(), str_extract(), str_replace() and str_remove(). Test them with str_view().
Dates and times: ymd(), dmy(), mdy() and friends, parse_date_time() for mixed styles, and year(), month(), wday() and hour() to take them apart.
Spans and zones: difftime() with units, durations versus periods, with_tz() to display a moment on another clock, and UTC for storage.
Factors: levels decide the order. fct_relevel(), fct_infreq(), fct_reorder(), fct_recode(), fct_collapse() and fct_lump_n() change them, and ordered factors know which level is bigger.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download lab_results_raw.csv and batches.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

A cleaning script. Start R/02-clean-lab.R. Read the raw file, and add the columns batch_id, analyte and measured_at, with this lesson’s code. You’ll finish this script in the next lesson, when you clean the values.
Regex practice. The free site regex101.com explains any regex piece by piece. Use it to write a pattern that matches the lot codes, like L26-006, and nothing else. Test it in R with str_detect().
Batches by day. Count the batches started on each day of the week with wday(start_time, label = TRUE), and plot them with geom_bar(). Then make a second plot with the days ordered from the busiest to the quietest, using fct_infreq().
Your own time zone. Show the start times of the first five batches in your own time zone with with_tz(). OlsonNames() lists all the zone names R knows, and Sys.timezone() tells you your own.










NoteKey words from this lesson






String

A piece of text. R calls its type character.

Regular expression (regex)

A pattern that describes text, like "^B\\d{2}$" for “a B and two digits, and nothing else”.

Date and date-time

A day on the calendar, and an exact moment in time. In R, Date and POSIXct.

Time zone

The rules that turn a moment into a clock time in some place, including daylight saving time.

UTC

Coordinated Universal Time, the world’s reference clock, which never changes for daylight saving time.

Duration and period

An exact number of seconds, and a span on the calendar, like “one day later”.

Factor and levels

R’s type for categories, and its set of allowed values, in order.

Ordered factor

A factor whose levels have a natural order, so that comparisons like > make sense.











NoteWant to read more?






R for Data Science (2e): “Strings”, “Regular expressions”, “Factors” and “Dates and times”. Four friendly chapters on exactly this lesson’s topics.
The stringr, lubridate and forcats cheat sheets, from Posit’s cheat sheet collection. One page each, perfect to keep next to you.

title: Missing data I: patterns and mechanisms
text:
Module 1 · Lesson 12 of 14 Week 27 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Every real dataset has holes. A sensor drops out, a sample gets lost, a survey question is skipped. You’ve been handling NAs since Module 0, mostly with na.rm = TRUE. This lesson asks the questions that come first: how much is missing, why is it missing, and what does ignoring it do to your answers?
Our case study is the plant’s online analyzer, which measures the product’s concentration in the sample line, in g/L. For a study, the lab also measured all 160 samples by hand, and the analyzer missed 36 of them. That’s a rare luxury: normally you never learn what the missing values were. Here, the lab’s results let us check every method against the truth.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Missing data I: patterns and mechanisms
text:
How much is missing?

analyzer <- read_csv("data/analyzer_study.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(analyzer)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   sample_id temp_C flow_Lmin analyzer_gL lab_gL
#>   <chr>      <dbl>     <dbl>       <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 S001        175.     11.6         38.3   39.2
#> 2 S002        168.     12.9         36.6   36.5
#> 3 S003        179      13.9         34     32.8
#> 4 S004        168.      9.65        39.9   38.7
#> 5 S005        177      10.5         46.2   45.9
#> 6 S006        168.     11.3         36.9   36.1

Each row is a sample: its temperature in the sample line, the flow rate, the analyzer’s reading and the lab’s. A quick count of the NAs in each column:

colSums(is.na(analyzer))
#>   sample_id      temp_C   flow_Lmin analyzer_gL      lab_gL 
#>           0           0           8          36           0

The naniar package is built for exploring missing data. miss_var_summary() gives the count and percentage for each variable, and vis_miss() draws the whole table, with every missing cell in black:

library(naniar)
miss_var_summary(analyzer)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   variable    n_miss pct_miss
#>   <chr>        <int>    <num>
#> 1 analyzer_gL     36     22.5
#> 2 flow_Lmin        8      5  
#> 3 sample_id        0      0  
#> 4 temp_C           0      0  
#> 5 lab_gL           0      0
vis_miss(analyzer)








The analyzer is missing 22.5% of its readings, and the flowmeter 5%. The other columns are complete. You can also count by row: miss_case_table() shows how many samples have no gaps, one gap or two.

miss_case_table(analyzer)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   n_miss_in_case n_cases pct_cases
#>            <int>   <int>     <dbl>
#> 1              0     118     73.8 
#> 2              1      40     25   
#> 3              2       2      1.25










Your turn. How many samples are complete, with no missing value in any column? Base R’s complete.cases() gives TRUE for each complete row.









complete.cases(analyzer) is TRUE for every row with no NA. sum() counts the TRUEs.


sum(complete.cases(analyzer))
118 of the 160 samples are complete. Notice that 36 + 8 = 44 missing values only cost 42 rows, because two samples are missing both.

title: Missing data I: patterns and mechanisms
text:
Why is it missing?
The reason a value is missing matters more than how many are missing. Statisticians describe three missingness mechanisms:








Mechanism
Whether a value is missing depends on…
Plant example




MCAR, missing completely at random
nothing at all
the flowmeter’s logger skips a reading now and then, at random


MAR, missing at random
other variables that were recorded
the analyzer drops out when the sample line is hot, and the temperature is recorded


MNAR, missing not at random
the missing value itself
the water titrator fails on very wet samples, so the wettest results are the ones missing



The names are confusing, everybody agrees! “Missing at random” doesn’t mean that the values are missing randomly. It means that once you take the recorded variables into account, what’s left is random.
Why does this matter? Because each mechanism does different damage:

Under MCAR, the complete cases are a random sample of all cases. Analyzing only them is unbiased, just less precise.
Under MAR, the complete cases can be a biased sample. But the recorded variables hold the information needed to correct for it.
Under MNAR, the information needed to correct the bias is in the missing values themselves. No method can fix that from the data alone, and you have to make assumptions about the missing values.

One more thing to know: data can show you that values are not MCAR, but it can never prove whether they’re MAR or MNAR, because the evidence is exactly what’s missing. That part takes knowledge of the process: how the instrument works, why people skip questions, and so on.

title: Missing data I: patterns and mechanisms
text:
Looking for patterns
The first clue is to compare the samples with and without an analyzer reading. Here’s that comparison, using is.na() to make a group:

analyzer |>
  group_by(analyzer_missing = is.na(analyzer_gL)) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_temp = mean(temp_C), mean_lab = mean(lab_gL))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   analyzer_missing     n mean_temp mean_lab
#>   <lgl>            <int>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 FALSE              124      171.     37.6
#> 2 TRUE                36      185.     46.2

The samples without a reading were about 14 °C hotter, and their lab concentrations were much higher. A picture makes the pattern plain. Here’s the lab’s concentration against temperature, with the samples that the analyzer missed in rose:

analyzer |>
  mutate(analyzer = if_else(is.na(analyzer_gL), "missing", "recorded")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = temp_C, y = lab_gL, color = analyzer)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(missing = "#C2416C", recorded = "#2a78d6")) +
  labs(x = "Sample line temperature (°C)", y = "Lab concentration (g/L)", color = "Analyzer reading") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The missing readings cluster in the hot, concentrated corner. The values are clearly not MCAR, and naniar’s mcar_test() (Little’s test) agrees, with a tiny p-value:

mcar_test(select(analyzer, -sample_id))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   statistic    df       p.value missing.patterns
#>       <dbl> <dbl>         <dbl>            <int>
#> 1      53.7     8 0.00000000789                4

What about MAR versus MNAR? The analyzer’s manual explains why readings go missing: when the sample line runs hot, the analyzer can’t hold the sample at its measuring temperature, so it skips the reading, and the hotter the line, the more often that happens. So whether a reading is missing depends on the temperature, which is recorded. That’s MAR. (Without the manual, an analyzer that failed at high concentrations, which is MNAR, would look almost the same in this plot. That’s why process knowledge matters.)
Your turn. Split the temperatures into bands, and compute the percentage of missing analyzer readings in each band.









The mean of a logical vector is the proportion of TRUEs. So mean(is.na(analyzer_gL)) is the share of missing readings.


analyzer |>
  mutate(band = cut(temp_C, breaks = c(-Inf, 165, 175, 185, Inf))) |>
  group_by(band) |>
  summarise(n = n(), pct_missing = round(100 * mean(is.na(analyzer_gL))))
From none at all below 165 °C, to 85% above 185 °C. The hotter the line, the likelier the dropout.

title: Missing data I: patterns and mechanisms
text:
What deleting does
The simplest way to handle missing values is to leave out every incomplete case. That’s called complete-case analysis (or listwise deletion), and it’s what na.rm = TRUE does, and what lm() does without even asking. Is it safe here?
