Your turn. Compare the mean of the analyzer’s readings, ignoring the missing ones, with the mean of the lab’s results for all 160 samples.









na.rm = TRUE leaves out the missing readings.


analyzer |>
  summarise(analyzer_mean = mean(analyzer_gL, na.rm = TRUE),
            lab_mean = mean(lab_gL))
37.6 g/L against 39.6 g/L. The analyzer’s mean is 2 g/L too low, not because the analyzer reads low, but because it missed the hottest, most concentrated samples.




Is the analyzer just reading low? No. On the samples it did measure, it agrees with the lab almost perfectly (the correlation is 0.99), and the lab’s mean for those same samples is 37.6 g/L too. The complete cases are simply a cooler, more dilute subset of the samples.
Here’s a surprise, though. Complete-case analysis biased the mean, but a regression of concentration on temperature is still fine:

coef(lm(analyzer_gL ~ temp_C, data = analyzer))    # complete cases only
#> (Intercept)      temp_C 
#> -74.1561141   0.6540077
coef(lm(lab_gL ~ temp_C, data = analyzer))         # all 160 samples
#> (Intercept)      temp_C 
#>  -70.557380    0.632524

Both slopes are about 0.63 to 0.65 g/L per °C. When values are missing because of a predictor, and that predictor is in the model, the complete cases still show the right relationship. They just can’t give the right overall mean, because the hot samples are under-represented. Whether deleting is safe depends on the mechanism and on the question you’re asking.
Notice too that lm() deleted the incomplete rows silently. nobs() tells you how many rows a model really used:

nobs(lm(analyzer_gL ~ temp_C + flow_Lmin, data = analyzer))
#> [1] 118

118 of 160. Always check this number, especially when a model has many variables, because each one’s missing values remove more rows.

title: Missing data I: patterns and mechanisms
text:
Filling in: single imputation
Instead of deleting, you could impute, which means filling in each missing value with a guess. Here are the common single guesses, and what they do.
Mean imputation replaces every NA with the mean of the observed values. It keeps all the rows, but it leaves the mean exactly as biased as before, and it squeezes the spread. Every filled-in value sits at the same point, like a spike in the middle of a histogram:

analyzer |>
  mutate(filled = coalesce(analyzer_gL, mean(analyzer_gL, na.rm = TRUE)),
         source = if_else(is.na(analyzer_gL), "imputed", "recorded")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = filled, fill = source)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, boundary = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(imputed = "#C2416C", recorded = "#2a78d6")) +
  labs(x = "Analyzer reading after mean imputation (g/L)", y = "Samples", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Regression imputation predicts each missing value from the variables you do have, here the temperature. That uses the MAR information, so it fixes the mean. But every imputed value sits exactly on the regression line, with none of the natural scatter around it. That makes relationships look stronger and more certain than they really are.
Stochastic regression imputation adds random noise, the size of the regression’s residuals, to each prediction. That restores the scatter. You’ll try it in the challenge round.
Carrying the last value forward (LOCF) is common for time series. tidyr::fill() does it. Remember the R2 thermocouple’s three-reading dropout in the sensor log?

sensor <- read_csv("data/sensor_log.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
sensor[199:205, c("timestamp", "R2_temp_C")] |> fill(R2_temp_C)
#> # A tibble: 7 × 2
#>   timestamp           R2_temp_C
#>   <dttm>                  <dbl>
#> 1 2026-03-10 16:30:00      27  
#> 2 2026-03-10 16:35:00      27.1
#> 3 2026-03-10 16:40:00      27.1
#> 4 2026-03-10 16:45:00      27.1
#> 5 2026-03-10 16:50:00      27.1
#> 6 2026-03-10 16:55:00      27.1
#> 7 2026-03-10 17:00:00      27.9

That’s reasonable while the reactor sits idle at 27 °C. During a heat-up, at 6 °C a minute, it would be badly wrong.
And zero? In Lesson 4, the running total of alarms broke at batch B31, whose alarm log was lost, and you asked whether coalesce(alarms, 0) was a fair guess. Now you can answer: no, not really. The log was lost, not empty, and the other batches averaged about 1.3 alarms each, so zero quietly biases the total down. Every fill-in is an assumption about the missing value. Say it out loud, in your cleaning log.
The deepest problem with any single imputation is this: afterwards, the analysis treats your guesses as if they were real measurements. It doesn’t know that 36 of the values are invented, so its standard errors and p-values are too optimistic. Fixing that is the job of multiple imputation, in the next lesson.
Your turn. Fill in the missing readings with the mean, and compare the standard deviation before and after.









The value to fill in is the mean of the observed readings: mean(analyzer_gL, na.rm = TRUE).


analyzer |>
  mutate(filled = coalesce(analyzer_gL, mean(analyzer_gL, na.rm = TRUE))) |>
  summarise(sd_before = sd(analyzer_gL, na.rm = TRUE), sd_after = sd(filled))
The standard deviation shrank from 6.6 to 5.8 g/L, because 36 values now sit exactly at the mean. The true spread, from the lab, is 7.4 g/L.




Your turn. Now try regression imputation. Fit a regression of the analyzer reading on temperature, use it to predict every sample, and fill in the gaps with the predictions. What’s the new mean?









Fill each gap with that sample’s prediction: coalesce(analyzer_gL, predicted).


fit <- lm(analyzer_gL ~ temp_C, data = analyzer)
analyzer |>
  mutate(predicted = predict(fit, newdata = analyzer),
         filled = coalesce(analyzer_gL, predicted)) |>
  summarise(mean_filled = mean(filled))
39.7 g/L, very close to the lab’s 39.6. Using the temperature, which explains why readings are missing, removed the bias.

title: Missing data I: patterns and mechanisms
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Is the flowmeter MCAR? Eight flow readings are missing. Compare the samples with and without a flow reading: their number, mean temperature and mean lab concentration. Do the missing flows look special?









Group by is.na(flow_Lmin), just as you did for the analyzer readings.


group_by(flow_missing = is.na(flow_Lmin)) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_temp = mean(temp_C), mean_lab = mean(lab_gL))


analyzer |>
  group_by(flow_missing = is.na(flow_Lmin)) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_temp = mean(temp_C), mean_lab = mean(lab_gL))
The 8 samples without a flow reading look like the rest: a similar temperature (172 °C against 174 °C), and a concentration well within the normal scatter. With only 8, you can’t be sure. But nothing argues against MCAR, and the logger’s documentation says that it drops readings at random. Deleting these 8 rows costs some precision, but adds no bias.




Challenge 2 · Putting the scatter back. Stochastic regression imputation adds random noise to each prediction, with the standard deviation of the regression’s residuals, sigma(fit). Fill in the gaps that way, and compare the standard deviation with the plain regression imputation’s 7.54 g/L.









The residual standard deviation of the regression is sigma(fit).


set.seed(2026)
fit <- lm(analyzer_gL ~ temp_C, data = analyzer)
analyzer |>
  mutate(predicted = predict(fit, newdata = analyzer),
         noisy = predicted + rnorm(n(), mean = 0, sd = sigma(fit)),
         filled = coalesce(analyzer_gL, noisy)) |>
  summarise(mean_filled = mean(filled), sd_filled = sd(filled))
The mean is still about 39.7 g/L, and the spread is back up, to about 7.8 g/L. But change the seed, and every imputed value changes. Which version is the “right” one? None of them, and that uncertainty is exactly what multiple imputation keeps track of.

title: Missing data I: patterns and mechanisms
text:
Quick quiz

1. A data logger skips a reading now and then, for no reason related to anything in the data. What kind of missingness is that?

MCAR, missing completely at random
MAR, missing at random
MNAR, missing not at random


Nothing predicts which readings are missing, so the complete cases are a random sample.



2. The analyzer skips readings when the sample line is hot, and the line temperature is recorded. What kind of missingness is that?

MCAR
MAR
MNAR


Whether a value is missing depends on a variable that was recorded. That’s MAR, and the recorded temperature can be used to correct for it.



3. A water titrator fails on very wet samples, so the highest water contents are the ones missing. What kind of missingness is that?

MCAR
MAR
MNAR


Whether a value is missing depends on the value itself. The data can’t correct for that without extra assumptions.



4. In the analyzer study, what did leaving out the missing readings do to the mean concentration?

It made it too low, because the hottest, most concentrated samples were the ones missing
Nothing: deleting missing values is always safe
It made it too high


37.6 g/L instead of 39.6 g/L. The complete cases were a cooler, more dilute subset.



5. What does mean imputation do to the standard deviation of a variable?

It leaves it unchanged
It shrinks it, because every imputed value sits at the mean
It makes it bigger


In the study, the standard deviation fell from 6.6 to 5.8 g/L, even further from the true 7.4 g/L.



6. What’s the deepest problem with filling in a single guess for each missing value?

It’s too slow for big datasets
The analysis then treats the guesses as real measurements, so it’s overconfident
R can’t analyze imputed data


The analysis can’t tell invented values from measured ones, so its standard errors are too small. Multiple imputation fixes that.

title: Missing data I: patterns and mechanisms
text:
Wrap-up
You can look at a hole in your data and ask the right questions! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Measure it: colSums(is.na()), complete.cases(), and naniar’s miss_var_summary(), miss_case_table() and vis_miss().
Mechanisms: MCAR (missing for no reason), MAR (missing because of something recorded) and MNAR (missing because of the value itself). The data can rule out MCAR, but only process knowledge can separate MAR from MNAR.
Look for patterns: compare cases with and without missing values, plot them, and try mcar_test().
Deleting: complete-case analysis is unbiased under MCAR. Under MAR it can bias means, while a regression that includes the cause of the missingness can still be right. Check nobs().
Single imputation: the mean shrinks the spread and keeps the bias, regression imputation fixes the mean but overstates relationships, LOCF suits only slow-changing series, and zero is rarely a fair guess. All of them treat guesses as data.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download analyzer_study.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and run install.packages("naniar").

Shadow columns. bind_shadow(analyzer) adds a column like analyzer_gL_NA for each variable, saying whether its value is missing. Use it to draw the lab concentration’s distribution with geom_density(), colored by whether the analyzer reading is missing.
naniar’s scatterplot. geom_miss_point() draws missing values in the margins of a scatterplot, instead of dropping them. Plot analyzer_gL against temp_C with it.
Simulate the mechanisms. Start from the lab’s complete results. Make three copies, and delete 30% of the values in each: completely at random, more often when the temperature is high (MAR), and more often when the concentration itself is high (MNAR). Compare the complete-case means with the truth. Can you tell the MAR and MNAR copies apart from their data alone?
Your own data. Run miss_var_summary() and vis_miss() on any dataset you have, maybe one from Module 0. What’s missing, and can you guess why?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Missingness mechanism

The process that decides which values are missing.

MCAR, missing completely at random

Whether a value is missing has nothing to do with the data, observed or not.

MAR, missing at random

Whether a value is missing depends only on variables that were recorded.

MNAR, missing not at random

Whether a value is missing depends on the missing value itself.

Complete-case analysis

Analyzing only the rows with no missing values, also called listwise deletion.

Imputation

Filling in missing values with estimates.

Single imputation

Filling in one value for each gap, for example the mean, a regression prediction, or the last value carried forward.











NoteWant to read more?






Stef van Buuren, Flexible Imputation of Missing Data, chapters 1 and 2. The standard reference, free online. Chapter 1 covers exactly this lesson’s ideas.
R for Data Science (2e), “Missing values”. The practical side: explicit and implicit missing values, fill() and complete().
“Getting started with naniar”. A tour of naniar’s summaries and plots.

title: Working across statistical software
text:
Module 1 · Lesson 14 of 14 Week 29 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Statisticians rarely work in one language alone. A colleague from the pharmaceutical side sends you a SAS program, the quality team keeps its analyses in SPSS, and an economist down the hall swears by Stata. You don’t need to master all three. But you do need to read their code, reproduce their numbers in R, and pass data and results back and forth without anything getting lost. This last lesson of the module shows you how, and warns you about the traps where the same analysis gives different answers.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Working across statistical software
text:
One analysis, four languages
All four languages do the same jobs, with different words. Here’s a phrasebook:










Task
SAS
SPSS
Stata
R




Open a dataset
SET plant.batches;
GET FILE='batches.sav'.
use batches.dta
read_csv(), read_sav(), read_dta()


Make a variable
y = x / 100;
COMPUTE y = x / 100.
generate y = x / 100
mutate(y = x / 100)


Change values
IF x > 5 THEN y = 1;
RECODE x (1 2 = 1) INTO y.
replace y = 1 if x > 5
mutate() with if_else() or case_when()


Keep rows
WHERE x > 5;
SELECT IF x > 5.
keep if x > 5
filter(x > 5)


Sort
PROC SORT; BY x;
SORT CASES BY x.
sort x
arrange(x)


Summarize by group
PROC MEANS; CLASS g; VAR x;
MEANS TABLES=x BY g.
tabstat x, by(g) statistics(n mean sd)
group_by(g) |> summarise()


Count
PROC FREQ; TABLES a*b;
CROSSTABS a BY b.
tabulate a b
count(a, b)


Regression
PROC REG; MODEL y = x1 x2;
REGRESSION /DEPENDENT y /METHOD=ENTER x1 x2.
regress y x1 x2
lm(y ~ x1 + x2)


Merge
MERGE a b; BY id;
MATCH FILES /FILE=* /TABLE='b.sav' /BY id.
merge 1:1 id using b
left_join(a, b, by = "id")



A few habits show at once. SAS and SPSS end every statement with punctuation, a semicolon or a period. SAS, SPSS and Stata all work on one “current” dataset at a time, while R can hold as many data frames as you like. And SAS and SPSS don’t care about upper and lower case in their commands, while R and Stata do.

title: Working across statistical software
Working across statistical software
text:
Reading SPSS syntax
SPSS is mostly used through menus, but every menu action can be pasted as syntax, and analysts often share syntax files (.sps). Each command ends with a period, and options follow slashes:
GET FILE='operator_survey.sav'.
FREQUENCIES VARIABLES=role shift.
MEANS TABLES=overtime_h BY role
  /CELLS=COUNT MEAN STDDEV.
RECODE workload (1 2 = 1) (3 = 2) (4 5 = 3) INTO workload3.
VALUE LABELS workload3 1 'low' 2 'about right' 3 'high'.
FREQUENCIES counts each value, MEANS ... BY summarizes one variable by another, and RECODE ... INTO makes a new variable from an old one, leaving the original as it was. In R, with haven:

survey <- read_sav("data/operator_survey.sav")
count(survey, role = as_factor(role))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   role           n
#>   <fct>      <int>
#> 1 operator      24
#> 2 technician    15
#> 3 engineer       9
survey |>
  mutate(workload3 = case_when(workload %in% 1:2 ~ "low",
                               workload == 3 ~ "about right",
                               workload %in% 4:5 ~ "high")) |>
  count(workload3)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   workload3       n
#>   <chr>       <int>
#> 1 about right    18
#> 2 high           14
#> 3 low            13
#> 4 <NA>            3

Remember from Lesson 9 that read_sav() turns the user-defined missing code, 9 = “no answer”, into NA, so those three people end up in the NA row. In SPSS, the same three would be left out of the recode automatically, as missing. The results agree, but only because haven did the right thing for you.
Your turn. Translate MEANS TABLES=overtime_h BY shift. into R, with the shifts’ names.









shift is a labelled variable, so as_factor(shift) gives the names “day” and “night”.


survey |>
  group_by(shift = as_factor(shift)) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(overtime_h), sd = sd(overtime_h))
About 7.1 hours of overtime on the day shift, and 7.6 on nights.

title: Working across statistical software
text:
Reading Stata
Stata’s commands are short, and a script of them is called a do-file (.do). Most commands follow the same pattern: the command, the variables, then if conditions, and options after a comma:
use "batches.dta", clear
generate long_run = residence_min > 50
tabulate catalyst long_run
regress yield_pct temp_C residence_min
generate makes a new variable (replace changes an existing one), tabulate makes a frequency table, and regress fits a linear regression. clear throws away the dataset that was open before. In R:

stata <- read_dta("data/batches.dta")
stata |>
  mutate(long_run = residence_min > 50) |>
  count(catalyst, long_run)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>   catalyst long_run     n
#>   <chr>    <lgl>    <int>
#> 1 A        FALSE        6
#> 2 A        TRUE         4
#> 3 B        FALSE       10
#> 4 B        TRUE         2
#> 5 C        FALSE        7
#> 6 C        TRUE         2
#> 7 D        FALSE        5
#> 8 D        TRUE         4

Your turn. Translate regress yield_pct temp_C residence_min, and find the coefficient for the residence time.









In Stata, the first variable after regress is the outcome, and the rest are the predictors: yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min.


fit <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min, data = batches)
coef(fit)
Each extra minute of residence time adds about 0.64 percentage points of yield. Both Stata and R quietly drop the two batches with no temperature, so nobs(fit) is 38, in both. Regression is the whole of the next module!

title: Working across statistical software
text:
Same data, different numbers
Translate a program perfectly, and you can still get different numbers. Four differences cause most of the trouble.
1. Missing values in comparisons. Is a missing temperature less than 170? Each language answers differently:









Language
Is NA < 170?
Is NA > 185?
So the missing values are…




R
NA
NA
dropped by filter()


SPSS
missing
missing
dropped by SELECT IF


SAS
true
false
treated as smaller than every number


Stata
false
true
treated as larger than every number



So SAS’s WHERE temp_C < 170; keeps the two batches with missing temperatures, and Stata’s generate hot = temp_C > 185 marks them as hot! Both are famous sources of bugs. A careful SAS or Stata programmer adds a condition like AND NOT MISSING(temp_C), or & !missing(temp_C) in Stata. When you reproduce someone’s numbers, check whether they did.

sum(batches$temp_C < 170, na.rm = TRUE)            # R and SPSS
#> [1] 6
sum(batches$temp_C < 170 | is.na(batches$temp_C))  # SAS
#> [1] 8

2. Quantiles. There are at least nine reasonable ways to compute a quartile from a sample, and software disagrees about which to use. R’s default is type 7, SAS’s default is type 2, and SPSS uses type 6. quantile() can do all of them:

quantile(batches$yield_pct, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), type = 7)   # R
#>    25%    50%    75% 
#> 55.200 57.300 63.125
quantile(batches$yield_pct, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), type = 2)   # SAS
#>   25%   50%   75% 
#> 55.10 57.30 63.25

The medians agree, but the quartiles differ in the first decimal place. That’s not an error, just a different definition, but it’s a puzzling difference if you don’t know about it.
3. Rounding. What’s 2.5, rounded to a whole number? SAS, SPSS, Stata and Excel all say 3. R says 2:

round(c(0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5))
#> [1] 0 2 2 4

R follows the international standard for floating-point arithmetic (IEC 60559), which rounds a 5 to the even digit. Over many numbers, that avoids a slight upward bias. It rarely matters, but it explains the odd difference in the last digit of a table.
4. Reference levels. In a regression with a categorical predictor, one category is the baseline, and the coefficients compare the other categories with it. R and Stata use the first level as the baseline, while SAS’s PROC GLM and SPSS use the last. The fitted model is identical, but every coefficient looks different. You’ll meet this properly in the next module, and you’ll reproduce a SAS result in the challenge round.
Your turn. A colleague’s SPSS output gives the quartiles of the yield. Reproduce them in R.









SPSS uses type 6.


quantile(batches$yield_pct, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), type = 6)
55.0, 57.3 and 63.375, against R’s default of 55.2, 57.3 and 63.125.

title: Working across statistical software
text:
Moving data and results
Data. haven writes files for every one of these tools, and it keeps the variable and value labels: write_sav(), write_dta() and write_xpt(). But each format has its own rules, and haven stops you when you break one:

SAS transport files, version 5 (the one regulators ask for), allow variable names of at most 8 characters. write_xpt(df, "file.xpt", version = 5) refuses residence_min, so you have to rename first.
Stata names can only use letters, digits and underscores, up to 32 characters, so yield.pct isn’t allowed.
SPSS’s user-defined missing values don’t exist in Stata. If you read a survey with user_na = TRUE, and write it to Stata, the 9 = “no answer” becomes an ordinary 9. Turn such codes into NA first, with zap_missing().

For tools beyond these three, like Python or a database, use CSV or Parquet (Lesson 9).
Results. When you send results to a colleague, send a table, not a screenshot. The broom package turns model output into a tidy data frame, which you can then write to CSV or Excel:

fit <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min, data = batches)
broom::tidy(fit)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   term          estimate std.error statistic      p.value
#>   <chr>            <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept)      5.08    22.2        0.229 0.820       
#> 2 temp_C           0.132    0.124      1.06  0.296       
#> 3 residence_min    0.644    0.0960     6.71  0.0000000915

And whenever you can, send the code too. A result that someone else can re-run, in any language, is a result that they can trust.
Your turn. Save the survey as a Stata file, read it back, and check that the variable label of role survived the trip.









Read the file you just wrote: read_dta("survey.dta").


write_dta(survey, "survey.dta")
back <- read_dta("survey.dta")
attr(back$role, "label")
“Job role”: the variable label made it through, and so did the value labels. Try attr(back$role, "labels") to see them.

title: Working across statistical software
Working across statistical software
text:
Quick quiz

1. In a SAS program, what does RUN; do?

It ends a DATA or PROC step, so that the step runs
It restarts SAS
It runs the whole program from the start


SAS programs are made of steps, and each one ends with RUN;.



2. In Stata, a batch has a missing temperature. What does generate hot = temp_C > 185 give it?

Missing
0, false
1, true, because Stata treats missing values as larger than every number


A classic Stata trap. Add if !missing(temp_C), or the missing batches count as hot.



3. Which SAS statement keeps the batches with missing temperatures, as well as the cool ones?

WHERE temp_C < 170;
WHERE temp_C > 185;
Neither: SAS always drops missing values


In SAS, a missing number is smaller than every real number, so it passes any “less than” test.



4. You want R’s quartiles to match SPSS’s. Which quantile() type do you use?

Type 7, R’s default
Type 2
Type 6


SPSS (and Minitab) use type 6, and SAS’s default is type 2.



5. What does R’s round(2.5) give?

2
3
2.5


R rounds a 5 to the even digit, following the IEC 60559 standard. SAS, SPSS, Stata and Excel give 3.



6. SAS and R report different coefficients for the catalysts in the same regression. What’s the most likely reason?

One of them has a bug
They use different baseline categories: SAS the last, R the first
SAS can’t fit regressions with categories


The fitted models are identical. Only the baseline, and so the meaning of each coefficient, differs. relevel() changes R’s baseline.

title: Working across statistical software
text:
Wrap-up
That’s the last lesson of Module 1, and only the project is left! You can read your colleagues’ code now, whatever their language. Here’s what you’ve learned:

The phrasebook: SAS’s DATA steps and PROCs, SPSS’s period-terminated commands, and Stata’s do-files all map onto dplyr verbs and lm().
Missing values: R and SPSS drop them in comparisons, SAS treats them as smaller than every number, and Stata as larger. Check for NOT MISSING() and !missing() when you reproduce results.
Definitions: quantiles (R type 7, SAS type 2, SPSS type 6), rounding (R rounds a 5 to the even digit), and baselines (R and Stata the first level, SAS and SPSS the last).
Moving data: haven’s writers keep labels. Respect each format’s naming rules, and turn user-defined missing codes into NA before you leave SPSS behind.
Sharing results: tidy tables from broom::tidy(), written to CSV or Excel, together with the code that made them.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)






The translation workbook. UCLA’s statistical consulting pages show the same analyses in SAS, SPSS, Stata and R. Pick two of their SAS or Stata examples, translate them into R yourself, and then compare your version with theirs.
Write for SAS. Write the batch table as a version 5 transport file. First rename every variable longer than 8 characters (for example, residence_min to res_min), and keep a small table that maps the new names to the old ones.
A Stata round trip. Read the survey with user_na = TRUE, write it with write_dta(), and read it back. What happened to “no answer”? Repeat with zap_missing() before writing.
Your own phrasebook. Start a one-page cheat sheet of the commands from this lesson, in all four languages. It’ll come in handy whenever a colleague sends you their code.










NoteKey words from this lesson






DATA step and PROC step

In SAS, a step that builds a dataset, and a step that runs an analysis procedure.

Syntax file

A script of SPSS commands, saved as .sps.

Do-file

A script of Stata commands, saved as .do.

Library

In SAS, a named folder of datasets, like plant in plant.batches.

Quantile type

One of the several definitions of a sample quantile. R’s default is type 7.

Reference level

The category that a regression compares the others with, also called the baseline.

Transport file

A SAS .xpt file, an open format for moving SAS datasets between systems.











NoteWant to read more?






Robert Muenchen, R for SAS and SPSS Users (2nd edition, Springer, 2011), and Robert Muenchen and Joseph Hilbe, R for Stata Users (Springer, 2010). Side-by-side translations, for when you meet a lot of code from one tool.
UCLA’s Statistical Methods and Data Analytics pages. Hundreds of worked examples, many of them in all four languages.
Rick Wicklin, “Sample quantiles: A comparison of 9 definitions”, on The DO Loop blog (SAS, 2017). The quantile definitions, explained by a SAS developer.

title: Module 1 project: an analysis-ready database
text:
The pilot plant ran a second campaign in April 2026: 30 more batches, B41 to B70. And, just like in real life, the data didn’t arrive as one tidy table. The control room sent an Excel workbook, the lab sent a European CSV file, the stores department sent a JSON file about the raw-material lots, and the shift supervisor added a short note. Your job is to turn this handover into an analysis-ready database: one that the next analyst can trust, query and understand without ever having to ask you a question.
That’s the whole of Module 1 in one project: reproducible workflows, tidy data, joins, database design, SQL, importing, cleaning text and dates, validation and missing data.

title: Module 1 project: an analysis-ready database
text:
What you’ll make
Four things, all in your plant-study RStudio project from Lesson 1:

A script that builds the database from scratch. One Quarto document (or R script) that reads the raw files, cleans them, validates them and writes data/campaign2.sqlite. Delete the database, run the script, and it comes back, identical. The raw files are never edited by hand.
The database itself, in SQLite, with one table for each kind of thing, primary and foreign keys, and sensible constraints.
A codebook that describes every table and column: its type, units, allowed values, how missing values are recorded, and what it means.
A cleaning log: every decision you made, why you made it, and how many rows it touched.

Nobody grades it, but build it as if a colleague will depend on it tomorrow. Because in real work, they will.

title: Module 1 project: an analysis-ready database
text:
The handover
Download all five files into a new folder in your project, data-raw/campaign2/, and don’t edit them:

README.txt: the shift supervisor’s note. Read it first, but don’t assume that it’s complete.
campaign2_batches.xlsx: the control room’s batch log.
campaign2_lab.csv: the lab’s purity, water and color results.
campaign2_lots.json: the raw-material lots, with their suppliers.
suppliers.csv: the supplier table from March.

Then download the project template, save it in the top folder of your project as campaign2.qmd, and click Render. It reads the raw files and shows you what’s in them, with headings for every step. Fill it in, one section at a time, and render often.

title: Module 1 project: an analysis-ready database
text:
The brief, step by step

Explore before you clean. Read each file with the right tools (Lesson 9): the header row, the delimiter, the decimal mark, the encoding, the nesting. Then look hard at every column (Lessons 10 and 11). Make a list of every problem you find, with the README’s five as a start.
Design the database (Lesson 6). Decide on the tables, their primary keys, and the foreign keys that link them. Draw an entity-relationship diagram. Keep each fact in one place: a supplier’s name belongs in the supplier table, not in every lot. The lab results should be in long format, one row per measurement.
Clean (Lessons 10 and 11). Standardize the names and the batch codes, turn text into numbers, convert the times to UTC, separate duplicates from genuine repeats, and deal with the impossible values. Flag the results below the detection limit, rather than hiding them.
Validate (Lesson 11). Write validation rules for every table, check that every foreign key has a match (anti_join() is your friend), and end your cleaning with stopifnot() assertions that pass.
Handle the missing values (Lessons 12 and 13). Count them, think about why they’re missing, and record them as NA in a consistent way. Don’t impute in the database itself: a database should store what was measured. Imputation belongs in an analysis, where it can be documented and varied.
Load it into SQLite (Lessons 7 and 8). Create each table with CREATE TABLE, including PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES ..., NOT NULL and CHECK constraints. Run PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON, load the parent tables before the children with dbAppendTable(), and add indexes on the columns you’ll join on. If the database refuses a row, it has found a problem that your cleaning missed!
Document it. Write the codebook and the cleaning log, and a short README for the database: what’s in it, where it came from, and how to rebuild it.
Prove that it works. Answer these questions with SQL queries against your finished database:

How many batches are there, and how many results for each analyte?
Which lot, and which supplier, gave the wettest product this time? Is the story from March repeating?
What are the mean yield and purity for each catalyst?
Which batches have a comment from the control room, and what do their lab results look like?


Stretch goal. Combine both campaigns in one database. Start from a copy of plant.sqlite, and add campaign 2’s batches, lots and lab results to it. The two campaigns weren’t recorded in quite the same way, so you’ll have design decisions to make: which columns does one campaign have that the other doesn’t, and how will you record that? Then compare the two campaigns’ yields with a query.

title: Module 1 project: an analysis-ready database
text:
Check your own work
When you’ve finished, assess your project against this rubric. Aim for the right-hand column.










Needs work
Good
Excellent




Reproducibility
Some steps were done by hand
One script builds the database
The script rebuilds everything from the untouched raw files, after restarting R, with no errors or warnings left unexplained


Design
One big table
Separate tables with primary keys
Normalized tables, enforced foreign keys and constraints, and an entity-relationship diagram


Cleaning
The README’s problems are only partly fixed
The README’s five problems are fixed
Every problem found, including the ones that the README doesn’t mention, with each decision justified


Validation
No checks
Some validation rules
Rules for every table, foreign-key checks and assertions, all passing, and the results reported


Missing data
Missing values recorded inconsistently
All missing values stored as NA
Missing values counted, their likely causes discussed, censored values flagged, and the consequences for analyses explained


Documentation
No codebook
A codebook with the column names and types
A complete codebook (types, units, allowed values, missing codes, meanings), a cleaning log with row counts, and a README

title: Module 1 project: an analysis-ready database
text:
Tips

Trust, but verify. The README describes the problems that the supervisor knows about. Check every column yourself: the problems nobody noticed are the dangerous ones.
Count rows after every step. Especially after joins and distinct(). If a number changes when you didn’t expect it to, stop and find out why.
Keep the evidence. When you change a value, keep a flag or a note in the cleaning log. A reader should always be able to tell a measured value from a corrected one.
Don’t guess silently. If a value looks wrong but you can’t be sure what it should be, set it to NA, flag it, and say so. In a real project, you’d email the person who recorded it.
Store times in UTC, and say so in the codebook.
Let the database help you. Constraints and foreign keys catch mistakes at the moment you load the data, which is far better than finding them in an analysis next month.


When it’s done, you’ll have built something genuinely professional: a database with a codebook, a cleaning log and a script that rebuilds it all. Congratulations on finishing Module 1! Module 2 puts these clean data to work, with regression and ANOVA.

title: Simple linear regression
text:
Module 2 · Lesson 2 of 15 Week 32 of 160 About 5–7 hours
If you’ve done a lab course in analytical chemistry, you’ve made a calibration curve: measure some standards of known concentration, plot the readings, add a trendline in Excel, and use it to find the concentration of an unknown. That trendline is a simple linear regression, and this lesson opens the box. What makes one line the “best”? Where do its numbers come from? What do they mean, and how good is the fit?
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Simple linear regression
text:
The model
The lab’s UV-Vis spectrophotometer measures how much light a sample absorbs. By the Beer-Lambert law, the absorbance should be proportional to the concentration of the product. To calibrate the instrument, the lab measured 8 standards of known concentration, from 0 (a blank) to 50 mg/L, three times each:

calibration <- read_csv("data/calibration.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(calibration)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   standard conc_mgL replicate absorbance
#>   <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 Std01           0         1     0.0041
#> 2 Std01           0         2     0.0049
#> 3 Std01           0         3     0.0065
#> 4 Std02           5         1     0.110 
#> 5 Std02           5         2     0.106 
#> 6 Std02           5         3     0.106
ggplot(calibration, aes(x = conc_mgL, y = absorbance)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, color = "#C2416C") +
  labs(x = "Concentration (mg/L)", y = "Absorbance") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








A straight line describes this beautifully. In statistics, we write that idea as a model:

Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad i = 1, \dots, n.

Here Y_i is the response (the absorbance of reading i), and x_i is the predictor (the concentration). The intercept \beta_0 and the slope \beta_1 describe the true line. The error \varepsilon_i is everything else: electronic noise, small differences between the cuvettes, tiny pipetting errors. We assume the errors average zero, so the true line gives the average response at each x.
We never get to see \beta_0 and \beta_1. The data give us estimates, which we write b_0 and b_1 (many books write \hat\beta_0 and \hat\beta_1), and the fitted line \hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x. The rest of this lesson is about how to choose them.

title: Simple linear regression
text:
Least squares
For any line you might draw, each point misses it by a vertical distance, its residual:

e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i = y_i - (b_0 + b_1 x_i).

A good line has small residuals. The least-squares line is the one with the smallest sum of squared errors:

\text{SSE} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \bigl(y_i - b_0 - b_1 x_i\bigr)^2 .

Squaring stops positive and negative misses from cancelling out, and it punishes big misses more than small ones. Minimizing SSE is a calculus problem, and its solution has a neat form:

b_1 = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}} = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}, \qquad b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1 \bar{x}.

The slope is the covariance of x and y divided by the variance of x (the n - 1s cancel). Since the correlation is the covariance divided by both standard deviations, you can also write b_1 = r \, s_y / s_x: the slope is the correlation, converted into the units of y per unit of x. And the formula for b_0 means that the line always passes through the point of averages, (\bar{x}, \bar{y}).






NoteGo deeper: deriving the least-squares line





Treat SSE as a function of the two unknowns, b_0 and b_1, and set both partial derivatives to zero:

\frac{\partial\, \text{SSE}}{\partial b_0} = -2 \sum (y_i - b_0 - b_1 x_i) = 0,
\qquad
\frac{\partial\, \text{SSE}}{\partial b_1} = -2 \sum x_i (y_i - b_0 - b_1 x_i) = 0.

These are the normal equations from Lesson 0.14, written out for one predictor. The first says \sum e_i = 0. Dividing it by n gives \bar{y} - b_0 - b_1\bar{x} = 0, so b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1\bar{x}. Put that into the second equation:

\sum x_i \bigl[(y_i - \bar{y}) - b_1 (x_i - \bar{x})\bigr] = 0 .

Because \sum \bar{x}(y_i - \bar{y}) = 0 and \sum \bar{x}(x_i - \bar{x}) = 0, you can replace the x_i in front by x_i - \bar{x} for free, which gives S_{xy} - b_1 S_{xx} = 0, so b_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx}.
Is it a minimum? The matrix of second derivatives is 2\begin{pmatrix} n & \sum x_i \\ \sum x_i & \sum x_i^2 \end{pmatrix}, whose determinant is 4 n S_{xx}. That’s positive as long as the x values aren’t all equal, so SSE is a bowl with a single lowest point. (If all the xs were equal, any line through (\bar x, \bar y) would do as well as any other, and the slope couldn’t be estimated at all.)
The two normal equations also tell you two facts about the residuals of any least-squares line with an intercept: they sum to zero, and they’re uncorrelated with x. Whatever pattern was in the data along x, the line has taken it out.













Your turn. Compute the least-squares slope and intercept of the calibration line from the formulas.









The denominator is S_{xx} = \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2, so sum((x - mean(x))^2). Then b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1\bar{x}.


x <- calibration$conc_mgL
y <- calibration$absorbance
b1 <- sum((x - mean(x)) * (y - mean(y))) / sum((x - mean(x))^2)
b0 <- mean(y) - b1 * mean(x)
c(b0 = b0, b1 = b1)
An intercept of 0.0173 and a slope of 0.0192 absorbance units per mg/L.




Your turn. Can you beat least squares? Write a function that computes the SSE of any line, then compare the least-squares line with a line through the origin with a slope of 0.02, which looks just as good by eye.









Each residual is the absorbance minus the line’s prediction: calibration$absorbance - predicted.


sse <- function(b0, b1) {
  predicted <- b0 + b1 * calibration$conc_mgL
  sum((calibration$absorbance - predicted)^2)
}
c(least_squares = sse(0.01728051, 0.01919739), guess = sse(0, 0.02))
0.0027 against 0.0068: the guess has two and a half times the squared error. Try any other numbers you like. Nothing beats the least-squares line, by definition.










NoteGo deeper: why squares, and not distances?





You could minimize the sum of absolute residuals instead. That gives least absolute deviations regression, which is less sensitive to outliers (it’s to least squares what the median is to the mean). So why is least squares the default?

The calculus is easy, and there’s always exactly one answer, in a formula.
In Lesson 0.7, you saw that the mean is the single number with the smallest sum of squared deviations. Least squares is the same idea, with a line instead of a single number.
If the errors are normally distributed, the least-squares line is also the maximum-likelihood line, the one that makes the data most probable. Lesson 15 explains maximum likelihood.
Even without normality, the Gauss-Markov theorem says least squares gives the most precise estimates among all unbiased estimates that are linear in the ys. You’ll see what that means in Lesson 4.

And why vertical distances? Because the model treats x as known exactly, and puts all the error in y. That fits calibration well: the standards’ concentrations are known far more precisely than the absorbance readings. If both variables had big errors, other methods (like “orthogonal” or Deming regression) would be fairer.

title: Simple linear regression
text:
Fitting lines with lm()
You won’t compute those sums by hand again. lm(), for linear model, fits the least-squares line. Its formula reads “response tilde predictor”, as in “absorbance as a function of concentration”:

fit_cal <- lm(absorbance ~ conc_mgL, data = calibration)
coef(fit_cal)
#> (Intercept)    conc_mgL 
#>  0.01728051  0.01919739

What do the numbers mean?

The slope, 0.0192, is the instrument’s sensitivity: each extra mg/L adds 0.0192 absorbance units, on average.
The intercept, 0.0173, is the predicted absorbance of a blank, with no product at all. Keep an eye on that one: the three blanks actually measured 0.0052 on average. A gap like that is a clue, and you’ll find out what it means in Lesson 8.

Here’s the line on the data. geom_smooth(method = "lm") fits the same model for the plot:

ggplot(calibration, aes(x = conc_mgL, y = absorbance)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, color = "#C2416C") +
  labs(x = "Concentration (mg/L)", y = "Absorbance") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Your turn. Now a noisier relationship. Fit the yield of the March batches as a function of their residence time, and look at the coefficients.









The response goes on the left of the ~: yield_pct ~ residence_min.


fit <- lm(yield_pct ~ residence_min, data = batches)
coef(fit)
Each extra minute in the reactor goes with 0.67 percentage points more yield, on average. And the intercept, 27.7%? That’s the predicted yield after 0 minutes, which is nonsense: with no time in the reactor, nothing reacts. The shortest batch ran for 16 minutes, so the line has no data to stand on down there. The intercept is simply where the line crosses the axis, and it only means something when x = 0 is inside, or near, the range of the data.

title: Simple linear regression
text:
Fitted values and residuals
Every observation gets a fitted value, the line’s prediction for its x, and a residual, what’s left over. fitted() and resid() pull them out of a model:

batches <- read_csv("data/batches.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fit <- lm(yield_pct ~ residence_min, data = batches)
batches |>
  mutate(fitted = fitted(fit), residual = resid(fit)) |>
  select(batch_id, residence_min, yield_pct, fitted, residual) |>
  head(4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>   batch_id residence_min yield_pct fitted residual
#>   <chr>            <dbl>     <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 B01               47.2      70.2   59.3   10.9  
#> 2 B02               37.9      53.7   53.1    0.640
#> 3 B03               32.5      49.2   49.4   -0.244
#> 4 B04               60.7      65.3   68.3   -3.03

Batch B01 ran for 47.2 minutes, so the line predicts 59.3%. It made 70.2%, a residual of +10.9 points: it did better than its residence time alone would suggest. Here are all the residuals, as vertical lines from each batch to the fitted line:

batches |>
  mutate(fitted = fitted(fit)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = residence_min, y = yield_pct)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = residence_min, yend = fitted), color = "#F4C0D1", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(fit)[1], slope = coef(fit)[2], color = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, color = "#C2416C") +
  labs(x = "Residence time (min)", y = "Yield (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Least squares made the sum of the squares of these pink lines as small as it could be. And as the Go deeper box promised, the residuals add up to zero, apart from rounding errors: sum(resid(fit)) gives about 10^{-14}.
Residuals are the most useful diagnostic tool in regression. They’re what the model couldn’t explain, so any pattern in them is a pattern the model missed. Lesson 8 is all about reading them.
Your turn. Which batch did best compared to its residence time? Find the batch with the largest residual.









resid(fit) gives the residuals, in the same order as the rows of batches.


fit <- lm(yield_pct ~ residence_min, data = batches)
batches |>
  mutate(residual = resid(fit)) |>
  slice_max(residual) |>
  select(batch_id, residence_min, yield_pct, residual)
B11: 74.8% after only 45 minutes, 16.9 points above the line. Something else went right for that batch. Is it the catalyst, the temperature, or luck? Multiple regression (Lesson 5) can start to answer that.

title: Simple linear regression
section: How good is the fit? R²
text:
How good is the fit? R²
Start with how much the yields vary in total, around their mean. That’s the total sum of squares, SST. The line splits it into two parts: the part it explains, SSR (the regression sum of squares, how far the fitted values spread around the mean), and the part it doesn’t, SSE:

\underbrace{\sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2}_{\text{SST}} = \underbrace{\sum (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2}_{\text{SSR}} + \underbrace{\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}_{\text{SSE}} .

The coefficient of determination is the fraction that’s explained:

R^2 = \frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}} = 1 - \frac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}} .

It runs from 0 (the line explains nothing) to 1 (every point sits on the line). In simple regression, it’s exactly the square of the correlation. That’s why it’s written R^2.
summary() prints it, along with a lot more that the next lesson explains:

summary(fit)
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = yield_pct ~ residence_min, data = batches)
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
#> -14.3926  -1.9188   0.6458   2.8965  16.9181 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)   27.68057    4.12814   6.705 6.18e-08 ***
#> residence_min  0.66965    0.08954   7.479 5.58e-09 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Residual standard error: 6.282 on 38 degrees of freedom
#> Multiple R-squared:  0.5955, Adjusted R-squared:  0.5848 
#> F-statistic: 55.93 on 1 and 38 DF,  p-value: 5.584e-09

R^2 = 0.595: residence time accounts for about 60% of the batch-to-batch variation in yield. The calibration line’s R^2 is 0.9989.
The same output gives the residual standard error, s = \sqrt{\text{SSE}/(n-2)} = 6.28 points. It’s the typical size of a residual: the line usually misses a batch’s yield by up to about 6 points. Why divide by n - 2? Because the line used up two pieces of information, b_0 and b_1, to fit the data. It’s the same reason the sample standard deviation divides by n - 1.
Two warnings about R^2:

A high R^2 doesn’t mean the model is right. The calibration line has R^2 = 0.9989, and in Lesson 8 you’ll find it’s still the wrong shape. A straight line through a gentle curve fits “well” by this measure.
A low R^2 doesn’t mean x is unimportant. 0.67 points of yield per minute is a big effect for a plant. It’s just that other things move the yield too.

Your turn. Compute R^2 for the batches from its definition, 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}.









SST measures the spread around the mean: mean(batches$yield_pct).


fit <- lm(yield_pct ~ residence_min, data = batches)
sse <- sum(resid(fit)^2)
sst <- sum((batches$yield_pct - mean(batches$yield_pct))^2)
1 - sse / sst
0.595, the same as summary() reports, and the same as cor(batches$residence_min, batches$yield_pct)^2.

title: Simple linear regression
text:
Predicting, and calibrating
To predict, give predict() a data frame of new x values, with the same column name as in the model:

predict(fit, newdata = tibble(residence_min = c(45, 60)))
#>        1        2 
#> 57.81491 67.85969

A batch with 60 minutes of residence is predicted to make about 67.9%. How sure is that? The next lesson puts intervals around predictions. For now, remember the residual standard error: individual batches miss the line by around 6 points.
Be careful with extrapolation, predicting outside the range of the data. The March residence times ran from 16 to 72 minutes. Inside that range, the line is backed by data. Outside it, you’re assuming the straight line carries on, and in chemistry it rarely does for long: yields can’t pass 100%, and reactions slow down as the reactant runs out.
A calibration line is used the other way round. The lab measures an unknown sample’s absorbance, y_0, and wants its concentration. Solving y_0 = b_0 + b_1 x_0 for x_0 gives

\hat{x}_0 = \frac{y_0 - b_0}{b_1} .

This is called inverse prediction, or simply calibration.
Your turn. An unknown sample has an absorbance of 0.462. Use the calibration line to estimate its concentration.









Divide by the slope, which is the second coefficient: b[2].


fit_cal <- lm(absorbance ~ conc_mgL, data = calibration)
b <- coef(fit_cal)
(0.462 - b[1]) / b[2]
About 23.2 mg/L. Remember this sample: in Lessons 8 and 9, you’ll find out whether a straight line was the right tool.

title: Simple linear regression
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Through the origin? The Beer-Lambert law says that a blank should read zero, so why not force the line through the origin? lm(absorbance ~ 0 + conc_mgL) fits a line with no intercept. Fit it, and compare its SSE with the SSE of the ordinary line, 0.00267.









The SSE is the sum of the squared residuals: sum(resid(fit0)^2).


fit0 <- lm(absorbance ~ 0 + conc_mgL, data = calibration)
c(slope = coef(fit0), sse = sum(resid(fit0)^2))
The slope rises a little, to 0.0197, and the SSE doubles, to 0.0053. Forcing the line through zero costs fit, which already hints that the straight line isn’t telling the whole story.
Now look at summary(fit0)$r.squared: it says 0.9992, higher than the ordinary line’s 0.9989, despite the worse fit! Without an intercept, R computes R^2 around zero instead of around the mean, so the two numbers aren’t comparable. Never use R^2 to choose between models with and without an intercept.




Challenge 2 · Swapping x and y. If yield goes up 0.67 points per minute, residence time should go up 1/0.67 = 1.49 minutes per point of yield, right? Fit residence time as a function of yield and find out.









Now residence time is the response: residence_min ~ yield_pct.


c(one_over_slope = 1 / coef(lm(yield_pct ~ residence_min, data = batches))[2],
  swapped_slope = coef(lm(residence_min ~ yield_pct, data = batches))[2])
1.49 against 0.89. The two lines are different! Each one minimizes the errors in its own response, so each slope is “pulled in” towards zero, by the factor r. With the formula b_1 = r\,s_y/s_x, the two slopes multiply to r^2 = 0.595, not 1. It’s regression to the mean again: a batch with an extreme yield is predicted to have a less extreme residence time, and the other way round.
For the calibration data, with r = 0.9994, the two lines almost coincide: 52.03 against 52.09 mg/L per absorbance unit. That’s why the direction hardly matters for a good calibration, but matters a lot for noisy data.

title: Simple linear regression
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does the least-squares line minimize?

The sum of the residuals
The sum of the squared vertical distances from the points to the line
The sum of the shortest (perpendicular) distances from the points to the line


The residuals always sum to zero, so that can’t be the target. Least squares minimizes the sum of the squared vertical residuals.



2. The fitted line is \widehat{\text{yield}} = 27.7 + 0.67 \times \text{residence}. What does 0.67 mean?

Each extra minute of residence time goes with 0.67 percentage points more yield, on average
67% of the variation in yield is explained by residence time
A batch with a residence time of 1 minute has a yield of 0.67%


The slope is the change in the average response for each unit of the predictor. The share of variation explained is R^2, a different number.



3. What does the intercept, 27.7, mean for the batches?

Every batch makes at least 27.7% yield
The yield at the average residence time
The predicted yield at 0 minutes, far outside the data, so it has no practical meaning here


The intercept is the prediction at x = 0. The shortest batch ran for 16 minutes, so it’s an extrapolation. (The line does pass through the point of averages, though: 44.75 minutes and 57.6%.)



4. A regression of yield on residence time has R^2 = 0.595. Which statement is right?

The predictions are right 59.5% of the time
Residence time accounts for about 60% of the variation in yield
The slope is 0.595


R^2 is the fraction of the total sum of squares that the line explains.



5. The calibration line has R^2 = 0.9989. What can you conclude?

The relationship is certainly a straight line
The points lie very close to the line, but a straight line could still be the wrong shape
The intercept must be zero


R^2 measures closeness, not correctness. A gentle curve can still give a very high R^2 with a straight line. Residual plots (Lesson 8) are the way to check the shape.



6. Why does the residual standard error divide by n - 2?

To make it bigger, to be on the safe side
Because the line used two estimated numbers, b_0 and b_1, to fit the data
Because two batches had missing values


Each estimated parameter uses up one degree of freedom. With n - 2, s^2 is an unbiased estimate of the error variance.

title: Simple linear regression
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve fitted, interpreted and checked your first regression lines! Here’s what you’ve learned:

The model: Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon. The true line gives the average response at each x, and the error is everything else.
Least squares picks the line with the smallest sum of squared residuals: b_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx} = r\,s_y/s_x and b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1\bar{x}. The line passes through (\bar{x}, \bar{y}).
lm(y ~ x, data = ...) fits it. coef(), fitted(), resid(), summary() and predict() get the pieces out.
Interpreting: the slope is the change in the average response per unit of x. The intercept is the prediction at x = 0, which only means something if 0 is within the data.
Residuals sum to zero and are uncorrelated with x. Any pattern left in them is something the model missed.
Fit: R^2 = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST} is the fraction of variation explained (r^2 in simple regression), and s = \sqrt{\text{SSE}/(n-2)} is the typical size of a residual. Neither one proves the model is right.
Prediction: stay inside the range of the data. For calibration, invert the line: \hat{x}_0 = (y_0 - b_0)/b_1.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download calibration.csv and batches.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Excel against R. Open calibration.csv in Excel, add a linear trendline with its equation and R^2, and compare them with lm(). Then try Excel’s =SLOPE(), =INTERCEPT() and =RSQ() functions. They’re all least squares.
The broom package. Run broom::tidy(fit), broom::glance(fit) and broom::augment(fit) on the batch model. They return the coefficients, the fit statistics, and the data with fitted values and residuals, as tidy data frames that are easy to plot and filter.
Your own minimizer. Use optim(c(0, 0), function(b) sse(b[1], b[2])) with the SSE function from this lesson, and check that the numerical minimum lands on the least-squares formulas.
Least absolute deviations. Install the quantreg package and fit quantreg::rq(yield_pct ~ residence_min, data = batches). It fits the line with the smallest sum of absolute residuals. How different is its slope?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Simple linear regression

A model of a response as a straight-line function of one predictor, plus random error: Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon.

Response and predictor

The variable being modeled (y), and the variable used to model it (x). Also called the dependent and independent variables.

Fitted value

The line’s prediction for an observation, \hat{y}_i = b_0 + b_1 x_i.

Residual

What the line misses for an observation, e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i.

Least squares

Choosing the coefficients that minimize the sum of squared residuals.

Sums of squares (SST, SSR, SSE)

The total variation around the mean, the part the model explains, and the part it leaves in the residuals. SST = SSR + SSE.

Coefficient of determination (R^2)

The fraction of the total variation that the model explains, SSR/SST.

Residual standard error

s = \sqrt{\text{SSE}/(n-2)}, the typical size of a residual.

Extrapolation

Predicting outside the range of the data the model was fitted to.

Inverse prediction (calibration)

Using a fitted line backwards, to estimate the x that produced an observed y.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 501, Lesson 1: Simple Linear Regression. Sections 1.1 to 1.5 cover the least-squares line, the error variance and R^2, with many examples.
Introduction to Modern Statistics, “Linear regression with a single predictor”. A gentle, picture-rich introduction to fitting and interpreting lines.
NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, “Calibration”. How measurement labs build and use calibration curves, including the inverse prediction you did here.

title: Regression in matrix notation
text:
Module 2 · Lesson 4 of 15 Week 34 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The formulas for simple regression were tidy: a slope, an intercept, a couple of sums of squares. But the March batches have a temperature, a pressure, a catalyst and an alarm count too, and writing out separate formulas for models with three or five predictors would be hopeless. Matrices fix that. With them, every linear model, with any number of predictors, has the same few formulas.
You met the main one in Lesson 0.14: the least-squares coefficients are \mathbf{b} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\mathbf{y}. This lesson builds on it. You’ll see what’s inside X^\top X, meet the matrix that turns data into fitted values, and find every standard error in a single matrix.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Regression in matrix notation
section: One equation for the whole dataset
text:
One equation for the whole dataset
The simple regression model is really 40 equations, one for each batch:

\begin{aligned}
y_1 &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \varepsilon_1 \\
y_2 &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_2 + \varepsilon_2 \\
&\;\;\vdots \\
y_{40} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{40} + \varepsilon_{40}
\end{aligned}

Stack them up, and they become one equation between vectors and a matrix:

\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_{40} \end{pmatrix}}_{\mathbf{y}}
=
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & x_1 \\ 1 & x_2 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & x_{40} \end{pmatrix}}_{X}
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} \beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \end{pmatrix}}_{\boldsymbol\beta}
+
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} \varepsilon_1 \\ \varepsilon_2 \\ \vdots \\ \varepsilon_{40} \end{pmatrix}}_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon},
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\mathbf{y} = X\boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon .

X is the design matrix: one row per observation, and one column per coefficient. The column of 1s carries the intercept. With p coefficients and n observations, X is n \times p, and the model looks the same whatever p is. A second predictor is just another column.
The assumptions get a compact form too. “The errors average zero” becomes E(\boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \mathbf{0}. “Independent errors with equal variance” becomes \text{Var}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \sigma^2 I: a covariance matrix with \sigma^2 all along its diagonal (equal variances) and zeros everywhere else (no correlation between errors).
model.matrix() shows you the design matrix that lm() builds:

fit <- lm(yield_pct ~ residence_min, data = batches)
head(model.matrix(fit), 4)
#>   (Intercept) residence_min
#> 1           1          47.2
#> 2           1          37.9
#> 3           1          32.5
#> 4           1          60.7












Your turn. The design matrix X and the yields y are ready for you. Compute X^\top X with crossprod(). What do its four numbers mean?









crossprod(X) computes t(X) %*% X, a little faster.


crossprod(X)
Each entry is a column of X multiplied by another column, then summed. The 1s column times itself counts the batches, 40. The 1s column times the residence column gives the sum of the residence times, 1,790 minutes, and the residence column times itself gives the sum of their squares, 85,025. So X^\top X holds n, \sum x_i and \sum x_i^2: everything least squares needs to know about the xs.

title: Regression in matrix notation
text:
The least-squares solution
Least squares minimizes \text{SSE} = (\mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{b})^\top(\mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{b}). Setting its gradient to zero, as in Lesson 0.14, gives the normal equations and their solution:

X^\top X\,\mathbf{b} = X^\top \mathbf{y}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{b} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y} .

For one predictor, this reproduces b_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx} and b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1\bar{x} from Lesson 2. But it works unchanged for any number of predictors. That’s the whole point.
In code, solve(A, b) solves the system A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} directly, which is faster and more accurate than computing the inverse first:

X <- model.matrix(fit)
y <- batches$yield_pct
solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, y))
#>                    [,1]
#> (Intercept)   27.680575
#> residence_min  0.669652

The same 27.68 and 0.670 that lm() found. (lm() itself uses an even more stable method, the QR decomposition, but the answer is the same.)
Your turn. Now add a second predictor. Build the design matrix for yield_pct ~ residence_min + temp_C and solve the normal equations. model.matrix() leaves out the two batches with no temperature, so drop them from the yields too.









Exactly as before: solve(crossprod(X2), crossprod(X2, y2)).


b2 <- filter(batches, !is.na(temp_C))
X2 <- model.matrix(~ residence_min + temp_C, data = b2)
y2 <- b2$yield_pct
solve(crossprod(X2), crossprod(X2, y2))
An intercept of 5.08, 0.644 points per minute of residence time, and 0.132 points per degree. Check it with coef(lm(yield_pct ~ residence_min + temp_C, data = b2)). What these coefficients mean, now that there are two of them, is the subject of the next lesson.

title: Regression in matrix notation
text:
The hat matrix
Put the solution back into the model to get the fitted values:

\hat{\mathbf{y}} = X\mathbf{b} = \underbrace{X (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top}_{H}\, \mathbf{y} = H\mathbf{y} .

The n \times n matrix H is called the hat matrix, because it puts the hat on \mathbf{y}. Each fitted value is a weighted sum of all the observed responses: \hat{y}_i = \sum_j h_{ij} y_j. Notice that H depends only on X. The weights are set by the predictors, before any yield is measured.
H has three neat properties:

It’s symmetric: H^\top = H.
It’s idempotent: HH = H. Applying it twice changes nothing, because the fitted values already lie on the fitted line. Fitting a line to points that are on a line gives the same line.
Its trace, the sum of its diagonal, equals p, the number of coefficients.







NoteGo deeper: least squares is a projection





Think of \mathbf{y} as a single point in 40-dimensional space, one coordinate per batch. The columns of X are two more points in that space, and all their combinations X\mathbf{b} form a flat two-dimensional plane through the origin: every possible set of fitted values that a straight line could produce.
Least squares finds the point of that plane closest to \mathbf{y}. The closest point is the one you reach by dropping a perpendicular, so \hat{\mathbf{y}} is the orthogonal projection of \mathbf{y} onto the plane, and H is the matrix that performs it. That’s why HH = H (projecting a point that’s already on the plane leaves it where it is), and why the residual vector \mathbf{e} = \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}} is perpendicular to the plane, which is the next section’s X^\top\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}.
Pythagoras finishes the picture. \hat{\mathbf{y}} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1} lies in the plane, \mathbf{e} is perpendicular to it, and their sum is \mathbf{y} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1}. So the squared lengths add up: \text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}. The decomposition from Lesson 2 is a right-angled triangle in 40 dimensions!



Your turn. Build the hat matrix for the simple model, and check its trace.









The trace is the sum of the diagonal: diag(H) pulls the diagonal out.


H <- X %*% solve(crossprod(X)) %*% t(X)
sum(diag(H))
Exactly 2, the number of coefficients. You can also check that max(abs(H %*% y - fitted(fit))) is essentially zero, and that H %*% H equals H.

title: Regression in matrix notation
Regression in matrix notation
text:
Residuals in matrix form
The residuals are what’s left after the fit:

\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}} = (I - H)\,\mathbf{y} .

Rearrange the normal equations, X^\top(\mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{0}, and you get one of the most useful facts in regression:

X^\top \mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0} .

Each row of this equation multiplies one column of X by the residuals and sums. The 1s column gives \sum e_i = 0: the residuals sum to zero. Every other column says that the residuals are orthogonal to that predictor, which, together with the zero sum, means they’re uncorrelated with it. With five predictors, you get six such equations. Whatever linear pattern the predictors could explain, the fit has already taken out.
One more fact about the residuals, which matters in Lesson 10. Since \text{Var}(\mathbf{e}) = \sigma^2 (I - H), each residual has variance \sigma^2(1 - h_{ii}). They’re not all equally variable: high-leverage observations have smaller residuals, because they pull the line towards themselves. B40’s residual has only 81% of the variance that an average-leverage batch’s would have.
Your turn. Compute the residuals with the hat matrix, then check that X^\top \mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}.









crossprod(X, e) computes X^\top \mathbf{e}.


H <- X %*% solve(crossprod(X)) %*% t(X)
e <- y - H %*% y
crossprod(X, e)
Both entries are around 10^{-11} or smaller: zero, apart from rounding errors in the computer’s arithmetic.

title: Regression in matrix notation
text:
The variance of the estimates
Now the payoff. Substitute the model into the solution: \mathbf{b} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top(X\boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \boldsymbol\beta + (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\boldsymbol\varepsilon. Two results follow in a line each:

E(\mathbf{b}) = \boldsymbol\beta, \qquad \text{Var}(\mathbf{b}) = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top (\sigma^2 I)\, X (X^\top X)^{-1} = \sigma^2 (X^\top X)^{-1} .

The estimates are unbiased, and their whole covariance matrix is \sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1}. Replace \sigma^2 by s^2, and its diagonal holds the squared standard errors. vcov() returns it:

vcov(fit)
#>               (Intercept) residence_min
#> (Intercept)    17.0415230  -0.358769075
#> residence_min  -0.3587691   0.008017186
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))
#>   (Intercept) residence_min 
#>    4.12813796    0.08953874

There are the standard errors from summary(), 4.13 and 0.0895, for any model you’ll ever fit. The off-diagonal entry is the covariance of the intercept and slope estimates. Converted to a correlation, cov2cor(vcov(fit)), it’s −0.97! The fitted line pivots around (\bar{x}, \bar{y}), and since \bar{x} = 44.75 is far from 0, a line that comes out a little too steep must cross the axis a little too low. So the two estimates are tied together, which matters whenever you combine them, as in a prediction.






NoteGo deeper: the Gauss-Markov theorem





Least squares isn’t just a way of estimating \boldsymbol\beta. Among all estimators that are linear in \mathbf{y} and unbiased, it has the smallest variance. That’s the Gauss-Markov theorem, and it needs only E(\boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \mathbf{0} and \text{Var}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \sigma^2 I, not normality.
The proof is short. Any linear estimator is \tilde{\mathbf{b}} = C\mathbf{y} for some matrix C. Write C = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top + D. Unbiasedness, E(\tilde{\mathbf{b}}) = CX\boldsymbol\beta = \boldsymbol\beta for every \boldsymbol\beta, forces DX = 0. Then

\text{Var}(\tilde{\mathbf{b}}) = \sigma^2 CC^\top = \sigma^2\left[(X^\top X)^{-1} + DD^\top\right],

because the cross terms contain DX = 0. DD^\top can never reduce a variance (each diagonal entry is a sum of squares), so the best choice is D = 0: least squares. Statisticians call it BLUE, the best linear unbiased estimator.
The conditions matter, though. If the errors have unequal variances or are correlated, least squares is no longer best, and Lesson 9’s weighted least squares can beat it.



Your turn. Compute the covariance matrix of the estimates from the formula, s^2(X^\top X)^{-1}, and take the square roots of its diagonal.









The matrix to invert is X^\top X: crossprod(X).


V <- sigma(fit)^2 * solve(crossprod(X))
sqrt(diag(V))
4.13 for the intercept and 0.0895 for the slope, the same as summary().

title: Regression in matrix notation
text:
The variance of a prediction
A prediction at new settings is a linear combination of the estimates: \hat{y}_0 = \mathbf{x}_0^\top \mathbf{b}, where \mathbf{x}_0 is a row of a design matrix, like (1, 60) for a 60-minute batch. A linear combination’s variance comes straight from the covariance matrix:

\text{Var}(\hat{y}_0) = \mathbf{x}_0^\top\, \text{Var}(\mathbf{b})\, \mathbf{x}_0 = \sigma^2\, \mathbf{x}_0^\top (X^\top X)^{-1} \mathbf{x}_0 .

For simple regression, this works out to the confidence interval formula from Lesson 3, s^2\left[1/n + (x_0 - \bar{x})^2/S_{xx}\right]. But it works for any model, and it uses the covariance of the estimates, which is why you can’t just add up their separate standard errors.
Your turn. Compute the standard error of the predicted mean yield at 60 minutes. Last lesson, predict() gave 1.69.









The new row of the design matrix is a 1 for the intercept and the residence time, 60.


V <- vcov(fit)
x0 <- c(1, 60)
sqrt(t(x0) %*% V %*% x0)
1.69, matching predict(fit, tibble(residence_min = 60), se.fit = TRUE)$se.fit. If you had ignored the covariance and added the two variances, 17.04 + 60^2 \times 0.008, you’d get a standard error of 6.8, four times too big.

title: Regression in matrix notation
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Centering untangles the estimates. Subtract the average residence time from every residence time, refit, and look at the correlation between the intercept and slope estimates.









Subtract mean(residence_min).


centered <- mutate(batches, res_c = residence_min - mean(residence_min))
fit_c <- lm(yield_pct ~ res_c, data = centered)
list(coefficients = coef(fit_c), correlation = cov2cor(vcov(fit_c))[1, 2])
The slope is unchanged, 0.670. The intercept is now 57.65, the mean yield: the predicted yield at an average residence time, which actually means something. And the correlation between the two estimates is zero. With a centered predictor, the 1s column and the residence column are orthogonal, so X^\top X is diagonal, and its inverse is too. You’ll use centering again with interactions (Lesson 7) and polynomials (Lesson 11).




Challenge 2 · Categories as columns. A design matrix can hold categories too. Build the design matrix for ~ catalyst and solve the normal equations. Then compare the four coefficients with the mean yield of each catalyst. What do they mean?









The response is still the yield, y.


Xd <- model.matrix(~ catalyst, data = batches)
head(Xd)
solve(crossprod(Xd), crossprod(Xd, y))
R made a column of 0s and 1s for catalysts B, C and D, but none for A. The intercept, 59.98, is the mean yield of catalyst A. Each other coefficient is the difference from A: catalyst B averaged 4.26 points less (55.73), C 5.18 less (54.80), and D 0.49 more (60.47). Check with tapply(batches$yield_pct, batches$catalyst, mean). Columns like these are called dummy variables, and Lesson 7 is all about them.

title: Regression in matrix notation
text:
Quick quiz

1. A model has an intercept and two predictors, fitted to 38 batches. What are the dimensions of its design matrix?

2 × 38
38 × 2
38 × 3


One row per observation and one column per coefficient: the intercept’s column of 1s plus one column for each predictor.



2. What does the hat matrix do?

It turns the observed responses into the fitted values: \hat{\mathbf{y}} = H\mathbf{y}
It turns the predictors into the coefficients
It removes the outliers from the data


H = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top projects \mathbf{y} onto the space spanned by the columns of X.



3. The diagonal of the hat matrix always adds up to…

the number of observations, n
the number of coefficients, p
1


The trace of H is p, so the average leverage is p/n.



4. What does an observation’s leverage depend on?

Only its predictor values, compared with the others’
Only its response value
Both, equally


H is built from X alone. An observation has high leverage when its x values are far from the rest, whatever its y.



5. How do you get the standard errors of the coefficients from \text{Var}(\mathbf{b}) = s^2(X^\top X)^{-1}?

Add up each row
Take the square roots of its diagonal entries
Invert it again


The diagonal holds the variances of the estimates, and the off-diagonal entries hold their covariances.



6. The residuals of a least-squares fit with an intercept are always…

normally distributed
all the same size
orthogonal to every column of X, so they sum to zero and are uncorrelated with every predictor


That’s X^\top\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}, a direct consequence of the normal equations. Normality is an assumption about the errors, not a property of the residuals.

title: Regression in matrix notation
text:
Wrap-up
You now have the matrix machinery that every regression program runs on! Here’s what you’ve learned:

The model: \mathbf{y} = X\boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon, with E(\boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \mathbf{0} and \text{Var}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \sigma^2 I. The design matrix X has a row per observation and a column per coefficient. model.matrix() shows it.
Least squares: X^\top X\,\mathbf{b} = X^\top\mathbf{y}, so \mathbf{b} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\mathbf{y}, for any number of predictors.
The hat matrix H = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top turns \mathbf{y} into \hat{\mathbf{y}}. It’s symmetric and idempotent, with trace p. Geometrically, it’s a projection.
Leverage is h_{ii}, the diagonal of H. It’s large for observations with unusual x values, and it averages p/n.
Residuals: \mathbf{e} = (I - H)\mathbf{y}, with X^\top\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0} and \text{Var}(e_i) = \sigma^2(1 - h_{ii}).
Uncertainty: \text{Var}(\mathbf{b}) = \sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1} gives every standard error and covariance (vcov()), and \text{Var}(\mathbf{x}_0^\top\mathbf{b}) = \sigma^2\mathbf{x}_0^\top(X^\top X)^{-1}\mathbf{x}_0 gives a prediction’s.
Gauss-Markov: with uncorrelated, equal-variance errors, least squares is the best linear unbiased estimator.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download batches.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

A bigger model by hand. Fit yield_pct ~ residence_min + temp_C + alarms with matrices: build X with model.matrix(), solve the normal equations, compute s^2 = \text{SSE}/(n - p), and the standard errors. Check every number against summary(). Watch the missing values: model.matrix() drops incomplete rows, so drop them from \mathbf{y} too.
QR, the way lm() does it. Compute qr.coef(qr(X), y) and compare it with the normal-equations solution. Then look up why the QR decomposition is more numerically stable.
Leverage formula. For the simple model, check that hatvalues(fit) equals 1/n + (x - mean(x))^2 / sum((x - mean(x))^2).
The seesaw. Simulate 1,000 campaigns from a known line, as in Lesson 3, and plot the fitted intercepts against the fitted slopes. Then do the same with centered residence times. The correlation of −0.97 should be plain to see, and then gone.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Design matrix (X)

The n \times p matrix of predictor values, with a column of 1s for the intercept: one row per observation and one column per coefficient.

Normal equations

X^\top X\,\mathbf{b} = X^\top\mathbf{y}, the equations that the least-squares coefficients solve.

Hat matrix (H)

H = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top, the matrix that turns the responses into the fitted values.

Idempotent

A matrix that equals its own square, HH = H, like every projection.

Leverage

An observation’s diagonal entry h_{ii} of the hat matrix, which measures how unusual its predictor values are and how much it can pull the fit.

Orthogonal

Perpendicular. Two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero, as the residuals are to every column of X.

Covariance matrix of the estimates

\text{Var}(\mathbf{b}) = \sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1}, with the variances of the coefficients on its diagonal and their covariances off it.

Gauss-Markov theorem

With uncorrelated errors of equal variance, least squares has the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators (BLUE).











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 501, Lesson 5: Multiple Linear Regression, especially section 5.4, “A Matrix Formulation of the Multiple Regression Model”.
Stephen Boyd and Lieven Vandenberghe, Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra, chapters 12 and 13. Least squares as linear algebra, with lots of engineering examples. Free online, and the same book Lesson 0.14 recommended.
