Essence of Linear Algebra (3Blue1Brown videos), “Dot products and duality”. The geometry behind orthogonality and projections.

title: Hypothesis tests in multiple regression
text:
Module 2 · Lesson 6 of 15 Week 36 of 160 About 5–7 hours
With one predictor, there was one question to test: is the slope zero? With several, the questions multiply. Does the model explain anything at all? Do the catalysts differ? Are catalysts B and C equally good? Does the old rule of thumb for residence time still hold, now that we account for temperature and feed water? All these questions have the same shape: a simpler model against a bigger one. And one test, the F-test, answers all of them.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Hypothesis tests in multiple regression
text:
One coefficient at a time
Let’s add the catalyst to last lesson’s model. It has three types, so R gives it two dummy columns, for B and C, with A as the baseline:

fit <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst, data = study)
summary(fit)
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + 
#>     catalyst, data = study)
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
#> -11.2341  -2.3093  -0.2512   2.5678  19.5736 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)    -45.422203   6.155362  -7.379 2.78e-11 ***
#> temp_C           0.539246   0.031414  17.166  < 2e-16 ***
#> residence_min    0.358441   0.030701  11.675  < 2e-16 ***
#> feed_water_ppm  -0.062179   0.008689  -7.156 8.61e-11 ***
#> catalystB        3.607356   0.932780   3.867 0.000184 ***
#> catalystC       -1.949850   0.926036  -2.106 0.037435 *  
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Residual standard error: 4.077 on 114 degrees of freedom
#> Multiple R-squared:  0.7975, Adjusted R-squared:  0.7887 
#> F-statistic: 89.81 on 5 and 114 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

Each row’s t-test asks whether that coefficient is zero, given all the other predictors in the model. So the feed_water_ppm row tests whether water matters for runs with the same temperature, residence time and catalyst. That’s a different question from last lesson’s simple regression, which is why it can give a different answer.
Two catalyst rows, two separate questions: is B different from A (t = 3.87, p = 0.0002)? Is C different from A (p = 0.037)? But neither row asks the obvious one: do the catalysts differ at all? And neither compares B with C. For those, you need a test of more than one coefficient at a time.

title: Hypothesis tests in multiple regression
text:
The overall F-test
The broadest question of all: does the model explain anything? The null hypothesis is that every slope is zero:

H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \dots = \beta_k = 0 .

The test is the ANOVA F-test from Lesson 3, with k slopes instead of one:

F = \frac{\text{SSR}/k}{\text{SSE}/(n - p)} = \frac{R^2/k}{(1 - R^2)/(n - p)},

where p = k + 1 counts the intercept too. summary() prints it on its last line: here F = 89.8 on 5 and 114 degrees of freedom. A p-value that small says that at least one predictor matters. It doesn’t say which.
In practice, the overall F-test is rarely interesting: you usually know that something matters before you fit a model. But it’s the simplest example of the idea that drives the rest of this lesson.










Your turn. Last lesson’s three-predictor model, fit3, had R^2 = 0.7336 with 120 runs. Compute its overall F statistic from R^2.









The residual degrees of freedom are n - p, and p = k + 1 includes the intercept: n - k - 1.


r2 <- summary(fit3)$r.squared
n <- 120
k <- 3
(r2 / k) / ((1 - r2) / (n - k - 1))
F = 106.5 on 3 and 116 degrees of freedom, the same as the last line of summary(fit3).

title: Hypothesis tests in multiple regression
text:
Comparing nested models
Here’s the general idea. Two models are nested if the smaller one is a special case of the bigger one, which you get by setting some of the bigger model’s coefficients to zero (or, as you’ll see, by fixing them in some other way). The smaller one is called the reduced model, and the bigger one the full model.
The full model always fits at least as well: \text{SSE}_F \le \text{SSE}_R. The question is whether it fits enough better to justify its extra coefficients. The partial F-test compares the drop in SSE with what you’d expect from luck alone:

F = \frac{(\text{SSE}_R - \text{SSE}_F)/q}{\text{SSE}_F/(n - p_F)},

where q is the number of coefficients the reduced model leaves out, and p_F counts the full model’s coefficients. If the extra coefficients are all really zero, F follows an F distribution with q and n - p_F degrees of freedom. anova(reduced, full) does the arithmetic.
The overall F-test is the special case where the reduced model has only an intercept. A t-test is the special case where q = 1: then F = t^2, as you’ll check in the challenge round.
Your turn. In Lesson 5, adding the outdoor temperature, the stirrer speed and the operator to fit3 nudged R^2 up, and adjusted R^2 down. Test all seven extra coefficients at once.









Put the reduced model first and the full model second: anova(fit3, bigger).


bigger <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + ambient_C + stir_rpm + operator_id,
             data = study)
anova(fit3, bigger)
The seven coefficients reduced the SSE by 73 out of 2,494. F = 0.47 on 7 and 109 degrees of freedom, p = 0.85. No evidence that any of them matters.

title: Hypothesis tests in multiple regression
text:
Testing a categorical predictor
The catalyst is one predictor, but two coefficients. “Do the catalysts differ?” means “are both dummy coefficients zero?”, and that’s a partial F-test with q = 2: the model without the catalyst against the model with it.
Why not just look at the two t-tests? Because they depend on the baseline. They compare B with A and C with A, but with B as the baseline, you’d get two different t-tests. The F-test asks the question about the catalyst as a whole, and it gives the same answer whichever catalyst is the baseline.
Your turn. Compute the partial F statistic for the catalyst by hand, from the two models’ SSEs. deviance() returns a linear model’s SSE.









The full model has two more coefficients than the reduced one: the dummies for B and C.


sse_r <- deviance(fit3)
sse_f <- deviance(fit)
q <- 2
((sse_r - sse_f) / q) / (sse_f / df.residual(fit))
F = 18.0 on 2 and 114 degrees of freedom, and anova(fit3, fit) gives p = 1.6 \times 10^{-7}. The catalysts clearly differ. Adding them cut the SSE from 2,494 to 1,895.

title: Hypothesis tests in multiple regression
text:
General linear hypotheses
Setting coefficients to zero isn’t the only way to make a reduced model. Any claim of the form “some combination of the coefficients equals some number” is a general linear hypothesis, and it can be tested the same way: build the model in which the claim is true, and compare.
Are catalysts B and C equally good? That’s H_0: \beta_B = \beta_C. If it’s true, B and C are really one catalyst, so the reduced model merges them into a single category, “B or C”:

study2 <- mutate(study, catalyst2 = if_else(catalyst == "A", "A", "B or C"))
merged <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst2, data = study2)

Does the rule of thumb hold? The full model says each minute adds 0.358 points. Is that consistent with the pilot plant’s long-standing figure of 0.35? H_0: \beta_{\text{res}} = 0.35 is a reduced model in which the residence coefficient isn’t estimated at all, but fixed. offset() adds a term with a fixed coefficient of 1:

fixed <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + offset(0.35 * residence_min) + feed_water_ppm + catalyst, data = study)

Both are nested in the full model, so anova() tests them. You’ll do that next. For hypotheses with several parts, the car package’s linearHypothesis() builds the reduced model for you from the hypothesis written as text, and gives the same F-tests:

car::linearHypothesis(fit, "catalystB = catalystC")
#> 
#> Linear hypothesis test:
#> catalystB - catalystC = 0
#> 
#> Model 1: restricted model
#> Model 2: yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst
#> 
#>   Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
#> 1    115 2478.1                                  
#> 2    114 1895.3  1    582.79 35.053 3.455e-08 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Your turn. Test whether catalysts B and C are equally good, by comparing the merged model with the full one.









The merged model is the reduced one, so it goes first: anova(merged, fit).


study2 <- mutate(study, catalyst2 = if_else(catalyst == "A", "A", "B or C"))
merged <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst2, data = study2)
anova(merged, fit)
F = 35.1 on 1 and 114 degrees of freedom, p = 3.5 \times 10^{-8}. B and C are clearly different: B beats A by 3.6 points, while C trails A by 1.9, so B beats C by about 5.6 points.




Your turn. Now test the rule of thumb, \beta_{\text{res}} = 0.35.









The offset fixes the residence coefficient at the rule-of-thumb value, 0.35.


fixed <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + offset(0.35 * residence_min) + feed_water_ppm + catalyst, data = study)
anova(fixed, fit)
F = 0.076, p = 0.78. The rule of thumb fits these data fine. (The simple regression in Lesson 5 said 0.21 per minute, which would have contradicted it: that was the confounded estimate.) This is the same test as the t-test t = (0.358 - 0.35)/\text{SE}, squared.

title: Hypothesis tests in multiple regression
section: Sequential and partial sums of squares
text:
Sequential and partial sums of squares
There’s one more way to split up the variation, and it causes a lot of confusion. Give anova() a single model, and it prints a table of sequential sums of squares (also called Type I): each row is the reduction in SSE from adding that predictor after the ones above it:

anova(lm(yield_pct ~ feed_water_ppm + residence_min + temp_C + catalyst, data = study))
#> Analysis of Variance Table
#> 
#> Response: yield_pct
#>                 Df Sum Sq Mean Sq  F value    Pr(>F)    
#> feed_water_ppm   1   59.0    59.0   3.5485   0.06215 .  
#> residence_min    1 1398.0  1398.0  84.0880 2.379e-15 ***
#> temp_C           1 5410.2  5410.2 325.4114 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> catalyst         2  598.9   299.4  18.0107 1.595e-07 ***
#> Residuals      114 1895.3    16.6                       
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Put the water first, and it explains only 59 units of the SSE (p = 0.062), because on its own the water’s effect is hidden by its confounding with residence time. Now put it after residence time:

anova(lm(yield_pct ~ residence_min + feed_water_ppm + temp_C + catalyst, data = study))
#> Analysis of Variance Table
#> 
#> Response: yield_pct
#>                 Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
#> residence_min    1  968.9   968.9  58.277 7.577e-12 ***
#> feed_water_ppm   1  488.1   488.1  29.360 3.393e-07 ***
#> temp_C           1 5410.2  5410.2 325.411 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> catalyst         2  598.9   299.4  18.011 1.595e-07 ***
#> Residuals      114 1895.3    16.6                      
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Now the water accounts for 488 units, and residence time’s own row shrinks from 1,398 to 969. When predictors are correlated, sequential sums of squares depend on the order, because each row only gets credit for what the predictors above it didn’t already explain. The rows always add up to the same total, SSR. Only the split between them changes.
The partial sums of squares (Type II) avoid this: each predictor is added last, after all the others, so the order doesn’t matter. Each row is then a partial F-test of that predictor. drop1() computes them, as does car::Anova():

drop1(fit, test = "F")
#> Single term deletions
#> 
#> Model:
#> yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst
#>                Df Sum of Sq    RSS    AIC F value    Pr(>F)    
#> <none>                      1895.3 343.16                      
#> temp_C          1    4899.1 6794.5 494.36 294.671 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> residence_min   1    2266.2 4161.5 435.54 136.306 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> feed_water_ppm  1     851.3 2746.7 385.68  51.205 8.614e-11 ***
#> catalyst        2     598.9 2494.2 372.11  18.011 1.595e-07 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Water, added last, accounts for 851 units, with F = 51.2. Which table should you use?

To test each predictor’s contribution given the others, which is usually the question, use the partial sums of squares: drop1() or car::Anova().
Sequential sums of squares suit a model built up in a meaningful order, like a polynomial (does the squared term add to the linear one?), or “does the catalyst matter after the process conditions?”.
In a designed experiment where the predictors are uncorrelated, the two tables agree, and the question goes away. That’s one more reason to design experiments. Lesson 14 meets a third kind, Type III, for unbalanced experiments.

Your turn. Find the water’s sequential sum of squares when it’s entered first, and its partial sum of squares (entered last).









In drop1()’s table, the column is called "Sum of Sq".


first <- anova(lm(yield_pct ~ feed_water_ppm + residence_min + temp_C + catalyst, data = study))
last <- drop1(fit, test = "F")
c(first = first["feed_water_ppm", "Sum Sq"], last = last["feed_water_ppm", "Sum of Sq"])
59 when entered first, 851 when entered last: a factor of 14, for the same predictor in the same data. When someone reports “variable X explains Y% of the variation”, always ask: entered in which order?

title: Hypothesis tests in multiple regression
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · A t-test is an F-test. For a single coefficient, the partial F statistic is the square of its t statistic. Check it for the water: square the t value from summary(fit), and compare it with the F value in drop1(fit, test = "F").









The t statistics are in the column called "t value".


t_water <- summary(fit)$coefficients["feed_water_ppm", "t value"]
c(t_squared = t_water^2, F = drop1(fit, test = "F")["feed_water_ppm", "F value"])
Both are 51.2: (-7.16)^2 = 51.2. The t-tests in summary() are partial F-tests with q = 1, which is why they’re “given all the other predictors”.




Challenge 2 · Fishing. Add 20 columns of pure random noise to the model, and count how many of them get a p-value below 0.05 in summary(). Then test all 20 together with a partial F-test.









Compare the model without the noise, fit, with the one with it, fished.


set.seed(2037)
noise <- as.data.frame(matrix(rnorm(120 * 20), nrow = 120))
fished <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst + .,
             data = bind_cols(select(study, yield_pct, temp_C, residence_min, feed_water_ppm, catalyst), noise))
p_noise <- summary(fished)$coefficients[paste0("V", 1:20), "Pr(>|t|)"]
c(significant = sum(p_noise < 0.05), joint_p = anova(fit, fished)[2, "Pr(>F)"])
Three of the twenty noise columns look “significant”! (On average, you’d expect one in twenty, since each test has a 5% false-alarm rate. This seed was a little unlucky, which happens.) Yet the partial F-test of all twenty together gives p = 0.11: no evidence that the noise matters, which is the truth. Testing many coefficients one at a time and reporting the winners is called fishing, and it’s one of the commonest ways to fool yourself. A joint test asks the question once.

title: Hypothesis tests in multiple regression
text:
Quick quiz

1. What’s the null hypothesis of the overall F-test?

The intercept is zero
All the slopes are zero
At least one slope is zero


It tests whether the model explains anything at all. Rejecting it says at least one predictor matters, not which.



2. In a model with temperature, residence time, water and catalyst, what does the t-test for catalystC test?

Whether catalyst C matters at all
Whether catalyst C differs from the baseline catalyst A, for runs with the same temperature, residence time and water
Whether catalyst C differs from catalyst B


Each dummy coefficient compares one category with the baseline, given the other predictors. To test the catalyst as a whole, use a partial F-test of both dummies.



3. Which pair of models is nested?

y ~ temp_C and y ~ residence_min
y ~ temp_C + residence_min and y ~ temp_C + residence_min + catalyst
y ~ temp_C and log(y) ~ temp_C


The smaller model is the bigger one with the catalyst coefficients set to zero. The other pairs can’t be turned into one another that way.



4. How do you test H_0: \beta_B = \beta_C with a partial F-test?

Drop the catalyst from the model
Merge catalysts B and C into one category, and compare that model with the full one
Look at the t-test for catalystB


If \beta_B = \beta_C, the model can’t tell B and C apart, so the reduced model treats them as one category.



5. When do sequential (Type I) sums of squares depend on the order of the predictors?

When the predictors are correlated with one another
Always
Never: the order never matters in regression


Each row only gets credit for what the rows above it didn’t explain. With uncorrelated predictors, as in a balanced designed experiment, there’s no shared credit to argue over.



6. You test 20 predictors that have no effect at all, each at the 5% level. How many would you expect to look significant?

None
About one
About five


Each test has a 5% chance of a false alarm, and 20 \times 0.05 = 1. A single joint F-test avoids this.

title: Hypothesis tests in multiple regression
text:
Wrap-up
You can now test almost any question about a linear model! Here’s what you’ve learned:

t-tests in summary() test one coefficient at a time, given all the other predictors.
The overall F-test tests whether all the slopes are zero: F = (R^2/k)/((1-R^2)/(n-p)).
Nested models: a reduced model is the full one with some coefficients constrained. The partial F-test, anova(reduced, full), compares their SSEs: F = [(\text{SSE}_R - \text{SSE}_F)/q] / [\text{SSE}_F/(n-p_F)].
Categorical predictors are tested as a whole with a partial F-test of all their dummies.
General linear hypotheses like \beta_B = \beta_C or \beta_{\text{res}} = 0.35 are partial F-tests too: merge categories, use offset(), or let car::linearHypothesis() build the reduced model.
Sums of squares: sequential ones (anova(fit)) depend on the order when predictors are correlated. Partial ones (drop1(), car::Anova()) add each predictor last.
Fishing: many separate tests produce false alarms. Ask the question once, with a joint test.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download process_study.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install the car package if you haven’t yet.

linearHypothesis() for everything. Use car::linearHypothesis() to redo this lesson’s tests: "catalystB = 0", c("catalystB = 0", "catalystC = 0"), "residence_min = 0.35". Check that each matches the test you did another way.
A trade-off test. Is 10 minutes of residence time worth as much as 6 degrees of temperature? Write that as "10 * residence_min = 6 * temp_C", and test it.
The baseline doesn’t matter to F. Make B the baseline catalyst with relevel(factor(study$catalyst), ref = "B"), refit, and compare the t-tests and the partial F-test for the catalyst with the ones in this lesson.
Type I, II and III. Compare anova(fit), car::Anova(fit, type = 2) and car::Anova(fit, type = 3). For this model, which ones agree?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Overall F-test

A test of whether all the slopes in a model are zero.

Nested models

A reduced model that’s a special case of a full model, obtained by constraining some of its coefficients.

Partial F-test

A test comparing nested models by how much the full model reduces the SSE, per extra coefficient.

General linear hypothesis

A claim that some linear combination of the coefficients equals a given value, such as \beta_B - \beta_C = 0.

Offset

A term added to a model with its coefficient fixed at 1, used to fix a coefficient at a chosen value.

Sequential (Type I) sums of squares

The reduction in SSE from adding each predictor after the ones listed before it.

Partial (Type II) sums of squares

The reduction in SSE from adding each predictor after all the others.

Fishing

Running many tests and reporting the significant ones, which produces false discoveries.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 501, Lesson 6: MLR Model Evaluation. The general linear F-test, sequential sums of squares and partial F-tests, step by step.
John Fox and Sanford Weisberg, An R Companion to Applied Regression, chapter 5. Written by the authors of the car package: Anova(), linearHypothesis() and the types of sums of squares.
Introduction to Modern Statistics, “Inference for linear regression with multiple predictors”. The same ideas with a lighter touch.

title: Checking model assumptions
text:
Module 2 · Lesson 8 of 15 Week 38 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Every standard error, test and interval since Lesson 3 has rested on four assumptions: a Linear mean, Independent errors, Normal errors and Equal variance. Until now, we took them on trust. This lesson checks them, and the evidence is in the residuals: everything the model couldn’t explain. A good model leaves residuals that look like pure, patternless noise. Any pattern you find is something the model missed, and it usually tells you what to do next.
Two models are on trial today: Lesson 7’s interaction model for the process study, and Lesson 2’s calibration line, the one with R^2 = 0.9989.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Checking model assumptions
text:
The residuals and their plots
Here’s the model from last lesson, with its residuals added to the data:

fit <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C * catalyst + residence_min + feed_water_ppm, data = study)
study <- mutate(study, fitted = fitted(fit), resid = resid(fit))

The most basic plot is the residuals against the fitted values. If the model is right, the points should form a shapeless horizontal band around zero, the same width everywhere:

ggplot(study, aes(x = fitted, y = resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, color = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Fitted yield (%)", y = "Residual (points)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The rose curve is a loess smoother, a flexible local average that follows any trend in the residuals. Here it stays close to zero. Mostly a band, then, apart from one point way up at +14 and another down at −11. Good so far, but this plot mixes all the predictors together. The next steps look at each assumption on its own.
Base R draws four standard diagnostic plots with a single command, plot(fit), and you’ll see them in many books. This lesson draws its own, to look at one thing at a time.

title: Checking model assumptions
text:
Linearity
A missing curve shows up best when you plot the residuals against each numerical predictor in turn:

ggplot(study, aes(x = temp_C, y = resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, color = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 158.1, y = 12.3, label = "P066", size = 3.5, color = "grey30") +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Residual (points)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Two things jump out. One run, P066, sits all alone at 158 °C, far to the left of every other run, with a huge residual (it drags the smoother up at the far left, too). And between 170 and 205 °C, the residuals form a gentle arch: below zero at both ends, above zero in the middle. That’s what a missing curve looks like. The yield rises with temperature, but more slowly at the top, and a straight line can’t bend to follow it. (You’ll add the curve in Lesson 9.)










Your turn. Put a number on the arch. Split the temperatures into four bands, and compute the mean residual in each. The residuals are already in study$resid.









Average the resid column.


study |>
  mutate(band = cut(temp_C, breaks = c(-Inf, 175, 185, 195, Inf))) |>
  group_by(band) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_resid = mean(resid))
−1.25 below 175 °C, +0.13 and +1.53 in the middle bands, −0.38 above 195 °C. Down, up, down: the straight line runs too high at both ends and too low in the middle. (And the lowest band’s mean includes P066’s +14, without which it would be lower still.)

title: Checking model assumptions
text:
Constant variance
The calibration line tells the next story. Here are its residuals against concentration:

fit_cal <- lm(absorbance ~ conc_mgL, data = calibration)
calibration |>
  mutate(resid = resid(fit_cal)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = conc_mgL, y = resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "#C2416C") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Concentration (mg/L)", y = "Residual (absorbance)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Remember, this line has R^2 = 0.9989. Its residuals show two problems at once:

Another arch, much clearer than the process study’s: negative at both ends, positive in the middle. The absorbance bends down at high concentrations, which is the detector starting to saturate. That’s why the line’s intercept missed the blanks in Lesson 2: the straight line tilts to compromise with the curve, and lifts its left end off the blanks.
A funnel. The triplicates at the top of the range are far more spread out than the ones at the bottom. Their scatter grows with the absorbance, as it often does for instruments. That breaks the equal-variance assumption.

Why does unequal variance matter? Least squares gives every point the same weight, so the noisy high standards get as much say as the precise low ones. The estimates stay unbiased, but they’re less precise than they could be, and the standard errors, which assume one \sigma for every point, are wrong: too narrow in some places, too wide in others. A prediction interval for a low-concentration sample would be far too wide, and one for a high-concentration sample too narrow.
There are formal tests, too. The Breusch-Pagan test regresses the squared residuals on the predictors: if the spread changes with them, it finds the trend. When the data have replicates, as the calibration does, you can compare the replicates’ variances directly with Bartlett’s test: bartlett.test(absorbance ~ factor(conc_mgL), data = calibration) gives p = 0.036.
Your turn. Measure the funnel. Compute the standard deviation of the three replicates at each concentration.









sd(absorbance) within each group.


calibration |>
  group_by(conc_mgL) |>
  summarise(sd = sd(absorbance))
About 0.0015 for the standards from 0 to 10 mg/L, and about 0.009 for those from 30 to 50 mg/L: six times as big. These replicate standard deviations don’t depend on any model, so they show the funnel even more cleanly than the residuals do. With only three readings per standard, each one is rough, but the trend is clear.

title: Checking model assumptions
text:
Normality
To check whether the residuals look normal, plot them in a normal Q-Q plot (Lesson 0.10): sorted residuals against the values you’d expect from a normal distribution. Normal residuals fall along a straight line. It’s best to use standardized residuals, which are divided by their estimated standard deviation, s\sqrt{1 - h_{ii}} (Lesson 4), so that they’re all on the same scale and values beyond ±3 stand out. rstandard() computes them:

study |>
  mutate(std_resid = rstandard(fit)) |>
  ggplot(aes(sample = std_resid)) +
  geom_qq_line(color = "grey60") +
  geom_qq(size = 1.8, color = "#2a78d6") +
  annotate("text", x = c(2.15, -2.15), y = c(4.4, -3.1), label = c("P066", "P047"), size = 3.5, color = "grey30", hjust = c(1.2, -0.2)) +
  labs(x = "Theoretical normal quantiles", y = "Standardized residual") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The middle of the plot hugs the line nicely. But at the ends, two runs break away: P066, 4.4 standard deviations above its fitted value, and P047, 3.1 below. With 120 normal residuals, the most extreme ones would usually be around ±2.5 to ±3, so 4.4 is very unusual indeed. The Shapiro-Wilk test puts a number on it: shapiro.test(resid(fit)) gives p = 0.030.
Before testing anything else, look at what these two runs are:

study |>
  filter(run_id %in% c("P047", "P066")) |>
  select(run_id, temp_C, jacket_C, residence_min, yield_pct, resid, notes)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 7
#>   run_id temp_C jacket_C residence_min yield_pct resid notes                    
#>   <chr>   <dbl>    <dbl>         <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl> <chr>                    
#> 1 P047     183.     194.          57.6      41.6 -10.6 Stirrer tripped twice, r…
#> 2 P066     158.     196.          38.6      64.6  13.9 <NA>

P047 has an explanation in the notes: the stirrer tripped twice, so of course it underperformed. P066 has no note. But its temperature of 158.1 °C is more than nine degrees below any other run, in a study whose lowest set point was 170 °C. Its jacket, which normally runs 8 to 14 °C hotter than the reactor, was at 196.3 °C, 38 degrees hotter. Smells like a typo… Lesson 10 is about unusual points like these: how to find them systematically, how much damage they do, and what to do with them. For now, just keep them in mind.
How much does normality matter? Less than the other three assumptions, for the coefficients: thanks to the central limit theorem, their sampling distributions are close to normal in large samples even when the errors aren’t. It matters more for prediction intervals, which are about single observations, and a single wild residual matters a lot, normal or not.
Your turn. Run the Shapiro-Wilk test on the residuals of the same model fitted without P047 and P066. Does the rest look normal?









The other run to leave out is "P066".


rest <- filter(study, !run_id %in% c("P047", "P066"))
fit_rest <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C * catalyst + residence_min + feed_water_ppm, data = rest)
shapiro.test(resid(fit_rest))
p = 0.85: without those two runs, the residuals look perfectly normal. The “non-normality” was really two outliers. That’s common, and it’s why you should look at a Q-Q plot instead of just reading a test’s p-value.

title: Checking model assumptions
text:
Independence
The last assumption is the sneakiest: the errors shouldn’t be related to one another. The usual way to break it is time. If something drifts while the data are collected, runs close together in time share part of their error, and their residuals are correlated. That’s called autocorrelation, and the way to look for it is to plot the residuals in the order the runs were made:

run_order <- seq_len(nrow(study))
ggplot(mutate(study, run = run_order), aes(x = run, y = resid)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = seq(20.5, 100.5, by = 20), color = "#F4C0D1", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, color = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, span = 0.15, se = FALSE, color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Run order", y = "Residual (points)") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-12, 12)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The pink lines mark the days when both reactors got a fresh catalyst charge, every 20 runs. Between them, the residuals slide downhill: high just after a change, low just before the next one. A sawtooth! The model doesn’t know that the catalyst loses activity as it ages, so the ageing ends up in the residuals, and neighbouring runs share it.
Why does that matter? Correlated errors carry less information than independent ones: ten runs on one tired catalyst charge aren’t ten independent looks at the process. The model then overstates its precision, so the standard errors are too small, and the tests too confident.
Two ways to measure it:

The lag-1 autocorrelation: the correlation between each residual and the next one. Here it’s 0.23.
The Durbin-Watson statistic, d = \sum_{t=2}^{n}(e_t - e_{t-1})^2 \big/ \sum_{t=1}^{n} e_t^2. It’s about 2(1 - r_1), where r_1 is the lag-1 autocorrelation, so independent residuals give about 2, and positive autocorrelation pushes it towards 0. lmtest::dwtest(fit) gives its p-value.

The independence assumption depends on the order of the rows, so the residuals must be in time order, as they are here. And “time” isn’t the only way to be related: runs from the same feed lot, samples from the same batch, or measurements from the same analyst can share errors too.
Your turn. The sawtooth suggests a culprit: the catalyst charge’s age, which the data record as catalyst_age (1 to 10). Compute the mean residual for each age.









Group by catalyst_age.


study |>
  group_by(catalyst_age) |>
  summarise(mean_resid = mean(resid))
From +2.6 and +3.3 on a fresh charge down to −2.7 on its tenth run. Plotting residuals against a variable that’s not in the model is one of the best diagnostics there is: if they’re related to it, it belongs in the model.




Your turn. Compute the Durbin-Watson statistic by hand.









The denominator is the sum of the squared residuals, e^2. (diff(e) gives each residual minus the one before it.)


e <- study$resid
sum(diff(e)^2) / sum(e^2)
d = 1.53, below 2, which signals positive autocorrelation. lmtest::dwtest(fit) gives p = 0.004: strong evidence that the errors aren’t independent.

title: Checking model assumptions
section: Lack of fit: a test with replicates
text:
Lack of fit: a test with replicates
The calibration’s arch can be tested formally, thanks to its triplicates. The idea: the three readings at each concentration differ only by pure measurement error, since they have the same x. So the scatter within the triplicates estimates \sigma^2 without using any model at all. That’s called pure error. Whatever residual variation is left beyond pure error must come from the straight line missing the averages: lack of fit.
The test compares the straight line with a model that fits each concentration’s average exactly, by treating the concentration as a category. The line is nested in it (it’s the special case where the eight averages fall on a line), so anova() can compare them:

anova(fit_cal, lm(absorbance ~ factor(conc_mgL), data = calibration))
#> Analysis of Variance Table
#> 
#> Model 1: absorbance ~ conc_mgL
#> Model 2: absorbance ~ factor(conc_mgL)
#>   Res.Df        RSS Df Sum of Sq     F    Pr(>F)    
#> 1     22 0.00266578                                 
#> 2     16 0.00071282  6  0.001953 7.306 0.0006843 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The straight line’s SSE is 0.00267, and pure error accounts for only 0.00071 of it. The other 0.00195 is lack of fit: F = 7.3 on 6 and 16 degrees of freedom, p = 0.0007. The straight line is definitely the wrong shape, R^2 = 0.9989 notwithstanding. Analytical chemists, take note: a high R^2 is not a test of linearity. This is.
This test needs replicates, real repeated measurements at the same x. When you design a calibration or an experiment, include a few. They give you an estimate of \sigma that doesn’t trust the model.
Your turn. Run the lack-of-fit test.









Treat the concentration as a category: factor(conc_mgL).


saturated <- lm(absorbance ~ factor(conc_mgL), data = calibration)
anova(fit_cal, saturated)
F = 7.3, p = 0.0007: significant lack of fit. In Lesson 9, a curve will pass the same test.

title: Checking model assumptions
text:
When an assumption fails
Finding a problem is half the job. Here’s what usually fixes each one:








Problem
What you see
What to try




Curvature
an arch or a trend in the residuals against a predictor
add a curved term, like x^2, or transform x or y (Lesson 9)


Non-constant variance
a funnel
transform y, or use weighted least squares (Lesson 9)


Outliers
points far from the rest, in any plot
investigate them before anything else (Lesson 10)


Non-normality
a curved Q-Q plot
often a sign of outliers or a missing variable. Otherwise, with plenty of data, it matters little for the coefficients. Transform, or use robust methods


Dependence
patterns in time or groups
add the missing variable (here, the catalyst age), or use models for correlated data (Module 6)



Two more pieces of advice:

Plots first, tests second. With lots of data, formal tests flag deviations too small to matter. With little data, they miss big ones. Every test in this lesson was backed by a plot.
Fix one thing at a time. The problems interact: P066 inflated the non-normality, and it also distorted the arch. Deal with the outliers first, then look again.

title: Checking model assumptions
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · What does “good” look like? It’s easy to see patterns in pure noise. To calibrate your eye, compute the Durbin-Watson statistic for 120 independent random numbers.









Use the same formula as before, on z: sum(diff(z)^2) / sum(z^2).


set.seed(2026)
z <- rnorm(120)
sum(diff(z)^2) / sum(z^2)
2.2, close to 2, as independent errors should give. Try a few other seeds: you’ll see values from about 1.7 to 2.3. That’s the natural wobble, and it’s why 1.53, with the p-value to back it, counts as real evidence.




Challenge 2 · Fixing the independence problem. Add catalyst_age to the model, and recompute the Durbin-Watson statistic. How much yield does each run of catalyst age cost?









Add catalyst_age to the formula.


fit_age <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C * catalyst + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst_age, data = study)
e <- resid(fit_age)
c(age_coef = unname(coef(fit_age)["catalyst_age"]), dw = sum(diff(e)^2) / sum(e^2))
Each extra run on a charge costs 0.62 points of yield, so a charge’s tenth run makes about 5.5 points less than its first. And the Durbin-Watson statistic is back up to 1.93 (p = 0.32): the dependence is gone, because it was never in the errors at all. It was a missing variable. That’s a useful question to ask of any pattern in the residuals: what’s causing it, and did you measure it? (Whether replacing the catalyst more often is worth it is now a sum the plant can do.)

title: Checking model assumptions
text:
Quick quiz

1. The residuals against temperature form an arch: negative at both ends, positive in the middle. What does that suggest?

The errors aren’t normal
The relationship is curved, and the model needs a curved term
The variance isn’t constant


A systematic shape in the residuals against a predictor means the mean isn’t linear in that predictor.



2. The residuals fan out as the concentration grows. Which assumption fails, and what’s the consequence?

Normality, so the coefficients are biased
Equal variance, so the standard errors and prediction intervals are wrong
Independence, so the residuals don’t sum to zero


Least squares stays unbiased, but it weights the noisy points as heavily as the precise ones, and its standard errors assume one \sigma everywhere.



3. The Shapiro-Wilk test rejects normality, but the Q-Q plot shows two wild points and a straight line for everything else. What’s the best next step?

Investigate the two points
Transform the response straight away
Ignore it: normality never matters


The “non-normality” here is really two outliers. Without them, the residuals passed the test easily. Find out what happened in those runs.



4. The Durbin-Watson statistic is 1.53 for 120 residuals in time order. What does it suggest?

Negative autocorrelation
Positive autocorrelation: neighbouring residuals tend to be alike
Nothing: anything between 0 and 4 is fine


Independent errors give values close to 2, and positive autocorrelation pushes it towards 0. Here the p-value was 0.004.



5. What does a lack-of-fit test need?

At least 100 observations
Replicates: repeated observations at the same x
Normally distributed predictors


The replicates give an estimate of pure error that doesn’t depend on the model. Lack of fit is whatever the model’s residuals have beyond that.



6. The calibration line has R^2 = 0.9989 and fails the lack-of-fit test with p = 0.0007. How can both be true?

One of them must be miscalculated
R^2 measures how close the points are to the line, not whether the line is the right shape
A high R^2 makes the lack-of-fit test unreliable


With very precise measurements, even a small, systematic bend is detectable, and the line is close to the points everywhere anyway.

title: Checking model assumptions
text:
Wrap-up
You can now cross-examine a model’s residuals! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Residual plots are the main tool: against the fitted values, against each predictor, against variables not in the model, in a Q-Q plot, and in time order. A good model leaves a patternless band.
Linearity: an arch or trend against a predictor means a missing curve. Both models had one.
Equal variance: a funnel means the spread changes. Replicates show it directly. Breusch-Pagan and Bartlett test it.
Normality: check with a Q-Q plot of standardized residuals (rstandard()). Shapiro-Wilk tests it. Wild points matter more than mild skewness.
Independence: plot the residuals in time order. Durbin-Watson (\approx 2 when independent) and the lag-1 autocorrelation measure it. Here, a missing variable, the catalyst age, caused the dependence.
Lack of fit: with replicates, compare the model with one that fits each group’s mean, anova(fit, lm(y ~ factor(x))). R^2 is not a linearity test.
Two suspects: P047 (a stirrer trip, in the notes) and P066 (a temperature that doesn’t match its jacket). Lesson 10 takes the case.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download process_study.csv and calibration.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install the lmtest package.

The four standard plots. Run par(mfrow = c(2, 2)); plot(fit) for the process study model. Which plots show P066 and P047? What’s the “Residuals vs Leverage” plot? (Lesson 10 explains it.)
Formal tests. Run lmtest::bptest(fit), lmtest::dwtest(fit) and shapiro.test(resid(fit)), then repeat them without P047 and P066. Which results change?
Residuals against everything. Plot the residuals against every column of study that isn’t in the model: reactor, stir_rpm, ambient_C, operator_id, supplier, lot_id. Do any of them show a pattern? (Use boxplots for the categorical ones.)
A lineup. Simulate four sets of residuals from a correct model (rnorm(120)), plot them next to the real ones in a random order, and ask a friend which plot is the real one. If they can pick it out, the pattern is real. This trick has a name: the lineup protocol.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Residual plot

A plot of the residuals against the fitted values, a predictor, a variable not in the model, or the run order, used to look for patterns the model missed.

Loess smoother

A flexible curve, computed from local weighted averages, that follows trends in a scatterplot without assuming a shape.

Standardized residual

A residual divided by its estimated standard deviation, s\sqrt{1 - h_{ii}}, so that all residuals are on the same scale.

Heteroscedasticity

Non-constant error variance. The opposite is homoscedasticity.

Breusch-Pagan test

A test for non-constant variance that regresses the squared residuals on the predictors.

Autocorrelation

Correlation between errors that are close together in time (or space).

Durbin-Watson statistic

d = \sum (e_t - e_{t-1})^2 / \sum e_t^2, about 2 for independent errors and closer to 0 for positive autocorrelation.

Pure error and lack of fit

With replicates, the residual variation splits into the scatter within replicates (pure error) and the model’s failure to fit the group means (lack of fit).











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 501, Lesson 4: SLR Model Assumptions. Residual plots for each assumption, with many examples. (The lack-of-fit test is in Lesson 2, sections 2.8 to 2.10.)
NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, “How can I tell if a model fits my data?”. Engineering-flavored residual analysis, including lack of fit.
Hadley Wickham, Dianne Cook, Heike Hofmann and Andreas Buja, “Graphical inference for infovis”, IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2010). The paper behind the lineup protocol in the practice exercises.

title: Outliers and influence
text:
Module 2 · Lesson 10 of 15 Week 40 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Two runs have been following us around. P047 had a huge negative residual, and a note about a stirrer. P066 had an even bigger positive one, and a temperature that didn’t match its jacket. Lesson 7’s flatter slope for catalyst B vanished when Lesson 9 set P066 aside, and the curve in the yield only showed up clearly without it. This lesson opens the case properly: how do you find the points that matter, measure how much they matter, and decide what to do about them, fairly and on the record?
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Outliers and influence
text:
Three kinds of unusual
It’s easiest to see in two dimensions. Here’s the March batches’ yield against residence time, with one made-up batch added in each panel (in rose). The blue line is the fit without the extra batch, and the rose line the fit with it:

batches <- read_csv("data/batches.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
extras <- tibble(case = c("1. An outlier", "2. High leverage, on the line", "3. High leverage, off the line"),
                 residence_min = c(45, 100, 100), yield_pct = c(35, 94.6, 60))
lines <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(extras)), function(i) {
  with_extra <- bind_rows(select(batches, residence_min, yield_pct), extras[i, c("residence_min", "yield_pct")])
  b <- coef(lm(yield_pct ~ residence_min, data = with_extra))
  tibble(case = extras$case[i], intercept = b[1], slope = b[2])
}))
base <- coef(lm(yield_pct ~ residence_min, data = batches))
ggplot(batches, aes(x = residence_min, y = yield_pct)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, color = "grey55") +
  geom_abline(intercept = base[1], slope = base[2], color = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_abline(data = lines, aes(intercept = intercept, slope = slope), color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(data = extras, color = "#C2416C", size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ case) +
  labs(x = "Residence time (min)", y = "Yield (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)









An outlier is a point whose response is far from what the model predicts. The first extra batch has a typical residence time and a terrible yield. It drags the line down a little, but hardly tilts it: its slope stays at 0.67.
High leverage means unusual predictor values. The second batch ran for 100 minutes, far beyond the others, but its yield is exactly what the line predicts. It changes nothing, and it even makes the slope more precise.
An influential point is one whose removal would change the fit a lot. The third batch has high leverage and sits far off the line, so it pulls the slope from 0.67 down to 0.43 on its own.

Influence needs both ingredients: an unusual x gives a point the lever, and a large residual gives it a reason to pull. With many predictors you can’t see all this in one scatterplot, so you need numbers. The rest of this lesson computes them for the process study’s best model so far: last lesson’s curved interaction model, plus Lesson 8’s catalyst age. It’s fitted to all 120 runs, suspects included:

fit <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C * catalyst + I((temp_C - 185)^2) + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst_age,
          data = study)

title: Outliers and influence
Outliers and influence
text:
Outliers: studentized residuals
A raw residual is hard to judge on its own: is −11 big? Lesson 8’s standardized residuals divide each residual by its standard deviation, s\sqrt{1 - h_{ii}}. But there’s a catch. An outlier inflates s, and if it has high leverage, it also pulls the fit towards itself. Either way, it hides.
The cure is to judge each point by a model fitted without it. The studentized residual (also called the externally studentized, or deleted, residual) does exactly that:

t_i = \frac{e_i}{s_{(i)}\sqrt{1 - h_{ii}}},

where s_{(i)} is the residual standard error with observation i left out. If the model is right, t_i follows a t distribution with n - p - 1 degrees of freedom. rstudent() computes them all at once, without actually refitting 120 times (there’s a neat formula for it).

study |>
  mutate(t = rstudent(fit)) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(t))) |>
  select(run_id, temp_C, yield_pct, t) |>
  head(4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   run_id temp_C yield_pct     t
#>   <chr>   <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 P066     158.      64.6  8.68
#> 2 P047     183.      41.6 -4.36
#> 3 P040     185.      67.5  2.08
#> 4 P104     184       67.3  2.06

P066’s studentized residual is 8.7, and P047’s is −4.4. Everything else is within ±2.1. Are they significantly unusual? Be careful: you’re looking at the most extreme of 120 residuals, so a fair test must allow for picking the worst. The Bonferroni outlier test multiplies each two-sided p-value by n, the number of residuals you looked at. car::outlierTest(fit) does it for you, too.
Your turn. Compute P047’s Bonferroni-adjusted p-value.









Multiply by the number of residuals examined, nrow(study), which is 120.


t_47 <- rstudent(fit)[study$run_id == "P047"]
df <- nrow(study) - length(coef(fit)) - 1
p_one <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_47), df = df)
unname(min(1, nrow(study) * p_one))
0.0036: even allowing for having picked the most extreme residuals out of 120, P047 is a genuine outlier. P066’s adjusted p-value is 5 \times 10^{-12}. These two runs don’t belong to the same pattern as the others.

title: Outliers and influence
text:
Influence: Cook’s distance
Neither leverage nor residuals measure influence directly. Cook’s distance does: it measures how far all the fitted values move when observation i is left out, scaled by the model’s uncertainty. It also has a formula that shows the two ingredients multiplied together:

D_i = \frac{r_i^2}{p} \cdot \frac{h_{ii}}{1 - h_{ii}},

where r_i is the standardized residual. A big residual with tiny leverage has a small D_i, and so does a big leverage with a tiny residual. Two rough flags are common: D_i > 4/n deserves a look, and D_i > 1 means the point moves the fit about as much as the whole confidence region for the coefficients.

study |>
  mutate(cook = cooks.distance(fit)) |>
  arrange(desc(cook)) |>
  select(run_id, cook) |>
  head(4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   run_id   cook
#>   <chr>   <dbl>
#> 1 P066   2.82  
#> 2 P047   0.117 
#> 3 P019   0.0467
#> 4 P080   0.0427

P066’s Cook’s distance is 2.8. No other run comes close: P047 is next at 0.12, and every other run is below 0.05. P047 is a big outlier with ordinary leverage. P066 is a big outlier with a big lever, and that combination is what makes it dangerous.
Your turn. Check the formula for P066 by building its Cook’s distance from its standardized residual and its leverage.









The second factor is h_{ii}/(1 - h_{ii}).


i <- which(study$run_id == "P066")
r <- rstandard(fit)[i]
h <- hatvalues(fit)[i]
p <- length(coef(fit))
unname(r^2 / p * h / (1 - h))
2.82, the same as cooks.distance(fit). Its standardized residual, 6.7, squared and divided by p, gives 4.5, and its leverage factor, 0.39/0.61 = 0.63, scales that to 2.8.

title: Outliers and influence
section: Which coefficients move? DFFITS and DFBETAS
text:
Which coefficients move? DFFITS and DFBETAS
Cook’s distance says how much a point moves the fit. Two more measures say where:

DFFITS is the change in a point’s own fitted value when it’s left out, in standard errors. A common flag is |\text{DFFITS}| > 2\sqrt{p/n}.
DFBETAS is the change in each coefficient when the point is left out, in standard errors: one number per point per coefficient. A common flag is |\text{DFBETAS}| > 2/\sqrt{n}, here 0.18. Values above 1 mean the point alone moves a coefficient by more than its standard error.

DFBETAS answer the question that matters most: which conclusions depend on this point? dfbetas(fit) returns the whole matrix. Here’s P066’s row:

round(dfbetas(fit)[study$run_id == "P066", ], 2)
#>         (Intercept)              temp_C           catalystB           catalystC 
#>                0.89               -0.99                2.95                0.02 
#> I((temp_C - 185)^2)       residence_min      feed_water_ppm        catalyst_age 
#>                4.78                0.35               -0.53               -0.65 
#>    temp_C:catalystB    temp_C:catalystC 
#>               -2.87               -0.03

That’s the smoking gun. P066 moves the squared temperature term by 4.8 standard errors, and catalyst B’s main effect and its temperature interaction by about 3 each. With P066 in the data, the squared term in this model is barely distinguishable from zero (p = 0.07), and B looks less temperature-sensitive than A, as it did in Lesson 7. A catalyst B run, recorded at an impossibly low temperature with a perfectly normal yield, makes B look as if temperature hardly matters to it, and straightens the curve.
P047 is different: its biggest DFBETAS is −0.80, for the feed water. It was a wet Kestrel run that failed for another reason, the stirrer, so it exaggerates how much water hurts.
Your turn. Find the coefficient that P047 moves the most, using its row of DFBETAS.









Find the largest absolute value in row_47.


row_47 <- dfbetas(fit)[study$run_id == "P047", ]
row_47[which.max(abs(row_47))]
The feed water coefficient, by −0.80 standard errors: with P047 in the data, water looks a little more harmful than it is.

title: Outliers and influence
section: The verdict: what to do with unusual points
text:
The verdict: what to do with unusual points
Diagnostics find suspects. They don’t convict. Here’s a fair procedure:

Investigate. Check the records: the notes, the logbooks, the sensor data, the people. Is there a mistake, or a known cause?
Correct errors you can confirm, and record the correction and its evidence.
Exclude points with a known cause that puts them outside the question you’re asking. Record that too.
Keep everything else, however inconvenient. Never delete a point just because it doesn’t fit: that’s how real discoveries get thrown away.
When you can’t decide, report both fits, with and without the point, and say how much the conclusions change. Robust regression (below) is a good third opinion.

Now the evidence. P066. Its recorded temperature is 158.1 °C, but its jacket read 196.3 °C. In every other run, the reactor temperature can be predicted from the jacket temperature to within a couple of degrees, and for P066 that prediction is 185.3 °C. The reactor pressure, which also tracks the temperature, points the same way. And “185.1” with two digits swapped is “158.1”. The evidence for a typing error is overwhelming, so correct it to 185.1 °C, and write the correction in the cleaning log (Module 1, Lesson 11).
P047. The operators noted that its stirrer tripped twice. The study’s question is how the process behaves when it’s running properly, and a batch with a failed stirrer isn’t an example of that. So exclude it from the model, with that reason recorded. (If the question were “how often do batches fail, and what does it cost?”, P047 would be essential data.)
P115, the deliberate 95-minute trial? Unusual settings, but a studentized residual of 0.2 and a Cook’s distance of 0.001. It fits the model perfectly, and it’s the only evidence about long runs. Keep it.
Here’s what the decisions change:









Coefficient
All 120 runs
P066 corrected
P066 corrected, P047 excluded




squared temperature
−0.0038
−0.0115
−0.0126


temperature × catalyst B
−0.115

0.010

0.263

0.255


feed water
−0.0660
−0.0634
−0.0580

−0.602

residual standard error
3.02
