One wrong digit was hiding the curvature, faking an interaction, and inflating the residual standard error by 30%. The C interaction, which never depended on P066, barely moves. From now on, the module uses the cleaned study: P066 corrected and P047 excluded.
Your turn. Apply both decisions, refit the model, and look at the B interaction’s test.









The corrected temperature is 185.1.


clean <- study |>
  mutate(temp_C = if_else(run_id == "P066", 185.1, temp_C)) |>
  filter(run_id != "P047")
fit_clean <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C * catalyst + I((temp_C - 185)^2) + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst_age,
                data = clean)
summary(fit_clean)$coefficients["temp_C:catalystB", ]
An estimate of 0.010, with p = 0.80: catalysts A and B respond to temperature in the same way after all. Lesson 7’s “B is less temperature-sensitive” was P066 all along.

title: Outliers and influence
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · A robust third opinion. Robust regression fits the model in a way that gives less weight to points with big residuals, automatically. MASS::rlm() uses Huber weights: points with small residuals get full weight, and large ones get less and less. Fit it to the uncleaned data, and look at the weights it gave P066 and P047.









The other run is "P066".


fit_r <- MASS::rlm(yield_pct ~ temp_C * catalyst + I((temp_C - 185)^2) + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst_age,
                   data = study)
weights <- fit_r$w
weights[study$run_id %in% c("P047", "P066")]
0.19 for P047 and 0.10 for P066, while every other run got at least 0.47. Without being told anything, robust regression found the same two suspects, and its squared-temperature coefficient, −0.0107, lands close to the cleaned fit’s −0.0126. It’s a great cross-check. But it isn’t a substitute for investigating: it would have downweighted P066 forever without ever finding the typo, and it’s less effective against high-leverage points, which can pull the fit close enough to hide their residuals.




Challenge 2 · Everything at once. influence.measures(fit) computes the DFBETAS, DFFITS, covariance ratios, Cook’s distances and leverages for every run, and its $is.inf element marks which ones pass each flag. Which runs are flagged by at least one measure?









A run is flagged if any() of its measures is flagged: apply(inf$is.inf, 1, any).


inf <- influence.measures(fit)
flagged <- apply(inf$is.inf, 1, any)
study$run_id[flagged]
P047, P066 and P115. P115 is flagged by the covariance ratio, which measures how much a point changes the precision of the coefficients. P115’s ratio is 1.28, above 1: it makes the estimates more precise, because it’s the only long run. Flags are invitations to look, not verdicts. (influence.measures() uses stricter, size-adjusted cut-offs than the rules of thumb in this lesson, so it flags fewer runs.)

title: Outliers and influence
text:
Quick quiz

1. What gives an observation high leverage?

A large residual
Predictor values far from the rest of the data
A large response value


Leverage comes from the hat matrix, which depends on X alone.



2. A run with very high leverage sits exactly on the fitted line. Is it a problem?

Yes: high-leverage points should be removed
No: it agrees with the model, and it makes the estimates more precise
Only if its residual is negative


Influence needs both a long lever and a large residual. P115, the 95-minute trial, is a high-leverage point of this good kind.



3. Why do studentized residuals leave each point out of the estimate of s?

So that an outlier can’t hide by inflating the residual standard error, or by pulling the fit towards itself
To make the residuals sum to zero
To speed up the computation


Judging each point against a fit that doesn’t include it makes outliers stand out, and gives the residual an exact t distribution under the model.



4. Why multiply an outlier test’s p-value by n?

To make outliers easier to find
Because you picked the most extreme of n residuals, and some residual is always the biggest
Because the residuals aren’t normal


That’s the Bonferroni correction for looking at all n residuals. Without it, you’d “find” an outlier in almost every dataset.



5. A point’s DFBETAS for the squared temperature term is 4.8. What does it mean?

The point has a residual of 4.8
Leaving the point out moves that coefficient by 4.8 of its standard errors
The point’s leverage is 4.8 times the average


DFBETAS measure the change in each coefficient when a point is deleted, scaled by the coefficient’s standard error.



6. An influential point has no explanation in the records. What should you do?

Delete it, since it’s influential
Keep it and say nothing
Keep investigating, and report the fit with and without it


Without evidence of an error or a known cause, the point is data. Showing both fits lets readers see which conclusions depend on it.

title: Outliers and influence
text:
Wrap-up
Case closed! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Three kinds of unusual point: outliers (unusual y given x), high-leverage points (unusual x), and influential points (removing them changes the fit). Influence needs both a long lever and a large residual.
Leverage is h_{ii} (hatvalues()). It averages p/n. Flag values above 2p/n.
Studentized residuals (rstudent()) judge each point against a fit without it. Test the most extreme with a Bonferroni correction (car::outlierTest()).
Cook’s distance (cooks.distance()) combines the residual and the leverage: D_i = (r_i^2/p)\,h_{ii}/(1 - h_{ii}). Values above 1 are alarming.
DFFITS and DFBETAS (dffits(), dfbetas()) show how much a point moves its own prediction and each coefficient, in standard errors. influence.measures() computes everything.
The verdict: investigate, correct what you can confirm, exclude only with a known reason that puts a point outside the question, keep the rest, and record every decision. Report both fits when in doubt. Robust regression (MASS::rlm()) is a cross-check, not a replacement.
The process study’s verdict: P066’s temperature was a typo (185.1 °C, confirmed by the jacket and pressure), and it had hidden the curvature and faked a B interaction. P047, with its failed stirrer, is excluded. P115 stays.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download process_study.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install the car package if you haven’t yet.

The car package’s influence plots. Run car::influencePlot(fit): a bubble plot of studentized residuals against leverage, with bubbles sized by Cook’s distance. Then car::outlierTest(fit) and car::infIndexPlot(fit).
The fourth standard plot. plot(fit, which = 5) is “Residuals vs Leverage”, with contours of Cook’s distance. Find P066 on it.
Leave-one-out by brute force. For each run, refit the model without it, and store the squared-temperature coefficient. Plot the 120 values. Check that P066 is the one that changes it most, and that the change matches its DFBETAS times the standard error (roughly: DFBETAS uses s_{(i)}).
The project’s typos. The handover for the module project (R3 commissioning) was typed by hand too. When you get there, run this lesson’s diagnostics before you trust any model.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Outlier

An observation whose response is far from what the model predicts for its predictor values.

Leverage

An observation’s diagonal element of the hat matrix, h_{ii}, measuring how unusual its predictor values are.

Influential observation

An observation whose removal would change the fitted model substantially.

Studentized (deleted) residual

A residual divided by its standard error estimated without that observation, e_i / (s_{(i)}\sqrt{1 - h_{ii}}).

Bonferroni outlier test

A test of the most extreme studentized residual that multiplies its p-value by the number of residuals examined.

Cook’s distance

A measure of how much all the fitted values change when an observation is removed.

DFFITS and DFBETAS

The change in an observation’s own fitted value (DFFITS) and in each coefficient (DFBETAS) when it’s removed, in standard errors.

Robust regression

Fitting methods that downweight observations with large residuals, so that a few outliers can’t dominate the fit.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 501, Lesson 11: Influential Points. Leverage, studentized residuals, Cook’s distance, DFFITS and DFBETAS, with clear examples.
John Fox, Regression Diagnostics: An Introduction (Sage, 2nd edition, 2020). A short book by the author of the car package that covers this lesson and Lesson 8 in depth.
NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, “Detection of outliers”. Outlier tests from the engineering side, including why repeated testing needs care.

title: Model building and selection
text:
Module 2 · Lesson 12 of 15 Week 42 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Over the last seven lessons, you built a model for the process study one decision at a time: the water as a confounder, the catalyst and its interaction with temperature, a curve, the catalyst’s age, two runs dealt with. Each decision came from chemistry, a plot or a test. But the study recorded 19 columns. What if you’d simply thrown everything in? Or let the computer choose? This lesson is about choosing a model: the tools that help, and the traps that make it easy to fool yourself.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Model building and selection
text:
What is the model for?
Two very different goals lead to two different ways of choosing:

Explanation. You want to know how much each factor affects the yield: what does a degree, a minute or 100 ppm of water do? Then the model must include the confounders (Lesson 5), whether or not they’re “significant”, and it should be chosen with subject knowledge, ideally before looking at the data, so that its tests mean what they say.
Prediction. You want to predict the yield of next week’s batches as accurately as possible. Then any predictor that helps is welcome, and the test of a model is how well it predicts data it hasn’t seen.

Most real projects need some of both. A sensible strategy goes like this: start from what the science says should matter, build a model with those variables, check it with the diagnostics of Lessons 8 to 11, and use the tools of this lesson to compare a few serious candidates. Automatic searches can suggest candidates, but they’re no substitute for thinking.
In this lesson, the candidates are:

the small model: temperature, residence time and water, from Lesson 5;
the chemist’s model: the model you built through Lessons 7 to 10, with the curved temperature effect, the catalyst and its interaction with temperature, the residence time, the water and the catalyst age;
the kitchen sink: the chemist’s model plus every other predictor in the study, including the reactor, stirrer speed, outdoor temperature, operator, jacket temperature, pressure and feed rate.


study <- read_csv("data/process_study.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(temp_C = if_else(run_id == "P066", 185.1, temp_C)) |>
  filter(run_id != "P047") |>
  mutate(tc = temp_C - 185)
fit_small <- lm(yield_pct ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm, data = study)
fit_chem <- lm(yield_pct ~ tc * catalyst + I(tc^2) + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst_age, data = study)
fit_sink <- lm(yield_pct ~ tc * catalyst + I(tc^2) + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst_age +
                 reactor + stir_rpm + ambient_C + operator_id + jacket_C + pressure_bar + feed_rate_Lmin,
               data = study)

The temperature is centered at 185 °C, as usual, in the column tc.

title: Model building and selection
text:
More terms always fit better
Lesson 5 showed that R^2 can only go up when you add a predictor. Push that idea further: replace the curved temperature term in the chemist’s model with polynomials of higher and higher degree, from a straight line up to an 8th-degree polynomial. On the data used to fit them, they get better and better. But how well do they predict runs they haven’t seen? The rose line below answers that with cross-validation, which you’ll meet properly later in this lesson:

set.seed(2026)
folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(study)))
cv_rmse <- function(formula) {
  pred <- numeric(nrow(study))
  for (f in 1:10) pred[folds == f] <- predict(lm(formula, data = study[folds != f, ]), study[folds == f, ])
  sqrt(mean((study$yield_pct - pred)^2))
}
degrees <- 1:8
errors <- bind_rows(lapply(degrees, function(d) {
  f <- as.formula(paste0("yield_pct ~ poly(tc, ", d, ", raw = TRUE) + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst + catalyst_age"))
  tibble(degree = d, `fitted runs` = sqrt(mean(resid(lm(f, data = study))^2)), `new runs (cross-validated)` = cv_rmse(f))
}))
errors |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-degree, names_to = "error on", values_to = "rmse") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = degree, y = rmse, color = `error on`)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("fitted runs" = "#2a78d6", "new runs (cross-validated)" = "#C2416C")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = degrees) +
  labs(x = "Degree of the temperature polynomial", y = "Prediction error (RMSE, points)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The error on the fitted runs (blue) keeps falling, from 2.8 points for a straight line to 2.2 for degree 8. The error on new runs (rose) falls from degree 1 to degree 2, then rises. Beyond degree 2, the extra terms aren’t learning about the process. They’re learning the noise in these particular 119 runs, which won’t repeat. That’s overfitting.
It’s a trade-off between two kinds of error. A model that’s too simple is biased: it misses real structure, like the straight line missing the curve. A model that’s too complex has high variance: its coefficients chase noise, so they’d come out differently with different data. The best predictions come from the right balance between the two.










Your turn. Compare the R^2 of the degree-2 and degree-8 polynomial models.









The second model uses a polynomial of degree 8.


fit2 <- lm(yield_pct ~ poly(tc, 2, raw = TRUE) + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst + catalyst_age, data = study)
fit8 <- lm(yield_pct ~ poly(tc, 8, raw = TRUE) + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst + catalyst_age, data = study)
c(degree2 = summary(fit2)$r.squared, degree8 = summary(fit8)$r.squared)
0.929 against 0.934. The six extra terms “explain” a little more of these runs, and predict new runs worse. R^2 can’t tell you when to stop.

title: Model building and selection
text:
Criteria that charge for complexity
Several criteria balance fit against complexity. Each combines the SSE with a penalty for the number of coefficients, p:









Criterion
Formula (up to a constant)
Prefer
Penalty per coefficient




adjusted R^2
1 - \frac{\text{SSE}/(n-p)}{\text{SST}/(n-1)}
larger
mild


AIC, Akaike’s information criterion
n \ln(\text{SSE}/n) + 2p
smaller
2


BIC, the Bayesian information criterion
n \ln(\text{SSE}/n) + p \ln n
smaller
\ln n, about 4.8 here


Mallows’ C_p
\text{SSE}_p / \hat\sigma^2_{\text{full}} - n + 2p
smaller, and close to p
2



The n\ln(\text{SSE}/n) part rewards fit, and the second part punishes size. AIC aims at the model that predicts best. BIC charges more per coefficient (whenever n > 7), so it picks smaller models, and with enough data it tends to find the true model if it’s among the candidates. C_p compares each model’s SSE with the error variance estimated from the biggest model: a model that leaves out nothing important has C_p \approx p, and one that misses something has C_p much bigger than p. All four penalize with the same ingredients, so they often agree.
The absolute values of AIC and BIC mean nothing: only differences between models fitted to the same data matter. A difference of 2 or less is small, and more than 10 is decisive. R’s AIC() and BIC() compute them from the log-likelihood, which adds a constant but gives the same differences.

tibble(model = c("small", "chemist's", "kitchen sink"),
       coefficients = sapply(list(fit_small, fit_chem, fit_sink), function(m) length(coef(m))),
       r2 = sapply(list(fit_small, fit_chem, fit_sink), function(m) summary(m)$r.squared),
       adj_r2 = sapply(list(fit_small, fit_chem, fit_sink), function(m) summary(m)$adj.r.squared),
       AIC = sapply(list(fit_small, fit_chem, fit_sink), AIC),
       BIC = sapply(list(fit_small, fit_chem, fit_sink), BIC))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   model        coefficients    r2 adj_r2   AIC   BIC
#>   <chr>               <int> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 small                   4 0.799  0.794  672.  686.
#> 2 chemist's              10 0.954  0.950  510.  540.
#> 3 kitchen sink           21 0.956  0.948  524.  585.

The kitchen sink has the highest R^2, as it must. But every criterion that charges for complexity prefers the chemist’s model: higher adjusted R^2, an AIC 14 lower, and a BIC 45 lower. The 11 extra coefficients don’t earn their keep.
Your turn. Compute the AIC and BIC of the chemist’s model and the kitchen sink.









BIC(fit_sink).


c(AIC_chem = AIC(fit_chem), AIC_sink = AIC(fit_sink),
  BIC_chem = BIC(fit_chem), BIC_sink = BIC(fit_sink))
AIC: 509.7 against 523.9. BIC: 540.3 against 585.0. Both favor the chemist’s model, BIC more strongly, because it charges more for each of the sink’s extra coefficients.




Your turn. Compute Mallows’ C_p for the chemist’s model, using the kitchen sink to estimate \sigma^2.









The penalty is 2p: 2 * p.


sigma2_full <- deviance(fit_sink) / df.residual(fit_sink)
n <- nrow(study)
p <- length(coef(fit_chem))
deviance(fit_chem) / sigma2_full - n + 2 * p
C_p = 5.7 with p = 10: below p, so the chemist’s model has left out nothing that the kitchen sink captures. The small model’s C_p is 341, with p = 4: it’s missing a lot.

title: Model building and selection
text:
Best-subset selection
With criteria in hand, you could let the computer search. Best-subset selection fits every combination of candidate columns, and reports the best model of each size. With k candidates there are 2^k subsets, which sounds hopeless, but the leaps package uses a clever “branch and bound” search that avoids fitting most of them. Here, the kitchen sink’s 20 columns (more than a million subsets) take a fraction of a second:

X <- model.matrix(fit_sink)[, -1]
subsets <- leaps::regsubsets(x = X, y = study$yield_pct, nvmax = ncol(X))
s <- summary(subsets)
ggplot(tibble(size = seq_along(s$bic), bic = s$bic), aes(x = size, y = bic)) +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "#C2416C") +
  labs(x = "Number of columns (besides the intercept)", y = "BIC of the best model of that size") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








BIC drops steeply up to 8 columns, and then rises slowly: every extra column costs more than it gains. regsubsets() works with columns, not variables, so it can choose some dummies of a factor and not others. That’s both a strength and a weakness: it found a model with only C’s temperature interaction, not B’s, which fits what Lesson 10 discovered, but it would just as happily keep one operator’s dummy and drop the rest, which would make no sense.
Your turn. Which 8 columns does the best model of size 8 use?









s$which has one row per model size. Pick the row of the best one: best.


X <- model.matrix(fit_sink)[, -1]
subsets <- leaps::regsubsets(x = X, y = study$yield_pct, nvmax = ncol(X))
s <- summary(subsets)
best <- which.min(s$bic)
names(which(s$which[best, -1]))
The temperature and its square, the two catalyst dummies, C’s temperature interaction, the residence time, the water and the catalyst age: the chemist’s model, minus B’s (non-existent) interaction. None of the seven extra variables made it. C_p picks the same 8 columns.

title: Model building and selection
text:
Stepwise selection
Stepwise selection is a greedier search. Backward elimination starts from the biggest model and repeatedly drops the term whose removal improves the criterion most, until no removal helps. Forward selection starts from nothing and adds terms one at a time. R’s step() does either (or both), using AIC by default, and it works with whole terms: a factor’s dummies go in or out together, and it never drops a main effect while its interaction is still in the model.

step(fit_sink, trace = 0)
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = yield_pct ~ tc + catalyst + I(tc^2) + residence_min + 
#>     feed_water_ppm + catalyst_age + tc:catalyst, data = study)
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>    (Intercept)              tc       catalystB       catalystC         I(tc^2)  
#>      59.054152        0.557778        3.144974       -1.719019       -0.012647  
#>  residence_min  feed_water_ppm    catalyst_age    tc:catalystB    tc:catalystC  
#>       0.342829       -0.058007       -0.569067        0.009974        0.254990

Starting from the kitchen sink, backward elimination lands on exactly the chemist’s model. With k = log(nrow(study)), step() uses BIC instead, and here it lands on the same model. Forward selection from an empty model gets there too.
That’s reassuring, but don’t read too much into it. This dataset was generated from a model like this one, its signal is strong, and the junk variables really are junk. With weaker signals and more correlated candidates, stepwise searches often disagree with one another, depend on the starting point, and change their minds with small changes in the data. Try it: on bootstrap resamples of these same runs, backward elimination keeps the operator in about two out of three, purely by chance.
Your turn. Run backward elimination from the kitchen sink, and list the terms it keeps.









Start from the biggest model, fit_sink.


chosen <- step(fit_sink, trace = 0)
attr(terms(chosen), "term.labels")
The chemist’s terms, and nothing else. (trace = 0 hides the long printout of every step. Try trace = 1 to watch it work.)

title: Model building and selection
text:
Cross-validation
The most direct test of a model meant for prediction is to predict. If you had new data, you’d fit the model to the old data and measure its errors on the new. Cross-validation fakes new data from the data you have:

Split the runs at random into k groups, called folds, usually 5 or 10.
Hold out one fold, fit the model to the others, and predict the held-out runs.
Repeat for every fold, so that each run is predicted exactly once by a model that never saw it.
Summarize the prediction errors, often by their root mean square (RMSE).

The model with the smallest cross-validated error predicts best. It’s an honest estimate because no run helps predict itself. Unlike AIC and BIC, it doesn’t rest on the model’s assumptions, and it works for any prediction method at all, which is why Module 7 uses it everywhere.
For our three models, 10-fold cross-validation gives prediction errors of 4.04 points for the small model, 2.05 for the chemist’s model, and 2.23 for the kitchen sink. The sink fits its own runs better than the chemist’s model does, and predicts new runs worse. With 37 coefficients (adding every two-way interaction), the error on new runs climbs to 2.67.
Your turn. Write the cross-validation loop for the chemist’s model. The folds are already assigned.









Predict the held-out fold, test.


set.seed(2026)
folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(study)))
pred <- numeric(nrow(study))
for (f in 1:10) {
  train <- study[folds != f, ]
  test <- study[folds == f, ]
  model <- lm(yield_pct ~ tc * catalyst + I(tc^2) + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst_age, data = train)
  pred[folds == f] <- predict(model, newdata = test)
}
sqrt(mean((study$yield_pct - pred)^2))
2.05 points. The same model’s error on the runs it was fitted to is 1.88: a little optimistic, as fitted errors always are. The cross-validated number is the one to quote for “how well will this predict next month’s batches?”.

title: Model building and selection
text:
Selection and honesty
Selection has a hidden cost. The p-values, confidence intervals and R^2 of a selected model are too optimistic, because the same data chose the model and then tested it. A predictor that made it through selection did so partly because, in this sample, it happened to look good. Its “p = 0.01” was earned in a contest that it was always going to win.
You’ll see this vividly in the second challenge, where selection on pure noise produces “significant” predictors. Some habits that keep you honest:

Pre-specify the model for the main question, from the science, before looking at the outcome. Test that model.
Use selection to explore, and say that you did, and how.
Judge prediction models by cross-validation, or better, on genuinely new data.
Check stability: does the chosen model survive bootstrap resamples, or different criteria?
Don’t drop confounders because they aren’t significant: a confounder’s job is to remove bias from other coefficients.

title: Model building and selection
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Choosing the degree by cross-validation. Compute the cross-validated RMSE of the polynomial models of degree 1 to 6, and find the best degree.









which.min(errors) gives the degree with the smallest error.


set.seed(2026)
folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(study)))
cv_rmse <- function(formula) {
  pred <- numeric(nrow(study))
  for (f in 1:10) pred[folds == f] <- predict(lm(formula, data = study[folds != f, ]), study[folds == f, ])
  sqrt(mean((study$yield_pct - pred)^2))
}
errors <- sapply(1:6, function(d) {
  cv_rmse(as.formula(paste0("yield_pct ~ poly(tc, ", d, ", raw = TRUE) + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst + catalyst_age")))
})
round(errors, 3)
which.min(errors)
Degree 2, with an error of 2.53 points, against 2.99 for a straight line and 2.55 to 2.63 for degrees 3 to 6. Cross-validation, AIC and BIC all agree with the residual plot from Lesson 8: a single bend.




Challenge 2 · Selecting from noise. Make a dataset where nothing is related to anything: a random response and 20 random predictors. Let backward elimination choose a model, and look at the p-values of the predictors it keeps.









Count the kept predictors with p_values below 0.05.


set.seed(2030)
noise <- as.data.frame(matrix(rnorm(119 * 20), nrow = 119))
noise$y <- rnorm(119)
chosen <- step(lm(y ~ ., data = noise), trace = 0)
p_values <- summary(chosen)$coefficients[-1, "Pr(>|t|)"]
round(p_values, 4)
sum(p_values < 0.05)
Selection kept 3 of the 20 noise columns, and 2 of them have p-values below 0.05. The selected model’s overall F-test even gives p = 0.001. Every one of those numbers is a fiction: there’s nothing in these data at all. Selection found the luckiest columns, and then the tests congratulated it. That’s why p-values from a selected model can’t be read at face value.

title: Model building and selection
text:
Quick quiz

1. As you add terms to a model, what happens to the error on the data it was fitted to?

It keeps falling, or stays the same
It falls, then rises
It rises


The fitted error can only go down, which is why it can’t be used to choose the size of a model. The error on new data falls, then rises.



2. What is overfitting?

Using too few predictors
A model that fits the noise in its data, so that it predicts new data worse than a simpler model would
A model with a very high R^2, which is always bad


An overfitted model has learned the quirks of one sample. Its high R^2 is real, but useless for prediction.



3. Two models have AICs of 509.7 and 523.9. Which is preferred?

The one with an AIC of 509.7
The one with an AIC of 523.9
You can’t tell without the p-values


Smaller is better, for both AIC and BIC. A difference of 14 is decisive.



4. Why does BIC tend to choose smaller models than AIC?

It uses the residuals differently
It charges \ln n per coefficient instead of 2, which is more whenever n > 7
It ignores the intercept


With 119 runs, BIC charges 4.8 per coefficient, more than twice AIC’s 2.



5. What makes cross-validation an honest estimate of prediction error?

It uses more data than the usual fit
Each observation is predicted by a model fitted without it
It assumes the errors are normal


No observation helps predict itself, so the errors are like errors on new data.



6. You let stepwise selection choose a model, and a predictor it kept has p = 0.01. How should you read that p-value?

At face value: the predictor is significant at the 1% level
As too optimistic, because the same data chose the predictor and then tested it
As too pessimistic


Selection keeps the predictors that look best in this sample. Their p-values don’t account for the search, as the noise challenge showed.

title: Model building and selection
text:
Wrap-up
You can now choose a model without fooling yourself! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Purpose first: a model for explanation should be chosen with subject knowledge and include the confounders. A model for prediction should be judged by how well it predicts new data.
Overfitting: more terms always fit the data better, but beyond a point they fit the noise, and predict worse. It’s a trade-off between bias and variance.
Criteria: adjusted R^2 (larger is better), AIC and BIC (smaller is better, BIC stricter), and Mallows’ C_p (smaller, and close to p) all trade fit against size.
Searches: leaps::regsubsets() finds the best subset of each size, and step() adds or drops whole terms by AIC (or BIC, with k = log(n)). Both are tools for suggesting candidates.
Cross-validation estimates prediction error by predicting each fold from the others. The chemist’s model predicted best: 2.05 points, against 2.23 for the kitchen sink.
Honesty: p-values after selection are too optimistic. Pre-specify the main model, report how you chose, check stability, and keep the confounders.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download process_study.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and apply Lesson 10’s cleaning.

Stepwise, every way. Run step() backward from the kitchen sink, forward from lm(yield_pct ~ 1) with scope = formula(fit_sink), and in both directions. Repeat with k = log(nrow(study)). Do they all agree?
Instability. Write a loop that draws 50 bootstrap resamples of the runs and runs backward elimination on each. Count how often each term is kept. Which junk variables sneak in most often?
Leave-one-out. For linear models, leave-one-out cross-validation has a shortcut: the prediction error for run i is e_i/(1 - h_{ii}). Compute sqrt(mean((resid(fit_chem) / (1 - hatvalues(fit_chem)))^2)) and compare it with the 10-fold result.
The purity model. Build a model for purity_pct the same way: start from the chemistry (which variables should affect purity?), check the diagnostics, and compare a few candidates by AIC, BIC and cross-validation.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Overfitting

Fitting the noise in a sample as well as the signal, so that the model predicts new data worse than a simpler one.

Bias-variance trade-off

Simple models err by missing structure (bias), and complex ones by chasing noise (variance). The best predictions balance the two.

AIC (Akaike’s information criterion)

n\ln(\text{SSE}/n) + 2p up to a constant. Smaller is better. It aims at the best predictive model.

BIC (Bayesian information criterion)

n\ln(\text{SSE}/n) + p\ln n up to a constant. Smaller is better. It charges more per coefficient than AIC.

Mallows’ C_p

\text{SSE}_p/\hat\sigma^2_{\text{full}} - n + 2p. A model that misses nothing important has C_p \approx p.

Best-subset selection

Comparing the best model of every size, found by an exhaustive (or branch-and-bound) search.

Stepwise selection

Adding (forward) or removing (backward) terms one at a time, guided by a criterion such as AIC.

Cross-validation

Estimating prediction error by repeatedly fitting the model to part of the data and predicting the rest.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 501, Lesson 10: Model Building. The model-building process, stepwise regression and best-subset selection, with the criteria.
Gareth James, Daniela Witten, Trevor Hastie and Robert Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning, chapters 5 and 6. Cross-validation, subset selection and their modern alternatives. The book is free online, and Module 7 uses it.
Frank Harrell, Regression Modeling Strategies (Springer, 2nd edition), chapter 4. A forceful case against stepwise selection, and what to do instead.

title: Multifactor ANOVA
text:
Module 2 · Lesson 14 of 15 Week 44 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The screening experiment found a winner: F2 beat the standard catalyst by about 6 points at 185 °C. The obvious next question for a process engineer: does that hold at other temperatures? Lesson 7 showed that catalysts can respond to heat differently. So the team ran a follow-up experiment with two factors at once, the catalyst and the temperature, and it ran into a classic complication along the way: the feed came from three different lots. This lesson analyzes it.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Multifactor ANOVA
text:
The follow-up experiment
The design crosses two factors: the catalyst at two levels (standard and F2) and the temperature at three (175, 185 and 195 °C). That gives 2 \times 3 = 6 treatment combinations, and the experiment ran every one of them: a full factorial design.
The feed came from three lots, L1 to L3, and the team knew that lots can differ. So each lot was used for a complete set of the six combinations, twice, in a random order within the lot. That’s 3 \times 6 \times 2 = 36 runs, and the lots are blocks: groups of runs that are alike, within which every treatment appears.

factorial <- read_csv("data/factorial.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(catalyst = factor(catalyst, levels = c("standard", "F2")),
         temp = factor(temp_C), lot = factor(lot))
head(factorial)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>     run lot   catalyst temp_C feed_water_ppm yield_pct temp 
#>   <dbl> <fct> <fct>     <dbl>          <dbl>     <dbl> <fct>
#> 1     1 L1    standard    195            200      66.2 195  
#> 2     2 L1    F2          185            211      67.9 185  
#> 3     3 L1    F2          185            213      67.4 185  
#> 4     4 L1    standard    175            209      58.4 175  
#> 5     5 L1    F2          175            212      59.3 175  
#> 6     6 L1    F2          195            208      72.5 195

The temperature goes into the model as a factor, temp, rather than a number. With only three levels, a factor makes no assumption about the shape of the temperature effect: it gets one mean for each level.
Why not vary one factor at a time, the way many engineers are taught? Compare the catalysts at 185 °C, then try the temperatures with the better catalyst? That one-factor-at-a-time approach has two problems. It’s wasteful: in a factorial, every run tells you about both factors, so each comparison uses all 36 runs. And it’s blind to interactions: if F2’s advantage depends on the temperature, you can’t find out by testing the catalysts at only one temperature.

title: Multifactor ANOVA
text:
Main effects and interactions
Start with the mean yield of each of the six combinations, the cell means:

factorial |>
  group_by(catalyst, temp) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(yield_pct), .groups = "drop") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = temp, values_from = mean_yield)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   catalyst `175` `185` `195`
#>   <fct>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 standard  57.4  61.0  63.9
#> 2 F2        60.0  65.6  71.7

An interaction plot draws them, with one line per catalyst:

cell_means <- factorial |> group_by(catalyst, temp) |> summarise(yield_pct = mean(yield_pct), .groups = "drop")
ggplot(factorial, aes(x = temp, y = yield_pct, color = catalyst, group = catalyst)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.06, height = 0, seed = 1), alpha = 0.45, size = 1.8) +
  geom_line(data = cell_means, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = cell_means, size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(standard = "#2a78d6", F2 = "#C2416C")) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Yield (%)", color = "Catalyst") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The two factors each have a main effect: averaged over the temperatures, F2 beats the standard (65.8% against 60.8%), and averaged over the catalysts, hotter is better. But the lines aren’t parallel. F2’s advantage grows with the temperature: 2.7 points at 175 °C, 4.5 at 185 °C and 7.9 at 195 °C. That’s an interaction: the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other. In an interaction plot, parallel lines mean no interaction, and lines that diverge, converge or cross mean an interaction.
The model behind a two-way ANOVA writes each run’s yield as

y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk},

where \alpha_i is catalyst i’s main effect, \beta_j temperature j’s, and (\alpha\beta)_{ij} the interaction: whatever’s special about that particular combination. It’s Lesson 7’s dummy variables and interaction columns again, with both predictors categorical.










Your turn. What’s the mean yield of F2 at 195 °C? Compute all six cell means.









Group by both factors: catalyst and temp.


factorial |>
  group_by(catalyst, temp) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(yield_pct), .groups = "drop")
71.7% for F2 at 195 °C, the best of the six combinations, against 63.9% for the standard catalyst at the same temperature.

title: Multifactor ANOVA
text:
The two-way ANOVA
aov() fits the model, and catalyst * temp means both main effects and their interaction, as in Lesson 7:

summary(aov(yield_pct ~ catalyst * temp, data = factorial))
#>               Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
#> catalyst       1  226.0  226.00  31.174 4.49e-06 ***
#> temp           2  495.1  247.53  34.144 1.86e-08 ***
#> catalyst:temp  2   41.6   20.79   2.868   0.0725 .  
#> Residuals     30  217.5    7.25                     
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Each factor gets its own F-test, and so does the interaction. Both main effects are clear. The interaction, the most interesting part for the plant, has F = 2.9 and p = 0.072: suggestive, but not convincing at the usual 5% level. Should the engineers conclude that F2’s advantage is the same at every temperature?
Not yet. Look at the residual mean square, 7.2, so the run-to-run standard deviation is \sqrt{7.2} = 2.7 points. In the screening experiment, with a single feed lot, it was 2.3. Something extra is adding noise.
Your turn. Fit the two-way ANOVA, and pull out the interaction’s p-value.









The second factor is temp.


fit_2way <- aov(yield_pct ~ catalyst * temp, data = factorial)
summary(fit_2way)[[1]]["catalyst:temp", "Pr(>F)"]
p = 0.072. (The [[1]] is needed because summary() of an aov returns a list of tables, one per error stratum. Here there’s only one.)

title: Multifactor ANOVA
text:
Blocking
The something extra is the feed lots. Their mean yields differ by up to 5 points: 64.3% for L1, 60.3% for L2 and 65.2% for L3. In the two-way ANOVA, those lot-to-lot differences are part of the residuals, so they inflate the noise against which every effect is judged.
Because each lot contains every treatment combination equally often, the lot differences can be taken out by adding the lot to the model as a block:

summary(aov(yield_pct ~ lot + catalyst * temp, data = factorial))
#>               Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
#> lot            2  167.4   83.72   46.83 1.17e-09 ***
#> catalyst       1  226.0  226.00  126.43 6.81e-12 ***
#> temp           2  495.1  247.53  138.47 3.03e-15 ***
#> catalyst:temp  2   41.6   20.79   11.63  0.00021 ***
#> Residuals     28   50.1    1.79                     
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The lots soak up 167 units of the residual sum of squares, and the residual mean square drops from 7.2 to 1.8, so the run-to-run noise halves, from 2.7 to 1.3 points. Every F statistic grows, and the interaction is now unmistakable: F = 11.6, p = 0.0002. The catalyst and temperature effects didn’t change at all (look at their sums of squares, 226 and 495 in both tables), because the design is balanced: each lot saw every combination equally often, so the lots are uncorrelated with the treatments. Only the noise changed.
This is a randomized complete block design: complete because every block gets every treatment, and randomized because the order is random within each block. The motto of experimental design sums it up: block what you can, randomize what you can’t. You can’t block on things you don’t know about, so randomization protects you against those, as in Lesson 13. But when you know a nuisance factor will matter, like the feed lot, the day, the reactor or the analyst, building it into the design as a block removes its noise completely.
The lot is a nuisance, not a question, so nobody needs its F-test. It’s in the model to clean up the residuals.
Your turn. Fit the blocked model, and find the interaction’s p-value and the residual mean square.









Put the block, lot, first.


fit_block <- aov(yield_pct ~ lot + catalyst * temp, data = factorial)
tab <- summary(fit_block)[[1]]
c(p_interaction = tab["catalyst:temp", "Pr(>F)"], residual_ms = tab["Residuals", "Mean Sq"])
p = 0.0002 and a residual mean square of 1.79. The interaction was there all along. The lots’ noise was hiding it.

title: Multifactor ANOVA
text:
Reading the interaction
When the interaction is real, the main effects don’t tell the whole story: “F2 is 5 points better” is an average over temperatures that hides how the advantage changes. Report the simple effects instead: the effect of one factor at each level of the other. Here, F2’s advantage at each temperature is the difference of two cell means, each the average of 6 runs, so its standard error is \sqrt{\text{MSE}\,(1/6 + 1/6)} = 0.77 points, using the blocked model’s MSE.



Temperature
F2’s advantage
95% interval




175 °C
2.7 points
1.1 to 4.2


185 °C
4.5 points
3.0 to 6.1


195 °C
7.9 points
6.3 to 9.4



F2 is better at every temperature, and much better when hot. For the plant, the conclusion is concrete: switch to F2, and run it hot, since that’s where it shines. (Before going above 195 °C, though, remember Lesson 9’s warning about extrapolating curves, and check the purity, which falls with temperature.)
Your turn. Compute F2’s advantage over the standard at each temperature.









Subtract the standard catalyst’s row, "standard".


m <- tapply(factorial$yield_pct, list(factorial$catalyst, factorial$temp), mean)
m["F2", ] - m["standard", ]
2.65, 4.53 and 7.85 points at 175, 185 and 195 °C.

title: Multifactor ANOVA
text:
Unbalanced data
Real experiments lose runs. Suppose four samples had been lost (runs 3, 11, 20 and 28), leaving the cells with 4 to 6 runs each instead of 6. The design is now unbalanced, and the factors are no longer uncorrelated with each other. That brings back Lesson 6’s problem: sequential (Type I) sums of squares depend on the order of the terms.

unbalanced <- filter(factorial, !run %in% c(3, 11, 20, 28))
anova(lm(yield_pct ~ lot + catalyst * temp, data = unbalanced))
#> Analysis of Variance Table
#> 
#> Response: yield_pct
#>               Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
#> lot            2  81.42  40.709  21.831 3.966e-06 ***
#> catalyst       1 127.78 127.776  68.523 1.716e-08 ***
#> temp           2 426.32 213.160 114.312 5.406e-13 ***
#> catalyst:temp  2  44.51  22.254  11.934 0.0002523 ***
#> Residuals     24  44.75   1.865                      
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
anova(lm(yield_pct ~ lot + temp * catalyst, data = unbalanced))
#> Analysis of Variance Table
#> 
#> Response: yield_pct
#>               Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
#> lot            2  81.42  40.709  21.831 3.966e-06 ***
#> temp           2 359.76 179.878  96.463 3.363e-12 ***
#> catalyst       1 194.34 194.341 104.219 3.278e-10 ***
#> temp:catalyst  2  44.51  22.254  11.934 0.0002523 ***
#> Residuals     24  44.75   1.865                      
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The catalyst’s sum of squares is 128 when it comes before the temperature, and 194 after it. Same data, same model, different answer. Three types of sums of squares deal with this differently:

Type I (sequential): each term after the ones listed before it. Order-dependent. Use only when the order means something.
Type II: each main effect after the other main effects, but not after its own interactions. That’s the natural test of a main effect when there’s no interaction. car::Anova(fit, type = 2).
Type III: each term after all the others, interactions included. It needs sum-to-zero contrasts (Lesson 7) to make sense, and it tests main effects averaged equally over the levels of the other factor. car::Anova(fit, type = 3), after setting contrasts = list(catalyst = "contr.sum", temp = "contr.sum").

All three give the same test for the interaction, the last term. And that’s the practical advice: test the interaction first. If it’s real, as here, the main-effect tests aren’t very meaningful whatever their type, and the simple effects or cell means are what to report. If it isn’t, Type II tests of the main effects are the usual choice. Statisticians argue a lot about Type II against Type III. Knowing that the argument exists, and what each type tests, puts you ahead of most software users.
Your turn. Find the catalyst’s sequential sum of squares in both orders.









In the second model, the temperature comes before the catalyst: temp * catalyst.


unbalanced <- filter(factorial, !run %in% c(3, 11, 20, 28))
first <- anova(lm(yield_pct ~ lot + catalyst * temp, data = unbalanced))
second <- anova(lm(yield_pct ~ lot + temp * catalyst, data = unbalanced))
c(catalyst_first = first["catalyst", "Sum Sq"], catalyst_after_temp = second["catalyst", "Sum Sq"])
128 and 194. Three of the four lost runs were F2 runs, two of them at 195 °C, so in the unbalanced data the catalyst is tangled up with the temperature, and the credit depends on who goes first. In the full, balanced data, both orders give 226.

title: Multifactor ANOVA
text:
ANCOVA: adjusting for a covariate
Why did the lots differ? The lab measured the water content of the feed for every run, and the lots were very different: about 207 ppm for L1, 265 for L2 and 180 for L3. Water lowers the yield (Lesson 5). So instead of a block for each lot, you could adjust for the measured water directly. A model with categorical factors plus a numerical covariate is called an analysis of covariance, or ANCOVA:

fit_ancova <- lm(yield_pct ~ feed_water_ppm + catalyst * temp, data = factorial)
summary(fit_ancova)$coefficients
#>                      Estimate  Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
#> (Intercept)        70.0130339 1.534579597 45.623592 1.482362e-28
#> feed_water_ppm     -0.0583358 0.006563582 -8.887799 8.921316e-10
#> catalystF2          2.5041605 0.819492571  3.055745 4.782757e-03
#> temp185             3.5749975 0.819354564  4.363187 1.480943e-04
#> temp195             6.6583407 0.819564852  8.124239 5.857099e-09
#> catalystF2:temp185  2.3889103 1.160100631  2.059227 4.855169e-02
#> catalystF2:temp195  5.1027737 1.158756795  4.403662 1.324658e-04
car::Anova(fit_ancova, type = 2)
#> Anova Table (Type II tests)
#> 
#> Response: yield_pct
#>                Sum Sq Df  F value    Pr(>F)    
#> feed_water_ppm 159.08  1  78.9930 8.921e-10 ***
#> catalyst       225.12  1 111.7827 1.838e-11 ***
#> temp           508.89  2 126.3455 4.820e-15 ***
#> catalyst:temp   39.10  2   9.7088 0.0005919 ***
#> Residuals       58.40 29                       
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Each ppm of water costs 0.058 points of yield, very close to the process study’s estimate, and the interaction is clear (p = 0.0006). The residual standard deviation is 1.42 points, almost as small as with the lot blocks (1.34). The water explains nearly all of the lot-to-lot variation.
ANCOVA is regression with both factors and numerical predictors, so everything from Lessons 5 to 12 applies. Two things to know:

Its assumption is that the covariate has the same slope in every group (no covariate × treatment interaction). Check it by adding feed_water_ppm:catalyst and testing it.
It gives adjusted means: the predicted mean of each treatment at the same value of the covariate, usually its average. When the covariate differs between groups, comparing adjusted means is fairer than comparing raw means.

Blocking and ANCOVA are two ways of removing the same nuisance. Blocking needs nothing measured, and removes everything that differs between blocks. ANCOVA needs a measurement, and removes only what that measurement explains, but it works even when the covariate varies within blocks, and it can be used after the fact.
Your turn. Fit the ANCOVA, and find the water coefficient.









The covariate is feed_water_ppm.


fit_ancova <- lm(yield_pct ~ feed_water_ppm + catalyst * temp, data = factorial)
coef(fit_ancova)["feed_water_ppm"]
−0.058 points per ppm. L2’s feed, about 58 ppm wetter than L1’s, costs about 3.4 points: most of the 4-point gap between their mean yields.

title: Multifactor ANOVA
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Is the lot just its water? If the water explains the lot differences completely, adding the water to the blocked model should add nothing. Test it with a partial F-test.









Add feed_water_ppm to the blocked model.


blocked <- lm(yield_pct ~ lot + catalyst * temp, data = factorial)
both <- lm(yield_pct ~ lot + feed_water_ppm + catalyst * temp, data = factorial)
anova(blocked, both)
p = 0.92: once the lots are in the model, the water adds nothing. The run-to-run variation in water within a lot is small, so all the water’s information is already in the lot differences. Blocks and covariate tell the same story, which is reassuring: it means we know why the lots differed.




Challenge 2 · Adjusted means. Use the ANCOVA to predict the mean yield of each of the six combinations at the average water content of all 36 runs. These are the adjusted means. Which combination is best?









The average water content is mean(factorial$feed_water_ppm).


fit_ancova <- lm(yield_pct ~ feed_water_ppm + catalyst * temp, data = factorial)
grid <- expand.grid(catalyst = levels(factorial$catalyst), temp = levels(factorial$temp),
                    feed_water_ppm = mean(factorial$feed_water_ppm))
grid$adjusted_mean <- predict(fit_ancova, newdata = grid)
grid
At the average water content of 217 ppm, F2 at 195 °C is best, at 71.6%, and the standard catalyst at 175 °C is worst, at 57.3%. Here they’re almost identical to the raw cell means, because the design is balanced over the lots, so every combination saw the same mix of water. The adjustment matters most when the covariate differs between treatments.

title: Multifactor ANOVA
text:
Quick quiz

1. What’s the main advantage of a factorial design over varying one factor at a time?

It needs no randomization
Every run informs every factor, and it can reveal interactions
It always needs fewer factor levels


One-factor-at-a-time experiments use their runs less efficiently, and they can’t see whether one factor’s effect depends on another.



2. In an interaction plot, the lines for the two catalysts are parallel. What does that mean?

The catalysts have the same yield
There’s no interaction: the catalyst’s effect is the same at every temperature
The temperature has no effect


Parallel lines mean a constant gap between the catalysts. Non-parallel lines mean an interaction.



3. Adding the lots as blocks made the interaction significant. Why?

Blocks change the treatment means
The lot-to-lot differences were inflating the residual variance, and the blocks removed them
Blocking always makes effects significant


The effects’ sums of squares were the same in both analyses. Only the noise they were compared with shrank, from a mean square of 7.2 to 1.8.



4. “Block what you can, randomize what you can’t.” What does it mean?

Build known nuisance factors into the design as blocks, and use randomization to protect against the unknown ones
Randomize the blocks instead of the treatments
Only randomize when blocking is impossible


Blocking removes the noise from nuisance factors you know about. Randomization stops the ones you don’t know about from lining up with the treatments.



5. In unbalanced data, which sums of squares depend on the order of the terms in the model?

Type I (sequential)
Type II
Type III


Type I gives each term credit only for what the terms before it didn’t explain. Types II and III don’t depend on the order.



6. What does ANCOVA assume about the covariate?

That it’s categorical
That its slope is the same in every treatment group
That it’s unrelated to the response


The basic ANCOVA fits parallel lines, one per group. If the slopes differ, the covariate interacts with the treatment, and the adjusted differences depend on the covariate’s value.

title: Multifactor ANOVA
text:
Wrap-up
You can now design and analyze real multifactor experiments! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Factorial designs run every combination of the factors’ levels. They’re more efficient than one-factor-at-a-time, and they reveal interactions.
Main effects and interactions: the two-way model is \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij}. aov(y ~ A * B) tests each part. Interaction plots show non-parallel lines when the factors interact.
Blocking groups similar runs, like those from the same feed lot, and gives every block every treatment. It removes nuisance variation from the residuals: here it cut the noise in half and revealed the interaction (p = 0.072 became p = 0.0002).
When there’s an interaction, report the simple effects: F2’s advantage grew from 2.7 points at 175 °C to 7.9 at 195 °C.
Unbalanced data make Type I sums of squares order-dependent. Test the interaction first, use Type II for main effects without an interaction, and know what Type III tests.
ANCOVA adds a numerical covariate to a factorial model. Here, the feed water explained the lot differences. It assumes parallel slopes, and it gives adjusted means.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download factorial.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install the emmeans package if you haven’t yet.

Simple effects with emmeans. Fit fit <- lm(yield_pct ~ lot + catalyst * temp, data = factorial), then run emmeans::emmeans(fit, pairwise ~ catalyst | temp) for F2’s advantage at each temperature, with standard errors and tests. Compare them with the table in this lesson.
Temperature as a number. Refit with temp_C as a numerical predictor instead of the factor, with and without a squared term. Does a straight line in temperature fit as well as the factor? (Test it: the straight-line model is nested in the factor model.)
Base R’s interaction plot. Try with(factorial, interaction.plot(temp, catalyst, yield_pct)).
Plan your own. Design a 2 \times 2 \times 2 factorial for three factors you’d like to test in a lab (say, temperature, catalyst and stirring speed), with two replicates. Use expand.grid() to list the runs and sample() to randomize them. How many runs is it, and which interactions could you estimate?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Factor and level

In an experiment, a variable you set (a factor), and the values you set it to (its levels).

Full factorial design

An experiment that runs every combination of the factors’ levels.

Main effect

The effect of one factor, averaged over the levels of the other factors.

Interaction

When the effect of one factor depends on the level of another.

Interaction plot

A plot of the cell means against one factor, with a line for each level of another. Non-parallel lines suggest an interaction.

Block

A group of similar runs, such as those using the same feed lot, within which the treatments are compared.

Randomized complete block design

A design in which every block receives every treatment, in a random order within the block.

Simple effect

The effect of one factor at a fixed level of another.

Type I, II and III sums of squares

Sequential tests (order-dependent), tests of each main effect after the other main effects, and tests of each term after all the others.

Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA)

A model with categorical factors and a numerical covariate, used to compare treatments after adjusting for the covariate.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 502, Lesson 5: Multi-Factor ANOVA and Lesson 7: Randomization Design Part I. Factorial designs and interactions, then completely randomized and randomized complete block designs. Its Lessons 9 and 10 cover ANCOVA.
NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, “Process improvement”. The whole chapter on designed experiments for engineers, from full factorials to response surfaces.
Douglas Montgomery, Design and Analysis of Experiments (Wiley), chapters 4 and 5. Blocking and factorial designs, with many chemical-engineering examples.

title: Multivariate data and matrix algebra
text:
Module 3 · Lesson 1 of 13 Week 47 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The customer’s specification for our product doesn’t have one number on it. It has four: the purity, the water content, the color and the acid value. Every batch gets all four measured, and a batch is only good if all four are good. So far in this course, we’ve analyzed one response at a time. This module is about analyzing several together, which answers questions that one-at-a-time analyses get wrong: is this batch unusual as a whole? Is the product on target on all four properties at once? Which properties really tell two suppliers apart?
The first step is the language: vectors and matrices, which you met in Lessons 0.14 and 2.4. This lesson puts them to work describing multivariate data.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Multivariate data and matrix algebra
text:
Four properties per batch
The data are last quarter’s 80 batches from the full-scale plant. For each batch, they record a few process conditions, and the four properties on the customer’s specification sheet:

quality <- read_csv("data/batch_quality.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(quality)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 9
#>   batch_id temp_C residence_min feed_water_ppm catalyst purity_pct water_ppm
#>   <chr>     <dbl>         <dbl>          <dbl> <chr>         <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 FS01       181.          36.4            321 B              99.0       205
#> 2 FS02       191.          48.2            196 B              99.2       122
#> 3 FS03       176.          62.8            275 A              99.3       133
#> 4 FS04       179.          62.5            329 B              99.1       176
#> 5 FS05       175.          52.3            190 A              99.6       133
#> 6 FS06       184.          52.1            207 B              99.2       118
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: color_apha <dbl>, acid_mgKOH <dbl>








Column
What it is




purity_pct
the product’s purity, %


water_ppm
its water content, ppm


color_apha
its color on the APHA (Hazen) scale: 0 is water-white, and higher is yellower


acid_mgKOH
its acid value: mg of potassium hydroxide needed to neutralize the acid in 1 g



The process columns (temp_C, residence_min, feed_water_ppm and catalyst) will matter in Lessons 11 and 12. For now, take the four properties. Arranged with one row per batch and one column per property, they form the data matrix:

X = \begin{pmatrix} x_{11} & x_{12} & \cdots & x_{1p} \\ x_{21} & x_{22} & \cdots & x_{2p} \\ \vdots & & & \vdots \\ x_{n1} & x_{n2} & \cdots & x_{np} \end{pmatrix},
\qquad n = 80 \text{ batches}, \quad p = 4 \text{ variables.}

Row i, written \mathbf{x}_i, is batch i’s observation vector: four numbers that belong together. Here’s every pair of variables at once:

Y <- as.matrix(quality[, c("purity_pct", "water_ppm", "color_apha", "acid_mgKOH")])
pairs(Y, pch = 19, cex = 0.8, col = adjustcolor("#C2416C", 0.65), gap = 0.4,
      labels = c("Purity (%)", "Water (ppm)", "Color (APHA)", "Acid (mg KOH/g)"))








The properties aren’t independent of each other. Purer batches are paler and less acidic. Wetter batches are more acidic, because water hydrolyzes the product into acid. Those relationships are part of the data, and multivariate methods use them.

title: Multivariate data and matrix algebra
text:
The mean vector
The mean vector collects the four means:

\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \begin{pmatrix} \bar{x}_1 \\ \vdots \\ \bar{x}_p \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{n} X^\top \mathbf{1},

where \mathbf{1} is a column of n ones: multiplying by it adds up each column. It’s the “center of the cloud” in four-dimensional space.










Your turn. The matrix Y holds the four properties. Compute the mean vector.









colMeans() averages each column of a matrix.


colMeans(Y)
The average batch is 99.17% pure, with 131 ppm of water, a color of 15.4 APHA and an acid value of 0.210 mg KOH/g.

title: Multivariate data and matrix algebra
text:
Covariance and correlation matrices
The covariance matrix collects every variance and covariance:

S = \frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}})(\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}})^\top = \frac{1}{n - 1}\, X_c^\top X_c ,

where X_c is the centered data matrix (Lesson 0.14). It’s p \times p and symmetric: the variance of variable j is on the diagonal at s_{jj}, and the covariance of variables j and k is at s_{jk} (and s_{kj}).

S <- cov(Y)
S
#>              purity_pct   water_ppm   color_apha    acid_mgKOH
#> purity_pct  0.134454035  -1.5689636  -1.15469225 -0.0072952690
#> water_ppm  -1.568963608 816.2897152 -21.41466772  0.5053313291
#> color_apha -1.154692247 -21.4146677  17.92753006  0.0540924367
#> acid_mgKOH -0.007295269   0.5053313   0.05409244  0.0009221259

Covariances are hard to read, because each one carries the units of two variables: the covariance of purity and water is in “%·ppm”. The correlation matrix removes the units. Divide each covariance by the two standard deviations, r_{jk} = s_{jk}/\sqrt{s_{jj}s_{kk}}. In matrix form, with D the diagonal matrix of the variances,

R = D^{-1/2}\, S\, D^{-1/2} .

D^{-1/2} is diagonal with entries 1/s_j, so multiplying on the left scales the rows and multiplying on the right scales the columns.

round(cor(Y), 2)
#>            purity_pct water_ppm color_apha acid_mgKOH
#> purity_pct       1.00     -0.15      -0.74      -0.66
#> water_ppm       -0.15      1.00      -0.18       0.58
#> color_apha      -0.74     -0.18       1.00       0.42
#> acid_mgKOH      -0.66      0.58       0.42       1.00

The strongest relationships: purity with color (r = -0.74) and with acid (-0.66), and water with acid (0.58).
Your turn. Compute the correlation matrix from S with the matrix formula, and check that it matches cor(Y).









Multiply by D_half_inv on both sides.


D_half_inv <- diag(1 / sqrt(diag(S)))
R_mine <- D_half_inv %*% S %*% D_half_inv
max(abs(R_mine - cor(Y)))
The largest difference is around 10^{-16}: the same matrix, up to rounding. (cov2cor(S) does the same in one step.)

title: Multivariate data and matrix algebra
text:
Linear combinations
Many useful quantities are weighted sums of the variables. For instance, the customer’s contract caps the total impurity, in percent: everything that isn’t product, which is 100 - \text{purity} plus the water converted from ppm to percent:

\text{total impurity} = 100 - x_1 + 0.0001\,x_2 .

Apart from the constant, that’s \mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x} with \mathbf{a} = (-1, 0.0001, 0, 0). Any linear combination has a simple mean and variance:

\text{mean of } \mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a}^\top \bar{\mathbf{x}}, \qquad
\text{variance of } \mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a}^\top S\, \mathbf{a} = \sum_j \sum_k a_j a_k s_{jk} .

The variance formula includes every covariance, not just the variances, and that’s where correlated variables matter: the variance of a sum of positively correlated variables is bigger than the sum of their variances. The covariance between two combinations, \mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x} and \mathbf{b}^\top\mathbf{x}, is \mathbf{a}^\top S\,\mathbf{b}. These two formulas run through the whole module.






NoteGo deeper: why the variance is \mathbf{a}^\top S \mathbf{a}





For one observation, \mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{a}^\top\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{a}^\top(\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}}). Squaring a number is multiplying it by itself, and since a number equals its own transpose,

\left(\mathbf{a}^\top(\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}})\right)^2 = \mathbf{a}^\top(\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}})(\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}})^\top\mathbf{a} .

Add these up over the observations and divide by n - 1: the middle part becomes S. The same steps give \mathbf{a}^\top S\,\mathbf{b} for a covariance. And since a variance can’t be negative, \mathbf{a}^\top S\,\mathbf{a} \ge 0 for every \mathbf{a}: a covariance matrix is always positive semi-definite. When no combination of the variables is constant, it’s strictly positive, and S is positive definite, which is what lets us invert it.



Your turn. Compute the variance of the total impurity with the formula \mathbf{a}^\top S\,\mathbf{a}.









The same vector goes on both sides: t(a) %*% S %*% a.


a <- c(-1, 0.0001, 0, 0)
t(a) %*% S %*% a
0.1348, a standard deviation of 0.37 percentage points. Check it with var(100 - Y[, 1] + 0.0001 * Y[, 2]). Almost all of it is the purity’s own variance (0.1345): the water term is tiny in percent. But not quite all: purity and water are negatively correlated, and \mathbf{a} gives them opposite signs, so their covariance adds a little to the variance.




Your turn. The color isn’t part of the total impurity, but the two are related. Compute their covariance with \mathbf{a}^\top S\,\mathbf{b}, where \mathbf{b} picks out the color.









The color is the third variable, so \mathbf{b} = (0, 0, 1, 0).


a <- c(-1, 0.0001, 0, 0)
b <- c(0, 0, 1, 0)
t(a) %*% S %*% b
1.15: batches with more impurity tend to be yellower, which makes sense, since both come from the same side reactions.

title: Multivariate data and matrix algebra
text:
Total and generalized variance
Sometimes you want a single number for the spread of the whole cloud. There are two common ones:

The total variance is the sum of the variances, the trace of S: \text{tr}(S) = \sum_j s_{jj}. Here it’s 834, and 816 of that is the water’s, simply because water is measured in ppm, where numbers are big. The total variance depends completely on the units, so it only makes sense when the variables share them.
The generalized variance is the determinant, |S|. It measures the volume of the cloud, and it accounts for the correlations: strongly correlated variables squash the cloud into a thinner shape, with less volume. On the correlation scale, |R| runs from 1 (all the variables uncorrelated) to 0 (some variable is a perfect combination of the others, the perfect collinearity of Lesson 2.11).

For two variables, |R| = 1 - r^2, so it’s a direct measure of how much the pair overlaps. For all four properties, |R| = 0.11: the four measurements carry a lot of shared information.
Your turn. Compute |R| for all four properties, and for water and acid alone.









Pick the same rows and columns: R[c(2, 4), c(2, 4)].


c(all_four = det(R), water_acid = det(R[c(2, 4), c(2, 4)]))
0.111 for all four, and 0.661 for water and acid, which is exactly 1 - 0.582^2.

title: Multivariate data and matrix algebra
text:
Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
Lesson 0.14 showed that the eigenvectors of a correlation matrix point along the directions in which the data spread out, and that the eigenvalues are the variances in those directions. Every covariance or correlation matrix can be rebuilt from them, by the spectral decomposition:

R = P \Lambda P^\top = \sum_{j=1}^{p} \lambda_j\, \mathbf{e}_j \mathbf{e}_j^\top ,

where the columns of P are the eigenvectors \mathbf{e}_j (each of length 1, and at right angles to the others) and \Lambda is the diagonal matrix of the eigenvalues. The eigenvalues are never negative, and they add up to the total variance: for R, that’s p = 4.

e <- eigen(cor(Y))
e$values
#> [1] 2.3044267 1.3117847 0.1946988 0.1890898
round(e$vectors, 2)
#>       [,1]  [,2]  [,3]  [,4]
#> [1,]  0.60  0.21  0.64 -0.43
#> [2,] -0.26  0.77 -0.33 -0.48
#> [3,] -0.49 -0.52  0.17 -0.68
#> [4,] -0.58  0.31  0.67  0.35


tibble(property = rep(c("purity", "water", "color", "acid"), 2),
       direction = rep(c("1st eigenvector (λ = 2.30)", "2nd eigenvector (λ = 1.31)"), each = 4),
       weight = c(e$vectors[, 1], e$vectors[, 2])) |>
  mutate(property = factor(property, levels = c("purity", "water", "color", "acid"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = property, y = weight, fill = weight > 0)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#2a78d6", `FALSE` = "#C2416C")) +
  facet_wrap(~ direction) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Weight") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The two biggest eigenvalues, 2.30 and 1.31, account for (2.30 + 1.31)/4 = 90\% of the total variance. So the four properties really vary along about two directions, and each one has a chemical meaning:

The first contrasts purity (positive) with color and acid (negative): batches are either pure, pale and low in acid, or impure, yellow and acidic. That’s the signature of thermal degradation, which makes colored, acidic by-products.
The second is mostly water, with acid going the same way and color the opposite way: wetter batches are more acidic, and paler. That’s hydrolysis (water makes acid), mixed with the residence time: short runs leave the product wetter, but give it less time to darken.

The last two eigenvalues are small, about 0.19 each. Very little happens in those directions: for example, the four properties hardly ever all rise together. (The signs of an eigenvector are arbitrary: -\mathbf{e} is just as good an eigenvector as \mathbf{e}, so read the pattern of the signs, not the signs themselves.) Using these directions as new variables is called principal components analysis, which Module 7 covers.
Why the correlation matrix and not S? Do it with S, and the first eigenvector is almost pure water, with 98% of the “variance”: the ppm units drown everything else out. As with the total variance, when the variables have different units, standardize first.
Your turn. What fraction of the total variance does each eigenvalue of R account for?









The eigenvalues of a correlation matrix add up to the number of variables, sum(ev), which is 4.


ev <- eigen(R)$values
ev / sum(ev)
58%, 33%, 5% and 5%. Two directions carry 90% of the variation.

title: Multivariate data and matrix algebra
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Units change the total variance. Convert the water from ppm to percent (divide by 10,000), and recompute the total variance of the four properties. What happens?









Compute the covariance matrix of the converted data, cov(Y_pct).


Y_pct <- Y
Y_pct[, "water_ppm"] <- Y_pct[, "water_ppm"] / 10000
c(ppm = sum(diag(cov(Y))), percent = sum(diag(cov(Y_pct))))
From 834 down to 18. The data didn’t change, only the units, and now the color dominates instead of the water. Any summary that adds up variances across variables, including the eigen-analysis of S, inherits this. The correlation matrix doesn’t: it’s the same in any units.




Challenge 2 · An inverse from eigenvalues. The spectral decomposition makes functions of a matrix easy: R^{-1} = P \Lambda^{-1} P^\top, because inverting \Lambda just inverts each eigenvalue. Build R^{-1} that way, and compare it with solve(R). (Next lesson’s Mahalanobis distance uses the inverse of a covariance matrix.)









Invert the eigenvalues, e$values.


e <- eigen(R)
P <- e$vectors
R_inv <- P %*% diag(1 / e$values) %*% t(P)
max(abs(R_inv - solve(R)))
A difference of about 10^{-15}: the same matrix. Notice what this says about small eigenvalues: 1/\lambda is large when \lambda is small, so the inverse greatly magnifies the directions in which the data hardly vary. Keep that in mind for the next lesson.

title: Multivariate data and matrix algebra
text:
Quick quiz

1. In a data matrix with 80 batches and 4 properties, what is a row?

One property, measured on every batch
One batch’s observation vector: its four measurements
A mean vector


Rows are units (batches), and columns are variables (properties).



2. What’s on the diagonal of a covariance matrix?

The variances of the variables
The correlations of each variable with itself, which are all 1
The means


The diagonal of S holds the variances, and the off-diagonal entries hold the covariances. A correlation matrix has 1s on its diagonal.



3. What’s the variance of the linear combination \mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x}?

\mathbf{a}^\top\bar{\mathbf{x}}
\sum_j a_j s_{jj}
\mathbf{a}^\top S\,\mathbf{a}, which includes every covariance


\mathbf{a}^\top S\,\mathbf{a} = \sum_j\sum_k a_j a_k s_{jk}. Ignoring the covariances is only right when the variables are uncorrelated.



4. Why is the total variance \text{tr}(S) a poor summary for the four properties?

Because it ignores the means
Because it depends on the units: the water, in ppm, dominates it
Because it can be negative


Changing the water from ppm to percent cut it from 834 to 18. Standardize first, or use the correlation matrix.



5. For two variables, the determinant of their correlation matrix is 1 - r^2. What does |R| = 0 mean?

The variables are independent
One variable is a perfect linear function of the other
Both variables are constant


A determinant of zero means the matrix has no inverse: perfect collinearity, as in Lesson 2.11.



6. The first eigenvector of R has weights +0.60, -0.26, -0.49, -0.58 for purity, water, color and acid. What does it describe?

Batches that are high in everything
A trade-off between purity and color and acid: batches are either pure, pale and low in acid, or the opposite
The water content alone


Purity goes one way, and color and acid the other. It’s the direction of thermal degradation, and it carries 58% of the variance.

title: Multivariate data and matrix algebra
text:
Wrap-up
You can now describe multivariate data in the language of matrices! Here’s what you’ve learned:

The data matrix X has one row per unit (an observation vector) and one column per variable.
The mean vector \bar{\mathbf{x}} (colMeans()) is the center of the cloud.
The covariance matrix S (cov()) holds the variances and covariances. The correlation matrix R = D^{-1/2} S D^{-1/2} (cor(), cov2cor()) removes the units.
Linear combinations: \mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x} has mean \mathbf{a}^\top\bar{\mathbf{x}} and variance \mathbf{a}^\top S\,\mathbf{a}, and two combinations have covariance \mathbf{a}^\top S\,\mathbf{b}.
Total variance \text{tr}(S) depends on the units. Generalized variance |S| measures the cloud’s volume, and |R| runs from 1 (uncorrelated) to 0 (redundant).
Eigen-decomposition: R = P\Lambda P^\top. The eigenvectors are the directions of spread, and the eigenvalues the variances along them. For the four properties, two directions, thermal degradation and hydrolysis, carry 90% of the variance.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download batch_quality.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

A nicer scatterplot matrix. Install the GGally package and run GGally::ggpairs(quality, columns = c("purity_pct", "water_ppm", "color_apha", "acid_mgKOH")). It shows the scatterplots, the correlations and each variable’s distribution at once.
Covariance by hand. Compute S from the formula X_c^\top X_c/(n - 1), with scale(Y, scale = FALSE) for X_c, and check it against cov(Y).
Mixing units. Convert the purity to an impurity in ppm, 10^4 \times (100 - \text{purity}), and redo the eigen-analysis of S. Which variable dominates now? What about the eigen-analysis of R?
The two directions as scores. Compute each batch’s coordinates along the first two eigenvectors of R: scale(Y) %*% e$vectors[, 1:2]. Plot them against each other. Which batches are the most degraded, and which are the wettest?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Data matrix

An n \times p array with one row per unit and one column per variable.

Observation vector

One unit’s measurements on all p variables: a row of the data matrix.

Mean vector

The vector of the p variables’ means.

Covariance matrix

The p \times p matrix of variances (on the diagonal) and covariances (off the diagonal).

Correlation matrix

The covariance matrix of the standardized variables, with 1s on the diagonal.

Linear combination

A weighted sum of the variables, \mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x}, with mean \mathbf{a}^\top\bar{\mathbf{x}} and variance \mathbf{a}^\top S\mathbf{a}.

Total and generalized variance

The trace \text{tr}(S), the sum of the variances, and the determinant |S|, a measure of the volume of the data cloud.

Positive definite

A matrix S with \mathbf{a}^\top S\mathbf{a} > 0 for every non-zero \mathbf{a}, like any covariance matrix in which no combination of the variables is constant.

Spectral decomposition

Writing a symmetric matrix as P\Lambda P^\top, from its eigenvectors and eigenvalues.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 505, Lesson 1: Measures of Central Tendency, Dispersion and Association and Lesson 2: Linear Combinations of Random Variables. The same ideas, with clear worked examples.
Richard Johnson and Dean Wichern, Applied Multivariate Statistical Analysis (6th edition), chapters 1 to 3. The standard textbook for this course. Chapter 2 is a compact review of the matrix algebra.
Essence of Linear Algebra (3Blue1Brown videos), “Eigenvectors and eigenvalues”. The geometry of eigenvectors, beautifully animated.

title: The multivariate normal distribution
text:
Module 3 · Lesson 3 of 13 Week 49 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The normal distribution is the foundation of the t-tests, intervals and regressions of Modules 0 to 2. Its multivariate version plays the same role for this module: Hotelling’s T^2, MANOVA and discriminant analysis are all built on it. This lesson introduces the multivariate normal distribution, shows the properties that make it so convenient, and, just as important, shows how to check whether your data are anywhere near it.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: The multivariate normal distribution
text:
The density
A random vector \mathbf{X} with p components has a multivariate normal distribution, N_p(\boldsymbol\mu, \Sigma), when its density is

f(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{p/2}\,|\Sigma|^{1/2}} \exp\!\left( -\tfrac12 (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol\mu) \right).

Compare it with the one-variable normal density, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12 (x - \mu)^2/\sigma^2\right). Everything has its matrix counterpart: the squared z-score becomes the squared Mahalanobis distance, and \sigma becomes |\Sigma|^{1/2}, the square root of the generalized variance. The distribution is completely described by two things, the mean vector \boldsymbol\mu and the covariance matrix \Sigma (Greek letters, because these are the true, population values).
The density depends on \mathbf{x} only through its Mahalanobis distance from \boldsymbol\mu. So all the points at the same distance have the same density: the contours of the hill are exactly last lesson’s ellipses. Here’s the bivariate normal fitted to the batches’ water and acid:

W <- Y[, c("water_ppm", "acid_mgKOH")]
mu <- colMeans(W)
Sigma <- cov(W)
grid <- expand.grid(water_ppm = seq(60, 230, length.out = 120), acid_mgKOH = seq(0.12, 0.31, length.out = 120))
