grid$density <- mvtnorm::dmvnorm(as.matrix(grid), mean = mu, sigma = Sigma)
ggplot(grid, aes(x = water_ppm, y = acid_mgKOH)) +
  geom_contour_filled(aes(z = density), bins = 8, alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = as.data.frame(W), shape = 21, fill = "white", color = "#3A1F35", size = 1.6, stroke = 0.4) +
  geom_point(data = as.data.frame(W)["FS73", ], shape = 21, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "#3A1F35", size = 2.6) +
  annotate("text", x = W["FS73", 1], y = W["FS73", 2], label = "FS73", vjust = -1, size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colorRampPalette(c("#FDF2F6", "#F4C0D1", "#C2416C", "#5c1a33"))(8), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Water (ppm)", y = "Acid (mg KOH/g)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The darkest region is the peak, at the mean vector, and the density falls off in elliptical rings. FS73 sits out in the pale area at the top left, at 84 ppm and 0.261 mg KOH/g.










Your turn. Compute the fitted bivariate normal density at FS73’s water and acid, from the formula. Compare it with mvtnorm::dmvnorm().









The quadratic form is \mathbf{d}^\top \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{d}, so the last factor is d again. With p = 2, (2\pi)^{-p/2} = (2\pi)^{-1}.


mu <- colMeans(W)
Sigma <- cov(W)
d <- W["FS73", ] - mu
by_hand <- (2 * pi)^(-1) * det(Sigma)^(-1/2) * exp(-0.5 * t(d) %*% solve(Sigma) %*% d)
c(by_hand = as.numeric(by_hand), mvtnorm = mvtnorm::dmvnorm(W["FS73", ], mean = mu, sigma = Sigma))
Both give 0.00029, against 0.226 at the peak: 0.13% of the peak height, which is e^{-13.3/2}, from FS73’s squared distance of 13.3. (The density’s units are “per ppm per mg KOH/g”, so its size on its own means little. Ratios like this one do.)

title: The multivariate normal distribution
text:
What makes it so convenient
If \mathbf{X} \sim N_p(\boldsymbol\mu, \Sigma), then:

Every linear combination is normal: \mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{X} \sim N(\mathbf{a}^\top\boldsymbol\mu,\ \mathbf{a}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{a}). That’s Lesson 1’s mean and variance formulas, and the shape is normal too. (In fact, it works the other way round as well: if every linear combination is normal, the vector is multivariate normal.)
Every subset of the variables is multivariate normal, with the corresponding parts of \boldsymbol\mu and \Sigma. In particular, each variable on its own is normal.
Zero correlation means independence. For most distributions, uncorrelated variables can still depend on each other in curved ways (remember cor(x, x^2) from Lesson 0.7). For multivariate normal variables, a zero covariance means they’re completely independent.
Squared Mahalanobis distances are chi-square: (\mathbf{X} - \boldsymbol\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{X} - \boldsymbol\mu) \sim \chi^2_p. That’s last lesson’s yardstick, and it’s exact when \boldsymbol\mu and \Sigma are known.
Slices are normal too, and they’re the next step.

The converse of property 2 is not true, and it’s a classic trap: every variable can be normal on its own while the vector isn’t multivariate normal. Checking the variables one at a time isn’t enough, which is why this lesson ends with checks that look at all of them together.
To simulate multivariate normal data, use MASS::mvrnorm(n, mu, Sigma). It’s how every dataset in this module was made.
Your turn. Simulate 10,000 batches from a multivariate normal with the same mean vector and covariance matrix as the real ones. What fraction have a squared distance below the 95% point of \chi^2_4?









There are 4 variables, so 4 degrees of freedom.


set.seed(2026)
sim <- MASS::mvrnorm(10000, mu = colMeans(Y), Sigma = cov(Y))
d2 <- mahalanobis(sim, colMeans(Y), cov(Y))
mean(d2 <= qchisq(0.95, df = 4))
95.1%, as property 4 promises. You can check property 1 the same way: sd(sim %*% c(-1, 0.0001, 0, 0)) gives 0.368, Lesson 1’s total-impurity standard deviation.

title: The multivariate normal distribution
text:
Conditional distributions are regressions
Suppose you know a batch’s water content. What does that tell you about its acid? Split the vector into the part you know, \mathbf{x}_2, and the part you don’t, \mathbf{x}_1, and split the mean and covariance the same way:

\boldsymbol\mu = \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol\mu_1 \\ \boldsymbol\mu_2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma_{11} & \Sigma_{12} \\ \Sigma_{21} & \Sigma_{22} \end{pmatrix} .

For a multivariate normal, the conditional distribution of \mathbf{X}_1 given \mathbf{X}_2 = \mathbf{x}_2 is normal again, with

\text{mean } \boldsymbol\mu_1 + \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_2 - \boldsymbol\mu_2), \qquad
\text{covariance } \Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21} .

Look closely at the mean. It’s a straight line in \mathbf{x}_2, with slope \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}: for one predictor, that’s s_{xy}/s_x^2, the least-squares slope from Lesson 2.2! The conditional mean of a multivariate normal is the regression line. And the conditional variance is the residual variance: it’s smaller than the marginal variance \Sigma_{11} (knowing \mathbf{x}_2 helps), and it’s the same whatever value \mathbf{x}_2 takes, which is exactly regression’s equal-variance assumption. When data are multivariate normal, linear regression isn’t an approximation: it’s exactly right.
That gives a sharper look at FS73. Given its water content, 84 ppm, what acid value should it have had?
Your turn. Compute the conditional mean and standard deviation of the acid, given a water content of 84 ppm, with the formulas.









\Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}^2/\Sigma_{22}: divide by the water’s variance, S["water_ppm", "water_ppm"].


mu <- colMeans(W)
S <- cov(W)
cond_mean <- mu["acid_mgKOH"] + S["acid_mgKOH", "water_ppm"] / S["water_ppm", "water_ppm"] * (84 - mu["water_ppm"])
cond_var <- S["acid_mgKOH", "acid_mgKOH"] - S["acid_mgKOH", "water_ppm"]^2 / S["water_ppm", "water_ppm"]
c(mean = unname(cond_mean), sd = sqrt(cond_var))
A batch with 84 ppm of water should have an acid value of about 0.181, give or take 0.025. FS73 had 0.261, 3.3 conditional standard deviations too high. The marginal standard deviation of the acid is 0.030, so knowing the water shrinks the uncertainty by about a fifth: the variance shrinks by the factor 1 - r^2 = 0.66. Check the mean against predict(lm(acid_mgKOH ~ water_ppm, data = quality), data.frame(water_ppm = 84)).




Your turn. Now condition on two variables at once: the acid given both FS73’s purity and its water. Use the matrix formulas.









The last factor is \Sigma_{21}: rows i2, column i1.


mu <- colMeans(Y)
S <- cov(Y)
i1 <- 4                 # acid
i2 <- c(1, 2)           # purity and water
x2 <- Y["FS73", i2]
cond_mean <- mu[i1] + S[i1, i2] %*% solve(S[i2, i2]) %*% (x2 - mu[i2])
cond_var <- S[i1, i1] - S[i1, i2] %*% solve(S[i2, i2]) %*% S[i2, i1]
(Y["FS73", i1] - cond_mean) / sqrt(cond_var)
5.5 conditional standard deviations! Given its high purity and its low water, FS73’s acid should have been about 0.165, with a standard deviation of only 0.017. Knowing more makes the prediction sharper, and the anomaly starker. (This is a multiple regression of the acid on the purity and the water, which lm() reproduces exactly.)

title: The multivariate normal distribution
text:
Checking multivariate normality
Real data are never exactly multivariate normal. The question is whether they’re close enough for methods that assume it. Check in three ways.
1. Each variable on its own. If any variable is clearly non-normal, the vector can’t be multivariate normal. Q-Q plots and the Shapiro-Wilk test (Lesson 2.8) do the job. Here, the color is right-skewed (as color scales often are), and the water is a little odd too, with p = 0.03.
2. All the variables together: a chi-square Q-Q plot. If the data are multivariate normal, the squared Mahalanobis distances should behave like a sample from \chi^2_p. So sort them, and plot them against the matching chi-square quantiles: the points should fall along the line y = x.

d2 <- mahalanobis(Y, colMeans(Y), cov(Y))
n <- nrow(Y)
tibble(batch = names(sort(d2)), observed = sort(d2), theoretical = qchisq((seq_len(n) - 0.5) / n, df = 4)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = theoretical, y = observed)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(color = "#2a78d6", size = 1.8) +
  annotate("text", x = max(qchisq((seq_len(n) - 0.5) / n, 4)), y = max(d2), label = "FS73", hjust = 1.4, size = 3.5) +
  labs(x = "Chi-square quantile (4 df)", y = "Squared Mahalanobis distance") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Most points follow the line, with one glaring exception: FS73, at 34.6, where the largest of 80 chi-square values would typically be about 14. One point that far from the line says more than any test could.
3. Formal tests. Mardia’s tests measure multivariate skewness and kurtosis. The skewness statistic is near zero for symmetric data and the kurtosis statistic near p(p+2) for normal data. Both come with p-values. The setup code for the exercises defines a small mardia() function that computes them. For the raw data, both reject strongly (skewness p < 10^{-13}, kurtosis z = 6.5). The MVN package offers these and several other tests.
What to do when the data aren’t multivariate normal?

Look for outliers first. One point like FS73 can wreck every test. Investigate it (Lesson 2.10), and decide what to do with it.
Transform skewed variables. Logs often fix concentrations and color scales, as here.
Remember robustness. Tests about means, like the ones in the next three lessons, lean on the central limit theorem, so mild non-normality matters little when n is reasonably large. Outliers matter much more.
Check the errors, not the raw variables. When a variable depends on something else, like the product’s water on the feed’s water, its raw distribution can be a mixture, and look non-normal for that reason alone. For a model, what matters is the normality of what the model leaves over: the second challenge shows this.

Your turn. Compare the Shapiro-Wilk p-values for the color and for its logarithm.









Test log(Y[, "color_apha"]).


c(color = shapiro.test(Y[, "color_apha"])$p.value,
  log_color = shapiro.test(log(Y[, "color_apha"]))$p.value)
0.083 for the raw color (its skewness is 0.54), and 0.86 for its log: on the log scale, the color looks perfectly normal. Color comes from degradation products whose amount grows exponentially with temperature (Arrhenius again, Lesson 2.9), so a log is natural.




Your turn. How far is FS73 from where the chi-square Q-Q plot says the largest of 80 distances should be? Compute the theoretical quantile that matches the largest observation, \chi^2_4 at (n - 0.5)/n.









The largest observation is matched with the quantile at (n - 0.5)/n.


n <- nrow(Y)
d2 <- mahalanobis(Y, colMeans(Y), cov(Y))
c(observed = max(d2), expected = qchisq((n - 0.5) / n, df = 4))
34.6 observed against about 14.4 expected: more than twice as far out as the most extreme of 80 normal batches would typically be. The second largest, FS51 at 12.4, is right on target (11.8).

title: The multivariate normal distribution
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Mardia’s tests after cleaning up. Log the color, leave out FS73, and run Mardia’s tests with the mardia() function from the setup code.









Leave out the row named "FS73".


Y_fixed <- Y
Y_fixed[, "color_apha"] <- log(Y_fixed[, "color_apha"])
Y_fixed <- Y_fixed[rownames(Y_fixed) != "FS73", ]
mardia(Y_fixed)
Skewness p = 0.20, kurtosis p = 0.17: no evidence against multivariate normality any more. Leaving out FS73 alone gets the kurtosis right but not the skewness (p = 0.02), and logging the color alone fixes neither, so both steps were needed. The FS73 decision isn’t a statistical one, though: it was excluded because of its acid wash, not because it spoiled a test.




Challenge 2 · Normal errors, non-normal data. The product’s water content failed the Shapiro-Wilk test (p = 0.03). But about a quarter of the batches used Kestrel’s wet feed, so the water is really a mixture of two groups. Regress the product’s water on the feed’s water, and test the residuals.









The predictor is feed_water_ppm.


fit <- lm(water_ppm ~ feed_water_ppm, data = quality)
shapiro.test(resid(fit))$p.value
p = 0.39: once the feed’s water is accounted for, the rest looks normal. The “non-normality” was the mixture of wet and dry feed lots. Most methods in this module assume normal errors within groups or around a model, not normal raw variables, so this is the kind of check that matters.

title: The multivariate normal distribution
text:
Quick quiz

1. What two things completely describe a multivariate normal distribution?

Its mean and its standard deviation
Its mean vector and its covariance matrix
Its median and its correlation matrix


N_p(\boldsymbol\mu, \Sigma): the density depends on nothing else.



2. What shape are the contours of a bivariate normal density?

Circles, always
Ellipses of constant Mahalanobis distance
Squares


The density depends on \mathbf{x} only through (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol\mu). They’re circles only when the variables are uncorrelated with equal variances.



3. Each of four variables has a normal distribution on its own. Is the vector of all four multivariate normal?

Yes, always
Not necessarily: normal margins don’t guarantee a multivariate normal
Only if they’re correlated


That’s why multivariate checks, like the chi-square Q-Q plot, look at the variables together.



4. For a multivariate normal, what’s the conditional mean of one variable given another?

A straight-line function of the other variable: the regression line
Its marginal mean, always
A curve that depends on the skewness


\mu_1 + \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(x_2 - \mu_2) is linear in x_2, and its slope is the least-squares slope.



5. Two components of a multivariate normal vector have zero correlation. What can you conclude?

Nothing more
They’re independent
One of them is constant


For multivariate normal variables, and only then in general, zero covariance means independence.



6. In a chi-square Q-Q plot of squared Mahalanobis distances, one point lies far above the line, and the rest follow it closely. What’s the most likely story?

An outlier in otherwise roughly multivariate normal data
The data are heavily skewed throughout
The number of variables is wrong


A single point far off the line is an outlier, like FS73. A systematic curve away from the line would suggest skewness or heavy tails.

title: The multivariate normal distribution
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve met the distribution that the rest of the module stands on! Here’s what you’ve learned:

The density of N_p(\boldsymbol\mu, \Sigma) depends on the squared Mahalanobis distance, so its contours are ellipses. mvtnorm::dmvnorm() evaluates it, and MASS::mvrnorm() simulates from it.
Properties: linear combinations are normal, with mean \mathbf{a}^\top\boldsymbol\mu and variance \mathbf{a}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{a}; subsets are multivariate normal; zero correlation means independence; and D^2 \sim \chi^2_p.
Conditional distributions are normal, with mean \boldsymbol\mu_1 + \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_2 - \boldsymbol\mu_2), a regression, and covariance \Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21}, a residual variance.
Checking normality: look at each variable, then at all of them with a chi-square Q-Q plot of the distances, and Mardia’s tests. Normal margins aren’t enough.
The batches: FS73 is an outlier (its acid is 5.5 conditional standard deviations too high for its purity and water), the color is log-normal, and the product’s water is a mixture driven by the feed. Deal with those, and the rest is close to multivariate normal.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download batch_quality.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install the MVN package.

The MVN package. Run MVN::mvn(Y) (see ?MVN::mvn for the options in your version) to get Mardia’s tests, the Henze-Zirkler test and univariate tests together, then try it on Y_fixed from the challenge.
A 3D picture. Use plotly to draw the fitted bivariate normal density of water and acid as a surface: compute it on a grid with mvtnorm::dmvnorm() and pass it to plotly::plot_ly(z = ~..., type = "surface").
The classic trap. Simulate x <- rnorm(1000) and y <- ifelse(abs(x) > 1, x, -x). Show that y is exactly normal on its own, and plot y against x. Is the pair bivariate normal? What’s their correlation?
Conditional regression. Verify that the conditional mean formula with two conditioning variables matches lm(acid_mgKOH ~ purity_pct + water_ppm). Why does the residual standard error of the lm() fit differ very slightly from the conditional standard deviation? (Hint: degrees of freedom.)










NoteKey words from this lesson






Multivariate normal distribution

The distribution N_p(\boldsymbol\mu, \Sigma), whose density depends on \mathbf{x} through its squared Mahalanobis distance from \boldsymbol\mu.

Bivariate normal

The multivariate normal with p = 2.

Marginal distribution

The distribution of a subset of the variables, ignoring the others. For a multivariate normal, it’s multivariate normal too.

Conditional distribution

The distribution of some variables given fixed values of others. For a multivariate normal, its mean is a linear regression and its covariance is a residual covariance.

Chi-square Q-Q plot

A plot of the sorted squared Mahalanobis distances against chi-square quantiles, used to check multivariate normality.

Mardia’s tests

Tests of multivariate normality based on multivariate measures of skewness and kurtosis.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 505, Lesson 4: Multivariate Normal Distribution and Lesson 6: Multivariate Conditional Distribution and Partial Correlation. The density, its geometry, outliers, and conditional distributions.
Johnson and Wichern, Applied Multivariate Statistical Analysis, chapter 4. The multivariate normal’s properties with proofs, and section 4.6 on assessing normality.
Korkmaz, Goksuluk and Zararsiz, “MVN: An R package for assessing multivariate normality”, The R Journal 6(2), 2014. A practical tour of the tests and plots.

title: Comparing two mean vectors
text:
Module 3 · Lesson 5 of 13 Week 51 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Most comparisons in a plant come in two flavors. Sometimes the same items are measured twice, by two instruments, or before and after a change: that’s a paired comparison. Sometimes two different groups are compared, like the lots from two suppliers: that’s an independent-samples comparison. Lesson 0.13 did both with one variable at a time. This lesson does them with several variables at once, using Hotelling’s T^2, and both examples have a twist that one-at-a-time tests would miss or misread.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Comparing two mean vectors
section: Paired comparisons: is the analyzer biased?
text:
Paired comparisons: is the analyzer biased?
The plant’s online NIR analyzer reads the purity, water and acid of the product every few minutes, without waiting for the lab. For an audit, 30 samples were analyzed both ways:

pairs_data <- read_csv("data/analyzer_pairs.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(pairs_data, 4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 7
#>   sample_id lab_purity nir_purity lab_water nir_water lab_acid nir_acid
#>   <chr>          <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 N01             98.8       98.7       199       203    0.209    0.196
#> 2 N02             99.0       99.1       150       140    0.164    0.165
#> 3 N03             99.2       99.3       223       214    0.181    0.203
#> 4 N04             98.9       98.9       208       216    0.218    0.217

Each sample’s two results belong together, so the right thing to analyze is the differences, NIR minus lab, one vector per sample. If the analyzer is unbiased, the mean difference vector is zero, so the question is a one-sample test of H_0: \boldsymbol\delta = \mathbf{0}, exactly last lesson’s T^2 with \boldsymbol\mu_0 = \mathbf{0}:

T^2 = n\,\bar{\mathbf{d}}^\top S_d^{-1}\,\bar{\mathbf{d}}, \qquad \frac{n - p}{p(n - 1)}\,T^2 \sim F_{p,\,n-p} .

Pairing removes the big sample-to-sample differences (the lab’s purities range over about 1.5 percentage points), so that only the analyzer’s errors remain. That’s what makes a paired comparison so much more sensitive than comparing two independent sets of measurements.










Your turn. Build the matrix of differences, NIR minus lab, and compute its mean vector.









The third column is nir_acid - lab_acid.


D <- with(pairs_data, cbind(purity = nir_purity - lab_purity,
                            water = nir_water - lab_water,
                            acid = nir_acid - lab_acid))
colMeans(D)
On average, the NIR reads 0.019 points of purity higher than the lab, 3.3 ppm more water, and 0.002 more acid. Small differences, and all in the same direction.




Your turn. Test each difference on its own, with a paired t-test (a one-sample t-test of the differences).









Test the differences in column j: t.test(D[, j]).


D <- with(pairs_data, cbind(nir_purity - lab_purity, nir_water - lab_water, nir_acid - lab_acid))
sapply(1:3, function(j) t.test(D[, j])$p.value)
0.072, 0.077 and 0.25. None is significant at 5%: on these tests, the audit would pass the analyzer.




Your turn. Now test all three differences at once with T^2.









Use the covariance matrix of the differences, cov(D).


D <- with(pairs_data, cbind(nir_purity - lab_purity, nir_water - lab_water, nir_acid - lab_acid))
n <- nrow(D); p <- ncol(D)
d_bar <- colMeans(D)
T2 <- n * t(d_bar) %*% solve(cov(D)) %*% d_bar
F_stat <- (n - p) / (p * (n - 1)) * T2
c(T2 = T2, p = pf(F_stat, p, n - p, lower.tail = FALSE))
T^2 = 15.8, p = 0.0076. The analyzer is biased, and the joint test is sure of it.




Why is the joint test so much surer? Look at how the analyzer’s errors behave:

D <- with(pairs_data, tibble(purity = nir_purity - lab_purity, water = nir_water - lab_water))
ggplot(D, aes(x = purity, y = water)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey75") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey75") +
  geom_point(color = "#2a78d6", size = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = mean(purity), y = mean(water)), color = "#C2416C", size = 4, shape = 18) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(D$purity), y = mean(D$water), label = "mean difference", vjust = -1.3, size = 3.5) +
  labs(x = "Purity: NIR minus lab (points)", y = "Water: NIR minus lab (ppm)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
#> Warning in geom_point(aes(x = mean(purity), y = mean(water)), color = "#C2416C", : All aesthetics have length 1, but the data has 30 rows.
#> ℹ Please consider using `annotate()` or provide this layer with data containing
#>   a single row.








The NIR reads purity and water from overlapping bands of the same spectrum, so when it overestimates one, it tends to underestimate the other: its errors are negatively correlated (r = -0.55). The cloud of differences runs from top left to bottom right. The bias, though, pushes both readings up, which is the direction across the cloud, where the errors are smallest. In that direction, even a small shift stands out. The one-at-a-time tests can’t see it, because each of them looks along an axis, where the errors are large.

title: Comparing two mean vectors
text:
Two independent groups
Now the incoming feed lots. The lab measures every delivered lot for water, aldehyde, acid and iron:

feed <- read_csv("data/feed_lots.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
feed |> group_by(supplier) |> summarise(lots = n(), across(water_ppm:iron_ppb, mean))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>   supplier     lots water_ppm aldehyde_ppm acid_mgKOH iron_ppb
#>   <chr>       <int>     <dbl>        <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 Fizzwell       16      191.         44.0     0.0986     30.7
#> 2 Kestrel        15      297          48.8     0.147      37.2
#> 3 Plum Valley    14      194.         47.6     0.105      43.0
#> 4 Rosewater      13      208.         68.5     0.111      32.8

Kestrel’s lots are wet, as you know, and Rosewater’s carry aldehyde. Fizzwell and Plum Valley look like twins. Purchasing would like to know: is there any real difference between those two? That’s a comparison of two independent mean vectors, H_0: \boldsymbol\mu_1 = \boldsymbol\mu_2.
If the two suppliers’ lots have the same covariance matrix, it’s best estimated by pooling the two sample covariance matrices, as the pooled variance does in a two-sample t-test:

S_p = \frac{(n_1 - 1)S_1 + (n_2 - 1)S_2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2} .

The covariance matrix of the difference between the two sample means is then S_p\,(1/n_1 + 1/n_2), and the two-sample T^2 is

T^2 = (\bar{\mathbf{x}}_1 - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_2)^\top \left[ S_p \left( \tfrac{1}{n_1} + \tfrac{1}{n_2} \right) \right]^{-1} (\bar{\mathbf{x}}_1 - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_2),
\qquad
\frac{n_1 + n_2 - p - 1}{p\,(n_1 + n_2 - 2)}\,T^2 \sim F_{p,\ n_1 + n_2 - p - 1} .

The same test comes out of manova(), which the next lesson introduces: with two groups, its “Hotelling-Lawley” statistic is T^2/(n_1 + n_2 - 2), with the same F and p-value.
Your turn. The setup code has made X1 (Fizzwell’s 16 lots) and X2 (Plum Valley’s 14). Compute the pooled covariance matrix, the two-sample T^2 and its p-value.









The covariance of the difference of means is S_p(1/n_1 + 1/n_2).


n1 <- nrow(X1); n2 <- nrow(X2); p <- ncol(X1)
Sp <- ((n1 - 1) * cov(X1) + (n2 - 1) * cov(X2)) / (n1 + n2 - 2)
d <- colMeans(X1) - colMeans(X2)
T2 <- t(d) %*% solve(Sp * (1 / n1 + 1 / n2)) %*% d
F_stat <- (n1 + n2 - p - 1) / (p * (n1 + n2 - 2)) * T2
c(T2 = T2, p = pf(F_stat, p, n1 + n2 - p - 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
T^2 = 24.3, F = 5.42 on 4 and 25 degrees of freedom, p = 0.0028. The twins aren’t identical.

title: Comparing two mean vectors
text:
Which variables differ?
After a significant joint test, the natural question is where the difference is. The simultaneous intervals from Lesson 4 carry over, with the two-sample multiplier

c = \sqrt{\frac{p\,(n_1 + n_2 - 2)}{n_1 + n_2 - p - 1}\,F_{p,\ n_1 + n_2 - p - 1}(0.95)},
\qquad
(\bar{x}_{1j} - \bar{x}_{2j}) \pm c\,\sqrt{s_{p,jj}\left(\tfrac{1}{n_1} + \tfrac{1}{n_2}\right)} ,

and Bonferroni intervals use t_{n_1 + n_2 - 2}(\alpha/2p) instead of c. Here, c = 3.52 and the Bonferroni multiplier is 2.67.
A profile plot shows the two mean vectors side by side. Since the variables have different units, put each one in standard units first, here using the standard deviation of all 58 lots:

vars <- c("water_ppm", "aldehyde_ppm", "acid_mgKOH", "iron_ppb")
centers <- colMeans(feed[, vars]); spreads <- apply(feed[, vars], 2, sd)
feed |>
  filter(supplier %in% c("Fizzwell", "Plum Valley")) |>
  group_by(supplier) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(vars), mean)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-supplier, names_to = "property", values_to = "mean") |>
  mutate(z = (mean - centers[property]) / spreads[property],
         property = factor(sub("_.*", "", property), levels = c("water", "aldehyde", "acid", "iron"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = property, y = z, color = supplier, group = supplier)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Fizzwell = "#2a78d6", `Plum Valley` = "#C2416C")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean, in standard units", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The two profiles run close together on water, aldehyde and acid, then split apart on iron: Plum Valley’s lots carry about 12 ppb more. Profile plots are worth drawing for any multivariate comparison: Lesson 9 turns them into a formal analysis.
Your turn. Compute the simultaneous T^2 interval for the difference in mean iron, Fizzwell minus Plum Valley.









Multiply the standard error by the simultaneous multiplier, c_mult.


n1 <- nrow(X1); n2 <- nrow(X2); p <- ncol(X1)
Sp <- ((n1 - 1) * cov(X1) + (n2 - 1) * cov(X2)) / (n1 + n2 - 2)
c_mult <- sqrt(p * (n1 + n2 - 2) / (n1 + n2 - p - 1) * qf(0.95, p, n1 + n2 - p - 1))
d_iron <- mean(X1[, "iron_ppb"]) - mean(X2[, "iron_ppb"])
se_iron <- sqrt(Sp["iron_ppb", "iron_ppb"] * (1 / n1 + 1 / n2))
d_iron + c(-1, 1) * c_mult * se_iron
From −23.6 to −1.0 ppb: Fizzwell’s lots carry less iron than Plum Valley’s, by somewhere between 1 and 24 ppb. The simultaneous intervals for the water, aldehyde and acid all contain zero. Iron is the difference, probably from Plum Valley’s older, steel-lined storage tanks.

title: Comparing two mean vectors
text:
When the covariance matrices differ
Pooling assumes that both groups have the same covariance matrix. When they clearly don’t, and especially when the group sizes differ too, the pooled T^2 can be misleading, as the pooled t-test can be in one dimension. The fix is the same as Welch’s t-test: don’t pool. Use each group’s own covariance matrix,

T^2 = (\bar{\mathbf{x}}_1 - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_2)^\top \left( \frac{S_1}{n_1} + \frac{S_2}{n_2} \right)^{-1} (\bar{\mathbf{x}}_1 - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_2) .

For large samples, this is approximately \chi^2_p. For smaller ones, there are F approximations with estimated degrees of freedom (Yao’s, and Nel and Van der Merwe’s), much like Welch’s.
How do you tell whether the covariance matrices differ? Look at the standard deviations and the correlations group by group. The formal test is Box’s M test (heplots::boxM()), which you’ll meet properly in the next lesson. It’s sensitive to non-normality, so treat it as a warning light rather than a verdict. For Fizzwell and Plum Valley, the spreads are similar (Box’s M p = 0.74), so pooling is fine. Kestrel would be another story: its water content varies twice as much as anyone else’s.
Your turn. Compute the unpooled T^2 for Fizzwell against Plum Valley, and its large-sample chi-square p-value.









Divide the second covariance matrix by its own group size, nrow(X2).


d <- colMeans(X1) - colMeans(X2)
S_unpooled <- cov(X1) / nrow(X1) + cov(X2) / nrow(X2)
T2 <- t(d) %*% solve(S_unpooled) %*% d
c(T2 = T2, p = pchisq(T2, df = 4, lower.tail = FALSE))
T^2 = 23.1, close to the pooled 24.3, since the two covariance matrices are similar. The chi-square p-value, 0.0001, is smaller than the pooled F test’s 0.0028, but don’t read anything into that: with only 14 and 16 lots, the chi-square approximation is too optimistic, and the F version is the one to trust.

title: Comparing two mean vectors
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The analyzer’s bias direction. As in Lesson 4, the combination that differs most is \mathbf{a} = S_d^{-1}\bar{\mathbf{d}}. Compute it, and scale each weight by its variable’s standard deviation to compare them.









Scale by the standard deviations of the differences: diag(cov(D)).


D <- with(pairs_data, cbind(purity = nir_purity - lab_purity, water = nir_water - lab_water, acid = nir_acid - lab_acid))
a <- solve(cov(D)) %*% colMeans(D)
scaled <- a * sqrt(diag(cov(D)))
round(scaled[, 1] / max(abs(scaled)), 2)
1.00 for the purity, 0.99 for the water, 0.21 for the acid: the bias shows up as “purity and water both read high”, the combination that the analyzer’s negatively correlated errors rarely produce on their own. A sensible next step for the plant: recalibrate the NIR’s purity and water models together, against a fresh set of lab samples.




Challenge 2 · Do the spreads differ? Run Box’s M test for Fizzwell against Plum Valley, and for Fizzwell against Kestrel.









The second group is Kestrel’s lots, X3.


X3 <- as.matrix(filter(feed, supplier == "Kestrel")[, vars])
p_pv <- heplots::boxM(rbind(X1, X2), rep(c("Fizzwell", "Plum Valley"), c(nrow(X1), nrow(X2))))$p.value
p_k <- heplots::boxM(rbind(X1, X3), rep(c("Fizzwell", "Kestrel"), c(nrow(X1), nrow(X3))))$p.value
c(plum_valley = unname(p_pv), kestrel = unname(p_k))
p = 0.74 for Plum Valley, and p = 0.0009 for Kestrel, whose water varies with a standard deviation of 29 ppm against Fizzwell’s 14. Comparing Fizzwell with Kestrel, you’d use the unpooled T^2 (not that it would matter much here: their water contents differ by 100 ppm).

title: Comparing two mean vectors
text:
Quick quiz

1. Thirty samples are each analyzed by two instruments. How should you compare the instruments?

With a two-sample T^2 test, treating the instruments as two groups
With a one-sample T^2 test on the differences, one per sample
By comparing the two covariance matrices


The measurements are paired, so analyze the differences. That removes the sample-to-sample variation.



2. The analyzer’s three paired t-tests had p-values of 0.07, 0.08 and 0.25, but the paired T^2 gave 0.0076. Why?

T^2 ignores the correlations
The bias pushes purity and water the same way, while the analyzer’s errors in them are negatively correlated, so the bias stands out in that direction
The t-tests used the wrong data


T^2 looks in every direction, and finds the one where the shift is largest compared with the noise.



3. What does the two-sample T^2 test assume about the two groups’ covariance matrices?

That they’re equal, so they can be pooled
That they’re diagonal
Nothing at all


The pooled S_p is a weighted average of the two. When they clearly differ, use the unpooled version, S_1/n_1 + S_2/n_2.



4. After a significant two-sample T^2 test, how do you find which variables differ?

Rerun the T^2 test on each variable
Use simultaneous T^2 or Bonferroni intervals for each variable’s difference
Look for the variable with the largest mean


Simultaneous intervals keep the overall error rate at 5%. Here, only the iron’s interval excluded zero.



5. What’s a profile plot?

A plot of the residuals against each variable
A plot of each group’s mean on every variable, joined by lines, usually in standard units
A scatterplot matrix


It shows at a glance where two mean vectors agree and where they part, as on iron here.



6. With two groups, how is the two-sample T^2 related to manova()?

They test different hypotheses
They give the same F-test: the Hotelling-Lawley statistic is T^2/(n_1 + n_2 - 2)
manova() only works for one variable


MANOVA generalizes the two-sample T^2 to more than two groups, in the next lesson.

title: Comparing two mean vectors
text:
Wrap-up
You can now compare two mean vectors, paired or independent! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Paired data: analyze the differences with a one-sample T^2 against zero. The NIR analyzer passed three t-tests but failed the joint test (p = 0.0076), because its bias goes across its error structure.
Two independent groups: the two-sample T^2 with the pooled covariance S_p, and \frac{n_1+n_2-p-1}{p(n_1+n_2-2)}T^2 \sim F_{p,\,n_1+n_2-p-1}. Fizzwell and Plum Valley differ (p = 0.0028).
Where they differ: simultaneous T^2 or Bonferroni intervals, and a profile plot. The difference is in iron.
Unequal covariances: use S_1/n_1 + S_2/n_2, with a chi-square approximation for large samples. Box’s M test is a warning light: Kestrel’s spreads differ from the others’.
The direction of a difference is S^{-1} times the mean difference, the combination with the largest t^2.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download analyzer_pairs.csv and feed_lots.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

The wrong analysis. Compare the NIR and lab results as if they were two independent groups of 30 samples, with the two-sample T^2. What p-value do you get, and why is it so much larger than the paired one?
manova() for two groups. Run summary(manova(cbind(water_ppm, aldehyde_ppm, acid_mgKOH, iron_ppb) ~ supplier, data = filter(feed, supplier %in% c("Fizzwell", "Plum Valley"))), test = "Hotelling-Lawley"), and check the F statistic against your T^2.
A Bland-Altman plot. For each property, plot the NIR-minus-lab difference against the average of the two readings. It’s the standard way chemists compare two measurement methods. Is the bias constant across the range?
Kestrel against Fizzwell. Compute both the pooled and the unpooled T^2 for Kestrel against Fizzwell, and their simultaneous intervals. Which properties differ, besides the water?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Paired comparison

A comparison of two measurements on the same units, analyzed through their differences.

Two-sample T^2 test

A test of whether two independent groups have the same mean vector, using the pooled covariance matrix.

Pooled covariance matrix

S_p = [(n_1-1)S_1 + (n_2-1)S_2]/(n_1+n_2-2), the combined estimate of a covariance matrix that two groups share.

Unpooled (Behrens-Fisher) T^2

A two-sample T^2 that uses S_1/n_1 + S_2/n_2, for groups with different covariance matrices.

Box’s M test

A test of whether several groups share the same covariance matrix. It’s sensitive to non-normality.

Profile plot

A plot of the groups’ mean vectors, one line per group, across the variables.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 505, Lesson 7: Inferences Regarding Multivariate Population Mean, sections 7.1.6 to 7.1.15 (paired and two-sample tests) and 7.2.4 to 7.2.8 (intervals, profile plots and unequal covariance matrices).
Johnson and Wichern, Applied Multivariate Statistical Analysis, chapter 6, sections 6.1 to 6.3. Paired comparisons and the comparison of two mean vectors.
J. Martin Bland and Douglas Altman, “Statistical methods for assessing agreement between two methods of clinical measurement”, The Lancet (1986). The classic on comparing two measurement methods, just as useful in a chemistry lab.

title: Linear contrasts and simultaneous inference
text:
Module 3 · Lesson 7 of 13 Week 53 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The MANOVA said the four suppliers’ lots differ, with a p-value too small to print sensibly. That’s not much use to the purchasing department on its own. They have specific questions. Is Kestrel different from everyone else, and in what? Is Rosewater? And what about the twins, Fizzwell and Plum Valley? This lesson answers questions like these with contrasts, the planned comparisons of Lesson 2.13, now with mean vectors, and with intervals that stay honest when you look at many comparisons at once.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Linear contrasts and simultaneous inference
text:
Contrasts of mean vectors
A contrast is a weighted combination of the group means, with weights that add up to zero (Lesson 2.13). With mean vectors, it’s a vector:

\boldsymbol\psi = c_1\boldsymbol\mu_1 + c_2\boldsymbol\mu_2 + \dots + c_k\boldsymbol\mu_k, \qquad \sum_i c_i = 0 .

The suppliers are in alphabetical order: Fizzwell, Kestrel, Plum Valley, Rosewater. So “Kestrel against the average of the other three” has weights \mathbf{c} = (-\tfrac13, 1, -\tfrac13, -\tfrac13), and “Fizzwell against Plum Valley” has (1, 0, -1, 0).
The contrast is estimated by the same combination of the sample mean vectors, \hat{\boldsymbol\psi} = \sum c_i\bar{\mathbf{x}}_i. Because the groups are independent, its covariance matrix is \left(\sum c_i^2/n_i\right)\Sigma, and \Sigma is estimated by the pooled within-group covariance matrix of all the groups, S_p = E/(N - k). To test H_0: \boldsymbol\psi = \mathbf{0}, use a T^2 statistic:

T^2 = \hat{\boldsymbol\psi}^\top \left[ \Big(\sum_i \frac{c_i^2}{n_i}\Big) S_p \right]^{-1} \hat{\boldsymbol\psi},
\qquad
\frac{N - k - p + 1}{p\,(N - k)}\,T^2 \sim F_{p,\ N - k - p + 1} .

With 58 lots, 4 suppliers and 4 properties, that’s an F distribution with 4 and 51 degrees of freedom.










Your turn. The setup code has made means, a matrix with one row of means per supplier, and n_i, the group sizes. Estimate the contrast “Kestrel against the other three”.









Rosewater, the fourth supplier, gets the same weight as the other two: -1/3.


cc <- c(-1/3, 1, -1/3, -1/3)
colSums(cc * means)
Compared with the average of the other three, Kestrel’s lots carry 99 ppm more water, 4.5 ppm less aldehyde, 0.042 mg KOH/g more acid and 1.7 ppb more iron. (cc * means multiplies each row of means by its supplier’s weight, and colSums() adds them up.)




Your turn. Test the Kestrel contrast with T^2.









The covariance of the contrast is \left(\sum c_i^2/n_i\right) S_p.


cc <- c(-1/3, 1, -1/3, -1/3)
psi <- colSums(cc * means)
T2 <- t(psi) %*% solve(sum(cc^2 / n_i) * Sp) %*% psi
F_stat <- (N - k - p + 1) / (p * (N - k)) * T2
c(F = F_stat, p = pf(F_stat, p, N - k - p + 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
F = 69.7 on 4 and 51 degrees of freedom, p = 5 \times 10^{-20}. No doubt at all: Kestrel’s lots are different.

title: Linear contrasts and simultaneous inference
text:
Contrasts with car::linearHypothesis()
The car package tests contrasts directly on a multivariate linear model. Fit the model with one coefficient per group (the “cell means” model, with 0 + to drop the intercept), and give linearHypothesis() the contrast weights as a hypothesis matrix, one row per contrast:

mlm <- lm(cbind(water_ppm, aldehyde_ppm, acid_mgKOH, iron_ppb) ~ 0 + supplier, data = feed)
car::linearHypothesis(mlm, hypothesis.matrix = rbind(c(-1/3, 1, -1/3, -1/3)))
#> 
#> Sum of squares and products for the hypothesis:
#>                 water_ppm aldehyde_ppm  acid_mgKOH     iron_ppb
#> water_ppm    109469.94968  -4998.82908 46.01704939 1899.6022915
#> aldehyde_ppm  -4998.82908    228.26623 -2.10131973  -86.7433227
#> acid_mgKOH       46.01705     -2.10132  0.01934384    0.7985214
#> iron_ppb       1899.60229    -86.74332  0.79852135   32.9632824
#> 
#> Sum of squares and products for error:
#>               water_ppm aldehyde_ppm  acid_mgKOH    iron_ppb
#> water_ppm    21466.0192   616.557692 11.37120192 -721.476923
#> aldehyde_ppm   616.5577  2321.584696  1.26538196 -310.138674
#> acid_mgKOH      11.3712     1.265382  0.01921501   -1.584202
#> iron_ppb      -721.4769  -310.138674 -1.58420174 3009.947168
#> 
#> Multivariate Tests: 
#>                  Df test stat approx F num Df den Df     Pr(>F)    
#> Pillai            1  0.845267 69.65012      4     51 < 2.22e-16 ***
#> Wilks             1  0.154733 69.65012      4     51 < 2.22e-16 ***
#> Hotelling-Lawley  1  5.462755 69.65012      4     51 < 2.22e-16 ***
#> Roy               1  5.462755 69.65012      4     51 < 2.22e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

It prints the contrast’s SSCP matrix, the error matrix E, and all four MANOVA statistics. For a single contrast, they all give the same F-test as the T^2, F = 69.7, because a one-row contrast has only one non-zero eigenvalue. A hypothesis matrix with several rows tests several contrasts jointly, with \min(p, \text{rows}) eigenvalues, and then the four statistics differ again.






NoteGo deeper: orthogonal contrasts split H





With k groups, you can find k - 1 contrasts that together carry all of the between-group information, so that their SSCP matrices add up to H exactly, like the sums of squares of orthogonal contrasts in ANOVA. Each contrast’s SSCP matrix is \hat{\boldsymbol\psi}\hat{\boldsymbol\psi}^\top / \sum (c_i^2/n_i).
The condition for two contrasts \mathbf{c} and \mathbf{d} to be orthogonal is \sum c_i d_i/n_i = 0. With equal group sizes, that’s the familiar \sum c_i d_i = 0. With unequal sizes, as here (16, 15, 14 and 13 lots), “Kestrel against the rest” and “Rosewater against Fizzwell and Plum Valley” aren’t quite orthogonal, so their SSCP matrices overlap a little, and don’t add up to H. That’s harmless for testing each one. It matters only if you want a neat decomposition of H. Then weight the averages by the group sizes: for example, Kestrel against the pooled mean of the other 43 lots is \mathbf{c} = (-\tfrac{16}{43}, 1, -\tfrac{14}{43}, -\tfrac{13}{43}). Practice item 3 at the end builds a full orthogonal set.



Your turn. Test “Fizzwell against Plum Valley” with linearHypothesis().









Plum Valley, the third supplier, gets the weight -1.


mlm <- lm(cbind(water_ppm, aldehyde_ppm, acid_mgKOH, iron_ppb) ~ 0 + supplier, data = feed)
test <- car::linearHypothesis(mlm, hypothesis.matrix = rbind(c(1, 0, -1, 0)))
test
F = 6.42 on 4 and 51 degrees of freedom, p = 0.0003. Lesson 5’s two-sample test of the same pair gave p = 0.0028. Why the difference? This test estimates the covariance matrix from all four suppliers’ lots, so it has 54 error degrees of freedom instead of 28, which sharpens the test. That’s one of the advantages of following up a MANOVA instead of running separate two-group tests, as long as the groups share a covariance matrix. Here they don’t quite: Kestrel’s water varies about twice as much as the others’ (Box’s M flagged it in Lesson 6), and pooling it in inflates the water variance. A careful analyst checks that this doesn’t drive the conclusion. Pooling only the other three suppliers gives p = 0.001, so it doesn’t.

title: Linear contrasts and simultaneous inference
text:
Which properties drive a contrast?
A significant contrast says the two sides differ somewhere in their four properties. To see where, build an interval for the contrast on each property. For property j,

\hat\psi_j \pm m \sqrt{\Big(\sum_i \frac{c_i^2}{n_i}\Big)\, s_{p,jj}} ,

where s_{p,jj} is the pooled variance of property j, and the multiplier m depends on how many intervals you look at:

Bonferroni, for a planned set of r intervals: m = t_{N-k}(\alpha/2r). For one contrast on four properties, r = 4.
Simultaneous T^2-type intervals, for every contrast on every combination of properties you might want, even after looking at the data: m = \sqrt{\frac{p(N-k)}{N-k-p+1}F_{p,\,N-k-p+1}(\alpha)}, like Lesson 4’s. They’re wider, the price of complete freedom.

Here, the Bonferroni multiplier for four intervals is t_{54}(0.05/8) = 2.58, and the T^2-type multiplier is 3.29.
Your turn. Compute the Bonferroni intervals for the Kestrel contrast on all four properties.









There are four intervals, one per property: r = 4.


cc <- c(-1/3, 1, -1/3, -1/3)
psi <- colSums(cc * means)
se <- sqrt(sum(cc^2 / n_i) * diag(Sp))
m <- qt(1 - 0.05 / (2 * 4), df = N - k)
cbind(estimate = psi, lower = psi - m * se, upper = psi + m * se)
The water’s interval runs from about 84 to 115 ppm, and the acid’s from 0.027 to 0.056: both far from zero. The aldehyde’s and the iron’s intervals both include zero. Kestrel’s lots are wetter and more acidic than the others, and that’s all.

title: Linear contrasts and simultaneous inference
text:
All pairs of groups
When there’s no specific plan, the usual follow-up is to compare every pair of groups on every property. Here, that’s \binom{4}{2} = 6 pairs times 4 properties: r = 24 intervals, so the Bonferroni multiplier is t_{54}(0.05/48) = 3.23. Here are the intervals that exclude zero:

levs <- levels(supplier)
means <- t(sapply(levs, function(s) colMeans(X[supplier == s, , drop = FALSE])))
n_i <- as.numeric(table(supplier))
E <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(levs, function(s) {
  Xs <- X[supplier == s, , drop = FALSE]
  crossprod(sweep(Xs, 2, colMeans(Xs)))
}))
Sp <- E / (nrow(X) - 4)
m <- qt(1 - 0.05 / (2 * 24), df = nrow(X) - 4)
pairs_list <- combn(4, 2)
intervals <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(ncol(pairs_list)), function(j) {
  a <- pairs_list[1, j]; b <- pairs_list[2, j]
  d <- means[a, ] - means[b, ]
  se <- sqrt(diag(Sp) * (1 / n_i[a] + 1 / n_i[b]))
  tibble(pair = paste(levs[a], "-", levs[b]), property = vars, difference = d, lower = d - m * se, upper = d + m * se)
}))
filter(intervals, lower > 0 | upper < 0)
#> # A tibble: 11 × 5
#>    pair                    property     difference     lower    upper
#>    <chr>                   <chr>             <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#>  1 Fizzwell - Kestrel      water_ppm     -106.     -129.     -82.9   
#>  2 Fizzwell - Kestrel      acid_mgKOH      -0.0481   -0.0700  -0.0262
#>  3 Fizzwell - Plum Valley  iron_ppb       -12.3     -21.1     -3.45  
#>  4 Fizzwell - Rosewater    aldehyde_ppm   -24.5     -32.4    -16.5   
#>  5 Kestrel - Plum Valley   water_ppm      102.       78.5    126.    
#>  6 Kestrel - Plum Valley   acid_mgKOH       0.0412    0.0186   0.0639
#>  7 Kestrel - Rosewater     water_ppm       89.3      64.9    114.    
#>  8 Kestrel - Rosewater     aldehyde_ppm   -19.6     -27.7    -11.6   
#>  9 Kestrel - Rosewater     acid_mgKOH       0.0359    0.0128   0.0590
#> 10 Plum Valley - Rosewater aldehyde_ppm   -20.8     -29.0    -12.7   
#> 11 Plum Valley - Rosewater iron_ppb        10.1       0.833   19.4

And here are all 24, one panel per property:

intervals |>
  mutate(property = factor(property, levels = vars, labels = c("Water (ppm)", "Aldehyde (ppm)", "Acid (mg KOH/g)", "Iron (ppb)")),
         pair = factor(pair, levels = rev(unique(pair))),
         excludes_zero = ifelse(lower > 0 | upper < 0, "Excludes zero", "Includes zero")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = difference, y = pair, xmin = lower, xmax = upper, color = excludes_zero)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_pointrange(size = 0.3, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Excludes zero" = "#C2416C", "Includes zero" = "grey65"), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ property, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Difference between the two suppliers' means (first minus second)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Eleven of the 24 intervals exclude zero, and they tell a tidy story:

Kestrel differs from every other supplier in water and acid (and from Rosewater in aldehyde too).
Rosewater differs from every other supplier in aldehyde.
Plum Valley differs from Fizzwell and Rosewater in iron.
Fizzwell has no distinguishing feature of its own: it’s the clean baseline.

Your turn. Compute the Bonferroni interval for Fizzwell minus Plum Valley on the iron, with the multiplier for all 24 pairwise intervals.









Plum Valley is the third group, so its size is n_i[3].


m <- qt(1 - 0.05 / (2 * 24), df = N - k)
d <- means["Fizzwell", "iron_ppb"] - means["Plum Valley", "iron_ppb"]
se <- sqrt(Sp["iron_ppb", "iron_ppb"] * (1 / n_i[1] + 1 / n_i[3]))
d + c(-1, 1) * m * se
From −21.1 to −3.5 ppb. Even with the strict multiplier for 24 intervals, Plum Valley’s lots carry more iron than Fizzwell’s.

title: Linear contrasts and simultaneous inference
section: Is one difference explained by another?
text:
Is one difference explained by another?
Kestrel’s lots are more acidic. But water hydrolyzes the product into acid, and Kestrel’s lots are also much wetter. Is the extra acid just the extra water, or is something else wrong with Kestrel’s feed? A contrast can’t tell you, but a model that adjusts for the water can: compare the suppliers’ acid values at the same water content. That’s an ANCOVA (Lesson 2.14), and in a multivariate follow-up it’s called a step-down analysis: test a response after adjusting for the ones that cause it.
Your turn. Fit the acid against the water, then add the supplier, and test whether the supplier adds anything.









Add supplier to the second model.


water_only <- lm(acid_mgKOH ~ water_ppm, data = feed)
with_supplier <- lm(acid_mgKOH ~ water_ppm + supplier, data = feed)
anova(water_only, with_supplier)
F = 0.62, p = 0.61. Once the water content is known, the supplier tells you nothing more about the acid: each extra ppm of water brings 0.00053 mg KOH/g of acid, whoever supplied the lot. So Kestrel’s acid problem is really its water problem. Fix the water (dry the feed, or tighten the contract), and the acid follows. That’s a much more useful message for purchasing than “Kestrel differs on two properties”.

title: Linear contrasts and simultaneous inference
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Rosewater. Test the contrast “Rosewater against Fizzwell and Plum Valley” with T^2.









Plum Valley, the third supplier, gets the same weight as Fizzwell: -1/2. Kestrel gets 0.


cc <- c(-1/2, 0, -1/2, 1)
psi <- colSums(cc * means)
T2 <- t(psi) %*% solve(sum(cc^2 / n_i) * Sp) %*% psi
F_stat <- (N - k - p + 1) / (p * (N - k)) * T2
c(F = F_stat, p = pf(F_stat, p, N - k - p + 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
F = 26.6, p = 6 \times 10^{-12}. Rosewater’s lots carry about 23 ppm more aldehyde than the other two dry suppliers’.




Challenge 2 · Counting the differences. Using the pairwise intervals built above (the setup has all the pieces), count how many of the 24 Bonferroni intervals exclude zero.









An interval excludes zero when the difference is more than m standard errors away from it.


m <- qt(1 - 0.05 / (2 * 24), df = N - k)
pairs_list <- combn(4, 2)
excludes_zero <- sapply(seq_len(ncol(pairs_list)), function(j) {
  a <- pairs_list[1, j]; b <- pairs_list[2, j]
  d <- means[a, ] - means[b, ]
  se <- sqrt(diag(Sp) * (1 / n_i[a] + 1 / n_i[b]))
  abs(d) > m * se
})
sum(excludes_zero)
11 of the 24. With ordinary 95% intervals, you’d expect more than one false alarm among 24 comparisons, even if nothing differed. Bonferroni keeps the chance of any false alarm at 5%.

title: Linear contrasts and simultaneous inference
text:
Quick quiz

1. What makes a set of weights a contrast?

They’re all positive
They add up to zero
They add up to one


Then the contrast is zero whenever all the group means are equal.



2. Which covariance matrix does a contrast test after MANOVA use?

The covariance matrix of the two groups being compared only
The pooled within-group covariance matrix of all the groups, E/(N - k)
The total covariance matrix


Pooling all the groups gives more degrees of freedom, as long as the groups share a covariance matrix.



3. For a single contrast, why do all four MANOVA statistics give the same F?

Because they’re all approximations
Because a one-row hypothesis has only one non-zero eigenvalue
Because the groups are of equal size


With one eigenvalue, Wilks, Pillai, Hotelling-Lawley and Roy are all functions of the same number, so they’re exact and equivalent.



4. You’ll look at 24 pairwise intervals. What should the Bonferroni multiplier be, with N - k = 54 error degrees of freedom?

t_{54}(0.025), about 2.0
t_{54}(0.05/48), about 3.2
t_{54}(0.05/24), about 3.0


Each of the 24 two-sided intervals gets \alpha/24, so each tail gets \alpha/48.



5. When are simultaneous T^2-type intervals better than Bonferroni intervals?

Always: they’re narrower
When you want to explore contrasts and combinations that you didn’t plan before seeing the data
When there’s only one comparison


They’re wider, but they cover every contrast and combination at once. For a few planned intervals, Bonferroni is narrower.



6. Kestrel’s lots are wetter and more acidic. After adjusting the acid for the water, the supplier has no effect (p = 0.61). What does that suggest?

Kestrel’s lots aren’t really more acidic
Kestrel’s extra acid comes from its extra water, so fixing the water would fix the acid
The water and the acid are unrelated


The acid is higher, but no higher than its water content predicts. That’s what a step-down (covariate-adjusted) follow-up can reveal.

title: Linear contrasts and simultaneous inference
text:
Wrap-up
You can now turn a significant MANOVA into specific findings! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Contrasts of mean vectors: \boldsymbol\psi = \sum c_i\boldsymbol\mu_i with \sum c_i = 0, estimated by \sum c_i\bar{\mathbf{x}}_i with covariance (\sum c_i^2/n_i)\Sigma, and tested with T^2 and an F_{p,\,N-k-p+1} distribution.
car::linearHypothesis() tests contrasts on a cell-means model, lm(cbind(...) ~ 0 + group), from a hypothesis matrix of weights.
Which properties: Bonferroni intervals for planned contrasts, or wider T^2-type intervals for unplanned ones.
All pairs: with g groups and p properties, Bonferroni uses \alpha/2r per tail for r = p\,g(g-1)/2 intervals.
The feed lots: Kestrel is wetter and more acidic, Rosewater carries aldehyde, Plum Valley iron, and Fizzwell is the clean baseline.
Step-down follow-ups ask whether a difference survives adjustment for its cause. Kestrel’s acid doesn’t: it’s a water problem.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download feed_lots.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Several contrasts at once. Test the three contrasts of this lesson jointly with a three-row hypothesis matrix in car::linearHypothesis(). Do the four statistics agree now? Compare the result with Lesson 6’s MANOVA. Why are they the same? (Hint: what do three different contrasts of four groups span?)
T²-type intervals. Compute the T^2-type intervals for the Kestrel contrast, with the multiplier 3.29, and compare them with the Bonferroni ones. Which conclusions change?
An orthogonal set. With weights proportional to the group sizes, the contrasts (-\tfrac{16}{43}, 1, -\tfrac{14}{43}, -\tfrac{13}{43}), (-\tfrac{16}{30}, 0, -\tfrac{14}{30}, 1) and (1, 0, -1, 0) are orthogonal. Check that \sum c_i d_i/n_i = 0 for each pair, compute each contrast’s SSCP matrix, \hat{\boldsymbol\psi}\hat{\boldsymbol\psi}^\top/\sum(c_i^2/n_i), and check that the three add up to Lesson 6’s H.
A full step-down analysis. Order the properties by your chemistry (water first, since it causes acid, then the others), and test each one after adjusting for the ones before it. Which supplier differences remain?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Contrast

A weighted combination of group means whose weights add up to zero, used to answer a specific comparison.

Hypothesis matrix

A matrix whose rows are contrast weights, used to test one or several contrasts at once.

Cell-means model

A model with one mean (coefficient) per group and no intercept, ~ 0 + group, convenient for writing contrasts.

Orthogonal contrasts

Contrasts with \sum c_i d_i/n_i = 0, whose sums of squares (or SSCP matrices) add up to the between-group total.

Pairwise comparisons

Comparisons of every pair of groups, which need a multiple-comparison adjustment such as Bonferroni.

Step-down analysis

Testing each response after adjusting for responses that come before it in a meaningful order, to see whether a difference is explained by another.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 505, Lesson 8: Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA), sections 8.6 to 8.8. Orthogonal contrasts, how to build them, and their tests.
Johnson and Wichern, Applied Multivariate Statistical Analysis, chapter 6, section 6.5, “Simultaneous confidence intervals for treatment effects”. The Bonferroni intervals for every pair and every variable.
John Fox and Sanford Weisberg, Multivariate linear models in R, a free online appendix to An R Companion to Applied Regression. How car::linearHypothesis() and car::Anova() test hypotheses in multivariate models, including repeated-measures designs.

title: Repeated-measures designs
text:
Module 3 · Lesson 9 of 13 Week 55 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The kinetics lab wants to know how fast three catalysts work, not just how far each batch gets. So they ran 24 batches, eight with each catalyst, and sampled every batch at 15, 30, 45, 60 and 90 minutes to measure the conversion. That’s a repeated-measures design: each batch is measured five times.
Five samples of the same batch aren’t five independent runs. A batch that’s ahead at 15 minutes is usually still ahead at 90 minutes, so the five measurements are correlated. That’s exactly the situation multivariate methods are made for: treat each batch’s five measurements as one vector. This lesson shows that approach, the classical univariate one and its main assumption, and a third approach that uses the chemistry.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Repeated-measures designs
text:
The kinetics study
The data come in wide format, one row per batch and one column per sampling time. Here are all 24 batches, with each catalyst’s mean profile in bold:

long_num <- pr |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(starts_with("conv_"), names_to = "time", names_prefix = "conv_", values_to = "conversion") |>
  mutate(time = as.numeric(time))
mean_profiles <- long_num |> group_by(catalyst, time) |> summarise(conversion = mean(conversion), .groups = "drop")
ggplot(long_num, aes(x = time, y = conversion, color = catalyst)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = batch_id), alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = mean_profiles, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(data = mean_profiles, size = 2.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(A = "#2a78d6", B = "#C2416C", C = "#1baf7a"), name = "Catalyst") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(15, 30, 45, 60, 90)) +
  labs(x = "Time (minutes)", y = "Conversion (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Catalyst B is the fastest, and C the slowest. Every curve rises steeply at first and then levels off as the conversion approaches 100%, which is what first-order kinetics predicts. The batches also spread out within each catalyst: some B batches are well ahead of others from the first sample on.
The batch is the subject here: the unit that’s measured repeatedly. The catalyst is a between-subjects factor, since each batch has one catalyst. The time is a within-subjects factor, since every batch is measured at every time.










Your turn. How strongly are the five measurements of a batch correlated? Compute the correlations of the residuals from a model with one mean profile per catalyst. Removing each catalyst’s mean profile leaves the way batches with the same catalyst vary together.









Take the correlations of r, the residuals.


r <- resid(lm(cbind(conv_15, conv_30, conv_45, conv_60, conv_90) ~ catalyst, data = pr))
round(cor(r), 2)
All the correlations are between 0.81 and 0.97: a batch that’s ahead stays ahead. They’re highest for samples close in time (0.97 for 15 and 30 minutes) and lowest for the samples furthest apart (0.81 for 15 and 90 minutes). Treating the 120 measurements as independent would be badly wrong.

title: Repeated-measures designs
text:
Profile analysis
In Lesson 5, a profile plot drew a mean vector as a line across its variables. When the variables are the same measurement at different times, that line is a profile over time, and comparing the groups’ profiles is called profile analysis. It asks three questions, in order:

Are the profiles parallel? That’s the catalyst × time interaction: does the conversion change over time in the same way with every catalyst?
Are the profiles at the same level? That’s the catalyst’s main effect: averaged over the five times, is the conversion the same?
Are the profiles flat? That’s the time’s main effect: averaged over the catalysts, does the conversion change with time?

The trick is to transform each batch’s five measurements. Parallel profiles have the same gains from one sample to the next. So parallelism is a one-way MANOVA of the four gains, \mathbf{d} = (x_{30} - x_{15},\ x_{45} - x_{30},\ x_{60} - x_{45},\ x_{90} - x_{60}). The level is a one-way ANOVA of each batch’s average. And flatness is a test that the mean gains are all zero.
Your turn. The setup code has stored the five measurements as the matrix Y. Compute the gains between consecutive samples.









Y[, -1] drops the first column. Drop the last column, the fifth, from the other copy.


D <- Y[, -1] - Y[, -5]
colnames(D) <- c("gain_15_30", "gain_30_45", "gain_45_60", "gain_60_90")
colMeans(D)
Y[, -1] holds the samples from 30 to 90 minutes and Y[, -5] those from 15 to 60, so their difference is each sample minus the one before it. On average, the conversion rises by 23 points from 15 to 30 minutes, 14 points from 30 to 45, 9 from 45 to 60, and 9 from 60 to 90. (The last gain covers 30 minutes, not 15.)




Your turn. Test whether the profiles are parallel: a MANOVA of the four gains on the catalyst.









The gains are compared between the catalysts: D ~ catalyst.


summary(manova(D ~ catalyst, data = pr))
Pillai’s trace 0.89, F = 3.84 on 8 and 38 degrees of freedom, p = 0.002. The profiles aren’t parallel: the catalysts gain conversion at different rates over time. B gains the most early on, and then has the least left to gain: from 60 to 90 minutes, B’s batches gain 5 points and C’s 12.




Your turn. Test whether the profiles are at the same level: an ANOVA of each batch’s average conversion.









Average each row of Y, the five measurements.


pr$average <- rowMeans(Y)
anova(lm(average ~ catalyst, data = pr))
F = 17.1 on 2 and 21 degrees of freedom, p = 0.00004. Averaged over the five samples, the conversion is 77.6% with B, 68.4% with A and 61.4% with C. Since the profiles aren’t parallel, this level test is an average over differences that change with time, much like a main effect with an interaction in Lesson 8. Here, though, B leads at every time and C trails at every time, so the summary is fair.




The third question hardly needs asking here: the conversion obviously rises with time. The flatness test agrees, with F = 3276.

title: Repeated-measures designs
text:
The multivariate approach in R
car::Anova() runs all three tests in one call, on the multivariate model of the five measurements. You tell it how the five columns are organized with an intra-subject design: idata is a data frame with one row per column of the response (here, a time factor), and idesign is a formula in its variables.
Your turn. The setup code has fitted mlm, the model of the five measurements on the catalyst, and stored times, a data frame with the five times as a factor. Run the repeated-measures analysis.









The within-subjects factor is time.


car::Anova(mlm, idata = times, idesign = ~ time)
Three tests you’ve already done by hand:

catalyst is the level test, F = 17.1, p = 0.00004.
time is the flatness test, F = 3276.
catalyst:time is the parallelism test: Pillai’s trace 0.89, p = 0.002.

(The (Intercept) line tests whether the overall average conversion is zero, which is of no interest.)

title: Repeated-measures designs
text:
The univariate approach and sphericity
The classical alternative is a repeated-measures ANOVA, which is a split-plot ANOVA in disguise. Each batch is a whole plot that gets one catalyst, and the five times are its subplots. aov() fits it from the data in long format, one row per measurement, with an Error() term that says the times are nested in the batches:

long <- pr |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(starts_with("conv_"), names_to = "time", names_prefix = "conv_", values_to = "conversion") |>
  mutate(time = factor(time, levels = c("15", "30", "45", "60", "90")))
summary(aov(conversion ~ catalyst * time + Error(batch_id / time), data = long))
#> 
#> Error: batch_id
#>           Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
#> catalyst   2   5271  2635.7   17.11 3.91e-05 ***
#> Residuals 21   3236   154.1                     
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Error: batch_id:time
#>               Df Sum Sq Mean Sq  F value   Pr(>F)    
#> time           4  44431   11108 2397.246  < 2e-16 ***
#> catalyst:time  8    290      36    7.823 8.49e-08 ***
#> Residuals     84    389       5                      
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

There are two error strata. The catalyst is tested against the variation between batches, with 21 degrees of freedom, and gives the level test again. The time and the interaction are tested against the variation within batches, with 84 degrees of freedom. These F-tests are more powerful than the multivariate ones: the interaction has F = 7.8 and p = 10^{-7}, against p = 0.002.
That power comes from an assumption called sphericity: the difference between the measurements at any two times has the same variance, whichever two times they are. (Equal variances at every time, with equal correlations between every pair of times, is enough for it.) Here, the variance of the gain from 15 to 30 minutes is 3.7, and of the gain from 30 to 90 minutes 19.9. That’s far from equal.
Mauchly’s test checks sphericity. When it fails, the usual fix is to multiply both degrees of freedom of each within-subjects F-test by a correction factor \varepsilon between 1/(t - 1) and 1, where t is the number of times. Two estimates of \varepsilon are common: the Greenhouse-Geisser estimate, which is a little conservative, and the Huynh-Feldt estimate, which is a little less so.
Your turn. The setup code has stored the result of car::Anova() as av. Ask for its univariate tests, which come with Mauchly’s test and both corrections.









multivariate = FALSE leaves out the multivariate tests.


summary(av, multivariate = FALSE)
Mauchly’s test rejects sphericity (W = 0.18, p = 0.0001), and the Greenhouse-Geisser estimate is \hat\varepsilon = 0.52: well below 1, which would mean no problem, though above the worst case, 0.25. With the correction, the interaction’s p-value goes from 10^{-7} to 0.00007.




Here are all the tests of the interaction side by side:



Test of the catalyst × time interaction
p-value




Univariate, assuming sphericity
0.00000008


Univariate, Greenhouse-Geisser corrected
0.00007


Univariate, Huynh-Feldt corrected
0.00003


Multivariate (Pillai’s trace)
0.002



They agree that the profiles aren’t parallel, but the uncorrected test is far too optimistic. Which should you report? The multivariate test makes no sphericity assumption at all, but it needs enough subjects (at least t - 1 error degrees of freedom), and with few subjects it has less power. The corrected univariate tests are the usual choice with small samples. Reporting the multivariate test and a corrected univariate test together is common, and when they agree, as here, the conclusion is safe. The modern alternative is a mixed model that describes the correlations directly and copes with missing samples, which the next lesson introduces.

title: Repeated-measures designs
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Epsilon by hand. Sphericity has a neat matrix form. Take t - 1 = 4 orthonormal contrasts of the five times: columns that each sum to zero, have length 1, and are orthogonal to each other. contr.poly(5) is one such set. If C holds them, then M = C^\top S_p C is the covariance matrix of the four contrasts, where S_p is the pooled within-catalyst covariance matrix. Sphericity means that M is a multiple of the identity matrix, with all its eigenvalues equal. The Greenhouse-Geisser estimate measures how unequal they are:

\hat\varepsilon = \frac{\big(\operatorname{tr} M\big)^2}{(t - 1)\operatorname{tr}\big(M^2\big)} = \frac{\big(\sum \lambda_j\big)^2}{(t - 1)\sum \lambda_j^2} .

It’s 1 when the eigenvalues are equal, and 1/(t-1) when only one isn’t zero. Compute it. (The setup code has stored S_p as Sp.)









\operatorname{tr}(M^2) is sum(diag(M %*% M)).


C <- contr.poly(5)
M <- t(C) %*% Sp %*% C
sum(diag(M))^2 / (4 * sum(diag(M %*% M)))
0.5168, the same as car reported. The eigenvalues of M are 12.3, 3.4, 1.5 and 1.3: far from equal. (contr.poly() is designed for equally spaced levels, and the times aren’t. That doesn’t matter here: every set of orthonormal contrasts gives the same eigenvalues, and so the same \hat\varepsilon.)




Challenge 2 · Let the chemistry summarize. A chemical engineer would summarize each batch by its rate constant. For a first-order reaction, the conversion is X = 100\,(1 - e^{-kt}) percent at time t. The setup code has a function, fit_k(), that fits this curve to one batch’s five samples by nonlinear least squares (nls()), and returns k. Apply it to every row of Y, then compare the catalysts’ rate constants with a one-way ANOVA.









apply(Y, 1, f) applies f to each row of Y.


pr$k <- apply(Y, 1, fit_k)
anova(lm(k ~ catalyst, data = pr))
F = 14.3 on 2 and 21 degrees of freedom, p = 0.0001. The mean rate constants are 0.030 per minute for A, 0.042 for B and 0.023 for C. In half-lives, \ln 2/k, a typical batch is half converted after 23 minutes with A, 17 with B and 30 with C.
That’s the summary-statistic approach: reduce each subject’s profile to one meaningful number, then use an ordinary method. It sidesteps sphericity entirely, and it answers the question the lab actually asked. It also explains why the profiles can’t be parallel: a faster first-order reaction gains more early and then has less left to gain.

title: Repeated-measures designs
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why can’t the 120 conversion measurements be analyzed as 120 independent runs?

Because there are too many of them
Because the five measurements of the same batch are correlated
Because the conversion can’t exceed 100%


A batch that’s ahead stays ahead: the within-catalyst correlations are 0.81 to 0.97.



2. In profile analysis, what do parallel profiles mean?

No difference between the groups at all
No group × time interaction: the groups change over time in the same way
No change over time


Parallel profiles have the same gains between consecutive times, which is why parallelism is tested with a MANOVA of the gains.



3. In the split-plot ANOVA, what is the catalyst tested against?

The variation between batches
The variation within batches
The variation between times


Each batch gets one catalyst, so the batches are the catalyst’s replicates.



4. What does sphericity mean?

All the measurements have the same mean
The difference between any two times has the same variance
The measurements are uncorrelated


Equal variances and equal correlations are enough for it. Here, the variances of the differences range from 3.7 to 19.9.



5. Mauchly’s test gives p = 0.0001, and \hat\varepsilon = 0.52. What should you do?

Report the univariate tests that assume sphericity
Use the Greenhouse-Geisser or Huynh-Feldt corrected tests, or the multivariate tests
Drop the time factor from the model


The corrections multiply the degrees of freedom by \hat\varepsilon. The multivariate tests don’t assume sphericity at all.



6. What’s the summary-statistic approach?

Reporting the means and standard deviations at each time
Reducing each subject’s profile to one meaningful number, such as a rate constant, and analyzing those numbers
Averaging the p-values of the univariate and multivariate tests


With a good summary, the analysis is simple and answers the real question.

title: Repeated-measures designs
text:
Wrap-up
You can now analyze measurements repeated over time! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Repeated measures on the same subject are correlated, so the subject, not the measurement, is the unit of replication.
Profile analysis asks whether the profiles are parallel (a MANOVA of the gains), at the same level (an ANOVA of the averages) and flat (a test that the mean gains are zero).
car::Anova(mlm, idata, idesign) runs the multivariate tests in one call, and summary(..., multivariate = FALSE) adds the univariate ones.
The univariate approach is a split-plot ANOVA. It assumes sphericity. Check it with Mauchly’s test, and correct for it with the Greenhouse-Geisser or Huynh-Feldt \varepsilon.
The multivariate approach makes no sphericity assumption, but needs enough subjects, and has less power when there are few.
The summary-statistic approach reduces each profile to a meaningful number. For the kinetics study, first-order rate constants show that B is the fastest catalyst and C the slowest.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download profiles.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

A first mixed model. With the long data, fit lme4::lmer(conversion ~ catalyst * time + (1 | batch_id), data = long) and look at anova() of it. Its F values match the univariate ANOVA that assumes sphericity. Why? (Hint: a random intercept for each batch gives every pair of times the same correlation.)
Half-lives. Compute each batch’s half-life, \ln 2/k, and compare the catalysts with a one-way ANOVA and Tukey’s intervals. Which pairs of catalysts differ?
A linearized fit. Compute k instead as the slope through the origin of -\ln(1 - X/100) against t. Batches K13 and K15 reached the analyzer’s upper limit of 99.9% at 90 minutes. What happens to their linearized rate constants, and why does the nonlinear fit cope better?
Profile plots of the gains. Plot each catalyst’s mean gains between consecutive samples. How does the plot show the non-parallel profiles?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Repeated-measures design

A design in which each subject is measured several times, under different conditions or at different times.

Within-subjects and between-subjects factors

A within-subjects factor varies within each subject (here, the time). A between-subjects factor is fixed for each subject (here, the catalyst).

Profile analysis

Comparing groups’ mean profiles by testing whether they’re parallel, at the same level and flat.

Sphericity

The assumption that the difference between any two repeated measurements has the same variance. The univariate repeated-measures F-tests need it.

Mauchly’s test

A test of sphericity.

Greenhouse-Geisser and Huynh-Feldt corrections

Estimates of \varepsilon, the factor by which the degrees of freedom of the within-subjects F-tests are multiplied when sphericity fails.

Summary-statistic approach

Reducing each subject’s repeated measurements to one meaningful number, then analyzing those numbers.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 505, Lesson 9: Repeated Measures Analysis. The split-plot ANOVA, its criticisms, and the MANOVA approach, with a worked example.
Penn State STAT 502, Lesson 11: Introduction to Repeated Measures. The univariate view: the historical methods, correlated residuals and covariance structures.
John Fox and Sanford Weisberg, Multivariate linear models in R, section 3, “Handling repeated measures”. How idata and idesign work in car::Anova().
Johnson and Wichern, Applied Multivariate Statistical Analysis, chapter 6, sections 6.8 and 6.9, “Profile analysis” and “Repeated measures designs and growth curves”.

title: Multivariate regression and correlation
text:
Module 3 · Lesson 11 of 13 Week 57 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lessons 1 to 4 described the four quality properties of the 80 batches: purity, water, color and acid. Now the process engineers want to know what drives them. Each batch also has a record of its process conditions: the reactor temperature, the residence time, the water content of the feed, and the catalyst. That’s four responses and four predictors.
One regression per property would give the coefficients, as in Module 2. But some questions involve all four properties at once. Does the residence time matter for the product’s quality at all? Are two properties linked directly, or only because the same conditions drive both? This lesson answers them with multivariate multiple regression and partial correlation.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Multivariate regression and correlation
text:
The model
As in Lesson 4, FS73, the batch with the acid-wash residue, is left out. The color goes in on the log scale, which Lesson 3 found closer to normal:

bq <- read_csv("data/batch_quality.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(batch_id != "FS73") |>
  mutate(log_color = log(color_apha), catalyst = factor(catalyst))
select(bq, batch_id, temp_C:catalyst, purity_pct, water_ppm, log_color, acid_mgKOH) |> head(4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 9
#>   batch_id temp_C residence_min feed_water_ppm catalyst purity_pct water_ppm
#>   <chr>     <dbl>         <dbl>          <dbl> <fct>         <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 FS01       181.          36.4            321 B              99.0       205
#> 2 FS02       191.          48.2            196 B              99.2       122
#> 3 FS03       176.          62.8            275 A              99.3       133
#> 4 FS04       179.          62.5            329 B              99.1       176
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: log_color <dbl>, acid_mgKOH <dbl>

With n batches, q responses and k predictors, the multivariate multiple regression model is

\underset{n \times q}{Y} = \underset{n \times (k+1)}{X}\ \underset{(k+1) \times q}{B} + \underset{n \times q}{\mathcal{E}},

where each row of \mathcal{E} is a N_q(\mathbf{0}, \Sigma) error vector. Y holds the four responses as columns, X is the usual design matrix of Lesson 2.4, and B has one column of coefficients per response. The least-squares estimate is the familiar formula with a matrix in place of a vector:

\hat B = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top Y .

So each column of \hat B is exactly what a separate regression of that response would give.
