What’s new is everything that involves the responses together: the error covariance matrix \Sigma, estimated by \hat\Sigma = \hat{\mathcal{E}}^\top\hat{\mathcal{E}}/(n - k - 1), and the tests built on it. In R, lm() fits the model when the response is a matrix, cbind() of the response columns.










Your turn. The setup code has loaded the 79 batches as bq. Fit the multivariate regression of the four properties on the four process conditions, and look at its coefficients.









The fourth response is the acid, acid_mgKOH.


mlm <- lm(cbind(purity_pct, water_ppm, log_color, acid_mgKOH) ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst, data = bq)
coef(mlm)
A 5 × 4 matrix: one column per response, one row per coefficient. Reading down the water’s column: each extra minute of residence time takes out 1.09 ppm of water, and each extra ppm of water in the feed leaves 0.51 ppm more in the product. Fit lm(water_ppm ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst, data = bq) on its own, and you’ll get the same numbers.

title: Multivariate regression and correlation
section: Testing a predictor on all the responses
text:
Testing a predictor on all the responses
Does the residence time matter for the product’s quality? In the multivariate model, that’s the hypothesis that its whole row of B is zero: no effect on any of the four properties. Each predictor gets an SSCP matrix H, which compares the model’s fit with and without it, and H is tested against the error matrix E with the four statistics of Lesson 6. A predictor with one coefficient per response has a rank-1 H, so all four statistics give the same F-test.
car::Anova() runs these tests for every predictor. Its Type II tests compare the full model with the model that drops one predictor, so the order of the predictors doesn’t matter.
Your turn. The setup code has fitted the model as mlm. Run the multivariate tests.









The function is car::Anova(), with a capital A.


car::Anova(mlm)
Every process condition matters for the quality as a whole. The temperature (Pillai’s trace 0.93) and the feed water (0.79) have enormous effects. The residence time’s is smaller but clear (0.37, p = 10^{-6}), and the catalyst’s is the smallest (p = 0.001).




Which properties does each condition affect? summary(mlm) prints the four separate regressions’ coefficient tables. Here they are, with each condition’s effect on each property and its p-value:











Purity (%)
Water (ppm)
log color
Acid (mg KOH/g)




Temperature (per °C)
−0.051 (< 0.0001)
−0.07 (0.78)
+0.037 (< 0.0001)
+0.0030 (< 0.0001)


Residence time (per minute)
+0.001 (0.54)
−1.09 (< 0.0001)
+0.007 (0.0001)
−0.0010 (< 0.0001)


Feed water (per ppm)
−0.0027 (< 0.0001)
+0.51 (< 0.0001)
+0.0003 (0.37)
+0.0004 (< 0.0001)


Catalyst B (against A)
+0.127 (0.00002)
−0.3 (0.93)
+0.010 (0.71)
−0.0011 (0.75)



The heat lowers the purity and darkens the product. A longer residence time dries it, but darkens it a little. Wet feed makes wet, slightly less pure product. And catalyst B seems to raise the purity, by 0.13 percentage points, and to do nothing else.
Your turn. Is that last impression right? Test the catalyst’s effect on the other three properties together, with a multivariate regression of the water, the log color and the acid.









The third of the other properties is acid_mgKOH.


others <- lm(cbind(water_ppm, log_color, acid_mgKOH) ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst, data = bq)
car::Anova(others)
For the catalyst, Pillai’s trace is 0.0035 and p = 0.97. There’s no sign that catalyst B changes the water, the color or the acid, in any combination. Its only effect is on the purity.




Your turn. Next week’s campaign will run at 190 °C with 45 minutes of residence time, on catalyst A, with feed from Kestrel, at about 250 ppm of water. Predict all four properties at once.









The feed water is 250 ppm.


planned <- data.frame(temp_C = 190, residence_min = 45, feed_water_ppm = 250, catalyst = "A")
predict(mlm, newdata = planned)
Purity 98.72%, water 152 ppm, log color 2.88 (that’s e^{2.88} = 17.8 APHA), and acid 0.245 mg KOH/g. Wet feed, a hot reactor and a short residence time make a wet, acidic product. With the estimated error covariance matrix, you could also put a joint prediction region around these four numbers, like the ellipses of Lesson 2.

title: Multivariate regression and correlation
text:
Multiple correlation
How well do the process conditions predict each property? The multiple correlation R between a response and a set of predictors is the largest correlation between the response and any linear combination of the predictors. That combination is the regression’s fitted value, so R is the correlation between y and \hat y, and R^2 is the regression’s coefficient of determination from Module 2. Its test is the regression’s overall F-test.
Your turn. summary(mlm) is a list of four regression summaries, one per response. Pull out each one’s R^2.









A regression summary stores its R^2 as r.squared.


sapply(summary(mlm), function(s) s$r.squared)
The process conditions explain 89% of the variation in purity, 81% in log color, 75% in acid and 74% in water. The multiple correlations, the square roots, are 0.95, 0.90, 0.87 and 0.86.

title: Multivariate regression and correlation
text:
Partial correlation
The four properties are strongly correlated with each other. For example, the purity and the log color have a correlation of −0.78, and the water and the acid 0.64. Are these direct links? Or are they there only because the same process conditions drive both properties?
The partial correlation of two variables, given a set of other variables, answers that. It’s the correlation between what’s left of the two after the linear effect of the others is taken out: the correlation of the two sets of residuals. Here, the residuals of the multivariate regression do the job at once. Their correlation matrix is the matrix of partial correlations of the responses, given the process conditions.
Here are the two pairs before and after the process conditions are taken out:

mlm <- lm(cbind(purity_pct, water_ppm, log_color, acid_mgKOH) ~ temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst, data = bq)
res <- as.data.frame(resid(mlm))
panel_levels <- c("Purity and log color, as measured", "Purity and log color, after the process conditions",
                  "Water and acid, as measured", "Water and acid, after the process conditions")
scatter <- bind_rows(
  tibble(panel = panel_levels[1], x = bq$purity_pct, y = bq$log_color),
  tibble(panel = panel_levels[2], x = res$purity_pct, y = res$log_color),
  tibble(panel = panel_levels[3], x = bq$water_ppm, y = bq$acid_mgKOH),
  tibble(panel = panel_levels[4], x = res$water_ppm, y = res$acid_mgKOH)
) |>
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = panel_levels))
r_labels <- scatter |> group_by(panel) |> summarise(r = sprintf("r = %.2f", cor(x, y)))
ggplot(scatter, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(color = "#3A1F35", alpha = 0.7, size = 1.5) +
  geom_text(data = r_labels, aes(label = r), x = -Inf, y = Inf, hjust = -0.15, vjust = 1.5, color = "#C2416C", size = 3.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "First property", y = "Second property") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)








The purity and the color look tightly linked, but the link disappears completely once the process conditions are taken out: their partial correlation is 0.00. Hot batches are both less pure and darker, and that’s all. The water and the acid keep their whole correlation, 0.64. That’s a direct link, and the chemistry explains it: water hydrolyzes the product into acid.
Your turn. Compute the correlation matrix of the residuals: the partial correlations of the four properties, given the process conditions.









The residuals of a model are resid(mlm).


round(cor(resid(mlm)), 2)
Every partial correlation is close to zero, except the water’s and the acid’s, 0.64. Once the process conditions are known, the four properties vary independently, except for the water-acid link. That’s the multivariate regression’s estimate of \Sigma, rescaled to a correlation matrix.










NoteGo deeper: partial correlations from the inverse correlation matrix





There’s a neat shortcut. If P = R^{-1} is the inverse of the correlation matrix of a set of variables, the partial correlation of variables i and j, given all the others in the set, is

r_{ij \cdot \text{rest}} = -\frac{P_{ij}}{\sqrt{P_{ii}\,P_{jj}}} .

That’s how software computes partial correlation networks, which draw a line between two variables only when their partial correlation isn’t zero. Try it with the four process conditions (with the catalyst as a 0/1 column) and the four properties: the water-acid partial correlation, given everything else, is still 0.64.

title: Multivariate regression and correlation
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Testing a partial correlation. Is the water-acid partial correlation, r = 0.64, more than chance? A partial correlation given m variables is tested like an ordinary correlation, with m fewer degrees of freedom:

t = \frac{r\sqrt{n - 2 - m}}{\sqrt{1 - r^2}}, \quad \text{on } n - 2 - m \text{ degrees of freedom.}

Here, n = 79 and m = 4: temperature, residence time, feed water and the catalyst’s 0/1 column. Compute t and its p-value. (cor.test() on the two sets of residuals would use n - 2 = 77 degrees of freedom, which is slightly too many.)









Four variables are partialled out: m = 4.


r <- cor(resid(mlm))["water_ppm", "acid_mgKOH"]
df <- 79 - 2 - 4
t_stat <- r * sqrt(df) / sqrt(1 - r^2)
c(t = t_stat, p = 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), df))
t = 7.12 on 73 degrees of freedom, p = 6 \times 10^{-10}. The water-acid link is real.




Challenge 2 · Through the water. The residence time and the feed water both affect the acid, according to the table above. Do they act on the acid directly, or only through the water they leave in the product? Fit the acid on the water and the temperature, then test whether the other three conditions add anything.









The third condition to add is the catalyst.


small <- lm(acid_mgKOH ~ water_ppm + temp_C, data = bq)
large <- lm(acid_mgKOH ~ water_ppm + temp_C + residence_min + feed_water_ppm + catalyst, data = bq)
anova(small, large)
F = 0.90, p = 0.44. Once the product’s water and the temperature are known, the residence time, the feed water and the catalyst tell you nothing more about the acid. They affect the acid only through the water, which fits the hydrolysis story: to control the acid, control the water and the temperature. That’s the step-down idea of Lesson 7 again.

title: Multivariate regression and correlation
text:
Quick quiz

1. How do the coefficients of a multivariate multiple regression compare with separate regressions of each response?

They’re exactly the same
They’re smaller, because the responses are correlated
They’re different, because the model uses \Sigma


\hat B = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top Y works column by column. What the multivariate model adds is joint inference.



2. What does car::Anova(mlm) test for the residence time?

Whether it affects the water
Whether it affects any of the four responses, in any combination
Whether it’s correlated with the other predictors


It tests that the residence time’s whole row of B is zero.



3. What’s the multiple correlation of a response with a set of predictors?

The average of the response’s correlations with each predictor
The correlation between the response and its fitted values, the best linear combination of the predictors
The correlation between two responses, given the predictors


Its square is the regression’s R^2.



4. The purity and the log color have a correlation of −0.78, but a partial correlation of 0.00 given the process conditions. What does that mean?

The correlation of −0.78 was a calculation error
The link comes from shared causes: hot batches are both less pure and darker
Purity and color are measured badly


Once the temperature and the other conditions are accounted for, nothing links the two.



5. How many degrees of freedom does the t-test for a partial correlation given 4 variables have, with n = 79?

77
73
75


n - 2 - m = 79 - 2 - 4 = 73.



6. Given the water and the temperature, the residence time and the feed water add nothing to the model of the acid. What does that suggest?

They don’t affect the acid at all
They affect the acid only through the water they leave in the product
The water should be removed from the model


Their effect on the acid is real, but it’s carried by the water.

title: Multivariate regression and correlation
text:
Wrap-up
You can now model several responses on the same predictors! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Multivariate multiple regression, Y = XB + \mathcal{E}, is fitted by lm(cbind(...) ~ ...). Its coefficients are those of separate regressions.
Multivariate tests of each predictor, car::Anova(), ask whether it affects any response. Here, catalyst B affects only the purity.
Prediction with predict() gives all the responses at once.
The multiple correlation R is the correlation between a response and its fitted values, with R^2 the familiar coefficient of determination.
Partial correlations, the correlations of residuals, separate direct links from shared causes. Purity and color share causes; water and acid are linked directly.
A partial correlation given m variables is tested with n - 2 - m degrees of freedom.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download batch_quality.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

The inverse correlation matrix. Build the partial correlations of all eight variables (the catalyst as a 0/1 column) from the inverse of their correlation matrix, as in the “Go deeper” box. Which links survive among the process conditions themselves?
With FS73. Refit the model with FS73 included. Which residual stands out, and how does it change the water-acid partial correlation?
Interaction terms. Does the temperature’s effect on the color depend on the residence time? Add temp_C:residence_min to the multivariate model, and test it with car::Anova().
Two predictors together. Use car::linearHypothesis(mlm, c("temp_C = 0", "residence_min = 0")) to test two predictors together on all four responses. How many non-zero eigenvalues does its E^{-1}H have, and why?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Multivariate multiple regression

A regression of several responses on the same predictors, Y = XB + \mathcal{E}, with correlated errors.

Coefficient matrix

B, with one column of regression coefficients per response.

Error covariance matrix

\Sigma, the covariance matrix of a row of errors, estimated from the residuals.

Multiple correlation

The correlation between a response and its best linear prediction from a set of predictors. Its square is R^2.

Partial correlation

The correlation between two variables after the linear effects of a set of other variables have been removed from both.

Shared cause

A variable that drives two others, making them correlated even when neither affects the other.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 505, Lesson 6: Multivariate Conditional Distribution and Partial Correlation. Conditional distributions, partial correlations and their tests.
John Fox and Sanford Weisberg, Multivariate linear models in R, section 2. Fitting and testing multivariate regressions with lm() and car.
Johnson and Wichern, Applied Multivariate Statistical Analysis, chapter 7, “Multivariate linear regression models”, especially section 7.7. The model, its tests and prediction regions.

title: Linear discriminant analysis
text:
Module 3 · Lesson 13 of 13 Week 59 of 160 About 5–7 hours
A forklift accident in the warehouse knocked over a pallet, and six drums of feed lost their labels. Nobody knows which supplier sent which drum. The lab sampled each one and measured the same four properties as the incoming lots of Lessons 5 to 7:
drums
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   drum_id water_ppm aldehyde_ppm acid_mgKOH iron_ppb
#>   <chr>       <dbl>        <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 U1            206         56.1      0.1       38  
#> 2 U2            174         43.2      0.091     32.4
#> 3 U3            348         54.7      0.157     36.8
#> 4 U4            205         56.4      0.086     56  
#> 5 U5            197         40.4      0.082     34.6
#> 6 U6            215         41.4      0.134     48.1
The 58 labeled lots of Lessons 5 to 7 show what each supplier’s feed looks like. Discriminant analysis turns them into a rule that assigns a new case to one of several known groups. It’s a classification method, like the logistic regression of Lesson 2.15 but for several groups at once, and Module 7 builds many more.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Linear discriminant analysis
text:
Fisher’s linear discriminants
In 1936, R. A. Fisher asked: which linear combination \mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x} of the variables separates the groups best? “Best” means the largest ratio of the between-group variation to the within-group variation of the combination:

\frac{\mathbf{a}^\top H \mathbf{a}}{\mathbf{a}^\top E \mathbf{a}},

with H and E the between-group and within-group SSCP matrices of one-way MANOVA (Lesson 6). The answer is the eigenvector of E^{-1}H with the largest eigenvalue: the first linear discriminant. The next eigenvectors give the second and third discriminants, each the best separator among the combinations uncorrelated with the earlier ones. With k groups and p variables, there are \min(p, k - 1) of them, here 3.
So the eigenvalues that Lesson 6 turned into Wilks’ lambda, 5.50, 2.14 and 0.46, also measure how well each discriminant separates the suppliers. The first carries 5.50/(5.50 + 2.14 + 0.46) = 68\% of the separation.










Your turn. The setup code has loaded the 58 lots as feed and the six drums as drums. Fit the linear discriminant analysis with MASS::lda().









The groups go on the left of the formula: supplier.


fit <- MASS::lda(supplier ~ water_ppm + aldehyde_ppm + acid_mgKOH + iron_ppb, data = feed)
fit
The printout shows the prior probabilities (the suppliers’ shares of the 58 lots), the group means, the coefficients of the three discriminants, and the “proportion of trace”: 68%, 26% and 6% of the separation. The coefficients depend on the units, so they’re hard to read directly. The next exercise interprets the discriminants a better way.




Your turn. predict(fit)$x holds each lot’s scores on the three discriminants. As with canonical variates in Lesson 12, correlate them with the original variables to see what each discriminant measures.









The scores are in the x component: predict(fit)$x.


scores <- predict(fit)$x
round(cor(X, scores), 2)
Each discriminant is essentially one property. LD1 is the water (0.99), with the acid along for the ride (0.77): it separates Kestrel. LD2 is the aldehyde (0.99): it separates Rosewater. LD3 is the iron (−0.94): it separates Plum Valley from Fizzwell. These are the fingerprints of Lessons 6 and 7, found automatically.




Here are the 58 lots and the six drums on the discriminants. The left panel shows LD1 against LD2, and the right panel LD3 against LD2:

fit <- MASS::lda(supplier ~ water_ppm + aldehyde_ppm + acid_mgKOH + iron_ppb, data = feed)
lot_scores <- as.data.frame(predict(fit)$x) |> mutate(supplier = feed$supplier)
drum_scores <- as.data.frame(predict(fit, newdata = drums)$x) |> mutate(drum = drums$drum_id)
long_scores <- function(d) {
  bind_rows(mutate(d, panel = "LD1 against LD2", horizontal = LD1),
            mutate(d, panel = "LD3 against LD2", horizontal = LD3))
}
drum_points <- long_scores(drum_scores) |>
  mutate(hjust = c(1.4, -0.4, 1.4, -0.4, 1.4, -0.4,    # label sides in the left panel, U1 to U6,
                   -0.4, 1.4, 1.4, -0.4, -0.4, -0.4))  # and the right panel, so no labels overlap
ggplot(long_scores(lot_scores), aes(x = horizontal, y = LD2)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = supplier, shape = supplier), size = 2.2, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_point(data = drum_points, shape = 21, fill = "white", color = "black", size = 3, stroke = 0.9) +
  geom_text(data = drum_points, aes(label = drum, hjust = hjust), size = 3.4, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Fizzwell = "#2a78d6", Kestrel = "#1baf7a", `Plum Valley` = "#C2416C", Rosewater = "#d18a12"), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(Fizzwell = 16, Kestrel = 17, `Plum Valley` = 15, Rosewater = 18), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "LD2") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Kestrel is unmistakable, and so is drum U3. Rosewater sits at the top. Fizzwell and Plum Valley overlap in the left panel and only come apart on LD3, the weakest discriminant, so they’ll be the hardest to tell apart. Drum U1 sits between three suppliers.

title: Linear discriminant analysis
text:
Classifying the drums
Classification needs a rule. Suppose each supplier’s lots are multivariate normal with a common covariance matrix \Sigma (MANOVA’s assumption). Then the probability that a new case \mathbf{x} came from group j is its posterior probability, by Bayes’ theorem:

P(\text{group } j \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{\pi_j f_j(\mathbf{x})}{\sum_i \pi_i f_i(\mathbf{x})},

where f_j is group j’s normal density and \pi_j its prior probability, how common the group is before you look at \mathbf{x}. The rule assigns \mathbf{x} to the group with the largest posterior probability. Because the groups share \Sigma, the boundaries between the groups are straight lines (planes, in four dimensions): that’s why it’s called linear. By default, lda() uses the groups’ shares of the training data as the priors.
Your turn. Classify the six drums, and look at the posterior probabilities.









Predict for the drums data frame.


pred <- predict(fit, newdata = drums)
data.frame(drum = drums$drum_id, supplier = pred$class, round(pred$posterior, 3))
Five clear verdicts: U2 and U5 are Fizzwell’s (posteriors 0.86 and 0.88), U3 is Kestrel’s (1.00), and U4 and U6 are Plum Valley’s (0.90 and 0.96). U1 is assigned to Plum Valley, but with a posterior of only 0.49, against 0.34 for Rosewater and 0.17 for Fizzwell. The rule is guessing. The honest report says so: “U1 is probably Plum Valley’s or Rosewater’s: test it further before using it.”

title: Linear discriminant analysis
text:
LDA is a distance rule
There’s a simpler way to see the rule. Take logs of \pi_j f_j(\mathbf{x}), drop what’s the same for every group, and you’re left with

-\tfrac12 D_j^2(\mathbf{x}) + \ln \pi_j, \qquad D_j^2(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_j)^\top S_p^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_j),

where D_j^2 is the squared Mahalanobis distance of Lesson 2 from \mathbf{x} to group j’s mean, measured with the pooled covariance matrix S_p. So with equal priors, LDA assigns each case to the nearest group mean, in Mahalanobis distance. Unequal priors just give the more common groups a small head start.
Your turn. The setup code has stored the suppliers’ mean vectors as the rows of means, and the pooled covariance matrix as Sp. Compute each drum’s squared distance to each supplier.









Measure the distances with the pooled covariance matrix, Sp.


D2 <- sapply(levs, function(s) mahalanobis(as.matrix(drums[, vars]), means[s, ], Sp))
rownames(D2) <- drums$drum_id
round(D2, 1)
Each drum’s smallest distance picks the same supplier as lda() did. For U1, the distances to Plum Valley (3.2), Rosewater (3.9) and Fizzwell (5.6) are all small: U1 would be an ordinary lot from any of the three. That’s why its posterior probabilities are so evenly split. U3, at a distance of 8.4 from Kestrel, is a slightly unusual Kestrel lot, but it’s 59 or more from everyone else.

title: Linear discriminant analysis
section: How often is the rule wrong?
text:
How often is the rule wrong?
Before trusting the rule, estimate its error rate. The obvious way is to classify the 58 training lots and count the mistakes. That’s the apparent error rate, and it’s optimistic: the rule was fitted to those very lots, so it does better on them than it will on new ones.
The honest way is cross-validation, as in Lesson 2.12: classify each lot with a rule fitted to the other 57. With CV = TRUE, lda() does exactly that (leave-one-out cross-validation), and returns each lot’s cross-validated class.
Your turn. Compute the apparent error rate and the confusion table, which crosses the true suppliers with the predicted ones.









Compare the predictions with the true suppliers, feed$supplier.


predicted <- predict(fit)$class
print(table(true = feed$supplier, predicted = predicted))
mean(predicted != feed$supplier)
6 of the 58 lots are misclassified, an apparent error rate of 10%. Every Kestrel and Rosewater lot is right. The mistakes are mostly between the twins: four Plum Valley lots called Fizzwell’s, and one the other way round. The sixth is a Fizzwell lot called Rosewater’s.




Your turn. Now the honest estimate: the leave-one-out cross-validated error rate.









Set CV = TRUE.


cv <- MASS::lda(supplier ~ water_ppm + aldehyde_ppm + acid_mgKOH + iron_ppb, data = feed, CV = TRUE)
mean(cv$class != feed$supplier)
8 of the 58 lots are misclassified, 14%. On new drums, expect the rule to be wrong about one time in seven, mostly when a drum comes from Fizzwell or Plum Valley. The apparent rate, 10%, was a little optimistic, as expected.

title: Linear discriminant analysis
text:
Quadratic discriminant analysis
LDA assumes that the groups share a covariance matrix. Lesson 6’s Box’s M test said they don’t: Kestrel’s water varies about twice as much as anyone else’s. Quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA) drops the assumption. Each group keeps its own covariance matrix S_j, so the distance to group j is measured with S_j, and the rule adds a term for the size of S_j:

-\tfrac12 \ln\det S_j - \tfrac12 (\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_j)^\top S_j^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_j) + \ln \pi_j .

The boundaries between the groups become curved (quadratic). That’s more flexible, but it costs something. QDA estimates four separate covariance matrices, 40 parameters in all, from 13 to 16 lots per supplier, against 10 parameters for LDA’s single pooled matrix. With small groups, that extra noise can outweigh the better fit.

title: Linear discriminant analysis
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · QDA. Compute QDA’s cross-validated error rate, and compare it with LDA’s 14%.









The function is MASS::qda().


qcv <- MASS::qda(supplier ~ water_ppm + aldehyde_ppm + acid_mgKOH + iron_ppb, data = feed, CV = TRUE)
mean(qcv$class != feed$supplier)
21%: 12 of the 58 lots, worse than LDA’s 8. Its apparent error rate is better than LDA’s (9% against 10%), but that’s the extra flexibility fitting noise. With these small groups, the simpler rule generalizes better, even though its assumption is a little wrong. QDA would earn its keep with larger groups, or with covariance matrices that differ much more.




Challenge 2 · Better priors. The warehouse manager remembers that the pallet was half Rosewater’s drums, with the rest from the other three suppliers. Use priors of 1/2 for Rosewater and 1/6 for each of the others (in the order Fizzwell, Kestrel, Plum Valley, Rosewater), and classify the drums again.









Rosewater’s prior is 1/2.


pred2 <- predict(fit, newdata = drums, prior = c(1/6, 1/6, 1/6, 1/2))
data.frame(drum = drums$drum_id, supplier = pred2$class, round(pred2$posterior, 3))
U1 switches to Rosewater, with a posterior of 0.63. The other five verdicts don’t change, though U4’s posterior for Rosewater rises to 0.26. The data hardly distinguished Rosewater from Plum Valley for U1, so the prior information tipped the balance. For the clear-cut drums, the data overwhelm any reasonable prior.




Postscript. The delivery notes turned up a week later. U2 and U5 were Fizzwell’s, U3 Kestrel’s, U4 and U6 Plum Valley’s, and U1 was Rosewater’s. The LDA rule with the default priors got five of the six drums right, and the one it got wrong was exactly the one whose posterior probabilities said “not sure”.

title: Linear discriminant analysis
text:
Quick quiz

1. How many linear discriminants are there with 4 groups and 4 variables?

4
3
16


There are \min(p, k - 1) = \min(4, 3) = 3.



2. Where do Fisher’s discriminants come from?

The eigenvectors of the total covariance matrix
The eigenvectors of E^{-1}H, the same matrix as in one-way MANOVA
The group means


Each discriminant maximizes the ratio of between-group to within-group variation, \mathbf{a}^\top H\mathbf{a}/\mathbf{a}^\top E\mathbf{a}.



3. With equal priors, which group does LDA assign a case to?

The group with the most training cases
The group whose mean is nearest in Mahalanobis distance, with the pooled covariance matrix
The group whose mean is nearest in Euclidean distance


That’s why LDA works with the variables’ correlations and units, like Lesson 2’s distances.



4. Why is the apparent error rate optimistic?

Because it ignores the priors
Because the rule is tested on the same cases it was fitted to
Because it uses too few cases


Cross-validation tests each case with a rule fitted without it.



5. QDA has a better apparent error rate but a worse cross-validated error rate than LDA. What does that suggest?

QDA is always worse
QDA’s extra flexibility is fitting noise: with small groups, the separate covariance matrices are poorly estimated
The cross-validation is wrong


More parameters fit the training data better, but can predict new data worse.



6. A drum’s posterior probabilities are 0.49, 0.34 and 0.17 for three suppliers. What should you report?

It’s from the first supplier
It’s uncertain: probably the first or the second supplier, and it needs a further test
The rule has failed and should be discarded


Posterior probabilities tell you how sure the rule is, not just what it guesses.

title: Linear discriminant analysis
text:
Wrap-up
You can now classify new cases into known groups! Here’s what you’ve learned:

Fisher’s linear discriminants are the eigenvectors of E^{-1}H: the combinations that best separate the groups. Here, each one is essentially one property: water, aldehyde, iron.
The classification rule assigns a case to the group with the largest posterior probability. With a common covariance matrix, that’s the nearest group mean in Mahalanobis distance, adjusted for the priors.
Posterior probabilities say how sure the rule is. U1’s split posteriors flagged the one drum the rule got wrong.
Error rates: the apparent rate (10%) is optimistic, and leave-one-out cross-validation (14%) is honest.
Priors matter when the data can’t decide. Half-Rosewater priors switched U1 to Rosewater.
QDA gives each group its own covariance matrix. With small groups, it can do worse than LDA, as here (21%).







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download feed_lots.csv and unlabeled_drums.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Fewer variables. Refit the LDA with only the water and the aldehyde. What happens to the cross-validated error rate, and which suppliers get confused? Which property would you add first?
Plot the boundaries. With two variables, LDA’s boundaries are straight lines. Make a fine grid of water and aldehyde values with expand.grid(), classify each grid point, and draw the regions with geom_tile(). Try the same with QDA, and see the curves.
Costs. Sending a Kestrel drum into production unnoticed is expensive, because its water ruins a batch. How would you change the rule to make that mistake rarer? (Hint: what do the priors do?)
A canonical view. candisc::candisc(lm(cbind(water_ppm, aldehyde_ppm, acid_mgKOH, iron_ppb) ~ supplier, data = feed)) gives canonical discriminant analysis, which is the same as LDA’s discriminants with MANOVA’s tests attached. Compare its canonical correlations with the square roots of \lambda/(1 + \lambda) for Lesson 6’s eigenvalues.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Discriminant analysis

A method that builds a rule to assign new cases to one of several known groups.

Linear discriminant

A linear combination of the variables that best separates the groups, an eigenvector of E^{-1}H.

Prior probability

A group’s probability before the case’s measurements are seen, such as its share of all cases.

Posterior probability

A group’s probability after the measurements are seen, by Bayes’ theorem.

Apparent error rate

The share of the training cases that the rule misclassifies. It’s optimistic.

Cross-validated error rate

The share of cases misclassified by rules fitted without them, an honest estimate of the error on new cases.

Quadratic discriminant analysis

Discriminant analysis with a separate covariance matrix for each group, giving curved boundaries.











NoteWant to read more?






Penn State STAT 505, Lesson 10: Discriminant Analysis. Linear and quadratic discriminant analysis, error rates and an example, with sections 10.3 to 10.5 on this lesson’s topics.
Gareth James and others, An Introduction to Statistical Learning, chapter 4, “Classification”. LDA and QDA alongside logistic regression, with R labs. A preview of Module 7.
Johnson and Wichern, Applied Multivariate Statistical Analysis, chapter 11, “Discrimination and classification”. The rules, the costs and priors, and Fisher’s method, in depth.

title: Module 3 project: a multivariate study
text:
A customer has complained about a shipment that arrived labeled as the plant’s product. They say it behaved differently in their process, and they suspect that some of the drums aren’t the plant’s at all: a distributor may have filled the order partly with a competitor’s product. Priya, the quality manager, has sent you everything the lab has: 75 reference samples of known origin, and 8 samples from the customer’s drums, each with five trace impurities measured by the plant’s GC method. Her question: which of these drums are ours?
That’s the whole of Module 3 in one project. You’ll check the data with distances, compare groups with MANOVA and contrasts, and build a discriminant rule with honest error rates. And because this may end up in a dispute with the distributor, you’ll have to be precise about what the data can and can’t show.

title: Module 3 project: a multivariate study
text:
What you’ll make
One report, written in Quarto in your plant-study RStudio project, that Priya could pass on to the company’s lawyer. It should contain:

A summary for Priya, at the top, in plain words: which questioned samples are consistent with the plant’s product, which aren’t, whose they most likely are, and how sure you are.
The fingerprints: how the three products differ, and which impurities tell them apart.
The rule: how you classify a sample, how often it’s wrong, and how you know.
The eight questioned samples, one by one: the most likely source, the posterior probabilities, and whether the sample looks like a typical sample of that source.
A cleaning log and a list of limitations: every change you made to the reference set, and why, and everything these data can’t show.

Nobody grades it, but write it as if it will be read by someone looking for holes in it. In a dispute, it would be.

title: Module 3 project: a multivariate study
text:
The handover
Download the three files into a new folder in your project, data-raw/shipment/, and don’t edit them:

README.txt: Priya’s note, with the questions, the columns and the known issues. Read it first.
reference_samples.csv: the 75 reference samples: 25 of the plant’s product, and 25 each of Competitor X’s and Competitor Y’s, bought on the open market.
questioned_samples.csv: the 8 samples from the customer’s drums.

Then download the project template, save it in the top folder of your project as shipment-analysis.qmd, and click Render. It reads the data, prints a first look and draws the impurities by source, with headings for every step. Fill it in one section at a time, and render often.

title: Module 3 project: a multivariate study
text:
The brief, step by step

Explore (Lessons 1, 3). Summarize each impurity by source, and plot them. Draw a scatterplot matrix colored by source. Which impurities look different between the products? Does any value look impossible?
Check the reference set (Lessons 2, 13). The results were copied into the file by hand. Look for values that can’t be right, and for samples that don’t look like their own source. Two good tools are each sample’s Mahalanobis distance from its source’s mean, computed without the sample itself, and a cross-validated LDA: a reference sample that the rule confidently assigns to another source deserves a hard look. Correct what you can justify, set aside what you can’t trust, and log every decision.
Compare the fingerprints (Lessons 3, 6, 7). Fit a one-way MANOVA of the five impurities on the source, and check its assumptions: residual normality and Box’s M. Follow up with univariate ANOVAs. Then test the two contrasts Priya cares about, the plant’s product against X’s and against Y’s, with Bonferroni intervals for each impurity. Which impurities tell the plant’s product apart from each competitor’s?
Build a rule (Lesson 13). Fit an LDA, and interpret its discriminants with structure correlations. Estimate its error rate by leave-one-out cross-validation, and show the confusion table. Compare QDA. Which rule would you defend, and why?
Classify the questioned samples (Lesson 13). For each one, give the most likely source and the posterior probabilities. Q6 is missing its chloride result: build a second rule from the other four impurities, check its error rate too, and use it for Q6. Don’t fill in the missing value with a guess.
Ask whether each sample fits at all (Lessons 2, 4). LDA always picks one of the three sources, even for a sample from a fourth manufacturer. For each questioned sample, compute its Mahalanobis distance to the mean of the source it’s assigned to, with the pooled covariance matrix, and a p-value from the chi-square distribution with 5 degrees of freedom (4 for Q6). Would any sample be unusual for every source?
Say how sure you are, and what you can’t say. Posterior probabilities depend on the priors. What did you use, and would a different reasonable choice change any verdict? Are the reference samples, bought on the open market, representative of each manufacturer’s production? Are the eight questioned samples from eight different drums?
Write it up. Summary first, in words a lawyer could follow. One table with the eight verdicts, plots that make each point, and the limitations at the end.

Stretch goal. Lesson 3’s conditional distributions give a second way to handle Q6. Within each source, predict Q6’s chloride from its other four impurities with the conditional mean, and see whether the verdict changes. Then try other priors: if the distributor’s records show that 90% of what it sells is the plant’s product, use priors of 0.90, 0.05 and 0.05. Which verdicts survive? And if the customer only needs to know “ours or not ours”, is there a better way to set up the rule?

title: Module 3 project: a multivariate study
text:
Check your own work
When you’ve finished, assess your project against this rubric. Aim for the right-hand column.










Needs work
Good
Excellent




The reference set
The data are used as received
The impossible value is found and dealt with
The impossible value and the sample that doesn’t match its label are both found, with distances and cross-validation, each decision is justified, and the cleaning log is complete


Fingerprints
A MANOVA p-value only
A MANOVA with univariate follow-ups
A MANOVA with checked assumptions, contrasts of the plant’s product against each competitor’s, and Bonferroni intervals that say which impurities differ


The rule
The apparent error rate only
A cross-validated error rate
Cross-validated error rates for LDA and QDA, a confusion table, interpreted discriminants, and a justified choice


The questioned samples
A source for each
Sources with posterior probabilities
Sources, posterior probabilities, a separately validated rule for Q6, and a check that each sample is typical of its source


Honesty
Verdicts stated as facts
The uncertainty is mentioned
Clear about what the data can and can’t show: posteriors and error rates, the priors, the three-candidate assumption, and how representative the reference samples are


Communication
Code output with little text
A report that explains its steps
A report Priya could pass on: a plain summary, one table of verdicts, plots that make each point, honest limitations

title: Module 3 project: a multivariate study
text:
Tips

Look before you model. summary() of the reference data shows one value that can’t be right. Is there a simple explanation for it?
A mislabeled reference sample is worse than a missing one. It teaches the rule the wrong fingerprint, and it inflates its group’s covariance matrix. Look at the reference samples that cross-validation assigns, with high confidence, to another source.
A bad sample hides itself. Its own group’s mean and covariance matrix are pulled toward it, so compute its distance with the sample left out.
One distance is always the largest. With 75 samples, the biggest distance will look large even in perfect data. Judge it with a Bonferroni-adjusted p-value, as in Lesson 2, and ask whether the sample looks like a typical member of another source.
Fix the reference set first, then fit everything again. The MANOVA, the rule, the error rates and the verdicts all depend on it. Say in the report whether your cleaning changed any verdict.
“Consistent with” isn’t “proven”. A posterior probability of 0.99 is strong evidence, and the rule’s cross-validated error rate says how often strong-looking evidence has misled it. Use careful words, such as “consistent with Competitor X’s product, and not with ours”.
A rule is only as good as its candidates. It can’t name a manufacturer that isn’t in the reference set. The typicality check in step 6 is your protection.
Write for the reader. Priya knows the chemistry, and the lawyer knows neither the chemistry nor the statistics. Neither needs the formula for Wilks’ lambda. They need to know what you did, what you found, and how sure you are.


When it’s done, you’ll have taken a real question from messy measurements to a careful verdict, with every multivariate tool of the module: distances, MANOVA, contrasts and discriminant analysis. Congratulations on finishing Module 3! Module 4 opens up the algorithms behind modern statistics: simulation, resampling, optimization and more.

title: Numbers inside the computer
text:
Module 4 · Lesson 2 of 14 Week 62 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The plant’s new batch-control script adds catalyst in doses of 0.1 kg, and it’s supposed to stop when the total reaches 0.3 kg. Here’s its logic, with a safety limit of 10 doses:
total <- 0
doses <- 0
while (total != 0.3 && doses < 10) {
  total <- total + 0.1
  doses <- doses + 1
}
doses
#> [1] 10
It never stopped at 0.3 kg. It added all 10 doses, a full kilogram of catalyst. The code looks right, and in ordinary arithmetic it is right. But the computer doesn’t do ordinary arithmetic:
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3
#> [1] FALSE
This lesson is about how computers store numbers, and when that matters for statistics. Most of the time, it doesn’t. But when it does, the results can be silently, badly wrong, and every algorithm in this module has to be written with it in mind.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Numbers inside the computer
text:
Numbers in binary
R stores numbers as double-precision floating-point numbers, or doubles: in binary, with about 16 significant decimal digits. Some decimal fractions are exact in binary, such as 0.5 (one half) and 0.375 (three eighths). Most aren’t. In binary, one tenth is the never-ending fraction 0.000110011001100…, just as one third is 0.333… in decimal. The computer cuts it off after 53 binary digits, so 0.1 is stored as the nearest double, a tiny bit too big. Ask R for 20 digits and you can see it:

print(0.1, digits = 20)
#> [1] 0.10000000000000000555
print(0.1 + 0.2, digits = 20)
#> [1] 0.30000000000000004441
print(0.3, digits = 20)
#> [1] 0.2999999999999999889

The errors in 0.1 and 0.2 add up, and their sum lands on a different double from the one nearest 0.3. The difference is 5.6 \times 10^{-17}, but == asks for exact equality, so it says FALSE.
The fix is to compare with a tolerance: two computed numbers are “equal” if they’re closer than some small amount. abs(x - y) < 1e-9 does that, and so does isTRUE(all.equal(x, y)), whose default tolerance is 1.5 \times 10^{-8} in relative terms.











Your turn. Fix the batch-control loop: make it stop when the total is within 10^{-9} kg of 0.3.









The tolerance is 1e-9.


total <- 0
doses <- 0
while (abs(total - 0.3) > 1e-9 && doses < 10) {
  total <- total + 0.1
  doses <- doses + 1
}
doses
Three doses, as intended. After three doses, total is 0.30000000000000004, which is within 10^{-9} of 0.3, so the loop stops. The rule: never test computed doubles with ==. Integers that came from counting are fine, and so are numbers you typed in and never calculated with.

title: Numbers inside the computer
text:
How precise is a double?
A double has 53 binary digits of precision. So the gap between 1 and the next double above it is 2^{-52} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-16}. That’s the machine epsilon: add anything much smaller than it to 1, and you get 1 back. In relative terms, every double is stored with an error of at most half of it, which is about 16 significant digits.
The gap between neighboring doubles grows with their size. Near 1, doubles are 2.2 \times 10^{-16} apart. Near a billion, they’re 1.2 \times 10^{-7} apart. Near 10^{18}, they’re 128 apart: between 10^{18} and 10^{18} + 128, there’s no other double at all.

x <- c(1, 1000, 1e9, 1e16, 1e18)
data.frame(x = x, gap_to_next_double = 2^(floor(log2(x)) - 52))
#>       x gap_to_next_double
#> 1 1e+00       2.220446e-16
#> 2 1e+03       1.136868e-13
#> 3 1e+09       1.192093e-07
#> 4 1e+16       2.000000e+00
#> 5 1e+18       1.280000e+02

Integers are exact up to 2^{53} \approx 9 \times 10^{15}. Beyond that, there are gaps:

2^53 + 1 == 2^53
#> [1] TRUE







NoteGo deeper: what’s inside a double





A double is 64 bits: 1 for the sign, 11 for the exponent, and 52 for the fraction. It stands for

(-1)^{\text{sign}} \times 1.f \times 2^{\,e - 1023},

where 1.f is a binary number between 1 and 2 (the leading 1 isn’t stored, which gives 53 digits of precision from 52 bits), and e is the exponent, from 1 to 2046. That gives a range from about 2.2 \times 10^{-308} to 1.8 \times 10^{308}: R reports them as .Machine$double.xmin and .Machine$double.xmax. The two exponents left over are used for zero, Inf, NaN, and some extra-tiny “subnormal” numbers. The standard that defines all this is IEEE 754, and nearly every computer since the 1980s follows it.



Your turn. Find the machine epsilon yourself: start with e <- 1, and keep halving it while adding e / 2 to 1 still changes it.









Stop when 1 + e / 2 equals 1.


e <- 1
for (k in 1:100) {
  if (1 + e / 2 == 1) break    # stop when adding e/2 no longer changes 1
  e <- e / 2
}
c(e = e, machine_eps = .Machine$double.eps)
After 52 halvings, e = 2^{-52} = 2.2 \times 10^{-16}, exactly R’s .Machine$double.eps. (This is one of the few places where == is the right test: you want to know whether the result is exactly 1.)

title: Numbers inside the computer
text:
Too big and too small
Doubles stop at about 1.8 \times 10^{308}. Anything bigger overflows to Inf. At the other end, numbers smaller than about 10^{-308} lose precision, and below 5 \times 10^{-324} they underflow to 0:

factorial(170)
#> [1] 7.257416e+306
factorial(171)
#> [1] Inf
1e-320
#> [1] 9.999889e-321
5e-324 / 2
#> [1] 0

Overflow and underflow are common in statistics, because probabilities of whole datasets are tiny. Lesson 3 will test random number generators, and one simple test counts the ones in 2,000 random bits. The probability of exactly 1,000 ones is the binomial probability

\binom{2000}{1000} \, 0.5^{1000} \, (1 - 0.5)^{1000}.

The binomial coefficient is about 10^{600}, which overflows, and 0.5^{2000} underflows to 0. The formula, typed as written, gives \infty \times 0, which is NaN (not a number). The cure is to work with logarithms: \log \binom{2000}{1000} \approx 1382 is no problem at all, and lchoose() computes it directly.
Your turn. Compute the probability on the log scale, and then take the exponential.









Each of the 2,000 bits contributes a factor of 0.5: log(0.5).


choose(2000, 1000) * 0.5^2000                        # as written: Inf times 0
exp(lchoose(2000, 1000) + 2000 * log(0.5))
0.0178, a perfectly ordinary number made from two numbers that a double can’t hold. It’s what dbinom(1000, 2000, 0.5) gives: R’s distribution functions are written to avoid overflow and underflow, and most have a log = TRUE argument that gives you the logarithm directly.

title: Numbers inside the computer
text:
Subtracting nearly equal numbers
Each double carries about 16 significant digits. When you subtract two numbers that agree in their first 14 digits, only 2 meaningful digits are left, and the rounding errors, which were in the 16th digit, are now in the 2nd. This is catastrophic cancellation, and it’s the most common way that a correct formula gives a wrong answer.
The lab checks its balance every morning with a 1 kg reference weight. The balance reads in micrograms, so a reading is about a billion: 10^9 µg. Here are 20 mornings:

print(w, digits = 12)
#>  [1]  999999999 1000000004 1000000017  999999997 1000000018 1000000001
#>  [7] 1000000006 1000000015  999999999 1000000004 1000000004 1000000003
#> [13]  999999999 1000000011  999999997 1000000010 1000000010 1000000006
#> [19] 1000000012 1000000003

Many textbooks give a “computational formula” for the variance, which needs only one pass through the data:

s^2 = \frac{\sum x_i^2 - n \bar{x}^2}{n - 1}.

It’s exact in ordinary arithmetic. But here, \sum x_i^2 and n\bar{x}^2 are both about 2 \times 10^{19}, where doubles are 4,096 apart, and their difference is about 800. All the digits that matter are lost in the subtraction. The two-pass formula subtracts the mean first, from each reading, and then squares numbers of about 10:

s^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}.

Your turn. Compute the variance of the readings both ways, and compare them with var().









Subtract the mean first: w - mean(w).


n <- length(w)
one_pass <- (sum(w^2) - n * mean(w)^2) / (n - 1)
two_pass <- sum((w - mean(w))^2) / (n - 1)
c(one_pass = one_pass, two_pass = two_pass, var = var(w))
The two-pass formula gives 42.2 µg², an SD of 6.5 µg, just like var(). The one-pass formula gives nonsense, probably 0 or a multiple of about 200 (the exact nonsense depends on the computer). A variance of 0 would say the balance is perfect, and a negative one is impossible. Nothing warns you: the formula just quietly returns the wrong number.




Another fix is to shift the data before you start: subtract a round number near the mean, such as 10^9, which changes nothing about the variance. Stable algorithms are designed so that they never subtract big, nearly equal numbers. Challenge 1 builds one that works even when the readings arrive one at a time.

title: Numbers inside the computer
text:
Working on the log scale
The likelihood of a dataset is a product of densities, one for each observation (Lesson 9 will maximize likelihoods). With a thousand observations, the product underflows, even though every density is a reasonable number:

set.seed(4022)
x <- rnorm(1000, 185, 1.5)
prod(dnorm(x, 185, 1.5))
#> [1] 0
sum(dnorm(x, 185, 1.5, log = TRUE))
#> [1] -1792.041

So statisticians work with the log-likelihood, a sum of logs, which is no trouble at all. That raises a new problem: sometimes you need to add probabilities that you’ve stored as logs. For example, a mixture model (Lesson 10) adds up the probability of an observation under each group. If a_1 and a_2 are log-probabilities, you want \log(e^{a_1} + e^{a_2}). With a = -1000 and -1001, both exponentials underflow to 0, and the log of 0 is -\infty.
The trick is to factor out the biggest term. With m = \max_i a_i,

\log \sum_i e^{a_i} = m + \log \sum_i e^{a_i - m}.

Now the biggest exponential is e^0 = 1, and none of them can overflow. Any that underflow were too small to matter anyway. It’s called the log-sum-exp trick.
Your turn. Write the function.









Subtract the maximum, m, before taking the exponentials.


logsumexp <- function(a) {
  m <- max(a)
  m + log(sum(exp(a - m)))
}
log(sum(exp(c(-1000, -1001))))     # the direct way
logsumexp(c(-1000, -1001))
The direct way gives -Inf. The trick gives −999.687, which is right: -1000 + \log(1 + e^{-1}) = -1000 + 0.313. It works for big numbers too, where the direct way overflows: logsumexp(c(800, 801)) is 801.313.

title: Numbers inside the computer
text:
Ill-conditioned problems
Some problems magnify rounding errors, however carefully you compute. Here’s the heat capacity of carbon dioxide gas, measured from 300 to 1500 K:

ggplot(hc, aes(x = T_K, y = cp_J_molK)) +
  geom_point(color = "#C2416C", size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (K)", y = "Heat capacity (J/(mol·K))") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Engineers fit curves like this with a polynomial, c_p = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T + \beta_2 T^2 + \beta_3 T^3. As a regression, its model matrix X has columns 1, T, T^2 and T^3, and Lesson 2.4 gave the least-squares estimates as the solution of the normal equations, X^\top X \boldsymbol\beta = X^\top \mathbf{y}. Solve them directly, and R refuses:

X <- cbind(1, hc$T_K, hc$T_K^2, hc$T_K^3)
tryCatch(solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, hc$cp_J_molK)), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "system is computationally singular: reciprocal condition number = 1.7397e-21"

The columns are wildly different in size: 1, about a thousand, a million, a billion. And over this range, T^2 and T^3 are almost perfectly correlated (0.99), so the problem is almost singular. The condition number measures how much a problem can magnify errors. A condition number of 10^k can cost you about k of your 16 digits. kappa() computes it.
Your turn. Compute the condition numbers of X and of X^\top X.









crossprod(X) computes X^\top X.


X <- cbind(1, hc$T_K, hc$T_K^2, hc$T_K^3)
c(X = kappa(X, exact = TRUE), XtX = kappa(crossprod(X), exact = TRUE))
X has a condition number of 2.4 \times 10^{10}, which would cost about 10 digits. X^\top X has 5.7 \times 10^{20}, exactly the square: more than all 16 digits. That’s why solve() gave up. Forming X^\top X squares the condition number, and that’s the trouble with the normal equations.




lm() fits the same model without complaint, because it never forms X^\top X. It uses the QR decomposition of X itself, which only meets X’s condition number. That’s why statistical software uses QR, and why you should use lm() (or qr.solve()) rather than coding the textbook formula (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top \mathbf{y} directly.
The other fix is to rescale the predictor. Centering and scaling the temperature to t = (T - 900)/600, which runs from −1 to 1, makes the columns similar in size and far less alike.
Your turn. Rescale the temperature, check the new condition number, and solve the normal equations.









The middle of the range, 300 to 1500 K, is 900.


t <- (hc$T_K - 900) / 600       # from -1 to 1
Xs <- cbind(1, t, t^2, t^3)
kappa(Xs, exact = TRUE)
b <- solve(crossprod(Xs), crossprod(Xs, hc$cp_J_molK))
drop(b)
The condition number drops from 2.4 \times 10^{10} to 7.8, and even the normal equations now work. The coefficients are for t, not T, so they look different, but the fitted curve is the same: both predict 54.33 J/(mol·K) at 1000 K. poly(), which Lesson 2.9 mentioned, goes one step further: it builds columns that are exactly uncorrelated with each other.

title: Numbers inside the computer
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · One reading at a time. The historian of Lesson 1 sends readings one at a time, and there may be too many to store. Welford’s algorithm updates the mean and the variance with each new reading, without ever subtracting big, nearly equal numbers. After reading x_n, with d = x_n - m_{n-1}:

m_n = m_{n-1} + \frac{d}{n}, \qquad S_n = S_{n-1} + d\,(x_n - m_n),

and the variance is S_n/(n-1). Complete the function, and try it on the balance readings.









The second factor uses the updated mean: xi - m.


welford <- function(x) {
  n <- 0; m <- 0; S <- 0
  for (xi in x) {
    n <- n + 1
    d <- xi - m
    m <- m + d / n
    S <- S + d * (xi - m)
  }
  c(mean = m, var = S / (n - 1))
}
welford(w)
The variance is 42.2 µg², the same as var() to ten digits, in one pass. Each step only multiplies small differences, of about 10 µg, so nothing cancels. It’s the algorithm inside many data loggers and streaming systems.




Challenge 2 · Posterior probabilities. In Lesson 3.13, discriminant analysis turned each group’s likelihood into a posterior probability: each likelihood divided by their sum (with equal priors). For a large sample, the log-likelihoods might be −1520.3, −1522.8 and −1530.1. Every likelihood underflows to 0, and 0/0 is NaN. Compute the probabilities with your log-sum-exp.









Divide by the sum on the log scale: subtract logsumexp(loglik).


logsumexp <- function(a) {
  m <- max(a)
  m + log(sum(exp(a - m)))
}
loglik <- c(Fizzwell = -1520.3, Kestrel = -1522.8, `Plum Valley` = -1530.1)
exp(loglik) / sum(exp(loglik))           # 0 / 0
exp(loglik - logsumexp(loglik))
0.924, 0.076 and 0.00005. Only the differences between the log-likelihoods matter: Kestrel is 2.5 log units behind Fizzwell, so it’s e^{-2.5} = 0.08 times as likely. Classification software computes its probabilities this way.

title: Numbers inside the computer
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why is 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 false in R?

R has a bug in its addition
0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 can’t be stored exactly in binary, and the sum lands on a different double from 0.3
== doesn’t work for decimals


In binary, one tenth is a never-ending fraction, like one third in decimal.



2. How should you check whether two computed numbers are equal?

With ==
With a tolerance, such as abs(x - y) < 1e-9 or isTRUE(all.equal(x, y))
By rounding both to 2 decimals


Rounding can fail too, when the two numbers fall on either side of a rounding boundary.



3. About how many significant decimal digits does a double carry?

7
16
53


53 binary digits, which is about 16 decimal digits. The machine epsilon is 2^{-52} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-16}.



4. Why does the one-pass formula \left(\sum x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2\right)/(n-1) fail for the balance readings?

The readings aren’t normal
It subtracts two huge, nearly equal numbers, and the digits that matter are lost
It needs more readings


That’s catastrophic cancellation. Subtracting the mean first keeps the numbers small.



5. Why do statisticians maximize the log-likelihood instead of the likelihood?

Because the log-likelihood has a different maximum
Because a product of many densities underflows to 0, while a sum of logs doesn’t
Because logs are faster to compute


The log is increasing, so both have their maximum in the same place. Only the log is safe to compute.



6. Why does lm() work where solve(t(X) %*% X, t(X) %*% y) fails?

lm() uses more digits
lm() uses the QR decomposition of X, and never forms X^\top X, whose condition number is the square of X’s
lm() drops the hard columns


Squaring a condition number of 10^{10} gives 10^{20}, which is beyond what 16 digits can handle.

title: Numbers inside the computer
text:
Wrap-up
You can now see the machine’s numbers for what they are. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Doubles store numbers in binary, with 53 binary digits: about 16 decimal digits. Most decimal fractions, such as 0.1, are stored with a tiny error.
Compare with a tolerance, never with ==, or a loop that waits for 0.3 kg adds a whole kilogram.
The machine epsilon, 2^{-52} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-16}, is the relative precision of a double. The gaps between doubles grow with their size.
Overflow and underflow: doubles run from about 10^{-308} to 10^{308}. Work with logarithms: lchoose(), log = TRUE, log-likelihoods, and the log-sum-exp trick.
Catastrophic cancellation: subtracting nearly equal numbers loses digits. The two-pass variance, shifted data and Welford’s algorithm avoid it.
Ill-conditioning: a condition number of 10^k can cost k digits. X^\top X squares it, so use lm() or the QR decomposition, and rescale predictors.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download heat_capacity.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Where do the digits go? For x = 10^k with k = 1, 2, \dots, 16, compute (x + 0.1) - x. How close to 0.1 is the answer, and when does it go badly wrong? Explain it with the gaps between doubles.
A sum that depends on the order. Compute sum(1 / (1:1e6)) and sum(1 / (1e6:1)), and print both with 20 digits. Are they the same? Then try cumsum() and take the last element. Adding the small numbers first is usually more accurate. Why?
The quadratic formula. The roots of x^2 - 10^8 x + 1 = 0 are about 10^8 and 10^{-8}. Compute the small one with the usual formula, (b - \sqrt{b^2 - 4c})/2 with b = 10^8, and then with the stable form, 2c/(b + \sqrt{b^2 - 4c}). Which is right, and why?
Polynomial fits. Fit the heat capacity with lm(cp_J_molK ~ poly(T_K, 3)) and with lm(cp_J_molK ~ T_K + I(T_K^2) + I(T_K^3)). Compare the fitted values and the condition numbers of the two model matrices (model.matrix()). Then try degree 6 with raw powers: what does lm() do?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Floating-point number

A number stored as a sign, a fraction and an exponent, like scientific notation in binary. R’s doubles use 64 bits.

Machine epsilon

The gap between 1 and the next larger double, 2^{-52} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-16}: the relative precision of a double.

Overflow and underflow

A result too big for a double becomes Inf (overflow), and one too small becomes 0 (underflow).

Catastrophic cancellation

The loss of significant digits when two nearly equal numbers are subtracted.

Log-sum-exp

Computing \log \sum e^{a_i} as m + \log \sum e^{a_i - m}, with m the largest a_i, so that nothing overflows or underflows.

Condition number

A measure of how much a problem can magnify small errors. A condition number of 10^k can cost about k significant digits.

QR decomposition

Writing a matrix as an orthogonal matrix times a triangular one. Least squares by QR avoids forming X^\top X.











NoteWant to read more?






The R FAQ, question 7.31, “Why doesn’t R think these numbers are equal?”. The short official answer, with links.
Patrick Burns, The R Inferno, circle 1, “Falling into the floating point trap”. The same traps, told with humor.
David Goldberg, “What every computer scientist should know about floating-point arithmetic” (1991). The classic paper: rounding, cancellation and the IEEE standard, in depth.

title: Simulating from distributions
text:
Module 4 · Lesson 4 of 14 Week 64 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 3 turned uniform random numbers into Weibull lifetimes by inverting the CDF. That works whenever you can write down F^{-1}. Often you can’t: the normal distribution’s CDF has no formula, and many distributions in science come as a density and nothing more. This lesson collects the other tools: transformations, rejection sampling and mixtures. Then you’ll put random numbers to work in a simulation study, the statistician’s experiment, to find out whether a method the lab uses every day really does what it claims.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Simulating from distributions
text:
Transformations
If you can make one kind of random number, you can often make another by transforming it. Some may be familiar: if Z is standard normal, then e^Z is lognormal and Z^2 is chi-square with 1 degree of freedom. The most famous transformation makes normals out of uniforms. If U_1 and U_2 are independent uniforms, then

Z_1 = \sqrt{-2 \log U_1}\, \cos(2\pi U_2), \qquad Z_2 = \sqrt{-2 \log U_1}\, \sin(2\pi U_2)

are two independent standard normals. It’s the Box-Muller transformation, from 1958.






NoteGo deeper: why Box-Muller works





Think of (Z_1, Z_2) as a point in the plane, in polar coordinates: a radius R and an angle \Theta. Two independent standard normals have the joint density \frac{1}{2\pi} e^{-(z_1^2 + z_2^2)/2}, which depends only on the radius. So the angle is uniform on (0, 2\pi): that’s 2\pi U_2. And the squared radius R^2 = Z_1^2 + Z_2^2 is chi-square with 2 degrees of freedom, which is the exponential distribution with mean 2, so by inversion (Lesson 3), R^2 = -2\log U_1. Taking the cosine and the sine of the angle turns the polar point back into the two coordinates.












Your turn. Make 10,000 standard normals with the Box-Muller transformation, from 5,000 pairs of uniforms, and check their mean, their SD, and the share beyond ±2 (it should be 4.55%).









The second normal uses the sine: sin().


set.seed(4041)
u1 <- runif(5000)
u2 <- runif(5000)
r <- sqrt(-2 * log(u1))
z <- c(r * cos(2 * pi * u2), r * sin(2 * pi * u2))
c(mean = mean(z), sd = sd(z), beyond_2 = mean(abs(z) > 2))
A mean of 0.005, an SD of 1.007, and 4.9% beyond ±2: standard normals, within the wobble you’d expect from 10,000 random numbers. R’s own rnorm() uses a different method, as Lesson 3’s RNGkind() showed: inversion, with qnorm() applied to a uniform number.

title: Simulating from distributions
text:
Molecular speeds
Here’s a transformation with physics in it. The molecules of a gas move in random directions at random speeds. In each direction, a molecule’s velocity is normal with mean 0 and SD a = \sqrt{k_B T/m}, where k_B is Boltzmann’s constant, T the temperature in kelvin and m the mass of one molecule. Its speed is the length of its velocity vector,

s = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2 + v_z^2},

and speeds follow the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. Its mean, from kinetic theory, is \sqrt{8/\pi}\; a.
Your turn. Simulate the speeds of 10,000 nitrogen molecules at 300 K (about room temperature). The setup code has computed a, 298 m/s. Draw three normal velocity components per molecule, and compute the speeds.









Square the components: v^2.


set.seed(4042)
v <- matrix(rnorm(3 * 10000, 0, a), ncol = 3)     # one row per molecule
speed <- sqrt(rowSums(v^2))
c(a = a, mean_speed = mean(speed), theory = sqrt(8 / pi) * a)
A mean speed of 478 m/s, against 476 m/s from kinetic theory. Nitrogen molecules in your room move at about 1,700 km/h, faster than the speed of sound, which isn’t a coincidence: sound is carried by these molecules.

title: Simulating from distributions
text:
Rejection sampling
Suppose you only knew the density of the speeds, from a physics textbook:

f(s) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\; \frac{s^2}{a^3}\, \exp\!\left(-\frac{s^2}{2a^2}\right), \qquad s > 0.

There’s no formula for F^{-1}, and no transformation in sight. Rejection sampling needs only the density. Choose a proposal distribution g that’s easy to sample from, and a constant M so that the envelope M g(s) is never below f(s). Then repeat:

Draw a proposal s from g.
Accept it with probability f(s)/(M g(s)): draw a uniform u, and accept if u < f(s)/(M g(s)).

The accepted values have exactly the density f. Here, the proposal is uniform from 0 to 2,000 m/s, so g(s) = 1/2000 (practically no molecule is faster than 2,000 m/s: the chance is 10^{-9}). The envelope must reach the density’s peak, which is at the most likely speed, \sqrt{2}\,a = 422 m/s, so M = 2000 \times f(\sqrt2\, a) = 3.93.
The picture shows why it works. Each proposal is a point, placed at a random height under the envelope. The points that land under the curve are accepted, and they’re spread over the speeds in proportion to the density:

set.seed(4048)
pts <- data.frame(s = runif(2000, 0, 2000))
pts$height <- runif(2000) * M * g(pts$s)
pts$result <- ifelse(pts$height < f(pts$s), "accepted", "rejected")
curve_df <- data.frame(s = seq(0, 2000, length.out = 400))
ggplot(pts, aes(x = s, y = height)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = result), size = 0.9, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(data = curve_df, aes(x = s, y = f(s)), color = "#3A1F35", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = M / 2000, linetype = "dashed", color = "#3A1F35") +
  annotate("text", x = 1980, y = M / 2000 * 1.05, label = "envelope M g(s)", hjust = 1, size = 3.6, color = "#3A1F35") +
  annotate("text", x = 700, y = f(700) * 1.12, label = "density f(s)", hjust = 0, size = 3.6, color = "#3A1F35") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(accepted = "#C2416C", rejected = "grey75"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Speed (m/s)", y = "Height") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








On average, a fraction 1/M of the proposals is accepted, here about 25%. The other three quarters are wasted, which is the price of a crude envelope.






NoteGo deeper: why the accepted values have density f





A proposal X has density g, and it’s accepted with probability f(x)/(Mg(x)). So the chance that a proposal lands below x and is accepted is

\int_{-\infty}^{x} g(t)\, \frac{f(t)}{M g(t)}\, dt = \frac{F(x)}{M},

and the chance that it’s accepted at all is the same integral over everything, 1/M. Dividing, P(X \le x \mid \text{accepted}) = F(x): the accepted values have the CDF F. The density only appears as a ratio, f/(Mg), so f only needs to be known up to a constant. That’s the feature that makes rejection sampling useful for the posterior distributions of Module 5.



Your turn. Run the rejection sampler with 20,000 proposals. The setup code has defined the density f() and the proposal density g().









Divide by the envelope, M * g(s).


M <- 2000 * f(sqrt(2) * a)                  # the envelope M g(s) touches the peak of f
set.seed(4043)
s <- runif(20000, 0, 2000)                  # proposals from g
accept <- runif(20000) < f(s) / (M * g(s))
speed <- s[accept]
c(acceptance = mean(accept), theory = 1 / M, mean_speed = mean(speed))
25.3% of the proposals were accepted, against 1/M = 25.4\% in theory, which leaves 5,068 speeds. Their mean, 475 m/s, matches the transformation method and the theory. Two very different methods, the same distribution.




The better the envelope fits the density, the fewer proposals are wasted. A proposal shaped more like the density, such as a gamma distribution, can accept over 70%. Rejection sampling also gets worse quickly in higher dimensions, where even a good envelope wastes most of its volume. Lessons 11 and 12 meet methods that don’t have that problem.

title: Simulating from distributions
text:
Mixtures
The crystallizer makes two kinds of crystals. Most grow to about 210 µm, but secondary nucleation, new crystals breaking off old ones, makes a population of fines at about 85 µm. If 35% of the crystals are fines, the size distribution is a mixture:

f(x) = 0.35\, f_{\text{fines}}(x) + 0.65\, f_{\text{main}}(x).

To simulate from a mixture, follow the story: first choose each crystal’s population, with probabilities 0.35 and 0.65, then draw its size from that population’s distribution.
Your turn. Simulate 250 crystals. Fines are normal with mean 85 µm and SD 18 µm, and the main population with mean 210 µm and SD 38 µm.









A crystal is a fine with probability 0.35.


set.seed(4044)
n <- 250
fines <- runif(n) < 0.35                 # TRUE for a fine crystal
size <- ifelse(fines, rnorm(n, 85, 18), rnorm(n, 210, 38))
c(fines = mean(fines), mean_size = mean(size), sd_size = sd(size))
34% fines, a mean size of 170 µm and an SD of 69 µm. The SD is much bigger than either population’s, because it includes the gap between them: in theory, it’s \sqrt{0.35 \cdot 18^2 + 0.65 \cdot 38^2 + 0.35 \cdot 0.65 \cdot 125^2} = 68 µm. (ifelse() draws 250 sizes from each population and keeps one per crystal. It’s a little wasteful, but simple.) Lesson 10 runs this story backwards: given only the sizes, it works out the two populations.

title: Simulating from distributions
text:
Designing a simulation study
Now for what all this is for. A simulation study is an experiment on a statistical method: generate many datasets from a model where you know the truth, apply the method to each one, and see how well it does. It answers questions that the mathematics can’t, or can only answer for large samples.
Here’s one. The lab measures a trace impurity in ten samples from each campaign and reports a 95% t-interval for the mean, \bar{x} \pm t_{0.975,\,9}\, s/\sqrt{10}. But impurity levels are right-skewed: most samples are low and a few are high. The t-interval assumes normal data. Does it still cover the true mean 95% of the time?
A good plan for a simulation study has five parts, known as ADEMP:

Aim: find the coverage of the t-interval for skewed impurity data, with n = 10.
Data: lognormal, with meanlog = log(20) and sdlog = 0.8, which looks like the lab’s results.
Estimand: the true mean, e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2} = 27.5 ppm.
Method: the t-interval.
Performance measure: the coverage, the share of intervals that contain the true mean.

The setup code has a function that does one replicate: it simulates ten results, computes the interval, and returns TRUE if the interval covers the true mean.

covers <- function(n) {
  x <- rlnorm(n, log(20), 0.8)
  ci <- mean(x) + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, n - 1) * sd(x) / sqrt(n)
  ci[1] < true_mean && true_mean < ci[2]
}

A simulation’s estimate has its own uncertainty, because it’s based on a finite number of replicates. Report it. A coverage estimated from R replicates is a proportion, so its Monte Carlo standard error is \sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)/R}.
Your turn. Run 4,000 replicates with n = 10, and report the coverage with its Monte Carlo standard error.









Each replicate has ten samples: covers(10).


set.seed(4045)
hits <- replicate(4000, covers(10))
coverage <- mean(hits)
c(coverage = coverage, mcse = sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / 4000))
88.0%, with a Monte Carlo standard error of 0.5 percentage points. So the true coverage is somewhere around 87% to 89%: clearly short of the promised 95%. The “95% interval” misses the true mean about one time in eight, not one in twenty.




Here are 40 more simulated campaigns, with their intervals:

set.seed(4061)
ints <- t(replicate(40, {
  x <- rlnorm(10, log(20), 0.8)
  mean(x) + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, 9) * sd(x) / sqrt(10)
}))
ints <- data.frame(rep = 1:40, lower = ints[, 1], upper = ints[, 2])
ints$result <- ifelse(ints$lower < true_mean & true_mean < ints$upper, "covers", "misses")
ggplot(ints, aes(y = rep)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, yend = rep, color = result), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_mean, color = "#3A1F35", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = true_mean + 0.5, y = 41.5, label = "true mean, 27.5 ppm", hjust = 0, size = 3.6, color = "#3A1F35") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(covers = "grey70", misses = "#C2416C"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL) +
  labs(x = "95% t-interval for the mean impurity (ppm)", y = "Simulated campaign") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Every miss is on the same side: the interval is too low. In 4,000 replicates, 476 intervals were entirely below the true mean, and only 6 were above it. With skewed data, a sample that happens to miss the rare high values has both a low mean and a low SD, so its interval is short and low at the same time. A report that treats the upper limit as a safe upper bound on the mean would be wrong about 12% of the time, not 2.5%. That’s worth knowing before a customer asks. The module project builds a bigger simulation study of this kind.

title: Simulating from distributions
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Does a bigger sample help? Find the coverage for samples of 5, 10, 30 and 100, with 2,000 replicates each.









Inside the function, the sample size is n.


set.seed(4046)
sizes <- c(5, 10, 30, 100)
coverage <- sapply(sizes, function(n) mean(replicate(2000, covers(n))))
names(coverage) <- sizes
coverage
87%, 88%, 91% and 93%. The coverage creeps toward 95% as the sample grows, because the central limit theorem makes the mean more normal. But even with 100 samples it’s short, and the lab has 10. Each estimate has a Monte Carlo standard error of about 0.7 percentage points, so the small difference between n = 5 and n = 10 could be simulation noise.




Challenge 2 · What the customer sees. The plant’s purity is normal, with mean 99.1% and SD 0.3%, but only product within the specification, 98.5% to 99.5%, is shipped. So the customer sees a truncated normal distribution. Simulate it by inversion: draw uniforms between F(98.5) and F(99.5) instead of between 0 and 1, and apply qnorm().









The upper end is the upper specification limit, hi.


mu <- 99.1; s <- 0.3; lo <- 98.5; hi <- 99.5
set.seed(4047)
u <- runif(10000, pnorm(lo, mu, s), pnorm(hi, mu, s))
shipped <- qnorm(u, mu, s)
c(in_spec = pnorm(hi, mu, s) - pnorm(lo, mu, s), mean = mean(shipped), sd = sd(shipped))
89% of production is in specification. The shipped product has a mean of 99.07%, a little below the plant’s 99.1%, because the cut at 99.5% removes more of the upper tail than the cut at 98.5% removes of the lower. And its SD is 0.23%, not 0.3%. Every one of the 10,000 draws is in specification, and none was wasted. Rejection (draw normals and throw away the ones outside the specification) would also work, but it would waste 11% of the draws.

title: Simulating from distributions
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does the Box-Muller transformation produce from two independent uniforms?

One normal random number
Two independent standard normal random numbers
Two uniforms on a circle


A radius from one uniform and an angle from the other, turned back into two coordinates.



2. A rejection sampler uses an envelope with M = 4. About what share of its proposals is accepted?

4%
25%
75%


The acceptance rate is 1/M.



3. Why does rejection sampling only need the density up to a constant?

Because the constant is always 1
Because the density only enters as the ratio f(x)/(Mg(x)), and any constant can be absorbed into M
Because it never uses the density


That’s what makes it useful for densities whose normalizing constant is unknown.



4. How do you simulate one value from a mixture of two populations?

Average one draw from each population
Choose a population with its mixing probability, then draw from that population
Draw from the population with the larger probability


Averaging would give a single narrow peak, not two populations.



5. A simulation study estimates a coverage of 0.880 from 4,000 replicates. What’s its Monte Carlo standard error?

0.0001
About 0.005
About 0.05


\sqrt{0.88 \times 0.12/4000} = 0.0051. So 0.880 is clearly below 0.95.



6. In the ADEMP plan for a simulation study, what does the “E” stand for?

The error rate
The estimand, the true quantity that the method is trying to estimate
The number of experiments


Aims, Data-generating mechanisms, Estimands, Methods and Performance measures.

title: Simulating from distributions
text:
Wrap-up
You can now simulate from almost anything, and use simulations to test methods. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Transformations turn one distribution into another. Box-Muller makes normals from uniforms, and the length of a normal velocity vector is a Maxwell-Boltzmann speed.
Rejection sampling needs only a density (up to a constant) and an envelope Mg above it. It accepts a share 1/M of the proposals, so a close envelope saves work.
