Mixtures are simulated by following the story: choose a population, then draw from it.
Truncated distributions can be simulated by inversion, with uniforms on a shorter interval.
Simulation studies test methods where you know the truth. Plan them with ADEMP, and report Monte Carlo standard errors.
The lab’s t-interval for skewed data covers the true mean only 88% of the time with ten samples, and its misses are all too low.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)






Hot and cold gas. Simulate nitrogen speeds at 77 K (liquid nitrogen’s boiling point) and at 1000 K. How does the mean speed change with temperature? Check it against \sqrt{8 k_B T/(\pi m)}. Then try hydrogen, m = 2.016 \times 10^{-3}/N_A kg.
A better envelope. The speed density is a gamma-like curve. Try a gamma proposal, rgamma(n, shape = 3, rate = 3 / 476), with its density dgamma(). Find the smallest M that keeps Mg(s) \ge f(s) (plot f/g on a fine grid and take its maximum). What’s the new acceptance rate?
A better interval? In the coverage study, replace the t-interval with one computed on the log scale: a t-interval for the mean of \log x, transformed back with exp(). What does it estimate, and why doesn’t it cover 27.5 ppm? (Hint: the mean of the logs isn’t the log of the mean.)
Your own ADEMP. Write an ADEMP plan for this question: does the two-sample t-test keep its 5% false-alarm rate when the two groups have different SDs and different sizes? Then run it, comparing t.test(var.equal = TRUE) with Welch’s default.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Box-Muller transformation

A way to make two independent standard normals from two independent uniforms.

Rejection sampling

Simulating from a density f by drawing proposals from a density g and accepting each with probability f/(Mg).

Envelope

The function M g(x) in rejection sampling, which must never be below the target density.

Mixture distribution

A distribution made of several populations, each with its own probability: f = \sum_j p_j f_j.

Truncated distribution

A distribution restricted to an interval, such as the product that passes a specification.

Simulation study

An experiment that tests a statistical method on many datasets generated from a known model.

Monte Carlo standard error

The standard error of an estimate that comes from a simulation, due to its finite number of replicates.

Coverage

The share of confidence intervals that contain the true value.











NoteWant to read more?






Roger Peng, Advanced Statistical Computing, section 6.3, “Rejection sampling”. The algorithm, why it works, and how to choose the envelope.
Tim Morris, Ian White and Michael Crowther, “Using simulation studies to evaluate statistical methods”, Statistics in Medicine (2019), free to read. The ADEMP plan, performance measures and their Monte Carlo standard errors, with advice on reporting.
Luc Devroye, Non-Uniform Random Variate Generation, chapter 2. The general principles: inversion, rejection, mixtures and transformations.

title: The bootstrap
text:
Module 4 · Lesson 6 of 14 Week 66 of 160 About 5–7 hours
After filtration, each batch goes into the dryer until its moisture is below 0.5%. The planners book the dryer for a fixed time per batch, and if a batch isn’t dry in time, the next one waits. They’d like to book a time that’s long enough for 90% of batches. Here are the last 30 batches’ drying times, in hours:
sort(dry$drying_h)
#>  [1]  3.04  3.45  4.01  4.07  4.82  5.11  5.14  5.18  5.31  5.59  5.93  5.94
#> [13]  6.18  6.18  6.53  6.62  6.97  7.10  7.27  7.53  7.83  7.90  8.54  8.66
#> [25]  9.07  9.41 10.27 10.40 10.53 12.33
quantile(dry$drying_h, 0.9)
#>    90% 
#> 10.283
So the answer is about 10.3 hours. But how sure is that? Thirty batches is not many, and a different thirty would give a different 90th percentile. For a mean, the standard error is s/\sqrt{n}. For a 90th percentile there’s no simple formula, and for many statistics there’s none at all.
The bootstrap, invented by Bradley Efron in 1979, answers “how uncertain?” for almost any statistic, with one idea and a loop. It’s the most widely used tool in this module.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: The bootstrap
section: The sample stands in for the population
text:
The sample stands in for the population
To know how much the 90th percentile varies from sample to sample, you’d want many samples of 30 batches. You only have one. The bootstrap’s idea is to treat that sample as if it were the population. Draw a new sample of 30 from it, with replacement, so that some batches appear twice and others not at all. That’s a bootstrap resample. Compute the statistic on it. Repeat a few thousand times. The spread of the results imitates the spread you’d see over real new samples:

Draw a resample of size n from the data, with replacement.
Compute the statistic on the resample.
Repeat B times, for B = 2,000, say.
The standard deviation of the B results is the bootstrap standard error.

It works because the sample’s distribution is our best estimate of the population’s distribution. With replacement matters: without it, every resample would be the original data in a different order.










Your turn. Start with the median drying time, 6.58 hours. Estimate its standard error from 2,000 bootstrap resamples.









Resample with replacement: replace = TRUE.


set.seed(4061)
boot_medians <- replicate(2000, median(sample(dry$drying_h, replace = TRUE)))
c(median = median(dry$drying_h), boot_se = sd(boot_medians))
The median is 6.58 hours, with a bootstrap standard error of 0.53 hours. sample(x, replace = TRUE) draws length(x) values from x with replacement, which is exactly a bootstrap resample. (With replace = FALSE, every resample has the same median, and the standard error is 0.)

title: The bootstrap
text:
Bootstrap confidence intervals
The simplest bootstrap confidence interval is the percentile interval: the middle 95% of the bootstrap results, from their 2.5th to their 97.5th percentile. It needs no formula and no normality.
Your turn. Bootstrap the 90th percentile, the planners’ number. The setup code has a function q90() that computes it. Find the standard error and the 95% percentile interval.









The upper end of a 95% interval is the 97.5th percentile: 0.975.


set.seed(4062)
boot_q90 <- replicate(2000, q90(sample(dry$drying_h, replace = TRUE)))
c(estimate = q90(dry$drying_h), se = sd(boot_q90), quantile(boot_q90, c(0.025, 0.975)))
10.3 hours, with a standard error of 0.76 hours and a percentile interval from 8.6 to 10.7 hours. That’s a lot of uncertainty for a booking time: with 30 batches, only three of them are in the slowest tenth.




Here’s the bootstrap distribution of the 90th percentile:

set.seed(4062)
boot_q90 <- replicate(2000, q90(sample(dry$drying_h, replace = TRUE)))
ggplot(data.frame(q = boot_q90), aes(x = q)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, boundary = 0, fill = "#C2416C") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = q90(dry$drying_h), linetype = "dashed", color = "#3A1F35") +
  annotate("text", x = q90(dry$drying_h) - 0.08, y = 480, label = "estimate, 10.3 h", hjust = 1, size = 3.6, color = "#3A1F35") +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap 90th percentile (hours)", y = "Number of resamples") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








It’s not a smooth curve, but a set of spikes. A resample’s 90th percentile is always near one of the few slowest batches, so only 51 different values ever appear. And on average, the resamples’ 90th percentiles are 0.38 hours below the original estimate: the bootstrap is telling you that the estimate itself is probably biased low. Both are warning signs that the simple percentile interval may not be accurate here.

title: The bootstrap
text:
Better intervals: BCa
The BCa interval (bias-corrected and accelerated) adjusts the percentile interval for the bias, and for a standard error that changes with the true value. It’s more accurate in many problems, and it’s what statisticians usually recommend. The boot package computes it, along with other bootstrap intervals. boot() needs the statistic as a function of the data and a vector of indices i, which says which observations are in each resample.
Your turn. Compute the percentile and BCa intervals with boot.









The function picks the resample with the indices: x[i].


set.seed(4063)
b <- boot::boot(dry$drying_h, statistic = function(x, i) q90(x[i]), R = 2000)
boot::boot.ci(b, type = c("perc", "bca"))
The percentile interval is 8.0 to 10.7 hours, and the BCa interval is 8.6 to 12.3 hours, shifted up to correct the bias. Its upper end is the longest drying time in the data, 12.33 hours: the bootstrap can’t imagine a drying time longer than any it has seen. The honest summary for the planners: “about 10.3 hours, but with 30 batches it could easily be 12”.

title: The bootstrap
text:
The parametric bootstrap
The bootstrap above resamples the data, so it’s called nonparametric: it assumes nothing about the shape of the distribution. If you trust a model, the parametric bootstrap simulates new samples from the fitted model instead. Drying times are right-skewed, and their logarithms look normal (a Shapiro-Wilk test gives p = 0.93), so a lognormal model is reasonable. Its 90th percentile is \exp(\hat\mu + z_{0.9}\,\hat\sigma), where \hat\mu and \hat\sigma are the mean and SD of the log drying times, and z_{0.9} = 1.28.
Your turn. Bootstrap the lognormal model’s 90th percentile: simulate 2,000 samples of 30 from the fitted lognormal, and compute the model’s 90th percentile for each.









Simulate from the fitted model, with sdlog = sl.


ml <- mean(log(dry$drying_h))
sl <- sd(log(dry$drying_h))
q90_model <- function(x) exp(mean(log(x)) + qnorm(0.9) * sd(log(x)))
set.seed(4064)
boot_param <- replicate(2000, q90_model(rlnorm(30, ml, sl)))
c(estimate = q90_model(dry$drying_h), se = sd(boot_param), quantile(boot_param, c(0.025, 0.975)))
The model’s 90th percentile is 10.1 hours, with a standard error of 0.83 hours and an interval from 8.6 to 11.8 hours. The interval reaches higher than the nonparametric percentile interval, because the model can imagine batches slower than any in the data. If the model is right, the parametric bootstrap is more accurate, especially for small samples and tail quantities like this one. If it’s wrong, it’s confidently wrong. Both answers agree on the message: book about 10 hours, and expect some batches to need 12.

title: The bootstrap
text:
Bootstrapping a regression
The lab measures an impurity by gas chromatography (GC). The GC doesn’t report concentrations, only peak areas, so the lab runs a calibration: 14 injections of standards with known concentrations, from 0.5 to 20 ppm. A straight line through them converts areas into concentrations. Then the sample of interest is injected three times, and its concentration is read off the line:

\hat{x}_0 = \frac{\bar{y}_0 - b_0}{b_1},

where \bar{y}_0 is the sample’s mean area, and b_0 and b_1 are the line’s intercept and slope.

ggplot(std, aes(x = conc_ppm, y = area)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(fit)[[1]], slope = coef(fit)[[2]], color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(color = "#2a78d6", size = 2.2) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = x0_hat, y = y0, yend = y0, linetype = "dashed", color = "#C2416C") +
  annotate("segment", x = x0_hat, xend = x0_hat, y = y0, yend = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "#C2416C") +
  annotate("point", x = x0_hat, y = y0, color = "#C2416C", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = x0_hat + 0.4, y = y0 - 1500, label = "sample: 7.41 ppm", hjust = 0, size = 3.6, color = "#C2416C") +
  labs(x = "Concentration (ppm)", y = "Peak area") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The result, 7.41 ppm, depends on three uncertain things: the intercept, the slope and the sample’s mean area. It’s a ratio of them, so its standard error isn’t simple. The bootstrap handles it by rebuilding the whole experiment:

A new calibration. The standards’ concentrations were chosen by the lab, so keep them fixed, and give each one a new random error: its fitted area plus a residual drawn at random from the 14 residuals. This is residual resampling.
New injections of the sample. Its mean area plus the mean of three resampled residuals.
A new result, read off the new line.

Your turn. Run the residual bootstrap. The setup code has the fitted areas fitted_area, the residuals res, the sample’s mean area y0, and a quick function line_coef() that returns a line’s intercept and slope (lm() would work too, but it’s slower in a loop).









The sample was injected three times: draw 3 residuals.


set.seed(4065)
x0_star <- replicate(2000, {
  y_star <- fitted_area + sample(res, replace = TRUE)            # a new calibration
  b <- line_coef(std$conc_ppm, y_star)
  y0_star <- y0 + mean(sample(res, 3, replace = TRUE))            # three new injections
  (y0_star - b[1]) / b[2]
})
c(x0 = x0_hat, boot_se = sd(x0_star), quantile(x0_star, c(0.025, 0.975)))
7.41 ppm, with a bootstrap standard error of 0.030 ppm, and a 95% interval from 7.35 to 7.47 ppm. So the lab can report “7.41 ± 0.06 ppm”. Most of the uncertainty comes from the sample’s own three injections, not from the calibration line.




Analytical chemistry textbooks have a formula for this standard error, derived with the delta method:

s_{\hat{x}_0} = \frac{s}{b_1} \sqrt{\frac{1}{m} + \frac{1}{n} + \frac{(\bar{y}_0 - \bar{y})^2}{b_1^2\, S_{xx}}},

with s the residual standard error, m = 3 injections of the sample, n = 14 standards, and S_{xx} = \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2.
Your turn. Compute the formula’s standard error, and compare it with the bootstrap’s 0.030 ppm.









The last term divides by b_1^2 S_{xx}: Sxx.


s <- summary(fit)$sigma
b1 <- coef(fit)[[2]]
Sxx <- sum((std$conc_ppm - mean(std$conc_ppm))^2)
s / b1 * sqrt(1 / 3 + 1 / 14 + (y0 - mean(std$area))^2 / (b1^2 * Sxx))
0.033 ppm, close to the bootstrap’s 0.030. The bootstrap is a little smaller because residuals are a little smaller than the true errors: the line was fitted to make them small. Multiplying the residuals by \sqrt{n/(n-2)} = 1.08 before resampling corrects most of that. When a formula exists, the two should agree, and that’s a good check of your bootstrap. The bootstrap’s value is for the problems where no formula exists.

title: The bootstrap
text:
When the bootstrap fails
The bootstrap works for most statistics, but not all. It needs the statistic to depend smoothly on the data, and it needs the resamples to imitate the way the data were collected. Watch out for:

Extremes. The largest value of a resample can never exceed the largest value in the data, so the bootstrap can’t tell you anything about values beyond it (Challenge 2).
Dependent data. Hourly readings from the historian are correlated with their neighbors. Resampling single readings breaks that, and the standard errors come out too small. Resample blocks of consecutive readings instead (the block bootstrap), or use a time series model (Module 6).
Very small samples. With 5 observations, there are only 126 different resamples, and the sample may not look much like the population.
The design. Resample the way the data were produced. The calibration’s concentrations were fixed by the lab, so the residual bootstrap kept them fixed. Challenge 1 resamples whole standards instead.

title: The bootstrap
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Resampling cases. Another way to bootstrap a regression is to resample the cases, the (concentration, area) pairs, with replacement. Some resamples then have the 20 ppm standard twice and the 0.5 ppm standard not at all. Compute the bootstrap standard error this way, and compare it with the residual bootstrap’s 0.030.









Use the same indices i for the areas as for the concentrations.


set.seed(4066)
x0_cases <- replicate(2000, {
  i <- sample(14, replace = TRUE)                  # which standards are in the resample
  b <- line_coef(std$conc_ppm[i], std$area[i])
  y0_star <- y0 + mean(sample(res, 3, replace = TRUE))
  (y0_star - b[1]) / b[2]
})
sd(x0_cases)
0.031 ppm, almost the same here. Case resampling treats the concentrations as random, which suits observational data, where the x values aren’t chosen. It’s also safer when the errors’ spread changes with x, because each residual stays with its own standard. Residual resampling matches a designed experiment like a calibration, and it relies on the line being the right model.




Challenge 2 · The bootstrap and the maximum. The slowest batch took 12.33 hours. Bootstrap the maximum drying time, and find the share of resamples whose maximum is exactly the sample’s maximum.









Compare with the largest drying time, max(dry$drying_h).


set.seed(4067)
boot_max <- replicate(2000, max(sample(dry$drying_h, replace = TRUE)))
mean(boot_max == max(dry$drying_h))
66% of the resamples have exactly 12.33 hours as their maximum. In theory, it’s the chance that the slowest batch appears at least once in 30 draws, 1 - (29/30)^{30} = 64\%. So the bootstrap distribution is mostly one spike at the observed maximum, and nothing at all above it, while the true maximum of a new sample of 30 could well be higher. For extremes, use a model of the tail, such as the lognormal, or extreme value theory.

title: The bootstrap
text:
Quick quiz

1. How is a bootstrap resample drawn?

Half of the data, without replacement
As many values as the data has, drawn from the data with replacement
New data from a normal distribution


With replacement, each resample is a slightly different version of the data.



2. What is the bootstrap standard error?

The standard deviation of the data
The standard deviation of the statistic over the bootstrap resamples
The mean of the bootstrap resamples


It measures how much the statistic varies from resample to resample.



3. The bootstrap replicates of a statistic average 0.38 below the original estimate. What does that suggest?

The bootstrap has failed
The estimate is probably biased low, and a bias-corrected interval such as BCa is a good idea
The standard error is 0.38


The bootstrap estimates the bias as the average replicate minus the estimate.



4. How does the parametric bootstrap differ from the nonparametric one?

It uses more resamples
It simulates new samples from a fitted model, instead of resampling the data
It doesn’t need a computer


It’s more accurate when the model is right, and misleading when it’s wrong.



5. Why does the calibration’s bootstrap keep the standards’ concentrations fixed?

Because concentrations can’t be resampled
Because the lab chose them by design, so new experiments would use the same ones
Because it makes the standard error smaller


Resample the way the data were produced.



6. For which of these does the simple bootstrap fail?

The median of 50 values
The maximum of 50 values
The mean of 50 values


A resample’s maximum can never exceed the data’s maximum, so the bootstrap can’t see what lies above it.

title: The bootstrap
text:
Wrap-up
You can now put an error bar on almost anything. Here’s what you’ve learned:

The bootstrap treats the sample as the population: resample it with replacement, recompute the statistic, and repeat. The SD of the results is the bootstrap standard error.
Percentile intervals are the middle 95% of the bootstrap results. BCa intervals correct them for bias and skewness, and are usually better. The boot package computes both.
The planners’ number: the 90th percentile of drying times is about 10.3 hours, but with only 30 batches the truth could easily be 12.
The parametric bootstrap resamples from a fitted model. It can see beyond the data, which helps for tail quantities, as long as the model is right.
Regression: residual resampling for designed experiments, and case resampling for observational data. The calibration result is 7.41 ± 0.06 ppm, in agreement with the textbook formula.
Failures: extremes, dependent data, tiny samples, and resampling that doesn’t match the design.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download drying_times.csv and gc_calibration.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

How many resamples? Bootstrap the median’s standard error with B = 50, 200, 1,000 and 10,000, five times each with different seeds. How much do the estimates vary at each B? For standard errors, a few hundred resamples are usually enough. Percentile intervals need more, because they depend on the tails.
Rescaled residuals. Multiply the calibration’s residuals by \sqrt{14/12} before resampling. Does the bootstrap standard error move closer to the formula’s 0.033?
Check the bootstrap with a simulation. Simulate 500 samples of 30 from a lognormal with meanlog = 1.88 and sdlog = 0.34. For each one, compute the percentile interval for the 90th percentile with 500 resamples. What share of the intervals contains the true 90th percentile, qlnorm(0.9, 1.88, 0.34)? (This is a simulation study of the bootstrap itself. It takes a minute or two.)
The block bootstrap. For a time series, resample blocks of consecutive values. Simulate 200 values of an autocorrelated series with stats::filter(rnorm(200), 0.8, method = "recursive"), and compare the bootstrap standard error of its mean from resampling single values with resampling blocks of 20 (pick 10 random block starts). Which is larger, and why?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Bootstrap

Estimating the sampling distribution of a statistic by recomputing it on many resamples of the data.

Bootstrap resample

A sample of the same size as the data, drawn from the data with replacement.

Bootstrap standard error

The standard deviation of a statistic over the bootstrap resamples.

Percentile interval

A confidence interval made of the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap results.

BCa interval

A bootstrap interval corrected for bias and for a standard error that changes with the true value (“bias-corrected and accelerated”).

Parametric bootstrap

A bootstrap that simulates new samples from a fitted model, instead of resampling the data.

Residual resampling

Bootstrapping a regression by keeping the x values fixed and adding resampled residuals to the fitted values.











NoteWant to read more?






Tim Hesterberg, “What teachers should know about the bootstrap”, The American Statistician (2015), free on arXiv. When the bootstrap works, when it doesn’t, and which intervals to trust, with many pictures.
Gareth James and others, An Introduction to Statistical Learning, section 5.2, “The bootstrap”, with an R lab in section 5.3. A short, friendly introduction.
Bradley Efron and Robert Tibshirani, An Introduction to the Bootstrap (Chapman & Hall, 1993). The classic book, by the bootstrap’s inventor. Not free.

title: Root finding and one-dimensional optimization
text:
Module 4 · Lesson 8 of 14 Week 68 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Many problems end with an equation that has no formula for its solution. You can write it down, and you can check any proposed answer, but you can’t rearrange it into “x = something”. Maximum likelihood is full of them: the estimate is where the derivative of the log-likelihood is zero, and for most models that equation can’t be solved by algebra. So statisticians solve it numerically, with the algorithms of this lesson and the next.
The first example comes from your separations course. A liquid mixture of three hydrocarbons, a light, a middle and a heavy one, enters a flash drum, where it partly boils. What fraction V of the feed leaves as vapor? With feed mole fractions z_i and equilibrium ratios K_i = y_i/x_i, the answer is the root of the Rachford-Rice equation,
g(V) = \sum_i \frac{z_i (K_i - 1)}{1 + V(K_i - 1)} = 0, \qquad 0 < V < 1.
Here, \mathbf{z} = (0.30, 0.50, 0.20) and \mathbf{K} = (3.2, 0.95, 0.25). There’s no formula for V with three or more components.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Root finding and one-dimensional optimization
text:
Bisection
g(0) = 0.485 and g(1) = -0.420. The function is continuous and changes sign between 0 and 1, so it must cross zero somewhere in between. Bisection closes in on the crossing:

Evaluate g at the midpoint of the interval.
Keep the half where g still changes sign.
Repeat until the interval is as short as you need.

Each step halves the interval, so after n steps the root is pinned down to within (b - a)/2^n. Bisection never fails, as long as you start with a sign change. But it’s slow: each step gains one binary digit, so 10 decimal digits take 34 steps.









Your turn. The setup code has the Rachford-Rice function rr(). Complete the bisection function: when the midpoint’s sign matches the lower end’s, the root is in the upper half, and otherwise it’s in the lower half.









Otherwise the root is in the lower half, so the midpoint becomes the new upper end, hi.


bisect <- function(g, lo, hi, tol = 1e-10) {
  iterations <- 0
  while (hi - lo > tol) {
    mid <- (lo + hi) / 2
    if (sign(g(mid)) == sign(g(lo))) lo <- mid else hi <- mid
    iterations <- iterations + 1
  }
  c(root = (lo + hi) / 2, iterations = iterations)
}
bisect(rr, 0, 1)
V = 0.5780: 57.8% of the feed leaves as vapor, after 34 halvings, exactly \lceil \log_2(1/10^{-10}) \rceil. From V, the phase compositions follow: the liquid is x_i = z_i/(1 + V(K_i - 1)), which is 13% light, 51% middle and 35% heavy, and the vapor y_i = K_i x_i is 42% light and only 9% heavy.

title: Root finding and one-dimensional optimization
text:
Newton’s method
Newton’s method (or Newton-Raphson) uses the slope. At the current guess x_n, replace g by its tangent line, and jump to where the tangent crosses zero:

x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{g(x_n)}{g'(x_n)} .

Near the root, the tangent is an excellent approximation, and the error is roughly squared at every step: 10^{-2}, then 10^{-4}, then 10^{-8}. That’s quadratic convergence, where the number of correct digits doubles with each step. Bisection’s convergence is linear: a fixed factor, one half, per step.
The price is that Newton’s method needs the derivative, and a starting point close enough to the root. Far from it, the tangent can point anywhere.
Your turn. Run Newton’s method on the Rachford-Rice equation from V = 0.5, and watch the digits. The setup code has the derivative, rr_prime().









Divide by the derivative, rr_prime(V).


V <- 0.5
for (iteration in 1:20) {
  step <- rr(V) / rr_prime(V)
  V <- V - step
  cat(iteration, format(V, digits = 15), "\n")
  if (abs(step) < 1e-12) break
}
After one step, V = 0.5786, which is 3 correct digits. After two, the error is about 10^{-7}. After three, all 15 digits that a double can show are right. Bisection needed 34 steps for 10 digits. The Rachford-Rice function is smooth and has no turning points between 0 and 1, which is the ideal case for Newton.




Here are the errors of the two methods, step by step:

Vr <- uniroot(rr, c(0, 1), tol = 1e-15)$root
lo <- 0; hi <- 1; err_b <- numeric(34)
for (i in 1:34) {
  mid <- (lo + hi) / 2
  if (sign(rr(mid)) == sign(rr(lo))) lo <- mid else hi <- mid
  err_b[i] <- abs((lo + hi) / 2 - Vr)
}
V <- 0.5; err_n <- numeric(4)
for (i in 1:4) { V <- V - rr(V) / rr_prime(V); err_n[i] <- abs(V - Vr) }
errs <- rbind(data.frame(step = 1:34, error = pmax(err_b, 1e-16), method = "bisection"),
              data.frame(step = 1:4, error = pmax(err_n, 1e-16), method = "Newton"))
ggplot(errs, aes(x = step, y = error, color = method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 22, y = 3e-5, label = "bisection", color = "#2a78d6", size = 3.6) +
  annotate("text", x = 6.5, y = 1e-11, label = "Newton", color = "#C2416C", size = 3.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(bisection = "#2a78d6", Newton = "#C2416C"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = 10^c(0, -4, -8, -12, -16), labels = c("1", "1e-4", "1e-8", "1e-12", "1e-16")) +
  labs(x = "Iteration", y = "Error (log scale)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








In practice, use R’s uniroot(). It implements Brent’s method, which combines the safety of bisection with faster steps that need no derivative: it keeps a bracket with a sign change, like bisection, and tries a faster interpolation step whenever that stays inside the bracket.

title: Root finding and one-dimensional optimization
text:
A maximum likelihood estimate
Now a statistical root. The test rig ran 20 pump seals until they failed:

sort(x)
#>  [1] 139.7 147.6 161.8 266.1 279.7 299.6 374.4 419.4 420.6 424.4 439.0 465.4
#> [13] 470.0 538.1 637.1 644.2 646.3 686.5 697.9 745.7

Lesson 3 described seal lifetimes with the Weibull distribution. Which shape k and scale \lambda fit these 20 seals best? The maximum likelihood estimates make the observed data as probable as possible. The Weibull log-likelihood is

\ell(k, \lambda) = n \log k - n k \log \lambda + (k - 1) \sum_i \log x_i - \sum_i \left(\frac{x_i}{\lambda}\right)^k .

At the maximum, both partial derivatives are zero. Setting \partial \ell/\partial \lambda = 0 gives \lambda in terms of k: \hat\lambda(k) = \left(\frac{1}{n}\sum x_i^k\right)^{1/k}. Substituting it into \partial \ell / \partial k = 0 leaves one equation in k alone, the score equation:

\frac{1}{k} + \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \log x_i - \frac{\sum_i x_i^k \log x_i}{\sum_i x_i^k} = 0 .

No algebra can solve it for k, but uniroot() can.
Your turn. The setup code has the seal lifetimes as x. Complete the score function, solve it, and compute the scale.









The denominator is \sum x_i^k: sum(x^k).


score <- function(k) 1 / k + mean(log(x)) - sum(x^k * log(x)) / sum(x^k)
k_hat <- uniroot(score, c(0.5, 10), tol = 1e-10)$root
c(shape = k_hat, scale = mean(x^k_hat)^(1 / k_hat))
A shape of 2.65 and a scale of 502 hours. The shape is well above 1, so these seals wear out: the longer they’ve run, the more likely they are to fail soon. (The seals were simulated from a shape of 2.3 and a scale of 480, so 20 seals pin the shape down only roughly. Lesson 9 computes its standard error.) Without tol = 1e-10, uniroot() stops at its default tolerance of about 10^{-4}, which gives 2.64587: plenty for the seals, but it’s worth knowing the default.




General-purpose software doesn’t always get this right. MASS::fitdistr() fits distributions by maximizing the likelihood with a general optimizer, and on these data it gives up:

tryCatch(MASS::fitdistr(x, "weibull"), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "optimization failed"
MASS::fitdistr(x / 100, "weibull")
#>      shape       scale  
#>   2.6459005   5.0183372 
#>  (0.4864730) (0.4453867)

With the lifetimes in hundreds of hours, it finds the same shape, 2.65, and a scale of 5.02 hundred hours. The optimizer struggles when the two parameters are on very different scales, here 2.6 and 500. That’s one of the lessons of Lesson 9. Solving the one-dimensional score equation sidesteps the problem.

title: Root finding and one-dimensional optimization
text:
One-dimensional optimization
Instead of solving the score equation, you can maximize the log-likelihood itself. Substituting \hat\lambda(k) into \ell gives the profile log-likelihood of k alone, which the setup code has as loglik_k():

\ell_p(k) = n \log k - n \log\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i^k\right) + (k-1)\sum_i \log x_i - n.


ks <- seq(1, 5, by = 0.02)
ggplot(data.frame(k = ks, ll = sapply(ks, loglik_k)), aes(x = k, y = ll)) +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("point", x = 2.6459, y = loglik_k(2.6459), color = "#3A1F35", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.75, y = loglik_k(2.6459) + 0.4, label = "maximum at k = 2.65", hjust = 0, size = 3.6, color = "#3A1F35") +
  labs(x = "Weibull shape k", y = "Profile log-likelihood") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Golden-section search is bisection’s cousin for finding a maximum. Bisection keeps an interval with a sign change. Golden-section search keeps an interval that contains the maximum, and shrinks it by comparing the function at two interior points: if the left point is higher, the maximum can’t be to the right of the right point, so that part is discarded, and vice versa. Each step keeps 61.8% of the interval, the golden ratio’s (\sqrt5 - 1)/2. That choice means one of the two interior points can be reused in the next step (this short version just recomputes both). It works for any function with a single peak in the interval, and needs no derivatives.
Your turn. Complete the golden-section search: when the right point is at least as high, the maximum is to the right of the left point, so the left end moves up to it.









The left end moves up to the left interior point, x1.


golden <- function(f, a, b, tol = 1e-8) {
  phi <- (sqrt(5) - 1) / 2                         # 0.618...
  x1 <- b - phi * (b - a)
  x2 <- a + phi * (b - a)
  while (b - a > tol) {
    if (f(x1) > f(x2)) b <- x2 else a <- x1
    x1 <- b - phi * (b - a)
    x2 <- a + phi * (b - a)
  }
  (a + b) / 2
}
golden(loglik_k, 0.5, 10)
2.6459, the same as the root of the score equation, as it must be: the maximum of a smooth function is where its derivative is zero. It took 43 steps to shrink the interval from 9.5 to 10^{-8}, because 0.618^{43} \approx 10^{-9}. Like bisection, it converges linearly.




R’s version is optimize(). Like uniroot(), it’s based on Brent’s ideas: golden-section steps, sped up by fitting parabolas through the last three points.
Your turn. Maximize the profile log-likelihood with optimize(). By default it minimizes, so tell it to maximize.









maximum = TRUE.


optimize(loglik_k, interval = c(0.5, 10), maximum = TRUE)
The maximum is at 2.6459, where the log-likelihood is −132.49. Without maximum = TRUE, optimize() would search for the lowest point of the curve in the interval, which is at one of its ends. (Another common way is to minimize the negative log-likelihood, which Lesson 9 does.)

title: Root finding and one-dimensional optimization
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The Colebrook equation. Another classic from your fluid mechanics course: the Darcy friction factor f for turbulent flow in a rough pipe solves the Colebrook equation,

\frac{1}{\sqrt f} = -2 \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\varepsilon/D}{3.7} + \frac{2.51}{\text{Re}\,\sqrt f}\right).

Writing u = 1/\sqrt f turns it into u = h(u), so it can be solved by fixed-point iteration: start with a guess, and keep applying h. That converges when |h'(u)| < 1 near the solution, which it is here. Find f for Re = 100,000 and a relative roughness \varepsilon/D = 0.0001.









2.51/(\text{Re}\sqrt f) = 2.51\,u/\text{Re}, so the blank is u.


Re <- 1e5
rel_rough <- 1e-4
u <- 5                                   # u = 1 / sqrt(f), a first guess
for (i in 1:10) {
  u <- -2 * log10(rel_rough / 3.7 + 2.51 * u / Re)
  cat(i, format(1 / u^2, digits = 10), "\n")
}
c(friction_factor = 1 / u^2)
f = 0.01851, the value you’d read from a Moody chart. The iterations gain about one digit each time: linear convergence, with the error shrinking by a factor of about |h'(u)| \approx 0.1 per step. Explicit approximations, such as the Swamee-Jain formula, give 0.01845, within half a percent.




Challenge 2 · When Newton goes wrong. Newton’s method on the Weibull score equation needs the score’s derivative, which the code below has. Run six Newton steps from a starting shape of 2, and then from 6.









Divide by the derivative, dscore(k).


dscore <- function(k) {
  S0 <- sum(x^k); S1 <- sum(x^k * log(x)); S2 <- sum(x^k * log(x)^2)
  -1 / k^2 - (S2 * S0 - S1^2) / S0^2
}
newton_path <- function(k) {
  path <- k
  for (i in 1:6) {
    k <- k - score(k) / dscore(k)
    path <- c(path, k)
  }
  path
}
rbind(from_2 = newton_path(2), from_6 = newton_path(6))
From 2, Newton reaches 2.6459 in four steps. From 6, its first step jumps to −1.12, and then it converges, quickly and confidently, to −1.82. That is a root of the score function, but a negative shape is meaningless: Newton found a solution of the equation that isn’t a solution of the problem. Far from the root, the score curve is flat, so the tangent line crosses zero far away. Safe practice: start close (from a rough estimate or a plot), keep the parameter in its valid range (Lesson 9 does that by working with \log k), and check the answer, ideally with a method that keeps a bracket, like uniroot().

title: Root finding and one-dimensional optimization
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does bisection need to get started?

The derivative of g
An interval where the continuous function g changes sign
A guess close to the root


A sign change guarantees a root inside, and bisection never loses it.



2. Bisection starts with an interval of length 1. How long is it after 20 steps?

1/20
2^{-20}, about 10^{-6}
10^{-20}


Each step halves it: linear convergence, one binary digit per step.



3. What is Newton’s update for solving g(x) = 0?

x - g'(x)/g(x)
x - g(x)/g'(x)
x - g(x)


It’s where the tangent line at x crosses zero.



4. Near the root, Newton’s error goes 10^{-2}, 10^{-4}, \dots. What comes next?

10^{-6}
10^{-8}
10^{-5}


Quadratic convergence squares the error, doubling the number of correct digits at each step.



5. Why is the maximum likelihood estimate a root-finding problem?

Because likelihoods are always zero at the maximum
Because the maximum of a smooth log-likelihood is where its derivative, the score, is zero
Because optimize() can’t find maxima


Solving the score equation and maximizing the log-likelihood give the same answer, as uniroot() and optimize() did.



6. What does golden-section search require of the function on the interval?

A known derivative
A sign change
A single peak (no other local maxima)


With several peaks, it can close in on the wrong one, and no warning is given.

title: Root finding and one-dimensional optimization
text:
Wrap-up
You can now solve equations that algebra can’t. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Bisection keeps a bracket with a sign change and halves it each step. It always works and converges linearly: 34 steps for 10 digits of the flash drum’s vapor fraction, 0.578.
Newton’s method follows the tangent line. It converges quadratically, here to 15 digits in 3 steps, but it needs the derivative and a good start.
uniroot() (Brent’s method) combines both: a safe bracket and fast steps. Remember its default tolerance.
Maximum likelihood leads to score equations. The seal test’s Weibull shape is 2.65, and the scale is 502 hours.
Golden-section search and optimize() maximize a function with one peak in an interval, without derivatives, and found the same 2.65.
Check your answers. From a bad start, Newton converged to a negative shape: a root of the equation, but not a solution of the problem.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download seal_test.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

The secant method. Replace the derivative in Newton’s method by the slope through the last two guesses: x_{n+1} = x_n - g(x_n)(x_n - x_{n-1})/(g(x_n) - g(x_{n-1})). Solve the Rachford-Rice equation from x_0 = 0 and x_1 = 1. How many steps does it need for 12 digits? (Its convergence is “superlinear”, with an order of about 1.6.)
A dew point. The flash drum is at its dew point when V = 1 and the first drop of liquid forms. Suppose K_i = P_i^{\text{sat}}(T)/P with Antoine equations for each component. Write g(T) = \sum z_i/K_i(T) - 1, and find the dew temperature with uniroot(). (Look up Antoine constants for propane, n-butane and n-pentane.)
Count the work. Count how many times uniroot() and optimize() evaluate their function: wrap it in a function that adds 1 to a counter every time it’s called (use <<-). Compare with your bisection and golden-section codes.
A second peak. Make a function with two peaks, such as function(x) dnorm(x, 2, 0.5) + 0.8 * dnorm(x, 5, 0.5). Run optimize() on the interval from 0 to 7, then on 0 to 4 and on 3 to 7. Which peak does it find each time?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Root finding

Solving an equation g(x) = 0 numerically.

Bisection

A root-finding method that repeatedly halves an interval in which the function changes sign.

Newton’s method

A root-finding method that jumps to where the tangent line crosses zero: x_{n+1} = x_n - g(x_n)/g'(x_n).

Linear and quadratic convergence

The error shrinks by a constant factor per step (linear), or is roughly squared per step (quadratic).

Score equation

The equation that sets the derivative of the log-likelihood to zero. Its root is the maximum likelihood estimate.

Profile log-likelihood

The log-likelihood maximized over the other parameters, as a function of one parameter.

Golden-section search

A method that finds the maximum of a single-peaked function by shrinking an interval by a factor of 0.618 per step.

Fixed-point iteration

Solving u = h(u) by repeatedly applying h. It converges when |h'| < 1 near the solution.











NoteWant to read more?






Roger Peng, Advanced Statistical Computing, chapter 2, “Solving nonlinear equations”. Bisection, rates of convergence, fixed-point iteration and Newton’s method, including Newton’s method for maximum likelihood.
R’s help pages for uniroot() and optimize(). Their tolerances and their algorithms, with references to Brent’s book.
Geof Givens and Jennifer Hoeting, Computational Statistics (Wiley, 2nd edition, 2013), chapter 2, “Optimization and solving nonlinear equations”. The standard textbook for this course. Not free.

title: The EM algorithm
text:
Module 4 · Lesson 10 of 14 Week 70 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Some likelihoods would be easy, if only you knew one more thing. In Lesson 1.11, the lab’s titrator reported some water results as “<20 ppm”, and the database stored them as 10 ppm, half the detection limit, “so that the choice can be revisited”. Now we revisit it. If you knew those results exactly, estimating the mean would be trivial. You don’t, but you do know something: each one is below the limit.
The EM algorithm (expectation-maximization, named and generalized by Dempster, Laird and Rubin in 1977) turns that situation into a simple loop. Fill in what you can’t see with its expected value, given your current estimates (the E-step). Estimate the parameters as if the filled-in data were real (the M-step). Repeat. Each round, the likelihood goes up, and the estimates converge to the maximum likelihood estimates.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: The EM algorithm
text:
Results below the detection limit
The GC can’t quantify toluene below 5 ppm. Of the last 40 batches, 27 have a result, and 13 were reported as “<5 ppm”:

head(tol)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   batch_id toluene_ppm lod_ppm below_lod
#>   <chr>          <dbl>   <dbl> <lgl>    
#> 1 T01             6.09       5 FALSE    
#> 2 T02             5.19       5 FALSE    
#> 3 T03            11.6        5 FALSE    
#> 4 T04             5.8        5 FALSE    
#> 5 T05             6.17       5 FALSE    
#> 6 T06            NA          5 TRUE
sort(detected)
#>  [1]  5.11  5.19  5.69  5.80  5.86  6.09  6.12  6.17  6.39  6.75  6.84  7.10
#> [13]  7.30  7.42  7.69  7.80  8.03  8.17  8.56  8.67  8.67  8.89  9.23  9.32
#> [25]  9.67 10.45 11.65

What’s the mean toluene level? There are several quick answers, and they disagree:

Drop the censored results and average the other 27. That ignores that the 13 missing results are all low, so it’s biased upward.
Substitute the limit, 5 ppm, which overstates every censored result.
Substitute half the limit, 2.5 ppm, the plant’s convention.
Substitute zero, which understates them all.











Your turn. The setup code has the 27 detected results as detected, and the number below the limit as n_below. Compute the mean the first three ways.









Half the limit is 2.5 ppm.


c(drop = mean(detected),
  limit = (sum(detected) + n_below * 5) / 40,
  half_limit = (sum(detected) + n_below * 2.5) / 40)
7.58, 6.74 and 5.93 ppm: a spread of more than 1.6 ppm, just from how the 13 results are handled. Which is right? None of them, quite. The substitution methods also wreck the SD: with every censored result at exactly 2.5 ppm, the data get an artificial spike, and the SD comes out at 2.76. EM does better.

title: The EM algorithm
text:
EM for censored data
Suppose the toluene levels are normal with mean \mu and SD \sigma. If we had all 40 values, the maximum likelihood estimates would be the mean and the (divide-by-n) SD, which only need two sums: \sum x_i and \sum x_i^2. EM fills in the censored results’ contributions to those two sums with their expected values, given that each one is below L = 5 and given the current estimates.
For a normal variable below L, with c = (L - \mu)/\sigma and \lambda = \phi(c)/\Phi(c) (the normal density over the normal CDF at c), the truncated normal distribution gives

E[X \mid X < L] = \mu - \sigma\lambda, \qquad E[X^2 \mid X < L] = \mu^2 + \sigma^2 - \sigma(L + \mu)\lambda .

So one round of EM is:

E-step: compute E[X \mid X < L] and E[X^2 \mid X < L] at the current \mu and \sigma.
M-step: \mu_{\text{new}} = \left(\sum_{\text{detected}} x_i + n_{\text{below}}\, E[X \mid X < L]\right)/n, and \sigma^2_{\text{new}} = \left(\sum_{\text{detected}} x_i^2 + n_{\text{below}}\, E[X^2 \mid X < L]\right)/n - \mu_{\text{new}}^2.

Your turn. Write the E-step function, and evaluate it at \mu = 6 and \sigma = 2.5.









\lambda divides the normal density by the normal CDF, pnorm().


e_step <- function(mu, sigma) {
  cc <- (L - mu) / sigma
  lam <- dnorm(cc) / pnorm(cc)
  c(EX = mu - sigma * lam, EX2 = mu^2 + sigma^2 - sigma * (L + mu) * lam)
}
e_step(6, 2.5)
If the toluene levels were N(6, 2.5^2), a result below 5 ppm would be 3.33 ppm on average. That’s more than half the limit, 2.5 ppm. A numerical integral of x times the truncated density gives the same 3.33, which is a good check of the formula.




Your turn. Now run EM: start from the mean and SD of the detected results, and repeat the E-step and the M-step 100 times.









The mean uses the expected value of X: e[["EX"]].


e_step <- function(mu, sigma) {                 # your E-step, from the last exercise
  cc <- (L - mu) / sigma
  lam <- dnorm(cc) / pnorm(cc)
  c(EX = mu - sigma * lam, EX2 = mu^2 + sigma^2 - sigma * (L + mu) * lam)
}
mu <- mean(detected)
sigma <- sd(detected)
for (i in 1:100) {
  e <- e_step(mu, sigma)                                       # E-step
  mu_new <- (sum(detected) + n_below * e[["EX"]]) / n          # M-step
  sigma <- sqrt((sum(detected^2) + n_below * e[["EX2"]]) / n - mu_new^2)
  mu <- mu_new
}
c(mu = mu, sigma = sigma)
\hat\mu = 6.22 ppm and \hat\sigma = 2.48 ppm. Maximizing the censored likelihood directly with optim(), as in Lesson 9 (detected results contribute the density, censored ones \Phi(c)), gives the same values to six digits. The data were simulated from a mean of 6.0 and an SD of 2.5, so EM is close to the truth, and much closer than dropping the censored results (7.58). Half the limit gave 5.93, not too far off here, but its SD is wrong, and the module project shows that its error depends on how much is censored.




Here are the detected results, with the fitted normal distribution. EM accounts for the part of the curve below the limit, where the 13 censored results must be:

mu_hat <- 6.222980; sigma_hat <- 2.478307
curve_df <- data.frame(t = seq(-1, 13, by = 0.05))
curve_df$y <- 40 * dnorm(curve_df$t, mu_hat, sigma_hat)
ggplot(data.frame(t = detected), aes(x = t)) +
  geom_area(data = subset(curve_df, t <= 5), aes(x = t, y = y), fill = "#F4C0D1") +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(count)), binwidth = 1, boundary = 5, fill = "#C2416C", color = "white") +
  geom_line(data = curve_df, aes(x = t, y = y), color = "#3A1F35", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5, linetype = "dashed", color = "#3A1F35") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.6, y = 7.2, label = "13 results\nbelow 5 ppm", size = 3.6, color = "#3A1F35") +
  annotate("text", x = 5.1, y = 7.9, label = "detection limit", hjust = 0, size = 3.6, color = "#3A1F35") +
  labs(x = "Toluene (ppm)", y = "Number of batches") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: The EM algorithm
text:
Mixture models
The second kind of hidden information is a latent variable: a label that every observation has, but nobody recorded. Lesson 4 simulated crystal sizes from two populations, fines and the main population. Here are 250 real crystals from the crystallizer’s image analyzer:

ggplot(crystals, aes(x = size_um)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, boundary = 0, fill = "#C2416C", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Crystal size (µm)", y = "Number of crystals") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Two humps. The model is a two-component normal mixture: each crystal is a fine with probability p, with size N(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2), and otherwise from the main population, N(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2). If we knew which crystals were fines, we’d just compute the two groups’ means and SDs. We don’t, so EM fills in the labels with probabilities.

E-step: for each crystal, the responsibility of the fines is the posterior probability that it’s a fine, by Bayes’ theorem (as in Lesson 3.13): 
r_i = \frac{p\, \phi(x_i; \mu_1, \sigma_1)}{p\, \phi(x_i; \mu_1, \sigma_1) + (1 - p)\, \phi(x_i; \mu_2, \sigma_2)}.

M-step: weighted versions of the obvious estimates: p = \bar r, \mu_1 = \sum r_i x_i / \sum r_i, \sigma_1^2 = \sum r_i (x_i - \mu_1)^2 / \sum r_i, and the same for the main population with weights 1 - r_i.

Your turn. Start from p = 0.5, \mu_1 = 100, \mu_2 = 200 and both SDs 30. Compute the responsibilities.









The main population’s mean is m2.


p <- 0.5; m1 <- 100; s1 <- 30; m2 <- 200; s2 <- 30
a <- p * dnorm(x, m1, s1)                 # fines
b <- (1 - p) * dnorm(x, m2, s2)           # main population
r <- a / (a + b)
data.frame(size = head(x), responsibility = round(head(r), 4))
The 71.6 µm crystal is almost surely a fine (0.9998), and the 228.8 µm one almost surely not (0.0002). The 151.8 µm crystal, halfway between the two means, is a coin toss: 0.45. EM doesn’t force a decision. It keeps the uncertainty, and each crystal counts as 0.45 of a fine and 0.55 of a main-population crystal in the M-step.




Your turn. Now the M-step: update the five parameters from the responsibilities.









A weighted mean divides by the sum of the weights, sum(r).


p <- 0.5; m1 <- 100; s1 <- 30; m2 <- 200; s2 <- 30
a <- p * dnorm(x, m1, s1); b <- (1 - p) * dnorm(x, m2, s2); r <- a / (a + b)
p_new <- mean(r)
m1_new <- sum(r * x) / sum(r)
m2_new <- sum((1 - r) * x) / sum(1 - r)
s1_new <- sqrt(sum(r * (x - m1_new)^2) / sum(r))
s2_new <- sqrt(sum((1 - r) * (x - m2_new)^2) / sum(1 - r))
c(p = p_new, mu1 = m1_new, s1 = s1_new, mu2 = m2_new, s2 = s2_new)
After one round: 41% fines, with means of 90.7 and 220.8 µm and SDs of 24.3 and 35.7 µm. The fines already look narrower than the starting guess, and the main population broader. Now repeat.

title: The EM algorithm
text:
Convergence
EM has a remarkable property: the likelihood never goes down. Each E-step builds a function that touches the log-likelihood at the current estimates and lies below it everywhere else, and each M-step climbs to that function’s maximum. So the log-likelihood rises at every step until it levels off at a maximum. A good stopping rule is to stop when it rises by less than a tiny amount, such as 10^{-8}.
Your turn. Put the E- and M-steps in a loop, record the log-likelihood after every round, and stop when it stops rising.









Stop when the gain is below 1e-8.


p <- 0.5; m1 <- 100; s1 <- 30; m2 <- 200; s2 <- 30
ll <- mixll(p, m1, s1, m2, s2)                    # the log-likelihood at the start
for (i in 1:1000) {
  a <- p * dnorm(x, m1, s1); b <- (1 - p) * dnorm(x, m2, s2); r <- a / (a + b)
  p <- mean(r); m1 <- sum(r * x) / sum(r); m2 <- sum((1 - r) * x) / sum(1 - r)
  s1 <- sqrt(sum(r * (x - m1)^2) / sum(r)); s2 <- sqrt(sum((1 - r) * (x - m2)^2) / sum(1 - r))
  ll <- c(ll, mixll(p, m1, s1, m2, s2))
  if (ll[length(ll)] - ll[length(ll) - 1] < 1e-8) break
}
c(iterations = i, loglik = ll[length(ll)], p = p, mu1 = m1, s1 = s1, mu2 = m2, s2 = s2)
14 rounds. 37.5% of the crystals are fines, of 85.5 \pm 16.8 µm, and the main population is 216.9 \pm 38.6 µm. The log-likelihood rose from −1416.3 to −1349.4, and all(diff(ll) >= 0) confirms it never fell. (The crystals were simulated from 35% fines of 85 \pm 18 µm and 210 \pm 38 µm, so EM recovered the populations well from 250 crystals.)




Here’s the fitted mixture on the histogram, with its two components:

pr <- fit_mix$par
dens <- data.frame(s = seq(30, 340, by = 1))
dens$fines <- pr[["p"]] * dnorm(dens$s, pr[["mu1"]], pr[["s1"]]) * 250 * 10
dens$main <- (1 - pr[["p"]]) * dnorm(dens$s, pr[["mu2"]], pr[["s2"]]) * 250 * 10
dens$mixture <- dens$fines + dens$main
ggplot(crystals, aes(x = size_um)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, boundary = 0, fill = "grey85", color = "white") +
  geom_line(data = dens, aes(x = s, y = fines), color = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = dens, aes(x = s, y = main), color = "#1baf7a", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = dens, aes(x = s, y = mixture), color = "#3A1F35", linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 62, y = 24, label = "fines, 37.5%", color = "#2a78d6", size = 3.6, hjust = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 268, y = 19, label = "main population", color = "#1baf7a", size = 3.6, hjust = 0) +
  labs(x = "Crystal size (µm)", y = "Number of crystals") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)














NoteGo deeper: why EM is slow, and when it struggles





EM converges linearly, like bisection. Its rate depends on how much information is missing: when the populations overlap heavily, each round only improves the estimates a little, and EM can need thousands of rounds. Newton’s method on the same likelihood would converge quadratically, but EM’s steps are simpler, never leave the valid range (probabilities stay between 0 and 1, and SDs stay positive) and never decrease the likelihood. That’s why EM is so popular.
Two traps. EM finds a maximum, not necessarily the highest one, so run it from several starting values and keep the best. And a mixture’s likelihood is unbounded: if one component shrinks onto a single data point, its SD goes to 0 and the likelihood to infinity. Starting values with sensible SDs, and a check that no SD collapses, avoid that.

title: The EM algorithm
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Starting values. The setup code has em_mix(), which runs this lesson’s EM from any starting values. Run it from three starts: the sensible one (100 and 200 µm), a start where the two components are identical (both 170 µm, SD 60), and a start with the labels swapped (250 and 80 µm). Compare where they end up.









For identical components, the second SD is also 60.


fits <- list(sensible = em_mix(0.5, 100, 30, 200, 30),
             identical = em_mix(0.5, 170, 60, 170, 60),
             swapped = em_mix(0.5, 250, 30, 80, 30))
t(sapply(fits, function(f) c(round(f$par, 3), loglik = tail(f$loglik, 1))))
The swapped start finds the same fit with the labels exchanged: 62.5% in “component 1”, which is now the main population. That’s label switching, and it’s harmless. The identical start is stuck: both components stay at 167.6 µm with an SD of 71.3, a single normal distribution, with a much worse log-likelihood (−1421.5 against −1349.4). With identical components, every crystal gets a responsibility of exactly 0.5, so the M-step keeps them identical forever. It’s a stationary point, but not a maximum, and EM can’t escape it. Always try several different starts.




Challenge 2 · Counting the fines. Use the fitted mixture to classify each crystal: a fine if its responsibility is above 0.5. How many fines are there, and how many crystals are genuinely uncertain (a responsibility between 0.1 and 0.9)?









A crystal is a fine if its responsibility is above 0.5: sum(r > 0.5) counts them.


fit <- em_mix(0.5, 100, 30, 200, 30)$par
a <- fit[["p"]] * dnorm(x, fit[["mu1"]], fit[["s1"]])
b <- (1 - fit[["p"]]) * dnorm(x, fit[["mu2"]], fit[["s2"]])
r <- a / (a + b)
c(fines = sum(r > 0.5), uncertain = sum(r > 0.1 & r < 0.9))
95 fines, 38% of the crystals, close to the mixture’s estimated 37.5%. Only 5 crystals are genuinely uncertain, all between 115 and 135 µm, near the point where the two weighted components cross, 127 µm. The populations are well separated, so a sieve at about 127 µm would remove the fines almost exactly. That’s the kind of practical answer a mixture model can give.

title: The EM algorithm
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does the E-step of EM compute?

The maximum likelihood estimates
The expected values of the missing information (or of the sums that need it), given the data and the current estimates
A random guess for the missing values


For censored data, the expected censored values. For a mixture, the probabilities of each label.



2. Why is “drop the results below the detection limit” biased?

Because it reduces the sample size
Because the dropped results are all low, so the average of the rest is too high
Because the limit is uncertain


The missing values aren’t missing at random: they’re missing because they’re low.



3. What happens to the log-likelihood from one EM iteration to the next?

It can go up or down
It never decreases
It always doubles


That’s EM’s guarantee, and a good check of your code: if it ever falls, there’s a bug.



4. In a two-component mixture, what’s a crystal’s responsibility?

Its size divided by the mean size
The posterior probability that it came from the first component, given its size and the current estimates
0 or 1, depending on which mean is closer


EM keeps the uncertainty: a crystal halfway between the populations counts half in each.



5. EM started with two identical components stays stuck. Why?

The data have only one population
Every observation gets a responsibility of 0.5, so the M-step keeps both components identical
EM needs at least 1,000 iterations


It’s a stationary point of the likelihood, but not a maximum. Start from different values.



6. Compared with Newton’s method, EM usually converges…

Faster, quadratically
More slowly (linearly), but with simple, stable steps that never decrease the likelihood
Only for normal distributions


Its rate depends on the share of information that’s missing.

title: The EM algorithm
text:
Wrap-up
You can now maximize likelihoods with missing pieces. Here’s what you’ve learned:

The EM algorithm alternates an E-step (fill in the missing information with its expectation, given the current estimates) and an M-step (maximize as if the data were complete).
Censored data: the expected value of a result below the limit comes from the truncated normal. The mean toluene level is 6.22 ppm with an SD of 2.48, where dropping the censored results gave 7.58 and half the limit 5.93 (with the wrong SD).
Mixtures: the responsibilities are posterior probabilities of the hidden labels. The crystallizer makes 37.5% fines of 85.5 µm, and a main population of 217 µm.
Convergence: the log-likelihood never falls. EM converges linearly, here in 14 to 17 rounds. Stop when the gain is tiny.
Starting values: identical components get stuck, swapped labels are harmless, and in general EM finds a local maximum, so try several starts.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download impurity_lod.csv and crystal_sizes.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

How fast? Record \hat\mu at every iteration of the censored EM, and plot |\hat\mu_t - \hat\mu| on a log scale against t. A straight line means linear convergence. Estimate the rate (the ratio of successive errors), and compare it with the share of censored results, 13/40.
A different limit. Pretend the limit were 7 ppm: censor every detected result below 7 too. Rerun the naive methods and EM. Which methods get worse as more data are censored? (The module project studies this properly, with a simulation.)
Three components. Extend em_mix() to three components, and fit it to the crystal sizes. Does the log-likelihood improve by much? Compare the two models with AIC (Lesson 2.12): \text{AIC} = -2\ell + 2 \times (number of parameters).
The mclust way. The mclust package fits mixtures with EM and chooses the number of components by BIC. Install it, run summary(mclust::Mclust(crystals$size_um)), and compare its answer with yours.










NoteKey words from this lesson






EM algorithm

An algorithm for maximum likelihood with missing information, alternating an expectation step and a maximization step.

Censored data

Values known only to lie in a range, such as results below a detection limit.

Detection limit

The lowest value a measurement method can report reliably. Results below it are reported as “<limit”.

Latent variable

A variable that every observation has but that wasn’t observed, such as the population a crystal came from.

Mixture model

A model in which each observation comes from one of several distributions, each with its own probability.

Responsibility

In a mixture, the posterior probability that an observation came from a given component.

Label switching

The same mixture fit, with the components numbered in a different order.











NoteWant to read more?






Roger Peng, Advanced Statistical Computing, chapter 4, “The EM algorithm”, with the two-part normal mixture and censored data as its examples, and why the likelihood never falls.
Arthur Dempster, Nan Laird and Donald Rubin, “Maximum likelihood from incomplete data via the EM algorithm”, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B (1977). The paper that named EM and proved its properties. One of the most cited papers in statistics.
Dennis Helsel, Statistics for Censored Environmental Data Using Minitab and R (Wiley, 2nd edition, 2012). Detection limits in practice, and why substitution fails. Not free, but the module project draws on its ideas.

title: Gibbs sampling
text:
Module 4 · Lesson 12 of 14 Week 72 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The Metropolis algorithm of Lesson 11 proposes a random step and sometimes rejects it. For many models, there’s a smarter way. Often the posterior of all the parameters together is complicated, but the posterior of one parameter, with all the others held fixed, is a familiar distribution that R can sample directly. Gibbs sampling takes advantage of that: it updates the parameters one at a time, each drawn from its full conditional distribution, given the data and the current values of all the others. Every draw is accepted. Repeat, and the chain’s stationary distribution is the full posterior.
Named after the physicist Josiah Willard Gibbs by the brothers Geman, who used it to restore noisy images in 1984, it made Bayesian statistics practical in the 1990s. It’s the engine inside software such as BUGS and JAGS.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Gibbs sampling
text:
One coordinate at a time
Start with a target you can check: two standard normal variables X and Y with correlation \rho. Their full conditionals are normal (it’s a property of the multivariate normal, from Lesson 3.3):

X \mid Y = y \;\sim\; N\!\left(\rho y,\; 1 - \rho^2\right), \qquad Y \mid X = x \;\sim\; N\!\left(\rho x,\; 1 - \rho^2\right).

So a Gibbs sampler alternates: draw X given the current Y, then Y given the new X, and so on. Each move is parallel to one axis, so the chain moves in a staircase:

set.seed(4127)
x <- 0; y <- 0; path <- data.frame(x = 0, y = 0)
for (i in 1:25) {
  x <- rnorm(1, 0.6 * y, sqrt(1 - 0.36)); path <- rbind(path, c(x, y))
  y <- rnorm(1, 0.6 * x, sqrt(1 - 0.36)); path <- rbind(path, c(x, y))
}
grid <- expand.grid(x = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 100), y = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 100))
grid$d <- exp(-(grid$x^2 - 1.2 * grid$x * grid$y + grid$y^2) / (2 * 0.64))
ggplot(grid, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_contour(aes(z = d), bins = 6, color = "grey75") +
  geom_path(data = path, color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(data = path[seq(1, nrow(path), by = 2), ], color = "#C2416C", size = 1.6) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "X", y = "Y") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)


















Your turn. Run 5,000 rounds of the Gibbs sampler for \rho = 0.6, and check the correlation of the draws.









Y’s conditional mean is \rho x, using the new x.


rho <- 0.6
set.seed(4121)
xs <- ys <- numeric(5000)
x <- 0; y <- 0
for (i in 1:5000) {
  x <- rnorm(1, rho * y, sqrt(1 - rho^2))           # X given the current Y
  y <- rnorm(1, rho * x, sqrt(1 - rho^2))           # Y given the new X
  xs[i] <- x; ys[i] <- y
}
c(correlation = cor(xs, ys), mean_x = mean(xs), sd_x = sd(xs))
A correlation of 0.599, a mean of −0.04 and an SD of 0.99: a sample from the right bivariate normal, built from nothing but one-dimensional normal draws.

title: Gibbs sampling
text:
The reference material
Lesson 7’s audit question comes back. The lab analyzed a certified reference material, whose iron content is certified as 50.0 mg/kg, 15 times:

iron
#>  [1] 52.43 50.64 50.35 53.27 52.10 49.34 50.76 50.09 51.44 50.13 50.38 52.95
#> [13] 49.83 51.38 51.28

The mean is 51.09. Is the method biased, and by how much? Model the results as N(\mu, \sigma^2), with both \mu and \sigma unknown. It’s convenient to work with the precision \tau = 1/\sigma^2. With a normal prior for \mu and a gamma prior for \tau, the full conditionals are:

\mu \mid \tau, \mathbf{y} \sim N(m, v), \qquad v = \frac{1}{1/s_0^2 + n\tau}, \quad m = v\left(\frac{\mu_0}{s_0^2} + \tau \sum y_i\right),


\tau \mid \mu, \mathbf{y} \sim \text{Gamma}\!\left(a_0 + \frac{n}{2},\; b_0 + \frac12 \sum (y_i - \mu)^2\right).

The first says: given the precision, the posterior mean of \mu is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean \mu_0 and the data. The second: given \mu, the precision is set by the sum of squared deviations from it. We’ll use vague priors that let the data speak: \mu_0 = 50 with s_0 = 10 mg/kg, and a_0 = b_0 = 0.01. (Module 5 derives these, and discusses choosing priors.)
Your turn. Complete the Gibbs sampler, run 5,000 rounds, and drop 500 as burn-in.









The deviations are from the current mu.


mu0 <- 50; s0 <- 10
n <- length(iron)
set.seed(4122)
draws <- matrix(NA, 5000, 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("mu", "sigma")))
mu <- mean(iron); tau <- 1 / var(iron)
for (i in 1:5000) {
  v <- 1 / (1 / s0^2 + n * tau)
  m <- v * (mu0 / s0^2 + tau * sum(iron))
  mu <- rnorm(1, m, sqrt(v))                                        # mu given tau
  tau <- rgamma(1, a0 + n / 2, b0 + sum((iron - mu)^2) / 2)          # tau given mu
  draws[i, ] <- c(mu, 1 / sqrt(tau))
}
keep <- draws[-(1:500), ]
c(mu = mean(keep[, "mu"]), quantile(keep[, "mu"], c(0.025, 0.975)), sigma = mean(keep[, "sigma"]))
The posterior mean of \mu is 51.10 mg/kg, with a 95% credible interval from 50.46 to 51.75, and \sigma is about 1.24 mg/kg. The t-interval of Module 0 gives 50.44 to 51.74: with vague priors, the Bayesian and the classical answers nearly agree. Here, the draws are almost independent: their effective sample size is about 4,500 out of 4,500.




The posterior gives direct answers to the auditor’s questions. The lab’s bias is \mu - 50.0, and with draws of \mu, the posterior of the bias, and the probability that the method reads high, are one line each.
Your turn. The setup code has the sampler as a function, gibbs_normal(y, n_iter, mu0, s0). Find the posterior mean bias, its 95% credible interval, and the probability that the method reads high.









The method reads high when the bias is above 0.


set.seed(4122)
keep <- gibbs_normal(iron, 5000, mu0 = 50, s0 = 10)[-(1:500), ]
bias <- keep[, "mu"] - 50.0
c(bias = mean(bias), quantile(bias, c(0.025, 0.975)), p_reads_high = mean(bias > 0))
A bias of +1.10 mg/kg, between 0.46 and 1.75, and a 99.8% posterior probability that the method reads high. That’s a statement the auditor can use directly: “the method almost certainly reads about 2% high, so correct the results or recalibrate”. A p-value can’t be phrased that way.

title: Gibbs sampling
text:
Data augmentation
Lesson 10’s toluene results had 13 values below the 5 ppm detection limit. EM filled them in with their expected values. The Gibbs way, called data augmentation, treats the missing values as extra unknowns, and draws them too:

Impute: draw each censored value from its full conditional: the normal N(\mu, \sigma^2), truncated to values below 5 ppm.
Update: with the data now complete, draw \mu and \tau exactly as for the reference material.

Drawing from a truncated normal is Lesson 3’s inverse-transform method, as in Lesson 4’s second challenge: draw u uniformly between 0 and \Phi\big((5 - \mu)/\sigma\big), the CDF at the limit, and transform it back with qnorm().
Your turn. Write the imputation step as a function, and test it: 10,000 imputed values at \mu = 6 and \sigma = 2.5 should all be below 5, and their mean should match Lesson 10’s E-step, 3.33.









The upper end is the normal CDF at the limit, pnorm(L, mu, sigma).


impute <- function(k, mu, sigma) {
  u <- runif(k, 0, pnorm(L, mu, sigma))      # uniform below the CDF at the limit
  qnorm(u, mu, sigma)
}
set.seed(4123)
z <- impute(10000, 6, 2.5)
c(largest = max(z), mean = mean(z))
Every value is below 5 ppm (the largest is 4.9995), and their mean is 3.33, the same as Lesson 10’s E[X \mid X < 5]. EM uses the average, and data augmentation uses random draws whose average it is.




Your turn. Now the full data-augmentation sampler for the toluene, with vague priors (\mu_0 = 5, s_0 = 10). Complete the line that joins the detected and the imputed values.









Join the detected results and the imputed ones, z.


impute <- function(k, mu, sigma) qnorm(runif(k, 0, pnorm(L, mu, sigma)), mu, sigma)
mu0 <- 5; s0 <- 10
set.seed(4124)
draws <- matrix(NA, 5000, 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("mu", "sigma")))
mu <- mean(detected); tau <- 1 / var(detected)
for (i in 1:5000) {
  z <- impute(n_below, mu, 1 / sqrt(tau))             # 1. impute the 13 censored results
  y <- c(detected, z)                                 #    the completed data
  n <- length(y)
  v <- 1 / (1 / s0^2 + n * tau); m <- v * (mu0 / s0^2 + tau * sum(y))
  mu <- rnorm(1, m, sqrt(v))                           # 2. update mu and tau
  tau <- rgamma(1, a0 + n / 2, b0 + sum((y - mu)^2) / 2)
  draws[i, ] <- c(mu, 1 / sqrt(tau))
}
keep <- draws[-(1:500), ]
c(mu = mean(keep[, "mu"]), quantile(keep[, "mu"], c(0.025, 0.975)), sigma = mean(keep[, "sigma"]))
The posterior mean toluene level is 6.18 ppm, with a 95% credible interval from 5.20 to 7.03, and \sigma about 2.62 ppm. EM gave 6.22 and 2.48: the same picture, plus an honest interval that includes the uncertainty about the 13 missing values. (The posterior mean of \sigma is a little above the maximum likelihood estimate, as usual for a scale parameter with 40 observations.)

title: Gibbs sampling
text:
When Gibbs is slow: blocking
Gibbs sampling moves parallel to the axes. When two parameters are strongly correlated in the posterior, the posterior is a narrow diagonal ridge, and axis-parallel steps can only inch along it. Each draw is then almost the same as the last, and the chain explores slowly.
Your turn. Run the bivariate normal sampler again with \rho = 0.99, and compare the effective sample size of its 5,000 draws of X with 5,000 independent draws.









Draw 5,000 standard normals: rnorm(5000).


rho <- 0.99
set.seed(4125)
xs <- numeric(5000)
x <- 0; y <- 0
for (i in 1:5000) {
  x <- rnorm(1, rho * y, sqrt(1 - rho^2))
  y <- rnorm(1, rho * x, sqrt(1 - rho^2))
  xs[i] <- x
}
independent <- rnorm(5000)                   # 5,000 independent draws of X
c(ess_gibbs = coda::effectiveSize(xs), ess_independent = coda::effectiveSize(independent))
The Gibbs chain’s 5,000 draws are worth about 58 independent ones: a correlation of 0.98 between successive draws. With \rho = 0.6, the same sampler gives an effective sample size of about 2,300. Independent draws are worth about 5,000, as they should be.




The fixes all aim to stop moving along the axes. Blocking draws the correlated parameters together, from their joint conditional distribution, when that’s possible: here, drawing (X, Y) jointly from the bivariate normal gives independent draws. Reparameterizing changes the parameters so that they’re less correlated, such as centering a predictor in a regression (Lesson 2.11). And Metropolis steps with correlated proposals (Lesson 11’s last practice exercise) follow the ridge instead of crossing it.






NoteGo deeper: Gibbs is a special case of Metropolis-Hastings





A Gibbs update of one parameter is a Metropolis-Hastings step whose proposal is that parameter’s full conditional distribution. Plug that proposal into the Hastings acceptance ratio, \frac{\pi(\theta^*)\, q(\theta^* \to \theta)}{\pi(\theta)\, q(\theta \to \theta^*)}, and everything cancels to exactly 1, which is why Gibbs never rejects. When some full conditionals aren’t standard distributions, you can mix the two: Gibbs steps for the parameters with easy conditionals, and Metropolis steps for the rest. That’s called Metropolis-within-Gibbs, and it’s how many real samplers work.

title: Gibbs sampling
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The next analysis. The posterior predictive distribution describes a future observation, with all the uncertainty about \mu and \sigma included. Simulate it: for each posterior draw, draw one new analysis from N(\mu, \sigma^2). What’s the chance that the next analysis of the reference material reads above 53 mg/kg, the lab’s alarm limit?









Use each draw’s own SD, keep[, "sigma"].


set.seed(4122)
keep <- gibbs_normal(iron, 5000, mu0 = 50, s0 = 10)[-(1:500), ]
set.seed(4126)
y_new <- rnorm(nrow(keep), keep[, "mu"], keep[, "sigma"])
c(quantile(y_new, c(0.025, 0.975)), p_over_53 = mean(y_new > 53))
The next analysis will be between 48.5 and 53.6 mg/kg with 95% probability, almost the same as the classical prediction interval for a new observation, \bar y \pm t_{0.975,\,14}\, s\sqrt{1 + 1/15}, which runs from 48.5 to 53.7. There’s a 6% chance that the next analysis trips the alarm at 53. If the alarm is meant to catch a broken method, it will raise a false alarm about once in 16 analyses of a working one, partly because of the bias.




Challenge 2 · How many batches are over the limit? A customer’s specification allows at most 10 ppm of toluene. For each posterior draw of (\mu, \sigma) from the data-augmentation sampler, compute the share of batches above 10 ppm, 1 - \Phi\big((10 - \mu)/\sigma\big), and summarize its posterior.









The specification limit is 10 ppm.


set.seed(4124)
keep <- augmented_draws(5000)[-(1:500), ]       # the setup code's version of your sampler
p_over_10 <- 1 - pnorm(10, keep[, "mu"], keep[, "sigma"])
c(mean = mean(p_over_10), quantile(p_over_10, c(0.025, 0.975)))
About 7.4% of batches are over 10 ppm, but it could be anywhere from 2.4% to 15.6%. Plugging in Lesson 10’s maximum likelihood estimates gives a single number, 6.4%, with no sense of its uncertainty. In the data, 2 of the 40 batches were over 10 ppm, which is consistent. A nonlinear quantity like this one gets its full posterior for free from the draws.

title: Gibbs sampling
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does a Gibbs sampler draw at each step?

A proposal that it might reject
One parameter (or block) from its full conditional distribution, given the data and the current values of the others
All the parameters independently from their priors


Every draw is accepted.



2. In the normal model, what is \mu’s full conditional posterior mean?

The sample mean
The prior mean
A precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the data


With a vague prior (s_0 large), the data dominate, and it’s close to the sample mean.



3. What’s the difference between EM and data augmentation for censored values?

There’s none
EM fills in their expected values and finds the maximum likelihood estimate; data augmentation draws them at random and samples the posterior
Data augmentation ignores the censored values


Both fill in the missing values from their conditional distribution, one with its average and one with draws.



4. Why does Gibbs sampling slow down when two parameters are highly correlated?

Because it rejects more proposals
Because its moves are parallel to the axes, so it can only inch along a narrow diagonal ridge
Because the full conditionals become non-normal


With \rho = 0.99, 5,000 draws were worth about 58.



5. What is blocking?

Throwing away blocks of draws
Drawing correlated parameters together, from their joint conditional distribution
Running several chains


It removes the zigzag along the ridge.



6. How do you get the posterior of a quantity such as the share of batches above 10 ppm?

With the delta method
Compute it for each posterior draw of the parameters, and summarize the results
Plug the posterior means into the formula


Plugging in posterior means gives a single number. The draws give the whole distribution.

title: Gibbs sampling
text:
Wrap-up
You can now sample posteriors one parameter at a time. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Gibbs sampling draws each parameter from its full conditional distribution in turn, and never rejects.
The normal model: \mu is normal given \tau, and \tau is gamma given \mu. The lab’s method reads 1.10 mg/kg high (0.46 to 1.75), with a 99.8% posterior probability of reading high.
Data augmentation draws the missing values too: below a detection limit, from a truncated normal by inversion. The toluene mean is 6.18 ppm (5.20 to 7.03), close to EM’s 6.22, with honest uncertainty.
Posterior summaries of anything: the next analysis reads above 53 with a 6% chance, and 7.4% of batches (2.4% to 15.6%) exceed 10 ppm.
Slow mixing: with strongly correlated parameters, Gibbs moves in tiny steps. Block, reparameterize, or use better Metropolis proposals.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download qc_repeats.csv and impurity_lod.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

An informative prior. The method’s validation report says its bias is 0 \pm 0.5 mg/kg. Use \mu_0 = 50 and s_0 = 0.5, and rerun the reference material sampler. How far does the posterior bias move toward 0? How much would more analyses help?
Blocking for real. Write a sampler for the bivariate normal with \rho = 0.99 that draws (X, Y) jointly in each step (draw X from its marginal, N(0, 1), and then Y given X). Compare its trace plot with the one-at-a-time sampler’s.
A mixture, the Gibbs way. Write a Gibbs sampler for Lesson 10’s two-component crystal mixture: draw each crystal’s label (fine or not) from its responsibility, then p from a beta distribution, and each component’s mean and precision given its crystals. Compare the posterior means with EM’s estimates. Watch out for label switching.
JAGS. If you’d like a preview of Module 5, install JAGS and the rjags package, and fit the reference material model in the BUGS language. It writes the Gibbs sampler for you.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Gibbs sampling

An MCMC method that updates each parameter in turn by drawing from its full conditional distribution.

Full conditional distribution

The distribution of one parameter given the data and the current values of all the other parameters.

Precision

One over the variance, \tau = 1/\sigma^2, which often makes formulas simpler.

Data augmentation

Treating missing or censored values as unknowns and drawing them inside a Gibbs sampler.

Posterior predictive distribution

The distribution of a future observation, averaged over the posterior uncertainty in the parameters.

Blocking

Updating several correlated parameters together, from their joint conditional distribution.

Metropolis-within-Gibbs

A sampler that uses Gibbs steps for some parameters and Metropolis steps for others.











NoteWant to read more?
