Roger Peng, Advanced Statistical Computing, section 7.3, “Gibbs sampler”. The bivariate normal and the normal model with unknown mean and variance, as in this lesson, and Gibbs as a case of Metropolis-Hastings.
Andrew Gelman and others, Bayesian Data Analysis (3rd edition), free PDF on the book’s site, section 11.1, “Gibbs sampler”, and chapter 12 on making samplers efficient.
George Casella and Edward George, “Explaining the Gibbs sampler”, The American Statistician (1992). A short, classic introduction, with the bivariate examples.

title: Data mining: clustering and classification
text:
Module 4 · Lesson 14 of 14 Week 74 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Data mining means finding useful patterns in data, usually with algorithms that make few assumptions. Its two classic tasks are clustering, finding groups in data that have no labels, and classification, learning to predict labels from data that has them. Modules 7 and 8 are all about them. This lesson is a first look, with the algorithms written out, so you can see how they work.
The data are an old friend: Lesson 3.13’s 58 incoming feed lots from four suppliers, with four inspection results each.
head(lots)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   lot_id  supplier    water_ppm aldehyde_ppm acid_mgKOH iron_ppb
#>   <chr>   <fct>           <dbl>        <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 F26-001 Kestrel           273         51.8      0.148     39  
#> 2 F26-002 Plum Valley       188         30.2      0.08      54.5
#> 3 F26-003 Plum Valley       205         57.2      0.115     39.7
#> 4 F26-004 Rosewater         244         57.7      0.126     26.4
#> 5 F26-005 Rosewater         184         74.8      0.1       28.5
#> 6 F26-006 Fizzwell          215         40.7      0.137     29.3
table(lots$supplier)
#> 
#>    Fizzwell     Kestrel Plum Valley   Rosewater 
#>          16          15          14          13
Lesson 3.13 classified them with linear discriminant analysis, which assumes that each supplier’s lots are multivariate normal with a common covariance matrix, and its leave-one-out error was 8 out of 58, 13.8%. This lesson asks two questions. If the labels had been lost, could you have found the four suppliers anyway? And do methods that assume much less than LDA classify any better?
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Data mining: clustering and classification
text:
k-means clustering
Distance-based methods need the variables on comparable scales. The water content varies by about 50 ppm, and the acid value by about 0.03 mg KOH/g, so in raw units, the water would decide everything (Challenge 1 shows how badly). The setup code has standardized the four variables to mean 0 and SD 1, as Z.
k-means looks for k clusters whose points are as close as possible to their cluster’s mean, the center. It minimizes the total within-cluster sum of squares, and it does so with Lloyd’s algorithm, which alternates two steps:

Assign each point to its nearest center.
Update each center to the mean of the points assigned to it.

Each step can only lower the within-cluster sum of squares, so the algorithm converges, usually in a few rounds. But it converges to a local minimum that depends on the starting centers, which is why kmeans() has an nstart argument: it runs many random starts, and keeps the best.











Your turn. Do one assignment step by hand: choose 4 random lots as the starting centers, compute every lot’s squared distance to each center, and assign each lot to the nearest one.









For each row, find the position of the smallest distance: which.min.


set.seed(4141)
centers <- Z[sample(nrow(Z), 4), ]                         # 4 random lots as the first centers
d2 <- sapply(1:4, function(j) colSums((t(Z) - centers[j, ])^2))   # 58 x 4 squared distances
cluster <- apply(d2, 1, which.min)                         # the nearest center for each lot
table(cluster = cluster, supplier = lots$supplier)
After one step from random centers, the clusters are a mess: one has 25 lots from three suppliers, though cluster 2 is already pure Kestrel. The update step would move each center to its cluster’s mean, and a few more rounds of assign-and-update would sort things out. t(Z) - centers[j, ] subtracts the center from every lot at once, because R recycles the center down each column of the transposed matrix.




Your turn. Now let kmeans() run the whole algorithm, with 25 random starts, and compare its four clusters with the true suppliers.









nstart = 25.


set.seed(4142)
km <- kmeans(Z, centers = 4, nstart = 25)
tb <- table(cluster = km$cluster, supplier = lots$supplier)
print(tb)
c(within_ss = km$tot.withinss, purity = purity(tb))
Without ever seeing a label, k-means found Kestrel perfectly (all 15 of its wet lots in one cluster) and Rosewater mostly (12 of 13, by their aldehyde). Fizzwell and Plum Valley, the twins of Lesson 3.13, are mixed across two clusters. The purity, the share of lots that belong to their cluster’s main supplier, is 81%. (The cluster numbers are arbitrary: rerun with another seed, and they may be shuffled.)





set.seed(4142)
km <- kmeans(Z, centers = 4, nstart = 25)
plot_df <- data.frame(water = Z[, "water_ppm"], aldehyde = Z[, "aldehyde_ppm"],
                      cluster = factor(km$cluster), supplier = lots$supplier)
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = water, y = aldehyde, color = cluster, shape = supplier)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#C2416C", "#2a78d6", "#1baf7a", "#d18a12"), name = "k-means cluster") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15, 18), name = "True supplier") +
  labs(x = "Water (standardized)", y = "Aldehyde (standardized)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: Data mining: clustering and classification
text:
How many clusters?
In a real clustering problem, nobody tells you k. Two common guides:

The elbow. The within-cluster sum of squares always falls as k grows, all the way to 0 when every point is its own cluster. Plot it against k, and look for an “elbow”, where adding clusters stops helping much. Here it falls 228, 151, 105, 74, 63, 55: the drops shrink after k = 4.
The silhouette. For each point, compare a, its average distance to the other points of its own cluster, with b, its average distance to the points of the nearest other cluster. Its silhouette width is (b - a)/\max(a, b): near 1 if it sits snugly in its cluster, near 0 if it’s on a border, and negative if it’s probably in the wrong cluster. The average silhouette width over all points measures how well separated the clusters are, and you choose the k that maximizes it.

Your turn. Compute the average silhouette width for k = 2 to 7, with cluster::silhouette().









silhouette() needs the distances, D.


set.seed(4144)
D <- dist(Z)
widths <- sapply(2:7, function(k) {
  km <- kmeans(Z, k, nstart = 25)
  mean(cluster::silhouette(km$cluster, D)[, "sil_width"])
})
names(widths) <- 2:7
round(widths, 3)
The widths are 0.34, 0.35, 0.38, 0.38, 0.33 and 0.30: k = 4 and k = 5 are practically tied, and both beat fewer or more clusters. That’s typical. The data suggest “four or five groups”, and deciding between them needs outside knowledge, such as knowing that there are four suppliers. Average silhouette widths around 0.4 also say that the clusters overlap: well-separated clusters score above 0.7.

title: Data mining: clustering and classification
text:
Hierarchical clustering
Hierarchical clustering doesn’t need k in advance. Start with every lot as its own cluster, and repeatedly merge the two closest clusters, until one is left. The record of the merges is a tree, the dendrogram, and cutting it at any height gives clusters.
How far apart two clusters are is a choice, called the linkage. Complete linkage uses their two farthest points, average linkage the average distance, and single linkage the two closest points (which tends to make long chains). Ward’s method merges the pair that increases the within-cluster sum of squares the least, the same criterion as k-means.

hc <- hclust(dist(Z), method = "ward.D2")
par(mar = c(1, 4, 1, 1))
plot(hc, labels = FALSE, hang = -1, main = "", sub = "", xlab = "", ylab = "Merge height", col = "#3A1F35")
rect.hclust(hc, k = 4, border = "#C2416C")








Your turn. Cluster the lots with Ward’s method, cut the tree into four clusters, and compare them with the suppliers.









Cut into k = 4 clusters.


hc <- hclust(dist(Z), method = "ward.D2")
groups <- cutree(hc, k = 4)
tb <- table(cluster = groups, supplier = lots$supplier)
print(tb)
purity(tb)
A purity of 86%, better than k-means’ 81%: Kestrel (15 of 15) and Rosewater (13 of 13) each get their own cluster, Fizzwell is mostly in one (14 of 16), and Plum Valley mostly in another (8 of 14). Ward’s method is deterministic (there are no random starts), and the dendrogram shows the structure at every level at once. With other linkages, the purity is 62% (complete), 86% (average) and 31% (single linkage, which chains 55 of the 58 lots into one cluster).

title: Data mining: clustering and classification
text:
k-nearest neighbors
Now use the labels. k-nearest neighbors (kNN) is the simplest classifier there is: to classify a lot, find the k labeled lots nearest to it, and take a vote. There’s no model and no fitting, just distances. Small k follows the data closely, and is noisy. Large k is smooth, but blurs the boundaries. It’s the bias-variance trade-off of Lesson 13 again, and cross-validation chooses k.
class::knn.cv() does leave-one-out cross-validation directly: it classifies each lot by its k nearest other lots. (It breaks tied votes at random, hence the seed.)
Your turn. Compute the leave-one-out error rate for k = 1 to 15.









Inside the function, the number of neighbors is k.


errors <- sapply(1:15, function(k) {
  set.seed(4145)
  predicted <- class::knn.cv(Z, lots$supplier, k = k)
  mean(predicted != lots$supplier)
})
round(errors, 3)
One neighbor misclassifies 28% of the lots, and the error falls, unevenly, to a minimum of 15.5% (9 lots) at k = 12. That’s close to LDA’s 13.8%, and it’s a little optimistic, because k was chosen to minimize this same error. Almost all of kNN’s mistakes are Plum Valley lots: only 7 of its 14 are classified correctly. kNN needs no assumptions, but LDA’s assumptions were close to true for these data, and a correct assumption is worth a lot of data.

title: Data mining: clustering and classification
text:
Classification trees
A classification tree asks a sequence of yes-or-no questions about one variable at a time: “is the water above 250 ppm?”, then, for the lots below, “is the aldehyde above 57?”, and so on. Each question splits a group of lots into two, choosing the variable and the threshold that make the two halves as pure as possible. The rpart package grows such trees. Its trees are easy to read and explain, and they need no standardizing, because each split looks at one variable on its own scale.
Your turn. Grow a tree for the supplier on the raw inspection results, and find its apparent error rate.









Compare with the true labels, lots$supplier.


tree <- rpart::rpart(supplier ~ water_ppm + aldehyde_ppm + acid_mgKOH + iron_ppb, data = lots)
print(tree)
mean(predict(tree, type = "class") != lots$supplier)
Three questions: water of 250 ppm or more means Kestrel (all 15 lots, no mistakes); otherwise, aldehyde of 57.45 ppm or more means Rosewater; otherwise, iron of 38.55 ppb or more means Plum Valley, and less means Fizzwell. That’s Lesson 3.13’s discriminants in plain language: water, aldehyde and iron, one at a time. The apparent error is 12.1%, 7 of 58. As in Lesson 3.13, the apparent error is optimistic, and the honest one needs cross-validation.




Your turn. Estimate the tree’s error honestly by leave-one-out: grow a tree without each lot, and classify that lot with it.









Classify the left-out lot, lots[i, ].


loo <- sapply(1:nrow(lots), function(i) {
  t_i <- rpart::rpart(supplier ~ water_ppm + aldehyde_ppm + acid_mgKOH + iron_ppb, data = lots[-i, ])
  as.character(predict(t_i, lots[i, ], type = "class"))
})
c(wrong = sum(loo != lots$supplier), error_rate = mean(loo != lots$supplier))
8 of 58 wrong, 13.8%: exactly LDA’s leave-one-out error, from three yes-or-no questions. So here’s the scorecard, all honest leave-one-out error rates: LDA 13.8%, the tree 13.8%, kNN 15.5% (and that one’s a little optimistic). And without labels at all, Ward’s clustering grouped 86% of the lots with their own supplier.










NoteGo deeper: how a tree chooses its splits





At each node, rpart() tries every variable and every threshold between consecutive values, and picks the split that most reduces the Gini impurity, \sum_j p_j(1 - p_j), where p_j is the share of class j in a node. A pure node has impurity 0. Left alone, it keeps splitting until the nodes are tiny, and a tree that big fits the training data perfectly and generalizes badly. rpart() stops early by default: a split must improve the fit by a complexity parameter cp (0.01 of the root’s error, by default), and nodes must have at least 20 lots to be split. The modern approach is to grow a big tree and prune it back with cross-validation (Challenge 2). Module 8 goes much further: random forests and boosting combine hundreds of trees, and they’re among the most accurate classifiers known.

title: Data mining: clustering and classification
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Forget to standardize. Run k-means with 4 clusters on the raw inspection results, and compute the purity.









Compute the purity of this table, tb.


set.seed(4147)
km_raw <- kmeans(lots[, vars], centers = 4, nstart = 25)
tb <- table(cluster = km_raw$cluster, supplier = lots$supplier)
print(tb)
print(tapply(lots$water_ppm, km_raw$cluster, range))
purity(tb)
The purity drops to 64%. The four clusters are just four bands of water content: 155 to 215, 207 to 244, 256 to 301 and 315 to 353 ppm. The water’s SD, 49 ppm, is so much bigger than the acid’s, 0.027, that the other variables hardly count in the distances. Kestrel is split in two by its water, and Fizzwell, Plum Valley and half of Rosewater are lumped together. Standardize before clustering, unless the units are genuinely comparable.




Challenge 2 · Grow big, then prune. Grow a tree with no stopping rules (cp = 0 and minsplit = 2), so that it fits every lot. rpart() cross-validates it internally (10-fold, hence the seed), and its cptable lists the cross-validated error, xerror, of every smaller tree. Prune to the complexity with the smallest xerror.









Choose the row with the smallest cross-validated error, "xerror".


set.seed(4146)
big <- rpart::rpart(supplier ~ water_ppm + aldehyde_ppm + acid_mgKOH + iron_ppb, data = lots,
                    control = rpart::rpart.control(cp = 0, minsplit = 2))
print(big$cptable)
best_cp <- big$cptable[which.min(big$cptable[, "xerror"]), "CP"]
pruned <- rpart::prune(big, cp = best_cp)
c(leaves_big = sum(big$frame$var == "<leaf>"), leaves_pruned = sum(pruned$frame$var == "<leaf>"))
The big tree has 13 leaves and fits all 58 lots perfectly (a relative training error of 0). But its cross-validated error is lowest with just 3 splits and 4 leaves (an xerror of 0.19, against 0.29 for the full tree), and pruning gives back exactly the default tree, with its water, aldehyde and iron questions. The extra 9 leaves were fitting individual lots: Lesson 7’s overfitting, in tree form.

title: Data mining: clustering and classification
text:
Quick quiz

1. What’s the difference between clustering and classification?

Clustering uses more variables
Clustering finds groups in data without labels, and classification learns to predict known labels
Classification can’t use distances


Data miners call them unsupervised and supervised learning.



2. What are the two steps of Lloyd’s algorithm for k-means?

Split and merge
Assign each point to its nearest center, then move each center to its cluster’s mean
Shuffle the labels, then count


Each step lowers the within-cluster sum of squares, so it converges, to a local minimum.



3. Why standardize the variables before k-means or kNN?

It makes the algorithms faster
Distances are dominated by the variables with the largest spread, whatever their importance
It makes the data normal


Unstandardized, the water decided everything, and the purity fell from 81% to 64%.



4. What does a silhouette width near 0 mean for a point?

It’s in the center of its cluster
It’s on the border between two clusters
It’s an outlier far from every cluster


Near 1 means snugly in its cluster, and negative means probably in the wrong one.



5. How does kNN with k = 12 classify a lot?

With the label of its single nearest lot
By a vote of the 12 labeled lots nearest to it
With the most common supplier overall


Larger k smooths the boundaries between classes.



6. A tree grown with no stopping rules fits the training data perfectly. What’s the problem?

There’s none
It’s overfitting the training lots, and it predicts new lots worse than a pruned tree
It can’t be used for prediction


Its cross-validated error was 0.29, against 0.19 for the pruned tree.

title: Data mining: clustering and classification
text:
Wrap-up
You can now find groups, and learn to predict them. Here’s what you’ve learned:

k-means alternates assigning points to their nearest center and moving the centers. Use many random starts, and standardize first. It found Kestrel and Rosewater without labels, with a purity of 81%.
Choosing k: the elbow and the silhouette both pointed to four or five clusters.
Hierarchical clustering builds a dendrogram of merges. Ward’s method reached a purity of 86%, and single linkage chained everything together.
k-nearest neighbors classifies by a vote of the nearest labeled points, with k chosen by cross-validation: 15.5% error at k = 12.
Classification trees ask yes-or-no questions, one variable at a time. Three questions (water, aldehyde, iron) gave a leave-one-out error of 13.8%, the same as LDA’s.
Prune by cross-validation: a 13-leaf tree that fits every lot predicts worse than the 4-leaf tree.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download feed_lots.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Draw the tree. Install rpart.plot, and draw the tree with rpart.plot::rpart.plot(tree). Each box shows the predicted supplier, the class shares and the percentage of lots.
Plot the silhouettes. plot(cluster::silhouette(km$cluster, dist(Z))) draws every lot’s silhouette width, by cluster. Which lots have negative widths? Which suppliers are they from?
The unlabeled drums. Download Lesson 3.13’s unlabeled_drums.csv. Standardize the drums with the lots’ means and SDs (scale(drums[, vars], center = attr(Z, "scaled:center"), scale = attr(Z, "scaled:scale"))), then classify them with class::knn() (k = 12) and with predict(tree, drums, type = "class"). Do they agree with LDA’s verdicts?
A random forest. Install randomForest, and fit randomForest::randomForest(supplier ~ ., data = lots[, c("supplier", vars)]). Its printout includes an “out-of-bag” error rate, an honest estimate like cross-validation’s. Is it better than the single tree? (Module 8 explains how forests work.)










NoteKey words from this lesson






Clustering

Finding groups of similar observations in data without labels (unsupervised learning).

Classification

Learning to predict a categorical label from data in which the labels are known (supervised learning).

k-means

A clustering method that finds k clusters minimizing the within-cluster sum of squares, by alternating assignment and update steps.

Silhouette width

A measure of how well a point fits its cluster compared with the nearest other cluster, from −1 to 1.

Hierarchical clustering

Building a tree of clusters by repeatedly merging the closest pair. The linkage defines the distance between clusters.

Dendrogram

The tree diagram of a hierarchical clustering, cut at a chosen height to give clusters.

k-nearest neighbors

A classifier that predicts by a vote of the k nearest labeled observations.

Classification tree

A classifier that splits the data with a sequence of yes-or-no questions about single variables.

Pruning

Cutting a large tree back to a smaller one, chosen by cross-validation, to avoid overfitting.











NoteWant to read more?






Gareth James and others, An Introduction to Statistical Learning, chapters 2.2.3 (kNN), 8.1 (classification trees) and 12.4 (k-means and hierarchical clustering), with R labs. The friendliest introduction, and the main reading for Modules 7 and 8.
Leonard Kaufman and Peter Rousseeuw, Finding Groups in Data (Wiley, 1990). The book behind the cluster package, including the silhouette, by its inventor. Not free.
The rpart package’s long introduction, “An introduction to recursive partitioning using the RPART routines”, by Terry Therneau and Elizabeth Atkinson. How trees are grown, pruned and cross-validated.

title: Module 4 project: a simulation study
text:
The plant’s treated wastewater goes to the river, and its discharge permit limits the phenol in it. Every Tuesday, the lab analyzes a sample. But many results come back below the lab’s detection limit, as “<10 µg/L”, and for years the plant’s annual report has replaced them with half the limit before averaging. Now the regulator’s new guidance says that substitution “can bias the results”, and asks the plant to justify it, or to switch to a method designed for censored data.
Hana, the environmental engineer, wants evidence, not opinions. That’s what a simulation study is for: in a world where you know the truth, you can measure how wrong each method is. Then the better method answers this year’s question: is the plant within its permit?

title: Module 4 project: a simulation study
text:
What you’ll make
One report, written in Quarto in your plant-study RStudio project, that Hana could send to the regulator. It should contain:

A summary for Hana, at the top, in plain words: is half the detection limit good enough for the plant’s data, what should replace it if not, and is the plant within its permit this year?
The method: your EM algorithm for censored data, checked against a direct maximum likelihood fit.
The simulation study: its plan, its results with Monte Carlo standard errors, and what they mean.
This year’s answer: the annual average and 95th percentile, with confidence intervals, compared with the permit limits.
A cleaning log and a list of limitations: every change you made to the data, and what the study can’t show.

Nobody grades it, but write it as if the regulator’s statistician will read it. In real life, one would.

title: Module 4 project: a simulation study
text:
The handover
Download the two files into a new folder in your project, data-raw/wastewater/, and don’t edit them:

README.txt: Hana’s note, with the permit limits, the questions, the columns and a known issue. Read it first.
wastewater_2026.csv: this year’s 43 weekly results, January to October.

Then download the project template, save it in the top folder of your project as wastewater-study.qmd, and click Render. It reads the data, prints a first look and plots the results over time, with headings and code skeletons for every step. Fill it in one section at a time, and render often.

title: Module 4 project: a simulation study
text:
The brief, step by step

Explore (Lessons 1, 10). Plot the results over time, with the detection limits. How many results are censored before and after July? Look for any value that can’t be right: what would a detected result below its own detection limit mean? Fix what you can justify, and log it.
Write the EM algorithm (Lessons 9, 10). Concentrations like these are close to lognormal, so work with the logarithms: they’re normal, with mean \mu and SD \sigma, and a censored result is a log concentration below the log of its own detection limit. Generalize Lesson 10’s E-step to a different limit for each result. Check your estimates against a direct maximum likelihood fit with optim(), where each censored result contributes \Phi\big((\log L_i - \mu)/\sigma\big). Then the annual mean is e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}, and the 95th percentile is e^{\mu + 1.645\sigma}.
Plan the simulation study (Lesson 4). Write its ADEMP plan in the report before you run anything:

Aims: does half the detection limit give accurate estimates of the annual mean and the 95th percentile for data like the plant’s, and does EM do better?
Data-generating mechanisms: 43 weekly lognormal results, with this year’s detection limits (10 µg/L until July, then 5). Vary the geometric mean, e^\mu (11, 7 and 4 µg/L, giving roughly 35%, 55% and 75% censored), and \sigma (0.85 and 1.2): six scenarios.
Estimands: the true annual mean and the true 95th percentile of each scenario’s lognormal distribution.
Methods: half the detection limit (the mean of the substituted results, and their 95th percentile with quantile()), and EM (the formulas in step 2).
Performance measures: the bias and the root mean squared error (RMSE), as percentages of the truth, each with its Monte Carlo standard error (Lesson 5).

Run it (Lessons 1, 3). 1,000 replicates per scenario. Set the seed once, at the start. Write functions: one that simulates a year, one that applies both methods, one that runs a scenario. Try 50 replicates first, to debug quickly.
Report the results. One table and one plot. Which method is less biased, for which estimand, in which scenarios? Are the differences bigger than their Monte Carlo standard errors? Which scenario is closest to the plant’s data?
This year’s answer (Lesson 6). With the method your study supports, estimate this year’s annual mean and 95th percentile. Get 95% confidence intervals with the parametric bootstrap: simulate 2,000 years from the fitted lognormal, with this year’s detection limits, and apply EM to each. Compare a nonparametric bootstrap.
Answer Hana. Is the annual average below 20 µg/L? Is the 95th percentile below 50 µg/L? How sure are you? If the answer to “is half the limit good enough?” depends on the estimand, say so plainly.
Write it up. Summary first. Then the method, the simulation study, this year’s answer, and the limitations, with the cleaning log at the end.

Stretch goal. Bias and RMSE judge point estimates. The regulator will also look at the intervals. For one scenario close to the plant’s, compare the coverage of two 95% intervals for the mean: the t-interval on the half-limit data, and the parametric bootstrap interval for EM. (A bootstrap inside a simulation is slow: use 300 replicates and 200 bootstrap resamples, and expect it to run for a few minutes.) Which one keeps its promise? Or take the Bayesian route instead: extend Lesson 12’s data augmentation to lognormal data with sample-specific limits, and report the posterior probability that the 95th percentile is above 50 µg/L.

title: Module 4 project: a simulation study
text:
Check your own work
When you’ve finished, assess your project against this rubric. Aim for the right-hand column.










Needs work
Good
Excellent




The data
Used as received
The detection-limit change is handled
The impossible value is found, fixed with a justification, and its effect on the methods is shown; everything is in the cleaning log


The EM algorithm
Copied from Lesson 10
Works with this year’s two detection limits
Handles sample-specific limits on the log scale, converges with a stopping rule, and agrees with optim()


The study design
Results without a plan
An ADEMP plan
An ADEMP plan written before running, scenarios that bracket the plant’s data, a seed set once, and a sensible number of replicates


The results
Bias only
Bias and RMSE for both estimands
Bias and RMSE with Monte Carlo standard errors, one clear table and plot, and conclusions that separate the mean from the 95th percentile


This year’s answer
Point estimates only
Estimates with bootstrap intervals
Estimates with parametric and nonparametric bootstrap intervals, compared with both permit limits, with honest wording about how sure you are


Communication
Code output with little text
A report that explains its steps
A report Hana could send to the regulator: a plain summary, a clear recommendation, and stated limitations

title: Module 4 project: a simulation study
text:
Tips

Work on the log scale. Fit the normal distribution to the log concentrations, censored below \log L_i, and transform back only at the end. The mean of the logs isn’t the log of the mean: the annual mean is e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}.
A detected value below its own detection limit is impossible. Look at the smallest detected result. A misplaced decimal point or a mix-up of units (µg/L and mg/L differ by a factor of 1,000) is the usual explanation. Then try EM with the value left in: on the log scale, one wild value can move everything.
Check EM against optim(). If the two disagree in the fourth digit, one of them has a bug.
Simulate the design you have. Keep the 43 samples and this year’s detection-limit pattern fixed in the simulation, and vary only the concentrations. That’s what makes the study relevant to the plant.
Start small, then go big. Debug with 50 replicates. When it works, run 1,000, and save the results with saveRDS() so that rendering the report doesn’t rerun the simulation every time.
Report the Monte Carlo error. The Monte Carlo standard error of a bias is the SD of the estimates divided by \sqrt{R}, for R replicates. A difference of 1% with an MCSE of 0.5% is noise.
“Good enough” depends on the question. A method can be fine for the mean and poor for the 95th percentile, or fine at 35% censoring and poor at 75%. Hana needs that level of detail, and the regulator will appreciate it.
Be careful with the word “compliant”. An estimate below the limit with an interval that crosses it says “probably within the permit, but not demonstrably”. Say which one you mean.


When it’s done, you’ll have done what statisticians do when nobody knows the answer: built a world where you do know it, and tested the methods there. Congratulations on finishing Module 4! Module 5 takes the posterior distributions you sampled here and makes them the center of everything: Bayesian statistics.

title: The beta-binomial model
text:
Module 5 · Lesson 2 of 13 Week 77 of 160 About 5–7 hours
In Lesson 1, you computed the recipe’s posterior on a grid of 1,001 rates. It worked, but it was approximate, and it gets slow with more parameters. For some combinations of prior and likelihood there’s a shortcut: the posterior belongs to the same family as the prior, with updated parameters, and you can write it down with no computing at all. Such a prior is called conjugate, and for an unknown proportion, the conjugate prior is the beta distribution.
Conjugate models are rarely the last word in a real analysis. But they show exactly how a prior and data combine, they’re the building blocks of bigger models, and they give answers you can check by hand. This lesson uses them to finish the recipe trial: 2 off-spec batches out of 30, against the old recipe’s 7.9%.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: The beta-binomial model
text:
The beta distribution
The beta distribution lives on the interval from 0 to 1, so it’s a natural way to describe what you believe about a proportion. It has two shape parameters, a and b:

p(\theta) = \frac{\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}}{B(a, b)}, \qquad \text{mean} = \frac{a}{a+b},

where B(a, b) is the beta function, the constant that makes it integrate to 1. A useful way to think about it: a and b act like prior counts of successes and failures. Beta(1, 1) is flat. Beta(5, 95) is what you might believe after seeing 5 off-spec batches in 100, and Beta(50, 950) is the same belief held ten times more firmly. The total a + b is the prior’s effective sample size.
The development team’s lab work suggested an off-spec rate of about 5%, and they’d be surprised by anything over 15%. They chose a prior worth 20 batches: Beta(1, 19).











Your turn. Check that the prior matches what the team said: its mean, the probability it gives to a rate above 15%, and its 95th percentile.









Quantiles of the beta distribution come from qbeta().


a <- 1
b <- 19
c(mean = a / (a + b), p_over_15 = pbeta(0.15, a, b, lower.tail = FALSE), q95 = qbeta(0.95, a, b))
A prior mean of 5%, a 4.6% chance of a rate above 15%, and a 95th percentile of 14.6%. That’s the team’s belief, in numbers. As always in R, dbeta(), pbeta(), qbeta() and rbeta() give the density, the cumulative probability, the quantiles and random draws.

title: The beta-binomial model
text:
Conjugate updating
Multiply the Beta(a, b) prior by the binomial likelihood for y off-spec batches out of n:

\underbrace{\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}}_{\text{prior}} \times \underbrace{\theta^{y}(1-\theta)^{n-y}}_{\text{likelihood}} = \theta^{a+y-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-y-1}.

That’s another beta distribution. The posterior is

\theta \mid y \;\sim\; \text{Beta}(a + y,\; b + n - y).

Add the off-spec batches to a, and the good ones to b. That’s all.
Your turn. The setup code has y and n. Find the posterior’s parameters, its mean and its mode, (a' - 1)/(a' + b' - 2).









The good batches are n - y.


a <- 1
b <- 19
a_post <- a + y
b_post <- b + n - y
c(a_post = a_post, b_post = b_post, mean = a_post / (a_post + b_post), mode = (a_post - 1) / (a_post + b_post - 2))
The posterior is Beta(3, 47), with a mean of 6.0% and a mode of 4.2%. It’s worth 50 batches: the prior’s 20 plus the trial’s 30.




Your turn. Check the formula against Lesson 1’s grid method. On a grid with steps of 0.001, the posterior probabilities divided by 0.001 approximate the posterior density.









Compare with the density of Beta(3, 47).


grid <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.001)
post <- dbeta(grid, 1, 19) * dbinom(y, n, grid)
post <- post / sum(post)
max(abs(post / 0.001 - dbeta(grid, 3, 47)))       # the largest difference from the formula
The largest difference is 0.0000003, against a peak density of 13.5. The grid and the formula agree, as they should: they’re the same calculation, done two ways.




Here are the prior, the likelihood and the posterior together. The likelihood is scaled to have area 1, which makes it the flat-prior posterior, Beta(3, 29):

th <- seq(0, 0.3, by = 0.001)
curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(theta = th, density = dbeta(th, 1, 19), what = "prior"),
  data.frame(theta = th, density = dbeta(th, 3, 29), what = "likelihood"),
  data.frame(theta = th, density = dbeta(th, 3, 47), what = "posterior")
)
ggplot(curves, aes(x = theta, y = density, color = what)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = c(0.016, 0.135, 0.075), y = c(17.5, 5.6, 13.5), label = c("prior", "likelihood", "posterior"),
           color = c("#2a78d6", "#1baf7a", "#C2416C"), hjust = 0, size = 3.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(prior = "#2a78d6", likelihood = "#1baf7a", posterior = "#C2416C"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Off-spec rate", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The posterior sits between the prior and the likelihood, and it’s narrower than either: it combines two sources of information.

title: The beta-binomial model
text:
The posterior as a compromise
The posterior mean can be written as a weighted average of the prior mean and the trial’s own proportion:

\frac{a + y}{a + b + n} \;=\; \frac{a + b}{a + b + n}\cdot\frac{a}{a+b} \;+\; \frac{n}{a + b + n}\cdot\frac{y}{n}.

The weights are the two sample sizes: the prior’s 20 “batches” and the trial’s 30. As the trial grows, the data’s weight goes to 1, and the prior stops mattering.
Your turn. Compute the data’s weight, and the posterior mean as the weighted average.









The data’s own estimate is the proportion y / n.


a <- 1
b <- 19
w <- n / (a + b + n)                              # the weight of the data
c(weight = w, mean = (1 - w) * a / (a + b) + w * y / n)
The data get 60% of the weight and the prior 40%, so the posterior mean is 0.4 \times 5\% + 0.6 \times 6.7\% = 6.0\%, as before. This kind of compromise is called shrinkage: the data’s estimate is pulled, or shrunk, toward the prior. It’s at the heart of hierarchical models, in Lessons 11 and 12.

title: The beta-binomial model
text:
Credible intervals and probabilities
A 95% credible interval is any interval with 95% posterior probability. The usual choice is the equal-tailed one, from the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile, and with a beta posterior that’s two calls to qbeta(). Posterior probabilities of statements about \theta come from pbeta().
Your turn. Find the 95% credible interval for the new recipe’s off-spec rate.









The upper end is the 97.5th percentile, 0.975.


qbeta(c(0.025, 0.975), 3, 47)
From 1.3% to 14.0%. Given the trial and the team’s prior, there’s a 95% probability that the rate is in that range. Compare the classical 95% confidence interval from 0.8% to 22%. It doesn’t use the prior, and its meaning is more roundabout: 95% of intervals made this way, in repeated trials, would contain the true rate.




Your turn. Find the posterior probability that the new recipe is better than the old one, whose rate is old_rate in the setup code.









pbeta(x, 3, 47) is the posterior probability that \theta is below x.


pbeta(old_rate, 3, 47)
76%. With a flat prior, Beta(1, 1), the posterior would be Beta(3, 29), and the probability 44.9%: Lesson 1’s grid gave 45.2%, close but not exact. The team’s prior raised it to 76%, because it said lower rates were more plausible to begin with.

title: The beta-binomial model
text:
How strong a prior?
The team’s prior had a mean of 5%, worth 20 batches. A team member who trusts the lab results more might argue for 200 batches. Someone who trusts them less, for 2. With prior mean m and effective sample size s, the prior is Beta(ms, (1-m)s).
Your turn. For prior sample sizes of 2, 20 and 200, all with a prior mean of 5%, compute the posterior mean and the probability that the new recipe is better.









The posterior’s second parameter is b + n - y.


t(sapply(c(2, 20, 200), function(s) {
  a <- 0.05 * s
  b <- 0.95 * s
  c(prior_size = s, mean = (a + y) / (a + b + n), p_better = pbeta(old_rate, a + y, b + n - y))
}))



Prior worth
Posterior mean
P(better)




2 batches
6.6%
69%


20 batches
6.0%
76%


200 batches
5.2%
95%



The conclusion depends on how much the team trusts its lab work. A prior worth 200 batches nearly settles the question before the trial starts, which is a lot to ask of lab results for a recipe that has never run at full scale. When the answer depends this much on the prior, say so, and collect more data. This is a sensitivity analysis, and Lesson 3 does more of them.

title: The beta-binomial model
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · How many more batches? The plant manager wants a 95% probability that the new recipe is better before switching over. Starting from the Beta(3, 47) posterior, suppose the next k batches are all on spec. What’s the smallest k that does it?









Each good batch adds 1 to the second parameter: 47 + k.


k <- 0:200
p_better <- pbeta(old_rate, 3, 47 + k)
c(k = k[min(which(p_better > 0.95))], p_better = p_better[min(which(p_better > 0.95))])
29 more batches in a row on spec would push the probability to 95.2%. A single off-spec batch along the way would push the target back, as you can check by changing the 3 to 4. Because Bayesian updating has no penalty for looking at the data as it arrives (Lesson 1), the plant can recompute after every batch and stop as soon as it’s sure.




Challenge 2 · The next 50 batches. How many of the next 50 batches will be off spec? Averaging the binomial over the beta posterior gives the beta-binomial distribution:

P(Y = k) = \binom{50}{k} \frac{B(k + a',\; 50 - k + b')}{B(a', b')}.

Compute it for k = 0, \ldots, 50, and find the probability of at most 2 off-spec batches. Compare it with the plug-in binomial probability, which uses the posterior mean as if it were the true rate.









The denominator is the beta function of the posterior’s parameters, beta(3, 47).


k <- 0:50
prob <- choose(50, k) * beta(k + 3, 50 - k + 47) / beta(3, 47)
c(total = sum(prob), at_most_2 = sum(prob[k <= 2]), plug_in = pbinom(2, 50, 0.06))
The probabilities sum to 1, and there’s a 49% chance of at most 2 off-spec batches, against 42% from the plug-in binomial. Both predict 3 on average, but the beta-binomial is more spread out, because it allows for the uncertainty in the rate. Here, that puts more probability on the low counts. It also puts more on the high ones: the chance of 8 or more is 4.9%, against 0.9%. You can get the same distribution by simulation: draw a rate from rbeta(1, 3, 47), then a count from rbinom(1, 50, rate), many times.

title: The beta-binomial model
text:
Quick quiz

1. What makes a prior conjugate to a likelihood?

It’s flat
The posterior is in the same family as the prior
It’s based on previous data


A beta prior with a binomial likelihood gives a beta posterior. You’ll meet more conjugate pairs in Lesson 4.



2. A Beta(2, 8) prior is updated with 6 successes in 10 trials. What’s the posterior?

Beta(6, 4)
Beta(8, 12)
Beta(8, 18)


Add the 6 successes to a and the 4 failures to b.



3. Which prior expresses the most confidence in a rate of 10%?

Beta(1, 9)
Beta(10, 90)
Beta(100, 900)


All three have a mean of 10%, but Beta(100, 900) is worth 1,000 observations, so it’s the narrowest.



4. As the trial gets bigger, what happens to the posterior mean?

It moves toward the prior mean
It moves toward the sample proportion, as the data’s weight n/(a + b + n) approaches 1
It stays at the prior mean


With enough data, the prior stops mattering, unless it rules some values out completely.



5. What does a 95% credible interval of 1.3% to 14.0% mean?

Given the data and the prior, there’s a 95% probability that the rate is between 1.3% and 14.0%
95% of batches have an off-spec rate in that range
If you repeated the trial, 95% of the intervals would contain the true rate


The third answer describes a confidence interval. The credible interval makes the direct probability statement.



6. Why is the beta-binomial distribution more spread out than the binomial with the posterior mean plugged in?

Because the beta-binomial uses a flat prior
Because it includes the uncertainty about the rate, as well as the batch-to-batch randomness
Because it counts the prior batches too


Two sources of uncertainty give a wider prediction than one.

title: The beta-binomial model
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve done a complete Bayesian analysis with nothing but formulas. Here’s what you’ve learned:

The beta distribution describes beliefs about a proportion. Its parameters act like prior counts, and a + b is the prior’s effective sample size.
Conjugate updating: a Beta(a, b) prior and y successes in n trials give a Beta(a + y, b + n - y) posterior. The recipe’s is Beta(3, 47).
Shrinkage: the posterior mean, 6.0%, is a weighted average of the prior mean, 5%, and the data’s 6.7%, with weights 40% and 60%.
Credible intervals and probabilities: a 95% credible interval from 1.3% to 14.0%, and a 76% probability that the new recipe is better.
Sensitivity: with prior sample sizes of 2, 20 and 200, that probability is 69%, 76% and 95%.
The beta-binomial distribution predicts future counts, with the uncertainty in the rate included.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download recipe_trial.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

A posterior after every batch. Starting from Beta(1, 19), update after each of the 30 batches in turn. Plot the posterior mean and the 95% credible interval against the batch number. When did the interval first drop below 20% at its upper end?
The bayesrules package. Install it with install.packages("bayesrules"), and try plot_beta_binomial(alpha = 1, beta = 19, y = 2, n = 30) and summarize_beta_binomial(1, 19, y = 2, n = 30). Do they agree with your numbers?
Elicit your own prior. Think of a proportion you know something about, such as the share of days your commute is late. Choose a beta prior whose mean and 90th percentile match your belief (adjust a and b by trial and error with qbeta()). Then record a week of data and update it.
The old recipe, properly. Give the old recipe’s rate a Beta(1, 1) prior and update it with 38 in 480. Simulate 100,000 draws from each posterior, and find the probability that the new recipe is better, and the posterior distribution of the difference in rates.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Conjugate prior

A prior for which the posterior belongs to the same family, so the update is a formula.

Beta distribution

A distribution on the interval from 0 to 1 with two shape parameters, used for beliefs about proportions.

Effective sample size of a prior

How many observations the prior is worth. For Beta(a, b), it’s a + b.

Shrinkage

The pull of an estimate toward the prior mean, or toward a group average. The posterior mean is a weighted average of the prior mean and the data’s estimate.

Credible interval

An interval with a stated posterior probability of containing the parameter. The equal-tailed interval runs from the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile.

Sensitivity analysis

Repeating an analysis with different reasonable priors, to see how much the conclusions depend on them.

Beta-binomial distribution

The distribution of a future binomial count, averaged over a beta distribution for the probability.











NoteWant to read more?






Alicia Johnson, Miles Ott and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, chapters 3, “The Beta-Binomial Bayesian model” and 4, “Balance and sequentiality in Bayesian analyses”, with R code using the bayesrules package.
Andrew Gelman and others, Bayesian Data Analysis (3rd edition), sections 2.1 to 2.4: the binomial model, the posterior as a compromise, and summaries of the posterior.
Allen Downey, Think Bayes (2nd edition), free online. Python rather than R, but its grid-based approach is a good match for Lessons 1 and 2.

title: More conjugate models
text:
Module 5 · Lesson 4 of 13 Week 79 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The beta-binomial model handles proportions. Two other kinds of data turn up all the time in a plant: counts of events over time, such as trips, alarms and leaks, and measurements with a known instrument error. Each has its own conjugate prior, and this lesson works through both.
It also takes prediction further. A posterior describes the parameters, but the people who run the plant care about what will happen: how many trips next quarter, or what the next reading will be. The posterior predictive distribution answers that, and it’s where Bayesian methods are often most useful.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: More conjugate models
text:
The gamma-Poisson model
The plant’s new air compressor, C-7, was installed in May 2025. Unplanned trips, when it shuts down on a fault and the standby has to take over, are a real cost. Over its first 18 months, it tripped 6 times. Trips happen at random moments at some average rate, so the number in a month is a Poisson count with rate \lambda trips per month.
The conjugate prior for a Poisson rate is the gamma distribution, with shape \alpha and rate \beta:

p(\lambda) \propto \lambda^{\alpha - 1} e^{-\beta\lambda}, \qquad \text{mean} = \frac{\alpha}{\beta}.

Like the beta’s a and b, the gamma’s parameters act like prior data: \alpha prior events in \beta prior months. After observing counts y_1, \ldots, y_n in n months, the posterior is

\lambda \mid y \;\sim\; \text{Gamma}\Big(\alpha + \textstyle\sum y_i,\; \beta + n\Big).

Add the trips to \alpha and the months to \beta.
The prior comes from the plant’s other compressors, which trip about 0.7 times a month. C-7 is a newer model, so the reliability engineer wanted only a modest prior: worth 6 months of data, Gamma(4.2, 6).











Your turn. Check the prior: its mean, its 95% interval, and the probability it gives to a rate above 1.5 trips a month. In R, the gamma functions take the shape and the rate: pgamma(x, shape, rate).









The rate in question is 1.5 trips a month.


alpha <- 4.2
beta <- 6
c(mean = alpha / beta, qgamma(c(0.025, 0.975), alpha, beta), p_over_1.5 = pgamma(1.5, alpha, beta, lower.tail = FALSE))
A prior mean of 0.7 trips a month, a 95% interval from 0.20 to 1.51, and a 2.6% chance of more than 1.5. A careful warning: R’s gamma functions also accept a scale, which is 1/\beta. Write pgamma(x, 4.2, scale = 6) by mistake and you get a prior with a mean of 25 trips a month. Always check a prior’s mean after writing it down.




Your turn. Update the prior with C-7’s 18 months. Find the posterior’s parameters, its mean and its 95% credible interval.









Add the number of months, length(y).


alpha_post <- 4.2 + sum(y)
beta_post <- 6 + length(y)
c(alpha_post = alpha_post, beta_post = beta_post, mean = alpha_post / beta_post, qgamma(c(0.025, 0.975), alpha_post, beta_post))
The posterior is Gamma(10.2, 24), with a mean of 0.425 trips a month and a 95% credible interval from 0.21 to 0.72. As with the beta, the mean is a compromise: the data’s own rate, 6/18 = 0.33, gets weight 18/(6 + 18) = 75\%, and the fleet’s 0.7 gets 25%.




Your turn. What’s the posterior probability that C-7 trips less often than the fleet average of 0.7 a month?









pgamma(0.7, 10.2, 24) is the posterior probability that \lambda is below 0.7.


pgamma(0.7, 10.2, 24)
97%. Even with a prior centered on the fleet’s rate, 18 months of data make it very probable that the new model trips less often. That’s useful evidence for the next compressor purchase.

title: More conjugate models
text:
Predicting next quarter
The maintenance planner wants to know how many trips to expect in the next three months. If \lambda were known, the count would be Poisson with mean 3\lambda. Averaging that Poisson over the gamma posterior gives the negative binomial distribution, with size \alpha' and probability \beta'/(\beta' + 3):

P(Y = k) = \int_0^\infty \text{Poisson}(k \mid 3\lambda)\;\text{Gamma}(\lambda \mid \alpha', \beta')\; d\lambda = \text{NegBin}\Big(k \;\Big|\; \alpha',\ \tfrac{\beta'}{\beta' + 3}\Big).

Your turn. Find the probability of no trips at all next quarter, and of 3 or more. Compare the second with the plug-in Poisson, which uses the posterior mean as if it were the true rate.









Use the same prob in both negative binomial calls.


prob <- 24 / (24 + 3)
c(none = dnbinom(0, size = 10.2, prob = prob),
  three_plus = pnbinom(2, size = 10.2, prob = prob, lower.tail = FALSE),
  plug_in = ppois(2, 3 * 0.425, lower.tail = FALSE))
A 30% chance of a trip-free quarter, and a 14.6% chance of 3 or more trips, against 13.7% from the plug-in Poisson. The difference is small here, because 18 months pin the rate down fairly well. With a few months of data, it would be much larger. The predictive distribution is always more spread out than the plug-in, because it includes the uncertainty in \lambda.




You don’t need to know the negative binomial to get these numbers. Simulation does the averaging for you: draw a rate from the posterior, then a count with that rate, and repeat. This two-step recipe works for any model, conjugate or not.
Your turn. Simulate 100,000 quarters this way, and estimate the two probabilities.









Each quarter uses its own drawn rate, lambda.


set.seed(5041)
lambda <- rgamma(100000, 10.2, 24)             # step 1: a rate from the posterior
quarter <- rpois(100000, 3 * lambda)           # step 2: a quarter's trips at that rate
c(none = mean(quarter == 0), three_plus = mean(quarter >= 3))
30.1% and 14.9%, within simulation error of the exact 30.1% and 14.6%. When rpois() gets a vector of rates, it uses a different one for each draw, which is exactly what the recipe needs.




Here’s the predictive distribution, next to the plug-in Poisson:

k <- 0:7
pred <- rbind(
  data.frame(trips = k, prob = dnbinom(k, size = 10.2, prob = 24 / 27), what = "posterior predictive"),
  data.frame(trips = k, prob = dpois(k, 3 * 0.425), what = "plug-in Poisson")
)
ggplot(pred, aes(x = factor(trips), y = prob, fill = what)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`posterior predictive` = "#C2416C", `plug-in Poisson` = "#F4C0D1"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Trips next quarter", y = "Probability") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: More conjugate models
text:
The normal-normal model
A tanker of solvent has arrived, and its density is a quick check of its purity: water contamination pushes it up. The specification is 0.8700 to 0.8740 g/mL. The supplier’s certificate says 0.8720, and from experience, certificates are within about ±0.0020 of the truth (a normal prior with mean 0.8720 and SD 0.0010). The lab’s densitometer has a known measurement SD of \sigma = 0.0004 g/mL, and four readings came back: 0.8731, 0.8736, 0.8729 and 0.8734.
For a normal mean \mu with known measurement SD \sigma, the conjugate prior is normal, \mu \sim N(\mu_0, \tau_0^2). The posterior is normal too, and the cleanest way to write it uses precisions, one over the variances:

\frac{1}{\tau_n^2} = \frac{1}{\tau_0^2} + \frac{n}{\sigma^2}, \qquad \mu_n = \tau_n^2\left(\frac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2} + \frac{n\bar y}{\sigma^2}\right).

Precisions add, and the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the data’s mean.
Your turn. Compute the posterior mean and SD of the tanker’s density, and the weight the data get. The readings are in the setup code’s density.









The data’s term is n\bar y/\sigma^2, which is sum(density) / sigma^2.


mu0 <- 0.8720
tau0 <- 0.0010
sigma <- 0.0004
n <- length(density)
precision <- 1 / tau0^2 + n / sigma^2
mu_n <- (mu0 / tau0^2 + sum(density) / sigma^2) / precision
c(mean = mu_n, sd = sqrt(1 / precision), data_weight = (n / sigma^2) / precision)
A posterior mean of 0.87320 g/mL, with an SD of 0.00020. The four readings average 0.87325, and they get 96% of the weight: four precise readings say much more than a certificate that’s only good to ±0.0020. The posterior’s 95% credible interval, 0.87282 to 0.87359, is well inside the spec, though higher than the certificate claimed.




Your turn. The quality inspector will take one more reading from the tanker’s outlet. Its predictive distribution is normal with the posterior mean and a variance of \sigma^2 + \tau_n^2: the measurement error plus the uncertainty about \mu. Find the 95% predictive interval, and the probability that the reading comes out above the spec limit of 0.8740 (which would start an argument with the supplier).









The predictive variance is sigma^2 + tau_n^2.


mu_n <- 0.8732019
tau_n <- 0.0001961
sigma <- 0.0004
pred_sd <- sqrt(sigma^2 + tau_n^2)
c(mu_n + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * pred_sd, p_over_spec = pnorm(0.8740, mu_n, pred_sd, lower.tail = FALSE))
The next reading will probably be between 0.8723 and 0.8741, and there’s a 3.7% chance that it’s over the limit, even though the tanker’s true density almost certainly isn’t (the posterior probability of that is 0.002%). That distinction, between the uncertainty about a parameter and the spread of the next observation, is one of the most important in applied statistics. A single reading above the limit isn’t evidence of a bad tanker. Several would be.

title: More conjugate models
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · New against old. C-7 replaced an older compressor in the same service, which had 22 trips in its last 30 months. With the same fleet prior for both, draw 100,000 rates from each posterior, and find the probability that C-7 trips less often, and a 95% interval for the ratio of the rates.









The old compressor was watched for 30 months.


set.seed(5042)
new <- rgamma(100000, 4.2 + 6, 6 + 18)
old <- rgamma(100000, 4.2 + 22, 6 + 30)
c(p_new_better = mean(new < old), quantile(new / old, c(0.025, 0.975)))
A 94% probability that C-7 is better. The ratio of the rates has a posterior median of 0.57 (C-7 trips about 43% less often), but its 95% interval, from 0.26 to 1.15, still includes “no better”. The posterior of any function of the parameters, such as a ratio, comes straight from the draws.




Challenge 2 · Trust, but verify. Check the gamma-Poisson formula against Lesson 1’s grid method. Compute the posterior on a grid of rates from 0.001 to 3, using the product of the 18 Poisson probabilities as the likelihood, and compare it with the Gamma(10.2, 24) density.









Inside the function, the rate is lambda.


grid <- seq(0.001, 3, by = 0.001)
lik <- sapply(grid, function(lambda) prod(dpois(y, lambda)))
post <- dgamma(grid, 4.2, 6) * lik
post <- post / sum(post)
max(abs(post / 0.001 - dgamma(grid, 10.2, 24)))
A difference of about 10^{-14}, against a peak density of 3.1: the formula is right. Only the total number of trips and months mattered, not which months the trips happened in. They’re sufficient statistics, and conjugate models always have them.

title: More conjugate models
text:
Quick quiz

1. A Gamma(2, 4) prior for a Poisson rate is updated with 10 events in 20 periods. What’s the posterior?

Gamma(10, 20)
Gamma(12, 24)
Gamma(22, 14)


Add the events to the shape and the periods to the rate.



2. You type rgamma(1000, 4.2, scale = 6) for a prior with mean 0.7. What’s wrong?

The prior’s mean is now 25, because scale is one over the rate
Nothing, scale and rate are the same thing
The prior is now improper


Shape times scale is 25.2. Use rate = 6, or just pass the rate as the third argument.



3. Why is the negative binomial predictive distribution wider than the plug-in Poisson?

Because it’s discrete
Because it also includes the uncertainty in the rate
Because the prior was informative


The Poisson’s variance equals its mean. Averaging over an uncertain rate adds the rate’s variance.



4. In the normal-normal model, how is the posterior precision related to the prior and the data?

It’s the average of their precisions
It’s the sum of the prior precision and n times the measurement precision
It’s the larger of the two


1/\tau_n^2 = 1/\tau_0^2 + n/\sigma^2. Every reading adds precision.



5. The posterior SD of the tanker’s density is 0.0002. Why is the next reading’s predictive SD bigger, 0.00045?

Because the prior was wide
Because the reading also has its own measurement error, \sigma = 0.0004
Because of rounding


The predictive variance is \sigma^2 + \tau_n^2: the noise in one reading plus the uncertainty about the mean.



6. What’s the general recipe for a posterior predictive simulation?

Simulate data from the prior
Draw parameters from the posterior, then draw new data from the model with those parameters
Resample the observed data


Two steps, repeated many times. It works for any model, whether or not you know a formula.

title: More conjugate models
text:
Wrap-up
You now know the three classic conjugate models. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Gamma-Poisson: a Gamma(\alpha, \beta) prior and \sum y events in n periods give a Gamma(\alpha + \sum y, \beta + n) posterior. C-7’s is Gamma(10.2, 24): 0.425 trips a month, 95% credible interval 0.21 to 0.72.
Comparisons: a 97% probability that C-7 trips less often than the fleet, and 94% that it’s better than its predecessor.
The negative binomial predicts next quarter’s trips: a 30% chance of none, and 14.6% of 3 or more.
Normal-normal: precisions add, and the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average. Four readings outweighed the certificate 96 to 4.
Prediction for a measurement: the next reading’s variance is the measurement variance plus the posterior variance.
Simulation gives any predictive distribution: draw the parameters, then the data.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download compressor_trips.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Month by month. Update C-7’s posterior one month at a time, from the fleet prior, and plot the posterior mean and 95% interval against the month. Add the fleet’s 0.7 as a horizontal line. When did the interval first fall entirely below it?
Exposure. Suppose C-7 was shut down for maintenance for half of month 7 and all of month 12. With a Poisson rate per operating month, the posterior is Gamma(\alpha + \sum y_i, \beta + \sum t_i), where t_i is the operating time in month i. Recompute it.
A predictive check. If the gamma-Poisson model is right, C-7’s monthly counts should look like draws from the posterior predictive. Simulate 1,000 sets of 18 months, and compare the number of months with no trips in each with the observed 12. Is 12 unusual?
The prior’s influence. With the normal-normal model, how wide would the certificate’s prior have to be before the four readings got 99% of the weight? How narrow before they got only 50%?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Poisson distribution

The distribution of the number of events in a fixed time when events happen at random at a constant rate.

Gamma distribution

A distribution for positive quantities, with a shape and a rate parameter. It’s the conjugate prior for a Poisson rate.

Negative binomial distribution

The distribution of a Poisson count whose rate has a gamma distribution, and so the posterior predictive distribution of the gamma-Poisson model.

Precision

One over the variance. In the normal-normal model, the posterior precision is the sum of the prior and data precisions.

Posterior predictive distribution

The distribution of future data given the observed data, averaging the model over the posterior.

Predictive interval

An interval that will contain a future observation with a stated probability. It’s wider than the credible interval for the mean.

Sufficient statistic

A summary of the data that carries all the information the likelihood needs, such as the total count and total time for Poisson data.











NoteWant to read more?






Alicia Johnson, Miles Ott and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, chapter 5, “Conjugate families”, with the gamma-Poisson and normal-normal models.
Andrew Gelman and others, Bayesian Data Analysis (3rd edition), sections 2.5 to 2.7: the normal model with known variance, and the Poisson model, with the negative binomial as its predictive distribution.
Peter Hoff, A First Course in Bayesian Statistical Methods (Springer, 2009), chapter 3, “One-parameter models”. A clear and careful treatment of all three conjugate models, with R.

title: Multiparameter models
text:
Module 5 · Lesson 6 of 13 Week 81 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The fixed-bed reactor’s catalyst is due for replacement, and two suppliers are bidding. Catalyst pellets have to be strong: weak ones crush under the weight of the bed, and the fragments block the gaps between pellets and push up the pressure drop. The lab crush-tested samples from both: 14 pellets from Brightwater and 10 from Calloway. The reactor’s specification says that at least 95% of pellets must withstand 45 N.
So far, every model in this module had one parameter. A normal model for crush strength has two, the mean \mu and the SD \sigma, and both are unknown. That changes the mechanics, but not the idea: the posterior is now a joint distribution of (\mu, \sigma), and posterior draws of both answer any question about them. It also lets us ask the question the reactor actually cares about, which depends on both.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Multiparameter models
text:
The joint posterior
With the standard noninformative prior, p(\mu, \sigma^2) \propto 1/\sigma^2 (flat in \mu and in \log\sigma), the posterior factors into two familiar pieces:

\sigma^2 \mid y \;\sim\; \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{n-1}}, \qquad \mu \mid \sigma^2, y \;\sim\; N\!\left(\bar y,\ \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).

That suggests a two-step simulation: draw \sigma^2 from its marginal posterior, then \mu from its conditional posterior given that \sigma^2. Each pair is a draw from the joint posterior. It’s the same “draw one, then the other” recipe as the predictive simulation in Lesson 4.











Your turn. Start with the data: the number of pellets, the mean and the SD for each supplier.









The SD is sd(x).


aggregate(strength_N ~ supplier, data = pellets, FUN = function(x) c(n = length(x), mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)))
Brightwater’s pellets average 52.2 N with an SD of 3.8, and Calloway’s 59.8 N with an SD of 9.3. Calloway’s are stronger on average, but more than twice as variable.




Your turn. For Brightwater, draw 10,000 values of \sigma^2 from its marginal posterior, and summarize \sigma with its posterior median and 95% credible interval.









The chi-squared distribution has n - 1 degrees of freedom.


set.seed(5061)
n <- length(bright)
sigma2 <- (n - 1) * var(bright) / rchisq(10000, df = n - 1)
c(median = median(sqrt(sigma2)), quantile(sqrt(sigma2), c(0.025, 0.975)))
A posterior median of 3.9 N, with a 95% credible interval from 2.8 to 6.2 N. It’s skewed to the right: with 14 pellets, the SD could be well above the sample’s 3.8, but it can’t be much below it. (With this noninformative prior, it’s the same as the classical chi-squared confidence interval for an SD.)




Your turn. Now the second step: for each \sigma^2 draw, draw \mu from its conditional posterior. Summarize the \mu draws, which are draws from its marginal posterior.









Each \mu draw uses its own \sigma^2 draw: sqrt(sigma2 / n).


set.seed(5061)
n <- length(bright)
sigma2 <- (n - 1) * var(bright) / rchisq(10000, df = n - 1)
mu <- rnorm(10000, mean = mean(bright), sd = sqrt(sigma2 / n))
c(mean = mean(mu), quantile(mu, c(0.025, 0.975)))
A posterior mean of 52.2 N, with a 95% credible interval from 50.0 to 54.4 N. By drawing \mu with a different \sigma^2 each time, the simulation averaged over the uncertainty in \sigma, which is what a marginal posterior is. That’s how Bayesian methods handle nuisance parameters, the ones you need in the model but don’t care about: integrate them out.




Your turn. The marginal posterior of \mu can also be worked out exactly: it’s a t distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom, centered at \bar y with scale s/\sqrt{n}. Compute its 95% interval.









The degrees of freedom are n - 1.


n <- length(bright)
mean(bright) + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * sd(bright) / sqrt(n)
From 50.0 to 54.4 N, matching the simulation. It’s also exactly the t confidence interval of Module 0, Lesson 12. With the noninformative prior, the Bayesian and classical intervals for a normal mean are numerically identical, and only their interpretation differs. This is why p(\mu, \sigma^2) \propto 1/\sigma^2 is called the “reference” prior for the normal model.

title: Multiparameter models
text:
Comparing the suppliers
With draws for each supplier, comparing them is easy. The posterior of the difference in means is the difference of the draws, and nothing requires the two SDs to be equal. (Classically, comparing two means with unequal variances is the “Behrens-Fisher problem”, which has no exact solution. Welch’s t-test is an approximation.)
Your turn. The setup code’s post_draws() does the two-step simulation for one supplier. Use it for both, and find the posterior of \mu_C - \mu_B: its mean, its 95% credible interval and the probability that it’s positive.









Subtract Brightwater’s draws, B$mu.


set.seed(5062)
B <- post_draws(bright)
C <- post_draws(callo)
diff <- C$mu - B$mu
c(mean = mean(diff), quantile(diff, c(0.025, 0.975)), p_calloway_stronger = mean(diff > 0))
Calloway’s mean is higher by 7.6 N (95% credible interval 0.7 to 14.8 N), with a 98% posterior probability. If average strength were all that mattered, Calloway would win.




Your turn. And the spread: what’s the probability that Calloway’s SD is larger?









Compare with B$sigma.


set.seed(5062)
B <- post_draws(bright)
C <- post_draws(callo)
mean(C$sigma > B$sigma)
99.8%. Calloway’s pellets are almost certainly more variable. A stronger average with a wider spread: for a specification on the weakest pellets, that could go either way.

title: Multiparameter models
section: The question the reactor cares about
text:
The question the reactor cares about
The specification is about individual pellets, not means: what share of each supplier’s pellets would crush below 45 N? Answer it with the posterior predictive distribution: for each draw of (\mu, \sigma), draw a new pellet.
Your turn. Simulate one new pellet per posterior draw for each supplier, and estimate the probability that a pellet is weaker than 45 N.









Each new Calloway pellet uses its own SD draw, C$sigma.


set.seed(5063)
B <- post_draws(bright)
C <- post_draws(callo)
new_B <- rnorm(10000, B$mu, B$sigma)
new_C <- rnorm(10000, C$mu, C$sigma)
c(brightwater = mean(new_B < 45), calloway = mean(new_C < 45))
5.1% of Brightwater’s pellets and 8.1% of Calloway’s are predicted to crush below 45 N. The supplier with the stronger average sends more weak pellets, because of its spread. The comparison of means answered a question nobody needed answered. Brightwater is right at the specification’s 5% limit, so this isn’t over yet.




Here are the two joint posteriors. The dashed line is where the 5th percentile, \mu - 1.645\,\sigma, is exactly 45 N. Draws to the upper left of it meet the specification:

set.seed(5064)
draws <- rbind(cbind(post_draws(pellets$strength_N[pellets$supplier == "Brightwater"], 3000), supplier = "Brightwater"),
               cbind(post_draws(pellets$strength_N[pellets$supplier == "Calloway"], 3000), supplier = "Calloway"))
ggplot(draws, aes(x = sigma, y = mu, color = supplier)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 45, slope = qnorm(0.95), linetype = "dashed", color = "#3A1F35") +
  annotate("text", x = 2.2, y = 57.5, label = "Brightwater", color = "#2a78d6", hjust = 0, size = 3.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 15, y = 51, label = "Calloway", color = "#C2416C", hjust = 0, size = 3.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 6.4, y = 46.5, label = "dashed line: 5th percentile = 45 N", color = "#3A1F35", hjust = 0, size = 3.4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Brightwater = "#2a78d6", Calloway = "#C2416C"), guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(2, 20), ylim = c(42, 78)) +
  labs(x = "SD of crush strength, σ (N)", y = "Mean crush strength, μ (N)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: Multiparameter models
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Does each supplier meet the specification? “At least 95% of pellets withstand 45 N” means the 5th percentile of the strength distribution, \mu - 1.645\,\sigma, is above 45. That’s a function of both parameters, so its posterior comes from applying it to each draw. Find the posterior probability that each supplier meets the specification.









Calloway’s 5th percentile uses C$sigma.


set.seed(5064)
B <- post_draws(bright)
C <- post_draws(callo)
p5_B <- B$mu - qnorm(0.95) * B$sigma
p5_C <- C$mu - qnorm(0.95) * C$sigma
c(brightwater = mean(p5_B > 45), calloway = mean(p5_C > 45), median_B = median(p5_B), median_C = median(p5_C))
A 67% probability that Brightwater meets the specification, and 41% for Calloway. The posterior medians of the 5th percentiles are 45.8 N and 44.0 N. Neither supplier has demonstrated compliance with 14 and 10 pellets, so the recommendation is: Brightwater is the better bet, and test 30 more of its pellets before signing. Classically, this is a “tolerance interval” problem, with awkward formulas. With posterior draws, it took two lines.




Challenge 2 · A posterior on a two-dimensional grid. Without the formulas, you could still use Lesson 1’s grid, in two dimensions. Make a grid of 301 means from 45 to 60 N and 301 values of \log\sigma, compute the log-likelihood at every point (the prior is flat on this scale), and sum over \sigma to get the marginal posterior of \mu. Find its 95% interval.









The marginal posterior sums over the other parameter: sum.


g <- expand.grid(mu = seq(45, 60, length.out = 301), log_sigma = seq(log(1.5), log(12), length.out = 301))
log_lik <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(g)), function(i) sum(dnorm(bright, g$mu[i], exp(g$log_sigma[i]), log = TRUE)))
post <- exp(log_lik - max(log_lik))                  # subtract the maximum to avoid underflow
post <- post / sum(post)
marginal <- tapply(post, g$mu, sum)                  # add up over sigma for each mu
mus <- as.numeric(names(marginal))
c(lower = mus[min(which(cumsum(marginal) >= 0.025))], upper = mus[min(which(cumsum(marginal) >= 0.975))])
From 50.0 to 54.4 N, the same as the t-interval, to the grid’s resolution of 0.05 N. The grid needed 90,601 likelihood evaluations for two parameters. With ten parameters and 301 points each, it would need 301^{10} \approx 6 \times 10^{24}, which is why grids stop here and simulation takes over.

title: Multiparameter models
text:
Quick quiz

1. How do you get draws from the joint posterior of (\mu, \sigma^2) for the normal model?

Draw \mu and \sigma^2 independently from their own distributions
Draw \sigma^2 from its marginal posterior, then \mu from its conditional posterior given that \sigma^2
Draw from the prior and reject the bad ones


Marginal, then conditional, gives a draw from the joint distribution.



2. What’s the marginal posterior of \mu under the noninformative prior?

A normal distribution with variance s^2/n
A t distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom, centered at \bar y with scale s/\sqrt{n}
A chi-squared distribution


Averaging the normal over the uncertainty in \sigma gives the heavier-tailed t.



3. What is a nuisance parameter, and how does a Bayesian analysis handle it?

A parameter with an improper prior, which is dropped
A parameter you need in the model but don’t care about, which is integrated out of the posterior
A parameter that’s fixed at its estimate


With draws, integrating out is simply ignoring that column.



4. Why didn’t the comparison of suppliers need equal variances?

Because the variances were nearly equal
Because each supplier had its own posterior for (\mu, \sigma), and the difference of means came from the draws
Because the prior assumed them equal


The Behrens-Fisher problem disappears when you simulate.



5. Calloway’s pellets are stronger on average. Why do they send more weak pellets?

Because of the prior
Because their SD is much larger, so more of them fall in the lower tail
Because they were tested on a different rig


The share below a limit depends on both the mean and the spread.



6. Why don’t grid methods work for models with many parameters?

Because the posterior isn’t defined
Because the number of grid points grows exponentially with the number of parameters
Because grids can’t handle correlated parameters


k points per parameter means k^d points in d dimensions. Simulation, like MCMC, scales much better.

title: Multiparameter models
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve analyzed a model with two unknowns, and answered a question that depends on both. Here’s what you’ve learned:

The joint posterior of a normal mean and variance can be simulated in two steps: \sigma^2 from its marginal posterior, then \mu given \sigma^2.
Marginal posteriors integrate out nuisance parameters. The marginal posterior of \mu is a t distribution, and its interval, 50.0 to 54.4 N for Brightwater, equals the classical t-interval.
Comparing groups with draws needs no equal-variance assumption: Calloway’s mean is 7.6 N higher, with 98% probability.
Predictions answer the engineering question: 5.1% of Brightwater’s pellets and 8.1% of Calloway’s would crush below 45 N.
Functions of several parameters, such as the 5th percentile, get their posteriors from the draws: a 67% probability that Brightwater meets the specification, and 41% for Calloway.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download pellet_strength.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Plot the marginal posteriors. Plot the posterior densities of \mu and of \sigma for both suppliers, with geom_density(), in two panels.
Welch’s test. Run t.test(strength_N ~ supplier, data = pellets). How does its 95% confidence interval for the difference compare with the posterior interval from this lesson?
An informative prior. Brightwater’s pellets have been used at a sister plant, where 200 tested pellets had an SD of 4.2 N. Use it as a prior for \sigma (for example, \sigma^2 \sim 200 \cdot 4.2^2/\chi^2_{200} before seeing the new data), and redo the 5th-percentile calculation with a Gibbs sampler (Module 4, Lesson 12). How much does the probability of meeting the specification change?
How many more pellets? Simulate the result of testing 30 more Brightwater pellets: draw a (\mu, \sigma) from the posterior, simulate 30 pellets, add them to the data, and recompute the probability of meeting the specification. Repeat 200 times. How often would the extra tests push it above 90%?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Joint posterior

The posterior distribution of several parameters together.

Marginal posterior

The posterior of one parameter, averaged over the others. With draws, it’s that column alone.

Conditional posterior

The posterior of one parameter given fixed values of the others.

Nuisance parameter

A parameter needed in the model but not of interest in itself, such as \sigma when the question is about \mu.

Reference prior

A standard noninformative prior, such as p(\mu, \sigma^2) \propto 1/\sigma^2 for the normal model.

Behrens-Fisher problem

Comparing two normal means with unknown, unequal variances, which has no exact classical solution.

Tolerance limit

A limit that a stated share of the population exceeds, such as the 5th percentile. Its posterior comes directly from the draws.











NoteWant to read more?






Andrew Gelman and others, Bayesian Data Analysis (3rd edition), chapter 3, “Introduction to multiparameter models”: the normal model with unknown mean and variance, done exactly as in this lesson.
Alicia Johnson, Miles Ott and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, chapter 6, “Approximating the posterior”, on grid approximation and why it stops working as the dimension grows.
Peter Hoff, A First Course in Bayesian Statistical Methods (Springer, 2009), chapter 5, “The normal model”, including conjugate priors for both parameters.

title: MCMC in practice
text:
Module 5 · Lesson 8 of 13 Week 83 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Module 4 built two MCMC samplers: random-walk Metropolis and Gibbs. Both work, and both have a weakness. Metropolis proposes blind steps, so in more than a few dimensions it either crawls or gets rejected. Gibbs needs every conditional posterior to have a formula. The sampler inside Stan, which the next lesson introduces, avoids both problems: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) uses the gradient of the log-posterior to make long, well-aimed moves, and it’s accepted almost every time.
This lesson builds HMC by hand on the flammability posterior from Lesson 7, so that nothing in Stan is a black box. Then it turns to the practical question every MCMC user faces: how do you know the chain is telling the truth? You’ll use the diagnostics that Stan reports, from the posterior package.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: MCMC in practice
text:
Metropolis, revisited











The setup code has Lesson 7’s log_post(), now for a single pair \theta = (\alpha, \beta), and Module 4’s metropolis(), which takes the number of steps, a start and a step SD for each parameter. For effective sample sizes, we’ll use posterior::ess_bulk(), a modern version of Module 4’s coda::effectiveSize().
Your turn. Run 5,000 Metropolis steps from near the mode, with step SDs of 0.5 for \alpha and 3 for \beta (about the posterior SDs), and find the acceptance rate and the effective sample size of the \beta draws.









The step SD for \beta is 3.


set.seed(5081)
run <- metropolis(5000, start = c(-0.3, 9.7), step = c(0.5, 3))
