c(acceptance = run$acceptance, ess_beta = posterior::ess_bulk(run$draws[, 2]))
60% accepted, and 5,000 draws worth 372 independent ones for \beta: an efficiency of 7%. With two parameters, that’s tolerable. With 50 parameters, the step size would have to shrink so much to keep any proposals accepted that the efficiency would fall to a fraction of a percent.

title: MCMC in practice
text:
The gradient
HMC treats the parameters as the position of a particle, and the negative log-posterior as a landscape it slides on: low where the posterior is high. To simulate the slide, it needs the gradient, the direction and steepness of the slope at each point. For logistic regression, it has a simple form. With p_i = \text{logit}^{-1}(\alpha + \beta x_i),

\frac{\partial \log p}{\partial \alpha} = \sum_i (y_i - m_i p_i) - \frac{\alpha}{2.5^2}, \qquad \frac{\partial \log p}{\partial \beta} = \sum_i (y_i - m_i p_i)\, x_i - \frac{\beta}{25^2}.

The first part of each comes from the likelihood (observed minus expected ignitions), and the second from the normal priors.
Your turn. Write the gradient function, and evaluate it at \alpha = 0, \beta = 10.









The \beta component weights each residual by its concentration, x.


grad_log_post <- function(th) {
  r <- y - m * plogis(th[1] + th[2] * x)              # observed minus expected ignitions
  c(sum(r) - th[1] / 2.5^2, sum(r * x) - th[2] / 25^2)
}
grad_log_post(c(0, 10))
(-1.00, -0.04). At \alpha = 0, the model expects one more ignition in total than the 14 observed, so the slope says: lower \alpha. The \beta component is nearly 0: \beta = 10 is close to the best steepness. A quick check of a hand-written gradient is to compare it with a finite difference, (log_post(th + c(1e-6, 0)) - log_post(th)) / 1e-6. Stan computes gradients automatically, by automatic differentiation, so you’ll never have to write one by hand again.

title: MCMC in practice
text:
The leapfrog integrator
Each HMC iteration gives the particle a random momentum, a kick in a random direction, and lets it slide for a while under the “force” of the gradient. Its total energy, the Hamiltonian, is the potential energy (the negative log-posterior) plus the kinetic energy of its momentum:

H(\theta, p) = -\log p(\theta \mid y) + \tfrac12 \sum_k M_k^{-1} p_k^2 .

The inverse mass M^{-1} scales each direction to the posterior’s width; here it’s about the posterior variances, 0.32 for \alpha and 10.7 for \beta. On a frictionless surface, energy is conserved, so a perfect simulation of the slide could be accepted every time. The leapfrog method simulates it in small time steps of length \varepsilon: half a step of momentum, a full step of position, half a step of momentum. It conserves energy very nearly, and the small error is fixed by a Metropolis test at the end: accept with probability \min(1, e^{H_0 - H_1}).
Your turn. Starting from the mode with a random momentum, slide for a fixed time of 2 with step sizes of 0.05, 0.2 and 0.8, and see how well each conserves energy. The setup code has leapfrog().









Compare with the energy at the start, with the starting momentum mom.


inv_mass <- c(0.32, 10.7)
H <- function(th, mom) -log_post(th) + sum(inv_mass * mom^2) / 2      # the total energy
set.seed(5082)
mom <- rnorm(2, 0, sqrt(1 / inv_mass))                                 # a random kick
th0 <- c(-0.3, 9.7)
sapply(c(0.05, 0.2, 0.8), function(eps) {
  end <- leapfrog(th0, mom, eps, L = round(2 / eps), inv_mass)
  H(end$th, end$mom) - H(th0, mom)                                     # the energy error
})
Energy errors of 0.0002, 0.003 and 0.07. The acceptance probability is e^{-\Delta H}, so even the largest step would be accepted 94% of the time. Smaller steps conserve energy better but need more gradient evaluations to travel the same distance: 40 for a step of 0.05, 10 for 0.2 and 2 for 0.8. Tuning \varepsilon is HMC’s balancing act, and Stan does it automatically during warmup, aiming for an average acceptance of about 80%.




Here is one HMC trajectory, on the posterior’s contours. Pushed by its random momentum and steered by the gradient, the particle travels in one smooth sweep, slowing down as it climbs the side of the bowl, and ends a long way from where it started, all within a single iteration. A random walk covers that distance only by luck, in many steps that keep doubling back:

ag <- seq(-2.2, 1.6, length.out = 120); bg <- seq(0, 26, length.out = 120)
gr <- expand.grid(a = ag, b = bg)
gr$lp <- apply(gr, 1, function(r) log_post(c(r[["a"]], r[["b"]])))
gr$z <- exp(gr$lp - max(gr$lp))
inv_mass <- c(0.32, 10.7)
mom <- c(-1.5, 0.5)
path <- data.frame(a = -0.3, b = 9.7); th <- c(-0.3, 9.7)
for (k in 1:20) { lf <- leapfrog(th, mom, 0.15, 1, inv_mass); th <- lf$th; mom <- lf$mom; path <- rbind(path, data.frame(a = th[1], b = th[2])) }
ggplot(gr, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
  geom_contour(aes(z = z), breaks = c(0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8), color = "grey70") +
  geom_path(data = path, color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = path, color = "#C2416C", size = 1.6) +
  annotate("point", x = -0.3, y = 9.7, size = 3.2, color = "#3A1F35") +
  annotate("text", x = -0.22, y = 9.0, label = "start", hjust = 0, size = 3.4, color = "#3A1F35") +
  annotate("text", x = -0.85, y = 18.3, label = "one HMC iteration: 20 leapfrog steps", hjust = 0, size = 3.4, color = "#C2416C") +
  labs(x = "α (log-odds at 1.4%)", y = "β (slope)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: MCMC in practice
text:
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
Each HMC iteration draws a fresh momentum, runs L leapfrog steps, and accepts or rejects the end point. The setup code’s hmc() does that.
Your turn. Run 1,000 HMC iterations with a step size of 0.25 and 8 leapfrog steps, and compare the acceptance rate and the effective sample size for \beta with Metropolis’s.









Use 8 leapfrog steps.


set.seed(5083)
run <- hmc(1000, start = c(-0.3, 9.7), eps = 0.25, L = 8)
c(acceptance = run$acceptance, ess_beta = posterior::ess_bulk(run$draws[, 2]), mean_beta = mean(run$draws[, 2]))
99.7% accepted, and 1,000 draws worth 855: an efficiency of 85%, against Metropolis’s 7%. Each HMC iteration cost 8 gradient evaluations, so per unit of computing the gain is smaller, about a factor of 1.5 here. But that gap grows quickly with the number of parameters, which is why HMC can sample models with thousands of them. The posterior mean of \beta, 11.6, agrees with Lesson 7’s grid.





set.seed(5081)
rw <- metropolis(500, c(-0.3, 9.7), c(0.5, 3))$draws[, 2]
set.seed(5083)
hm <- hmc(500, c(-0.3, 9.7), 0.25, 8)$draws[, 2]
traces <- data.frame(iteration = rep(1:500, 2), beta = c(rw, hm),
                     sampler = factor(rep(c("random-walk Metropolis", "Hamiltonian Monte Carlo"), each = 500),
                                      levels = c("random-walk Metropolis", "Hamiltonian Monte Carlo")))
ggplot(traces, aes(x = iteration, y = beta)) +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.35) +
  facet_wrap(~ sampler, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Iteration", y = "β") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: MCMC in practice
text:
Trusting a chain
Module 4 checked convergence with \hat R and the effective sample size from the coda package. Since then, the definitions have been improved, and the versions in the posterior package are what Stan and brms report:

R-hat splits each chain in half and compares all the halves, after converting the draws to ranks, so it catches chains that drift, and it works for heavy-tailed posteriors. Use the draws only if it’s below 1.01.
Bulk ESS is the effective sample size for the center of the distribution (means and medians). Tail ESS is the effective sample size for the 5% and 95% quantiles, which matter for intervals. Both should be at least about 400 (100 per chain, for 4 chains).

These functions take a matrix with one column per chain.
Your turn. Run 4 HMC chains of 600 iterations from four widely spread starting points, drop the first 100 of each as warmup, and compute R-hat, the bulk ESS and the tail ESS for \beta.









The tail ESS is posterior::ess_tail().


set.seed(5084)
starts <- list(c(-3, 2), c(3, 2), c(-3, 40), c(3, 40))
chains <- sapply(starts, function(s) hmc(600, s, eps = 0.25, L = 8)$draws[-(1:100), 2])    # 500 x 4
c(rhat = posterior::rhat(chains), ess_bulk = posterior::ess_bulk(chains), ess_tail = posterior::ess_tail(chains))
R-hat is 1.001, the bulk ESS is 2,770 and the tail ESS 1,655, all from 2,000 kept draws. A bulk ESS above the number of draws isn’t a mistake: HMC’s draws can be negatively correlated, so that each one partly cancels the last one’s error. The four chains started at very different places and agree, so we can trust them.

title: MCMC in practice
text:
When HMC goes wrong
HMC’s errors aren’t quiet. If the step size is too large for the posterior’s curvature somewhere, the leapfrog simulation becomes unstable, and the energy shoots off: the particle “flies off the bowl”. Stan calls that a divergent transition, and reports every one. Divergences mean the sampler couldn’t explore some region of the posterior, often a narrow one, so the draws may be biased. One divergence in a fit deserves attention. Many mean that the results can’t be trusted.
Your turn. Run 500 iterations with a step size of 1.5, six times too big, and count the acceptances and the divergent transitions, iterations where the energy error exceeded 1,000.









Use a step size of 1.5.


set.seed(5085)
run <- hmc(500, start = c(-0.3, 9.7), eps = 1.5, L = 8)
c(acceptance = run$acceptance, divergent = run$divergent)
Only 26% accepted, and 12 divergent transitions. In Stan, the usual fix is to make the warmup tune the step size more cautiously, with a higher target acceptance (adapt_delta = 0.95 or 0.99), or better, to reparameterize the model so that its posterior has a friendlier shape. Lesson 11 shows the most famous case, the hierarchical model.

title: MCMC in practice
text:
Monte Carlo standard errors
Every number computed from MCMC draws has a simulation error, on top of the posterior uncertainty. For a posterior mean, the Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE) is the posterior SD divided by the square root of the effective sample size, and posterior::mcse_mean() computes it. Report enough digits for the MCSE to be small in the last one, and no more.
Your turn. From the 1,000 HMC draws, compute the posterior mean of the LFL50, 1.4 - \alpha/\beta, and its MCSE.









The MCSE of a mean is posterior::mcse_mean().


set.seed(5083)
run <- hmc(1000, start = c(-0.3, 9.7), eps = 0.25, L = 8)
lfl50 <- 1.4 - run$draws[, 1] / run$draws[, 2]
c(mean = mean(lfl50), mcse = posterior::mcse_mean(lfl50), ess = posterior::ess_bulk(lfl50))
A posterior mean of 1.4336% with an MCSE of 0.0013, from an ESS of 1,650. So the third decimal is uncertain, and the right way to report it is “1.43%”. The posterior SD, 0.05, is about 40 times larger than the MCSE: the uncertainty about the LFL50 comes almost entirely from the 30 tests, not from the simulation.

title: MCMC in practice
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The same check for Metropolis. Run four Metropolis chains of 600 iterations from the same four starts, drop 100 from each, and compute R-hat and the bulk ESS for \beta. Would you trust them?









The sampler is metropolis().


set.seed(5084)
starts <- list(c(-3, 2), c(3, 2), c(-3, 40), c(3, 40))
chains <- sapply(starts, function(s) metropolis(600, s, step = c(0.5, 3))$draws[-(1:100), 2])
c(rhat = posterior::rhat(chains), ess_bulk = posterior::ess_bulk(chains))
R-hat is 1.02 and the bulk ESS 124. Both fail the thresholds: R-hat above 1.01, and fewer than 400 effective draws. The chains need to run much longer. Per evaluation of the log-posterior or its gradient, HMC got 0.14 effective draws and Metropolis 0.05, almost three times fewer, and only HMC passed the checks.




Challenge 2 · Gibbs, revisited. Module 4’s Gibbs sampler alternates between the conditional posteriors. For Brightwater’s pellets from Lesson 6, with the prior p(\mu, \sigma^2) \propto 1/\sigma^2, they are: \sigma^2 \mid \mu, y \sim \sum(y_i - \mu)^2/\chi^2_n and \mu \mid \sigma^2, y \sim N(\bar y, \sigma^2/n). Run 5,000 iterations, drop 500, and compare the 95% interval for \mu with Lesson 6’s exact t-interval, 50.00 to 54.40 N.









\mu’s conditional variance is \sigma^2/n, with the current draw s2.


pellets <- read_csv("data/pellet_strength.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
bright <- pellets$strength_N[pellets$supplier == "Brightwater"]
set.seed(5086)
n <- length(bright)
mu <- mean(bright)
out <- matrix(NA, 5000, 2)
for (g in 1:5000) {
  s2 <- sum((bright - mu)^2) / rchisq(1, n)            # sigma^2 given mu
  mu <- rnorm(1, mean(bright), sqrt(s2 / n))           # mu given sigma^2
  out[g, ] <- c(mu, sqrt(s2))
}
quantile(out[-(1:500), 1], c(0.025, 0.975))
From 49.98 to 54.45 N, within Monte Carlo error of the exact 50.00 to 54.40. Gibbs works perfectly when the conditionals have formulas, as here. When they don’t, as in the flammability model, you need Metropolis steps inside it, or HMC.

title: MCMC in practice
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does HMC use that random-walk Metropolis doesn’t?

The normalizing constant of the posterior
The gradient of the log-posterior, to make long, directed moves
Conjugate conditional distributions


The gradient lets the particle follow the posterior’s shape instead of stepping blindly.



2. Why does HMC accept almost every proposal?

Because it never moves far
Because the leapfrog integrator nearly conserves the total energy, and the acceptance probability is e^{-\Delta H}
Because it ignores the likelihood


With a well-tuned step size, \Delta H is small, so the acceptance probability is close to 1.



3. A fit reports R-hat = 1.04 for one parameter. What should you do?

Nothing, it’s close to 1
Not use the results yet: run longer, or look for a problem with the model or sampler
Drop that chain


The current guideline is R-hat below 1.01 for every parameter.



4. What’s the difference between bulk ESS and tail ESS?

Bulk ESS counts all draws, tail ESS only the last ones
Bulk ESS measures precision for the center of the distribution, tail ESS for its extreme quantiles
They’re two names for the same thing


A chain can estimate a mean well and a 95% interval badly. Check both.



5. Stan reports 37 divergent transitions. What do they suggest?

The prior is too strong
The sampler couldn’t follow the posterior’s curvature somewhere, so the draws may be biased
The chains have converged


Try a higher adapt_delta, and if that doesn’t fix it, reparameterize the model.



6. A posterior mean is 1.4336 with an MCSE of 0.0013. How should you report it?

1.4336
1.43
1


The third decimal is already uncertain, so report two.

title: MCMC in practice
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve built the algorithm inside Stan, and you know how to check its work. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Random-walk Metropolis is simple but inefficient: 5,000 draws worth 372 for the flammability model’s \beta.
HMC gives the parameters momentum and slides them along the log-posterior’s gradient with the leapfrog integrator. Energy is nearly conserved, so nearly every proposal is accepted: 1,000 draws worth 855.
Step size balances accuracy against cost. Too big, and the simulation diverges: 12 divergent transitions with a step of 1.5.
Diagnostics from the posterior package: R-hat below 1.01, and bulk and tail ESS above about 400. Four HMC chains passed, and four Metropolis chains of the same length didn’t.
Monte Carlo standard errors say how many digits to report: the LFL50 is 1.43%, with an MCSE of 0.0013.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download flammability.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

The posterior package. Combine four chains into a draws object with posterior::as_draws_array(), and try posterior::summarise_draws(). Which columns are there? Compare them with this lesson’s numbers.
The number of leapfrog steps. With a step size of 0.25, run HMC with L = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32, and plot the ESS per gradient evaluation against L. Why does it fall off for large L? (The trajectory starts to turn back on itself. Stan’s NUTS, the “No-U-Turn Sampler”, stops each trajectory when that happens.)
A unit mass. Rerun HMC with inv_mass = c(1, 1). What happens to the acceptance rate and the ESS? Why does the mass matrix matter so much when the parameters have such different scales?
Check the gradient. Write a function that compares grad_lp() with finite differences at 100 random points from the posterior. What’s the largest relative difference?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)

An MCMC method that gives the parameters a random momentum and simulates their motion on the negative log-posterior, using its gradient.

Gradient

The vector of partial derivatives of the log-posterior: the direction and steepness of its slope.

Leapfrog integrator

The numerical method HMC uses to simulate the motion: half a momentum step, a position step, half a momentum step.

Hamiltonian

The total energy, the negative log-posterior plus the kinetic energy. HMC accepts with probability \min(1, e^{H_0 - H_1}).

Mass matrix

Scales the momentum in each direction to match the posterior’s width. Stan estimates it during warmup.

Divergent transition

An HMC trajectory whose energy error blew up, a sign that the sampler can’t explore part of the posterior.

R-hat (rank-normalized, split)

The modern convergence diagnostic, comparing halves of all the chains. Values below 1.01 are acceptable.

Bulk and tail ESS

Effective sample sizes for the center and for the tails of the posterior.

Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE)

The simulation error of an MCMC estimate, such as the posterior SD over the square root of the ESS for a mean.











NoteWant to read more?






Michael Betancourt, “A conceptual introduction to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo” (2017). Why HMC works in high dimensions, with pictures instead of proofs, by one of Stan’s developers.
Aki Vehtari, Andrew Gelman, Daniel Simpson, Bob Carpenter and Paul-Christian Bürkner, “Rank-normalization, folding, and localization: an improved R-hat for assessing convergence of MCMC”, Bayesian Analysis (2021). The R-hat, bulk ESS and tail ESS used in this lesson, and the thresholds.
Radford Neal, “MCMC using Hamiltonian dynamics”, chapter 5 of the Handbook of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (2011). The standard reference, including the leapfrog method and the choice of step size.
Richard McElreath, Statistical Rethinking lectures, lecture 8, “Markov chain Monte Carlo”, with an animated HMC.

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
Module 5 · Lesson 10 of 13 Week 85 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Module 2 fitted the Arrhenius equation to the rate constants of the plant’s main reaction, measured twice at each of eight temperatures from 140 to 210 °C:
k = A\, e^{-E_a/(RT)} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \log k = \log A - \frac{E_a}{1000R}\cdot\frac{1000}{T}.
A straight line of \log k against 1000/T, with T in kelvin, whose slope b gives the activation energy: E_a = -bR kJ/mol, with R = 8.314 J/(mol K). Least squares found E_a = 82 kJ/mol.
The Bayesian version of linear regression has the same model, with a prior on the coefficients and the residual SD, and a posterior instead of estimates and standard errors. This lesson shows what that adds: the prior’s say when data are scarce, predictions that carry every source of uncertainty, and a new way of checking whether the model fits, the posterior predictive check.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Bayesian linear regression
section: Least squares, and the flat-prior posterior
text:
Least squares, and the flat-prior posterior











Your turn. Fit the line with lm(), and convert the slope and its 95% confidence interval to an activation energy.









Every slope converts to an activation energy by multiplying by -R.


fit <- lm(log_k ~ inv_T, data = kin)
c(Ea = -coef(fit)[["inv_T"]] * R, -confint(fit)["inv_T", 2:1] * R)
E_a = 82.3 kJ/mol, with a 95% confidence interval from 80.4 to 84.2. (The interval’s ends swap places because multiplying by a negative number reverses the order.)




With the noninformative prior p(\beta, \sigma^2) \propto 1/\sigma^2, the posterior of a linear regression is Lesson 6’s normal model, generalized. With \hat\beta the least squares coefficients and s^2 the residual variance, on n - p degrees of freedom:

\sigma^2 \mid y \;\sim\; \frac{(n-p)\,s^2}{\chi^2_{n-p}}, \qquad \beta \mid \sigma^2, y \;\sim\; N\!\left(\hat\beta,\ \sigma^2 (X^\top X)^{-1}\right).

So the posterior can be simulated exactly in Lesson 6’s two steps: \sigma^2, then the coefficients.
Your turn. Draw 10,000 values from the posterior, and summarize the activation energy. The multivariate normal draws use the Cholesky factor of (X^\top X)^{-1}, as in Module 4.









Each row of coefficient draws is scaled by its own \sigma: sqrt(sigma2).


fit <- lm(log_k ~ inv_T, data = kin)
X <- model.matrix(fit)
n <- nrow(X); p <- ncol(X)
s2 <- sum(resid(fit)^2) / (n - p)
set.seed(5101)
sigma2 <- (n - p) * s2 / rchisq(10000, df = n - p)
Z <- matrix(rnorm(10000 * 2), 10000, 2)
beta <- matrix(coef(fit), 10000, 2, byrow = TRUE) + (Z %*% chol(solve(crossprod(X)))) * sqrt(sigma2)
Ea <- -beta[, 2] * R
c(mean = mean(Ea), quantile(Ea, c(0.025, 0.975)))
A posterior mean of 82.3 kJ/mol, and a 95% credible interval from 80.4 to 84.2: the confidence interval, to the first decimal. As in Lesson 6, with this prior the Bayesian and classical answers are numerically identical. Everything Module 2 did with lm() was, in that sense, already a Bayesian analysis with a flat prior.

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
A prior from the literature
Reactions of this type, the process chemists say, have activation energies of 70 to 100 kJ/mol: a normal prior for E_a with mean 85 and SD 10 kJ/mol. On the slope’s scale, that’s a normal prior with mean -85/R = -10.22 and SD 10/R = 1.20.
When the data’s information about a coefficient is roughly normal, with estimate \hat b and standard error \text{se}, combining it with a normal prior is Lesson 4’s normal-normal model: the precisions add.
Your turn. Combine the literature prior with the slope from lm(), and find the posterior activation energy, its SD, and the weight the data get.









The data’s term is \hat b/\text{se}^2.


fit <- lm(log_k ~ inv_T, data = kin)
b_hat <- coef(fit)[["inv_T"]]
se <- summary(fit)$coefficients["inv_T", "Std. Error"]
m0 <- -85 / R; t0 <- 10 / R                                  # the prior, on the slope's scale
precision <- 1 / t0^2 + 1 / se^2
b_post <- (m0 / t0^2 + b_hat / se^2) / precision
c(Ea = -b_post * R, Ea_sd = R / sqrt(precision), data_weight = (1 / se^2) / precision)
82.3 kJ/mol, with a posterior SD of 0.87: the data get 99.2% of the weight. Sixteen good measurements over a 70 °C range say far more than the literature’s ±10 kJ/mol, and the prior hardly moves the answer.




When does the prior matter? When the data are thin. Suppose the lab had only measured at the two lowest temperatures, 140 and 150 °C: four runs over a 10-degree range.
Your turn. Repeat the combination with only those four runs.









Keep the runs at 150 °C and below.


few <- subset(kin, temp_C <= 150)
fit_few <- lm(log_k ~ inv_T, data = few)
b_hat <- coef(fit_few)[["inv_T"]]
se <- summary(fit_few)$coefficients["inv_T", "Std. Error"]
m0 <- -85 / R; t0 <- 10 / R
precision <- 1 / t0^2 + 1 / se^2
b_post <- (m0 / t0^2 + b_hat / se^2) / precision
c(data_Ea = -b_hat * R, data_se = se * R, Ea = -b_post * R, Ea_sd = R / sqrt(precision), data_weight = (1 / se^2) / precision)
The four runs alone say 87 ± 6.9 kJ/mol. The prior gets a third of the weight now, and the posterior is 86.5 ± 5.7: about 20% narrower than the data alone. That’s the typical pattern. An informative prior helps most when the data are weak, and it’s honest only if it really comes from earlier knowledge, here the chemistry of similar reactions. (With these four runs, the classical 95% interval would use a t distribution with 2 degrees of freedom, which makes it very wide. This quick calculation treats \sigma as known. A full analysis, like brms’s, would account for it.)

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
The full model in brms
brms fits the whole model, with priors on all three parameters, and samples them jointly:
kin$inv_T <- 1000 / (kin$temp_C + 273.15)
kin$log_k <- log(kin$k_per_min)
fit <- brm(
  log_k ~ inv_T, data = kin,
  prior = c(prior(normal(-10.2, 1.2), class = b),          # Ea about 85 kJ/mol, give or take 10
            prior(normal(-3, 2), class = Intercept),        # log k at the average temperature
            prior(exponential(10), class = sigma)),         # residual SD, about 0.1 on the log scale
  seed = 5101
)
Here’s its summary:

#>  Family: gaussian 
#>   Links: mu = identity 
#> Formula: log_k ~ inv_T 
#>    Data: kin (Number of observations: 16) 
#>   Draws: 4 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1;
#>          total post-warmup draws = 4000
#> 
#> Regression Coefficients:
#>           Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> Intercept    18.77      0.26    18.28    19.28 1.00     3512     2588
#> inv_T        -9.90      0.11   -10.13    -9.68 1.00     3519     2599
#> 
#> Further Distributional Parameters:
#>       Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> sigma     0.05      0.01     0.04     0.08 1.00     2646     2659
#> 
#> Draws were sampled using sample(hmc). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
#> and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
#> scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).

One detail: brms’s prior on the Intercept applies to the intercept with the predictors centered, here \log k at the average 1000/T, which is much easier to have a prior belief about than \log A. The summary reports the uncentered intercept, \log A = 18.8.
Your turn. The setup code has brms’s draws in draws, with columns intercept, slope and sigma. Summarize the activation energy.









The activation energy comes from the slope.


Ea <- -draws$slope * R
c(mean = mean(Ea), quantile(Ea, c(0.025, 0.975)))
82.3 kJ/mol (80.5 to 84.2), as the quick calculation said. The interval is the same width as the flat-prior one: the prior hardly matters here.

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
Predictions
The plant is considering running at 230 °C, above any measured temperature. What rate constant would a new run there give? The posterior predictive distribution combines the uncertainty in the line with the run-to-run scatter: for each draw, compute the line at 230 °C, add a normal residual with that draw’s \sigma, and transform back with exp().
Your turn. Find the median and the 95% predictive interval of a new run’s rate constant at 230 °C.









Each draw’s residual has its own SD, draws$sigma.


x_new <- 1000 / (230 + 273.15)
set.seed(5102)
log_k_new <- draws$intercept + draws$slope * x_new + rnorm(nrow(draws), 0, draws$sigma)
k_new <- exp(log_k_new)
c(median = median(k_new), quantile(k_new, c(0.025, 0.975)))
A median of 0.40 per minute, with a 95% predictive interval from 0.36 to 0.45. Without the residual, the interval for the average run would be 0.38 to 0.43. Both assume that the Arrhenius line continues straight beyond 210 °C. No posterior can check that: it’s an assumption about chemistry, not statistics, and the report should say so.

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
Posterior predictive checks
A model can fit the data badly and still give a confident posterior. The posterior predictive check asks: if the model were right, would data like ours be typical? Simulate many replicated datasets from the posterior predictive distribution, at the same temperatures, and compare them with the real data using a test statistic T(y) chosen to probe a possible failure. The posterior predictive p-value is the share of replicated datasets with T(y^{\text{rep}}) \geq T(y). Values near 0 or 1 mean the real data are unusual for the model.
Suppose someone had fitted a straight line to k itself against the temperature in °C. The Arrhenius equation says k curves upward, so a good test statistic is the curvature: the average of k at the two ends, 140 and 210 °C, minus the average in the middle, 170 and 180 °C. For a straight line, it’s close to 0. For the real data, it’s 0.053.
Your turn. Simulate 4,000 replicated datasets from the flat-prior posterior of the straight-line model, compute the curvature of each, and find the posterior predictive p-value.









Compare with the observed data’s curvature, curvature(kin$k_per_min).


curvature <- function(k) mean(k[kin$temp_C %in% c(140, 210)]) - mean(k[kin$temp_C %in% c(170, 180)])
line <- lm(k_per_min ~ temp_C, data = kin)
X <- model.matrix(line)
n <- nrow(X)
s2 <- sum(resid(line)^2) / (n - 2)
set.seed(5103)
sigma2 <- (n - 2) * s2 / rchisq(4000, n - 2)
beta <- matrix(coef(line), 4000, 2, byrow = TRUE) + (matrix(rnorm(8000), 4000, 2) %*% chol(solve(crossprod(X)))) * sqrt(sigma2)
T_rep <- sapply(1:4000, function(s) curvature(X %*% beta[s, ] + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(sigma2[s]))))
c(T_observed = curvature(kin$k_per_min), p_value = mean(T_rep >= curvature(kin$k_per_min)))
A posterior predictive p-value of 0.004: only 15 of 4,000 replicated datasets curve as much as the real data. The straight line can’t produce data like these, and the check says so, without reference to any other model. It has a second giveaway, too: in 97% of the posterior draws, the line predicts a negative rate constant somewhere in the range. A good test statistic targets what a model might get wrong, and that takes knowing the science.




Here are the two models’ 90% predictive bands for a new run, on the rate constant’s own scale:

grid_T <- seq(140, 210, by = 1)
set.seed(5105)
arr <- t(sapply(grid_T, function(tc) quantile(exp(draws$intercept + draws$slope * 1000 / (tc + 273.15) + rnorm(nrow(draws), 0, draws$sigma)), c(0.05, 0.95))))
line <- lm(k_per_min ~ temp_C, data = kin)
lin <- predict(line, data.frame(temp_C = grid_T), interval = "prediction", level = 0.9)
bands <- rbind(data.frame(temp = grid_T, lo = arr[, 1], hi = arr[, 2], model = "Arrhenius (log k against 1/T)"),
               data.frame(temp = grid_T, lo = lin[, "lwr"], hi = lin[, "upr"], model = "straight line (k against T)"))
ggplot(bands, aes(x = temp)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi, fill = model), alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_point(data = kin, aes(x = temp_C, y = k_per_min), color = "#3A1F35", size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`Arrhenius (log k against 1/T)` = "#C2416C", `straight line (k against T)` = "#2a78d6"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Rate constant k (per minute)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The same check for the Arrhenius model. Use brms’s draws to simulate a replicated dataset for each draw, from the Arrhenius model, and compute the posterior predictive p-value for the curvature.









The observed statistic is curvature(kin$k_per_min).


curvature <- function(k) mean(k[kin$temp_C %in% c(140, 210)]) - mean(k[kin$temp_C %in% c(170, 180)])
X <- cbind(1, kin$inv_T)
set.seed(5104)
T_rep <- sapply(1:nrow(draws), function(s) curvature(exp(X %*% c(draws$intercept[s], draws$slope[s]) + rnorm(nrow(kin), 0, draws$sigma[s]))))
mean(T_rep >= curvature(kin$k_per_min))
0.72: the real data’s curvature is entirely typical for the Arrhenius model. A posterior predictive check can’t prove that a model is right, only find ways in which it’s wrong. This one found none. Lesson 13 adds more checks, and ways to compare models.




Challenge 2 · How long does a batch take? The reaction is first order, so the time to 99% conversion is \log(100)/k. At 200 °C, what’s its posterior median and 95% credible interval, for the average run (no residual)?









99% conversion leaves 1% of the reactant, so the time is \log(100)/k.


k_200 <- exp(draws$intercept + draws$slope * 1000 / (200 + 273.15))
t99 <- log(100) / k_200
c(median = median(t99), quantile(t99, c(0.025, 0.975)))
A median of 39.9 minutes, with a 95% credible interval from 38.4 to 41.5. Any quantity computed from the parameters, however nonlinear, gets its posterior from the draws, without the delta method or any other approximation. That’s often the most practical advantage of a Bayesian regression.

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
Quick quiz

1. With the prior p(\beta, \sigma^2) \propto 1/\sigma^2, how do the posterior credible intervals of a linear regression compare with the least squares confidence intervals?

They’re always wider
They’re numerically identical
They’re always narrower


The posterior of each coefficient is a t distribution centered at the estimate, with the standard error as its scale.



2. When does an informative prior on a coefficient change the answer most?

When there are many observations over a wide range
When the data say little about the coefficient, for example a narrow range or few observations
When the residual SD is small


With precisions adding, the prior’s share is large only when the data’s precision is small.



3. In brms, what does a prior on class = Intercept apply to, by default?

The intercept at x = 0
The intercept with the predictors centered at their means
The residual SD


brms centers the predictors internally, which makes the intercept easier to have a belief about, and helps the sampler.



4. What does a posterior predictive interval include that a credible interval for the regression line doesn’t?

The prior
The scatter of a new observation around the line
Nothing, they’re the same


The line’s uncertainty plus the residual variation.



5. A posterior predictive check gives a p-value of 0.004. What does that suggest?

The model fits very well
The real data are very unusual for the model, in the respect the test statistic measures
The prior is too weak


It points to a specific failure, here curvature that a straight line can’t produce.



6. What’s a good test statistic for a posterior predictive check?

The sample mean, always
One that targets a way the model might fail, chosen from knowledge of the problem
The one with the smallest p-value


The mean is usually fitted well by any model. Curvature, extremes, or runs of residuals are more revealing.

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
Wrap-up
You can now do Bayesian regression, and check the models you fit. Here’s what you’ve learned:

The flat-prior posterior of a linear regression can be simulated exactly. For the Arrhenius model, it gives E_a = 82.3 kJ/mol (80.4 to 84.2), the same as least squares.
Informative priors matter when the data are thin: with all 16 runs, the literature prior got 0.8% of the weight. With 4 runs over 10 degrees, it got a third.
brms fits the full model with priors on every parameter, and centers the predictors for its intercept prior.
Predictions come from the draws: a run at 230 °C would give 0.40 per minute (0.36 to 0.45), if the line continues straight.
Posterior predictive checks catch misfit: a straight line in k couldn’t reproduce the data’s curvature (p = 0.004), but the Arrhenius model could (p = 0.72).







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download kinetics.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder. Steps 2 and 3 need brms (Lesson 9).

Plot the posterior of E_a and \log A together. They’re strongly correlated. Why? Center 1000/T at its mean and refit with lm(): what happens to the correlation of the intercept and slope?
Fit it with brms with the lesson’s priors, and run pp_check(fit), pp_check(fit, type = "intervals") and pp_check(fit, type = "stat", stat = "max"). What does each one show?
A misleading prior. Refit with a prior on E_a of 120 ± 5 kJ/mol, strongly at odds with the data. Where does the posterior end up? Would a prior predictive check, or a posterior predictive check, have warned you?
The straight line, done properly. For the straight-line model of k against T, plot the residuals against temperature. Would you have needed the posterior predictive check to see the problem?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Bayesian linear regression

A linear regression with a prior on the coefficients and the residual SD, giving a posterior for all of them.

Activation energy

The E_a in the Arrhenius equation, k = A e^{-E_a/(RT)}: how strongly a reaction’s rate depends on temperature.

Posterior predictive distribution

The distribution of a new observation, combining the uncertainty in the parameters with the residual variation.

Posterior predictive check

Comparing the observed data with datasets simulated from the posterior predictive distribution, to look for misfit.

Replicated data

A dataset simulated from the model with parameters drawn from the posterior, at the same predictor values as the real data.

Test statistic

A summary of a dataset, chosen to probe a possible failure of the model, compared between the real and replicated data.

Posterior predictive p-value

The share of replicated datasets whose test statistic is at least as extreme as the observed one.











NoteWant to read more?






Andrew Gelman and others, Bayesian Data Analysis (3rd edition), chapter 14, “Introduction to regression models”, and chapter 6, “Model checking”, the source of posterior predictive checks.
Andrew Gelman, Jennifer Hill and Aki Vehtari, Regression and Other Stories (2020). Bayesian regression for practitioners, with free code and data for every example.
Alicia Johnson, Miles Ott and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, chapters 9, “Simple normal regression” and 10, “Evaluating regression models”, with posterior predictive checks in rstanarm.

title: Hierarchical models II
text:
Module 5 · Lesson 12 of 13 Week 87 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 11’s hierarchical model had one parameter per group. Most real problems have more: each group has its own regression line, or its own logistic curve. This lesson takes the same idea, partial pooling, to hierarchical regression.
The first problem is about catalyst. The plant’s eight hydrogenation reactors use the same catalyst, and its relative activity falls roughly linearly over time until it’s replaced, at 80% of its starting activity. The lab measures each reactor’s activity about every three weeks. Reactors R1 to R7 have eight to ten months of data. R8 was started only six weeks ago, and its three measurements fell steeply: on their own, they say it’ll need new catalyst after only 228 days, months earlier than any other reactor. Ordering catalyst takes four months, so the planner needs to decide soon.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Hierarchical models II
text:
No pooling












Your turn. Fit a separate straight line to each reactor’s activity against time (in units of 100 days), and look at R8’s slope and its standard error.









The row name is the reactor’s name, "R8".


fits <- lapply(split(deact, deact$reactor), function(d) lm(activity_pct ~ day100, data = d))
coefs <- t(sapply(fits, function(f) c(coef(f), se = summary(f)$coefficients["day100", "Std. Error"])))
round(coefs, 2)
coefs["R8", c("day100", "se")]
Reactors R1 to R7 lose 3.6 to 6.8 percentage points of activity per 100 days, with standard errors from 0.25 to 0.55. R8’s three points say 10.6, with a standard error of 1.9: far steeper than any other, and far less certain. And with only three points, that standard error is itself very uncertain. No pooling ignores what the other seven reactors say about how this catalyst behaves.

title: Hierarchical models II
text:
Varying intercepts and slopes
The hierarchical version gives each reactor j its own starting activity a_j and decline rate b_j, and treats the pairs as draws from a common bivariate normal distribution:

y_{ij} \sim N(a_j + b_j t_{ij},\ \sigma^2), \qquad \begin{pmatrix} a_j \\ b_j \end{pmatrix} \sim N\!\left(\begin{pmatrix} \mu_a \\ \mu_b \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} \tau_a^2 & \rho\,\tau_a\tau_b \\ \rho\,\tau_a\tau_b & \tau_b^2 \end{pmatrix}\right).

\mu_a and \mu_b describe the typical reactor, \tau_a and \tau_b how much reactors vary, and \rho whether reactors that start higher also decline faster. In brms, it’s one formula, the same as lmer()’s in Module 3:
deact$day100 <- deact$day / 100
fit <- brm(
  activity_pct ~ day100 + (day100 | reactor), data = deact,
  prior = c(prior(normal(95, 10), class = Intercept), prior(normal(0, 10), class = b),
            prior(exponential(0.5), class = sigma), prior(exponential(0.5), class = sd),
            prior(lkj(2), class = cor)),                 # a mild preference for small correlations
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99), seed = 5123
)
The (day100 | reactor) term means “an intercept and a slope for each reactor, correlated”. The LKJ prior is the standard prior for a correlation matrix: lkj(1) is flat over all correlations, and larger values prefer correlations near 0. A first run with adapt_delta raised from brms’s default of 0.8 to 0.95 still had one divergent transition, so this fit raised it to 0.99, which makes Stan take smaller steps. Here’s the summary:

#>  Family: gaussian 
#>   Links: mu = identity 
#> Formula: activity_pct ~ day100 + (day100 | reactor) 
#>    Data: deact (Number of observations: 114) 
#>   Draws: 4 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1;
#>          total post-warmup draws = 4000
#> 
#> Multilevel Hyperparameters:
#> ~reactor (Number of levels: 8) 
#>                       Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS
#> sd(Intercept)             2.25      0.63     1.34     3.81 1.00     1600
#> sd(day100)                1.15      0.40     0.62     2.09 1.00     1688
#> cor(Intercept,day100)    -0.47      0.27    -0.86     0.17 1.00     1980
#>                       Tail_ESS
#> sd(Intercept)             2421
#> sd(day100)                2411
#> cor(Intercept,day100)     2270
#> 
#> Regression Coefficients:
#>           Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> Intercept   101.18      0.84    99.48   102.81 1.00     1409     1830
#> day100       -5.65      0.46    -6.57    -4.73 1.00     1458     1999
#> 
#> Further Distributional Parameters:
#>       Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> sigma     1.21      0.09     1.06     1.39 1.00     3235     2834
#> 
#> Draws were sampled using sample(hmc). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
#> and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
#> scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).

The typical reactor starts at 101.2% and loses 5.65 points per 100 days. Reactors differ by about 2.2 points in starting activity (\tau_a) and 1.15 points per 100 days in decline rate (\tau_b). The setup code has the posterior draws of every reactor’s coefficients, in slopes: columns a_R1 to a_R8 and b_R1 to b_R8, and the hyperparameters mu_a, mu_b, sd_a, sd_b and cor_ab.
Your turn. Find R8’s partially pooled decline rate: its posterior mean and 95% credible interval.









R8’s slope draws are in the column b_R8.


c(mean = mean(slopes$b_R8), quantile(slopes$b_R8, c(0.025, 0.975)))
−6.3 points per 100 days (−8.9 to −4.1), pulled most of the way from R8’s own −10.6 toward the typical −5.65. R8’s three points are still in there: its posterior mean is steeper than the typical reactor’s, and its interval is three to four times as wide as the others’. That’s partial pooling working as it should, with the other reactors supplying what three points can’t.




Here are the eight reactors’ data, with the no-pooling lines (dashed) and the partially pooled ones (solid):

grid_d <- seq(0, 360, by = 10)
np <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(deact, deact$reactor), function(d) {
  f <- lm(activity_pct ~ I(day / 100), data = d)
  data.frame(reactor = d$reactor[1], day = grid_d, activity = coef(f)[1] + coef(f)[2] * grid_d / 100, fit = "no pooling")
}))
pp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(paste0("R", 1:8), function(r) {
  data.frame(reactor = r, day = grid_d, activity = mean(slopes[[paste0("a_", r)]]) + mean(slopes[[paste0("b_", r)]]) * grid_d / 100, fit = "partial pooling")
}))
ggplot(deact, aes(x = day, y = activity_pct)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 80, color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(data = np, aes(y = activity), linetype = "dashed", color = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_line(data = pp, aes(y = activity), color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1, color = "#3A1F35") +
  facet_wrap(~ reactor, nrow = 2) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(68, 106)) +
  labs(x = "Days on stream", y = "Catalyst activity (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The grey line is the replacement level, 80%. For R1 to R7, with plenty of data, the two methods agree. Only R8 differs.
Your turn. What will R8’s activity be at day 300? Compare the no-pooling prediction, 104.15 - 10.57 \times 3, with the partially pooled posterior, and find the posterior probability that R8 is already below 80% by then.









Time is in units of 100 days, so day 300 is 3.


at_300 <- slopes$a_R8 + slopes$b_R8 * 3                # day 300 is 3 units of 100 days
c(no_pooling = 104.1473 - 10.57007 * 3, partial = mean(at_300), quantile(at_300, c(0.025, 0.975)), p_below_80 = mean(at_300 < 80))
No pooling says R8 will be at 72% by day 300, well past replacement. Partial pooling says 84% (77% to 91%), with a 7% probability that it’s below 80%. The planner can wait for more data before ordering catalyst, and check again in a month.




Your turn. When will R8 reach 80%? For each draw, the time is (a_j - 80)/(-b_j), in units of 100 days. Find its posterior median and 95% interval, in days.









Convert from units of 100 days to days: multiply by 100.


t80 <- (slopes$a_R8 - 80) / (-slopes$b_R8) * 100        # in days
c(median = median(t80), quantile(t80, c(0.025, 0.975)))
A median of 369 days, with a 95% interval from 271 to 557. No pooling said 228 days. (Since these data are simulated, we know the truth: R8’s catalyst was set to decline by 4.0 points per 100 days, so it would reach 80% after about 550 days. Partial pooling’s interval includes that, at its upper end. No pooling missed it by almost a year.) Ordering catalyst for day 300, the lower end of the interval, would be a sensible, cautious plan.

title: Hierarchical models II
section: Predicting a new reactor, and the correlation
text:
Predicting a new reactor, and the correlation
The plant is planning a ninth reactor. Before it starts, what decline rate should the planner expect? For each draw of the hyperparameters, a new reactor’s slope is a draw from N(\mu_b, \tau_b^2).
Your turn. Simulate a new reactor’s decline rate, and find its 95% predictive interval.









The between-reactor SD of the slopes is sd_b.


set.seed(5121)
b_new <- rnorm(nrow(slopes), mean = slopes$mu_b, sd = slopes$sd_b)
c(mean = mean(b_new), quantile(b_new, c(0.025, 0.975)))
A new reactor will probably lose between 3.0 and 8.4 points per 100 days, with a mean of 5.6. That interval is the honest range for planning the ninth reactor’s catalyst budget. Like Lesson 11’s new lab, it includes the uncertainty about the hyperparameters, not just the spread between reactors.




Your turn. Do reactors whose catalyst starts more active also lose activity faster? Summarize the posterior of the correlation \rho between the intercepts and slopes, and the probability that it’s negative (a higher start goes with a more negative slope, a faster decline).









Negative means below 0.


c(mean = mean(slopes$cor_ab), p_negative = mean(slopes$cor_ab < 0))
A posterior mean of −0.48, and a 95% probability that the correlation is negative: catalyst that starts more active tends to fade faster. That’s chemically plausible, since the most active sites are often the first to be poisoned. With eight reactors, the interval is wide, from −0.86 to 0.17, so it’s a lead to follow, not a finding. The correlation also helps R8: its high starting activity, about 103%, suggests a somewhat faster decline than average, which is part of why its posterior slope is steeper than the typical reactor’s.

title: Hierarchical models II
text:
Hierarchical logistic regression
The second problem is about leaks. Under the plant’s leak detection and repair (LDAR) program, every valve, flange and pump seal in a process unit is checked for leaking vapor once a year. This year’s survey covered 18 units, with very different numbers of components, from 30 to 960.
Three units stand out on raw rates: U05 had 54 leaks in 520 components (10.4%), U09 had none in 400, and U11 had none in 30. The hierarchical model gives each unit a leak probability p_j on the log-odds scale, with the logits drawn from a common normal distribution: Lesson 11’s model, inside a logistic regression.
fit <- brm(
  leaks | trials(components) ~ 1 + (1 | unit), family = binomial(), data = ldar,
  prior = c(prior(normal(-4, 1.5), class = Intercept),     # about 2% leak, give or take
            prior(exponential(1), class = sd)),
  seed = 5124
)

#>  Family: binomial 
#>   Links: mu = logit 
#> Formula: leaks | trials(components) ~ 1 + (1 | unit) 
#>    Data: ldar (Number of observations: 18) 
#>   Draws: 4 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1;
#>          total post-warmup draws = 4000
#> 
#> Multilevel Hyperparameters:
#> ~unit (Number of levels: 18) 
#>               Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> sd(Intercept)     0.75      0.19     0.45     1.20 1.00     1026     1795
#> 
#> Regression Coefficients:
#>           Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> Intercept    -3.73      0.22    -4.20    -3.34 1.00     1001     1529
#> 
#> Draws were sampled using sample(hmc). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
#> and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
#> scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).

The typical unit’s log-odds is −3.73, a leak rate of 2.4%, and units vary with an SD of 0.75 on the log-odds scale: some units leak two or three times as often as others. The setup code has the draws of each unit’s leak probability in ldar_draws, in columns U01 to U18.
Your turn. Compare the partially pooled leak probabilities of U09, U11 and U05 with their raw rates of 0%, 0% and 10.4%.









U05’s draws are in the column U05.


c(U09 = mean(ldar_draws$U09), U11 = mean(ldar_draws$U11), U05 = mean(ldar_draws$U05))
U09’s 0 out of 400 becomes 0.7%, and U11’s 0 out of 30 becomes 2.1%, almost the plant’s typical rate: 30 components say very little, while 400 say quite a lot. U05’s 10.4% barely moves, to 9.8%, because 54 leaks out of 520 is strong evidence. A raw rate of 0% would have suggested that U11 needs no attention, which no engineer would believe from 30 components.




Your turn. The regulator requires a unit with a leak rate above 5% to be resurveyed every quarter. What’s the posterior probability that U05, U03 (2 leaks in 45 components, 4.4%) and U11 are above 5%?









The limit is 5%, 0.05.


c(U05 = mean(ldar_draws$U05 > 0.05), U03 = mean(ldar_draws$U03 > 0.05), U11 = mean(ldar_draws$U11 > 0.05))
U05 is above 5% in every draw: resurvey it quarterly, and find out why it leaks so much more than the rest of the plant. U03, whose raw rate was 4.4%, has a 16% probability, and U11 4%. Neither needs quarterly surveys, but U03 deserves a closer look next year.

title: Hierarchical models II
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Which unit is the worst? League tables of raw rates are dominated by small groups, which have the most extreme rates by chance. With posterior draws, you can compute the probability that each unit has the highest leak rate: in each draw, find the unit with the largest probability, and count.









which.max gives the position of the largest value in each row.


p_matrix <- as.matrix(ldar_draws[, ldar$unit])               # one column per unit
worst <- apply(p_matrix, 1, which.max)                       # the column of the largest rate, in each draw
round(table(factor(ldar$unit[worst], levels = ldar$unit)) / nrow(p_matrix), 3)
U05 is the worst unit in 98% of the draws. U03, with only 45 components, comes second, with about 1%. Ranks are notoriously uncertain, and this is the honest way to report them: the probability of each rank, not just the ranking of point estimates.




Challenge 2 · Varying intercepts only. A simpler model gives each reactor its own intercept but one common slope: activity_pct ~ day100 + (1 | reactor). Its draws are in data/brms_deact_intercepts_draws.csv, with the same column names (every b_ column is the same common slope). What does it predict for R8 at day 300?









Use R8’s slope column, b_R8, which in this model is the common slope.


intercepts <- read_csv("data/brms_deact_intercepts_draws.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
at_300 <- intercepts$a_R8 + intercepts$b_R8 * 3
c(mean = mean(at_300), quantile(at_300, c(0.025, 0.975)), p_below_80 = mean(at_300 < 80))
85.8% (83.9% to 87.6%), and no chance at all of being below 80%. This model is too confident: it assumes that R8 declines exactly like the average reactor, when the other seven clearly differ, from 3.6 to 6.8 points per 100 days. Complete pooling of the slopes, no pooling, partial pooling: which is best? Lesson 13 compares them properly.

title: Hierarchical models II
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does the brms term (day100 | reactor) mean?

One slope for all reactors
An intercept and a slope for each reactor, drawn from a common bivariate normal distribution
A separate model for each reactor


It’s the same notation as lme4’s lmer(). (1 | reactor) would give varying intercepts only.



2. R8’s own slope is −10.6 from three points, and its partially pooled slope −6.3. Why so much shrinkage?

Because R8 is an outlier
Because three points over 41 days say little about the slope, compared with what the other reactors say
Because the prior on the slope is strong


As in Lesson 11, shrinkage depends on how precise the group’s own data are.



3. What does the LKJ prior describe?

The residual SD
A correlation matrix, here the correlation between the intercepts and slopes
The intercept


lkj(1) is flat over correlations, and larger values prefer correlations near 0.



4. A unit had 0 leaks in 30 components. Why is its partially pooled leak rate 2.1%, not 0%?

Because the model adds one leak to every unit
Because 30 components can’t distinguish a rate of 0% from 2%, so the estimate is pulled toward the plant’s typical rate
Because of rounding


Zero events in a small sample is weak evidence of a zero rate.



5. Why are league tables of raw rates misleading?

Because they use too many decimals
Because small groups have the most extreme rates by chance, so they crowd the top and the bottom
Because larger groups are always better


Partial pooling, and rank probabilities, correct for that.



6. How do you predict a reactor that doesn’t exist yet?

Use the average of the eight reactors’ estimates
For each posterior draw, draw its coefficients from the group-level distribution, with that draw’s hyperparameters
You can’t, without data


That carries both the spread between reactors and the uncertainty about the hyperparameters.

title: Hierarchical models II
text:
Wrap-up
You can now fit hierarchical regression models, for measurements and for counts. Here’s what you’ve learned:

No pooling gave R8, with three points, a slope of −10.6 per 100 days, and a replacement date of day 228.
Varying intercepts and slopes pooled R8 with the other reactors: −6.3 (−8.9 to −4.1), and a replacement date around day 369 (271 to 557), much closer to the simulated truth.
A new reactor will probably lose 3.0 to 8.4 points per 100 days, and reactors that start more active tend to fade faster (95% probability).
Hierarchical logistic regression shrinks small units’ rates toward the plant’s typical 2.4%: U11’s 0 out of 30 became 2.1%, while U05’s 10.4% from 520 components stayed at 9.8%.
Rank probabilities report league tables honestly: U05 is the worst unit with 98% probability.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download deactivation.csv and ldar_survey.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder. Steps 2 to 4 need brms (Lesson 9).

The classical version. Fit lme4::lmer(activity_pct ~ day100 + (day100 | reactor), data = deact), and compare coef() for R8 with the posterior mean. Why are they close? What does lmer not give you?
Refit with brms, and use ranef(fit) and coef(fit) to see each reactor’s deviations and coefficients. Plot them with conditional_effects(fit, re_formula = NULL).
A predictor for units. Some units handle heavy liquids, which usually leak less. Add a made-up service column, and fit leaks | trials(components) ~ service + (1 | unit). How does a unit-level predictor change the shrinkage?
More data for R8. Add two more made-up measurements for R8, at days 62 and 83, at 97.6% and 96.7%, refit, and see how R8’s posterior slope changes.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Hierarchical regression

A regression whose coefficients vary by group, drawn from a common distribution.

Varying intercepts

A separate intercept for each group, as in (1 | group).

Varying slopes

A separate slope for each group, usually together with varying intercepts, as in (x | group).

Bivariate normal distribution

A normal distribution for two quantities together, with two means, two SDs and a correlation.

LKJ prior

The standard prior for correlation matrices. Its parameter sets how strongly it prefers correlations near 0.

Hierarchical logistic regression

A logistic regression with group-level parameters on the log-odds scale, drawn from a common distribution.

Rank probability

The posterior probability that a group has a particular rank, such as the highest rate.











NoteWant to read more?

Alicia Johnson, Miles Ott and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, chapters 17, “(Normal) hierarchical models with predictors” and 18, “Non-normal hierarchical regression & classification”.
Richard McElreath, Statistical Rethinking lectures, lectures 12 to 14, on multilevel models, varying slopes and correlated effects.
Paul-Christian Bürkner, “Advanced Bayesian multilevel modeling with the R package brms”, The R Journal (2018).

title: Time series data
text:
Module 6 · Lesson 1 of 13 Week 90 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Every dataset in this course so far has had a hidden assumption: the observations are independent. Batch 17’s yield says nothing about batch 18’s, and shuffling the rows changes nothing. For a lot of plant data, that’s false. Today’s steam demand is a lot like yesterday’s, this January is a lot like last January, and if you shuffle the months, you destroy exactly the information you need. Data recorded in time order, where the order matters, is a time series, and this module is about the methods built for it.
The first series is the plant’s steam demand: how many thousand tonnes (kt) of steam the boilers made each month, from January 2014 to December 2025. Steam drives turbines and reboilers, but it also heats buildings and keeps pipes from freezing, so demand rises in winter. The utilities engineer also has each month’s heating degree days (HDD): the sum, over the month’s days, of how far the average outdoor temperature fell below 15.5 °C. A cold month has many, a summer month almost none.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Time series data
text:
Time series objects
R’s built-in ts class stores a series of equally spaced observations with its timing: the time of the first observation, and the frequency, the number of observations per unit of time. For monthly data with years as the unit, the frequency is 12: quarterly data has 4, weekly about 52.18, and hourly data with days as the unit 24.











Your turn. Make a monthly ts object of the steam demand, starting in January 2014, and look at its time attributes with tsp(): the start, the end and the frequency.









Monthly data with years as the unit has a frequency of 12.


steam_ts <- ts(steam$steam_kt, start = c(2014, 1), frequency = 12)
tsp(steam_ts)
The series starts at 2014.000 and ends at 2025.917, December 2025, which is 2025 + 11/12, with 12 observations per year. start = c(2014, 1) means “year 2014, period 1”, January. Once R knows the timing, plots get a proper time axis, and functions like window(), cycle() and aggregate() work by date.




Your turn. The setup code has the series as y. Use window() to pick out 2020, and find its average monthly demand.









The year ends in period 12, December.


y2020 <- window(y, start = c(2020, 1), end = c(2020, 12))
mean(y2020)
39.34 kt a month in 2020. window() keeps the result a ts object, with the right start date, so you can keep using time series functions on it.




Your turn. Add up each year’s months with aggregate(), which sums a monthly series into a yearly one.









Total demand is the sum: FUN = sum.


annual <- aggregate(y, FUN = sum)
annual
From 447 kt in 2014 to 525 kt in 2025. The yearly totals rise in most years, but not all: 2015 and 2017 were slightly lower than the year before. Mild winters use less steam, so the yearly totals mix the growth of the plant with the weather.

title: Time series data
text:
Trend, seasonality and cycles
Here’s the series over time, a time plot:

autoplot(y, color = "#C2416C") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Steam demand (kt per month)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Three kinds of pattern show up in time series, and this one has two of them:

A trend is a long-term rise or fall. Steam demand drifts upward as the plant grows.
Seasonality is a pattern that repeats with a fixed period, tied to the calendar: here, every 12 months, high in winter and low in summer.
A cycle is a rise and fall without a fixed period, like a business cycle that lasts anywhere from two to ten years. Cycles are much harder to forecast than seasons. Lesson 13 meets a series with long, irregular swings.

A seasonal plot draws each year as its own line against the months, which makes the seasonal pattern, and any year that breaks it, easy to see:

ggseasonplot(y, year.labels = FALSE) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "magma", end = 0.85, name = "Year") +
  labs(title = NULL, x = NULL, y = "Steam demand (kt per month)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Your turn. cycle() gives each observation’s position in the cycle, here the month, 1 to 12. Use it to find the average demand for each calendar month.









The grouping is the month, cycle(y).


round(tapply(y, cycle(y), mean), 2)
January averages 45.5 kt and August 34.4: a seasonal swing of 11 kt, about a quarter of the average demand. The pattern is smooth, falling from January to August and rising again, as the heating degree days do.




Your turn. Fit a straight-line trend with lm(), using time(y), the time in years, as the predictor. How much does demand grow per year?









The predictor is the time, time(y).


trend <- lm(y ~ time(y))
coef(trend)[2]                  # kt per month, gained each year
0.60 kt per month per year: monthly demand grows by about 1.5% a year. Careful with the standard error that summary(trend) would print, though. It assumes independent residuals, and the residuals of this series are anything but, as the next section shows.

title: Time series data
text:
Autocorrelation
The defining feature of a time series is that each observation is related to its own past. A lag plot shows it: each month’s demand against the demand k months earlier.

lagged <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 6, 12), function(k) data.frame(now = y[-(1:k)], before = y[1:(length(y) - k)], lag = paste("lag", k))))
lagged$lag <- factor(lagged$lag, levels = paste("lag", c(1, 6, 12)))
ggplot(lagged, aes(x = before, y = now)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, color = "#C2416C", alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ lag) +
  labs(x = "Demand k months earlier (kt)", y = "Demand (kt)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The autocorrelation at lag k, r_k, is the correlation in each of those panels, computed in a standard way: with the overall mean and variance of the series, rather than each panel’s own. Together, the r_k are the autocorrelation function (ACF), which Lesson 3 uses to tell models apart.
Your turn. Compute the ACF with acf(..., plot = FALSE), and pick out the autocorrelations at lags 1, 6 and 12. (The first element is lag 0, which is always 1.)









Lag k is element k + 1, so lag 12 is element 13.


r <- acf(y, lag.max = 24, plot = FALSE)$acf
c(lag1 = r[2], lag6 = r[7], lag12 = r[13])
0.83 at lag 1, −0.49 at lag 6, and 0.81 at lag 12. Consecutive months are strongly alike, months half a year apart are opposites, and the same month a year apart is alike again. For independent data, every autocorrelation beyond lag 0 would be near 0. Here, knowing one month tells you a lot about the next. That’s useful for forecasting, and fatal for any method that assumes independence: standard errors, t-tests and confidence intervals that ignore it are too small, sometimes by a factor of several.




Your turn. How closely does steam demand follow the weather? Find the correlation between the monthly demand and the heating degree days.









The heating degree days are in the column hdd.


cor(steam$steam_kt, steam$hdd)
0.86. Most of the seasonal swing is the weather, so a model that uses the heating degree days can explain the seasonality instead of just copying it. That’s Lesson 10, regression with time series errors. A warning from the same lesson: two series that both trend or both have seasons can be highly correlated without being related at all.

title: Time series data
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Year over year. Comparing each month with the same month a year earlier removes the seasonality: diff(y, lag = 12). That’s a seasonal difference, and Lesson 9 builds models on it. Find the average year-over-year change, and its SD.









A year is 12 months.


yoy <- diff(y, lag = 12)
c(mean = mean(yoy), sd = sd(yoy))
An average rise of 0.59 kt over the same month last year, close to the trend’s 0.60 per year, but with an SD of 1.9: from one year to the next, the weather moves a month’s demand by much more than the plant’s growth does. The 132 year-over-year changes have no seasonality left, which makes the trend much easier to see.




Challenge 2 · When is the peak? In which month did each year’s demand peak? Group the series by year, floor(time(y)), and find the position of each year’s maximum.









which.max(v) gives the position of the largest value.


tapply(y, floor(time(y)), function(v) which.max(v))
The peak came in January (1) in three years, February (2) in four, and December (12) in five. The seasonal pattern is fixed, but the coldest month isn’t: it depends on the weather. A model with a fixed seasonal shape would put the peak in January every year, so it’d be off in most years by a month or so. A model with the heating degree days wouldn’t.

title: Time series data
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does the frequency of a ts object mean?

How often the series was revised
The number of observations per unit of time, such as 12 for monthly data in years
The number of seasons in the data


With the start time, it gives every observation its date.



2. What distinguishes a cycle from seasonality?

Seasonality has a fixed period tied to the calendar; a cycle rises and falls without a fixed period
Cycles are always longer than a year
There’s no difference


That’s why seasons are easy to forecast and cycles aren’t.



3. A monthly series has an autocorrelation of 0.81 at lag 12. What does that suggest?

A downward trend
Strong seasonality: each month is like the same month a year earlier
No pattern at all


Seasonal series have large autocorrelations at multiples of the seasonal period.



4. Why is autocorrelation a problem for an ordinary regression’s standard errors?

It isn’t
They assume independent residuals, so with positively autocorrelated data they’re too small
It makes them too large


Twelve correlated months carry less information than twelve independent ones. Lesson 10 fixes this.



5. What does diff(y, lag = 12) compute for a monthly series?

The change from one month to the next
The change from each month to the same month a year earlier
The 12-month moving average


A seasonal difference. It removes a stable seasonal pattern.



6. What does a seasonal plot show that a time plot doesn’t?

The trend
Each year as its own line against the season, so the seasonal shape and unusual years stand out
The autocorrelation


In a time plot, the seasonal shape is spread across the years. A seasonal plot stacks them.

title: Time series data
text:
Wrap-up
You can now read a time series. Here’s what you’ve learned:

ts objects store a series with its start and frequency, so that window(), cycle(), time() and aggregate() work by date.
Trend: steam demand grows by 0.60 kt per month each year, from 447 kt a year in 2014 to 525 kt in 2025.
Seasonality: January averages 45.5 kt and August 34.4, following the heating degree days (correlation 0.86).
Plots: time plots show trend and seasonality, seasonal plots the seasonal shape, and lag plots the relation of a series to its past.
Autocorrelation: 0.83 at lag 1 and 0.81 at lag 12. Observations in time aren’t independent, which is useful for forecasting and dangerous for ordinary standard errors.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download steam_demand.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder. Install the forecast package, which the rest of this module uses: install.packages("forecast").

Plots from forecast. Try autoplot(y), ggseasonplot(y), ggseasonplot(y, polar = TRUE), ggsubseriesplot(y) and gglagplot(y). Which one shows the seasonal pattern most clearly? Which shows the trend in each month?
The ACF plot. Plot ggAcf(y, lag.max = 36). Describe its shape. Then plot ggAcf(diff(y, lag = 12)): what’s left after removing the seasonality?
Other frequencies. Make a weekly series from Lesson 6’s feed_impurity.csv with ts(x, start = c(2019, 1), frequency = 365.25 / 7). What do tsp() and time() give?
Steam per degree day. Plot the steam demand against the heating degree days, colored by year. What does the color pattern tell you?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Time series

Observations recorded in time order, where the order matters.

Frequency

The number of observations per unit of time in a ts object: 12 for monthly data in years.

Trend

A long-term rise or fall in a series.

Seasonality

A pattern that repeats with a fixed, known period, such as every 12 months.

Cycle

Rises and falls without a fixed period.

Lag

The number of time steps between two observations being compared.

Autocorrelation function (ACF)

The correlations of a series with its own past at each lag.

Seasonal difference

The change from each observation to the one a full season earlier, such as diff(y, lag = 12).











NoteWant to read more?






Rob Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd edition), chapter 2, “Time series graphics”. The best introduction to time series there is, free online. It uses the newer fable packages; the 2nd edition uses the forecast package, like this module.
Penn State’s STAT 510, Applied Time Series Analysis, lesson 1, on time series plots and the ACF.
Robert Shumway and David Stoffer, Time Series: A Data Analysis Approach Using R (CRC Press, 2019), chapter 1. Its code and data, in the astsa package, are on the book’s GitHub page.

title: Stationarity and autocorrelation
text:
Module 6 · Lesson 3 of 13 Week 92 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Most time series models, including the ARMA models of the next three lessons, assume that the series is stationary: its behavior doesn’t depend on when you look at it. Its mean and variance are constant, and the correlation between two observations depends only on how far apart they are, not on the date. A stationary series fluctuates around a fixed level and keeps coming back to it.
Many real series aren’t like that. They wander, trend, or have seasons. This lesson is about telling the two kinds apart, and about the simplest way of turning one into the other, differencing. The examples come from the plant’s control system: 600 minutes of a reactor temperature’s deviation from its set point, under PID control, and the level of an intermediate tank, which simply accumulates whatever flows in minus whatever flows out.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Stationarity and autocorrelation
text:
White noise
The simplest stationary series is white noise: independent draws with mean 0 and a constant variance. It has no memory at all, so its autocorrelations at every lag beyond 0 are 0. In a sample, they won’t be exactly 0, but for white noise of length n, about 95% of them should be within \pm 1.96/\sqrt n. Those are the dashed lines on every ACF plot.












Your turn. Simulate 600 values of white noise, compute their autocorrelations at lags 1 to 20, and count how many fall outside \pm 1.96/\sqrt{600}.









The series has 600 values.


set.seed(6031)
e <- rnorm(600)
r <- acf(e, lag.max = 20, plot = FALSE)$acf[-1]          # drop lag 0
c(lag1 = r[1], outside = sum(abs(r) > 1.96 / sqrt(600)))
The lag-1 autocorrelation is 0.05, and none of the 20 is outside \pm 0.080. On average, 1 in 20 would be, by chance, so a single autocorrelation just outside the lines is no evidence of anything. A pattern, or a large spike at a meaningful lag such as 1 or 12, is.

title: Stationarity and autocorrelation
text:
Random walks
Add up white noise, and you get a random walk: y_t = y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t. Each step is independent, but the level is the sum of all of them, so it wanders off and never comes back on purpose. Its variance grows with time, \text{Var}(y_t) = t\sigma^2, so it isn’t stationary. A random walk is said to have a unit root, because the coefficient on y_{t-1} is exactly 1.
Your turn. Simulate a random walk of 600 steps, and look at its autocorrelations at lags 1 and 30.









A random walk is the cumulative sum of the steps: cumsum().


set.seed(6032)
w <- cumsum(rnorm(600))
r <- acf(w, lag.max = 30, plot = FALSE)$acf
c(lag1 = r[2], lag30 = r[31])
0.99 at lag 1, and still 0.82 at lag 30. That slow, almost linear decay is the signature of a non-stationary series in an ACF plot. (Strictly, a random walk has no ACF, since it isn’t stationary. The sample ACF still computes, and that’s what it looks like.)

title: Stationarity and autocorrelation
text:
Two process signals
Here are the plant’s two signals:

sig <- rbind(data.frame(minute = ps$minute, value = ps$temp_dev_C, signal = "reactor temperature, deviation from set point (°C)"),
             data.frame(minute = ps$minute, value = ps$tank_level_pct, signal = "tank level (%)"))
ggplot(sig, aes(x = minute, y = value)) +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ signal, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Minute", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The temperature keeps returning to 0: the controller sees to that. The tank level has no controller holding it at a target, so it goes wherever the flows take it.
Your turn. Compute the tank level’s autocorrelations at lags 1, 10 and 30.









The tank level is in the setup code’s tank.


r <- acf(tank, lag.max = 30, plot = FALSE)$acf
c(lag1 = r[2], lag10 = r[11], lag30 = r[31])
0.99, 0.86 and 0.52: the slow decay of a random walk. Half an hour later, the level still remembers where it was, because it’s an accumulation, an integral of the flow imbalance. In chemical engineering terms, a tank without level control is an integrating process, and integrating processes are non-stationary.

title: Stationarity and autocorrelation
text:
Differencing
If the level is a random walk, its changes are white noise. Differencing, y'_t = y_t - y_{t-1}, removes a unit root, and often makes a wandering series stationary. Lesson 1’s seasonal difference, diff(y, lag = 12), does the same for a seasonal pattern.
Your turn. Difference the tank level, and look at the lag-1 autocorrelation, the mean and the SD of the changes.









diff() computes the differences.


changes <- diff(tank)
c(lag1 = acf(changes, plot = FALSE)$acf[2], mean = mean(changes), sd = sd(changes))
A lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.009: the changes look like white noise, with an SD of 0.34 percentage points a minute, and a mean of 0.01, so essentially no drift. The tank level is a random walk, a model with no parameters to estimate beyond that SD. The next lessons build models for series whose differences, or whose levels, still have structure.

title: Stationarity and autocorrelation
text:
Unit-root tests
Looking at plots is the first step, but there are formal tests too. The augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test regresses the change \Delta y_t on the previous level y_{t-1} (and some lagged changes). If the series has a unit root, the coefficient on y_{t-1} is 0. The null hypothesis is a unit root (non-stationary), so a small p-value is evidence of stationarity. tseries::adf.test() runs it.
Your turn. Run the ADF test on the tank level and on its differences.









Test the differenced series, diff(tank), too.


c(level = tseries::adf.test(tank)$p.value, changes = tseries::adf.test(diff(tank))$p.value)
p = 0.52 for the level: no evidence against a unit root. For the changes, p = 0.01 (the test only reports p-values down to 0.01, and warns when the real one is smaller): strong evidence that they’re stationary. So the tank level is integrated of order 1, I(1): one difference makes it stationary.




The KPSS test turns the hypotheses around: its null is stationarity, so a small p-value is evidence of a unit root. Using both is good practice, since unit-root tests have low power, and a large p-value from either isn’t proof.
Your turn. Run the KPSS test on the tank level and on the temperature.









Use kpss.test() for both.


c(tank = tseries::kpss.test(tank)$p.value, temperature = tseries::kpss.test(temp)$p.value)
For the tank, p = 0.01 (or smaller): KPSS rejects stationarity. For the temperature, p = 0.10 (or larger): no evidence against stationarity. The two tests agree on both signals. (KPSS reports p-values only between 0.01 and 0.10, from a table, and warns at the ends.)

title: Stationarity and autocorrelation
text:
The partial autocorrelation function
The temperature is stationary, but far from white noise. Its ACF falls off fast, oscillating as it goes, and that alone doesn’t say what model would describe it. The partial autocorrelation function (PACF) helps: the partial autocorrelation at lag k is the correlation between y_t and y_{t-k} after removing the effect of the lags in between, 1 to k - 1. It’s the last coefficient in a regression of y_t on its first k lags.

a <- acf(ps$temp_dev_C, lag.max = 20, plot = FALSE)$acf[-1]
pa <- pacf(ps$temp_dev_C, lag.max = 20, plot = FALSE)$acf
cf <- rbind(data.frame(lag = 1:20, value = a, fn = "ACF"), data.frame(lag = 1:20, value = as.numeric(pa), fn = "PACF"))
ggplot(cf, aes(x = lag, y = value)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1, 1) * 1.96 / sqrt(600), linetype = "dashed", color = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0), color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ fn) +
  labs(x = "Lag (minutes)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Your turn. Find the temperature’s partial autocorrelations at lags 1 to 4. (Unlike acf(), pacf() starts at lag 1.)









Lags 1 to 4 are the first 4 elements.


pacf(temp, lag.max = 5, plot = FALSE)$acf[1:4]
0.81, −0.59, −0.02 and 0.04.
