Two large partial autocorrelations, then nothing: each minute’s temperature depends directly on the last two minutes, and once those are known, earlier minutes add nothing. That pattern points to an autoregressive model of order 2, AR(2), the subject of Lesson 4. The negative second coefficient is what makes a controlled loop oscillate: an overshoot is followed by a correction.




Your turn. The forecast package’s ndiffs() runs a unit-root test repeatedly to decide how many differences a series needs. Ask it about both signals.









The temperature is temp.


c(tank = forecast::ndiffs(tank), temperature = forecast::ndiffs(temp))
One difference for the tank, none for the temperature. Lesson 6’s auto.arima() uses ndiffs() this way to choose the “I” in ARIMA. Differencing a stationary series, overdifferencing, would be a mistake: it adds a characteristic pattern to the ACF, a large negative autocorrelation at lag 1, that Lesson 5 explains.

title: Stationarity and autocorrelation
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Any autocorrelation at all? Testing each autocorrelation separately invites false alarms. The Ljung-Box test combines the first h of them into one statistic, Q = n(n+2)\sum_{k=1}^h r_k^2/(n-k), whose null hypothesis is white noise. Run it with 10 lags on the white noise from earlier and on the temperature.









Use type = "Ljung-Box" for both.


set.seed(6031)
e <- rnorm(600)
c(white_noise = Box.test(e, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value,
  temperature = Box.test(temp, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value)
p = 0.63 for the white noise, and effectively 0 for the temperature, with Q = 600 on 10 degrees of freedom. Lesson 7 uses this test on a model’s residuals: if the model has captured the structure, they should look like white noise.




Challenge 2 · A random walk’s variance. Simulate 2,000 random walks of 400 steps each, and compare the variance of their values at step 100 with the variance at step 400. The theory says t\sigma^2.









Row 400 holds the 400th step of every walk.


set.seed(6033)
walks <- replicate(2000, cumsum(rnorm(400)))       # 400 steps x 2,000 walks
c(step_100 = var(walks[100, ]), step_400 = var(walks[400, ]))
101 and 396, close to the theoretical 100 and 400: the variance grows in proportion to time, so the spread grows with its square root. That’s why a random walk’s forecasts have prediction intervals that keep widening without limit, while a stationary series’ intervals settle at a fixed width.

title: Stationarity and autocorrelation
text:
Quick quiz

1. What makes a series stationary?

It has no trend
Its mean, variance and autocorrelations don’t depend on time
It’s normally distributed


No trend is necessary, but not sufficient: a random walk has no trend and still isn’t stationary.



2. A sample ACF decays very slowly, almost linearly, from 0.99. What does that suggest?

White noise
A non-stationary series, such as a random walk
Strong seasonality


Difference it and look again.



3. What is the null hypothesis of the augmented Dickey-Fuller test?

The series has a unit root
The series is stationary
The series is white noise


A small p-value is evidence of stationarity. KPSS has the opposite null.



4. The PACF has two large spikes, at lags 1 and 2, and nothing after. Which model does that suggest?

MA(2)
AR(2)
A random walk


An AR(p) process has partial autocorrelations of 0 beyond lag p.



5. Why is an uncontrolled tank level non-stationary?

Because tanks are always filling
Because the level accumulates the flow imbalance, so it’s an integral of noise: a random walk
Because level sensors drift


Integrating processes have a unit root. A level controller would make the level stationary.



6. What does a Ljung-Box test on 10 lags check?

Whether the series has a trend
Whether the first 10 autocorrelations are, together, consistent with white noise
Whether the series needs 10 differences


It’s most useful on a model’s residuals, in Lesson 7.

title: Stationarity and autocorrelation
text:
Wrap-up
You can now tell a series that settles from one that wanders. Here’s what you’ve learned:

White noise has autocorrelations near 0, within \pm 1.96/\sqrt n, and passes the Ljung-Box test (p = 0.63).
A random walk is the sum of white noise. Its variance grows with time, and its sample ACF decays slowly: 0.99 at lag 1 and 0.82 at lag 30.
The tank level is a random walk, an integrating process, and differencing makes it stationary.
Unit-root tests agree: ADF finds a unit root in the level (p = 0.52) but not in the changes, and KPSS rejects stationarity for the tank but not for the temperature.
The PACF of the controlled temperature cuts off after lag 2 (0.81, −0.59), pointing to an AR(2) model.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download process_signals.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

ACF plots. Plot ggAcf() and ggPacf() for the temperature, the tank level and its differences. Practice describing each one in a sentence.
The ADF test’s regression. Fit the regression behind the ADF test yourself: lm(diff(tank) ~ tank[-600]). What’s the coefficient on the lagged level? Why can’t you use its ordinary t-test p-value? (Under a unit root, the t statistic doesn’t follow a t distribution: that’s why Dickey and Fuller needed their own tables.)
Overdifferencing. Difference the temperature, which is already stationary, and plot the ACF of the result. What happens at lag 1?
A drifting random walk. Simulate cumsum(rnorm(600, mean = 0.05)). What does the ADF test say? Try tseries::adf.test() and urca::ur.df(x, type = "trend"), which allows a trend, and compare.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Stationary series

A series whose mean, variance and autocorrelations don’t change over time.

White noise

Independent observations with mean 0 and constant variance: no autocorrelation at any lag.

Random walk

A series whose changes are white noise: y_t = y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t. It has a unit root and isn’t stationary.

Unit root

A coefficient of exactly 1 on the previous value, which makes a series non-stationary.

Differencing

Replacing a series by its changes, y_t - y_{t-1}, to remove a unit root.

Integrated of order d, I(d)

A series that becomes stationary after d differences.

Augmented Dickey-Fuller test

A test whose null hypothesis is a unit root.

KPSS test

A test whose null hypothesis is stationarity.

Partial autocorrelation function (PACF)

The correlation between y_t and y_{t-k} after removing the effect of the lags in between.

Ljung-Box test

A test of whether the first h autocorrelations, taken together, are consistent with white noise.











NoteWant to read more?






Rob Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd edition), section 9.1, “Stationarity and differencing”, including unit-root tests.
Penn State’s STAT 510, lesson 1, on stationarity and the ACF, and lesson 2, on the PACF.
Robert Shumway and David Stoffer, Time Series: A Data Analysis Approach Using R (2019), chapters 2 and 3, on correlation and stationarity, with plenty of examples.

title: Moving-average and ARMA models
text:
Module 6 · Lesson 5 of 13 Week 94 of 160 About 5–7 hours
An AR model remembers the series’ own past values. A moving-average model remembers past shocks:
y_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t + \theta_1 \varepsilon_{t-1} + \cdots + \theta_q \varepsilon_{t-q}.
Each disturbance affects the series for exactly q steps, then it’s gone. (The name is unfortunate: it has nothing to do with Lesson 2’s moving averages of the data.) MA terms appear when something smears each disturbance over a few periods, like a mixing tank, a sample that spans two hours, or a filter in an analyzer. And combining both kinds of memory gives the ARMA(p, q) model, which describes most stationary series with only a few parameters.
The example is a product blend whose viscosity the lab measures every hour. The specification is 120 ± 2 cSt.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Moving-average and ARMA models
text:
MA(1)












In an MA(1), y_t = \varepsilon_t + \theta\varepsilon_{t-1}, each value shares one shock with its neighbor and none with anything further away. So its autocorrelation at lag 1 is \theta/(1 + \theta^2), and at every lag beyond 1, exactly 0. An MA(q)’s ACF cuts off after lag q, the mirror image of an AR(p)’s PACF.
Your turn. Simulate 3,000 values of an MA(1) with \theta = 0.6, and compare the autocorrelations at lags 1 and 2 with the theory.









e[-1] drops the first shock, so the previous shocks are e[-3001], which drops the last.


set.seed(6051)
e <- rnorm(3001)
y <- e[-1] + 0.6 * e[-3001]                     # each value plus 0.6 times the shock before it
r <- acf(y, lag.max = 3, plot = FALSE)$acf
c(lag1 = r[2], lag2 = r[3], theory_lag1 = 0.6 / (1 + 0.6^2))
0.42 at lag 1, close to the theoretical 0.44, and −0.02 at lag 2: nothing beyond lag 1. Even with \theta much larger, an MA(1)’s lag-1 autocorrelation can’t exceed 0.5, since \theta/(1 + \theta^2) is at most \frac12, at \theta = 1. A sample ACF with a spike of 0.8 at lag 1 and nothing else isn’t an MA(1).

title: Moving-average and ARMA models
text:
Invertibility
Your turn. Compare the theoretical ACFs of two MA(1) models, \theta = 0.6 and \theta = 1/0.6.









The second model has \theta = 1/0.6.


rbind(theta_0.6 = ARMAacf(ma = 0.6, lag.max = 3), theta_1.67 = ARMAacf(ma = 1 / 0.6, lag.max = 3))
Identical: 0.441 at lag 1 for both. Since \theta/(1 + \theta^2) doesn’t change when \theta is replaced by 1/\theta, the data can’t tell the two apart. The convention is to choose the invertible one, |\theta| < 1, for which the shocks can be recovered from the past data, \varepsilon_t = y_t - \theta y_{t-1} + \theta^2 y_{t-2} - \cdots. That’s what forecasting needs. With |\theta| > 1, that sum blows up.




The condition for an MA(q) to be invertible mirrors Lesson 4’s stationarity condition: every root of 1 + \theta_1 z + \cdots + \theta_q z^q must lie outside the unit circle.
Your turn. Check both models’ roots.









The polynomial for \theta = 1/0.6 is 1 + (1/0.6)z.


c(theta_0.6 = Mod(polyroot(c(1, 0.6))), theta_1.67 = Mod(polyroot(c(1, 1 / 0.6))))
1.67 for \theta = 0.6, outside the unit circle: invertible. 0.6 for \theta = 1.67, inside: not invertible. arima() always reports the invertible version. Any MA model is stationary, whatever its coefficients, so for MA models the question is only invertibility, and for AR models only stationarity.

title: Moving-average and ARMA models
text:
The fingerprint of overdifferencing
Lesson 3 warned against differencing a series that’s already stationary. Here’s why. Differencing white noise gives \varepsilon_t - \varepsilon_{t-1}: an MA(1) with \theta = -1, exactly on the edge of invertibility.
Your turn. Difference 2,000 values of white noise, and look at the lag-1 autocorrelation and the MA(1) coefficient arima() finds.









An MA(1) has q = 1.


set.seed(6052)
w <- rnorm(2000)
d <- diff(w)
c(lag1 = acf(d, plot = FALSE)$acf[2], theta = coef(arima(d, order = c(0, 0, 1), include.mean = FALSE)))
A lag-1 autocorrelation of −0.50 and \hat\theta = -0.999. That’s the fingerprint of overdifferencing: a large negative spike at lag 1, about −0.5, and an MA coefficient near −1. If you see it after differencing, you’ve probably differenced once too often. Go back one step.

title: Moving-average and ARMA models
text:
Identifying a model
Here’s the rule of thumb, from Box and Jenkins:



Model
ACF
PACF




AR(p)
decays gradually
cuts off after lag p


MA(q)
cuts off after lag q
decays gradually


ARMA(p, q)
decays gradually
decays gradually



Here’s the viscosity, with its ACF and PACF:

ggplot(data.frame(hour = seq_along(visc), v = visc), aes(x = hour, y = v)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(118, 122), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.35) +
  labs(x = "Hour", y = "Viscosity (cSt)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









cf <- rbind(data.frame(lag = 1:20, value = acf(visc, lag.max = 20, plot = FALSE)$acf[-1], fn = "ACF"),
            data.frame(lag = 1:20, value = as.numeric(pacf(visc, lag.max = 20, plot = FALSE)$acf), fn = "PACF"))
ggplot(cf, aes(x = lag, y = value)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1, 1) * 1.96 / sqrt(400), linetype = "dashed", color = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0), color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ fn) +
  labs(x = "Lag (hours)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The dashed lines on the time plot are the specification limits, 118 and 122 cSt.
Your turn. Look at the numbers behind the plots: the ACF and PACF at lags 1 to 5.









The partial autocorrelations come from pacf().


rbind(acf = acf(visc, lag.max = 5, plot = FALSE)$acf[2:6],
      pacf = pacf(visc, lag.max = 5, plot = FALSE)$acf[1:5])
The ACF decays smoothly, 0.78, 0.47, 0.28, 0.18, 0.13, so it isn’t a low-order MA. The PACF doesn’t quite cut off either: 0.78, −0.35, then 0.16 at lag 3, outside the bounds of ±0.10, and alternating after that. Neither function cuts off cleanly, which points to a mixed ARMA model. Real data rarely follow the table exactly, so the next step is to fit a few candidates and compare them.




Your turn. Fit five candidates, AR(1), MA(1), ARMA(1,1), AR(2) and MA(2), and compare their AIC values. Lower is better.









AIC() works on arima() fits.


orders <- list(ar1 = c(1, 0, 0), ma1 = c(0, 0, 1), arma11 = c(1, 0, 1), ar2 = c(2, 0, 0), ma2 = c(0, 0, 2))
sapply(orders, function(o) AIC(arima(visc, order = o)))
ARMA(1,1) has the lowest AIC, 942.1, followed by AR(2) at 953.0. AR(1) and MA(1) are far behind, at 1002 and 1060. The ARMA(1,1) does with three parameters (plus the mean) what a pure AR or MA would need several more terms for. That’s the principle of parsimony: the simplest model that captures the structure.

title: Moving-average and ARMA models
text:
ARMA(1,1)
Your turn. Fit the ARMA(1,1), y_t - \mu = \phi(y_{t-1} - \mu) + \varepsilon_t + \theta\varepsilon_{t-1}, and look at its estimates and standard errors.









One MA term: q = 1.


fit <- arima(visc, order = c(1, 0, 1))
rbind(estimate = coef(fit), se = sqrt(diag(vcov(fit))))
\hat\phi = 0.62 (SE 0.05), \hat\theta = 0.49 (SE 0.05), and a mean of 120.03 cSt (SE 0.15), right on target. Both coefficients are many standard errors from 0, so neither part of the model can be dropped. A physical reading: the blend tank smooths the composition (the AR part), and each hourly sample averages over a stretch of flow that overlaps the next one (the MA part).




Any stationary ARMA model can be written as an infinite MA, y_t - \mu = \varepsilon_t + \psi_1\varepsilon_{t-1} + \psi_2\varepsilon_{t-2} + \cdots. The \psi weights are the impulse response: the effect of one shock on the following hours. ARMAtoMA() computes them.
Your turn. Find the fitted model’s first six \psi weights.









The MA coefficient is the second, coef(fit)[2].


fit <- arima(visc, order = c(1, 0, 1))
ARMAtoMA(ar = coef(fit)[1], ma = coef(fit)[2], lag.max = 6)
1.10, 0.68, 0.42, 0.26, 0.16, 0.10. A disturbance of 1 cSt is still 1.1 cSt an hour later, larger than at first because the MA term adds to the AR carry-over, and then it fades by a factor of 0.62 an hour: after six hours, a tenth is left. So if the blend goes off spec, it’ll stay off for several hours unless someone corrects it. That’s useful to know for setting up alarms.

title: Moving-average and ARMA models
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Let the computer choose. The forecast package’s auto.arima() searches over ARIMA orders by AICc, testing for differencing first. What does it choose for the viscosity?









The function is forecast::auto.arima().


fit <- forecast::auto.arima(visc)
forecast::arimaorder(fit)
(1, 0, 1): ARMA(1,1), no differencing, the same as the hand-built comparison. auto.arima() is a good assistant, but not a substitute for looking at the data: Lesson 6 shows its search and its limits, and Lesson 7 how to check whatever it chooses.




Challenge 2 · How often is the blend off spec? The fitted model implies a stationary distribution for the viscosity: normal, with the model’s mean and variance \gamma_0 = \sigma^2(1 + 2\phi\theta + \theta^2)/(1 - \phi^2). Use it to compute the probability that an hour’s viscosity is above the upper limit, 122 cSt, and compare it with the share of hours that actually were.









The SD is the square root of gamma0.


fit <- arima(visc, order = c(1, 0, 1))
phi <- coef(fit)[[1]]; theta <- coef(fit)[[2]]; mu <- coef(fit)[[3]]
gamma0 <- fit$sigma2 * (1 + 2 * phi * theta + theta^2) / (1 - phi^2)
c(model_sd = sqrt(gamma0), data_sd = sd(visc), p_above_122 = pnorm(122, mu, sqrt(gamma0), lower.tail = FALSE), share_above_122 = mean(visc > 122))
The model’s SD, 1.339 cSt, matches the data’s, 1.342. It predicts that 7.0% of hours are above 122 cSt, and 7.8% actually were. The shock SD is only 0.78 cSt, but the dynamics amplify it by 1.7 times. To narrow the blend’s spread, it’s the persistence, the AR part, that the process engineers should attack, for example with faster feedback from the analyzer.

title: Moving-average and ARMA models
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does an MA(q) model’s ACF look like?

It decays gradually
It cuts off after lag q
It’s 0 at every lag


Each shock affects only q steps, so observations more than q apart share none.



2. Why do we require MA models to be invertible?

Because non-invertible models are non-stationary
Because for each ACF there are two MA models, and only the invertible one lets the shocks be recovered from past data
Because it makes the coefficients positive


Recovering the shocks is what forecasting needs.



3. After differencing, the ACF has a spike of −0.5 at lag 1 and an MA(1) fit gives \theta \approx -1. What does that suggest?

An AR(1) model
The series was overdifferenced
A seasonal pattern


Differencing a stationary series creates exactly that MA(1).



4. Neither the ACF nor the PACF cuts off. Which model family should you try?

Pure AR
Pure MA
ARMA


Then compare a few low-order candidates by AIC.



5. What does the principle of parsimony say?

Use as many parameters as the data allow
Prefer the simplest model that captures the structure
Always use ARMA(1,1)


Extra parameters add estimation error to every forecast.



6. What are the \psi weights of an ARMA model?

Its AR coefficients
The effect of one shock on the following periods: the impulse response
Its forecast errors


They come from writing the model as an infinite MA.

title: Moving-average and ARMA models
text:
Wrap-up
You can now identify and fit ARMA models. Here’s what you’ve learned:

MA(q) models remember the last q shocks, so their ACF cuts off after lag q: an MA(1) with \theta = 0.6 has 0.44 at lag 1 and nothing beyond.
Invertibility: \theta and 1/\theta give the same ACF, and the convention is |\theta| < 1.
Overdifferencing leaves a fingerprint: a lag-1 autocorrelation near −0.5, and \theta near −1.
Identification: the viscosity’s ACF and PACF both decay, AIC prefers ARMA(1,1) (942.1) to AR(2) (953.0), and auto.arima() agrees.
Interpretation: \hat\phi = 0.62 and \hat\theta = 0.49. A disturbance fades to a tenth in six hours, and the model predicts 7.0% of hours above the 122 cSt limit, against 7.8% observed.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download blend_viscosity.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Identify from simulations. Simulate 400 points from MA(2) with \theta = (0.5, 0.4), AR(1) with \phi = 0.7, and ARMA(1,1) with \phi = 0.7, \theta = 0.4 with arima.sim(), and plot each one’s ACF and PACF with ggtsdisplay(). Could you tell them apart without knowing which is which?
The extended ACF. The TSA package’s eacf(visc) prints a table of symbols that helps identify p and q together. Install it and try it. Where’s the triangle of “o”s?
Overfitting. Fit ARMA(2,1) and ARMA(1,2) to the viscosity. Are the extra coefficients significant? Do the AIC values improve?
Off-spec alarms. Using the \psi weights, how large a single shock would it take to push the viscosity from 120 to above 122 an hour later?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Moving-average model, MA(q)

A model in which each value is a linear combination of the current shock and the previous q shocks.

ARMA(p, q) model

A model with p autoregressive and q moving-average terms.

Invertibility

The condition that an MA model’s shocks can be recovered from past data: all roots of 1 + \theta_1 z + \cdots + \theta_q z^q outside the unit circle.

Overdifferencing

Differencing a series that’s already stationary. It creates an MA(1) with \theta near −1.

Model identification

Choosing candidate orders p and q from the ACF and PACF.

Parsimony

Preferring the simplest adequate model.

\psi weights

The coefficients of a model’s infinite-MA form, which give the impulse response to one shock.











NoteWant to read more?






Rob Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd edition), sections 9.4, “Moving average models” and 9.5, “Non-seasonal ARIMA models”.
Penn State’s STAT 510, lesson 2, on MA models and the identification table, and lesson 3, on fitting ARIMA models.
Robert Shumway and David Stoffer, Time Series: A Data Analysis Approach Using R (2019), chapter 4, on ARMA models, including invertibility and the \psi weights.

title: Model diagnostics
text:
Module 6 · Lesson 7 of 13 Week 96 of 160 About 5–7 hours
A fitted model is a claim: “everything predictable in this series is captured by these few parameters, and what’s left is white noise.” The residuals, the one-step-ahead forecast errors e_t = y_t - \hat y_{t \mid t-1}, test that claim. If the model is right, they should be uncorrelated, with mean 0 and constant variance, and ideally normal. If they still have structure, the model has missed something, and its forecasts and intervals are wrong.
This is step 3 of the Box-Jenkins approach, and it’s the one most often skipped. This lesson checks Lesson 6’s sulfur model, and shows what failing models look like.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Model diagnostics
text:
Looking at the residuals












Your turn. Fit Lesson 6’s ARIMA(1,1,0), and check its residuals’ mean, SD and lag-1 autocorrelation.









residuals(fit) extracts them.


fit <- forecast::Arima(x, order = c(1, 1, 0))
e <- residuals(fit)
c(mean = mean(e), sd = sd(e), lag1 = acf(e, plot = FALSE)$acf[2])
A mean of −0.001 wt%, essentially 0: no bias. An SD of 0.026, matching the model’s estimate of the shock SD, \sqrt{\hat\sigma^2} = 0.026. And a lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.02, well inside \pm 1.96/\sqrt{364} = \pm 0.10. So far, so good.




Here’s the standard set of residual plots: the residuals over time, their ACF and their histogram. forecast::checkresiduals() draws the same three.

e <- residuals(Arima(x, order = c(1, 1, 0)))
d1 <- data.frame(week = seq_along(e), e = as.numeric(e))
r <- acf(e, lag.max = 24, plot = FALSE)$acf[-1]
long <- rbind(data.frame(panel = "residuals over time", x = d1$week, y = d1$e))
g1 <- ggplot(d1, aes(x = week, y = e)) + geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.4) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Residual (wt%)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
g2 <- ggplot(data.frame(lag = 1:24, r = r), aes(x = lag, y = r)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1, 1) * 1.96 / sqrt(length(e)), linetype = "dashed", color = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0), color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 1) + labs(x = "Lag (weeks)", y = "ACF") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
g3 <- ggplot(d1, aes(x = e)) + geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 30, fill = "#F4C0D1", color = "white") +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = sd(e)), color = "#3A1F35") + labs(x = "Residual (wt%)", y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
gridExtra::grid.arrange(g1, g2, g3, layout_matrix = rbind(c(1, 1), c(2, 3)))

title: Model diagnostics
text:
The Ljung-Box test, again
Lesson 3’s Ljung-Box test combines the first h autocorrelations into one test. Applied to residuals, there’s one adjustment: the model’s p + q estimated coefficients have used up some of the freedom, so the test’s degrees of freedom are h - (p + q), not h. Box.test() does that with its fitdf argument.
Your turn. Test the residuals with 10 lags, and fitdf = 1 for the one AR coefficient.









The model estimated one ARMA coefficient: fitdf = 1.


fit <- forecast::Arima(x, order = c(1, 1, 0))
Box.test(residuals(fit), lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 1)
Q = 9.10 on 9 degrees of freedom, p = 0.43: no evidence of remaining autocorrelation. How many lags? A common rule is 10 for non-seasonal data and 2m for seasonal data with period m, and no more than a fifth of the series’ length.




Your turn. Now an underfitted model: ARIMA(0,1,0), the random walk, which treats the weekly changes as white noise. Test its residuals.









The random walk is ARIMA(0,1,0).


rw <- forecast::Arima(x, order = c(0, 1, 0))
c(lag1 = acf(residuals(rw), plot = FALSE)$acf[2], p_value = Box.test(residuals(rw), lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value)
A lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.57 in the residuals, and a p-value of essentially 0. The random walk’s residuals are just the weekly changes, which, as Lesson 6 found, are an AR(1). The test catches the missing term, and the residuals’ ACF says where it is. That’s the Box-Jenkins loop: a failed check sends you back to identification, with a clue.




Your turn. forecast::checkresiduals() runs the Ljung-Box test with the right degrees of freedom automatically, and draws the plots. Run it on the ARIMA(1,1,0) without the plots.









plot = FALSE prints the test only.


fit <- forecast::Arima(x, order = c(1, 1, 0))
test <- forecast::checkresiduals(fit, plot = FALSE)
c(p_value = test$p.value, df = test$parameter)
The same p = 0.43 on 9 degrees of freedom: it chose 10 lags and subtracted the 1 coefficient itself. In RStudio, drop plot = FALSE to get the three plots too. It’s the quickest complete check there is.

title: Model diagnostics
text:
Overfitting
The opposite check: add a term the model doesn’t have, and see whether it’s needed. If the model is adequate, the extra coefficient should be small compared with its standard error, and the others shouldn’t change much.
Your turn. Fit ARIMA(2,1,0) and ARIMA(1,1,1), and look at each extra coefficient, its standard error, and the AR(1) coefficient in the second.









ARIMA(1,1,1) adds one MA term.


ar2 <- forecast::Arima(x, order = c(2, 1, 0))
arma11 <- forecast::Arima(x, order = c(1, 1, 1))
c(ar2 = coef(ar2)[[2]], se_ar2 = sqrt(vcov(ar2)[2, 2]), ma1 = coef(arma11)[[2]], se_ma1 = sqrt(vcov(arma11)[2, 2]), ar1_with_ma = coef(arma11)[[1]])
The extra AR term is −0.047 (SE 0.053), and the extra MA term 0.086 (SE 0.093): both less than one standard error from 0. With the MA term, the AR coefficient moves from 0.575 to 0.518, compensating, because the two terms describe overlapping structure. Neither extension is needed. Overfitting checks protect against a model that passes the Ljung-Box test only because the test has low power.




Your turn. The prediction intervals from Lesson 6 assumed normal shocks. Test the residuals’ normality with the Shapiro-Wilk test.









shapiro.test() runs the Shapiro-Wilk test.


fit <- forecast::Arima(x, order = c(1, 1, 0))
shapiro.test(as.numeric(residuals(fit)))$p.value
p = 0.18: no evidence against normality, so the intervals are trustworthy as they are. Non-normal residuals don’t spoil the point forecasts, but they make the intervals wrong. If the residuals have heavy tails, forecast(fit, bootstrap = TRUE) builds intervals by resampling the residuals instead.

title: Model diagnostics
text:
The viscosity, checked
Your turn. Lesson 5’s viscosity had a simpler candidate than ARMA(1,1): an AR(1). Test both models’ residuals with 10 lags, each with its own fitdf.









ARMA(1,1) has two coefficients: fitdf = 2.


ar1 <- forecast::Arima(visc, order = c(1, 0, 0))
arma11 <- forecast::Arima(visc, order = c(1, 0, 1))
c(ar1 = Box.test(residuals(ar1), lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 1)$p.value,
  arma11 = Box.test(residuals(arma11), lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 2)$p.value)
The AR(1) fails badly, p = 8 \times 10^{-9}: its residuals still carry the MA structure. ARMA(1,1) passes, p = 0.31. The diagnostics agree with Lesson 5’s AIC comparison. When they don’t, the diagnostics win: a model with a better AIC but autocorrelated residuals is still wrong.




Your turn. How much does fitdf matter? Test the ARMA(1,1)’s residuals with fitdf = 0 and fitdf = 2.









The first test ignores the fitted coefficients: fitdf = 0.


arma11 <- forecast::Arima(visc, order = c(1, 0, 1))
c(fitdf_0 = Box.test(residuals(arma11), lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 0)$p.value,
  fitdf_2 = Box.test(residuals(arma11), lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 2)$p.value)
0.50 without the adjustment, 0.31 with it. Fitting the model makes its residuals look whiter than true shocks would be, because the estimates chose the coefficients to remove autocorrelation. Ignoring that makes the test too lenient. With few lags and many coefficients, the difference can decide the result.

title: Model diagnostics
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · A lab error. Suppose week 200’s result had been typed as 0.3 wt% too high, a slipped digit. Refit the model to the corrupted series, find the three largest standardized residuals (residuals divided by \hat\sigma) and where they are, and see what happened to \hat\phi.









The shock variance is fit2$sigma2.


x2 <- x
x2[200] <- x2[200] + 0.3
fit2 <- forecast::Arima(x2, order = c(1, 1, 0))
z <- residuals(fit2) / sqrt(fit2$sigma2)
top <- order(-abs(z))[1:3]
c(weeks = top, z = z[top], phi = coef(fit2)[[1]])
Weeks 201 and 200 stand out, at −9.6 and +7.2 standard deviations. The next largest is −2.6. In a differenced model, one bad value makes two bad changes, up into it and down out of it, so outliers come in pairs of opposite sign. The damage is worse than two big residuals: \hat\phi fell from 0.575 to 0.24, because the pair looks like a sharp reversal. One typo halved the estimated persistence, and every forecast with it. That’s why the residual plot comes before anything else.




Challenge 2 · Is the model stable? A model fitted to seven years assumes that the same dynamics held throughout. Fit ARIMA(1,1,0) separately to the first and second halves, 182 weeks each, and compare \hat\phi, its standard error, and the shock SD.









The second half starts at week 183.


first <- forecast::Arima(x[1:182], order = c(1, 1, 0))
second <- forecast::Arima(x[183:364], order = c(1, 1, 0))
rbind(first = c(phi = coef(first)[[1]], se = sqrt(vcov(first)[1, 1]), shock_sd = sqrt(first$sigma2)),
      second = c(coef(second)[[1]], sqrt(vcov(second)[1, 1]), sqrt(second$sigma2)))
\hat\phi = 0.52 (SE 0.064) in the first half and 0.63 (SE 0.058) in the second. The difference, 0.11, is about 1.3 times its standard error, \sqrt{0.064^2 + 0.058^2} = 0.086: within what chance would produce. The shock SDs, 0.028 and 0.025, are similar too. So one model for the whole period is reasonable. If the crude supply had changed, for example after a new pipeline, the two halves would differ, and the forecasts should use the recent dynamics.

title: Model diagnostics
text:
Quick quiz

1. What should the residuals of an adequate time series model look like?

A smooth trend
White noise: uncorrelated, with mean 0 and constant variance
The same as the original series


Anything predictable left in them is something the model missed.



2. Why does the Ljung-Box test on an ARMA(p, q) model’s residuals use h - p - q degrees of freedom?

Because the residuals are shorter than the series
Because the fitted coefficients have already removed some autocorrelation, so the residuals look whiter than true shocks
Because of differencing


Without the adjustment, the test is too lenient.



3. A random walk model’s residuals have a lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.57. What should you do?

Accept the model
Add an AR term for the differences: ARIMA(1,1,0)
Difference again


The residuals’ ACF points to what’s missing.



4. An overfitting check adds an MA term, which comes out at 0.09 with a standard error of 0.09. What does that suggest?

The MA term is essential
It isn’t needed: the simpler model is adequate
The model is non-stationary


An extra term less than a couple of standard errors from 0 adds nothing but estimation error.



5. In a model with one difference, a single outlier in the data typically shows up as what in the residuals?

One large residual
Two large residuals of opposite sign, next to each other
Nothing


The changes into and out of the bad value are both wrong.



6. The residuals pass the Ljung-Box test but are clearly not normal. What’s affected?

The point forecasts
The prediction intervals, which assume normal shocks
Nothing at all


Bootstrapped intervals, from resampled residuals, avoid the assumption.

title: Model diagnostics
text:
Wrap-up
You can now check a time series model properly. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Residual checks: the ARIMA(1,1,0)’s residuals have mean −0.001, SD 0.026, and a lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.02.
The Ljung-Box test with fitdf = p + q: p = 0.43 on 9 degrees of freedom, a pass. checkresiduals() does it automatically.
Underfitting and overfitting: the random walk fails (residual lag-1 autocorrelation 0.57), and the extra AR or MA terms are less than a standard error from 0.
Normality holds (Shapiro-Wilk p = 0.18), so the normal prediction intervals are fine.
For the viscosity, AR(1) fails and ARMA(1,1) passes, and ignoring fitdf would make the test too lenient (0.50 instead of 0.31).
Outliers show up as pairs of large standardized residuals, and a single typo cut \hat\phi from 0.575 to 0.24.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download feed_impurity.csv and blend_viscosity.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

The full check. Run checkresiduals() with its plots on the sulfur model, the random walk and the viscosity’s AR(1). Describe what each plot shows, and what it should look like.
Ljung-Box with more lags. Repeat the test on the sulfur model with 5, 10, 20 and 50 lags. Does the conclusion change? Why might a very large number of lags be a poor choice?
Robust to the outlier. For the corrupted series, use forecast::tsoutliers(x2), which detects outliers and suggests replacements. Does it find week 200? Fit the model to tsclean(x2) and compare \hat\phi with the clean fit.
Rolling estimates. Fit ARIMA(1,1,0) to every window of 104 weeks, moving one week at a time, and plot \hat\phi against the window’s end. Is it stable?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Residuals

The one-step-ahead forecast errors of a fitted model, y_t - \hat y_{t \mid t-1}.

Diagnostic checking

Step 3 of the Box-Jenkins approach: testing whether the residuals are white noise.

Ljung-Box test on residuals

The Ljung-Box test with h - p - q degrees of freedom, for an ARMA(p, q) model.

Underfitting

Leaving out structure the data have, so the residuals stay autocorrelated.

Overfitting check

Adding a term to a model to confirm it isn’t needed.

Standardized residual

A residual divided by the estimated shock SD. Values beyond about ±3 deserve investigation.

Parameter stability

Whether a model’s coefficients stay the same over different stretches of the data.











NoteWant to read more?






Rob Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd edition), section 5.4, “Residual diagnostics”, with the Ljung-Box test and the rule of thumb for the number of lags.
Penn State’s STAT 510, lesson 3, section 3.2, “Diagnostics”.
George Box, Gwilym Jenkins, Gregory Reinsel and Greta Ljung, Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control (5th edition, Wiley, 2015), chapter 8, “Model diagnostic checking”, including the overfitting method.

title: Seasonal ARIMA
text:
Module 6 · Lesson 9 of 13 Week 98 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The steam demand’s strongest memory isn’t last month, it’s last year: Lesson 1 found an autocorrelation of 0.81 at lag 12. A seasonal ARIMA model has terms for that. It’s written ARIMA(p, d, q)(P, D, Q)_m: the usual non-seasonal part, plus seasonal AR, differencing and MA terms of orders P, D and Q at multiples of the period m, here 12. In backshift notation, where B y_t = y_{t-1} and B^{12} y_t = y_{t-12}, the seasonal and non-seasonal parts multiply:
\underbrace{(1 - \phi B)}_{\text{AR}}\underbrace{(1 - B)^d}_{\text{difference}}\underbrace{(1 - B^{12})^D}_{\text{seasonal difference}}\, y_t = \underbrace{(1 + \theta B)}_{\text{MA}}\underbrace{(1 + \Theta B^{12})}_{\text{seasonal MA}}\,\varepsilon_t .
That multiplication means the terms interact: an MA(1) and a seasonal MA(1) together put structure at lags 1, 12 and 13.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Seasonal ARIMA
text:
Seasonal differencing












The seasonal difference, y_t - y_{t-12}, removes a seasonal pattern that repeats from year to year. nsdiffs() tests whether it’s needed, using a measure of seasonal strength.
Your turn. Ask how many seasonal differences the steam demand needs, and then how many ordinary differences the seasonally differenced series needs.









A seasonal difference for monthly data uses lag = 12.


c(seasonal = nsdiffs(y), ordinary_after = ndiffs(diff(y, lag = 12)))
One seasonal difference, D = 1, and then no ordinary difference, d = 0, according to the KPSS test. That decision is closer than it looks, as you’ll see. A rule worth knowing: d + D should rarely exceed 2, and with a seasonal difference, a drift term means a steady trend in the year-over-year changes.

title: Seasonal ARIMA
text:
Identifying seasonal terms
Seasonal terms show up in the ACF and PACF at the seasonal lags, 12, 24, 36. The same rules as Lesson 5 apply there: a seasonal MA(1) gives an ACF spike at lag 12 and nothing at 24, with the PACF decaying across 12, 24, 36. A seasonal AR(1) does the opposite.
Your turn. Look at the seasonally differenced series’ ACF at lags 1, 2, 12 and 24, and its PACF at 12 and 24.









The ACF at lag 24 is element 25.


sd12 <- diff(y, lag = 12)
r <- acf(sd12, lag.max = 36, plot = FALSE)$acf
pr <- pacf(sd12, lag.max = 36, plot = FALSE)$acf
c(acf1 = r[2], acf2 = r[3], acf12 = r[13], acf24 = r[25], pacf12 = pr[12], pacf24 = pr[24])
At the seasonal lags, the ACF has one large spike, −0.50 at lag 12, and nothing at 24 (−0.01), while the PACF decays, −0.51 then −0.25. That’s a seasonal MA(1), with a negative coefficient. At the short lags, the ACF is 0.22 then 0.11: a small AR(1). So the first candidate is ARIMA(1, 0, 0)(0, 1, 1)_{12}. The negative spike at lag 12 is typical after seasonal differencing: it often means the seasonal pattern is nearly constant, and the difference partly overdid it, as in Lesson 5’s overdifferencing.




Your turn. Check the signature with the theoretical ACF of a pure seasonal MA(1), y_t = \varepsilon_t + \Theta\varepsilon_{t-12}, with \Theta = -0.8. In ARMAacf(), that’s an MA(12) whose first eleven coefficients are 0.









Eleven zeros, then the coefficient at lag 12.


r <- ARMAacf(ma = c(rep(0, 11), -0.8), lag.max = 13)
r[c("1", "11", "12", "13")]
0 everywhere except lag 12, where it’s -0.8/(1 + 0.64) = -0.49: Lesson 5’s MA(1) formula, stretched to the seasonal period. Close to the sample’s −0.50.

title: Seasonal ARIMA
text:
The airline model
The most famous seasonal model is ARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)_{12}, called the airline model because Box and Jenkins first fitted it to airline passenger numbers, Lesson 2’s AirPassengers. It takes both an ordinary and a seasonal difference, and has one MA term for each. It’s a natural first try for monthly data with a trend and a stable season.
Your turn. Fit the airline model to the steam demand.









One seasonal difference: D = 1.


airline <- Arima(y, order = c(0, 1, 1), seasonal = c(0, 1, 1))
c(coef(airline), aicc = airline$aicc)
\hat\theta = -0.86 and \hat\Theta = -0.91, with an AICc of 476.6. Both MA coefficients are close to −1. As Lesson 5 showed, an MA coefficient near −1 after differencing means the difference nearly cancels out: here, the trend and the seasonal pattern are both nearly deterministic, changing very slowly. That’s consistent with Lesson 2’s ETS fit, whose trend and seasonal smoothing parameters were almost 0.

title: Seasonal ARIMA
text:
Choosing between candidates
Your turn. Fit the candidate you identified, ARIMA(1,0,0)(0,1,1)_{12} with drift (the drift handles the trend, since there’s no ordinary difference), and check its residuals with the Ljung-Box test over 24 lags, two seasons, with fitdf = 2 for its two ARMA coefficients.









Two ARMA coefficients, the AR and the seasonal MA: fitdf = 2.


fit <- Arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0), seasonal = c(0, 1, 1), include.drift = TRUE)
c(coef(fit), aicc = fit$aicc, ljung_box_p = Box.test(residuals(fit), lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 2)$p.value)
\hat\phi = 0.34, \hat\Theta = -0.88, and a drift of 0.052 kt a month in the year-over-year changes, about Lesson 1’s 0.6 kt a year. But the residuals fail: p = 0.017. The model misses something. Its AICc, 478.4, can’t be compared with the airline model’s, because the two have different differencing (d = 0 against d = 1). So the residual checks have to decide.




Your turn. Within the d = D = 1 family, which AICc can compare, try ARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)_{12}, the airline model plus an AR term. Compare its AICc with the airline’s 476.6, and check its residuals.









One AR term: p = 1.


fit <- Arima(y, order = c(1, 1, 1), seasonal = c(0, 1, 1))
c(coef(fit), aicc = fit$aicc, ljung_box_p = Box.test(residuals(fit), lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 3)$p.value)
\hat\phi = 0.21 (SE 0.09), and an AICc of 474.1, 2.5 better than the airline model. Its residuals pass, p = 0.10, though not by much. Of the dozen seasonal models one might try here, this is among the best on both counts. Seasonal model selection is rarely clean: several models are nearly as good, and the forecasts they give are usually close too.

title: Seasonal ARIMA
text:
Forecasting a seasonal series
Your turn. Forecast 2026 with ARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)_{12}, and find the forecasts and 95% intervals for January and July.









July 2026 is the seventh month ahead.


fit <- Arima(y, order = c(1, 1, 1), seasonal = c(0, 1, 1))
fc <- forecast(fit, h = 12)
rbind(january = c(fc$mean[1], fc$lower[1, 2], fc$upper[1, 2]),
      july = c(fc$mean[7], fc$lower[7, 2], fc$upper[7, 2]))
January 2026: 50.2 kt (47.6 to 52.9). July 2026: 39.3 kt (36.4 to 42.1). Very close to Lesson 2’s ETS forecast for January, 50.0. The intervals are about ±2.7 kt in January and ±2.9 in July: the winter peak is more predictable than you might think, because the model knows it’s coming. What it can’t know is next winter’s weather.





fit <- Arima(y, order = c(1, 1, 1), seasonal = c(0, 1, 1))
fc <- forecast(fit, h = 12)
autoplot(window(y, start = 2021), color = "#C2416C") +
  autolayer(fc, color = "#3A1F35", fill = "#F4C0D1", alpha = 0.7, showgap = FALSE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Steam demand (kt per month)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Your turn. The utilities budget needs 2026’s total. Adding up the monthly forecasts gives its point forecast, but the monthly errors are correlated, so their intervals can’t simply be added. Simulate 2,000 future years from the model instead, and take the 5th and 95th percentiles of their totals.









future = TRUE simulates forward from the end of the data.


fit <- Arima(y, order = c(1, 1, 1), seasonal = c(0, 1, 1))
fc <- forecast(fit, h = 12)
set.seed(6091)
totals <- replicate(2000, sum(simulate(fit, nsim = 12, future = TRUE)))
c(point = sum(fc$mean), quantile(totals, c(0.05, 0.95)), total_2025 = sum(window(y, start = 2025)))
A total of 532 kt for 2026, with a 90% interval from 518 to 547, against 525 kt in 2025. It’s the predictive simulation recipe from Module 5 again: draw future paths, compute the quantity you care about on each, and summarize. It works for any function of the forecasts, such as the number of months above a capacity limit.

title: Seasonal ARIMA
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Seasonal naive is an ARIMA model. ARIMA(0,0,0)(0,1,0)_{12} says the seasonal differences are white noise: this year’s month equals last year’s, plus noise. Check that its forecasts are the seasonal naive method’s.









One seasonal difference, D = 1.


fit <- Arima(y, order = c(0, 0, 0), seasonal = c(0, 1, 0))
rbind(arima = forecast(fit, h = 2)$mean, snaive = snaive(y, h = 2)$mean)
49.05 and 48.97 both ways: January and February 2025, copied. Every benchmark of Lesson 8 is an ARIMA model: naive is ARIMA(0,1,0), drift is ARIMA(0,1,0) with drift, and seasonal naive is this one. That’s another way to see why they’re benchmarks: they’re the simplest members of the family.




Challenge 2 · What’s left over? The identified model with drift failed its residual check. Find which of its residual autocorrelations, at lags 1 to 24, are outside \pm 1.96/\sqrt{144}.









The series has 144 months.


fit <- Arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0), seasonal = c(0, 1, 1), include.drift = TRUE)
r <- acf(residuals(fit), lag.max = 24, plot = FALSE)$acf[-1]
big <- which(abs(r) > 1.96 / sqrt(144))
rbind(lag = big, autocorrelation = r[big])
Lags 5, 9 and 18, at 0.21, 0.19 and 0.26. No simple ARMA term explains a pattern at lags 5, 9 and 18. It’s the weather: a cold spell that lasts a few months, or a mild winter, leaves its mark on the residuals, because the model only knows the calendar, not the temperature. Every pure seasonal model here has some of this left over. Lesson 10 adds the heating degree days to the model, and the leftover structure goes away.

title: Seasonal ARIMA
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does ARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)_{12} mean?

Twelve AR terms
One ordinary and one seasonal difference, an AR(1) and an MA(1), and a seasonal MA(1) at lag 12
A model for data with a 1-month period


The capital letters are the seasonal orders, and the subscript is the period.



2. After a seasonal difference, the ACF has a single spike at lag 12 and the PACF decays across 12, 24, 36. Which seasonal term does that suggest?

A seasonal AR(1)
A seasonal MA(1)
Another seasonal difference


The same rule as for non-seasonal MA terms, at the seasonal lags.



3. Why is it called the airline model?

Because Box and Jenkins first fitted ARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)_{12} to monthly airline passenger numbers
Because it’s used for flight schedules
Because it has two engines


That’s AirPassengers, 1949 to 1960.



4. Two seasonal models have AICc values of 474.1 and 478.4, but one has d = 1 and the other d = 0. Which is better?

The one with 474.1
You can’t tell from AICc: models with different differencing aren’t comparable that way
The one with d = 0


Use residual checks, or test-set accuracy and cross-validation (Lesson 8).



5. Why can’t you add up twelve monthly 95% intervals to get an interval for the year’s total?

Because intervals can’t be added
Because the monthly errors are correlated, so the total’s uncertainty isn’t the sum or any simple combination; simulate instead
Because the year has 365 days


Simulating future paths handles the correlation automatically.



6. The residuals of a seasonal model have autocorrelations at lags 5, 9 and 18. What’s the most likely explanation?

The model needs an AR(18) term
Something outside the model, here the weather, drives the series, and no calendar-based model can capture it
The series is overdifferenced


That’s the motivation for regression with ARIMA errors.

title: Seasonal ARIMA
text:
Wrap-up
You can now model and forecast seasonal series. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Seasonal differencing: the steam demand needs one seasonal difference, D = 1.
Identification: after it, a single ACF spike at lag 12 (−0.50) and a decaying PACF point to a seasonal MA(1).
Fitting: the airline model, ARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)_{12}, has both MA coefficients near −1. Adding an AR term, ARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)_{12}, improves AICc to 474.1, and its residuals pass (p = 0.10). The d = 0 alternative fails (p = 0.017).
Forecasts: 50.2 kt for January 2026 (47.6 to 52.9) and 39.3 for July, and a 2026 total of 532 kt (90% interval 518 to 547), by simulation.
What’s left: residual autocorrelations at lags 5, 9 and 18 that only the weather can explain.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download steam_demand.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

auto.arima(). Run auto.arima(y) and auto.arima(y, stepwise = FALSE, approximation = FALSE). Which models do they choose? Check each one’s residuals with checkresiduals().
The airline model on AirPassengers. Fit Arima(log(AirPassengers), order = c(0, 1, 1), seasonal = c(0, 1, 1)). Why the log? Compare its coefficients with Box and Jenkins’s published 0.40 and 0.61, written in their sign convention, which puts a minus in front of MA terms.
Seasonal AR. Fit ARIMA(1,0,0)(1,1,0)_{12} with drift, a seasonal AR instead of MA. How do its residuals compare? What does a seasonal AR(1) predict for a month that was unusually cold last year?
Cross-validate. Compare ARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)_{12} with ETS(A,A,A) by tsCV() with h = 12 and initial = 60. Which forecasts better a year ahead?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Seasonal ARIMA, ARIMA(p, d, q)(P, D, Q)_m

An ARIMA model with seasonal AR, differencing and MA terms at multiples of the period m.

Seasonal difference

y_t - y_{t-m}. D is the number of seasonal differences.

Backshift operator

B y_t = y_{t-1}. Seasonal models multiply polynomials in B and B^m.

Seasonal MA term

A moving-average term at lag m, shown by a single ACF spike at the seasonal lag.

Airline model

ARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)_{12}, the classic model for monthly data with trend and seasonality.

Simulated forecast paths

Future series drawn from a fitted model, used for the distribution of totals or other functions of the forecasts.











NoteWant to read more?






Rob Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd edition), section 9.9, “Seasonal ARIMA models”, with worked examples.
Penn State’s STAT 510, lesson 4, “Seasonal models”, with the identification rules for seasonal terms.
George Box, Gwilym Jenkins, Gregory Reinsel and Greta Ljung, Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control (5th edition, Wiley, 2015), chapter 9, “Analysis of seasonal time series”, where the airline model comes from.

title: Multivariate time series
text:
Module 6 · Lesson 11 of 13 Week 100 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Every model so far has had one series on the left-hand side. Lesson 10 let another series into the right-hand side, as a predictor, but it treated that predictor as given. In a process plant, signals drive each other. In a distillation column, more heat from the reboiler raises the bottom temperature, which pushes more of the heavy component up the column, which lowers the top product’s purity. And the control system feeds back the other way.
A vector autoregression (VAR) treats all the signals as one system: each is regressed on the past of all of them. With three signals and one lag, a VAR(1) is
\mathbf y_t = \mathbf c + A\,\mathbf y_{t-1} + \boldsymbol\varepsilon_t, \qquad \mathbf y_t = \begin{pmatrix} \text{duty}_t \\ \text{temperature}_t \\ \text{purity}_t \end{pmatrix},
where A is a 3 \times 3 matrix: entry (i, j) is the effect of signal j last hour on signal i this hour. The vars package fits it. The data are 500 hours of the column’s reboiler duty (MW), bottom temperature (°C) and top purity (%).
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Multivariate time series
text:
Cross-correlations













long <- rbind(data.frame(hour = cs$hour, value = cs$duty_MW, signal = "reboiler duty (MW)"),
              data.frame(hour = cs$hour, value = cs$bottom_temp_C, signal = "bottom temperature (°C)"),
              data.frame(hour = cs$hour, value = cs$top_purity_pct, signal = "top purity (%)"))
long$signal <- factor(long$signal, levels = unique(long$signal))
ggplot(long, aes(x = hour, y = value)) +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.35) +
  facet_wrap(~ signal, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Hour", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The cross-correlation function (CCF) correlates one series with another at each lag. In R, ccf(x, y) at lag k is the correlation of x_{t+k} with y_t, so a peak at a negative lag means x leads y.
Your turn. Compute the cross-correlations of the duty with the temperature at lags −6 to 6, and find the lag with the largest one.









The temperature column is bottom_temp_C.


cc <- ccf(Y$duty_MW, Y$bottom_temp_C, lag.max = 6, plot = FALSE)
r <- setNames(round(cc$acf[, 1, 1], 3), cc$lag[, 1, 1])
c(r, best_lag = as.numeric(names(which.max(r))))
The peak is at lag −1, 0.81: the duty one hour ago correlates best with the temperature now. The duty leads. The correlations are large at every lag, though, because both series are themselves autocorrelated, which smears any relationship across lags. A CCF hints at direction, but to separate the dynamics properly, you need a model of the whole system.

title: Multivariate time series
text:
Fitting a VAR
Your turn. Choose the VAR’s order with VARselect(), which compares orders 1 to 6 by four criteria.









Compare up to 6 lags.


vars::VARselect(Y, lag.max = 6)$selection
All four criteria, AIC, Hannan-Quinn, Schwarz (BIC) and the final prediction error, choose 1 lag. When they disagree, AIC tends to choose more lags than BIC. With three series, each extra lag adds nine coefficients, so parsimony matters even more than for one series.




Your turn. Fit the VAR(1), and look at its coefficient matrix A (plus the constants) with Bcoef().









One lag: p = 1.


v <- vars::VAR(Y, p = 1)
round(vars::Bcoef(v), 3)
Read it row by row, as equations. The temperature row: 0.35 times last hour’s duty, plus 0.60 times last hour’s temperature, and almost nothing from the purity (0.03). The purity row: −0.33 times last hour’s temperature, plus 0.67 times its own past. The duty row: 0.80 times its own past, and very little from the others. So the arrows run duty → temperature → purity, exactly the column’s physics, and there’s no direct effect of the duty on the purity (0.007): it acts only through the temperature.




Your turn. A VAR is nothing more than a set of ordinary regressions, one per series, with the same lagged predictors. Fit the temperature equation with lm().









Every predictor is the previous hour: drop the last observation, [-n].


n <- nrow(Y)
coef(lm(Y$bottom_temp_C[-1] ~ Y$duty_MW[-n] + Y$bottom_temp_C[-n] + Y$top_purity_pct[-n]))
0.353, 0.599 and 0.028, with a constant of 52.3: identical to VAR()’s temperature row. Because every equation has the same predictors, least squares equation by equation is the efficient estimator for the whole system. What VAR() adds is the joint covariance of the shocks, and the tools built on it: Granger tests, impulse responses and joint forecasts.

title: Multivariate time series
text:
Granger causality
A series x Granger-causes y if x’s past helps predict y, beyond what y’s own past (and the other series’ past) already does. In a VAR, that’s an F-test that x’s coefficients in the other equations are all 0. It’s prediction, not causation in the physical sense: a common cause, or a missing variable, can produce it. But in a well-instrumented process, it often lines up with the physics.
Your turn. Test whether the duty Granger-causes the other two signals.









The cause is the duty column, "duty_MW".


v <- vars::VAR(Y, p = 1)
g <- vars::causality(v, cause = "duty_MW")$Granger
c(F = g$statistic, df1 = g$parameter[1], p_value = g$p.value)
F = 160 on 2 and 1,485 degrees of freedom, p ≈ 0: the duty’s past improves the forecasts of the temperature and the purity (together, hence the 2 restrictions). The large second degrees of freedom count every equation’s observations together.




Your turn. And the other way: does the purity Granger-cause the duty and the temperature?









The purity column is "top_purity_pct".


v <- vars::VAR(Y, p = 1)
vars::causality(v, cause = "top_purity_pct")$Granger$p.value
p = 0.57: no evidence that the purity’s past helps predict the other two. So in this data, there’s no feedback from the purity to the reboiler, for example from a purity controller adjusting the duty. That’s worth knowing: if the column has such a controller, these data suggest it’s switched off, or too slow to see at hourly resolution.

title: Multivariate time series
text:
Impulse responses
The coefficient matrix shows the effects one hour ahead. Effects spread through the system over several hours: the duty raises the temperature, which then lowers the purity, and each persists. An impulse response function traces the full path: the effect, over the following hours, of a one-unit shock to one series on another. It’s computed by running the VAR forward from the shock. (With ortho = FALSE, the shock hits one series alone. Orthogonalized responses, the default, also let it move the others in the same hour, in proportion to the shocks’ correlation.)
Your turn. Find the response of the purity, over 10 hours, to a 1 MW shock in the duty, and when it’s largest.









The response is the purity, "top_purity_pct".


v <- vars::VAR(Y, p = 1)
ir <- vars::irf(v, impulse = "duty_MW", response = "top_purity_pct", n.ahead = 10, ortho = FALSE, boot = FALSE)
response <- ir$irf$duty_MW[, 1]
c(round(response, 3), largest = min(response), hours_after = which.min(response) - 1)
Nothing in the first hour, then the purity falls, by 0.10 points after 2 hours, and most, 0.40 points, after 6 hours, before slowly recovering. The delay is the column’s dynamics: the temperature has to rise first (its own response peaks at 0.53 °C after 3 hours), and then the composition takes time to move up the trays. For the operators, that’s the practical rule: a 1 MW step in the duty costs about 0.4% of purity, six hours later.





v <- VAR(Y, p = 1)
irs <- irf(v, impulse = "duty_MW", response = c("bottom_temp_C", "top_purity_pct"), n.ahead = 10, ortho = FALSE, boot = FALSE)$irf$duty_MW
df <- rbind(data.frame(hour = 0:10, value = irs[, 1], response = "bottom temperature (°C)"),
            data.frame(hour = 0:10, value = irs[, 2], response = "top purity (%)"))
ggplot(df, aes(x = hour, y = value)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#C2416C", size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ response, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Hours after a 1 MW step in the reboiler duty", y = "Response") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: Multivariate time series
text:
Forecasting the system
Your turn. Forecast all three signals 6 hours ahead with predict(), and look at the purity’s forecasts and 95% intervals.









Six hours ahead: n.ahead = 6.


v <- vars::VAR(Y, p = 1)
fc <- predict(v, n.ahead = 6)
round(fc$fcst$top_purity_pct, 3)
The purity was 96.49% in the last hour, low, and the forecast climbs back toward the system’s mean: 96.47 in the next hour, then 97.26 six hours out, with the 95% interval widening from ±0.30 to ±0.85. The VAR uses all three signals to get there: the last hour’s duty and temperature tell it where the purity is headed, not just the purity’s own past.

title: Multivariate time series
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Is the VAR stable? A VAR(1) is stationary if all the eigenvalues of A have modulus less than 1. (That’s Lesson 4’s condition, in matrix form.) vars::roots() computes them.









The function is vars::roots().


v <- vars::VAR(Y, p = 1)
vars::roots(v)
0.78, 0.77 and 0.52, all inside the unit circle: the system is stable, and every shock dies out. The slowest, 0.78, sets how long the system remembers: about 9 hours to fall to a tenth. The eigenvalues are close to the diagonal of A (0.80, 0.60 and 0.67) but not equal, because the off-diagonal links couple the signals.




Challenge 2 · Are the residuals white noise? The multivariate version of the Ljung-Box test, the portmanteau test, checks all the residuals’ auto- and cross-correlations at once. Run vars::serial.test() with 10 lags.









Ten lags: lags.pt = 10.


v <- vars::VAR(Y, p = 1)
vars::serial.test(v, lags.pt = 10, type = "PT.asymptotic")$serial$p.value
p = 0.73: no remaining correlation, within or between the three residual series. The VAR(1) has captured the system’s dynamics. If it hadn’t, the next step would be more lags, or a VARMA model, which adds moving-average terms in matrix form. VARMA models are harder to estimate and identify, which is why VARs dominate in practice.

title: Multivariate time series
text:
Quick quiz

1. In a VAR(1) with three series, how many lag coefficients are there?

3
9
27


A 3 \times 3 matrix: each series on the previous value of each. Each extra lag adds 9 more.



2. ccf(x, y) peaks at lag −2. What does that suggest?

x leads y by about two periods
y leads x by two periods
The series are unrelated


R’s convention: lag k is the correlation of x_{t+k} with y_t.



3. What does “x Granger-causes y” mean?

x physically causes y
x’s past improves the prediction of y, beyond y’s own past
x and y are correlated


It’s about prediction. A common cause can produce Granger causality without a physical link.



4. The duty has almost no direct coefficient on the purity, but its impulse response on the purity is large. How?

It’s a mistake in the model
The effect travels through the temperature: duty raises temperature, which lowers purity
The purity is non-stationary


Impulse responses show indirect effects that the coefficient matrix alone hides.



5. When is a VAR(1) stable?

When all coefficients are positive
When all the eigenvalues of its coefficient matrix have modulus less than 1
When the series are uncorrelated


The matrix version of |\phi| < 1.



6. Why can a VAR be estimated by least squares, one equation at a time?

Because the series are independent
Because every equation has the same predictors, so equation-by-equation least squares is efficient
Because VARs have no shocks


The shocks’ cross-correlations matter for inference and impulse responses, not for the coefficients.

title: Multivariate time series
text:
Wrap-up
You can now model several series as one system. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Cross-correlations suggest the duty leads the temperature by an hour (0.81 at lag −1), but autocorrelation blurs them.
A VAR(1), chosen by every criterion, shows the arrows: duty → temperature (0.35) → purity (−0.33), and no direct duty → purity effect. It’s a set of ordinary regressions.
Granger causality: the duty helps predict the others (F = 160), and the purity doesn’t feed back (p = 0.57).
Impulse responses: a 1 MW step in the duty raises the temperature by up to 0.53 °C after 3 hours, and costs 0.40% of purity after 6 hours.
Forecasts and checks: the system is stable (largest eigenvalue 0.78), and its residuals pass the portmanteau test (p = 0.73).







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download column_signals.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install vars: install.packages("vars").

Plots. Try plot(irf(v, impulse = "duty_MW", n.ahead = 12)), which adds bootstrap confidence bands, and plot(predict(v, n.ahead = 24)). How wide are the bands on the purity’s response?
Orthogonal responses. Compare irf(v, ortho = TRUE) with ortho = FALSE. Why do they differ? Change the order of the columns of Y and refit: which responses change?
Forecast error variance decomposition. Run fevd(v, n.ahead = 12). How much of the purity’s 12-hour forecast uncertainty comes from shocks to the duty?
A two-signal VAR. Fit a VAR to the duty and the purity only, leaving out the temperature. What does it say about duty → purity now? Why is the omitted middle variable a problem?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Cross-correlation function (CCF)

The correlations between one series and another at each lag.

Vector autoregression, VAR(p)

A model in which each of several series is regressed on the previous p values of all of them.

Granger causality

x Granger-causes y if x’s past improves the prediction of y beyond y’s own past.

Impulse response function

The effect, over time, of a shock to one series on another, in a multivariate model.

Orthogonalized impulse response

An impulse response that also lets the shock move the other series in the same period, according to the shocks’ correlation.

Portmanteau test

The multivariate Ljung-Box test, for auto- and cross-correlation in a VAR’s residuals.

VARMA model

A VAR with matrix moving-average terms added.











NoteWant to read more?






Rob Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd edition), section 12.3, “Vector autoregressions”.
Bernhard Pfaff, “VAR, SVAR and SVEC models: Implementation within R package vars”, Journal of Statistical Software (2008). The vars package’s own guide, with every function used in this lesson.
Penn State’s STAT 510, lesson 11, “Vector autoregressive models, ARCH/GARCH models”.

title: Volatility and long memory
text:
Module 6 · Lesson 13 of 13 Week 102 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Every model so far has assumed that the shocks have a constant variance. For many series, especially prices, that’s wrong in an interesting way. The plant’s gas buyers know it well: some weeks the gas price barely moves, and some weeks it swings by 5% a day, and turbulent days come in clusters. The direction of tomorrow’s change is unpredictable, but its size isn’t. That’s volatility clustering, and Robert Engle’s ARCH model, and its generalization GARCH, describe it. It’s the other half of the 2003 Nobel Prize from Lesson 12.
The lesson’s second half is about the opposite extreme of Lesson 3’s random walk: a stationary series whose memory fades so slowly that ARMA models can’t describe it. That’s long memory, and its classic example is a real series: the yearly minimum level of the Nile at Cairo, recorded from 622 to 1284.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Volatility and long memory
text:
Returns and their squares












Prices are analyzed through their log returns, r_t = \log(P_t/P_{t-1}), roughly the daily percentage change. Lesson 12 found the gas price is a random walk, so its returns should be close to white noise.
Your turn. Compute the returns, and look at their mean, SD, lag-1 autocorrelation, and the lag-1 autocorrelation of their squares.









Square the returns: r^2.


r <- diff(log(gp$gas_eur_mwh))
c(mean = mean(r), sd = sd(r), lag1 = acf(r, plot = FALSE)$acf[2], lag1_squared = acf(r^2, plot = FALSE)$acf[2])
A mean of 0.06% a day and an SD of 2.1%. The returns have no autocorrelation to speak of, −0.02: yesterday’s direction says nothing about today’s. But the squared returns have a lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.09: a big move, in either direction, tends to be followed by another big move. The returns are uncorrelated, but not independent.




Your turn. Test both with the Ljung-Box test at 10 lags. On the squared returns, it’s a test for ARCH effects.









Test the squared returns, r^2.


c(returns = Box.test(r, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value,
  squared = Box.test(r^2, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value)
p = 0.97 for the returns: white noise, as far as the mean goes. For the squared returns, p ≈ 0: strong evidence that the variance is predictable. An ARIMA model would say “nothing to model here”, and would get the risk wrong on every calm and every turbulent day.

title: Volatility and long memory
text:
GARCH(1,1)
The GARCH(1,1) model lets each day’s variance \sigma_t^2 depend on yesterday’s squared shock and yesterday’s variance:

r_t = \mu + \sigma_t z_t, \quad z_t \sim N(0, 1), \qquad \sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha\, (r_{t-1} - \mu)^2 + \beta\, \sigma_{t-1}^2 .

A big shock raises tomorrow’s variance through \alpha, and the raised variance persists through \beta. It’s an ARMA(1,1) for the squared shocks, which is why the squares were autocorrelated. The fGarch package fits it by maximum likelihood with garchFit().
Your turn. Fit a GARCH(1,1) to the returns, and look at the coefficients, their standard errors, and the persistence, \alpha + \beta.









trace = FALSE keeps the optimizer quiet.


fit <- fGarch::garchFit(~ garch(1, 1), data = r, trace = FALSE)
cf <- coef(fit)
c(cf, se = fit@fit$se.coef, persistence = cf[["alpha1"]] + cf[["beta1"]])
\hat\alpha = 0.10 (SE 0.026) and \hat\beta = 0.86 (SE 0.038), close to the 0.10 and 0.85 the prices were simulated with. The persistence, 0.96, means a volatility shock decays by only 4% a day: its half-life is \log 0.5/\log 0.96 \approx 16 trading days. That’s typical of real commodity and financial markets, where persistence is often 0.95 to 0.99. If \alpha + \beta reached 1, shocks to the variance would never die out.




Your turn. The long-run (unconditional) variance of a GARCH(1,1) is \omega/(1 - \alpha - \beta). Compute it, the long-run daily volatility (its square root), and the annualized volatility, assuming 250 trading days a year.









Subtract both \alpha and \beta: the second is "beta1".


fit <- fGarch::garchFit(~ garch(1, 1), data = r, trace = FALSE)
cf <- coef(fit)
long_run_var <- cf[["omega"]] / (1 - cf[["alpha1"]] - cf[["beta1"]])
c(daily = sqrt(long_run_var), annual = sqrt(long_run_var * 250))
A long-run volatility of 2.1% a day, or 34% a year: in a typical year, the gas price could rise or fall by a third. The day-to-day volatility moves around that level, from 1.4% in the calmest stretch of these four years to 3.5% in the most turbulent.




Here’s the estimated volatility over the four years, with the returns:

fit <- garchFit(~ garch(1, 1), data = r, trace = FALSE)
df <- rbind(data.frame(day = seq_along(r), value = r, panel = "daily return"),
            data.frame(day = seq_along(r), value = volatility(fit), panel = "GARCH volatility (daily SD)"))
ggplot(df, aes(x = day, y = value)) +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.35) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Trading day", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: Volatility and long memory
text:
Forecasting volatility
Your turn. The last day’s volatility was above average. Forecast the volatility for the next 10 trading days with predict().









Ten days: n.ahead = 10.


fit <- fGarch::garchFit(~ garch(1, 1), data = r, trace = FALSE)
fc <- predict(fit, n.ahead = 10)
c(today = tail(fGarch::volatility(fit), 1), round(fc$standardDeviation, 5))
The last day’s volatility was 2.43%, above the long-run 2.14%. The forecast falls from 2.40% tomorrow to 2.32% in ten days, slowly, at the persistence rate of 0.96 a day, toward the long-run level. A constant-variance model would say 2.08% (the sample SD) for every day, no matter what had just happened.




Your turn. The gas buyers’ risk measure is a one-day 99% value-at-risk: how much the price could rise tomorrow, in €/MWh, with only a 1% chance of rising more. With the GARCH forecast, that’s the 99th percentile of tomorrow’s return, \hat\mu + 2.33\,\hat\sigma_{t+1}, applied to today’s price. Compare it with the constant-variance version.









The 99th percentile of a standard normal is qnorm(0.99).


fit <- fGarch::garchFit(~ garch(1, 1), data = r, trace = FALSE)
fc <- predict(fit, n.ahead = 1)
price <- tail(gp$gas_eur_mwh, 1)
q99 <- fc$meanForecast[1] + qnorm(0.99) * fc$standardDeviation[1]
c(price = price, garch_var = price * (exp(q99) - 1), constant_var = price * (exp(mean(r) + qnorm(0.99) * sd(r)) - 1))
At €63.68/MWh, the GARCH value-at-risk says the price could rise by €3.67 tomorrow, against €3.19 from the constant-variance model: 15% more risk, because the market is in a turbulent spell. On a calm day, it would go the other way. A risk measure that ignores volatility clustering is too high when things are calm, and too low exactly when they aren’t.

title: Volatility and long memory
text:
Long memory
Now the Nile. Its yearly minimum level at the Roda gauge in Cairo was recorded, by hand, for over 600 years. The hydrologist Harold Hurst, studying it in the 1950s to design the Aswan dams, found something strange: long stretches of high years and long stretches of low ones, far longer than a random process with short memory would produce. That’s long memory.

ggplot(nile, aes(x = year, y = min_level_cm)) +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.35) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Minimum level (cm)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Your turn. Compute its autocorrelations at lags 1, 10 and 50, and compare them with what an AR(1) fitted to the same data would imply, \hat\phi^k.









Lag 50 is element 51.


r_nile <- acf(nile, lag.max = 50, plot = FALSE)$acf
phi <- coef(arima(nile, order = c(1, 0, 0)))[[1]]
rbind(sample = c(lag1 = r_nile[2], lag10 = r_nile[11], lag50 = r_nile[51]), ar1 = phi^c(1, 10, 50))
At lag 1, both say 0.57. But at lag 10, the sample autocorrelation is still 0.28, while the AR(1) implies 0.004, and at lag 50, half a century apart, the data still have 0.13, against an AR(1)’s 10^{-12}. An ARMA model’s autocorrelations decay exponentially. The Nile’s decay like a power of the lag, \rho_k \sim k^{2d-1}, much more slowly. Yet the series is stationary: it doesn’t wander off like a random walk.

title: Volatility and long memory
text:
ARFIMA models
The ARFIMA model handles long memory by allowing the differencing order d in ARIMA to be a fraction: (1 - B)^d y_t = \varepsilon_t, with (1 - B)^d expanded as a binomial series. With 0 < d < 0.5, the process is stationary but has long memory: its autocorrelations decay like k^{2d - 1}. With d = 0, it’s white noise, and with d = 1, a random walk. The fracdiff package estimates d.
Your turn. Estimate d for the Nile minima (after subtracting their mean).









Subtract the mean, mean(nile).


fd <- fracdiff::fracdiff(nile - mean(nile))
fd$d
\hat d = 0.39: strong long memory, inside the stationary range. Hurst’s own measure, the Hurst exponent, is H = d + \frac12 \approx 0.9, the figure usually quoted for the Nile, against 0.5 for short memory. For the dam designers, this mattered: with long memory, droughts last longer, and a reservoir sized for a short-memory river would run dry. Long memory shows up in many natural and engineered series: river flows, climate records, network traffic, and some process measurements over very long periods.

title: Volatility and long memory
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Did GARCH capture the clustering? If the model is right, the standardized residuals, (r_t - \hat\mu)/\hat\sigma_t, should have no ARCH effects left. Test their squares with the Ljung-Box test, with fitdf = 2 for \alpha and \beta.









standardize = TRUE divides by the conditional SD.


fit <- fGarch::garchFit(~ garch(1, 1), data = r, trace = FALSE)
z <- residuals(fit, standardize = TRUE)
Box.test(z^2, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 2)$p.value
p = 0.91: no clustering left. The GARCH(1,1) has captured the volatility dynamics completely, as it should, since the data were simulated from one. With real prices, check the standardized residuals’ tails too: real returns usually have more extreme days than a normal distribution allows, and garchFit(..., cond.dist = "std") uses a t distribution for z_t instead.




Challenge 2 · Long memory from block averages. The variance of the mean of m consecutive observations falls like 1/m for short memory, but like m^{2d - 1} for long memory. Average the Nile minima in blocks of 1, 2, 4, …, 32 years, regress the log variance of the block means on \log m, and estimate d from the slope, 2d - 1. This is the aggregated variance method.









Regress on the log of the block size, log(m).


m <- c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32)
v <- sapply(m, function(k) {
  blocks <- floor(length(nile) / k)
  var(colMeans(matrix(nile[1:(blocks * k)], nrow = k)))      # the variance of the block means
})
slope <- coef(lm(log(v) ~ log(m)))[[2]]
c(slope = slope, d = (slope + 1) / 2)
A slope of −0.31, so \hat d = 0.34: for short memory, it would be −1, and d = 0. A simpler estimate than fracdiff()’s 0.39, but it tells the same story. Long memory has a practical consequence for every average: the uncertainty of a 32-year mean of the Nile falls much more slowly than 1/\sqrt{32}, so long-run averages are far less precise than the usual formula claims.

title: Volatility and long memory
text:
Quick quiz

1. The returns of a price have no autocorrelation, but their squares do. What does that mean?

The price is predictable
The direction of changes is unpredictable, but their size isn’t: volatility clustering
The returns are independent


Uncorrelated isn’t the same as independent.



2. In a GARCH(1,1), what does \alpha + \beta = 0.96 say?

The returns are 96% predictable
Volatility shocks persist, decaying by only 4% a day
The model is non-stationary


Its half-life is about 16 days. At \alpha + \beta = 1, shocks would never decay.



3. What’s the long-run variance of a GARCH(1,1)?

\omega
\omega/(1 - \alpha - \beta)
\alpha + \beta


The level that volatility forecasts return to.



4. Why does a value-at-risk with constant variance mislead?

It’s always too high
It’s too high in calm periods and too low in turbulent ones, exactly when it matters
It ignores the mean


GARCH lets the risk measure follow the market’s current state.



5. How do the autocorrelations of a long-memory process decay?

Exponentially, like an AR(1)
Like a power of the lag, much more slowly
They don’t decay at all


\rho_k \sim k^{2d - 1}. A random walk’s sample ACF barely decays, but it isn’t stationary.



6. An ARFIMA model has d = 0.39. What kind of process is it?

A random walk
Stationary, with long memory
White noise


0 < d < 0.5 is stationary long memory. d \geq 0.5 is non-stationary.

title: Volatility and long memory
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve reached the end of Module 6. Here’s what you’ve learned in this lesson:

Volatility clustering: the gas returns are white noise (Ljung-Box p = 0.97), but their squares aren’t (p ≈ 0).
GARCH(1,1): \hat\alpha = 0.10, \hat\beta = 0.86, a persistence of 0.96, and a long-run volatility of 2.1% a day, 34% a year. The standardized residuals show no clustering left (p = 0.91).
Volatility forecasts decay toward the long-run level: from 2.43% to 2.32% over ten days. The one-day 99% value-at-risk is €3.67/MWh, against €3.19 with constant variance.
Long memory: the Nile minima’s autocorrelation is still 0.13 at lag 50, where an AR(1) implies 10^{-12}.
ARFIMA: a fractional d of 0.39 (Hurst exponent about 0.9), and the aggregated variance method agrees, at 0.34.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download gas_prices.csv and nile_minima.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install fGarch and fracdiff.

The news impact curve. For the fitted GARCH, plot tomorrow’s variance, \omega + \alpha\varepsilon^2 + \beta\bar\sigma^2, against today’s shock \varepsilon, at the long-run variance \bar\sigma^2. It’s a parabola. An EGARCH or GJR-GARCH model makes it asymmetric, with bad news raising volatility more than good news. Would that make sense for a gas buyer?
Student’s t shocks. Refit with cond.dist = "std". What does it estimate for the degrees of freedom? Do the \alpha and \beta estimates change?
Real prices. Download a real daily commodity price series (for example, from an exchange’s website) and repeat the analysis. Is the persistence higher or lower than this lesson’s 0.96?
