Forecasting the Nile. Fit forecast::arfima(nile), and forecast 50 years ahead. Compare the forecast’s return to the mean with an AR(1)’s. Which one remembers longer?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Log return

\log(P_t/P_{t-1}): roughly the percentage change of a price.

Volatility clustering

Large changes followed by large changes, and small by small, in either direction.

ARCH and GARCH models

Models in which the variance of the shocks depends on past squared shocks (ARCH), and on past variances too (GARCH).

Persistence

\alpha + \beta in a GARCH(1,1): how slowly volatility shocks decay.

Value-at-risk

A loss, or price move, that will be exceeded with only a stated small probability over a given horizon.

Standardized residuals

Residuals divided by their conditional SD. In a good GARCH model, they show no remaining clustering.

Long memory

Autocorrelations that decay like a power of the lag, much more slowly than any ARMA model’s.

ARFIMA model

An ARIMA model with a fractional differencing order d. With 0 < d < 0.5, it’s stationary with long memory.

Hurst exponent

H = d + \frac12: 0.5 for short memory, larger for long memory.











NoteWant to read more?






Robert Engle, “GARCH 101: the use of ARCH/GARCH models in applied econometrics”, Journal of Economic Perspectives (2001). The friendliest introduction there is, by the inventor of ARCH.
Penn State’s STAT 510, lesson 11, which covers ARCH and GARCH models after VARs, and lesson 13, on fractional differencing and long memory.
Jan Beran, Statistics for Long-Memory Processes (Chapman & Hall, 1994). The standard reference, with the Nile minima as its running example, and the source of the longmemo package.
Harold Edwin Hurst, “Long-term storage capacity of reservoirs”, Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers (1951). Where long memory was discovered, from the Nile.

title: Module 6 project: a forecasting study
text:
Every October, the plant renews its electricity contract, and the supplier wants a forecast for the coming year, month by month. The contract has two numbers that matter: the year’s total, which sets the budget, and a monthly cap of 11,000 MWh, above which every MWh is billed at the spot price, often two or three times the contract price. Last year’s forecast came from a spreadsheet trend, and it was off by 7% in some months.
Tomas, the energy manager, wants something better: a forecast he can defend, with uncertainty he can plan around. That’s a forecasting study: model the series, compare methods fairly on data they haven’t seen, and report the winner’s forecasts with honest intervals.

title: Module 6 project: a forecasting study
text:
What you’ll make
One report, written in Quarto in your plant-study RStudio project, that Tomas could send to the supplier, with a page for the plant’s management. It should contain:

A summary for Tomas, at the top, in plain words: the forecast for each month of the contract year with its range, the year’s total with an interval, which months risk going over the cap and how likely that is, and why this forecast deserves more trust than the spreadsheet’s.
The data and its cleaning: the series, its trend and season, and every problem you found and how you handled it.
The model comparison: at least four methods, including the benchmarks, compared on a test set and by time-series cross-validation.
The chosen model: its specification, its diagnostics, and its forecasts.
A cleaning log and a list of limitations.

Nobody grades it, but write it as if the supplier’s analyst will check your numbers. In real life, one would.

title: Module 6 project: a forecasting study
text:
The handover
Download the two files into a new folder in your project, data-raw/electricity/, and don’t edit them:

README.txt: Tomas’s note, with the contract terms, the questions, the columns and a known issue. Read it first.
electricity_2026.csv: the main meter’s monthly readings, January 2015 to September 2026.

Then download the project template, save it in the top folder of your project as electricity-forecast.qmd, and click Render. It reads the data, plots it, and shows a seasonal plot, with headings and code skeletons for every step. Fill it in one section at a time, and render often. It uses the tidyverse and the forecast package.

title: Module 6 project: a forecasting study
text:
The brief, step by step

Explore (Lessons 1 and 2). Plot the series, a seasonal plot and an STL decomposition. Describe the trend and the season. Look closely at 2021: is any value missing, or impossible? A missing month next to one that’s twice its usual size has a likely explanation. Fix what you can justify, and log it.
Handle the step change (Lesson 10). The new compressor house started in March 2023 and added a steady load. Model it with a step variable, 0 before March 2023 and 1 from then on, as a predictor. How big is the step, in percent?
Choose a scale (Lesson 2). Is the seasonal swing proportional to the level? If so, model the logarithm and transform the forecasts back with exp().
Set up a fair comparison (Lesson 8). Hold out the last 24 months, October 2024 to September 2026, as a test set. Fit every method to the earlier data only.
Compare methods (Lessons 2, 8, 9 and 10). At least: the seasonal naive benchmark, ETS, a seasonal ARIMA without the step, and a seasonal ARIMA with the step as a regressor. Add the spreadsheet’s method, a straight-line trend, tslm(y ~ trend), to show what it gets wrong. Compare RMSE and MAPE on the test set, and check the coverage of the 80% and 95% intervals.
Cross-validate (Lesson 8). With tsCV(), compare the best two or three methods at a 12-month horizon, over many forecast origins. Does the ranking agree with the test set?
Check the chosen model (Lessons 7 and 9). Refit it to all the data. Residual plots, the Ljung-Box test with the right degrees of freedom, and an overfitting check.
Forecast (Lessons 8 and 9). October 2026 to September 2027, month by month, with 80% and 95% intervals. Simulate 4,000 future years from the model for the annual total’s interval, the probability that each month exceeds 11,000 MWh, and the probability that at least one month does.
Write it up. Summary first. Then the data, the cleaning, the comparison, the model and its checks, the forecasts, and the limitations, with the cleaning log at the end.

Stretch goal. The forecast assumes the plant runs as it has. Two things could change that: a planned three-week shutdown in August 2027, and a new chiller that would add about 4% to the summer load from June 2027. Build both as scenarios, with their own predictors or adjustments, and show how the cap risk changes. Which one matters more?

title: Module 6 project: a forecasting study
text:
Check your own work
When you’ve finished, assess your project against this rubric. Aim for the right-hand column.










Needs work
Good
Excellent




The data
Used as received
The meter problem is noticed
The missing and doubled months are found, split with a justification, and the effect of leaving them in is shown; everything is in the cleaning log


The step change
Ignored
Modeled with a step variable
Its size is estimated with an interval, and forecasts with and without it are compared


The comparison
One model
Several models on a test set
Benchmarks, ETS and ARIMA with and without the step, compared on a test set and by cross-validation, with interval coverage


The chosen model
Chosen by AIC alone
Diagnostics checked
Residual checks passed, overfitting checked, and the choice justified by out-of-sample accuracy


The forecasts
Point forecasts only
Monthly forecasts with intervals
Monthly intervals, a simulated annual total, and cap probabilities for each month and for the year


Communication
Code output with little text
A report that explains its steps
A report Tomas could send to the supplier: a plain summary, a clear recommendation, honest uncertainty and stated limitations

title: Module 6 project: a forecasting study
text:
Tips

Read the README’s dates against the data. The meter was replaced in spring 2021. Where the reading for one month is missing and the next is twice the usual, the meter’s first reading probably covered both. Split it in proportion to the days in each month.
Log scale, then back. If you model log(y), the forecasts’ exp() is the median, not the mean, of the original scale. For the annual total, simulate paths and add them up on the original scale.
Future values of the step. Forecasting with a regressor needs its future values: here, rep(1, 12), since the compressor house is staying.
Don’t let the test set choose for you twice. Pick the method on the test set and by cross-validation, then refit it to all the data for the final forecast. Don’t go back and tweak it to look better on the test set.
auto.arima() is slow with seasonal data. Expect a few seconds per fit. For cross-validation, fix the model’s orders from one auto.arima() run, and refit only the coefficients at each origin with Arima(x, model = ...), or with the orders given explicitly.
“At risk” needs a number. “Summer is at risk” is less useful than “this month has a 1-in-4 chance of exceeding the cap”. Simulate.
Explain the spreadsheet’s error. A straight-line trend ignores the season and the step. Show its test-set errors month by month: that’s what will convince management.


When it’s done, you’ll have done a complete forecasting study: cleaning, comparing, checking and communicating. Congratulations on finishing Module 6! Module 7 turns from time series to machine learning: models that learn patterns from many predictors at once.

title: Resampling and model assessment
text:
Module 7 · Lesson 2 of 14 Week 105 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 1 had a luxury that real problems never have: 2,000 extra runs from the same process, to measure the test error directly. In practice, all the data you have is the data you fit the model to. This lesson is about resampling: reusing that data cleverly, to estimate how well a model will do on data it hasn’t seen.
The example for the next few lessons is a soft sensor. The plant’s gas-phase polyethylene reactor makes four grades of polymer, and the property that defines a grade is its melt index (MI): how many grams of molten polymer flow through a standard die in 10 minutes. The lab measures it every 8 hours, and a result takes about two hours. If the MI drifts off target, the plant makes off-grade polymer for hours before anyone knows. A soft sensor predicts the MI from process tags that are measured every second, so the operators can see a drift as it happens.
soft_sensor.csv has 500 lab results, from June to November 2025, with the hourly averages of 20 process tags at each sample’s time. The chemistry says that the MI depends mostly on the hydrogen/ethylene ratio (hydrogen ends the polymer chains, and shorter chains flow more easily), and also on the reactor temperature, the comonomer ratio and the ethylene pressure. The other tags are there because they were in the historian.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Resampling and model assessment
text:
The soft sensor
The MI varies by a factor of 30 across the grades, and its errors scale with its size, so models work on \log(\text{MI}). The chemistry predicts a straight line between \log(\text{MI}) and \log(\text{H}_2/\text{C}_2):

ggplot(mi, aes(h2_ratio, melt_index, color = grade)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(A = "#C2416C", B = "#2a78d6", C = "#1baf7a", D = "#8a5a00")) +
  labs(x = "Hydrogen/ethylene ratio (log scale)", y = "Melt index, g/10 min (log scale)", color = "Grade") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The setup code reads the data and adds the two logs. It also defines three candidate models, from simple to complicated, and a helper that computes the root mean squared error (RMSE) of a fitted model on some data. On the log scale, an RMSE of 0.17 means a typical error of about 17% of the MI.













Your turn. Find the correlation between the MI and the hydrogen ratio, first on the original scales, then on the log scales.









The log of the hydrogen ratio is the column log_h2.


c(original = cor(mi$melt_index, mi$h2_ratio),
  log = cor(mi$log_mi, mi$log_h2))
0.934 on the original scales and 0.973 on the log scales. The hydrogen ratio alone explains 0.973^2 = 95\% of the variation in \log(\text{MI}). The question for the soft sensor is whether the other tags can explain part of the remaining 5%, and how to tell, honestly.

title: Resampling and model assessment
text:
The validation set approach
The simplest honest estimate: split the data at random into a training set, to fit each model, and a validation set (or hold-out set), to measure its error.
Your turn. Put 350 samples into a training set and keep 150 for validation. Fit the three models to the training set, and compute each one’s RMSE on the validation set.









The validation set is every row not in train: mi[-train, ].


set.seed(7021)
train <- sample(500, 350)
c(a = rmse(lm(f_a, mi[train, ]), mi[-train, ]),
  b = rmse(lm(f_b, mi[train, ]), mi[-train, ]),
  c = rmse(lm(f_c, mi[train, ]), mi[-train, ]))
0.225 for hydrogen alone, 0.176 for the chemistry model, and 0.176 for all 20 tags. The three extra chemical variables cut the error by a fifth. The other 16 tags add nothing: model c’s validation error is a hair higher than model b’s (0.1764 against 0.1756), even though its training error is lower (0.163 against 0.166). More predictors always fit the training data better.




The validation set approach has two weaknesses. Only 350 of the 500 samples train each model, so the models are a little worse than they’d be with all the data, and the error estimate is a little pessimistic. And the estimate depends on which samples happened to land in the validation set.
Your turn. Repeat the split with seeds 1 to 10, and find model b’s validation RMSE for each.









Each split uses its own seed, s.


val_b <- sapply(1:10, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  train <- sample(500, 350)
  rmse(lm(f_b, mi[train, ]), mi[-train, ])
})
round(val_b, 4)
range(val_b)
From 0.161 to 0.183: the same model, the same data, and estimates that differ by 14%, just from the split. Over the same ten splits, model c beats model b in one, and comes within 0.001 of it in three more. With one split, you could easily conclude that the extra 16 tags help. Cross-validation fixes both weaknesses.

title: Resampling and model assessment
text:
Leave-one-out cross-validation
Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) takes the split to its extreme: leave out one sample, fit the model to the other 499, predict the one left out, and repeat for every sample. The estimate is the average of the 500 squared errors:

\text{CV}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \big(y_i - \hat y_{(i)}\big)^2 ,

where \hat y_{(i)} is the prediction from the model fitted without sample i. Every model trains on almost all the data, and there’s no randomness at all. It sounds expensive, but for least squares there’s a shortcut: one fit gives every leave-one-out residual, from the leverages h_i of Module 2,

y_i - \hat y_{(i)} = \frac{y_i - \hat y_i}{1 - h_i} .

Your turn. Compute model b’s LOOCV RMSE with the shortcut.









Divide each residual by 1 - h_i: (1 - h).


fit_b <- lm(f_b, data = mi)
h <- hatvalues(fit_b)
sqrt(mean((resid(fit_b) / (1 - h))^2))
0.1700. A loop that really refits the model 500 times gives exactly the same number. The shortcut works for any linear smoother, but not for most of the methods later in this module, where LOOCV would mean n refits. LOOCV also has a subtler problem: the 500 fitted models are almost identical, so their errors are highly correlated, and the average of correlated errors has a high variance.

title: Resampling and model assessment
text:
k-fold cross-validation
k-fold cross-validation is the workhorse. Divide the data at random into k groups, or folds, of about equal size. Hold out the first fold, fit the model to the other k - 1, and compute its error on the fold that was held out. Repeat for each fold, and average:

\text{CV}_{(k)} = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^k \text{MSE}_j .

With k = 5 or 10, each model trains on 80% or 90% of the data, and it takes only 5 or 10 fits. It’s less variable than LOOCV, and a little more biased, and in practice, k = 5 or 10 is the standard compromise.
Your turn. Assign each sample to one of 10 folds at random, then compute the 10-fold cross-validated RMSE of the three models.









Predict for the fold that was held out: mi[fold == j, ].


cv_rmse <- function(formula, fold) {
  err <- numeric(nrow(mi))
  for (j in unique(fold)) {
    fit <- lm(formula, data = mi[fold != j, ])
    err[fold == j] <- mi$log_mi[fold == j] - predict(fit, mi[fold == j, ])
  }
  sqrt(mean(err^2))
}
set.seed(7022)
fold <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = 500))
c(a = cv_rmse(f_a, fold), b = cv_rmse(f_b, fold), c = cv_rmse(f_c, fold))
0.217, 0.170 and 0.174. Every sample is predicted exactly once, by a model that didn’t see it, and the verdict is clearer than any single split: the chemistry model is best, and adding the other 16 tags makes it slightly worse. sample(rep(1:10, length.out = 500)) makes folds of exactly 50, in random order.










NoteGo deeper: the bias and variance of cross-validation





Each CV estimate is itself a statistic, with a bias and a variance. Its bias comes from training on less than all the data: with k = 2, each model sees half the data and is worse than the final model will be, so the estimate is pessimistic. LOOCV is nearly unbiased. Its variance comes from two sources: which observations happen to be in the data, and how they’re split. LOOCV’s n fits overlap almost completely, so their errors are strongly positively correlated, and the mean of correlated quantities is more variable than the mean of independent ones. Folds of 5 or 10 overlap less. Kohavi’s 1995 study (“A Study of Cross-Validation and Bootstrap for Accuracy Estimation and Model Selection”, IJCAI) found 10-fold CV the best choice on real datasets, and The Elements of Statistical Learning, section 7.10, discusses why. Neither bias nor variance can be computed from the data alone, which is why repeating k-fold CV with different random folds (Challenge 1) is a good habit.

title: Resampling and model assessment
text:
The bootstrap
Cross-validation estimates prediction error. The bootstrap is a more general tool, from Module 4: it estimates the uncertainty of almost any statistic, by recomputing it on resamples of the data drawn with replacement.
Your turn. Estimate the standard error of model b’s reactor temperature coefficient from 1,000 bootstrap resamples, and compare it with the one from summary().









A bootstrap resample is drawn with replacement: replace = TRUE.


set.seed(7023)
boot_coef <- replicate(1000, {
  rows <- sample(500, replace = TRUE)
  coef(lm(f_b, data = mi[rows, ]))[["reactor_temp_C"]]
})
c(bootstrap = sd(boot_coef),
  formula = summary(lm(f_b, data = mi))$coefficients["reactor_temp_C", "Std. Error"])
0.0073 from the bootstrap, 0.0069 from the formula, for a coefficient of 0.100: each degree raises the MI by about 10%. The two agree well. The formula assumes constant error variance; the bootstrap doesn’t, and it works just as well for statistics with no formula at all, like a test RMSE or a lasso coefficient. But both assume that the 500 samples are independent, and the last step shows they aren’t.

title: Resampling and model assessment
section: Data leakage I: choosing predictors outside the CV
text:
Data leakage I: choosing predictors outside the CV
Data leakage is when information from the data used to judge a model gets into the model itself. It makes the CV estimate optimistic, sometimes absurdly so, and it’s the most common way that machine-learning results fail to hold up.
The classic case: with many candidate predictors, a common recipe is to keep the ones most correlated with the response, then cross-validate a model on those. The trap is that the screening used all the data, including every fold that’s later held out.
Your turn. Simulate 50 samples of 1,000 predictors and a response that are all pure noise. Keep the 10 predictors most correlated with the response, then 5-fold cross-validate a linear model on them. Compare its CV mean squared error with the variance of the response, which is the MSE of just predicting the mean.









Predict the held-out fold, d[fold == j, ].


set.seed(7024)
X <- matrix(rnorm(50 * 1000), 50)
y <- rnorm(50)
top <- order(abs(cor(X, y)), decreasing = TRUE)[1:10]
d <- data.frame(y = y, X[, top])
fold <- rep(1:5, length.out = 50)
err <- numeric(50)
for (j in 1:5) {
  fit <- lm(y ~ ., data = d[fold != j, ])
  err[fold == j] <- y[fold == j] - predict(fit, d[fold == j, ])
}
c(cv_mse = mean(err^2), var_y = var(y))
A CV MSE of 0.49, against 0.91 for predicting the mean: the model seems to explain almost half the variance of pure noise. Out of 1,000 noise predictors, some are correlated with y by chance, and they stay correlated with it in every fold, because the folds were part of the data that chose them.




The fix is to treat the screening as part of the model: every step that learns from the data happens inside each fold, using only that fold’s training data. That includes choosing predictors, but also standardizing, imputing missing values, and choosing tuning settings.
Your turn. Redo the cross-validation, choosing the top 10 predictors inside each fold, from that fold’s training rows only.









Correlate the training rows of X with the training rows of y: y[tr].


set.seed(7024)
X <- matrix(rnorm(50 * 1000), 50)
y <- rnorm(50)
fold <- rep(1:5, length.out = 50)
err <- numeric(50)
for (j in 1:5) {
  tr <- fold != j
  top_j <- order(abs(cor(X[tr, ], y[tr])), decreasing = TRUE)[1:10]
  d <- data.frame(y = y, X[, top_j])
  fit <- lm(y ~ ., data = d[tr, ])
  err[!tr] <- y[!tr] - predict(fit, d[!tr, ])
}
mean(err^2)
1.27: worse than predicting the mean (0.91), which is the truth. The model is useless, and now the CV says so. This example is from The Elements of Statistical Learning, section 7.10.2, “The Wrong and Right Way to Do Cross-validation”, and it’s still one of the most common mistakes in published work.

title: Resampling and model assessment
section: Data leakage II: samples close in time
text:
Data leakage II: samples close in time
Random folds assume that the samples are independent, so that a held-out sample is as new to the model as a future one. For the soft sensor, that’s false. The catalyst’s activity drifts slowly, and nobody measures it, so it shows up in the residuals:

fit_b <- lm(log_mi ~ log_h2 + reactor_temp_C + comonomer_ratio + c2_pressure_bar, data = mi)
ggplot(data.frame(time = as.POSIXct(mi$time, tz = "UTC"), res = resid(fit_b)), aes(time, res)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Residual, log(MI)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The lag-1 autocorrelation of these residuals is 0.80: each sample’s error is a lot like the previous one’s. With random folds, every held-out sample has neighbors 8 hours before and after it in the training data, sharing its drift, so the model “knows” the drift it’s being tested on. A soft sensor in use only ever predicts the future. The honest test holds out blocks of consecutive samples, so the model has to predict a stretch of time it hasn’t seen.
Your turn. Make 10 folds of 50 consecutive samples each (about 17 days), and compute the blocked CV RMSE of the three models.









Blocks of 50: ceiling(seq_len(500) / 50) gives 1 to 50 a fold number of 1, 51 to 100 a 2, and so on.


cv_rmse <- function(formula, fold) {
  err <- numeric(nrow(mi))
  for (j in unique(fold)) {
    fit <- lm(formula, data = mi[fold != j, ])
    err[fold == j] <- mi$log_mi[fold == j] - predict(fit, mi[fold == j, ])
  }
  sqrt(mean(err^2))
}
block <- ceiling(seq_len(500) / 50)
c(a = cv_rmse(f_a, block), b = cv_rmse(f_b, block), c = cv_rmse(f_c, block))
0.235, 0.194 and 0.216, all higher than the random-fold estimates (0.217, 0.170 and 0.174). Model b’s honest error is about 19%, not 17%. And the penalty for using all 20 tags is much bigger, 0.216 against 0.194: random folds let the extra tags fit the drift, through accidental patterns that hold for a few days and then stop. In this case, the leakage didn’t just flatter the models; it hid how much the extra tags hurt.




The same goes for any grouping in the data. If a dataset has several samples from each batch, each patient or each pump, the folds should keep each group together (grouped CV). Otherwise a model can do well by recognizing the group, not by learning anything that carries over to new ones. Module 6’s time-series cross-validation, with its rolling forecast origin, is the strictest version for time series.

title: Resampling and model assessment
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Repeated cross-validation. One run of 10-fold CV still depends on the random folds. Repeat it 5 times, with seeds 7031 to 7035, for model b, and find the mean and the range of the five estimates.









Cross-validate model b, f_b.


cv_rmse <- function(formula, fold) {
  err <- numeric(nrow(mi))
  for (j in unique(fold)) {
    fit <- lm(formula, data = mi[fold != j, ])
    err[fold == j] <- mi$log_mi[fold == j] - predict(fit, mi[fold == j, ])
  }
  sqrt(mean(err^2))
}
reps <- sapply(7031:7035, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  fold <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = 500))
  cv_rmse(f_b, fold)
})
c(mean = mean(reps), min = min(reps), max = max(reps))
A mean of 0.1703, and the five estimates span only 0.1697 to 0.1706. Compare the ten validation splits, which spanned 0.161 to 0.183: because every sample is predicted once in each run, k-fold CV is far more stable than a single split. Repeating it costs a little more computing, and it shows how much the folds matter.




Challenge 2 · A block bootstrap. The ordinary bootstrap also assumes independent samples. A moving-block bootstrap resamples blocks of consecutive samples instead, so that each block keeps its drift. Resample 20 blocks of 25 consecutive samples, with replacement, to make each 500-sample resample, and find the standard error of the temperature coefficient.









A block that starts at s and has 25 samples ends at s + 24.


set.seed(7025)
boot_block <- replicate(1000, {
  starts <- sample(1:476, 20, replace = TRUE)
  rows <- as.vector(sapply(starts, function(s) s:(s + 24)))
  coef(lm(f_b, data = mi[rows, ]))[["reactor_temp_C"]]
})
sd(boot_block)
0.0146: twice the ordinary bootstrap’s 0.0073, and twice the formula’s. Because neighboring samples share their drift, 500 samples carry less information than 500 independent ones would, and an honest 95% interval for the temperature effect is about twice as wide, roughly 0.07 to 0.13. The block length is a judgment call: long enough to keep most of the dependence (the drift lasts days, so 25 samples, about 8 days, is reasonable), and short enough to leave many blocks to resample.

title: Resampling and model assessment
text:
Quick quiz

1. What is the main weakness of a single validation set?

It takes too long to compute
The estimate depends heavily on which samples land in it
It’s biased toward complex models


Ten random splits gave estimates from 0.161 to 0.183 for the same model.



2. In 10-fold cross-validation, how many times is each sample predicted?

Once, by a model that didn’t see it
Ten times
Nine times


Each sample is in exactly one held-out fold.



3. Why is k = 5 or 10 usually preferred to LOOCV?

LOOCV is always biased
LOOCV’s fits overlap almost completely, so its estimate has a high variance, and it needs n fits
LOOCV can’t be used for regression


LOOCV is nearly unbiased, but its estimate is variable, and for most methods it’s expensive.



4. You standardize all the predictors using the whole dataset’s means and SDs, then cross-validate. Is that leakage?

No, standardizing doesn’t use the response
Yes, a little: the held-out folds influenced the means and SDs
Only for classification


It’s usually mild, but the rule is simple: every step that learns from data happens inside each fold. Lesson 14’s recipes do that automatically.



5. Why was random-fold CV optimistic for the soft sensor?

There were too few samples
Neighboring samples share the catalyst drift, so held-out samples weren’t really new
The response was on a log scale


Blocked CV, which holds out stretches of time, gave higher and more honest errors.



6. What does the bootstrap estimate?

Only the test error
The sampling variability of almost any statistic
The true value of a parameter


By recomputing the statistic on resamples drawn with replacement.

title: Resampling and model assessment
text:
Wrap-up
You can now estimate how well a model will predict, and avoid the traps that make it look better than it is. Here’s what you’ve learned:

A validation set is simple, but its estimate depends on the split: 0.161 to 0.183 for the same model.
LOOCV fits n models, each without one sample. For least squares, one fit and the leverages give it: 0.170 for the chemistry model.
k-fold CV with k = 5 or 10 is the standard: stable, cheap and nearly unbiased. It chose the chemistry model over all 20 tags, 0.170 against 0.174.
The bootstrap gives standard errors for almost any statistic: 0.0073 for the temperature coefficient.
Leakage from screening: choosing predictors on all the data made pure noise look predictive. Every step that learns from data belongs inside the folds.
Leakage from dependence: samples close in time share the drift. Blocked CV gave 0.194 for the chemistry model, and showed that the extra tags hurt more than random folds said.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download soft_sensor.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

The bias of small training sets. Compute the k-fold CV RMSE of model b for k = 2, 5, 10, 25 and LOOCV. Repeat each 10 times with different folds, and plot the means and spreads.
Group by grade. Use the grade as the fold: train on three grades, and predict the fourth. How well does the soft sensor extrapolate to a grade it has never seen? Which grade is hardest?
The boot package. Redo the bootstrap with boot::boot(), and get a percentile and a BCa interval for the temperature coefficient with boot::boot.ci().
Forward in time. Train on the first 300 samples and test on the last 200. Compare with the blocked CV estimate.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Resampling

Reusing the data, by repeatedly fitting models to subsets or resamples of it, to estimate a model’s performance or a statistic’s uncertainty.

Validation set approach

Splitting the data once into a training set and a validation (hold-out) set.

Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV)

Fitting the model n times, each time leaving out one observation and predicting it.

k-fold cross-validation

Splitting the data into k folds, and using each fold once as the validation set for a model trained on the others.

Bootstrap

Estimating a statistic’s sampling distribution by recomputing it on resamples drawn with replacement.

Data leakage

Information from the data used to evaluate a model getting into the model, which makes the evaluation optimistic.

Blocked (grouped) cross-validation

Cross-validation whose folds keep related observations together: consecutive samples, or samples from the same group.

Soft sensor

A model that estimates a hard-to-measure quality from process measurements that are easy to get.











NoteWant to read more?






James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition), chapter 5, “Resampling Methods”.
Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, sections 7.10 and 7.11, including “The Wrong and Right Way to Do Cross-validation”.
Sebastian Raschka, “Model Evaluation, Model Selection, and Algorithm Selection in Machine Learning”, 2018, arXiv:1811.12808. A readable survey of the whole topic.
Petr Kadlec, Bogdan Gabrys and Sibylle Strandt, “Data-driven Soft Sensors in the process industry”, Computers & Chemical Engineering 33(4), 2009, doi:10.1016/j.compchemeng.2008.12.012. A review of soft sensors, written for chemical engineers.

title: Logistic and multinomial regression
text:
Module 7 · Lesson 4 of 14 Week 107 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The reactor’s high-temperature alarm goes off a few times a week. Half the time it’s a false alarm: a load change that the controller brings back within minutes. The other half, something is wrong: the cooling has dropped, the feed has surged, or the cooling-water valve is sticking. The engineers labeled 800 past alarms with the cause they found afterwards, and each alarm comes with six measurements from the 10 minutes after it:
Lesson 3’s nearest neighbors misdiagnosed 20% of them. This lesson models the probabilities directly: first, the probability that an alarm is a real fault, with logistic regression, which you met in Module 2; then, the probability of each of the four causes, with its generalization to many classes, multinomial logistic regression.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Logistic and multinomial regression
text:
Real fault or false alarm?
For a 0/1 response, logistic regression models the probability p(x) = P(Y = 1 \mid x) through its log-odds, which it takes to be linear in the predictors:

\log \frac{p(x)}{1 - p(x)} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p,
\qquad
p(x) = \frac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots}} .

A one-unit increase in x_j adds \beta_j to the log-odds, which multiplies the odds by e^{\beta_j}, the odds ratio. The coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood, with glm(..., family = binomial).
The setup code reads the alarms, makes “normal” the first level of cause, and adds a 0/1 column fault: 1 for a real fault, 0 for a false alarm.












Your turn. Fit a logistic regression of fault on the temperature deviation alone, and find the odds ratio for each extra degree.









Logistic regression is family = binomial.


fit1 <- glm(fault ~ temp_dev_C, family = binomial, data = faults)
exp(coef(fit1))
An odds ratio of 3.41: each extra degree above the set point multiplies the odds that the alarm is real by 3.4. At the set point itself, the odds are 0.52 (the exponentiated intercept), a probability of 0.52/1.52 = 34\%. An odds ratio isn’t a ratio of probabilities: going from odds of 0.52 to 1.76 (one degree higher) moves the probability from 34% to 64%, but the same factor moves 90% only to 97%.





fit1 <- glm(fault ~ temp_dev_C, family = binomial, data = faults)
g <- data.frame(temp_dev_C = seq(-2.5, 4.5, by = 0.05))
g$p <- predict(fit1, g, type = "response")
ggplot(faults, aes(temp_dev_C, fault)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.04, width = 0, color = "grey60", size = 0.8, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = g, aes(y = p), color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Temperature deviation (°C)", y = "P(real fault)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: Logistic and multinomial regression
section: Predicted probabilities and the decision boundary
text:
Predicted probabilities and the decision boundary
Temperature alone leaves a lot of overlap. A sticking valve announces itself by the valve’s restlessness, so the valve’s SD should help.
Your turn. Fit fault ~ temp_dev_C + valve_sd_pct, and predict the probability of a real fault for the first three alarms.









type = "response" gives probabilities. The default, type = "link", gives log-odds.


fit2 <- glm(fault ~ temp_dev_C + valve_sd_pct, family = binomial, data = faults)
predict(fit2, faults[1:3, ], type = "response")
0.78, 0.95 and 0.18. Alarm A001 (a loss of cooling, as Lesson 3 found the hard way) is probably real, at 78%. The usual rule turns a probability into a class at 0.5, but the cut-off is a choice: if a missed fault costs much more than a false alarm, it should be lower. Lesson 6 is about choosing it.




The decision boundary is where p(x) = 0.5, which is where the log-odds are 0: \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 = 0. That’s a straight line. Logistic regression is a linear classifier: however curved its probability surface, the boundary between its classes is a straight line (a plane, in more dimensions).
Your turn. Solve \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{temp} + \beta_2 \cdot \text{valve SD} = 0 for the valve SD, and find the boundary line’s intercept and slope.









valve SD = -\beta_0/\beta_2 - (\beta_1/\beta_2)\,temp. The slope uses \beta_1, which is b[[2]].


b <- coef(glm(fault ~ temp_dev_C + valve_sd_pct, family = binomial, data = faults))
c(intercept = -b[[1]] / b[[3]], slope = -b[[2]] / b[[3]])
The boundary is valve SD = 1.88 - 0.89 \times temperature deviation. At the set point, a valve SD above 1.88% tips the call to “real fault”; at 1 °C above it, 0.99% is enough. The two measurements trade off against each other along a straight line, shown below.





b <- coef(glm(fault ~ temp_dev_C + valve_sd_pct, family = binomial, data = faults))
ggplot(faults, aes(temp_dev_C, valve_sd_pct, color = factor(fault, labels = c("false alarm", "real fault")))) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_abline(intercept = -b[1] / b[3], slope = -b[2] / b[3], linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("grey60", "#C2416C"), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 8)) +
  labs(x = "Temperature deviation (°C)", y = "Valve position SD (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Logistic and multinomial regression
text:
All six measurements
Your turn. Fit the logistic regression with all six measurements, and look at the temperature and pressure rows of the coefficient table.









The response is the 0/1 column fault.


fit6 <- glm(reformulate(vars, response = "fault"), family = binomial, data = faults)
round(summary(fit6)$coefficients[c("temp_dev_C", "pressure_dev_bar"), ], 3)
Temperature is strongly significant, with a coefficient of 1.11 and a z of 5.2. Pressure’s coefficient is -0.10 with a standard error of 2.57, and a p-value of 0.97: on its own, pressure is a decent predictor, but it adds nothing once temperature is known. The two are correlated at 0.87 within every class (a hotter reactor has a higher vapor pressure), so the model can’t tell their effects apart. This is Module 2’s multicollinearity: coefficients that are unstable and hard to interpret, while the predictions are fine. For prediction, it’s mostly harmless. For inference, it means “pressure doesn’t matter” is the wrong conclusion.




Your turn. Compare the 10-fold CV error rates of the two-measurement and six-measurement models, classifying an alarm as real when \hat p > 0.5.









Classify as a real fault when the probability is over 0.5.


cv_glm <- function(formula) {
  p <- numeric(nrow(faults))
  for (j in 1:10) {
    fit <- glm(formula, family = binomial, data = faults[fold != j, ])
    p[fold == j] <- predict(fit, faults[fold == j, ], type = "response")
  }
  mean((p > 0.5) != faults$fault)
}
c(two = cv_glm(fault ~ temp_dev_C + valve_sd_pct), six = cv_glm(reformulate(vars, "fault")))
21.4% wrong with two measurements, 18.6% with six. The feed deviation and the valve position, both strongly significant in the six-measurement model, catch faults that the temperature and the valve’s SD miss.

title: Logistic and multinomial regression
text:
Multinomial logistic regression
Knowing that an alarm is real isn’t enough: the operator needs to know what to do, and the response to a cooling loss (open the valve, cut the feed) is different from the response to a sticking valve (switch to manual). With K classes, multinomial logistic regression picks one class as the baseline (here, “normal”) and models the log-odds of each other class against it, each with its own coefficients:

\log \frac{P(Y = k \mid x)}{P(Y = \text{normal} \mid x)} = \beta_{k0} + \beta_{k1} x_1 + \cdots + \beta_{kp} x_p, \qquad k = 1, \ldots, K - 1 .

That’s K - 1 logistic regressions, fitted together so that the probabilities add up to 1. In R, nnet::multinom() fits it. (The function is in the nnet package because the model is a neural network with no hidden layer, as Lesson 11 shows.)
Your turn. Fit the multinomial model of cause on all six measurements, and find the odds ratio, for “cooling loss” against “normal”, for each extra degree of coolant temperature rise.









The coefficient is in the row "cooling_loss" and the column "coolant_dt_C".


mn <- nnet::multinom(reformulate(vars, response = "cause"), data = faults, trace = FALSE)
round(coef(mn), 3)
exp(coef(mn)["cooling_loss", "coolant_dt_C"])
The coefficient matrix has 3 rows (one per cause, against “normal”) and 7 columns. The odds ratio is 0.40: each extra degree of warming across the jacket cuts the odds of “cooling loss” against “normal” by 60%. It makes physical sense: when the cooling water flow drops, the alarm comes with less heat being carried away. For a feed upset, the same coefficient is positive (+1.06): more feed, more heat of reaction, more heat carried away. One measurement, opposite signs for two causes: that’s how the model tells them apart.

title: Logistic and multinomial regression
text:
The softmax function
The K - 1 log-odds turn into probabilities with the softmax function. Give the baseline a linear predictor of \eta_{\text{normal}} = 0, and each other class its \eta_k = \beta_{k0} + \beta_k^\top x. Then

P(Y = k \mid x) = \frac{e^{\eta_k}}{\sum_{l} e^{\eta_l}} .

Each probability is positive, and they add up to 1. The same function turns a neural network’s outputs into class probabilities, in Lesson 11 and in almost every classifier you’ll meet.
Your turn. Compute alarm A001’s four probabilities by hand from the coefficients, and check them against predict(mn, faults[1, ], type = "probs").









Divide each exp(eta) by the sum of all of them.


mn <- nnet::multinom(reformulate(vars, response = "cause"), data = faults, trace = FALSE)
x1 <- c(1, unlist(faults[1, vars]))
eta <- c(normal = 0, coef(mn) %*% x1)
names(eta)[2:4] <- rownames(coef(mn))
exp(eta) / sum(exp(eta))
45% normal, 29% cooling loss, 2% feed upset and 24% sticking valve, exactly what predict() gives. The model would call A001 “normal”, like kNN did, but only just. The probabilities say more than the class: an operator told “45% false alarm, 29% cooling loss, 24% sticking valve” knows to check the cooling water and the valve, not to silence the alarm.

title: Logistic and multinomial regression
text:
Cross-validating the diagnosis
Your turn. Cross-validate the multinomial model on the same 10 folds, then make the confusion matrix of predicted against actual causes.









Predict the held-out fold, faults[fold == j, ].


pred <- factor(rep(NA, nrow(faults)), levels = levels(faults$cause))
for (j in 1:10) {
  fit <- nnet::multinom(reformulate(vars, "cause"), data = faults[fold != j, ], trace = FALSE)
  pred[fold == j] <- predict(fit, faults[fold == j, ])
}
print(table(predicted = pred, actual = faults$cause))
mean(pred != faults$cause)
20.1% misdiagnosed, the same as kNN. The confusion matrix shows where: 78 real faults are called “normal” (24 cooling losses, 31 feed upsets and 23 sticking valves), and only 52 of the 100 sticking valves are recognized. The sticking valve is the hardest: its average temperature and pressure are close to normal, and its signature, a restless valve, also shows up, more weakly, in the other faults. The next lesson finds a better model for it.










NoteGo deeper: why the baseline doesn’t matter





Choosing “normal” as the baseline only changes how the coefficients are written, not the model. If \beta_k are the coefficients against “normal”, the coefficients of class k against class l are \beta_k - \beta_l, because

\log \frac{P(k \mid x)}{P(l \mid x)} = \log \frac{P(k \mid x)}{P(\text{normal} \mid x)} - \log \frac{P(l \mid x)}{P(\text{normal} \mid x)} .

The fitted probabilities are identical whichever baseline you choose. Some books use the symmetric form, with coefficients for all K classes and a constraint (they sum to zero, say) to make them identifiable. That’s how glmnet fits multinomial models, in Lesson 8, where the penalty makes the symmetric form the natural one. The softmax function is the same either way: adding the same number to every \eta_k doesn’t change e^{\eta_k}/\sum_l e^{\eta_l}.

title: Logistic and multinomial regression
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Curved boundaries. Multinomial regression’s boundaries are straight, because its log-odds are linear in x. Add the square of each measurement as a predictor, and cross-validate again.









Squares: ^2. paste0() writes terms like I(temp_dev_C^2).


fq <- reformulate(c(vars, paste0("I(", vars, "^2)")), response = "cause")
pred <- factor(rep(NA, nrow(faults)), levels = levels(faults$cause))
for (j in 1:10) {
  fit <- nnet::multinom(fq, data = faults[fold != j, ], trace = FALSE, maxit = 500)
  pred[fold == j] <- predict(fit, faults[fold == j, ])
}
mean(pred != faults$cause)
16.9%, down from 20.1%. Squared terms make each log-odds a quadratic function of the measurements, so the boundaries can curve. The biggest gain is for the sticking valve, whose measurements are more variable than the other causes’ rather than shifted: a curved boundary can wrap around a spread-out cloud, and a straight one can’t. maxit = 500 gives the optimizer more iterations, because 13 coefficients per cause take longer to converge. The next lesson reaches curved boundaries another way, by modeling each class’s spread directly.




Challenge 2 · Which measurement matters most? A likelihood ratio test compares the full multinomial model with one that drops a measurement: the drop in deviance has a chi-squared distribution with 3 degrees of freedom (one coefficient per non-baseline cause). Test the coolant temperature rise.









Dropping one measurement removes 3 coefficients, one for each cause against “normal”.


full <- nnet::multinom(reformulate(vars, "cause"), data = faults, trace = FALSE)
reduced <- nnet::multinom(reformulate(setdiff(vars, "coolant_dt_C"), "cause"), data = faults, trace = FALSE)
lr <- deviance(reduced) - deviance(full)
c(LR = lr, p = pchisq(lr, df = 3, lower.tail = FALSE))
A deviance drop of 231 on 3 degrees of freedom, p \approx 10^{-49}. Dropping each measurement in turn gives a ranking: the valve’s SD (253), the coolant temperature rise (231), the feed deviation (121), the valve position (73), the temperature (28) and the pressure (0.05). In the yes/no model, the coolant rise didn’t matter at all (p = 0.60); for telling the causes apart, it’s the second most important measurement. And pressure adds nothing that temperature doesn’t already say.

title: Logistic and multinomial regression
text:
Quick quiz

1. A logistic regression coefficient is 1.23. What does a one-unit increase in that predictor do?

Adds 1.23 to the probability
Multiplies the odds by e^{1.23} = 3.4
Multiplies the probability by 3.4


Coefficients act on the log-odds. Their effect on the probability depends on where you start.



2. What shape is a logistic regression’s decision boundary between two classes?

An S-shaped curve
A straight line (a plane, in more dimensions)
A circle


The boundary is where the log-odds are zero, and the log-odds are linear in x.



3. Pressure had a p-value of 0.97 in the six-measurement model. What’s the right conclusion?

Pressure is unrelated to faults
Pressure adds nothing once temperature is known, because the two are highly correlated
The model is wrong


On its own, pressure predicts faults well. It’s redundant given temperature.



4. With 4 classes and 6 predictors, how many coefficients does a multinomial logistic model have?

7
28
21


3 non-baseline classes, each with an intercept and 6 slopes.



5. What does the softmax function do?

Picks the largest class
Turns a set of linear predictors into probabilities that are positive and add up to 1
Smooths the decision boundary


P(k) = e^{\eta_k}/\sum_l e^{\eta_l}.



6. Which cause did the multinomial model diagnose worst?

Normal
Feed upset
Sticking valve


Only 52 of 100. Its signature, a restless valve, isn’t captured well by a linear model.

title: Logistic and multinomial regression
text:
Wrap-up
You can now model class probabilities, for two classes or many. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Logistic regression models the log-odds as linear in the predictors. Its coefficients are log odds ratios: each degree of temperature deviation multiplies the odds of a real fault by 3.4.
Its decision boundary is linear: for two measurements, valve SD = 1.88 - 0.89 \times temperature deviation.
Correlated predictors make individual coefficients unstable (pressure’s SE was 2.6) without harming the predictions. The six-measurement model misclassified 18.6% of alarms as real or false.
Multinomial logistic regression fits K - 1 log-odds against a baseline, and the softmax turns them into probabilities.
Diagnosing the cause was 20.1% wrong, with the sticking valve hardest. Squared terms, which curve the boundaries, brought it down.
Likelihood ratio tests rank the measurements: the valve’s SD and the coolant temperature rise matter most for telling the causes apart.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download process_faults.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Plot the probabilities. For the multinomial model, plot each alarm’s predicted probability of its true cause, by cause, as box plots. Which cause gets the least confident predictions?
A different baseline. Refit with “sticking_valve” as the baseline (relevel()), and check that the predicted probabilities don’t change. How do the coefficients change?
Interactions. Add the interaction temp_dev_C:valve_sd_pct to the binary model. Is it significant? Does it improve the CV error?
broom. Use broom::tidy(mn, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) to get odds ratios with confidence intervals for every cause.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Logistic regression

A model for a binary response in which the log-odds of the event are linear in the predictors.

Log-odds (logit)

\log\big(p/(1 - p)\big).

Odds ratio

The factor by which the odds are multiplied when a predictor increases by one unit, e^{\beta_j}.

Decision boundary

The set of inputs where a classifier is undecided between two classes. For logistic regression, a line or plane.

Linear classifier

A classifier whose decision boundaries are linear in the inputs.

Multinomial logistic regression

The generalization of logistic regression to more than two unordered classes, with the log-odds of each class against a baseline linear in the predictors.

Softmax function

The function e^{\eta_k}/\sum_l e^{\eta_l}, which turns linear predictors into class probabilities.

Confusion matrix

A table of predicted against actual classes.











NoteWant to read more?






James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition), sections 4.1 to 4.3, on logistic regression, including multinomial logistic regression (section 4.3.5).
Alan Agresti, An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis (3rd edition, Wiley, 2019), chapter 6, “Multicategory Logit Models”.
William Venables and Brian Ripley, Modern Applied Statistics with S (4th edition, Springer, 2002), section 7.3, by the authors of nnet::multinom().

title: Evaluating classifiers
text:
Module 7 · Lesson 6 of 14 Week 109 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The plant has 125 pumps at two sites, and each month the reliability team records their condition: vibration, bearing temperature, motor current, seal flush pressure and hours since the last service. When a pump fails unexpectedly, it costs about €20,000: lost production, emergency repairs, and sometimes a seal fire. An inspection, which catches most failures before they happen, costs about €800. The team wants a model that says which pumps to inspect this month.
pump_failures.csv has 3,000 monthly records, each labeled with whether the pump failed within the next 30 days. Only about 1 in 15 did. That makes this a different problem from the alarms of Lessons 3 to 5, where the classes were balanced: with rare events, the error rate, the measure used so far, can be badly misleading. This lesson is about better measures, and about turning a model’s probabilities into decisions.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Evaluating classifiers
section: The setup, and a useless model
text:
The setup, and a useless model
The setup code drops the 150 records whose bearing temperature sensor was offline, splits the remaining 2,850 at random into 1,900 for training and 950 for testing, and fits a logistic regression on the training set. p holds its predicted failure probabilities for the 950 test records.













Your turn. Find the share of test records that failed, and the accuracy of a “model” that predicts that no pump ever fails.









“Never fails” predicts 0 for every record. It’s right whenever test$failed == 0.


c(failure_rate = mean(test$failed),
  accuracy_of_never = mean(test$failed == 0))
6.8% of the test records failed, so predicting “no failure” every time is 93.2% accurate, and completely useless: it never catches a failure. Any model’s accuracy has to be judged against this, and for rare events, accuracy hardly moves when the model gets better or worse at the thing that matters.

title: Evaluating classifiers
text:
The confusion matrix
A classifier that flags a pump when \hat p \ge t makes two kinds of mistakes, and the confusion matrix counts them:




Actually failed
Didn’t fail




Flagged
true positive (TP)
false positive (FP)


Not flagged
false negative (FN)
true negative (TN)



Your turn. Make the confusion matrix for the logistic model at the usual threshold of 0.5.









Flag a pump when its probability is at least 0.5.


flag <- p >= 0.5
table(flagged = flag, failed = test$failed)
Of the 65 failures, the model flags 19 and misses 46. It also flags 7 pumps that were fine. Its accuracy is (878 + 19)/950 = 94.4\%, barely better than “never fails”. But it does catch 19 failures that “never fails” would miss, at the cost of 7 needless inspections. Accuracy can’t see that difference; the confusion matrix can.




From the four counts come the measures that matter:








Measure
Formula
The question it answers




Sensitivity (recall, true positive rate)
TP / (TP + FN)
Of the pumps that failed, what share did we flag?


Specificity (true negative rate)
TN / (TN + FP)
Of the pumps that were fine, what share did we leave alone?


Precision (positive predictive value)
TP / (TP + FP)
Of the pumps we flagged, what share were really going to fail?


False positive rate
FP / (FP + TN) = 1 − specificity
Of the pumps that were fine, what share did we flag?



Medicine speaks of sensitivity and specificity; information retrieval of precision and recall. They’re the same four counts, seen from different sides.
Your turn. Write a function that computes sensitivity, specificity and precision for any threshold, and use it at 0.5.









Precision divides the true positives by everything flagged: sum(flag).


rates <- function(t) {
  flag <- p >= t
  y <- test$failed == 1
  c(sensitivity = sum(flag & y) / sum(y),
    specificity = sum(!flag & !y) / sum(!y),
    precision = sum(flag & y) / sum(flag))
}
rates(0.5)
A sensitivity of 29%, a specificity of 99.2% and a precision of 73%. When this model flags a pump, it’s usually right, but it flags too few: 71% of the failures go unflagged. For the reliability team, that’s the wrong balance.

title: Evaluating classifiers
text:
Moving the threshold
Nothing forces the threshold to be 0.5. Lowering it flags more pumps: more failures caught (higher sensitivity), more needless inspections (lower specificity and precision).
Your turn. Compute the three rates at a threshold of 0.1.









Call rates(0.1).


rates <- function(t) {
  flag <- p >= t
  y <- test$failed == 1
  c(sensitivity = sum(flag & y) / sum(y),
    specificity = sum(!flag & !y) / sum(!y),
    precision = sum(flag & y) / sum(flag))
}
rbind(t0.5 = rates(0.5), t0.1 = rates(0.1))
At 0.1, the model catches 68% of the failures (44 of 65), against 29%. The price: specificity falls to 90.6%, and precision to 35%, so about two of every three inspections find nothing wrong. Whether that’s a good trade depends on what the mistakes cost, which is a question for the reliability team, not for the model.

title: Evaluating classifiers
section: The ROC curve and the AUC
text:
The ROC curve and the AUC
Every threshold gives a pair (false positive rate, sensitivity). Tracing them all, from t = 1 (flag nothing) to t = 0 (flag everything), draws the ROC curve (receiver operating characteristic, a name from radar engineering):

r <- pROC::roc(test$failed, p, quiet = TRUE)
roc_df <- data.frame(fpr = 1 - r$specificities, tpr = r$sensitivities)
pts <- data.frame(t = c(0.5, 0.1), fpr = c(mean(p[test$failed == 0] >= 0.5), mean(p[test$failed == 0] >= 0.1)),
                  tpr = c(mean(p[test$failed == 1] >= 0.5), mean(p[test$failed == 1] >= 0.1)))
ggplot(roc_df[order(roc_df$fpr, roc_df$tpr), ], aes(fpr, tpr)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_step(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = pts, size = 2.5, color = "#3A1F35") +
  geom_text(data = pts, aes(label = paste("t =", t)), nudge_x = 0.13, size = 3.5) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "False positive rate (1 − specificity)", y = "Sensitivity") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








A perfect classifier’s curve goes straight up the left side to the top-left corner; a useless one follows the diagonal. The area under the curve (AUC) summarizes it in one number, from 0.5 (useless) to 1 (perfect). It measures how well the model ranks the records, regardless of any threshold.
Your turn. Compute the AUC with pROC::roc() and pROC::auc().









The predictor is the model’s probabilities, p.


r <- pROC::roc(response = test$failed, predictor = p, quiet = TRUE)
as.numeric(pROC::auc(r))
0.852. pROC::ci.auc(r) gives a 95% interval of 0.79 to 0.91: with only 65 failures in the test set, the AUC itself is uncertain. Rules of thumb call 0.8 to 0.9 “good”, but the AUC is best used to compare models on the same data, not as a grade.




The AUC has a direct meaning: it’s the probability that a randomly chosen failure gets a higher predicted probability than a randomly chosen non-failure. That’s the Mann-Whitney (Wilcoxon rank-sum) statistic, and it gives a way to compute the AUC from ranks.
Your turn. Compute the AUC from the ranks of p: the sum of the failures’ ranks, minus its smallest possible value, divided by the number of failure/non-failure pairs.









There are n_1 \times n_0 pairs.


rk <- rank(p)
n1 <- sum(test$failed == 1)
n0 <- sum(test$failed == 0)
(sum(rk[test$failed == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
0.852 again, exactly. Of the 65 \times 885 = 57{,}525 pairs of a failure and a non-failure, the model ranks the failure higher in 85% of them. This is why the AUC ignores the threshold, and also why it can’t tell you whether the probabilities are right: multiplying every \hat p by 10 leaves the ranks, and the AUC, unchanged.

title: Evaluating classifiers
section: Precision and recall with rare events
text:
Precision and recall with rare events
The ROC curve’s horizontal axis, the false positive rate, divides by the 885 healthy pumps, so even a lot of needless inspections look like a small rate. For rare events, the precision-recall view is often more honest: as you flag more pumps to raise recall, what share of your inspections are worth it?
Your turn. Sort the test records from the highest \hat p to the lowest, and find the threshold that first reaches 80% recall, with the precision and the number of pumps flagged there.









80% recall is recall >= 0.8.


o <- order(p, decreasing = TRUE)
caught <- cumsum(test$failed[o])
recall <- caught / sum(test$failed)
precision <- caught / seq_along(o)
k <- which(recall >= 0.8)[1]
c(threshold = p[o][k], precision = precision[k], flagged = k)
To catch 80% of the failures (52 of 65), the team would have to inspect 302 of the 950 pumps, with a threshold of 0.028, and only 17% of those inspections would find a pump about to fail. On the ROC curve, the same point is a comfortable-looking false positive rate of 28%. The precision tells the reliability team what their week will look like.

title: Evaluating classifiers
text:
Choosing a threshold from costs
The right threshold comes from the costs. If a missed failure costs C_{FN} and an inspection costs C_{FP}, inspecting a pump with failure probability p is worth it when the expected saving beats the inspection’s cost:

p \cdot C_{FN} > C_{FP} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p > \frac{C_{FP}}{C_{FN}} .

This assumes that an inspection always prevents the failure, and costs the same whether or not the pump was going to fail. With €800 and €20,000, the threshold is 0.04: a pump with a 1-in-25 chance of failing is worth inspecting. That assumes the probabilities are right, which the next step checks.
Your turn. Compute the total cost on the test set, for thresholds from 0.01 to 0.5: €800 for every pump flagged, plus €20,000 for every failure missed. Find the cheapest threshold, and compare its cost with flagging nothing and flagging everything.









A missed failure is a pump that wasn’t flagged and did fail: test$failed == 1.


thr <- seq(0.01, 0.5, by = 0.01)
cost <- sapply(thr, function(t) {
  flag <- p >= t
  800 * sum(flag) + 20000 * sum(!flag & test$failed == 1)
})
c(best_threshold = thr[which.min(cost)], best_cost = min(cost), cost_at_0.04 = cost[thr == 0.04],
  flag_none = 20000 * sum(test$failed), flag_all = 800 * nrow(test))
The cheapest threshold on the test set is 0.07, at €471,200, and the theoretical 0.04 costs €484,800, within 3%. Doing nothing would cost €1.3 million, and inspecting every pump €760,000. The model saves €275,000 to €289,000 against the better of the two simple policies (inspecting everything), on 950 pump-months. With only 65 failures, the cost curve is bumpy, and its exact minimum is partly luck: the theoretical threshold, which comes from the costs alone, is the more trustworthy choice, if the probabilities are calibrated.





thr <- seq(0.01, 0.5, by = 0.01)
cost <- sapply(thr, function(t) { flag <- p >= t; 800 * sum(flag) + 20000 * sum(!flag & test$failed == 1) })
ggplot(data.frame(thr, cost), aes(thr, cost / 1000)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.04, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "Threshold", y = "Total cost (thousand €)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: Evaluating classifiers
text:
Are the probabilities right?
A model is calibrated if, among the records it gives a probability near p, about a share p really fail. The AUC can’t check this (it only uses ranks), but cost-based thresholds depend on it.
Your turn. Split the test records into five equal groups by \hat p, and compare each group’s average predicted probability with its observed failure rate.









Five groups need the quantiles at 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1: by = 0.2.


group <- cut(p, breaks = quantile(p, probs = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2)), include.lowest = TRUE)
round(cbind(predicted = tapply(p, group, mean), observed = tapply(test$failed, group, mean)), 3)
The top group’s predicted 24.7% matches its observed 25.3%, and the middle groups are close. In the bottom two, the model predicts 0.2% and 0.5%, but 1.6% and 2.1% failed: 7 failures in pumps the model was nearly sure about. With 190 records per group, those differences are partly noise, but they’re worth a closer look. The next challenge finds where they come from.










NoteGo deeper: scoring rules





Thresholded measures (sensitivity, precision) depend on t, and the AUC ignores the probabilities’ values. A proper scoring rule judges the probabilities themselves, and is minimized, on average, by the true probabilities. The two common ones:

the Brier score, \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (\hat p_i - y_i)^2, the mean squared error of the probabilities. Here it’s 0.044, against 0.064 for predicting the training failure rate for every pump;
the log loss, -\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \big[y_i \log \hat p_i + (1 - y_i)\log(1 - \hat p_i)\big], the negative log-likelihood per record, which logistic regression minimizes on the training data.

Both reward calibration and discrimination at once. Gneiting and Raftery’s “Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation” (Journal of the American Statistical Association, 2007) is the standard reference.

title: Evaluating classifiers
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Weighting the rare class. A common remedy for imbalance is to give the failures more weight in the fit. Refit the logistic regression on the training set with a weight of 10 for each failure, and compare its AUC and its average predicted probability with the original model’s.









Give each failure a weight of 10.


tr <- pumps[train, ]
w <- ifelse(tr$failed == 1, 10, 1)
fit_w <- suppressWarnings(glm(failed ~ vibration_mm_s + bearing_temp_C + hours_since_service + pump_type + seal_flush_bar + motor_current_pct,
                              family = binomial, data = tr, weights = w))
p_w <- predict(fit_w, test, type = "response")
c(auc_original = as.numeric(pROC::auc(pROC::roc(test$failed, p, quiet = TRUE))),
  auc_weighted = as.numeric(pROC::auc(pROC::roc(test$failed, p_w, quiet = TRUE))),
  mean_p_original = mean(p), mean_p_weighted = mean(p_w))
The AUC hardly changes (0.852 both ways), but the average predicted probability jumps from 6% to 22%, while the real failure rate is still 6.8%. Weighting the failures is, roughly, the same as moving the threshold: it changes where the 0.5 line falls, not how well the model ranks. It also destroys the calibration, so the weighted model’s “22%” means nothing as a probability. For a model like logistic regression, it’s usually better to fit it unweighted and choose the threshold from the costs. (glm() warns about non-integer successes with weights; suppressWarnings() hides it.)




Challenge 2 · Calibrated everywhere? Compare the average predicted probability with the observed failure rate at each site, in the test set.









Group by test$site.


round(cbind(predicted = tapply(p, test$site, mean), observed = tapply(test$failed, test$site, mean)), 3)
At North, the model predicts 7.6% and 7.2% failed: fine. At South, it predicts 3.7%, but 6.3% failed: the model under-predicts South’s failures by almost half. At a threshold of 0.1, it catches 73% of North’s failures but only 60% of South’s. The model didn’t use the site, and something about South’s measurements misleads it. (The reliability team later found the cause: South’s vibration sensors are a different brand, which reads about 25% lower.) An overall calibration check can hide a group the model serves badly. Lesson 14 comes back to this.

title: Evaluating classifiers
text:
Quick quiz

1. 7% of records are failures. A model is 93% accurate. What do you know?

It’s a good model
Nothing yet: “never fails” is also 93% accurate
It catches 93% of failures


With rare events, compare against the trivial model, and look at sensitivity and precision.



2. What does sensitivity measure?

The share of actual failures that the model flags
The share of flagged pumps that actually fail
The share of healthy pumps left alone


The second is precision, the third specificity.



3. What happens when you lower the threshold?

Sensitivity and specificity both rise
Sensitivity rises and specificity falls
The AUC rises


More pumps are flagged. The AUC doesn’t depend on the threshold.



4. What does an AUC of 0.85 mean?

85% of predictions are correct
A random failure gets a higher predicted probability than a random non-failure 85% of the time
The model is 85% calibrated


It’s a rank statistic, the Mann-Whitney probability.



5. A miss costs €20,000 and an inspection €800. Above what probability should a pump be inspected, if the probabilities are calibrated?

0.5
0.04
0.96


800 / 20{,}000 = 0.04.



6. Weighting the failures by 10 left the AUC unchanged. What did it change?

Nothing
The probabilities, which became much too high, so they’re no longer calibrated
The ranking of the pumps


It moved the 0.5 line, much as lowering the threshold would.

title: Evaluating classifiers
text:
Wrap-up
You can now judge a classifier by what matters, and turn its probabilities into decisions. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Accuracy misleads with rare events: “never fails” is 93.2% accurate.
The confusion matrix gives sensitivity, specificity and precision. At 0.5, the pump model caught 29% of failures, with 73% precision.
Moving the threshold trades sensitivity for specificity: at 0.1, it caught 68%.
The ROC curve traces every threshold, and its AUC, 0.852, is the probability of ranking a failure above a non-failure.
Precision-recall shows the workload: 80% recall meant 302 inspections, 17% of them useful.
Costs choose the threshold: C_{FP}/C_{FN} = 0.04 saved €275,000 on the test set against the best simple policy, if the probabilities are calibrated.
Calibration checks the probabilities themselves. They were good overall, but South’s failures were under-predicted by almost half.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download pump_failures.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install pROC.

Plot the curves. plot(pROC::roc(...)) draws the ROC curve. Draw the precision-recall curve yourself from precision and recall, and compare the two.
Compare two models. Fit a second model that adds site as a predictor. Compare the two ROC curves with pROC::roc.test(). Is the difference significant?
Cross-validate the AUC. Instead of one test set, use 10-fold CV with folds that keep each pump together (grouped by pump). How does the AUC compare?
A calibration plot. Plot the observed failure rate against the predicted probability in 10 groups, with the diagonal. ggplot2::geom_smooth() on the 0/1 outcomes against \hat p gives a smooth version.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Confusion matrix

A table of predicted against actual classes, counting true and false positives and negatives.

Sensitivity (recall, true positive rate)

TP / (TP + FN): the share of actual positives that are flagged.

Specificity

TN / (TN + FP): the share of actual negatives that aren’t flagged.

Precision (positive predictive value)

TP / (TP + FP): the share of flagged cases that are actual positives.

ROC curve

Sensitivity against the false positive rate, over all thresholds.

AUC

The area under the ROC curve: the probability that a random positive is ranked above a random negative.

Calibration

Agreement between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies.

Class imbalance

When one class is much rarer than the other, which makes accuracy a poor measure.











NoteWant to read more?






James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition), section 4.4.2, on the confusion matrix, thresholds and the ROC curve.
Tom Fawcett, “An introduction to ROC analysis”, Pattern Recognition Letters 27(8), 2006, doi:10.1016/j.patrec.2005.10.010. The standard tutorial.
Takaya Saito and Marc Rehmsmeier, “The Precision-Recall Plot Is More Informative than the ROC Plot When Evaluating Binary Classifiers on Imbalanced Datasets”, PLOS ONE 10(3), 2015, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0118432.
Charles Elkan, “The Foundations of Cost-Sensitive Learning”, IJCAI 2001. The derivation of the cost-based threshold, and why weighting and moving the threshold are related.

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
Module 7 · Lesson 8 of 14 Week 111 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Ridge regression kept every predictor and shrank them all. That’s ideal for spectra, where every wavelength carries a little of the signal. But the soft sensor of Lesson 2 is a different kind of problem: 20 candidate tags, of which the chemistry says only four should matter. There, you’d like a method that selects: sets the useless coefficients to exactly zero, and leaves a model that an engineer can read.
Module 2 selected predictors with stepwise searches, which are greedy, unstable and hard to cross-validate properly. The lasso (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) does it in one smooth optimization, with a single tuning parameter. Its only change from ridge is the penalty:
\hat\beta^{\text{lasso}} = \arg\min_\beta \; \sum_{i=1}^n \Big(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_j x_{ij}\beta_j\Big)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j| .
That small change, |\beta_j| instead of \beta_j^2, makes coefficients hit exactly zero, as the Go deeper box explains.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
The lasso path
The setup code builds the soft sensor’s predictor matrix Xs (the log hydrogen ratio and the 19 other tags) and response ys (log MI), and the time blocks from Lesson 2: 10 folds of 50 consecutive samples. It also loads the spectra and the pump data, for later.












Your turn. Fit the lasso path to the soft-sensor data with glmnet(..., alpha = 1), and find the order in which the tags enter the model as \lambda falls: for each tag, the largest \lambda at which its coefficient is nonzero.









The lasso is alpha = 1 (it’s glmnet’s default, too).


fit <- glmnet::glmnet(Xs, ys, alpha = 1)
enter <- apply(as.matrix(fit$beta) != 0, 1, function(nz) fit$lambda[which(nz)[1]])
head(sort(enter, decreasing = TRUE), 5)
The hydrogen ratio enters first, at \lambda = 0.83, then the reactor temperature (0.097), the ethylene pressure (0.056) and the comonomer ratio (0.032): the four chemistry tags, in order of importance, before any of the others. The fifth, the isopentane concentration, comes in at 0.014, by which point the lasso is starting to fit noise. fit$beta is the matrix of coefficients, one column per \lambda.





fit <- glmnet(Xs, ys, alpha = 1)
B <- as.matrix(fit$beta)
paths <- data.frame(loglam = rep(log(fit$lambda), each = 20), beta = as.vector(B),
                    tag = rep(rownames(B), length(fit$lambda)))
paths$group <- ifelse(paths$tag %in% c("log_h2", "reactor_temp_C", "c2_pressure_bar", "comonomer_ratio"), paths$tag, "the other 16 tags")
ggplot(paths, aes(loglam, beta, group = tag, color = group)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey80") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(log_h2 = "#C2416C", reactor_temp_C = "#2a78d6", c2_pressure_bar = "#1baf7a",
                                comonomer_ratio = "#8a5a00", `the other 16 tags` = "grey70"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "log(λ), decreasing →", y = "Coefficient") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "top")














NoteGo deeper: why the lasso gives exact zeros





Both penalized problems can be written as constrained ones: minimize the RSS subject to \sum_j \beta_j^2 \le s (ridge) or \sum_j |\beta_j| \le s (lasso). In two dimensions, ridge’s constraint region is a disk, and the lasso’s is a diamond with corners on the axes. The RSS has elliptical contours around the least-squares estimate. The solution is where the smallest contour touches the region, and an ellipse usually touches a diamond at a corner, where one coefficient is zero; a disk has no corners. Algebraically, with orthonormal predictors, the two have simple forms in terms of the least-squares \hat\beta_j: ridge gives \hat\beta_j/(1 + \lambda), a proportional shrink, and the lasso gives \text{sign}(\hat\beta_j)\,(|\hat\beta_j| - \lambda/2)_+, soft thresholding: subtract a constant, and set to zero anything that would cross zero. glmnet fits the lasso by cyclic coordinate descent, applying soft thresholding to one coefficient at a time. ISLR’s figure 6.7 draws the diamond and the disk, and its section 6.2.2 does the algebra.

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
Choosing λ, honestly
Lesson 2 found that random folds flatter models on the soft-sensor data, because neighboring samples share the catalyst drift. cv.glmnet() takes the folds you give it through foldid.
Your turn. Cross-validate the lasso with the time blocks as folds, and list the tags with nonzero coefficients at lambda.min.









The folds are the time blocks: foldid = block.


cv <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(Xs, ys, alpha = 1, foldid = block)
b <- coef(cv, s = "lambda.min")
setNames(as.numeric(b), rownames(b))[as.numeric(b) != 0]
Exactly the four chemistry tags, and none of the other 16: the lasso has rediscovered the chemistry from the data. The blocked CV RMSE at lambda.min is 0.207. With foldid, no random numbers are used, so the result is the same every time.




Your turn. Find the tags kept at lambda.1se, and compare the blocked CV RMSE at the two values of \lambda.









Compare with cv$lambda.1se.


cv <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(Xs, ys, alpha = 1, foldid = block)
b1 <- coef(cv, s = "lambda.1se")
print(rownames(b1)[as.numeric(b1) != 0])
sqrt(c(at_min = cv$cvm[cv$lambda == cv$lambda.min], at_1se = cv$cvm[cv$lambda == cv$lambda.1se]))
At lambda.1se, the comonomer ratio drops out, leaving three tags, and the CV RMSE rises from 0.207 to 0.226. cvm holds the CV mean squared errors, hence the square root. The comonomer is a real but small effect, and the one-standard-error rule, which prefers simpler models, sacrifices it. Neither choice is wrong; the rule is a heuristic. Here, the chemistry says the comonomer matters, which argues for lambda.min.

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
The lasso’s bias, and refitting
The lasso’s blocked CV RMSE, 0.207, is worse than Lesson 2’s least-squares fit on the same four tags (0.194, on the same blocks). That’s not a contradiction. The penalty shrinks the coefficients it keeps, not just the ones it drops, so the selected coefficients are biased toward zero. When the selection is right, that bias is pure cost.
Your turn. Compare the lasso’s coefficients at lambda.min with a least-squares fit of the same four tags.









Refit with the kept columns: Xs[, kept].


cv <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(Xs, ys, alpha = 1, foldid = block)
b <- as.matrix(coef(cv, s = "lambda.min"))[-1, 1]
kept <- names(b)[b != 0]
refit <- lm(ys ~ Xs[, kept])
round(rbind(lasso = b[kept], least_squares = coef(refit)[-1]), 4)
Every lasso coefficient is smaller in size than least squares’: hydrogen 0.997 against 1.035, temperature 0.083 against 0.100, and the comonomer ratio 4.2 against 8.1, half its size. The comonomer entered the path last, so it has been shrunk the most. Using the lasso to select and least squares to estimate is called the relaxed lasso (glmnet does a tuned version with relax = TRUE), and least squares on these four tags had a blocked CV RMSE of 0.194 in Lesson 2. The catch: the least-squares standard errors after selection are too small, because they ignore that the data chose the model. Honest inference after selection is a research topic of its own.

title: Lasso and elastic net
section: Correlated predictors: where the lasso struggles
text:
Correlated predictors: where the lasso struggles
The soft sensor suits the lasso: a few clear signals among independent-ish noise. The spectra are the opposite: the signal is spread over many wavelengths that are all correlated with each other.
Your turn. Fit the lasso to the spectra (the same 80 calibration samples and the same long \lambda grid as in Lesson 7), and find the number of wavelengths it keeps and the test RMSE.









The lasso is alpha = 1.


set.seed(7053)
cv_l <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = 1, lambda = lam)
b <- as.numeric(coef(cv_l, s = "lambda.min"))[-1]
