c(kept = sum(b != 0), test_rmse = sqrt(mean((y[-train] - predict(cv_l, X[-train, ], s = "lambda.min"))^2)))
41 wavelengths, and a test RMSE of 0.49, against ridge’s 0.416. Among a group of highly correlated predictors, the lasso tends to keep one or a few and drop the rest, more or less arbitrarily. On spectra, averaging over many neighboring wavelengths is what cancels the noise, and that’s what ridge does and the lasso refuses to do.




The elastic net mixes the two penalties:

\lambda \Big( \alpha \sum_j |\beta_j| + \frac{1 - \alpha}{2} \sum_j \beta_j^2 \Big),

with \alpha = 1 the lasso and \alpha = 0 ridge, which is what glmnet’s alpha argument has meant all along. The ridge part makes correlated predictors share their coefficient, the grouping effect, while the lasso part still sets the useless ones to zero.
Your turn. Compare \alpha = 1, 0.5, 0.1 and 0 on the spectra: the number of wavelengths kept and the test RMSE.









Use the function’s argument: alpha = a.


t(sapply(c(1, 0.5, 0.1, 0), function(a) {
  set.seed(7053)
  cv_a <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = a, lambda = lam)
  b <- as.numeric(coef(cv_a, s = "lambda.min"))[-1]
  c(alpha = a, kept = sum(b != 0), test_rmse = sqrt(mean((y[-train] - predict(cv_a, X[-train, ], s = "lambda.min"))^2)))
}))
As \alpha falls from 1 to 0, the number of wavelengths kept rises (41, 52, 70, 100) and the test RMSE falls (0.49, 0.45, 0.43, 0.42). For spectra, the more ridge, the better. For the soft sensor, it would be the other way round. \alpha is a second tuning parameter, and it can be chosen by cross-validation too: Lesson 14’s tools tune both at once.

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
Lasso logistic regression
The same penalties work for any likelihood: glmnet maximizes the log-likelihood minus the penalty. With family = "binomial", that’s penalized logistic regression, and type.measure = "auc" makes cv.glmnet() choose \lambda by the cross-validated AUC of Lesson 6. glmnet needs a numeric matrix, so categorical predictors become dummy columns with model.matrix().
Your turn. Fit a lasso logistic regression to the pump failures, with all seven measurements and the site as candidates, and look at the coefficients at lambda.min.









Logistic regression is family = "binomial".


Xp <- model.matrix(~ vibration_mm_s + bearing_temp_C + motor_current_pct + seal_flush_bar +
                     hours_since_service + pump_type + site, data = pumps)[, -1]
yp <- as.integer(pumps$failed_30d == "yes")
set.seed(7082)
cvp <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(Xp, yp, family = "binomial", type.measure = "auc")
print(max(cvp$cvm))
round(as.matrix(coef(cvp, s = "lambda.min")), 4)
A cross-validated AUC of 0.894, and at lambda.min the lasso keeps everything, including the site, with a coefficient of +1.42 for South. That’s Lesson 6’s calibration problem, found by the model itself: at the same vibration reading, a South pump is about e^{1.42} = 4 times as likely (in odds) to fail, because South’s sensors read low. [, -1] drops model.matrix()’s intercept column, since glmnet adds its own.




Your turn. Look at the coefficients at lambda.1se instead.









s = "lambda.1se".


Xp <- model.matrix(~ vibration_mm_s + bearing_temp_C + motor_current_pct + seal_flush_bar +
                     hours_since_service + pump_type + site, data = pumps)[, -1]
yp <- as.integer(pumps$failed_30d == "yes")
set.seed(7082)
cvp <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(Xp, yp, family = "binomial", type.measure = "auc")
b <- as.matrix(coef(cvp, s = "lambda.1se"))[, 1]
b[b != 0]
Only the vibration and the bearing temperature survive, with smaller coefficients than at lambda.min. The one-standard-error rule trades a slightly lower AUC for a model with two inputs, which is easier to explain to the reliability team, and to check. But it has also dropped the site, and with it the correction for South’s sensors. A sparser model isn’t automatically a better one: here, it’s simpler partly by ignoring a real problem.

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Random folds choose differently. Cross-validate the soft-sensor lasso with ordinary random folds (nfolds = 10, after set.seed(7081)), and count the tags kept at lambda.min.









nfolds = 10.


set.seed(7081)
cv_r <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(Xs, ys, alpha = 1, nfolds = 10)
b <- coef(cv_r, s = "lambda.min")
rownames(b)[as.numeric(b) != 0]
Seven tags: the four chemistry tags, plus the bed level, the superficial gas velocity and the isopentane concentration. With random folds, every held-out sample has neighbors in the training data that share its catalyst drift, and a tag that happens to track the drift over a few weeks looks predictive. The blocked folds didn’t fall for it. Leakage doesn’t just make the error estimate optimistic; it changes which model you choose.




Challenge 2 · How stable is the selection? Draw 10 bootstrap resamples of the 80 calibration spectra, fit the cross-validated lasso to each, and count how often each wavelength is selected.









Bootstrap resamples are drawn with replacement.


sel <- sapply(1:10, function(k) {
  set.seed(7100 + k)
  rows <- sample(train, replace = TRUE)
  cv_b <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(X[rows, ], y[rows], alpha = 1, lambda = lam)
  as.numeric(coef(cv_b, s = "lambda.min"))[-1] != 0
})
freq <- rowSums(sel)
c(always = sum(freq == 10), sometimes = sum(freq > 0 & freq < 10), never = sum(freq == 0))
15 wavelengths are selected in all 10 resamples, the other 85 in some but not all, and none is never selected. Every wavelength gets picked by some resample, so a list of “the wavelengths the lasso chose” from one fit would mean very little. When predictors are this correlated, the lasso’s choice among them is close to arbitrary, and a small change in the data changes it. Stability selection (Meinshausen and Bühlmann, 2010) builds on exactly this: keep only the predictors chosen in most resamples.

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
Quick quiz

1. What’s the only difference between the lasso and ridge?

The lasso uses cross-validation
The penalty: \lambda\sum|\beta_j| instead of \lambda\sum\beta_j^2
The lasso standardizes the predictors


That one change makes some coefficients exactly zero.



2. Why does the lasso give exact zeros, and ridge doesn’t?

The lasso rounds small coefficients
Its constraint region has corners on the axes, where the RSS contours usually touch it
Ridge’s \lambda is always smaller


A diamond has corners; a disk doesn’t. With orthonormal predictors, the lasso soft-thresholds.



3. The lasso selected the right four tags, but its CV error was worse than least squares on those tags. Why?

The lasso chose the wrong tags
The penalty also shrinks the coefficients it keeps, biasing them toward zero
Least squares overfits less


Refitting the selected model by least squares removes that bias.



4. On the spectra, which did best?

The lasso
The elastic net with \alpha = 0.5
Ridge


When the signal is spread over many correlated predictors, averaging beats selecting.



5. What does the elastic net’s ridge part add?

Exact zeros
The grouping effect: correlated predictors share their coefficient
A second response


The lasso part still sets useless coefficients to zero.



6. Random folds let a noise tag into the soft sensor. Why?

Random folds are always worse
Neighboring samples share the drift, so a tag that tracks the drift by chance looks predictive
glmnet’s random numbers are biased


Blocked folds, which respect time, chose exactly the chemistry tags.

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
Wrap-up
You can now select predictors and shrink them in one step. Here’s what you’ve learned:

The lasso penalizes \sum|\beta_j|, which sets some coefficients exactly to zero. The soft sensor’s four chemistry tags entered its path first.
Blocked CV chose exactly those four tags at lambda.min; lambda.1se dropped the comonomer too.
The lasso shrinks what it keeps: the comonomer’s coefficient was half its least-squares size. Refitting the selected tags by least squares removes the bias (Lesson 2’s blocked CV RMSE for them was 0.194, against the lasso’s 0.207).
Correlated predictors defeat the lasso: on spectra, it kept 41 wavelengths, unstably, with a test RMSE of 0.49, against ridge’s 0.416.
The elastic net (0 < \alpha < 1) blends the two, with the grouping effect.
Penalized logistic regression (family = "binomial") found the pump data’s site effect, with a CV AUC of 0.894.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download the three data files into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Plot the CV curves. plot(cv) for the blocked lasso on the soft sensor: the numbers along the top are the nonzero counts. Where do lambda.min and lambda.1se fall?
The relaxed lasso. cv.glmnet(..., relax = TRUE) blends the lasso with the refitted model, and tunes the blend. Try it on the soft sensor with the time blocks.
Choose α by CV. On the spectra, cross-validate \alpha = 0, 0.1, …, 1 with the same folds (foldid), and plot the best CV error against \alpha.
Multinomial lasso. cv.glmnet(..., family = "multinomial") on the alarm data of Lessons 4 and 5. Which measurements does it drop for which cause?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Lasso

Least squares (or another likelihood) with a penalty \lambda\sum_j|\beta_j|, which shrinks the coefficients and sets some exactly to zero.

Sparsity

Having many coefficients exactly equal to zero.

Soft thresholding

Shrinking a value toward zero by a constant, and setting it to zero if it would cross zero.

Elastic net

A penalty that mixes the lasso and ridge penalties, controlled by \alpha.

Grouping effect

The tendency of the elastic net to give correlated predictors similar coefficients.

Relaxed lasso

Using the lasso to select the predictors, then refitting them with less (or no) shrinkage.

Coordinate descent

An optimization method that updates one parameter at a time, cycling through them, as glmnet does.











NoteWant to read more?






James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition), section 6.2.2, “The Lasso”, and the lab in section 6.5.2.
Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani and Martin Wainwright, Statistical Learning with Sparsity: The Lasso and Generalizations (CRC Press, 2015, free PDF). Everything about the lasso, by its developers.
Robert Tibshirani, “Regression Shrinkage and Selection via the Lasso”, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 58(1), 1996, doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1996.tb02080.x. The original paper.
Hui Zou and Trevor Hastie, “Regularization and Variable Selection via the Elastic Net”, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 67(2), 2005, doi:10.1111/j.1467-9868.2005.00503.x.

title: Support vector machines
text:
Module 7 · Lesson 10 of 14 Week 113 of 160 About 5–7 hours
A distillation tray works only inside a window of vapor and liquid flows. Push too much vapor up through it, and the liquid can’t drain down: the tray floods, separation collapses, and the column has to be backed off. Too little vapor, and liquid rains through the holes instead of flowing across: the tray weeps, and efficiency falls. Every tray design has an operating chart showing that window, but the real column rarely matches the vendor’s chart exactly.
The plant has 300 operating points from a revamped column, each with its liquid load (m³ of liquid per m² of tray area per hour) and its F-factor (the vapor velocity times the square root of its density, a measure of vapor load), labeled from the operators’ logs as weeping, normal or flooding:
ggplot(col, aes(liquid_load_m3_m2h, f_factor_Pa05, color = state)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = scol, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Liquid load (m³/m²h)", y = "F-factor (Pa^0.5)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "top")
The window is curved, and it closes at high liquid loads, where the flooding and weeping limits meet. This lesson maps it with support vector machines (SVMs), which come from computer science rather than statistics, and were among the best off-the-shelf classifiers in the 1990s and 2000s. They’re built on a geometric idea, the widest possible street between the classes, and a trick, kernels, that bends that street into any shape.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Support vector machines
text:
The widest street
Start with two classes, flooding or not. If the two classes could be separated by a straight line, there would be infinitely many such lines. The maximal margin classifier chooses the one that’s as far as possible from the nearest points of each class: the middle of the widest street that separates them. Only the points on the edges of the street matter. They’re the support vectors, and moving any other point (without crossing the street) changes nothing.
Real classes overlap, so no street is perfectly clear. The support vector classifier allows some points inside the street, or even on the wrong side, at a price. In e1071::svm(), the price is the cost parameter C: a small cost tolerates many violations and gives a wide street, held up by many support vectors; a large cost tolerates few, and gives a narrow street. Cost plays the part that 1/\lambda played in ridge regression: small cost, more regularization.
The setup code reads the 300 points and makes two factors: state, with all three classes, and flood, flooding or not.












Your turn. Count the operating points in each state.









Tabulate col$state.


table(col$state)
42 weeping, 126 normal and 132 flooding points. The operators clearly spent a lot of time near the flood limit, where the column makes the most product. That’s typical of historical data: it’s dense where operations were interesting, and sparse elsewhere.




Your turn. Fit a support vector classifier for flooding with a linear kernel and a cost of 1. Find the number of support vectors and the training error rate.









kernel = "linear".


fit <- e1071::svm(flood ~ liquid_load_m3_m2h + f_factor_Pa05, data = col, kernel = "linear", cost = 1)
c(support_vectors = fit$tot.nSV, training_error = mean(predict(fit) != col$flood))
63 support vectors out of 300 points, and a training error of 7.3%. Only those 63 points determine the boundary; the other 237 could be deleted without changing it. svm() standardizes both predictors by default (scale = TRUE), which matters for the same reason as in kNN: the margin is a distance.




Here is that classifier: the solid line is the boundary, the dashed lines are the edges of the street, and the circled points are the support vectors.

fit <- svm(flood ~ liquid_load_m3_m2h + f_factor_Pa05, data = col, kernel = "linear", cost = 1)
grid <- expand.grid(liquid_load_m3_m2h = seq(5, 60, length.out = 150), f_factor_Pa05 = seq(0.4, 3, length.out = 150))
grid$dv <- -as.numeric(attr(predict(fit, grid, decision.values = TRUE), "decision.values"))
ggplot(col, aes(liquid_load_m3_m2h, f_factor_Pa05)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = flood), size = 1.4) +
  geom_point(data = col[fit$index, ], shape = 21, size = 3, stroke = 0.6, color = "#3A1F35") +
  geom_contour(data = grid, aes(z = dv), breaks = 0, color = "#3A1F35", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_contour(data = grid, aes(z = dv), breaks = c(-1, 1), color = "#3A1F35", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(not = "grey60", flooding = "#C2416C"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Liquid load (m³/m²h)", y = "F-factor (Pa^0.5)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "top")








Your turn. Fit the same classifier with costs of 0.1, 1, 10, 100 and 1,000, and count the support vectors for each.









Use the function’s argument: cost = C.


sapply(c(0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000), function(C) {
  e1071::svm(flood ~ liquid_load_m3_m2h + f_factor_Pa05, data = col, kernel = "linear", cost = C)$tot.nSV
})
111, 63, 47, 42 and 42. A low cost makes violations cheap, so the street widens until it holds a third of the data, and every point inside it is a support vector: the boundary is an average over many points, stable but possibly biased. A high cost narrows the street to the few points that are hardest to separate: low bias, high variance. Past a cost of 100 nothing changes, because the street is already as narrow as the overlap allows.










NoteGo deeper: the optimization behind the street





Code the classes as y_i = \pm 1. The support vector classifier solves

\min_{\beta_0, \beta, \xi} \; \tfrac12 \|\beta\|^2 + C \sum_i \xi_i \quad \text{subject to} \quad y_i(\beta_0 + x_i^\top\beta) \ge 1 - \xi_i, \;\; \xi_i \ge 0 .

The street’s half-width is 1/\|\beta\|, so minimizing \|\beta\| widens it; the slack variables \xi_i measure each point’s violation (\xi_i > 1 means it’s on the wrong side). It’s a quadratic program. Its solution has the form \hat\beta = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i x_i, with \alpha_i > 0 only for the support vectors, and the decision function is f(x) = \beta_0 + \sum_i \alpha_i y_i \langle x, x_i\rangle: it depends on the data only through inner products \langle x, x_i\rangle. Replacing them with a kernel K(x, x_i) gives the SVM. Equivalently, the problem is \min \sum_i \max\big(0, 1 - y_i f(x_i)\big) + \lambda\|\beta\|^2: the hinge loss plus a ridge penalty. Logistic regression with a ridge penalty has almost the same form, with the log loss instead, which is why the two often give similar answers. ISLR section 9.5 makes the comparison.

title: Support vector machines
text:
Tuning the cost
The cost is a tuning parameter, chosen by cross-validation. e1071::tune() does it: give it the fitting function, the model, and a list of values to try, and it runs 10-fold CV on each.
Your turn. Tune the linear classifier’s cost over 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10 and 100.









The last cost to try is 100.


set.seed(7101)
tl <- e1071::tune(e1071::svm, flood ~ liquid_load_m3_m2h + f_factor_Pa05, data = col, kernel = "linear",
                  ranges = list(cost = c(0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100)))
tl$performances
A cost of 10 is best, with a CV error of 6.3%, but every cost is within 2 points of it, and the dispersion column (the SD of the error across folds) is about 5 points. The cost hardly matters here, because the real limitation is the straight line: the flood limit bends at high liquid loads, and no straight street can follow it.

title: Support vector machines
text:
Kernels: bending the street
Here is the trick that turns a support vector classifier into a support vector machine. The classifier depends on the data only through inner products \langle x, x_i \rangle, a measure of how similar two points are. Replace that with another similarity measure, a kernel K(x, x_i), and the boundary is still a straight line, but in a transformed space that may have many (even infinitely many) dimensions. Back in the original space, it’s curved. The two common kernels:

polynomial: K(x, x') = (\text{coef0} + \gamma\langle x, x'\rangle)^d, for boundaries that are polynomials of degree d;
radial (Gaussian): K(x, x') = \exp(-\gamma \|x - x'\|^2). Points close together are similar, and far apart, not at all. The boundary is then built from bumps around the support vectors, and \gamma sets how narrow they are: a large \gamma gives a wiggly, local boundary, like kNN with a small k.

Your turn. Tune a radial-kernel SVM for flooding over costs of 1, 10 and 100 and \gamma of 0.5, 1 and 2, and find the best combination and its CV error.









kernel = "radial".


set.seed(7102)
tr <- e1071::tune(e1071::svm, flood ~ liquid_load_m3_m2h + f_factor_Pa05, data = col, kernel = "radial",
                  ranges = list(cost = c(1, 10, 100), gamma = c(0.5, 1, 2)))
c(tr$best.parameters, error = tr$best.performance)
A cost of 10 and \gamma = 2, with a CV error of 2.0%, a third of the linear classifier’s 6.3%. The radial kernel follows the flood limit’s bend. With two predictors, you can see the gain on a plot; with twenty, you can’t, which is exactly when kernels are most useful.

title: Support vector machines
text:
Three classes
SVMs are built for two classes. For more, svm() uses the one-versus-one approach: it fits a classifier for every pair of classes (K(K-1)/2 of them, here 3), and each new point gets the class that wins the most pairwise votes.
Your turn. Tune a linear SVM for the three states over costs of 0.1, 1, 10 and 100.









The response with all three classes is state.


set.seed(7103)
tl3 <- e1071::tune(e1071::svm, state ~ liquid_load_m3_m2h + f_factor_Pa05, data = col, kernel = "linear",
                   ranges = list(cost = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100)))
tl3$best.performance
A CV error of 7.7%, at a cost of 100. Three straight boundaries can’t follow the window’s curved edges, especially at the right, where it closes.




Your turn. Tune a radial SVM for the three states, over costs of 1, 10 and 100 and \gamma of 0.1, 0.5, 1 and 2.









The last \gamma is 2.


set.seed(7104)
tr3 <- e1071::tune(e1071::svm, state ~ liquid_load_m3_m2h + f_factor_Pa05, data = col, kernel = "radial",
                   ranges = list(cost = c(1, 10, 100), gamma = c(0.1, 0.5, 1, 2)))
c(tr3$best.parameters, error = tr3$best.performance)
A cost of 10 and \gamma = 0.1, with a CV error of 3.3%, against 7.7% for straight lines. Most of the 12 combinations are between 3.3% and 4.7%: the radial SVM isn’t fussy, as long as \gamma and the cost aren’t both large. A polynomial kernel of degree 2 (kernel = "polynomial", degree = 2, coef0 = 1) does about as well, 3.7%.





grid <- expand.grid(liquid_load_m3_m2h = seq(5, 60, length.out = 150), f_factor_Pa05 = seq(0.4, 3, length.out = 150))
lin <- svm(state ~ liquid_load_m3_m2h + f_factor_Pa05, col, kernel = "linear", cost = 100)
rad <- svm(state ~ liquid_load_m3_m2h + f_factor_Pa05, col, kernel = "radial", cost = 10, gamma = 0.1)
reg <- rbind(cbind(grid, state = predict(lin, grid), k = "linear kernel"),
             cbind(grid, state = predict(rad, grid), k = "radial kernel"))
ggplot(reg, aes(liquid_load_m3_m2h, f_factor_Pa05)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = state), alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_point(data = col, aes(color = state), size = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = scol, name = NULL) + scale_color_manual(values = scol, guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~k) + coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Liquid load (m³/m²h)", y = "F-factor (Pa^0.5)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Support vector machines
text:
Probabilities near the edge
An SVM’s raw output is a class, or a signed distance from the boundary, not a probability. With probability = TRUE, svm() fits an extra model (Platt scaling: a logistic regression on the decision values, by internal cross-validation) that converts them into probabilities.
Your turn. Fit the tuned radial SVM with probability = TRUE, and find the class probabilities at four operating points: (10, 0.6), (30, 1.5), (50, 1.4) and (55, 0.9), as (liquid load, F-factor).









probability = TRUE, both when fitting and when predicting.


set.seed(7105)
fit <- e1071::svm(state ~ liquid_load_m3_m2h + f_factor_Pa05, data = col, kernel = "radial",
                  cost = 10, gamma = 0.1, probability = TRUE)
new <- data.frame(liquid_load_m3_m2h = c(10, 30, 50, 55), f_factor_Pa05 = c(0.6, 1.5, 1.4, 0.9))
p <- predict(fit, new, probability = TRUE)
round(attr(p, "probabilities")[, c("weeping", "normal", "flooding")], 3)
At (10, 0.6), low vapor at a low liquid load, it’s 80% weeping. At (30, 1.5), right in the middle of the window, it’s normal with near certainty. At (50, 1.4), 91% flooding: at high liquid loads, the flood limit has dropped below an F-factor of 1.4. And at (55, 0.9), the model is split: 57% flooding, 39% weeping, and only 4% normal. That’s the corner where the window closes: at that liquid load, the vapor rate that stops the weeping is already enough to flood the tray. The engineer’s conclusion is not about statistics: at liquid loads above about 55 m³/m²h, this tray has no safe operating point, and the column needs a higher-capacity tray or less liquid.

title: Support vector machines
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Too narrow bumps. Fit radial SVMs for the three states with a cost of 100 and \gamma of 1, 10, 50 and 200. For each, find the training error, the number of support vectors, and the CV error (with tune() and a single value of each parameter).









Use the function’s argument: gamma = g.


t(sapply(c(1, 10, 50, 200), function(g) {
  fit <- e1071::svm(state ~ liquid_load_m3_m2h + f_factor_Pa05, data = col, kernel = "radial", cost = 100, gamma = g)
  set.seed(7106)
  cv <- e1071::tune(e1071::svm, state ~ liquid_load_m3_m2h + f_factor_Pa05, data = col, kernel = "radial",
                    ranges = list(cost = 100, gamma = g))
  c(gamma = g, train_error = mean(predict(fit) != col$state), n_sv = fit$tot.nSV, cv_error = cv$best.performance)
}))
From \gamma = 10 on, the training error is 0: every point is classified correctly, mislabeled ones included. But the CV error climbs from 4.3% to 7.7% to 19.7%, and at \gamma = 200, 293 of the 300 points are support vectors: the model is a bump around each point, a lookup table that has memorized the data. It’s Lesson 1’s overfitting, and Lesson 3’s k = 1, in kernel form.




Challenge 2 · A curved logistic regression. SVMs aren’t the only way to curve a boundary. Cross-validate a multinomial logistic regression with squared terms and the interaction, on 10 random folds.









Predict the held-out fold, col[fold == j, ].


set.seed(7107)
fold <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = 300))
pred <- factor(rep(NA, 300), levels = levels(col$state))
fq <- state ~ liquid_load_m3_m2h + f_factor_Pa05 + I(liquid_load_m3_m2h^2) + I(f_factor_Pa05^2) + liquid_load_m3_m2h:f_factor_Pa05
for (j in 1:10) {
  fit <- nnet::multinom(fq, data = col[fold != j, ], trace = FALSE, maxit = 1000)
  pred[fold == j] <- predict(fit, col[fold == j, ])
}
mean(pred != col$state)
4.0%, close to the radial SVM’s 3.3% (on different folds, so the gap is within noise). With a few predictors and a smooth boundary, a logistic regression with the right terms does nearly as well as an SVM, and it gives calibrated probabilities and readable coefficients. SVMs earn their keep when there are many predictors and nobody knows which terms to add.

title: Support vector machines
text:
Quick quiz

1. What are the support vectors?

All the training points
The points on or inside the margin, or on the wrong side, which alone determine the boundary
The class means


Moving any other point, without crossing the margin, doesn’t change the classifier.



2. What happens as the cost C increases?

The margin widens and there are more support vectors
The margin narrows and there are fewer support vectors
The boundary becomes curved


Violations get more expensive. Low cost is more regularization, like a large \lambda.



3. What does a kernel do?

It removes outliers
It replaces the inner product with another similarity measure, which makes the boundary curved in the original space
It scales the predictors


The boundary is linear in a transformed space that’s never computed explicitly.



4. What does a large \gamma do in a radial kernel?

Makes the boundary smoother
Makes the kernel’s bumps narrow, so the boundary becomes wiggly and can overfit
Increases the margin


At \gamma = 200, 293 of 300 points were support vectors, and the CV error was 20%.



5. How does svm() handle three classes?

It can’t
One-versus-one: a classifier for each pair, then a vote
It fits one classifier with three margins


With K classes, K(K-1)/2 classifiers.



6. Where do an SVM’s probabilities come from?

Directly from the margin
From an extra logistic model fitted to the decision values (Platt scaling)
From Bayes’ theorem


That’s what probability = TRUE adds.

title: Support vector machines
text:
Wrap-up
You can now fit, tune and read support vector machines. Here’s what you’ve learned:

The support vector classifier finds the widest street between the classes, allowing violations at a price C. Only the support vectors (63 of 300 at C = 1) define it.
The cost sets the trade-off: low cost, a wide street and many support vectors; high cost, a narrow one. tune() chooses it by CV.
Kernels curve the boundary. For flooding, a radial kernel cut the CV error from 6.3% to 2.0%.
Three classes are handled one-versus-one: 7.7% wrong with straight boundaries, 3.3% with a radial kernel.
Probabilities come from Platt scaling. Near the corner where the window closes, the model was split between weeping and flooding.
Large \gamma overfits: zero training error, and a CV error that rose to 20%.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download column_operating.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install e1071.

Plot the classifier. plot(fit, col, f_factor_Pa05 ~ liquid_load_m3_m2h) draws an svm() fit’s regions and marks the support vectors with crosses.
The full grid. Tune the radial SVM over costs from 0.1 to 1,000 and \gamma from 0.01 to 100, both on log scales. Plot the CV error as a heat map (plot(tune_result) does it). Where’s the good region?
Kernlab. The kernlab package’s ksvm() is another SVM implementation, with more kernels. Fit the three-state model with kernel = "rbfdot" and compare.
The window’s corner. Using the probabilities, find the liquid load beyond which no F-factor gives “normal” with a probability above 0.5.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Maximal margin classifier

The linear boundary that separates two classes with the widest possible margin.

Margin

The distance from the boundary to the nearest training points.

Support vector classifier

A maximal margin classifier that allows violations of the margin, at a cost C.

Support vectors

The training points on or inside the margin, or on the wrong side; they alone determine the classifier.

Kernel

A function K(x, x') that measures similarity, replacing the inner product to give curved boundaries.

Radial (Gaussian) kernel

K(x, x') = \exp(-\gamma\|x - x'\|^2).

Support vector machine (SVM)

A support vector classifier with a kernel.

One-versus-one

Handling K classes by fitting a classifier to every pair and taking a vote.

Hinge loss

\max(0, 1 - y f(x)), the loss that the support vector classifier minimizes, plus a penalty.











NoteWant to read more?






James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition), chapter 9, “Support Vector Machines”, with its lab in section 9.6, which uses e1071.
Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, chapter 12, on SVMs as penalized methods.
Corinna Cortes and Vladimir Vapnik, “Support-Vector Networks”, Machine Learning 20, 1995, doi:10.1007/BF00994018. The paper that introduced the soft margin.
Henry Kister, Distillation Operation (McGraw-Hill, 1990). The practitioner’s classic on tray flooding, weeping and troubleshooting columns.

title: Principal components analysis
text:
Module 7 · Lesson 12 of 14 Week 115 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Every lesson so far has been supervised: a response to predict. The last two lessons of this module are about unsupervised learning, where there’s no response, only a set of variables and a question about their structure.
A tubular reactor’s control room shows 16 sensors: six temperatures along the tube, the inlet and outlet pressures and the pressure drop, the feed, recycle and coolant flows, the coolant’s inlet and outlet temperatures, and two online analyzers for conversion and selectivity. reactor_sensors.csv has 400 hourly snapshots of all 16, from one catalyst run. An operator watching 16 trends is watching far fewer independent things than that, because the sensors move together: more feed raises the flows, the pressures and the temperatures at once. Principal components analysis (PCA) finds the few directions in which the 16 sensors really vary, and the result is often a short list of things an engineer can name.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Principal components analysis
text:
Directions of maximum variance
The first principal component is the direction in the 16-dimensional space of the (standardized) sensors along which the snapshots vary the most: the linear combination

z_1 = \phi_{11} x_1 + \phi_{21} x_2 + \cdots + \phi_{p1} x_p, \qquad \sum_j \phi_{j1}^2 = 1,

with the largest variance. The \phi_{j1} are its loadings, and the values z_{i1} for each snapshot are its scores. The second component is the direction of largest variance that’s uncorrelated with the first, and so on, up to p components. Together they’re just a rotation of the original axes, but ordered so that the first few carry as much of the variation as possible. Module 3 used the same mathematics for multivariate normal data.
The setup code reads the 400 snapshots into the matrix R (one column per sensor), and the spectra from Lessons 7 and 8.












Your turn. How many of the 120 pairs of sensors have a correlation stronger than 0.5 in size?









Compare the absolute correlations with 0.5.


r <- cor(R)
sum(abs(r[upper.tri(r)]) > 0.5)
67 of the 120 pairs. upper.tri(r) picks each pair once, leaving out the diagonal. With that much correlation, 16 sensors can’t be carrying 16 independent pieces of information.




The components come from the eigendecomposition of the correlation matrix (the covariance matrix of the standardized sensors). The eigenvectors are the loadings, and each eigenvalue is the variance of that component’s scores. The eigenvalues add up to p = 16, the total variance of 16 standardized variables, so each one divided by 16 is that component’s proportion of variance explained.
Your turn. Find the eigenvalues of the correlation matrix, and the proportion of the variance that each of the first four components explains.









Divide by the sum of all the eigenvalues, sum(ev), which is 16.


ev <- eigen(cor(R))$values
round(ev, 3)
round(ev[1:4] / sum(ev), 4)
The eigenvalues are 8.72, 4.20 and 1.07, then a sudden drop to 0.29, and the other twelve are between 0.08 and 0.21. The first component explains 54.5% of the variation, the second 26.2%, the third 6.7%, and the fourth only 1.8%. Three components carry 87% of what 16 sensors say. The small eigenvalues are each sensor’s own noise.

title: Principal components analysis
text:
prcomp() and the scree plot
prcomp(x, scale. = TRUE) standardizes the variables and does the same calculation, more accurately, with the singular value decomposition. It returns the loadings in rotation, the scores in x, and the components’ standard deviations in sdev (the square roots of the eigenvalues).
Your turn. Run prcomp() on the standardized sensors, and find the cumulative proportion of variance explained by the first five components.









Standardize: scale. = TRUE.


pca <- prcomp(R, scale. = TRUE)
summary(pca)$importance["Cumulative Proportion", 1:5]
0.545, 0.807, 0.874, 0.892 and 0.905. The third component adds 6.7%, the fourth and fifth less than 2% each. How many to keep is a judgment, and three common rules agree here: the elbow of the scree plot (below), where the eigenvalues flatten out, is after the third; the Kaiser rule (keep components with eigenvalues above 1, the variance of a single standardized sensor) keeps three; and three components pass a typical 85% target.





ggplot(data.frame(k = 1:16, ev = pca$sdev^2), aes(k, ev)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(color = "#C2416C") + geom_point(color = "#C2416C", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:16) +
  labs(x = "Component", y = "Variance (eigenvalue)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: Principal components analysis
text:
Reading the components
A component means what its loadings say. In the biplot below, each arrow is a sensor’s loadings on the first two components, and each point is a snapshot’s scores:

sc <- as.data.frame(pca$x[, 1:2]); ld <- as.data.frame(pca$rotation[, 1:2] * 7); ld$sensor <- rownames(ld)
bundle <- c("P_in", "P_out", "dP", "F_feed", "F_recycle"); temps <- paste0("T", 1:6)
lab <- ld[!(ld$sensor %in% c(bundle, temps)), ]
lab <- rbind(lab, data.frame(PC1 = mean(ld[bundle, 1]), PC2 = mean(ld[bundle, 2]), sensor = "pressures, feed\nand recycle flows"),
             data.frame(PC1 = mean(ld[temps, 1]), PC2 = mean(ld[temps, 2]), sensor = "T1 to T6"))
ggplot(sc, aes(PC1, PC2)) + geom_point(color = "grey80", size = 0.8) +
  geom_segment(data = ld, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC2), color = "#C2416C",
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm"))) +
  geom_text(data = lab, aes(x = PC1 * 1.25, y = PC2 * 1.25, label = sensor), size = 3, color = "#3A1F35", lineheight = 0.9) +
  coord_equal() + labs(x = "PC1 (54.5%)", y = "PC2 (26.2%)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11)








PC1 has negative loadings, of similar size, on almost everything: the pressures, the flows and the temperatures all rise together. It’s throughput: when the plant pushes more feed through, everything goes up. (The sign is arbitrary; flipping every loading and score describes the same component.) PC2 contrasts the coolant temperatures, which load positively, with the flows and pressures: it’s the coolant temperature, which heats the whole tube when it rises, independently of the throughput. What’s PC3?
Your turn. List PC3’s loadings, sorted by size.









The third column of the loadings: pca$rotation[, 3].


pca <- prcomp(R, scale. = TRUE)
l3 <- pca$rotation[, 3]
round(l3[order(abs(l3), decreasing = TRUE)], 3)
The largest loadings are the conversion (+0.61), the coolant flow (+0.43), the last tube temperature, T6 (-0.37), and the coolant inlet temperature (-0.32), with the first temperatures, T1 to T3, positive and the last ones negative. High PC3 means high conversion with the heat released early in the tube; low PC3 means lower conversion, with the reaction smeared further down the tube. To a reaction engineer, that pattern means catalyst activity.




Your turn. If PC3 is catalyst activity, it should decline over the run. Find the correlation between each of the first three components’ scores and the snapshot number (time).









Time is the column snapshot.


pca <- prcomp(R, scale. = TRUE)
cor(pca$x[, 1:3], rs$snapshot)
0.11 for PC1, -0.01 for PC2 and -0.82 for PC3. Throughput and coolant temperature come and go with the plant’s schedule, but PC3 falls steadily through the run: the catalyst is deactivating. No single sensor shows this clearly, because each is dominated by throughput and coolant changes, but a weighted combination of all 16 does. That’s the most useful thing PCA does in a plant: it separates the things that are driven on purpose from the ones that drift.





ggplot(data.frame(t = rs$snapshot, pc3 = pca$x[, 3]), aes(t, pc3)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey60", size = 0.8) + geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = "#C2416C", formula = y ~ x) +
  labs(x = "Hour of the catalyst run", y = "PC3 score (catalyst activity)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12)














NoteGo deeper: PCA for process monitoring





Multivariate statistical process control uses PCA routinely. Fit the components to a period of normal operation, keep k of them, and monitor two statistics for every new snapshot: Hotelling’s T^2 on the k scores (Module 3’s statistical distance, within the model’s plane), which flags unusual but consistent combinations, like an extreme throughput; and the squared prediction error (SPE, or Q), the squared distance from the snapshot to the plane, which flags combinations the model has never seen, like a sensor that stops agreeing with its neighbors. Two charts replace sixteen. MacGregor and Kourti’s “Statistical process control of multivariate processes” (Control Engineering Practice 3(3), 1995) introduced the method to chemical engineers, and Challenge 1 computes the ingredient of the SPE.

title: Principal components analysis
text:
Standardize, or not?
PCA finds directions of maximum variance, and variance depends on units. The coolant flow is in tonnes per hour, with an SD of 13.4; the pressure drop is in bar, with an SD of 0.15.
Your turn. Run PCA without standardizing, and find the proportion of variance of the first component and its largest loading.









Don’t standardize: scale. = FALSE.


raw <- prcomp(R, scale. = FALSE)
l1 <- raw$rotation[, 1]
c(prop_pc1 = summary(raw)$importance["Proportion of Variance", 1], largest_loading = l1[which.max(abs(l1))])
The first component explains 64.5%, and its loading on the coolant flow is -0.94: it’s essentially the coolant flow alone, because that sensor’s numbers are the biggest. The second mixes the tube temperatures and the recycle flow, the sensors with the next-largest spreads. In raw units, PCA describes whichever sensors happen to have large numbers. Standardize unless the variables share units and their variances are comparable, as for the spectra below.

title: Principal components analysis
text:
Principal components regression
Lesson 7’s ridge regression found that the NIR spectra have about five strong directions. Principal components regression (PCR) uses them directly: compute the spectra’s first M principal components, and regress the ethanol on their scores. With M chosen by cross-validation, it’s a regularized method too: instead of shrinking every direction a little, as ridge does, it keeps the first M directions whole and drops the rest. (Spectra share their units, and the absorbance’s variation carries meaning, so they’re usually left unstandardized.)
Your turn. Cross-validate PCR on the 80 calibration samples, for M = 1 to 12 components. The PCA must be refitted inside each fold, to avoid leakage.









Use the fitted regression’s coefficients: coef(fit).


Xt <- X[train, ]; yt <- y[train]
set.seed(7121)
fold <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = 80))
cv_pcr <- sapply(1:12, function(M) {
  err <- numeric(80)
  for (j in 1:10) {
    tr <- fold != j
    pc <- prcomp(Xt[tr, ])
    fit <- lm(yt[tr] ~ pc$x[, 1:M, drop = FALSE])
    new_scores <- predict(pc, Xt[!tr, , drop = FALSE])[, 1:M, drop = FALSE]
    err[!tr] <- yt[!tr] - cbind(1, new_scores) %*% coef(fit)
  }
  sqrt(mean(err^2))
})
round(cv_pcr, 3)
which.min(cv_pcr)
5 components, with a CV RMSE of 0.371. The curve drops sharply: 5.4 with one component, 3.3 with two or three, 0.92 with four, then 0.37 with five, and flat after that. Five components: the three chemicals, the baseline offset and the baseline slope. predict(pc, newdata) projects new spectra onto the training components, centering them with the training means.




Your turn. Fit PCR with 5 components to all 80 calibration samples, and find its test RMSE on the other 40.









Use the first 5 components: 1:5.


pc <- prcomp(X[train, ])
fit <- lm(y[train] ~ pc$x[, 1:5])
pred <- cbind(1, predict(pc, X[-train, ])[, 1:5]) %*% coef(fit)
sqrt(mean((y[-train] - pred)^2))
0.409, as good as ridge regression (0.416) and better than the lasso (0.49). Ridge and PCR are close cousins: ridge shrinks each principal direction by d_j^2/(d_j^2 + \lambda), smoothly, and PCR shrinks the first M by nothing and the rest to zero, a hard cut-off. With five clear directions and noise beyond, both work.

title: Principal components analysis
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · What three components miss. Reconstruct the standardized sensors from their first three components’ scores and loadings, and find the R^2 for each sensor: the share of its variance that the three components capture. Which sensor is captured worst?









Use the same three components’ loadings: pca$rotation[, 1:3].


pca <- prcomp(R, scale. = TRUE)
Z <- scale(R)
Z_hat <- pca$x[, 1:3] %*% t(pca$rotation[, 1:3])
r2 <- 1 - colSums((Z - Z_hat)^2) / colSums(Z^2)
round(sort(r2), 3)
The selectivity analyzer is captured worst, at 77%; every other sensor is between 86% and 91%. The rest of each sensor’s variance is its own noise, which no shared component explains. In process monitoring, the difference Z - \hat Z is the residual whose squared length is the SPE: if one sensor’s residual suddenly grows, that sensor has stopped agreeing with the others, which usually means it’s drifting or broken.




Challenge 2 · Variance isn’t relevance. PCR picks components by how much they vary, not by how well they predict. Find the correlation between ethanol and each of the first six principal component scores of the calibration spectra, and their proportions of variance.









Correlate with the calibration samples’ ethanol, y[train].


pc <- prcomp(X[train, ])
rbind(prop_variance = summary(pc)$importance["Proportion of Variance", 1:6],
      cor_with_ethanol = as.numeric(cor(pc$x[, 1:6], y[train])))
PC4 explains only 0.6% of the spectra’s variance, but its correlation with ethanol is 0.42, more than PC3’s 0.06 with 3.2% of the variance. That’s why PCR needed four or five components, and why it was poor with three. When the response’s signal sits in a low-variance direction, PCR has to keep every larger direction first. Partial least squares (PLS), the chemometricians’ standard, fixes this: it chooses directions that have both high variance and high covariance with the response. The pls package fits it in R.

title: Principal components analysis
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does the first principal component maximize?

Its correlation with the response
The variance of the scores, among all unit-length combinations of the variables
The number of variables it uses


PCA is unsupervised: it never looks at a response.



2. The eigenvalues of a 16 \times 16 correlation matrix add up to what?

1
16
The number of observations


The total variance of 16 standardized variables. Each eigenvalue over 16 is a proportion explained.



3. Why standardize before PCA, usually?

To make the components uncorrelated
Otherwise the variables with the largest numbers dominate the components
prcomp() needs it


Unstandardized, PC1 was just the coolant flow, in t/h.



4. What does the Kaiser rule keep?

The first three components
Components with eigenvalues above 1, more variance than a single standardized variable
Components explaining 85%


Here it kept three, in agreement with the elbow.



5. PC3’s scores fell steadily over the run. What did that reveal?

A sensor fault
The catalyst’s activity was declining
The throughput was falling


No single sensor showed it clearly; a weighted combination did.



6. What’s the main weakness of principal components regression?

It can’t handle more variables than samples
It chooses components by their variance, not by their relevance to the response
It’s always worse than least squares


Partial least squares chooses directions that also covary with the response.

title: Principal components analysis
text:
Wrap-up
You can now find, read and use the main directions of variation in many correlated variables. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Principal components are uncorrelated combinations of the variables, ordered by variance. Their loadings are the eigenvectors of the correlation matrix, and their variances its eigenvalues.
Three components carried 87% of the 16 sensors’ variation, by the elbow, the Kaiser rule and the 85% rule alike.
Interpreting loadings named them: throughput, coolant temperature, and catalyst activity, whose scores fell through the run (correlation with time -0.82).
Standardize variables in different units, or the largest numbers take over.
PCR with 5 components predicted ethanol with a test RMSE of 0.409, as well as ridge. But PCA ignores the response, so a relevant low-variance direction can be missed.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download reactor_sensors.csv and nir_spectra.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

The built-in biplot. biplot(prcomp(R, scale. = TRUE)). Then try factoextra::fviz_pca_biplot(), if you install factoextra.
A monitoring chart. Fit PCA on the first 200 snapshots only. Compute Hotelling’s T^2 for the 3 scores, and the SPE, for all 400, and plot both over time. What happens as the catalyst ages?
Partial least squares. Install pls, and fit plsr(ethanol_pct ~ ., ncomp = 10, data = ..., validation = "CV") to the calibration spectra. How many components does it need, compared with PCR?
Loadings as spectra. Plot the first five loading vectors of the spectra against the wavelength. Which one looks like ethanol’s spectrum?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Principal components analysis (PCA)

Finding uncorrelated linear combinations of the variables, ordered by how much variance each explains.

Loadings

The weights \phi_{jm} that define each component; the eigenvectors of the correlation (or covariance) matrix.

Scores

The values of the components for each observation.

Proportion of variance explained

A component’s variance divided by the total variance.

Scree plot

A plot of the components’ variances against their number, used to choose how many to keep.

Biplot

A plot of the observations’ scores and the variables’ loadings on the same axes.

Principal components regression (PCR)

Regressing the response on the first M principal component scores.

Partial least squares (PLS)

A regression method that chooses directions with high covariance with the response, rather than high variance alone.











NoteWant to read more?






James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition), section 12.2, “Principal Components Analysis”, and section 6.3, on PCR and PLS.
Ian Jolliffe and Jorge Cadima, “Principal component analysis: a review and recent developments”, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 374, 2016, doi:10.1098/rsta.2015.0202. A short, readable review.
John MacGregor and Theodora Kourti, “Statistical process control of multivariate processes”, Control Engineering Practice 3(3), 1995, doi:10.1016/0967-0661(95)00014-L. PCA for monitoring chemical plants.

title: The machine-learning workflow
text:
Module 7 · Lesson 14 of 14 Week 117 of 160 About 5–7 hours
This module has used a dozen methods, and every one of them came with the same chores: split the data, preprocess it (inside each fold, to avoid leakage), set up cross-validation (with the right folds), tune, refit, test once, check. Each lesson wrote those chores by hand, in a slightly different way. That’s fine for learning, and error-prone for real work.
tidymodels is a set of R packages that gives each chore its own tool, with a consistent grammar:
This lesson rebuilds Lesson 6’s pump-failure model the tidymodels way, end to end, and adds the two last steps a model needs before anyone relies on it: an explanation of what it uses, and a check that it works for everyone it will serve.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: The machine-learning workflow
text:
Spending the data
The setup code reads the pump data and makes the response a factor, failed, with “yes” as its first level (yardstick treats the first level as the event of interest). Unlike Lesson 6, it keeps the 125 records with a missing bearing temperature: the recipe will deal with them. It then builds everything this lesson uses, step by step, so that each exercise can start from it; the exercises rebuild the pieces one at a time.













The test set is set aside first, and touched once, at the very end. With rare failures, a purely random split could leave the test set with noticeably more or fewer failures than the training set, so the split is stratified: it samples within each class separately, keeping the failure rate the same in both.
Your turn. Split the data 75/25, stratified by failed, and compare the sizes and the failure rates of the two sets.









Stratify by the response, failed.


set.seed(7141)
split <- initial_split(pumps, prop = 0.75, strata = failed)
train <- training(split)
test <- testing(split)
c(n_train = nrow(train), n_test = nrow(test),
  rate_train = mean(train$failed == "yes"), rate_test = mean(test$failed == "yes"))
2,250 records for training and 750 for testing, with failure rates of 6.8% and 6.7%: matched, as stratification promises. Everything that follows (preprocessing, tuning, choosing the model) uses only the 2,250 training records.

title: The machine-learning workflow
text:
Preprocessing as a recipe
A recipe lists the preprocessing steps, in order, without doing them yet:

update_role(record, pump, new_role = "id") keeps the record and pump identifiers in the data but out of the model;
step_impute_median() fills in missing bearing temperatures with the training median;
step_dummy() turns the categorical predictors (site and pump type) into 0/1 columns;
step_normalize() standardizes every numeric predictor.

prep() learns what each step needs (the median, the means and SDs) from the data it’s given; bake() applies them, to that data or to new data. Inside cross-validation, tidymodels preps the recipe on each fold’s analysis set only, so the held-out records never influence the medians or the SDs. That’s Lesson 2’s rule, enforced automatically.
Your turn. Prep the recipe on the training set, bake it, and check that no missing values remain. Also find the median the imputation step learned.









new_data = NULL returns the processed training data.


prepped <- prep(rec, training = train)
baked <- bake(prepped, new_data = NULL)
print(names(baked))
c(missing_before = sum(is.na(train$bearing_temp_C)), missing_after = sum(is.na(baked)),
  median_used = prepped$steps[[1]]$medians$bearing_temp_C)
125 missing bearing temperatures before, none after: each was filled with the training median, 57.8 °C. The baked data has the identifiers, the five numeric predictors (now standardized), the response, and three dummy columns: site_South, pump_type_multistage and pump_type_screw (centrifugal and North are the baselines). Module 1’s lessons on missing data would point out that median imputation is crude; step_impute_bag() or step_impute_knn() are better ones, and drop into the same recipe.

title: The machine-learning workflow
text:
Folds that respect the pumps
The 2,250 training records come from 125 pumps, about 18 records each, and a pump’s records are alike: the same pump type, similar vibration levels from month to month. With random folds, a pump’s other months would sit in the analysis set while some of its months are held out, and the model would be judged partly on pumps it has already seen. The model will be used on next month’s records of the same pumps, so this leak is milder than Lesson 2’s, but a model that’s meant to work on newly installed pumps needs grouped folds, which hold out whole pumps.
Your turn. Make 5 folds grouped by pump, and check that no pump appears in both the analysis and the assessment set of any fold.









Group by pump.


set.seed(7142)
folds <- group_vfold_cv(train, group = pump, v = 5)
sapply(folds$splits, function(s) length(intersect(analysis(s)$pump, assessment(s)$pump)))
0, 0, 0, 0, 0: every fold holds out about 25 whole pumps. In rsample, “analysis” and “assessment” are the names for a fold’s training and held-out parts, to keep them distinct from the overall training and test sets.

title: The machine-learning workflow
text:
Model, workflow and tuning
A parsnip model specification says what model to fit, not how: logistic_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 1) is a lasso logistic regression (glmnet’s alpha is parsnip’s mixture), with the penalty marked as a parameter to tune; set_engine("glmnet") says which package fits it. A workflow bundles the recipe and the model, so that they’re always prepped, fitted and applied together. tune_grid() then cross-validates the workflow at every value in a grid, re-prepping the recipe in each fold.
Your turn. Tune the workflow over the grid of 10 penalties from 10^{-4} to 10^{-1}, with the grouped folds, scoring by AUC. Look at the best mean AUCs.









Resample with the grouped folds, folds.


res <- tune_grid(wf, resamples = folds, grid = grid, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc))
show_best(res, metric = "roc_auc", n = 3)
The best penalty is 0.0022, with a mean CV AUC of 0.892 (standard error 0.018). Every penalty up to 0.01 is within 0.004 of it, and the AUC falls only above that, to 0.863 at 0.1, as the lasso drops predictors. collect_metrics(res) gives the whole table, and autoplot(res) plots it.




Your turn. select_best() picks the penalty with the highest mean AUC. select_by_one_std_err() applies the one-standard-error rule: it sorts the candidates from simplest to most complex (here, from the largest penalty down) and picks the first within one standard error of the best. Find both.









The simplest model has the largest penalty: sort by desc(penalty).


res <- tune_grid(wf, resamples = folds, grid = grid, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc))
c(best = select_best(res, metric = "roc_auc")$penalty,
  one_se = select_by_one_std_err(res, desc(penalty), metric = "roc_auc")$penalty)
0.0022 for the best, and 0.022, ten times more shrinkage, by the one-standard-error rule, with a mean AUC of 0.877. The rest of the lesson uses the best value: with failures this costly, a few points of AUC matter more than a simpler model.

title: The machine-learning workflow
section: The final fit, and the one test
text:
The final fit, and the one test
With the penalty chosen, finalize_workflow() writes it into the workflow, and last_fit() does the last two steps in one call: it fits the workflow to the whole training set, and evaluates it, once, on the test set.
Your turn. Finalize the workflow with the best penalty, 0.00215, run last_fit(), and find the test AUC.









last_fit() takes the initial split, split, so it knows which rows are training and which are test.


final_wf <- finalize_workflow(wf, data.frame(penalty = 0.00215443469))
lf <- last_fit(final_wf, split = split, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc))
collect_metrics(lf)$.estimate
A test AUC of 0.885, close to the CV estimate of 0.892, as it should be when nothing has leaked. That number is the honest estimate to report. If you now went back and changed the model to improve it, the test set would become part of the tuning, and you’d need new data to get an honest estimate again. collect_predictions(lf) has the test-set probabilities, and extract_workflow(lf) the fitted workflow, ready to predict new records.

title: The machine-learning workflow
text:
Explaining the model
A model that will decide which pumps get inspected needs an explanation that the reliability team can check against their experience. For a penalized linear model, the coefficients are one explanation.
Your turn. Extract the fitted model and look at its coefficients with tidy().









Extract the model from the last fit, lf.


lf <- last_fit(finalize_workflow(wf, data.frame(penalty = 0.00215443469)), split, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc))
co <- tidy(extract_fit_parsnip(lf))
setNames(round(co$estimate, 3), co$term)
The vibration coefficient is -1.47, the bearing temperature -0.48, the hours since service -0.39, and South -0.67. They’re negative because glmnet models the probability of the second level of the response, “no”, so every sign is flipped: on the failure scale, vibration is +1.47 per SD. It’s an easy trap. And since the predictors are standardized, the sizes are comparable: vibration matters three times as much as anything else. The motor current, the seal flush and the pump types have coefficients near zero.




Coefficients only explain models that have them. Permutation importance works for any model: shuffle one predictor’s values in the test set, breaking its link with the response, and see how much the model’s AUC drops. A big drop means the model relies on that predictor.
Your turn. Compute the permutation importance of each of the seven predictors.









Shuffle the predictor’s own column: shuffled[[v]].


lf <- last_fit(finalize_workflow(wf, data.frame(penalty = 0.00215443469)), split, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc))
final <- extract_workflow(lf)
auc_of <- function(d) roc_auc_vec(d$failed, predict(final, d, type = "prob")$.pred_yes)
base <- auc_of(test)
preds <- c("vibration_mm_s", "bearing_temp_C", "hours_since_service", "site", "pump_type", "motor_current_pct", "seal_flush_bar")
sapply(preds, function(v) {
  set.seed(7143)
  shuffled <- test
  shuffled[[v]] <- sample(shuffled[[v]])
  base - auc_of(shuffled)
})
Shuffling the vibration drops the AUC by 0.29, from 0.885 to about 0.60. The hours since service (0.019), the bearing temperature (0.014) and the site (0.008) matter a little, and the rest not at all. The model is, above all, a vibration alarm with corrections, which the reliability team will find reassuring: it’s what their own experience says. One shuffle is noisy; repeating each one several times and averaging is better practice (the iml package does this, with FeatureImp()).










NoteGo deeper: other ways to explain a model





Permutation importance says how much a model relies on each predictor, not how. Partial dependence plots show how the average prediction changes as one predictor varies, with the others held at their observed values: a model-agnostic version of Lesson 9’s partial effects. SHAP values split each single prediction into contributions from each predictor, which is useful for explaining one decision (“this pump was flagged mainly because of its vibration”). Module 8 uses both for tree ensembles, where there are no coefficients to read. Christoph Molnar’s free book Interpretable Machine Learning covers all of them, with their pitfalls: with correlated predictors, shuffling one creates impossible combinations (a hot bearing on a calm pump), and the importances can mislead.

title: The machine-learning workflow
text:
Does it work for everyone?
An overall AUC can hide a group that the model serves badly, as Lesson 6 found for the South site. The last check before deployment is to compare the model’s performance across the groups it will be used on: sites, pump types, shifts, or, for models about people, groups of people. The questions are always the same: are the predictions calibrated in each group, and does each group get the same sensitivity at the chosen threshold?
Your turn. For each site, compare the average predicted failure probability with the observed failure rate in the test set, and find the sensitivity at Lesson 6’s cost-based threshold of 0.04.









Use the threshold 0.04.


lf <- last_fit(finalize_workflow(wf, data.frame(penalty = 0.00215443469)), split, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc))
p <- predict(extract_workflow(lf), test, type = "prob")$.pred_yes
by_site <- function(p) sapply(c("North", "South"), function(s) {
  k <- test$site == s
  c(predicted = mean(p[k]), observed = mean(test$failed[k] == "yes"),
    sensitivity = mean(p[k & test$failed == "yes"] >= 0.04))
})
round(by_site(p), 3)
Well calibrated at both sites: 7.1% predicted against 6.7% observed at North, and 7.1% against 6.6% at South. At a threshold of 0.04, the model catches 77% of North’s failures and 90% of South’s. Unlike Lesson 6’s model, this one includes the site as a predictor, and its South coefficient corrects for the South sensors’ low readings. Including the group variable was the right fix here, because the group difference is a measurement artifact with a known cause. In models about people, using a group variable can be illegal or harmful, and the fixes are harder; the check, though, is the same.

title: The machine-learning workflow
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Without the site. Remove the site from the model by adding step_rm(site_South) to the recipe (after the dummy step has made that column), refit with a penalty of 0.001 (the best for that model), and repeat the comparison by site. Also find its test AUC.









Remove the dummy column site_South.


rec_ns <- rec |> step_rm(site_South)
wf_ns <- workflow() |> add_recipe(rec_ns) |> add_model(spec)
lf_ns <- last_fit(finalize_workflow(wf_ns, data.frame(penalty = 0.001)), split, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc))
p <- predict(extract_workflow(lf_ns), test, type = "prob")$.pred_yes
print(collect_metrics(lf_ns)$.estimate)
round(sapply(c("North", "South"), function(s) {
  k <- test$site == s
  c(predicted = mean(p[k]), observed = mean(test$failed[k] == "yes"))
}), 3)
A test AUC of 0.886, the same as the model with the site (0.885). By the usual headline metric, the two models are equally good. But without the site, the model predicts 9.4% failures at North, where 6.7% failed, and 4.6% at South, where 6.6% failed: it under-predicts South by a third and over-predicts North. The AUC can’t see this, because within each site the ranking of the pumps is still good; only the probabilities are off, in opposite directions. With cost-based thresholds, that means too many inspections at North and too few at South. Two models, one number, and only a check by group tells them apart.




Challenge 2 · What it saves. Using the final model’s test-set predictions from collect_predictions(), find the cost of inspecting every pump with \hat p \ge 0.04 (€800 per inspection, €20,000 per missed failure), and compare it with inspecting none and inspecting all.









The threshold is 0.04.


lf <- last_fit(finalize_workflow(wf, data.frame(penalty = 0.00215443469)), split, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc))
pr <- collect_predictions(lf)
y <- pr$failed == "yes"
flag <- pr$.pred_yes >= 0.04
c(model = 800 * sum(flag) + 20000 * sum(!flag & y), none = 20000 * sum(y), all = 800 * length(y))
€360,800 with the model, against €1.0 million for inspecting nothing and €600,000 for inspecting everything: a saving of €239,000 over the better simple policy, on 750 pump-months, about €320 per pump-month. That’s the number that gets a model deployed. Like every number from the test set, it’s an estimate with an uncertainty (only 50 failures), and the bootstrap of Lesson 2 could put an interval on it.

title: The machine-learning workflow
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why stratify the initial split by the response?

To make the training set larger
To keep the failure rate the same in the training and test sets
To remove the class imbalance


With rare events, a random split can give the test set noticeably more or fewer of them.



2. What’s the difference between prep() and bake()?

There is none
prep() learns the steps’ parameters (medians, means, SDs) from data; bake() applies them
bake() fits the model


Inside resampling, the recipe is prepped on each fold’s analysis set only.



3. Why group the folds by pump?

To make them equal in size
So that no pump has records on both sides of a fold, and the CV estimate reflects unseen pumps
Because glmnet requires it


It’s Lesson 2’s grouped CV, with group_vfold_cv().



4. What does last_fit() do?

It tunes the model
It fits the finalized workflow to the training set and evaluates it once on the test set
It refits the model on all the data, test set included


For deployment, some practitioners then refit on all the data; the test estimate stays the one from last_fit().



5. How does permutation importance work?

It counts how often a predictor is used
It shuffles one predictor and measures how much the model’s performance drops
It removes a predictor and refits the model


It works for any model, which is why it’s so widely used.



6. Two models have the same test AUC, but one is well calibrated at both sites and the other under-predicts one site by a third. What does that show?

They’re equally good
An overall metric can hide a group the model serves badly, so check performance by group
The AUC is wrong


Subgroup checks of calibration and sensitivity are part of evaluating any model before it’s used.

title: The machine-learning workflow
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve put the whole machine-learning workflow together. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Spend the data once: a stratified 75/25 split, with the test set untouched until the end.
Recipes hold the preprocessing (imputation, dummies, standardization), and tidymodels re-learns them inside every fold, so the leaks of Lesson 2 can’t happen.
Grouped folds held out whole pumps. Workflows bundled the recipe and a lasso logistic model, and tune_grid() chose a penalty of 0.0022, with a CV AUC of 0.892.
last_fit() gave the honest test AUC, 0.885.
Explanation: permutation importance showed a model that’s mostly a vibration alarm, which matches the engineers’ experience.
Fairness: with the site included, the model was calibrated at both sites. Without it, the overall AUC was unchanged, but South’s failures were under-predicted by a third.
The business case: the model would have cost €360,800 on the test set, against €600,000 for inspecting every pump.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download pump_failures.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install the tidymodels meta-package with install.packages("tidymodels"), which loads all of these packages with library(tidymodels).

Tune two parameters. Change the model to logistic_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = tune()), and tune both with grid_regular(penalty(), mixture(), levels = 5).
Compare models. Use the workflowsets package to tune a lasso, a kNN model (nearest_neighbor(neighbors = tune())) and a neural network (mlp(hidden_units = tune(), penalty = tune())) with the same recipe and folds, and rank them.
Better imputation. Replace step_impute_median() with step_impute_knn(). Does the CV AUC change?
A curve for vibration. Add step_ns(vibration_mm_s, deg_free = 3) before the dummy step. The true effect is curved; does the spline help on the test set?










NoteKey words from this lesson






tidymodels

A collection of R packages for modeling that share a consistent grammar: rsample, recipes, parsnip, workflows, tune, dials and yardstick, among others.

Stratified split

A split that samples within each class separately, so that every part has the same class proportions.

Recipe

A specification of preprocessing steps that’s learned (prep()) from training data and applied (bake()) to any data.

Model specification

A description of a model’s type, its parameters and the engine that fits it, separate from the data.

Workflow

A bundle of a recipe and a model that’s fitted and applied as one object.

Analysis and assessment sets

The parts of a resampling fold used to fit and to evaluate a model.

Permutation importance

The drop in a model’s performance when one predictor’s values are randomly shuffled.

Subgroup evaluation

Checking a model’s calibration, error rates and sensitivity separately for each group it will be used on.











NoteWant to read more?






Max Kuhn and Julia Silge, Tidy Modeling with R (free online). The tidymodels book: chapters 5 to 10 cover this lesson’s workflow, and chapter 18 explaining models.
The tidymodels website, with its five-part “Get Started” tutorial.
Christoph Molnar, Interpretable Machine Learning (free online), on permutation importance, partial dependence and SHAP.
Solon Barocas, Moritz Hardt and Arvind Narayanan, Fairness and Machine Learning (free online). What “working for everyone” means, and why it’s harder than one table.

title: Module 7 project: a prediction challenge
text:
The plant crystallizes its main product in batches, and about one batch in five fails the particle-size test: too many fines, which clog the filters and fail the customer’s specification. A failed batch has to be redissolved and recrystallized, at about €12,000 a time. There’s a rescue: at the end of the seeding step, the operator can switch a batch to the slow cooling program, which almost always passes, but it costs about €1,500 in lost capacity, too much to do for every batch.
Ines, who runs the crystallization unit, wants a model that says, at the end of seeding, which batches to switch. That’s a prediction challenge: build several models, compare them honestly, choose one with a rule for using it, and show what it would have saved, on batches it has never seen.

title: Module 7 project: a prediction challenge
text:
What you’ll make
One report, written in Quarto in your plant-study RStudio project, that Ines could take to the plant’s management. It should contain:

A summary for Ines, at the top, in plain words: the model you recommend and the rule for using it, what it would have saved on the new batches, what drives the failures, and how it does on reactor R3.
The data and its problems: what you found, and what you did about it.
The model comparison: at least five methods from this module, tuned and compared by cross-validation on the 1,000 batches with known results.
The chosen model and its threshold, with its test on the 250 new batches.
An explanation and a fairness check, and a list of limitations.

Nobody grades it, but write it as if the plant manager will decide on your numbers. In real life, they would.

title: Module 7 project: a prediction challenge
text:
The handover
Download the four files into a new folder in your project, data-raw/crystallization/, and don’t edit them:

README.txt: Ines’s note, with the costs, the questions, the columns and a known issue. Read it first.
crystallization_batches.csv: 1,000 batches from January 2023 to June 2026, with their particle-size results.
new_batches.csv: 250 batches from July to October 2026, without results.
new_batch_results.csv: the results for those 250 batches. Don’t open it until you’ve chosen your model and your threshold. That’s the whole point of a test set: once you’ve looked, every later change is tuned to it.

Then download the project template, save it in the top folder of your project as batch-failure-model.qmd, and click Render. It reads the data and summarizes it, with headings and code skeletons for every step. Fill it in one section at a time, and render often. It uses the tidyverse, glmnet, mgcv, e1071 and nnet, and optionally the tidymodels packages of Lesson 14.

title: Module 7 project: a prediction challenge
text:
The brief, step by step

Explore (Lessons 1 and 2). Summarize every column. What’s the failure rate, overall and by reactor? Plot the failure rate against each process variable. Look hard at anything that couldn’t be known at the end of seeding, which is when the model will be used.
Clean (Module 1, Lesson 3). Some values are in the wrong units. Some are missing: is the missingness informative? Decide what to do with each problem, and log it.
Set up an honest comparison (Lessons 2 and 14). Use the 1,000 batches with results for everything: tuning, comparing and choosing. Use 10-fold CV, stratified by the outcome. Keep all preprocessing (imputation, scaling) inside the folds.
Compare methods (Lessons 3 to 11). At least: logistic regression with main effects, a lasso logistic regression, kNN, an SVM and a neural network. Then use what you’ve learned about the process: does a logistic regression with an interaction or a curved term, or a GAM, do better? Compare the CV AUC and the CV log loss.
Choose a threshold (Lesson 6). From the costs, at what probability is switching a batch worth it? Check your model’s calibration before you trust that threshold.
Test once (Lessons 6 and 14). Refit the chosen model to all 1,000 batches. Predict the 250 new batches, open new_batch_results.csv, and report the AUC, the confusion matrix at your threshold, and the cost, against switching no batches and switching all of them.
Explain (Lessons 4, 9 and 14). What drives the failures? Coefficients, partial effects or permutation importance, in words a process engineer can act on. Is there a best agitator speed?
Check fairness (Lessons 6 and 14). Does the model work as well on R3 as on R1 and R2? Compare the calibration, the AUC and the sensitivity by reactor, on the new batches.
Write it up. Summary first. Then the data, the cleaning, the comparison, the model, the test, the explanation and the fairness check, the limitations, and the cleaning log at the end.

Stretch goal. Ines could also run a partial rescue, a slower cooling program for only the last third of the batch, which costs €600 and prevents about 60% of failures. Work out the expected cost of each action (nothing, partial, full rescue) as a function of the failure probability, and turn your model into a three-way rule. How much more would it save?

title: Module 7 project: a prediction challenge
text:
Check your own work
When you’ve finished, assess your project against this rubric. Aim for the right-hand column.










Needs work
Good
Excellent




The data
Used as received
The unit error is fixed
The leak is found and excluded with a reason, the unit error and the missing values are handled and logged, and the effect of the leak on the CV AUC is shown


The comparison
One model
Several models by CV
Five or more methods, tuned inside the CV, with preprocessing inside the folds, compared by AUC and log loss, plus a model built from process insight


The threshold
0.5
Chosen from the costs
Derived from the costs, with a calibration check, and the cost curve shown


The test
None, or repeated
The chosen model tested on the new batches
Tested once, after choosing; AUC, confusion matrix and cost against both simple policies


The explanation
None
The main predictors listed
Drivers explained in process terms, with the interaction and the agitator’s sweet spot quantified


Fairness
Not checked
Results by reactor
Calibration, AUC and sensitivity by reactor, with the consequences for R3 spelled out


Communication
Code output with little text
A report that explains its steps
A report Ines could take to management: a plain summary, a clear rule, money saved, honest uncertainty and stated limitations

title: Module 7 project: a prediction challenge
text:
Tips

Ask “when is this known?” of every column. A predictor that’s measured after the outcome, or because of it, makes a model look brilliant in CV and useless in practice. A CV AUC near 0.99 for a messy industrial process is a warning, not a triumph.
Units. Plot each variable’s distribution. A handful of values in another unit stands out a long way from the rest.
Missing values can carry information. Compare the failure rate of batches with and without an impurity reading before you impute. A missingness indicator is a legitimate predictor.
The process knows things. Crystallization engineers know that fines form when the cooling outpaces the growth that the seed surface can absorb, so cooling rate and seed mass may interact, and that agitation has a sweet spot. Try those terms; a GAM can check the shapes.
Tune inside the folds. The lasso’s \lambda, kNN’s k, the SVM’s cost and \gamma, and the network’s size and decay should all be chosen within each training fold, or you’ll fool yourself. cv.glmnet() and tune() do this, or use tidymodels.
The threshold is 1{,}500 / 12{,}000. Switching costs €1,500 for sure; not switching costs €12,000 times the probability of failure. Switch when the probability is above 0.125, if your probabilities are calibrated.
R3 is new. It has only 74 batches in the training data, and the new batches include 90 from R3. How does the model treat a reactor it has seen little of?


When it’s done, you’ll have run a complete machine-learning project, from a leaky spreadsheet to a deployable rule with a price tag. Congratulations on finishing Module 7! Module 8 continues with decision trees and their ensembles, the methods that win most prediction contests on tables of data like these.

title: How decision trees work
text:
Module 8 · Lesson 2 of 13 Week 120 of 160 About 5–7 hours
A decision tree is a sequence of yes/no questions. “Did the account have three or more late deliveries? If so, is it in Pharma or Food?” Each answer sends an account down one branch, and at the end of the branches, the leaves, the tree makes its prediction: the churn rate of the training accounts that ended up there.
Sales managers like trees because they read like the rules of thumb they already use. Statisticians like them because they find thresholds and interactions on their own, without being told where to look.
