This lesson grows one by hand, so that nothing the rpart package does later is a mystery. The method is recursive partitioning, the heart of CART (classification and regression trees, Breiman, Friedman, Olshen and Stone, 1984):
In this lesson you’ll:

title: How decision trees work
text:
Impurity
A node is pure if all its accounts have the same outcome. For a node in which a share p churned, two common measures of impurity are

\text{Gini} = 1 - p^2 - (1 - p)^2 = 2p(1 - p), \qquad \text{entropy} = -p \log_2 p - (1 - p) \log_2 (1 - p) .

Both are 0 for a pure node and largest at p = 0.5. The Gini index is the probability that two accounts drawn at random from the node have different outcomes; entropy is the information theorist’s measure of surprise, in bits.

pp <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 300)
imp <- rbind(data.frame(p = pp, v = 2 * pp * (1 - pp), m = "Gini"),
             data.frame(p = pp, v = -(pp * log2(pp) + (1 - pp) * log2(1 - pp)) / 2, m = "entropy / 2"),
             data.frame(p = pp, v = pmin(pp, 1 - pp), m = "misclassification rate"))
ggplot(imp, aes(p, v, color = m)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Gini = "#C2416C", `entropy / 2` = "#2a78d6", `misclassification rate` = "#1baf7a"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Share of churners in the node, p", y = "Impurity") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "top")








The setup code makes Lesson 1’s partition and keeps the training set, train. It also defines y, a TRUE/FALSE vector of which training accounts churned, and the function gini().












Your turn. Compute the Gini index and the entropy of the root node: all 1,962 training accounts.









The second term uses the share that didn’t churn, 1 - p.


p <- mean(y)
c(p = p, gini = 2 * p * (1 - p), entropy = -(p * log2(p) + (1 - p) * log2(1 - p)))
p = 0.198, a Gini index of 0.317 and an entropy of 0.717 bits. Every split will be judged by how much it lowers this.

title: How decision trees work
text:
The best threshold
A split sends the accounts with x < t left and the rest right. Its quality is the decrease in impurity: the parent’s impurity minus the size-weighted impurity of the two children,

\Delta = G(\text{parent}) - \Big( \tfrac{n_L}{n} G(L) + \tfrac{n_R}{n} G(R) \Big) .

Your turn. Compute the Gini decrease for the split “three or more late deliveries”, and the churn rate of the accounts that go right.









The right child’s impurity is gini(y[right]).


right <- train$late_deliveries >= 3
decrease <- gini(y) - (mean(!right) * gini(y[!right]) + mean(right) * gini(y[right]))
c(decrease = decrease, n_right = sum(right), churn_right = mean(y[right]))
A decrease of 0.0456. The 255 accounts with three or more late deliveries churned at 58.8%, three times the base rate, and the other 1,707 at 13.9%. One question already separates high risk from low.




Your turn. Why three? Compute the decrease for every threshold from 0.5 to 5.5.









Use the function’s argument, t.


dec <- function(x, t) {
  L <- x < t
  gini(y) - (mean(L) * gini(y[L]) + mean(!L) * gini(y[!L]))
}
thresholds <- seq(0.5, 5.5, by = 1)
d <- sapply(thresholds, function(t) dec(train$late_deliveries, t))
round(d, 5)
thresholds[which.max(d)]
2.5 wins, with 0.0456; the next best, 3.5 and 1.5, manage only 0.016. That’s the threshold built into the data: customers tolerate one or two late deliveries a year, and start looking elsewhere at three. A tree finds thresholds like that by brute force, and with only the values that occur in the data as candidates (midway between them), the search is cheap.

title: How decision trees work
text:
The best input
Your turn. Find the best threshold, and its decrease, for each of seven numeric inputs.









Report the largest decrease, max(d).


dec <- function(x, t) {
  L <- x < t
  gini(y) - (mean(L) * gini(y[L]) + mean(!L) * gini(y[!L]))
}
best <- function(x) {
  u <- sort(unique(x))
  th <- (head(u, -1) + tail(u, -1)) / 2
  d <- sapply(th, function(t) dec(x, t))
  c(threshold = th[which.max(d)], decrease = max(d))
}
inputs <- c("late_deliveries", "volume_change_pct", "price_index", "account_years", "complaints", "volume_t", "visits")
round(t(sapply(train[inputs], best)), 5)
The late deliveries win easily (0.0456), then a volume drop of more than 14.5% (0.0180), a price index above 1.0465 (0.0133) and an account younger than 2.5 years (0.0128). The volume and the visits barely matter. Each best threshold is a fact the sales team can use: “a customer whose volume has dropped by 15% is a warning sign; a price 5% above the market is another”.




Here’s the search for one input, the volume change: every candidate threshold and its decrease.

u <- sort(unique(train$volume_change_pct)); th <- (head(u, -1) + tail(u, -1)) / 2
dd <- sapply(th, function(t) { L <- train$volume_change_pct < t; gini(y) - (mean(L) * gini(y[L]) + mean(!L) * gini(y[!L])) })
ggplot(data.frame(th, dd), aes(th, dd)) + geom_line(color = "#C2416C") + geom_point(color = "#C2416C", size = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Threshold for volume change (%)", y = "Gini decrease") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: How decision trees work
text:
Splitting a categorical input
A categorical input with k levels can be split into two groups in 2^{k-1} - 1 ways: 127 for the 8 segments, and about 5.8 \times 10^{17} for the 60 sales reps. For a two-class target, there’s a shortcut: order the levels by their churn rate, and only consider splits that keep that order. One of those k - 1 splits is guaranteed to be the best of all 2^{k-1} - 1.
Your turn. Order the segments by their training churn rate, and find the best of the 7 ordered splits.









The best split is at which.max(d).


rate <- tapply(y, train$segment, mean)
ordered <- names(sort(rate))
d <- sapply(1:7, function(k) {
  L <- train$segment %in% ordered[1:k]
  gini(y) - (mean(L) * gini(y[L]) + mean(!L) * gini(y[!L]))
})
round(d, 5)
ordered[1:which.max(d)]
Pharma and Food against the rest, with a decrease of 0.0028: real, but far weaker than the late deliveries. The ordering trick is why CART can split categorical inputs quickly. It’s also a danger: with 60 sales reps, the tree can always find some grouping of reps that looks good on the training data, as Lesson 1’s logistic regression found for itself. Lesson 7 shows how badly that biases trees.

title: How decision trees work
text:
rpart does the same
Your turn. Grow a tree with a single split (maxdepth = 1) with rpart(), leaving out the sales reps and the satisfaction score for now, and compare its improve value for the first split with n \times \Delta from your calculation.









A single split: maxdepth = 1.


stump <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep - satisfaction, data = train, method = "class", maxdepth = 1)
print(stump)
right <- train$late_deliveries >= 3
c(rpart_improve = stump$splits[1, "improve"],
  n_times_decrease = nrow(train) * (gini(y) - (mean(!right) * gini(y[!right]) + mean(right) * gini(y[right]))))
Both are 89.38: rpart chose late_deliveries < 2.5 by exactly your calculation, and reports the decrease multiplied by the node’s size. The printout reads: node 1 is the root, with 1,962 accounts, 388 of them “lost” (misclassified if the node predicts “no”), and class proportions 0.802 and 0.198. Nodes 2 and 3 are its children; a * marks a leaf.




Your turn. Let the tree grow to depth 2, and look at it.









In yval2, column 5 holds the share of the second class, “yes”.


tree2 <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep - satisfaction, data = train, method = "class", maxdepth = 2)
print(tree2)
tree2$frame$yval2[tree2$frame$var == "<leaf>", 5]
The tree split the high-risk branch again, by segment: of the 255 accounts with three or more late deliveries, the 58 in Food and Pharma churned at 31%, and the other 197 at 67%. The low-risk branch wasn’t split at all, because no split there improved the fit by enough to pass rpart’s default threshold (the complexity parameter, cp = 0.01, which Lesson 5 is about). So the leaves predict 13.9%, 31.0% and 67.0%. The tree has found an interaction: segment matters, but only for accounts with delivery problems. A logistic regression would only find that if someone added the interaction term.




Here it is, drawn with the rpart.plot package (each box shows the predicted class, the churn probability and the share of training accounts):

tree2 <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep - satisfaction, data = train, method = "class", maxdepth = 2)
rpart.plot(tree2, type = 4, extra = 106, box.palette = list("#F4C0D1", "#C2416C"), branch.lty = 1, roundint = FALSE, digits = 3)








Your turn. Predict the churn probability of an account with four late deliveries in Mining, and of one with one late delivery.









type = "prob" returns the class probabilities.


tree2 <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep - satisfaction, data = train, method = "class", maxdepth = 2)
new <- train[c(1, 1), ]
new$late_deliveries <- c(4, 1)
new$segment <- factor(c("Mining", "Mining"), levels = levels(train$segment))
predict(tree2, new, type = "prob")[, "yes"]
0.670 and 0.139: each account falls into a leaf and gets its churn rate. Nothing else about the accounts matters to this tree, so a tree’s predictions take only as many different values as it has leaves. That makes trees coarse rankers, which is one reason a single tree’s AUC is often lower than a logistic regression’s, and why Lessons 12 and 13 average many trees.










NoteGo deeper: why not split on the misclassification rate?





The obvious measure of a node’s quality is its misclassification rate, \min(p, 1 - p). CART doesn’t use it to grow trees, for two reasons. First, it’s often blind to good splits: a node with 80 stayers and 20 leavers, split into (60, 0) and (20, 20), has the same misclassification count before and after (20 errors), yet the split has found a pure group. The Gini index and entropy reward it, because they’re strictly concave: any split that changes the class proportions lowers them. Second, the misclassification rate isn’t differentiable, which makes it a poor guide when comparing many candidate splits. It’s the right measure for pruning and evaluating a finished tree, though, and rpart uses it (or a cost-weighted version) there. Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman’s Elements of Statistical Learning, section 9.2.3, discusses the three measures.

title: How decision trees work
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Entropy instead. Grow the depth-2 tree with the entropy criterion, parms = list(split = "information"), and check whether it makes the same splits.









rpart calls entropy "information".


g <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep - satisfaction, data = train, method = "class", maxdepth = 2)
e <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep - satisfaction, data = train, method = "class", maxdepth = 2,
           parms = list(split = "information"))
identical(g$frame$var, e$frame$var) && identical(g$frame$n, e$frame$n)
TRUE: the same splits, with the same accounts in every node. The two criteria almost always agree near the top of a tree, where the splits are strong; they occasionally differ deeper down, between nearly equal candidates. The choice rarely matters much, and Gini is rpart’s default.




Challenge 2 · Stopping rules. With cp = 0 (no improvement threshold), the only thing stopping the tree is minbucket, the smallest number of accounts allowed in a leaf. Count the leaves for minbucket = 7, 20, 50 and 100.









Use the function’s argument: minbucket = mb.


sapply(c(7, 20, 50, 100), function(mb) {
  fit <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep - satisfaction, data = train, method = "class",
               control = rpart.control(minbucket = mb, cp = 0))
  sum(fit$frame$var == "<leaf>")
})
38, 15, 6 and 2 leaves. With leaves as small as 7 accounts, the tree keeps splitting until it’s describing small groups of training accounts, noise included. Stopping rules like minbucket, maxdepth and cp are crude ways to stop that early. The better way, in Lesson 5, is to grow a big tree and prune it back, with cross-validation choosing how far.

title: How decision trees work
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does a classification tree predict in a leaf?

The most common input value
The class proportions of the training cases in that leaf
A logistic regression fitted in the leaf


Its predicted class is the majority, and its probability the leaf’s share.



2. The Gini index of a node with 30% churners?

0.30
0.42
0.09


2 \times 0.3 \times 0.7 = 0.42.



3. How does CART choose a split?

At random
It tries every input and every possible split, and picks the one with the largest decrease in impurity
It uses the input most correlated with the target


That’s a greedy search: the best split now, without looking ahead.



4. Why does CART order a categorical input’s levels by their churn rate?

To make the tree easier to read
For a two-class target, the best binary split is one that keeps that order, so only k - 1 splits need checking
Because rpart can’t handle factors


Instead of 2^{k-1} - 1 possible groupings.



5. The tree split on segment only for accounts with three or more late deliveries. What has it found?

A main effect of segment
An interaction between segment and late deliveries
An error


Trees find interactions automatically, because each split happens within a branch.



6. What does minbucket control?

The tree’s depth
The smallest number of cases allowed in a leaf
The number of trees


Small leaves let the tree fit noise.

title: How decision trees work
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve grown a tree by hand and checked it against rpart. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Impurity: the Gini index 2p(1-p) and entropy measure how mixed a node is. The root: 0.317 and 0.717.
The best split maximizes the size-weighted decrease in impurity: three or more late deliveries, \Delta = 0.0456, separating 58.8% churners from 13.9%.
Every input is scanned; the late deliveries beat a volume drop past 14.5%, a price 4.65% above the market and an account under 2.5 years old.
Categorical inputs are split by ordering their levels by churn rate: Pharma and Food against the rest.
rpart found exactly the same split, and its depth-2 tree found an interaction: segment matters only for accounts with delivery problems.
Stopping rules like minbucket control the size: 38 leaves at minbucket = 7, 2 at 100.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download customer_churn.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install rpart.plot.

The second split by hand. Within the 255 accounts with three or more late deliveries, repeat the search over all the inputs. Do you find rpart’s segment split?
Draw the tree. Try rpart.plot() with type 0 to 5 and extra 101 to 106. Which version would you show Lena?
Read the rules. rpart.plot::rpart.rules(tree2) writes each leaf as an if-then rule. Turn them into a paragraph for the sales team.
A tree on two inputs. Grow a tree on volume_change_pct and price_index only, and plot the training accounts in those two dimensions with the tree’s rectangles drawn on top.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Decision tree

A model that predicts by sending each case down a sequence of yes/no questions to a leaf.

Recursive partitioning

Growing a tree by repeatedly splitting each node in the way that most reduces impurity.

Node, leaf (terminal node)

A group of cases at a point in the tree; a leaf is a node that isn’t split further.

Impurity

A measure of how mixed a node’s classes are: zero for a pure node.

Gini index

\sum_k p_k(1 - p_k), which is 2p(1-p) for two classes.

Entropy

-\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k, in bits.

Greedy algorithm

A method that makes the best choice at each step, without looking ahead.

Stopping rule

A rule that stops a node from being split, such as a minimum leaf size or a maximum depth.











NoteWant to read more?






James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition), section 8.1, “The Basics of Decision Trees”.
Boehmke and Greenwell, Hands-On Machine Learning with R, chapter 9, “Decision Trees”.
Terry Therneau and Elizabeth Atkinson, “An Introduction to Recursive Partitioning Using the RPART Routines”, the rpart package’s long introduction, sections 1 to 3.
Leo Breiman, Jerome Friedman, Richard Olshen and Charles Stone, Classification and Regression Trees (Wadsworth, 1984). The book that started it all.

title: CART regression trees
text:
Module 8 · Lesson 4 of 13 Week 122 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Trees aren’t only for classes. A regression tree predicts a number, and the plant has a number that matters a lot: how long a charge of hydrotreating catalyst lasts before it has to be regenerated or replaced. A changeout means a shutdown of several days and a catalyst bill of hundreds of thousands of euros, so planners want to know, for a given set of operating conditions, how many days a charge will run.
The process engineers have a feel for what shortens catalyst life. Above a certain inlet temperature, the active metal sinters. Hydrogen sulfide above a few ppm in the feed poisons it. Each regeneration costs some activity. catalyst_life.csv has 600 past charges, with their average operating conditions and how many days each lasted:
Effects like “above 365 °C” and “above 5 ppm” are thresholds, and a regression tree is built from thresholds.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: CART regression trees
section: Splitting on the sum of squares
text:
Splitting on the sum of squares
For a numeric target, a node’s impurity is its sum of squares around its mean, \sum_i (y_i - \bar y)^2, and its prediction is the mean. The best split is the one that reduces the sum of squares the most:

\Delta = \text{SS}(\text{parent}) - \text{SS}(L) - \text{SS}(R) .

Equivalently, it’s the split whose two groups have the most different means, weighted by their sizes, which is a one-way ANOVA with two groups. That’s why rpart calls it method = "anova".
The setup code reads the 600 charges, and puts 400 of them, chosen at random, in a training set, and the other 200 in a test set.












Your turn. Find the correlation of each numeric input with the life.









Take the column for life_days.


num <- sapply(train, is.numeric)
round(cor(train[num])[, "life_days"], 3)
The inlet temperature (-0.47), the H₂S (-0.35) and the regenerations (-0.34) have the strongest correlations, the space velocity a weaker one, and the pressure almost none. Correlations measure straight-line association, so they understate effects that are thresholds, which the next steps find.




Your turn. Compute the share of the training sum of squares removed by splitting at an H₂S of 5 ppm.









The other child is the charges with low H₂S, y[!high].


y <- train$life_days
ss <- function(v) sum((v - mean(v))^2)
high <- train$h2s_ppm >= 5
(ss(y) - ss(y[high]) - ss(y[!high])) / ss(y)
26.9%: one question about the feed’s H₂S explains more than a quarter of the variation in catalyst life. That’s the split’s R^2.




Your turn. Find the best threshold for each numeric input, and the share of the sum of squares it removes.









Divide by the parent’s sum of squares, ss(y).


y <- train$life_days
ss <- function(v) sum((v - mean(v))^2)
best <- function(x) {
  u <- sort(unique(x))
  th <- (head(u, -1) + tail(u, -1)) / 2
  d <- sapply(th, function(t) ss(y) - ss(y[x < t]) - ss(y[x >= t]))
  c(threshold = th[which.max(d)], share = max(d) / ss(y))
}
round(t(sapply(train[c("inlet_temp_C", "h2s_ppm", "space_velocity_h", "pressure_bar", "regenerations")], best)), 4)
The H₂S wins, at 5.03 ppm (26.9%), ahead of the temperature at 381.75 °C (19.9%) and the regenerations at 2.5 (10.3%). By correlation, temperature was first; by splits, H₂S is. Poisoning is a threshold effect, and a split measures exactly that: the H₂S’s correlation was diluted by all the charges below 5 ppm, where it hardly matters.

title: CART regression trees
text:
A regression tree
Your turn. Grow a regression tree with rpart’s defaults, and count its leaves.









A regression tree is method = "anova".


tree <- rpart(life_days ~ ., data = train, method = "anova")
print(tree)
sum(tree$frame$var == "<leaf>")
12 leaves. The root splits on H₂S at 5.03 ppm; both branches then split on temperature, near 375 °C; then the feed source C (a heavier feed) appears in almost every branch, and the regenerations and space velocity further down. The leaves’ predictions range from 494 days (high H₂S and high temperature together) to 1,091 days (clean feed, moderate temperature, few regenerations, low space velocity). Each leaf prints its number of charges, its sum of squares (“deviance”) and its mean.




Your turn. Compare the tree with a linear regression on all six inputs, by their RMSE on the 200 test charges.









Predict the test charges, test.


tree <- rpart(life_days ~ ., data = train, method = "anova")
line <- lm(life_days ~ ., data = train)
c(tree = rmse(predict(tree, test), test$life_days),
  linear = rmse(predict(line, test), test$life_days),
  sd = sd(test$life_days))
85 days for the tree and 125 for the linear model, against a standard deviation of 165. The tree wins clearly, because the true effects are thresholds and an interaction, which a straight-line model can only approximate. On data with smooth, additive effects, the order is usually reversed.

title: CART regression trees
text:
An interaction, found
Your turn. Grow a tree of depth 2, and look at the four leaves’ means.









maxdepth = 2.


tree2 <- rpart(life_days ~ ., data = train, method = "anova", maxdepth = 2)
print(tree2)
round(tree2$frame$yval[tree2$frame$var == "<leaf>"])
494, 753, 831 and 964 days. Going above about 375 °C costs 259 days when the feed has more than 5 ppm of H₂S (753 to 494), but only 134 days when it’s clean (964 to 831): the sintering and the poisoning compound each other. That’s an interaction, and the tree found it simply by splitting on temperature separately in each H₂S branch. In a regression, you’d have to think of adding temperature × H₂S yourself.

title: CART regression trees
text:
The staircase, and its edges
A tree’s predictions are constant within each leaf, so as one input changes, with the others fixed, the prediction moves in steps.
Your turn. Predict the life of a charge with clean feed (2 ppm), source A, no regenerations, a space velocity of 2,000 and 30 bar, at inlet temperatures of 350, 370, 380, 395, 420 and 450 °C, with the tree and with the linear model.









Predict new with the linear model too.


tree <- rpart(life_days ~ ., data = train, method = "anova")
line <- lm(life_days ~ ., data = train)
new <- data.frame(inlet_temp_C = c(350, 370, 380, 395, 420, 450), h2s_ppm = 2, space_velocity_h = 2000,
                  pressure_bar = 30, feed_source = factor("A", levels = levels(train$feed_source)), regenerations = 0)
round(cbind(temp = new$inlet_temp_C, tree = predict(tree, new), linear = predict(line, new)))
The tree says 1,000 days at 350 and 370 °C, 900 at 380, and 852 at 395, 420 and 450 °C. The data stop at 395 °C, and beyond the last split the tree’s prediction is frozen: it has no idea that a charge at 450 °C would sinter in weeks. The linear model keeps falling (655 days at 450), which is at least the right direction. Trees, like kNN in Module 7, can’t extrapolate; they always predict an average of training cases. Inside the data, the tree’s steps are crude too: real catalyst life doesn’t jump by 100 days between 374 and 375 °C.





tree <- rpart(life_days ~ ., data = train, method = "anova"); line <- lm(life_days ~ ., data = train)
g <- data.frame(inlet_temp_C = seq(330, 460, by = 0.5), h2s_ppm = 2, space_velocity_h = 2000, pressure_bar = 30,
                feed_source = factor("A", levels = levels(train$feed_source)), regenerations = 0)
pp <- rbind(data.frame(t = g$inlet_temp_C, life = predict(tree, g), m = "regression tree"),
            data.frame(t = g$inlet_temp_C, life = predict(line, g), m = "linear model"))
ggplot(pp, aes(t, life, color = m)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 335, xmax = 395, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey93") +
  geom_step(data = pp[pp$m == "regression tree", ], linewidth = 0.9) + geom_line(data = pp[pp$m == "linear model", ], linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`regression tree` = "#C2416C", `linear model` = "#2a78d6"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Inlet temperature (°C), gray: the training range", y = "Predicted life (days)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "top")








Your turn. Compare the tree’s R^2 on the training and test charges.









Use the test charges’ life, test$life_days.


tree <- rpart(life_days ~ ., data = train, method = "anova")
r2 <- function(p, y) 1 - sum((y - p)^2) / sum((y - mean(y))^2)
c(train = r2(predict(tree), train$life_days), test = r2(predict(tree, test), test$life_days))
0.763 on the training charges, 0.730 on the test charges: a small drop, so this 12-leaf tree generalizes well. rpart’s default cp = 0.01 stopped it before it fitted much noise; a tree grown with cp = 0 would fit the training data almost perfectly and do worse on the test set. Lesson 5 chooses the size properly.










NoteGo deeper: trees as basis functions





A regression tree with M leaves R_1, \ldots, R_M is the model

\hat f(x) = \sum_{m=1}^M c_m \, I(x \in R_m),

a linear combination of indicator functions of boxes, with c_m the mean of the training cases in box m. It’s a linear model with a basis chosen by the data, like Module 7’s splines, but with discontinuous, box-shaped basis functions. Two extensions smooth the steps: MARS (multivariate adaptive regression splines, the earth package) builds the same kind of greedy partition from hinge functions \max(0, x - t), so its predictions are continuous; model trees (the Cubist package, or partykit’s lmtree()) fit a regression in each leaf instead of a constant. The Elements of Statistical Learning, sections 9.2 and 9.4, covers both.

title: CART regression trees
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · From tree to regression. The tree’s findings suggest a better linear model: a hinge in temperature (no effect below a threshold, a linear decline above it), a step at 5 ppm of H₂S, their interaction, and linear terms for the rest. Fit it with the hinge at 365 °C, and find its test RMSE.









Put the hinge at 365 °C.


hinge <- lm(life_days ~ pmax(inlet_temp_C - 365, 0) * I(h2s_ppm > 5) + space_velocity_h + pressure_bar +
              feed_source + regenerations, data = train)
round(coef(hinge), 3)
rmse(predict(hinge, test), test$life_days)
A test RMSE of 59 days: better than the tree (85) and much better than the plain linear model (125). Its coefficients read like an engineering rule: each °C above 365 costs 7.3 days, or 10.8 with a poisoned feed; more than 5 ppm of H₂S costs 217 days; each regeneration 35 days; feed C 113 days. This is a common, and very effective, way to use trees: as an exploration tool that shows where the thresholds and interactions are, so that a simpler, smoother model can be built around them.




Challenge 2 · Where’s the kink? The tree put its temperature split near 375 °C. Search for the hinge point k from 350 to 385 °C that gives the hinge model the smallest training residual sum of squares.









deviance(fit) is the residual sum of squares.


ks <- 350:385
rss <- sapply(ks, function(k) {
  fit <- lm(life_days ~ pmax(inlet_temp_C - k, 0) * I(h2s_ppm > 5) + space_velocity_h + pressure_bar +
              feed_source + regenerations, data = train)
  deviance(fit)
})
ks[which.min(rss)]
363 °C, close to the sintering threshold that the engineers expected. The tree’s split, near 375 °C, was about 10 °C too high: a tree puts its threshold where a step best separates the means, and a gradual decline that starts at 363 °C looks most step-like further up. Tree thresholds are a good first guess for where something happens, not a precise estimate of it.

title: CART regression trees
text:
Quick quiz

1. What does a regression tree predict in a leaf?

A regression line
The mean of the training cases in that leaf
The median of all the data


That’s why its predictions form a staircase.



2. How does a regression tree choose a split?

By correlation
By the largest reduction in the sum of squares
By the Gini index


Equivalently, the split whose two group means differ most, weighted by size.



3. Why did the tree beat the linear model on catalyst life?

Trees always beat linear models
The true effects are thresholds and an interaction, which straight lines can’t follow
The linear model had too few inputs


On smooth, additive relationships, linear models usually win.



4. What does a tree predict for an input value far beyond the training data?

A trend continued from the data
The same as for the most extreme training values in that direction
An error


Its prediction is frozen beyond the last split.



5. How did the tree show the interaction between temperature and H₂S?

With an interaction coefficient
By splitting on temperature separately within each H₂S branch, with different effects
It didn’t


High temperature cost 259 days with a poisoned feed and 134 with a clean one.



6. What’s a good use of a regression tree, besides predicting?

Estimating thresholds precisely
Finding thresholds and interactions to build into a smoother model
Extrapolating


The hinge model built from the tree’s findings beat the tree.

title: CART regression trees
text:
Wrap-up
You can now grow and use regression trees. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Regression trees split on the reduction in the sum of squares, and predict each leaf’s mean.
The best first split was H₂S at 5.03 ppm, removing 26.9% of the sum of squares, even though temperature had the stronger correlation.
The 12-leaf tree had a test RMSE of 85 days, against 125 for a linear model, and generalized well (R^2 0.763 on training, 0.730 on test).
It found the interaction: high temperature cost 259 days with a poisoned feed, 134 with a clean one.
Its staircase can’t extrapolate: frozen at 852 days beyond 389 °C.
Tree-inspired regression, with a hinge at 365 °C and a step at 5 ppm, beat both, at 59 days, and the best hinge was at 363 °C.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download catalyst_life.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Draw it. rpart.plot::rpart.plot(tree) for the regression tree. Write its rules with rpart.rules().
Residuals. Plot the tree’s test residuals against each input. Which input’s effect is the tree approximating worst?
MARS. Install earth, and fit earth(life_days ~ ., data = train). Does it find the hinge at about 363 °C? Compare its test RMSE.
A model tree. partykit::lmtree(life_days ~ inlet_temp_C | h2s_ppm + feed_source + regenerations, data = train) fits a temperature regression in each leaf. How does it compare?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Regression tree

A tree that predicts a numeric target by the mean of the training cases in each leaf.

Sum of squares (deviance)

\sum(y_i - \bar y)^2 within a node: a regression tree’s impurity.

Piecewise-constant prediction

A prediction that is constant within regions and jumps between them: a staircase.

Interaction

When one input’s effect depends on another’s value.

Extrapolation

Predicting outside the range of the training data, which trees can’t do.

Hinge function

\max(0, x - t): zero below a threshold t, linear above it.











NoteWant to read more?






James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition), section 8.1.1, “Regression Trees”, and the comparison with linear models in section 8.1.3.
Therneau and Atkinson, “An Introduction to Recursive Partitioning Using the RPART Routines”, section 8, on regression trees (“anova” splitting).
Calvin Bartholomew, “Mechanisms of catalyst deactivation”, Applied Catalysis A 212, 2001, doi:10.1016/S0926-860X(00)00843-7. Why catalysts die by poisoning and sintering, for the chemistry behind this lesson’s thresholds.

title: CHAID
text:
Module 8 · Lesson 6 of 13 Week 124 of 160 About 5–7 hours
CART comes from statistics and computer science. CHAID, chi-squared automatic interaction detection, comes from market research: Gordon Kass designed it in 1980 to find segments in survey data, where nearly every variable is a category (“age band”, “region”, “brand used”). It’s still the default tree in SPSS and one of the standard ones in SAS Enterprise Miner, which is why STAT 585 teaches it. It differs from CART in three ways:
The CHAID package isn’t available in this course’s browser R, so this lesson builds CHAID by hand, which is the best way to understand it anyway. (In RStudio, the CHAID package from R-Forge does it all; the Practice section shows how.)
In this lesson you’ll:

title: CHAID
text:
The chi-square test
The setup code makes Lesson 1’s partition and keeps the training accounts. It also defines three helpers that the later steps use, each of which you’ll first meet in its simplest form:

chisq_p(g, y): the p-value of a chi-square test of a grouping g against the target y;
merge_levels(x, y, ordinal): CHAID’s merging loop, which returns the merged groups of categories;
chaid_test(x, y, ordinal): merges an input’s categories and returns its groups and its Bonferroni-adjusted p-value.













Your turn. Test the segment against churn with a chi-square test.









Cross-tabulate the segment with the target, y.


test <- chisq.test(table(train$segment, y), correct = FALSE)
c(statistic = unname(test$statistic), df = unname(test$parameter), p = test$p.value)
\chi^2 = 18.5 on 7 degrees of freedom, p = 0.0097: churn rates differ between the segments. But the test says nothing about which segments differ. With 8 segments, many may be alike, and CHAID’s next step finds out which.

title: CHAID
text:
Merging categories
CHAID merges categories one pair at a time. For a nominal input (no natural order), any two categories may be merged; for an ordinal one (like a number of late deliveries), only neighbors. At each step:

For every allowed pair of groups, test the pair against the target (a 2 \times 2 chi-square test).
Find the pair with the largest p-value: the two groups that are most alike.
If that p-value is above the merging threshold (0.05), merge them and go back to step 1. Otherwise, stop.

Your turn. Do step 1 and 2 for the segments: test every pair, and find the five most similar.









Use the same accounts for the target: y[k].


pairs <- t(combn(levels(train$segment), 2))
p <- apply(pairs, 1, function(ab) {
  k <- train$segment %in% ab
  chisq_p(droplevels(train$segment[k]), y[k])
})
o <- order(p, decreasing = TRUE)
data.frame(pairs[o, ], p = round(p[o], 4))[1:5, ]
Mining and Plastics are the most alike (p = 0.974), then Adhesives and Plastics (0.930), Adhesives and Textiles (0.918). These segments have churn rates within a point or two of each other, so CHAID merges Mining and Plastics first, then tests again with the merged group.




Your turn. Run the whole merging loop for the segments with merge_levels().









The segment is nominal: ordinal = FALSE.


groups <- merge_levels(train$segment, y, ordinal = FALSE)
groups
Two groups: Food and Pharma, and the other six segments. The merging stopped when the only remaining pair, these two groups, differed with p \le 0.05. It’s the same split as CART’s ordering trick found in Lesson 2, reached by a different road: CART asked which grouping lowers the impurity most, CHAID asked which segments can’t be told apart.




Your turn. CHAID works with categories, so numeric inputs are first grouped. The setup code made late5, the late deliveries as 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5+. Tabulate it against churn, then merge it as an ordinal input.









The late deliveries are ordered: ordinal = TRUE.


print(table(late5, y))
merge_levels(late5, y, ordinal = TRUE)
Three groups: no late deliveries, one or two, and three or more. As an ordinal input, only neighboring counts may merge, so the groups stay ranges. CART, which splits in two, found only the threshold at three; CHAID also finds that accounts with no late deliveries are a little safer than those with one or two.

title: CHAID
text:
Adjusting for the merging
After merging, CHAID tests the merged table: the input’s groups against the target. But that p-value is too optimistic, because the groups were chosen to look as different as possible. CHAID corrects it with a Bonferroni multiplier: the number of ways the original c categories could have been merged into r groups.

For an ordinal input, the groups are ranges, so the number of ways is the number of ways to place r - 1 cut points in c - 1 gaps: \binom{c-1}{r-1}.
For a nominal input, any grouping is allowed, and the number of ways is the Stirling number of the second kind, S(c, r).

Your turn. Compute the multipliers for the segments (8 categories merged into 2 groups) and the late deliveries (6 categories into 3 ordered groups).









Six ordered categories have 6 - 1 = 5 gaps.


c(segment = stirling2(8, 2), late_deliveries = choose(6 - 1, 3 - 1))
127 for the segments and 10 for the late deliveries. Nominal inputs with many categories pay a heavy price: 8 categories can be merged into 3 groups in 966 ways, and the 60 sales reps into 2 groups in about 5.8 \times 10^{17}. That’s exactly what protects CHAID from Lesson 2’s danger, inputs with many levels that look good by chance, and it’s the main statistical advantage CHAID has over CART.




Your turn. Use chaid_test() for the segment, and check its adjusted p-value against the raw p-value times the multiplier.









The adjusted p-value is r$p_adj.


r <- chaid_test(train$segment, y, ordinal = FALSE)
c(raw_p = r$p, multiplier = r$multiplier, adjusted = r$p_adj)
The merged table (Food and Pharma against the rest) has a raw p-value of 2.8 \times 10^{-5}, and after multiplying by 127, an adjusted p-value of 0.0036. Still significant, but 127 times less impressive. Compare the unmerged test, with 8 categories, at p = 0.0097: merging made the test sharper, and the Bonferroni adjustment paid for the search.

title: CHAID
text:
Choosing the split
Your turn. Run chaid_test() for nine inputs, with the numeric ones grouped (deciles for the volume change and the price, quintiles for the account’s age, counts capped for the rest), and find the most significant.









Each input’s second element says whether it’s ordinal: inp[[2]].


inputs <- list(
  segment = list(train$segment, FALSE), region = list(train$region, FALSE), tech_service = list(train$tech_service, FALSE),
  late = list(late5, TRUE), complaints = list(factor(pmin(train$complaints, 3)), TRUE),
  volume_change = list(bin(train$volume_change_pct), TRUE), price = list(bin(train$price_index), TRUE),
  years = list(bin(train$account_years, 5), TRUE), visits = list(factor(pmin(train$visits, 8)), TRUE))
res <- t(sapply(inputs, function(inp) {
  r <- chaid_test(inp[[1]], y, ordinal = inp[[2]])
  c(groups = length(r$groups), p_adj = r$p_adj)
}))
signif(res[order(res[, "p_adj"]), ], 3)
The late deliveries win by a mile (p = 1.4 \times 10^{-61}, three groups), then the volume change (4.3 \times 10^{-20}), the account’s age, the price and the complaints (all near 10^{-17}), the service contract (7 \times 10^{-6}) and, much further back, the segment and the visits (0.0035). The region isn’t significant at all (p = 0.61). The ranking is close to CART’s, as it should be when the signal is strong.




Your turn. The root splits three ways, on the late-delivery groups. Find the number of accounts and the churn rate in each branch.









Group by branch.


gr <- merge_levels(late5, y, ordinal = TRUE)
branch <- integer(nrow(train))
for (i in seq_along(gr)) branch[late5 %in% gr[[i]]] <- i
rbind(n = table(branch), churn_rate = round(tapply(y == "yes", branch, mean), 3))
558 accounts with no late deliveries (11.5% churned), 1,149 with one or two (15.1%), and 255 with three or more (58.8%). The third branch is CART’s right-hand node exactly; CHAID has split CART’s left-hand node into two as well, in one step. Multiway splits make for wide, shallow trees, which business users often find easier to read: “zero, one or two, three or more” is how a sales manager thinks about late deliveries.



















NoteGo deeper: CHAID’s full algorithm and its variants





Kass’s original algorithm (Applied Statistics 29(2), 1980) has one more step: after merging, any group of three or more original categories is tested for a significant binary re-split, which can undo an early merge. Exhaustive CHAID (Biggs, de Ville and Suen, 1991) keeps merging until only two groups remain, recording the most significant grouping along the way, which avoids stopping too early. For a numeric target, CHAID uses F tests instead of chi-square tests; for an ordinal target, likelihood-ratio tests. All versions grow until no adjusted p-value passes the threshold, or a minimum node size is reached, and none prunes. The price of significance testing is that a node with few cases can’t produce a significant test, so CHAID trees stop where the data run thin, which is sensible, but they can also miss strong effects in small branches.

title: CHAID
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The second level. Within the branch with no late deliveries (558 accounts), run chaid_test() for the same nine inputs. Which input splits it?









Use only the branch’s accounts for the target as well: y[k].


k <- late5 == "0"
inputs <- list(
  segment = list(train$segment, FALSE), region = list(train$region, FALSE), tech_service = list(train$tech_service, FALSE),
  complaints = list(factor(pmin(train$complaints, 3)), TRUE), volume_change = list(bin(train$volume_change_pct), TRUE),
  price = list(bin(train$price_index), TRUE), years = list(bin(train$account_years, 5), TRUE),
  visits = list(factor(pmin(train$visits, 8)), TRUE))
res <- t(sapply(inputs, function(inp) {
  r <- chaid_test(inp[[1]][k], y[k], ordinal = inp[[2]])
  c(groups = length(r$groups), p_adj = r$p_adj)
}))
signif(res[order(res[, "p_adj"]), ], 3)
The volume change (p = 5.8 \times 10^{-10}), into two groups, closely followed by the account’s age (2.2 \times 10^{-9}), then the price and the service contract. The region and the complaints can’t even be merged into two significant groups (their adjusted p-value is 1), and the segment (p = 0.22) is no longer significant within this branch. CHAID would now split these 558 accounts by volume change, and carry on in each branch until no test passes. Within the busy branch with three or more late deliveries, the segment does matter, as CART found: that’s the interaction again.




Challenge 2 · CHAID’s stopping rule. Why will CHAID never split on the region? Use chaid_test() for the region on all the training accounts, and look at its groups and adjusted p-value.









Report r$p_adj.


r <- chaid_test(train$region, y, ordinal = FALSE)
list(groups = r$groups, p_adj = r$p_adj)
The merging leaves two groups, and the adjusted p-value is 0.61, far above 0.05, so the region is never a candidate. In the data, the region really has no effect on churn. CART has no equivalent test: given a node where nothing matters, it still finds the best split by impurity, and only pruning removes it. CHAID’s significance-based stopping is its built-in protection against fitting noise; its weakness is that the threshold, 0.05, is arbitrary, and with big samples, tiny effects pass it.

title: CHAID
text:
Quick quiz

1. How does CHAID choose a split?

By the largest impurity decrease
By the smallest Bonferroni-adjusted p-value of a chi-square test
By cross-validation


CART uses impurity; CHAID uses significance tests.



2. When does CHAID merge two categories?

When their pair is the most alike and its chi-square p-value is above the merging threshold
When they have the same number of cases
Always, until two groups remain


Merging stops when every remaining pair differs significantly.



3. For an ordinal input, which categories can be merged?

Any two
Only neighbors, so the groups stay ranges
None


“1 or 2 late deliveries” is allowed; “0 or 3” isn’t.



4. Why multiply the p-value by a Bonferroni factor?

To make it smaller
The groups were chosen to look as different as possible, so the raw p-value is too optimistic
Because chi-square tests are inaccurate


The multiplier counts the ways the merging could have gone.



5. How many ways can 8 nominal categories be merged into 2 groups?

8
28
127


The Stirling number S(8, 2) = 2^7 - 1 = 127.



6. What’s a key difference between CHAID and CART trees?

CHAID can’t use numeric inputs at all
CHAID splits multiway and stops by significance; CART splits in two and prunes
CART can’t use categorical inputs


CHAID groups numeric inputs into categories first.

title: CHAID
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve built CHAID from its parts. Here’s what you’ve learned:

CHAID tests each input against the target with a chi-square test: the segment, unmerged, had p = 0.0097.
Merging joins the most similar pair of categories (any pair for nominal inputs, neighbors for ordinal ones) while their p-value is above 0.05. The segments merged into Food and Pharma against the rest; the late deliveries into 0, 1 to 2, and 3 or more.
Bonferroni multipliers pay for the merging: 127 for the segments, 10 for the late deliveries.
The split goes to the smallest adjusted p-value: the late deliveries (10^{-61}), splitting the root three ways (11.5%, 15.1%, 58.8%).
Stopping by significance: the region (p = 0.61) is never split on.
Compared with CART: the same main structure, with wider, shallower trees, and built-in protection against many-level inputs.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download customer_churn.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder. Install CHAID from R-Forge with install.packages("CHAID", repos = "http://R-Forge.R-project.org"); it needs partykit.

A full CHAID tree. CHAID needs factors: make late5, deciles of the numeric inputs and so on, then run chaid(churned ~ ., data = ..., control = chaid_control(minsplit = 100, minbucket = 50)) and plot() it.
Compare it with your hand-built first level. Does the package find the same three-way split?
The sales reps. Add sales_rep as an input. What’s its adjusted p-value at the root, compared with its raw one?
Validation. Score the validation accounts with the CHAID tree, and compare its AUC with Lesson 5’s pruned CART tree.










NoteKey words from this lesson






CHAID

Chi-squared automatic interaction detection: a tree that splits by significance tests, with multiway splits and merged categories.

Multiway split

A split into more than two branches, one per group of categories.

Merging categories

Combining categories whose relationship with the target doesn’t differ significantly.

Nominal and ordinal inputs

Categories with no natural order, and categories with one; CHAID merges ordinal categories only with their neighbors.

Bonferroni adjustment

Multiplying a p-value by the number of tests (here, of possible groupings) it was chosen from.

Stirling number of the second kind, S(c, r)

The number of ways to partition c items into r non-empty groups.











NoteWant to read more?






Gordon Kass, “An Exploratory Technique for Investigating Large Quantities of Categorical Data”, Applied Statistics 29(2), 1980, doi:10.2307/2986296. The original CHAID paper.
Barry de Ville, Decision Trees for Business Intelligence and Data Mining: Using SAS Enterprise Miner (SAS Institute, 2006), chapter 2, on CHAID and CART as STAT 585’s software uses them.
Wei-Yin Loh, “Fifty Years of Classification and Regression Trees”, International Statistical Review 82(3), 2014, doi:10.1111/insr.12016. A history of tree methods, from AID and CHAID to CART and beyond.

title: Missing values and categorical inputs
text:
Module 8 · Lesson 8 of 13 Week 126 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Two things in the churn data have been set aside since Lesson 1: the satisfaction score, missing for almost a third of the accounts, and the sales rep, an input with 60 levels. Both are typical of business data, and both need care, for opposite reasons. Missing values are a gap in the information; a 60-level category is too much freedom for a tree to search. This lesson deals with each.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Missing values and categorical inputs
text:
Is missing informative?
The setup code makes Lesson 1’s partition, and defines auc().












Your turn. Compare the churn rate and the average number of complaints of the training accounts with and without a satisfaction score.









The input with gaps is satisfaction.


miss <- is.na(train$satisfaction)
rbind(n = table(miss), churn_rate = tapply(train$churned == "yes", miss, mean),
      complaints = tapply(train$complaints, miss, mean))
599 of the 1,962 training accounts have no score. They churned at 22.7%, against 18.5% for those who answered, and they complained more (0.85 complaints a year, against 0.65). Unhappy customers are less likely to fill in a survey. In Module 1’s terms, the data are missing not at random: the missingness depends on the very thing the score would have measured. So the gap is itself information, and a model should be able to use it.

title: Missing values and categorical inputs
text:
Surrogate splits
When rpart splits a node on an input, it also looks for surrogate splits: splits on other inputs that send the cases to the same side as the primary split as often as possible. When a case’s primary input is missing, rpart uses the best available surrogate; if none is available, it sends the case in the majority direction.
Your turn. Grow a one-split tree on four inputs, chosen so that the root splits on the satisfaction score, and look at its splits table: the primary split and its surrogates.









One split: maxdepth = 1.


stump <- rpart(churned ~ satisfaction + complaints + visits + payment_days, data = train, method = "class",
               control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 1, cp = 0))
print(stump)
stump$splits
The root splits on a satisfaction score below 4.5: 76 accounts, 54% of them churners, against 18% for the rest. The splits table lists the primary split and the runners-up (count is the number of cases with the input observed), and below them the surrogate: complaints of 4.5 or more, with an adj of 0.027. adj measures how much better the surrogate predicts the primary split’s direction than simply following the majority: 0 means no better, 1 means perfectly. Here the surrogate is barely better than the majority rule, so for the 599 accounts without a score, rpart is close to guessing.




Your turn. Predict the validation accounts without a score, with surrogates (the default) and with surrogates switched off (usesurrogate = 0).









usesurrogate = 0 switches them off.


f <- churned ~ satisfaction + complaints + visits + payment_days
with_s <- rpart(f, data = train, method = "class", control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 1, cp = 0))
without_s <- rpart(f, data = train, method = "class", control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 1, cp = 0, usesurrogate = 0))
na <- is.na(valid$satisfaction)
list(with_surrogates = table(round(predict(with_s, valid[na, ])[, "yes"], 3)),
     without = table(round(predict(without_s, valid[na, ])[, "yes"], 3)))
With surrogates, all 330 validation accounts without a score get 0.184: none of them has 5 or more complaints, so the surrogate sends every one to the large, low-risk side. Without surrogates, they stop at the root and get its rate, 0.198. Neither knows what the data say: that non-responders churn more than average. Surrogates are designed for values missing at random, where another input can stand in; when the missingness is the signal, they throw it away.

title: Missing values and categorical inputs
section: Three ways to handle the gaps
text:
Three ways to handle the gaps
The alternatives to surrogates:

Imputation: fill the gaps with a typical value, such as the training median. Simple, but it pretends the non-responders are average.
A missingness code: fill the gaps with a value outside the real range (here -1, below every real score), and add an indicator column. A tree can then split the missing cases off on their own, on either input, whenever that helps.

Your turn. Grow a tree three ways, with surrogates, with median imputation, and with the code and indicator, and compare their validation AUCs.









Code the gaps as -1.


f <- churned ~ . - sales_rep
med <- median(train$satisfaction, na.rm = TRUE)
impute <- function(d) { d$satisfaction[is.na(d$satisfaction)] <- med; d }
code <- function(d) {
  d$sat_missing <- factor(ifelse(is.na(d$satisfaction), "yes", "no"))
  d$satisfaction[is.na(d$satisfaction)] <- -1
  d
}
t_sur <- rpart(f, data = train, method = "class", cp = 0.005)
t_imp <- rpart(f, data = impute(train), method = "class", cp = 0.005)
t_code <- rpart(f, data = code(train), method = "class", cp = 0.005)
c(surrogates = auc(predict(t_sur, valid)[, "yes"], valid$churned),
  median = auc(predict(t_imp, impute(valid))[, "yes"], valid$churned),
  code = auc(predict(t_code, code(valid))[, "yes"], valid$churned))
0.762, 0.768 and 0.766: practically the same. On these data, the satisfaction score is mostly redundant (the complaints and late deliveries that drive it are already in the model), so how its gaps are handled hardly matters. That’s often the case, and worth checking before investing in elaborate imputation. When an input with informative gaps matters more, as the financial ratios do in this module’s project, the code-and-indicator approach is usually the safest for trees, because it lets the tree decide.




Your turn. Trees only use the order of a numeric input. Check that taking the log of the volume (a monotone transformation) leaves the tree’s predictions unchanged.









The log tree needs the log-transformed validation data, valid_log.


f <- churned ~ . - sales_rep
t_raw <- rpart(f, data = train, method = "class", cp = 0.005)
train_log <- train; train_log$volume_t <- log(train$volume_t)
valid_log <- valid; valid_log$volume_t <- log(valid$volume_t)
t_log <- rpart(f, data = train_log, method = "class", cp = 0.005)
identical(predict(t_raw, valid), predict(t_log, valid_log))
TRUE. A split at “volume < 120 t” and one at “log(volume) < 4.79” send exactly the same accounts left. So trees need none of the transformations that regression needs (logs, standardizing, dealing with skew), and outliers in an input can’t pull a split around. That robustness is a large part of why trees are so easy to use on raw business data. The target is different: for regression trees, a log transformation of the target does change the tree.

title: Missing values and categorical inputs
text:
Sixty sales reps
Your turn. Find how many training accounts each sales rep has, and the range of the reps’ churn rates.









The range of the reps’ rates: range(rate_rep).


n_rep <- table(train$sales_rep)
rate_rep <- tapply(train$churned == "yes", train$sales_rep, mean)
print(summary(as.numeric(n_rep)))
round(sort(rate_rep, decreasing = TRUE)[1:6], 3)
round(range(rate_rep), 3)
Each rep has 21 to 47 training accounts (33 on average), and their churn rates run from 4.0% to 44.1%. With about 33 accounts and a true rate near 20%, a rep’s observed rate has a standard error of about \sqrt{0.2 \times 0.8 / 33} = 7 points, so a spread from 4% to 44% is mostly noise. (Because these data are simulated, we know the truth: three reps, R07, R23 and R41, really do lose customers. R07 and R23 top the list; R41 isn’t in the top six, and R10, R20 and R40 are there by chance.)




Smoothed target encoding replaces each level with a number: its churn rate, shrunk toward the overall rate in proportion to how little data it has,

\text{encoded} = \frac{n_k \bar y_k + m \, \bar y}{n_k + m},

where n_k and \bar y_k are the level’s count and churn rate, \bar y the overall rate, and m a smoothing constant: a level with m accounts is pulled halfway. It’s the partial pooling of Module 5’s hierarchical models, in one line. The encoded rep becomes a single numeric input with one sensible order, instead of 60 levels with 5.8 \times 10^{17} groupings.
Your turn. Encode the reps with m = 20, and look at the top six and the new range.









The denominator is n_k + m.


n_rep <- table(train$sales_rep)
rate_rep <- tapply(train$churned == "yes", train$sales_rep, mean)
prior <- mean(train$churned == "yes")
m <- 20
enc <- (n_rep * rate_rep + m * prior) / (n_rep + m)
round(sort(enc, decreasing = TRUE)[1:6], 3)
round(range(enc), 3)
The range shrinks to 11.0% to 35.1%, and R07 stays clearly on top (35.1%), with R23 second (26.3%). R10 is now level with R23 at 26.2%, and R41, the third truly bad rep, ranks only 25th of 60. Shrinkage tames the noise, but it can’t create information that isn’t there: with 32 accounts each, the data can find the worst rep, and not much more.




There’s a trap in using the encoding: a training account’s own outcome is part of its rep’s rate, so the encoded input contains a little of the target. That’s leakage, and with small levels it’s not little. The fix is to encode out of fold: split the training set into folds, and encode each fold’s accounts with rates computed from the other folds. Validation accounts are encoded with the full training rates.
Your turn. Encode the reps out of fold (5 folds), grow a tree with the encoded rep in place of the raw one, and find its validation AUC and whether it uses the encoded rep.









Encode fold j’s accounts: train[fold == j, ].


m <- 20
encode <- function(from, to) {
  n <- table(from$sales_rep); r <- tapply(from$churned == "yes", from$sales_rep, mean)
  e <- (n * r + m * mean(from$churned == "yes")) / (n + m)
  as.numeric(e[as.character(to$sales_rep)])
}
set.seed(8082)
fold <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(train)))
train_e <- train; valid_e <- valid
train_e$rep_rate <- NA_real_
for (j in 1:5) train_e$rep_rate[fold == j] <- encode(train[fold != j, ], train[fold == j, ])
valid_e$rep_rate <- encode(train, valid)
t_enc <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train_e, method = "class", cp = 0.005)
c(auc = auc(predict(t_enc, valid_e)[, "yes"], valid$churned), uses_rep_rate = "rep_rate" %in% t_enc$frame$var)
A validation AUC of 0.762, the same as without the reps, and the tree doesn’t split on the encoded rep at all (uses_rep_rate is 0, FALSE). Encoded honestly, the reps carry too little reliable signal to earn a split, which is the right answer: their effect is real but too thinly spread to estimate well from 1,962 accounts. Compare the next two challenges, where it goes wrong.










NoteGo deeper: other ways to handle many levels





Besides target encoding: lumping rare levels into an “other” level (forcats::fct_lump_min() does it), which helps when a few levels are big and many tiny; grouping by domain knowledge (reps into regions or teams), often the best option; frequency encoding (the level’s count), useful when size matters; and hierarchical models (Module 5), which estimate each level’s effect with partial pooling inside the model, the principled version of smoothed encoding. For trees specifically, ctree (Lesson 7) and CHAID (Lesson 6) test a many-level factor fairly, and C5.0 and some implementations of gradient boosting have their own handling. Micci-Barreca’s “A Preprocessing Scheme for High-Cardinality Categorical Attributes” (SIGKDD Explorations, 2001) introduced smoothed target encoding.

title: Missing values and categorical inputs
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The leak. Encode the reps with their raw, in-sample training churn rates (no smoothing, no folds), grow the tree, and compare its training and validation AUCs and the encoded rep’s importance.









Predict the encoded validation data, valid_l.


rate_rep <- tapply(train$churned == "yes", train$sales_rep, mean)
train_l <- train; valid_l <- valid
train_l$rep_rate <- as.numeric(rate_rep[as.character(train$sales_rep)])
valid_l$rep_rate <- as.numeric(rate_rep[as.character(valid$sales_rep)])
t_leak <- rpart(churned ~ . - sales_rep, data = train_l, method = "class", cp = 0.005)
c(train_auc = auc(predict(t_leak, train_l)[, "yes"], train$churned),
  valid_auc = auc(predict(t_leak, valid_l)[, "yes"], valid$churned),
  importance = unname(t_leak$variable.importance["rep_rate"]))
A training AUC of 0.833 and a validation AUC of 0.758, lower than the honest tree’s 0.762, with the leaky encoded rep as an important input (17.9). In the training data, each account’s own churn is part of its encoded value, so the encoded rep looks predictive; on new accounts, it isn’t. This is one of the most common leaks in practice, because target encoding is so useful.




Challenge 2 · The raw factor. Grow the same tree with the raw 60-level sales_rep factor, and find its validation AUC.









Fit on train, with every input.


t_raw <- rpart(churned ~ ., data = train, method = "class", cp = 0.005)
auc(predict(t_raw, valid)[, "yes"], valid$churned)
0.716, the worst of all the versions: five points below leaving the reps out (0.762). CART searches the 60 levels for groupings at every node, finds ones that fit the training accounts’ noise, and spends splits on them that new accounts don’t follow. Out of the three ways to use the reps, ignoring them, encoding them honestly, or handing the raw factor to CART, the last is the only one that hurts.

title: Missing values and categorical inputs
text:
Quick quiz

1. Accounts without a satisfaction score churned more. What does that mean?

The missing values should be deleted
The missingness is informative: missing not at random
The survey is broken


A model can use the gap itself, with a missingness indicator.



2. What is a surrogate split?

A random split
A split on another input that mimics the primary split, used when the primary input is missing
A split that replaces a pruned branch


Its adj measures how much better it does than the majority direction.



3. When are surrogate splits a poor way to handle missing values?

When values are missing at random
When the fact of being missing carries information that other inputs don’t
Never


Surrogates route missing cases like similar complete ones, throwing the signal away.



4. Why didn’t taking the log of the volume change the tree?

rpart ignores the volume
Trees split on the order of an input’s values, which a monotone transformation preserves
The log was too small


Trees need no scaling or transformation of their inputs.



5. What does smoothed target encoding do with a sales rep who has few accounts?

Drops the rep
Pulls the rep’s churn rate strongly toward the overall rate
Gives the rep the highest rate


(n_k \bar y_k + m\bar y)/(n_k + m): partial pooling.



6. Why encode out of fold?

It’s faster
An account’s own outcome would otherwise be part of its encoded value, which is leakage
To use fewer levels


In-sample encoding gave a training AUC of 0.833 and a worse validation AUC.

title: Missing values and categorical inputs
text:
Wrap-up
You can now deal with gaps and messy categories in tree models. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Missingness can be information: accounts without a satisfaction score churned at 22.7%, against 18.5%.
Surrogate splits route missing cases by other inputs; here the best surrogate barely beat the majority, and sent every gap to the low-risk side.
Surrogates, median imputation and a missingness code gave validation AUCs of 0.762, 0.768 and 0.766: when the input is redundant, the choice hardly matters.
Monotone transformations don’t change a tree.
The 60 reps’ churn rates ran from 4% to 44%, mostly noise. Smoothed target encoding with m = 20 shrank them to 11% to 35%.
Out of fold, the encoded rep earned no split (AUC 0.762); in-sample, it leaked (training 0.833, validation 0.758); as a raw factor, CART overfitted it (0.716).







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download customer_churn.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Read the surrogates. summary() of the default churn tree prints every node’s primary split and surrogates. Find the nodes where a surrogate has an adj above 0.3.
Choose m. Repeat the out-of-fold encoding with m = 0, 5, 20 and 100. Does any value make the encoded rep useful on the validation set?
Missingness indicators everywhere. Write a function that adds an indicator for every input with missing values and codes the gaps. Use it on the credit data in this module’s project.
Lump the levels. Use forcats::fct_lump_min(train$sales_rep, min = 40) to keep only the biggest reps, and grow the tree. What happens?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Surrogate split

A split on another input that best mimics the primary split, used to route cases whose primary input is missing.

Missing not at random

Missingness that depends on the unobserved value itself, so that the gap carries information.

Missingness indicator

A 0/1 input recording whether a value was missing.

High-cardinality categorical input

A categorical input with many levels, such as a sales rep or a postcode.

Target (mean) encoding

Replacing each level of a categorical input with the average target for that level.

Smoothing (shrinkage)

Pulling a level’s estimate toward the overall average, more strongly when the level has few cases.

Out-of-fold encoding

Computing each training case’s encoding from the other folds only, so that its own target isn’t used.











NoteWant to read more?






Therneau and Atkinson, “An Introduction to Recursive Partitioning Using the RPART Routines”, section 5, “Missing data”, on surrogates and adj.
Boehmke and Greenwell, Hands-On Machine Learning with R, chapter 3, “Feature & Target Engineering”, on imputation, lumping and encoding.
Max Kuhn and Kjell Johnson, Feature Engineering and Selection (free online), sections 5.4 (“Supervised encoding methods”) and 8.1 (“Understanding the nature and severity of missing information”).

title: Neural networks for prediction
text:
Module 8 · Lesson 10 of 13 Week 128 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Neural networks are STAT 585’s third classic predictive model, next to trees and logistic regression. In SAS Enterprise Miner, a “Neural Network” node sits beside the “Decision Tree” and “Regression” nodes, and an analyst runs all three on the same data and compares them. Module 7 built networks from their parts. This lesson uses them the way a business analyst does: on a real prediction problem, with the validation set as the referee.
The big difference from Module 7 is the stakes: a churn network that memorizes the training accounts will send the engineers to the wrong customers. So most of the lesson is about restraint.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Neural networks for prediction
text:
Preparing the inputs
Networks need numbers on comparable scales. The setup code prepares the accounts as in Lesson 9 (satisfaction filled, with a missingness flag; sales reps dropped), turns the factors into dummy columns with model.matrix(), and standardizes everything with the training means and SDs. Dtr is the training data, with the 0/1 target churn, and Dva the validation inputs; yva holds the validation target as 0/1. It also defines auc() and ll(), the log loss.












Your turn. How many input columns does the network get, and what are the means and SDs of the standardized training columns?









Apply sd to each column.


inputs <- Dtr[, names(Dtr) != "churn"]
c(columns = ncol(inputs), max_abs_mean = max(abs(colMeans(inputs))), mean_sd = mean(apply(inputs, 2, sd)))
22 columns: the 9 numeric inputs, the missingness flag, and 12 dummy columns for the segment (7), the region (4) and the service contract (1). Every column has mean 0 and SD 1. The validation inputs are scaled with the training means and SDs, so their columns aren’t exactly 0 and 1, as it should be: anything else would leak information from the validation set into the preparation.

title: Neural networks for prediction
text:
A network that memorizes
Your turn. Fit a network with 10 hidden units, no weight decay and up to 2,000 iterations, with the cross-entropy loss (entropy = TRUE, the right loss for a 0/1 target). Compare its training and validation AUCs.









No weight decay: decay = 0.


set.seed(8101)
net <- nnet(churn ~ ., data = Dtr, size = 10, decay = 0, maxit = 2000, entropy = TRUE, trace = FALSE)
c(weights = length(net$wts), train = auc(predict(net, Dtr), Dtr$churn), valid = auc(predict(net, Dva), yva))
241 weights for 1,962 accounts, a training AUC of 0.959 and a validation AUC of 0.668. The network has memorized the training accounts, noise and all, and on new accounts it’s worse than Lesson 1’s five-input logistic regression (0.766). The exact numbers can differ slightly between computers, because the optimizer’s path is sensitive to rounding.

title: Neural networks for prediction
text:
Early stopping
A network starts from small random weights, which make it nearly linear, and becomes more complex as training goes on. Stopping the training early, at the point where the validation error is lowest, is the classic way to keep a network simple. It’s what SAS Enterprise Miner’s neural network node does by default, with the validation set as the judge. With nnet, the same random start (the same set.seed()) and a smaller maxit give the same path, cut short.
Your turn. Fit the 10-unit network with maxit of 5, 10, 20, 50, 100 and 500, from the same start, and find the validation log loss and AUC of each.









Use the function’s argument: maxit = it.


t(sapply(c(5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 500), function(it) {
  set.seed(8102)
  net <- nnet(churn ~ ., data = Dtr, size = 10, decay = 0, maxit = it, entropy = TRUE, trace = FALSE)
  p <- predict(net, Dva)
  c(iterations = it, valid_log_loss = ll(p, yva), valid_auc = auc(p, yva), train_auc = auc(predict(net, Dtr), Dtr$churn))
}))
The validation log loss is lowest after about 10 iterations (0.460), and then climbs steadily, to 0.96 by 100 iterations, while the training AUC keeps rising, from 0.79 to 0.97. The validation AUC is best even earlier, at 5 iterations (0.761), and falls to 0.69. So the right amount of training is very little: after 10 iterations, every further one fits noise. Early stopping picks the network at the bottom of the validation curve. Its weakness is that the validation set now does two jobs, stopping and judging, so a separate test set is needed for an honest estimate.

title: Neural networks for prediction
text:
Weight decay and size
Your turn. The other leash is weight decay, a ridge penalty on the weights. Fit the 10-unit network to convergence with decays of 0, 0.01, 0.1, 1 and 5, and compare the validation AUCs.









Use decay = d.


t(sapply(c(0, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 5), function(d) {
  set.seed(8103)
  net <- nnet(churn ~ ., data = Dtr, size = 10, decay = d, maxit = 1000, entropy = TRUE, trace = FALSE)
  c(decay = d, train = auc(predict(net, Dtr), Dtr$churn), valid = auc(predict(net, Dva), yva))
}))
The validation AUC climbs from 0.64 without decay to 0.71, 0.72, 0.78 and 0.79 as the decay grows to 5, while the training AUC ends at 0.81 with a decay of 5, against 0.92 to 0.96 with little or no decay. A large decay keeps the weights small, so the hidden units stay in the nearly linear part of their curves, and the network behaves almost like a logistic regression. That’s a hint about these data.




Your turn. With a decay of 1, compare networks with 1, 2, 5, 10 and 20 hidden units.









Use size = h.


sapply(c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20), function(h) {
  set.seed(8104)
  net <- nnet(churn ~ ., data = Dtr, size = h, decay = 1, maxit = 1000, entropy = TRUE, trace = FALSE, MaxNWts = 5000)
  c(size = h, valid = auc(predict(net, Dva), yva))
})
0.788 with a single hidden unit, 0.785 with 2, 0.770 with 5, 0.768 with 10 and 0.782 with 20. One hidden unit with a sigmoid output is a logistic regression passed through an extra S-curve, and it’s as good as anything bigger. The network can’t find the thresholds and the interaction on its own from 1,962 accounts: with weight decay to keep it stable, it ends up close to a logistic regression on the raw inputs (0.787).




Your turn. Networks from different random starts disagree. Average the predictions of five networks (5 hidden units, decay 1, seeds 8111 to 8115), and compare the average’s validation AUC with each network’s.









Average across the five columns: rowMeans(preds).


preds <- sapply(8111:8115, function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  net <- nnet(churn ~ ., data = Dtr, size = 5, decay = 1, maxit = 1000, entropy = TRUE, trace = FALSE)
  predict(net, Dva)
})
c(each = apply(preds, 2, auc, y = yva), average = auc(rowMeans(preds), yva))
The five networks score 0.770 to 0.789, and their average 0.794, better than any of them. Each network has fitted the noise in its own way, and averaging cancels part of it. It’s the same idea as bagging and random forests, next lesson but one, and the standard practice for networks in production.

title: Neural networks for prediction
text:
Looking inside
A network’s weights mean nothing one by one, but two summaries help. Input importance combines the weights along every path from an input to the output; Olden’s method multiplies the input-to-hidden and hidden-to-output weights and sums them, keeping the signs. A partial dependence curve sets one input to a value for every account, averages the predictions, and repeats across the input’s range: it shows the model’s average response to that input.
Your turn. Fit a network with 5 hidden units and decay 1, and find its six most important inputs by Olden’s method.









bar_plot = FALSE returns the numbers instead of a plot.


set.seed(8105)
best <- nnet(churn ~ ., data = Dtr, size = 5, decay = 1, maxit = 1000, entropy = TRUE, trace = FALSE)
imp <- olden(best, bar_plot = FALSE)
head(imp[order(-abs(imp$importance)), , drop = FALSE], 6)
The price index (+4.3), the volume change (-3.9), the late deliveries (+3.9), the account’s age (-3.6), the service contract (-2.2) and the satisfaction (-2.2). The same inputs as every tree and regression in this module, with sensible signs: higher prices and more late deliveries raise the risk; growing volume, longer relationships, a service contract and satisfied customers lower it. Agreement between very different models is reassuring evidence that these effects are real.




Your turn. Compute the network’s partial dependence on the late deliveries, from 0 to 6: set every validation account’s late deliveries to each value in turn (before scaling), and average the predicted probabilities.









Set the column to the function’s argument, v.


set.seed(8105)
best <- nnet(churn ~ ., data = Dtr, size = 5, decay = 1, maxit = 1000, entropy = TRUE, trace = FALSE)
pd <- sapply(0:6, function(v) {
  X <- Xva
  X[, "late_deliveries"] <- v
  mean(predict(best, data.frame(scale(X, mu, s))))
})
round(setNames(pd, 0:6), 3)
From 12.6% with no late deliveries to 54.8% with six, rising fastest between two and four. The network has learned that late deliveries matter, and roughly where, but as a smooth S-curve. The data, as the bars in the plot below show, have a step: the churn rate is 14% with none or one late delivery, 22% with two, and jumps to 50% at three. (The bars for five and six come from only ten accounts, so don’t read much into them.) The network, held back by its weight decay, can’t make a step that sharp, which is one reason the engineered logistic regression of Lesson 9, with its 0/1-2/3+ groups, did better.





set.seed(8105)
best <- nnet(churn ~ ., data = Dtr, size = 5, decay = 1, maxit = 1000, entropy = TRUE, trace = FALSE)
pd <- sapply(0:6, function(v) { X <- Xva; X[, "late_deliveries"] <- v; mean(predict(best, data.frame(scale(X, mu, s)))) })
obs <- tapply(yva, pmin(valid$late_deliveries, 6), mean)
ggplot() +
  geom_col(aes(x = as.numeric(names(obs)), y = as.numeric(obs)), fill = "grey80", width = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(x = 0:6, y = pd), color = "#C2416C", linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(aes(x = 0:6, y = pd), color = "#C2416C", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  labs(x = "Late deliveries (6 = 6 or more for the bars)", y = "Churn probability") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12)














NoteGo deeper: why the network didn’t find the threshold





A sigmoid hidden unit can make a step, but only if its weights are large, and a step at exactly three late deliveries needs the weight on that input to be large and the others small. Weight decay, which kept the network from overfitting, penalizes exactly such large weights. Without decay, the network can make steps, and it makes far too many, fitting noise. With 1,962 accounts and 22 inputs, there isn’t enough data for the network to tell the real step from the noisy ones, so the best it can do is a smooth compromise. That’s the general pattern: flexible models need data in proportion to their flexibility, and a few hand-crafted inputs can stand in for a lot of data. Ripley’s Pattern Recognition and Neural Networks (Cambridge, 1996), by nnet’s author, discusses weight decay and early stopping as forms of regularization.

title: Neural networks for prediction
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Price. Compute the network’s partial dependence on the price index at 0.90, 0.95, 1.00, 1.03, 1.05, 1.08 and 1.12.









The column is "price_index".


set.seed(8105)
best <- nnet(churn ~ ., data = Dtr, size = 5, decay = 1, maxit = 1000, entropy = TRUE, trace = FALSE)
prices <- c(0.90, 0.95, 1.00, 1.03, 1.05, 1.08, 1.12)
pd <- sapply(prices, function(v) {
  X <- Xva
  X[, "price_index"] <- v
  mean(predict(best, data.frame(scale(X, mu, s))))
})
round(setNames(pd, prices), 3)
From 9.5% at 10% below the market to 37.2% at 12% above it, rising smoothly the whole way. Again a smooth version of what the data hold: in truth, the risk jumps above 1.04, and mainly for accounts without a service contract, which a partial dependence curve, by averaging over all accounts, can’t show. (Lesson 13 meets two-way partial dependence, which can.) For Lena, the network’s message is still useful: every point above the market costs retention.




Challenge 2 · Against the engineered regression. Lesson 9’s engineered logistic regression had a validation AUC of 0.853. Feed the same engineered inputs to a network (5 hidden units, decay 1), and compare.









Predict the engineered validation data, Eva_d.


engineer <- function(d) {
  d$late_grp <- cut(d$late_deliveries, c(-1, 0, 2, Inf), labels = c("0", "1-2", "3+"))
  d$vol_drop <- as.integer(d$volume_change_pct < -15)
  d$high_price <- as.integer(d$price_index > 1.04)
  d$new_account <- as.integer(d$account_years <= 2)
  d
}
Etr <- model.matrix(churned ~ ., engineer(train))[, -1]; Eva <- model.matrix(churned ~ ., engineer(valid))[, -1]
m_e <- colMeans(Etr); s_e <- apply(Etr, 2, sd)
Etr_d <- data.frame(scale(Etr, m_e, s_e), churn = Dtr$churn); Eva_d <- data.frame(scale(Eva, m_e, s_e))
set.seed(8106)
net_e <- nnet(churn ~ ., data = Etr_d, size = 5, decay = 1, maxit = 1000, entropy = TRUE, trace = FALSE)
auc(predict(net_e, Eva_d), yva)
0.826, up from 0.79 with the raw inputs, but still below the engineered logistic regression (0.853) with the very same inputs. With the thresholds built in, there’s little left for the hidden layer to discover, and its extra flexibility only adds variance. On data with a few strong, simple effects, a well-specified regression is hard to beat; networks earn their keep on large datasets with complex, unknown structure, like images, text or sensor streams, which business tables rarely are.

title: Neural networks for prediction
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why standardize the inputs with the training means and SDs, not the validation set’s?

The validation set is too small
