Using the validation set’s own statistics would leak information from it into the preparation
It doesn’t matter


New data must be prepared exactly as the training data were.



2. A network has a training AUC of 0.96 and a validation AUC of 0.67. What’s happening?

It’s underfitting
It has memorized the training data
The validation set is mislabeled


241 weights for 1,962 accounts, without any restraint.



3. How does early stopping restrain a network?

It removes hidden units
It stops training when the validation error is lowest, before the weights grow large enough to fit noise
It adds a penalty


Training starts nearly linear, and gets more complex with each iteration.



4. What does a large weight decay make a network behave like?

A decision tree
A nearly linear model, close to logistic regression
A random guess


Small weights keep the hidden units in the linear part of their curves.



5. What does a partial dependence curve show?

One account’s prediction
The average prediction as one input is set to each value for every account
The network’s weights


It averages over the other inputs, so it can hide interactions.



6. Why didn’t the network beat the engineered logistic regression?

Networks are always worse
The structure is a few thresholds and an interaction, which the regression was given and the network couldn’t learn reliably from this much data
The network had too few inputs


Good inputs can be worth more than a flexible model.

title: Neural networks for prediction
text:
Wrap-up
You can now use neural networks as a predictive model, and keep them honest. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Prepare with dummy columns and training-set standardization: 22 inputs.
Unrestrained, a 10-unit network memorized the training accounts: AUC 0.96 on training, 0.67 on validation.
Early stopping and weight decay restrain it; with a decay of 5, the validation AUC reached about 0.79, and one hidden unit was as good as twenty.
Averaging five networks beat each one: 0.794.
Input importance and partial dependence show what a network uses: price, volume change, late deliveries and age, with smooth responses where the truth has steps.
Good inputs beat flexibility: the engineered logistic regression (0.853) remained the best model so far.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download customer_churn.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install NeuralNetTools.

Draw the network. plotnet(best) draws the 5-unit network with its weights as line widths.
A full early-stopping curve. Fit the 10-unit, no-decay network with maxit from 1 to 60, and plot the training and validation log loss against the iterations.
Tune both together. Make a grid of sizes (1, 3, 5, 10) and decays (0.1, 1, 3, 10), and find the best validation AUC. How flat is the surface?
Garson’s method. garson(best) measures importance without signs. Does it rank the inputs like Olden’s?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Multilayer perceptron

A neural network with one or more hidden layers of units between the inputs and the output.

Early stopping

Stopping training when the validation error stops improving, to prevent overfitting.

Weight decay

A ridge penalty on a network’s weights.

Cross-entropy (log loss)

The loss -\sum[y\log p + (1-y)\log(1-p)] for a binary target; entropy = TRUE in nnet.

Ensemble of networks

Averaging the predictions of several networks trained from different starts.

Input importance

A summary of how strongly a network’s output depends on each input, from its weights (Garson’s, Olden’s) or from permutations.

Partial dependence

The average prediction as one input is fixed at each value for every case.











NoteWant to read more?






Boehmke and Greenwell, Hands-On Machine Learning with R, chapter 13, “Deep Learning”, sections on network architecture and regularization.
Julian Olden, Michael Joy and Russell Death, “An accurate comparison of methods for quantifying variable importance in artificial neural networks using simulated data”, Ecological Modelling 178, 2004, doi:10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2004.03.013.
Christoph Molnar, Interpretable Machine Learning, the chapter on partial dependence plots.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Module 8 · Lesson 12 of 13 Week 130 of 160 About 5–7 hours
A single tree has a deep flaw that pruning only partly fixes: it’s unstable. Change a few training accounts, and the first split can move, and with it everything below. That’s high variance, in the bias-variance sense of Module 7, and it’s why single trees, however well pruned, rank accounts poorly. Leo Breiman’s fix, in two steps (1996 and 2001), is one of the great ideas of machine learning: grow many trees on different samples, and average them.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Unstable trees
The setup code prepares the accounts as in Lesson 9: satisfaction filled with a missingness flag, and no sales reps (randomForest can’t handle a factor with more than 53 levels). It makes Lesson 1’s partition, and defines auc(), which here takes the “no”/“yes” factor.












Your turn. Draw two bootstrap samples of the training accounts (sampling with replacement), grow a deep, unpruned tree on each, and compare their first splits and the correlation of their validation predictions.









A bootstrap sample is drawn with replacement.


set.seed(8121)
b1 <- train[sample(nrow(train), replace = TRUE), ]
b2 <- train[sample(nrow(train), replace = TRUE), ]
t1 <- rpart(churned ~ ., data = b1, method = "class", control = deep)
t2 <- rpart(churned ~ ., data = b2, method = "class", control = deep)
p1 <- predict(t1, valid)[, "yes"]; p2 <- predict(t2, valid)[, "yes"]
list(first_splits = c(as.character(t1$frame$var[2]), as.character(t2$frame$var[2])),
     correlation = cor(p1, p2), aucs = c(auc(p1, valid$churned), auc(p2, valid$churned)))
The two trees split first on different inputs below the root’s late-delivery split (the volume change in one, the price in the other), and their predictions for the validation accounts are correlated at only 0.45. Same population, same method, two quite different models, with validation AUCs of 0.777 and 0.756. Each deep tree has captured the real structure plus a different helping of noise. Averaging them should keep the structure and cancel some of the noise.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Bagging by hand
Bagging (bootstrap aggregating): grow B deep trees, each on its own bootstrap sample of the training data, and average their predicted probabilities. Each tree is unbiased-ish and very variable; their average keeps the low bias and has a much lower variance.
Your turn. Bag 50 deep trees, and compare the validation AUC of the average with that of a single tree.









Average across the 50 columns: rowMeans(P).


set.seed(8122)
B <- 50
P <- matrix(NA, nrow(valid), B)
for (b in 1:B) {
  i <- sample(nrow(train), replace = TRUE)
  tree_b <- rpart(churned ~ ., data = train[i, ], method = "class", control = deep)
  P[, b] <- predict(tree_b, valid)[, "yes"]
}
c(single_tree = auc(P[, 1], valid$churned), mean_single = mean(apply(P, 2, auc, y = valid$churned)),
  bagged = auc(rowMeans(P), valid$churned))
The first tree alone has an AUC of 0.721, and the 50 trees average 0.745 each. Their average has 0.826, better than any single tree in this module, without any pruning or tuning. The averaged probabilities also take hundreds of distinct values, so the ranking is fine-grained, which was the other weakness of single trees.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Out-of-bag error
A bootstrap sample of n accounts leaves out each account with probability (1 - 1/n)^n \approx e^{-1} = 0.368. So every tree has about 37% of the accounts out of bag (OOB): unseen. Predicting each account with only the trees that didn’t see it gives an honest error estimate for free, with no validation set.
Your turn. For one bootstrap sample of the 1,962 training accounts, find the share that’s out of bag, and compare with e^{-1}.









An account is out of bag if it isn’t in the sample i.


set.seed(8122)
i <- sample(nrow(train), replace = TRUE)
c(share_out_of_bag = mean(!(seq_len(nrow(train)) %in% i)), e_minus_1 = exp(-1))
36.95% of the accounts are out of bag, against e^{-1} = 36.79\%. The other 63% are in the sample, many of them more than once.




Your turn. Bag the 50 trees again, but this time also record each tree’s predictions for its out-of-bag training accounts. Average each account’s out-of-bag predictions, and find the OOB AUC.









Predict the out-of-bag accounts, train[out, ].


set.seed(8122)
B <- 50
oob <- matrix(NA, nrow(train), B)
for (b in 1:B) {
  i <- sample(nrow(train), replace = TRUE)
  tree_b <- rpart(churned ~ ., data = train[i, ], method = "class", control = deep)
  out <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(train)), i)
  oob[out, b] <- predict(tree_b, train[out, ])[, "yes"]
}
p_oob <- rowMeans(oob, na.rm = TRUE)
auc(p_oob, train$churned)
An OOB AUC of 0.841, on the training accounts, each judged only by trees that never saw it. It’s close to the validation AUC (0.826), and costs nothing extra. (Each account is averaged over about 18 of the 50 trees, so the OOB estimate is slightly pessimistic, as for a smaller forest.) With bagging and forests, the OOB error can replace cross-validation for tuning.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Random forests
Bagged trees are correlated with each other: the late deliveries are such a strong first split that almost every bootstrap tree uses them, and the trees end up similar. Averaging correlated trees cancels less of the noise. A random forest decorrelates them with one more source of randomness: at each split, only a random subset of mtry inputs is considered. With p inputs, the default for classification is \sqrt p. Weaker inputs then get their chance at the top of some trees, and the trees disagree in more useful ways.
Your turn. Fit a random forest of 300 trees with the default mtry, and a bagged forest (mtry = all 13 inputs), and compare their validation AUCs and OOB error rates.









300 trees for both: ntree = 300.


p <- ncol(train) - 1
set.seed(8123)
bag <- randomForest(churned ~ ., data = train, mtry = p, ntree = 300)
set.seed(8123)
rf <- randomForest(churned ~ ., data = train, ntree = 300)
rbind(mtry = c(bag$mtry, rf$mtry),
      oob_error = c(bag$err.rate[300, "OOB"], rf$err.rate[300, "OOB"]),
      valid_auc = c(auc(predict(bag, valid, type = "prob")[, "yes"], valid$churned),
                    auc(predict(rf, valid, type = "prob")[, "yes"], valid$churned)))
The bagged forest has an OOB error of 15.9% and a validation AUC of 0.823; the random forest, with mtry = 3, 15.0% and 0.832. Sampling inputs helped, a little, here; it helps more when a few inputs dominate and many others carry weaker signal. randomForest’s trees are grown fully deep (down to leaves of one case for classification), which is fine: the averaging does the regularizing.




Your turn. How many trees are enough? Look at the random forest’s OOB error after 1, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200 and 300 trees.









The overall OOB error is the "OOB" column.


set.seed(8123)
rf <- randomForest(churned ~ ., data = train, ntree = 300)
round(rf$err.rate[c(1, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 300), "OOB"], 4)
20.4% after one tree, 20.1% after 10, 16.8% after 25, then 15.8%, 15.1%, 14.9% and 15.0%: the error falls quickly and levels off after about 100 trees. Unlike a tree’s depth or a network’s training time, more trees never cause overfitting; past the plateau, they only cost computing time. A few hundred is usually plenty.




Your turn. Tune mtry: fit forests with mtry of 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and 13, and compare their OOB AUC (from the OOB votes, rf$votes) and validation AUC.









Use the function’s argument: mtry = m.


t(sapply(c(1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13), function(m) {
  set.seed(8124)
  f <- randomForest(churned ~ ., data = train, mtry = m, ntree = 300)
  c(mtry = m, oob_auc = auc(f$votes[, "yes"], train$churned),
    valid_auc = auc(predict(f, valid, type = "prob")[, "yes"], valid$churned))
}))
The OOB AUC peaks at mtry 2 or 3 (0.853), and the validation AUC agrees (0.834 and 0.833), with mtry = 1 (each split on a random input) and mtry = 13 (bagging) the worst. The default, \lfloor\sqrt{13}\rfloor = 3, is a good choice here, as it often is. Tuning by OOB, without touching the validation set, picked the same answer.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Variable importance
A forest has two importance measures. The Gini importance (MeanDecreaseGini) adds up each input’s impurity decreases over all the trees, as rpart does for one tree. The permutation importance (MeanDecreaseAccuracy) shuffles each input in each tree’s out-of-bag cases and measures how much the accuracy drops, as Module 7 did by hand.
Your turn. Fit a forest with importance = TRUE, and compare the two measures.









importance = TRUE computes the permutation importance.


set.seed(8125)
rf_i <- randomForest(churned ~ ., data = train, ntree = 300, importance = TRUE)
im <- importance(rf_i)[, c("MeanDecreaseAccuracy", "MeanDecreaseGini")]
round(im[order(-im[, "MeanDecreaseAccuracy"]), ], 1)
By permutation, the late deliveries (45.4), the volume change (23.0), the price (18.8) and the account’s age (16.1) lead, and the volume, the region and the payment terms are near zero: exactly the inputs that matter in the data, and the ones that don’t. The Gini importance agrees at the top, but it gives the useless volume (59.9) and region (36.6) high scores, above the complaints and the service contract. Gini importance rewards inputs with many possible split points (the volume is continuous) or many levels, for the same reason as Lesson 7’s selection bias. Trust the permutation importance.










NoteGo deeper: why averaging works, and where it stops





If B identically distributed predictions each have variance \sigma^2 and pairwise correlation \rho, their average has variance

\rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1 - \rho}{B}\sigma^2 .

As B grows, the second term vanishes, but the first stays: averaging can’t remove the variance the trees share. Bagging reduces \sigma^2’s share by averaging; random forests also reduce \rho, by sampling inputs, at the cost of a little extra bias in each tree. That’s why mtry has an optimum, and why more trees stop helping. It also explains what forests can’t do: they reduce variance, not bias. A forest of trees that all miss a smooth trend (trees can’t extrapolate, Lesson 4) misses it too. The Elements of Statistical Learning, chapter 15, has the analysis, and Breiman’s “Random Forests” (Machine Learning 45, 2001) is the original.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · A regression forest. Grow a random forest of 500 trees for catalyst life (Lesson 4’s 400 training charges), with the default mtry and with mtry = 4, and compare their test RMSEs with the tree’s (85 days) and the hinge regression’s (59).









mtry = 4.


cat_life <- read.csv("data/catalyst_life.csv", stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
cat_life$charge <- NULL
set.seed(8022); tr <- sample(600, 400)
rmse <- function(f) sqrt(mean((cat_life$life_days[-tr] - predict(f, cat_life[-tr, ]))^2))
set.seed(8126)
rf_default <- randomForest(life_days ~ ., data = cat_life[tr, ], ntree = 500)
set.seed(8126)
rf_4 <- randomForest(life_days ~ ., data = cat_life[tr, ], ntree = 500, mtry = 4)
c(default_mtry = rf_default$mtry, rmse_default = rmse(rf_default), rmse_mtry4 = rmse(rf_4),
  oob_rmse_default = sqrt(rf_default$mse[500]))
For regression, the default mtry is p/3, here 2, with a test RMSE of 73.6 days (OOB RMSE 65.4); with mtry = 4, 69.2. Both beat the single tree (85) by a lot, but neither beats the hinge regression built from the tree’s findings (59). The forest averages staircases, so its predictions are smoother than one tree’s, but it still can’t produce a clean hinge or extrapolate it. Where the structure is simple and known, a good parametric model wins; forests win when it’s complicated and unknown.




Challenge 2 · A pure-noise input. Add a column of random numbers to the training and validation accounts, fit a forest with importance, and find the noise column’s rank among the 14 inputs by each importance measure.









The Gini importance is "MeanDecreaseGini".


set.seed(8127)
train_n <- train; train_n$noise <- rnorm(nrow(train))
rf_n <- randomForest(churned ~ ., data = train_n, ntree = 300, importance = TRUE)
im <- importance(rf_n)
c(rank_permutation = rank(-im[, "MeanDecreaseAccuracy"])[["noise"]],
  rank_gini = rank(-im[, "MeanDecreaseGini"])[["noise"]])
By permutation importance, the noise column ranks 13th of 14, at the bottom with the payment terms and the missingness flag, where it belongs. By Gini importance, it ranks 7th, above the complaints, the satisfaction and the service contract, all of which really matter. A continuous column of random numbers offers a split point between every pair of values, and deep trees use them to fit noise in small nodes, which the Gini importance adds up as if it were useful. Adding a noise column is a good sanity check for any importance measure: anything ranked below it can’t be trusted.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why do single deep trees predict poorly?

They’re biased
They’re unstable: small changes in the data change the tree a lot, so their variance is high
They can’t handle factors


Two trees on bootstrap samples had predictions correlated at only 0.45.



2. What is bagging?

Pruning many trees
Averaging the predictions of trees grown on bootstrap samples
Growing trees on random subsets of the inputs


Random forests add the input sampling.



3. About what share of the training cases is out of bag for each tree?

10%
37%
63%


(1 - 1/n)^n \approx e^{-1} = 0.368.



4. What does mtry control in a random forest?

The number of trees
The number of inputs considered at each split
The depth of each tree


Smaller mtry decorrelates the trees, at some cost in each tree’s accuracy.



5. Can adding more trees to a random forest cause overfitting?

Yes, like growing a deeper tree
No; the error levels off, and more trees only cost time
Only for regression


The number of trees isn’t a flexibility setting.



6. Why prefer permutation importance to Gini importance?

It’s faster
Gini importance favors inputs with many split points or levels, even useless ones
Gini importance can’t be computed for forests


The useless volume had a Gini importance above the complaints’.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Wrap-up
You can now build and tune tree ensembles that average away variance. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Deep trees are unstable: two bootstrap trees’ predictions correlated at 0.45.
Bagging 50 deep trees lifted the validation AUC from about 0.745 per tree to 0.826.
Out-of-bag cases (37% per tree) give an honest error estimate for free: an OOB AUC of 0.841.
Random forests sample mtry inputs per split, decorrelating the trees: 0.832 with the default mtry = 3, against 0.823 for bagging. The OOB error levels off after about 100 trees.
Permutation importance found exactly the inputs that matter; Gini importance flattered the useless volume and region.
Regression forests cut catalyst life’s RMSE from 85 days (one tree) to 69 to 74, but didn’t beat the tree-inspired hinge regression.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download customer_churn.csv and catalyst_life.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install randomForest (and, if you like, ranger, a faster implementation).

The OOB curve. plot(rf) draws the OOB error and each class’s error against the number of trees. Why is the “yes” class’s error so much higher?
Balanced forests. randomForest(..., sampsize = c(400, 400)) draws equal numbers of each class for every tree. How does it change the OOB error by class, and the validation AUC?
ranger. Refit the churn forest with ranger::ranger(churned ~ ., data = train, probability = TRUE, importance = "permutation"). Is it the same model, and how much faster?
Partial dependence. partialPlot(rf, train, late_deliveries, which.class = "yes") draws a forest’s partial dependence. Compare it with Lesson 10’s network.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Bagging (bootstrap aggregating)

Averaging the predictions of models fitted to bootstrap samples of the training data.

Bootstrap sample

A sample of n cases drawn with replacement from n.

Out-of-bag (OOB) cases

The training cases not in a given tree’s bootstrap sample; about 37% of them.

OOB error

The error of predicting each training case with only the trees that didn’t see it.

Random forest

Bagged trees in which each split considers only a random subset of mtry inputs.

Decorrelation

Making the ensemble’s members less similar, so that averaging cancels more of their errors.

Gini importance

The total impurity decrease from an input’s splits across a forest.

Permutation importance

The drop in out-of-bag accuracy when an input’s values are shuffled.











NoteWant to read more?






James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition), section 8.2.1 and 8.2.2, “Bagging” and “Random Forests”.
Boehmke and Greenwell, Hands-On Machine Learning with R, chapters 10 and 11, “Bagging” and “Random Forests”.
Leo Breiman, “Random Forests”, Machine Learning 45, 2001, doi:10.1023/A:1010933404324.
Carolin Strobl, Anne-Laure Boulesteix, Achim Zeileis and Torsten Hothorn, “Bias in random forest variable importance measures”, BMC Bioinformatics 8, 2007, doi:10.1186/1471-2105-8-25.

title: Spatial data and maps
text:
Module 9 · Lesson 1 of 13 Week 133 of 160 About 5–7 hours
So far, every observation in this course has been a row that could be shuffled without losing anything. Module 9 follows STAT 586, spatial-temporal statistics, where that’s no longer true: each observation has a place, often a time, and observations close together tend to be alike. That’s both a problem (the methods of Modules 2 and 7 assume independence) and an opportunity (a measurement tells you something about its neighbours, so you can predict where you haven’t measured).
The plant’s history gives us plenty to work with. Until 2017, it made chlorine in a mercury cell room, as many chlor-alkali plants did, and for fifty years a little mercury escaped through the roof vents and settled on the land around. Hana, from environmental engineering, has the results of two soil surveys, and the questions every regulator asks: where is the contamination, how much is there, and how sure are we?
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Spatial data and maps
text:
Three kinds of spatial data
Spatial statistics has three branches, one for each kind of data, and this module covers all three:

Geostatistical data: a quantity that exists everywhere, measured at chosen points. Mercury in soil, groundwater levels, air temperature. The question is usually what is it at the places we didn’t measure? Lessons 2 to 5.
Areal (lattice) data: one value per area, such as a district’s population or its number of hospital admissions. There’s nothing between the areas to predict; the questions are about patterns and their causes. Lessons 6 and 7.
Point patterns: the locations of events, such as leaks, corrosion pits or crystals. The locations themselves are the data, and the question is whether they cluster, repel, or follow a covariate. Lessons 8 and 9.

Then Lessons 10 to 13 add time: measurements at fixed places that change from day to day, and fields that evolve.
Here’s the soil survey. soil_mercury.csv has 200 topsoil samples (0 to 10 cm deep):







Column
What it is




sample
sample ID


x, y
coordinates, metres (UTM zone 32N, EPSG:32632)


campaign
“plant 2018”: 56 samples targeted within 600 m of the cell room; “grid 2019”: 144 on a 250 m grid over 3 × 3 km


land_use
plant site, residential, farmland or woodland


hg_mgkg
total mercury, mg per kg of dry soil



The setup code reads it, and stores the cell room’s coordinates.

title: Spatial data and maps
text:
Coordinates and sf objects
A coordinate pair means nothing without its coordinate reference system (CRS): the rules that connect the numbers to a place on Earth. There are two families:

Geographic CRSs give longitude and latitude, in degrees, on an ellipsoid. EPSG:4326 (WGS 84, what GPS uses) is the standard one.
Projected CRSs flatten a region of the Earth onto a plane, so that coordinates are in metres and distances can be computed with Pythagoras. The UTM system cuts the world into 60 zones, each 6° of longitude wide; inside its zone, a UTM projection distorts distances by less than 0.1%. This plant is in zone 32N, EPSG:32632.

The sf package (“simple features”) stores spatial data as a data frame with a geometry column, plus the CRS. st_as_sf() builds one from a table with coordinate columns.
Your turn. Make soil_sf, telling st_as_sf() which columns are the coordinates and which CRS they’re in. Print the first three rows and find the CRS’s EPSG code.









UTM zone 32N is EPSG code 32632.


soil_sf <- st_as_sf(soil, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
print(soil_sf[1:3, ])
st_crs(soil_sf)$epsg
The x and y columns have become a geometry column of POINTs, and the header says “Projected CRS: WGS 84 / UTM zone 32N” and gives the bounding box: the survey covers 480,860 to 483,744 m east and 5,699,776 to 5,702,642 m north, a square about 2.9 km across. Every other column is carried along unchanged, so soil_sf still works like a data frame.




Your turn. How far is each sample from the cell room? Make the cell room a point with st_sfc(st_point(...)), in the same CRS, then use st_distance(). Summarize the distances, and count the samples within 500 m.









The distance from every sample to cell_room.


soil_sf <- st_as_sf(soil, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
cell_room <- st_sfc(st_point(cell_room_xy), crs = 32632)
d <- as.numeric(st_distance(soil_sf, cell_room))      # metres
print(summary(d))
sum(d < 500)
From 9 m to 2,038 m, with a median of 915 m; 53 samples lie within 500 m. st_distance() returns a matrix (here 200 × 1) with units attached (“[m]”); as.numeric() drops them. In a projected CRS, this is just Pythagoras on the coordinates.




Your turn. A buffer is the area within a given distance of a geometry. Draw a 1 km buffer around the cell room, find which samples fall inside it with st_intersects(), and compare the median mercury inside and outside.









The distance is in the CRS’s units: metres.


soil_sf <- st_as_sf(soil, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
cell_room <- st_sfc(st_point(cell_room_xy), crs = 32632)
zone <- st_buffer(cell_room, 1000)                       # a disc, 1 km radius
inside <- st_intersects(soil_sf, zone, sparse = FALSE)[, 1]
c(n_inside = sum(inside), median_inside = median(soil$hg_mgkg[inside]),
  median_outside = median(soil$hg_mgkg[!inside]))
108 samples within 1 km, with a median of 1.19 mg/kg, against 0.25 mg/kg outside. Natural background for mercury in topsoil is about 0.05 to 0.1 mg/kg, so even the outside median is raised. st_intersects() is one of a family of spatial predicates (st_within(), st_touches(), st_crosses(), …); with sparse = FALSE it returns a TRUE/FALSE matrix.

title: Spatial data and maps
text:
Longitude and latitude aren’t distances
Your turn. The regulator’s database wants the cell room’s location in longitude and latitude. Transform the point to EPSG:4326 with st_transform().









WGS 84 longitude and latitude is EPSG:4326.


cell_room <- st_sfc(st_point(cell_room_xy), crs = 32632)
st_coordinates(st_transform(cell_room, 4326))
8.7452° east, 51.4617° north. st_transform() doesn’t just relabel the CRS; it recomputes every coordinate (st_set_crs(), by contrast, only relabels, which is how wrong maps get made). The location is invented, by the way: the course’s data use a real CRS so that the tools work, but don’t describe a real place.




A degree of latitude is always about 111 km. A degree of longitude is 111 km at the equator, and 111 \cos(\text{latitude}) km elsewhere: at 51.5° north, only 69 km. So distances computed with Pythagoras on longitude and latitude are wrong, and wrong differently in different directions.
Your turn. Take samples 1 and 200, and compute their distance three ways: in UTM, with st_distance() on their longitudes and latitudes (sf then computes the distance on the sphere), and naively, as the Euclidean distance in degrees times 111,320 m.









Multiply by 111320, the metres in one degree at the equator.


soil_sf <- st_as_sf(soil, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
two <- soil_sf[c(1, 200), ]
two_ll <- st_transform(two, 4326)
xy <- st_coordinates(two_ll)
c(utm = as.numeric(st_distance(two[1, ], two[2, ])),
  sphere = as.numeric(st_distance(two_ll[1, ], two_ll[2, ])),
  naive = sqrt(sum((xy[1, ] - xy[2, ])^2)) * 111320)
2,149 m in UTM and 2,145 m on the sphere (UTM’s distortion is tiny), but 3,115 m naively, 45% too much, because the two samples are mostly east-west of each other and a degree of longitude here is only 69 km. Every method in this module (variograms, kriging, neighbours, K functions) computes distances, so the first step of every analysis is to put the data in a projected CRS.

title: Spatial data and maps
text:
Polygons: the districts
The county’s 60 districts come as a GeoJSON file, a text format for geometries that’s always in longitude and latitude (EPSG:4326). district_health.csv has each district’s population and health data, which Lessons 6 and 7 analyze.
Your turn. Read the districts with st_read(), check their CRS, transform them to UTM, and compute the total area in km².









Transform to the same CRS as the soil data, 32632.


dis <- st_read("data/districts.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
print(st_crs(dis)$epsg)
dis <- st_transform(dis, 32632)
sum(as.numeric(st_area(dis))) / 1e6                     # km2
The file is in EPSG:4326, as GeoJSON always is. In UTM, the county covers 693.5 km², from districts of 0.7 km² in the town to 45 km² in the countryside. (st_area() on the longitude and latitude version also works, on the sphere, and gives 691.5 km²; the 0.3% difference is UTM’s distortion at the edges of the zone and the sphere’s simplification of the Earth’s shape.)




Your turn. Attach the health data to the polygons with merge() (an sf object merged with a data frame stays an sf object), compute the population density, and find the three densest districts.









Both tables have a district column.


dis <- st_transform(st_read("data/districts.geojson", quiet = TRUE), 32632)
health <- read.csv("data/district_health.csv")
dis <- merge(dis, health, by = "district")
dis$density <- dis$population / (as.numeric(st_area(dis)) / 1e6)   # people per km2
st_drop_geometry(dis[order(-dis$density), c("district", "name", "density")])[1:3, ]
Castle Gate (D26), with 3,965 people per km², then Market Hill (1,940) and Station Road (1,834), all in the town north-east of the plant. st_drop_geometry() turns the result back into a plain data frame, which prints more compactly.

title: Spatial data and maps
text:
Spatial joins and maps
A spatial join attaches to each feature the attributes of the features it intersects: here, to each soil sample, the district it lies in.
Your turn. Join the samples to the districts with st_join(), and count the samples in each district.









Keep the districts’ name column.


soil_sf <- st_as_sf(soil, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
dis <- st_transform(st_read("data/districts.geojson", quiet = TRUE), 32632)
joined <- st_join(soil_sf, dis[, "name"])
table(joined$name)
The 200 samples fall in six districts: 100 in Canal Side, the district that contains the plant, 49 in Kingsmead, 32 in Dunham, 10 in Lime Kiln, 5 in Chapel End and 4 in Barton. Both layers must be in the same CRS; sf refuses to join layers whose CRSs differ, which is a good thing.




ggplot2 draws sf objects with geom_sf(), which reads the geometry and the CRS by itself. Mercury varies over two orders of magnitude, so a log color scale shows it best.
Your turn. Map the samples, colored by mercury on a log scale, on top of the district boundaries, cropped to the survey area.









A log scale: trans = "log10".


soil_sf <- st_as_sf(soil, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
dis <- st_transform(st_read("data/districts.geojson", quiet = TRUE), 32632)
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = dis, fill = "white", color = "grey60") +
  geom_sf(data = soil_sf, aes(color = hg_mgkg), size = 2) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(trans = "log10", name = "Hg, mg/kg") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(480800, 483800), ylim = c(5699700, 5702700), datum = st_crs(32632)) +
  theme_minimal()
The highest values cluster around the cell room, in the middle, but the cloud of raised values isn’t round: it stretches toward the north-east, the direction the prevailing south-westerly wind blew the vent emissions. That stretch will come back in Lesson 3 as anisotropy. datum = st_crs(32632) labels the axes in UTM metres instead of degrees.

title: Spatial data and maps
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Land use. For each land use, find the share of samples above 1 mg/kg, a common screening value for gardens and play areas.









Compare with 1.


round(tapply(soil$hg_mgkg > 1, soil$land_use, mean), 3)
75% on the plant site, 14% of the farmland, 10% of the residential samples (2 of 20) and none in the woodland. The two residential samples are the ones that matter most, and they lie to the north-east. But this table treats the samples as if they were a random sample of each land use, and they aren’t: 50 of the 65 plant-site samples come from the targeted 2018 campaign, which went where mercury was expected. A share of samples isn’t a share of area. Kriging (Lesson 4) turns samples into an estimate for every square metre, which can be summed honestly.




Challenge 2 · The third kind of data. The plant’s 2025 leak survey found leaking flanges and valves. Their locations are in site_leaks.csv, in site coordinates: metres from the south-west corner of the fence, a local CRS that sf knows nothing about. Read them, count the leaks by component, and work out why sf’s crs = NA is the right choice here.









The column is component.


leaks <- read.csv("data/site_leaks.csv")
leaks_sf <- st_as_sf(leaks, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = NA)
print(st_crs(leaks_sf))
table(leaks_sf$component)
205 leaks: 85 flanges, 69 valves, 29 connectors and 22 pump seals. With crs = NA, sf treats the coordinates as plain Cartesian numbers, which is exactly what local site coordinates are: distances and areas work, in metres, but sf won’t pretend to know where on Earth they are. Pretending (say, by labelling them UTM) would silently put the plant in the wrong place. For a point pattern, the interesting thing is the locations themselves, and Lessons 8 and 9 analyze them with the spatstat package.

title: Spatial data and maps
text:
Quick quiz

1. Mercury measured at 200 soil samples is an example of:

Geostatistical data
Areal data
A point pattern


The quantity exists everywhere; the samples are where it was measured.



2. The number of hospital admissions in each of 60 districts is:

Geostatistical data
Areal data
A point pattern


One value per area, with nothing in between to predict.



3. Why put data in a projected CRS such as UTM before analyzing it?

It makes the maps prettier
Coordinates are then in metres, so distances can be computed with Pythagoras
GeoJSON requires it


In longitude and latitude, a degree east and a degree north are different distances.



4. What does st_transform() do?

Relabels the CRS, keeping the numbers
Recomputes every coordinate in the new CRS
Moves the geometry


st_set_crs() relabels; st_transform() converts.



5. What does st_join(points, polygons) add to each point?

The distance to the nearest polygon
The attributes of the polygon it falls in
The polygon’s area


By default it joins by intersection.



6. 75% of the plant-site samples exceed 1 mg/kg. Why isn’t that 75% of the plant site’s area?

Because of the CRS
Because most plant-site samples were targeted where mercury was expected
Because mercury evaporates


Preferential sampling: a share of samples is only a share of area if the samples were spread at random or on a grid.

title: Spatial data and maps
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve set up the machinery for the whole module. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Three kinds of spatial data: geostatistical (soil mercury), areal (district admissions) and point patterns (leaks).
A CRS gives coordinates their meaning. Work in a projected CRS (UTM zone 32N, EPSG:32632, here); longitude and latitude distances computed naively were 45% wrong.
sf objects are data frames with a geometry column: st_as_sf(), st_read(), st_transform(), st_distance(), st_buffer(), st_area(), st_join().
The soil survey: within 1 km of the cell room, a median of 1.19 mg/kg against 0.25 outside, with raised values stretched toward the north-east.
Samples aren’t area: the targeted campaign makes simple shares misleading, which is a reason for the spatial prediction of Lessons 3 to 5.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download soil_mercury.csv and districts.geojson into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install sf.

Write a GeoPackage. Save the soil samples with st_write(soil_sf, "soil.gpkg") and open it in QGIS (free) if you have it. GeoPackage is the modern replacement for shapefiles.
An interactive map. Install mapview and run mapview::mapview(soil_sf, zcol = "hg_mgkg"). Since the location is invented, the background map will show wherever 8.75° E, 51.46° N happens to be.
Distances to a line. Make the motorway a line with st_linestring() (it runs from (487200, 5689000) to (488400, 5715000)), and compute each district’s distance to it with st_distance().
Areas by land use. Make a 50 m grid over the survey square with st_make_grid(), and count how many cells lie within 1 km of the cell room. What area is that, and how does it compare with the 108 samples?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Geostatistical data

Measurements of a quantity that exists everywhere, taken at chosen locations.

Areal (lattice) data

One value for each area of a partition, such as districts.

Point pattern

The locations of events in a region; the locations themselves are the data.

Coordinate reference system (CRS)

The rules connecting coordinates to places on Earth, identified by an EPSG code.

Geographic and projected CRS

Longitude and latitude in degrees (EPSG:4326) versus flat coordinates in metres (such as UTM).

Simple features (sf)

The standard way to store points, lines and polygons with their attributes; in R, the sf package.

Buffer

The area within a given distance of a geometry.

Spatial join

Attaching to each feature the attributes of the features it intersects.

Preferential sampling

Choosing sampling locations where high (or low) values are expected, which biases simple summaries.











NoteWant to read more?






Edzer Pebesma and Roger Bivand, Spatial Data Science with Applications in R (free online), chapters 1 to 3 and 7, on coordinates, geometries and sf. This module’s main reading for Lessons 1 to 9.
Robin Lovelace, Jakub Nowosad and Jannes Muenchow, Geocomputation with R (free online), chapters 2 to 4 and 7, on spatial data, operations and reprojection, with many more examples.
Noel Cressie, Statistics for Spatial Data (revised edition, Wiley, 1993), chapter 1, the classic statement of the three kinds of spatial data.

title: Variograms
text:
Module 9 · Lesson 3 of 13 Week 135 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 2 measured spatial dependence with correlations. Geostatistics, which grew up in the 1950s and 1960s in South African gold mines and French mining schools, uses a different tool: the variogram. It asks how different two measurements are, on average, as a function of the distance between them. Close together, they’re similar; far apart, as different as two random samples. How fast the difference grows, and where it stops growing, is what kriging (Lesson 4) needs to predict between the samples.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Variograms
text:
The semivariance
For a quantity Z measured at locations s, the semivariogram (usually just “variogram”) is

\gamma(h) = \tfrac{1}{2} \, \mathrm{E}\big[(Z(s + h) - Z(s))^2\big],

half the expected squared difference between two values a distance h apart. (The half makes \gamma equal to the variance for far-apart, uncorrelated pairs.) That only makes sense if \gamma depends on the separation h and not on where you are: the assumption of stationarity. If it also depends only on the length of h, not its direction, the field is isotropic.
For two specific samples i and j, \frac{1}{2}(z_i - z_j)^2 is a single noisy estimate of \gamma(h_{ij}). All of them together form the variogram cloud: 200 \times 199 / 2 = 19{,}900 pairs here. The empirical variogram averages the cloud within distance bins.
The setup code reads the soil data, takes logs, and computes the distance to the cell room in kilometres.












Your turn. Build the variogram cloud: every pair’s distance and half squared difference. Then average the semivariance over the pairs less than 100 m apart.









Squared: ^2.


D <- as.matrix(dist(soil[, c("x", "y")]))                  # distances, m
G <- 0.5 * outer(soil$z, soil$z, "-")^2                     # half squared differences
keep <- lower.tri(D)                                        # each pair once
h <- D[keep]; g <- G[keep]
c(pairs = length(h), close_pairs = sum(h < 100), gamma_close = mean(g[h < 100]))
19,900 pairs, of which 79 are within 100 m, with an average semivariance of 0.081. The variance of all 200 log values is 1.34, so samples less than 100 m apart differ by only a small fraction of the overall variation. Each single pair’s value is very noisy (a squared difference is a chi-squared-like quantity with one degree of freedom), which is why the cloud itself is hard to read and is always averaged.




Your turn. Now average the semivariance for pairs 1,400 to 1,500 m apart, and compare it with the variance of the log values.









Up to 1,500 m.


D <- as.matrix(dist(soil[, c("x", "y")]))
G <- 0.5 * outer(soil$z, soil$z, "-")^2
keep <- lower.tri(D); h <- D[keep]; g <- G[keep]
c(gamma_far = mean(g[h > 1400 & h < 1500]), variance = var(soil$z))
2.09, more than the variance of 1.34. For a stationary field that can’t happen: the semivariance of far-apart pairs should level off at the variance (the sill). Here it keeps growing, because pairs 1.4 km apart are typically one sample near the cell room and one far away. That’s the trend from Lesson 2: the mean isn’t constant, so the field isn’t stationary, and the raw variogram mixes the trend with the dependence.

title: Variograms
text:
The empirical variogram
gstat’s variogram() does the binning: cutoff is the largest distance considered (a common rule is up to half the largest distance in the data), and width the bin width. The formula’s left side is the variable, its right side the trend (~ 1 for a constant mean), and locations = ~x + y names the coordinates.
Your turn. Compute the empirical variogram of log mercury up to 1.5 km in 100 m bins, and check its first bin against your hand calculation.









Bins 100 m wide.


v <- variogram(z ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = soil, cutoff = 1500, width = 100)
print(v[, c("np", "dist", "gamma")])
v$gamma[1]
The first bin has the same 79 pairs and the same 0.081. np is the number of pairs in each bin and dist their average distance. The semivariance climbs steadily, from 0.08 to 2.09, without levelling off: the trend again.




Your turn. Put the trend in the formula: z ~ dist_km computes the variogram of the residuals from a regression on the distance to the cell room. Compare its first and last bins with the raw variogram’s.









The trend is the distance, dist_km.


vr <- variogram(z ~ dist_km, locations = ~x + y, data = soil, cutoff = 1500, width = 100)
print(vr[, c("np", "dist", "gamma")])
vr$gamma[c(1, 15)]
0.074 at the shortest distances, much as before, but only 0.71 at 1.45 km instead of 2.09. The residual variogram rises quickly to about 0.4 at 500 m, flattens, and rises slowly again beyond a kilometre, toward the residuals’ variance of 0.64 and a bit beyond. The slow rise at large distances is real: as you’ll see below, the dependence reaches much farther in one direction than in the other.

title: Variograms
text:
Variogram models
Kriging needs \gamma(h) at every distance, not just at the bin centres, and it needs a function that’s guaranteed to give valid (non-negative) variances for every combination of locations. So we fit a model from a family known to be valid. Every model has three features:

the nugget c_0: the jump at the origin, \gamma(0^+). Measurement error plus variation at scales smaller than the closest samples (the name comes from gold nuggets: two samples a centimetre apart can differ completely).
the sill c_0 + c_1: the plateau, the variance of far-apart values; c_1 is the partial sill.
the range a: how far the dependence reaches.

The common models, with c_1 and a:








Model
\gamma(h) - c_0 for h > 0
Reaches 95% of the sill at




Spherical
c_1\left(\frac{3h}{2a} - \frac{h^3}{2a^3}\right) for h \le a, c_1 beyond
exactly a (and stops)


Exponential
c_1(1 - e^{-h/a})
3a (the practical range)


Gaussian
c_1(1 - e^{-h^2/a^2})
\sqrt{3}\,a



The Matérn family adds a smoothness parameter \kappa: \kappa = 0.5 is the exponential, \kappa \to \infty the Gaussian. Rough fields (soil, ore grades) have small \kappa and rise linearly from the nugget; smooth ones (groundwater levels, temperature) have large \kappa and rise like a parabola.
fit.variogram() fits a model to the empirical variogram by weighted least squares (by default, each bin’s weight is its number of pairs divided by its distance squared, so the short distances that matter most for kriging count most). You give it a starting model with vgm(psill, model, range, nugget).
Your turn. Fit an exponential model to the residual variogram, and compute its practical range.









The exponential model is "Exp".


vr <- variogram(z ~ dist_km, ~x + y, data = soil, cutoff = 1500, width = 100)
fe <- fit.variogram(vr, vgm(psill = 0.6, model = "Exp", range = 300, nugget = 0.05))
print(fe)
c(nugget = fe$psill[1], partial_sill = fe$psill[2], range = fe$range[2], practical_range = 3 * fe$range[2])
A nugget of 0.018, a partial sill of 0.692 (so a sill of 0.71), and a range parameter of 693 m, which means a practical range of 2.1 km. The nugget is only 2.6% of the sill: two samples a few metres apart would differ very little, so the laboratory’s measurement error and the soil’s very-small-scale patchiness are small. The starting values only need to be roughly right; the fit adjusts them.




Your turn. Fit a spherical model, which reaches its sill at a finite range, and compare.









The spherical model is "Sph".


vr <- variogram(z ~ dist_km, ~x + y, data = soil, cutoff = 1500, width = 100)
fs <- fit.variogram(vr, vgm(0.6, "Sph", 900, 0.05))
c(nugget = fs$psill[1], partial_sill = fs$psill[2], range = fs$range[2])
A nugget of 0.059, a partial sill of 0.587 and a range of 1,440 m. To fit the steep rise at short distances and the slow rise beyond a kilometre with a curve that must stop at its range, the spherical model compromises: a bigger nugget, a lower sill. Different models can describe the same points quite differently near the origin, and the origin is what matters for kriging.




Your turn. Compare the weighted sums of squared errors (attr(fit, "SSErr")) of the exponential, spherical and Gaussian fits.









The attribute is "SSErr".


vr <- variogram(z ~ dist_km, ~x + y, data = soil, cutoff = 1500, width = 100)
fits <- list(Exp = fit.variogram(vr, vgm(0.6, "Exp", 300, 0.05)),
             Sph = fit.variogram(vr, vgm(0.6, "Sph", 900, 0.05)),
             Gau = fit.variogram(vr, vgm(0.6, "Gau", 500, 0.05)))
sapply(fits, attr, "SSErr")
The exponential fits best (5.6 \times 10^{-5}), then the spherical (9.0 \times 10^{-5}), and the Gaussian worst (1.4 \times 10^{-4}): soil contamination is rough, and the Gaussian model, which describes very smooth fields, rises too slowly at short distances. The SSErr is a weighted least-squares criterion, useful for comparing models fitted to the same variogram, but not a measure of predictive skill; Lesson 4’s cross-validation is the better judge.

title: Variograms
text:
Anisotropy
Isotropy means the dependence is the same in every direction. A wind that blew mostly from the south-west for fifty years, though, would spread mercury further along the wind than across it. A directional variogram uses only pairs whose direction is within a tolerance (by default ±22.5°) of a given angle, measured clockwise from north: 45° is north-east (along the wind), 135° south-east (across it).
Your turn. Compute the residual variogram in the two directions, and average each direction’s semivariance over the bins below 600 m.









Across the wind: 135°.


vd <- variogram(z ~ dist_km, ~x + y, data = soil, cutoff = 1200, width = 150, alpha = c(45, 135))
print(vd[, c("np", "dist", "gamma", "dir.hor")])
short <- vd$dist < 600
tapply(vd$gamma[short], vd$dir.hor[short], mean)
Below 600 m, the average semivariance is 0.21 along the wind and 0.33 across it. At 380 m, for example, it’s 0.23 north-east and 0.48 south-east: samples 380 m apart along the wind are as alike as samples about 200 m apart across it. The dependence reaches roughly twice as far along the wind. That’s geometric anisotropy: the same variogram shape, with a range that depends on direction, which a stretch of the coordinates turns back into isotropy. Lesson 5 puts it into kriging.










NoteGo deeper: why not just any curve?





A variogram model must be conditionally negative definite: for any locations s_1, \dots, s_n and weights \lambda_i that sum to zero, \sum_i \sum_j \lambda_i \lambda_j \gamma(s_i - s_j) \le 0. That’s equivalent to saying that the variance of every linear combination \sum \lambda_i Z(s_i) with weights summing to zero, -\sum_i\sum_j \lambda_i\lambda_j\gamma(s_i - s_j), is non-negative. A curve drawn through the empirical points by hand, or a polynomial, can violate it, and then kriging can give negative variances. Bochner’s theorem characterizes the valid covariance functions as the Fourier transforms of non-negative measures, which is how families like the Matérn are proven valid. Also note: a model valid in one dimension may not be valid in two or three; the spherical model is valid only up to three dimensions. Noel Cressie’s Statistics for Spatial Data (Wiley, 1993), chapter 2, has the details.

title: Variograms
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Matérn. Fit a Matérn model with its smoothness \kappa estimated too (fit.kappa = TRUE), starting from \kappa = 1. What \kappa does it choose, and what does that say about the field?









fit.kappa = TRUE.


vr <- variogram(z ~ dist_km, ~x + y, data = soil, cutoff = 1500, width = 100)
fm <- suppressWarnings(fit.variogram(vr, vgm(0.6, "Mat", 300, 0.05, kappa = 1), fit.kappa = TRUE))
print(fm)
fm$kappa[2]
\kappa = 0.4, a little rougher than the exponential’s 0.5, with no nugget at all: the rough Matérn absorbs the small nugget into its steep start. gstat searches \kappa over a grid (0.3, 0.4, …, up to 5) and keeps the best, which is why it’s a round number. The fit (SSErr 5.2 \times 10^{-5}) is barely better than the exponential’s: the data say “rough, about exponential”, and the simpler model is the usual choice.




Challenge 2 · Only the grid. The 56 samples of the 2018 campaign cluster near the cell room. Fit the exponential model to the 144 grid samples only. What happens to the shortest-distance bins, and to the fitted nugget?









The grid campaign is "grid 2019".


grid <- soil[soil$campaign == "grid 2019", ]
vg <- variogram(z ~ dist_km, ~x + y, data = grid, cutoff = 1500, width = 100)
print(vg[, c("np", "dist", "gamma")])
fg <- fit.variogram(vg, vgm(0.6, "Exp", 300, 0.05))
c(nugget = fg$psill[1], partial_sill = fg$psill[2], range = fg$range[2])
With the grid alone, no two samples are closer than 100 m (they’re 250 m apart, jittered), so the first bin is at 176 m, with 57 pairs. The fitted nugget jumps to 0.107, six times the 0.018 from all the samples, and the range parameter grows to 1,117 m: below 175 m, the model has no data and has to extrapolate. That’s why survey designers add some close pairs to a grid: without them, the nugget, the most important number for kriging at short range, is a guess.

title: Variograms
text:
Quick quiz

1. What is \gamma(h)?

The correlation at distance h
Half the expected squared difference between values a distance h apart
The number of pairs at distance h


For a stationary field, \gamma(h) = \sigma^2 - C(h), the variance minus the covariance.



2. The raw variogram kept rising above the variance. Why?

Too few pairs
A trend: the mean changes with distance from the cell room
A large nugget


A stationary variogram levels off at the variance; a trend makes it keep climbing.



3. The nugget represents:

The largest value
Measurement error plus variation at scales below the closest sample spacing
The range


It’s the jump of the variogram at the origin.



4. An exponential model with range parameter 693 m reaches 95% of its sill at about:

693 m
2.1 km
230 m


The practical range of the exponential model is three times its range parameter.



5. Why fit a model instead of using the empirical variogram directly?

It’s faster
Kriging needs values at every distance, from a function guaranteed to give valid variances
The empirical variogram is biased


Only conditionally negative definite functions are safe.



6. The semivariance at 380 m was 0.23 toward the north-east and 0.48 toward the south-east. That’s:

A trend
A nugget effect
Anisotropy: the dependence reaches further along the wind


Geometric anisotropy, from fifty years of south-westerly wind.

title: Variograms
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve built the geostatistician’s main tool. Here’s what you’ve learned:

The semivariance \frac{1}{2}(z_i - z_j)^2, averaged over pairs in distance bins, is the empirical variogram: 0.081 for pairs within 100 m.
A trend makes the variogram climb without limit (2.09 at 1.45 km, above the variance of 1.34). Model the trend (z ~ dist_km) and look at the residuals’ variogram.
Models have a nugget, a sill and a range. The exponential fits best here: nugget 0.018, sill 0.71, practical range 2.1 km.
Anisotropy: the dependence reaches about twice as far along the wind (north-east) as across it.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download soil_mercury.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install gstat.

Plot the variogram and the model. plot(vr, fe) draws both. Try plot(variogram(z ~ dist_km, ~x + y, soil, cloud = TRUE)) for the cloud.
A variogram map. plot(variogram(z ~ dist_km, ~x + y, soil, cutoff = 1000, width = 100, map = TRUE)) shows the semivariance for every separation vector. Where is the long axis of the low values?
Bin widths. Recompute the variogram with widths of 50, 100 and 200 m. How do the noise and the fitted range change?
Raw mercury. Fit a variogram to hg_mgkg itself instead of its log. Why is it so much noisier?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Semivariogram (variogram)

\gamma(h) = \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{E}[(Z(s+h) - Z(s))^2], half the expected squared difference at separation h.

Variogram cloud

The half squared differences of all pairs, against their distances.

Stationarity

The statistical properties don’t depend on location; for the variogram, a constant mean and a \gamma that depends only on the separation.

Isotropy and anisotropy

Dependence that’s the same in every direction, or that depends on direction.

Nugget, sill, range

The variogram’s jump at the origin, its plateau, and the distance at which it reaches the plateau.

Practical range

The distance at which a model reaches 95% of its sill: 3a for the exponential model.

Matérn model

A family of variogram models with a smoothness parameter \kappa; \kappa = 0.5 is the exponential.











NoteWant to read more?






Edzer Pebesma and Roger Bivand, Spatial Data Science with Applications in R (free online), chapter 12, “Spatial Interpolation”, on variograms and kriging with gstat, by its author.
Peter Diggle and Paulo Ribeiro, Model-based Geostatistics (Springer, 2007), chapters 3 and 5, on covariance models and on estimating them.
Hans Wackernagel, Multivariate Geostatistics (3rd edition, Springer, 2003), chapters 2 to 9, the classical treatment from the French school of geostatistics.

title: Beyond ordinary kriging
text:
Module 9 · Lesson 5 of 13 Week 137 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 4’s ordinary kriging assumed a constant mean, at least within each neighbourhood. But we know the mean isn’t constant: mercury falls with the distance from the cell room. And we know the dependence isn’t the same in every direction: the wind stretched it toward the north-east. This lesson puts both into the model, and then steps back to see kriging as what it is underneath: prediction from a Gaussian process.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Beyond ordinary kriging
text:
Universal kriging
Universal kriging (also called kriging with a trend) models the value as a regression on covariates plus a spatially correlated residual:

Z(s) = \mathbf x(s)^\top \boldsymbol\beta + \varepsilon(s), \qquad \varepsilon \text{ with variogram } \gamma .

The kriging weights are now constrained so that the prediction is unbiased for any \boldsymbol\beta, and the variogram is the residuals’ variogram (Lesson 3). In gstat, it’s one change: the formula’s right side.
The setup code reads the data, computes the distance in kilometres, and fits both variograms: m, Lesson 4’s model for log mercury, and mr, Lesson 3’s model for the residuals from the distance trend.












Your turn. First, the trend on its own: an ordinary regression of log mercury on the distance.









Regress on dist_km.


fit <- lm(z ~ dist_km, data = soil)
c(coef(fit), r_squared = summary(fit)$r.squared)
An intercept of 0.83 (2.3 mg/kg at the cell room) and a slope of -1.66 per km: mercury falls by a factor of e^{1.66} = 5.2 per kilometre. The distance alone explains 52% of the variation in log mercury; the residuals carry the rest, and they’re spatially correlated (Lesson 2’s Moran’s I of 0.62).




Your turn. Krige the garden with the trend, using the residuals’ variogram mr. The new location needs the covariate too: garden has its dist_km.









The same trend as the regression: z ~ dist_km.


krige(z ~ dist_km, ~x + y, soil, newdata = garden, model = mr, debug.level = 0)
0.0115 with a variance of 0.131, against ordinary kriging’s 0.0135 and 0.136 in Lesson 4: practically the same. The garden is surrounded by samples, so the neighbours tell kriging almost everything, with or without a trend. Trends matter most where the samples are sparse.




Your turn. Cross-validate universal kriging and compare it with ordinary kriging.









Universal kriging uses the residuals’ variogram, mr.


cv_ok <- krige.cv(z ~ 1, ~x + y, soil, model = m, debug.level = 0)
cv_uk <- krige.cv(z ~ dist_km, ~x + y, soil, model = mr, debug.level = 0)
score <- function(cv) c(rmse = sqrt(mean(cv$residual^2)), mean_sq_z = mean(cv$zscore^2))
rbind(ordinary = score(cv_ok), universal = score(cv_uk))
An RMSE of 0.440 for universal kriging against 0.443 for ordinary kriging: a tiny gain. Its variances are a little too small (mean squared z-score 1.10). With 200 well-spread samples, the data already “know” about the trend locally, and ordinary kriging with a nearly linear variogram follows it.




Regression kriging does the same in two steps: fit the trend by ordinary least squares, krige the residuals (with a known mean of zero, simple kriging), and add the two.
Your turn. Predict the garden by regression kriging.









Simple kriging of the residuals, whose mean is 0: beta = 0.


fit <- lm(z ~ dist_km, data = soil)
soil$res <- residuals(fit)
k_res <- krige(res ~ 1, ~x + y, soil, newdata = garden, model = mr, beta = 0, debug.level = 0)
c(trend = unname(predict(fit, garden)), residual = k_res$var1.pred,
  prediction = unname(predict(fit, garden)) + k_res$var1.pred)
The trend says -0.69 (0.50 mg/kg) (the garden is 0.92 km from the cell room), and the kriged residual adds +0.70, because the nearby samples are higher than the trend predicts: that’s the north-east plume. Total: 0.0124, within 0.001 of universal kriging. The difference is that universal kriging estimates the trend accounting for the correlation (by generalized least squares) and includes the trend’s uncertainty in its variance; regression kriging ignores both, which matters when the trend is poorly determined.

title: Beyond ordinary kriging
text:
Trends far from the data
Inside the data, the trend hardly matters. Outside, it takes over: with no neighbours to correct it, universal kriging returns to the trend, and ordinary kriging to the mean.
Your turn. Predict at a point 4.3 km north-east of the cell room, well outside the survey square, by both methods.









Back-transform uk.


far <- data.frame(x = 485500, y = 5704000)
far$dist_km <- sqrt((far$x - 482300)^2 + (far$y - 5701200)^2) / 1000
ok <- krige(z ~ 1, ~x + y, soil, newdata = far, model = m, debug.level = 0)$var1.pred
uk <- krige(z ~ dist_km, ~x + y, soil, newdata = far, model = mr, debug.level = 0)$var1.pred
c(ordinary_mgkg = exp(ok), universal_mgkg = exp(uk))
Ordinary kriging says 0.15 mg/kg, close to the survey’s typical outer values; universal kriging says 0.009 mg/kg, a tenth of the natural background of about 0.08. The straight-line trend in log mercury can’t level off at the background, so beyond the data it keeps falling, to impossibly clean soil. A trend fitted over 2 km says nothing reliable at 4 km; if you must extrapolate, use a trend with the right shape (one that levels off at the background), and treat the result with suspicion anyway.

title: Beyond ordinary kriging
text:
Anisotropy in kriging
Lesson 3 found that the dependence reaches further toward the north-east. In gstat, geometric anisotropy is anis = c(angle, ratio) in vgm(): the range applies along the angle (clockwise from north), and range × ratio across it. The isotropic fit’s range of 693 m is a compromise between the two directions, so to compare like with like, keep their geometric mean at 693 m: major range 693/\sqrt{r}, minor 693\sqrt{r}.
The variogram fit can’t choose the ratio well from 200 samples, but cross-validation can.
Your turn. Cross-validate universal kriging with ratios 0.3, 0.5, 0.7 and 1 (isotropic), along 45°.









The long axis points north-east: 45°.


rmse_for <- function(r) {
  ma <- vgm(mr$psill[2], "Exp", mr$range[2] / sqrt(r), mr$psill[1], anis = c(45, r))
  cv <- krige.cv(z ~ dist_km, ~x + y, soil, model = ma, debug.level = 0)
  sqrt(mean(cv$residual^2))
}
ratios <- c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1)
setNames(sapply(ratios, rmse_for), ratios)
An RMSE of 0.437 with a ratio of 0.3, 0.423 with 0.5, 0.426 with 0.7, and 0.440 isotropic. The best ratio, 0.5, means a range of 980 m along the wind and 490 m across it, and it cuts the RMSE from 0.440 (isotropic) to 0.423, about 4%. A modest gain. With 200 samples, the data already show the ellipse, so the map changes little; anisotropy matters most where samples are sparse, because it decides which far samples count for the gaps between them.

title: Beyond ordinary kriging
text:
The Gaussian-process view
Behind the variograms and the weights is a simple model: the vector of log mercury values is multivariate normal,

\mathbf z \sim N\big(X\boldsymbol\beta,\; \Sigma(\boldsymbol\theta)\big), \qquad \Sigma_{ij} = \sigma^2 \rho(\lVert s_i - s_j \rVert; \phi) + \tau^2 \,\mathbb 1[i = j],

with a correlation function \rho (here exponential, with range \phi), a partial sill \sigma^2 and a nugget \tau^2. A random function whose values at any set of points are jointly normal is a Gaussian process, and kriging is nothing but the conditional mean of the unknown value given the observed ones (Module 3’s conditional normal distribution). Machine learning uses the same model under the name Gaussian-process regression.
With a likelihood, everything can be estimated at once, by maximum likelihood: the trend \boldsymbol\beta and the covariance parameters \boldsymbol\theta, instead of fitting a variogram to residuals from a trend fitted as if the data were independent. nlme::gls() (Module 3, Lesson 11) does it, with corExp() for the exponential correlation.
Your turn. Fit the Gaussian-process model by maximum likelihood, and read the estimated range and nugget.









Include a nugget: nugget = TRUE.


g <- gls(z ~ dist_km, data = soil, method = "ML",
         correlation = corExp(form = ~ x + y, nugget = TRUE, value = c(500, 0.05)))
c(coef(g), coef(g$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE), sigma2 = g$sigma^2)
A range of 591 m (the variogram fit had 693), a nugget that’s 0.6% of the total variance of 0.77 (nlme reports the nugget as a proportion), and a different trend: a slope of -1.21 per km instead of the ordinary regression’s -1.66. Maximum likelihood lets the correlated residuals absorb part of what the ordinary regression had attributed to distance: the samples near the cell room are clustered, and a correlated cluster counts for less than as many independent samples.




Your turn. Compare the slope’s standard error from the ordinary regression with the one from the Gaussian-process model.









The standard error is the table’s second column.


fit <- lm(z ~ dist_km, data = soil)
g <- gls(z ~ dist_km, data = soil, method = "ML",
         correlation = corExp(form = ~ x + y, nugget = TRUE, value = c(500, 0.05)))
se <- c(ols = coef(summary(fit))[2, 2], gls = summary(g)$tTable[2, 2])
c(se, ratio = se[["gls"]] / se[["ols"]])
0.11 from the ordinary regression, 0.41 from the spatial model: 3.7 times larger. The ordinary regression treats 200 correlated samples as 200 independent pieces of evidence; there’s much less information in them than that, roughly as much as in 200 / 3.7^2 \approx 15 independent samples. A trend is still clearly there (t = -2.9), but a confidence interval from lm() would be far too narrow. This is the most important practical lesson of spatial statistics for anyone who fits regressions to spatial data: test the residuals for autocorrelation, and if it’s there, model it.




Your turn. Compare the two models’ AIC.









AIC(g).


fit <- lm(z ~ dist_km, data = soil)
g <- gls(z ~ dist_km, data = soil, method = "ML",
         correlation = corExp(form = ~ x + y, nugget = TRUE, value = c(500, 0.05)))
c(independent = AIC(fit), spatial = AIC(g))
483 for the independent model, 295 for the spatial one: a difference of 188, with two extra parameters. The spatial correlation isn’t a refinement; it’s most of the story. (Both are maximum-likelihood fits of the same data, so their AICs are comparable.)










NoteGo deeper: REML, big data, and Bayesian geostatistics





Maximum likelihood underestimates variance parameters slightly, because it ignores the degrees of freedom used by \boldsymbol\beta; restricted maximum likelihood (REML, method = "REML", nlme’s default) corrects that, as in mixed models. Each likelihood evaluation needs the Cholesky factor of the n \times n matrix \Sigma, which costs O(n^3): fine for 200 samples, hopeless for 100,000. Large-data methods replace \Sigma with something cheaper: low-rank basis functions (Lesson 12), sparse precision matrices (the SPDE approach of Lindgren, Rue and Lindström, 2011, implemented in INLA), or nearest-neighbour Gaussian processes (Datta and others, 2016). A Bayesian treatment puts priors on \boldsymbol\theta and averages the predictions over their posterior, which carries the uncertainty about the variogram into the kriging variance, something plug-in kriging ignores. Diggle and Ribeiro’s Model-based Geostatistics (Springer, 2007) is the standard account.

title: Beyond ordinary kriging
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · The final map. Krige the grid with the trend and the best anisotropy, and recompute the areas where the probability of exceeding 1 mg/kg is above 0.9, 0.5 and 0.1. Compare them with Lesson 4’s 0.49, 1.21 and 2.53 km².









The third threshold is 0.1.


grid <- expand.grid(x = seq(480825, 483775, by = 50), y = seq(5699725, 5702675, by = 50))
grid$dist_km <- sqrt((grid$x - 482300)^2 + (grid$y - 5701200)^2) / 1000
best <- vgm(mr$psill[2], "Exp", mr$range[2] / sqrt(0.5), mr$psill[1], anis = c(45, 0.5))
ku <- krige(z ~ dist_km, ~x + y, soil, newdata = grid, model = best, debug.level = 0)
p1 <- 1 - pnorm((0 - ku$var1.pred) / sqrt(pmax(ku$var1.var, 1e-12)))
sapply(c(0.9, 0.5, 0.1), function(p) sum(p1 > p) * 0.0025)
0.48, 1.17 and 2.50 km², within 4% of ordinary kriging’s areas, and the residential area with a probability above 10% hardly changes (94 cells instead of 95). With samples this dense, the refinements sharpen the cross-validation but barely move the map: the decision about where to sample gardens doesn’t depend on the model choice, which is reassuring. On a sparser survey, it would. (pmax() guards against tiny negative variances from rounding, at grid cells that coincide with samples.)




Challenge 2 · The likelihood by hand. In RStudio, write the negative log-likelihood of the Gaussian-process model yourself: for given (\sigma^2, \phi, \tau^2), build \Sigma, compute the generalized least-squares \hat{\boldsymbol\beta}, and evaluate \frac{1}{2}\log\lvert\Sigma\rvert + \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf z - X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf z - X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) with chol(). Minimize it with optim() over the logs of the three parameters, and check that you get gls()’s answer.

title: Beyond ordinary kriging
text:
Quick quiz

1. Universal kriging differs from ordinary kriging by:

Using more neighbours
Modelling the mean as a regression on covariates
Ignoring the nugget


The kriging weights become unbiased for any trend coefficients.



2. Inside the survey, universal kriging barely beat ordinary kriging (0.440 against 0.443). Why?

The trend was wrong
With dense samples, the neighbours already carry the trend’s information
Cross-validation can’t detect trends


Trends matter where data are sparse, and they dominate where there are none.



3. Far outside the survey, universal kriging predicted 0.009 mg/kg. What went wrong?

The straight-line trend was extrapolated beyond the data
The variogram was anisotropic
The nugget was too small


Without neighbours, the prediction is the trend, and this trend doesn’t level off.



4. In anis = c(45, 0.5), what’s the range toward the south-east?

Twice the north-east range
Half the north-east range
The same


The ratio applies across the main direction.



5. In the Gaussian-process view, the kriging prediction is:

The trend
The conditional mean of the unknown value given the observations
The maximum of the likelihood


For jointly normal values, the best predictor is the conditional mean.



6. The slope’s standard error was 0.11 with lm() and 0.41 with gls(). Which is right, and why?

0.11: it has fewer assumptions
0.41: correlated samples carry less information than independent ones
Both: they answer different questions


Ignoring spatial correlation makes standard errors too small and tests too confident.

title: Beyond ordinary kriging
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve taken kriging beyond a constant mean. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Universal kriging adds a trend (z ~ dist_km) and uses the residuals’ variogram; regression kriging does it in two steps. Inside the data both match ordinary kriging (RMSE 0.440 against 0.443).
Trends extrapolate badly: 4.3 km out, the straight-line trend predicted a tenth of the natural background.
Anisotropy along the wind (ratio 0.5: 980 m along, 490 m across) lowered the cross-validated RMSE to 0.423, though with samples this dense the map hardly changed.
The Gaussian-process view: fitting trend and covariance together by maximum likelihood changed the slope from -1.66 to -1.21 per km, multiplied its standard error by 3.7, and lowered the AIC by 188.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download soil_mercury.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

A better trend. Replace dist_km with exp(-dist_km), which levels off far from the plant. Does it extrapolate more sensibly to the far point? Does the cross-validation change?
Kriging from gls. Write the kriging predictor \hat z_0 = \mathbf x_0^\top\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} + \mathbf c_0^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf z - X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) using gls()’s estimates, and compare it with gstat’s universal kriging at the garden.
Matérn by likelihood. Install geoR (in RStudio) or fields, and fit a Matérn model by maximum likelihood. Is the smoothness close to Lesson 3’s 0.4?
Land use as a covariate. Add land_use to the trend. Is the plant site different from what distance predicts?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Universal kriging

Kriging with a mean that’s a linear function of covariates, unbiased for any coefficients.

Regression kriging

Fitting the trend by regression, kriging its residuals, and adding the two.

Geometric anisotropy

A variogram whose range depends on direction, described by an angle and a ratio.

Gaussian process

A random function whose values at any set of locations are jointly normal; geostatistics’ underlying model.

Generalized least squares (GLS)

Regression that accounts for correlated errors through their covariance matrix.

Restricted maximum likelihood (REML)

A likelihood for the covariance parameters that accounts for the estimated trend.











NoteWant to read more?






Peter Diggle and Paulo Ribeiro, Model-based Geostatistics (Springer, 2007), chapters 3 to 7, the Gaussian-process view from start to finish.
Edzer Pebesma and Roger Bivand, Spatial Data Science with Applications in R (free online), chapter 12, on universal kriging with gstat.
Carl Rasmussen and Christopher Williams, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning (MIT Press, 2006, free online), chapter 2, the same model as seen from machine learning.

title: Models for areal data
text:
Module 9 · Lesson 7 of 13 Week 139 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 6 showed that the newspaper’s pattern is real: admission ratios cluster, and they’re higher near the plant. It also showed that the districts near the plant are the most deprived. Deprivation is one of the strongest predictors of respiratory illness everywhere (through smoking, damp housing, occupations and access to care), and so is traffic. So the question for this lesson is precise: after accounting for deprivation and traffic, is there any association left with the distance from the plant?
Two complications make it a spatial-statistics question. The counts vary more than a Poisson model allows, and whatever the covariates miss is spatially correlated, so ordinary regression standard errors are too small, exactly as in Lesson 5.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Models for areal data
text:
Poisson regression with an offset
For counts O_i with expected counts E_i, the natural model is

O_i \sim \text{Poisson}(E_i \,\theta_i), \qquad \log\theta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \dots,

so \log \mathrm{E}[O_i] = \log E_i + \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \dots: the log of the expected count enters with a coefficient fixed at 1, as an offset. Each e^{\beta_j} is a relative risk per unit of x_j.
The setup code reads and merges the data, and builds the row-standardized contiguity weights from Lesson 6.













Your turn. Fit the newspaper’s model: admissions on the distance from the plant only.









The offset is the log of the expected counts.


g1 <- glm(admissions ~ offset(log(expected)) + dist_plant_km, family = poisson, data = dis)
print(coef(summary(g1)))
exp(coef(g1)[["dist_plant_km"]])                               # relative risk per km
A relative risk of 0.967 per km: 3.3% fewer admissions for every kilometre from the plant, with z = -10. Over 10 km, that’s a factor of 0.967^{10} = 0.72. Taken at face value, a district next to the plant has 40% more admissions than one 10 km away. Don’t take it at face value yet.




Your turn. Add deprivation and traffic.









Traffic is traffic_km_per_km2.


g2 <- glm(admissions ~ offset(log(expected)) + deprivation + traffic_km_per_km2 + dist_plant_km,
          family = poisson, data = dis)
print(coef(summary(g2)))
exp(coef(g2))
Deprivation: a relative risk of 1.21 per standard deviation. Traffic: 1.07 per km of main road per km². Distance from the plant: 0.998 per km, with p = 0.65. The plant’s apparent effect has vanished; it was deprivation and traffic, which are both higher near the plant (the old industrial housing, the motorway). That’s confounding, and the reason no study of a local health complaint should stop at the map.




Your turn. A Poisson model’s residual deviance should be about its degrees of freedom. Check, and refit as quasi-Poisson, which scales the standard errors by the estimated dispersion.









family = quasipoisson.


g2 <- glm(admissions ~ offset(log(expected)) + deprivation + traffic_km_per_km2 + dist_plant_km,
          family = poisson, data = dis)
q2 <- glm(admissions ~ offset(log(expected)) + deprivation + traffic_km_per_km2 + dist_plant_km,
          family = quasipoisson, data = dis)
c(deviance_per_df = deviance(g2) / df.residual(g2), dispersion = summary(q2)$dispersion,
  p_distance = coef(summary(q2))["dist_plant_km", 4])
A deviance of 2.2 per degree of freedom, and an estimated dispersion of 2.2: the counts vary more than Poisson, because districts differ in ways the covariates don’t capture. The quasi-Poisson standard errors are \sqrt{2.2} = 1.49 times larger, and the distance’s p-value rises to 0.76. Overdispersion is the rule, not the exception, for area counts.

title: Models for areal data
text:
Are the residuals spatially correlated?
The extra variation might be spatially structured: neighbouring districts sharing whatever the covariates miss (housing stock, a GP practice’s referral habits, a valley with poor air). If it is, the districts aren’t independent pieces of evidence, and even the quasi-Poisson standard errors are too small.
Your turn. Compute Moran’s I of the Poisson model’s Pearson residuals.









type = "pearson".


g2 <- glm(admissions ~ offset(log(expected)) + deprivation + traffic_km_per_km2 + dist_plant_km,
          family = poisson, data = dis)
res <- residuals(g2, type = "pearson")
moran.test(res, lw)$estimate
I = 0.39, against an expected -0.017: strong positive autocorrelation in the residuals. The covariates explain the plant-distance pattern, but they leave a smooth spatial pattern behind. A model for that pattern is needed, both for honest standard errors and for better estimates of each district’s risk.

title: Models for areal data
text:
Spatial regression models
The spatialreg package fits the two classical spatial regression models, for a continuous response y (here the log standardized ratio, which is roughly normal with expected counts this size):

the spatial error model (SEM): y = X\boldsymbol\beta + \mathbf u, \mathbf u = \lambda W \mathbf u + \boldsymbol\varepsilon. The errors are spatially correlated: something unmeasured and smooth. The coefficients mean what they mean in an ordinary regression.
the spatial lag model (SLM, or SAR lag): y = \rho W y + X\boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon. The response itself spills over between neighbours (house prices, contagious behaviour). A covariate change in one district then affects its neighbours too, so the coefficients aren’t the full effects.
