Both are simultaneous autoregressive (SAR) models. The conditional autoregressive (CAR) model specifies instead each district’s error given its neighbours’, \mathrm{E}[u_i \mid u_{-i}] = \lambda \sum_j w_{ij} u_j, and is the basis of most disease-mapping models.
First, the ordinary regression on the log ratio.
Your turn. Fit it, and test its residuals with lm.morantest().









lm.morantest.


m0 <- lm(lsmr ~ deprivation + traffic_km_per_km2 + dist_plant_km, data = dis)
print(coef(summary(m0)))
lm.morantest(m0, lw)$estimate
The same story as the Poisson model (deprivation and traffic strong, distance not), and the residuals’ I is 0.32 (standard deviate 4.9, p < 10^{-6}). Note the expected value under no autocorrelation: -0.047, not -0.017, because regression residuals are correlated with each other through the fitted coefficients, which lm.morantest() accounts for.




Which spatial model? Lagrange multiplier (Rao score) tests, computed from the ordinary regression alone, test for a spatial error term and for a spatial lag. Their robust (adjusted) versions test each one allowing for the other. The usual rule (Anselin, 1996): if only one robust test is significant, choose that model.
Your turn. Run all five tests with lm.RStests().









test = "all".


m0 <- lm(lsmr ~ deprivation + traffic_km_per_km2 + dist_plant_km, data = dis)
rs <- lm.RStests(m0, lw, test = "all")
sapply(rs, function(t) c(statistic = unname(t$statistic), p = t$p.value))
Both simple tests are significant (error: p = 0.0001; lag: p = 0.009), but of the robust versions, only the error test is (adjusted error: p = 0.004; adjusted lag: p = 0.53). The lag test was only significant because it picks up error autocorrelation. So: a spatial error model. That also makes sense: respiratory admissions don’t “spill over” between districts, but unmeasured risk factors vary smoothly.




Your turn. Fit the spatial error model with errorsarlm().









The function is errorsarlm.


sem <- errorsarlm(lsmr ~ deprivation + traffic_km_per_km2 + dist_plant_km, data = dis, listw = lw)
print(summary(sem)$Coef)
c(lambda = unname(sem$lambda), lambda_se = unname(sem$lambda.se))
\lambda = 0.61 (standard error 0.12): strong spatial correlation in the errors. Deprivation’s coefficient is 0.20 (a 22% higher risk per standard deviation) and traffic’s 0.066, both still clear; the distance from the plant has a coefficient of +0.0024 per km, standard error 0.0089, p = 0.79. Compared with the ordinary regression, the standard errors are larger (distance: 0.0089 against 0.0066), as they should be. The residuals of this model have a Moran’s I of 0.006: the error model has absorbed the spatial pattern.




Your turn. Fit the spatial lag model with lagsarlm() too, and compare the three models’ AIC.









The lag model is lagsarlm.


f <- lsmr ~ deprivation + traffic_km_per_km2 + dist_plant_km
m0 <- lm(f, data = dis)
sem <- errorsarlm(f, data = dis, listw = lw)
slm <- lagsarlm(f, data = dis, listw = lw)
c(ols = AIC(m0), error = AIC(sem), lag = AIC(slm), rho = unname(slm$rho))
AICs of -38.6 for the ordinary regression, -50.2 for the error model and -42.6 for the lag model (\rho = 0.34). The error model wins clearly, as the robust tests said. In the lag model, a coefficient isn’t the whole effect: a change in one district’s deprivation also raises its neighbours’ predicted ratios through \rho W y. impacts(slm, listw = lw) splits the effects into direct and indirect (spillover) parts; for deprivation, the total effect is 0.24, of which 0.08 is spillover.




Your turn. Fit a CAR model with spautolm(..., family = "CAR"). CAR models need symmetric weights, so use binary weights (style "B").









Binary weights: style "B".


lwB <- nb2listw(poly2nb(dis), style = "B")
car <- spautolm(lsmr ~ deprivation + traffic_km_per_km2 + dist_plant_km, data = dis, listw = lwB, family = "CAR")
print(summary(car)$Coef)
c(lambda = unname(car$lambda), AIC = AIC(car))
\lambda = 0.166 with binary weights, close to the largest value the model allows, 1/5.88 = 0.170 (one over the largest eigenvalue of the weights matrix; \lambda’s scale depends on the weights): strong spatial correlation, as in the error model. An AIC of -48.6, close to the error model’s -50.2, and the same conclusions: deprivation and traffic matter, distance doesn’t. SAR and CAR are two ways to write down a smooth unmeasured pattern; they rarely disagree on the substance.

title: Models for areal data
section: What can we say about the plant?
text:
What can we say about the plant?
“Not significant” isn’t “no effect”. The useful answer is a confidence interval: how large an effect is still compatible with the data?
Your turn. From the spatial error model, compute a 95% confidence interval for the distance coefficient, and turn it into a relative risk for a district 5 km closer to the plant.









The standard error is the second element of est.


sem <- errorsarlm(lsmr ~ deprivation + traffic_km_per_km2 + dist_plant_km, data = dis, listw = lw)
est <- summary(sem)$Coef["dist_plant_km", ]
ci <- est[1] + c(-1.96, 1.96) * est[2]
c(ci_per_km = ci, rr_5km_closer = rev(exp(-5 * ci)))
The distance coefficient lies between -0.015 and +0.020 per km. For a district 5 km closer to the plant, the relative risk lies between 0.91 and 1.08. So the data are compatible with the plant raising admissions in nearby districts by up to about 8% (or lowering them by up to 10%), and not with the 18% that the newspaper’s model implied (0.967^{-5}). That’s what Hana can tell the council: the pattern on the map is explained by deprivation and traffic; any remaining effect of the plant on respiratory admissions, at the district level, is small, at most a few percent. It’s not proof that the plant is harmless (district data can’t see effects concentrated in a few streets, Lesson 6’s ecological fallacy), but it’s what these data can say.










NoteGo deeper: disease mapping with BYM models





The log ratio works here because every district expects at least 24 admissions. With small counts (a rare cancer, a small area), the log of O/E is unstable or undefined at zero, and the model should stay on the count scale: O_i \sim \text{Poisson}(E_i\theta_i) with \log\theta_i = \mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta + u_i + v_i, where u_i is a spatially structured CAR effect and v_i an unstructured one. That’s the Besag-York-Mollié (BYM) model (1991), the workhorse of disease mapping, fitted by MCMC (the CARBayes package, or Stan, as in Module 5) or by INLA. Its maps of \theta_i borrow strength both from the whole county (like Lesson 6’s empirical Bayes) and from each district’s neighbours. Riebler and others’ “BYM2” reparametrization (2016) makes its priors easier to set. Waller and Gotway’s Applied Spatial Statistics for Public Health Data (Wiley, 2004), chapter 9, explains it from the ground up.

title: Models for areal data
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · A likelihood ratio test. Test the distance term in the spatial error model with a likelihood ratio test: fit the model without it, and compare with LR.Sarlm().









Drop only the distance: keep traffic_km_per_km2.


sem <- errorsarlm(lsmr ~ deprivation + traffic_km_per_km2 + dist_plant_km, data = dis, listw = lw)
sem0 <- errorsarlm(lsmr ~ deprivation + traffic_km_per_km2, data = dis, listw = lw)
lr <- LR.Sarlm(sem, sem0)
c(statistic = unname(lr$statistic), p = lr$p.value)
A likelihood ratio of 0.066 on 1 degree of freedom, p = 0.80: adding the distance from the plant doesn’t improve the spatial error model at all. Compare with a spatial error model on the distance alone (lsmr ~ dist_plant_km): there the coefficient is -0.039 per km with p = 0.00002. Even with the spatial correlation modelled, leaving out the confounders makes the plant look guilty.




Challenge 2 · Spillovers. In RStudio, run impacts(slm, listw = lw, R = 500) for the lag model, which simulates standard errors for the direct, indirect and total effects, and summary() the result. Is the indirect effect of deprivation significant? What would it mean if it were?

title: Models for areal data
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why is \log E_i an offset rather than a covariate?

It’s not significant
The expected count should scale the mean exactly, with a coefficient of 1
Offsets are faster


Then the other coefficients describe the relative risk, O/E.



2. The distance’s effect vanished when deprivation and traffic were added. That’s:

Overdispersion
Confounding
Spatial autocorrelation


Deprivation and traffic are correlated with the distance and with admissions.



3. A deviance of 2.2 per degree of freedom in a Poisson model means:

The counts vary more than Poisson; standard errors need scaling up
The model fits too well
The offset is wrong


Overdispersion; quasi-Poisson multiplies the standard errors by \sqrt{2.2}.



4. Only the robust error test was significant. Which model?

Spatial error
Spatial lag
Ordinary regression


The simple lag test was significant only because it picks up error autocorrelation.



5. In a spatial lag model, why isn’t a coefficient the full effect of its covariate?

Because of the offset
A change in one area also changes its neighbours’ responses through \rho W y
Because of overdispersion


Direct plus indirect (spillover) impacts make the total.



6. What’s the best summary of the analysis for the council?

The plant has no effect on health
The plant raises admissions by 18% within 5 km
The pattern is explained by deprivation and traffic; any district-level effect of the plant is at most a few percent


A confidence interval, with the limits of district-level data stated.

title: Models for areal data
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve answered the newspaper’s question, carefully. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Poisson regression with an offset models relative risks. On distance alone, admissions fell 3.3% per km; with deprivation (1.21 per SD) and traffic (1.07 per unit) in the model, the distance’s effect was 0.998 per km, p = 0.65.
Overdispersion (2.2) and residual autocorrelation (Moran’s I 0.39) both make ordinary standard errors too small.
Lagrange multiplier tests chose the spatial error model (\lambda = 0.61, AIC -50.2 against -38.6 for ordinary regression and -42.6 for the lag model); a CAR model agreed.
The honest answer is an interval: for a district 5 km closer to the plant, a relative risk between 0.91 and 1.08.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download districts.geojson and district_health.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install spatialreg.

The Durbin model. lagsarlm(..., Durbin = TRUE) adds the neighbours’ covariates (WX) to the lag model. Does any neighbour effect appear?
A BYM model. Install CARBayes and fit S.CARbym(admissions ~ offset(log(expected)) + deprivation + traffic_km_per_km2 + dist_plant_km, family = "poisson", data = dis, W = nb2mat(poly2nb(dis), style = "B"), burnin = 5000, n.sample = 25000). Compare its coefficients with the spatial error model’s.
Mapped risk. Map the BYM model’s fitted relative risks next to Lesson 6’s raw and empirical Bayes ratios.
Weights matter? Refit the error model with k = 4 nearest-neighbour weights. Do the conclusions change?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Offset

A term with a coefficient fixed at 1, such as the log of the expected count in a Poisson model for rates.

Relative risk

The ratio of the rate in one group to the rate in another; in a log-linear model, e^\beta per unit of the covariate.

Overdispersion

More variation in counts than the Poisson model allows.

Spatial error model (SEM)

A regression whose errors follow a simultaneous autoregression, \mathbf u = \lambda W\mathbf u + \boldsymbol\varepsilon.

Spatial lag model (SLM)

A regression with the neighbours’ average response as a predictor, y = \rho W y + X\boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon.

Conditional autoregressive (CAR) model

A model specifying each area’s value given its neighbours’; the basis of most disease-mapping models.

Lagrange multiplier (Rao score) tests

Tests for spatial error and spatial lag dependence computed from the ordinary regression; their robust versions separate the two.

Direct and indirect impacts

In a spatial lag model, the effect of a covariate change on the same area and the spillover effect on others.











NoteWant to read more?






Edzer Pebesma and Roger Bivand, Spatial Data Science with Applications in R (free online), chapters 16 and 17, on spatial regression and its econometric models, by spatialreg’s author.
Luc Anselin, Spatial Econometrics: Methods and Models (Kluwer, 1988), the classic treatment of the error and lag models and their tests.
Julian Besag, Jeremy York and Annie Mollié, “Bayesian Image Restoration, with Two Applications in Spatial Statistics”, Annals of the Institute of Statistical Mathematics 43, 1991, pages 1 to 59, where the BYM model was introduced.

title: Point patterns II
text:
Module 9 · Lesson 9 of 13 Week 141 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 8 asked how many points there are where. This lesson asks how the points relate to each other. Two very different physical processes can make points deviate from complete randomness:
And a third thing that looks like clustering but isn’t: an inhomogeneous intensity, like the leaks near the old units. Telling these apart is this lesson’s job.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Point patterns II
text:
Ripley’s K and L functions
Ripley’s K function counts, for each point, the other points within distance r, averages over the points, and divides by the intensity:

K(r) = \frac{1}{\lambda}\,\mathrm{E}[\text{number of other points within } r \text{ of a typical point}].

Under CSR, K(r) = \pi r^2, the area of a disc of radius r. More than that means more neighbours than random (clustering at scale r), less means fewer (inhibition). The L function, L(r) = \sqrt{K(r)/\pi}, turns the parabola into a straight line, L(r) = r under CSR, so L(r) - r is easy to read: positive for clustering, negative for inhibition. Both need edge corrections, since the discs around points near the edge stick out of the window.
The data: tank_pits.csv, the 265 pits found on tank T-104’s floor (a disc 14 m across; coordinates in metres from its centre); crystal_nuclei.csv, 170 crystals in a 1 × 1 mm microscope field (coordinates in micrometres). The setup code reads both, and the leaks.












Your turn. Compute K for the pits, and compare K(0.5) with its CSR value \pi \times 0.5^2.









The area of a disc: \pi r^2.


K <- Kest(P, r = seq(0, 1.5, by = 0.05), correction = "isotropic")
k <- K$iso[K$r == 0.5]
c(K = k, csr = pi * 0.5^2, L = sqrt(k / pi))
K(0.5) = 2.43 against 0.79 for CSR: a typical pit has three times as many other pits within 50 cm as random pits would. L(0.5) = 0.88, against 0.5. The isotropic correction (Ripley’s) weights each pair by the share of the circle through the second point that lies inside the window.




Your turn. Compute L(r) - r for the pits at 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 m.









Subtract the distances, L$r.


L <- Lest(P, r = seq(0, 1.5, by = 0.05), correction = "isotropic")
keep <- round(L$r, 2) %in% c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1, 1.5)
setNames(round(L$iso[keep] - L$r[keep], 3), L$r[keep])
0.083 at 10 cm, 0.225 at 30 cm, 0.379 at 50 cm, 0.460 at 1 m, then down to 0.367 at 1.5 m. L(r) - r rises while r is within the clusters, peaks around 1 m, a rough guide to the clusters’ size, and falls beyond it, where pairs from different clusters dominate.

title: Point patterns II
text:
Simulation envelopes
How far from L(r) = r is “far”? There’s no simple formula, so we simulate: generate many CSR patterns with the same number of points in the same window, compute L for each, and draw the band between the highest and lowest simulated values at each r. That’s a simulation envelope. With 39 simulations, the observed curve has a 1 in 40 (2.5%) chance of being above the band at a given r under CSR, and 2.5% below.
Your turn. Compute the envelope for the pits, and find where the observed L is above it.









39 simulations.


set.seed(9091)
e <- envelope(P, Lest, nsim = 39, r = seq(0, 1.5, by = 0.05), correction = "isotropic", verbose = FALSE)
above <- e$r[e$obs > e$hi]
c(L_obs = e$obs[e$r == 0.5], upper = e$hi[e$r == 0.5], from = min(above), to = max(above))
At 50 cm, the observed L = 0.88 against an upper envelope of 0.53, and the curve is above the envelope at every distance from 10 cm to 1.5 m. The pits are clustered, at all these scales. (Checking many r values against a pointwise envelope inflates the error rate, like multiple testing; spatstat’s global = TRUE option gives a band with a proper overall level.)













Your turn. Now the crystals. Compute L(r) - r at 45 µm, the smallest nearest-neighbour distance, and the share of crystals whose nearest neighbour is closer than 45 µm.









Closer than 45 µm.


L <- Lest(C, r = seq(0, 120, by = 5), correction = "isotropic")
nn <- nndist(C)
c(L_minus_r_45 = L$iso[L$r == 45] - 45, min_nn = min(nn), share_closer = mean(nn < 45))
L(45) - 45 = -23.4: a typical crystal has far fewer neighbours within 45 µm than random points would. Yet the closest pair is only 8.9 µm apart, and 24% of the crystals have a neighbour closer than 45 µm: the inhibition is strong but not absolute. A crystal nucleating near another one isn’t impossible, just much less likely.




Your turn. Compute the envelope for the crystals, and find the distances at which the observed L is below it.









The lower envelope is e$lo.


set.seed(9092)
e <- envelope(C, Lest, nsim = 39, r = seq(0, 120, by = 5), correction = "isotropic", verbose = FALSE)
below <- e$r[e$obs < e$lo]
range(below)
Below the envelope from 10 µm to 115 µm: inhibition, detectable well beyond the 45 µm radius, because a crystal’s empty neighbourhood also changes the counts at somewhat larger distances.

title: Point patterns II
text:
Models: clusters and inhibition
Summary functions describe; models explain, and their parameters are physical quantities.
A Thomas process (a Neyman-Scott cluster process) places invisible “parent” points by CSR, with intensity \kappa; each parent has a Poisson number of “offspring”, with mean \mu, scattered around it with a Gaussian of standard deviation \sigma; only the offspring are seen. For the tank floor: \kappa is the density of water pockets under the plates, \mu the pits per pocket, \sigma the pocket’s size. kppm() fits it by matching the theoretical K function to the observed one.
Your turn. Fit a Thomas process to the pits.









clusters = "Thomas".


fit <- kppm(P ~ 1, clusters = "Thomas")
c(kappa_per_m2 = fit$clustpar[["kappa"]], sigma_m = fit$clustpar[["scale"]], mu = fit$mu)
About 0.29 clusters per m² (44 water pockets on the 154 m² floor), each with an average of 6 pits spread with \sigma = 0.32 m: most of a cluster’s pits lie within 65 cm (2\sigma) of its centre. For the inspection engineer, that says: where you find one pit, look within a metre for five more, and the pockets are a few metres apart. An envelope of L simulated from the fitted Thomas model contains the observed curve at every distance: the model fits.




A Strauss process describes inhibition: each pair of points closer than R multiplies the pattern’s probability density by \gamma (0 \le \gamma \le 1). \gamma = 1 is CSR; \gamma = 0 is a hard core, no pairs closer than R at all; in between, close pairs are discouraged. It’s fitted with ppm() and an interaction term.
Your turn. Fit a Strauss process with R = 45 µm to the crystals, and compute \gamma.









The interaction is Strauss.


fit <- ppm(C ~ 1, Strauss(r = 45))
print(coef(fit))
exp(coef(fit)[["Interaction"]])                                 # gamma
\gamma = 0.17: each pair of crystals closer than 45 µm makes a configuration about 6 times less likely. In physical terms, the depletion zone around a growing crystal suppresses nucleation by roughly that factor. ppm() fits Gibbs processes like this by maximizing the pseudolikelihood, since the true likelihood’s normalizing constant is intractable.




Your turn. Why 45 µm? Choose R by profile pseudolikelihood: fit the model for R = 20, 25, …, 80 µm and keep the best.









Steps of 5 µm.


prof <- profilepl(data.frame(r = seq(20, 80, by = 5)), Strauss, C ~ 1)
prof$param[which.max(prof$prof), ]
45 µm, the radius used above. The lab’s crystallization model says the depletion zone after 10 minutes should be 40 to 50 µm; the point pattern agrees. A point pattern can measure a physical length scale that’s hard to measure directly.

title: Point patterns II
text:
The leaks: clustered or inhomogeneous?
The L function of the leaks, computed as if their intensity were constant, lies above its CSR envelope at most distances up to 150 m. Are the leaks clustered? Not necessarily: an inhomogeneous Poisson process (independent points, varying intensity) also has more close pairs than CSR, simply because the points crowd where the intensity is high. To tell the two apart, model the intensity, then check what’s left.
An inhomogeneous Poisson model with a log-linear intensity, \log\lambda(u) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 d(u), is fitted by ppm() with the covariate as a function.
Your turn. Fit it with the distance from the old units, and compare its AIC with the homogeneous model’s.









X ~ dist_old.


dist_old <- function(x, y) sqrt((x - 300)^2 + (y - 560)^2)
f0 <- ppm(X ~ 1)
f1 <- ppm(X ~ dist_old)
c(coef(f1), per_100m = exp(100 * coef(f1)[["dist_old"]]), AIC_homogeneous = AIC(f0), AIC_distance = AIC(f1))
The intensity falls by a factor of 0.71 for every 100 m from the old units (it halves every 200 m), and the AIC drops from 3,849 to 3,751. That’s Lesson 8’s distance bands as a model: a Poisson regression for point patterns, fitted by the Berman-Turner device, which turns the likelihood into a weighted Poisson GLM on a fine set of quadrature points.




Your turn. Now compare the ordinary L function with the inhomogeneous L function, which divides each pair’s contribution by the fitted intensities at its two points, so that an inhomogeneous Poisson process gives L(r) = r.









Give it the fitted model, f1.


dist_old <- function(x, y) sqrt((x - 300)^2 + (y - 560)^2)
f1 <- ppm(X ~ dist_old)
rr <- seq(0, 150, by = 5)
L <- Lest(X, r = rr, correction = "border")
Li <- Linhom(X, lambda = f1, r = rr, correction = "border")
keep <- rr %in% c(25, 50, 100)
rbind(homogeneous = L$border[keep] - rr[keep], inhomogeneous = Li$border[keep] - rr[keep])
With a constant intensity, L(r) - r is 1.9 m at 25 m, 12.7 at 50 m and 24.4 at 100 m: apparent clustering, growing with distance. With the fitted intensity, it’s -1.0, 7.5 and 6.8, much smaller, and an envelope simulated from the fitted inhomogeneous Poisson model contains the observed inhomogeneous L at every distance. The leaks are an inhomogeneous Poisson pattern: they don’t cluster around each other; they’re more frequent where the equipment is old. For maintenance, that’s the difference between “a leak predicts another leak nearby” (it doesn’t) and “old units leak more” (they do).










NoteGo deeper: Cox processes, and why one pattern can’t always tell





A Cox process is a Poisson process whose intensity is itself random, for example \lambda(u) = e^{Z(u)} with Z a Gaussian process: the log-Gaussian Cox process, which connects point patterns to Lessons 3 to 5’s geostatistics. Thomas processes are Cox processes too (the random intensity is the sum of the Gaussian bumps around the parents). Here’s the catch: from a single pattern, a cluster process and an inhomogeneous Poisson process with the right intensity surface can be indistinguishable. Bartlett pointed this out in 1964. What separates them is outside information: a covariate that explains the intensity (the old units’ distance, here), replicated patterns (several tank floors), or physical knowledge. That’s why the leak analysis used the distance covariate, not just the L function. Baddeley, Rubak and Turner’s Spatial Point Patterns (CRC, 2015), chapter 12, covers both.

title: Point patterns II
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Does the cluster model fit? In RStudio, simulate an envelope of L from the fitted Thomas model (envelope(fit, Lest, nsim = 39)) and plot it with the observed curve. Then fit a homogeneous Poisson model to the pits and do the same. Which model’s envelope contains the observed curve?
Challenge 2 · A likelihood ratio test. In RStudio, test the distance term in the leaks’ model with anova(f0, f1, test = "LRT"). The deviance drops by 99.4 on one degree of freedom. Then add a term for the tank farm (x > 800 & y < 330) and test it too. Does it improve the model, and why might it, even with the distance term in?

title: Point patterns II
text:
Quick quiz

1. Under complete spatial randomness, K(r) equals:

r
\pi r^2
1


The expected number of neighbours within r, divided by the intensity: the disc’s area.



2. L(r) - r below zero means:

Clustering
Inhibition: fewer neighbours than random
An edge effect


The crystals’ curve dipped to -23 µm at 45 µm.



3. What does a simulation envelope show?

The range of the summary function in patterns simulated under the null model
A confidence interval for the intensity
The edge correction


With 39 simulations, a pointwise envelope gives a 5% two-sided test at each distance.



4. In a Thomas process, \sigma is:

The number of clusters
The number of points per cluster
The spread of each cluster’s points around its centre


For the pits, 0.32 m: the size of a water pocket.



5. In a Strauss process, \gamma = 0 means:

Complete spatial randomness
A hard core: no two points closer than R
Clustering


\gamma = 1 is CSR; the crystals had \gamma = 0.17.



6. The leaks’ ordinary L function showed “clustering”, but the inhomogeneous L didn’t. Conclusion?

The leaks cluster around each other
The leaks are independent, with an intensity that varies with the equipment’s age
The L function is wrong


An inhomogeneous intensity makes an ordinary K or L look clustered.

title: Point patterns II
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve looked at how points relate to each other. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Ripley’s K and L functions count neighbours at every distance; L(r) = r under CSR, above for clustering, below for inhibition. Simulation envelopes judge the departures.
The pits cluster: L(0.5) = 0.88 against an envelope of 0.53. A Thomas process describes them: about 44 water pockets on the floor, 6 pits each, spread over \sigma = 0.32 m.
The crystals repel: L(45) - 45 = -23 µm, below the envelope from 10 to 115 µm. A Strauss process with R = 45 µm (chosen by profile pseudolikelihood) has \gamma = 0.17.
The leaks are inhomogeneous, not clustered: an inhomogeneous Poisson model (intensity × 0.71 per 100 m from the old units) explains their apparent clustering, as the inhomogeneous L shows.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download tank_pits.csv, crystal_nuclei.csv, site_leaks.csv and site_boundary.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install spatstat.

The pair correlation function. plot(pcf(P)) shows clustering as g(r) > 1, scale by scale, without K’s accumulation. Where does the pits’ g fall to 1?
Other cluster models. Fit kppm(P ~ 1, "MatClust") (uniform discs instead of Gaussians) and "LGCP". Compare their envelopes and AICs (AIC() works for kppm fits with method = "palm").
Simulate from the fits. plot(simulate(fit)) for the Thomas and Strauss fits. Do the simulated patterns look like the real ones?
Pit depth. The pits have a mark, depth_mm. Use markcorr() to see whether deep pits are near other deep pits.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Ripley’s K function

The expected number of other points within distance r of a typical point, divided by the intensity; \pi r^2 under CSR.

L function

L(r) = \sqrt{K(r)/\pi}, equal to r under CSR.

Simulation envelope

The band of a summary function’s values in patterns simulated from a null model.

Clustering and inhibition

More, or fewer, close pairs of points than complete spatial randomness gives.

Thomas process

A cluster process: Poisson parents, each with a Poisson number of offspring scattered as a Gaussian around it.

Strauss process

An inhibition process in which each pair closer than R multiplies the density by \gamma.

Inhomogeneous Poisson process

Independent points with an intensity that varies with location, often modelled log-linearly in covariates.

Inhomogeneous K and L functions

Versions of K and L that account for a varying intensity, so that they detect interaction rather than inhomogeneity.











NoteWant to read more?






Adrian Baddeley, Ege Rubak and Rolf Turner, Spatial Point Patterns: Methodology and Applications with R (CRC Press, 2015), chapters 7, 9, 12 and 13, on K functions, Poisson models, cluster processes and Gibbs models.
Brian Ripley, “Modelling Spatial Patterns”, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 39, 1977, pages 172 to 212, where the K function was introduced.
Janine Illian, Antti Penttinen, Helga Stoyan and Dietrich Stoyan, Statistical Analysis and Modelling of Spatial Point Patterns (Wiley, 2008), chapters 4 and 6, with many examples from materials science and forestry.

title: Spatio-temporal covariance and kriging
text:
Module 9 · Lesson 11 of 13 Week 143 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 10 found that the network’s space-time interaction (what’s left after the station and day effects) is correlated over a few kilometres and a few days. Geostatistics in Lessons 3 to 5 used correlation in space to predict where nobody measured. With time, there’s a second source of information: a station’s own yesterday and tomorrow. Spatio-temporal kriging uses both, through a covariance function of the distance in space and the lag in time.
Tomás has a practical reason to care. Analyzers fail, and the EU’s air-quality rules require 90% data capture for a station’s annual mean to count; good gap-filling, with honest uncertainty, is part of running a network.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Spatio-temporal covariance and kriging
text:
Covariance in space and time
For a field Z(s, t) with mean zero, the spatio-temporal covariance is C(h, u) = \mathrm{Cov}(Z(s, t), Z(s + h, t + u)): a function of the spatial distance h and the time lag u, if the field is stationary in both. It’s separable if it factors into a spatial and a temporal part,

C(h, u) = \frac{C(h, 0)\, C(0, u)}{C(0, 0)},

which means that the spatial pattern of correlation is the same at every time lag, only scaled down. Separable models are convenient (their covariance matrices are Kronecker products, cheap to invert), but physical processes like wind-driven transport usually aren’t separable.
The setup code computes the interaction from Lesson 10 (log NO₂ minus station and day effects), as a 365 × 24 matrix R, and the station coordinates in kilometres.












Your turn. Compute the covariance between every pair of stations at lag 0, and average it in distance bands.









Average by band.


C0 <- cov(R, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
pair <- lower.tri(D)
band <- cut(D[pair], c(0, 3, 6, 10, 15, 30))
c(variance = mean(diag(C0)), round(tapply(C0[pair], band, mean), 4))
The anomalies’ variance is 0.036 (a standard deviation of 0.19 on the log scale, roughly ±20%). Stations within 3 km of each other share a covariance of 0.013, about 37% of the variance; from 3 km on, the covariances are slightly negative (-0.005 to -0.006) and close to zero beyond 15 km. The negative values are a side effect of removing the day effect: the anomalies of all stations average zero every day, so a positive cluster of stations must be balanced by negative ones elsewhere.




Your turn. Now in time: the covariance of each station with itself one day later, averaged over the stations, and its ratio to the variance.









Tomorrow drops the first day: R[-1, ].


today <- R[-365, ]; tomorrow <- R[-1, ]
C1 <- cov(tomorrow, today, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")      # C1[i, j]: station i tomorrow, station j today
C0 <- cov(R, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
c(lag0 = mean(diag(C0)), lag1 = mean(diag(C1)), ratio = mean(diag(C1)) / mean(diag(C0)))
A lag-1 covariance of 0.012, 34% of the variance: a station’s anomaly today has a correlation of about 0.34 with its anomaly yesterday (Lesson 10’s average autocorrelation, 0.38, weighed every station equally).




Your turn. Is the covariance separable? Compare the observed lag-1 covariance between different stations, by distance band, with the separable prediction C(h, 0) \times C(0, 1) / C(0, 0).









Multiply by the temporal ratio, ratio.


C0 <- cov(R, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
C1 <- cov(R[-1, ], R[-365, ], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
C1s <- (C1 + t(C1)) / 2                                          # average the two directions
pair <- lower.tri(D); band <- cut(D[pair], c(0, 3, 6, 10, 15, 30))
ratio <- mean(diag(C1)) / mean(diag(C0))
round(rbind(lag0 = tapply(C0[pair], band, mean), lag1 = tapply(C1s[pair], band, mean),
            separable = tapply(C0[pair], band, mean) * ratio), 4)
Within 3 km, the observed lag-1 covariance between different stations is 0.0039, and the separable prediction 0.0046, a little higher; beyond 3 km both are near zero. They’re close enough that a separable model is a reasonable first approximation. A clear mismatch, such as a lag-1 covariance between two stations that’s larger than their lag-0 covariance (which a plume moving from one to the other would produce), would rule it out.

title: Spatio-temporal covariance and kriging
text:
The spatio-temporal variogram
gstat works with the spacetime package’s STFDF class (Lesson 10’s “full grid”): a set of locations, a set of times, and a data frame with one row per location-time, space varying fastest (all stations for day 1, then all for day 2, …). variogramST() then computes \gamma(h, u) for distance bins h and time lags u. To keep it quick, the lesson uses the first quarter of 2025.
Your turn. Build the STFDF for January to March, and check its dimensions.









Use the logical vector q1 to keep the rows for January to March, and leave the column index empty to keep all the stations: R[q1, ]. t() makes the stations vary fastest.


q1 <- as.Date(rownames(R)) < as.Date("2025-04-01")
days <- as.Date(rownames(R))[q1]
stf <- STFDF(SpatialPoints(xy), days, data.frame(r = as.vector(t(R[q1, ]))))
dim(stf)
24 locations × 90 days × 1 variable. Transposing the days × stations matrix before as.vector() is what puts the stations fastest; getting this order wrong silently scrambles the data, so check a value or two (stf[3, 5]$r should be R[5, 3]).




Your turn. Compute the spatio-temporal variogram for time lags 0 to 3 days, up to 20 km in 2 km bins.









Lags 0 to 3: tlags = 0:3.


q1 <- as.Date(rownames(R)) < as.Date("2025-04-01")
stf <- STFDF(SpatialPoints(xy), as.Date(rownames(R))[q1], data.frame(r = as.vector(t(R[q1, ]))))
vst <- variogramST(r ~ 1, stf, tlags = 0:3, cutoff = 20, width = 2, na.omit = TRUE, progress = FALSE)
vst[1:6, c("np", "dist", "timelag", "gamma")]
At lag 0, the semivariance rises from 0.011 at 1.4 km to 0.041 at 5 km, then levels off (the missing first row, distance 0 at lag 0, would be each station with itself on the same day). The plot below shows all four lags: at short distances, the curves for longer lags start higher, and at large distances they level off together, just below the lag-0 curve.

title: Spatio-temporal covariance and kriging
text:
Fitting models
A separable model in gstat has a spatial variogram, a temporal variogram (each with sill 1) and a joint sill. A metric model treats time as a third coordinate, with a space-time anisotropy factor converting days into kilometres: \gamma(\sqrt{h^2 + (\kappa u)^2}). There are others (product-sum, sum-metric), with more parameters. fit.StVariogram() fits them by weighted least squares, like fit.variogram(), and works much better when the distances are in kilometres than in metres (the optimizer’s step sizes don’t adapt to the scale of each parameter).
Your turn. Fit a separable model with exponential spatial and temporal parts.









The model type is "separable".


q1 <- as.Date(rownames(R)) < as.Date("2025-04-01")
stf <- STFDF(SpatialPoints(xy), as.Date(rownames(R))[q1], data.frame(r = as.vector(t(R[q1, ]))))
vst <- variogramST(r ~ 1, stf, tlags = 0:3, cutoff = 20, width = 2, na.omit = TRUE, progress = FALSE)
start <- vgmST("separable", space = vgm(0.8, "Exp", 3, 0.2), time = vgm(0.8, "Exp", 1.5, 0.2), sill = 0.04)
fs <- fit.StVariogram(vst, start, method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = c(0.1, 0, 0.1, 0, 0.001), upper = c(50, 1, 20, 1, 1))
c(space_range_km = fs$space$range[2], time_range_days = fs$time$range[2], sill = fs$sill,
  lag1_correlation = exp(-1 / fs$time$range[2]), MSE = attr(fs, "MSE"))
A spatial range parameter of 2.3 km (a practical range of about 7 km), a temporal range of 3.1 days, and a joint sill of 0.036, matching the variance. The temporal range implies a correlation of 0.72 between consecutive days, much higher than the 0.34 you computed by hand. The difference matters: the fitted model has essentially no nugget, so it treats all of the variance as smooth and persistent, while part of it (measurement noise, the plume’s jumps from day to day) is neither. Remember that for the validation.




Your turn. Fit a metric model, and compare its fit.









Start the anisotropy at 3 km per day.


q1 <- as.Date(rownames(R)) < as.Date("2025-04-01")
stf <- STFDF(SpatialPoints(xy), as.Date(rownames(R))[q1], data.frame(r = as.vector(t(R[q1, ]))))
vst <- variogramST(r ~ 1, stf, tlags = 0:3, cutoff = 20, width = 2, na.omit = TRUE, progress = FALSE)
start <- vgmST("metric", joint = vgm(0.04, "Exp", 3, 0.01), stAni = 3)
fm <- fit.StVariogram(vst, start, method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = c(0.001, 0.1, 0, 0.1))
c(range_km = fm$joint$range[2], km_per_day = fm$stAni, MSE = attr(fm, "MSE"))
A joint range of 2.5 km and an anisotropy of 0.97 km per day: one day apart counts like about a kilometre apart. Its MSE, 1.35 \times 10^{-5}, is practically the same as the separable model’s 1.37 \times 10^{-5}: the empirical variogram can’t tell the two apart.

title: Spatio-temporal covariance and kriging
section: Space-time kriging, and an honest test
text:
Space-time kriging, and an honest test
To test the method, hide a random 15% of January’s measurements, predict them with krigeST() from everything else, and compare with two simpler methods: kriging each day from that day’s other stations (space only), and averaging the station’s own previous and next day (time only).
krigeST() takes the observations as an STSDF (sparse: only the observed combinations) and the targets as another STSDF, whose index lists each target’s station and day.
Your turn. Run the test.









The fitted model is fs.


q1 <- as.Date(rownames(R)) < as.Date("2025-04-01")
stf <- STFDF(SpatialPoints(xy), as.Date(rownames(R))[q1], data.frame(r = as.vector(t(R[q1, ]))))
vst <- variogramST(r ~ 1, stf, tlags = 0:3, cutoff = 20, width = 2, na.omit = TRUE, progress = FALSE)
fs <- fit.StVariogram(vst, vgmST("separable", space = vgm(0.8, "Exp", 3, 0.2), time = vgm(0.8, "Exp", 1.5, 0.2), sill = 0.04),
                      method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = c(0.1, 0, 0.1, 0, 0.001), upper = c(50, 1, 20, 1, 1))
jan <- as.Date(rownames(R)) < as.Date("2025-02-01"); dj <- as.Date(rownames(R))[jan]
Rj <- R[jan, ]
set.seed(9111)
hide <- matrix(runif(length(Rj)) < 0.15, nrow(Rj)) & !is.na(Rj)          # 15% of the measurements
obs <- Rj; obs[hide] <- NA
sts <- as(STFDF(SpatialPoints(xy), dj, data.frame(r = as.vector(t(obs)))), "STSDF")
sts <- sts[!is.na(sts$r), ]
h <- which(t(hide))                                                        # stations fastest
s_i <- (h - 1) %% ncol(Rj) + 1; t_i <- (h - 1) %/% ncol(Rj) + 1
target <- STSDF(SpatialPoints(xy), dj, data.frame(id = seq_along(h)), index = cbind(s_i, t_i))
k <- krigeST(r ~ 1, data = sts, newdata = target, modelList = fs, computeVar = TRUE)
truth <- Rj[cbind(t_i, s_i)]
sm <- fs$space; sm$psill <- sm$psill * fs$sill                             # the spatial part alone
space_only <- sapply(seq_along(h), function(i) {
  d <- data.frame(xy, r = obs[t_i[i], ]); d <- d[!is.na(d$r), ]
  krige(r ~ 1, ~x + y, d, newdata = xy[s_i[i], , drop = FALSE], model = sm, debug.level = 0)$var1.pred })
time_only <- sapply(seq_along(h), function(i) {
  z <- obs[, s_i[i]]; nb <- z[c(t_i[i] - 1, t_i[i] + 1)[c(t_i[i] > 1, t_i[i] < nrow(obs))]]
  if (all(is.na(nb))) 0 else mean(nb, na.rm = TRUE) })
rmse <- function(p) sqrt(mean((p - truth)^2))
c(hidden = length(h), spacetime = rmse(k$var1.pred), space = rmse(space_only), time = rmse(time_only), zero = rmse(0))
116 values hidden. Space-time kriging’s RMSE is 0.162, exactly as good as kriging each day in space alone (0.162). The station’s own neighbouring days alone give 0.183, and predicting zero (only the station and day effects) 0.204. So, on average, adding time didn’t help at all. Is that the whole story?




Your turn. An average hides a lot. Break the space-time and space-only errors down by station type.









Each hidden value’s station is s_i.


q1 <- as.Date(rownames(R)) < as.Date("2025-04-01")
stf <- STFDF(SpatialPoints(xy), as.Date(rownames(R))[q1], data.frame(r = as.vector(t(R[q1, ]))))
vst <- variogramST(r ~ 1, stf, tlags = 0:3, cutoff = 20, width = 2, na.omit = TRUE, progress = FALSE)
fs <- fit.StVariogram(vst, vgmST("separable", space = vgm(0.8, "Exp", 3, 0.2), time = vgm(0.8, "Exp", 1.5, 0.2), sill = 0.04),
                      method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = c(0.1, 0, 0.1, 0, 0.001), upper = c(50, 1, 20, 1, 1))
jan <- as.Date(rownames(R)) < as.Date("2025-02-01"); dj <- as.Date(rownames(R))[jan]
Rj <- R[jan, ]
set.seed(9111)
hide <- matrix(runif(length(Rj)) < 0.15, nrow(Rj)) & !is.na(Rj)
obs <- Rj; obs[hide] <- NA
sts <- as(STFDF(SpatialPoints(xy), dj, data.frame(r = as.vector(t(obs)))), "STSDF"); sts <- sts[!is.na(sts$r), ]
h <- which(t(hide)); s_i <- (h - 1) %% ncol(Rj) + 1; t_i <- (h - 1) %/% ncol(Rj) + 1
target <- STSDF(SpatialPoints(xy), dj, data.frame(id = seq_along(h)), index = cbind(s_i, t_i))
k <- krigeST(r ~ 1, data = sts, newdata = target, modelList = fs, computeVar = TRUE)
truth <- Rj[cbind(t_i, s_i)]
sm <- fs$space; sm$psill <- sm$psill * fs$sill
space_only <- sapply(seq_along(h), function(i) {
  d <- data.frame(xy, r = obs[t_i[i], ]); d <- d[!is.na(d$r), ]
  krige(r ~ 1, ~x + y, d, newdata = xy[s_i[i], , drop = FALSE], model = sm, debug.level = 0)$var1.pred })
type <- stations$type[match(colnames(Rj), stations$station)][s_i]
round(rbind(spacetime = tapply((k$var1.pred - truth)^2, type, function(e) sqrt(mean(e))),
            space = tapply((space_only - truth)^2, type, function(e) sqrt(mean(e)))), 3)
No: it depends entirely on the station. At the roadside stations, strung along the motorway 5 to 6.5 km apart, space-time kriging cuts the error from 0.158 to 0.118, and at the rural stations, far from everything, from 0.171 to 0.148: there, the station’s own previous and next days are the best information available. In the town, where the urban stations are 1 to 2 km apart, it’s worse (0.129 against 0.106): with its too-strong temporal correlation, the model gives the station’s own neighbouring days too much weight compared with its close neighbours on the same day. At the industrial stations it’s worse too (0.220 against 0.196): their anomalies are driven by the plume, which switches on and off with the wind, and no stationary covariance can represent that. The average of 0.162 against 0.162 was hiding a gain in one place and a loss in another.










NoteGo deeper: non-separable covariances and physics





Separable covariances can’t represent transport: if a pollution episode moves east at 10 km a day, then station B, 10 km east of A, is most correlated with A one day earlier, not on the same day, and the correlation’s peak shifts with the lag. Non-separable families handle this: Gneiting’s class (2002) lets the spatial range change with the time lag; Lagrangian (frozen-field) models C(h - vu, 0) move a spatial covariance with a velocity v; and models from stochastic partial differential equations (advection-diffusion) build the physics in. With a dominant wind direction, the covariance is also asymmetric in space-time, which none of gstat’s built-in models allow. Wikle, Zammit-Mangion and Cressie’s Spatio-Temporal Statistics with R, chapter 4, and Gneiting’s “Nonseparable, Stationary Covariance Functions for Space-Time Data” (Journal of the American Statistical Association 97, 2002) are the places to start.

title: Spatio-temporal covariance and kriging
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Calibration. Are the kriging variances honest? Compute the mean squared z-score, overall and by station type.









Divide by the kriging variance, k$var1.var.


q1 <- as.Date(rownames(R)) < as.Date("2025-04-01")
stf <- STFDF(SpatialPoints(xy), as.Date(rownames(R))[q1], data.frame(r = as.vector(t(R[q1, ]))))
vst <- variogramST(r ~ 1, stf, tlags = 0:3, cutoff = 20, width = 2, na.omit = TRUE, progress = FALSE)
fs <- fit.StVariogram(vst, vgmST("separable", space = vgm(0.8, "Exp", 3, 0.2), time = vgm(0.8, "Exp", 1.5, 0.2), sill = 0.04),
                      method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = c(0.1, 0, 0.1, 0, 0.001), upper = c(50, 1, 20, 1, 1))
jan <- as.Date(rownames(R)) < as.Date("2025-02-01"); dj <- as.Date(rownames(R))[jan]
Rj <- R[jan, ]
set.seed(9111)
hide <- matrix(runif(length(Rj)) < 0.15, nrow(Rj)) & !is.na(Rj)
obs <- Rj; obs[hide] <- NA
sts <- as(STFDF(SpatialPoints(xy), dj, data.frame(r = as.vector(t(obs)))), "STSDF"); sts <- sts[!is.na(sts$r), ]
h <- which(t(hide)); s_i <- (h - 1) %% ncol(Rj) + 1; t_i <- (h - 1) %/% ncol(Rj) + 1
target <- STSDF(SpatialPoints(xy), dj, data.frame(id = seq_along(h)), index = cbind(s_i, t_i))
k <- krigeST(r ~ 1, data = sts, newdata = target, modelList = fs, computeVar = TRUE)
z2 <- (k$var1.pred - Rj[cbind(t_i, s_i)])^2 / k$var1.var
type <- stations$type[match(colnames(Rj), stations$station)][s_i]
round(c(all = mean(z2), tapply(z2, type, mean)), 2)
A mean squared z-score of 3.19 overall: the errors are, on average, \sqrt{3.19} = 1.8 times as large as the kriging standard errors claim. At the roadside stations (1.17) the variances are about right, at the rural ones (1.70) somewhat optimistic, and in the town (2.92) and at the industrial stations (6.44) badly so. That’s the missing nugget and the too-strong temporal correlation, plus the plume. A model can predict reasonably and still misstate its uncertainty, and only validation reveals it. Compare Lesson 4’s soil kriging, whose z-scores were honest (1.03).




Challenge 2 · Put the wind in the mean. In RStudio, add the plume to the model as a covariate: for each station and day, a “downwind” variable equal to 1 for stations within 30° of the downwind direction from the plant and within 6 km, 0 otherwise. Regress the interaction on it, krige the residuals in space and time, and add the two back (regression kriging, Lesson 5, in space-time). Do the industrial stations’ errors and z-scores improve?

title: Spatio-temporal covariance and kriging
text:
Quick quiz

1. A spatio-temporal covariance C(h, u) is separable when:

It doesn’t depend on time
It factors into a spatial part times a temporal part
Space and time are independent variables


Then the spatial pattern of correlation is the same at every lag, only scaled.



2. In a gstat STFDF, the data must be ordered:

With space varying fastest: all stations for day 1, then day 2, …
With time varying fastest
In any order


Hence as.vector(t(R)) from a days × stations matrix.



3. A metric model’s anisotropy factor is measured in:

Days
Kilometres per day: it converts time lags into distances
It has no units


The model then treats space-time as a three-dimensional space.



4. Why did space-time kriging help most at the roadside and rural stations?

Their measurements are more accurate
Their spatial neighbours are far away, so their own previous and next days carry more information
They have more missing values


Where same-day neighbours are close (the town), time adds little.



5. At the industrial stations, space-time kriging did worse and its z-scores were far too large. The most likely reason:

Too few hidden values
The wind-driven plume is a non-stationary signal that a stationary covariance can’t represent
The separable model has too many parameters


Put the plume into the mean (a covariate), and krige what’s left.



6. What’s the main lesson of the validation?

Space-time kriging is always better
Space-time kriging is never worth it
Validate by subgroup: a method can help in one place and fail in another, and the average hides it


Honest validation decides where to use a method.

title: Spatio-temporal covariance and kriging
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve modelled correlation in space and time together. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Spatio-temporal covariance C(h, u), estimated by hand from the stations’ series; separable if it factors as space times time.
gstat’s tools: STFDF objects (space fastest), variogramST(), and fit.StVariogram() for separable and metric models (in kilometres).
Space-time kriging fills in hidden measurements from both the neighbouring stations and the neighbouring days.
Validation by station type showed where it helps (stations far from their neighbours) and where it fails (the plume’s non-stationarity), and that its variances were overconfident there.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download air_stations.csv and air_no2_daily.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install sp, spacetime and gstat.

Plot the variogram surface. plot(vst, fs, wireframe = TRUE, all = TRUE) shows the empirical and fitted variograms side by side.
Other models. Fit "productSum" and "sumMetric" models. Do they converge? Compare their MSE with the separable and metric fits.
A09’s annual mean. Fill A09’s three-week June gap by space-time kriging (fit the model to May to July), and recompute its annual mean. How much does it change compared with ignoring the gap?
The school. A new primary school is planned at (484000, 5704600). Predict its daily NO₂ for January with space-time kriging of the full log values (including the station effects, which you’ll need to krige too).










NoteKey words from this lesson






Spatio-temporal covariance

C(h, u), the covariance between values a distance h and a time lag u apart.

Separable covariance

A covariance that factors into a purely spatial and a purely temporal part.

Spatio-temporal variogram

\gamma(h, u) = \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Var}[Z(s+h, t+u) - Z(s, t)], estimated for distance bins and time lags.

Metric model

A spatio-temporal variogram that treats time as a scaled third dimension.

Space-time anisotropy

The factor converting time lags into equivalent distances (km per day).

Space-time kriging

Kriging with a spatio-temporal covariance, using neighbours in both space and time.

Non-stationarity

Statistical properties that change with location or time, such as a plume that appears only with certain winds.











NoteWant to read more?






Christopher Wikle, Andrew Zammit-Mangion and Noel Cressie, Spatio-Temporal Statistics with R (CRC Press, 2019, free online), chapter 4, on descriptive spatio-temporal models and kriging.
Benedikt Gräler, Edzer Pebesma and Gerard Heuvelink, “Spatio-Temporal Interpolation using gstat”, The R Journal 8(1), 2016, pages 204 to 218, the guide to variogramST(), fit.StVariogram() and krigeST(), with an air-quality example.
Tilmann Gneiting, “Nonseparable, Stationary Covariance Functions for Space-Time Data”, Journal of the American Statistical Association 97, 2002, pages 590 to 600.

title: Dynamic spatio-temporal models
text:
Module 9 · Lesson 13 of 13 Week 145 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Lesson 12 found that three patterns carry the lake’s interesting variation: the wind’s tilt, the cooling-water plume and the shallow bay. Their amplitudes are three time series, with gaps where the clouds hid the lake. Two questions remain, and they’re the questions most environmental monitoring ends with:
Both need a model of the dynamics: how the state at one time produces the state at the next. That’s a dynamic spatio-temporal model, the last idea of the module, and it brings together Module 6’s autoregressions, Lesson 12’s dimension reduction, and the Kalman filter.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Dynamic spatio-temporal models
text:
The hierarchical view
Wikle, Zammit-Mangion and Cressie organize spatio-temporal statistics as a hierarchy of three models:

the data model: how the observations relate to the true process. Here, the satellite measures the lake’s surface temperature with some error, and sometimes not at all (clouds).
the process model: how the true field evolves. Here, \boldsymbol\alpha_t = M\boldsymbol\alpha_{t-1} + G\mathbf u_t + \boldsymbol\eta_t: next week’s pattern amplitudes are a linear function of this week’s, plus the effect of the inputs \mathbf u_t (load and wind), plus an innovation \boldsymbol\eta_t.
the parameter model: what we assume about M, G and the variances (here, nothing: we estimate them; a Bayesian would put priors on them, as in Module 5).

Working with the EOF amplitudes \boldsymbol\alpha_t instead of the 258 pixels is what makes the process model feasible: a 3 \times 3 matrix M instead of 258 \times 258. This reduced-rank approach is how most large dynamic spatio-temporal models work.
The setup code reads the data, computes Lesson 12’s anomalies and first three EOFs (V, a 258 × 3 matrix), and defines the Kalman filter and smoother used at the end of the lesson.












Your turn. Project each clear week’s anomaly map onto the three EOFs to get its amplitudes, and put them in a 156 × 3 matrix with NA for the cloudy weeks.









Multiply the anomalies by the EOFs, V.


alpha <- matrix(NA, nrow(plant), 3)
obs <- match(rownames(Z), plant$week)                                 # rows of the clear weeks
alpha[obs, ] <- A %*% V
c(weeks = nrow(alpha), clear = sum(!is.na(alpha[, 1])), round(apply(alpha, 2, sd, na.rm = TRUE), 2))
156 weeks, 124 of them clear. The amplitudes’ standard deviations are 2.91, 2.52 and 1.57: these are UD from Lesson 12, the weight of each pattern in each week’s map, and their variances are in the same proportions as the EOFs’ shares of the variance. Projecting onto the EOFs is how a new image (next week’s, or a cloudy week’s partial one) would be reduced too.

title: Dynamic spatio-temporal models
text:
A vector autoregression
A first-order vector autoregression, VAR(1) (Module 6, Lesson 12), predicts each amplitude from all three amplitudes of the week before: \boldsymbol\alpha_t = M\boldsymbol\alpha_{t-1} + \boldsymbol\eta_t. It can only be fitted from pairs of consecutive clear weeks. To test it honestly, fit it on 2023 and 2024, and keep 2025 for testing.
Your turn. Find the pairs of consecutive clear weeks, and how many fall in each period.









The comparison is shifted by one week: add 1 to get week t.


alpha <- matrix(NA, nrow(plant), 3); obs <- match(rownames(Z), plant$week); alpha[obs, ] <- A %*% V
pair <- which(!is.na(alpha[-1, 1]) & !is.na(alpha[-nrow(alpha), 1])) + 1   # week t, with t - 1 clear too
c(pairs = length(pair), training = sum(yr[pair] < 2025), test = sum(yr[pair] == 2025))
100 pairs: 66 for training (2023 and 2024) and 34 for testing (2025). Clouds cost more than their 20% of the weeks: every cloudy week breaks two pairs. That’s the first argument for a method, like the Kalman filter, that doesn’t need complete data.




Your turn. Fit the VAR(1) on the training pairs by least squares, one regression for all three amplitudes, without an intercept (the amplitudes have mean zero).









The predictors are last week’s amplitudes: tr - 1.


alpha <- matrix(NA, nrow(plant), 3); obs <- match(rownames(Z), plant$week); alpha[obs, ] <- A %*% V
pair <- which(!is.na(alpha[-1, 1]) & !is.na(alpha[-nrow(alpha), 1])) + 1
tr <- pair[yr[pair] < 2025]
fit <- lm(alpha[tr, ] ~ alpha[tr - 1, ] - 1)
M_var <- t(coef(fit))                                                 # rows: this week; columns: last week
round(M_var, 3)
The diagonal (0.67, 0.74 and 0.71) is each pattern’s persistence from one week to the next; the off-diagonal terms are interactions, mostly small, except that the shallow bay last week (-0.52) feeds into the tilt this week, which is probably the season showing through both. With 66 pairs and 9 coefficients, M is estimated quite roughly.




Your turn. A VAR(1) is stable (its effects die away, rather than growing) if all the eigenvalues of M have modulus less than 1. Check, and compute how many weeks it takes the slowest mode to halve.









The eigenvalues are eigen(M)$values.


alpha <- matrix(NA, nrow(plant), 3); obs <- match(rownames(Z), plant$week); alpha[obs, ] <- A %*% V
pair <- which(!is.na(alpha[-1, 1]) & !is.na(alpha[-nrow(alpha), 1])) + 1
tr <- pair[yr[pair] < 2025]
M_var <- t(coef(lm(alpha[tr, ] ~ alpha[tr - 1, ] - 1)))
lambda <- Mod(eigen(M_var)$values)
c(round(lambda, 3), half_life_weeks = log(0.5) / log(max(lambda)))
Moduli of 0.91, 0.61 and 0.60, all below 1: stable. The slowest mode halves in about 7 weeks; the other two in about a week and a half. (Complex eigenvalues, which come in pairs with the same modulus, mean oscillation: a pattern that rotates into another and back.)

title: Dynamic spatio-temporal models
text:
Adding the inputs
The lake doesn’t evolve on its own: the plant’s load drives the plume, and the wind drives the tilt. Add them to the process model: \boldsymbol\alpha_t = M\boldsymbol\alpha_{t-1} + G\mathbf u_t + \boldsymbol\eta_t. (This is a VAR with exogenous inputs, a VARX.)
Your turn. Fit it, and look at G, the effects of this week’s load and wind.









This week’s inputs: u[tr, ].


alpha <- matrix(NA, nrow(plant), 3); obs <- match(rownames(Z), plant$week); alpha[obs, ] <- A %*% V
pair <- which(!is.na(alpha[-1, 1]) & !is.na(alpha[-nrow(alpha), 1])) + 1
tr <- pair[yr[pair] < 2025]
fit <- lm(alpha[tr, ] ~ cbind(alpha[tr - 1, ], u[tr, ]) - 1)
B <- t(coef(fit)); M <- B[, 1:3]; G <- B[, 4:5]
round(G, 3)
A west wind of 1 m/s adds 0.69 to amplitude 1 (the tilt), and full load changes all three amplitudes, by -1.29, -0.26 and -0.49 respectively, not just the plume’s. That’s less tidy than “load drives the plume, wind drives the tilt”, because the EOFs are statistical patterns (they mix the physical modes a little, and their signs are arbitrary), and because with M in the model, part of the load’s effect is already carried by last week’s amplitudes. The forecasts are the better test.




Your turn. Forecast each 2025 test week from the previous week, with four methods, and compare their errors on the lake’s pixels (reconstructing each forecast map from the three EOFs): the VARX, the VAR without inputs, persistence (next week = this week) and climatology (anomaly zero, the average lake).









Reconstruct the maps with the EOFs: t(V).


alpha <- matrix(NA, nrow(plant), 3); obs <- match(rownames(Z), plant$week); alpha[obs, ] <- A %*% V
pair <- which(!is.na(alpha[-1, 1]) & !is.na(alpha[-nrow(alpha), 1])) + 1
tr <- pair[yr[pair] < 2025]; te <- pair[yr[pair] == 2025]
B <- t(coef(lm(alpha[tr, ] ~ cbind(alpha[tr - 1, ], u[tr, ]) - 1)))
M_var <- t(coef(lm(alpha[tr, ] ~ alpha[tr - 1, ] - 1)))
fc <- list(varx = cbind(alpha[te - 1, ], u[te, ]) %*% t(B),
           var = alpha[te - 1, ] %*% t(M_var),
           persistence = alpha[te - 1, ],
           climatology = matrix(0, length(te), 3))
truth <- A[match(te, obs), ]                                         # the observed anomaly maps
sapply(fc, function(f) sqrt(mean((f %*% t(V) - truth)^2)))      # RMSE over pixels, degrees C
On the 34 test weeks of 2025: 0.309 °C for the VARX, 0.325 for the VAR, 0.337 for persistence and 0.372 for climatology. Each step adds skill: dynamics beat the average lake, and knowing next week’s load and wind beats dynamics alone. Remember that even a perfect forecast of the three amplitudes would leave an error of about 0.27 °C (Lesson 12’s reconstruction error with three EOFs): the small-scale noise isn’t predictable. So the VARX captures about 60% of the predictable part that climatology misses. (In real use, the load is planned and the wind forecast, so next week’s inputs are available, with some error.)

title: Dynamic spatio-temporal models
text:
The Kalman filter
For the cloudy weeks, the Kalman filter combines the process model with whatever data exist. At each week, it carries an estimate \mathbf a_t of the state and its covariance P_t:

Predict from last week: \mathbf a_{t|t-1} = M\mathbf a_{t-1} + G\mathbf u_t, with covariance P_{t|t-1} = MP_{t-1}M^\top + Q (the process model’s uncertainty, Q, adds to what was already uncertain).
Update if there’s an image: \mathbf a_t = \mathbf a_{t|t-1} + K_t(\mathbf y_t - \mathbf a_{t|t-1}), with the Kalman gain K_t = P_{t|t-1}(P_{t|t-1} + R)^{-1}, where R is the observation error’s covariance (the data model). The gain weighs the prediction against the observation by their uncertainties, exactly like Module 5’s posterior mean weighs a prior against data.

In a cloudy week, there’s no update: the estimate is the prediction, and its uncertainty grows. The setup code’s kf() does both steps; here R is tiny (the projected amplitudes are measured almost without error), so a clear week’s estimate is essentially its observation.
Your turn. Run the filter with the VARX’s matrices, and compare the estimated plume amplitude (the second) in the turnaround of April 2024, when the plant was shut down and one week was cloudy.









The plume is the second amplitude: element [2, 2] of each covariance matrix.


alpha <- matrix(NA, nrow(plant), 3); obs <- match(rownames(Z), plant$week); alpha[obs, ] <- A %*% V
pair <- which(!is.na(alpha[-1, 1]) & !is.na(alpha[-nrow(alpha), 1])) + 1
tr <- pair[yr[pair] < 2025]
fit <- lm(alpha[tr, ] ~ cbind(alpha[tr - 1, ], u[tr, ]) - 1)
B <- t(coef(fit)); M <- B[, 1:3]; G <- B[, 4:5]; Q <- cov(residuals(fit))
f <- kf(alpha, u, M, G, Q, R = diag(1e-4, 3))
turn <- which(plant$week >= "2024-04-08" & plant$week <= "2024-05-06")
rbind(observed = alpha[turn, 2], filtered = f$a[turn, 2], se = sqrt(sapply(turn, function(t) f$P[[t]][2, 2])))
In the four clear weeks, the filter’s estimate is the observation, with a tiny standard error (0.01). The plume amplitude climbs from 3.0 to 7.8; with this EOF’s sign, a positive value means a cooler outfall area, so that’s the plume fading as the plant shuts down. In the cloudy week of 29 April, the filter has only its prediction from the week before: 5.55, with a standard error of 1.62, below the clear weeks on either side (7.45 and 7.78). The filter can’t know that the following week was 7.78, and the model’s estimate of the shutdown’s effect falls short. Its standard error says how little it knows: a 95% interval of about \pm 3.2.




Your turn. Validate: hide 15 clear weeks of 2025, fill them with the filter, and compare with linear interpolation between the neighbouring clear weeks, on the pixels.









Interpolate at the hidden weeks, hid.


alpha <- matrix(NA, nrow(plant), 3); obs <- match(rownames(Z), plant$week); alpha[obs, ] <- A %*% V
pair <- which(!is.na(alpha[-1, 1]) & !is.na(alpha[-nrow(alpha), 1])) + 1
tr <- pair[yr[pair] < 2025]
fit <- lm(alpha[tr, ] ~ cbind(alpha[tr - 1, ], u[tr, ]) - 1)
B <- t(coef(fit)); M <- B[, 1:3]; G <- B[, 4:5]; Q <- cov(residuals(fit))
set.seed(9131)
hid <- sample(which(!is.na(alpha[, 1]) & yr == 2025), 15)
a2 <- alpha; a2[hid, ] <- NA
f <- kf(a2, u, M, G, Q, R = diag(1e-4, 3))
lin <- sapply(1:3, function(j) approx(seq_len(nrow(a2)), a2[, j], xout = hid, rule = 2)$y)
truth <- A[match(hid, obs), ]
c(filter = sqrt(mean((f$a[hid, ] %*% t(V) - truth)^2)), linear = sqrt(mean((lin %*% t(V) - truth)^2)),
  climatology = sqrt(mean(truth^2)))
0.308 °C for the filter, 0.312 for linear interpolation and 0.358 for the average lake. The filter only edges out interpolation, and that’s not a fair contest: the filter only uses the weeks before each gap, while interpolation uses the week after too. The smoother, next, fixes that.




The Kalman smoother (Rauch, Tung and Striebel, 1965) runs backwards after the filter, revising each week’s estimate with everything that happened afterwards. For filling past gaps, it’s the right tool; the filter is for real time.
Your turn. Smooth the filtered estimates with ks(), and compare again.









Smooth the filter’s output, f.


alpha <- matrix(NA, nrow(plant), 3); obs <- match(rownames(Z), plant$week); alpha[obs, ] <- A %*% V
pair <- which(!is.na(alpha[-1, 1]) & !is.na(alpha[-nrow(alpha), 1])) + 1
tr <- pair[yr[pair] < 2025]
fit <- lm(alpha[tr, ] ~ cbind(alpha[tr - 1, ], u[tr, ]) - 1)
B <- t(coef(fit)); M <- B[, 1:3]; G <- B[, 4:5]; Q <- cov(residuals(fit))
set.seed(9131)
hid <- sample(which(!is.na(alpha[, 1]) & yr == 2025), 15)
a2 <- alpha; a2[hid, ] <- NA
f <- kf(a2, u, M, G, Q, R = diag(1e-4, 3))
s <- ks(f, u, M, G, Q)
lin <- sapply(1:3, function(j) approx(seq_len(nrow(a2)), a2[, j], xout = hid, rule = 2)$y)
truth <- A[match(hid, obs), ]
c(smoother = sqrt(mean((s$a[hid, ] %*% t(V) - truth)^2)), linear = sqrt(mean((lin %*% t(V) - truth)^2)))
0.293 °C for the smoother against 0.312 for interpolation: with information from both sides of each gap, plus the model’s knowledge of what the load and the wind were doing, the smoother wins clearly, and it’s within 0.02 °C of the best any three-EOF reconstruction could do (about 0.27). By amplitude, it’s much better for the tilt (RMSE 0.94 against 1.97: the wind is known even when the lake isn’t seen) and for the shallow bay (0.90 against 1.01), and slightly worse for the plume (1.31 against 1.21), whose week-to-week changes are smooth enough for interpolation.



















NoteGo deeper: integro-difference equations and physical dynamics





Fitting M freely works for three amplitudes, but not for a full field: a 258 \times 258 matrix has 66,564 entries. Physical dynamics give it structure. An integro-difference equation (IDE) model writes the next field as a smoothed, shifted version of the current one, Y_t(s) = \int k(s, r; \boldsymbol\theta) Y_{t-1}(r)\,dr + \eta_t(s), where the kernel k (often a Gaussian whose centre is offset by a velocity) describes diffusion and advection with a handful of parameters \boldsymbol\theta. With a spatially varying velocity, it can represent a plume drifting with the currents. The IDE package fits such models, and with basis functions (Lesson 12) the integral becomes a small matrix. The models connect directly to the advection-diffusion equations of transport phenomena. Wikle, Zammit-Mangion and Cressie’s Spatio-Temporal Statistics with R, chapter 5, develops them, with R code.

title: Dynamic spatio-temporal models
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Calibration. Are the smoother’s standard errors honest? For the 15 hidden weeks, compute the mean squared z-score of each amplitude.









Divide by the standard errors, se.


alpha <- matrix(NA, nrow(plant), 3); obs <- match(rownames(Z), plant$week); alpha[obs, ] <- A %*% V
pair <- which(!is.na(alpha[-1, 1]) & !is.na(alpha[-nrow(alpha), 1])) + 1
tr <- pair[yr[pair] < 2025]
fit <- lm(alpha[tr, ] ~ cbind(alpha[tr - 1, ], u[tr, ]) - 1)
B <- t(coef(fit)); M <- B[, 1:3]; G <- B[, 4:5]; Q <- cov(residuals(fit))
set.seed(9131)
hid <- sample(which(!is.na(alpha[, 1]) & yr == 2025), 15)
a2 <- alpha; a2[hid, ] <- NA
s <- ks(kf(a2, u, M, G, Q, R = diag(1e-4, 3)), u, M, G, Q)
se <- t(sapply(hid, function(t) sqrt(diag(s$P[[t]]))))
round(colMeans(((s$a[hid, ] - alpha[hid, ]) / se)^2), 2)
0.45, 0.85 and 0.84: all below 1, so the smoother’s uncertainty is, if anything, a little pessimistic (more so for the tilt, which the known wind predicts better than the model’s Q assumes). With only 15 hidden weeks, these are rough. Unlike Lesson 11’s space-time kriging, the dynamic model’s error bands can be reported as they are. For Hana’s permit report, that means a plume estimate for every one of the 156 weeks, with an honest band, and the cloudy weeks no longer a gap in the record.




Challenge 2 · Partly cloudy. In real satellite data, clouds often cover only part of the lake. In RStudio, hide a random half of the pixels in some weeks, and change the data model: instead of observing \boldsymbol\alpha_t directly, observe the visible pixels, \mathbf y_t = V_{\text{vis}}\boldsymbol\alpha_t + \boldsymbol\varepsilon_t, with V_{\text{vis}} the EOFs’ rows for those pixels. The Kalman update becomes K_t = P_{t|t-1}H^\top(HP_{t|t-1}H^\top + R)^{-1} with H = V_{\text{vis}}. How well does it reconstruct the hidden half?

title: Dynamic spatio-temporal models
text:
Quick quiz

1. In the hierarchical view, the process model describes:

How the satellite measures the lake
How the true field evolves over time
The priors on the parameters


Data model, process model, parameter model.



2. Why model the three EOF amplitudes instead of the 258 pixels?

The pixels are inaccurate
A 3 \times 3 transition matrix can be estimated; a 258 \times 258 one can’t
EOFs are smoother


Reduced-rank dynamics: the standard approach for large fields.



3. A VAR(1) is stable when:

All entries of M are positive
All eigenvalues of M have modulus less than 1
M is symmetric


Then disturbances die away instead of growing.



4. Which forecast was best on the 2025 test weeks?

Climatology
Persistence
The VAR with the load and wind as inputs


0.309 °C, against 0.337 for persistence and 0.372 for climatology.



5. The Kalman gain K_t:

Is always 1
Weighs the prediction against the new observation according to their uncertainties
Measures the forecast error


Like a posterior mean weighing a prior and data.



6. Why is the smoother, not the filter, the right tool for filling past cloudy weeks?

It’s faster
It uses the observations after each gap as well as before
It doesn’t need a process model


The filter is for real time; the smoother for reconstructing the past.

title: Dynamic spatio-temporal models
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve built a dynamic model of a spatio-temporal field. Here’s what you’ve learned:

The hierarchy: a data model (the satellite, with clouds), a process model (how the field evolves) and a parameter model.
Reduced-rank dynamics: three EOF amplitudes, 124 clear weeks of 156, only 100 consecutive pairs.
A VAR(1) is stable (eigenvalue moduli 0.91, 0.61, 0.60); with the load and the wind as inputs, it forecasts next week’s lake to 0.309 °C, against 0.337 for persistence and 0.372 for climatology.
The Kalman filter and smoother fill the cloudy weeks; on 15 hidden weeks, the smoother’s error was 0.293 °C, against 0.312 for interpolation, with slightly conservative standard errors.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download lake_temperature.csv and plant_weekly.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

More EOFs. Repeat the forecasts with 2, 4 and 6 EOFs. Does more dimensions mean better forecasts, or just more parameters?
Multi-step forecasts. Forecast 1, 2, 4 and 8 weeks ahead by iterating the VARX. How fast does the skill decay toward climatology?
KFAS. Install KFAS and fit the same state-space model with SSModel() and fitSSM(), which estimates Q and R by maximum likelihood instead of from regression residuals. Do the estimates and the smoothed gaps change?
The permit, every week. Using the smoothed amplitudes for all 156 weeks, reconstruct the plume map each week, and count the weeks in which more than 1 km² (16 pixels) was 3 °C above the lake’s mean. How many were cloudy?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Dynamic spatio-temporal model

A model of how a spatial field at one time produces the field at the next.

Data, process and parameter models

The three levels of a hierarchical spatio-temporal model: measurement, evolution, and parameters.

Reduced-rank dynamics

Modelling the evolution of a few basis-function or EOF amplitudes instead of the whole field.

Vector autoregression with inputs (VARX)

\boldsymbol\alpha_t = M\boldsymbol\alpha_{t-1} + G\mathbf u_t + \boldsymbol\eta_t.

Persistence and climatology forecasts

The baselines: next time equals this time, or next time equals the average.

Kalman filter

A recursive estimator of a state-space model’s state, alternating prediction and update.

Kalman gain

The weight given to a new observation relative to the prediction.

Kalman (Rauch-Tung-Striebel) smoother

A backward pass that revises the filter’s estimates using later observations.

Integro-difference equation (IDE)

A process model in which the next field is an integral (a kernel smoothing) of the current one, representing diffusion and advection.











NoteWant to read more?






Christopher Wikle, Andrew Zammit-Mangion and Noel Cressie, Spatio-Temporal Statistics with R (CRC Press, 2019, free online), chapters 5 and 6, on dynamic spatio-temporal models, IDEs and model evaluation.
Noel Cressie and Christopher Wikle, Statistics for Spatio-Temporal Data (Wiley, 2011), chapter 7, the full theory of hierarchical dynamic models.
Jacques Commandeur and Siem Jan Koopman, An Introduction to State Space Time Series Analysis (Oxford, 2007), a short, gentle introduction to the Kalman filter and smoother.

title: Module 9 project: an environmental spatio-temporal analysis
text:
In 1994, a buried pipe at the plant’s old tank farm leaked petrol-grade benzene into the ground. The free product was removed in 1996, but a dissolved plume remains in the shallow aquifer, and the groundwater flows east, toward the town’s drinking-water well, PW-1, 1.8 km away. Hana has persuaded the regulator to accept monitored natural attenuation (letting bacteria break the benzene down, and proving it with data) instead of pumping and treating the groundwater for decades. The regulator agreed, on three conditions, and wants a report on all three.
That’s an environmental spatio-temporal analysis: data at fixed places, measured again and again, with a map of today, a trend over time, a prediction, and an honest account of the uncertainty in each.

title: Module 9 project: an environmental spatio-temporal analysis
text:
What you’ll make
One report, written in Quarto in your plant-study RStudio project, that Hana could send to the regulator. It should contain:

A summary for the regulator, at the top, in plain words: where benzene is above 10 µg/L today (with a map and its uncertainty), whether the plume is shrinking (how fast) and moving (how fast, which way), and whether the sentinel wells, between the plume and PW-1, are at risk.
The data and its problems: what you found, and what you did about each.
The map of today: a kriged map of the 2026 Q3 round, a map of its standard error, and a map of the probability of exceeding 10 µg/L, with the variogram and the cross-validation behind them.
The trend: how the plume’s size, mass and position have changed since 2019.
The sentinel wells: what the data say about MW-36 and MW-37, and what they can’t say yet.
Limitations, and a recommendation.

Nobody grades it, but write it as if the regulator’s hydrogeologist will check every number. In real life, they would.

title: Module 9 project: an environmental spatio-temporal analysis
text:
The handover
Download the three files into a new folder in your project, data-raw/groundwater/, and don’t edit them:

README.txt: Hana’s note, with the three conditions, the questions, the columns and a known issue. Read it first.
wells.csv: the 40 monitoring wells, with their coordinates and screen depths.
groundwater_benzene.csv: every result since February 2019, as the labs reported it.

Then download the project template, save it in the top folder of your project as groundwater-benzene.qmd, and click Render. It reads the data and summarizes it, with headings and code skeletons for every step. Fill it in one section at a time, and render often. It uses the tidyverse, sf and gstat.

title: Module 9 project: an environmental spatio-temporal analysis
text:
The brief, step by step

Explore (Lessons 1 and 10). Map the wells. How many results per well and per round? How do the values range, and what does a time series look like at the source and at the edge?
Clean (Lesson 1, and Modules 1 and 4). Check every well’s coordinates against the others (is one in a different CRS?). Look for duplicated results, for values that can’t be numbers, and for a round whose values look a thousand times too small. Decide how to treat results below the detection limit: they’re information, not missing values (Module 4, Lesson 11).
Map today (Lessons 3 to 5). Work on the log scale. Compute and fit a variogram for the 2026 Q3 round (consider a trend, or the distance from the tank farm), krige a grid, map the prediction and its standard error, cross-validate, and map the probability of exceeding 10 µg/L.
The trend (Lessons 10 and 11, and Module 6). For each round, estimate the plume’s total “mass” (the sum of kriged concentrations over the grid, which is proportional to the mass if porosity and thickness are constant), its area above 10 µg/L, and its centre of mass. Is the mass falling, and at what half-life? Is the centre moving?
The sentinels (Module 4, Lesson 11, and Module 6). MW-36 and MW-37 are mostly below the detection limit. What can you say about their trend? If it continues, when would they reach 1 µg/L?
Write it up. Summary first. Then the data, the cleaning, today’s map, the trend, the sentinels, the limitations and a recommendation, and the cleaning log at the end.

Stretch goal. Fit a spatio-temporal model to all the rounds at once: for example, universal kriging with a trend in time and in the distance downstream of the tank farm, or a space-time variogram (Lesson 11) of the residuals. Does it give a sharper map of today than the 2026 Q3 round alone? Does it let you predict at the sentinel wells with an uncertainty?

title: Module 9 project: an environmental spatio-temporal analysis
text:
Check your own work
When you’ve finished, assess your project against this rubric. Aim for the right-hand column.










Needs work
Good
Excellent




The data
Used as received
The duplicate and the dry samples removed
The CRS error, the mg/L round, the duplicate, the dry samples and the censored results all found and handled with reasons, and logged


Today’s map
Points coloured by value
A kriged map on the log scale
Kriged map, standard-error map and exceedance-probability map, with a fitted variogram and cross-validation that checks the calibration


The trend
Graphs of a few wells
Trends at several wells
Mass, area and centroid over the rounds, a half-life with an interval, and the plume’s speed and direction


The sentinels
Ignored
Their results listed
Their trend estimated with the censoring handled, and a prediction with its uncertainty, with its limits stated


Uncertainty
None
Some standard errors
Every key number has an uncertainty, and the report says which conclusions are firm and which aren’t


Communication
Code output with little text
A report that explains its steps
A report Hana could send to the regulator: a plain summary, clear maps, honest uncertainty, a recommendation and stated limitations

title: Module 9 project: an environmental spatio-temporal analysis
text:
Tips

Coordinates first. One well with coordinates near (8.76, 51.46) is in longitude and latitude. Convert it with st_transform() from EPSG:4326 to EPSG:32632; don’t drop it.
Censored values. Substituting half the detection limit is a common start (Module 4 showed when it’s good enough).
