With the log scale and kriging, a value at half the limit is a reasonable plug-in for a map; for the sentinel trends, where most values are censored, consider a censored regression (survival::survreg() with type = "left"), as in Module 4.
The unit error. Compare the median of each round and each lab. A round from one lab a thousand times lower than the rounds before and after isn’t a sudden clean-up.
The variogram of one round. With only 40 wells and a strong trend, the raw variogram may not level off. Try a trend in the distance from the tank farm, or in the distance downstream (x), and fit the residuals’ variogram.
Mass and centroid. Krige every round on the same grid with the same variogram model, then sum e^{\hat z} over the grid (the mass proxy) and weight the coordinates by it (the centroid). Regress the log of the mass on time for a half-life.
Don’t over-claim. The sentinel wells’ trend is estimated from a few small numbers near the detection limit. Say what it suggests, how uncertain it is, and what more data would settle it (more frequent sampling at MW-36 and MW-37, a lower detection limit).


When it’s done, you’ll have carried out a complete environmental spatio-temporal analysis, from a messy monitoring database to maps, trends and a recommendation with its uncertainty. Congratulations on finishing Module 9! Module 10, the last one, takes statistics into biology: sequences, genes and the trees of life.

title: Biological databases and file formats
text:
Module 10 · Lesson 2 of 13 Week 148 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Bioinformatics runs on shared data. Every sequence published in a journal is deposited in a public database, and the databases exchange their data every day. Before Amaya’s team writes a word about PL-7, they’ll compare its genes with millions already known. This lesson is about where those sequences live and the plain-text formats they travel in.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Biological databases and file formats
text:
The databases
The core public databases, all free:








Database
Holds
Run by




GenBank / ENA / DDBJ
every published nucleotide sequence, with annotation (the three mirror each other daily: the INSDC)
NCBI (USA), EMBL-EBI (Europe), NIG (Japan)


RefSeq
a curated, non-redundant selection of GenBank: one reference record per gene, transcript and protein
NCBI


UniProt
protein sequences and their functions; Swiss-Prot is its hand-curated half, TrEMBL the automatic rest
UniProt consortium


PDB
experimentally determined 3D structures of proteins and nucleic acids
wwPDB


AlphaFold DB
predicted structures for over 200 million proteins (Lesson 11)
EMBL-EBI, Google DeepMind


Ensembl
annotated genomes of animals and plants, with genes, variants and comparative data
EMBL-EBI


GEO / ArrayExpress
gene-expression datasets, including microarrays (Lessons 12, 13)
NCBI, EMBL-EBI



Records are identified by accession numbers (GenBank’s look like CP012345.1, UniProt’s like P0A9Q7, the PDB’s like 1ZEM); the number after the dot is the version, which changes when the sequence does. In R, Bioconductor’s packages (Biostrings, GenomicRanges, and many more) read all these formats; the web services can be queried with packages like rentrez, but this lesson works offline, with files for PL-7.
The setup code loads Biostrings.

title: Biological databases and file formats
text:
A GenBank record
pl7_fragment.gb is the fragment of Lesson 1 as a GenBank flat file. Its header lines (LOCUS, DEFINITION, SOURCE, …) describe the record; the FEATURES table lists annotated regions, each with a location and qualifiers (/gene=, /product=, /translation=); ORIGIN starts the sequence, in numbered blocks of ten; // ends the record.
Your turn. Read the record, and list its feature lines (those with a key in columns 6 to 20).









value = TRUE returns the lines themselves.


gb <- readLines("data/pl7_fragment.gb")
feat <- grep("^     [a-zA-Z]", gb, value = TRUE)
feat
Five features: the source (the whole record, 1..3000), two gene features and two CDS features (coding sequences): one at 301..600, a hypothetical protein, and one at complement(1101..1859), the kred gene. In a GenBank feature table, the key starts in column 6 and the location in column 22, a fixed layout that dates from punched cards.




Your turn. Parse the kred CDS location into a strand, a start and an end with regular expressions.









A reverse-strand location starts with complement.


gb <- readLines("data/pl7_fragment.gb")
loc <- sub("^ +CDS +", "", grep("^     CDS", gb, value = TRUE)[2])
nums <- as.numeric(regmatches(loc, gregexpr("[0-9]+", loc))[[1]])
c(location = loc, strand = ifelse(grepl("complement", loc), "-", "+"), start = nums[1], end = nums[2])
Strand -, from 1,101 to 1,859. GenBank locations can be more complex: join(100..200,300..400) for a gene in pieces (eukaryotic exons), <1..500 for a gene that starts before the record does, and combinations like complement(join(...)). Biological coordinates are 1-based and include both ends, unlike most programming languages’ 0-based, half-open ranges, a classic source of off-by-one errors.




Your turn. The /translation qualifier holds the protein, spread over several lines. Collect it.









The capital letters are the range A-Z.


gb <- readLines("data/pl7_fragment.gb")
i <- grep("/translation=", gb)
j <- grep("^ORIGIN", gb) - 1                            # the qualifier runs until ORIGIN
prot <- gsub("[^A-Z]", "", paste(gb[i:j], collapse = ""))  # keep only capital letters
c(length = nchar(prot), start = substr(prot, 1, 20))
252 residues, starting MCRKHPMKESGTGAASGIGL: the same protein you translated by hand in Lesson 1, without the stop (GenBank translations omit the *). Removing every character that isn’t a capital letter takes care of the spaces, the quotes, the line breaks and the lower-case word translation in one step.




Your turn. Read the sequence after ORIGIN, and check that it matches the FASTA file.









Compare with identical().


gb <- readLines("data/pl7_fragment.gb")
o <- grep("^ORIGIN", gb); e <- grep("^//", gb)
seq_gb <- toupper(gsub("[^a-z]", "", paste(gb[(o + 1):(e - 1)], collapse = "")))
seq_fa <- paste(readLines("data/pl7_fragment.fasta")[-1], collapse = "")
c(length = nchar(seq_gb), identical = identical(seq_gb, seq_fa))
3,000 bases, identical to the FASTA file. GenBank writes sequences in lower case, in blocks of ten, sixty per line, with the position of each line’s first base; removing everything that isn’t a lower-case letter strips the numbers and spaces.

title: Biological databases and file formats
text:
FASTA with Biostrings
Parsing by hand teaches the format; for real work, use Biostrings, Bioconductor’s package for sequences. It stores them compactly (a genome of billions of bases fits in memory), and provides DNAString, RNAString and AAString objects, sets of them (DNAStringSet), and fast functions for everything in Lesson 3.
Your turn. Read the fragment with readDNAStringSet(), and check its name, width and GC content.









As a proportion: as.prob = TRUE.


fa <- readDNAStringSet("data/pl7_fragment.fasta")
print(fa)
c(names = names(fa), width = width(fa), gc = letterFrequency(fa, "GC", as.prob = TRUE))
One sequence of width 3,000, named by its FASTA header, with a GC content of 0.633, as in Lesson 1. A DNAStringSet checks its letters: only A, C, G, T, the gap -, and the IUPAC ambiguity codes (N for any base, R for A or G, Y for C or T, and so on) are allowed.

title: Biological databases and file formats
text:
FASTQ: reads and their qualities
A sequencer doesn’t read a genome in one piece; it produces millions of short reads, here of 150 bases. FASTQ stores each read in four lines: @ and a name, the bases, +, and a quality string with one character per base. Each character encodes a Phred quality score Q = -10\log_{10} P(\text{error}): Q = 30 means a 1-in-1,000 chance that the base is wrong, Q = 20 1 in 100. The character is the one whose ASCII code is Q + 33.
Your turn. Read the FASTQ file’s lines, count the reads, and decode the first read’s qualities.









The quality strings are every fourth line, starting at line 4.


fq <- readLines("data/pl7_reads.fastq")
reads <- fq[seq(2, length(fq), 4)]
qual <- fq[seq(4, length(fq), 4)]
q1 <- utf8ToInt(qual[1]) - 33                             # ASCII code minus 33
c(n_reads = length(reads), read_length = nchar(reads[1]), first_q = q1[1], last_q = q1[150])
400 reads of 150 bases. The first read’s first base has Q = 37 (an error probability of 0.0002) and its last Q = 27 (0.002): quality falls along the read, as the sequencing chemistry runs down.




Your turn. Decode every read’s qualities into a 400 × 150 matrix, and compute the mean quality at each position and the expected number of errors per read.









P = 10^{-Q/10}.


fq <- readLines("data/pl7_reads.fastq")
qual <- fq[seq(4, length(fq), 4)]
Q <- t(sapply(qual, function(q) utf8ToInt(q) - 33))      # reads x positions
p_err <- 10^(-Q / 10)
c(mean_q_first = mean(Q[, 1]), mean_q_last = mean(Q[, 150]), errors_per_read = mean(rowSums(p_err)))
The mean quality is 36.7 at the first position and 24.6 at the last, and a read has on average 0.67 expected errors in its 150 bases (the sum of its error probabilities). The plot below shows the decline along the read.













Your turn. Some reads are poor throughout (a cluster on the flow cell that went wrong). Count the reads whose mean quality is below 20.









Below 20.


fq <- readLines("data/pl7_reads.fastq")
qual <- fq[seq(4, length(fq), 4)]
mean_q <- sapply(qual, function(q) mean(utf8ToInt(q) - 33))
c(poor = sum(mean_q < 20), share = mean(mean_q < 20), median_q = median(mean_q))
24 reads, 6%, have a mean quality below 20, against a median of 33.9. Their bases are wrong about once in ten, and they’re usually discarded whole.




Your turn. When the DNA fragment being sequenced is shorter than the read, the sequencer reads on into the adapter, a synthetic sequence attached during library preparation. The common Illumina adapter starts AGATCGGAAGAGC. Find the reads that contain it, and where.









Search for "AGATCGGAAGAGC".


fq <- readLines("data/pl7_reads.fastq")
reads <- fq[seq(2, length(fq), 4)]
hits <- regexpr("AGATCGGAAGAGC", reads, fixed = TRUE)
c(reads_with_adapter = sum(hits > 0), median_start = median(hits[hits > 0]))
6 reads contain the adapter’s first 13 bases exactly, starting at a median position of 114 (one more contains it with a single sequencing error, which a fuzzy search like agrep() finds). Everything from the adapter on isn’t PL-7’s DNA, and left in, it would make reads fail to align or, worse, align wrongly.










NoteGo deeper: where Phred scores come from





Phil Green’s phred program (1998) estimated the error probability of each base from features of the sequencing trace (peak spacing, the ratio of called to uncalled peaks) by calibrating against sequences of known truth, and the logarithmic scale stuck. Modern sequencers calibrate their own scores the same way, and recalibration tools (like GATK’s base quality score recalibration) re-estimate them from known variants, because the reported scores are often optimistic. Older Illumina files used an offset of 64 instead of 33 (“Phred+64”), so a FASTQ file’s quality characters, if they’re all above @, may need a different offset. Brent Ewing and Phil Green, “Base-calling of automated sequencer traces using phred. II. Error probabilities”, Genome Research 8, 1998, pages 186 to 194.

title: Biological databases and file formats
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Trimming. Trim each read at the first position where the quality drops below 20, and at the adapter if there is one, whichever comes first. Then drop reads shorter than 50 bases, and report how many survive and their mean length.









Keep the bases before the cut: subtract 1.


fq <- readLines("data/pl7_reads.fastq")
reads <- fq[seq(2, length(fq), 4)]; qual <- fq[seq(4, length(fq), 4)]
keep_len <- mapply(function(r, q) {
  qs <- utf8ToInt(q) - 33
  cut_q <- which(qs < 20)[1]; if (is.na(cut_q)) cut_q <- nchar(r) + 1
  cut_a <- regexpr("AGATCGGAAGAGC", r, fixed = TRUE); if (cut_a < 0) cut_a <- nchar(r) + 1
  min(cut_q, cut_a) - 1
}, reads, qual)
c(surviving = sum(keep_len >= 50), mean_length = mean(keep_len[keep_len >= 50]))
376 reads survive, with a mean length of 149.5 bases: most good reads never drop below Q20, so they’re kept whole; the adapter reads are cut back to about 110 bases, and the 24 poor reads mostly fall below 50 bases at their first bad base and are dropped. Real pipelines (Trimmomatic, cutadapt, fastp) do the same with more care.




Challenge 2 · A gentler trimmer. Cutting at the first base below Q20 throws away a lot of good sequence after a single bad base. In RStudio, write a sliding-window trimmer instead (cut where the mean quality of 4 consecutive bases drops below 20, as Trimmomatic does), and compare the surviving bases.

title: Biological databases and file formats
text:
Quick quiz

1. Which database holds experimentally determined protein structures?

GenBank
UniProt
The PDB


UniProt holds sequences and functions; AlphaFold DB holds predicted structures.



2. A GenBank location complement(1101..1859) means:

Positions 1,101 to 1,859 are missing
The feature is on the reverse strand, between those positions
The gene is 1,859 bases long


Read the region, then reverse-complement it.



3. A Phred score of 30 means an error probability of:

1 in 30
1 in 100
1 in 1,000


10^{-30/10}.



4. How is a Phred score stored in a FASTQ file?

As a number after each base
As the character with ASCII code Q + 33
In a separate file


One character per base, on the fourth line of each record.



5. Adapter sequence appears in a read when:

The sequencer makes an error
The DNA fragment is shorter than the read, so the sequencer reads into the adapter
The read is from the other strand


It must be trimmed before the read is used.



6. Biological coordinates are usually:

1-based and inclusive at both ends
0-based and half-open
Counted from the end


A frequent source of off-by-one errors when mixing tools.

title: Biological databases and file formats
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve read biology’s file formats. Here’s what you’ve learned:

The databases: GenBank for nucleotide sequences, UniProt for proteins, the PDB for structures, Ensembl for genomes, GEO for expression data; records have versioned accession numbers.
GenBank records: a header, a feature table with locations and qualifiers, and the sequence; the kred CDS is at complement(1101..1859), and its /translation matches Lesson 1’s.
Biostrings reads FASTA into DNAStringSet objects.
FASTQ stores reads with Phred qualities, Q = -10\log_{10}P, as characters with ASCII code Q + 33; quality falls along the read, 6% of the reads were poor, and a few had adapter sequence.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download pl7_fragment.gb and pl7_reads.fastq into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install Biostrings with BiocManager::install("Biostrings").

A real record. Install rentrez and download a real GenBank record, for example entrez_fetch(db = "nuccore", id = "NC_000913.3", rettype = "gb") (the E. coli K-12 genome; it’s big, so try a gene record instead). Parse its features with your code from this lesson.
Biostrings for FASTQ. readQualityScaledDNAStringSet("pl7_reads.fastq") reads the reads with their qualities. Use as(quality(x), "matrix") to get the score matrix, and compare it with yours.
Map the reads. Use matchPattern() (Lesson 3) to find where the first 20 bases of each good read occur in the fragment, on either strand. How evenly do the reads cover the fragment?
UniProt. Look up a real short-chain dehydrogenase on uniprot.org, for example by searching for “short-chain dehydrogenase Rhodococcus”, and read its entry: function, catalytic activity, sequence and structure links.










NoteKey words from this lesson






GenBank, RefSeq, UniProt, PDB, Ensembl, GEO

The main public databases for nucleotide sequences, curated references, proteins, structures, genomes and expression data.

Accession number

A database record’s stable identifier, with a version number after the dot.

Feature table

The part of a GenBank record listing annotated regions with their locations and qualifiers.

FASTA

A text format for sequences: a > header line, then the sequence.

FASTQ

A text format for sequencing reads: name, bases, +, and a quality string.

Phred quality score

Q = -10\log_{10} P(\text{error}) for a base call.

Adapter

A synthetic sequence attached to DNA fragments for sequencing, which appears in reads longer than their fragment.

Bioconductor, Biostrings

The project of R packages for genomics, and its core package for biological sequences.











NoteWant to read more?






Susan Holmes and Wolfgang Huber, Modern Statistics for Modern Biology (free online), chapter 2, with Biostrings examples.
The Bioconductor website, whose Biostrings vignettes cover reading, writing and manipulating sequences.
The NCBI’s “GenBank sample record” page, which explains every field of a GenBank record.

title: Pairwise alignment I: global alignment
text:
Module 10 · Lesson 4 of 13 Week 150 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Amaya’s group has found 24 enzymes in public databases that look like relatives of PL-7’s ketoreductase. Their first question is always the same: how similar is each one to ours, and which residues correspond? Sequences of related proteins differ by substitutions, and also by insertions and deletions (indels), so comparing them position by position doesn’t work: a single extra residue shifts everything after it. An alignment puts the two sequences in rows, with gaps where one has residues the other lacks, so that corresponding residues share a column.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Pairwise alignment I: global alignment
text:
Dot plots
A dot plot puts one sequence along each axis and marks a dot wherever the two have the same letter. Identical stretches show as diagonal lines; an insertion shifts the line sideways; a repeat shows as parallel lines. Noise is reduced with a window: put a dot only where, say, at least 3 of the 5 letters in a window match.
kred_family.fasta has the 25 family members; the first is PL7_KRED. The setup code reads them.












Your turn. Make a windowed dot plot of the first 80 residues of PL7_KRED and SDR_01: a dot where at least 3 of 5 residues match along the diagonal. Count the dots, and the dots on the main diagonal.









At least 3 matches in the window of 5.


a <- strsplit(as.character(subseq(fam[[1]], 1, 80)), "")[[1]]
b <- strsplit(as.character(subseq(fam[[2]], 1, 80)), "")[[1]]
match <- outer(a, b, "==")                                  # 80 x 80 TRUE/FALSE
w <- 5
dots <- matrix(FALSE, 76, 76)
for (i in 1:76) for (j in 1:76) dots[i, j] <- sum(match[cbind(i:(i + 4), j:(j + 4))]) >= 3
c(dots = sum(dots), on_diagonal = sum(diag(dots)))
53 dots, 52 of them on the main diagonal: over its first 80 residues, SDR_01 lines up with PL7_KRED without any shift, and there’s only one chance dot off the diagonal. The full plot below shows the diagonal running through the whole length, with small sideways steps where one of the sequences has an insertion.

title: Pairwise alignment I: global alignment
text:
Scoring an alignment
To choose between alignments, give each a score: add a reward for each column with two identical residues (a match), a penalty for each mismatch, and a penalty for each gap. With DNA, a common simple scheme is match +1, mismatch -1, gap -1 (this lesson’s) or -2. Higher is better, and the best alignment is the one with the highest score.
Your turn. Score this alignment of GATTACA and GCATGCT with match +1, mismatch -1 and gap -1:
G-ATTACA
GCAT-GCT









A mismatch scores -1.


top <- strsplit("G-ATTACA", "")[[1]]
bot <- strsplit("GCAT-GCT", "")[[1]]
gap <- top == "-" | bot == "-"
sum(ifelse(gap, -1, ifelse(top == bot, 1, -1)))
A score of 0. Column by column: G/G match, -/C gap, A/A match, T/T match, T/- gap, A/G mismatch, C/C match, A/T mismatch: 4 matches, 2 mismatches and 2 gaps, 4 - 2 - 2 = 0. Is that the best possible? Checking every alignment is hopeless, as the challenge shows; the next section finds the best one directly.

title: Pairwise alignment I: global alignment
text:
Needleman-Wunsch: dynamic programming
How do we find the best alignment? Saul Needleman and Christian Wunsch (1970) used dynamic programming. Let F(i, j) be the best score for aligning the first i letters of x with the first j letters of y. The last column of that best alignment is one of three things: x_i against y_j, x_i against a gap, or a gap against y_j. So

F(i, j) = \max\begin{cases}
F(i-1, j-1) + s(x_i, y_j)\\
F(i-1, j) + g\\
F(i, j-1) + g
\end{cases}

with s the match/mismatch score and g the gap score (negative), starting from F(0, 0) = 0, F(i, 0) = ig and F(0, j) = jg (aligning a prefix against nothing at all). Fill the table row by row; F(n, m) is the best score; tracing back the choices gives the alignment. The work is proportional to nm, not to the astronomical number of alignments.
Your turn. Set up the (n+1) \times (m+1) matrix for x = GATTACA and y = GCATGCT, and fill its first row and column.









The first row is j \times g too.


x <- strsplit("GATTACA", "")[[1]]; y <- strsplit("GCATGCT", "")[[1]]
g <- -1
F <- matrix(NA, length(x) + 1, length(y) + 1, dimnames = list(c("", x), c("", y)))
F[, 1] <- (0:length(x)) * g
F[1, ] <- (0:length(y)) * g
F
An 8 × 8 matrix whose first column runs 0, -1, …, -7 (aligning GATTACA’s first i letters against nothing costs i gaps) and first row likewise, with everything else still to fill.




Your turn. Fill in the rest with the recurrence, and read off the best score.









Every gap costs g.


x <- strsplit("GATTACA", "")[[1]]; y <- strsplit("GCATGCT", "")[[1]]
g <- -1; s <- function(a, b) ifelse(a == b, 1, -1)
F <- matrix(NA, length(x) + 1, length(y) + 1, dimnames = list(c("", x), c("", y)))
F[, 1] <- (0:length(x)) * g; F[1, ] <- (0:length(y)) * g
for (i in 2:(length(x) + 1)) for (j in 2:(length(y) + 1)) {
  F[i, j] <- max(F[i - 1, j - 1] + s(x[i - 1], y[j - 1]),       # diagonal: align x and y
                 F[i - 1, j] + g,                               # up: x against a gap
                 F[i, j - 1] + g)                               # left: y against a gap
}
print(F)
F[length(x) + 1, length(y) + 1]
The bottom-right cell is 0: the best global alignment of GATTACA and GCATGCT scores 0, so the alignment you scored above is one of the best. Each cell was computed once from three neighbours: 49 cells, instead of examining millions of alignments.




Your turn. Trace back from the bottom-right cell: at each step, move to the neighbour that produced the cell’s value (preferring the diagonal), and build the alignment from the end.









A left move uses one letter of y: j - 1.


x <- strsplit("GATTACA", "")[[1]]; y <- strsplit("GCATGCT", "")[[1]]
g <- -1; s <- function(a, b) ifelse(a == b, 1, -1)
F <- matrix(NA, length(x) + 1, length(y) + 1)
F[, 1] <- (0:length(x)) * g; F[1, ] <- (0:length(y)) * g
for (i in 2:(length(x) + 1)) for (j in 2:(length(y) + 1))
  F[i, j] <- max(F[i - 1, j - 1] + s(x[i - 1], y[j - 1]), F[i - 1, j] + g, F[i, j - 1] + g)
i <- length(x) + 1; j <- length(y) + 1; top <- bot <- character(0)
while (i > 1 || j > 1) {
  if (i > 1 && j > 1 && F[i, j] == F[i - 1, j - 1] + s(x[i - 1], y[j - 1])) {
    top <- c(x[i - 1], top); bot <- c(y[j - 1], bot); i <- i - 1; j <- j - 1
  } else if (i > 1 && F[i, j] == F[i - 1, j] + g) {
    top <- c(x[i - 1], top); bot <- c("-", bot); i <- i - 1
  } else {
    top <- c("-", top); bot <- c(y[j - 1], bot); j <- j - 1
  }
}
c(paste(top, collapse = ""), paste(bot, collapse = ""))
G-ATTACA over GCA-TGCT: a different alignment from the one you scored (G-ATTACA over GCAT-GCT), with the same score of 0. There are often several optimal alignments, and which one the traceback returns depends on how ties are broken (here, the diagonal first, then up).

title: Pairwise alignment I: global alignment
text:
With pwalign
Your turn. Do the same with pwalign::pairwiseAlignment(). Its gap penalty for a gap of length k is gapOpening + k \times gapExtension, so a linear gap of 1 per position is gapOpening = 0, gapExtension = 1.









One per gap position.


sm <- nucleotideSubstitutionMatrix(match = 1, mismatch = -1)
al <- pairwiseAlignment(DNAString("GATTACA"), DNAString("GCATGCT"), type = "global",
                        substitutionMatrix = sm, gapOpening = 0, gapExtension = 1)
print(al)
score(al)
A score of 0, the same as yours, and pwalign’s alignment is G-ATTACA over GCATG-CT, a third optimal one. The score is what’s guaranteed; the alignment is one of the best.

title: Pairwise alignment I: global alignment
text:
Aligning two enzymes
For proteins, matches and mismatches aren’t all equal: replacing leucine with isoleucine (both hydrophobic, similar size) is common in evolution and rarely harmful, while replacing it with aspartate is rare. A substitution matrix gives each pair of amino acids a score from how often they replace each other in real alignments; Lesson 5 explains where BLOSUM62, the standard one, comes from. Gaps are scored affinely: a larger penalty to open a gap, a smaller one to extend it, because a single indel event often inserts or deletes several residues at once.
Your turn. Align PL7_KRED globally with SDR_01, using BLOSUM62, a gap-opening penalty of 10 and an extension penalty of 1, and compute the percentage identity with pid().









The matrix is "BLOSUM62".


al <- pairwiseAlignment(fam[[1]], fam[[2]], type = "global", substitutionMatrix = "BLOSUM62",
                        gapOpening = 10, gapExtension = 1)
c(score = score(al), identity = pid(al), gaps = nindel(al)@insertion[1] + nindel(al)@deletion[1])
A score of 757, 60.6% identity and 2 gap events: SDR_01 is a close relative. pid() counts identical columns as a percentage of the aligned columns, including gaps inside the alignment (there are several conventions; pid(al, "PID2") and others give the alternatives). Lesson 6 puts scores like 757 on a probability scale.




Your turn. The gap penalties change the alignment. Align PL7_KRED with SDR_01 with gap-opening penalties of 2, 10 and 25, and count the gap events.









The third opening penalty is 25.


sapply(c(open2 = 2, open10 = 10, open25 = 25), function(o) {
  al <- pairwiseAlignment(fam[[1]], fam[[2]], type = "global", substitutionMatrix = "BLOSUM62", gapOpening = o, gapExtension = 1)
  c(gap_events = nindel(al)@insertion[1] + nindel(al)@deletion[1], identity = pid(al))
})
With a cheap gap opening (2), the alignment uses 7 gap events to squeeze in a few more identities (61.3%); with 10, 2 gap events (60.6%); with 25, a single one (59.8%). Cheap gaps over-fit, opening gaps to line up residues that match by chance; expensive gaps miss real indels. For proteins with BLOSUM62, gap-opening penalties of 10 to 11 and extensions of 1 are the usual compromise.










NoteGo deeper: affine gaps in three matrices, and linear space





With affine gaps, the recurrence needs three matrices (Gotoh, 1982): M(i, j) for alignments ending in a match column, I_x(i, j) for those ending with a gap in y, and I_y(i, j) for those ending with a gap in x. A gap is opened from M (paying open plus extend) and extended within I_x or I_y (paying extend only). The work is still O(nm). Memory is O(nm) too, which is a problem for long sequences (two bacterial genomes would need 10^{13} cells), but Hirschberg’s algorithm (1975) finds the same alignment in linear memory by divide and conquer, computing the middle row’s scores from both ends. Richard Durbin, Sean Eddy, Anders Krogh and Graeme Mitchison, Biological Sequence Analysis (Cambridge, 1998), chapter 2, is the classic account.

title: Pairwise alignment I: global alignment
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · How many alignments? The number of global alignments of two sequences of lengths n and m satisfies N(i, j) = N(i-1, j-1) + N(i-1, j) + N(i, j-1), with N(i, 0) = N(0, j) = 1 (the Delannoy numbers). Compute it for two sequences of 10 and of 250 letters.









The third term is the left neighbour: j - 1.


count_alignments <- function(n) {
  N <- matrix(1, n + 1, n + 1)
  for (i in 2:(n + 1)) for (j in 2:(n + 1)) N[i, j] <- N[i - 1, j - 1] + N[i - 1, j] + N[i, j - 1]
  N[n + 1, n + 1]
}
c(n10 = count_alignments(10), log10_n250 = log10(count_alignments(250)))
8,097,453 alignments for two sequences of 10 letters, and about 10^{190} for two of 250, far more than the roughly 10^{80} atoms in the observable universe. The Needleman-Wunsch table for 250 × 250 has 62,500 cells.




Challenge 2 · End gaps. A global alignment penalizes gaps at the ends, which is wrong when one sequence is a fragment of the other (a read and a gene). Align the first 100 residues of SDR_01 to the whole of PL7_KRED globally and with type = "global-local" (the second sequence’s ends are free), and compare the scores.









The type is "global-local".


piece <- subseq(fam[[2]], 1, 100)
sapply(c("global", "global-local"), function(ty)
  score(pairwiseAlignment(piece, fam[[1]], type = ty, substitutionMatrix = "BLOSUM62", gapOpening = 10, gapExtension = 1)))
131 globally against 293 with free end gaps. The global alignment has to pay for PL7_KRED’s other 150 residues as gaps; the global-local alignment fits the 100 residues where they belong, and leaves the rest unaligned at no cost.

title: Pairwise alignment I: global alignment
text:
Quick quiz

1. In a dot plot of two related sequences, an insertion in one appears as:

A gap in the diagonal with no shift
A sideways shift of the diagonal line
A second parallel line


Parallel lines indicate repeats.



2. F(i, j) in the Needleman-Wunsch matrix is:

The score of aligning x_i with y_j
The best score for aligning the first i letters of x with the first j letters of y
The number of alignments


That’s the subproblem that dynamic programming solves.



3. Why is dynamic programming necessary?

It gives higher scores
There are astronomically many alignments, but only nm subproblems
It aligns more than two sequences


Two sequences of 250 letters have over 10^{190} alignments.



4. What does the traceback do?

Computes the score
Recovers the alignment by following the choices back from the final cell
Fills the first row


Ties give several optimal alignments.



5. With affine gap penalties, a gap of length 5 costs:

5 times the opening penalty
The opening penalty plus 5 times the extension penalty
The same as a gap of length 1


In pwalign’s convention: gapOpening + k * gapExtension.



6. When should end gaps be free?

Never
When one sequence may be a fragment of the other
Always, for proteins


Semi-global (“global-local”, “overlap”) alignment.

title: Pairwise alignment I: global alignment
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve aligned sequences optimally. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Dot plots show similarity as diagonals, shifted by indels.
An alignment’s score adds match rewards and mismatch and gap penalties.
Needleman-Wunsch finds the best global alignment by dynamic programming in O(nm); the traceback recovers it. GATTACA and GCATGCT’s best score is 0.
pwalign does the same, with substitution matrices and affine gaps; PL7_KRED and SDR_01 are 61% identical.
The number of alignments is astronomical (8 million for two sequences of 10), which is why the algorithm matters.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download kred_family.fasta into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install pwalign with BiocManager::install("pwalign").

All against all. Align PL7_KRED with all 24 relatives and plot the percentage identity against the alignment score. Is the relation straight?
Gotoh by hand. Extend your Needleman-Wunsch code to affine gaps with three matrices, and check it against pwalign on two short proteins.
A dot plot function. Write a function that draws a windowed dot plot with ggplot2 for any two sequences, window and threshold. Try a sequence against itself, and against its reverse.
Timing. Time your R implementation against pwalign for sequences of 100, 200 and 400 letters. How do both scale?










NoteKey words from this lesson






Alignment

An arrangement of two (or more) sequences in rows, with gaps, so that corresponding letters share columns.

Dot plot

A plot with one sequence on each axis and a dot wherever they match (in a window).

Indel

An insertion or a deletion, shown as a gap in an alignment.

Global alignment

An alignment of the whole of both sequences, end to end.

Dynamic programming

Solving a problem by combining the solutions of overlapping subproblems, stored in a table.

Needleman-Wunsch algorithm

The dynamic programming algorithm for optimal global alignment.

Traceback

Following the choices back through the matrix to recover the optimal alignment.

Substitution matrix

Scores for aligning each pair of letters, such as BLOSUM62 for amino acids.

Affine gap penalty

A gap cost of an opening penalty plus an extension penalty per position.











NoteWant to read more?






Richard Durbin, Sean Eddy, Anders Krogh and Graeme Mitchison, Biological Sequence Analysis (Cambridge, 1998), chapter 2, on pairwise alignment. The standard text for Lessons 4 to 7 and 10.
Saul Needleman and Christian Wunsch, “A general method applicable to the search for similarities in the amino acid sequence of two proteins”, Journal of Molecular Biology 48, 1970, pages 443 to 453.
Phillip Compeau and Pavel Pevzner, Bioinformatics Algorithms (3rd edition, 2018), chapter 5, “How Do We Compare Biological Sequences?”, which builds dynamic programming from the “Manhattan tourist” problem.

title: Database searching
text:
Module 10 · Lesson 6 of 13 Week 152 of 160 About 5–7 hours
When Amaya’s group sequenced PL-7, the first thing they did with every gene was a database search: compare its protein with every protein known, and list the ones that look related. Relatives with known functions tell you what a new protein probably does. The search tool of choice since 1990 is BLAST (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool), run millions of times a day against databases of hundreds of millions of proteins.
Here, the database is a small one: 600 proteins, among which are PL-7’s enzyme’s relatives. It’s small enough to align the query with every entry by Smith-Waterman, which is what BLAST approximates, so you can see both the shortcut and the exact answer.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Database searching
text:
The database
protein_db.fasta has 600 proteins, each with a header like a real database’s: an identifier, a description and the organism. The setup code reads it and the query (PL7_KRED), and aligns the query with every entry, scores only, in one vectorized call (it takes well under a second).












Your turn. Count the entries and residues, and look at the lengths.









The lengths are width(db).


print(head(names(db), 3))
c(entries = length(db), residues = sum(width(db)), shortest = min(width(db)), longest = max(width(db)))
600 entries, 171,888 residues, from 120 to 450 residues long. Real databases are a million times larger (UniProt holds about 250 million proteins), which is why search speed matters.

title: Database searching
text:
BLAST’s shortcut: words
Aligning a query with every protein in a database of hundreds of millions takes too long. BLAST (Altschul and others, 1990) exploits the fact that a real alignment almost always contains a short stretch of high similarity. It breaks the query into words of 3 amino acids, and for each word builds its neighbourhood: all 8,000 three-letter words that score at least a threshold T (11, with BLOSUM62) against it. Database sequences containing a neighbourhood word are seeds, extended into alignments; everything else is skipped.
Your turn. For the query word TGA (from the TGxxxGxG motif), find all three-letter words with a BLOSUM62 score of at least 11.









The threshold is 11.


data(BLOSUM62, package = "pwalign")
aa <- c("A", "R", "N", "D", "C", "Q", "E", "G", "H", "I", "L", "K", "M", "F", "P", "S", "T", "W", "Y", "V")
w <- c("T", "G", "A")
all3 <- expand.grid(a = aa, b = aa, c = aa, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)       # 8,000 words
s3 <- BLOSUM62[w[1], all3$a] + BLOSUM62[w[2], all3$b] + BLOSUM62[w[3], all3$c]
nb <- paste0(all3$a, all3$b, all3$c)[s3 >= 11]
c(score_of_itself = sum(diag(BLOSUM62[w, w])), neighbourhood = length(nb), examples = paste(head(nb, 5), collapse = " "))
TGA scores 15 against itself (5 + 6 + 4), and its neighbourhood at T = 11 has 7 words, including SGA, TGC, TGG and TGS: one conservative change is allowed, mostly at the first or third position, because the glycine’s score of 6 is hard to make up elsewhere. A typical query word has a few dozen neighbours; the threshold trades sensitivity (more seeds) against speed (more extensions).




Your turn. A simpler filter: count, for every database entry, how many of the query’s distinct 3-letter words it contains exactly, and compare the family members (identifiers starting with PL7, SDR or RMT) with the rest.









Count the entry’s words found among the query’s words, qw.


words_of <- function(s) { s <- as.character(s); unique(substring(s, 1:(nchar(s) - 2), 3:nchar(s))) }
qw <- words_of(query)
shared <- sapply(seq_along(db), function(i) sum(words_of(db[[i]]) %in% qw))
family <- grepl("^(PL7|SDR|RMT)", names(db))
rbind(family = summary(shared[family]), others = summary(shared[!family]))
Family members share a median of 43 of the query’s words (from 17 up to all 243 of the query itself); unrelated entries share a median of 12 and at most 32. Exact 3-letter words are a crude test, but they already separate most relatives from the rest.




Your turn. Use the shared-word count as a filter: keep only entries sharing at least 25 of the query’s words. How many entries pass, and how many of the 29 family members?









At least 25 shared words.


words_of <- function(s) { s <- as.character(s); unique(substring(s, 1:(nchar(s) - 2), 3:nchar(s))) }
qw <- words_of(query)
shared <- sapply(seq_along(db), function(i) sum(words_of(db[[i]]) %in% qw))
family <- grepl("^(PL7|SDR|RMT)", names(db))
keep <- shared >= 25
c(passed = sum(keep), family_kept = sum(keep & family), family_total = sum(family), others_kept = sum(keep & !family))
35 entries pass: 25 of the 29 family members and 10 unrelated ones. Aligning 35 entries instead of 600 is 17 times less work, but 4 relatives were lost. That’s the trade-off every heuristic makes, and BLAST’s neighbourhood words and two-hit seeds are a far better filter than shared exact words.

title: Database searching
section: The exact search, and its statistics
text:
The exact search, and its statistics
Your turn. The setup aligned the query with all 600 entries. Look at the score distribution: the top ten, and the bulk.









Add the 99th percentile, 0.99.


top <- order(sc, decreasing = TRUE)[1:10]
print(data.frame(score = sc[top], entry = substr(names(db)[top], 1, 60)))
quantile(sc, c(0.5, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99))
The query finds itself (1,333), then 9 family members with scores of 634 to 892. The median of all 600 scores is 31, the 95th percentile 49, but the 99th percentile jumps to 750: the top 5% includes the family, which is completely separated from the bulk.




Most entries are unrelated to the query, so their scores are the null distribution, and BLAST-like programs estimate it from the search itself. Your turn. Fit a Gumbel distribution by the method of moments to the scores below 100 (the clearly unrelated bulk), and compute every entry’s E-value, E = N \times P(S \ge s), with N = 600.









Below 100.


bulk <- sc[sc < 100]
lambda <- pi / (sd(bulk) * sqrt(6)); mu <- mean(bulk) - 0.5772 / lambda
log10_p <- ifelse(sc < 150, log10(1 - exp(-exp(-lambda * (sc - mu)))), -lambda * (sc - mu) / log(10))
log10_E <- log10(length(db)) + log10_p
c(n_bulk = length(bulk), lambda = lambda, mu = mu, log10_E_top = max(-log10_E) * -1)
572 scores below 100 make up the bulk. The fitted Gumbel has \lambda = 0.256 and \mu = 29.4, close to Lesson 5’s fit from shuffles (0.248 and 29.9). The best hit (the query itself) has E = 10^{-142}. The code uses the exact formula for moderate scores and the tail approximation e^{-\lambda(x-\mu)} for large ones, where the exact one rounds to 0.













Your turn. List the significant hits, at E < 0.001, and check what they are.









E below 0.001.


bulk <- sc[sc < 100]
lambda <- pi / (sd(bulk) * sqrt(6)); mu <- mean(bulk) - 0.5772 / lambda
log10_p <- ifelse(sc < 150, log10(1 - exp(-exp(-lambda * (sc - mu)))), -lambda * (sc - mu) / log(10))
log10_E <- log10(length(db)) + log10_p
hits <- which(log10_E < log10(0.001))
table(substr(names(db)[hits], 1, 3))
28 significant hits: the query itself, 24 SDR family members and 3 of the remote relatives, RMT_01 to RMT_03. No unrelated protein reaches E < 0.001; the score needed is about 80, and the best unrelated entry scored 54.




Your turn. For the hits, compute the percentage identity of their local alignments, and find the least similar significant hit.









pid(al).


hit_ids <- which(sc > 100)
al <- pairwiseAlignment(db[hit_ids], query, type = "local", substitutionMatrix = "BLOSUM62", gapOpening = 10, gapExtension = 1)
res <- data.frame(entry = substr(names(db)[hit_ids], 1, 7), score = score(al), identity = round(pid(al), 1))
res <- res[order(res$identity), ]
head(res, 4)
The least similar significant hit, RMT_03, shares only 27.4% of the residues in its local alignment (score 127), followed by RMT_02 at 31.6% and SDR_05 at 36.5%. That’s the twilight zone, around 20 to 30% identity, where unrelated proteins can also align with similar identities over short stretches, and only the score’s significance (which accounts for the alignment’s length) can tell them apart.




Your turn. The database contains a fourth remote relative, RMT_04, a true member of the family that diverged a very long time ago. Find its score and E-value.









Search for "RMT_04".


bulk <- sc[sc < 100]
lambda <- pi / (sd(bulk) * sqrt(6)); mu <- mean(bulk) - 0.5772 / lambda
i <- grep("^RMT_04", names(db))
p <- 1 - exp(-exp(-lambda * (sc[i] - mu)))
c(score = sc[i], rank = rank(-sc)[i], E = length(db) * p)
A score of 33, ranked 218th of 600, with an E-value of 198: indistinguishable from unrelated proteins. RMT_04 has the same fold and function as PL7_KRED (it’s simulated from the same ancestor), but after so many substitutions, its sequence carries no detectable trace of the relationship. Structural comparison (Lesson 11) or profile methods (the box below) can sometimes still find such relatives.










NoteGo deeper: what BLAST adds, and PSI-BLAST and profile HMMs





Real BLAST adds several refinements: the two-hit method (extend only when two seeds lie on the same diagonal within 40 residues, which cuts extensions tenfold), X-drop extension (stop extending when the score falls too far below its maximum), gapped extension only for the best ungapped hits, low-complexity filtering (to stop repeats like QQQQQQ from matching everything), and compositional adjustment of the scores. Its E-values use \lambda and K precomputed for each scoring system, with corrections for the edges of the sequences. To reach further into the twilight zone, PSI-BLAST iterates: it builds a position-specific scoring matrix from the first round’s hits and searches again with it; HMMER searches with profile hidden Markov models (Lessons 7 and 10) built from whole family alignments, and finds relatives that pairwise search misses. Stephen Altschul and others, “Gapped BLAST and PSI-BLAST: a new generation of protein database search programs”, Nucleic Acids Research 25, 1997, pages 3389 to 3402.

title: Database searching
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Annotation transfer. Most database descriptions are themselves predicted by similarity, so errors spread. Tabulate the descriptions of all entries with E < 0.001, then of those between rank 30 and 40 (the best non-significant hits). Would you trust a description transferred from those?









Ranks 30 to 40: ord[30:40].


desc <- sub("^\\S+ ", "", sub(" \\[.*$", "", names(db)))
ord <- order(sc, decreasing = TRUE)
list(significant = table(desc[ord[1:28]]), next_ten = table(desc[ord[30:40]]))
All 28 significant hits are described as short-chain dehydrogenases or reductases. The next eleven, just below significance, have eleven different descriptions (methyltransferases, regulators, transporters, …): nothing to transfer. In a real database, a hit’s description is only as good as its own evidence, and the chain of transfers behind it.




Challenge 2 · Real BLAST. In a web browser, paste PL7_KRED’s sequence (from kred_family.fasta) into NCBI’s protein BLAST and search the “nr” database. The sequence is fictional, but it was built to look like a short-chain dehydrogenase: does BLAST find real SDRs? What are their E-values and identities, and which conserved domain does it report?

title: Database searching
text:
Quick quiz

1. Why doesn’t BLAST align the query with every database sequence?

It would give wrong answers
It would be too slow; word seeds pick the few sequences worth aligning
Databases don’t allow it


Smith-Waterman on every entry is exact, but too slow for hundreds of millions of sequences.



2. A word’s neighbourhood is:

The words next to it in the query
All words that score at least T against it
The database sequences containing it


Seeds can be similar words, not only identical ones.



3. Where does a database search’s null distribution come from?

Largely from the scores of the many unrelated entries (or from simulation)
From the best hit
From the query’s composition only


Most of a database is unrelated to any given query.



4. The same alignment gives E = 0.0001 in a small database and E = 10 in a large one. Why?

The alignment changed
The E-value counts the chance hits expected in a search of that size
Large databases use different matrices


More comparisons, more chance high scores.



5. RMT_04 is a true relative but scored like random proteins. What does that show?

It isn’t a relative
Sequence similarity can decay below detection, beyond the “twilight zone”
The E-value is wrong


Profile methods and structure comparison reach further.



6. Why can transferring a function from a database hit be risky?

Hits are always wrong
Many descriptions were themselves transferred by similarity, so errors propagate, especially from weak hits
Functions can’t be transferred


Prefer hits with experimental evidence, such as Swiss-Prot entries.

title: Database searching
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve searched a database like BLAST. Here’s what you’ve learned:

The database: 600 proteins, 171,888 residues.
BLAST’s shortcut: 3-letter words and their neighbourhoods as seeds; even a crude shared-word filter keeps the family and drops most of the rest.
The exact search: Smith-Waterman against every entry; the unrelated bulk gives the Gumbel null; E-values = N \times P.
The hits: 28 significant hits, all family members, down to about 30% identity.
The limit: RMT_04, a true but very distant relative, scores like noise: sequence search has a horizon.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download protein_db.fasta and kred_family.fasta into your project’s data-raw/ folder.

Sensitivity and specificity. For score thresholds from 40 to 200, count the family members found and the unrelated entries passing. Draw the ROC curve (Module 7).
The filter’s trade-off. Vary the shared-word threshold from 5 to 60, and plot the share of entries that must be aligned against the share of family members kept.
Search with another member. Use SDR_24 as the query. Does it find RMT_04? What about the family members closest to PL7_KRED?
BLAST+ locally. Install NCBI’s BLAST+ command-line tools, make a database with makeblastdb -in protein_db.fasta -dbtype prot, and search it with blastp. Compare its E-values with yours.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Database search

Comparing a query sequence with every entry of a database to find similar sequences.

BLAST

The Basic Local Alignment Search Tool: a heuristic local alignment search with word seeds and E-values.

Word, neighbourhood, seed

A short substring of the query; the words scoring at least T against it; a database position matching a neighbourhood word.

Hit list

The database entries ranked by score or E-value.

E-value

The expected number of chance hits at least as good, in a search of this size.

Twilight zone

Sequence identities of about 20 to 30%, where alignment can no longer reliably distinguish relatives from chance.

Annotation transfer

Assigning a function to a new protein from its database hits.











NoteWant to read more?






Stephen Altschul, Warren Gish, Webb Miller, Eugene Myers and David Lipman, “Basic local alignment search tool”, Journal of Molecular Biology 215, 1990, pages 403 to 410, one of the most cited papers in all of science.
Richard Durbin and others, Biological Sequence Analysis (Cambridge, 1998), chapter 2, section 2.5, on fast heuristic search.
The NCBI’s BLAST help pages, with a clear explanation of E-values, bit scores and the program’s options.

title: Phylogenetic trees I
text:
Module 10 · Lesson 8 of 13 Week 154 of 160 About 5–7 hours
The plant’s wastewater treatment unit runs on bacteria: they eat the organic waste, turn ammonia into nitrate and then into nitrogen gas, and store phosphate. Its operators care which bacteria are there, because a change in the community warns of trouble before the effluent does. Hana’s colleagues sequenced the 16S ribosomal RNA gene of 14 bacteria isolated from the bioreactor, PL-7 among them. The 16S gene is in every bacterium, changes slowly, and is the standard ruler of bacterial relationships.
A phylogenetic tree is a hypothesis about how sequences (and the organisms that carry them) descend from common ancestors. This lesson builds trees from distances; Lesson 9 builds them from the characters directly.
In this lesson you’ll:

title: Phylogenetic trees I
text:
Trees and their vocabulary
A tree’s tips (leaves) are the sequences; its internal nodes are inferred ancestors; branch lengths measure change, usually in substitutions per site. A clade is an ancestor and all its descendants. A rooted tree has a node marking the oldest ancestor, so it shows the direction of time; an unrooted tree shows only relationships. Most methods produce unrooted trees, rooted afterwards with an outgroup, a group known to have branched off first.
The ape package stores trees as phylo objects and reads and writes the Newick format, in which a tree is a nested set of parentheses: ((A:0.1,B:0.2):0.05,C:0.3);.
bioreactor_16s.fasta has 1,200 aligned positions of the 14 bacteria’s 16S genes. Because the course’s sequences are simulated, the true tree is known too (bioreactor_true_tree.nwk): a luxury real studies never have, and a way to see which methods work. The setup code reads the alignment.












Your turn. Check the alignment’s dimensions and base composition.









base.freq(s16).


print(s16)
round(base.freq(s16), 3)
14 sequences of 1,200 aligned positions, with 24.7% A, 26.4% C, 28.8% G and 20.1% T: slightly GC-rich, as 16S genes usually are, because their RNA must fold into a stable structure. A DNAbin object stores the bases compactly as bytes.

title: Phylogenetic trees I
text:
Distances
The simplest distance is the p-distance: the share of sites at which two sequences differ. But it underestimates evolution: a site can change twice (A to G and back to A, or A to G to C), and only the net change is visible. Over long times, two random DNA sequences can’t be more than 75% different, however long ago they split.
Your turn. Compute the p-distances, and find the closest and the most distant pairs.









The p-distance is model = "raw".


p <- dist.dna(s16, model = "raw")
m <- as.matrix(p); diag(m) <- NA
c(min = min(m, na.rm = TRUE), max = max(m, na.rm = TRUE), closest = paste(rownames(which(m == min(m, na.rm = TRUE), arr.ind = TRUE)), collapse = " + "))
From 5.9% (Gordonia and Rhodococcus PL-7, close relatives) to 26.8% different. At 27% raw difference, many sites have changed more than once.




The Jukes-Cantor model (1969) assumes every base changes to each other base at the same rate. Under it, the expected number of substitutions per site behind an observed p-distance p is

d_{\text{JC}} = -\tfrac{3}{4}\ln\left(1 - \tfrac{4}{3}p\right),

always larger than p, more so for large p, and infinite at p = 0.75.
Your turn. Correct the largest p-distance by hand, and compare with dist.dna(model = "JC69").









Correct pmax.


p <- as.matrix(dist.dna(s16, model = "raw"))
jc <- as.matrix(dist.dna(s16, model = "JC69"))
pmax <- max(p)
c(p = pmax, jc_by_hand = -3 / 4 * log(1 - 4 / 3 * pmax), jc_ape = max(jc))
The largest p-distance, 0.268, corrects to 0.332 substitutions per site: about a quarter more change than the raw count shows. Your formula and ape agree exactly.




Real DNA isn’t that simple: transitions (A↔︎G, C↔︎T, between bases of the same shape) happen more often than transversions (the other eight changes). The Kimura two-parameter model (K80) allows the two rates to differ.
Your turn. Count the transitions and transversions between every pair of sequences, and compute their overall ratio.









model = "TV".


ts <- dist.dna(s16, model = "TS")                    # number of transitions, per pair
tv <- dist.dna(s16, model = "TV")                    # number of transversions
c(transitions = sum(ts), transversions = sum(tv), ratio = sum(ts) / sum(tv))
12,530 transitions and 8,875 transversions over all pairs: a ratio of 1.41, although there are twice as many kinds of transversion as of transition. Per possible change, transitions are almost three times as frequent; the Kimura model’s ratio \kappa estimates the rate ratio itself, corrected for multiple hits (the simulation used 4).

title: Phylogenetic trees I
text:
Building trees
UPGMA (unweighted pair group method with arithmetic mean) is average-linkage clustering (Module 7): repeatedly join the two closest clusters, and define the distance between clusters as the average of their members’ distances. It produces a rooted tree in which every tip is the same distance from the root, an ultrametric tree. That’s correct only if all lineages evolve at the same rate: the molecular clock.
Neighbour joining (Saitou and Nei, 1987) doesn’t assume a clock. At each step, it joins the pair i, j that minimizes Q(i, j) = (n - 2) d_{ij} - \sum_k d_{ik} - \sum_k d_{jk}, which corrects each distance for how far the two sequences are from everything else, so a fast-evolving sequence isn’t mistaken for a distant one. It produces an unrooted tree, and it’s exact if the distances are exactly additive along some tree.
The Robinson-Foulds distance (dist.topo()) counts the splits (bipartitions of the tips) that are in one tree but not the other: 0 for identical topologies.
Your turn. Build a UPGMA tree from the Kimura distances, check that it’s ultrametric, and compare it with the true tree.









UPGMA is average linkage.


truth <- read.tree("data/bioreactor_true_tree.nwk")
d <- dist.dna(s16, model = "K80")
up <- as.phylo(hclust(d, method = "average"))
c(ultrametric = is.ultrametric(up), rf_to_truth = dist.topo(unroot(up), unroot(truth)))
Ultrametric, as UPGMA trees always are, and 4 splits away from the truth. The plot below shows what went wrong: the two Accumulibacter sequences, which evolve three times faster than the rest, are torn apart. Accumulibacter_B branches off alone near the root, as if it were the most distant organism of all, and Accumulibacter_A sits on its own deep branch. To UPGMA, a long branch looks like an old one.




Your turn. Build neighbour-joining trees from the raw, Jukes-Cantor and Kimura distances, and compare each with the true tree.









The function is nj.


truth <- read.tree("data/bioreactor_true_tree.nwk")
sapply(c("raw", "JC69", "K80"), function(model) {
  tr <- nj(dist.dna(s16, model = model))
  dist.topo(unroot(tr), unroot(truth))
})
With Jukes-Cantor distances, neighbour joining recovers the true tree exactly (distance 0); with raw distances it’s 2 splits off, and with the Kimura distances 2 as well, placing the Accumulibacter pair one node too deep. The internal branch that decides it is short (0.03 substitutions per site), and with 1,200 sites the data can’t pin it down reliably; Lesson 9’s bootstrap measures that uncertainty. Note that the Kimura model, which matches how the data were simulated, didn’t do better here: with this little data, sampling noise can matter more than the model.













Your turn. Root the neighbour-joining tree with the Bacteroidetes outgroup, and check that the outgroup forms a clade.









Use outgroup.


tr <- nj(dist.dna(s16, model = "JC69"))
rooted <- root(tr, outgroup = outgroup, resolve.root = TRUE)
c(rooted = is.rooted(rooted), outgroup_is_a_clade = is.monophyletic(rooted, outgroup))
Rooted, and the three Bacteroidetes form a clade. An outgroup works only if it really did branch off first; here that’s known from many other studies (the Bacteroidetes are far from both the Proteobacteria and the Actinobacteria). is.monophyletic() checks whether a set of tips forms a clade.




Your turn. Is there a molecular clock? In the rooted neighbour-joining tree, compute each tip’s distance from the root, and find the extremes.









Largest first: decreasing = TRUE.


rooted <- root(nj(dist.dna(s16, model = "JC69")), outgroup = outgroup, resolve.root = TRUE)
depth <- node.depth.edgelength(rooted)[1:Ntip(rooted)]       # distance from the root to each tip
names(depth) <- rooted$tip.label
round(sort(depth, decreasing = TRUE), 3)[1:4]
Accumulibacter_B (0.239) and Accumulibacter_A (0.222) are the farthest from the root, followed by the two Nitrospira (0.188 and 0.177). With a molecular clock, all tips would be the same distance from the root; here the Accumulibacter lineage has evolved much faster. (Polyphosphate-accumulating bacteria like Accumulibacter really are under unusual selection in wastewater plants, though the speed-up here is the simulation’s.)




Your turn. How well does each tree represent the data? Compare the distances along each tree (cophenetic()) with the Kimura distances they were built from.









The neighbour-joining tree is nt.


d <- dist.dna(s16, model = "K80")
up <- as.phylo(hclust(d, "average")); nt <- nj(d)
tips <- labels(d)
dd <- as.vector(as.dist(as.matrix(d)[tips, tips]))
c(upgma = cor(dd, as.vector(as.dist(cophenetic(up)[tips, tips]))),
  nj = cor(dd, as.vector(as.dist(cophenetic(nt)[tips, tips]))))
A correlation of 0.930 between the UPGMA tree’s distances and the data, and 0.991 for neighbour joining: NJ’s unequal branch lengths can represent the data, UPGMA’s clock can’t.










NoteGo deeper: why distances need models, and how many trees there are





Distance corrections are models of evolution in disguise. The Jukes-Cantor formula comes from a Markov chain on the four bases (Module 4’s Markov chains) with equal rates: the probability that a site differs after time t is \frac34(1 - e^{-4\alpha t}), and inverting it gives d_{\text{JC}}. Kimura’s adds a transition/transversion ratio; the general time-reversible (GTR) model allows six rates and unequal base frequencies; and gamma-distributed rates across sites (some sites nearly invariant, others fast) matter as much as the substitution model. Under-correcting distances can create long-branch attraction, where fast lineages are wrongly grouped together. As for search: the number of unrooted binary trees of n tips is (2n-5)!! = 3 \times 5 \times 7 \times \dots \times (2n-5), already 2 million for 10 tips and 8 \times 10^{21} for 20, which is why fast algorithms like neighbour joining matter. Joseph Felsenstein’s Inferring Phylogenies (Sinauer, 2004), chapters 3, 11 and 13, is the standard reference.

title: Phylogenetic trees I
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · PL-7’s relatives. In the rooted neighbour-joining tree, find the smallest clade containing Rhodococcus_PL7 and Mycobacterium, and list its members.









The most recent common ancestor of PL-7 and "Mycobacterium".


rooted <- root(nj(dist.dna(s16, model = "JC69")), outgroup = outgroup, resolve.root = TRUE)
node <- getMRCA(rooted, c("Rhodococcus_PL7", "Mycobacterium"))
sort(extract.clade(rooted, node)$tip.label)
Gordonia, Mycobacterium and Rhodococcus PL-7: the three Actinobacteria (Mycobacteriales) form a clade, with PL-7 closest to Gordonia, as the 16S distances suggested. Genus names on sequences are hypotheses too; a 16S tree is how a new isolate’s genus is checked.




Challenge 2 · How many trees? In RStudio, compute (2n - 5)!! for n = 4 to 20 tips, and plot it on a log scale. For 14 tips, how long would it take to evaluate every tree at a million trees per second?

title: Phylogenetic trees I
text:
Quick quiz

1. A clade is:

Any group of tips
An ancestor and all of its descendants
The root of a tree


is.monophyletic() checks whether tips form one.



2. Why is the Jukes-Cantor distance larger than the p-distance?

It counts gaps
It corrects for multiple substitutions at the same site, which the p-distance can’t see
It uses a different alignment


The correction grows with distance.



3. UPGMA assumes:

A molecular clock: all lineages evolve at the same rate
Equal base frequencies
No gaps


That’s why its trees are ultrametric.



4. Why did neighbour joining recover the true tree when UPGMA didn’t?

It uses more data
It doesn’t assume a clock, so the fast-evolving Accumulibacter lineage wasn’t misplaced
It’s a maximum likelihood method


NJ corrects each distance for each sequence’s overall divergence.



5. A Robinson-Foulds distance of 0 means:

The branch lengths are identical
The two trees have the same topology (the same splits)
The trees have no splits


It ignores branch lengths.



6. What does an outgroup do?

Improves the alignment
Roots an unrooted tree, assuming the outgroup branched off first
Removes long branches


A wrong outgroup gives a wrong root.

title: Phylogenetic trees I
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve built your first phylogenies. Here’s what you’ve learned:

Trees: tips, nodes, branches, clades; rooted or unrooted; Newick format.
Distances: p-distances underestimate evolution; the Jukes-Cantor and Kimura corrections account for multiple hits; transitions outnumber transversions 1.4 to 1.
UPGMA assumes a clock and misplaced the fast Accumulibacter lineage (Robinson-Foulds distance 4 from the truth).
Neighbour joining on Jukes-Cantor distances recovered the true topology exactly; rooted with the Bacteroidetes, PL-7 groups with Gordonia and Mycobacterium.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download bioreactor_16s.fasta and bioreactor_true_tree.nwk into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install ape.

Neighbour joining by hand. Implement the Q criterion for one step: compute Q for all pairs of the Kimura distances and find the pair to join first. Is it the same as nj()’s first join?
Gamma rates. dist.dna(..., gamma = 0.5) corrects for rate variation across sites (the simulation used a shape of 0.5). Do the distances and the tree change?
Plot the truth. Plot the true tree next to the NJ tree with cophyloplot() from ape. Where do the branch lengths differ most?
Real 16S. Download a few real 16S sequences from NCBI (for example of Rhodococcus, Gordonia, Nitrosomonas and Escherichia coli), align them with the msa package, and build an NJ tree.










NoteKey words from this lesson






Phylogenetic tree

A branching diagram of descent from common ancestors.

Tip, node, branch, clade

A sequence, an inferred ancestor, the line connecting them, and an ancestor with all its descendants.

Rooted and unrooted trees

Trees with and without a marked oldest ancestor.

Outgroup

Taxa known to have branched off first, used to root a tree.

p-distance

The proportion of differing sites between two sequences.

Jukes-Cantor and Kimura (K80) distances

Distances corrected for multiple substitutions, under equal rates or with a transition/transversion ratio.

UPGMA

Average-linkage clustering, which assumes a molecular clock.

Neighbour joining

A distance method that doesn’t assume a clock.

Robinson-Foulds distance

The number of splits present in one tree but not the other.

Molecular clock

The hypothesis that all lineages evolve at the same rate.











NoteWant to read more?






Joseph Felsenstein, Inferring Phylogenies (Sinauer, 2004), chapters 1 to 3 and 11, on trees, counting trees and distance methods.
Emmanuel Paradis, Analysis of Phylogenetics and Evolution with R (3rd edition, Springer, 2020), chapters 3 to 5, by ape’s author.
Naruya Saitou and Masatoshi Nei, “The neighbor-joining method: a new method for reconstructing phylogenetic trees”, Molecular Biology and Evolution 4, 1987, pages 406 to 425.

title: Hidden Markov models for sequences
text:
Module 10 · Lesson 10 of 13 Week 156 of 160 About 5–7 hours
Genomes aren’t uniform. In vertebrates, most of the genome is poor in the dinucleotide CG, but stretches of a few hundred to a few thousand bases, CpG islands, are rich in C, G and CG, and they mark the starts of many genes. Finding them is a classic problem because their boundaries aren’t marked: the composition shifts gradually, and short random stretches can look island-like. The same problem, with more states, is gene finding: exons, introns and intergenic regions, each with its own statistics.
The tool is the hidden Markov model (HMM): a hidden sequence of states (island or background) that follows a Markov chain (Module 4), each state emitting bases with its own probabilities. We see the bases; we infer the states.
This lesson’s 30,000 bases are a fictional genome segment, simulated with islands at known positions (cpg_islands.csv), so that the methods can be checked against the truth.
In this lesson you’ll:
The setup code reads the sequence (as a vector of letters) and the islands, and builds the true state of every base.
Your turn. Compare the base composition inside and outside the islands.
Your turn. First, the naive approach: call a base “island” if the GC content of the 200 bases around it is above 0.6, and measure the share of bases classified correctly.

title: Hidden Markov models for sequences
text:
The model
An HMM has:

states, here background and island, forming a Markov chain with transition probabilities a_{kl} = P(\text{state } l \text{ next} \mid \text{state } k \text{ now}). A state with stay-probability a_{kk} lasts on average 1/(1 - a_{kk}) bases.
emission probabilities e_k(b): the probability of base b in state k.
start probabilities for the first state.

Your turn. Estimate the parameters from the annotation: the emission probabilities as each state’s base frequencies, and the transition probabilities from the number of switches.









Pair each base’s state with the next one: drop the first, truth[-1].


emis <- prop.table(table(truth, x), 1)
switches <- table(from = truth[-length(truth)], to = truth[-1])
trans <- prop.table(switches, 1)
list(emission = round(emis, 3), transition = trans, mean_island_length = 1 / trans["island", "bg"])
The emission probabilities are the composition table above. The background stays background with probability 0.99970 (a switch every 3,309 bases on average) and an island stays island with probability 0.99898: islands last 977 bases on average. These are maximum likelihood estimates from labelled data; Baum-Welch (the challenge) estimates them without labels.

title: Hidden Markov models for sequences
text:
The Viterbi algorithm
The Viterbi algorithm (1967) finds the single most probable state path, by dynamic programming again (Lesson 4). Let v_k(i) be the probability of the best path for the first i bases ending in state k. Then

v_l(i + 1) = e_l(x_{i+1}) \max_k \big(v_k(i)\,a_{kl}\big),

remembering which k gave the maximum; the best final state, traced back, gives the path. Products of thousands of probabilities underflow, so it’s done with logarithms: products become sums.
Your turn. Run Viterbi by hand on the 18 bases ATATGCGCGCGCGCATAT with a toy model (staying probability 0.9 in both states).









The pointer for position i.


obs <- strsplit("ATATGCGCGCGCGCATAT", "")[[1]]
E <- rbind(bg = c(A = 0.3, C = 0.2, G = 0.2, T = 0.3), island = c(A = 0.15, C = 0.35, G = 0.35, T = 0.15))
A <- matrix(c(0.9, 0.1, 0.1, 0.9), 2, dimnames = list(c("bg", "island"), c("bg", "island")))
v <- matrix(NA, 2, length(obs), dimnames = list(rownames(E), NULL)); back <- v
v[, 1] <- log(0.5) + log(E[, obs[1]])
for (i in 2:length(obs)) for (l in 1:2) {
  cand <- v[, i - 1] + log(A[, l])                             # from each state k into l
  v[l, i] <- log(E[l, obs[i]]) + max(cand); back[l, i] <- which.max(cand)
}
path <- integer(length(obs)); path[length(obs)] <- which.max(v[, length(obs)])
for (i in length(obs):2) path[i - 1] <- back[path[i], i]
paste(c("b", "I")[path], collapse = "")
bbbbIIIIIIIIIIbbbb: background for ATAT, island for the ten bases GCGCGCGCGC, background again for ATAT. Switching state costs \log 0.1 each way instead of \log 0.9 for staying, while each G or C gains \log(0.35/0.20) in the island: ten of them pay for the two switches. With the twelve-base sequence ATATGCGCGCAT, only six GC bases, the best path stays in the background throughout: short GC runs aren’t worth a switch. That’s the transition probabilities doing what the window’s threshold did, but in a principled way.




Your turn. Build the model with the HMM package from the estimated parameters, and decode the whole 30,000 bases with viterbi().









viterbi(h, x).


emis <- prop.table(table(truth, x), 1)
trans <- prop.table(table(truth[-length(truth)], truth[-1]), 1)
h <- initHMM(States = c("bg", "island"), Symbols = c("A", "C", "G", "T"), startProbs = c(0.9, 0.1),
             transProbs = unclass(trans), emissionProbs = unclass(emis))
path <- viterbi(h, x)
c(accuracy = mean(path == truth), island_found = mean(path[truth == "island"] == "island"),
  false_island = mean(path[truth == "bg"] == "island"))
99.66% of bases decoded correctly, 99.4% of island bases found, and 0.28% of background bases called island: better than the window rule on every count, and with no tuning, just the estimated parameters.




Your turn. Turn the decoded path into islands (runs of “island”), and compare their starts with the true islands’.









The runs whose value is "island".


emis <- prop.table(table(truth, x), 1)
trans <- prop.table(table(truth[-length(truth)], truth[-1]), 1)
h <- initHMM(c("bg", "island"), c("A", "C", "G", "T"), c(0.9, 0.1), unclass(trans), unclass(emis))
path <- viterbi(h, x)
r <- rle(path)
ends <- cumsum(r$lengths); starts <- ends - r$lengths + 1
pred_start <- starts[r$values == "island"]
c(n_predicted = length(pred_start), n_true = nrow(isl), mean_start_error = mean(abs(pred_start - isl$start)))
7 predicted islands for 7 true ones, with starts off by 7.4 bases on average. Boundaries are where all methods disagree, because the composition change is gradual on the scale of a few bases.

title: Hidden Markov models for sequences
text:
Forward and posterior
The forward algorithm replaces Viterbi’s maximum by a sum: f_l(i+1) = e_l(x_{i+1}) \sum_k f_k(i)\,a_{kl}, so \sum_k f_k(n) is the probability of the whole sequence under the model, summed over every possible path. To avoid underflow without logarithms of sums, the forward variables are rescaled at each step to sum to 1, and the logs of the scaling factors add up to the log-likelihood.
Your turn. Write the scaled forward algorithm and compare its log-likelihood with the HMM package’s forward().









Rescale by the sum, s.


emis <- prop.table(table(truth, x), 1)
trans <- unclass(prop.table(table(truth[-length(truth)], truth[-1]), 1))
f <- c(0.9, 0.1) * emis[, x[1]]; ll <- log(sum(f)); f <- f / sum(f)
for (i in 2:length(x)) {
  f <- emis[, x[i]] * as.vector(f %*% trans)                 # sum over the previous state
  s <- sum(f); ll <- ll + log(s); f <- f / s
}
h <- initHMM(c("bg", "island"), c("A", "C", "G", "T"), c(0.9, 0.1), trans, unclass(emis))
fw <- forward(h, x); last <- fw[, length(x)]
c(by_hand = ll, hmm_package = max(last) + log(sum(exp(last - max(last)))))
-40{,}533.13 both ways. The scaling trick is how the HMM package’s forward() avoids underflow too (it returns log forward variables), and it’s how gene finders handle chromosomes of millions of bases.




Combining the forward algorithm with its mirror image, the backward algorithm, gives each base’s posterior probability of being in each state, given the whole sequence: P(\pi_i = k \mid x). Viterbi gives one best path; the posterior says how sure the model is at each position.
Your turn. Compute the posterior probabilities with posterior(), and count the bases where the model is unsure (posterior of island between 0.1 and 0.9).









The island row: "island".


emis <- prop.table(table(truth, x), 1)
trans <- prop.table(table(truth[-length(truth)], truth[-1]), 1)
h <- initHMM(c("bg", "island"), c("A", "C", "G", "T"), c(0.9, 0.1), unclass(trans), unclass(emis))
post <- posterior(h, x)["island", ]
c(mean_in_islands = mean(post[truth == "island"]), mean_outside = mean(post[truth == "bg"]),
  unsure_bases = sum(post > 0.1 & post < 0.9))
The posterior probability of island averages 0.993 inside the true islands and 0.004 outside, and 230 bases (less than 1%) have a posterior between 0.1 and 0.9: they’re at the islands’ edges. The plot below shows how sharp the boundaries are, and where the model hesitates.













Your turn. How much better does the HMM explain the sequence than a model with a single composition everywhere? Compute the log-likelihood ratio.









Look up each base’s probability: p_all[x].


emis <- prop.table(table(truth, x), 1)
trans <- unclass(prop.table(table(truth[-length(truth)], truth[-1]), 1))
h <- initHMM(c("bg", "island"), c("A", "C", "G", "T"), c(0.9, 0.1), trans, unclass(emis))
last <- forward(h, x)[, length(x)]
ll_hmm <- max(last) + log(sum(exp(last - max(last))))
p_all <- prop.table(table(x))
ll_one <- sum(log(p_all[x]))                              # every base independently, one composition
c(hmm = ll_hmm, one_state = ll_one, log_ratio = ll_hmm - ll_one)
A log-likelihood of -40{,}533 for the HMM against -41{,}520 for a single composition: a log-likelihood ratio of 986. For six extra parameters (a second set of three free emission probabilities, two transition probabilities and a start probability), that’s overwhelming evidence that the sequence has two kinds of region.










NoteGo deeper: real CpG models and gene finders





The two-state model here emits each base independently, so it sees only composition. Durbin and others’ classic CpG model has eight states (A+, C+, G+, T+ in islands and A−, C−, G−, T− outside), so that transitions between states encode dinucleotide frequencies, and the CG step itself carries information; a CpG island is then a run of “+” states. Gene finders like GENSCAN and AUGUSTUS use generalized HMMs, in which each state emits a whole segment (an exon, an intron) with an explicit length distribution, and emissions model codon structure, splice-site motifs and start and stop codons. The algorithms stay Viterbi, forward-backward and Baum-Welch, generalized. Richard Durbin and others, Biological Sequence Analysis (Cambridge, 1998), chapter 3, and Christopher Burge and Samuel Karlin, “Prediction of complete gene structures in human genomic DNA”, Journal of Molecular Biology 268, 1997 (GENSCAN).

title: Hidden Markov models for sequences
text:
Challenge round
Challenge 1 · Learning without labels. Usually there’s no annotation. The Baum-Welch algorithm (an EM algorithm, Module 4, Lesson 10) estimates the parameters from the sequence alone: compute the posterior expected transitions and emissions, update the parameters, repeat. Start from nearly uniform emissions and run 5 iterations on the first 10,000 bases.









5 iterations.


x10 <- x[1:10000]
h0 <- initHMM(c("bg", "island"), c("A", "C", "G", "T"), startProbs = c(0.5, 0.5),
              transProbs = matrix(c(0.999, 0.001, 0.001, 0.999), 2, byrow = TRUE),
              emissionProbs = matrix(c(0.26, 0.24, 0.24, 0.26, 0.24, 0.26, 0.26, 0.24), 2, byrow = TRUE))
bw <- baumWelch(h0, x10, maxIterations = 5)
round(bw$hmm$emissionProbs, 3)
From nearly uniform starting values, 5 iterations recover a background of 30.2% A, 20.3% C, 19.9% G and 29.7% T and islands of 14.3% A, 36.8% C, 35.8% G and 13.1% T, close to the true values, without being told where a single island is. Baum-Welch can converge to a local maximum, so in practice it’s run from several starting points, and its states have no names: here the second state became the island because the starting values leaned that way.




Challenge 2 · Dinucleotides. In RStudio, compute the CG dinucleotide’s observed-to-expected ratio (Lesson 3) inside and outside the true islands. The simulation emitted bases independently, so both should be near 1; in real vertebrate DNA, the background ratio is about 0.2 and the islands’ about 0.6 to 1. How would you change the model to use that signal?

title: Hidden Markov models for sequences
text:
Quick quiz

1. In an HMM, what’s hidden?

The bases
The states (island or background) that produced them
The emission probabilities


We observe the emissions and infer the states.



2. A state with a stay-probability of 0.999 lasts on average:

999 bases
1,000 bases
1 base


1/(1 - 0.999): the length is geometric.



3. The Viterbi algorithm finds:

The single most probable sequence of states
The probability of the sequence
Each base’s posterior probability


Forward gives the probability, forward-backward the posteriors.



4. Why work with logarithms or scaling?

To make the algorithm exact
Products of thousands of small probabilities underflow to zero
To speed up the computation


0.25^{30000} is far below the smallest representable number.



5. A posterior probability of 0.5 at a base means:

The base is half island
Given the whole sequence, the model can’t tell whether this base is in an island
The model is wrong


Typical at island boundaries.



6. Baum-Welch is:

A decoding algorithm
An EM algorithm for estimating an HMM’s parameters without labelled states
A way to choose the number of states


It can converge to local maxima, so starting values matter.

title: Hidden Markov models for sequences
text:
Wrap-up
You’ve hunted islands with a hidden Markov model. Here’s what you’ve learned:

An HMM has hidden states in a Markov chain, transition probabilities and emission probabilities; the islands here are 70% C and G against 40% in the background.
A sliding window finds islands crudely (accuracy 98.6%); Viterbi decoding gets 99.7% of bases right and finds all 7 islands, with boundaries off by a few dozen bases.
The forward algorithm gives the sequence’s log-likelihood (by hand and with the package, the same); the HMM explains the sequence far better than a single composition.
Posterior decoding shows where the model is unsure: at the boundaries.
Baum-Welch learns the parameters from the sequence alone.







TipPractice in RStudio (optional, about an hour)





Download genome_segment.fasta and cpg_islands.csv into your project’s data-raw/ folder, and install HMM.

Simulate. Use simHMM() to simulate 30,000 bases from the estimated model, and plot the run lengths of each state. Are they geometric?
